Row.txt_code:
Rose Curtis with a sample Comfort Journa
Objective:
To provide participants with a window of time to think about what brings them comfort and nurturance and to collage related images onto a journal. The end product is a journal that can be used as an ongoing reference and source of comfort.

Materials:
Spiral binders or sketch books
Cover stock paper (in various colors and textures if possible)
Cardboard or poster board (for front and back of covers)
Construction paper or 20 lb copy paper (to glue onto the bound pages and then collage on top of)
Magazines (such as Home Beautiful, Arizona Highway, Sunset, Glamour, Bath and Body, Garden Botanica or Red Rose Collection)
Collage material (ribbon, scraps of fabric, greeting cards, calendar pictures, etc.)
Markers and metallic pens
Calligraphy pens
Crayons
Glue stiks
Scissors

Opening:
“This is a window of time to think about what brings comfort to you. The more we are able to nurture ourselves the easier it becomes to love ourselves. As we are guided through the relaxation try to let images of comfort flow through your mind. Scenes of peaceful places, bubbles floating through the air, scents of flowers, notes of windchimes tinkling... whatever sounds, scents or scenes comfort you, let them wash over you.”

Technical Demonstration:
“What we will be doing today is starting our own Comfort Journal. The plan is to have your cover done today and if you have time, to fill a few pages of your journal to get you started. “Comfort Journals are a way to comfort yourself when you are feeling blue, sad, lonely, and even when you are feeling good. We all need extra nurturing everyday. I hope you find working and looking through your comfort journal is like giving yourself a warm hug!”

Note: As a leader, if you feel comfortable showing examples, this can be a good idea because if your audience is new to the idea of self comfort they may need some examples just to get them started.





 
  Pages from a Comfort Journal

Guided Relaxation:
Speak slowly feeling very relaxed....

“Make yourself comfortable. If you are sitting, it is good to sit with your back straight, your feet flat on the floor and your hands lying loosely in your lap.

“Take a deep breath and exhale slowly....if it feels safe for you....close your eyes. This is a time for you to breath in love.... and breath out tension. In your mind, let comforting colors wash over you.

“Let’s start with your toes, picture them curling in soft sand....now move up to your calves and feel them gently relax....relax your thighs and feel the sun gently warming your body.

“Breathe in deeply and become aware of any holding you are doing in your body. Calmly release the tension....breathing in love.... breathing out tension....let your stomach relax....feel yourself relaxing more deeply.

“Move your awareness to your shoulders....feel the weight lifting off as if someone very kind was massaging your muscles....you feel the knots smoothing out as you smell your favorite fragrance drifting by....if there is any tension left...imagine it flowing down your arms....through your fingers.... slipping down onto the floor and seeping down into the earth.

“Relax your throat....relax your chin....relax your jaws.... breathing in love ....breathing out tension. Relax your scalp.... relax your eyelids....imagine your whole body totally relaxed.

“Now, move your awareness into a very deep place inside of you....Let images of comfort come into your mind....notice if any particular colors come to mind.... notice if any fragrance floats in.... open all your senses .....are there notes of music that relax you? ....let you mind wander....are there special places that feel safe for you? ....are there plants, flowers or perhaps tall grasses to lie in?......let yourself be whimsical.....

“Just think about what makes you feel good and start to gently bring yourself back into the room.... holding onto the peace....breath in love.....and when you are ready, gently open your eyes and begin to go through the materials in front of you....and begin to create comfort...”



 A Comfort Journal
Allow at least 30 minutes for the creation of the Comfort Journal Cover. Participants who complete their cover early may explore the first pages of their journal, filling it with whatever brings them comfort (see “Future Comfort Ideas” below).

Closing:
Ask the group to share their creations and how it felt for them to totally focus on comfort. Ask them if they are inspired to add to their journal and if they would like to share their ideas for future pages.

Future Comfort Ideas:
These are ideas of what to put inside your Comfort Journal...
Love Notes to yourself
Love Notes from others
Comfort Letters from friends
Affirmations
Inspirational Sayings
Photographs
Pressed Flowers/Leaves
Prayers
Poetry
Pictures of items that comforted you as a child i.e. teddy bears or dolls
Whatever is positive, loving, nurturing, and comforting to you, save it for your Comfort Journal!!!

Special Thanks:
I received inspiration from and give credit to The Women’s Comfort Book by Jennifer Louden.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants a window of time to think about what brings them comfort and nurturance and to collage related images onto a journal. End product is a journal that can be used as an ongoing reference and source of comfort.

Row.txt_code:
"Inner Me" Artist: Rose Curtis
 Objective:
To learn more about yourself by going within and discovering your inner self through creating a portrait!

Introduction:
This workshop will assist older children and teens to look inside and discovering more about their inner-self! We are used to looking at our outer selves, our looks, our clothes, our appearance, the image we try to portray!This workshop gives us an opportunity to go to a deeper level and get more in touch with our inner-self. You will have 3 options of materials, you can also combine them.

  Materials:   
 Timeframe:    
  Large Template  Introduction: 5 min
  Small Template  Opening Circle: 10 min
  11x14 Thick white paper (recommended)
 Journaling/Sharing: 20 min 
Technical: 5 min
  Journal Questions (You may want to print them on novelty paper   
Paper or Journals & Pen		 Relaxation: 5 min
Creation: 1 hour
Closing: 15 min
    Total: 2 hours













Below is a list of materials you may need  based on which medium you want to use:
 Collage
Option One
 Paper Mosaic
Option Two
 Oil Pastels Resist
Option Three
Magazines with images and words
Scissors
Glue sticks
Embellishments as wanted -
butterflies, flowers
Markers
 Novelty papers - patterns, textures, metallics
Pre-cut mosaic shapes are available at
Discount School Supply
Glue Sticks
Mod Podge with brushes
Scissors
 Oil Pastels
Watercolors         
Brushes
Cups
Spray Bottle
Water pitcher

Prep:
Have body and head templates ready, one for each participant. Print journal questions on special paper. Have samples on hand if available. If you are using watercolors, be sure to pre-moisten them with a spray bottle before the participants use them. It's great to make an example of each medium so the participants get an idea of what they can create.

 
  Pre-collage Without a background image
 
  Adding a background image
 Collaging with layers
Technical Demonstration:
Explain to the participants the materials that will be available, especially if you are giving all three options. It is important to demonstrate all of the materials you give to them.

Collage - You may want to show your participants the different effects you can get by layering. You can show them how adding a background image can add hidden meaning and also make a collage "pop"!

Another wonderful collage technique is to not use scissors. Tearing the paper creates a cool effect.

Finally, encourage participants that while choosing images they should try to follow their intuition. This process can be quite surprising and freeing.

Paper Mosaic
You may not need to show a technical demonstration of how to do a paper mosaic, but it's good to at least show an example of what a mosaic is. Participants may choose to use a pencil to outline the spaces they would like to fill with mosaic pieces. It's also important to remind them that mosaics don't necessarily have to be squares, they can do long strips for hair and use lots of shapes.

 
 Notice how the white oil pastel was used
 in the bubbles of this Inner self portrait		 
  
Oil Pastel Resist
Give a demonstration to the participants by drawing a shapes with oil pastel on card stock  then using the watercolor over pastel to show how the pastel resists the watercolor. Remind them to use a lot of water and a lot of paint on their brush to create richer color effects. Using a spray bottle is an easy way to add water to the paper to help the watercolors flow.

Opening Circle:
Remind the group that anything shared in this circle is anonymous and should not be shared with anyone outside of this room.  Have the participants introduce themselves and share one thing that others don't know about them!  Ask the clients to be brave when deciding what to share and remind them that everything that is said in group stays in group.

 
 Combination Collage and Paper Mosaic Inner-Self Portrait
Journaling & Sharing (optional): 
Have participants journal on the questions provided and then share what they feel comfortable sharing. It is sometimes helpful to give participants a time frame and play soft music to get them writing.

If you plan to use the journal questions provided, realize it takes a lot more time to write and then share. If you are doing this workshop with teens it may be a good idea to have them share in pairs. It may feel safer to share if they are not asked to share with the group. If they are not up for sharing, that is okay too. If you have the time use this step as you may notice participants tend to go to a deeper level when they write and share before they create.

Relaxation:
Feel free to adapt this relaxation to work with your group and time frame.  Ask the children/teens to close their eyes and or put their head down on the desk. If you fall asleep that is great! Just like with the art there is no right or wrong way to do the relaxation. Read slowly, pausing in between sentences to create a relaxing atmosphere. Encourage the children/teens to breath deeply and try the relaxation. Then read the following:

 
  Paper Mosaic Inner Self Portrait
“Get comfortable in your chair, it is good to sit with your feet flat and your hands just laying loosely in your lap. If it feels safe for you, you can close your eyes. Just notice your in-breath and out-breath. No need to change it, simply notice the breath as it enters your nose and fills your chest.

Move your thoughts to your mind... knowing you can relax your mind just like a muscle ... take a deep breathe and go deep within and begin to meet your inner-self. What colors come to mind for your inner-self? What shapes or images arise as you meet your inner-self, are they large or small, round or heart? Is your inner-self male or female, are they young or old, is your image clear or foggy?

Greet your inner self, and ask him or her what they need from you... maybe a hug?.. maybe they just need you to sit and listen... take a moment and just spend some time getting to know and loving your inner-self. Take a deep breath in and let it out, continue breathing comfortably and know that you can return to talk and share with your inner-self any time you want. Hold onto all the images you saw and felt, slowly open your eyes and begin to create a portrait of your inner-self, selecting one of the techniques.
  
Participants working on their Inner self portraits!
Creation:
Remind the children and teens that their portrait doesn't have to look like anything in particular, especially a person. If their inner self is just shapes and colors or even lots of words, that is okay.  Just have fun and enjoy the process! Reminder:  There are so many materials that it is good to give the participants time warnings.

Closing Circle:
Ask everyone to share their portrait and what it means to them. What did they discover?   What is important for them to share about the art.
Row.txt_description: This workshop will assist older children and teens to look inside and discovering more about their inner-self! We are used to looking at our outer selves, our looks, our clothes, our appearance, the image we try to portray! This workshop gives us an opportunity to go to a deeper level and get more in touch with our inner-self. You will have 3 options of material to work with, you can mix them up if you prefer.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Project Overview:    
The New Year's Wish-Markers are small collages similar to book-markers, but they can vary in size and shape.  They are something that you can carry with you or keep around the house to remind you of the wishes you have for the upcoming year.

In this workshop we will look at the upcoming year as if has already passed.  This way, rather than seeing our wishes as something to be reached, we will let
our imaginations and instincts show us these wishes as if they have already come to life and we can see even our wildest dreams come true.  We will use the wish-markers as personal reminders to affirm our power in the creation of our lives.    
       
      
 Seasons of Healing
"Cada estacion del año es para sanar y recuperar cuando el fruto de Dios esta en nuestro espiritú!"
"There is a season for healing and restoration when God is the fruit of our spirit!"


     

Materials Needed:
Tag board to collage on (Different sizes and shapes)
Glue stick
Magazines
Scissors
Hole-Puncher

Ribbons
Pens and Paper for writing
Relaxing music
Timer
Magnets (optional)
Laminator (if you don't have one, each participant may laminate their own at Kinko's, or you could take the group's markers there in a bunch.)

   
      
        Restoration Reunification Successfulnes
"Esto es de mi futuro, esperanza en mi familía, y de prosperidad en mi vida."
"This is about my future, hope in my family and prosperity in my life."

  

Time Frame: 2 1/2 hrs
Introduction: 15
Opening Circle: 20
Timed Writing: 15
Technical Demonstration: 10
Collaging: 75
Closing Circle: 15

Introduction:
Remember that this workshop is a window of time for you to appreciate yourself completely, to respect all of your efforts, struggles and triumphs of the past year, and to think about the up-coming year with full respect for all of your thoughts, dreams and wishes. 

We will be creating "New Year's Wish-Markers" (show samples).  They can serve as book markers, but they can also be magnets to be placed in the kitchen, bedroom, desk or whethever you need them most.  They will mark your place in your very own wish for the upcoming year. 

You can create as many as you need.  You don't have to figure out your wishes right now.  During the relaxation and writing portions of the workshop you will have the chance to reflect on the wishes that are vital to you.
 
 
  
 It's Behind Us ... A New Life
Todó se quedó atrás...Una nueva vida
   
     
Opening Circle:
Let's begin to notice that this is a safe space for each of us to respect what we are feeling by having an opening circle.  Let's start with everyone sharing your name, how you're feeling, and one thing you appreciate about yourself most during the past year.  You can also acknowledge how you feel after the holiday season ( ie. Christmas and New Year).

Technical Information:
Show all the materials that are available to work with.  Demonstrate tearing, cutting and gluing onto the marker.  Show some different sizes and shapes we have can work with and mention the possibility of using magnets.  State that there are no right or wrongs in their creations. 
 
Relaxation:
(adapted from Jennifer Louden's The Women's Comfort Book)  

Get yourself comfortable.  Take a deep breath.  Hold it for a moment, and then slowly let it go.  Inhale another deep breath.  Imagine you are breathing pure relaxation in.  Hold your breath.  Now exhale, and imagine you are breathing out all the tension of your day, your week, your life.  As you take another breath, keep noticing you are breathing in pure relaxation.  As you let it go, keep noticing that you are letting go of any tensions.  Notice your body.  Are there any areas of tension?  Inhale and send your breath curling around the knotted muscle, the stored stress.  Exhale and imagine your pure, relaxing breath melting any tension away.  
  
  Reflections of Fear
  

Writing Warm-up:
Set your timer to 15 minutes, and during that time, write without stopping, without crossing anything out, without censoring or criticizing yourself.  

Begin by writing about the past year.  Try starting with the phrase:  "2005 was the year I....  " and writing about it in a completely triumphant way.  Remember any compliments you received during the year.  Remember any new things you learned.  

If any negative thoughts come into your mind, take a deep breath and see if you can notice what was positive about each experience.  Notice the strength you showed in the face of challenges.  Notice the decisions you made.  Notice the steps you took and the insights you gained, even from your mistakes.  You deserve to be appreciated for all you have done and been during this past year.

Writing Ahead:

Now try writing about the year ahead.  Try pretending you are sitting here a year from today.  What are your wishes for the year ahead?  Write them as if they have already happened.  Begin with the phrase “2006 was the year I...”  Let your imagination run wild.  You can concentrate on the year as a whole or on each individual month.
  
As you finish your last sentence, look back at what you've written.  Circle what seems most significant to you, and see if you can choose what you'd like to focus on for your Wish-Markers.

  
 Angels Holding Our Hearts
"Veo el futuro positivamente. La mariposa representa libertad después de la lucha y el angel representa como sostiene nuestro corazón y cuida al mundo entero."
"I see the future very positively. The butterfly represents freedom after struggle and the angel represents how they hold our hearts and watch over the whole world."
  
    
Collaging:

When you're ready to start your collage, begin to look through magazines and pull out any images, colors, textures, words that you are drawn to, or that you feel are related to your wish.   When you are ready, begin to collage them together onto the tag boards.   

Wrap-up:

As you finish up, write what each marker means to you on the back.  The words you choose are an important part of your Wish-Markers.  You will be able to read them throughout the year when you feel like you’ve lost your way or when you need to congratulate yourself on what you have been able to accomplish.

(If people are not finished with their collages, welcome them to take their images so that they can finish at home.  They can also continue to work on them during the closing circle.)

 
 Life Is Not A Gamble
 

Lamination:

You can get your Wish-Marker Laminated inexpensively at a place like Kinko’s.  Lamination makes the Wish-Marker into something beautiful and strong that you can carry with you throughout the year ahead.

After lamination, holes can be added to the marker.  They can have a ribbon on top or they can be attached to one another.  The magnets can also be added at this time.

Throughout the Year:

Carry your Wish-Markers throughout the year and use them to remind you of your visions and wishes.  They can also become magnets you place around the house. Take notes throughout the year regarding your successes and challenges as you reach for your wishes.  We would love to hear your stories.
Row.txt_description: Gives each participant a relaxing opportunity to think positively about the year ahead, and to create a vision in collage that she can carry with her into the year.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
For survivors coming from an abusive environment, one way to manage their experience is to dissociate from their body. Instead of experiencing their reality and being fully present in body, mind, and soul, they are usually distracting their attention away. They may use drugs, alcohol, food, denial of food, TV, or an endless list of ways to be distracted from being present in their experience. This adaptive behavior unfortunately takes them so far from the sacred vessel they inhabit, that they have become disembodied. The body map is a way of getting back in touch with the body. Awareness of the relationship that is held with the body is the goal. This exercise also gives them another option in which to experience and relate to their body.



 
Body Image from Group Interactive Art Therapy
by Diane Waller
Materials:
Felt tip markers
Tempera paints
Pastels
Crayons
Collage material
Magazines
Glue
A roll of butcher paper/mural paper, Newsprint in rolls, or brown packaging paper

Timeframe:
This workshop can take between 1 1/2 and 2 hours to complete depending on the size of the group and their willingness to share.

Getting the Paper:
I was able to call some of the large paper suppliers nearby and asked for a roll of paper as a tax deductible donation to the shelter. If you need to get large paper, you might try this. The shelter should have a form to give you. You may also call some of the local craft or art suppliers, or even the local health food store that has a meat department. Locally owned stores are sometimes easier to get donations from than the larger chain stores. (You may also inquire at this time about any type of collage materials that the store can spare.) If you are unable to acquire the butcher paper, then use masking tape to tape pieces of paper together that are large enough for participants to lay down on and trace their body.

Note:
This is one of those exercises that include a guided meditation, and arrangements for the children to be occupied elsewhere would be ideal. If not, they can participate in the body tracing, and then set them up with crayons while you do the guided meditation with the participants.

Introduction and Preparation for Body Map Exercise:
Pair participants up. You can be a partner if there is an odd number. Have them take turns in tracing their partner’s body. They can move their arms and legs in whatever position they like. A dark felt marker works best for this if it’s available. When they are finished, have them lay down over their traced image. Explain that, “We will be doing a guided meditation to bring awareness to the body. We will then try to replicate any feelings, energy, numbness, cold, heat, tension, etc. onto the body map using the art materials.”

Relaxation:
[To be spoken in a calm, even, and slowly paced voice. Make pauses appropriately.]

“Take a couple of slow deep breaths and relax. Now let the floor support you... sink into it... allow the gravity of the earth to pull all your tension away... just let it sink into the earth. Now we’re going to focus on specific areas of our bodies. Just notice how it feels without judgment. Just bring your awareness and make a mental note of anything you notice. Let’s start with the head... is it tight? Is it soft? What color or colors might represent the way it feels? What sound or movement could represent the energy? Just allow any free associations you might have to come to your mind. [Pause] Now move to your neck and shoulder area. Again, what colors, images, or movements could represent the feelings you are experiencing there? You may not be feeling anything. How might you represent that? Spend a moment to notice your neck and shoulders... and now move down your arms and just notice how they feel. [Pause] Move your awareness now to your torso. Does your back feel different from your front area? Spend a moment to notice the feelings. [Pause] Now move to your abdomen area... notice how your buttocks support you on the floor... Does the left side of your body feel different from the right side? Just notice your experience. [Pause] Move your attention down to your upper legs and slowly move down as you feel ready to the very tip of your toes... Take a minute to do so...[Pause] When you are ready you may open your eyes.”



 

Body Image from Group Interactive Art Therapy

by Diane Waller


Art Directive/Creation:
Have participants use the available material to symbolize what they noticed in their bodies. Tell them they may need to refocus on each particular area as they try to represent what they experience with color, shape, movement, texture, etc. If they are having difficulties with the art media, suggest picking a color that would work with some words to express their experience. Tell them, “Let your imagination go and do whatever you feel to do. Feel free to explore and experiment.”



 
Body Image from
Group Interactive Art Therapy

by Diane Waller


Sharing:
Invite participants to hang up their images and talk about them if they choose to. After they finish, suggest to them to consider journaling about, and to, the image. Write a letter to your body! Write a poem to honor the vessel that makes it possible for you to be on this earth. Suggest that they may want to continue to add to their art piece. Just as you take the time to decorate your home, decorate your body image. Give it power symbols. Bring some magic into your image. Write some positive and powerful words on it. Feel free to explore and experiment. Communicate that the purpose of this exercise is to bring awareness to their own body, and awareness about their relationship to their body.

Note to Facilitator:
As always with art, but especially with the body map, strong emotions may come up for some of the participants. Be aware of this, and notify the staff if you are concerned about someone in particular. For instance if they withdraw from the group and choose not to talk, you can be supportive of their
choice and ask if they are OK. Then alert the staff
to her reaction to the art experience. Enjoy!
Row.txt_description: Gives survivors a way of renewing their relationships with their bodies after possibly managing their abuse through disassociation or addiction. Offers another option in which to experience and relate to their bodies.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide a family, or a group of families, with an opportunity for each member to create a symbolic representation of self and place it within a commonly created family context. The aim is to facilitate individual ex pression and encourage an atmosphere of tolerance for similarities and differences. Each family member will decide where to place their decorated hand cut-out on or around the family tree trunk. As a result, they will have the freedom to choose a comfortable level of closeness or distance in relation to each other.

 
 
 
 
 


 Materials
Materials:
Large white butcher paper
8 1/2 x 11 white and colored paper
Markers
Pastels
Crayons
Colored pencils
Scissors (adult and children’s)
Glue sticks
Optional: Glitter glue, stickers, stamps and ink pads.

Time Frame:
This workshop can last between 60-90 minutes depending on the age of the children participating. It is helpful to have some simple toys available (building blocks, cars, dolls, etc.) for the younger children who might not be able to participate or who might lose interest after a short time.


A family with their finished Family Tree 
Space:
If possible, it is nice to have a separate table and chairs for each family. Otherwise have the family sit together at one end of a table or clear a space for them on the floor. There should be enough art materials so that each family has their own and doesn’t have to keep getting up to go get things they need. I have done this workshop with one family working outside at a picnic table and others inside a room. The goal is to allow each family to focus on their particular group process and not get too distracted by the activities of other families. There will be time to share as a whole group at the end of the workshop.

Introduction:
“In the next hour or so each family here will have the chance to create a picture of their family tree. The ideas and suggestions I give you are just one approach to follow, so feel free at any time to select your own method and make any changes that you wish. I have asked you to sit together as a family so that you can make decisions as a group about how you want your picture to look and so that the adults in each family can assist the younger children if they need help. If anyone does not want to participate or would prefer to work independently, that is okay too. There is no right or wrong way to do this art project. The most important thing is to let yourself by guided by how you feel and respect each others choices.



 Family tracing and decorating their hands
“The first step in making a family tree is for each family member to trace their hand on a piece of construction paper. Choose colors that are expressive of who you are and feel free to draw or write any shapes, symbols, or words on your hand that are significant and meaningful to you. After you have finished coloring or decorating your hand, cut it out. Smaller children may need help with this. If there is an infant in your family, a small hand can be made for them.



 Mother drawing the tree trunk
“The second step is for the adult in each family to draw a tree trunk on the piece of large white butcher paper. Children can make suggestions to her as she draws. Next each family member decides where they would like to place their hand on the tree and glues it down. It may be necessary to discuss with each other the exact position of your hand so that you respect each other’s boundaries and need for space. If you wish to place your hand elsewhere on the large piece of paper, that is okay too.



 Creating the Family Tree's environment
“The last step is to talk together as a famly and decide what kind of environment you would like to have around your tree. You may use any of the art materials to decorate the areas of ground and sky. It may be helpful for the adult to assign each child a space to draw within, or you may decide to let everyone draw what and where they please. Finally, if your family would like to title the completed picture, dicuss this together and write it on the front. You might like to have everyone sign their names either on the front or back of the drawing.”

Creation:
Have the families begin the art process after you have answered any questions they might have. Multi-family groups can become a little noisy and chaotic, so know that this is normal! You will probably have to repeat the directives step-by-step individually to each family because they will progress at their own pace and be involved in different stages at different times.
 
 Example of Our Family Tree






Example #2 of Our Family Tree
  Example #3 of Our Family Tree

Sharing Circle and Closing:
When all the families have completed the art directive have them come together in a large circle, if possible, and take turns holding up their picture for everyone to see. Make sure that every individual in the family is given the opportunity to speak about both the content of their drawing and the process of doing it. Always offer the option of not sharing, but if they are willing, have them discuss the significance of their hand, it’s placement, and their contribution to the tree’s environment. Even if the experience was not a positive one it is important to listen to all feelings being expressed. Closing the circle can be done with a rousing round of applause in appreciation of the efforts of everyone and families are encouraged to hang their family tree in their rooms at the shelter.

Note: Some shelters create a shelter tree with a hand from each resident. Some children make a tree that includees other relatives and ancestors. Encourage participants to take it in whatever direction they want.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants an opportunity to explore their sense of family and their place within it by using their hands to create a "family tree."
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual Pg.87 TO DO: Create varation for adults (appropriate for all ages). TO DO: Check against manual’s version of same.

Row.txt_code:
< td style="vertical-align: top">
 
  
 
  
 
 Example of series from Watercolor Windows
Overview:
This workshop offers survivors an opportunity to notice their inner and outer worlds, and to express their sense of self-transformation. The simplicity of this project allows it to work successfully within a short time frame and with participants who may never have used watercolor before. Participants may discover how beautiful and rewarding watercolor can be as a form of self expression.

Materials:
4" x 4" watercolor paper (3 pieces per participant)
Masking tape (one per participant)
Watercolor sets (one per participant)
Brushes (one medium sized brush per participant)
Cups of water (2 per participant)
Paper towels
Writing paper
Pens (one per participant)
Relaxing music

Time Frame:
This workshop will take 1 1/2 - 2 hours to complete.

Note to Leaders:
With watercolors, many beginners miss out on the beauty and ease of this material because they paint with the full strength of the pigment rather than using water washes. This workshop puts the focus directly on the water wash, having the women select the shape of the wash and define it on the page before adding any color. Once the water wash is in place, the rest flows easily and beautifully.

This workshop focuses on this single-wash process. It does not teach participants how to use multiple washes to render objects in a representational way. That sort of thing takes more time for the washes to dry in between, and takes more training than this workshop involves.

Opening Circle:
“Share your name, how you're doing, and how you feel about art. As you share, remember that this is your time to really notice yourself. As you listen to the others in the circle, remember that your listening helps to create the safety and respect in this room.”

Introduction:

1. A window of time

“This workshop is a window of time for you to practice respecting yourself and all of your thoughts and feelings. We will be using watercolors, a material which is quite wonderful and surprising. As you use the watercolors today, try not to be critical of what you do. It's fine to make a mess on the paper. It's fine to leave the paper blank. Whatever you decide to do is fine, as long as you try to keep respecting yourself instead of criticizing yourself.”

2. About watercolors

“Watercolors are a great chance to let yourself loosen up and have fun witnessing what emerges. This kind of paint can be layered in delicate washes to create incredible paintings. To do that sort of layering takes a lot of time and patience. Today, we will be using them in a more simple way. This workshop is designed to share the full beauty of the watercolor, without the frustration.”

3. Today's project

“We will each choose a simple shape to represent ourselves. It can be as simple as a circle or line or triangle. You don't have to think of the shape right now. We'll be doing a relaxation, and you can just let it come to you.

We'll be creating the shape on all three pages with water, and then adding color. The three pages can represent whatever you want them to represent. They can represent how you feel on the inside, and how the world feels around you. They can represent your transformation and healing. They can represent your different states of mind. They can represent your past, your present and your future.”



Fig.1: Taping the paper down

 

 
Fig.2: Defining your shape
with watercolor

 

 
Fig.3: Dropping color into the water
 
Technical Demonstration:
Tape down the three pieces of paper. Explain the various supplies, (fig. 1) especially the reason for the two cups of water (one is to rinse the brush, and one is a source of clear water to paint with).

To demonstrate the use of the water washes, paint a shape with pure water on all three papers (fig. 2). Use plenty of water so that the shape remains wet like a lake on the page.
Begin to drop color into the shapes (fig. 3). Notice how the beauty of watercolor comes from what the color does by itself as it is carried through the water. When the paint is dropped into it, the magic begins effortlessly.

Show what it's like to drop it near the edge. Show what it's like as the color spreads and runs into other colors (fig. 5).

Show what it's like to paint the area outside the shape with color, leaving a space of dry paper between the shape and the background (fig. 6).

Show what it's like if you join the two wet spaces. You can work the three papers at the same time, or one at a time (fig. 7).
 
 Fig.4: General set-up of materials





Distribute Supplies:
Make sure everyone has her paper taped down, and make sure each has her paints, water cups, brush, writing paper and pen ready (fig. 4).



 
Fig.5: Filling the shape with color

 
 
Fig.6: Leaving an edge of dry paper between the shape and the ground

 
 Fig.7: Bridging the dry edge,
where desired
Relaxation:
(Adapted from Jennifer Louden's The Women's Comfort Book.)

Note: relaxation is optional. If you are leading a group of participants who won't be comfortable with a guided relaxation, go ahead and skip to the creating.

“Get yourself comfortable. Take a deep breath. Hold it for a moment, and then slowly let it go. Inhale another deep breath. Imagine you are breathing pure relaxation in. Hold your breath. Now exhale, and imagine you are breathing out all the tension of your day, your week, your life. As you take another breath, keep noticing you are breathing in pure relaxation. As you let it go, keep noticing that you are letting go of any tensions. Notice your body. Are there any areas of tension? Inhale and send your breath curling around the knotted muscle, the stored stress. Exhale and imagine your pure, relaxing breath melting any tension away.

“When you feel relaxed and ready, take a moment to think about how you feel. What shape would you choose to represent yourself?

“Once you have fixed upon a shape, go ahead and open your eyes and begin to create that shape on each of your papers in pure water.

Creation:
Each participant can go ahead and create her shape in water on the three pages and then begin to add color as she wishes.

As participants begin to finish up, encourage them to write about their paintings. This gives them a way to process what they have experienced while the paint dries and the others finish up.

Closing Circle:
When participants are finished, leave the papers taped down during the closing circle. This will give the water washes a chance to dry.

For the closing circle, encourage each woman to share what she created and what she discovered in doing her paintings.

After the circle, participants can go ahead and take the tape off. If the paint is still wet, they may want to wait longer, or use a hair dryer gently, to dry the water before taking the tape off.
Row.txt_description: Offers survivors an opportunity to notice their inner and outer worlds, and to express their sense of self-transformation through the use of watercolors. Allows participants an opportunity to work successfully with the medium in a short time with rewarding results regardless of experience.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Allows participants an opportunity to explore and understand their feelings, know that all feelings are acceptable, and notice what their relationship to their feelings is like today. Participants do a series of quick , intuitive drawings, the focus being more on their experience than on the final product.



 Materials
Materials:
Paper (8 sheets per participant)
Pastels (1 set per participant)
Pens
Extra writing paper

Note: If using this workshop to help the women release or process anger, it is important to begin by having a discussion on "What is Anger?" Please click here to see the entire Processing Anger Workshop Series.

Time Frame:
This exercise goes fast and will take up the entire hour. I encourage participants to discuss their experience, but find it best to do after you have gone through all the emotions in the experiential process. In this way they will talk about the most poignant awarenesses they came across, and it will be most conducive to your time allowance.

The introduction should be about ten minutes in length. Each feeling should get five minutes. One minute to access and express the feeling, and four minutes to write and contemplate in silence. Let them know that time will be allowed for discussion after the art experiential.

This workshop will take 1 1/2 - 2 hours to complete.

Set Up:
It helps to have a large piece of paper with the questions written on them and displayed on a wall where participants can refer to if needed. The first four questions are the important ones to include. In order, the questions keep the participants in their “here and now” body experience with the emotion, and then moves them into an intellectual understanding of the feeling and their relationship to it. So encourage them to answer the first four in order, and then draw a line and write optional for the rest of the questions, or anything else they might want to include.

Also, have the eight sheets of paper and pastels placed before each participant before you begin the introduction.

Introduction:
Part of our experience as human beings is the capacity to have emotions. They are called “feelings,” because we are supposed to feel them. It’s unfortunate that we live in a society that has marked certain feelings as acceptable, and others as not. Some feelings are only acceptable if you are a certain sex. (Everyone has probably experienced the implied message that boys are not supposed to cry, and that women are not to assert their anger).

The fact is that as a human being, regardless of our gender, we are all capable and expected to feel a full range of emotions. Love and empathy are for the purpose of connection. Fear and anger are to warn and prepare us to fight off that which threatens our survival. Grief provides a relief process when we experience loss. This physical body is like a faucet that opens up to allow the emotional waters to pour through. Emotions are meant to be fluid and move the energy of our reactions that we experience through our senses.

If we don’t allow the energy to flow by it’s natural process of emoting, then it may become stuck or turned inward. For instance, have you heard the expression that worry causes ulcers, or repressed anger turns inward into depression. These notions even carry truth in modern medicine, which is looking more towards the body/mind connection in regards to “dis-ease.” It’s very important to feel your feelings!!

“The purpose of this exercise today is to explore and understand how all feelings are acceptable, and notice what your own relationship to your feelings is like today.

“I would like to emphasize ‘explore and notice.’ To explore and notice is to take a curious look at something, noting it’s qualities. We are not here to judge or shame ourselves in regards to what we think we ‘should’ be. The simple act of awareness provides a space for change and transition to occur naturally in it’s own time and way.

“You have developed a very intricate and necessary adaptation in life in regards to your feelings. The way you relate has been the way you have needed to survive in the social setting that you grew up in and find yourself today. This information may give you some options as to how you will relate in the future. Change and new behavior seem to come too slowly at times, but remember to put it in perspective with it taking your whole life to get where you are now.

“So above all, be kind and loving and patient with yourself when it comes to learning new ways of being.”

Art Directive and Creation:
“We will do a series of drawings today. For each sheet of paper, you will take a moment to reflect on a feeling. You will then pick one color that best suits that feeling, and make a mark or series of marks that may represent the energy of the feeling. “Allow your hand to touch the paper with your chosen color and move it however it wants to move. Don’t worry about how it looks, but rather, trust that deep inside you know how to express this feeling, and to let it come out through you. Whatever you draw will be perfect, and it does not necessarily need to be a picture.

“Pay attention to how your body feels when you hold the thought of each feeling. Just notice any sensations, tensions, or numbness you may be feeling. You may notice that you don’t even seem to be in your body.

“We will take about thirty seconds to complete each emotional gesture drawing. After you finish each one, take a moment to just be with the expression. Again, just notice any thoughts, judgments, bodily sensations, or whatever goes on when you contemplate this particular feeling. You may not feel particularly charged about it one way or another.

“On the back of the picture write:

(1) The name of the feeling.

(2) How you feel about this feeling.

(3) How do you feel in your body with this emotion?

(4) What thoughts, judgments, or messages do you have about feeling this emotion?

(Optional questions and considerations:)

“Who influenced you on these judgments (Parent, peers, society)? You may have some wishes or concerns about this feeling.

“What are your fears or hopes in regards to this feeling?

“Spend a few minutes writing what ever comes to mind. These questions are merely a jumping off place.”

Visualization:
At the beginning of this exercise, and in between each feeling, it is very important to let go of the feeling they experienced prior.

Do this by having them close their eyes and take a couple of deep breaths...

“Now imagine a waterfall that starts at the top of your head and flows through your entire body... washing the last feeling experience (or for the beginning of the session just say washing any tension...) out of your body and soaking into the earth... Let go of all tension with your out breath...

“Now think of a time when you felt (Insert feeling here. Suggested order: sad, happy, disappointed, excited, fearful, hopeful, angry, peaceful. It is important to end with a positive emotion.), allow yourself to really imagine the situation in which you experienced this... engage your senses by trying to visualize, smell, hear, or feel whatever you can about this experience... and when you are ready, open your eyes and choose a color that best suits the feeling, and make a mark or movement that best shares the energy of the feeling you are experiencing.

“When you are finished with this quick gesture drawing, be with it for a moment and really take it in... then when you are ready, turn over the paper and refer to the questions here (on the wall).”

After the first drawing, you can continue by saying, “...and when your ready, open your eyes and draw your gesture drawing, contemplate, and reflect and write on the questions as before...”

Suggested Discussion and Closing:
Open the floor for discussion on anything that comes up for participants. Remember, no right or wrong, but just reflection and consideration.

They may want to take some of their concerns into therapy. As a further exploration, they might consider taking the emotional expressions that they felt most resistant to, and to pin them up in their room somewhere where they have contact with them often. Encourage them to notice how over one week’s time the resistance and feelings towards these emotions change and shift.

You may also encourage them to write in their journal each night: one or two sentences to each of the emotions in this workshop. At the end of the week, ask them to consider any changes that they have experienced.

Alternate Closing:
Brainstorm a "Safety Plan" with the women to help them process their anger. Some helpful tips include:
Talk to a friend you can trust
Count to 10
Take out art supplies and draw a picture of your anger
Journal about your anger
Take deep breaths
Listen to music
Walk away
Dance or exercise
Row.txt_description: Allows participants an opportunity to explore and understand their feelings, know that all feelings are acceptable, and notice what their relationship to their feelings is like today. Participants do a series of quick, intuitive drawings, the focus being more on their experience than on the final product.
Row.txt_notes: ER TO DO: Rewrite!
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding thei r comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Note About Anger Workshops
We recommend that you start anger workshops with a discussion; don't be afraid to talk to the women about their anger. Anger is nothing to be ashamed of, it is important to look at and talk about it to try to understand it.

Some anger prompts that we like are:
What is Anger? What does it look like and what does it sound like?
What was the trigger to your anger?
What did you think about it?
How did it make you feel?
How did you act?
What effect did it have on you and those around you?

Row.txt_code:
Designs by Sherrill Kahn, creator of
"Impress Me" rubber stamps compan
Background:
This workshop was developed for the “In Touch with Teens” Program at Monroe High School in Los Angeles County. It was inspired by the work of Sherrill Kahn, a wonderful artist who was my high school art teacher. I have adapted it here for your use in the shelters, and I hope you enjoy it!

Objective:
To provide an opportunity for participants to explore their own, violence-free definitions of love, power and identity. To guide each participant to put their own definitions into a visually powerful form that she can carry with her and use to reminder of what she stands for as she leaves the shelter.

Materials:
Shrinky Dinks paper (Frosted Ruff N’Ready type cut to 2”x2” in advance, at least 4 per person) You can order bulk online! Search for “The Magical Land of Shrinky Dinks.”
Permanent markers
Colored pencils
Hole punchers and scissors
String/ribbon/yarn
Beads
White paper
Pencil sharpener
Oven

Note: Ballpoint pens work wonderfully!

Timeframe:
This workshop takes about 2 hours to allow for participants to write, sketch and design their own definitions in visual form, and share what they come up with.

Introduction:
Perspective to share with participants, “Throughout your stay in the shelter, you have probably had a chance to look at your own definitions of love, power and personal identity. You’ve probably looked at violent forms of power, love, and identity and uncovered the ways that violent power isn’t really power at all, and violent love isn’t really love. Hopefully, you’ve had a chance to imagine what love, power and identity could be without violence.

“With so much violence all around, it can be hard to remember what these things might be without violence. It can be hard to remember what you stand for, and how you can stand against the violence.

“This workshop offers a chance to put what you have learned into a form you can remember easily. In this workshop, each person gets a chance to notice how you can personally stand for what you believe.

“By creating designs that represent your own violence-free definition of love, power and your own identity, you can take this chance to notice, explore and express what you stand for.”

As You Begin:
“Remember that this workshop is a window of time for you to respect your deepest hopes and visions. Defining violence-free power, love, relationships, and identity are no small task, but it is an important one. As you do this, make sure you respect your own thoughts. Remember that you count. Your visions count. Your actions count.”

Relaxation:
(Adapted from JenniferLouden's The Women's Comfort Book.)

“Get yourself comfortable. Take a deep breath. Hold it for a moment, and then slowly let it go. Inhale another deep breath. Imagine you are breathing pure relaxation in. Hold your breath. Now exhale, and imagine you are breathing out all the tension of your day, your week, your life. As you take another breath, keep noticing you are breathing in pure relaxation. As you let it go, keep noticing that you are letting go of any tensions. Notice your body. Are there any areas of tension? Inhale and send your breath curling around the knotted muscle, the stored stress. Exhale and imagine your pure, relaxing breath melting any tension away.”

Writing Warm-up:
“In the four corners of your page, write four concepts that you want to define, violence-free. You may choose power, love, relationships, or identity, or you may choose other concepts that are important to you.

“Once you have selected your four concepts, begin writing whatever comes to mind as a definition for each of your concepts, violence-free. As you write, remember to write without stopping, without crossing anything out, without censoring or criticizing yourself.

“When you feel done writing, move on to the sketching.”

Sketching:
“Begin to imagine shapes that express your definitions. You can sketch them out on scratch paper. Try to stay really loose and uncritical. Explore as many shapes as you can for each concept.”

Drawing:
“When you have one or more sketches that you want to use to create a final design, go ahead and put it onto a fresh piece of paper.

You may create a design for each of your four concepts, or you may create one. You might find that your one design expresses all of your ideas. Make as many or as few designs as you wish.”

Making the Shrinky Dinks:
Draw on the “rough” frosted side of the Shrinky Dink plastic. Draw and/or trace the image and/or word(s) that will remind you of what you stand for. If you want to change the shape of your plastic, use scissors to cut to the shape you want. Keep in mind that a hole will be punched on the top portion so don’t write/draw anything too crucial in that section. Once you are done coloring and drawing/tracing, punch your hole on the top so you can later put ribbon or string through it. The hole needs to be punched PRIOR to baking. (When you punch the hole, don’t punch it too close to the edge, or too far. The distance from the edge should be about a half the diameter of the hole-punch circle.)

Baking Instructions:
A toaster oven is ideal for baking Shrinky Dinks. However, your conventional oven will “shrink” your masterpieces just as well. Step 1: Pre-heat oven to 325°F (163°C). Step 2: Cut a rectangle shape out of a brown grocery bag and turn one corner up. (Turned-up corner will make it easy to remove from tray or cookie sheet). Step 3: Place Shrinky Dinks pieces, colored side up, on brown paper and place paper in tray or onto cookie sheet. Put into pre-heated oven. Step 4: Watch as your Shrinky Dinks shrink. Bake approximately 1 to 3 minutes. After pieces lay flat, allow an additional 30 seconds of baking time to complete the process. Step 5: Remove paper from tray or cookie sheet and lightly press flat with folded paper or a pad of paper (or book) until pieces have cooled. (Approximately 15 seconds.)

Using Your Creation:
Use your “What I Stand for” creation throughout the year to remind you of the definitions you take with you. Take notes throughout the year regarding your discoveries as you remember “what you stand for.”
Row.txt_description: Provides an opportunity for participants to explore their own definitions of love, power and identity and put these definitions into a visually powerful form. The end product can be carried on a key-chain or elsewhere as a reminder of what he or she believes in.
Row.txt_notes: PROG-both ER TO DO: Check scans. TO DO: Create variation for Children.

Row.txt_code:
“Story telling is the soul’s speech, and it is free to move between the realities of imagination and literal events.” -Shaun McNiff (from Art as Medicine).



 Story Doll, Shara Stevens
Objective:
The importance to tell one’s story is vital to rising above the shame, secrecy, and isolation that can accompany the abusive relationship. Another important aspect is using the imagination to create a new ending to the story. By making “story dolls” we give participants a voice to explore what has happened, and what direction they can choose to take for the future. By externalizing their own story onto the doll, it becomes a safer place to explore all of this. The doll often becomes a mirror, and a way for participants to discover feelings and thoughts she may have never claimed as her own before. A powerful transformation can occur when one is given the opportunity to truly speak their truth. The doll can also be used as a way to get in touch with their inner wisdom through dialogue. By asking a question to the doll, participants actually give the answer she needs to hear. Much like when we give advice to others, it’s the very thing we need to hear ourselves. This exercise allows participants to embrace their own advice and wisdom.

Materials Needed:
Fabric or felt
Beads
Buttons
Feathers
Miscellaneous collage material
Needles and thread or embroidery supplies
Scissors
Glue
Cotton batting or toilet paper for stuffing

Note:
This workshop can tap powerful emotions. If your group has established a sense of closeness and safety it might be a good workshop to try. Fabric stores are usually good resources for donations. I also frequent garage sales and thrift stores and buy articles for a dime or quarter and use those for material scraps.

Time Frame:
Participants may get very involved in their dolls so you might want to allow forty-five minutes for the making of them. If children are sitting in on this group, you can cut out ginger bread shaped persons on paper, and give them colors or magazines to decorate their own doll. After the dolls are finished, the participants can break up in groups of two or three to tell a story. A half an hour to forty-five minutes should be enough for each participant to have a turn.

Doll Making:
The doll can simply be two gingerbread person shapes that can be sewn together by hand and then stuffed. It could also be assembled in parts (body, head, arms and legs). It could also be as simple as a single sided hanging wall piece. If there is no material to work with, you can make the doll a single sided decorated paper cutout. Glue or sew on any items that seem appropriate and meaningful. Beans and pasta found in the kitchen pantry can be used. Be creative. Pull out colored markers and paints as well.

Introduction:
“In making our dolls today, think about the part of you that holds your inner wisdom. Think about the intuitive voice that resides within. Think about your soul or spirit, the energy that gives you life and yet is bigger than your life. Try to meditate on these aspects while creating your doll. Try not to worry about how the doll looks or how well it’s stitched together, but rather trust in the process of creating, understanding that the doll will be perfect exactly how it turns out. This doll is a part of you. When you talk to it and ask it questions, the immediate response that comes to mind will be coming from your own reservoir of wisdom and intuition. Sometimes it takes something outside of us to initially hear that wisdom and to trust it. This doll can be a part of you that needs to talk and tell a story. It may be literal or it may be a fantasy or symbolic of something bigger. Most importantly, this doll can be a window to your personal journey of discovering your self."

Sharing Exercise and Closing:
After the dolls are completed have participants pair up (if they are not done with their doll, try to encourage participants to finish them as they can during the week, but to use them as is for now). Groups of two are ideal because they will have more time to tell their story to one another. Give them a time limit for each person and also announce that you will let them know when they have five minutes left before switching. Have the owner of the doll tell its story. They can begin with “Once upon a time....” Make sure they include an ending. The ending can be however they wish things to be for themselves in the future. Some participants will take off immediately in this role play. However, others will not know how to start or what to say, or just not feel motivated to do anything. As an alternative idea, I have listed some questions here that they can ask of the doll. You may want to copy this and hand out for them to do at a later time on their own, if they engage well with the story telling. These are basic questions that can access the intuitive voice within on any given issue.

Possible Questions to Ask Your Doll:
“You may want to ask these questions with your doll in front of you, and either verbalize or write out the answers. It is important not to edit what you say or write. Trust the process and express what ever comes to mind without questioning or judgment. Be open to whatever response arises and just be available to hear it out. What comes up can be the intuitive wise part of you that you are getting more in touch with. It may also be old messages that are not true for you today. The important part is to let out what needs to be said, and be with that response to see what wisdom it has for you today.”
“What is it that you need from me?

“What do I need to know about my situation right now?

“What advice do you have for me in regards to this choice I need to make right now? (Verbalize the choice.)

“How can I achieve __________ right now in my life?

“Is there anything that you want to tell me?

“What is it that you feel I need to know about myself?”

Of course all these questions are being asked of your inner wise self. The doll just makes it easier to start these conversations and to connect to that wise part of you. Remember, trust the answers and the process. Trust your inner wisdom and intuition.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants a voice to explore their abuse and what directions they can choose to take for their future. By externalizing their own story onto a doll, it becomes a safe place to explore, often becoming a way to discover feelings and thoughts never before claimed.
Row.txt_notes: ER TO DO: Get scans

Row.txt_code:
Spring 1996 Hands Comforter #8 (Won County Fair Blue Ribbon)
"Hands are not for hurting. I will not use my hands for violence!"
Background on The Project:
Quilts have always evoked visions of comfort and nostalgia. The imagery and symbolism run very deep throughout the entire quilt process. Right from the start, participants being taking scraps of fabric, piecing them together into something beautiful and functional, and creating order out of chaos. Women are literally and figuratively stitching their lives together.

At Humbolt Women for Shelter (HWS), the Children's Comfort Project began in the Spring of 1993. Initially the comfort project was done just with children during childcare and/or kids groups. When HWS opened a shelter in the summer of 1995, the project was expanded to include adults. In this article,
I share the children’s quilting process, although it can be easily be adapted to use with adults.

The comforters are as varied as the children who have worked on them. At first, the comforters did not have themes. The children could draw anything they wanted. After 3-4 quilts, we began using themes. Some of the themes groups have chosen are; Hands are not for Hurting, Alcohol and Other Drug Prevention, Friendship, the Strength of Women, and My Favorite Things.

We have used our comforters in many different ways. Four have gone home with children, two remain in the children's room where they are used for stories, naps, picnics, etc. Two comforters are used for public display and community education (the names have been covered to protect confidentiality), two comforters are in use at our shelter house and two are used in our group room at our office. Three comforters have also been made by staff members for other staff members going through difficult times. Since the project began, fifteen comforters have been completed. We currently have three comforters in progress.

In August, 1996 the kids comforter, "Hands Are Not for Hurting" was entered in the Humboldt County Fair. It won a Blue Ribbon and a Special Award. The children are so proud when they come into HWS office and see the quilt on display with the ribbons pinned on.



 
Detail of Moon Stone House
 Comforter #1
Objectives:
Part of healing from the cycle of domestic violence is giving children a safe space to express their thoughts and feelings. The HWS Children's Comfort Project has been a wonderful and tangible way for this to happen--children are encouraged to share their unique ideas through the supportive creative process of making a group comforter.

The Comfort Project is very good for shelter houses on many levels. It gives adults and children a chance to share their stories and all of the pain, sorrow, love, joy and laughter... the strength and courage they have all shown in their lives. It brings comfort in the making and in the use of the finished product. Whether the comforter goes home with one family or stays in the shelter house to be used by all, adults and children are literally wrapping themselves in comfort and hope. It is a project that all ages are able to work on, from adult to young child. If a child can hold a crayon and make a mark, they can make a square. The squares can be as simple or as complex as the maker desires.

The creation of a group comforter takes place over a period of time. The children get to see a process. Some children will see the entire process, while others will see only certain stages. The first stage is the creation of the squares. The final stage is, of course, the completed comforter.

This particular comforter uses the theme: "Hands are not for hurting. I will not use my hands for violence!" In addition to making a pledge of non-violence, the children get to express themselves through the creation of the square. Each child gets to decide what colors and shapes they want to use. Then they can choose what fabric they want to frame their square. There is immediate gratification in the completion of the square. They also get to see the long term process and the eventual reward of the completed group project. Each child has an important part in the creation of the comforter. The finished comforter becomes a visual reminder of the group process and the support the group has to offer. It reminds the child they have a place where they belong and where they are safe.



 Detail of Moon Stone House Comforter #1
Materials:
Muslin fabric: 2-4 yards depending on size of comforter.
Pentel fabric crayons and fabric pens
Quilt batting:
45x69 for 12 square comforter,
72x90 for 20 square comforter.
Flannel or other fabric for backing
Fabric for 3" framing strips
Yarn and yarn needles
Masking tape
Basic sewing supplies
Iron and ironing board
Newsprint
Polaroid camera and film

Timeframe:
The entire group is about 90 minutes, for the children to make the quilt squares and choose the frame.
15-20 min: Snack, check-in
45-50 min: Making squares, choosing frame
15-20 min: Sharing squares, check out

(Sometimes there is enough time for the children to make more than one square. Then they can leave one for the comforter and have one to take home with them, if they want.)

Sometimes making the squares is all I have the children do. Then I take the squares home and bring back a finished comforter. Other times, I involve them in more steps along the way, depending on their interest level.

The average time that goes by from the completion of the first square to the completed comforter is about 6-12 months. Depending on how many squares I collect and what the finished size of the comforter is, it may take 1-6 months just to collect enough squares for the quilt.

Once the squares are collected it takes about 15-20 hours to complete the comforter. It takes longer if you bring the quilt back to the group for the various stages (see “Follow-up” for a list of all the stages.), if the names have to be covered, if the comforter is larger than 20 squares, or if this is your first time constructing a comforter.

If you can collect 12 squares in one group and have an eager volunteer (hopefully one who already knows how to construct a quilt) with 15-20 hours available, the comforter could be completed in a week. Usually the process takes a little longer than that.

I like to plan working on the comforter in one stage or another about one group a month for about 6-9 months. In the shelter house, adults and children get to see whatever stage is being worked on while they are at the house. If they continue coming to HWS ongoing support groups, they can see the quilt when it is finished.

There is also time spent documenting the comforters. I don't have an estimate on this as it is something I am just beginning. I have always had the adults and children tell their stories with the squares, but I haven't written them down until this most recent comforter started in the shelter house The Strength of Women. I have now started asking the women's permission to write down their story as they tell it. I want to make journals, books to stay with the comforters.

Preparation:
*Cut 25-30 8”x1/2" muslin squares (this is so you will be sure to have enough extra. Cut more if your quilt will be larger than 20 squares).

*Cut 80-100 fabric framing strips 3" x 15" from assorted fabric scraps (Lots of colors and prints are desired. The more variety the more choices available to the children.)

*Tape the muslin square to the table on all four sides. Tape in 1/2" from edge of fabric. This does three things: 1) It secures the fabric so it won't slip around while drawing on it. 2) It frames the drawing space, anything beyond the tape will probably be sewn into the seam and not show. 3) It is a chance to stretch the fabric and smooth out any wrinkles.

*Set up ironing board and newsprint. (If the children are very young or unable to contain their energy, you may want to iron the squares later for safety’s sake.)

*Notebook or journal and pen to record the stories that go with the squares. Always ask permission before writing anything down.

*Polaroid camera (to take pictures of each adult and child and their quilt square, so each person has something to keep from group, since they are leaving their squares for the comforter.)



 Detail of Hands Comforter #8

 
 Detail of Hands Comforter #8

 
 Detail of Hands Comforter #8
Opening Activity:
I have the group start with a snack and a quick check-in. We go around a circle with the following: say your name, how you are feeling right now, and is there anything you want to talk about today? After everyone has a chance to share, I describe the project:

“Today we're going to make quilt squares. The theme (you can use this theme or you can have the group choose a theme) for this comforter is: Hands are not for hurting. I will not use my hands for violence. So, what I want you to do is to trace your hand on the square. Then you can decorate it anyway that you want to. Now, I want you to think of the positive ways you can use your hands and write one way on your square. We have lots of extra squares, so if you don't like how yours is coming out and you can't fix it, you can start again on a fresh square."

While the squares are being made, the kids are talking about the different ways that hands can be used to hurt and the ways that hands can be used to help. When they have finished drawing and writing, the tape is removed from the fabric and the square is ironed to set the crayon. Place a piece of newsprint on the ironing board, then place the square face down, then another piece of newsprint. Now iron, holding the iron in place for 10 seconds, then move it over a couple of inches and hold 10 seconds. Repeat until the entire square has been ironed. Adults can do this themselves, older children may need help, and younger children need it done for them. The ironing melts the crayon and sets it into the fabric. It is an important step. Next the framing strips are chosen. The framing strips are 3"x15" strips of fabric. Each person can choose four to frame their square. They can all be the same, or they can all be different. Have each person pin the strips on, one on each side of the square.

Closing:
For closing we sit in a circle again. Each person has the chance to say anything they want to say about the group, share their square and say anything they want to say about their square, and close by saying something they like about themselves. (I may ask a question like "Do the colors, shapes, images have any special meaning for you?" if the person is hesitant or doesn't seem to know where to begin.) Remember to ask permission to record their story in the journal, and always respect it when they say no.



 1994 Comforter #4 (No Theme)
Follow-up:
There is quite a bit of follow-up involved for this project, but the end result is worth the effort! The following are 8 Basic Stages of the Comfort Project.

Stages of Comforter Construction:
1) Make squares
2) Sew frames on (volunteer)
3) Lay out quilt (group or volunteer)
4) Piece top (volunteer)
5) Tie it (group or volunteer)
6) Bind it (group or volunteer)
7) Label it (group or volunteer) Have group decide how quilt will be used. Cover names if it is to be used for public display.
8) Photograph it (volunteer) Reproduce to give photos of finished comforter to women and children who worked on comforter.

I have not included basic quilt making instructions. There are a lot of good books already written. Check your library or local Quilt Guild. Quilt Guilds are a good place to recruit volunteers for this project.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants a chance to share their stories and emotions in individual quilt squares and brings comfort in the making and in the use of the finished product, a comforter. Comforters are finished over a period of time and children will get to see some or all of the process, depending on their length of stay at the shelter.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
My objective is to address the subject of self-respect and respect for others in an engaging, powerful way through the vehicle of the ancient symbols of the circle, the ceremonial staff, and drumming. Our society has trained most of us to have difficulty saying no and drawing our boundaries (that would be considered unaccomodating and selfish!) Through this process we create some symbols of self-respect on which to focus and use as tools in our self-growth.

 
 Cate O'Hagan drums with "Ceremonial Staff" art workshop participants in Central Oregon



  
Materials:
Sticks of all sizes that no longer have bark
Paints (acrylic house paint or the less expensive acrylic artist colors)
Found materials
Feathers
Brass tacks
Leather
String for wrapping and tying
Beads
Trinkets
Bones 
Brushes
Paint rags
Water containers for cleaning brushes
Small plastic cups for individuals to work from
Scissors
Larger size needles
Fast drying glue
Tape player (for drumming and relaxing music)
Optional: woodburning tools, glue-guns, etc.

Note:
If the participants are given advance notice, they may be invited to gather their own stick to work with (from 24" or so to several feet tall) and to bring their own treasures to attach to their staff, such as beads, feathers, old jewelry, etc.

Note to Facilitator:
While inspiration for the Ceremonial Staff workshop came from Native American peoples, the staff has been used as a symbol of respect in all cultures throughout time. We think of it being associated with indigenous peoples, but if you watch the opening ceremonies for the United States Senate you will see a ceremonial staff used!

I have not yet encountered resistance to this process, or any alarm that it may hint at the pagan. If this occurs, it may be neutralized by pointing to such things as flags as forms of decorated staffs that symbolize national self-respect and healthy pride.

I suggest using a drumming tape, unless you have some familiarity with fast, rhythmic, regular beat drumming. I use a "double drumming" tape by Michael Harner, which should be widely available. It is this particular type of drumming, with the fast, regular beat, that naturally puts the listener into a relaxed state. (It actually relates to the brain wave function that causes relaxation.) Over the last five years, I have experienced only one person resistant to drumming, yet they made it through this process with flying colors. Again, the drum is common to all peoples, and is used just like we would use a tape of calming music.

Introduction:
While staffs are common to all cultures, the inspiration for this particular exercise originates with the Native American Sioux. During times of battle, some of the experienced and wise warriors would feel moved to ride into the heat of a battle armed with nothing more than a decorated stick, rather than a weapon. This stick is called a "coup stick" (pronounced koo and actually a French word). The warrior would ride up to the enemy and touch him with his coup stick, (which is the origin of the term "counting coup.") The warrior would touch his enemy with the stick, rather than wound or kill him. The enemy was therefore very aware that his life had been spared, and that he had been put on notice to never cross certain boundaries again.

We can use this imagery to represent our "inner warrior," that place in us that respects our boundaries and the boundaries of others. During the guided meditation we will look for or feel symbols that we can use to decorate our staff.



 
Touch drawing
by Daborah Koff-Chapin
Guided Meditation:
Let participants know that any part of this exercise is elective, and invite them to sit or lay in a comfortable position, with eyes open or closed. In a soothing, evenly-paced voice suggest they take three or more deep breaths, feeling each breath as it flows through the upper body, relaxing the neck shoulders, back and chest; then on to the lower body... releasing any tension in the lower back and abdomen, letting any excess tension flow out the toes. Let the mind wander, allowing the thoughts to pass through like a breeze.

“In your mind, find yourself in a totally comforting space... whether it be on a tropical beach or snuggled in a down comforter, whatever image or feeling works for you. While in this space, we will be listening to drumming to assist your relaxation. While listening to the drumming, create images of what your very own inner warrior may look like, or sound like or feel like.
