We will be bringing these images with us as inspiration for creating our staffs. Remember that if you feel you are not sensing any images, that's OK. This is your time to relax. Please enjoy about ten minutes of drumming, and when I turn down the sound at the end, slowly bring yourself back and we will begin.”

Facilitator’s Note:
After the meditation, suggest that each participant select a stick that feels right to her and dive into the materials. Invite them to paint or attach anything they want. There usually is a fair amount of interaction as participants share materials and methods of attaching items. I usually make no overt efforts to draw out comments at this time, but let the process take its natural course. I usually play soothing music during this part.

Closing Circle:
This is an opportunity for all of us to stand in a circle with our Ceremonial Staffs and talk about anything we feel moved to talk about, including about our staff and our inner warrior. As we stand in a circle we can notice that it is that self-respect and respect for each other that allows us all to co-exist harmoniously within the circle. For most of us that sense of safety within our family circle has been broken, and this is a way we can practice rebuilding it, beginning with self respect. So when you talk about your own staff or inner warrior, share with the group some ways you might begin to respect yourself more.

 
 "Ceremonial Staff" workshop participants
Row.txt_description: Addresses the subjects of boundaries, saying no, self-respect and respect for others in an engaging, powerful way through the vehicle of the ancient symbols of the circle, ceremonial staff, and drumming. The end product, the ceremonial staff acts as a symbol of self-respect on which to focus and use as a tool in self-growth.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for Children.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop helps the children to focus on identifying their own personal needs to feel happy and healthy. Each child will create a Paying Attention to Me Doll that can serve as a reminder that they have unique needs and the power to meet many of them on their own.

 
  Paying Attention to ME! supplies 

Materials:
Sculpey III (variety of colors) - 1  Sculpey III packet per person, 2 colors each
Handiwipes
Copy Paper for journaling (different colors) & Pens
Toothpicks/Skewers
Cookie sheet (covered in brown paper from a bag)
3" jewelry head pins (craft or bead stores)
Small beads
Jump ring (size work well
Pliers (needle-nose work well)
Ribbon (optional)
Manilla Folders(to act as the work surface - (Don't work directly on the table)

Timeframe: 
Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Discussion/Journaling: 10 minutes
Demonstration: 10 minutes
Creation: 40 minutes
Baking: Time varies: 275 degrees for 15 minutes for each ¼ inch of clay thickness
Assembling: 5 minutes
Closing Circle: 15 minutes

Workshop Preparation:
Today is helpful to preheat the oven before you begin creating; that way the oven is nice and hot when it's time to bake the clay.  We suggest using an oven thermometer to accurately maintain the correct temperature.

Keep in mind that this may be many of the participant's first experience working with the Sculpey/Polymer clay. The first time you do any project, it can be a bit more challenging. It always gets easier with practice. Show the children an example created by you or print this workshop to show them how "cool" their doll will look like when it is complete.

Introduction:
Today we are focusing on what each of us needs to be happy, healthy and feel safe. This workshop is called Paying Attention to ME doll.  Using clay that we'll bake in the oven, we will create cool looking dolls to remind us how important each of us is. Taking time to pay attention to our needs is very important part of being happy. When we feel good in our bodies hearts and minds we are stronger and healthy.

  
  Journaling Exercise

Opening Circle:
Start by having each child think about what they want or need in order to feel safe, happy and healthy.  Have each child share one word about a need they have right now.  It may help the children get started if you share an example of a need that they can relate to. For example, "My body's tired, I need sleep."

After all the children have shared, ask them to notice the similarities and/or differences in all of their needs.   Thank them for sharing their unique needs and acknowledge that all of these needs are  important!

Journaling/Discussion Warm-up:
Depending on the ages or composition of your group you may choose to skip the journaling and run this warm-up as a group discussion.

We all have 3 different types of needs: the needs of our body, our mind and our spirit.  We are now going to talk a little bit about each of these needs and then we are going to create a Paying Attention To ME doll to help us remember that our unique needs are important.

For Journaling Exercise: Ask each child to take a piece of paper (choose a color that makes them feel comfortable and safe, or even strong and hopeful).  Fold that paper into thirds lengthwise. On the top of the first column, write the word Physical, on the second Emotional, and on the third Spiritual. 

Now I'm going to talk a little bit about each of these three needs and give you a few minutes to write about your own needs. You can write sentences, words, lists, draw symbols, shapes, or anything you like.  The most important thing is you just allow your thoughts to flow onto your paper.  What you write does not have to make sense to anyone but you!  (You might want to play soft background music during this journaling portion).

For Discussion: On a board (dry erase, chalk, poster, etc.) create 3 columns. On the top of the first column, write the word Physical, on the second Emotional, and on the third Spiritual. After you review each type of need using the examples below,  have the children brainstorm and call out needs that fall in each category.

Physical needs are what we usually think about first.   What are your physical needs in order to be safe, happy and healthy?  For example: We need to have a safe place to live. We need to eat healthy food and drink clean water.   We need to play and be active, so our bodies are healthy and strong.   We need rest, so we have energy and can do well in school and at home.  In the first column, begin writing (or calling out) words, sentences, symbols or shapes to represent your physical needs. What do you need to feel heathy?

Another need that may be a little harder to think about, but just as important, are our emotional needs. Emotions are feelings like happiness and love. What emotional/feeling needs do you have?  For example: We all need to know we are loved and appreciated.  We need to feel understood when we tell others how we feel.   We need to have a loving family, and friends that are nice to us.  Now in the second column, begin writing (or calling out) about your emotional/feeling needs. What do you need to feel happy?

Finally, we will address our spiritual needs.  Our spiritual needs are things that feed your soul and help you feel peaceful.  What do you need to feel peaceful?   Do you need quiet time to pray?   Do you need to forgive or have more patience with members of your family?  Does doing nice things for others help you feel happy inside?  In the third column write (or calling out) words to reflect your spiritual needs. What kind of things do you need to feel peaceful?

Thank each child for taking the time to think about their needs and wants.

Creation:

 
    Sculpey "snake" using 3 colors
  
   Rolling Sculpey in a ball
  
   Rolling Sculpey in a ball

Today we're going to create a "Pay Attention to ME" doll.  It will remind you to take care of yourself, and notice what you need and want to be happy, healthy and feel safe!

Tell the children: "You get to decide how you want your clay person to look.  If you want, you can look back at the needs you wrote about in your journal (or during the group discussion).  You can choose to represent one aspect of your needs (physical, spiritual or emotional), or focus on one specific need (such as eight hours of sleep).   Or your clay person can be a reminder to pay attention to all of your needs!"  You can use shapes and colors to represent those needs. First I will show you how to make new colors and cool effects with the clay and then how to create the shapes to make your needs doll.

Demo 1: Show the children how to create new colors with the Sculpey clay.  The children can use the straight color (directly from the package), or they can use 2 or more colors and blend the clay. 

Step 1: To blend the clay, choose at least two colors.  Use no more than a pinch of each color.

Step 2: In order to soften and easily work with the clay, you will need to warm it up first. You're going to warm the clay by using your hands!  Break it apart into smaller pieces. Squeeze it and stretch it; you'll start to feel it getting softer.   Keep working with it, rolling it, kneading it and stretching it.   Join the pieces back together. When it's soft, roll it up into a ball.

Step 3: Roll each color ball into a "snake" by rolling it back and forth.

Step 4: Wrap each "snake" around each other like a candy-cane and twist together.

Step 5: Twist each little section of the roll until the colors are blended just the way you want them.

Step 6: Roll the "snakes" into a ball. If you want, you can make your ball into a snake and twist several times to create a more marbled effect.

Step 7: If you keep twisting and rolling, however, eventually the colors will form a new color! You decide!

Are you ready to create your own Paying Attention to ME Doll using the cool techniques you just learned?

Creation Process:
The children will start making 3 balls of clay (approximately 1/2 inch each): one for the head, one for the arms, and one for the legs.

Tell the children they can use a solid color for the head, body and arms?  Or, they may want to use marbled or blended colors?  Each ball can be different or they can all be the same. Whatever they choose is okay!   The only thing that is important as they create their 3 balls of clay is to remember that they are creating a doll that represents a them and their needs. 

 
   Piercing the head with a tooth pick
  
  Piercing legs and arms with tooth pick

Step 1(Conditioning the Clay): Let the children pick the colors they want to use for each ball. Help the children with the marbling and blending technique as needed.

Once they have the clay the way they want it for each of the body parts (the head, the arms, and the legs) - they can roll it with their hands into their three 1/2" balls.

Give them enough time to create their 3 balls

Step 2 (making the head): We're going to start with the head. Decide which ball you want to use.  Using a toothpick, you're going to make a hole that goes completely through the ball.  This is going to be used to attach the other body parts later.

Tip: Help children as needed.  The best way to make a hole is to put the ball on the table. Slowly punch though the ball with the toothpick until you feel it hitting the table.  Pick up the ball; push the toothpick all the way through and pull it out the other side.  If the ball distorts a little, you can use you fingers to reshape it.  Next, run the toothpick all the way through the ball, the opposite way, to make a clean hole!

Note: In making the hole, don't use anything wider than a toothpick.  We want the hole to be as small as possible!

Step 2 (making the arms): Next we're going to make the arms. Decide which ball you want to use for the arms. Using your hands, roll the ball into a hotdog-like shape.  You can pull the ends slightly to stretch it to the desired length.  Decide how you want the arms to look. You can have both arms go out straight.  Or, you can bend both arms slightly, by creating a "u" shape. For the arms you can face the "u" up or down. Or, you can make one arm look like it's waving by creating an "s" shape.  

Once your shape is done create a hole in the middle of the "u" or "s" curve.

Step 3 (making the legs): Now, we're going to make the legs.  Take the last colored ball and roll it into a hotdog-like shape.  Gently bend the shape in the middle to make a "v" shape, or to create a "u" curve.  Whatever feels good to you!  Using the same technique in Step 8, create a hole using a toothpick. The hole will go right in the middle of the bend.

Keep in mind that after baking the arms and legs will stay exactly as you positioned them. Manipulate the legs to be open or closed, or bend them how you see fit.

Step 4 (optional bead making): If you have time, you can make small beads from the leftover clay. You can add these extra beads to the ribbon if you wish to hang your creation.  Use your hands to shape the clay into small cubes or disks (about 1/4 inch). Make a hole where you want it; you can make it slightly bigger than before to accommodate the ribbon.

 
   Lining up the parts before baking

Step 5 (baking the clay): Next we're going to bake the head, arms and legs. Mount/slide each body part on a skewer.  Make sure the pieces aren't touching each other, or they will stick together during cooking.  Place the clay-filled skewers on a baking sheet/dish.  A glass baking sheet or dish is recommended, however, you can also use a cookie sheet covered in foil.

Cooking instructions will vary depending on the type of clay you use.  For Sculpey clay, baking directions are listed on each package.  Generally, you will be baking at 275 degrees for 15 minutes for each ¼" of clay thickness.  Sculpey Amazing Eraser Clay bakes for 10 minutes at 250 degrees. It is helpful to use an oven thermometer to accurately maintain these temperatures.

While the clay bakes have the children decide how they will hang their creation. Give them time to choose their ribbon and any additional beads you have provided.  Another option is to give them a healthy snack or do some stretching exercises to remind them of how important it is to meet your body's physical needs. If they prefer they can put their heads down and take a little rest.  Depending on the age group you may want read a book about feelings or ask the children to do more writing about their needs and how they will meet them.

Step 6 (Assembling your "Pay Attention to ME" doll):  Make sure your clay pieces have cooled down before assembling.  Take a 3" Head Pin; string one bead on the pin (the "head" of the pin should be facing down, so it holds the bead).  Next slide the legs of your clay person down the pin; then place another bead on top of the legs.  Next slide the arms down the pin; then place another bead on top of the arms (this will become the neck).  Slide the bead that serves as the head on top of the neck bead.  Place another bead on top of the head.  Using pliers, bend the head pin so it forms a closed circle around a jump ring.  (Note: help children with this part as needed - it can be tricky!). 

  
  Finished "Paying Attention to ME doll"
hanging from a beaded necklace

Step 7(optional):  Finally you can string a piece of ribbon through the jump ring to hang the clay person (and add any additional beads you created). Your "Paying Attention to ME" doll can be worn as a necklace or hung by your bed, etc. It will remind you of how valuable you are, and to take care of and honor your personal needs!

Closing Circle:
Ask each child to share about their "Paying Attention to ME" doll and anything they learned from this workshop. 

Encourage the children to continue journaling at home, and to keep looking at what they need or want.  They are worth it!  Remember: Noticing what we need to feel safe, happy and healthy in our lives is one of the most important jobs we will ever have, and one job that no one else can do for us!
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps the children to focus on identifying their own personal needs to feel happy and healthy. Each child will create a Paying Attention to Me Doll that can serve as a reminder that they have unique needs.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Offers a way of doing affirmations that focus on what participants want to believe and be, while acknowledging, challenging and learning about all the old beliefs. The project is a writing exercise geared to editing and ultimately deleting negative self-thought.

Materials:
Paper
Colored pens
Optional: Journal (to create into an "Affirmation Journal"), any other art supplies to decorate their affirmations.

Introduction:
Self-worth is an extremely important issue in dealing with survivors coming from abusive relationships. I don’t feel there are any easy ways to obtain this, but what we can do is offer some tools in order to help them move toward this goal. I think that it’s important to discuss the issue of raising self-worth as a process, rather than a point of arrival. Each small step is a victory toward this goal, and should be celebrated as such.

Sometimes it may seem like three steps forward and two steps back, but overall the general movement is toward health, healing, and gentleness and love towards oneself. It’s important to explain this to the women. Otherwise, they may be discouraged and feel “what’s the use in trying”. It is very hard to change a life time of internal messages about oneself: messages that are so ingrained that we experience them as who we are, rather than just the messages that we somehow took on and believed.

What if, as an infant, you were raised with parents who completely accepted you; they allowed you to be who you are without shame or guilt or disapproval; they encouraged you and allowed you to make mistakes and learn from them? You would have the belief system that you are OK. You are inherently lovable and perfect even with your human imperfections.

Instead, we have been raised with parents who only knew what they were taught and did only what they were capable of. Most of us grow up thinking that we are not OK, and we have this internal message ingrained into our beliefs about ourselves. Just because we believe this to be true doesn’t mean it is true. If you grew up in the other family, you would have the belief that you are OK. This analogy is important. It challenges our beliefs about ourselves by showing how we could have just as easily believed in our self-worth had we grown up in a different environment.

What we are faced with now is to unlearn and relearn. This is going to be challenging, but not impossible. This is where it’s very important to focus on celebrating small achievements as we move toward the goal of self-love.

What will be given in this art project is a way to do affirmations that affirm what you want to believe, while acknowledging, challenging and learning about all the old beliefs. These old beliefs are like a tape recorder that keeps playing the old messages over and over regardless of their validity. As an adult, we can challenge and eradicate these old beliefs.

Incorporating Art with the Affirmations:
Learning how to do the affirmations is really the main point of this exercise. In order to incorporate the art piece, I can suggest two options:

1) After participants have done the first affirmation exercise, they can write their affirmation on a piece of paper, decorate it and use it as the front page of an “Affirmation Journal;”

2) They may also simply make it into an art piece and hang it on their wall above their bed or next to the bathroom mirror.

Remember, the negative messages have been repeated by our own minds for years and years. So, it’s important to repeat the positive loving messages over and over in order to override the negative. You can learn the positive just as easily as the negative. Whatever gets repeated and given more attention will win out. It’s important to relate this to the participants. You must put some time and energy into relearning these new messages, but the end result is worth it. More importantly, you are worth it.

Affirmation Techniques:
Make two columns on a sheet of paper. On the left side, have the participants write out an affirmation (some suggestions are given below). On the right side, let them write the immediate response they have to the affirmation. Go back to the left side and write the affirmation again. Then write the immediate response again on the right side. Keep doing this until all the possible negative reactions are no longer coming to mind. Be patient, as this may take a while, but know that they will eventually stop. After they have stopped, write the affirmation on the left side of the paper twenty to thirty more times. Remember, repetition is tedious, but very necessary. The negative messages have been repeated over and over for years. So, put some time and energy into repeating the positive.

After participants have their successful affirmation, write it out on another piece of paper and decorate it with magazine pictures, positive word cut outs, drawings or whatever. Celebrate your new commitment to reinforcing the positive and challenge and dispute those old negative messages from now on. You deserve it.

Example Affirmations:
I am worthy of love from myself and others.
I deserve to be appreciated and loved.
I am worthy of being treated with gentleness and kindness.
I deserve to be happy.
I love myself.
I am gentle and nurturing towards myself.

You may have participants brainstorm with each other on other positive statements.

A Note on Wording:
Always keep affirmations in the positive rather than “I am not...” , “I cannot...”, “I don’t...”, etc. For some reason the mind does not acknowledge the “am not” part and sees it as “I am unworthy”, rather than the way you wrote it as “I am not unworthy”.

Example Exercise & Possible Reactions:
I am worthy of love         No you’re not
I am worthy of love         You are always fucking up
I am worthy of love         Not if you knew me
I am worthy of love         I want to believe it, but I don’t know how
I am worthy of love         Only if I earn it
I am worthy of love         Love doesn’t exist
I am worthy of love         Not the kind of love I am looking for
I am worthy of love         I want to be
I am worthy of love         Only if I love you first
I am worthy of love         Only if I am needed
I am worthy of love         I don’t believe you
I am worthy of love

Suggested Follow-up:
This exercise could be done everyday if possible, even twice a day if you can. You can even rip the page in half and take all the negative responses and tear them up and say good-bye to all that old conditioning and claim that this is not true for me today. I let these go. There is so much power in a simple ritual like this.
Row.txt_description: Offers a way of doing affirmations that focus on what participants want to believe and be, while acknowledging, challenging and learning about all the old beliefs. The project is a writing exercise geared to editing and ultimately deleting negative self-thought.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for Teens.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Shares a simple weaving method as a way for participants to express themselves creatively, learn about themselves and their world, and raise their self-esteem. A sketchbook/notebook is used as a loom, leading the fini shed product to be a woven journal cover.

 
 Yarn
Materials:
Small-to-medium size spiral sketchbooks/notebooks
Warp yarns
A variety of weft yarns
Pencils
Crayons
Watercolors
Scissors
Waving needles

Note:  Weavings are created by interlacing threads or yarns on a loom. The "warp" is the strong set of yearn or threads which run lengthwise in the loom, while the "weft" is the yarn or threads that are used to weave back and forth across the warp. Warp yarns need to be non-stretchy; cotton works well. Weft yarns, what you weave into the warp threads, can be anything!

Timeframe:
Classes can be 1-1&1/2 hours long. For a workshop, two hours would be great.

Introduction:
I love sitting in a circle, introducing ourselves and sharing what we know about weaving.

Guided Relaxation:
“This exercise is a way to get centered and visualize a cover for your weaving journal. If you feel safe, you can close your eyes. Become aware of your breathing. Think of a place that is very special to you, a place where you feel very safe. Smell the smells, listen to the noises, feel the breezes if you are outdoors, or the sand under your feet. This is your special place and because you are safe here, you can be your most creative. Let yourself begin to imagine the kind of picture you would like to bring back from this special place: the colors, the feelings, the words. When you are ready to come back from this place, begin to become aware of your breathing again.”

I usually sense when the group has had enough and begins to get restless and I respect their timing.

 
 
 
 Diagrams for creating weaving with sketchbook
Creation Process:
In this workshop we use the notebook as a loom. To do this we tie warp thread around it and tape it to the back. Keeping the tension even, wind the warp around the “loom,” keeping the yarns parallel but the spacing depends on personal choice. They can be wound close together, far apart, or both. It will affect the design and looseness or tightness of the woven piece. When you have as much warp on as the width of the piece you want to weave, tie off and tape at the end. Some people like to cut a small slit in the cardboard to anchor the weaving in with a knot.

Then, tie a piece of yarn (about a yard, not too long or it can tangle) to a needle or use your fingers to take the weft yarn over and under the warp threads. Leave an inch or so of the end thread hanging and weave it into the next row. To begin a new color do the same, weaving about an inch or more on either end back into the weaving. Keeping the edges straight is a new (and old) weaver’s biggest challenge.

To finish, cut the warp string down the middle of the back, 2-4 strings at a time and tie two strings at a time together. This prevents the weaving from unraveling and creates a fringe. Cut the fringe long enough so that the knots do not untie.

The sketchbook is for anything! I use mine to write in, do poetry, it's a scrapbook and a place to draw and design.

Towards the end of our time, I like to read a short story about weaving and life.

Reflection and Closing:
This time is very important and I am just learning how to incorporate this into my groups with a sharing of the work, comments on the experience and time to clean up the things they were using.

Background and Inspiration for Peace Weaving Project:
In 1991, The first Gulf War began and the first Peace Weaving was created. People from many ages, backgrounds, and beliefs have worked on these weavings. They have been sent with groups or individuals having a commitment to peace and restoration.

Iraq             -Physicians for Social Responsibility
Bosnia          -Halcyon Weavers
Haiti            -Bryan Sirchio
                   It now hangs in a hospital on a ward for
                   children with tuberculosis and AIDS.
Madison        -We are currently looking for a place to share
                   this weaving.
Israel           -There are plans to display this weaving with
                   the one for Palestine.
El Salvador    -Arcatao Sister City delegation, summer, 1996.
Burma          -In the process of being delivered to Burma.
Cuba            -Delivered to Havana, Cuba, January, 1997.
Nicaragua      -Being taken to our sister city, Managua,
                   Nicaragua, summer, 1997.
Palestine      -Current Peace Weaving.

Each weaving is a prayer or a thought of peace for a place in turmoil and pain. The hope is that each weaving will hang in a place of healing, such as hospitals, community centers, shelters, daycare centers, or homes for the elderly.

Project Variation:
Other than creating their own small weavings with the sketchbook/notebook as a loom, they can take part in creating larger Peace Weavings. Once they have the basic idea of their own looms I bring in a Navajo upright loom with a weaving in progress and I invite them to add a special color (obviously different for everyone) that feels like peace to them, or any symbolic piece they find, feathers, shells, etc. This can be worked on by, at most, four at a time. It is something they can turn to if they need a break from their project.

I choose the locations to send the Peace Weavings by my feelings. Sometimes, I am moved to send a weaving by the news, sometimes, friends have inspired me or social action groups, such as the Madison's Sister-City projects. I take my loom to family, friends, classes, churches, schools, the streets. It is a great way to open conversation and educate.
Row.txt_description: Shares a simple weaving method as a way for participants to express themselves creatively, learn about themselves and their world, and raise their self-esteem. The finished product is a woven journal cover.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide participants with a sense of safety in expressing all the negative things that have been said to them and they have thought about themselves so that they may:
-Write down anything, person or reason that they feel has held them back, kept them     from accomplishing (eg: ugly or negative secrets, fears, negative thinking or remarks,         etc.)
-Free themselves to grow and live a productive, spiritual and empowered life.
-Take responsibility and reclaim or establish their power. To stop claiming the negatives     and allowing them to "rent" space in the head.
 -Reclaim the positives and allow them to roam freely in the growing span of their             minds.
 -Discover a tool to use when the negatives are surrounding them and trying to break         their spirit and put them down.

This exercise will help the warrior inside come out and fight the negatives and will help your “empowered self” to increase in strength.  This workshop is especially useful when we are our functioning as own worst enemy by putting ourselves down.

Materials:
Pens
Pencils
Bright markers
Paper
Bucket or garbage pail
Water (to drown the papers)
Dirt (to dig a hole)
Match (to burn papers)
Area where there is a garbage bin, open grassy area, or dirt lot (for burial)

Music:
Music with drums or songs of empowerment (eg: Tracy Chapman, Gabriel Roth, Ubaka Hillor, Agape Choir). Uplifting songs work well with this workshop. It helps to evoke the emotions for release.

Time Format:
1-2 hrs., sometimes just 20-35 minutes. It depends on what place the group is in after completing this “Labor of Love” and how much they feel like talking.

Introduction:
“This excercise is a Labor of Love for oneself. It may not feel that way in the beginning, but hopefully it will in the end. Let's do this exercise in silence so that the ultimate in concentration can occur. There will be time of sharing if you choose to do so in the end. We can all agree not to share, but if someone wants to, they can do so without judgment and in the safety of this circle or room. Please do not ask to read someone else’s paper or comment on anyone else's sharing. Let's respect each other's needs and space.

Writing:
“Thank you for participating in this process! Each of you has a writing utensil and at least two pieces of paper. Please write down everything you hate about yourself. Put down what you can remember that was said to you: anything you want to let go of, any secrets that you want to release, anything that is hateful for you. You may also write down the person who has said harmful remarks or things to you if you so choose.”

Give about 5-20 minutes to write. Gauge your time by seeing what place everyone is in. Look around the room. No rescuing if someone is crying. Please don't run with a tissue. Let them ask for what they need, respecting they'll know when they need it. After completion of the list, ask the group if anyone wants to share. If no, move into the rest of the ceremony.

Creation:
One of two things can be done.
1. Each participant can fold their papers and tear it with all their might into tiny pieces. Then throw the paper into a trash can filled with water. Explain that it is important not to reclaim what was written, it is time to work towards the positive. If they do reclaim it at a later date, complete the ceremony again until they no longer reclaim the negatives back into their lives. Go out to that garbage bin. Let each participant either take a handful of water and paper flinging it into the bin or they may each pour some into the bin. Have them cheer and clap for themselves. Now is time for the closing and relaxation.

2. If you are in a grassy area or dirt filled place, dig a hole with a shovel and bury or burn the negatives in a deep hole. Let each participant share in digging the hole and placing the shredded paper in. The last person fills the hole in with water and dirt or covers the negatives. Let them cheer for themselves. This is where the ceremony ends and the relaxation and closing begin.

3. If there is a safe place to do it, i.e. a fireplace, the negatives can simply be burnt for a very satisfying finish followed by cheering, clapping and relaxation.

Relaxation & Closing:
The relaxation is the actual closing of the group. With a voice as soft as the wind and guided with a loving flow, begin the relaxation: “Please close your eyes, if this feels safe for you. [Open-eye meditation is still possible for those who are not safe closing their eyes.] Take a deep breath and let the air flow from your mouth slowly. Again this time follow the deep breath to your abdomen. Hold it for two seconds and release. This time make a soothing sound as the breath is exhaled. Inhale again deeper this time. Now release slowly making the soothing exhaling sound: sounds like music flowing from deep within you. For your last breath, go as deep as you can inhale. Picture yourself in a place that is peaceful for you. Exhale with a breath that is so soothing you send it to the center of the room. Whoever walks in this room afterward will feel all the good vibes you have left behind. Seek peace for yourself and do this relaxation before you go to bed at night or when you awaken. This has been a Labor of Love, a celebration of self. Note: If time permits, do a “feelings check” to make sure that everyone feels safe especially leaving the safety and support of the circle. This “feelings check” can be done quickly using one to two words or a sentence from each participant.
Row.txt_description: Provides participants with a sense of safety in expressing all of the negative things that have been said to them and they have thought about themselves. Allowing for a chance to free and reclaim their empowered, "warrior" selves from negative thoughts.

Row.txt_code:
“Disarming Your Critic” is the second part of the self-esteem art directive "Affirming Self-Worth" which appeared in the September Leader’s Update of 1997. Part of unlearning and replacing negative belief systems is through positive affirm ations. Another key part in this process is “disarming the internal critic.”



 "Flight of Escape!" by Twyla Swanson
Objective:
Offers participants the opportunity to explore the voice of their inner critic and then unlearn and replace negative belief systems through positive affirmations. The finished product is a two-part collage, one part is a vision of the critic's messages, the second is an image of a rescuer or some other kind of support against the critic.

Materials:
18” x 24” sheet of paper (or as large as you can find around this size)
Magazines
Glue
Scissors
Colored markers
Pencils

Note on Leading This Workshop:
It is important to impress upon the participants that this is a learning process and to look at progress rather than perfection. Explain to them that this internal critic has been having a big part in their mind for just about their entire life, and it probably won’t go away too easily or quickly. It’s important to celebrate small victories rather than expect huge changes right away. Impress upon them to be gentle with themselves as they grow and change into a new life of self-love and respect. Just as a caterpillar goes through many stages to become a butterfly, they too must go through a lifetime of transformation toward their own “becoming.”

Introduction:
What is this inner critic anyway? The internal critic is that “parental voice” inside you that condemns and criticizes you throughout the day. These messages are either ones that you heard directly when you were growing up, or messages that you internally believed that others felt about you or your behavior. This means that they are actually an “old tape” that continually plays in your head which was formed in your childhood. It may or may not be true for you today, yet you unknowingly keep replaying the tape.

In order to feel good about yourself, it’s important to be aware of the messages you believe and tell yourself. This way, you can begin to refute them.

For the purpose of this exercise, think back to a recent time when you made a mistake or accidentally did something which you felt bad about. Once you have that memory, recreate the scenario in your mind and listen to the things you told yourself about the mistake you made. It may be messages such as: “you can’t do anything right,” “you are such a screw-up”, “you’re such a klutz,” “you’re late again; that figures,” etc., etc., etc.

In this workshop, we will be exploring these messages so you can become more conscious of them. From this awareness of your critical messages, you can begin to change the way you treat yourself when they start in on you. In this workshop, we will accomplish this with some help from an imaginary or real person of your choosing.

This is very important! Just because you made a mistake or did something wrong does not make you a horrible person. Sometimes we need to talk to ourselves the way we would a child. We need to talk to ourselves about learning from our mistakes and giving ourselves an understanding and forgiving break. Human beings are not perfect. It’s human to make mistakes. It’s human to mess up and forget. Have kindness and gentleness in your heart when dealing with yourself.

Today’s art exercise will help you do two things: First, it will help you to be aware of the things you say to yourself, and second, it will give you creative ways to tame that critic in order to feel better about yourself. Have fun and learn about yourself. Use some humor if you can in dealing with the internal critic. Humor is very healing for something so harsh and critical.

Creation:
This workshop will take place in a two-part collage. On the first half of the page, we will create a collage of our inner critic’s messages. We will have a chance to explore all the things the critic says. On the other half, we will create a collage of an imaginary rescuer coming to support us against the critic. This will give us a chance to explore new, creative, loving ways of disarming our critic.

Part I.
The Critic’s Message:
Cut out symbols of your own “critical inner voice.” Messages or comments that you tell yourself can be written down or cut out from magazines: pictures that symbolize some part of the critical inner voice. The collage could also be about how you put “shoulds” on yourself. That is, things you feel that you should be, or should be doing, or should be doing better. Create a collage of the inner critic’s message on the left half of your page.

Part II.
Finding Support:
After the critic part of the collage is done, see if you can come up with a cartoon character who comes to the rescue. If the cartoon character doesn’t work, perhaps you can think of someone in your lifetime who seems loving, positive, and gentle. You could imagine that person coming to your rescue to deal with the inner critic.

Once you have found your “helper,” create a collage or symbol for it on the right half of the page. Add encouraging words or phrases the helper would say to you during the critic’s attack. By creating this symbol and adding these positive messages, they will more likely resurface automatically next time you begin to criticize yourself.

Note to Facilitator:
You may need to play around with ideas and help participants share with each other until each participant has a “helper” who will work with them. If they cannot come up with a person or cartoon figure, perhaps the good fairy in the Wizard of Oz or fairy godmother in Cinderella would suffice. Finding support is the main objective here.

You will probably also have to help participants brainstorm on positive messages to tell themselves. Get everyone’s input so they are personalized rather than you giving them the “answers.” However, if they are truly stuck, here are some options:

“It’s OK to make mistakes, I can learn from them.”
“I am doing the best I can with what I know.”
“I am a child of God, therefore I am valuable.”
“Silly me, I goofed up.”
“This is about a behavior and not about who I am.”
“I choose to let go of this old negative belief.”

Winding Down:
After the participants have finished creating ask them to sit in a comfortable position and close their eyes for a moment. Ask them to take a few long deep breaths. Then say the following:

“Now imagine yourself as you were when you were a five or six year old child, and imagine her sitting or standing in front of you. (Pause for a moment.) Imagine her innocence and magic of simply being the delightful child she is.... Now think of some of the messages you have realized today that you continually tell yourself. Think of how it would feel to this child if you told her those things. (Pause.) This is exactly what happens when you say those things to yourself. You are telling them to the five-year-old emotional child within yourself. Take a moment to understand that you actually did not realize what you were doing. But you can start watching what you say to yourself today. Forgiving yourself first and foremost, make a commitment to this five-year-old inside you. Tell the little child that you will start to lessen these critical messages as much as you can, and that you will work on being supportive and loving and forgiving to her. Love this little child, because she still lives within you. She is your soft heart and needs your continued nourishment. Treat yourself with gentleness and forgiveness, always.

Closing Circle:
Give each participant an opportunity to share one word, phrase or thought about what she takes with her from this workshop.

Further Resources:
There are many good books out there on building self-esteem. I would like to recommend the book Self-Esteem by Mathew McKay, Ph.D., & Patrick Fanning. This is a very thorough and practical guide, but may be too clinical for some. Two other very excellent books are: You Can Heal Your Life by Louise Hay and Healing The Shame That Binds You by John Bradshaw. These go beyond just self-esteem to include it in a more holistic way in your life. Bradshaw actually goes more into understanding the dysfunctional family system and its effects on the individual. This may be more appropriate and helpful for those leaving abusive situations.
Row.txt_description: Offers participants the opportunity to explore the voice of their inner critic and then unlearn and replace negative belief systems through positive affirmations. Finished product is a two-part collage, one part is a vision of the critic's messages, the second is an image of a rescuer or some other kind of support against the critic.

< /tr>


 Suzanne Karcher Rogers
  
About the Author:
My name is Suzanne Karcher Rogers.  I'm a survivor of domestic violence and have been a painter for fifteen years.  I've always thought of art as my home.  I decided to share this home of art experience with others last July in shelters in Ohio.  Showing others a place where they can gain clarity through their creations seems very important, or just inviting them to play with the idea of creating something seems to make a difference.  I'm not sure I'm always able to relate the home I've found in art to other people, but I come with the idea that we can all create meaningful things.  I've noticed the energy is uplifted during workshops.  If nothing else, it brings some good feelings and smiles, and sometimes more.

Objective:
To provide a space of time for survivors to think about dreams and goals for the future.  Since I've been running workshops, I've noticed that many of the adults have so many responsibilities in their lives - with children, finding new homes, and starting over - that they don't always give themselves time to think about their goals and visions.  My guess is some have long put their dreams on hold.  This is a chance to get back in touch with what they want for themselves, dreams they may have, but just forgotten.

Materials:
Plain greeting cards and envelopes
Masking tape (optional)
Oil pastels (sets can be shared)
Money saving option: assorted cattle markers or oil sticks
Pencils, Writing paper
Tape player and relaxing tapes

Note: This project can be done with any materials you have on hand, oil pastels are only one option.


 
 
 Example from Dreams and
Goals Card workshop
  

Note to Facilitator:
Plain greeting cards are sold in packs of 10 to 20, in craft stores, card stores, or some large super stores.  They are fairly inexpensive.  Cards could also be made from various paper (cut and folded) and standard envelopes.

Cattle markers are a type of oil stick.  They are sold in feed mills and art supply stores (they are made for marking cattle, therefore are much more reasonably priced than conventional oil sticks.)

Timeframe:
20 minutes - opening circle, taping off cards, materials explanation
10 minutes - relaxation/meditation
10 minutes - timed writing
15 to 30 minutes - card front creation time
20 minutes - closing circle
Total time - 1 1/2 hours

  


Detail of drawing by Sandy Stallings
 
  

Introduction:
“This is a time for you to think about yourself - your dreams, visions, and goals.  While we do this we'll be making a greeting card to ourselves.  I will not be asking you to read this card aloud, so it can say anything!  First we'll do a short relaxation exercise so you will have time to think about your dreams/goals, so if nothing comes to mind right this minute that's fine.”   I think it's important to explain to people that the relaxation-meditation exercise is nothing they have to do.  I always explain that all they need to do is sit there during it - this seems to make the idea more comfortable.

“After we do the meditation, we'll do 10 minutes of timed writing for the inside of the card.  This is a time to write your most unimaginable goals for your life.  No dream is too big!  This is a time to think, ‘I can do anything.’

Timed writing is - writing your first fresh thoughts.  Don't stop writing keep your hand moving across the page.  Don't cross anything out.  Don't hesitate to write any goal or dream no matter how silly it seems.  Imagine your life exactly how you would love it to be, and write about that.  Don't hesitate - write your first thoughts.”
You could begin with one of the following phrases:

My goal for my life is -
My dream for me & my family is -
I've always dreamed of -
If I could do anything with my life, I would -

“After this writing time (10 minutes) we will make an image that represents this dream on the front of the card, or you could continue writing on front and other sheets of paper.”


 
 
 Detail of drawing by Sandy Stallings
  

Technical Information:
“The materials available for these cards are oil sticks, oils pastels, and pencils.  Oils sticks make a greasy workable surface.  There is no wrong way to use these materials, and you may not want to use both sticks and pastels, but one way to use them is to apply the oil sticks first liberally and then work in pastels.  It's kind of a layering process, moving the paint around, changing and building the colors.  I've chosen these mediums because they are so changeable and you are not stuck with a surface.  The more you layer these paints (I think of them as paints, not crayons) the more interesting the image normally becomes.  Writing on the surface with pencil is also an option.  It creates very nice dark lines (writing) on the oil.”

Option: Taping off a square on the front of the card (with masking tape) before applying paints makes a nice crisp edge around your image.  (Show example of this.)

Relaxation:
This relaxation involves imagining colors as light or fog coming down into the room.  Some thoughts about meditation colors are included (page 4).  Feel free to copy and share these with participants.  Also, feel free to change the relaxation to better suit the needs of your particular group.

“Sit back in a relaxing position.  Take a deep breath and let it out slowly.  Think about any tension that may be in your body, and take a deep breath for that tension.  As you exhale, imagine the tension leaveing you.  (Continue taking breaths for arms, legs, stomach, neck, etc.)  Now imagine that a soft blue fog of light is coming down around you.  Breathe in the light and know that the light protects you.  Imagine violet light is coming down around you.  Breathe it in, and with this light you are free.  Imagine a soft yellow light coming down around you, and with it is your source of inner wisdom.  Imagine that a soft pink light comes down around you, and with it is an unconditional source of love.”

  


Detail of drawing by
Sandy Stallings
 
  

(You can continue with other light/colors if you like - I've found that passing out the Colors Meditation Thoughts tends to make people more interested in trying this relaxation technique and others.)

Lead-in to Timed Writing:
“Now start to think about dreams you have had in the past, and any that come to mind now, don't feel pressured, just let your thoughts flow through your mind.  When you're ready, open your eyes and begin writing.  Remember not to cross anything out, and don't stop writing.  Just write whatever comes to mind.  (Set timer when most of the group has begun writing.)

Painted Image:
When writing time is up (10 minutes) encourage participants to continue writing thoughts on other sheets of paper while making the card front image.

Closing Circle:
Give each person a chance to show the image on the front of their card, and share any thoughts about it.  Invite anyone to read their card,  explain there is no pressure to do so, or they could share how this experience has affected them.

Have everyone write their name on the front of a card envelope.

(Oil sticks take a few hours to dry, 2-10 hours according to the thickness applied) so the cards will not be placed in the envelopes right away.)

Keep your card to re-read occasionally!

Colors Meditation Thoughts:
This is a guide of colors you can meditate on, and the qualities known to these colors.  It is not meant to guide your art works, because the colors you choose then come from the inside of you.  I've included this because meditating with the idea of a color/light can be very relaxing, and can be done at any time.  The color is imagined, for example, as a soft blue fog or blue light coming down aroud you.  The color/light can be breathed in for a relaxed feeling of protection and faith.  Knowing as you breathe in the light you are safe and protected.

Light blue - Protection, Faith, Will
Shamrock Green - Healing, Supply
Violet - Freedom, Forgiveness, Transmutation
Light Yellow - Wisdom
Rose Pink - Love, Devotion
White - Purity
Purple - Service, Ministration
Row.txt_description: Provides a space of time for participants to think about dreams and goals for the future and to take those dreams and goals off "hold." The end product is a decorated greeting card that the participant writes to themselves, reminding themselves in a positive voice of their desires for the future.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for Teens.

Deborah Koff-Chapin


About the Author:
My name is Deborah Koff-Chapin.  I discovered Touch Drawing in 1974.  I was in the print shop on my last day of art school.  As I was about to clean an inked glass, I playfully moved my hands on the back of the paper towel.  Upon lifting it, I saw that lines had been transferred to the underside through the pressure of my fingers.  I became ecstatic with the realization that lines had just come directly from the movement of my fingertips on the paper towel.  I felt in this moment that ”Touch Drawing” was not for myself alone.  My calling in life is to share this healing creative process with others.  I am honored to be presenting it to you, who are doing such important work to support healing and creativity!  

Note:  Compared to other Windows workshops these materials are fairly expensive and the process is relatively messy and requires a lot of space.   

Objective:
“This workshop provides a very safe, deep and private space to be with yourself.  You draw whatever you feel in the moment.  Each drawing takes you to a new place in yourself, which you again draw.  There is room for all feelings; from pain and darkness to playfulness and joy.  All you need to do is draw what you feel in the moment, not thinking of what it ‘looks like.’  The sense of freedom and permission to draw whatever you feel allows a deeper part of yourself to emerge.  In one session you will do a whole series of drawings.   While reflecting on the drawings after they are done, you may be surprised by the beauty, strength, and honesty that came through; you may gain insight from these images that came from the non-verbal part of yourself.  In Touch Drawing you learn to trust yourself; that the deeper part of you can guide you through even the darkest times into the light.”

Materials:
Student grade oil paints, any colors
Printmaking rollers (two people can share one)
Any smooth surface: used glass, plastic lunch trays, Formica scraps from a cabinet-maker, or marker board from a lumberyard
Plenty of paper: at least 20 sheets per person.  Many types will work; I recommend tissue paper, available in packaging supply stores, because it is so sensitive to the touch.  Freezer paper, butcher paper, typing paper, and newsprint will all work.  

Note About Materials:  Touch Drawing books, videos, and Soul Cards are available at The Center for Touch Drawing (www.touchdrawing.com).





Hands in the midst of Touch Drawing.



Timeframe:
Two hours
Opening: 15 minutes
Activity: 45 minutes
Sharing with partner: 15 – 30 minutes
Closing circle: 30 minutes

Space Set-up:
If you are working on tables that need to be kept clean, cover them with newspaper or a plastic drop cloth.  Set a drawing board at each participant’s place.  Next to it place a roller, tubes of paint, and a generous supply of paper.  Completed drawings can be piled one on top of another on the floor next to each participant’s chair.

Opening Circle:
Demonstrate Touch Drawing.  Put a little paint on the board.  Show them that they do not need as much paint as they might think.  Roll the paint smooth.  Put a sheet of paper on top of the paint.  Move your hands upon the paper.  Lift it and show how the paint only sticks to the paper where you have touched it.  (Hence the name, Touch Drawing!)

Emphasize that this will be a safe and private time to be with your own feelings, that it is okay to allow whatever feelings to come up to be valid expressions.  Show how you can draw with your eyes closed or open, with both hands or either hand.  Show how even the feeling of “not being able to draw” can be turned into a drawing.  Encourage participants to just stay with the process and honor whatever they are feeling by drawing it.  Encourage them to just trust themselves to know what to do.  Say you will give some suggestions while they are drawing, but that it is most important that they draw what they are feeling; only following the suggestions if they feel right. 




Touch Drawing by Deborah
Koff-Chapin




Activity:
Have participants each go to their own drawing board.  Invite them to take a few moments in silence to be open to the possibility of having an experience that will be most helpful, healing and fulfilling for them.

Encourage participants to begin by closing their eyes and moving their hands on the page.  Lift the paper off and put another one on the board immediately.  Occasionally, you can make suggestions such as the following:

“Bring your attention to your face.  Draw what your face feels like right now.

“Become aware of what your body feels right now.  Draw from those feelings.

“If you could do anything right now that would express how you feel, what would that be?  Imagine yourself doing that and draw yourself.

“Become aware of how your body would like to feel right now.  Draw from those feelings.

“Think of a relationship or situation in your life that you would like to change.  First draw it the way it feels to you right now.

“Next, draw the change you would like to experience.  Allow yourself to feel as if it has actually happened.  Draw from that feeling.

“Allow yourself to just be free of any thoughts.  Look at the paper.  Do you ‘see’ any drawing that has begun by itself through paint sticking to the paper, or anything that just pops into your mind’s eye as you gaze at the paper?”

A few minutes before the end of the drawing time, let the participants know they will be coming to a close soon.





Touch Drawing by Deborah
Koff-Chapin



Sharing in Partners:
When the activity time is over, encourage participants to find a partner they feel safe with.  One at a time, honor each other’s experience by looking through the drawings from the first to the last.  It is not necessary to interpret the drawings.  Just being deeply “seen” can be enough.  The participants can talk about what their experiences were while drawing.

Closing Circle:
Encourage each participant to share something about her experience.  Invite them to share a drawing or two if they would like.  This is not required.  Suggest that participants look at their drawings again in a few days.  They will be able to appreciate them more over time.  Talk about how they can take their drawing experience further by working creatively with their drawings.  This could happen as a group in another session; journal writing, storytelling, movement; whatever modes of expression you are comfortable leading the group in.   

Close the session with a moment of quiet to give thanks for each participant’s experience.  State the intention that each participant will find her own way to integrate and use this experience in a positive way.
Row.txt_description: Provides a very safe, deep and private space to draw whatever participants feel in the moment. The end product is a series of quickly done, intuitive drawings.
Row.txt_notes: ER TO DO: Original Quark update lost, need to create new layout (text is already entered).

Row.txt_code:
Suzy Karcher with Art Festival participant
 
  
About the Author:
Suzy Karcher Rogers is an artist and survivor of domestic violence who traveled from Ohio to attend the Window’s Leadership Training in 1997.  Since then, she has launched weekly art workshops for the residents at two local Ohio shelters.  In the process, she has developed many of her own workshops, and this is the second one she has written up to share with all of us at AWBW.  

Because of staffing and childcare challenges at the shelters, Suzy has often found herself working with children and adults together.  While this situation has been less than ideal and Suzy has had her hands full, she has been able to make a success out of these situations.  Her flexibility, her willingness to prepare for the unexpected, and her relaxed delight in participants of all ages help make this possible.


 
 
 Freedom Beads
  

Objective:
This is a fun and lively workshop.  It is also a time to think about freedom, and its importance to us.  Being in an abusive relationship, or part of a family where abuse has taken place can make it hard to remember what freedom is.  This workshop gives us a period of time to think about freedom - what it means to us personally, and how we can also allow others (including our children) to feel a sense of freedom.

Materials:
Super Sculpey
Acrylic paint
Brushes
Palette paper, or paper plates
Bead string
Scissors
Writing paper
Markers
Relaxing music
Optional: Assorted colored beads (young children are not always able to complete the process of making and painting beads to string.  It’s nice to have assorted beads for them to string along with the others).

Note:  Plastic beads can be bought in a large bag fairly inexpensively.

Less Messy Option:  Instead of using acrylic paint, buy colored Sculpey.  It‘s more expensive than plain Sculpey but can save a lot of time and mess with the paints. 


 
 
 Freedom Necklace (enlarged detail)
  

Timeframe:
(Total time - 1 1/2 to 2 hours)
15 minutes - opening circle
30 minutes - making Super Sculpey beads
10 minutes - baking time  (This can be time spent experimenting with the paint - mixing colors on the palette.)
15 to 30 minutes - painting the beads
10 minutes - stringing beads (Children may need more time.)
10 minutes - closing circle

Note to Facilitator:  I’ve found during this workshop that adults and children really have a good time making these beads. Because they are making so many quick art works (beads), they are not bound by the idea that they all have to turn out good - as often happens when only making one thing.  The idea of making a bead necklace is just frivolous enough to take away some people’s hesitation of making “art,” and they become free to create however they want.

Working with Adults and Children:
I have had some very good workshops where both adults and children are involved, but I basically try to go with the flow of the residents.  If the group is small (3 to 5 people) it normally goes very well, but with larger groups it becomes a little hectic.  Ideally, there should be other volunteers or staff to help the children in this workshop, but it’s been my experience that volunteers are not abounding at the shelter, and staff usually have a lot of their own duties.  Still, planning ahead to have others help would certainly make the workshop run smoother.  Normally there is child care staff around and I invite them to help run the workshop.  If that is not an option, I try to arrange the group in a circle where adults and children are involved together.  Children like working with Super Sculpey, so they don’t get bored too quickly.  They can make a couple of large beads and then start stringing plastic beads while the adults are still working.  Children should be at least 3 or 4 years old to be in this workshop. 


 
 
 Freedom Necklace
  

Opening Circle:
“We’re going to be making beads out of Super Sculpey, painting them, and stringing a ‘Freedom Necklace.’  This necklace could be worn or hung on a nail on the wall to remind us of the freedom we want for ourselves and others.  We’ll begin with a discussion of what freedom is, and how we might bring this idea to the beads we’ll be making.”  (Everyone should have a chance to talk in the circle, or feel “free” not to.  I normally start the conversation and just invite anyone else to jump in, they always do, and it takes away the pressure of those who do not feel like talking.)

Exploring Ideas of Freedom/Creating the Beads:
“Freedom may be being able to make decisions for yourself, and voice them, without fear of what others will do.  You may just want to think of a time when you have felt very free.  You could allow yourself the freedom now to make these beads any way, any size, without concern for how they might look.  Think about what shape freedom is for you.  Maybe it’s just a round bead that you don’t have to do much to.  What color is it?”

I encourage the adults to write thoughts while making beads.  In addition, when working with the children, I have a large sheet of paper beside me.  I invite them to voice their thoughts, while making beads.  I write their thoughts on our “Together List.”  When everyone is finished making the beads they can place them on their own area of the baking pan (everyone needs their own space on a baking tray to keep people’s beads separate).

Baking Time/Paint Exploration:
Beads bake quickly (about 5 minutes) because they’re small.  Large beads should be put on a different pan to begin with so they can bake longer (10 minutes).  “While the beads are baking we will experiment with the paint on palette sheets.  Let’s not settle for the colors in the tube.  That may be what you want, but let’s see what we can make first.”  (This becomes a very interesting part of the workshop.  Many people have never really mixed colors, and discovered what paint can do.  If the palette becomes interesting, I suggest they keep it as a painting, and mix for the beads on another sheet.)
 
Painting and Stringing the Beads:
One suggestion for painting beads is to paint small lines on the palette paper and just roll the beads through it.  Some may want to paint intricate paintings on the beads.  Acrylic paint dries fast (about 5 minutes).  Children will finish first, so you could take them away from the table and do some stretching games, while the beads are drying, and the adults finish painting.  Children will also need help stringing the beads.  String at a new table, and have the plastic beads there to add to the necklaces.  Older children can help the younger ones string beads also.  

Closing Circle:
Everyone should have a chance to show their necklace and talk about it.  Some participants will want to read part of what they have written.  Let them know that their writing is a valid form of art as well as the necklace, and they should keep it.  The “Together List” should be read also - children like to know that their thoughts are important.

  


Freedom Pin, Super Sculpey
Row.txt_description: A fun and lively workshop, giving time to think about the importance of freedom. End product is a Freedom Beads necklace or other form of wearable art.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation specifically for adults and children together.

Row.txt_code:
Fig. 1: Unusual handmade book shape
  
As a volunteer staff person at AWBW, I participated in a handmade book-making workshop recently led by Sherrill Kahn. Sherrill is a dynamic artist and teacher and her energy is infectuous.  We had a great time making and sharing our books.  Since we had almost the whole day to explore book-making, Sherrill introduced a lot of techniques. However, since shelter workshops are limited to two hours or less, I’m going to share the basics of book-making in this update.

Objective:
This workshop is a wonderful opportunity for participants to create something deeply personal, something they can keep and cherish.  A book can be whatever shape, size or color the participant wants.  They can be used as journals for art or writing or photos.  The important thing is, as Sherrill stressed, is that there is no right or wrong.  She showed us some of the different shapes, colors and cover designs of books she had made.
 
Materials:
Cover-weight paper for book covers
Paper for inside pages (try to provide a variety of colors for both cover and inside paper)
Acrylic paint (include iridescents)
Sponges cut into 1” squares
Net/mesh bath sponges (you can buy one mesh sponge, undo the metal staple at the center, cut into several pieces, and restaple, to create many mesh sponges from one)
Stapler: Long-necked (if available) or standard (if using a standard stapler, you will need corrugated cardboard and a metal table knife or spoon to hand-close the staples)
Plastic forks
Edgers (scissors that cut an interesting edge design)
Rubber stamps (optional)
Scissors (one per participant)
Glue sticks (one per participant)
Paper plates (to use as pallettes)
Paper towels
Water bucket (for rinsing sponges and rubber stamps)

Timeframe:
(Total time - 1 1/2 to 2 hours)
15 minutes - opening circle
10 minutes - demonstration
60 minutes - making books
15 minutes - closing circle

Note on Preparation:
It is helpful to have a few examples of books you have made to show at the beginning of the workshop.  It’s good to show some unconventional shapes (see Fig. 1), and let participants know they can make any shape they want.  It doesn’t need to look a certain way. 

To create the samples, I recommend that you try the following 6 steps yourself.  It will be well worth the time and will make it much easier for you to assist the participants.

Opening:
“Today, we will be making hand-made books.  As we make our books, the most important thing to remember is that there is no right or wrong.  You get to make your book any shape, size, color you think of.  Here are some examples of hand-made books (show your samples).  I’ll be demonstrating some of the steps we can use to make the books, but I want you to remember, you never have to do it like I am.  You get to do it however you want to.”  (If you want to have an opening circle, with each person sharing something about how they are feeling, go ahead and incorporate that into your opening.)

Demonstration:
To best share the book-making steps, create a demonstration example in front of the group.  That way, you can show each step hands-on, while encouraging each participant to be creative and make their book however they want it. 

You can either do a full demonstration of the steps before the group begin their own books, or you can demonstrate each step along with them.  Use whichever way works best for you.

   



Fig. 2: Cutting triangular book cover
 Fig. 3: Cutting round book cover
   
Step 1: Cover
The first step is for each participant to select their cover paper and then fold and cut it into their desired size and shape.  Books can be large, small, square, round, triangular, or any shape the participant chooses.  Encourage each person to create their own cover (see Fig. 2&3).   

Step 2: Select Pages
Next, each participant selects the paper to put inside their cover (usually about 4 sheets, folded, is enough).  Trim the pages so that they are slightly smaller than the cover.  Again, remember that creativity is welcome.  Some women may want to design their books with the paper sticking out of the cover.

Step 3: Staple Pages
Third, participants can bind their books.  They can staple along the fold using a long-neck stapler, if one is available (see Fig. 4).  Otherwise, they can use a standard stapler.  Open it up so that it is flat, and use corrugated cardboard underneath to staple into (see Fig. 5).  The book will be stapled, with the staples sticking straight into the cardboard.  You will need to pull the book off of the cardboard and then use a knife or scissors to bend the ends of the staple down (see Fig. 6).
   



Fig. 4: Using long-necked Stapler
 Fig. 5: Using regular stapler, opened up,
pressed into corrugated cardboard
   


 
 
 Fig. 6: Using scissor tip to close staples
by hand
  
Step 4: Hiding the Staples
It’s amazing what a difference it can make to disguise the staples.  They can be hidden by gluing pieces of paper down the center of the booklet and/or down the outside edge of the cover (see Fig. 7&8).  (For decorative effect, you can sponge-paint the paper before gluing it over the staples.)



   



Fig. 7: Covering staples on
outside of book
 Fig. 8: Covering staples on inside of book

   
Step 5: Detailing the Edges 
Add a decorative edge to the pages either by using paper-edgers (see Fig. 9&10), or by lightly finger-painting the edges of the cover with paint (see Fig. 11).  Gold paint looks especially elegant as an edge.



   



Fig. 9: Using edgers on inner pages
 Fig. 10: Edged cover

   

  
Fig. 11: Finger-painting   
   

Step 6: Decorate Cover 
The surface of the covers can be decorated by stamping paint on in many ways.  Sponges, forks and rubber stamps are only a few suggestions we have included for you to demonstrate. 

Once participants get going, they may find all sorts of objects around the shelter to use to create interesting patterns.  Encourage them to experiment.


 
 
 Fig. 12: Plate palette with white paint
  

Preparing the palette:  To use these techniques, each participant will put paint onto a plate (this will be their palette).  Then they can use the sponges, net mesh, forks, and anything else they wish, to apply the paint from the palette to the book). Participants may also want to have some scratch paper at hand to experiment with creating stamp effects (see Fig. 12).

Sponge-effect:  Dab the sponge onto the pallette until the paint is the consistency you want.  The amount of paint on the sponge makes a big difference as to how the sponge-effect will look.  Experiment on the pallette with having different amounts of paint on your sponge. 

Web-effect:  Using a web-mesh bath sponge is a quick and easy way to decorate the booklet cover.   Similar to the sponge-effect, you will dab the mesh bath sponge onto your pallette.  It may take some vigorous dabbing to distribute the paint throughout the mesh for a web-like effect (see Fig. 14).  Experiment with amounts of paint.  For a fine web, it does not take very much paint, just a lot of dabbing.


 
 
 Fig. 13: Dabbing mesh into paint
  
 
 Fig. 14: Creating web pattern on cover
 
 Fig. 15: Fork pattern, white paint on black
  

Fork-effect:  The tip of a fork can be used to place paint onto the cover of the booklet.  The effect can be somewhat like shooting stars (see Fig. 15).  This was discovered during the workshop thanks to one of the participants.

Rubber stamps:  If you have rubber stamps available, these can provide a wonderful source of decoration for the covers.  Use sponges to dab the paint onto the rubber stamps.  Then press onto the cover.  Before stamping on your cover, you may want to experiment on scratch paper with the effects created by different amounts of paint.

Further Decorations: 
Sherrill had lots of wonderful ideas for decorative ideas for the cover.  She suggested wooden beads, charms, raffia, yarn, shells and anything else the leaders or the women come up with.  A lot of items can be sewn or glued to the book. 

Closing Circle:
Save some time for the group to share what they made, what feelings and thoughts went into their decisions.  Perhaps they will be open to sharing what they will use the book for, and perhaps the next workshop can be dedicated to creative word pieces or picture collages to put into their books.
Row.txt_description: A powerful opportunity for participants to create something deeply personal to keep and cherish. The books can be whatever shape, size or color they want and can be used as journals for art, writing, or photos.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variations for Children's and Teens.

Row.txt_code:
Rose Curtis
 
Background:
As an AWBW Art leader, I am forever grateful for the opportunity to lead and participate in workshops with those staying at the shelter.  I had this idea of a round, “pizza-shaped” collage for many months now, and recently Katlin, the Survivor's Art Circle Director, inspired me to lead a workshop that would become part of the Survivor's Art Letter.  I had a great time coming up with the "Center of My Universe" idea, and of course, Cathy Salser motivated me to write up the workshop formally to share it with all of you!

I believe a circle is a very powerful symbol and when we put ourselves at the center of our universe, we can only expect powerful changes to happen in our lives. As you lead and participate in this workshop, I hope you are truly inspired to boldly create your Universe.

Objective:
This workshop is an opportunity for participants to focus on placing themselves at the center of their universe.  Each person’s vision of what this would mean to her unfolds during the workshop and becomes clear and tangible throughout the collaging process.
 
 
Materials:
Collage material (magazines, photostock books, etc.)
Glue sticks and scissors
Round poster board, approximately 9 inches across

Timeframe:
(Total time - 1 1/2 to 2 hours)
15 minutes - opening circle
10 minutes - demonstration
5 minutes - relaxation
45 minutes - making books
15 minutes - closing circle 

Opening:
“This is a window of time to think about what exactly you want in your world. Put yourself in the center of your universe and decide what pleases you, what makes your life work, what is absolutely necessary to thrive.

As you are guided through the relaxation, see yourself as the
most important person in your universe and visualize what you want in your world. Be bold and feel free to see all your dreams come true!”

Demonstration:
“What we will be doing today is creating exactly what we want in our Universe. We are going to create a round collage. Put an image in the center of the collage to represent you. Then surround this image with all that you want in your world. When we know firmly in our hearts and our souls what we want, and when we put out to the Universe what we want, we are most likely to receive and achieve exactly what we want.”

Relaxation: 
Speak slowly, softly and very lovingly. “Make yourself comfortable. When you are sitting it is good to be sitting with your back straight, your feet flat on the floor and your hands lying loosely in your lap.
   


All the words featured in this
collage have a special meaning to me.  Especially
the phrase that surrounds
the woman who represents
me.  Now is the time to
think about me.  Many of the
words are things I look
forward to in my future such
as... the perfect marriage
and baby number two.  I look
at this collage and realize all
the words on the collage are
a part of me.

    -Jennifer Galvan

The Power of Words
1998, collage
Artist: Jennifer Galvan
  
   
“Take a deep breath and if it feels safe for you, you may close your eyes. This is a special time just for you...to breathe in love and breathe out any tension.

“Take another deep breath and exhale softly... move your awareness down to your feet and gently wiggle your toes... feel the relaxation moving up your calves... gently relax your thighs and your whole pelvic area. Breathe in slowly... exhale slowly and feel your stomach muscles gently relax.

“Breathe in love... breathe out tension and feel your shoulders relax. If there's any tension left in  your shoulder area, imagine it sliding off your shoulder.
Breathe in deeply and become aware of any last holding you are doing in your body, calmly release the tension... breathing in love... breathing out tension... feel yourself relaxing more and more deeply. Imagine your entire body is now totally relaxed.

“Now move your awareness into a very deep place inside of you... let images of the world you want float into your mind. See yourself strong and daring at the center of your universe... (pause) What do you want in your Universe? Notice what you want to surround yourself with... notice what your universe is made up of... breathing in love, visualize everything you desire in your Universe.

“Keeping those images with you bring yourself gently back to the room and when you are ready, open your eyes and begin to create a collage of your world with you boldly in the center of your Universe.”

Collage Activity:
Afer the relaxation, allow the next 45 minutes for participants to create their collages.

Closing Circle:
Ask the group to share their collage and any of the feelings that came up for them while creating their Universe.

Special Thanks:
The relaxation is adapted from "Meditations" by Shakti Gawain.

   


For me it means getting on with
life and becoming a better
person; learning to love myself
and having another person love
me and respect me.
