I might say "It's not okay for people to touch your private parts unless it's your Mommy or Daddy and they’re giving you a bath. (You know it depends on the age of the kid.) And then I'd say, "But maybe we can talk about that later." And then I might say to the group, "This is our body and we need to say ‘No’ to someone who does something that's not okay, and then we need to tell somebody."

And then, later I'd want to have some private time with the kid and find out more about what they were saying. With this workshop, that may come up in the group, and it’s important to be ready to treat it like a general thing, and then address it in more depth with the child later to assess the situation and take further steps as necessary.

(Depending on your particular staff of volunteer role at the shelter, you may need to seek assistance from other shelter staff to follow up on such a situation.)

“What We Put in our Bodies” Discussion:

 
 
 Children’s Leader’s
Workshop participant
  

This is another discussion I offer the children as we get ready for the Body Tracing activity:  “Now, what we eat is how we get to make our bodies get strong.  So what we put in our bodies is really important.  We have to eat good food.  What's good food?”

In addition to naming healthy foods, the children may offer some challenges of what they’ve seen adults doing, like coffee or smoking.  Possible responses might be "Mmmm. Maybe when you're grown-up, coffee.  Even so, you see a lot of grown-ups drink coffee and they're kind of irritable.  How about smoking?  Not good for the body, right?   But maybe a lot of grown-ups do it but it's hard when you're a kid.  But you can tell your Mommy or Daddy, please don't smoke around me?"

  


Children’s Leader’s Workshop participant
 
  
  
  

Introducing the Tracing Project:
“We're going to draw our bodies today and then you get to fill in like putting band-aids on 'owies' to feel better.  You can put colors on where it feels good in your body.  And you can do whatever you like.  It's your body and you can decorate it just the way you want.  You can imagine putting all the clothes on and maybe the clothes that nobody will let you wear, you can just draw them on your body.

“So, we're going to have a piece of paper here, and you’ll have a grown-up to help you get the outline drawn.”  

Talking Through the Tracing Process:
Adult says: "I'm going to trace around you but maybe it's going to tickle a little bit so tell me if it's not okay with you."  It’s important to let the child know what you're doing at each moment, otherwise they might be terrified.  So I say, "We're going to go gently around you so I can get a nice shape of your body, is that okay with you? Let me know if it tickles, okay.  Alright.”

Around the arm: “I'm taking the marker and moving down your arm now, I'm going around your fingers, okay?   And it may tickle a little bit.  Yeah, that's not scary.  Okay, I'm going up your arm now right and so lift your sweater a little bit there.”

Down the side: “I'm going to go down to your waist. You must have been growing since you've been here; you look like you're taller to me.”

Around the leg and foot: “Here you go, I'm going down your leg, does this tickle?  Okay.  Do you like tickling?  Okay, I'll try not to tickle you then.  This is a bit tricky and you know what, I'm going to have to move your leg a little bit so we can get your foot, okay. So let me know if it's okay.  So moving just a little bit here.”

Between the legs: “Okay, I go up your leg now, alright.  I go right up here because I want to do your legs okay?  So you might feel something right there.  There you go and now I'm going down your other leg and move it again so I can get your foot.  Yeah, you're getting the hang of it now.  Okay we're going to do your feet and go up your other leg.” 

Wrapping up:  “You're being so still,  I'm going to get a real good tracing of your body.  It's helping me a lot with you staying still.  Are you sleeping at night in the shelter?   Okay.  Now you get to decorate it.”

Decorating the Bodies:
“Okay, let's all sit around our bodies.  And here we have band-aids, so if you want to put them down where we've got 'Owies' and we want to make it better.  And we've got nice stickers, and we've got lots of glitter and glue.  And here's some markers.  Anything you want to do.  You can decorate your body any way you want.  You may have all the colors that you like.  Make your body really jazzy.”

For younger kids sometimes I like to have pre-cut images.  So I can say, you really like baseball, how about sticking this baseball picture on your body.

For a lot of kids they have so much fantasy about painting themselves.  I've noticed a lot of kids in the shelter draw on themselves.  So this is like their chance to get them out of doing that and they can use their bodies here.  I think marking yourself is sort of like a ritual.  For some kids it's about hurting themselves and its actually better that they're drawing on themselves than hurting themselves.   Body tracing gives your body a lot of importance. And of course kids make all these comments about DOA (chalk outlines) and so on.  I think when you work with older kids, when they're 8 and up then you might get more self-conscious stuff about the body and body image, especially pre-teen/teen girls.  With your younger kids its actually lovely to see kids being free with their bodies.

“Wow.  Look at this colorful body.  Would your Mom let you wear these colors?  See it's kind of fun to pretend.  Any 'owies' on your body?  None, that's good.  Is that a happy face? Do you always have to have a happy face?  Is it okay not to have a happy face?”

Closing Circle:
To close, I gather everyone around and ask, "What are some of the good things about our bodies?"  And I'd also have the drawings and talk about how colorful they are and the images... (i.e.:) "I can see you have these boots for walking and dancing.  And it's good to keep our bodies safe and strong.  And look at that, I see that you like to have all kinds of colors on your nails.  Do you like to play with your Mom's nail polish?"  So you kind of like to have kids talk about their drawings and things they like to do with their bodies.  And bring it to a close: "We're going to keep our bodies in a nice place.  Maybe you want to put them up in your room.  Or you can leave them here. You might want to show your Mom."
Row.txt_description: A supplement to "Celebrating My Body," a workshop in the Children's Windows Manual. Shares in detail the words and tone of Binah Taylor when working with young children; how she engages them in the process and specifically how she talks them through being traced.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
< td>Shyann Duncan, participating
in a workshop during the 1998
Children’s Windows Training.





About the Author:
Shyann Duncan is a wife of nine years and a mother of three beautiful children, with a fourth on the way.  She is a graduate of Honolulu Community College, Human Services, Early Childhood Education.  Shyann became involved with children of domestic violence in May of 1998, when she became Childcare Program Director at Oshun Village Family Services in Palmdale.  She has been involved in the field of early childhood education for the past six years.  Shyann conducts weekly workshops with the children and has begun "family" workshops.  These workshops allow the mother and child(ren) to work together in a peaceful, supportive environment.  These workshops have been a success at the shelter.  The women and children love it, and Shyann truly enjoys leading them.

Objectives:
To provide mother and child(ren) with a vision of the wonderful future they can have, free from domestic violence.  To give the family an opportunity to work together as one, promoting a sense of unity in creating a representation of what their future home might look like.  To allow the family to express their dreams through creating their new home.  To allow families the opportunity to express some of the feelings they have about leaving their old homes, and the thoughts and feelings they have about moving to a new home. 





Creating a Dream House sample.



Materials:
Sticks, grass, rocks, flowers, pine cones
Rulers
Pencils, marker, crayons
Hot glue guns, glue sticks
Glitter glue sticks
Extension cords for hot glue guns

Optional: You could do this workshop with other supplies if you dont’ have a safe ploace for a nature walk.  Lots can be built with ordinary construction paper, tape, and glue.  

Timeframe:
15 minutes:  Opening Circle
60 minutes:  Activity
15 minutes:  Closing Circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 families

Space Setup:


Creating a Dream House sample.




Choose a space outdoors, which can provide the families with the necessary nature materials needed.  This space can be the front yard or back yard of the shelter.  If this space is not available, perhaps the setting can be at a park.  Make sure this outdoor area is safe for the families to walk about freely for 10 to 15 minutes.  This outdoor environment will be the location of the nature walk.

Have all the other materials set up on the tables before the group begins in order to avoid any distraction.  If possible, give each family their own table with supplies so they can work together comfortably.  If this is not possible, set the tables and chairs where each family can sit together and work together independently.  Make sure that the environment is supportive so that each family has the ability to focus on their own project.

It is a good idea to have some toys (Legos, blocks, dolls, cars) for the younger children who do not have the ability to stay involved in the workshop.

Opening Circle:





Creating a Dream House sample.



Play soothing music in the background and have each family sit together on the floor (or ground), holding hands.  Begin by doing some deep breathing exercises from the Breathwork section of the Children’s Windows Manual.

Ask them to close their eyes.  As the leader, begin guiding them in focusing on a new environment, safe from hurt, harm, or danger.  Ask them to think of a big empty space, near the beach, mountains, desert, etc.  Ask them to imagine themselves having all the space, time, and money to build themselves a new house on the big empty space.  Give them possible images of what the yard, the street, the house might look like.  Ask them now to gather their own images and focus on those images.  Encourage them to be vivid in their imaginations.

Invite each family to share their images.  It has been my experience that some mothers do not feel comfortable talking.  This is okay.  The children love to share their images.  Allow them the opportunity to do so.







Creating a Dream House sample.



Activity:
This workshop begins with a nature walk.  Before going on the nature walk, explain to the families that the purpose of this walk is for them to gather and collect materials with which they will build their houses.  Encourage the family to work together in collecting their sticks, grass, leaves, rocks, etc.  Let the children know that they cannot run off and play during this walk.  They should stay with their mothers.  As leader, move along with the families, offering help or a supportive word.  This portion of the activity should take no more than 20 minutes.  Once everyone has collected his or her materials, return to the original location of the activity.

Then have each family choose a place to sit.  If each family has their own table, encourage them to begin working on their house.  If the families are sharing the tables, ask each family member to sit next to each other.  In my experience with this activity, many families have needed clarification on how to make their houses.  I showed them pictures of samples that I had.  I suggest that you make one beforehand to have as an example to show them.

If you don’t have time to make one for viewing, tell the families that the mat board is the foundation upon which the house will be built.  Explain that the sticks can be glued by laying one on top of the other, (like a log cabin) or they can be glued standing straight up (like stilts).  They have the freedom to make their house any way they want.  The houses can be large or small, wide or narrow.  The mat board can be landscaped or decorated with grass, rocks, or flowers, to represent the yard.  Try to create a sense of "we can do this" within the workshop.  Add soothing music to create a stimulating atmosphere.  As leader, circulate among the tables offering assistance when needed.  Remind mothers to supervise their children when using the hot glue guns.

Closing Circle:





Creating a Dream House sample.



Invite each family to share their houses with the other participants.  Ask them to describe their homes, where they will be located, and who will be living there.  The houses will still be fragile, and possibly wet with glue, and may not be ready to be brought to the circle.  I suggest having closing circles at the tables so the houses can be in view.  I like to end this activity with having each family making an affirmation statement.  For example:  "I know that my children and I will one day have a home like this.  You can bet on it!"
Row.txt_description: Provides adults and children with a vision of the wonderful future they can have, free from domestic violence. Gives the family an opportunity to work together as one, promoting a sense of unity in creating a representation of what their future home might look like.

Row.txt_code:
Some of the cigar boxes recently
donated to AWBW for “Wish Boxes”


Objective:
To give each child an opportunity to enjoy exploring their wishes as they layer colors and pictures onto their own personal box.   To give each child their own private place (the box) to store notes and treasures safely.

Materials:
Cigar boxes - one per participant
Colored tissue paper (torn into small pieces - 1”-2” wide)
Large margarine containers
Elmer's glue
Large, soft brushes
Magazines (pre-cut for young children)
Scissors
Newspapers
Permanent markers
Paper towels
Optional: Ribbons, Glue sticks, Feathers, Sequins, Beads, Buttons





Glue/Water mixture, ready to dip into



Timeframe:
Opening Warm-up: 10 min.
Activity:  40 min.
Closing Circle:  10 min.

Ratio:
1 adult for 4 children; 1 adult for 2 young children.

Space Setup:
Cover table well with several layers of newspaper.  Also, set up a “drying area” with newspaper.  This will be where the completed boxes can be set to dry.  Make a bowl of glue/water mixture (half glue, half water).  Depending on the number of children, you may need more than one bowl.  Each child should have one within reach.  Rip up plenty of multicolored tissue paper for the children to use.  Also, rip or cut out magazine pictures for the younger children to use, since cutting out pictures might be difficult for them.  (AWBW has pre-cut images available for use in the Children’s Windows Workshops).




Torn tissue paper, ready for gluing




Opening Warm-up:
Movement and Sound Warm-ups from the Children’s Windows Training Manual, pg. 36.  
Talking About Wishes:
If the focus level of the group allows, you may want to start with a brief sharing of ideas on wishes.  (If the group is too young or too energetic to focus, it’s fine to let each child begin their box right away.  The process of covering the box with tissue and pictures is plenty to pay attention to, without even mentioning the word “wishes”).  Here are some thoughts for a brief discussion of wishes:

“Sometimes it’s fun to make up wishes.  Do you make wishes?  Have you ever made a wish on your birthday as you blow out the candles?  Have you ever made a wish as you go to sleep at night?  Do you have a wish right now?  Sometimes we want to share a wish, and sometimes we want to keep our wish a secret.  Does anyone have a wish they want to share?  Does anyone have a wish about their family?  Does anyone have a wish about school?  Does anyone have a wish about their friends?  Sometimes I wish for lots of smiles in the day.  Sometimes I wish for a friend to feel better when she’s hurting.  Does anyone have a wish about a feeling?  Did anyone ever have a wish that came true?  It’s good to hear about your wishes.  My wish is for each of you to enjoy making your own box today.”





Tearing magazine pictures instead of
using scissors gives a wonderful edge



Activity:
“We each get to make our own ‘Wish Box.’  We get to decorate our box with all the colors and pictures we wish.”  

Assist the children in selecting their own cigar boxes to work on.  

Demonstrate the three-step process for gluing:
1. Brush glue onto the box.
2. Lay the tissue paper or picture onto the sticky surface.
3.  Brush more glue on top of the tissue or picture.

Assist the children as they begin to cover their boxes with colors and images.  Encourage them. 






Step 1:  Brush glue onto the surface

Step 2:  Lay tissue paper or picture onto glue



Demonstrate how the tissue paper can overlap and create beautiful see-through multicolored layers.





Step 3: Brush more glue over the paper



About Decorations:  
Beads, buttons, feathers, etc., are optional additions the children might enjoy using.  However, having these extras might distract the children from the basic process of tissue collaging.  The

tissue and magazines are really plenty to focus on.  They make a beautiful surface, and they actually need to be applied before putting any buttons or feathers on the boxes.  For this reason, you might want to leave out the extra decorations, or only bring them out at the end, after everyone has gotten far along into the tissue process.  

Writing (Optional):
As the children complete their boxes, ask them if they’d like anything written on the bottom of their box.  Some may want a wish written down, others may just want their name on the box.





“Wish Box” collage sample



Closing Circle:  
Allow the children time to talk about what their Wish Boxes mean to them and how it felt making them.  If they choose to, they can share how they would like to use their Wish Box.  

Variations:  
This technique works beautifully on many surfaces, not just cigar boxes.  You can use flat mat boards, metal cans, tennis ball cans, and even glass bottles, cups or jars.  If you are using glass, you might find the tissue paper sticks well, but not the magazine images.  It can be beautiful to work with just the tissue paper, then add designs with crayons or pens.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants an opportunity to enjoy exploring their wishes as they layer colors and pictures onto their own personal box. End product is a private place to store notes and treasures with a feeling of safety.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give each child the sense of fun, surprise, and satisfaction involved in the ghost painting process.  To give each child an opportunity to celebrate the holidays by creating their own hand-made cards.










“Ghost Painting” process









Materials:
Heavy white drawing paper or watercolor paper, pre-cut and folded into cards  (about 5 per child)
Waxed paper (one piece per white paper)
Blunt marking tools (pens with caps work well)
Watercolor paints





Sample “Ghost Painted” card


Paintbrushes
Containers of water
Paper towels
Blank Envelopes (enough for all the cards)

Optional: White crayons or white candles serve as a useful alternative (see “Variations” section)

Timeframe:
Opening Warm-up: 10 min.
Activity: 40 min.
Closing Circle: 10 min.

Ratio:
1 adult for 4 children; 1 adult for 2 young children.

Space Setup:
Cover table well with several layers of newspaper.  Also, set up a “drying area” for the finished cards with newspaper.  Prepare the blank cards and cut pieces of wax paper to fit the card size.

Before Leading:





Sample “Ghost Painted” cards.


As always, be sure to experiment yourself with the processes so you know how it feels to do them.  I recommend that you try the “Variation” methods too, if possible, so you have a sense of their strengths and differences.

Sharing about the Holidays:
Depending on the group you have and their religious backgrounds, you may wish to open with some sharing and warm-ups related to the holidays.  To help your awareness of the types of holidays celebrated by those in your group, find out what you can about those in your group and the holidays they may celebrate at this time of year (i.e. Chanukah, Kwanzaa, Christmas, etc.)   Work this awareness into the warm-up and your discussion time.  

“Does anyone know what time of year it is?   What are some good things about this time of year?  (allow time for the children to share their thoughts and feelings).  What are some good things about being here in the shelter at this time of year?  (allow time for sharing).”




“Ghost Painter,” pleased with his work.




Opening Warm-up:
“Sometimes this is a time of year when people celebrate together with candles.  Has anyone seen candles during their Holidays?  Sometimes people light candles to share good feelings, like love, and peace, and joy.  Sometimes they light candles to be thankful for the things they have in their lives like food and friends.  To celebrate this time of year together, let’s do a special warm-up about candles.  Let’s be Holiday candles (standing up).  Stand tall.  Let’s see your flame burning bright!  (Raising arms up and wiggling them like a flame.)  What color candle are you?  How bright are you?  Let’s see you sharing all your brightness, and lovingness and smiles all over the room (waving arms around.)  How far does your light go?  Are you melting?  (Getting smaller, kneeling down.)  Are you getting warmer and warmer?  Let’s see you melt all the way down (laying

on the floor).  And poof!  Let your flame go out (dropping head to the floor).  Now you get to rest, peaceful.  You’ve shared your warmth, all your smiles, your light, and you get to rest.  (Wait a few moments as everyone rests on the floor.)  What wonderful candles you are, each one of you!  I’m glad you’re in my Holiday, brightening my day.”





Step One:  Placing the wax
paper on the card.





Step Two:  Drawing heavily through
the waxed paper with the tool
(marking pen with cap on).





Step Three:  Removing the
waxed paper.





Step Four:  Painting the card, seeing
the white lines emerge.



Activity:
“Has anyone ever seen a Holiday card?  What is it?  What is it for?  Sending good thoughts to people you love?  Has anyone ever made a card?  Today we’re going to be making cards in a surprise way.  It’s called ‘Ghost Painting.’  Want to see how it works?”  (Demonstrate briefly).  

Step One:  Place waxed paper over your white paper.  
Step Two:  Press very heavily with a blunt tool to draw lines onto the wax paper.  
Step Three:  Remove the waxed paper
Step Four:  Paint watercolor over the surface of your paper.  You can use as many or few colors as you wish.  

Note:  Be sure to brush the paint over the paper lightly.  If you “scrub” the surface with the brush many times, the wax lines will dissappear.
Step Five:   Allow paint to dry.  Start another card!

Closing Circle:  
Let’s each share something we liked about our Windows time.  (You might begin by enthusiastically telling them a few things you liked about them as a group today.  It’s impossible to overdo appreciation.)  Encourage them to each share a thought of what they liked.

Variations:  
In addition to using the ghost writing technique with the waxed paper, you can create the wax lines using white crayons or white candles.  This may be simpler, and may create stronger wax lines.  Just use the crayons or candles to draw lines directly on the paper.

Be sure to press very hard to make the wax lines as thick as possible.

The crayons work much easier than the candles because you can see the white crayon on the paper as you draw.  You cannot see the candle wax lines, so you can’t tell what you have drawn with the candle wax without looking very very carefully.




Crayon can be used to create the wax lines.





Candles can be used to create the wax lines.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants the sense of fun, surprise, and satisfaction involved in the ghost painting process. Gives each participant an opportunity to celebrate the holidays by creating their own hand-made cards.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide the children with an opportunity to enjoy tearing the paper and making shapes.  To support each child in enjoying the surprise of selecting a shape and creating something out of it.





Blob picutre giraffe



Materials:
Construction paper
White backing paper
Large cardboard box
Crayons or CrayPas
Glue
Newspaper to cover tables
Old pair of sunglasses, covered with acrylic paint to become "surprise glasses"
Optional: Glitter, sequins, stickers

Timeframe:
Introduction - 5 minutes
Opening Circle - 15 minutes
Demonstration - 10 minutes
Supply Distribution - 10 minutes
Relaxation - 5 minutes
Creation - 45 minutes
Closing - 15 minutes

Ratio:
1 adult for 4 children; 1 adult for 2 young children.




Blob Picture dragon




Space Setup:
Make your "surprise glasses" in advance, covering the glasses with acrylic paint or masking tape to make them opaque.  Before the workshop, cover the tables with Newspaper, and place colored construction paper and the other supplies in the middle of the table.    You will want to have a clear space, away from the table, for the children to have their opening warm-up and “animal dance.”

Opening Warm-up:
“If you were going to be an animal today, what would you be, and why?”  (Example: "I'd be a lion because I've been really loud today.  I can roar!")  Give each child a turn in the circle to name their animal.  Note: Remember each animal that was brought up in the circle, for the animal dance.

Animal Dance:
Walk in a circle together and one at a time, taking about 20 seconds to be each animal that was named in the circle.  Make noises and movements to become the animal.  As leader, shout out the name of each animal one at a time, for example, "Now we are becoming lions!  Let's hear all the roars!"






Blob Picture bird


Introduction/ Demonstration:
Gather back into a seated circle to discuss today's project.  "Did anyone ever look at the shapes of clouds and see an animal or face or something?  What did you see?  It's wonderful how we can be creative in how we look at things.   That's what we are going to do today.  First, we are going to make blobs of paper, and put them into a big box.  Then we are going to use these special "surprise glasses" to cover our eyes as we each pick a surprise shape from the box.  Then we'll be looking at our blobs and making them into pictures.  (Show a sample)  Ready to begin?”

Tearing the Shapes:
“You can make any blob shape you want.  They can be long and skinny, they can be round, they can be zig zaggy.”

Selecting the Shapes:  
Have each child pick a piece without looking.  You can have them close their eyes, but that might be scary for some kids.  The children could pass around the special "surprise glasses" as they each pick their shapes.   

Creation:
Once everyone has a shape, they can move to the table to begin to create their picture.  Encourage them to look at it for a while, like they look at clouds, until they see something they can make out of it.  If someone wants to pick a different piece, you might let them put the "surprise glasses" back on and exchange it.

Optional Writing:
(If there are enough adults.)  As the children complete their drawings, ask them to tell the story of their picture.  Write the words next to the drawing.

Closing Circle:  
Share the pictures, and give each child a chance to share his/her stories.  






Blob Picture giraffe (detail)


Encourage them to talk about the process.  "How did it feel to tear up the paper?  How did it feel to pick a surprise piece?  Did anyone think they couldn't make anything out of their piece?  Did anyone surprise themselves?"

Variations:
Each child could use their own pieces, rather than picking a surprise piece.  

Rip up the left-over torn paper.  Make mosaic collages out of the colors.
Row.txt_description: Provides children with an opportunity to enjoy tearing the paper and making shapes, supporting each child in enjoying the surprise of selecting a shape and creating something out of it.

Row.txt_code:
Oceana Madrone
 
  
About the Author:
My name is Oceana Madrone. I'm a mother, grandmother, partner and sweetheart. I make fantasy clothing, quilts, dolls, jewelry and other bead objects. I also work at Humboldt Women for Shelter, as Children’s Services Coordinator. My favorite part of the job is the art groups I get to do with the women and children. Art has been a powerful tool in my life. I feel honored to be able to share art as a way of expressing oneself and exploring feelings. I, too, am a survivor of domestic violence and sexual assault.

Objective:
To rediscover and honor our intuition. The inner voices that guide us and tell us what to do if we allow ourselves to become quiet enough to hear them. The dolls are a visual reminder to listen to our intuition.

Materials:
-One and a half pipe cleaners per person (for body)
-Embroidery thread (for hair)

 
 
  

-Thin ribbon: 1/8" wide, 36" long per person (for skin)
-4"x7" fabric rectangles (wide range of colors, textures and patterns)
-Beads, fishing line
-Old jewelry
-Feathers
-Pin backs
-Scissors
-Jewelry pliers and wire cutters
-Paper and pens

Timeframe:
75-90 mins—Total Time
10 mins—Intro + Opening Circle
5 mins—Technical Demonstration
5 mins—Relaxation and Visualization
45-60 mins—Creation of Doll
10-15 mins—Closing Circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children; 1 adult for 2 young children.

Introduction:
“Today we are going to make Intuition Dolls. The dolls are symbols to remind you to listen to your own inner voice.

“There is a Russian folk tale called Vassilissa. It is the story of a girl who receives a doll from her mother, right before her mother dies. She tells Vassilisa to always keep the doll close to her and to listen to what the doll tells her. She also tells her to keep the doll a secret and tell no one. Vassilissa keeps the doll in her pocket. Through the story Vassilissa consults her doll, who always gives her good advice. When Vassilissa comes to a fork in the road, the doll seems to tell her which way to go; when she meets Baba-Yaga, the doll jumps up and down in her pocket to warn Vassilissa.

“Vassilissa's doll is like intuition. That voice inside ourselves that tells us which path to take and warns us of danger. Can you think of a time when you've felt your intuition? What happened? Where in your body did you feel your intuition? Children may talk about a funny tummy feeling, a tightness in their chest, a voice in their head. It is helpful for them to talk about where they feel their intuition. Then, they can begin to recognize it and learn to listen to it.”


 
 
  
 
  

Technical Info:
Body:
1. Fold full size pipe cleaner in half. Twist 1/2"-3/4" into loop at top to make "head".
2. Using 1/2 pipecleaner for arms twist on below "head"
3. For smaller dolls, about 1/2 way down arms & legs fold pipe cleaner in (towards body). Twist small loops for hands.
4. For larger dolls, make head loop slightly larger. Fold in arms and legs at desired length, leave full length if desired.

Hair:
1. Wrap embroidery thread around all 4 of your fingers to make loops.
2. Insert loops through "head"
3. Tie knot. Clip loops.

Skin:
1. Using thin ribbon, tie an X over the chest of the doll.
2. Wrap the ribbon tightly! around the arms (leave the "hands" unwrapped), neck, head and chest area. Legs do not need to be wrapped.
3. Knot tightly. Save any extra ribbon for belt.

Dress:
1. Use pattern to cut dress.
2. Cut fringe, if you wish.
3. Fold in 1/2 front to back, and then fold in 1/2 again side to side. Just barely clip folded corner. This makes the neckhole. It will stretch so make sure not to cut it too big.
4. Slide dress over head. Use ribbon to tie around waist. Adjust if necesary.

Final Touches:
1. Add beads, feathers, etc.
2. Glue pin on back. Or you canuse a little piece of ribbon to tie it on.
3. When you are done, take a few minutes to write a few words about your intuition doll, and what it means to you.


 
 
 
Deep rich
colors

Dark &
nurturing—
like soil is
for seeds

Shell brings
wisdom of sea

Feathers—
flight & freedom

One arm holding close, protecting

Other arm extended, releasing...
  

Relaxation/ Visualization:
Use your own favorite relaxation. One of my favorites is Rose Rothwell’s Comfort Relaxation (Comfort Journals Nov. 1996).

Near the end, I change talking about comfort to talking about intuition. “What does your intuition look like?... What colors and images come to mind?.... If you look for your intuition in your body where do you find it?.... How does your intuition speak to you?... When you are ready, gently bring your awareness back to this room. You can make your own Intuition Doll a symbol to remind you to listen to your own inner voice. When you feel ready, open your eyes and begin.”

I like to play the song "Inner Voices" by Sweet Honey in the Rock while we make the dolls.

Closing Circle:
Give each person a chance to share as much or as little as they would like to about their doll, or anything they want to share about the group. Validate the unique creativity of each person. Listen to and enjoy the Intuition Doll.
Row.txt_description: Encourages participants to (re)discover and honor their intuition, the inner voices that guide us and tell us what to do if we allow ourselves to become quiet enough to hear them. The dolls are a visual reminder to listen to our intuition.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create "Medicine Dolls" version for boys and Teens.
Row.txt_tips: If working with teens, this workshop can be used to talk about healthy body image.

Row.txt_code:
“My Garden” example (prints
used: hand side prints, thumb
prints, finger prints).


Objective:
To support each child to notice, explore, and express the ways they are like plants in a garden: alive, wonderful to see, strong, growing, and unique.  To provide the children with an opportunity to explore the beauty of painting without brushes.  

Materials:
White paper (about 9”x12”)
Paper plates for each participant
Spoons for each color
Containers for mixed paints
Tempera paints (pre-mix many green colors and many bright flower colors)
Two large trays
Newspaper to cover tables
Paper towels

Timeframe:
Garden Warm-up - 5 minutes
Idea Circle - 5 minutes
Intro/Demo - 10 minutes
Supply Distribution - 5 minutes
Creation - 20 minutes
Closing - 10 minutes

Ratio:
1 adult for 4 children; 1 adult for 2 young children.

Space Setup:
Preparing a range of colors for the children to use is a very important step to do in advance.  Allow at least half an hour for you to enjoy the mixing of the colors.  It’s a beautiful process!  Know that the colors you mix will make all the difference in how the children’s paintings are going to look.  

First, pre-mix the green colors.  To get various shades of green, try adding a bit of red in some, orange in others, or purple too in some of the containers.  See what happens with the various mixes.  To get different lightnesses and darknesses, add yellow or white, or peach.  When you have about 6 to 10 greens, set all of them on one tray.

Next, pre-mix various shades of bright flower colors.  Try to make light, middle, and dark versions of a few colors (for example, a light purple, a middle purple, and a dark purple).  Put all of the flower color containers onto a second tray.

Cover the table well, with lots of newsprint.  Put trays safely out of reach.  In the center of the table, place the paper and the paper plates.




“My Garden” example (prints used:
hand side prints, fingertip prints)




Garden Warm-up:
When the children arrive, begin with the Garden Warm-up:  “Let’s stand in a circle and pretend we’re plants in a garden.  Can you dig your roots down into the ground? (wiggling your feet into the floor)  Can you grow tall, like a tall plant?  (reaching arms up to the ceiling)  Where are your leaves?  Are they reaching out for the sunshine?  Let’s see them reach!  (stretching and waving your hands)  And how about flowers?  Do you have some flowers?  What colors are your flowers?  Are they little?  Or big?  How big are they?”  Encourage each child to share about his or her flowers.  Follow the children’s lead with this warm-up.  Ask them what they see in their gardens.  A butterfly?  A tree?  A bird?  A snail?  To close the warm-up, you might say “Okay, now it’s becoming night in the garden.  Have you ever seen a flower close up at night?  Can you close up?”  (Curl up and lay down on the ground for nighttime so the flowers can rest).  

Idea Circle:
After the physical warm-up, sit together in a circle to share thoughts about plants:

“Can anyone think of a way that you are like a plant?”  (Encourage the children to think of ways...  I grow, I am beautiful, I am alive, I am strong, I am unique, different from everyone else, like each flower is different...)  

“What do you do that a plant does too?”  (e.g., eating, growing, drinking, changing, etc.)

“Has anyone ever seen a plant growing where it’s not easy to grow?”  (like in the cracks in the sidewalk, between rocks, etc.)  “Well, that’s like us too.  We can grow even when it’s hard to grow; and we can be very beautiful, like a flower growing up through the concrete.  

“Sometimes it might feel hard to be in the shelter, but we all get to grow and be beautiful, even where it’s sometimes hard.  Today, we are going to be painting our own gardens... our very own plants.  You can be one of the plants in your garden, or you can be the whole garden.”  

Introduction/ Demonstration:
“Has anyone ever painted without using brushes?  How did you do it?  Today, we are going to use our hands to make prints.”  

Note: There are two ways of getting paint on the hands.  You might want to try both in advance to decide which way would work best for your group:  
1.  The children can rub their hands around the plate to coat it with the paint, and then press it into the paper (see figure 1).  
2.  Another way is to use brushes to paint the children’s hands, and then press the hands onto the paper (see figure 2).  

“What shapes can you make with your hands?”  Share with the children how many different shapes can be made with your hands.  (See attached “Handprint Illustrations.”)  You could hold samples up and ask them how they think the shapes were made, or you could demonstrate it to them.  You could also let the children experiment together in their own ways.  You could also dive in and have them start their paintings along with you while you demonstrate.  

Making the Gardens:
Green Shapes First





Figure 1: Pressing hand into
plate to apply paint





Figure 2: Painting hand with a brush



“Just like a plant grows with its greens first, and then the flowers later, that’s the way we get to start.”

Begin by putting the tray of greens out.  Spoon onto each child’s plate the colors of green they want to use, and encourage them to go ahead and fill their page with the greens of their garden.  

Flower Shapes Next  
After everyone has enough greenery, go ahead and bring out the flower colors.  Each child may need a second plate for the flower colors.  Spoon out the colors each child wants to use.  Encourage them to go ahead and add their flowers.  

A “Minimal Touch”:
Beautiful effects can be made quite quickly with minimal work.
Encourage the children to stop their paintings when they still have that “minimal touch,” and encourage them to make as many paintings as they have time for, instead of overworking one image.

Optional Writing:
(If there are enough adults)  As the children complete their drawings, ask them to tell the story of their garden.  Ask them how it is like them.  Is there one plant that is them?  Which plant would they be?  Write the words next to the drawing.




“My Garden” example (prints used:
palm base prints, fist side prints,
fingertip prints)




Closing Circle:  
Give each child a chance to share the stories of his or her garden.  
Encourage them to talk about the process.  "How did it feel to paint with your hands instead of a brush?  Did anyone surprise themselves?"
Row.txt_description: Suports each child in noticing, exploring and expressing the ways they are like plants in a garden: alive, wonderful to see, strong, growing, and unique. Also provides an opportunity to explore the beauty of painting without brushes.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create version for adults.

Row.txt_code:
The “Monster in Me” idea was inspired by the quilt made by Megan Torrey and the children at Good Shepherd Shelter in Los Angeles, CA. Thanks Megan!

  
About this Workshop:
Thanks to a generous donation from Sakura, each Children’s Windows Program has been given an ample supply of Cray-Pas for the year. Cray-Pas are oil pastels that can be used in many diverse and fabulous ways. “The Monster in Me” is the first in a series of workshops AWBW has developed to assist your workshop participants in fully enjoying and exploring the Cray-Pas. The technique used here is “watercolor-resist.” This technique, using the Cray-pas and watercolors in this three-step process, can be used to draw anything: landscapes, families, doodles, flowers, etc. The “Monster in Me” idea is just one way of using this technique. Enjoy, and feel free to use this technique in whatever ways you wish. Please join us in experimenting and sharing new project ideas.

Objective:
To give the children an opportunity to be playful in exploring some of the more difficult emotions they experience. To offer a process that will look bold and powerful, and be rewarding and satisfying for the children.

Age-Range: 3 and up

Ratio:
1 adult for 6 children; 1 adult for 3 young children.

Materials:
Craypas sets (one set per child)
Thick white paper (8 1/2” x 11” is good)
Spray bottle filled with water
Watercolor sets (one set per child)
Watercolor brushes (one per child)
Newsprint to cover the table
Cups of water for rinsing the brushes
Paper towels for drying the brushes

Note: If using this workshop to help children release or process anger it is important to begin by having a discussion on "What is Anger?" Please click here to see the entire Processing Anger Series.

Timeframe:
Opening: 5 min
Monster Dance warm-up: 5 min
Technical demonstration: 10 min
Creation: 30 min
Closing: 10 min

 
  Space Set-up
Space Setup:
Open the Craypas sets in advance. Open each watercolor set and spray lightly with water. The water helps soften the colors so that they will be easy to use when the children paint. Prepare the cups of water for brush rinsing. Place supplies out of reach, (if necessary, depending on the age level), and bring out when needed. Have a space for the “Monster Dance” to occur, away from the art supplies.

Opening:
“Today, we’re doing a workshop called ‘The Monster in Me.’ Have you ever felt like a monster? How did you feel? What kind of monster would you be today? Who has a mean monster in them? Who has a happy one? Who has a sad one?”

 
  

 
  Monster Dance
Monster Dance Warm-up:
“Let’s do a Monster Dance. First we can start by moving around in a circle being monsters. Now let’s all be scary monsters! Now let’s be happy monsters! Can you be really loud monsters? Can you be really quiet monsters?”

Note for Teen Workshops:
If you are working with a group of teens, the Monster Dance might not be the best way to start. You could try something more theatrical, like walking into the workshop with a scary mask on and asking them what they see. Talk about how we all have monsters inside of us, and it’s really important to take a look at those monsters and see who they are and what they need.

Technical Demonstration:
There are three steps. Demonstrate them to the children, but get them involved in the demonstration. Ask them to guide you as you go through the three steps, so you’re creating the monster they are telling you to make.

1. Drawing the Monster:
“What kind of nose should I put on this monster? What kind of eyes? What kind of ears? How about big teeth? Anything else I should add? How about a neck for the monster... Notice that I’m pressing really hard to make the lines. This is important because it makes the lines strong enough for when we put the paint on.” 
 
  
2. Watering the Monster:
“Now we get to make the monster all wet. (Spray the entire page with a spray bottle.) Did I get the whole monster wet? Is there anywhere I missed? (Keep spraying until the whole surface is wet. You could call the water “Monster Juice.”)” 
 
  
3. Coloring the Monster:
“Now we get to add the colors. Tell me what colors to use. We can just drop the colors into each space and see them spread. (Demonstrate how the watercolors spread in the water.) Isn’t that beautiful? What color should I make the eyes? How about the mouth? How about the space around the monster?” 




Creation:
“Now it’s your turn. Go ahead and draw your monster. What kind of eyes do you want to make? What kind of mouth? Teeth? Ears? Does your monster have hair? (Encourage the children as they draw.) When you are ready, raise your hand, so I can come water your monster. (Probably, you will want to be in charge of the spray bottle, and spray for the children. If a spray bottle is not available, you might use a big, broad, house-painting brush.)

“When your monster has been sprayed, you get to drop in the colors and watch them fill the spaces. Beautiful! (Encourage and assist the children as they add the watercolors.)”


  
  Monster in Me Samples
Closing Circle:
Each child has an opportunity to share his or her monster. You might encourage the children to share with questions like: “What does your monster feel like? What is it thinking?” If time allows, ask the children to think about what their monster needs, to feel better. Does it need to be loved? Does it need to be understood? Sometimes monsters have important things to say if you listen to what they need in order to feel better.

Alternate Closing:
Brainstorm a "Safety Plan" with the children to help them process their anger. Some helpful tips include:
Talk to a friend you can trust
Count to 10
Take out art supplies and draw a picture of your anger
Journal about your anger
Take deep breaths
Listen to music
Walk away
Dance or exercise
Row.txt_description: Gives children an opportunity to be playful in exploring some of the more difficult emotions they experience. Offers a process that will look bold and powerful, and be rewarding and satisfying for the children.
Row.txt_tips:
If you'd like to include journaling in this workshop, here is a journaling handout that you can give to older youth.

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Note About Anger Workshops
We recommend that you start anger workshops with a discussion; don't be afraid to talk to the children about their anger. Anger is nothing to be ashamed of, it is important to look at and talk about it to try to understand it.

Some anger prompts that we like are:
What is Anger? What does it look like and what does it sound like?
What was the trigger to your anger?
What did you think about it?
How did it make you feel?
How did you act?
What effect did it have on you and those around you?

Row.txt_code:
“Through the Mud” sample


&l dquo;Through the Mud” is the second in a series of workshops AWBW has developed to assist your workshop participants in fully enjoying and exploring the Cray-Pas.  Thanks to a generous donation from Sakura, each Children’s Windows Program has been given an ample supply of Cray-Pas for the year.  Cray-Pas are oil pastels that can be used in many diverse and fabulous ways.  The technique used here is “scratchboard.”  This technique can be used to draw anything- landscapes, families, doodles, flowers, etc.  The “Through the Mud” idea is just one way of using this technique.  Enjoy, and feel free to use this technique in whatever ways you wish.  Please join us in experimenting and sharing new project ideas.

Objective:
To provide a rare and fun freedom for “mess-making.”  To offer a chance for each child to see the wonderful beauty that can come from taking bold, messy risks with their creations.  To give the children an opportunity to enjoy being physically vigorous and push beyond any carefulness or hesitation they might experience.





“Through the Mud” sample



Materials:
Cray-Pas sets (one set per child)
Small, thick, white paper (4”x4” is good)
Newsprint to cover the table
Plastic forks for scraping

Timeframe:
60 min—Total Time
Opening:  5 min
Mess Warm-up:  5 min
Technical demonstration:  10 min
Creation:  30 min
Closing:  10 min

Age Range:
3 and up.  When we tested this workshop out with some Children’s Windows Leaders, they felt that teens would love this technique because they can become so absorbed in the details and create really amazing images.

Ratio:
One adult to 3 young children

Note: Because you will be covering the entire page with Cray-Pas for this project, it’s good to have small paper.

Space Setup:
Cover the table with newspapers.  Open the Cray-Pas sets in advance.  Place supplies out of reach, (if necessary, depending on the age level) to bring out when needed.

Opening:
“Today, we’re going to have fun making messes.  Let’s see if we can make mud, and then make a beautiful picture come shining through.  Did you ever take a bad situation and make it better?  Did you ever see a sad face and make the person laugh?   We get to do that on paper today.”

Messy Heap Circle:
“Let’s start with a ‘Messy Heap Circle.’  (This is a variation of the “Wiggle Down” warm-up.  Gather in a circle to do this warm-up.)   Let’s see if we can make a mess with our bodies.  Let’s start with our feet.  Can you make a mess with your feet?  (Wiggle and move your feet around, messy.)  Can you make a mess with your knees?  (Wiggle your knees around.)  How about your arms and shoulders?  Can you get messy?  How about your head?  Can you make a mess with your whole self?  (You might want to end the circle by everyone falling down on the floor into a happily messy heap.)    Close by saying “Sometimes it’s wonderful to make a mess!  That’s what we get to do today with ‘Through the Mud.’”






1. Light colors

2. Dark colors



Technical:
There are three steps.  Demonstrate them to the children, but get them involved in the demonstration.  Ask them to guide you as you go through the three steps, so you’re creating what they are telling you to make.





3. Scratches





4. Finished drawing



1.  Light colors:
“We’re going to make our mud - light colors first.  What colors are light?  Tell me which colors to put on.  It’s important to press really hard so the paper is filled with color.  Do you see any parts of the page I’ve missed?  (Leave some blank parts for the children to catch you on.  Go ahead and fill them in as they point it out.)  See how the colors look beautiful as they are layered on top of each other?  We’ve got our light mud!”

2. Dark colors: 
“Now we’re going to cover it with a mess of dark colors.  What colors are dark?  Which ones should I use?  See how it looks like mud?  Look at this beautiful mud we’re making!”

3. Scratches: 
“Now we get to scratch through the mud.  (Scratch a line across the page, so the children can see how the light colors come shining through.)  What should I scratch?  How about a person dancing?  A flower?  A sun?  Can we make a bright picture coming through the mud?  When you are doing your picture, you can scratch anything you want!” 

Creation: 
“Now it’s your turn.  Go ahead and make your mess of light colors.  Be sure to fill the page and press really hard!

“When you are ready, add the dark colors.  Have fun making the mud. 

“Now you get to scratch your way through!”





CrayPas Leader’s Workshop participant



Closing Circle:
Each child has an opportunity to share his or her picture.  “What was it like making the mud?   What did you make shining through your mud?”

Variations:
This technique can be used to create all sorts of images.  Here are some suggested variations you could try:

Imaginary Animals: You could ask the children to scratch into their pictures an imaginary animal.  “Would it have wings?  Would it have teeth?  Would it have a tail?  What can you make up?  What does your imaginary animal do?  Does your imaginary animal have a name?  Is it friendly?  Can your animal talk?  What would it say if it could talk?”  

Magazine Images:  Instead of drawing the light mud on paper, you could use magazine images.  Each child could pick a magazine image as their first layer.  Then they could make “mud” over the image, and then scratch through to the picture.  (Be sure to test this process out yourself first, before leading it!)
Row.txt_description: Provides a rare and fun freedom for "mess-making." Offers a chance for each child to see the wonderful beauty that can come from taking bold, messy risks with their creations and enjoy being physically vigorous and pushing beyond any carefulness or hesitation they might experience.

Row.txt_code:
“Fish Families” samples
  
“Fish Families” is the third in a series of workshops AWBW has developed to assist your workshop participants in fully enjoying and exploring Cray-Pas.  Thanks to a generous donation from Sakura, each Children’s Windows Program has been given an ample supply of Cray-Pas for the year.  Cray-Pas are oil pastels that can be used in many diverse and fabulous ways.  The technique used here is “scratchboard with tempera paint.”  This technique can be used to draw anything—landscapes, families, doodles, flowers, etc.  The “Fish Families” idea is just one way of using this technique.  Enjoy, and feel free to use this technique in whatever ways you wish.   Please join us in experimenting and sharing new project ideas.

Objective:
To provide a chance for children to express their feelings about themselves and their families by creating a family of fish.  To assist the children in finding a sense of pride in creating their pictures with this beautiful, vivid process.

Materials:
Cray-Pas sets (one set per child)
Small, thick white paper (4”x4” is good)
Newsprint to cover the table
Plastic forks for scraping
Tempera paint:  three strong colors that would be good for water (blue, green, black) plus one light color (you might try white or light blue)
Tempera paint brushes (one per color)
Cups of water for rinsing the brushes
Paper towels for drying the brushes

Note: Tempera glitter paint is especially beautiful and rewarding to use.

Timeframe:
60 min—Total Time
Opening:  5 min
Fish Circle Warm-up:  5 min
Technical Demonstration:  10 min
Creation:  30 min
Closing:  10 min

Age Range: 5 and up 

Ratio:
One adult to 3 young children

Note:
Because you will be covering the entire page with Cray-Pas for this project, it’s good to have small paper.

Space Setup:
Cover the table with newspapers.  Open the Cray-Pas sets in advance.  Prepare containers of the tempera paint.  Place supplies out of reach, (if necessary, depending on the age level) to bring out when needed.

Opening:
“Today, we’re going to make a family of fish.  Have you ever seen a fish?  What did it look like?  If you were a fish, what would you look like? Would you be big?  Or small?  How would your family be?  Who would be close?  Who would be far?”

Fish Circle Warm-up:
“For our warm-up today, we’re going to make a fish circle.  Can you become a fish?  How would your face look?  (Puff up your cheeks and open and close your mouth like a fish.)  Which way do you want to swim around the circle?  (Start swimming around the circle.  It’s okay to have everyone swimming in their own directions.)  Say ‘hello’ to the other fishes!”


 
 
 1. Fish colors
  
 
 2. Painting on the paint
  
 
 3. Making the Fish
  

Technical:
There are three steps.  Demonstrate them to the children, but get them involved in the demonstration.  Ask them to guide you as you go through the three steps, so you’re creating what they are telling you to make. 

1. Fish Colors:
“What colors should we make our fish?  Yellow?  Red?  Silver?  Many colors mixed together?  We’re going to cover the page with these colors.  Did I cover it all up?  (Cover all the parts of the page.  Bright colors look especially good with this technique.)  It’s important to press really hard so the page is filled with Cray-Pas.”

2. Painting on the Paint: 
“Now we’re going to cover the page with paint. Which color resembling water should we make for our fish?  (Note:  the paint color must be different from the Cray-Pas color for the scratches to show through.)  Paint over the Cray-Pas.  Try to paint as thinly as possible.  That makes it easier to scratch through.  Some colors may bead up on top of the Cray-Pas, but you can usually cover the page pretty well.”

3.  Making the Fish: 
“Now we get to make our fish.  (Scratch with a fork, so the children can see how the light colors come shining through.)  Here’s our fish.  Should we put some underwater plants around it?  Anything else?”  (Do whatever they suggest.)

Creation: 
“Now it’s your turn.  Go ahead and make your fish colors.  Be sure to fill the page and press really hard!

“When you are ready, let me know so we can add the paint.  (Go around the room as needed, with the tempera colors, assisting each child to put his water on.  For some children, you might put the paint on for them.  Others might wish to paint it themselves.)

“Now you get to make your fish family!  (Encourage each child as she creates.)  If time allows, write the children’s words about their fish family, or the title of their paintings.  Scratch the children’s names and the date at the bottom of their paintings, if they’d like
you to.”

  


“Fish Families” sample drawing
 
  

Closing Circle:
“Tell me about your fishes?  Which one are you?”  (Give each child an opportunity to share his or her picture.)
Row.txt_description: Provides a chance for children to express their feelings about themselves and their families by creating a family of fish. Assists them in finding a sense of pride in creating their pictures through a beautiful, vivid process.

Row.txt_code:
“A Day of Feelings” samples
  
“A Day of Feelings” is the fourth in a series of workshops AWBW has developed to assist your workshop participants in fully enjoying and exploring Cray-Pas.  Thanks to a generous donation from Sakura, each Children’s Windows Program has been given an ample supply of Cray-Pas for the year.  Cray-Pas are oil pastels that can be used in many diverse and fabulous ways.  The technique used here is “Cray-Pas etchings.”  This technique can be used to draw anything- landscapes, families, doodles, flowers, etc.  The “A Day of Feelings” idea is just one way of using this technique.  Enjoy, and feel free to use this technique in whatever ways you wish.   Please join us in experimenting and sharing new project ideas.

Objective:
First, to help the children identify emotions and express them with colors and a drawing. Second, to let them enjoy the element of surprise made possible with this technique.

Materials:
Cray-Pas sets (one set per child)
Small, thick white paper (4”x4” is good) - 4-6 pieces per child
Newsprint to cover the table
Pencils


 
 
 “A Day of Feelings” etching sample -
sunshine and smiles
  

Time-Frame:
60 min—Total Time
Opening:  5 min
Warm-up:  10 min
Technical Demonstration:  10 min
Creation:  25 min
Closing:  10 min

Age Range: 3 and up 

Ratio:
One adult to 3 young children

Note:
Because you will be covering the entire page with CrayPas for this project, it’s good to have small paper.

Space Setup:
Cover the table with newspapers.  Open the Cray-Pas sets in advance.  Make sure to have the paper cut and ready.  Place supplies out of reach (if necessary, depending on the age level), to bring out when needed.

Opening:
“Today, we’re going to draw feelings.  Have you ever had a feeling you liked?  Can you name it?  If you were going to draw it, what color would you make it?  (Encourage each child to share a feeling they like and a color for it.)  Have you ever had one you didn’t like?  Can you name it? What color would you make that feeling?”  (Encourage each child to share a feeling they don’t like and a color for it.)

Feelings Warm-up:
Play easy, rhythmic music.  Ask everyone to move around the room to the rhythm, pantomiming how they are feeling at the beginning of the workshop.  Allow a few minutes.  Then gather in a circle and ask for volunteers to share what feelings they saw expressed.  Ask for volunteers to share what feelings they pantomimed. 
 


 
 
 1. Feeling colors
  
 
 2. Creating the etching with pencil
on top of second paper
  
 
 3. Turning it over to see the etched
drawing in color
  
Technical:
There are three steps.  Demonstrate them to the children, but get them involved in the demonstration.  Ask them to guide you as you go through the three steps, so you’re creating what they are telling you to make.  

1. Feeling Colors:
“Let’s pick a feeling.  What feeling should I start with?  What colors would it be?  We’re going to cover the page with these colors.  Did I cover it all up?  (Cover all the parts of the page.)  It’s important to press really hard so the page is filled with the Cray-Pas.” 

2.  Etching: 
“Now we’re going to cover the page with another piece of paper, and draw on it.  I’m going to draw a picture of this feeling.  What should I draw?” 

3.  Turning it Over: 
“Now we can turn it over, and here’s our picture!”  (Show the children how the lines are etched in the Cray-Pas colors.)

Creation: 
“Now it’s your turn.  Go ahead and pick your feeling colors.  You can make more than one etching if you have more than one feeling you are trying to express.  Maybe you could pick a feeling you don’t like.  What are some feelings you don’t like?  What are some feelings you like?  Go ahead and begin with whatever feeling you want.  Be sure to fill the page and press really hard!

“When you are ready, let me know so I can give you another paper to cover your colors with.  (Go around the room as needed to give the second page.)  

  


“A Day of Feelings” sample - mad feelings
 
  

“Now you can draw your etching!”

Closing Circle:
“Tell me about your picture!”   (Give each child an opportunity to share his or her picture.)  Write words down to go with each picture if the child wants you to.


 
 
 “A Day of Feelings”
sample - smiles
Row.txt_description: Helps children identify emotions and express them with colors and a drawing. Lets them enjoy the element of surprise made possible with this technique.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
“Fork, Knife, Spoon” sample design


Objective:
To give the children an opportunity to use materials they are familiar with (spoons, knives, and forks) in an inventive way.  To provide them an opportunity for play and discovery with the creative process.

Materials:
Black construction paper (other dark colors work too)
White tempera paint (possibly other light colors too)
Containers for the paint
Water containers to rinse brushes
Paper towels





Step One:  covering the page



Plastic forks, knives, and spoons (one of each per child)
Wide paintbrushes
Newsprint to cover the table

Timeframe:
60 min—Total Time
Opening:  5 min
Warm-up:  10 min
Technical Demonstration:  10 min
Creation:  25 min
Closing:  10 min

Age Range: 3 and up  

Ratio:







One adult to 3 young children

Note:
Be sure to test the supplies in advance, so you will be familiar with the process, and you will know the paint you have will work well on the paper.  (If the paint is too thin, it won’t work for this technique.)   

Space Setup:
You will need to set up three areas:  1) Open floor space for the warm-up.  2) Cover the table area with plenty of newsprint, and place the supplies in the center of the table.  3) A drying area, covered with newsprint, where the paintings can be left to dry.  

Opening:
“Today, we’re doing ‘Fork, Knife, Spoon.’  Do you have a favorite?  If you had to be a fork or a knife or a spoon today, what would you be?  Why?  (Encourage everyone to share.)

“Has anyone ever used a fork or knife or spoon for something besides eating?  What did you use it for?  Has anyone ever made a drawing using a fork or knife or spoon?  Today we are going to use forks and knives and spoons to make art.  Ready?”  

Fork, Knife, Spoon Warm-up:





Fork lines





Knife lines





Spoon lines



“Let’s make a circle together holding hands.  There we go - everyone holding hands.  Now let’s see how big we can make the circle, with our hands still together.  How far can we stretch?  That’s great!  Look at how big our circle is!  Now imagine this circle is a great big table.  Does it have a table cloth?  What color?  Is there food on the table?  What kind?  Are there good smells?  What do you smell?  Now let’s lay our selves down on this table and get comfortable.  As we melt into the table, let’s imagine that we are the forks on the table.  Can you be a fork?  Can you stretch your arms out?  Can you make the pointy ends of the fork?  Good job!  And how about being knives?  Can you make yourself straight and pointy like a knife.  Great knives!  And how about a spoon?  Feel yourself relaxing and melting into the curving, smooth shape of a spoon.  Beautiful spoons!  Now let yourself melt down again and this time, become a part of the table.  Let your whole self relax and melt into this big round table.”  (Rest a few moments.)  

Technical:
There are two steps to demonstrate to the children.  Get them involved as you demonstrate.

1. Covering the page with paint:
Apply paint evenly, covering the entire page.   This workshop can be done with just white paint.  It’s up to you, how many colors you want to make available.  Also, depending on the capabilities of the participants, you might want to cover their pages for them, or you might welcome them to cover their own pages.  It’s up to what you, as leader, think will work best with your group.

2. Scratching designs:  
Demonstrate how the fork can scratch lines into the paint.  Likewise, with the spoon and knife.  Encourage the children to notice how many different kinds of marks can be made.  Cover the whole page with designs.  

Creation:  
Now it’s your turn.  (Assist the children in beginning their work.)  As they complete their drawings, help them move the wet pictures to the drying area.

Closing Circle:
Each child has an opportunity to share his or her design.  You might encourage the children to share with questions like: “Who used a fork? Who used a spoon?  Who used a knife?”  The paint may take an hour to dry after the children are finished.  It depends on how thick the paint is, and how damp the weather is.
Row.txt_description: To use familiar materials to enhance discovery and the creative process.

Row.txt_code:
Cheering Frog Flag examples



Objective:
To encourage the children to never give up on the ir dreams.  To help them notice and remember the supportive voices in their lives—voices that have cheered them on—and give the children a way to take those cheering voices with them, as encouragement forever.

Materials:
Colored construction paper
Cray-Pas oil sticks
Glue sticks





“I love you” — Cheering Flog Flags example



Colored yarn or string
Paper towels
Newspaper to cover the table

Timeframe:
60 min—Total Time
Opening Story:  10 min
Warm-up:  5 min
Technical Demonstration:  10 min
Creation:  25 min
Closing:  10 min

Age Range: 3 and up  

Ratio:
One adult to 3 young children

Note:
Be sure to test the supplies in advance, so you will be familiar with the process.   It will also help if you have an example to show the children.  

Space Setup:
Cover the table area with plenty of newspaper, and place the supplies in the center of the table.  If you are working with younger children, pre-cut and fold the construction paper for the flags, and pre-cut the string into 1-yard lengths.  







Extra Special Prep:
Special Advance Prep:  If you have time, it makes this workshop very special if you can add to each child’s chain, a few flags created by shelter staff.  In advance of the workshop, make 3-5 flags for each child and on each one, have a staff person write some simple, encouraging thoughts to cheer on that child.  During the workshop, you can go around the group and ask each child for permission to add some special flags on to their chain.  As you do this, you can read what the staff person wrote on the flag.  This way, each child will have a special thought from some staff people at the shelter.  

Opening:
“Today, our project is called ‘Cheering Frog Flags.’  I’m going to share a story about cheering.  It’s called Two Frogs in the Woods. After I share it, I want to hear what you think it means.  Ready?”

“Two Frogs in the Woods” Story:
(Feel free to change the story into your own words, instead of reading the words here):
“A group of frogs were traveling through the woods, and two of them fell into a deep pit.  All the other frogs gathered around the pit.  When they saw how deep the pit was, they told the frogs that they could never get out.  The two frogs ignored the comments and tried to jump out of the pit with all of their might.  The other frogs kept telling them to stop.  They said:  “There’s no way you’ll ever get out of there.  You might as well stop trying!”  Finally, one of the frogs decided they were right.  He believed what all the other frogs were saying and gave up.  But the other frog continued to jump and jump and jump as hard as he could.  Once again, the crowd of frogs yelled at him.  They said he could never make it and they shook their arms at him and told him it would be better if he just gave up.  He jumped even harder and finally he made it out.  When he got out, the other frogs were amazed.  They said “Didn’t you hear us?”  The frog explained to them that he was deaf.  He couldn’t hear them, but he saw them yelling, and he thought they were encouraging him and cheering him on the entire time.
 
After sharing the story ask the children, “What does this story teach?”  Encourage them to share what they think.  Here are some possible lessons:

- When someone is encouraged and cheered, it can help lift them up so they can make it through the day.  

- When someone is told negative things, it can make them want to give up.  

- It’s important to not believe the negative things people say about you.  

- If you can remember all the good things and all the people who have cheered you on, it can help you to do great things.

- Be thoughtful of what you say to people when they are struggling.  You can be that special person for someone else.  You can be someone who encourages them, so they don’t give up.  An encouraging word can go a long way.

The Wave Warm-up:





“You’re Smart” — Cheering Flog Flags



If possible, gather a circle of chairs so everyone can sit together in a circle.  This is a cheering warm-up. “Has anyone ever had a crowd of people cheering for them?   What did it feel like?  (Encourage the children to share their stories.)  That’s what we are going to do for a Windows warm-up today:  we are going to see what it’s like to cheer for each other!  Has anyone ever seen a crowd do “the wave” at a sports event?  It’s a way people cheer for their team (if you don’t know what the wave is, be sure to ask someone who does, so you know how to teach it).  Let’s do a couple of practice rounds.  Here we go--yay!--

You can start the wave yourself by yelling ‘yay!’ and standing up and putting your arms high in the air.  Then the next person follows, and so on around the circle in a wave.  After a few rounds, once the group has gotten comfortable with it, do a round of the wave for each person in the group.  Do one round for the young person sitting next to you.  Instead of saying “yay!”, say “yay Maria!” (whatever that child’s name is).  Then do a wave for the next child, and the next and the next, until you’ve cheered for each person in the group.  






Cutting and folding flags





Applying glue across the fold





Placing the string





Sealing the flag onto the string


If doing ‘the wave’ is too confusing or difficult for your group, you could just cheer each person in the group, one at a time.  Clap, cheer and yell their name for half a minute or so.  Then cheer the next person, and so on, around the circle.  

After the warm-up, ask each person what it felt like to be cheered on.   

Introduction:  
“For the frog who jumped out of the hole, it was very important that he was thinking about having a group of other frogs cheering him on.  Even though they weren’t really cheering for him, what mattered was that he was picturing them cheering for him.  What was in his mind was most important.  Just like for the frog, it’s very important for all of us to keep in our minds thoughts of people cheering for us.  To do that, we are going to make ‘Cheering Frog Flags’ today.  We can each make our own set of flags that will remind us of people who cheer us on.”

Technical Demonstration: 
1. First, pick your string.

2. Then fold and cut out your flags. (For younger children, have the pieces of paper already cut, so it’s just a matter of picking out the colors.)  You could make a flag for each person (or animal) in your life that is a support to you.  Who do you like?  Who do you feel safe with?  Make a flag for each one of them.  They are your “cheering frog flags.”   

3. Then attach your flags to the string.  Hint: It helps to fold them first, and then put the glue on.  Then you can lay the string along the crease and fold it up easily.  

4. Then decorate your flags.  Put words and colors on them that represent people who have cheered you on.  You might want to ask for help with the writing. (If you have made some flags for each child in advance, you might let them know you’ll be asking their permission to add some extra flags to their string.)

Creation:
Now it’s your turn.  (Assist the children in beginning their work.)  As they complete their flags, help them with writing any words they want on the flags.   You might need to encourage them to think about times someone has been nice to them. 

Closing:
Gather in one final circle and give each child an opportunity to share his or her Cheering Frog Flags.  You might want to do the “wave” warm-up again, but this time, each child can be holding their flags.  Encourage the children to think about where they want to keep their Cheering Frog Flags.  Do they want to hang them next to their bed?  Do they want to wear them like a necklace?  Do they want to keep them private, in an envelope, and just take them out to look at when they want to?  (Have envelopes available for those who want them).




“I love your imagination” — example flag




Age Variations:
Depending on the ages of the children, they may need help with the words.  For younger children, the flags may be just happy colors and no words at all.  For older children, each flag could represent someone who has cheered them on.
Row.txt_description: Encourages the children to never give up on their dreams. To help them notice and remember the supportive voices in their lives - voices that have cheered them on - and give the children a way to take those cheering voices with them, as encouragement forever.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create version for adults.

Row.txt_code:
< /tr>


 Silvia Gutierrez, Children’s
Windows leader at Women and
Children’s Crisis Center,
Whittier, CA..
  
In response to last month’s request for holiday-themed workshops, Silvia has contributed “My Scarecrow.” Thank you Silvia, for this beautiful and deeply meaningful workshop!

Objective:
Scarecrows have been used by farmers to frighten away intruders (crows) and keep them from eating their valuable crops. This activity can help the children focus on protection. They can make their own special scarecrow to scare off their intruders. It can also provide them with the opportunity to identify what is valuable to them. (For example: crops are valuable to farmers.) During this workshop, they can notice what, for them, needs protection.

Materials:
White paper (for watercolors)
Cray-Pas
Watercolors

 
 
 Supplies: Watercolor sets
and Cray-Pas sets
  
 
 Scarecrow in a field
  

Brushes
Spray bottle for water
Newspaper to cover tables

Timeframe:
60 min—Total Time
Warm Up: 5 minutes
Idea Circle: 5 minutes
Intro/Demo: 10 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes

Age Range: 3 and up

Ratio:
One adult for four children; one adult for two young children.

Space Setup:
Cover the table with newspapers. Open the Cray-Pas sets in advance. Open each watercolor set and spray lightly with water. The water helps soften the colors so that they will be easy to use when the children paint. Prepare the cups of water for brush rinsing. Place supplies out of reach, (if necessary, depending on the age level), and bring out when needed. Have a space for the “Monster Dance” to occur, away from the art supplies. You’ll also need a “drying area,” for the paintings to dry when the are finished.

Monster Dance Warm-up:
When the children arrive, the Monster Dance warm-up can be used to tie in the Halloween Theme:

“Let’s do a Monster Dance. First we can start by moving around in a circle being monsters. Now let’s all be scary monsters! Now let’s be happy monsters! Can you be really loud monsters? Can you be really quiet monsters?”


 
 
 Drawing the scarecrow
  
 
 Adding the paint
  
 
 Painted scarecrow
  

Idea Circle:
After the warm-up, sit together in a circle to share thoughts about:

a) What is a scarecrow? Have you ever seen one? What are they used for?

b) Why are crops important to farmers? To all of us? What is valuable to each of us?

“Sometimes things that are valuable to us need a little added protection. Today we are going to make our own special individual protection for what’s important to each of us. Today we will make our own scarecrows to keep us safe.”

Technical:
(Note: this is the same procedure as for “The Monster in Me” workshop.)

There are three steps. Demonstrate them to the children, but get them involved in the demonstration. Ask them to guide you as you go through the three steps, so you’re creating the Scarecrow they are telling you to make.

1. Drawing the Scarecrow:
