“Let’s start with a Rock warm-up today. Let’s all sit in a circle. Good. To start our Safe Rock Warm-up, let’s take a minute to think about rocks together. Have you ever seen a rock you liked? What did it look like? Take a rock now and hold it in your hand. How does it feel? (smooth, hard, cold... etc.) Have you ever sat on a big rock? Or jumped off of one? Where were you? Have you ever felt how wonderful it can be to sit on a cool rock on a hot day? Or when you’re cold have you ever sat on a rock that’s been warmed up by the sun? As you hold your rock now, you might notice it warming up.

“How old do you think your rock is? Is it older than you? Is it older than your parents? And your grandparents too? Rocks are very old. They were here before there were TVs, computers, or even cars. They were here before this country was created. As you hold your rock, notice that it has been here a long, long time. Some people feel that rocks have wisdom in them. They have seen so much.

“Look closely at your rock. Imagine how old it is, old and strong. Imagine that your special rock wants to help keep you safe and happy. It has been around a long, long time. It knows many things, and now it’s happy to be meeting you for the first time today. What do you think your Safe Rock is thinking right now? If it could talk, what would it say right now?” (Encourage each child to share.)

Introduction/Sharing:
“Today each of us will get a chance to make our own Safe Rocks that we can carry with us, or give to someone else who needs help staying safe. If you need to make more than one rock, that’s fine. There are plenty.

You’ve already had a chance to hold your rock and ‘listen’ to what it might say. Now you get to use paints and pens to draw on it whatever colors and shapes it wants to have. What colors and shapes help remind you of being safe? Ocean waves? A party full of friends? The sunshine? Some trees? The moon? What gives you a sense of safety and peacefulness? Maybe it’s a special person who helps you feel safe. Or maybe there are words your rock would like to have on it, to help you feel safe. What words would your rock have on it?”


 
  
Painting:
Assist each child as they paint their Safe Rock or Rocks. They may need special help putting words on with the paint pens. Help them out as needed. Encourage them to create more than one rock so they can keep one for themselves and also give some to others. They make wonderful, meaningful gifts.

Closing:
For the closing circle, give each child a chance to share their Safe Rocks.
Affirm each child’s experience.
Row.txt_description: Gives the children the chance to think about when they felt secure, and to create something solid as an expression of that safe feeling.
Row.txt_tips: If available, bigger rocks would allow for more creativity and self expression.

Row.txt_code:
Heart Story Example
  
  
 Table set-up
Overview:
This workshop offers participants an opportunity to listen to their hearts, and express their heart story. Using a simple watercolor technique, along with meditation and journaling, participants will connect and honor themselves exactly where they are.
Materials:
4" x 6" watercolor paper (up to 3 pieces per participant)
Masking tape
Watercolor sets with brush
Cups of water (2 per participant)
Paper towels
Journaling Page: "What is your Heart Story?"
Pens (one per participant)
Relaxing music

Time Frame:
Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Introduction: 5 minutes
Materials Demo 10 minutes
Relaxation: 5 minutes
Creation: 20 minutes
Journaling: 5 minutes
Paired Sharing: 5 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour, 10 minutes

Workshop Prep:
You might want to try out this watercolor technique beforehand so you are comfortable when demonstrating it. Also, if you create a sample prior to the workshop and leave the tape on, during the demonstration, you can remove the tape and show participants the border that is created.

Depending on the time you have, you may want to tape the watercolor paper down prior to the workshop or have the participants tape their own. (See Fig. 1 below)

Opening Circle:
Before you begin our Heart Story workshop, you can start with a "heart circle" check-in. Invite anyone, who wants to: "Please share a word about how your heart is feeling today:
Light? Heavy? Foggy? Clear? Full? Strong? Happy? Sad?"

After each participant has a chance to share, you can say: "Thank you for honoring what's in your heart, and exactly where you are!"

Introduction:
  
"Today we are going to share our Heart Stories. Each of us has a story to tell! Sometimes we think 'our' story is the narrative of what is happening all around us, or to us. But actually, our Heart Stories are something different. Our heart stories are created in our hearts; they are the feelings, experiences, hopes and colors that live inside of each of us. If we listen -pause- we can notice the learning, the wisdom and value that guides and shapes our lives and who we are, and inspires our life stories. Today we'll have a chance to listen to our hearts and tell their stories.

Our stories can be expressed in many different ways, though voice, movement and many art forms.Today we are going to use watercolors. I'll guide you through a process that lets your story emerge by listening to your heart and expressing it through colors, shapes and flowing imagination.

I'll show you a simple watercolor "wash" technique. Or feel free to play and explore if that is what feels right to you. Remember this is your window of time, to honor your thoughts, feelings, visions and needs. What you choose to do is completely up to you. If you want to just sit quietly with your hand on your heart, that's okay. There is no right or wrong way!

"The way the colors move and blend can express so much. We will each choose a simple shape to tell our story. It can be as simple as a circle or line or triangle. You don't have to think of the shape right now. We'll be doing a relaxation, and you can just let it come to you.

"You can use one, two, three, or more pages to tell your story. The page(s) can represent whatever you want them to represent. They can represent how you feel on the inside, and how the world feels around you. They can represent your transformation and healing. They can represent your past, your present and your future. Or moving from I Can't to I CAN.”

 

 Fig.1: Taping the paper
around the edges
 
 
 
 Fig.2: Defining your shape
with water
 
 
 
 Fig.3: Dropping color into the water
 
   
   
Technical Demonstration:
Show how to tape down the paper if you haven't taped it prior to the workshop (Fig.1). Let participants know the reasons for taping the paper down: 1) When the tape is removed, after the watercolor is dry, there will be a frame around the art like a window. 2) The tape helps to contain the water so it stays on the page.

Explain the various supplies, especially the reason for the two cups of water (one is to rinse the brush, and one is a source of clear water to paint with).

To demonstrate the use of the water wash, paint a shape with pure water on the paper (Fig. 2). Use plenty of water so that the shape remains wet like a lake on the page.
Begin to drop color into the shapes (Fig. 3). Notice how the beauty of watercolor comes from what the color does by itself as it is carried through the water. When the paint is dropped into it, the magic begins effortlessly.

Show what it's like to drop the color near the edge. Show what it's like as the color spreads and runs into other colors (Fig. 4).

Show what it's like to paint the area outside the shape with color, leaving a space of dry paper between the shape and the background (Fig. 5).

Show what it's like if you join the two wet spaces (Fig. 6). You can work the all your papers at the same time, or one at a time.
 


 
 
Fig.4: Filling the shape with color

 
 
 
 
Fig.5: Leaving an edge of dry paper between the shape and the ground

 
 
 
 Fig.6: Bridging the dry edge,
where they desire		 
Relaxation:
"This is an opportunity to look inward, to connect with our hearts, and ourselves exactly where we are.

"Get yourself comfortable in your chair and gently place both your hands over your heart. Take a moment to relax and release some of the tension your body carries. Let your eyes close if you feel like closing them, and take a deep breath in. As you let it go, picture letting go of any more tension in your body... and take another nice deep breath in... and let it go. As you breathe deeply, bring your attention to your hands resting on your heart. Notice that this is a special time to care for your heart-all the good things, all the challenging things, all that your heart carries inside. If you remain still, can you hear any special message your heart has? As you listen to your heart you might hear difficult things, and you might also hear wonderful things. Begin to breathe in love and compassion for yourself; if expectations or doubts come up, listen to the strength in the beats of your heart and breathe. You might hear strength, hope, courage, or pain... you may hear words, songs or see shapes and colors in your minds eye. Trust your heart and take a moment to listen.... Is it something personal? Is it a change you want to make in the world? No story is too big or too small. Whenever you are ready, you can open your eyes and begin to create what your heart tells you."

Creation:
Each participant can go ahead and create their shapes in water on the pages and then begin to add color as they wish.

If participants finish early, encourage them to start the journaling process.

Note: When participants are finished, leave the papers taped down until later. This will give the water washes a chance to dry.

 
 
  Participant journaling
 
   
Journaling:
After participants have created their heart stories, you can give them 5 minutes to journal or reflect on what they've created. You can offer the following prompt, "What is the story you see in front of you?" Or they are free to write whatever feels right or good to them in this moment.

Paired Sharing:
Ask participants to choose a partner, and give each person 2 minutes to share about their heart story, the process, or anything else that is coming up for them. Remind the listener to listen with their heart and not with their words!

Closing Circle:
Give everyone an opportunity to share with the group about their heart story or any discoveries they made through the process.

"Thank you for taking this time to connect and listen to your hearts, to honor yourselves and your stories exactly where you are. You are worth it! Each of your hearts are beautiful and unique in their own way, and each heart has an important story that deserves to be heard."

After the circle, participants can go ahead and carefully take the tape off their art. If the paint is still wet, they may want to wait longer.
Row.txt_description: This workshop offers participants an opportunity to listen to their hearts, and express their heart story. Using a simple watercolor technique, along with meditation and journaling, participants will connect and honor themselves exactly where they are.

Row.str_author_location: Antelope Valley Domestic Violence Council, Lancaster, California
Row.txt_code:
Expressing Feelings sample: Mad
  
Objective:
To let the children express themselves and their feelings. To allow them to create without criticism. To give them the opportunity to experience the magic and beauty of seeing something invisible become visible.

Materials:
White construction paper or watercolor paper
Watercolor sets w/ brushes
Cups of water (2 per participant)
Paper towels
White crayons
Children’s music
Feeling chart (see attached sample)
Spray bottle with water


 
 
 Happy feelings painting (using watercolor on
op of bubble letters drawn with white crayon).
  

Music Suggestion:
I love to use a children’s music CD called “On the Move with Greg and Steve.” My favorite song for this workshop’s Opening Section (see below) is “Friends Forever.” This CD is available at teacher’s supply stores. It’s a wonderful resource for the Children’s Windows Workshops.

Ratio:
1 adult to 5 children

Timeframe: At least 1 hr
20 minutes: opening circle
30 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle


 
 
 Supplies for this workshop: paper, white
crayons, and watercolors.
  

Space Setup and Prep:
Have an open space for the opening circle and tables for the activity.

Opening:
Introduce yourself and explain about the art project, “Expressing Feelings with Watercolor.” Show the chart to the children and talk about it as a group. Have each child introduce themselves and share how they feel at that time. Remind the children about respecting others’ work as well as their feelings.

Do an exercise with the children with music to shake their feelings out. Have the children share what they do when they feel a certain way. (For example: “When I feel sad, I cry in my room.”) Encourage the children to share their feelings.

  


Angry feelings watercolor.
 
  

Expression Time:
Allow the children to write or draw how they feel with the white crayons. If they are unable to write, they can dictate the words and have you or another leader write for them. Be sure everyone presses hard to make their crayon lines. The harder you press, the more the crayon will show up!

Because both the paper and crayon are white, it is sometimes hard to see exactly where you left off. Help the children know that that’s part of the creation and it’s okay.

Once they are done, let them paint with the watercolors.

If they wish to see more of the colors mixing together, spray the paper lightly with a spray bottle (set on light mist).


 
 
 Using bubble letters for “SAD.”
  

When the color appears, a white outline will appear where the crayon is. The writing or drawing will stand out.

Let the children know even if it’s not exactly what they expected, it’s okay.

Closing:
At the end, give all the children a chance to share how they feel then and what they think of the art they have created. You may need to remind everyone about respecting all the art and all the different feelings.
Row.txt_description: Allows the children time to express their feelings without criticism. Gives the opportunity to experience the magic and beauty of seeing something invisible become visible.
Row.txt_tips: Kids who are too young to write can use faces instead to express the emotions.

Row.txt_code:
Note: The images illustrating this workshop
are miscellaneous magazine pictures.


Objective:
To give the children an opportunity to express   all the things they feel about themselves in their own creative way.  To help them focus on positive things about themselves and each other.

Impact:
When I lead this project the children get very excited about it.  They enjoy having the freedom to draw and experience how they feel about themselves.  I can see them gain a sense of self-esteem, pride, and understanding of themselves.  I can see how they benefit from this project because it allows them to take control of themselves and their feelings. 

Materials:
Construction paper (assorted colors)
Coloring markers
Magazines or photo stock books
Pre-cut images (for younger children who cannot cut their own)
Scissors







Glue sticks
Ratio:
1 adult to 6 children

Timeframe: At least 1 hr
20 minutes: opening circle
30 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Space Setup and Prep:
Set up an art table with supplies for the project.  If possible, set up a separate space for the opening and relaxation where the children can sit in a circle, away from the distraction and temptation of the art supplies.

If you are working with younger children who cannot use scissors, it’s important to have pre-cut images for them to select and paste.







Opening:
For the opening circle, I like to have each child say one thing they like about themselves.  When I work with the children, I constantly tell them positive things about themselves, so it’s not hard for them to think of things they like.  Often they say “can I say two things?”  It’s wonderful to see them focus on the positive about themselves.  
 
Relaxation:
Every group, I lead a relaxation for the children.  I dim the lights and play soft music.  I have them all sit in a circle and close their eyes.  I tell them this is a “special time” out for them—a time they get to relax and learn how to calm themselves.  Each relaxation I lead is different.  Often I count backwards from 10 to 1.  I also use the breathing exercises from the Children’s Windows Manual (pages 34-35), Energizing Breaths, Breathe Hot/Breathe Cold, Butterfly Breaths, and Monkey Breaths are all exercises that can be adapted into the relaxation. 











For the “All About Me” workshop relaxation, I like to have the children focus on noticing things they like about themselves during the relaxation.

Note about resistance: There are sometimes children who have a hard time relaxing and can tend to be disruptive during this part of the workshop.  Our group is optional, so I ask any children who do not want to cooperate with the relaxation to leave and go back to class.  If I feel it’s appropriate, I invite them back when the relaxation is over.

Expression Time:
After the relaxation, it’s creation time.  I encourage the children to look through the pictures in the magazines and pick out what ever they think best gives a description of themselves.  They then paste it onto their construction paper.  
I encourage them to pick lots of pictures of all the things they like about themselves.  They can also use markers to write or draw things they like.  

Closing:







At the end, give all the children a chance to share what each of their pictures means to them.  Encourage them to especially focus on sharing the things they like about themselves.  

If time allows, during each person’s turn, have the other kids say something positive about that person too.   

It’s wonderful practice for them to focus on the good in themselves and in those around them.
Row.txt_description: Encourages children to express all the things they feel about themselves in their own creative way. Helps them focus on positive things about themselves and each other.

Row.txt_code:
This workshop came to AWBW from Bob Bowman of Free Arts for Abused Children (FAAC).  Bob has volunteered with FAAC for 12 years and has been leading this Life Masks project for 10 years now.  He led this project for AWBW during  our May Leader’s workshop where it was well received a nd enjoyed by all.






Leader’s Workshop participant holding
her finished Life Mask.



Objective:
To give the children the unique and powerful experience of having a mask formed on their own face.  To give them the opportunity to explore their feelings and sense of self by decorating their life mask.

Materials:
Quick dry plaster bandages, cut into strips
Vaseline
Large bowls/warm, salted water
Paper towels
Plastic garbage bags (1 per child, plus extras for trash)
Masking tape (to secure the bags)
Clear shower caps (1 per child)
Baby wipes
Assorted acrylic or tempera paints (watercolors can be used as a low-budget alternative)
Glitter, sequins and feathers
Brushes
Scissors
Elmers glue
Newspaper or butcher paper to cover tables (and maybe floor)

Sources:
3-inch plaster bandages can be ordered from McKesson (a medical supply company) at (626) 284-3221.  It’s about $33 for a box of 12 rolls.  Also, instead of shower caps, you can use bouffant caps from Smart and Final.

Ratio:
At Free Arts, the ratio is one volunteer per child.  In your group, you might have older children work on each others’ masks to lower the ratio.

Timeframe: At least 1 hour
10 minutes: opening
20 minutes: mask making
20 minutes: decorating
10 minutes: closing circle

Space Setup:
Cover all tables and the floor too, if you wish.  The plaster is messy.  It does turn to powder when dry and washes off easily.  Cut plaster bandages into strips.  Cut 3” diameter paper towel circles to cover eyes.  Place strips, vaseline, warm salted water (the warmth and salt make the plaster dry faster), 3” circles, shower caps, baby wipes, and garbage bags at each of the mask-making tables.  Have enough tables to set the vaseline and water on, plus one separate table set up for decorating.  Note: At the end of the activity, dump the plaster/water outside (not into the plumbing system).

Opening:
Tell the children what you're going to do: you're going to cover their faces with vaseline, apply strips of wet plaster gauze, let it harden, peel it off and then they're going to decorate it.  Ask them if this is all okay with them.  This enables them to agree to the process and grant you entry into their space.  Empower the children by letting them decide if they will do a mask or a hand.  If they do a mask, ask if they want their eyes and mouths open or covered.

Note:  Although it might seem like it would be scary for kids to have their faces covered with plaster, I’ve found that they actually enjoy it it greatly.  Once they decide they want a mask, they generally go along with the process and don’t get apprehensive or scared.  I have never seen a kid freak out and require removal of a partially completed mask.  They usually trust the volunteers and are enthusiastic about the activity.

Face Masks: 
Step 1: Check-in
With this project, we work in pairs, one volunteer per child.  When you are assisting a child, first check in about the different mask options: Does the child want their mouth open or closed?  Eyes can be left open or covered.  Or would they rather do their hand instead of their face?










Fig. 1: Protecting hair
with cap and shoulders
with trash bag.

Fig. 2: Applying vaseline
to face.

Fig. 3: Covering eyes with
cut-out paper towels.





Step 2: Protection
When they are ready to begin their mask, have them sit in a chair facing you (not laying down).  Drape the trash bag over their chest and tape it behind the neck.  (Cutting a hole and slipping the bags over the children’s heads is confining and can be uncomfortably hot).  Put shower cap over the child’s hair (see Fig. 1). 





Fig. 4: Applying and
smoothing wet plaster gauze
around edges of face.




Cover the child’s face with a healthy layer of vaseline (see Fig. 2).  Use LOTS of vaseline.  Add extra along hair lines.  This prevents plaster from adhering to skin and facial hair. 

If the child wants to have their eyes covered by the mask, first have them close their eyes.  Then cover each eye with a paper towel circlet (see Fig. 3).  Explain the importance of covering the eyes, as the plaster is painful and difficult to remove from them.  Once the eyes are covered, you are ready to begin with the plaster.









Step 3:  Plaster
Dip plaster strip into warm-salted water (the salt helps the plaster dry more quickly), squeeze extra water from plaster by running it through two fingers.  Frame jawline, then forehead to create a circle (see Fig. 4-5).  Framing first strengthens mask and reinforces the structure.





Fig. 5: Creating a circle of
gauze around face.



Frame nostrils and mouth (See Fig 6-8).  For example with open nose, see Fig 13.  Fill in rest of face area with plaster strips, leaving air space for nose and mouth.  Add 3-4 layers of plaster gauze.  When the plaster feels solid and does not give when touched, the mask is ready to be removed.  Ask the child to move his/her jaw back and forth as you slip your fingers under their lower jaw area.  Peel the mask up and off (see Fig. 9).

Step 4:  Decoration
Have the child wipe their face with baby wipes.  Once they have cleaned themselves off, they can take their mask to the decorating table (see Fig 10-11). 













Fig. 6: Working up
over mouth.

Fig. 7: Working down nose.

Fig. 8: Entire face is
covered with layers.










Fig. 9: Removing mask.

Fig. 10.: Painting masks
with acrylics.

Painting masks

with acrylics.





Hands Masks:
When doing a mask of the hand instead of face, have the child lay his/her hand flat on the table.  Apply vaseline.  For some reason, hands need a lot more vaseline than faces, so put extra.   At Free Arts, we require the hands to be flat (to avoid gang signs, etc.).  Apply strips of plaster to the fingers.  Apply only to the top surface.  Do not wrap around the fingers.  You will need extra layers in order to make the plaster solid (5-6 layers).





Fig. 11.: Completed Life Mask.





Fig. 12.: Completed hand mask.




Closing:
At the end, give all the children a chance to share their masks and what they mean to them.






Fig. 13.: Sample of mask with open nose.
Row.txt_description: Gives the children the unique and powerful experience of having masks formed from their own faces. Gives them the opportunity to explore their feelings and sense of self by decorating their masks.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for adults (appropriate for all ages).

Row.txt_code:
At AWBW we’ve been noticing how many children struggle with being extremely hard on themselves and afraid of making mistakes.  We looked into our files to find a project that could help the children to find a sense of humor, playfulness and acceptance about making mistakes.   We found this workshop from Erica Poellot.  We hope you enjoy it and have fun exploring mistakes with the children!

Objective:
To help the children learn to stop being so hard on themselves.  To give them a chance to build a sense of humor and acceptance about mistakes they (and those around them) have made.  

Impact:
When I led this project it was a very lighthearted group.  Everyone was very open and joked a lot about mistakes we had all made.  It was great to see the sense of camaraderie.  One of the children said “Erica, I think you are the biggest turkey!”    








Materials:
Construction paper (assorted colors)
Coloring markers
School glue
Feathers (lots)
“Googley” eyes
Scissors
Optional:  We did the workshop using pinecones instead of construction paper.  It took a lot of extra feathers to decorate them, but they looked great!!!

Ratio:
1 adult to 6 children

Timeframe: At least 1 hr
20 minutes: opening circle
30 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle









Space Setup:
Set up an art table with supplies for the project.  If possible, set up a separate space for the opening and Turkey Dance where the children can be away from the distraction and temptation of the art supplies.

Note:  If you are working with younger children who cannot use scissors, don’t cut out the turkeys.







Opening:
At the beginning of the workshop, I encourage the group to think about mistakes.  I help them be light about it.  It helps to have some silly mistakes in mind that I can share to inspire the group to be open and enjoy sharing their mistakes.

Turkey Dance Warm-up:
If you have a young group, you could begin with a “Turkey Dance”  Play up-beat music, and have everyone dance around the room as a turkey.  Ask: Would they be a big turkey?  A little turkey?  A fast turkey?  A slow turkey?  Encourage everyone to be silly and not worry about how they look!

Expression Time:
For making the Mistake Turkeys, begin choosing colors of paper and outlining hands with markers.  If the children are old enough, they could cut out their hand-tracing before decorating it and adding feathers.  If they are younger, it may be much easier and less frustrating for them to leave it on the full page.  After the Turkey is drawn, add glue, feathers, more drawing, and “googley” eyes to complete them.   

Closing:
At the end, give all the children a chance to share their Mistake Turkey and anything about what it means to them. 

Encourage them to remember that it’s okay to make mistakes, and it’s okay not to be perfect.  Remind them that it can be fun when they are not being too hard on themselves.
Row.txt_description: Helps the children learn to stop being so hard on themselves and gives them a chance to use humor to accept their mistakes and those of others.

Row.txt_code:
Introduction:







Color Discovery Maps is a workshop  adapted from an exercise in the book The Artist’s Way by Julia Cameron.  The exercise is called Color Schemes and is in the chapter—Recovering a Sense of Strength.

I feel this is a good exercise for all ages. I wanted to adapt and expand the idea for children.

Objective:
To gain a sense of strength in relating ourselves to a color.   To explore and accept our feelings in a different forum by noticing our own qualities—   as they relate to color.  When a child (or older person too!) begins to contemplate their favorite color, or a color they like, and relate it to themselves somehow, I’ve found that they naturally begin to associate the good in themselves with their color.  They can also accept aspects of themselves as true and “OK” by thinking about the color.  Because colors are strong, a sense of strength is gained in relating ourselves with a color.  (The following details and steps of this workshop will describe this idea better.)

Age Level:
Children age 4 to 104    







Materials:
Butcher paper - or any large white paper that can be put on the floor (like a map).
The idea is to be able to work freely with a lot of space around each person.
Acrylic paint or finger paint (many colors)
Large brushes (or children can use their fingers)
Water
Paper towels
Cray-Pas
Markers

Timeframe:
Total time: 1 1/2 hours
Relaxation—10 minutes
Painting shape—15 minutes
Drawing on and around the color (making the map)—30 to 45 minutes
Closing circle—15 minutes 







Relaxation:
This art work is a relaxation on its own—you may want to begin by explaining what we are doing and just letting the children begin while listening to relaxing music.  You can use this relaxation if they don’t seem able to jump right in:

“Imagine a box of crayons—it’s a really big box.  It has every color you can imagine.  The crayons are big and once you begin to draw with them they can turn into markers, they can turn into paint brushes.  The box has so many colors.  There is bright red, sky blue, pumpkin orange, lime green, bright green, dark green—like in a dark forest.  Bright yellow—like the sun, light yellow like a pretty small bird, light pink—like cotton candy, dream like and carefree, bright blue—very strong, but friendly and, there, there it is: your favorite color—what color is it?” 

Encourage the children to announce their color.  Ask them to try to describe it exactly.  Now we are going to try to make our color with paint in a shape on our paper.

Art Making Steps:
#1 Have the children paint a shape of the color they have chosen in the center of their paper (map). This is the color they have in their mind - it may not be straight out of the bottle.  Help them to mix their color—the exact color they want.

#2 Put the paint away (young children will get distracted and messy with paint for long periods of time).  We want to stay focused, so it’s best to introduce our new materials (Cray-Pas and markers) for that purpose.

#3 “We want to relate the color we have chosen to ourselves and our feelings.  This color you chose to put on your paper—does it have anything in common with you?
When you think about the color, how is it like you?  The map has our color in the middle and we can draw pictures and write around that, in order to discover what the color has in common with us.”

Examples:  I am blue like the sky—positive, expansive, full of hope.  I am red—wild, fun, sometimes I get mad.

The children should have a good amount of time to draw pictures and write things around their color.  Of course they may need help.  I would walk around and just talk to each child individually to help generate ideas.

Closing:
Allow a good amount of time to let children share and discuss their color map (15 minutes for the group). They will discover more as they talk about their color.

Note: I recently did a version of this exercise with a painting class I teach.  The group is mostly adults, but they came up with such beautiful writings about color and themselves that I wanted to share them with you:






I am blue, full of hope.
Sometimes I’m blue like in
the sky and free.






I am blue, strong.

I am blue - expansive.






Sometimes I’m a peaceful blue.





Emma:
I am Golden. I am lustrous; radiant in richness and splendor; of greatest value and importance. I am precious, marked by peace, prosperity and creativeness, very favorable, advantaged and excellent. I have a promising future, assured of success.

Lea:
I am blue. I come in many shades depending on the weather, time of day, or season. I am seen mostly in the sky. I represent cleanliness and hope. I am a calmer.

Angie:
I am blue/green. I am blue at times, yet strong and positive, and green at times, feeling clam and close to nature as the trees. Yet when blended I am the beautiful color blue/green.

Shari:
I am green, the life, breath and beauty of spring, I am green.

Carol:
I am taupe, neutral, flexible, compatible, almost rosy. I can stand alone, but prefer a colorful companion. 

About the Author:
I taught workshops at Choices in Columbus to women and children for almost five years.
I learned a lot about teaching with a spirit that comes from A Window Between Worlds.
I was involved in Women’s Windows training in 1997 and Children’s windows training in 2002. I basically teach classes that are not involved with the shelter now, but I keep the spirit of teaching that I learned with the residents. I learned to give the residents a window of time and freedom to enjoy and express themselves. I’ll take that idea and my experiences with me to all the students I teach in the future.
Row.txt_description: Helps each child gain a sense of strength by identifying with a color that he or she really likes. Offers time for exploration and acceptance of feelings in a different forum - by noticing our own qualities as they relate to color.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for adults (appropriate for all ages).

Helping Hands artwork on these pages
by Olivia Tamayo and Cathy Salser
  

Objective:
To focus on the positive things that can be gained and learned from difficult experiences.
To notice the importance of giving and receiving help. To give participants an opportunity to reflect on the events of September 11th in an atmosphere
of safety and support.

Materials:
Heavy paper
Scissors
Markers, collage supplies, glitter, watercolors
Hole punch
Thread, string or ribbon

Age Level:
All ages. For younger children, you will need to help with the cutting, or else do the project without cutting out the hands. (You can just trace and draw without cutting.) Depending on the age-levels, range, and size of the group you might decide to limit the materials to just markers for simplicity.

Timeframe:
Total: 1 hour
10 min: Introduction
5 min: Warm-up Circle

 
 
  


25 min: Creation
20 min: Sharing

Caution:
Be thoughtful about whether or not to bring up 9/11. If it’s not already on the children’s minds, there’s probably no need to remind them or focus on it.

You can adjust the workshop by just leaving out all references to 9/11 and focusing on general feelings about helping others and being helped.

If 9/11 is on the children’s minds, then this workshop may provide a helpful way to channel worries and memories in a positive direction.

Introduction:
“With September here, I know people around us are talking about 9/11 and what happened last year. Have you heard people talking? Do you remember what happened last year?

“There were lots of scary and difficult things about what happened last year. There were also some good things. It might be hard to remember, but let’s try. Do you remember anything good? Did you see anyone helping anyone else? What do you remember that was good?”

  


  

Depending on the age of your group and what they remember seeing on television you might encourage them to remember some of these things: Do you remember the rescue workers saving people? Do you remember how people sent support from all across the country to help? Do you remember the dog that helped the blind man out of the building? What are the good things you remember seeing people do to help each other? Do you remember how special it was for the people who got to hear “I love you” from their loved ones for the last time? Little things people did make a very big difference.

“So today, in honor of all the ways people have helped each other since 9/11, we will be creating Helping Hands. You can make one, and if you want to make more after that, that’s fine.”

Warm-up:
“For our warm-up today, we’re going to go around in a circle and each share about someone who has helped us, and someone we have helped. It could be someone in your family, or someone far away. It could be something from today, or it could be something from a long time ago.”


 
 
  

Creation:
As the children create their hands, encourage
them to trust
whatever comes
to them and not
criticize it. Assist
them as needed with
the cutting. For those
who finish early, encourage
them to add any words that go on their hand. Let them know it’s fine to make another Helping Hand to give to someone else if they wish.

Sharing:
Give everyone an opportunity to share their Helping Hands, what they mean to them, and anything they discovered in the process.

Closure:
It is important to take special care to end the workshop on a positive and hopeful note, especially since this is such a deeply difficult subject. If you think it would help, have a final sharing circle. Ask each participant: What is one good thing you take with you from this workshop?

You might want to end with a celebration of hanging all of the hands in the shelter.
Row.txt_description: Offers time for focus on the positive things that can be gained and learned from difficult experiences and to notice the importance of giving and receiving help.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for adults (appropriate for all ages).
Row.txt_tips: One way to start out this activity that works well is to read kids the book "Hands are Not for Hitting", by Martine Agassi.

Row.str_author_location: Friendship Center of Helena, Helena, Montana
Row.txt_code:
Awesome Essence sample drawing.
 
  


Mary Huigen developed this project for a women’s group.  The goal was to work on creating and maintaining personal boundaries.  She wrote it to be adaptable for all ages, so here we share an adaptation for working with children.  Feel free to change and adjust it as you need.  Enjoy!

Objective:
To explore our “essence” by noticing who we are, what makes us special, and what makes us strong.  To see how this “essence” comes through whatever we experience, and all the challenges can make us even stronger, more special, and more amazing. 

Note:  If the word “essence” throws the kids off too much, you could call this workshop “Who am I?” and just leave the word “essence” out.   

Materials:
Large paper bags (brown grocery bags)
Cray-Pas oil pastels
Watercolors (Prang makes good strong colors)
Large container of warm water
Tea candle

Timeframe:
Total:        1 hour
10 min:  Introduction
10 min:  Visualization
30 min:   Activity
10 min:   Closing Circle

Setup/Prep:
It is optimal to have an open area that has plenty of space for movement, yet is near the area they will be working.  Place one of each item from the materials list for each participant.  Place the candle in the middle of the table, but don't light it yet.  Have the container of water near by, but in a location separate from the working table, so spills don't occur where the work is being done.

Be sure to experiment with this project prior to doing the workshop, so you know how it feels to go through these steps.


 
 
 Step 1: Cut the paper bag to
the shape you desire.
  
 
 Step 2: Draw an image of yourself.
  
 
 Step 5: Paint with water
colors (after folded & wet).
  

If you are working with children who won’t be able to cut out their own shapes from the bags, you might cut the bags in advance.  You might choose one basic shape for the kids to work with (hearts, circles, squares, etc.)

Introduction:
“This workshop is an opportunity to discover the power at the root of ourselves.  One word for this is our “essence.”  Our essence is the wonderful strength and specialness inside of us that cannot be changed.  It is there no matter what we go through.  Today we’ll be making drawings with shapes and colors to show our “essence” and then we’ll see what happens when our drawings go through difficult changes.  We’ll actually be taking our drawings, crumpling them up, and dunking them in water.  Then when we open them up, we can add watercolor and see how amazing they look even after all they’ve been through.”  (Maybe do a demonstration of the Awesome Essence Making)

Visualization:
We did this standing and with eyes closed.  If a participant is too uncomfortable with eyes closed, perhaps they could stand near you or with their back to the wall and the exit door near them.  They may choose to do this with eyes open.

“First, it is important to feel centered in your body.  Find the center of the balls of your feet.  Find the center of your heels.  Rest in that place.  Find where your hips are square and comfortable.  Find where your shoulders are set and balanced.  Find where your head rests evenly on your neck.  Stay here for a moment.  This is a good time to thank your body for what it does for you.  In front of you, imagine there are four balls of energy: one blue, one green, one violet and one white. In a way that is most comfortable for you, bend, fold, twist, or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the blue ball.  This ball holds the question for you, ‘Who is in my family?’ Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball. In a way that is most comfortable for you, fold, bend, twist or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the green ball. This ball holds the question, ‘Who are my friends?’  Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball.  In a way that is most comfortable for you, fold, bend, twist, or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the violet ball.  This ball holds the question, ‘What makes me special?’  Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball.  In a way that is most comfortable for you, fold, bend, twist, or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the white ball.  This ball holds the question, ‘What makes me strong?’ Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball.  Now find and gather all the balls you have stored.  With the greatest care and with all the power you can muster, bring these balls together and merge them into one singular flame.  Remember to use your power, not force.  Rest with this flame.” 
 
For different age levels you might vary the questions.  You might include “What are my hopes and dreams?”  “What makes me feel happy?”  “What makes me feel peaceful?”  “Who do I feel supported by?”


 
 
 Step 3: Crumple, fold, or bend.
  
 
 Step 4: Immerse in water.
  
 
 Step 4 (continued): Take out of water
to begin painting.
  

After the visualization, light the candle and bring everyone to the table.

Awesome Essence Making:
Step 1.  Cut the paper bag into the size and shape you desire. You may need to show younger children how to get into the paper bag and cut the bottom off so it lays flat.

Step 2.  Ask the participants to use the Cray-Pas to draw an image of themselves.  Encourage them to press hard.  I let them know they are not bound to making a body.  Often the image is of abstract shape rather than an identifiable object.  What ever the image is, is fine.

Step 3.  Crumple, fold, or bend the image and the paper bag. This is often hard to do because we don't like to mess up our art!!!  This portion may also be representative of the pains we have endured, times we have felt folded, crumpled or otherwise “mutilated.”  The more the fold lines are accentuated (by pressing harder) the more vibrant the paint will appear on those lines. 

Step 4.  Immerse the crumpled piece into the water.  You may hold it there for about 15 seconds or more, swish it around, squeeze it, whatever. (This part allows the paper to absorb moisture, thus allowing the watercolors to do their job.  The more moisture in the paper allows the paint to fuse across the paper.)

Step 5.  Open the paper flat and begin painting with the water colors.  This process is much like the healing process. Washing our experiences, our perceptions of ourselves with what we believe to be helping us heal.  The areas covered by the Cray-Pas will repel the water colors, while the mist area will absorb the colors.  It is best to use Prang Professional water colors, as the pigment is more dense and shows better on the darker paper.

Closing:
Before sharing about this project, it might be helpful to go over the “ground rules” for the Windows time, so that the children are especially good, supportive listeners for each other.  I like to allow enough time for participants to express their sensations about the process as well as what the piece expresses. 

I ask, “What did I notice in my body as I worked through each part of this process?  How did it feel to make the drawing?  How did it feel to crumple it up?  How did it feel to paint on it?” 

   



Awesome Essence drawing
before the water and paint.
 Awesome Essence drawing after
the water and paint.
Row.txt_description: Participants explore their "essence" by noticing who they are, what makes them special, and what makes them strong; getting a chance to see how this essence comes through whatever we experience.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for adults (appropriate for all ages).
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Recently, many of the Women’s Windows leaders created wonderful workshops focused on hearts. We thought these would be wonderful with the children too, so here are some of the favorites. Feel free to adjust them and come up with new ideas!


 
 
 
Note: The art in this Update is from
the Women’s Windows workshops
  

Note: The art in this Update is from the Women’s Windows workshops

Objective:
To give the children a chance to notice their hearts—and share what is in them—hurts, hopes, strength, love, and healing. To give them a chance to see that their heart is precious and beautiful.

Materials:
See variations below and decide which materials your group would like best:
1. Watercolor
2. Collage
3. Heart ornaments
4. Lamination
(Or come up with your own supplies and process!)

Timeframe:
Total: 1 hour
10 min: Warm-up
30 min: Heart-making
20 min: Closing

Introduction:
“Today will be a special time for us to listen to our hearts. Our hearts are how we love and care about people (and animals and the world around us...). What are some things you love with your heart? Our hearts can get broken too, when something hurts our feelings a lot. Has your heart ever felt broken? And our hearts can heal too, even after they’ve been broken. How do you think hearts can heal?

Today we will be making hearts and sharing. This is an extra special time to practice having kindness for all that our hearts hold, and for each other’s hearts too. (Does anyone remember the groundrules for how we make our Windows time safe and special?) This is a special time to care for ourselves and our hearts.”


 
 
 “Shadows , darkness, and light...
Falling apart...”
  
 
 “Nurturing, growth, beauty.”
  
 
 “My heart can be beautiful again
with patience and time.”
  

Warm-up:
(It’s great if you have a comfortable area where the children can sit away from the art supplies for the warm-up.)

“Let’s sit in a circle together. Today, this is our special heart circle. Do you know where your heart is? Can you gently place both your hands over your heart? Be gentle, like your hands are protecting and caring for your heart. Let your eyes close if you feel like closing them, and take a nice deep breath. Notice that your heart is safe and sound in this circle. Notice that this is a special time to care for your heart—all the good things, all the difficult things, all that your heart carries inside... This is a time to protect and thank your heart. And this is a time to listen to it. Whenever you are ready, you can open your eyes.”

Heart-making:
1. Watercolor
Healing Hearts
from Kori Taylor, The Abbie
Materials: Watercolor paper (three small pieces per person), watercolor sets, brushes, water cups, paper towels, relaxing music, pens and paper for writing.

Process: Have the children use the watercolors to paint three pictures of their heart on its journey of healing. Watercolors are a wonderful way to explore and express what’s happened to our hearts and then how our hearts are changing The way the colors move and blend can tell so much. (See illustrations this page.)

2. Collage
What’s in My Heart?
from Silvio Velasco, YWCA Wings
Materials: Heart outlines copied onto colored paper (see enclosed outline), glue sticks, scissors, and magazines. For children who are too young to use scissors, you can have pre-cut images available.

Process: This is a very simple project. Hand out xeroxed colored paper with outlines of hearts and have the participants collage onto the paper to show what is in their heart. It’s fine if they don’t stay within the outline of the heart. They can make it however they wish in order to show what’s in their heart. (See sample this page.)

Comments: “The supplies are simple and familiar, so the participants really like it and feel comfortable with it. It was not too hard for them and at the end of the group, everyone shared.”


 
 
 “Remembering my children who are not
with me... These pictures signify how much I
love them and wish to have them with me
very soon.”
  

3. Heart Ornaments
Inside/Outside Hearts
Based on workshops by Cecilia Bendimez (WomenShelter of Long Beach) and Jeanne Anderson and Caroline Castleforte (Good Shepherd Shelter)
Materials: Hearts copied onto white paper (two per participant—see enclosed master or make your own), markers, colored pencils, beads, yarn, scissors and glue.
Note: It can also be helpful to have a chart of different colors and what they can mean in terms of emotions.

Project: In this project, the children create a two-sided heart ornament that shows how their heart feels on the inside and on the outside.

Begin with talking about color and how different colors can convey different emotions. (You can use a color chart, or just discuss various feelings and what colors might convey those feelings. Remember, there is not a right or wrong answer. Different colors can convey different things for different people.)

Give the children each two hearts (pre-cut for younger children) and ask them to use colors on one heart to show how their heart looks inside. Ask them to use colors on the other heart to show how their heart looks on the outside—the side that the world sees.
They can then glue the two hearts back to back with yarn in between so they can hang it and see both sides.

4. Lamination
Giving Hearts
from Obbie Brown, Valley Oasis
Materials: Construction paper, scissors, edger scissors, markers, Cray-Pas, glitter glue, contact paper or lamination equipment, yarn and hole puncher.

Note: This workshop is based on the Affirmation Hearts project (August 2000 Women’s Leader’s Update).

Process: In this project the kids create something to give away that will help someone else’s heart feel better.

Each child creates three cut-out hearts, decorates them, and writes something on each one that they would want said to them when they are feeling down. (Younger children will need help writing.)


 
 
 
Hearts from the “Affirmation Hearts”
workshop (August 2000 Update)

 
  

After the hearts are made, you can laminate them with clear contact paper or a laminator. Then holes can be punched in each heart and strings or ribbons attached.
When all the hearts are completed, ask each child to choose one of their hearts to give away and put in a grab bag. Then ask each child to pick one out of the bag without looking. This is their special heart to keep.

They can give their other two hearts to someone else if they want to—moms, teachers, anyone they wish.

Closing:
Close with a special “heart circle.” Give participants an opportunity to share what they are carrying in their hearts from the workshop.
Row.txt_description: Gives the children a chance to notice their hearts and share what is in them: hurts, hopes, strength, love, and healing. Gives them a chance to see that their heart is precious and beautiful.
Row.txt_notes: ER TO DO: Create 2 pages at end of Quark document for patterns.
Row.txt_tips: If the kids work on ideas first and brainstorm, it will help them to narrow their choices/pictures.

Row.txt_code:
Shining Stars
  
Objective:To aid in building self-esteem/ self-concept and confidence. After all, who wouldn’t want their face on a star?

Materials:
Construction paper (2-3 each)
Polaroid camera (if not available, see options, pg 2)
Markers, glue, and glitter
Paint - brushes, cups, etc.
Pencils, pens, or black markers
Scissors and yarn
Hole punch and pipe cleaners
Large star stencils
Coat hangers (3) (for hanging completed stars - see page 3)
Any other materials for gluing onto construction paper
Newspaper/shower curtain to cover work area
Star song, i.e. “Lucky Star” (Madonna), “Shining Star” (Earth, Wind, and Fire).

Ages:
1 (w/ assistance) and up

Timeframe:
Opening:        5 min
Warm-up:        5 min
Demonstration:    10 min
Creation:        15-30 min (depending on age)
Closing:        10 min

Space Setup:
Cover work area with newspaper/shower curtain in advance. For recycling glitter, you may want to also put one piece of construction paper/newspaper paper at each work station. This allows for easy funneling of glitter back into containers.
If paint is being used, have accessories such as water, etc., ready. Put out other materials to be used according to age.

Camera Options:
With regard to pictures, make sure the pictures are ready to be used when the children arrive.  Various ways to do this are:

Polaroid Camera:
Polaroid cameras are best because they are instant.  In the cases of new children, this can be especially useful.

Ordinary Camera:
Pictures are taken & then developed and then the actual picture is given to the child to cut & use.

Digital Camera:
Pictures can be downloaded into the computer and printed out on card stock/paper.

Camera & Scanner:
Pictures can be taken and then scanned into computers & printed out on card stock/paper.  This way, you always have a picture of the child at hand.

No Camera Available:
Have the child draw a picture of themselves.

  


Completed Shining Star
Moblile hanging in the shelter.
 
  

Construction Paper:
For younger children: Have pre-cut stars of various colors ready.  Two stars for each child.

For older children: Have them stencil and cut out their own stars.  
Two-three sheets of construction paper of various color per child.

Opening:
(This Opening and Warm-up are mainly for younger children.  For older children, you might skip to the Technical Demo.)  Have the children sit at the table.  Pose the question:
“How would it make you feel to have your picture on a star hanging high in the sky for the whole world to see?”
“How would it make you feel to see your friend's picture/face on a star hanging high in the sky for the whole world to see?”
“How do you think it would make your friends feel to see you high up in the sky?”
“Today, we are going to make this happen. Our faces are going to be on stars for everyone to see!”

Warm-up:
Everyone stand up.  
“Look up high, high at the sky!” (Heads look up.)
“Look down low, low to the ground.”  (Heads look down.)
“Look up high, high as the sky!”  (Heads look up again.)
“See the stars all around?”
“Reach for the stars! Grab them, touch them, reach for them.” (Hold arms up and reaching.)
“Do you have them?  Bring them down.  Put them in your palm.  Pack them tight.  Did any get away?”  (Mime packing them into the palms of your hands.)
“Okay now everyone put them into your pocket/away for safe keeping until later.”

Technical Demo:
(The demonstration is mainly for older children. With very young children, it is better to sit down with them and just begin.  Young children are affected the same with only the picture.  Nothing has to be written about them onto the actual star.)

1. Create a sample star as a demonstration.  Your sample can be a star for the whole program and it can hang in the middle of the mobile, lower than the rest of the stars.  To do this, have the symbol/name for your organization and the words “Shining Stars” on a piece of construction paper ready to glue onto a pre-cut star:

“See this star?  I am going to glue this symbol onto the star.  Who knows what this is the symbol for?  That's right!  Our program!”  While gluing the picture onto one of the stars, continue with asking questions that will focus on positive aspects.  It is okay if they answer negatively, but you want to try to bring it back around to a positive note:  “What are some things you like about being here?  Those are some good things about this place aren't they?  They are so good that I think they ought to be written down.”  (Write the children's positive responses onto the other star with a black magic marker.)

2.  While beginning to decorate your sample star, narrate with something like: “Now I am going to decorate this star and make it shiny and beautiful so that it will match all of the shiny and beautiful things said about it!  Then, later, once everything has dried, I am going to glue the backs of the two stars together and make it one star.  I’ll put a string in the middle so it can hang!”

3.  Now you get to make your own star with YOU on it.  (Explain that the next time the children come, their faces will be on stars hanging high, high in the sky.  If a mobile has already begun and is hanging in the room, you may point it out at this point.)


 
 
 Three hangers tied together with pipe cleaners
to hang stars from.
  

Creation:
Young Children:  Sit down with them at the table. Supervision should be about one adult per 2-3 toddlers.  Have everything pre-cut and ready.  Glue sticks work better with this age.  Use your judgment on what materials would be better with the age group you have, but keep whatever materials you choose to use out of reach/sight until you are ready for them, especially the glitter!

Talk them through it and do the project with them.  To give them a sense of independence, you can keep busy by making smaller stars with your program's name on it to hang.  However, if you do this, just make sure you are not strictly concentrating on what you are doing, but that you are watching and interacting with the children.  Also, if you do this, do not get ahead of what they are doing.  When it comes time for glitter, painting, or whatever you choose, let them take the lead with your assistance.  Again, use your judgment!  Remember, children at this age model you, but like to think you are modeling them!

Children at this age get immediate gratification out of simply seeing their face in a picture.  Of course, they will tend to paint, color, etc. right over that picture, but the gratification is there nevertheless.  Let them do as they please.  They may not, however, remember they did the star, so, the next few times they come into the room you may have to point their star out to them.

Pretty soon after that, they will point their stars out to you!  And you will notice the huge smiles and see the confidence that builds every time they do so!

Older Children:  (After the demo) “Now it is your turn!  There are star stencils and pencils to trace with.  Choose colors of your choice—at least two.  (If you want to, you can choose three and put one in the middle, turned a different way so the points stick out.  It's up to you, but if you want to use 3, go ahead and glue 2 of them together so that I won't miss it.  Only decorate one side of the two glued together though because the blank side will be glued to the other one.)

“Next, glue your picture on one of your stars and on the other star, write your name.  Now everyone is going to pass their star around the table.  Once a star gets to you, look at who it belongs to.  Write something you like or admire about that person onto the star with a black marker.  Continue until your star gets back around to you.

“Once you get your star back start decorating.  Make sure you create a star as wonderful and unique as you!”  

If the group is really small, you yourself may want to write something positive about the children on their stars!  You may want to do this in a large group too.  Children love it!

Closing Circle:
If you have an older group, have each child share one or two of their favorite things that
someone wrote on their stars.
For younger groups and maybe for older ones too, have everyone stand up for a star dance: “Remember the stars you are holding?  Now that they have been made even more beautiful and shiny and unique, it is time to release them for the whole world to see!  Everyone take them out and ... ready...” (Begin playing song in CD or tape-player) “Everybody put your hands up into the air!  Reach for the sky and boogie!!”  

Clean-up:
Allow them to leave everything where it is, just so it is not in the way.  When they are dry enough, glue each person’s two stars together with string and hang them up on the coat hangers.  You will actually hang them on the mobile yourself later because the glue, etc. will still be too wet right after the workshop.  To create the coat hanger base, entwine the coat hangers and secure at center with pipe cleaners.  You may want to decorate the coat hangers with pipe cleaners, etc. Hang it from the ceiling in the children's program room in a place the kids can see.  Remember that it will probably rain glitter forever, so put it in a place where it won't bother you too much!
Row.txt_description: Aids in building self-esteem/self-concept and confidence. After all, who wouldn't want their face on a star?

Row.txt_code:
Suzy Karcher Rogers
 Daisy in a New Year’s Garden.
   


Objective:
To give children a chance to make a garden representing the important people and things in their lives. To give them an opportunity to explore and express feelings about themselves and their world symbolically through shapes and colors.

  


Materials arranged to be inviting.
 
  

About this Workshop:
I created this workshop last January with a group of children. They loved it! Even the boys enjoyed making a flower garden that represented themselves and the people in their lives—now and in the past and future. I didn’t really tell them to include ideas from their past, present and future, because that’s a difficult concept for a child. But they did it naturally. I told them we were going to make a flower garden for the New Year and we could make flowers that symbolized important people and things in our lives. They were able to take it from there. Most children are comfortable making art, so they are able to take a simple idea and run with it. (I just wrote this up as a workshop for adults too, so it’s in the January Women’s Windows Update.)

Materials:
Card Stock (heavy background paper) 81/2” x 11”
Construction paper
Tissue paper
Cray-Pas
Elmers Glue or glue sticks
Scissors and hole punch
Yarn (various colors can be bought in one mixed-color roll)
Relaxing music


 
 
 Fig. 1. Leaving the strip open at the top.
  
 
 Fig. 2. Adding strings for stems.
  
 
 Fig. 3. Completed New Year’s Garden.
  

Setup:
Many shelters operate on a very tight budget. I know when I was running groups there always seemed to be a sense of lack in the shelter, lack of space, lack of basic needs for the residents. I didn't want that sense of lack to be part of my group, so I would set everything up in an inviting way before we began (see illustration above). The way I arranged the supplies made it special and welcoming.
So place all papers, yarn and Cray-Pas in the center of the table or a nearby table. Invite the children to use as much as they need. Each child should have their own scissors and glue.

Timeframe: 1 hour
Opening Circle 10 minutes
Demonstrations 10 minutes
Creation 30 minutes
Closing Circle 10 minutes

Preparation:
Be sure to make a New Year’s Garden yourself before this group so you will have an example if possible.

Opening Circle:
Explain that we will be making a “New Year’s Garden.” Show your example and start a discussion about what each flower could possibly mean or represent. Welcome each child to introduce him or herself and they can also give an example of what or who they may make a flower to symbolize.
Discuss how the way a flower looks or is made lends meaning to it. What do certain colors symbolize?

Possible step by step method:
#1: Each child will get a piece of colored cardstock (for background).

#2: Glue a 2” piece of construction paper at the bottom (see Fig. 1). Only glue the sides and bottom like an envelope.

#3: Glue yarn on for stems. Tuck the bottom of the stems into the envelope (see Fig. 2).

#4: They will draw and make flowers to symbolize the important things and people in their lives and attach these to the stems (see Fig. 3).

Possible demos:
-Draw daisies (open flowers).

-Draw rose buds or other closed fragile flowers.

-Demonstrate whatever you are comfortable drawing.

-Make cones out of tissue or construction paper. These can be glued to stems and other paper can be attached inside or out.

-Cut daisy petals out of paper (oval shapes).

-Use hole punch to make dots of different colors that can be glued onto the flowers.

Closing Circle:
Have each child show their garden and welcome them to talk about it. Children love to talk about their art!

See if the children wish to hang their art in the shelter to welcome in the New Year!
Row.txt_description: Gives children a chance to make a garden representing the important people and things in their lives and the opportunity to explore and express feelings about themselves and their world symbolically through shapes and colors.
Row.txt_tips: If yarn is not available, other random art supplies, such as gel pens, markers, sequins, and gems also work.

Row.txt_code:
Worry beads can be soothing to hold.


This workshop was inspired by AWBW volunteer, Pam Douglas.  After hearing some of you leaders sharing how much comfort the children find in the “Safe Rocks” project (Leaders Update, March 2002), it occurred to her that “worry beads” could also be powerful.  She shared an article from the Los Angeles Times about worry beads, called “komboloi” in the Greek culture.  According to the article, worry beads are “like a toy in our hands helping us to calm and also to have something to concentrate and gather.”  They have been used for centuries and are “small works of art as diverse as the people who use them.”  Enjoy creating them with the children!

Objective:
To give children a chance to explore their emotions and create a strand of beads to use as a source of comfort and self-soothing—a way of handling anxiety and worry.

Materials:
-Large ball with “Feelings Faces” taped on (for Warm-up Game)
-Sculpey or Fimo clay in assorted colors (and/or pre-made beads with large enough holes for easy stringing)
-Toothpicks
-Toaster oven
-Yarn, cord, and/or leather string
-A sharp knife (for the leader to help make “spiral beads”)
-Relaxing music

Setup:
Try making a strand of beads yourself first, so you are familiar with the process and have a sample to share.  Try the various methods on page 3, or come up with your own.  Enjoy!  Also, be sure to prepare the big ball for the warm-up in advance. 

Timeframe: 1 hour
Opening Circle    5 minutes
Intro and Demo    5 minutes
Creation        20 minutes
Baking/Stringing    20 minutes
Closing Circle        10 minutes

Ball of Feelings Warm-up Game:
(Special Thanks to Giovanna Martinez of WomenShelter of Longbeach for sharing this wonderful warm-up game.)
Cut out Feelings Faces and tape them onto a big ball (like a basketball) with clear tape.  For this game, everyone sits in a circle and rolls the ball to each other.  Whenever someone gets the ball, they look to see what Feelings Face their hand is closest to, and they explain the feeling and say when they feel that way.  Play until everyone’s had a turn.  Validate all the many feelings and sharing.





AWBW Volunteer, Tesi Lowe,
shares her special beads.



Intro and Demo:
“Thanks for sharing all those feelings!  There sure are a lot of emotions that we deal with every day.  Today we’re going to make something that can help us handle all the different feelings and worries that come up.  Sometimes it helps to have a special thing we can keep in our pocket or hold in our hands to calm us down when there are lots of feelings—something that helps us feel clear and peaceful. 

“Have you ever heard of ‘worry beads?’  In a country called Greece, people have a special strand of beads that they carry around and hold to help with their anxieties and worries.  They can be very beautiful works of art! 

“Today we each get to make our own Worry Beads.  You could make your beads all the same, or you could make them all different.  You could make a bead for each emotion you feel, or you could make beads with colors that help you feel calm, and peaceful, and strong.  Your beads can be whatever you want them to be.  There is no right or wrong.”

(Share some techniques for making beads.  See attachment for suggestions.  As the children start their own beads, help them along, especially with poking the holes!)

Simple Variation:
Instead of creating beads, you could have the children string pre-made beads.  Just be sure the holes are big enough for easy stringing.






Toothpicks make holes through the beads.

Once the toothpicks are removed the holes remain.



Make Holes:
Once the beads are made, you can gently poke holes with a toothpick (see above).  When you pull the toothpick out, the hole remains.  For the younger kids, being gentle may take some help.

Bake and String:
The beads can then be baked in a toaster oven (see clay labels for baking instructions).  While they cook, the children can select their string or cord.  When the beads come out of the oven, they cool quickly and can be strung.

Closing Circle:
Welcome each child to share their worry beads and talk about them.




Completed worry beads.
Row.txt_description: Gives children a chance to explore their emotions and create a strand of beads to use as a source of comfort and self-soothing - a way of handling anxiety and worry.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for adults (appropriate for all ages).

Row.txt_code:
Carolyn Isbrandt, Buffalo, New York.
  
About this Workshop:
I want to begin by stating that this has been one of my favorite projects. The kids and I all enjoyed this activity from beginning to end, and I hope that you will too!
A lot of the children that come into shelter have grown up in an environment that focuses on negativity—negative behavior, negative words and negative treatment between people who should care for one another. This project was designed to help children heal and overcome that negativity that they have been exposed to. In my experience, it does not help a child to make them feel as if they are wrong for feeling anger or resentment. This project helps them to accept their feelings and release them. It’s meant to validate the child’s feelings and help begin a process by which they can express the more difficult things they are feeling and experiencing in a positive manner and begin the healing process. Starting with the meditation, the children are instructed to think of their problems and release them into the air, causing them to feel lighter. When the children and I worked together on this project, they were encouraged to make the project their own, using colors that made them feel good and covering the paper to their own liking.

Every child who participated in the activity found themselves giggling with delight. It is my own personal opinion that it is impossible to be in a bad mood while blowing bubbles and the children proved that throughout the group. I hope that all of you enjoy this activity as much as we did here in Buffalo!


 
 
 Bubble paintings mounted with bubble-shaped cut-outs
make a beautiful display.
  

Objective:
To give the children an opportunity to express the more difficult things they are feeling and experiencing. To help them discover a non-critical way to release any sense of negativity they carry and break through to joy and laughter.

Materials:
Bubble solution and wands
Plastic cups
Powdered tempera paints - different colors
Paper towels
(Two parts bubble solution: one part paint)
White construction paper
Smocks/old shirts
Classical music + CD player


 
 
 Blowing bubbles.
  

Ratio:
1 adult to 3 children
(1 adult per child for children under 5)

Timeframe: 1 1/2 hours
10 minutes: opening
30 minutes: relaxation exercise
30 minutes: activity
20 minutes: closing circle

Setup:
Have the table covered with paper towels to protect it from the splattering paint. Each individual should have a piece of white paper at their spot. I would advise having paper towels close by for more convenient clean-up. Have several plastic cups with a mixture of bubble solution and tempera paint and a bubble wand, a different color in each cup. There should be two parts bubble solution and one part paint per cup. Have the kids wipe off excess paint after they dip the wand. This avoids a lot of dripping paint. Each child should be wearing a smock or an old shirt, as the paint splatters when the bubbles pop! (I found this out the hard way!)
  


Bubble colors mixed with paint.
 
  
  
  

Introduction/Opening Circle:
Explain to the children that they are going to do an exercise on healing. Have a brief open discussion on the feelings of anger or the individual problems and stressors individuals in the group may be experiencing due to their experience with domestic violence. Talk about the healing process and let the group know that there are many healthy and unhealthy ways to deal with feelings of anger and pain. Let them know that you are going to guide them through a relaxation exercise and activity to show them a peaceful way to begin the healing process.

Relaxation Exercise:
Have the children begin by lying flat on their backs or sitting straight on a chair and closing their eyes. Have the kids focus on the music and instruct them to take slow, deep breaths, in through their nose, out through their mouth, as if blowing through a straw. Give them a few minutes to relax. Have the children imagine a beam of emerald light shining down from above. Tell them to


 
 
 Releasing the Feelings Bubble Painting artwork.
  
imagine that the light is shimmering and falling on their feet. The light is warming. Beginning with their toes, work your way up the entire body slowly, having the light follow, warming them and relaxing each muscle, all the way up to the top of their head. Instruct them to breathe into any area of their body that feels tense, releasing the tension into the air. After the muscle relaxation, instruct the children to imagine a bubble. Take some time to describe the bubble in detail. Next, have the children think about a problem they have been having recently. Tell them to imagine their problem in detail, then have them imagine stuffing their problem inside a bubble, then releasing it into the air and letting it go. Have them imagine that as they watch their problem float away, they begin to feel lighter and their body lifts in the air. Have them release other problems, and as each problem is released, their bodies feel lighter, more peaceful and free, and their body lifts up higher and higher, surrounded by hundreds of beautiful bubbles. Allow time for the children to visualize, and then bring them down again. Have them open their eyes and get ready to begin the activity.
*Variation* Have children put their hopes and wishes into the bubbles and release them.

  


Releasing the Feelings Bubble Painting artwork. 
  

Blowing the Bubbles:
Inform the group that they will be using the wands to blow bubbles on the paper, using the different colors to create their painting. The clients should not touch the paper at any time during the exercise, but should move their heads around the paper to cover the area. Group members should stand above the paper, blowing the bubbles, allowing them to pop on the paper.

Drying Time:
Allow the paper to dry, and then laminate each piece (if you have access to a laminator).

Closing Circle:
Encourage group members to share their feelings about the activity. Affirm each member’s experience.

Display Ideas:

 
 
 Bubbles are
beautiful!
  

Feel free to be creative—cut the white paper out into different sized circular shapes and mount them onto a black background to make the paintings stand out even more! When I set up my display, I cut out various sized circles and colored them with different pastel colors so that they looked like bubbles, then scattered them on the wall around the pictures. It brightened up the entire display, and gave the observer a clear idea of what they were looking at.
Row.txt_description: Gives children an opportunity to express the more difficult things they are feeling and experiencing. Helps them discover a non-critical way to release negativity and break through to joy and laughter.
Row.txt_tips:
Be sure to mix the paints in a variety of colors so the kids have plenty of options.

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
About this Workshop:

 
 
 Completed Music Box.
  

At Haven House, the children really seem to respond to the music boxes.  Each child was eager for us all to hear their own music boxes.  They took turns and shared as a group.  The sounds were amazing and so beautiful.  They all worked so hard, each box displayed a very different and unique look and sound.  When we returned the children to their cottages they couldn’t wait to show their moms their works of art.... Music is a part of us all in some way or another and their response to this activity, was evidence of that.  I enjoyed sharing this activity with the children at Haven House very much. It brought much laughter into a room that is sometimes very quiet, especially when there's a lot of pain.

Objective:
To allow children to create their own guitar-like instruments, explore their emotions through sound and music, and find a safe outlet of expression through their own rhythm and movement.

Materials:
Shoe boxes (1 per participant)
Glue sticks, liquid glue (Elmer's)
Construction paper (assorted colors)
Magazines, photo stock books
Rubber bands (large)
Craft sticks (snap apart sticks)
Glitter, stickers
Scissors
Markers, crayons, Cray-Pas
Music
Optional: Oatmeal containers, masking tape, chopsticks (if you’re going to make drums too)

Timeframe: 1 hour (1 1/2 hrs for younger children)
