Warm-up         5 min.      
Intro/Demo     5 min.
Ground Rules   5 min.
Creation          30-45 min.
Sharing Circle   15 min.


 
 
 Close-up of craft sticks holding the rubber bands
off the box surface.
  

Ages:
6 yrs. & up

Preparation:
It’s important to try this out yourself first, so you can see how to make it.  You’ll be better able to help the kids.  Also, for the warm-up, you’ll need to pick three types of music in advance if you want to use music rather than just voices (see below).

Sound & Feeling Warm-up:
“Today, let’s start by standing in a circle and taking a nice deep breath... and letting it out.  That’s good!  For out warm-up today, we are going to explore sounds and feelings.  Different feelings can sound different ways.  Can you make a sad sound? (Make sad sounds together.)  And now can you make an angry sound? (Make angry sounds together.)  And now can you make a happy sound? (Make happy sounds together.)  Wonderful!  You guys are making wonderful sounds!

“Now let’s try putting the sounds together with movements.  Let’s try sad again.  Can you make your sad sound again?  And this time let’s all move around the room in a sad way...  And can you make sad faces too?  Good!  And now how about angry!  Let’s hear those angry sounds and make angry movements and faces!  Wonderful!  And now how about happy?  Let’s hear the happy sounds and make happy movements around the room!  Look at all those happy faces! Beautiful!”

  


Many different Music Boxes made during one Haven House workshop.
 
  

You could also try playing three different songs (fast, slow and in-between) and ask the how would they move to these sounds. “What parts of your body can you move?”  Invite them to join in and share.  If they talk about the feelings they’d connect to each type of music, it’s important to remember that each child may interpret each song differently and display something very different and unique from one another.  Remind them that there is no right or wrong way.  The important thing is to make the child feel safe within the immediate environment and free to express themselves.

Intro/Demo:
Share Music Box creation steps (see below).  If you have a sample, share it and how it sounds.

Ground Rules:

 
 
 Fig 1. Cutting the hole in the lid.
  
 
 Fig 2. The hole is cut from tracing
a plastic lid.
  
 
 Fig 3. Covering the box with paper.
  
 
 Fig 4. Making sure the hole stays open.
  
 
 Fig 5. Cutting out images to collage.
  
 
 Fig 6. Adding collage images
to the music box.
  

Go over the Windows time ground rules to help create an atmosphere of safety, cooperation, and creativity.

Music Box Creation:
Continue to play music while the children work on their boxes.  These are the steps.  Smaller children will need more help along the way.

1.  For making the Music Boxes, begin by having the children trace a circle on the top of their shoe box lid (use something round like a yogurt top as a guide). See Fig 1-2.

2.  Once they have done this they may choose a color of construction paper, to cover the outside of their box.  Use a glue stick to apply the paper to the shoe box lid, but remove the paper covering the circle.  See Fig 3-4.  Repeat the covering process with the bottom of the shoe box.  Once they have covered the entire box have the children put the pieces together, closing the box.  

3.  They may now begin to decorate the box using the materials in front of them. They can collage or Cray-Pas.  See Fig 5-6.  For glitter, it’s best to wait until after the rubber bands are in place.  

4.  When they are finished decorating their Music Box you may pass out the craft sticks and rubber bands.  Assist the children with the bands, they may need to be stretched before they are placed around the box.  Once the bands are in place slide the craft sticks underneath the bands and stand
them on their sides so the grooves are holding the rubber bands apart ( the sticks may need to be adjusted for sound).  See Fig 7.

5.  Add glitter at the end.   See Fig 7.

Optional Drum-Making:
Drums can be also made by covering an oatmeal box with masking tape, covering the sides with construction paper, decorating, and playing with chopsticks.  (See figure above.)

Closing:
At the end of the group have the children come together and share what they enjoyed about the activity.   Ask them if they would they like to share their sounds.   Have the group share their Music Boxes together.

  


Fig 7. Adding glue and glitter after the
rubber bands are in place.
 
  

 
Drum-making example.
Row.txt_description: In this workshop children create their own guitar-like instruments, explore their emotions through sound and music, and find a safe outlet of expression through their own rhythm and movement.

Row.txt_code:
Seeing Me mirrors.
 
  
About this Workshop:
Our shelter receives donations everyday and at times it is hard to decide what can be used for art and what should be passed on.  When we saw five boxes of small mirrors with plastic coating our creative side saw endless art projects.  The first project we created is “Seeing Me.”  When our children start to settle into the shelter they begin to see themselves in a different light.  This project gives the children a chance to symbolically and verbally express how they are feeling about their physical appearance as well as how the are feeling on the inside.  We were amazed at how hard it was for the kids to recognize their own beauty and how easy it was for them to recognize the beauty of their fellow classmates.  We hope you enjoy this workshop as much as we did!

Objective:
To give the children a chance to see the beauty within themselves and to know how their peers view them.  The goal of the project is for the kids’ self-esteem to be raised each time they look at the art they create in this workshop.


 
 
 Front of the mirror.
  

Materials:
Mirrors (3x4 size is what we had)
Magazines/Art Stock books (pre-cut small images if possible for young children)
Mod Podge or watered down glue
Paint Brushes (older brushes are the best because the glue is rough on them)                        
Sequins, beads and feathers
Stickers (with positive messages)
Scissors
Puffy Paint
Glue Gun (optional)
Relaxing music

Timeframe: 1 hour
Warm-up:             10 minutes
Opening Circle:         10 minutes
Creation Time :         30 minutes
Closing Circle:         10 minutes


 
 
 Back of the mirror, collaged.
  

Setup:
Set out equal amounts of supplies for each child.  You can choose to let the children use all of the items listed above or just use collage-making materials.  We suggest using pre-cut collage materials because the children have a small  surface area to work with on their mirrors and it can be difficult to cut images small enough—especially for young ones.

Movement Warm-up:
Have the children pair off.  Assign one in each twosome as leader and one as follower.  Tell the kids to stare into the eyes of their partner and not to talk.  Ask the leader to begin making very, very slow deliberate movements, while keeping their eyes connected to each other.  Ask the follower to “mirror” the movements without moving their eyes to see the movements.  With the older children the movement becomes synchronous.  You might need to remind them to go really, really slow, like how slow a snail or turtle goes.  (After a few minutes, you could have them switch so each gets to be leader and follower!  If they aren’t focusing well, you don’t need to have them switch.)

Note:  Matching the children with partners of about the same height makes it easiest for them to follow each other.


 
 
 Mirror decorated with collage, glitter, and sequins.
  
 
 Front of mirror decorated with collaged words.
  

Mirror Opening:
Have the children take their seats.  “In your warm-up you had to use your partners eyes to copy or ‘mirror’ their movements.  You did a wonderful job!  Now, pick-up the little mirror in front of you and look at your OWN eyes.  Pull your mirror back so you can see your entire face.  Do you like what you see?  Just look and see what you like about the way you look.  Are there any volunteers who would like to say one thing they like about the way they look?  (Encourage the children to share.)  Now look at your eyes again.  Look into the centers of them—into the black centers.  Look deep down inside yourself.    What kind of beauty do you see inside yourself?  Do you see kindness?  Do you see your beautiful creativity?  Do you see your strength?  Are there any volunteers who would like to share what they like about their personality?”

Creativity:
After they share what they saw in the mirror opening, explain the project: “Today, we are going to decorate our mirrors with things that remind us of all the beautiful things about ourselves, inside and outside.  You can use (list supplies) to express all of the things you like about yourself.  When you’re finished with your mirror, I want you to keep it in a special place.  When you are feeling bad you can pull it out and remind yourself of how wonderful you are.”  Support the children as they create.  

Safety Note: If you’re using a glue gun to attach things, be sure to have an adult handle the glue gun and keep it out of reach so no one can burn themselves.

  


Some participants may also decorate the
front of their mirror.
 
  

 
Mod Podge over the collaged images looks
cloudy until it dries.
 
  

Closing:
“Now that you have completed your project carefully bring your mirrors to our closing circle.  (Have everyone stand in a circle.)  Hold your mirror by the edges.  Now everyone turn to your left and hold your mirror up in front of you.  Position your mirror so you can see the person behind you.  Look at their face.  Do you see something beautiful in the mirror?  Can you think of something beautiful about their appearance and something about their inner beauty?  Someone volunteer to start and we will go around the circle telling each other one thing that we like about the other person’s outside appearance and one thing about their inner beauty.”  It can help for the leader to go first, and then go around the circle from there.
Row.txt_description: Gives children a chance to see the beauty within themselves and insight into how their peers view them. The goal of the project is for the kids' self-esteem to be raised each time they look at the art they create in this workshop.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
This workshop was created by Children’s Windows leader, Cathy Peverly. It is shared here by Silvio Velasco, who adapted it to the Women’s Windows Program. She found it
especially wonderful in that it gives participants the opportunity to think about themselves, sometimes for the first time.

 
Objective:
Offers children the opportunity to see themselves through their own eyes and notice the things that make them shine by creating a sun full of rays with the words, images, and colors that make them special.

Materials:
Yellow copy paper (orange and red paper are fine too - any colors that would be nice to use for a sun)
Pattern with a circle drawn on (see attached pattern)
Pattern with sun rays drawn on (see attached pattern)
Color markers
Glue sticks
Scissors
Optional decorations: glitter, sequins, feathers and school glue
Relaxing music

Timeframe: 1 1/2 hrs
Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Relaxation: 10 minutes
Demonstration: 5 minutes
Creation: 45 minutes
Closing Circle: 20 minutes

Preparation:
Copy the circles and rays onto yellow, orange and red paper before the workshop. Make enough for participants to each have their own circle and rays. If you have young children who can’t cut, you might cut out some circles and rays in advance.

  
 
  
Introduction/Window of Time:
“Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you - a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you do or say is voluntary. I'll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there's no right or wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. Please ask for what you need, and know that I'm here in support of you. If you can't think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just play with the materials."

Today we will be making a sun. Not a regular sun, but one that represents us. We will concentrate on the things that make us individual, as the unique and wonderful person that we each are.”

Opening Circle:
Younger Children: Ask each child to share one thing they feel is special or good about them.
Older Children: For older participants, you might start with a check-in. Give each person a chance to share anything about how they are doing and feeling, as well as one thing they feel is special and good about them.

Relaxation:
Dim down the lights and play relaxing music. Tell the participants to sit comfortably, to close their eyes, and focus on the music and your voice as you go.

“Take a deep breath and let it out slowly. Now, take another deep breath and hold it for a little longer, and as you breathe out, do so a little slower... Do these wonderful deep breaths a couple more times. At this point when you start to breathe out, start to relax your body. Each time you breathe out relax your body little more...

“As you are feeling more relaxed, start to imagine yourself sitting outside. Imagine that the sun is touching your face, arms and legs. The touch of the sun is soft soothing and comfortable. You also can feel the warm breeze, as it moves your hair a little to the side.
“Slowly, as you continue to breathe in and breathe out, you start to feel a sense of comfort, security and happiness. Give yourself time to enjoy this feeling. Feel the sensation that it gives your body as you continue to breathe in and out.

“At this point you can feel yourself to be very light. You almost have no weight. It’s as if you are starting to float in a very soft and comfortable cloud. As you float, continue to breathe in deeply and each time that you do so you can feel all the good energy passing through your whole body.

“Slowly you continue to float to a spot in the sky where you can see your favorite places. You are at a comfortable spot in the sky. Rest there comfortably and feel the soft breeze sway you gently and feel the warmth of your body.

“As you breathe in you notice how comfortable you are with yourself and your surroundings. How good you feel inside and how your skin feels as if it is glowing. Imagine your face glowing with all of the goodness that you have inside of you. Feel yourself becoming brilliant, like a sun, shining and noticing all the wonderful things, great emotions, and love that you have within you. Let it shine from within you. Feel it, welcome it. As you feel your glow, let this glow touch everything around you. Let yourself enjoy these feelings.

“Once you are ready, slowly open your eyes, and as you do so keep feeling the sense of the glow. Allow the feeling of the glow to give you all the words, images or colors to do this project with.”

  
 Write words, drawings, or add colors.
 
  
  
Creation:
Allow the participants to write all the words, or drawings, or just color each ray on the colored paper. After they write and color, they can cut out the rays and the circle and glue each ray on the circle to make their sun. For those who aren’t old enough to cut, you could use pre-cut rays and have them focus on assembling them and decorating with color, glitter, etc. You would help write any words they want on their sun.

Closing Circle:
Give the participants an opportunity to share how they felt during the relaxation and then to explain what the rays of their sun say or mean.

You might want to end the group with allowing the participants to place their suns on a board for everyone else to see.
Row.txt_description: Offers children the opportunity to see themselves through their own eyes and notice the things that make them shine by creating a sun full of rays with the words, images, and colors that make them special.
Row.txt_tips:
Have precut rays and sun for the little ones.

Some kids might want to draw their own suns rather than use the templates provided.

Row.str_author_location: Women's and Children's Crisis Shelter, California
Row.txt_code:
Persona Dolls: Batman and Peasant Girl.


About this Workshop:
Here is a lesson Rosy has led during Mommie & Me classes. It has been a fun experience for us to watch parents and children making their own Persona Dolls.  It is amazing to watch them using their imagination and it’s amazing to see the creative outcome.  We have seen so many different dolls: peasant girls, Powerpuff Girls, Batman, Rapunzel, bikers, and replicas of themselves. We thought this would be an amazing workshop for children at other shelters to find their identity or maybe just to have fun.  We hope you and the children at your shelter enjoy it!

Objective:
To provide an arena where children have the opportunity to make a character or a "persona" of any kind. Children are able to make up a new character of their choice. For example, the character can be a superhero, cartoon character, a member of the family, or themselves! It can be an outlet for children to explore and gain a sense of identity in themselves.





The front of the Persona Doll
when held by the stick.



Materials:
Pre-cut dolls of various brown hues of construction paper
Felt or fabric of various colors
Yarn of various colors (it can be used for hair)
Wiggly eyes, beans, beads, sequins, (any kind of small objects that can be used as a substitute to express parts of the face such as eyes, nose, mouth etc.)
Scissors
Markers
Glue (white Elmer's Glue works well)
Craft sticks
Tape
Optional: paint or puffy paint

Setup:
Before the workshop, you will need to cut out dolls of various brown hues of construction paper.  (See attached doll pattern.)  It's a good idea to make a completed doll yourself before leading the group so you can see how difficult it is to create.  Having your sample also gives the children a visual to work with as they begin.  It can help spark their imaginations. (Especially if the children have low self-esteem, they are usually afraid or embarrassed to express their concept of what a doll should look like. so seeing a sample is great.  This is coming from personal experience!)




The back of the Persona Doll has two
craft sticks taped together and taped onto
the doll to make a puppet stick.




Activity:
Give each child a blank doll to work with. The child can start by dressing up the doll using the different kinds of material. The child can trace the doll onto the fabric and draw what kind of clothes the child wants to make, i.e. a dress, skirt, shirt, pants etc. This technique is helpful in order not to make the attire too small; it gives it its perfect fit.  Next, children can make the doll’s face using markers if they want to draw or small objects to give a two-dimensional look. The small objects can also be used for personal attire such as buttons or designs.  Yarn can be using for the doll’s hair. You can make spiky hair by cutting the yarn pieces about 1/2 an inch and lining them up, placing them on top of the head like a fence (see above).  Pigtails or braids can be made: just make sure you have fairly long pieces.  Tie up the middle with a separate yarn piece and then braid each side closing it with another yarn piece.  Finally the children can place craft sticks on the back of the doll so they can hold them up like a puppet. You will need two craft sticks for each doll. Be sure to overlap the two sticks about 1/4 together, and tape together to give it some sturdiness.




Completed Persona Dolls.








Yarn can be braided and tied at both ends to make this
hairdo.  Bangs are added.





Yarn can be cut short and lined up to make this spiky hairdo.
Row.txt_description: Provides an arena where children have the opportunity to make a character or a 'persona' of any kind. Children make up a new character of their choice, superhero, cartoon character, family member, or even themselves!

Row.txt_code:
About this Workshop:


 Feeling Bird finger-puppet ready to fly.
  

When I taught pre-school, I learned many wonderful projects to do with really young children.  This is one I’ve adapted for the shelter setting.  It’s a wonderful way to give the children an opportunity to explore their feelings through color, movement, and words.

Objective:
The finger puppets made in this project allow children to identify their feelings through color.

Materials:
Colored felt
Wiggly eyes

 
 
 Pulling the wing piece through the slits in the
body piece, the bird is made.
  

Feathers – as many colors as possible
Elmer’s or white glue
Scissors

Ratio Adult to Children:
1 adult to 3 children

Timeframe:
45 minutes to 1 hour

Setup:
Depending on the age of the children you may want to precut the shapes.  Also, before the children arrive, lay out the materials in an organized manner.

Bird Dance Warm-up:
Find music that would be good for a "bird dance." Ask what birds do.  (fly, eat, clean themselves off, sit on the telephone wire)  "Now we’re going to start with a bird dance.  Can you show me your wings?  And beaks?  And tails?   Can you show me how you fly?  Beautiful!  And how to you land?  Are there any noises you make?  And how would you sound if you were an angry bird?  How would you move around?  And how about if you were a happy bird?  And how about if you were a sleepy bird?  Can you come back to your chair and get comfortable in your nest?  Wonderful!"

  


Wing Piece on left; Body Piece on right
 
  

Opening:
Introduce yourself and open with a discussion of feelings and colors.  Also be sure to go over the ground rules.  It’s especially important to emphasize respecting everyone — and that means not laughing at what they’re feeling.  

"Today, we’re going to talk about how we feel in colors.  Like today I’m feeling yellow—to me, yellow means happy.  Does anyone else feel happy today?  What color happy would YOU be?  Does anyone have a different feeling?  Is anyone mad?  Or sad?  What color would you be?"  (Encourage an open discussion of feelings and colors.  Be sure to let the children know that there’s no right or wrong about colors.)

Demonstration/Creation:
Explain and demonstrate the project.  For younger kids, remember to have all the felt pieces cut out in advance.  "What we’re going to make today is a feeling bird.  Your bird can represent how you’re feeling today."

 
 
 Completed bird: Ready to become a finger puppet.
  
 
 Underside of bird: Place your finger through the
flap made by the wing piece.
  
 
 From the top: This bird is ready to fly!
  



1. Trace the pattern
2. Cut the felt
3. Put your bird together
4. Decorate with eyes, feathers, etc.  Some kids may put on rainbow feathers.  Some may make mismatched eyes.  

Closing:
Encourage children to share the bird they made and what it means to them.  Have the leader start off, and then go around the room one at a time.  You can ask questions like, "What does the color you choose for your puppet mean to you?"   "Why did you pick the color ‘red’?"  "Why does it look the way it looks?"  "What feelings does it have inside it?"

Often:
Blue – sad
Red – angry
Yellow – happy
(Be aware that colors can have different meanings for each person – and that’s okay.)

After each child shares, give him/her a chance to fly his/her bird across the room.  "Now show us how your bird flies!"  Pay attention to their body language and after they fly their bird, you can talk about whatever feelings they have.  (For example one child flew his bird really low and slow because he was sad, and then we all talked about being sad and things you can do to feel better when you feel sad.)  If there’s anyone who doesn’t want to share, be sure to let them know it’s okay.

After everyone has a turn sharing and flying, you can all fly together across the room.
Row.txt_description: Allows time for exploration of feelings through colors and motion, the end result, "Feeling Birds," are finger puppets.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.str_title: Domestic Violence Awareness Month--Project Ideas for Raising our Voices.
Row.txt_code:
Qui lt squares created by Children’s Windows Leaders—a sample of what
could be made  with the Circle of Values workshop, theme 3, pages 3-4.
 
  
About this Workshop:
With Domestic Violence Awareness Month on the way, we’ve been making plans.  We’ll be working with East LA College to create a special day filled with events to involve our community in raising awareness to help stop violence against women.  

Our big day will be October 22nd.  During the day there will be a Resource Fair where Bienvenidos will have a display and hands-on project.  Then in the evening, there will be a candlelight vigil to commemorate Domestic Violence Awareness Month. 


 
 
 “The Violence in Me, The Peace in Me,” Cray-Pas on paper.
  

In planning it, we brainstormed with AWBW about art projects that would be good for the display, the hands-on activity, and the vigil.  Last year, we did the Clothesline Project, so this year we were looking for another project that would be accessible, visible, and a good way to involve people.  

In this Update, we share three themes we brainstormed, and some thoughts about possible materials to use.   Art is a great way to get the message out there, and involve everyone.  Enjoy!

Importance of Children’s Participation:
Through their art, children can play a very special role in Domestic Violence Awareness Month.  Their creations and messages can make a strong impact on others—even just a simple handprint and a single word.  Encouraging children to share their expressions as part of the month’s activities can give them a knowledge of the power of their voices and the significant role they play in creating a future free from domestic violence.

  


“The Violence in Me, The Peace in Me,” Cray-Pas on paper.
 
  

Objective:
To bring powerful voices, images, and broad participation to Domestic Violence Awareness Month events through art.  To offer a way for children to voice their experiences of violence so that their stories are seen and heard.  To involve community members hands-on in commemorating Domestic Violence Awareness Month.  



Materials:
For all these projects, you could use a range of materials.  In choosing, think about how you want to display it, hang it, etc.  Do you want to use fabric so you end up with banners that can be carried in a vigil?  Or paper that can be carried as signs?  Think about whether or not you want to create something that can last for a long time, or just for the one day.  

Paper:  
Using paper can be easier and less expensive than fabric.  It’s also an easy way to make sure you have very bright, bold colors.  You could cut bright squares for each person and then glue them to a big piece of butcher paper.  

If you are gluing to a hanging surface and there’s a possibility of wind, you might want to bring a glue gun, just in case it would help.  

Also remember, markers don’t show up very well on many colors of colored paper. To make the art visible, try using Cray-Pas or tempera paint, or even fabric paint.


 
 
 Theme 2.  “All Hands Can Help Stop the Violence.”  These quilted squares were
created by children to express how their hands can help stop the violence.
  

Fabric:  
Using fabric can be wonderful for creating a permanent quilt or banners to carry in a vigil.  Consider what color(s) of fabric you want to use.  The colors you provide will make a big difference.  

Also, think about whether you’d like everyone to decorate their own square to add to the quilt, or have everyone working mural-style on one big piece.  Cray-Pas, tempera paint or fabric paint work well on fabrics.  If there’s no time for sewing, squares can be safety pinned to the larger piece of fabric or a sheet.  They could later be sewn to create a permanent quilt.  

Note:  If you are planning to hang a really large piece of fabric remember, you might need to cut slits to let the wind through.  Otherwise, you might have a “sail.”


  


Theme 1.  “The Violence in Me, The Peace
in Me,” puffy paints on fabric.
 
  
Possible Themes:
1.  The Violence in Me/The Peace in Me
Concept:  Each person traces both their hands.  Then they color one hand to express the violence they have inside of them, and the other to express the peace they have inside of them.  All of us have a range of emotions inside and it’s important for us to be responsible about how we handle our emotions.  It is up to all of us to help create a safe community.   

(Thanks to Rose Curtis for this project idea.  She’s found it to be an excellent project with her teen groups.)

2.  All Hands Can Help Stop the Violence
Concept:  Each person puts their handprint(s) on their square and creates a message about stopping the violence in our community.  It could be their personal commitment to help stop the violence, or it could be whatever message they want others to know about violence.  Each and every one of us can make a difference in helping stop the violence and this project shows how it takes all our many hands together – big and small, many colors, many ideas, many ways.

(Thanks to Yanti Bing for this project idea, based on the simple action of the Coalition to End Hunger and Homelessness)

3.  Circle of Values
Concept: In this workshop, each person thinks of what they value most, what matters to them most in their life and in their community. Is it family?  Is it trust?  Is it honesty?  Is it faith?  Is it helping others?  Is it learning?  Whatever they value most, they decorate a square to express it.  We are each a part of the circle of our community.   It takes all of us, honoring our deepest values to create a safe community—a circle of safety.  Each person’s expression can be attached to a larger paper or cloth.  If possible, arrange large papers or cloths around the gathering to form a circle.  That way, everyone can see the circle of values taking shape as people add their squares.

(Thanks to Carlos Sanchez and Martin Romo for this project idea, based on their "circle of values" necklace project they do with teen guys.)

Let Us Know How It Goes:
Let AWBW know how your event(s) go.  We’d love to share your photos, discoveries, tips and insights with the other leaders for next year!

  


Theme 3.  “Dream” square.
Row.txt_description: Offers a way for children to voice their experiences of violence so that their stores are seen and heard. Also involves community members hands-on in commemorating Domestic Violence Awareness Month.

Row.txt_code:
“This is Me” drawings at Haven House.
 
  
About this Workshop:
This workshop was very cool! It works really well with a broad range of age levels and I learned so much from the group I was working with.

The excitement the children displayed through the art and the sharing was a sight to see. They felt safe and accepted amongst their peers. This workshop proved to be a self-esteem booster even with the children who had very little or none at all. I enjoyed being a part of this activity and it helped me realize how much children really need to be heard.

One child in particular stood out—a 17-year-old male, who has a heavy burden upon him. He shared his art and his very own words about it telling you how he feels (see below).

Objective:
To give children a safe opportunity to explore and express who they are and what is special about themselves.


 
 
 At work on their “This is Me” drawings.
  

Materials:
Pastel chalks/variety of colors
White construction paper/all sizes
Newspaper
Hair spray (Aqua Net)
Scissors/edgers
Laminator or clear contact paper
Relaxing music

Timeframe:
1 hour 15 minutes

Age Range:
Children 6 years & up

Setup:
Place newspaper on the tables. include following items for each place setting, a tray of chalk, scissors and paper.

  


  

Ground Rules:
Respect one another
Listen
Communicate your needs
Proper use of materials:
Do not blow chalk dust or clap your hands together
Be respectful toward others and their work
Quiet when others are speaking
Warm-Up:
Ask the children to please stand in a circle and hold hands. (With a group of all teens you might skip the hand-holding.) “We will all go around the room and say two words or a sentence about ourselves that make us special.” (This may be very difficult for some of the children, depending on their background.)


 
 
 Destiny at work on her “This is Me”
pastel drawing.
  

Ask them who would like to start the circle? Include yourself in the circle as well. What do we love about ourselves? Is there something unique or special we want to share with the group today? At the end of the warm up have the children clap for themselves and one another.

Workshop:
Have the children write their own name in the center of each paper in any format they choose (cursive, print, etc.). Encourage them to cover the entire paper, so there is no paper showing. Allow them the freedom to choose. The ending result may be very powerful.




   


Brandyn’s finished drawing and words
about what it means.

The whole paper is me.
But on the outside,
that’s what people see.
So the black is anger
what people see.
Pink is happiness people see.
Neon orange shows my talent that people see.
And the white is the
emptiness in my life.
On the inside shows
how I feel within.
The black shows
how I feel most of the time.
Green is my happiness
and the brown is my loneliness
that I feel sometimes.
The blue letters that say Brandyn represent how I control all of my emotions.
By being cool,
like the color I chose.

—Brandyn
17 yrs.

  
   
Closing:
Give each participant a chance to share what their drawing means to them. If needed, remind them of the groundrules, so it is truly safe for everyone to share.

For those who really get into it, you could encourage them to write the words that go with their drawing (see poem by Brandyn).

Enjoy!

   



Miguel at work on his drawing.
 Aaron’s finished piece.
Row.txt_description: Gives children a safe opportunity to explore and express who they are and what is special about themselves through the creation of art centered around their name.
Row.txt_tips:
Separate the younger children from the older ones, if you have the space.

Allow kids to use watercolor in addition to the other media if they would like.

Row.str_title: Fall Workshops: Show Me your Tail Feathers; Let Bad Feelings Fall Away
Row.txt_code:
About these Workshops:
These workshops provide a wonderful way to take the themes of the Fall season and use them to explore the emotions the children are going through in shelter.

  


Example of “Show Me Your Tail Feathers”
 

Objective:
To give children a chance to explore and express what they are proud of about themselves.


 
 
 Example of “Let Bad Feelings Fall Away”
  

Materials:
Construction Paper
Markers
Bulletin Board
Scissors

Timeframe:
1 hour

Age Range:
3 — 12 years old.

Setup:
Prepare your turkey on the bulletin board—but don’t include any feathers. I put a pilgrim hat on mine. If you have children that are too young to handle scissors, pre-cut feathers for them to use.

Introduction:
As an introduction, I asked the kids what was wrong with the turkey. After they responded that he had no feathers, I told them that they were going to make feathers for the turkey that he could be proud of by putting on the feathers something they are proud of.

“I Feel Good” Wiggle Down:
You can start with a warm-up that is a variation of the Wiggle Down. It’s called the “I Feel Good!” Wiggle Down.

“Before we help make the turkey feel proud, let’s take a moment to feel good about ourselves, all the way from head to toe. Everybody stand in a big circle. Make sure you have an arm’s length distance around you. Good! Now let’s start with our toes. Can you notice how they feel today? Let’s see those toes feeling good! Can you give them an “I feel good!” wiggle? Wonderful! And how about your legs? Can they wiggle too? And how about all of our butts! Let’s give them an “I feel good!” wiggle. And how about your shoulders! Good! And now the whole length of our arms! Good! And what about your head? Can you wiggle that too? And how does your body move when you feel really good? Can you do an “I feel good!” dance? (jumping, wiggling, etc.) And now let’s take all our wiggles and wiggle them down, down, down (begin to crouch down so your hands are touching the floor). Let all your extra wiggles go down into the floor, and take a nice deep breath. And you can sit down on the floor in our circle and take another deep breath. Wonderful! Now as you sit there, think of some things you feel proud of about yourself. Do you feel proud of how you are a good friend? Or how you draw well? Or how you run fast? Anything that you are proud of is fine. When you are ready, go to the art table and make two feathers representing what you are proud of about yourself.”

Activity:
Help each participant as they cut their tail feathers out of construction paper (they can make two feathers out of one piece of construction paper). On one side of the construction paper they can write their names. On the other side, they write the thing they are particularly proud of about themselves.

Closing:
Once they are finished with making the feathers, then I have them come up and share with the group the two things they are proud of and let them help me put them on the turkey.


   



Turkey with no tail feathers.
 Adding the tail feathers one by one.
   


Let the Bad Feelings Fall Away

Objective:
To give children a chance to practice letting go of bad feelings.

Materials:
Construction paper
Markers
Scissors
Bulletin or dry erase Board

Timeframe:
1 hour

Age Range:
3 — 12 years old.

Setup:
Prepare your bare tree on a board. Prepare huge oak leaves cut out of construction paper for the kids to use. Or you could have them draw and color their own on paper and then cut them out. Whatever you think will work best with your group.

Introduction:
“We’re going to start today with this tree. What do you notice about it? (It has no leaves.) Have you ever noticed a tree with no leaves? It’s something that happens to lots of trees at this time of the year. The trees let go of all their leaves. What happens to the leaves? (Yes, they dance in the wind and fall onto the ground!) It’s a beautiful thing when the trees let go of their leaves. They don’t need them for the winter, so they just let go. Then later, they grow new ones.”


 
 
 Leaves with bad feelings on them.
  

Tree Warm-up:
“For the warm-up today, let’s all pretend we are trees. How do trees start out? Yes - very small - as seeds! Let’s see you be a seed. Good! And then what happens? Yes! You start to grow! Let’s see you growing, sending up a little sprout, and growing some leaves. And as you grow and grow, let’s see how tall you become. And the shapes of your branches? Beautiful! What color are you? Do you have lots of leaves? Or just a few? Let your fingers be the leaves. Can you feel them blowing in the wind? And see if they feel like falling down to the ground yet. When they are ready, let them fall down, dancing down, all the way down to the ground. (Fall down gently to lay on the ground.) And as you rest on the ground, take a nice deep breath and feel how good it feels to let everything go.”

  


“Let the Bad Feelings Fall Away” tree.
 
  

Activity:
“Today, we are going to notice how just like trees let go of their leaves when they need to, we can let go of things too. Sometimes there are bad feelings that we have that we need to let go of (or else they can get to us!) This project is called ‘Let the Bad Feelings Fall Away.’ It’s a chance for each of us to notice any bad feelings we want to let go of.”

Have the children color/draw huge oak leaves. On them, they write a bad feeling they sometimes have. Let them know that it can be any bad feeling. Then they share what bad feelings they sometimes have and what causes them.

Closing:
After the children are done creating their leaves, we welcome them to each bring their leaves up and display them on the bottom of the board as if they are leaves that have fallen to the ground.

Then we discuss how we have to let bad feeling fall away or they can get to us. The technique we talk about is the one we also used for anger:

Letting Go Exercise:
Stop
Take a deep breath in
Clench fists and count to five
Let it out
And walk away!
(A flip of the head helps!)
Row.txt_description: Two workshops that provide a wonderful way to take the themes of the Fall season and use them to explore emotions; what we are proud of as well as letting go of bad feelings.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Inner Gifts creation.


Objective:
To give the children a chance to explore the gifts they have on the inside, and  notice that they are their best gifts–better than anything money can buy.

Note:  This workshop is written around a Christmas theme.  Feel free to adapt to other holidays or see the non-holiday variation, pg. 3-4 as needed.

Materials:
Colored construction paper
Marker, scissors, glue
Glitter, feathers, decorations

Timeframe:
1 hour

Age Range:
3 — teen (for ideas on how to adapt for older kids, see pg. 3)

Setup:
Make a sample in advance, so the kids can see how the window works and get ideas for doing their own. Set the supplies in the center of the table so they’re out of reach during the warm-up.  For really young ones, the whole project can be done without cutting out the figure shape.  You can just trace the shape, color it, and create your window.   Just  create a cardboard pattern they can trace. 






Tracing and cutting out the Inner Gifts figure.





Introduction:
Today we are going to explore inner gifts—the ones we have in our hearts.  These are the gifts we each have inside of us.  They do not cost any money, and they are our best gifts.

Warm-up (younger kids):
“Ready for warm-up time? Everyone gather around me.  Come close.  For this warm-up, I’m going to be a Christmas tree.  Here I am!  What should I do with my arms?  Put them out like branches?  Should I stand tall?  Okay, there I am, a big, tall Christmas tree.  And what does a tree have under it?  Yes, presents!  Can you be my presents?  Gather close!  (Encourage them to curl up into little boxes under the tree.)  What color are you?  Do you have a ribbon on you?  Good!  

“Now I want you to know that each one of you has a very, very, special present inside of you.  I can see it on the inside of each one of you!  I can see your heart —and that’s where the most special gifts of all live.  Your heart is where I can see your kindness, I can see your cooperation.  If I look really, really close, I see your laughter and smiles!  All these things live inside your special heart.   

“As you sit there, take a nice deep breath and see if you can put your hand on your heart.  You can close your eyes if you want to, and take another nice deep breath.  

“With your hand resting on your heart, think about what is in your heart.  Do you see the kindness?  Do you see caring?  Do you see smiles?  

“Now picture something that makes you feel happy inside your heart, or something you are thankful for.  It could be the face of someone you love or whatever you love to think of.   Notice what makes your heart feel happy. (Take time and encourage the kids until you think each of them has something in mind.)

“Now, imagine it filling up your heart.  Feel that happiness filling your heart so full it’s overflowing.  

“And now picture it filling your whole body – all your joy and happiness and good feeling…

“And now picture it filling up the whole room!  All your happiness, filling the room so full it’s going to burst!  It’s shining out of your heart like a sunshine, filling the whole room!

“And now picture it shining out from the room to the whole world.  Shining all the way from inside your heart out to the whole world around you.  

“Take a moment with your eyes still closed to notice how wonderful it feels, and when you’re ready, open your eyes, and stretch like a ray of sunshine, filling the room!”






Sample words of inner gifts (for older kids)


Adapting for Older Kids:
If you are working with older kids, you will probably want a different warm-up and you will want to encourage them to create their own shape person (not use the gingerbread-shaped pattern).  One idea for an alternate warm-up is to place words in a hat—words representing the inner gifts you think your group of kids/teens has in their hearts.  Have them each draw a word and then think about where that gift is inside of them and how they show it in their lives.  If you think it would work with your group, you could lead a visualization similar to the one for younger kids, but having them picture their word filling up their heart and shining out to the rest of the world.









Creation:
Show the example, and walk them through the steps as needed:

Step One:
Making the main person shape. (Could be traced, could be cut out and colored.)





Two pieces of paper to make
the inner window.





The first piece is glued down
and decorated.





The second piece creates the window.



Step Two:  
Making the Window into Your Inner Gifts

Step Three:
Decorating everything!

Closing:
Give each child an opportunity to share about his/her creation and Inner Gifts.

Optional:  As we end our workshop today, let’s notice what’s nice about having holidays here with each other in the shelter.   Can anyone think of something that’s nice about celebrating together?
Row.txt_description: Gives the children a chance to explore the gifts they have on the inside, and notice that they are their best gifts--better than anything money can buy.

Row.txt_code:
I Am Strong Because... puzzle drawings from a
participant in Ramona’s workshops.
 
  



Objective:
To build a sense of pride in oneself and build a sense of cohesion within the group about the obstacles and hard times that they have been through as a group. The finished artwork serves as a pride badge as well as a means to not give up when times are difficult. This project is especially good for teenagers.

Materials:
Construction paper, markers, crayons, colored pencils, and a ruler for each participant.


 
 
 I Am Strong Because... puzzle drawings
from workshop participants
  

Be aware that there is a lot of room for creativity so please have glue, scissors, pencils, and pens on hand they just might want to use them.

Also have writing paper available because they may want to write it out before doing the artwork.

You will also need an easel or a large poster board attached to the wall and a marker available for participants to write on it in a visible accessible part of the room.

Timeframe:
This workshop could take up to 2 hours, but the time can be adjusted by the leader depending on the amount of time spent on discussion.


 
 
 I Am Strong Because... puzzle drawings

from workshop participants
  

Age Range:
Designed for teen girls, but please adapt to others as needed.

Setup:
Make a sample before the group, so you have something to share and get them started. Also, prepare the large poster board entitled We are strong because... so it will be accessible during the workshop.

Introduction:
Begin the introduction by having the participants read the quotes and the poem “Still I Rise” (see attached). If you have male clients, possibly teenage boys, they can discuss the poem “Ability” instead because they will be able to relate to it better. As the clients read the quotes and poem ask them what they feel the overall message is that the poem and the quotes give. (If you are short on time you can have the clients read only the poem or fewer quotes.) From the discussion that has been generated the leader can make a transition statement by saying something like, “We all have been through good times and bad times and this makes us who we are today, strong. If we were not strong we would not be here today.” I also present a poem that I personally wrote. (See side bar.)

 
 

 
I Am Strong Because... puzzle drawings
 
   


 
 A Picture of Me

Vivid, lively, and imaginative,
Smiling, laughing,
Caring, sharing, and loving,
Always putting others before herself,
Always helping others
in any way she could,
Friends and family are
her pride and joy: #1 priority,
As a matter of fact, through her actions,
she shows that they come before her.

She is her own Women,
She's a nonconformist,
Her clothes: a vivid formulation
of the passionate color of purple,
A style that is unique to her and only her,
She's not about styling and profiling,
She dresses for her,
It must comfort her,
No validation is needed but hers,
The decision to change
is hers and only hers,
She does what she wants
when she and only she wants to.

To understand her,
Nobody does,
She's like a puzzle of many pieces,
Only she has them all,
Everybody else just has a few pieces,
So they can’t see.

What they can’t see,
is that the pieces
are all in the pictures of her
It’s not in the pose,
It’s not in the hair,
It’s not in the clothes,
It’s not in her eyes,
It’s not that she is conceited,
Every set of eyes has a different story,
A story of growth,
That only she knows and only she can see.

By Ramona Young
  
Project:
Next, you tell the clients that today we are going to create our individual puzzle pieces which represent all of the reasons we are strong. Tell the clients that they can design it anyway that they want to and the title is I am strong because... You can show them your example and present it as a way to help them get started. The rulers are there in case they want to draw straight edges.

As clients begin to work, point out the poster board that you have entitled We are strong because... and tell them to feel free at any time to come up and write something on that piece of paper or ask you to write it for them.

As clients complete their puzzle give them the opportunity to share their puzzle with the group. You can point out or ask the clients to point out similar points made and use those to add to the We are strong because... page.

If possible, post the clients’ work and post the We are strong because... page as well. You can format the We are strong because... page into a poem. (See attached for the example my group did.) Make sure when you format it that it is written in a way that applies to all.

  


  



Obstacles and Hard Times
We need the rock of the past under our feeet in order to spring forward into the future. -Madeline L’Engle

Obstacles are those frightful things you see when you take your eyes off your goal. -Hannah Moore

I’ve failed over and over again in my life. And that is why I succeed. -Michael Jordan

You need chaos in your life to give birth to a dancing star. -Friedrich Nietzsche

Obstacles don’t have to stop you. If you run into a wall, don’t turn around and give up. Figure out how to climb it, go through it, or work around it. -Michael Jordan

Being defeated is often a temporary condition. Giving up is what makes it permanent. -Marilyn vos Savant

It gets dark sometimes, but morning comes... Keep hope alive. -Jesse Jackson


Still I Rise - Maya Angelou

You may write me down in history
With your bitter, twisted lies,
You may trod me in the very dirt
But still, like dust, I’ll rise.

Does my sassiness upset you?
Why are you beset with gloom?
‘Cause I walk like I’ve got oil wells
Pumping in my living room.

Just like moons and like suns,
With the certainty of tides,
Just like hopes springing high.
Still I’ll rise.

Did you want to see me broken?
Bowed head and lowered eyes?
Shoulders falling down like teardrops,
Weakened by my soulful cries.

Does my haughtiness offend you?
Don’t you take it awful hard
‘Cause I laugh like I’ve got gold mines
Diggin’ in my own back yard.

You may shoot me with your words,
You may cut me with your eyes,
You may kill me with your hatefulness,
But still, like air, I’ll rise.

Does my sexiness upset you?
Does it come as a surprise
That I dance like I’ve got diamonds
At the meeting of my thighs?

Out of the huts of history’s shame
I rise
Up from a past that’s rooted in pain
I rise
I’m a black ocean, leaping and wide,
Welling and swelling I bear in the tide.
Leaving behind nights of terror and fear
I rise
Into a daybreak that’s wondrously clear
I rise
Bringing the gifts that my ancestors gave.
I am the dream and the hope of the slave.
I rise I rise I rise



Ability - Selina E. Matis

Ability is to look at a blank page,
And create a poem.
Ability is to stare into the eyes of fear,
And come out stronger because of it.
Ability is to walk into a room of strangers,
And come out with friends.
Ability is to admit you are wrong,
When you are wrong.
Ability is to get back up,
When you fall down.
Ability is to believe,
When everything seems lost.

Ability - a simple word, with complex meaning.
For many, ability is never found, but for all ability is within.
Ability stares everyone in the face at one time or another.
Whether your ability is how well you shoot hoops,
How well you flip at dancing,
How smart you are at school.
You have ability.
For some, ability is lost by never trying.
Whether never trying to shoot one more time,
Never trying to bend a little more,
Or never trying to score higher in school.

Ability is within.
Ability is yours.


We are Strong Because - The Poetry Club

We are patient (sometimes).
We all have experienced good times and bad times.
We are strong because we come from strong cultures.
We help each other even when we don’t all get along.
We’ve had similar experiences.
We’ve had similar pasts.
We come together to help each other through hard times.
If we weren’t, we wouldn’t be here today.
We are all loved and we need each other.
Row.txt_description: Offers the chance to build a sense of pride in oneself as well as a sense of cohesion within the group about the obstacles and hard times that they have been through. The finished artwork serves as a pride badge and reminder to not give up.
Row.txt_tips:
The collage technique is popular because it prevents frustration over not being able to draw.

The theme behind this workshop also works well with journaling and poetry projects.

Row.str_title: Children Throughout The World Are Victims Too
Row.txt_code:
Here ’s how the final mural looks at Women-Shelter
of Long Beach.
 
  
Objective:
To educate, discuss and have the children share their feelings about being in a family with domestic violence. While doing the workshop, children learn that some children of all ages all over the world have had or have domestic violence issues within their families.


 
 
 
These are some of the paper
dolls made at WomenShelter
of Long Beach.
  

Materials:
Wall space of 6 by 5 feet
Construction paper (assorted colors)
Large white paper (for 2-foot diameter drawing of the globe)
Blue, black, green, yellow, & brown yarn for the globe & for the hair.
Cray-Pas and markers
Glue, scissors, masking tape and a white paper plate
Patterns of boy and girl (see attached templates)
Patterns of clothes for the boys/girls
Patterns of hearts (see attached)
Optional: Real globe for discussion

Timeframe:
We did this project during a whole week, taking about an hour each day to work on it.  Once it was up, we decided to leave it up (it’s been 6 months now) and make it an on-going project adding new dolls when new children come to the shelter.  They really like it, and when they leave the shelter, we give them their doll to take with them.  This makes space for new dolls to be welcomed as new families come to the shelter.

Age Range:
We’ve done this project with mixed groups, ages 3-17.

Setup:
It might be a good idea to have made all the patterns (world, letters, hearts, clouds, sun, children, and paper clothes) before you start this workshop. It is a little long for the children ages 3 to 5.  Decide based on your group how much how is realistic for them to help cut out.  You might want to use the clouds as something the younger children can help cut out so they will feel included while older children cut out the more detailed parts.  If you have a mixture of age-levels, the school-age children like to help the younger children.  

Introduction:
Throughout the days of this workshop, as you create the paper “mural,” you’ll be talking with the children about the world and about domestic violence.  Ask them if they know what domestic violence is.  Ask the older children to give some examples of what they think it is.  Let the children know what domestic violence and what abuse are.  Ask them to share about their families if they want to.  Ask the children if they can come up with different countries around the world.  Let them know that in every country children are victims. Ask the children how they think other children may be feeling in homes with domestic violence.  Go with the flow of the children.

These are the stages we did day by day.  You could try it this way, or change it to fit the schedule at your shelter.

Monday:  World
Talk about the world.  (It helps if you have a three-dimensional globe to show, and of course, how you talk about it will depend on how old the children are.)  The way we shared it was: “Throughout the world there are many victims.  Does everybody know what the world is?  Do you know what countries are?  Can anyone name a country?  (Point out the countries they name on the globe.)  And where do you think there are children in the world?  Are there children here (point somewhere on the globe)?  Yes, there are.  There are children everywhere around the globe.”

  


This is how the whole thing looks when it’s
finished.  It’s about 6 feet wide and takes
the whole wall, with the sun and clouds at
the top.  You can see how big it is compared
to the chairs.
 
  



As you begin the artwork, be sure you have a nice big area to work in. Take the large white paper and make an even circle 2 to 2 1/2 feet in diameter for the world.  Invite the older kids to help you cut out the world, draw shapes on the circle to look like land masses of the earth and water.  Cut and glue different colored yarn to the outlines of different landmasses.  Ask the children to color inside each land mass using the Cray-Pas that match the yarn around the land. Use blue cray-pas to color in the water inside the blue yarn.

After the world is all done, the children can help the leader hang it on the wall with masking tape.   Be sure the world is hanging up high enough so the younger children cannot reach the pins if you decide to use push pins.

Tuesday:  Letters
The next day, we make the letters to spell “Children Throughout the World Are Victims Too.”  This is a good day to talk more about what it means to be a victim.  We say: “We often think about how your moms are victims of violence, but you are also victims.  There are many kinds of victims.  Can anyone tell me what a victim is?”  The children are really smart as they explore and express the many ways kids can be victims.  Talking about how children are victims around the world can help them feel connected rather than isolated.
As we cut out the words, we made them all black except for the word “children” which we made in many colors.  Making the letters for “children” we asked “What color do you want the ‘c’ to be?  And how about the ‘h’?  We will use many colors because there are many of you!”  The letters are traced from alphabet stencils, which are 2 1/2 inches tall onto construction paper.  Leaders and older children can cut out the letters.

Have the children help the leaders to stick the letters up on the wall. They need to be about 14 inches from the world so the paper dolls go in between the world and letters.  Remember to leave spaces for the hearts—or make them the same day as the letters! (See photo.)

Wednesday:  Hearts, clouds, and sun
The next day, we work on the hearts, clouds and sun. Use red construction paper to make hearts about 4 by 4 inches and cut out. Do the same with the clouds 6 by 12 blue or white paper. The sun is a cut out from a paper plate and colored yellow. Keep your patterns once you made them so you can use them again. Have the children help the leaders to stick hearts, clouds, and sun up on the wall.   If the children are ready, you might get them started on making the children this day (see below), or you can start that on Thursday.

Thursday:  Children
Now it is time to make the doll patterns for the children of the world.  Leaders trace around each pattern on different colored construction paper according to how many are in the group. Younger children need help to cut out patterns, in some cases the leader can cut them out for them. Older children can cut out their own pattern. Leaders and older children can make patterns for the different clothes for the paper children. Different colors, and different pieces of clothes such as t-shirts, pants, dresses, blouses and skirts, and anything else the children might like. (This part is sort of like playing with paper dolls for the leaders who use to do that way back when.) Make a pattern of each piece of clothing then have the older children trace on to construction paper and cut out. Younger children can pick out what pieces they want for their paper doll and leaders will trace and cut out. The children then will glue each piece of clothing to the proper place on their doll.  

Friday:  Putting it together
The last day can be for finishing up the dolls and getting them ready to put on the wall.  “Now that the paper dolls all have clothes on, it is time to put them up on the wall!”  The dolls go around the world under the letters and hearts (see photo, page 3).  Attach masking tape on the back of the paper dolls (three inches rolled) and stick it to the wall.  Be sure to put the children’s names on the backs of their dolls before you put them up on the wall.

Have fun!
Row.txt_description: Offers a chance to educate, discuss and have children share their feelings about being in a family with domestic violence. While doing the workshop, children learn that children all over the world have experienced domestic violence issues.
Row.txt_notes: ER TO DO: Photograph and enter pages with "THE" and drawing of heart into Quark.
