Row.txt_code:
Audrey is an AWBW Board member and author of The Money ToolBox for Women. The recent Leader’s Workshop she led gave participants a sense of inspiration about their finances.  Th ey left feeling they had the tools to make their dreams come true—some for the first time.  It was clear how these tools make a big difference!

  


Cookie Jar, Clarity Keeper, and Angel Envelopes from
one participant at the Leader’s Workshop.
 
  



This is a four-session workshop that can be used as individual workshops or together.  Each session shares a different “tool” — a creative process leading us to awareness about our wealth through observing, respecting, honoring and tracking.  They say “the rich get richer” and that’s no accident.  There is a focus and attention involved.  These projects are about finding creative, simple ways to build that focus and attention. 

Note: Each Tool takes about 45 minutes.  With Opening and Closing Circles added each session could stand alone as an entire workshop.

Money ToolBox Tool #1:  Clarity Keepers

Objective:
To create a tracking system to help us observe where we spend our money each and every day—a way of becoming conscious of that which we might overlook that cause the ‘holes’ in our ‘money buckets.’


 
 
 Participant shares her
Clarity Keeper.
  

Materials:
2”X3” spiral notebooks
Puffy paints, stickers
Ball point pens
Presentation pad
Music

Introduction:
“How many people here count their money?  How many count it when they get change?  How many count it when it comes out of the ATM?  Counting your money is a powerful thing to do.  Knowledge is freedom.  The Clarity Keepers we will be making today are a tool to give us knowledge and set us free.  This tool helps us track our daily expenses by giving us a place to list the items and the amounts we spend each day.  In a microscopic way, this will begin to help you become conscious of where you spend your money on a daily basis.  It will create money clarity.  This can be uncomfortable, but being uncomfortable is normal with growth.” 


 
 
 Participant shares her
Clarity Keeper.
  

Process:
Pass out the notebooks and supplies.  Before everyone starts decorating theirs, guide them to prepare the inside pages.  On a presentation pad, draw a chart of what goes on each page: 
At the top of each page:
Date:
Money Start:         $_____
Spending:         $_____
At the bottom of each page:
Money Spent:         $_____
Money Ending:    $_____

Walk the group through the chart and how the ‘Money Ending’ amount should be the difference between what you had in the morning for “Money Start” and what you have spent during the day.  Walk them through how they will use their Clarity Keeper: “Each morning, count the money in your purse.  Know how much you are starting out with today and every day from now on.  At the end of the spending day, recount the money.  This way you know how much you have for tomorrow.  This is not about being a miser and counting your money to hoard it.  This is about letting the energy flow of money find itself.  (If you have a secret money place, that’s fine.  However, keep it consistent so you can keep track of it, and count it with the rest of your money.)”

  


Participant shares her
Clarity Keeper.
 
  

Once they are ready, they can go ahead and decorate the cover.

I recommend that you use your Clarity Keeper every day for 60-90 days to bring clarity.  Then in the future, whenever you feel out of control with your spending, you can do another “dose” of your Clarity Keeper.







Money ToolBox Tool #2: Cookie Jars

Objective:
To give intention and rigor to the practice of nurturing ourselves.  To create a special way of saving for yourself, so that saving money can become a wonderful, joyous and sacred process, connected to treating ourselves well and appreciating the gifts in our lives.    

Materials:
Jars (6" high) (You can get these  from the 99 cents store.)
Puffy paints, sequins, glitter



 
 
 Cookie Jar decorated with words:
“my style” and “family.”
  

Introduction:
“This workshop is about paying yourself first.  It is about saving today for what you want tomorrow.  It is also about the magic of money magnets:  Money attracts money.  The concept of paying ourselves is normally foreign to us.  Women especially will tell you that they have to pay all the bills first and they make do with what is left over.  We share with others—but do we share with ourselves?  If we were with our best friend and had three cookies, we’d at least offer one of them to our friend.  Well, in this workshop we will each decide to offer some percentage of our paycheck to ourselves, as our best friend.  It doesn’t matter what percentage you begin with.  Start today.” (You could read the Cookie Jar story — see attached.)

Process:
Start by going around the table and sharing what you’d be saving for with your Cookie Jar.  The goal you’d be saving for could be big or small.  Here are some examples:  buying stocks one share at a time, a seminar, a vacation, a down payment for _______________, an anniversary present, flowers for garden, a spa day, a manicure, a dress, a sweater, a house in the country...”
(Note:  If people have more than one thought, encourage them to choose the one that has the most energy in it for them.  If they really need to, they could create two different jars, like one for something fun, and one for something very different, like real estate investments.)

  


Participant shares her Boat Jar.
 
  

Distribute the jars, paints, etc. and encourage them to begin.  “As you decorate you Cookie Jar, give it a name that represents your intention.  (For example, if you’re saving for a downpayment on a boat, it could be your Boat Jar.)  Your jar needs to know why you’re saving it.”   

“As you complete your jar, think about what percent you will put into it.  For example, you will put 10%—or whatever feels comfortable for you to do now—into your cookie jar whenever, wherever money flows to you (paycheck, unexpected gifts, tax returns… a percentage of any money that comes your way.)”

“As you use your jar, count the money in it and be grateful to have it.  Let the money know it’s honored and respected.  It is not a change jar where you throw coins in unconsciously, and it’s not a jar you can borrow from in a pinch.  It’s a jar where you consciously build toward your dreams.  It’s a way of honoring yourself, celebrating yourself, and loving the life you’re living.  Watch your riches grow.”  (I keep a slip of paper in the cookie jar with the total amount I am money-magneting towards.  I add in each amount that is put in the jar so that I know when I’ve reach the intended amount.)
 
Money ToolBox Tool #3: Angel Envelopes

Objective:
To help set up, divide and organize your expenses into segments, so that you have money put aside for emergencies, savings, and tithing.  To set up an easy way to become rigorous with your money and practice recognizing what you need and when you’ll need it so you can stay on the mark for monthly money requirements. 

Materials:
Envelopes (3 each)
Watercolors, crayons, markers
Optional: Have each participant decorate a box where she can store her Angel Envelopes—her Treasure Box.

Introduction:
“Today, we are going to create Angel Envelopes.  These are envelopes to divide and organize our expenses into segments and practice staying on the mark for monthly money requirements.  It’s an easy way to practice recognizing what you need and when you’ll need it.”







 





Decorated Angel Envelopes.


 

Process:
“What we’re going to do is decorate 3 envelopes each.  These envelopes each represent a different category of money.

One is for Savings (Think about building for your future.)
One is for Emergencies (Think about the expenses that creep up on you as
emergencies—oil changes, car insurance, medical bills, etc.)
One is for Tithing (Tithing is when you give back to the world around you.  It could be giving to a church, or an organization you love.)

Decorate each envelope, energizing it with Loving Energy.  The envelopes hold the monthly money focus.  They are your training wheels in the new money practice.

For each envelope, choose a percentage you want to set aside each time you get paid or you receive money, any money.  Example:
     Savings  10%
     Tithing   10%
     Emergencies  5%

When you decide your percentages, remember you are putting away money in your Cookie Jar as well for what you are aspiring to attain. 

Having money in your Angel Envelopes will take the burden off when emergencies arise (so the burden won’t get put on your credit card and you won’t be paying interest on your emergencies). 

Use this practice until you get the rhythm of the money in your life. 

Be patient with yourself… These are new behaviors.  It takes time and practice to get them into your cellular level and into your conditioning.  

Money ToolBox Tool #4: Cutting Edge

Objective:
To get you out of credit card debt and build really great habits and choices about how you spend.  To assist you in balancing your credit card statement each month.

Materials:
Markers and 2 X 3 post-its

Introduction:
“Today we are going to focus on credit card spending.  In our society, it’s useful to have a credit card as long as we treat it with respect.  Most people spend on their credit card unconsciously.  This Cutting Edge Post-its project will give a way to bring you into conscious spending and better choice-making.  It is not about lack or deprivation.  It is about always having choices.”

Process:
“You may wonder, ‘how can a little post-it do all that?’  The Cutting Edge post-its will give you a ‘window’ into your credit card.  This is how they work:  

1.  At the top of the post it, write your current credit card balance.  This is the balance you can get off your last credit card statement.

2.  Each time you make a purchase with this card, list the item purchased and the amount.  For example:
Gas             $20.00
Sweater       $50.00

3.  When your statement arrives, there will be no surprises.  You can use the post it as the credit card manager when you match the purchases you have on your post-it to the statement as you check it off and balance it out.

4.  Set a budget for your credit card use for the month.  That way when or if you reach the magic I-won’t-go-past-this $$$ amount, you will know it because you are keeping yourself on the cutting edge of your spending knowledge.

Today we will get our post-its ready to attach to your card(s).  You can make extras so you’ll have some to put a new one on your card each month when you receive your credit card statement.” 

Before having the group go ahead and decorate the post-its, you could have a check-in circle to give each person an opportunity to share her experiences with credit cards.  Then the decorating begins.  Add green edges – flowers – trees dogs cats you can either draw on the post-it or use stickers.)  After the post-its are decorated – each participant can affix them to the back of their credit card(s)…one for each card.  And share any plans for tracking her credit card spending.
 
All Money ToolBox information is copyrighted and cannot be reproduced without permission from Money ToolBox for Women.  Contact at 310 394-7687 or
www.moneytoolboxforwomen.com for further information, or to become part of their e-mail list.


Great Aunt Harriet’s Cookie Jar
“Tool Story” from The Money ToolBox for Women

Martha's Great Aunt Harriet used to sit each morning at her kitchen table counting the household money into a large jar. So much for her husband's lunches, so much for groceries, and a few pennies into a smaller jar. Martha watched this ritual each day. She and her mother lived with her great aunt and uncle for almost fourteen years. When she was younger, she would sit at the table while her aunt counted the money. She often wondered what the smaller jar was for, but did not have the proper question to ask her great aunt. They lived on a tiny farm, and although they were financially poor, they never seemed to want for anything. The family was rich in traditions and love. They laughed and loved the life they were living.

When Martha was seven, she asked her great aunt Harriet why she counted the money every morning. She asked her why she had three stacks of money and only two jars.
Auntie H. took both the jars off the cabinet shelf. She explained that the large jar was for the household money and the other, a small cookie jar had a large "H" and other symbols and signs painted boldly on it that were meaningful for her.

"When your great uncle Jacob and I got married, we decided, together, there would be three jars." Martha was surprised. She'd only seen two jars.  "Where's the third jar, Auntie, and what's it for?" Martha quizzed.  "The third jar I keep with my Spiritual things. It is the money for the Beloved, that we give (tithe) back for the bounty given to us," replied Harriet.

We took the other two jars and went into the master bedroom. There on her nightstand was the jar, also decorated with signs and symbols, this time of prosperity and abundance. Great Aunt Harriet explained, "The Large jar is for the House. The money that goes into that jar keeps us fed, clothed and sheltered. The jar in the bedroom is for our Spirit. It keeps the flame of grace and ease connected with the energy from which we receive to begin with. It keeps us connected to the Divine within and above."

"The other jar, so brightly painted and decorated, is for me," said Great Aunt Harriett. "It is the ten percent I pay myself. I give it a name or an intention and use it for what it is ordained to create. It is for whatever I want to manifest. I decorate it and name it and allow the mystery of the money magnet to do its work."

"Is it always for the same thing?" Martha asked.  "No, sometimes the gift is for me, sometimes a present for you, sometimes I want to buy something for Uncle Jacob and sometimes for your mother. We always pay into the jars and then celebrate the joy we bring into our lives. These cookie jars are a celebration of OUR BEING on the Planet."

Martha smiled, and asked if someday she could have her own jar. "Yes, right now. Come choose a jar and after dinner, you can decorate it. I'll help you with the colors and symbols if you like." Martha was delighted.

Today, Martha is a successful chiropractor and she continues to use this method of attracting abundance into her life. Her observation is that it has worked through the years. It has been a demonstration of how to have dominion over her fate. How to grow the abundance of life and celebrate herself with God's Divine Loving.

"I have grown to give to myself 10% of all money that flows into my hands and I share this abundance with God by tithing (giving-being philanthropic). It is my safety net, it is my loving privilege," Martha smiles. "The giving reminds me of the lessons and times I was privileged to spend with my aunt. She gave me 100% of her gentle, kind spirit; a Beloved Angel here on this earth."
Row.txt_description: Participants create a tracking system to help them observe where they spend their money each and every day--a way of becoming conscious of that which might be overlooked and causes the 'holes' in our 'money buckets'. End product are helpful and empowering reminders of what they have learned and hope to accomplish.

Row.txt_code:
Based on Soul Mate Dolls—Dollmaking as a Healing Art by Noreen Crone-Findlay




Group of Soul Mate Dolls created by Windows
participants in Wausau, Wisconsin.



About this Workshop:
The idea for this project came from the book, Soul Mate Dolls, Dollmaking as a Healing Art by Noreen Crone-Findlay. 
I practiced first with making some of the flat dolls in the book, then took the pattern (see attached) and made a stuffed cloth doll.  Clients in the shelter loved the idea and I brought my own sewing machine in so they could work on the dolls and outfits in the evening.  At the morning workshop, they finished their dolls with such delight.

Besides our weekly morning workshop, we wanted to offer it to our Wednesday evening Women’s Support Group and Thursday morning Women Over Fifty group.  They meet once a month for AWBW.  I started sewing more dolls at home, then contacted our Volunteer Center and two women offered to help.  They made almost thirty dolls for us. We also made available a variety of fabrics, ribbons, yarns, etc. along with an iron, stitch witchery and glue guns.

The group loved the project and the idea of having their own “Soul mate” who will love them unconditionally.  Some made dolls for their children also.  They made pockets or purses to tuck in their love notes.  They became very creative and each doll was unique.  They were very proud of them and showed staff and other shelter residents. 





Basic Soul Mate Dolls created by volunteers,
ready for the Windows workshop.

Objective:
To give each participant an opportunity to create her own Soul Mate doll — a doll that will love her unconditionally, a support to carry with her, talk to, and connect with when things are difficult — a reminder to love herself. 

Doll-making Materials:
Yarn
1/2 yard of muslin, linen, or other closely-woven fabric
Stuffing
Sewing machine or needle and thread
Pins and scissors
Vanishing ink fabric marking pen
Paper clip
Small dowel or bamboo skewer

“Making my Soul Mate Doll was one
of the best workshops. 
When I feel like everything is
coming down on me and I
don’t want to tell anyone else, I
talk to my Soul Mate Doll
and I feel a lot better.  I think
making a Soul Mate Doll was
a blessing.  Thank you for my doll.”

—Soul Mate Doll workshop participant

Decorating Materials:
Yarn and ribbons
Fabrics
Needles and thread
Iron
Stitch Witchery
Glue Guns
Beads, feathers, sequins, etc.

Preparation: 
The original preparation was quite time-consuming because the basic dolls are prepared in advance.  To accomplish this, I got support from volunteers—they helped create about 30 dolls, and the project remains an on-going one that new residents like to take part
in.   




Preparing Soul Mate Dolls.




Introduction:
“Today you will get to create your own Soul Mate doll.  This project was created by someone named Noreen who uses Doll-making as a healing art.  You get to start with one of these blank dolls and make her your own.  You can create hair, clothes, decorations, whatever you think of.  It’s okay to leave the face blank if you want, or create features.  And you can create a purse for her to carry “Soul-Mate Messages”—loving words about you that she wants you to remember.”

Creation:
As participants start their work, you can assist them individually with their sewing if needed.  In preparation for the second round of groups, other staff and I made simple outfits for the women to choose from if they had minimal sewing abilities.  Remind them to be sure to make the purse to carry the special “Soul Mate” messages.

How to Make the Basic Dolls
Instructions from Soul Mate Dolls, Dollmaking as a Healing Art by Noreen Crone-Findlay

1.  Cut out the basic patterns (see attached).

“I made a doll for my daughter. 
She loved her.  She carries her
everywhere.  We moved back
home (from the shelter) and the
first day back to school she took
her Soul Mate doll to school and
now her friends want one.”

—Soul Mate Doll workshop participant

2.  Paper clip the Upper and Lower arm parts together in the position you want the arms.

3.  Fold:  Get your fabric ready to trace onto:  Fold it in half.  (That way, when you cut out each part, you’ll automatically have two pieces, a front and a back to sew together and stuff.)

4.  Trace:  Trace each part onto cloth using the vanishing ink fabric marking pen.  (Leave at least a 1/4 inch border around each part for a seam allowance.)  You’ll need to trace the leg pattern twice, to make the two different legs.  Be sure to flip the pattern over before tracing for the second leg.  That way, the second leg’s foot will be pointing the other direction. Do the same for the arms.




A circle of women working on their Soul Mate Dolls.




5.  Sew:  Guess what!  You can sew before cutting out the parts!  Sew along the outline of the body and leave the bottom edge open for stuffing.  For the legs, leave the top edge open for stuffing.  And for the arms, leave a 2 inch opening for stuffing along one side.

6.  Cut:  After the sewing, you can cut out each part, leaving a 1/4 inch seam around each sewn edge.  Clip the curved edges of the seam allowance.  Then turn each piece right side out.

7.  Knee joint:  Lay the sewn leg on the leg pattern and draw a line across the knee with the vanishing ink marker.




Her hands at work dressing her Soul Mate.




8.  Stuff legs: To stuff the legs, use the bamboo skewer or dowel to push tiny amounts of stuffing into them.  Fill to about 1 inch below the knee line.  Then stitch across the knee line.  Finish by filling the legs with stuffing.

9.  Body:  Stuff the body and then attach the legs as you sew the bottom edge.  To do this, fold a 1/4 inch edge up inside of the body’s lower edge and pin the body together with one pin at the center of the lower edge.  Insert the top edge of the legs inside of the body’s lower edge.  Stitch in place across the front of the first leg.  Stitch the body front to the body back at the center pin.  Then stitch across the second leg and around the across the back of the legs.

10.  Arms:  Stuff arms and sew the opening shut.  Stitch the inside top of the arm to the body at the shoulder.  Optional:  draw finger lines on the hands and stitch through all layers to form fingers and thumbs. 

Closing Circle:
Give each participant an opportunity to share her doll and what it means to her.




“I really enjoyed doing the dolls. 
It made me relax and it keeps my
spirits up.  It showed that I can do
something and it really made me
feel good about myself.”

—Soul Mate Doll workshop participant

Completed Soul Mate Doll.
Row.txt_description: Gives each participant an opportunity to create her own Soul Mate doll--a doll that will love her unconditionally, a support to carry with her, talk to, and connect with when things are difficult--a reminder to love herself.

Row.str_title: Handprint workshops - Domestic Violence Awareness Month activities
Row.txt_code:
Quilt squares created by Children’s Windows leaders—a sample of
what could be made  with the Circle of Values workshop, theme 3.		 
  
About this Workshop:
With Domestic Violence Awareness Month on the way, we’ve been making plans.  We’ll be working with East LA College to create a special day filled with events to involve our community in raising awareness to help stop violence against women.  

Our big day will be October 22nd.  During the day there will be a Resource Fair where Bienvenidos will have a display and hands-on project.  Then in the evening, there will be a candlelight vigil to commemorate Domestic Violence Awareness Month. 


 
 
 “The Violence in Me, The Peace in Me,” CrayPas on paper.
  

In planning it, we brainstormed with AWBW about art projects that would be good for the display, the hands-on activity, and the vigil.  Last year, we did the Clothesline Project, so this year we were looking for another project that would be accessible, visible, and a good way to involve people.  

In this Update, we share three themes we brainstormed, and some thoughts about possible materials to use.  Art is a great way to get the message out there, and involve everyone.  Enjoy!

Objective:
To bring powerful voices, images, and broad participation to Domestic Violence Awareness Month events through art.  To offer a way for children to voice their experiences of violence so that their stories are seen and heard.  To involve community members hands-on in commemorating Domestic Violence Awareness Month.  

Materials:
For all these projects, you could use a range of materials.  In choosing, think about how you want to display it, hang it, etc.  Do you want to use fabric so you end up with banners that can be carried in a vigil?  Or paper that can be carried as signs?  Think about whether or not you want to create something that can last for a long time, or just for the one day. 

  


“The Violence in Me, The Peace in Me,” CrayPas on paper.
 
  

Paper:  
Using paper can be easier and less expensive than fabric.  It’s also an easy way to make sure you have very bright, bold colors.  You could cut bright squares for each person and then glue them to a big piece of butcher paper.  

If you are gluing to a hanging surface and there’s a possibility of wind, you might want to bring a glue gun, just in case it would help.  

Also remember, markers don’t show up very well on many colors of colored paper. To make the art visible, try using CrayPas or tempera paint, or even fabric paint.

Fabric:  
Using fabric can be wonderful for creating a permanent quilt or banners to carry in a vigil.  Consider what color(s) of fabric you want to use.  The colors you provide will make a big difference.  

Also, think about whether you’d like everyone to decorate their own square to add to the quilt, or have everyone working mural-style on one big piece.  CrayPas, tempera paint or fabric paint work well on fabrics.  If there’s no time for sewing, squares can be safety pinned to the larger piece of fabric or a sheet.  They could later be sewn to create a permanent quilt.  

Note: If you are planning to hang a really large piece of fabric remember, you might need to cut slits to let the wind through.  Otherwise, you might have a “sail.”

Possible Themes:


Theme 1.  “The Violence in Me, The
Peace in Me,”  puffy paints on fabric.
 
  

1.  The Violence in Me/The Peace in Me
Concept:  Each person traces both their hands.  Then they color one hand to express the violence they have inside of them, and the other to express the peace they have inside of them.  All of us have a range of emotions inside and it’s important for us to be responsible about how we handle our emotions.  It is up to all of us to help create a safe community.   

(Thanks to Rose Curtis for this project idea.  She’s found it to be an excellent project with her teen groups.)

2.  All Hands Can Help Stop the Violence
Concept:  Each person puts their handprint(s) on their square and creates a message about stopping the violence in our community.  
It could be their personal commitment to help stop the violence, or it could be whatever message they want others to know about violence.  Each and every one of us can make a difference in helping stop the violence and this project shows how it takes all our many hands together – big and small, many colors, many ideas, many ways.


 
 
 Theme 2.  “All Hands Can Help Stop the Violence.”  These quilted squares
were created by children to express how their hands can help stop the
violence.
  

(Thanks to Yanti Bing for this project idea, based on the simple action of the Coalition to End Hunger and Homelessness.)

3.  Circle of Values
Concept: In this workshop, each person thinks of what they value most, what matters to them most in their life and in their community. Is it family?  Is it trust?  Is it honesty?  Is it faith?  Is it helping others?  Is it learning?  Whatever they value most, they decorate a square to express it.  We are each a part of the circle of our community.   It takes all of us, honoring our deepest values to create a safe community—a circle of safety.  Each person’s expression can be attached to a larger paper or cloth.  If possible, arrange large papers or cloths around the gathering to form a circle.  That way, everyone can see the circle of values taking shape as people add their squares.

(Thanks to Carlos Sanchez and Martin Romo for this project idea, based on their "circle of values" necklace project they do with teen guys.)

Let Us Know How It Goes:
Let AWBW know how your event(s) go.  We’d love to share your photos, discoveries, tips and insights with the other leaders for next year!

   


Theme 3.  “Understanding” square.
 Theme 3.  “Dream” square.
Row.txt_description: A chance to bring powerful voices images, and broad participation to Domestic Violence Awareness Month events and the community through art.

Row.txt_code:
Personal Needs Flower< /td> 
Objective:
This workshop provides an opportunity for participants to notice their personal needs by creating a flower where each petal represents one need. They will begin to see the many layers of needs—physical, emotional and spiritual—and to honor all these layers. To notice that our needs are deeply linked to who we are as a unique and special person.




 Materials:
Colored journaling paper
Pens
Colored construction paper 
CrayPas
Sharpies
Glue sticks
Timer
Blank envelopes (optional)

          
Time frame:
Total Time: 1 hour 15 minutes
Introduction           5 min
Opening Circle      10 min
Demonstration        5 min
Journaling             10 min
Creation                30 min
Closing Circle         15 min


 












   
  Set up of supplies
 
Set-up / Prep:
Lay out all the materials in the center of the table so that each person will be able to reach all the colors. Prepare a sample so that your demonstration can go quickly and leave plenty of time for creating.

Introduction:
"This workshop is a window of time for you-a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you do or say is voluntary. I'll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there's no right or wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this window of time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. Please ask for what you need, and know that I'm here in support of you.

"Many of us are willing to give SO MUCH of ourselves to our families, our friends, our coworkers, etc. We're often willing to sacrifice so much for others, that we forget to acknowledge and honor our own needs. Sometimes we don't even take time to breathe. It can be such a blind spot for us and we are often not even aware of it!

"This workshop is called Personal Needs Flower. Today, we're going to take a window of time to notice and honor our needs... what we want more of in our lives, or what might be out of balance and need our attention. Tending to our needs (physical, emotional and spiritual) is a vital part of self-care and one of the most important jobs we have. It is not only important, it is necessary for each of us to respect and honor our needs so we can recharge our batteries and be there in greater ways for ourselves and others."

Opening Circle:
"We are going to start by thinking about what each of us wants or needs in order to feel safe, happy, and healthy. I am going to ask anyone who wants to, to share one word about a need that is coming to mind as we start this workshop. Is there some need that's asking for attention right now? First thoughts are fine!"

After participants have shared: "Thank you for sharing and acknowledging that your needs are valid and important!"

Demonstration:
“Before we create our Personal Needs Flower, we will start with a journaling exercise to help us notice our needs. I’ll demonstrate the materials and creation process now, so that at the end of the journaling process, you can dive right in. As I demonstrate the steps, remember that more than anything else, this is your special time to listen to and trust your own needs. There is no right or wrong to what you create. Just listen to the voice inside of you as you go. Whatever emerges is fine!

"Today, we're going to try something new, and 'tear' the paper to create our flower. This is an opportunity to let go and enjoy the freedom that tearing allows. Allowing ourselves to be curious and playful can help us discover needs we might not even be aware of!

"I am going to be demonstrating a flower, but your creation can be anything you like. It does not even have to look like a flower. For example, you could create a deck of cards, where each card represents a specific need."


  
 
 
 Step One: Tearing the center circle.
 
   
 
 
 Adding a face to represent the peaceful,
nurturing part of you.
 
   
  
 Step Two: Drawing/writing on petals.
 
1.  Creating the Center
The first step is creating the center of your flower. (Hold up a sample or demonstrate by making one). With the colored paper, tear a circle as small or as large as you like. You can create this center to represent you. You might want to draw a face that represents the peaceful, nurturing, supportive part of yourself that is here to help you. Whatever you choose is up to you.

2.  Creating the Petals
The next step is creating the petals, each one representing one of your needs. To make each petal, choose the paper and tear it into whatever shape or size you want. You may want to vary the size of the petals to illustrate the importance of each need. For example, one of your greatest needs might be "peace," so you can choose to tear a large piece to represent that and a smaller need of yours might be "entertainment" so you could use a smaller petal for that.

Then you’ll go ahead and draw a symbol or use words to represent each need. Use your imagination to create colorful representations of all you discover. Place each petal, adding layer upon layer to the flower-like shape.

3.  Completing your Flower
"The final step is deciding how you want to finish your flower. Using a glue stick you can attach your petals together or glue them onto a larger piece of construction paper or collect them into a pile that can travel with you. If you are going to keep your petals loose, you might want to decorate an envelope to keep them in. 

"You can finish your flower whichever way will best support you not only in being reminded of the needs you noticed today, but also in the ongoing process of discovering more of your needs. (You could even make some extra petals without anything on them yet so you can add more needs as you discover them).

“Any questions? Remember it is very special to take this window of time for ourselves—a need most of us never acknowledge. Ready for the relaxation?” 

   
  Journal page, showing flower construction
 
  
   Journal page, showing flower construction 
   
   Journal page, showing flower construction 
   
Journaling/Warm up:
First, pick a color paper that speaks to you or makes you feel strong or hopeful.

We are going to journal about 3 different types of needs we all have: the needs of our body, our mind and our spirit. You can fold that paper into thirds lengthwise (show example). On the top of the first column, write the word Physical, on the second Emotional, and on the third Spiritual.

I'm going to talk a little bit about each of these three needs and give you two minutes after each one to reflect on/write about this need for yourself. There is no right or wrong way to do this journaling exercise. You can write sentences, words, lists, draw symbols, shapes, or anything else you like. Just allow your thoughts to flow onto your paper without judgment. What you write does not have to make sense to anyone but you! It is also fine to just sit quietly and notice what comes up. Remember this is your window of time to connect with yourself and what's meaningful for you. You might want to play soft background music during this journaling portion.

Physical needs are what we usually think about first. What are your physical needs in order to be safe, happy, and healthy? (Ex. We need to be free from harm. We need shelter and a safe place to live. We need good nutrition: healthy food and clean water. We need exercise - keeping our bodies healthy and strong. We need rest, giving us energy to do what we need to do, like succeeding at work or going to school).

In the first column, begin writing words, sentences, symbols or shapes to represent your physical needs. (Give participants two minutes to write).

Another need that may be a little harder to think about is our emotional needs. What are your emotional needs in order to feel safe, happy, and healthy? (Ex. Feeling understood, accepted, and heard. Knowing that we are loved and appreciated also gives us the feeling of having emotional support. Relaxation, fun, and friendship help us to find emotional balance. Having boundaries, realistic expectations, and a positive attitude are other ways of supporting our emotional health).

Now in the second column, begin journaling about your emotional needs. (Give participants two minutes to write).

Finally, we will address our spiritual needs. What does your spirit need to give you peace? (Ex. The ability to forgive, have patience or acceptance of others? Do you need quiet time to reflect, meditate, or pray? Do you need to do good deeds or help others feel uplifted? Do you need "me" time to care for your soul?)

In the third column write words, begin journaling about your spiritual needs. (Give participants two minutes to write).

Thank you for taking the time to reflect on (and honor) your own personal needs. Remember that you are worth it and representing your needs shows that they are, too!

Creation:
As the participants create their flowers, gently remind them that there is no right or wrong way. The only important thing to keep noticing and honoring their own needs. Encourage them to keep asking the question, What are my needs?

Be sure to leave time for sharing at the end. Encourage each person to decide how they want to finish their flower. Do they want to glue it together? Do they want to create any extra petals to carry with them to add more needs as they are discovered?
  
 
 
   Keep your petals in a pile to carry with you
 Or glue your flower together 

Closing:
Give everyone an opportunity to share about their Personal Needs Flower, and any discoveries they made as they took time to notice their needs.

Remind participants: "This process does not end today; you can reflect back on it anytime, however it best serves you. Noticing what we need to feel safe, happy and healthy in our lives is one of the most important jobs we will ever have, and one job that no one else can do for us!"

Encourage participants to continue the journaling exercise at home and to keep identifying more of their physical, emotional and spiritual needs. They are worth it!
Row.txt_description: This workshop provides an opportunity for participants to notice their personal needs by creating a flower where each petal represents one need. They will begin to see the many layers of needs—physical, emotional and spiritual—and to honor all these layers.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Conflicting Needs
Sometimes a person might notice that their different needs seem to be in conflict with each other. (For example, the need to have more quiet alone time and the need to spend more playful, fun time with her children). This is okay. The purpose of this workshop is to reveal the many needs that can be seen as part of our entire makeup. It is okay not to be problem-solving at this time, but rather supporting participants as they reveal and learn to accept themselves at this creative stage, seeing not only the needs that can be fulfilled, but also those that seem far from resolution. By putting all the needs around a single circle, we allow our conscious mind to see how they all can coexist and we can begin to find safer and more creative ways to embrace and move through any conflicts.

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways.  Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
&ld quo;A Moment in Time” sample frame.
 
  
Objective:
To give participants a chance to remember a time when they were happy and to allow them to live in the moment for the time during the art workshop.  The product of the art workshop, a decorated picture frame, can be used for them to capture other moments in time or to frame something from the workshop today.  


 
 
 Frames from IKEA.
  

Materials:
Picture frames (they are available in packages of 3 for $1.50 at IKEA)
Strips of paper pre-cut (for the opening circle time where they write down things that make them happy)
Pens
Various colors and types of paper (tissue paper, other thin paper)
Mirror paper
Other decorations for the frames (decorative leaves, flowers, tin foil, glitter, etc.)
Matte medium
Paint brushes for the matte medium
Magazines for collage


 
 
 Assorted papers, leaves, etc.
  

Timeframe:
Total Time:         2 hours
Introduction:        5 min
Opening Circle:     15 min
Technical Info:       5 min
Relaxation:        5 min
Creation:          60 min
Closing Circle:    30 min

Setup/Prep:
Lay out all the materials in the center of the table so that each woman will be able to reach everything.  Place three strips of paper at each place.  Prepare an example picture frame to share with the group.

Introduction:
During and after being through a traumatic experience, such as domestic violence or sexual assault, there is a sense of loss and fear.  Sometimes the memories of sadness, anger, and other negative emotions far outweigh memories of a sense of calm, happiness, and togetherness that every human being has the right to feel.  Picture frames often hold photographs of times that were happy or maybe they have photos of a time you were pretending to be happy.  Today we are going to create our own safe space of happiness in this moment in time we have together.   

Opening Circle:
“When was a time when you felt content, safe, or happy?  If you feel comfortable, please describe with the group what it felt like or feels like when you are happy.”

Technical Info:
Show an example of a finished picture frame.  Explain that they  can decorate just the frame part or also the part where the picture goes.  Explain that also, we will be writing on the strips of the paper in front of you and these can also be put in the frame to remember this moment in time we are sharing here today.  The large sheets of paper can be ripped, cut, etc. however you like and then use the matte medium glue to glue the paper to the frame and also to glaze over the paper to make a shiny finish.  You can use multiple colors of paper or just one color.  Note:  DO NOT use the matte medium over the mirror paper if you are going to use that on your frame.

  


“A Moment in Time” frame decorated with foil.
 
  

Relaxation:
“If you feel comfortable, please close your eyes.  Try to think about a time when you were truly happy.  A time when you felt safe, comfortable, and cherished.  Picture the people that you were with when this moment happened.  What was going on in your life at that time?  Where you indoors or outdoors?  Was it a sunny day, or was it snowing or raining?  What did it feel like to be happy?  How did you know you were happy?  As you focus on this moment, look around in your mind at the people that were with you or the environment you were in.  Was everyone smiling?  Were they laughing and talking?  We all deserve these moments when we feel like we are truly ourselves… Where we do not have to wear a mask to fit in.  Where we feel safe to express ourselves or just sit back and enjoy what is going on around us.  Now think of something that makes you happy at this point in your life.  Is it school, your children, or the sunshine?  

“When you are ready, open your eyes as we share a moment in time as a group.  You will see three strips of paper in front of you.  On each one please write one thing that makes you happy or a statement about what it feels like to be safe.  When you are done, please place them in the basket.  Just so you know, these will be shared with the group later, but you do not have to write your name on it, if you want to remain anonymous.”  (If you have clients that are illiterate, you may want to alter this and ask them to draw something that makes them happy instead of writing).  

Creation:
Spend 45-60 minutes decorating the frames.  Invite everyone to decorate their frames however they feel.  Remind them that all art that they produce is beautiful.  

After everyone is done, walk around the table so that everyone can share what they created and how they decorated their frames.  

Closing:
When everyone is seated again, ask each participant to take a strip of paper from the basket.  Go around and share the comments that other participants wrote about what it means to be happy.  Then, invite the participants to frame the strips of paper that they received as a remembrance of this moment in time we have all shared together.  You can end the group by asking everyone to express how they are feeling in one word.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants a chance to remember a time when they were happy and to allow them to live in the moment for the time during the art workshop. The end product is a decorated picture frame used to capture other moments or even something from the workshop today.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create a Shrinky Dink version.

Row.txt_code:
Painted Prayer workshop (above).
Jody Uttal (in circle).
  
Jody Uttal, author of Painted Prayers, created a painted journal during her mother’s terminal illness.  It provided a private space for her to process the experience of her mother’s death and allowed her to work through the painful grieving period.  After her mother’s death she edited a collection of the pages, copied and bound them.  She began to share the ‘book’ with the friends who were with her during her mother’s last days and presented it to a class on death and dying.  She began using the painted journal process to help others through their difficult times.  In November, Jody came to the AWBW studio to share this process with the Women’s Windows leaders.  Here is some of what she shared.

Objective:
To offer watercolor painting as a vehicle we can use to connect on a deep level with where we are in the present moment and what we are feeling; to use the painted prayers process as a way to enter the inner landscape and as a way to connect with something outside ourselves.  

A Note About Prayer:
We are not referring to prayer in a religious sense, thus this workshop is not limited to those with any particular religious beliefs or practices.  Painted Prayers are a vehicle that can help us connect with what we know to be true inside of ourselves.  It is a kind of meditation.  It can mean taking a special “window of time” to practice respecting ourselves.

Caution:
The process outlined below is a very open one, guiding participants to notice what they are feeling and to put it onto the page.  Sometimes this can feel scary.  It can feel safer to have more specific guidance and focus.  See the “Variations” if you want to try something more focused.
  


Painted Prayer, “Breathe”
 
  
Materials:
Watercolor sets (1 per participant)
Brushes - large and small round brushes (one large and one small per participant)
Watercolor paper (10-15 sheets per participant)
Paper towels
Cups of water (2 per participant)
Pencils and blank copy paper for writing
Optional: inspirational quotes and poems (see pg 5)

Timeframe:
Total Time: 2 hours
Introduction: 5 min
Opening Circle: 15 min
Technical Info: 5 min
Relaxation: 5 min
Painted Prayers: 60 min
Sharing: 30 min

Introduction:
“Today we will paint in a way that is like a prayer or a meditation.  It’s okay if you don’t usually pray or meditate.  Just use this as your own special “window of time” to connect with what is most deeply true to you.  We will be using watercolors.

 
 
 Participants during a Painted Prayer workshop at AWBW.
  
It doesn’t matter what it looks like.  It’s about trusting the process.  Whatever comes to you is just fine.  There is no right or wrong way.”

Opening Circle:
“Share one thing you are noticing is in your heart today.  Whatever comes to your mind is fine, and it’s also fine if nothing comes to your mind yet.  You can see what comes to you through the process of the workshop.

Technical Info:
“When we do our Painted Prayers paintings, it doesn’t matter what it looks like.  Let’s do a warm-up together and just experiment with the colors.  Try a big brush and lots of color.  Try lots of water and let it be splashy.  (Demonstrate and encourage them to try it).  You can also use a brush to paint words.  Try painting your name.  You can also use a pencil to write words, or even scribble through the paint.  See how that feels.  You have two cups of water one to rinse your brush and one to get fresh clear water.  (Give them a few minutes to experiment).  Remember, there’s no right or wrong, just many possibilities. 

  


Painted Prayer, “Secret”
 
  

“So now let’s transition from our experimenting and get ready for our Painted Prayers.  Clear the area in front of you and rinse your brush.  I’ll be leading a relaxation and then we’ll start painting.  As we paint, I’ll be guiding you with a few words and directions every few minutes that you can use to spark ideas and images.

“We’ll be doing a series of paintings, sort of like peeling the layers of an onion, moving from one painting to the next.  As we go along, remember it doesn’t matter what the paintings look like.  You can respond to the words and thoughts I share, or follow wherever your own painted prayers take you.  Any questions?  Ready for the relaxation?”

Relaxation:
“Take a nice deep breath and get comfortable in your chair.  Close your eyes if you feel comfortable closing them, and take another nice deep breath.  This is your time just for you.  It’s your special ‘window’ of time to relax.  Imagine it’s a crisp, beautiful morning and you’re walking on the beach. Feel the air brushing by, washing over you.  Feel the sand between your toes as you walk.  Notice the temperature of the sand and how wonderful it feels.  There’s nobody else around.  Feel the sun on your skin and take another nice, deep breath in.  If you feel like resting, find yourself a wonderful spot to lay down in the sand.  Notice how it feels to just lay down.  Notice how the sand feels against your legs, your back, your shoulders.  Notice how it holds you head.  Let the sand hold you and notice that you can let everything go.  Take another deep breath in, and as you let it go, notice your whole body relaxed and calm.   As you relax, check in with your heart, and try to find out who you are today.   Do any shapes or colors come to mind?  Take as much time as you want with your eyes closed, and when you’re ready, you can open your eyes and begin to paint however you are feeling right now…  who are you today?   If you have any urge to use words in what you create, go ahead.  You can use words as well as colors.”

 
 
 Painted Prayer "Contemplation".
  

Creation:
As the group begins to paint, give them gentle guidance every 5-10 minutes with the words and thoughts below (or invent your own, or try words from the variations, page 4-5).   Encourage them to move from one painting to another, not worrying about what they look like.  Remind them that it’s okay if they follow their own process and don’t follow what you are saying.

1.  “Paint how you feel right now.  Is there any shape or colors you could paint to express how you’re feeling right now?”  (The relaxation, page 3, leads into this first painting.) (Paint 5-10 minutes)

2. “When you’re ready, finish this painting up.  If everyone could just do a little stretch and take a nice deep breath, we can get ready for the next painting.  You can close your eyes and try to reconnect with where you are.  Now try to think of a person you feel safe with.  Think of how you feel when you’re with them.  Are there any shapes and colors that come to mind?  (Wait a few minutes…)  To finish this painting up, take your medium sized brush and paint any words in watercolor about that person.  You can use another sheet of paper to write the words.”  (Paint 5-10 minutes)

  


"God Is Alive" Painted Prayer
 
  

3.  “Now get ready to finish this painting up…  Take a break and check in with yourself again.  Check in with the area around your heart.  Put your hands on your heart and breathe in.  Let your eyes close and just take some time with your heart.  Notice what’s coming from that part of you and see if you can express it with your paint.  And on another sheet you can paint words that go with it.” 
(Paint 5-10 minutes)

Transition to Closing:
About ten minutes before the closing circle, give the group some sign, so they have a chance to reflect on what they’ve created and write words if they wish: "We will take about ten minutes more before we have our closing circle. You can take this time to keep painting, or you can look at what you’ve painted and notice if there are any words that go with it. Write down whatever comes to your mind."

Closing:
“Share anything you want about what you have created, what it felt like as you painted, and what it means to you.”
Row.txt_description: Offers watercolor painting as a vehicle to connect on a deep level with where we are in the present moment and what we are feeling; participants use the process as a way to enter the inner landscape and as a way to connect with something outside ourselves.
Row.txt_tips:
Inspirational Quotes and Poems

You must love yourself before you love another. By accepting yourself and joyfully being what you are, you fulfill your own abilities, and your simple presence can make others happy.
- Jane Roberts, The Nature of Personal Reality

Success is a journey not a destination - half the fun is getting there.
- Gita Bellin

You will have wonderful surges forward. Then there must be a time of consolidating before the next forward surge. Accept this as part of the process and never become downhearted.
- Eileen Caddy, God Spoke to Me

It is important from time to time to slow down, to go away by yourself,and simply Be.
- Eileen Caddy, The Dawn of Change

Never be afraid to tread the path alone. Know which is your path and follow it wherever it may lead you; do not feel you have to follow in someone else's footsteps.
- Eileen Caddy, Footprints on the Path

Never give up.
This may be your moment for a miracle.
- Greg Anderson

Our deepest fear is not that we are inadequate; our deepest fear is that we are powerful beyond all measure.
- Marianne Williamson

We have to dare to be ourselves, however frightening or strange that may turn out to be.
- May Sarton

Because of our routines we forget that life is an ongoing adventure.
- Maya Angelou

We cannot do everything at once, but we can do something at once.
- Calvin Coolidge

Never tell a young person that something can't be done. God may have waited centuries for someone ignorant enough of the impossible to do that very thing.
- Michael LeBoeuf

The only journey is the journey within.
- Rainer Maria Rilke

Every end is a new beginning.
- Author Unknown

At least once a day, allow yourself the freedom to think and dream for yourself.
- Albert Einstein

The first step in the journey is to lose our way.
- Galway Kinnell

Discoveries are often made by not following instructions, by going off the main road, by trying the untried.
- Frank Tyger

As you walk and eat and travel, be where you are, otherwise you will miss most of your life.
- Buddha

The time is always right to do what is right.
- Martin Luther King, Jr.

If you do not change direction, you may end up where you are heading.
- Lao-Tzu

Until you try, you don't know what you can do.
- Henry James

Follow your bliss and don't be afraid, and doors will open where you didn't know they were going to be.
- Joseph Campbell

Your spark can become a flame and change everything.
- E.D. Nixon

We are the ones we've been waiting for.
- June Gordon

Reach for your dreams and they will reach for you.
- Hana Rose Zadra

Put your ear down next to your soul and listen hard.
- Anne Sexton

Deja ya de vivir en un pasado que se ha ido y en un mañana que todavía no ha llegado. La vida es sólo este lugar, este tiempo, este instante, simplemente ahora.

La actitud de aceptación es una oración continua.

Acepta tu divinidad; el Dios que habita en ti te capacita para levantarte de nuevo.

No rechaces parte alguna de ti mismo. Lo que tú consideras "basura," puede convertirse en terreno abonado para una nueva vida.

Confía en el futuro. Recuerda cuántas veces has visto que el bien surgía de la tragedia y que una nueva vida brotaba de la muerte.

Cuando la oscuridad te rodee y extinga toda esperanza, confía en que Dios volverá a reaviviar tu espíritu.

Aceptarse es la única verdadera fuente de serenidad. Cuenta con tus propios altibajos; es posible vivir con ellos y a pesar de ellos.

Puede que te sea imposible resolver un problema hoy mismo. Cuando sea así, acéptalo y olvídalo.

Cuando hayas hecho las cosas lo mejor posible, tranquilízate. Deja el resto en manos de Aquel cuyo amor y sabiduría envuelve todo cuanto haces.

Acéptate a ti mismo. Tu Hacedor se deleitó en la sencilla idea de tu ser antes de que existieras.

Ignora las críticas injustas. Los demás no pueden herirte si tú mismo no se lo permites.

No intentes dar gusto a todos. La caridad comienza por uno mismo: gústate a ti mismo.

Cuando parece que el mal está venciendo al bien, recuerda que la creación todavía no está terminada. Tú puedes ayudar a moldear la creación en sentido positivo.

- No te quedes dormido pensando que algo es imposible, puede despertarte el ruido de quien ya lo está realizando.

La felicidad no depende de lo que uno no tiene, sino del buen uso que hace de lo que tiene.

-Los sueños y la perseverancia son una poderosa combinación.

La grandeza de un ideal no es alcanzarlo, sino luchar por él. Alcanzarlo es sólo una recompensa.

La felicidad se parece al perfume, no puedes darla sin que te salpique un poco.

Como humanos, todos cometemos errores, y la vida es hermosa porque siempre encontrarás a alguien que te apoye y te quiera, pues ese alguien erestú.

Nada es más valioso que el día de hoy.

La imaginación es el cometa que mayores alturas puede alcanzar.

La alegría es la piedra filosofal, que todo lo convierte en oro.

Nunca desperdicies la oportunidad de expresar tu amor.

Si lloras por haber perdido el sol, las lágrimas te impediran ver las estrellas.

Conviertete en la clase de persona que ilumina una habitación simplemente por entrar en ella.

Tu mente puede sostener un solo pensamiento a la vez; que éste sea positivo y constructivo.

Autoevalúate bajo tu propio criterio, no el de los demás.

No midas el éxito por la opinión ajena, sino por tu esfuerzo.

Soy libre de soñar y dejar volar mi imaginación y único responsable de la frustración de tener una vida vacía sin estrellas que alcanzar.

Vivir es vibrar y sentir; es amar y gozar; es observar y superar; es dar y aceptar; es ser y permanecer; es comprender que nuestro tiempo es lo único que poseemos para realizar plenamente nuestro ser.

Los niños son como espejos: en presencia del amor, es amor lo que reflejan. Cuando el amor está ausente, no tienen nada que reflejar.

El fracaso es un incidente, jamás una persona.

No te desanimes ¡insiste! porque normalmente la última llave que pruebas es la que abre la puerta.

El futuro pertenece a quienes tienen el valor de creer en la belleza de sus sueños.

Si te atrae una lucecita, síguela. Si te conduce al pantano, ya saldrás de él; pero si no la sigues toda tu vida te arrepentirás pensando que pudo haber sido tu estrella.

Sube muy alto, ya que las estrellas están escondidas en tu alma. Sueña profundamente, pues todo sueño procede a la meta.

Row.txt_code:
I Am Strong Because... puzzle drawings from a
participant in Ramona's workshops.

Objective:
To build a sense of pride in oneself and build a sense of cohesion within the group about the obstacles and hard times that they have been through as a group.  The finished artwork serves as a pride badge as well as a means to not give up when times are difficult. This project is especially good for teenagers.
  


 
I Am Strong Because... puzzle drawings
from workshop participants.


Materials:
Construction paper, markers, crayons, coloring pencils, and a ruler for each participant.  
Be aware that there is a lot of room for creativity so please have glue, scissors, pencils, and pens on hand they just might want to use them.
Also have writing paper available because they may want to write it out before doing the artwork.
You will also need an easel or a large poster board attached to the wall and a marker available for participants to write on it in a visible accessible part of the room.

 


I Am Strong Because... puzzle drawings
from workshop participants.

 

Timeframe:
This workshop could take up to 2 hours, but the time can be adjusted by the leader  depending on the amount of time spent on discussion.

Age Range:
Designed for teens, but please adapt to others as needed.

Setup:
Make a sample before the group, so you have something to share and get them started.  Also, prepare the large poster board entitled We are strong because... so it will be accessible during the workshop.

Introduction:
Begin the introduction by having the participants read the quotes and the poem “Still I Rise” (see below).  If you have male clients, possibly teenage boys, they can discuss the poem “Ability” instead because they will be able to relate to it better.  As the clients read the quotes and poem ask them what they feel that the overall message the poem and the quotes give. (If you are short on time you can have the clients read only the poem or fewer quotes.)  From the discussion that has been generated the leader can make a transition statement by saying something like, “We all have been through good times and bad times and this makes us who we are today, strong.  If we were not strong we would not be here today.”  I also present a poem that I personally wrote.  (See below.)




I Am Strong Because... puzzle drawings.
  

Project:
Next, you tell the clients that today we are going to create our individual puzzle pieces which represent all of the reasons we are strong.  Tell the clients that they can design it anyway that they want to and the title is I am strong because...  You can show them your example and present it as a way to help them get started.  The rulers are there in case they want to draw straight edges.   
As clients begin to work, point out the poster board that you have entitled We are strong because... and tell them to feel free at any time to come up and write something on that piece of paper or ask you to write it for them.  
As clients complete their puzzle give them the opportunity to share their puzzle with the group. You can point out or ask the clients to point out similar points made and use those to add to the We are strong because... page.

If possible, post the clients’ work and post the We are strong because... page as well.  You can format the We are strong because... page into a poem. (See the below example my group did.)  Make sure when you format it that it is written in a way that it applies to all.





A Picture of Me

Vivid, lively, and imaginative,

Smiling, laughing,

Caring, sharing, and loving,

Always putting others before herself,

Always helping others

   in any way she could,

Friends and family are

   her pride and joy: #1 priority,

As a matter of fact, through her actions,   

   she shows that they come before her.



She is her own Women,

She's a nonconformist,

Her clothes: a vivid formulation

   of the passionate color of purple,

A style that is unique to her and only her,

She's not about styling and profiling,

She dresses for her,

It must comfort her,

No validation is needed but hers,

The decision to change

   is hers and only hers,

She does what she wants

   when she and only she wants to.



To understand her,

Nobody does,

She's like a puzzle of many pieces,

Only she has them all,

Everybody else just has a few pieces,

So they can’t see.



What they can’t see,

   is that the pieces

   are all in the pictures of her

It’s not in the pose,

It’s not in the hair,

It’s not in the clothes,

It’s not in her eyes,

It’s not that she is conceited,

Every set of eyes has a different story,

A story of growth,

That only she knows and only she can see.



By Ramona Young		 Still I Rise - Maya Angelou

You may write me down in history
With your bitter, twisted lies,
You may trod me in the very dirt
But still, like dust, I’ll rise.

Does my sassiness upset you?
Why are you beset with gloom?
‘Cause I walk like I’ve got oil wells
Pumping in my living room.

Just like moons and like suns,
With the certainty of tides,
Just like hopes springing high.
Still I’ll rise.

Did you want to see me broken?
Bowed head and lowered eyes?
Shoulders falling down like teardrops,
Weakened by my soulful cries.

Does my haughtiness offend you?
Don’t you take it awful hard
‘Cause I laugh like I’ve got gold mines
Diggin’ in my own back yard.

You may shoot me with your words,
You may cut me with your eyes,
You may kill me with your hatefulness,
But still, like air, I’ll rise.

Does my sexiness upset you?
Does it come as a surprise
That I dance like I’ve got diamonds
At the meeting of my thighs?

Out of the huts of history’s shame
I rise
Up from a past that’s rooted in pain
I rise
I’m a black ocean, leaping and wide,
Welling and swelling I bear in the tide.
Leaving behind nights of terror and fear
I rise
Into a daybreak that’s wondrously clear
I rise
Bringing the gifts that my ancestors gave.
I am the dream and the hope of the slave.
I rise  I rise  I rise


Obstacles and Hard Times

We need the rock of the past under our feeet in order to spring forward into the future. - Madeline L’Engle

Obstacles are those frightful things you see when you take your eyes off your goal. - Hannah Moore

I’ve failed over and over again in my life.  And that is why I succeed. - Michael Jordan

You need chaos in your life to give birth to a dancing star. - Friedrich Nietzsche

Obstacles don’t have to stop you.  If you run into a wall, don’t turn around and give up.  Figure out how to climb it, go through it, or work around it. - Michael Jordan

Being defeated is often a temporary condition.  Giving up is what makes it permanent. - Marilyn vos Savant

It gets dark sometimes, but morning comes... Keep hope alive. - Jesse Jackson


Ability - Selina E. Matis

Ability is to look at a blank page,
And create a poem.
Ability is to stare into the eyes of fear,
And come out stronger because of it.
Ability is to walk into a room of strangers,
And come out with friends.
Ability is to admit you are wrong,
When you are wrong.
Ability is to get back up,
When you fall down.
Ability is to believe,
When everything seems lost.

Ability - a simple word, with complex meaning.
For many, ability is never found, but for all ability is within.
Ability stares everyone in the face at one time or another.
Whether your ability is how well you shoot hoops,
How well you flip at dancing,
How smart you are at school.
You have ability.
For some, ability is lost by never trying.
Whether never trying to shoot one more time,
Never trying to bend a little more,
Or never trying to score higher in school.

Ability is within.
Ability is yours.


We are Strong Because - The Poetry Club

We are patient (sometimes).
We all have experienced good times and bad times.
We are strong because we come from strong cultures.
We help each other even when we don’t all get along.
We’ve had similar experiences.
We’ve had similar pasts.
We come together to help each other through hard times.
If we weren’t, we wouldn’t be here today.
We are all loved and we need each other.
Row.txt_description: Offers the chance to build a sense of pride in oneself as well as a sense of cohesion within the group about the obstacles and hard times that they have been through. The finished artwork serves as a pride badge and reminder to not give up.

Row.txt_code:
Deb Knaff at Women’s Windows
Training in Alaska, November,
2003, where she shared this
workshop.
  


The Story of this Workshop:
Our domestic violence education group night fell on Valentine’s Day.  I decided that instead of covering the usual topics such as the dynamics of domestic violence, what is emotional abuse, the impact of domestic violence on children, or the other myraid of things we could discuss, we should just love ourselves on this day of love.  
  


  

Making a collage about loving ourselves seemed to be a wonderful way to celebrate Valentine’s Day,
so I quickly gathered some frilly ribbon, sequins, feathers, red buttons, glue, paper, magazines, etc. and also cut out loving words (to get the main idea started).  

When the women arrived for group, I heard some brief moaning and groaning about doing this collage and learning to love ourselves.  We talked about the notion that is was impossible for others to love us if we first didn’t love ourselves.  Everyone set out making their own masterpiece and soon I heard them talking about how they were all considering going back to their abuser as this holiday was a vivid reminder of how lonely they were, what a failure they thought they were for not being able to fix their abusive relationship, and how they just wanted to be loved.  
  


  

They then talked about how this collage was so therapeutic.  They could feel that they were loved, they loved themselves, and they were loved by the women around them.  They were so glad that they did not return to their abusive relationships.  Because of their collages, they could feel that loving themselves was a first step in possibly having a healthy relationship in the future.

There were many healing tears that evening and it was the most powerful group that I have been part of in the ten years that I have been doing domestic violence education.  The women who attended also formed a very tight bond and are still all very close to this day.  They support one another, share childcare, and two of them are now roommates.  

This year we are planning another “loving yourself art night” on Valentine’s Day again.  It was responsible for doing what others cannot do for us… begin to heal.  
  


  

Objectives:  
To give participants the opportunity and support to focus on loving
themselves.  To turn a holiday that might feel lonely and shameful into
a source of deep self-love, self-care, and connection that will carry
through the entire year.

Materials:
Paper
Scissors
  


  

Glue
Magazines
Ribbon
Sequins
Feathers

Prep:
Cut out loving words from magazines before the workshop.  This will help focus the workshop in a positive direction, even if participants come to the table not feeling very loving of themselves.  Spread the supplies invitingly on the table so they can reach what they need.

Introduction:
“Today, to celebrate Valentine’s Day, we are going to focus on loving ourselves.  Have you ever heard the notion that it’s impossible for others to love us if we don’t first love ourselves?  What does that mean?  Today we will each make a collage about loving ourselves.  It’s okay if you don’t feel like you love yourself at the beginning.  Doing this collage is about learning to love ourselves.”  

Opening Circle (optional):
Depending on how structured you want the group to be, you could have a check-in circle so that each participant can share how she’s feeling about Valentine’s Day and about loving herself.  Or you could just dive in with the collaging and let the conversation emerge naturally as they create.  Sometimes more can be expressed when the pressure is off and everyone’s focused on what their hands are doing instead of looking at each other.  

Creation:
This is a very simple, open workshop.  Show the supplies and the pre-cut loving words and give them a chance to go for it!

Closing:
Be sure everyone has a chance to share her collage and what it means to her.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants the opportunity and support to focus on loving themselves. Also, a chance to turn a holiday (Valentine's Day) that might feel lonely and shameful into a source of deep self-love and connection.
