Row.str_author_location: Adapted from the book 'Mandala-Luminous Symbols for Healing' by Judith Cornell.
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To strengthen your will and mental powers so you can distribute healing energies throughout your body.  In this exercise you make a luminous drawing of your hand.  “All true sacred art is alive with the spiritual energies of the maker. If open and receptive, the maker is inwardly changed by the creative act.  Just as the viewer of these spiritually energized symbols is changed.”  I found this idea in the book “Mandala—Luminous Symbols for Healing” by Judith Cornell.

Hands Mandala from Wausau, Wisconsin
  


 
Women working on their Hands Mandalas.
  

Materials:
Black paper, on a roll if possible, cut into 20” by 20” squares.
Artist grade white color pencils (each person should have two if possible)
Pencil sharpeners

Prep:
Have black paper cut to size and two white pencils for each person.  Have plenty of pencil sharpeners available.

Timeframe:
Total time: 2 hours—allow more time if needed.  Can be taken home to work on if necessary.  
  


 
"Trying to break free into the Light."
  

Introduction:
20 min
Opening Circle: 10 min
Relaxation:
 5 min
Creation:
 70 min
Closing:
 15 min

Introduction:
“Everyone has the power within themselves to heal both emotional and physical pain.  We can learn to tap into that sacred space by asking the loving Universe to work through you.  Today we will discover the beauty we can create by allowing the light to radiate through our hands onto this black paper.”

Opening Circle:
“Where can you go to feel safe and loved?  How many have tried going inward?”  
  


"As I was working on this I thought of my children,
whose love helped me get through the hardest
time in my life.  Also, I thought about the workers
here at the shelter and all the support they gave
to my family.  Thank you so much!"
 
  


Technical Info:
Demonstrate on a scrap of black paper how to use the white pencil to make gradations of light.  Start out by pressing very hard on the pencil until the black is totally covered, then gradually lighten the pressure until you see black again.  

Relaxation:
Ask each person to close their eyes and try to feel the light energy flowing from the top of their heads, down their arms and through their fingers.  Can they feel the warmth from this loving light?  We are all connected to each other and the Universe.  This light burns in each one of us so let us try to draw its beauty on the black paper in front of us.   

Creation:
Have them practice with you until they feel comfortable.  Explain that you can draw as many hands as you want, in different positions, crossing over each other, etc.  Encourage each person to just do what feels comfortable.  When they have completed placement of the hands, they can work on the luminous part by using the white pencil.  Some may want to use other colors besides white, which is fine.  But encourage lighter ones such as yellow or light orange.  Have everyone walk around the table to see what others have done.
  


 
"Reaching for Peace with the Worlds.  My art describes peace and harmony.  May God bless us all, so let us continue to reach for the sky and stars."
  


Closing:
Ask each person to explain what their Mandala means to them.  Were they able to feel a different kind of energy coming through their hands?  If they are not finished, encourage them to take them home.  (They will need a white pencil to take along.)  

We found that clients came back asking for more paper to work on more Mandalas.  They found them very peaceful and relaxing.

Exhibit:
We displayed over 35 different mandalas during the month of October.  We used this occasion as our Open House.  We draped black, red, and violet fabric over the walls in the hallway and hung the Mandalas from the fabric.  
It was very beautiful.  

Many participants also added words, which were typed and hung on the bottom of each Mandala.  We cut them out in circles: then pasted them to white poster board.  

I hope you enjoy this workshop!




Details from some of the mandalas.
Row.txt_description: Offers participants the opportunity to strengthen their will and mental powers in order to distribute healing energies throughout the body. The end product is a luminous drawing of the artists' hands.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Completed Key Tag.
 
  
About this Workshop:
Creating this workshop was a way for me to explore how I wanted to creat e more balance in my life, and to make something beautiful that I could carry with me as a reminder.

I created it because my life was out of balance. I was having health problems because of being out of balance and my quality of life was going down.

Leading this project in the shelter, I found that the group really loved it. It’s amazing how satisfying the result can be, because of the Shrinky-Dink process. The end result is something they are all so proud of!
  


 
Tracing Circles
  
 
 
Drawing
  
 
 
Cutting Out
  
 
 
Punching Hole
  
  

Objective:
To explore how to be more in balance in your everyday life. You will discover what sections need to have more of your focus, and also try to identify the “thieves” of your energy. The key-rings will be daily reminders of those items that you are working on so that you can redirect some of your energy towards getting more balance in your life - which will mean a happier (more authentic) YOU!

Materials:
Pens and paper for writing
Creating Balance Worksheet (click here)
Additional advanced worksheet (click here for template)
Shrinky Dinks paper (Frosted Ruff N’Ready type - You can order bulk online: search for “The Magical Land of Shrinky Dinks”)
Colored Permanent Markers (Sharpees)
Rolls of tape, cups, or anything to trace 3-inch circles onto the plastic
Colored pencils and sharpeners
Scissors
Magazines/Stock books/coloring books, etc., for tracing
Letter stencils/word stencils (see attached samples)
Hole puncher and pliers
Key-ring hardware materials: 20 mm size, 6 mm size split rings
One grocery bag/toaster oven

Prep:
Try this out yourself first so you can get a feel for the process - especially the cooking part. If you’re not used to it, it can be scary to see the art curl and uncurl as it cooks and shrinks.

Timeframe:
At our agency, we only have an hour and 15 minutes for group, so we often skip the relaxation and opening circle in order to have more time for creating. You can add in an opening and relaxation if you have time.

Introduction

5 min
Writing
 15 min
Demonstration
 5 min
Creation
 40 min
Closing
 10 min

Introduction:
There are two things I’ll ask of you today.
1. Be brave (you cannot create in fear).
2. Have fun! (This is your time just for you to enjoy.)
We will be writing for 15 minutes to explore issues of balance in our lives. This is a time to notice what you’d like to focus on more, and what things might be like “thieves” of your energy. After the writing, I’ll share how to do the key chains.

Writing:
Use the Creating Balance Key Tag worksheet to explore issues of balance in your life. Write whatever comes to mind. Be brave!

Technical Info:
Once the group is finished writing, lead them through the Shrinky Dinks process:

Tracing Circles:
Have each participant take a sheet of the material and trace 6 circles about 3 inches in diameter (you can use the inside of a tape roll or even a jar lid) with a permanent fine point marker on the smooth side of your Shrinky Dinks plastic. This will be a guide only.

Drawing:
Once you have this outline (on the smooth side) turn the paper around to the “rough” frosted side and draw and/or trace (from magazines, coloring books, your imagination, etc.) the image and/or word that will remind you about that item or items that you are going to be focusing on to have more balance in your daily life. Keep in mind that a hole will be punched on the top portion of your circle – so don’t write/draw anything too crucial in that section. Be creative, let yourself go, allow that energy that is inside to guide you now! Even if you just use colors, a word or symbol – as long as it is a reminder to you, that is all that matters - your key ring will look great – that’s a guarantee!
  
 Cooking Process


 
1. Make sure holes are punched before
cooking. Pre-heat oven to 325°F.

 
 
2. Place on paper bag in toaster oven.
Turn up the bag corner so you can grab it
easily and pull all the Shrinky Dinks off the
pan when they are done. Cook for 1-2
minutes. They are done when they flatten
out.

 
 
3. When you pull them out, immediately
press between smooth books for 15
seconds.

 
 
4. They come out very small!
  

Hole Punching:
Once you are done coloring and drawing/tracing, you can cut out your circle. Punch a hole on the top of your circle so you can later put the key ring through it. The hole needs to be punched PRIOR to baking. (When you punch the hole, don’t punch it too close to the edge, or too far. The distance from the edge should be about half the diameter of the hole-punch circle.)

Baking:
Now you are ready to bake! Follow the instructions pictured on this page. Place a piece of the paper bag to line the toaster oven tray, plus make a small “handle” by tipping up one of the corners – this way you won’t get your hands burned when you pull the paper out. Most circles will be “done” in about 2 minutes. Be patient. Let the circle lie down flat before you take it out of the oven. Once you take it out, quickly put a book on top of it and press down hard for 15 seconds.

Adding the Rings:
Once the circles are baked, open up one of the small key rings with small pliers and put it through the hole on your balance circle. Before you close it, put the big key ring in there too and then close the small ring. (You can put more than one circle in the big key ring, but each circle must have it’s own small ring through it.)

Using your Key Tags:
Choose which key tags you want to carry with you. You could focus on one at a time, and as they each feel resolved, you can switch to new items and save the circles just in case you need to focus on that item again later on.

Closing:
Ask each person to share anything they want to about their key tags and what they mean. You might encourage the women to share how/if they want to use the tags during their everyday life to help remind them of the balance they’re creating.
Row.txt_description: Participants explore how to be more in balance in their everyday lives through the creation of Shrinky Dink key-tags that act as daily reminder of items they wish to work on.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Because of the severe psychological abuse of battering, most residents come into the shelter feeling hopeless, fearful, and unsure of what their future will bring. Staying in a familiar abusive relationship is often easier than the unknown outcome of leaving and trying to make it on their own. The shelter’s most important job besides being a “safe house” is to provide the residents with the education, psychological and emotional support, and the resources necessary in order to embark on this journey. This art directive is focused on the education as well as acknowledging the participants’ own inherent strengths to help them make the journey.

As facilitator, point out that they did what they did to emotionally survive, and that it required amazing strength to live through that abuse and trauma. Their shame can be transformed, and their strengths can be accessed along with evaluating areas to be developed.

Materials:
A long sheet of paper (preferably butcher paper)
Magazines
Paint
Pastels
Markers
Collage material 
Tape
Glue
Scissors

Opening:
Have participants stand up and stretch and breathe. Guide them through their body with each out breath to feel their head, their neck, their shoulders, their arms, their torso, etc. Allow them to sink into the earth as if they had roots growing out from their feet. Let them know that this is their time, and to really be here for themselves. Let all their worries and stresses go. Breathe and feel your body, mind, and spirit present for the next couple of hours.

Time Format:
5 min. with the breathing + stretching
15-30 min. of discussion /brainstorming
30 min. for the art
30 min. for the sharing and processing
10 min. for closure and clean-up

Brainstorming:
It might be helpful to use domestic violence handouts to encourage discussion, regardless, communicate with participants the basic ideas of “Why abusers/batterers hit,” “Why victims stay.” and “The cycle of violence.” Stress the importance that they did what they had to in order to survive a traumatic situation. This inherent strength can be drawn upon to embark on whatever journey they will now choose to go on. In assessing our strengths, it is also important to be aware of areas that need to be developed. Some qualities that fall into both categories could be:

1. The ability to ask for help.
2. Willingness to try new ideas and be open to possibilities.
3. Desire to experience self-love and self-respect.
4. The ability to experience and express all feelings.
5. Assertive rather than passive or aggressive behavior.
6. Ability to have fun and be yourself.
7. Reasonable discipline and structure.
8. Willingness to take necessary steps for training in a fulfilling job.
9. Patience and gentleness towards self and others.
10. Willingness to be honest and courageous in working through issues.
11. Commitment to goals and self.

This list can go on forever. Engage participants in a brainstorming session of their strengths and areas needing attention. Remind them that life is a process that unfolds, it took them a lifetime to get to where they are, and it will take some time to heal. The important thing is that they treat themselves as they would a friend, supporting risk taking, progress, and goals. Being gentle on themselves as they learn healthier ways of making choices. Encourage them to get help and support. Perhaps join a free self-help group such as Co-dependents anonymous or Adult Children of Alcoholics. These are support groups which model healthy behavior through sharing experiences, strength, and hope. Read books or find a therapist. Do whatever it is they can to support their healing and growth, putting themselves first for once.

Art Creation:
After the group discussion of strengths and areas needing attention, have participants divide the paper into three sections. Label them past, present, and future goals.

“For the past, focus on the things that you have learned from the past and symbolize through pictures, drawings, or words what your strengths are. In the same manner also include the areas that trip you up, and that you would like to change.

“For the present block, think about your life and all that you have learned. It could be things you have learned here recently. Express any insight you have acquired. Also include questions and concerns you may have.

“For the future section, express how you would like to see yourself. What are your goals? How would you like to see your relationships with yourself, your family, and friends? What about a spiritual relationship? If you can conceive it you can achieve it! So don’t hold back! Allow your dreams, visions, and goals to be known. Share them with the others. Write down some steps you can take to achieve these goals. The first step is a commitment to yourself. Perhaps you could write a poem about your hope for the future.”

Sharing:
As participants share what they have created, notice whether or not they seem to get bogged down in the weaknesses and mistakes. If they do, focus them on shifting their point of view. See the problem areas in the light of managing their experience in the most adaptive way they could at the time with what they knew. By gently assessing where they are in the present, they can focus on other possible choices in getting their needs met. They can lovingly respond to the areas needing attention. Kindness and gentleness are the keys. It should be suggested as one of the most important goals on their lists as well.
Row.txt_description: Offers participants the opportunity assess their strengths as well as areas needing attention, supporting them to take risks in their progress, focus on their goals, and get help and support whenever possible. The end product is a compilation of lists and/or drawings of participants individual strengths to help them return to a place of knowing their own potential.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide a safe environment symbolically, as well as in the group.  This workshop aims to assist participants in finding a safe place mentally and then recreating that place on the cover of their journal.  The journal is then used as a powerful tool for insight, emotional expression, and a path to articulate a sense of self.

Materials:
8x11 piece of cardboard or construction paper
Wire bound notebook
Collage materials and magazines
Paints
Pastels
Glue
Scissors

Note to the Facilitator:
I have included a guided meditation to take the participants to their safe place.  If you have your own ways, please feel free to adapt them into this exercise.  The main point that I feel is important in guided maditation is to include the cue words for visuals, auditories, and kinesthetics.  I am a visual, and I have made the mistake of doing strictly visual guided meditations.  This can leave those whose primary way of connecting information is through hearing or through a "felt" sense, back in the body relaxation part.  Another note of caution in this exercise: try to provide at least five to ten minutes of uninterrupted quiet for participants to get the benefits of the meditation.  This may not be possible if childcare is not provided.  Think about any arrangements you can make ahead of time with a staff member for those precious ten minutes!

Introduction:
It's very important to let the participants know ahead of time about the session. This alleviates anxiety and gives them a choice as to whether they want to participate or not. All that needs to be said about this session is that "we will be doing a relaxation technique that can be used by you at any time as a stress reducer, and then we will do a guided visualization to a 'safe place'. Afterwards, there will be time to symbolically recreate our safe place. This final picture will be the cover of our journal.”

   
 
   Rhumtek Monastery Gangtok, Sikkim 
Guided Meditation:
[To be spoken in a calm, even and slowly paced voice. Make pauses appropriately.]
Ask participants to sit in a comfortable position. (Best not to lay down as relaxation will induce sleep, if you notice this occurring, bring your voice and pace up a little.) “Take some time to take five deep breaths very slowly and consciously... Feel the air coming in through your nose, filling your lungs, and exhaling through the mouth... Just breathe and feel your body... Feel your presence... Let go of all the thoughts of yesterday... and let go of all the thoughts of tomorrow.... let all that go with each breath. Just be here.. right now... just be here with nothing but your breath. Continue to breathe at a normal pace... and now I want you to bring your attention to your toes and feet... let go of any tensions you may find there... if you find the tension not leaving, you may want to tighten the muscles real firmly and then let go... keep doing this until your feet are relaxed... and now bring your attention to your calves.. feel them relaxing... feel your calves relaxing into the floor with your feet... and when you’re ready, move to your thighs and allow the muscles to relax... feel yourself sink into your chair... continue to move up your torso... sensing a motion of relaxation sweeping through your torso... connecting to the relaxation in your legs and feet... and if you’re feeling any tension, just squeeze your muscles and let go... squeeze and let go... relax into your body... now feel your arms... feel the energy of relaxation move down into your hands and fingers... squeeze your hands and release the tension... now move up into your shoulders and neck area... once again, if you feel tension, squeeze and relax... and again... feel the relaxation of your whole body move up into your head... squeeze your facial muscles and relax... take a deep breath and let go... feel yourself in your body... feel yourself relaxed..."

“I now want to take you on a journey to your inner world. Imagine yourself at the top of a staircase. Try to notice how it feels as you begin to walk down... notice the sound of your footsteps... notice the air on your skin... looking down the steps, you see a door... as you walk down the steps, you wonder what's behind the door... some wise intuitive feeling within you senses that this is a very safe place... this place is especially for you... you start to feel some excitement about opening the door... you instinctively know that this is a magical place where you can create whatever you need to be safe here... your very own magical space to create just to you liking... created especially for you to feel free and how wonderful it feels to be safe. Look around and notice all that surrounds you... listen to any sounds that soothe you... touch and smell anything that interests you... let your body experience this beautiful place that you created for yourself... place any objects in here that you like... splash colors and fragrances freely... experience what you have created and remember it... and when you’re ready to come back to this space and time... close your door knowing that you can come back any time you want to... Take your time to come back... just breathe and feel your body being supported by the chair... come back by opening your eyes whenever you are ready.”

Directive and Creation:
“Instead of talking about our special places, let’s direct the energy of our experience into creating a symbol of the feeling of safety. This could be an actual depiction of what we found in our room, or maybe some of the colors or textures. You may want to use words with the colors. However you want to express it so that it has meaning to you. Remember that it is the permission to allow yourself to express that is important, and not so much about the end result. So don't let that get in your way of having fun and playing with this expression of safety. If you happened to get so relaxed during the meditation that sleep became your safe place, no need to worry! Just sit with your body and find a sense of a safe feeling and imagine what a place of your own creating might look like, and again, this could be a collage of colors and words if you wish. Let yourself play."

When participants are finished with their art pieces, have them protect their cover with clear contact paper or masking tape. This provides reinforcement that their journal is a safe place.

Facilitator Note:
If a participant has a difficult time in experiencing a safe place, let her think back to any time that she felt loved and protected. This can be expressed through the media however she feels. Also, the use of prose or poetry can be the creative expression. Even a body sense and the color that it may look like is enough to get started on an art piece.

Closing:
Talk about how to keep the journal safe from someone finding it. Each participant might have her own strategy. When I was living with my abuser, I used to write in my journal and then give it to my girlfriend to keep. The importance of expression and identification of our thoughts, feelings, hopes, and fears are of utmost importance to communicate to participants. Explain the importance of allowing a flow of expression in their life. Dammed up water can become stagnant and poisoning. The journal is a way of letting go of that, as well as making room for new ideas and impressions. It can be a valuable tool for self discovery and an indication of growth. Dreams and goals can be established here, and then go on into the actual making. Do not underestimate the power of creative visualization. If it can be imagined, then it can be done. Imagine loving yourself and act as if. Imagine forgiving yourself and act as if. Imagine, imagine, imagine..
Row.txt_description: Assists participants in finding a safe place mentally and then recreating that place on the cover of their journal. The journal is then used as a powerful tool for insight, emotional expression, and a path to articulate a sense of self.

Row.txt_code:
“The Fish Dance” warm-up
 
  
Binah is one of the co-authors of the Children’s Windows Training Manual.  Here, she shares supplemental warm-up activities to try with the children.  Next Update will include Binah’s rhythm and music warm-ups!

Introduction:
Children love to do playful, expressive warm-ups together.  It also gets them in the mood for the art project and helps everyone focus, including you, the leader.

The following are some suggestions to use with children either before a workshop or if you need a break during the workshop.  I am also including some “mini-exercises” to help gather children.  Shelters are typically high stimulation environments, and with all the coming and going around them, children have a tendency to “wander off.”  Most likely your artspace is just some itty-bitty space in between other activity areas, which makes it even more tempting for children to drift off.  So I’d like you to think of yourself as the Creative Shepherd/ess who gently and imaginatively brings your flock back to the fold when they wander.


 
 
 “The Fish Dance” warm-up
  

The Natural World:
My experience in working with children of all ages has been that children almost always respond to imagination and playfulness — where better than in the natural world around us that fascinates children so much: jungles and deserts, animals and insects, stars and planets, rain and shine: Be creative and design your own exercises.  Here are a few simple warm-ups that you can do any time during an art project.

The Fish Dance:
Use this exercise if you want to get the children to follow you from one space to another, or just to bring them into a quieter mood.

“Now we are going to pretend that we are all little fishes following each other so that we get through the ocean without being eaten by those big, big fish out there.  We must stick close together but nobody is to push or get in each other’s way. 

“Let’s put our hands out in front of us, just like a little fish (press palms together and have the hands in front of the chest with elbows sticking out) and we are going to go smoothly through the water...that’s right, let’s move our arms and hands, keeping our palms together like little fish, swaying from left to right, and we can make a swoosh, swoosh noise...but not loud...because did anybody ever hear a loud fish?  Oh no, we have to be quiet so the big fish don’t hear us.”

  


“Growing as a Tree” warm-up
 
  

As you do this and have the kids gather behind and around you, move either in a circle around the room, or move to the place where you want the children to be.  Model to the children the whole body swaying from side to side, or wriggling back and forth, as close to a fish as you can be.

Growing As A Tree:
This is a nice exercise to do on the spot — in fact, it is great if you want kids to stay in one spot!

Have the children gather either in a circle, or just ask them to find a favorite spot near you in the room.  Ask them to make space around them because they are going to grow from small to big.  Tell the children that they are going to be special trees that are going to grow big and strong.


 
 
 “Moving as Animals” — a bull with horns
  

“Now I first want you to be a small tree but with strong roots.  So let’s make sure our feet are on the ground and we have good roots that will help us grow.  Let’s hunker down close to the ground so we can be small trees.  Now we are going to grow, little by little.  First let’s put our arms up above our head and our fingers are like little leaves, wiggling about and then little bit by little bit we are going to get bigger, and bigger, and bigger (until you are standing up fully).  Now we are a strong, wise tree, upright and ready for anything.  Yes, let’s keep our arms and hands straight up in the air.  Now let’s imagine that a wind comes up — not too big a wind, but a wind that makes us move around and about.  Be careful, we can’t move our feet, because our roots are in the ground!  Let’s just move our bodies at the top just like a real tree.  Can anyone show me how the wind in the trees sounds?  Yes, that’s good...”

Moving As Animals:
This is an all-time favorite with young children, and you can make it more sophisticated for older children. 

First gather the children around you, starting off in a circle.  Have everyone choose an animal he/she wants to be and go around the circle naming that animal.  You may want to have them describe in detail (prompting them if need be) what their animal looks like and show how it moves.

“Now we are going to pretend that we are an animal and we are going to move around the room as the animal.  We just have one rule: that no animal can hurt another animal, OK?

“Before we move, I am going to put on some music and then we can begin to move.  So remember which animal you said you would be.”

You can even divide up the room (for older children) between deserts and jungles, so that the animals stay in different areas.

Choose ambient-type music that would be a good backdrop for animals to roam around in.  Tell the children that when the music stops, all the animals must lie down and rest.  You may want to debrief with the children what it felt like to be that animal.

On the Spot Exercises:
The following are fun to do either on their own or as part of another exercise. 
These exercises do not need a lot of room space as they don’t involve moving around.

Rag Dolls:
Have the children pretend they are a rag doll and little bit by little bit have them relax and go limp until they GENTLY fall to the floor.  You can then continue the exercise with having them relax even more by having them imagine their body safely floating on a cloud, while they are taking nice, deep breaths.

(You may want to play soft music to help them get in the mood once they are on the floor.)

  


“Stirring the Dough” warm-up
 
  

Sanding the Table/Stirring the Dough:
This exercise is done standing up and needs each child to have room in front of him/her.  Have the children stand in their own space with their feet apart (remind them not to lock their knees) and imagine they are sanding a table.  Really get their imagination going: “Now you are going to get that table so smooth, so let’s go around and around with our hands like sanding machines and get it just right.”  Let them do it enough times that they get into the relaxing rhythm. 

After you have had them sand for a bit then let them shift into stirring dough.  Again, pump up their imaginations.  “Now you have got some thick dough that’s going to make the yummiest bread (or cookies), so let’s imagine we have a big, wooden spoon and we are going to stir, and stir, and stir.”  Keep prompting them with dialogue so they really get into it.

The Cat’s Paw:
This is a weird exercise that children really like.  It helps them to feel powerful.



 
 
 “The Cat’s Paw” turning to the side
  
 
 “The Cat’s Paw” starting position
  
Have the children stand with their feet a little apart and knees bent, with elbows to their side and arms up (like a V) and hands up, thumbs in, like two paws of an animal.  Let them look around with their eyes and their head moving from side to side.

Remind them that they are like a super cat, that is very still and can see and hear everything.  Now they are to take in a big breath and move their paws to the left in a sharp move (like a submarine lookout scope) and then quickly strike down next to the left side of their body while letting out their breath in a hissing sound, quickly bringing up the “paws” and moving this time to the right side, striking down on the right side of the body just like they did on the other side, again with a hissing sound.  Then they move their paws (which always stay parallel to each other) in an infinity sign across the front of their body from right to left several times before striking down again on the left side and bringing their paws back up to the front to start again.  They breathe normally several times and then take a deep breath to start all over again.

You will have to show the children first, then have them do it.  This is an atmospheric exercise if you set it up with some drama around being the all-powerful, all-seeing cat.

Your Gathering Call:
Develop a simple cue or call that you can tell your children in advance so that if you need to gather a child or group of children at any time you can use the call.

Some typical cues are telling the children that they are to stop and listen if you click your fingers or clap your hands.  Some leaders have found the words “Simon Says” followed by an instruction effective because so many children know the Simon Says game.

Whatever you use, be sure the children understand it.  Also, be sure that is simple enough without being jarring and you use it consistently to build recognition.  Test it out on your kids to see if it works for them and you.

A Closing Word:

 
 
 “Growing as a Tree” warm-up
  

One thing to remember with these exercises is that they are more effective if you are in the spirit of it and if you are tuned in to your children, bearing in mind their moods, their situations in the shelter, their age group and so forth.  You may need to adjust an exercise to fit a particular child, for example one with a disability, so have a few backup exercises always in your mind so that you can shift gears at the last minute if you need to.  Always keep safety in mind.

Good luck and don’t be afraid to let your imagination loose!
Row.txt_description: Gives children the opportunity to do playful, expressive warm-ups together. Gets them in the mood for the art project and helps everyone focus, including you, the leader.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways.  Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Leaders enjoy warm-ups at training
  
Binah is one of the co-authors of the Children’s Windows Training Manual.  This Update is “part 2,” an addition to the previous month’s Update on Warm-ups and Circles.

Introduction:
My experience in working with children of all ages has been that children almost always respond to the world of music with its compelling beats and sounds.  

The following exercises are inspired by Flamenco, a dance form that is both arousing and soulful with strong rhythms and beautiful movements that people of all ages can do.

Be creative and design your own exercises.

Let’s start with music.  These exercises will energize and focus kids.  All you have to do as a leader is to loosen up any inhibitions you might have and give them the rhythm so they have something to follow.  Remember, you don’t have to be perfect, and trust your body. 

A Stomping and A Hollering:
Children love to stomp their feet and make noises.  When you’re needing the children to be energized for your project, getting them to stomp and shout will really raise the energy level but keep them focused at the same time. 

First Stillness...Then Kindle The Fire:
First gather your children in a circle before the activity and have them stand in a circle, placing their hands on their hips, elbows a little forward, and feet parallel and slightly apart.  This is the moment to introduce the children to the exercise and talk a little about dance: “I just want you to feel that space between your hips, you know the part inside you, just inside your tummy?  Well, that is where the fire sits, that is where the dragon sleeps.  And we’re going to let it out a little bit a time, just a little bit, you don’t want to give it all away.  And I want you to stand proud, with your backs straight, and your eyes straight ahead.  So we’re going to put that energy out with some stomping and some sounds and I need you to really, really listen to me and to each other.  When we all work together it will be fantastic.  But remember, behind all that energy, right there between your hips, is stillness and quiet, behind every sound and dance is stillness and quiet....so let’s be quiet and listen to how we’re going to stomp....”

Learning the Stomp Step:
“Everybody is being so good at standing still, holding that dragon inside your hips.  So what we’re going to do is stomp one foot at a time: first stomp with the left foot, then the right foot, then the left foot, and so on, okay?  When we stomp we don’t smash down our feet, because that can be too hard on our knees and it doesn’t make the best sound.  What we do is pull our leg up a little so our knees are bent and then we just let our foot fall completely to the ground.  Just like that.”  (Demonstrate how the foot falls, and then the other.)  Let the children try this a little. 

  


Sorgas Clap hand position
 
  

Rhythm And Clap:
“Now we’re going to practice the claps, because in our dance we are going to stomp, then clap, then finish with ‘HA’.  So, let’s go back to putting our hands on our hips with our feet apart (don’t push back the knees, everything is a little soft)  and now slowly, proudly take your hands up to your chest, that’s right, keep the hands at your chest but a little away from your chest and your elbows out and then your hands together, fitting like two pieces of a puzzle, with your palms making a nice little space inside.  We also call this clasping your hands.  When you clap like this we call it Sorgas because the palms make a soft, hollow sound.” Everybody practices the Sorgas clap.

“Now let’s try a different clap.  Move your right hand so that your fingers stay together and hit (gently!) the palm of your other hand.  It makes a loud, clear sound and we call that the Claras clap.”  Everybody practices the Claras clap, and then have them go back to the Sorgas clap until they get the hang of the different claps. 

The Stomp And Ha!:

 
 
 Claras Clap hand position
  

“Now we’re going to put it all together, just like magic, and wake up the dragon and let the fire out, just a little at a time.  Let’s stand with our feet apart and our hands on our hips, just tickling the dragon a little bit, and then we’re going to bring up our hands in front of our chests ready for the Sorgas clap just like this (demonstrate).  But remember one rule: we do not stomp and clap at the same time.  Oh, no, no, no.  We keep the stomp and clap separate so all the sounds don’t get mixed up like a bad radio....

“So let’s stomp with the left foot, stomp with the right, stomp with the left, then 3 Sorgas claps and finish with a ‘HA!’”

Have the children do this first with the Sorgas clapping and then with the Claras clapping....

Clap And Ole!:
“That’s so good, you’ve really got the hang of stomping and clapping.  So now we’ve got rhythm we can hold the stomps and let’s go with the clapping. 

“Let’s go back to standing with backs straight, feet apart and our hands on our hips — elbows forward, remember — being proud, eyes straight ahead, and let’s tickle the dragon a little.  Then when we’ve woken her up we can bring our hands up to our chests to be ready for clapping.  I’m going to call out SORGAS and we all clap in Sorgas style — remember, the soft clap with the palms together making a little space inside — and then I will call out CLARAS and you move your right hand so the fingers hit your other palm.  Then, I will shout OLE! and you all join me.  Okay?”

Really get a rhythm going with the clapping, and let it build to a crescendo, finishing with a resounding OLE!

Possible Additions:
These exercises work best if the children are in unison and so they must be encouraged to look at you and follow your instructions, as well as be sensitive to other children around them.  This simple rhythm with hands and feet can create a very beautiful atmosphere and really bring the group together. 

If your children are really catching on, you can finish with some typical flamenco hand movements where the fingers roll out in the shape of a fan with the arms above the head, wrists twirling as the arms move down to the front of the body.  Improvise, and bring in some turns with the hand movements, if you like.  This can create very graceful movements and bring the children to a quieter harmonic.  You may want to bring flamenco music to add to this exercise.  Be creative and proud, AND HAVE FUN!
Row.txt_description: Provides time to enjoy the experience of music and its abilitiy to energize and provide focus. The exercises included in this workshop are inspired by Flamenco.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:





Tupelo models Graduation Hat.



To provide the children an opportunity to see their new, everyday accomplishments as achievements worth celebrating.  To allow them time to notice and define their successes.  To help them remember past accomplishments as they undergo new and challenging experiences so that they can feel confident in their learning curve.  The finished artwork serves as a reminder of their achievements and can be used again and again to celebrate new successes.

Materials:
Thick paper or cardboard (at least 1 per participant)
Collage option materials – Glue sticks, photo stock books, magazines
Fabric option materials – Assortment of fabric, Super Glue, stapler
Assortment of ribbon and yarn for tassels and decoration
Scissors
Optional – Beads and other decorations to weight the end of the tassels
Note: The Graduation Hats can be decorated in so many ways, consider having other materials available - Paints, markers, crayons, oil pastels/Cray-Pas





Olivia models Graduation Hat.



Timeframe:
Total Time         1 hour
Introduction        5 min
Opening Circle     5 min
Warm-up         10 min
Creating Hats         25 min
Pomp & Circumstance Ceremony     5 min
Closing Circle     10 min

Age Range/Ratio:
Age-Range: 8-12 years old
Ratio:     1 adult for 3 children, 1 adult for 2 younger children

Setup and Prep:
If you are planning on making fabric decorated Graduation Hats it is helpful to make one yourself so that you know how best to work with the fabric and attach it to the board.  Also, when you are preparing the cardboard squares you may want to pre-punch the center hole for the tassel.  (You can use the tip of scissors to do this.)    




Graduation Hat detail.




Introduction:
Be aware that some children will have already gone through a graduation ceremony at the end of kindergarten, but some won’t.  Also, depending on age, even if they participated in a graduation the children might be unfamiliar with a “cap and gown.”  Begin by asking questions about graduation and what it means and feel free to answer questions yourself if the children aren’t forthcoming: “How many of you know what a graduation is?  What is it celebrating?  It is a celebration of doing some very hard work.    What happens at a graduation?  What do you wear?  At some graduation ceremonies everyone who is graduating wears a cap and gown.  Does anyone know what they look like?  The gown is like a big coat.  The cap is like a flat, square hat and is called a mortarboard.  There is a string that hangs off of the hat that is called a tassel.  Does anyone know what the tassel is for?  After the person has graduated the tassel is moved from one side of the hat to the other.  The move of the tassel is a symbol of the hard work the person has accomplished.           

“Today, we are going to think about hard work we have done in our lives and remember to celebrate those things.  We are going to notice our biggest accomplishments and remember that all of our accomplishments are like little graduations.  Everytime we go from not knowing something to knowing something, that is a graduation.  We are going to celebrate our learning by making graduation hats, mortarboards and tassels.  And we will celebrate our accomplishments by having our own graduation ceremony today.” 





Cathy models Graduation Hat.


 
Opening Circle:
“To start, let’s all share something we have learned that wasn’t so easy for us.  Some of these things probably seem small now because we have learned them so well that they are easy, but they are still important and still worth celebrating.  For example, I remember when I was learning to tie my shoes, it was so hard and even my cousin who is younger than me could do it and I couldn’t.  But now I know how to tie my shoes, it is so easy I don’t even think about it!”  (Feel free to choose an example that is personal for you.  Go around the circle and have each participant share a learning experience.)
 
Warm-up:
“Now that everyone remembers a time they learned something new and the hard steps it took to get there, it is time to celebrate our accomplishments!  First, we are going to celebrate them by having Inside Yourself Celebrations, we are going to celebrate in our minds and then we are going to celebrate them on the outside by making our Graduation Hats.    Are you ready to have an Inside Yourself Celebration?  

“Okay, go inside and imagine yourself standing on a grassy lawn.  It is a beautiful day and the sun is perfectly warm.  You are wearing a beautiful long robe and a hat in the same color, it is your favorite color, it is the color of your school, dark green, bright yellow, royal purple, robin’s egg blue…You watch the color shimmer and then you see the tassel from your hat swaying where it hangs on the right side of your head.  Today is your graduation day!

You are warmed by the sunshine and feel confident and comfortable and calm.  You take a moment to breathe in the warm sunshine and the green grass, you breathe in energy and courage… As you breathe you notice that there are steps in front of you that lead up to a a big stage.

You count these steps as you breathe, one step for each breath... 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.  As you breath out on number seven, you hear a loving voice calling your name from the stage.  The voice is full of love and pride for you and you are ready to climb the steps in front of you... 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.




Graduation Hat detail.




At the top you see a familiar face holding out a hand to help you up the last step, you take the hand and see that this person, this person congratulating you with love and pride, is you!  It is the you that always knew you would be able to learn everything you needed to learn, waiting patiently at the top of the steps to help you onto this stage and say, “Congratulations!”

As you stand on the stage you move your tassel from one side of your Graduation Hat to the other side and all around you you hear the warm sound of applause as everyone celebrates your accomplishment!”  Begin clapping and after a few seconds continue with workshop.  

Graduation Hats:
It is time to create the Graduation Hats!  Explain how each participant gets to make their own hat.  Encourage the participants to think about their learning experiences and express their pride over these accomplishments onto their hats.  They can create whatever makes them remember their achievements and successes.

Suggest to the participants that they begin creating when they feel ready. 





Tango, AWBW mascot,
models Graduation Hat.



Pomp & Circumstance:
As the participants complete their Graduation Hats, help them one at a time, to congratulate themselves and move their tassel from the right to the left of their hat.  If the group is cohesive enough consider doing this during the closing circle.  Remind them that they can have their own private graduation ceremony anytime they want by moving the tassel from one side to the other.  

Finishing Up:
If some participants finish before others, give them paper so they can draw and/or write the story of their Graduation Hats while the other participants finish making their Hats.

Closing Circle:
Encourage each participant to share about their experience of making their Graduation Hats.  They might share how it felt noticing their groundbreaking accomplishments or the ways that their Graduation Hats will help them remember their past successes as they face new learning experiences.




Graduation Hat detail.
Row.txt_description: Provides children an opportunity to see their new, everyday accomplishments as achievements worth celebrating. The finished artwork serves as a reminder of their achievements and can be used again and again to celebrate new successes.

Row.txt_code:
“My mask is about the pain and hope of relationships.
One side symbolizes the emotions; the other side
symbolizes hope and beauty.  Emotions can symbolize
pain, anger, agony, depression...  it can also
symbolize love and joy.”

   ;  —Eddie Urrutia, age 18
 
  
Objective:
Utilizing this mask process will allow youth to think about teen dating violence in a visual way.  The mask will demonstrate how people look when they are in an abusive relationship and are feeling angry, scared, sad, jealous, happy, in love, or having a combination of feelings.  

If you are utilizing the workshop at a high school it would be beneficial to first discuss “what is abuse?” and the dynamics of an abusive relationship. With youth in a shelter, it is still beneficial to educate first about teen dating violence. Help the youth think about their peer relationships and abuse that can happen in dating relationships.

Materials:
Newspaper for protecting the surface of the table & for creating the mold
Sculptamold (1 bag for every three clients - can order from Dick Blick via dickblick.com or 1-800-828-4548.  It costs about $1.50 per person.)
Plastic or glass bowls to mix the sculptamold (one per participant)
Pitcher with water

 
 
 This mask represents verbal abuse, with the words
coming out of the mouth on wires.
  

Relaxing music
Paper and pencil
Masking tape
Toothpicks
Mat boards or cardboard to store the mask on while it dries
Feelings Faces chart (see attached - it can be helpful for exploring different expressions.)

For Day 2 of Workshop:
Acrylic paint, brushes, water, etc.
Phone wire, colored wire, or pipe cleaners
Sand paper
Material for hair…yarn or raffia
Glue gun or FabriTac Glue (for attaching hair, etc.)
If you want to display mask afterwards, fishing wire & drill


 
 
 Detail from verbal abuse mask above.
  
 
 Detail from verbal abuse mask above.
  

Timeframe:
Day 1 :    1 - 1 1/2 hours
Initial mask can be created in 1 hour, but it’s great if you have an extra 30 minutes for opening and demo.

Intro:             5 min
Opening Circle:     10 min
Technical Demo:     10 min
Relaxation:         5 min
Creation Time:     60 min (or less)

Day 2:      1 to 2 hours
Hard to say because it depends on how into decorating the masks the youth are!

Age Range/Ratio:
Depending on the population and the setting this workshop was designed for teenagers but the workshop can easily be adapted for ages seven and up. Youth that are not yet involved in dating but who are living in an abusive home could use the mask to portray feelings they've seen Dad or Mom show, or feelings they themselves have felt during a violent episode or during the “honeymoon phase.”

  


Forming the Sculptamold clay.
 
  
  
  

Setup and Prep:
It is definitely helpful to experiment with this material before leading the workshop. The material can dry really fast depending on weather and/or air conditioning.  Plus, the consistency is important, too little or too much water can create problems. The desired consistency is like cottage cheese. As you use the mixture it begins to dry and you can keep shaping it and smoothing it. Once it’s dry in the bowl you cannot soften it up again with water!

Note:  Throw unused, dried clay in the trash, not down the sink.  Wipe away all extra clay so it doesn’t go down the drain when you wash the bowls.

Day 1: Introduction
“This workshop is chance to explore in a visual way abusive relationships. The workshop will help us to see what emotions look like.  Let’s reflect on how a teen would feel in an abusive relationship as the victim or the perpetrator…  Can you visualize how those feelings are reflected in facial expressions?  What do people’s faces look like when they’re angry? (Can you make an angry face?  Let’s all do one together and look around.)  And how about sad or depressed?  Scared?  Or when you’re in love?  Happy?  Think about all those emotions that can be a part of an abusive relationship.  During this workshop you will be creating a mask to represent one of these feelings or a combination of these feelings.  You can start thinking about what emotion you want your mask to portray, but it’s okay if you don’t know.  You might find out as you work with the clay and that’s fine.”


 
 
 Forming the Sculptamold clay.
  

Opening Circle:
Ask the youth what feeling they are thinking about portraying with their mask. It can be helpful to show drawings of mouths and eyebrows for different emotions (e.g. Feelings Faces Chart) or have the group demonstrate with their own faces different emotions. Talk about what shape the mouth makes and if the eyes are open, half closed, if the brow is furrowed, etc.  This will assist them later when they are creating the mask.

1: Newspaper
(This step can be done before, during, or after the technical demonstration, depending on how you like to lead groups.)

Have participants create a mold out of newspaper. They can ball it up and squish the newspaper into a head shape, squeezing it tight to make it pretty solid.  It’s good to make the face side as smooth as possible, and the back of the head flat so it won’t roll around. They can use masking tape to tape the back of the oval ball…so the paper stays in place. Sizes will vary on how much Sculptamold you have and how large each participant wants to make their mask.

2: Demonstration
For the technical demonstration, mix up your batch and show how to layer the mix onto the mold, covering it half way, the layer needs to be at least a half inch thick. Demonstrate how to begin to sculpt the facial expressions. Let them know if they don’t like their first attempt, you actually have time to flatten out the features and sculpt them again. Smooth out the roughness of the mixture with your hands.  Let them know that the more they smooth it out before the mask completely dries, the less sanding they will need to do before painting the mask.

Demonstrate how to make openings for the eyes if they plan to have eyes…and an opening for the mouth.  Once the mask dries you will be removing the newspaper…so the openings will show.

Be sure to demonstrate how to make holes with a toothpick so they can attach hair or wire so their mask can be hung on the wall.

Also, be sure everyone has their newspaper molded before the relaxation, so they can jump right in after the relaxation.

Note:  Depending on their age you can have them mix the Sculptamold themselves or mix it for them.  If they are going to mix their own, have the bowls and bags of mixture all laid out with water.  If you are going to mix it for them, be sure to mix it right before they are going to use it.  It dries quick and can’t sit around long.

3: Relaxation
Although youth often balk at the relaxation part, I find it really important to do!  I always tell youth that the relaxation is to assist them in going within to get in touch with their creative power.  It helps to guide them into relaxing and once relaxed to begin to visualize in their mind the emotion they want to portray…to notice what the eyes are doing, to notice the eyebrows, are they drawn down like when you frown? or are they raised like when you are scared? etc.  To ask them to think about the mouth and what shape the lips are taking, are they snarled, smiling, open in fear, thin, tight, angry lips? The relaxation should guide them right into making their mask.


 
 
 “My colors hurt your eyes, like the blows
hurt my face.  Flaming streaks of burning
lies, not even my hair can hide my
disgrace.  My lips no longer lush.  Merely
swollen with blood.  My eyes cannot hush,
tears cause my brain to flood.”

    —Frank Ramirez, age 17
  

4:  Creation
This is the Creation Time…enjoy the peace of everyone being engaged in creating a powerful expression mask!  Encourage them to know it’s okay to see what comes out - it’s fine if it’s different from what they imagined in their mind.  It’s good to have paper and pencil for them to write about their mask after they are done, to write what feelings they are portraying or what their mask says about abusive relationships or teen dating violence.  They may choose to write again after the mask is completely done, with paint and hair etc.  Some may even want to write a story about the mask.

5: Wrap-up/Storage
If you plan to display them once they are completely finished, double check to make sure the participants have created holes in the sides of the mask for hanging.   Hand out cardboard or mat boards for the teens to store their masks on while they dry.  The drying process can take a couple of days depending on location, and weather.  The directions on the bag say you can bake the mask in an oven to assist with the drying.  Be sure to watch the oven so they don’t burn!   

The next part of the workshop is when the masks almost come alive!  

Day 2: Decorating
Have the youth think about how they want to decorate the mask. They can paint the mask without sanding it down if they like the rough texture or they can sand it first.  Different grades of sandpaper will work, either fine or medium.

How much or how little they decorate is up to them, they can add wire for hair or to represent stuff coming out of the mouth, like verbal abuse or angry sounds. The wire is from disposed of phone wiring—if you strip off the plastic coating you will find many thin strands of multicolored wires.   They can be bent or shaped and attached to the mask.  (If they didn’t make holes to tie them to, you can use a fine drill to create holes, or use a glue glue gun or FabriTac glue.)   


 
 
 “I’m so stupid I can’t be worth more than this. 
Why does he do this to me?  I need him, so I can’t
leave.  When he hits me, I feel vulnerable, like a
baby.  He has complete control of me.  I’m stuck.
I’m scared.  I’m stupid.”

    —Jennifer De La Rosa, age 17
  

Again when they are completely done decorating the mask, they may want to write about the finished mask, either adding words to what they have already written or starting fresh.  Many may want to write a complete story about the mask!

When they are all done, it’s wonderful to put them up as a display with their words.  You will find the masks make a powerful statement.  (To hang, insert fishing wire into holes on sides of mask.  Again, you can drill holes if they weren’t created when the masks were wet.)
Row.txt_description: This mask process allows youth to think about teen dating violence in a visual way. The masks demonstrate how people look when they are in abusive relationships and are experiencing a combination of complex emotions.

Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Tupelo models Graduation Hat.



Objective:
To create Graduation Hats as a way of noticing and validating each participants accomplishments in taking steps toward their future.  To notice the significance of each achievement (little and big) in light of the remarkable evolutionary process they are undergoing.  To celebrate these achievements, allowing time to notice and define them.  To help them remember how much they are actually accomplishing even when things seem challenging.  To create something that can serve as a reminder of their achievements and can be used again and again to celebrate new successes.

Materials:
Thick paper or cardboard (at least 1 per participant)
Collage option materials – Glue sticks, photo stock books, magazines
Fabric option materials – Assortment of fabric, Super Glue, stapler
Assortment of ribbon and yarn for tassels and decoration





Olivia models Graduation Hat.



Scissors
Pens/pencils
Writing paper
Optional – Beads and other decorations to weight the end of the tassels
Note:  The Graduation Hats can be decorated in so many ways, consider having other materials available - Paints, markers, crayons, oil pastels/Cray-Pas

Space Setup/Preparation:
If you are planning on making fabric decorated Graduation Hats, it is helpful to make one yourself so that you know how best to manipulate the fabric and attach it to the board.  Also, when you are preparing the cardboard squares you may want to pre-punch the center hole for the tassel.  (Using the tip of scissors works fine.)   

Timeframe:





Graduation Hat detail.



Total Time

1 hour
Opening Circle

15 min
Warm-up

5 min
Graduation Hats

20 min
Pomp and Circumstance


Ceremony

5 min


Closing Circle

15 min



Introduction:
“Today, we are thinking about the things we have done that are a ‘first’ in our lives and in our family.  The ways we have broken out of previous molds and are creating a new generation of success.  We are going to notice the many steps we have taken in our lives that are steps that have never been taken in our families before.  We are going to notice how by making the choices we have made, we have graduated from an old pattern, an old way of being into another, more positive one.  We are going to celebrate our graduation into new ways of thinking, feeling, and being by making Graduation Hats – mortarboards and tassels.  Then we will celebrate our graduation into our new lives by having our own graduation ceremony, with the pomp and circumstance we deserve.”    




Cathy models Graduation Hat.




Opening Circle:
“For our opening circle let’s each share something we have succeeded in doing that we had to learn how to do for ourselves: maybe you’ve done something that had never been done in your family before.  Some of these things might seem small, like baby steps, but they are not, they are worth noticing because without these steps we could never have changed the path of our lives and the lives of our families.  For example, I am the First in my family to… Believe in Myself, Believe I Deserve More, Say No, Ask for Help, Draw Boundaries, Create a Safe Environment, Be Addiction Free, Make My Dreams Come True, Protect Myself, Protect My Children.  I am a First Generation… Survivor, American.
(As Leader, you may want to choose an example that is personal for you to help encourage each participant to share.)

Go around the circle and have the participants each share an accomplishment.

Visualization:
“Now that everyone has an accomplishment in mind and can remember the steps they took to achieve it, let us begin to celebrate these victories the way they deserve.  We will begin by sitting quietly and comfortably and taking some deep, calm breaths.  Now, imagine yourself standing before the steps of a large stage on a grassy lawn.  You are wearing a beautiful long graduation robe and a graduation hat in the same color, what color is it?  Maybe it is your favorite color, this beautiful color is the color of your school… dark green, bright yellow, royal purple, robin’s egg blue…  You watch the material of your robe glisten in the sun, is it silk? is it velvet?  You watch it shimmering and notice the tassel swaying gently from your hat.  You remember that this is your graduation day.  You feel warmed by the sunshine from the outside and warmed by pride on the inside, you feel confident and calm.  Take a moment to breathe in the warm sunshine and the green grass, breathe in the energy that you have taken to get here, breath in the courage you have shown to reach this moment… As you breathe, notice the steps leading up to the stage, count them, and as you count them, breathe, one breath for each step, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7…  As you reach the last number you hear a familiar, loving voice calling your name from the stage.  It is a voice you recognize and love, you breathe in this love as you begin to climb the steps in front of you, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7…  As you reach the top step you see a kind face holding out a hand to help you up the last step. You take the hand and see that this person, the person congratulating you with love and pride, is you.  It is the future you, the you that you have been in the process of becoming and she has been waiting patiently at the top of the steps to help you onto this stage.  She not only wants to help you, she wants to thank you.  She thanks you for making her life possible and her eyes are full of gratitude and love, she is so happy to see you today.  As she releases your hand she gently moves your tassel from one side of your hat to the other and says, ‘Congratulations,’ and then she hugs you, a perfect, gentle, loving, and warm hug.  As you breathe in her love, you hug yourself, a long, gentle, perfect, loving and warm hug.”




Graduation Hat detail.




Creation:
After the warm-up, it is time to create the Graduation Hats.  Explain how each participant gets to make their own hat.  Encourage the participants to think about their accomplishments and express their pride in these achievements onto their hats.  They can create whatever makes them remember their achievements and successes.

Suggest to the participants that they begin when they feel ready.  



Pomp & Circumstance:
As the participants complete their Graduation Hats, help them one at a time to congratulate themselves and move their tassel from the right to the left of their hat.  It is not necessary that the art work be placed on the participants head!  

If the group is cohesive enough, you might also consider celebrating the graduations during the closing circle.  

You might also consider having the participants partner off and do an echo listening exercise that ends with the listener moving her partner’s tassel to celebrate the graduation she has just echoed.  

Remind the participants that they can have their own private graduation ceremony anytime they want to celebrate a new accomplishment by moving the tassel from one side of the hat to the other.  





Tango, AWBW mascot, models Graduation Hat.



Closing
Encourage each participant to share about their experience of making their Graduation Hats.  They might share how it felt noticing their groundbreaking accomplishments or any insights they have gained into their ability to handle the challenges they currently face in making their dreams a reality.
Row.txt_description: Participants create Graduation Hats as a way of noticing and validating each participants accomplishments in taking steps toward their futures. The end product serves as a reminder of achievements and can be used again and again to celebrate new successes.
