Ask the participants what feeling they are thinking about portraying with their mask.  It can be helpful to show drawings of mouths and eyebrows for different emotions (e.g. Feelings Faces Chart) or have the group demonstrate with their own faces different emotions.  Talk about what shape the mouth makes and if the eyes are open, half closed, if the brow is furrowed, etc.  This will assist them later when they are creating the mask.

1: Newspaper
(This step can be done before, during, or after the technical demonstration, depending on how you like to lead groups.)
Have participants create a mold out of newspaper. They can ball it up and squish the newspaper into a head shape, squeezing it tight to make it pretty solid.  It’s good to make the face side as smooth as possible, and the back of the head flat so it won’t roll around.  They can use masking tape to tape the back of the oval ball… so the paper stays in place. Sizes will vary on how much Sculptamold you have and how large each participant wants to make their mask.

2: Demonstration
For the technical demonstration, mix up your batch and show how to layer the mix onto the mold, covering it half way, the layer needs to be at least a half inch thick.  Demonstrate how to begin to sculpt the facial expressions. Let them know if they don’t like their first attempt, you actually have time to flatten out the features and sculpt them again.  Smooth out the roughness of the mixture with your hands.  Let them know that the more they smooth it out before the mask completely dries, the less sanding they will need to do before painting the mask.
  


Forming the Sculptamold clay.
 
  
  

Demonstrate how to make openings for the eyes if they plan to have eyes… and an opening for the mouth.  Once the mask dries you will be removing the newspaper… so the openings will show.

Be sure to demonstrate how to make holes with a toothpick so they can attach hair or wire later on, or attach wire so their mask can be hung on the wall.

Be sure everyone has their newspaper molded before the relaxation, so they can jump right in after the relaxation.

Note:  You can have each participant mix her own Sculptamold or mix it for them.  If they are going to mix their own, have the bowls and bags of mixture all laid out with water.  If you are going to mix it for them, be sure to mix it right before they are going to use it.  It dries quick and can’t sit around long.

3: Relaxation
I find it really important to do a relaxation before beginning the masks.  I always tell the participants that the relaxation is to assist them in going within to get in touch with their creative power.  It helps to guide them into relaxing and once relaxed to begin to visualize in their mind the emotion they want to portray…to notice what the eyes are doing, to notice the eyebrows, are they drawn down like when you frown, or are they raised like when you are scared, etc.  To ask them to think about the mouth and what shape the lips are taking, are they snarled, smiling, open in fear, thin tight angry lips?  The relaxation should guide them right into making their mask.

4:  Creation
This is the Creation Time…enjoy the peace of everyone being engaged in creating a powerful expression mask!  Encourage them to know it’s okay to see what comes out - it’s fine if it’s different from what they imagined in their mind.  It’s good to have paper and pencil for them to write about their mask after they are done, to write what feelings they are portraying or what their mask says about abusive relationships.  They may choose to write again after the mask is complete done, with paint and hair etc.  Some may even want to write a story about the mask.

 
 
 “My colors hurt your eyes, like the blows
hurt my face.  Flaming streaks of burning
lies, not even my hair can hide my
disgrace.  My lips no longer lush.  Merely swollen with blood.  My eyes cannot hush, tears cause my brain to flood.”
—Frank Ramirez, age 17
  

5: Wrap-up/Storage
If you plan to display them once they are completely finished, double check to make sure the participants have created holes in the sides of the mask for hanging.  Hand out cardboard or mat boards for the teens to store their masks on while they dry.  The drying process can take a couple of days depending on location, and weather.  The directions on the bag say you can bake the mask in an oven to assist with the drying.  Be sure to watch the oven so they don’t burn!   

The next part of the workshop is when the masks almost come alive!  

Day 2: Decorating
Have the participants think about how they want to decorate their mask.  They can paint the mask without sanding it down if they like the rough texture or they can sand it first. Different grades of sandpaper will work, either fine or medium.

How much or how little they decorate is up to them, they can add wire for hair or to represent stuff coming out of the mouth, like verbal abuse or angry sounds. The wire is from disposed of phone wiring—if you strip off the plastic coating you will find many thin strands of multicolored wires.   They can be bent or shaped and attached to the mask.  (If they didn’t make holes to tie them to, you can use a fine drill to create holes, or use a hot glue gun or FabriTac glue.)    
  


“I’m so stupid I can’t be worth more than
this.  Why does he do this to me?  I need
him, so I can’t leave.  When he hits me, I
feel vulnerable, like a baby.  He has
complete control of me.  I’m stuck.  I’m
scared.  I’m stupid.”
—Jennifer De La Rosa, age 17
 
  

Again when they are completely done decorating the mask, they may want to write about the finished mask, either adding words to what they have already written or starting fresh.  Many may want to write a complete story about the mask!

When they are all done, it’s wonderful to put them up as a display with their words.  You will find the masks make a powerful statement.  (To hang, insert fishing wire into holes on sides of mask.  Again, you can drill holes if they weren’t created when the masks were wet.)








Optional Closing:
Brainstorm a "Safety Plan" with the women to help them process their anger. Some helpful tips include:
Talk to a friend you can trust
Count to 10
Take out art supplies and draw a picture of your anger
Journal about your anger
Take deep breaths
Listen to music
Walk away
Dance or exercise
Row.txt_description: This mask process allows participants to think about domestic violence in a visual way. The masks demonstrate how people look when they are in an abusive relationship and are feeling a combination of complex emotions.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Note About Anger Workshops
We recommend that you start anger workshops with a discussion; don't be afraid to talk to the women about their anger. Anger is nothing to be ashamed of, it is important to look at and talk about it to try to understand it.

Some anger prompts that we like are:
What is Anger? What does it look like and what does it sound like?
What was the trigger to your anger?
What did you think about it?
How did it make you feel?
How did you act?
What effect did it have on you and those around you?

Row.txt_code:
Past and Future Journey Footprints
 
Objective:
To allow each participant to create a collage that validates their unique journey through domestic violence using the outline of their own foot as the template of the collage.  For most of us life is a journey.  When we leave abusive situations our feet carry us out and those same feet can carry us into a new life free from violence.

Materials:
Poster board
Glue sticks
Scissors
Magazines
Markers
Construction paper
Feet template
Relaxing music
Laminating sheets, Contact paper or laminator (optional)

Workshop Preparation:
If you are worried about not having enough time for the participants to complete the workshop, an easy way to save time is to print the attached Feet Template on colored cardstock. Invite the participants to select which pre-printed colored footprints they want to collage on, rather than taking the time to trace their own feet. This is also a recommended alternative for participants who are uncomfortable revealing and tracing their own feet. If possible, we do recommend that you ask the participants to trace their own feet since it adds a personalized element to the workshop!

Introduction/Opening:
Have the participants introduce themselves and give one word describing how they are feeling today. Explain the Journey Footprints Workshop (it helps to have some examples for the clients to examine), emphasizing the importance of including their whole journey through domestic violence and encouraging them to add hopes and dreams for the future. Briefly explain the collage technique, while passing out scissors, glue sticks, etc.

    
  Cutting out the foot
 
Step 1: Trace the outline of each participant's foot onto poster board and have her cut it out.

Step 2:
Using relaxing music lead the participants through a simple deep breathing exercise.  Emphasize that this is to help them focus and center in on the activity at hand, honoring their own experiences and feelings.

You may want to end the relaxation with, “Now, as you sit breathing deeply and slowly, I want you to remember that this is a time for you.  A time for you to share some of your journey through domestic violence, as well as a time for you to envision a life free from domestic violence.  Think about your feet... where have they carried you in your journey through domestic violence?  What images, words, colors come to mind?  Where would you like your feet to carry you now?  What would a life free from violence look like?  What images, words, colors come to mind?  When you are ready you can open your eyes and begin your journey collage.”

Step 3:
 
 
  Gluing Images
 

Encourage the participants to use the collage materials in the way that best illustrates their journey.  Have them collage on only one side of the foot.  Note: If the participants have limited or no experience with collage I encourage them to choose a large picture or use construction paper to cover the whole foot and then add words or images on top of this. This way they can achieve an end result they are more pleased with. As they become more skilled at collage it becomes easier for them to piece together a seamless looking collage.

Remind them to include their whole journey through domestic violence; past, present, and future hopes and dreams. (I have found that it is sometimes easier to focus on the future exclusively. Gently reminding them during the process can encourage them to include the past and present also.)


 
 
  Journey Footprint
 
Step 4:
When participants finish their collages encourage them do some writing on the back of the collage regarding what the collage means. Remind them to sign and date their collage. This is good for tracking progress.

Step 5:
If possible, laminate the collages. Cover the entire footprint using self-laminating sheets or contact on both sides. Cut off any excess laminating material and voila...they look great and last longer! 

If you are using a laminator, the leader will most likely need to do the laminating, as lamination sheets can be tricky and unforgiving when you make a mistake.

Note: After laminating, small pieces of magnetic tape (adhesive backed) can be added to the back of the collages so they can be hung on a metal surface.

Closing:
Encourage participants to share something from their collages and/or the experience of making the collage and seeing their whole journey on their own foot. Affirm each person’s experience.
Row.txt_description: Participants create collages that validate their unique journey through domestic violence using the outline of their own feet as the template of the collage.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
AWIC Gratitude Mandala
 
“I am grateful for being connected to so many beautiful people: family, friends, work, and volunteers. Even people I don’t know but share that ‘look of understanding,’ that light bulb going on. We are all so different yet connected. Thank God for our connectedness.” —Denise Nyby
Coordinator of Windows activities in Redding, California

About this Workshop:
Alexa Singer-Telles created the “Gratitude Mandala Meditation” used in this workshop. She shared it with the group of AWBW leaders in Redding, California. We are happy that she put it into writing so that other leaders can use it. It is a very wonderful, powerful, and detailed relaxation and guided imagery.

 
  Arctic Women in Crisis
Gratitude Mandala Display
“Gratitude Mandala
For groundedness
of body and earth,
Love for all in my life,
Flames of spirit
that support me on my path.
Empty brain is transformed
into pearls of wisdom.”
—Alexa Singer-Telles

Objective:
To give each participant an opportunity to reflect on different aspects of herself—body, heart, mind, and spirit—and notice her gratitude for gifts and blessings she notices in each of these areas.

Materials:
Circles to draw on:
Use bowls and/or other round objects of various sizes so participants can trace their circle mandala shape onto large paper. (You could also use blank pizza rounds, or cut construction paper or poster board into circles.)

Something to decorate with:
You could provide markers, pens, pencils, pastels, paints, collage materials, etc. Choose whatever you think will work best with your group. Remember that too many choices can be overwhelming. Sometimes simplicity is best.

Relaxing music


 
 AWIC Gratitude Mandala
 
Introduction:
“Today we will be reflecting on gratitude. We’ll be starting with a gratitude meditation. I’ll lead it and it’s sort of like a ‘time-out’—a time to let your eyes close, rest your head on the table if you like, and completely relax. If you’re not comfortable closing your eyes, that’s okay. Do whatever helps you to relax. This will be a chance to notice the gifts and blessings you are grateful for in your life. We all have much to be thankful for. We have amazing bodies, minds, hearts, and spirits, that help us do the very best that we can, even during difficult times. So today is a sort of ‘time-out’ to notice these gifts we have. I will lead the meditation and then at the end we will have a chance to draw a mandala, using whatever images, shapes, colors, and words come to us during the meditation. A mandala is a drawing done in the shape of a circle. You can fill your circle however you like. You could start at the center and make layers of rings, each one different. You could create slices, like a pie. There is no right or wrong. Your circle is just a place where you can express whatever shapes and colors and images you wish.”

About Mandalas: Mandalas have been used throughout history as a meditative and healing type of drawing. In some parts of the world, people create mandalas as a form of prayer. They can be very intricate, circular designs. Sometimes people look at mandalas in order to meditate and find clarity.

Relaxation:
“Get comfortable. Close your eyes. Notice your in-breath and out-breath. No need to change it, simply notice the breath as it enters your nostrils, fills your chest. Notice the exhalation, the letting go. Allow each out-breath to be a release of tensions, of thoughts, of any stress that holds you back from being fully present.

“Take a few moments to let the awareness of breathing in and out calm and relax you. You may want to imagine a healing or calming color and with each in-breath feel that calm, healing color as energy filling your entire body, from your toes…all the way up your legs… into your pelvic area and inner organs… into your back – from the lower back, through the mid-back to your upper back. Feel the healing and calming energy come into your belly… your lungs… your chest… feel it relaxing your shoulders… your neck… and gently feel your face muscles, your jaw, your eyes and ears relaxing. Take another few moments and check to see if any part of your body is still carrying tension or stress. Breathe into it a sense of calmness, breathe out, letting the exhalation be a release of tension, a letting go.

“Allow your mind to rest. Let any thoughts that arise fall away with the breath. No need to dwell on your passing thoughts right now. Simply follow your breath, noticing the thought but not grasping it. Imagine the thoughts are like clouds that float by in a blue sky. Let your thoughts just float away.

“In this clear space, we will be taking some time to create a circle of gratitude in our mind’s eye. Know that each person will imagine in their own unique way. You may see images or pictures, or you may have a feeling sense, or an idea or a word. There is no right or wrong way, simply follow your own imaginary experience without judgment. Just let happen what happens.

 
  A Gratitude Mandala from an
 AWIC participant
“Imagine yourself in a place that is safe and comforting to you. It could be inside a dwelling or somewhere in nature. It could be a place that you know or one that you make up. Just know that the place that you find is safe and sacred, allowing you to relax and take some time for self-reflection. Notice what is around you in this place, what colors, textures, smells, and objects. Find a place to sit or lie down and get comfortable. For this is a time for you to acknowledge the gratitude you have for your own life and your ability to share those gifts with those you love. Imagine you are gathering those images, symbols and thoughts of gratitude into some sort of a basket to bring back with you.

“Beginning with your body, becoming aware of the gifts your body has given you in the recent past. Has it been strong, has it gotten you where you needed to go? What image or feelings of gratitude do you have for your body? Place whatever symbol arises into your basket.

“Next, allow yourself to experience your open-heartedness. What is in your heart that you are grateful for? Place those images or symbols or feelings into your basket.

“Next, allow yourself to be aware of your mind, of its strengths and gifts. Place those thoughts into your basket.

“And finally, how has your spirit or your connection to a Higher Power or the Divine served and supported you in your life? What image or symbol comes to your awareness to represent your spiritual connections? Place that symbol into your gratitude basket.

“Notice how full your basket is and how it shines with all the gifts of who you are. Take this full basket with you as you leave this sacred place in your mind’s eye and begin to return to this safe and special room. Take your time, slowly feel and wiggle your fingers and toes. Find yourself present in this room. Slowly open your eyes.

“When you are ready, create a mandala using the images, feelings, or sense of whatever came to you in the meditation.”

  
 Arigaa!-Inupiaq word means, “sweet,” or “so good 
Creation:
Individually encourage the participants as needed, as they choose their supplies and begin their mandalas. Remind them that there are no right or wrong ways of creating it.

Closing:
Give each participant an opportunity to share her mandala and/or the experience of going through the meditation. How did it feel, reflecting on all the different aspects of themselves for which they can be thankful? Affirm each person's experience.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants an opportunity to reflect on different aspects of themselves (body, heart, mind, and spirit) and notice their gratitude for gifts and blessings associated with each of these aspects.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give participants a chance to focus on lessons they’ve learned, express them, and carry them forward in their lives in a strong, solid form.  

Materials:
Smooth stones (available at building supply/garden stores)
Colored pencils and sharpener
Specialty pens: metalic, gel-roller, and/or paint pens
Acrylic paints
Paper plates
Small brushes
Water cups
Paper towels
Blank paper for drawing, painting, or writing


  


“Love, Rest...”
 
 

Note on Variations:
See the other options for working with the stones (at the end of this Update).  Choose whatever you think will work best with your particular group.    


Introduction:

 
 
 “Courage...”
  

“Today we will be making Learning Stones.  Have you ever heard the idea that rocks have wisdom in them?  Have you ever thought about how old they are, how many years they have been here?  Thousands?  Millions?  Some rocks are thousands and thousands of years old—much older than we are.  Some people believe that the rocks around us have spirits in them, and knowledge to share with us.  Sometimes when we are most tired, confused, or upset, it can be calming to sit against a big rock and just imagine how long that rock has been sitting there, how much it has seen, and what knowledge it might have to share and help us.  Today we will be reflecting on the lessons we have been learning in our lives—lessons we’ve learned from people, from nature, from deep within ourselves, from God or a higher power (if that is our faith).  We will each have a chance to create our Learning Stone.  With paint, pens, pencils, or whatever you want to use, you can express those lessons that have come to you.” 

  


“Where do you want to go?”
 
 

Opening Circle:
“Let’s start by each sharing thoughts about something we’ve learned.  What do you know deep in your heart?  What do you know that can never be taken away from you?  Whatever comes to mind is fine.  It can be serious or silly.  It can be personal or spiritual.  And it’s okay if nothing comes to mind.  This is just a chance to explore out loud together.”


Technical Info:  
“Before we begin with our stones, I’ll share a little about the supplies we have.  You can use them and combine them any way you want.  We have a few different things for you to use:  There are paints, pens, and colored pencils.  (Demonstrate each technique as needed).  Try not to worry about what you will create.  You can let it unfold and trust whatever comes to your mind.” 


 
 
 “Together we are strong!”
  

Relaxation:
“Take a stone and place it in front of you.  Hold it in your hand.  Notice the weight of it, the texture, the temperature.  Before beginning to create on it, just take some time holding it.  Let your eyes close if you feel comfortable closing them.  Take a nice deep breath in, and let it out.  Notice your breathing as it goes in… and out…  Picture letting go of any tension with your breath.  As you breathe, notice yourself becoming relaxed and calm.  As you breathe, notice the rock gently resting in your hand, becoming warmer against your skin.  If this rock had a message to tell you, what would it be?  Does anything come to mind?  Are there any lessons this rock wants to share?  What does it want to remind you that you already know?  Take as much time as you like just holding your rock, breathing in and out, relaxing and listening.  When you are ready, you can open your eyes and begin to draw, paint, or write on your stone.  Follow whatever comes to mind.  If you feel like you need to draw, paint, or write on paper instead of the stone, you are welcome to do that.  If you need to work on more than one stone, you are welcome to do that as well.  Follow whatever you are moved to express.”

  


“Soul...”
 
  

Creation:
“As you begin to create your Learning Stone, remember there is no right or wrong.  You can just trust whatever comes to your mind.  Try to give yourself complete freedom: freedom to explore, freedom to make a mess, freedom to learn.”

Closing:
Give each participant an opportunity to share her Learning Stone (or Stones) and what it (they) means to her.







“Love is not violence...”
Row.txt_description: Gives participants a chance to focus on lessons they’ve learned, express them, and carry them forward in their lives in a strong, solid form.

Row.txt_code:
It’s Behind Us... A New Life
Artist: Anonymous
 
  



 Rising Above All I Lost
Artist: Patty Owens Badgett
  
About this Workshop:
Often, while in the shelter, the clients want to create a reminder of this time that they can take with them when they leave.  Catherine’s workshop gives a very simple, direct, and wonderful way to do this.

Note: The illustrations on these pages are actually Journey Markers (see December, 1996 Update).

Objectives:
To give participants something they can take with them when they leave the shelter—a “Bookmark in Time” to remind them of when they were here.  To give them a marker that can help them remember the difficult circumstances and experiences that brought them to their courageous choice of coming into shelter.  To give them something to help them summon that resolve and courage when they need it after they leave the shelter. 


 
 
 No Holds Barred
Artist: Rose Curtis
  

Materials:
Heavy paper (pre-cut into bookmark sized pieces)
Magazines and/or photo stock books
Glue sticks
Scissors
Optional: Laminator

Introduction:
“Today we will each be making a Bookmark in Time.  This is something for you to have when you leave the shelter.  It is a reminder of when you were here.  It is a reminder of when you made this courageous choice to come into shelter.  

“This workshop is not about bright and shiny futures.  It’s about where you are now, and making a marker to remember it. 

“As each of us knows, life can be hard.  When you’re out of this shelter, you might need to remember where you started.  You might need some way to recall the courage inside of you that has brought you this far.  You can use your bookmark to help you remember this time when you left your abuser.  Your marker can be a reminder of why you left and the sacrifices you made in order to start a new life.” 

Opening Circle:
“Let’s start with a check-in.  Share you name, how you’re doing today, and anything you want to remember about why you made this brave decision to come to shelter.  Share anything you want to remember about this difficult and important time once you leave this shelter.”

  


And Still We Rise
Artist: M. I. Hernandez
 
  

Technical Info: 
“Here is the paper and supplies for collaging.  I’ll lead a relaxation and then everyone can begin to create a Bookmark in Time.” 

Relaxation:
“Get comfortable in your chair.  Take a deep breath in... and let it go.  Before we begin creating our bookmarks, I want us all to have a little time out—a time to just notice how we are feeling, here and now.  Let your eyes close if you feel comfortable closing them.  Take another nice deep breath in... and let it go.  As you breathe and relax, picture yourself walking in a nice, safe place—wherever you feel safe and warm.  Breathe in the fresh air as you walk along, safe and comfortable.  Notice what is around you.  Are you on a favorite street?  Are you on a beautiful hillside?  Are you at the ocean?  Wherever you are, breathe deep and feel the safety and relaxation.  As you walk along, take some time to notice how you’re feeling right now at this point in time.  You have come through many difficulties.  You are in the midst of such huge changes.  What do you want to remember about this time?  Notice whatever comes to your mind, and when you are ready, you can open your eyes and begin to create you bookmark in time.”

Creation:
“As you begin to create your bookmark, choose whatever images grab your attention.  See if you can trust your intuition.  See if you can create a marker of where you are now:  all the difficult things, all the newness, all the hard choices you’ve had to make.  See if you can find a way to place all of this onto your bookmark.”

Closing:
Give each participant an opportunity to share their bookmark and what it means to them.  Validate their courage and strength.  Encourage them to carry their bookmark with them.  Let them know their expressions are very important.

Lamination:
If possible, laminate each participant’s bookmark.  This will make it much more durable for them to carry with them on the journey ahead.
 
 
  An exhibit option from Deb Blackstone
at South Lane Mental Health in Oregon
Row.txt_description: Gives participants something they can take with them when they leave the shelter. The marker helps them to remember the difficult circumstances and experiences that brought them to their courageous choice of coming into shelter.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop will teach the children about using a new and fun material while empowering them to think about positive sides of themselves.  The books can be an expression of themselves plus the hidden pockets can be used to save private messages or store special things.

   
  Anna Reyner teaching The Many Sides of Me
 
Materials:
BioColor Foam Paint
Paper plate to use as a palette
White Paper Bags - lunch bag size (3 per person)
Craft Sticks (one per book)
Rubber Bands, medium sized (one per book)
Soft paper towels
Crayons (inexpensive crayons with a higher wax content are preferred)
Hole punch (a two- hole punch is ideal)
Glue sticks
White construction paper for warm-up
Plain paper for writing exercise
Pens or Markers
Wet wipes

NOTE: the workshop can be messy but the Foam Paint is washable.

Workshop supplies can be purchased at www.discountschoolsupply.com .   Remember to use the source code AWBW to receive your 15 % discount.

Timeframe:
Total approximately 1 hour 30 minutes (you might want to divide the group into 2 sessions)
Foam Paint Warm Up: 10 minutes
Introduction:  10 minutes
Book assembly: 10 minutes 
Writing exercise: 15 minutes
Creating book pages: 20 minutes
Cover design: 15 minutes

   
  Sample book
 
Preparation:
It is helpful to make a sample of the Paper Bag Book ahead of time to show the children.  First assemble your book, then follow the writing exercise to get your book content. Lastly, use your content to write and illustrate the book. For the illustrations you’ll use fluffy Foam Paint” with paper towel "rags" to apply the paint. Create your sample book from your own voice as a leader, someone who provides healing, compassion and positive solutions for children and families in need. Go to the Writing Exercise, Creation (Part 2) and begin by writing down 5 positive “I am” statements about you and your role as a caregiver.  You may consider including statements such as:  I am a caring person, I am an agent of change,  I am a positive role model, I am loving.

   
  Foam Paint
 
Set Up:
  • Prepare paint palettes, 1 palette (paper plates) for every two children. Spray a small “mound” of foam paint onto a paper plate. Use about ½ cup of each color, but don’t measure, just estimate.  Spray out 3-5 colors in total on each paper plate.  You can replenish colors later if needed. Light and bright colors work best.
  • Group supplies: In the middle of the table place paper towels, crayons & pre-prepared paint palettes.  
  • Individual supplies:  In front of each seat place 1 craft stick, 1 rubber band, 3 white paper bags, 1 piece of white construction paper
  • OPTIONAL:  Hole punching requires that each of the 3 paper bags have two holes punched (see Quick Paper Bag Book instructions).  You can pre-punch the holes before the workshop, or if you have a small group of children (8 or less), you can punch the holes as they watch.  Older children can punch their own holes or help you prep the book holes for younger children.  A two-hole office punch works best.
Introduction:
Today we are going to work with Foam Paint. It’s something you probably haven’t played with before. Let me show you a little about it.  The foam paint not only looks super cool, but it makes a crazy sound when it comes out of the bottle!  Now everyone stay very quiet and see if you can hear the noise it makes (spray some of the foam onto the palette).    Look, I can even paint like Michelangelo in the Sistine Chapel and paint upside down (turn the foam paint palette upside down)! See how the paint stays solid!  But today we’ll smear the foam paint with paper towel rags and you’ll see how bright and beautiful it is, and how easy it is to work with.

Because it’s so fun to work with, you’ll find that it brings out your creative side. Is everybody ready to try the foam paint?  Let’s get started with a little warm-up exercise.  


   
  Name Doodle warm-up
 
Warm Up:
A nice way to warm up is by making a “crayon resist” design with your name, we call it a name Doodle. 

Step 1:
Take the white construction paper and crayons and write your name in bold, block letters. Press hard with the crayons so you’ll lay down lots of wax.  The more inexpensive crayons lay down more wax than the expensive Crayola brand which is why we recommend you use them.  Then add more lines, shapes and colors to make a Name Doodle design out of your name.  Remember to press down hard to get lots of wax on your paper, and use at least 4 different colors so your Name Doodle will be nice and bright.

Step 2:
Next take a paper towel and bunch it up in your fingers to make a paint “rag.”  Press this rag gently onto Foam Paint, getting one or several different colors onto your rag.  Pat your colors all over the top of your crayon design, covering ALL the crayon and paper so no white shows through.
 
 Dabbing the Foam paint onto the crayon
drawing or words
 
 "Polishing" the Foam Paint
 
Binding the book with a craft stick
and rubber band
 
 Sharing in pairs
 
  Writing the "I Am" statements
 
 
 
 Create your pages
 
 
 Anna shows the secret pockets in the book
 
 
 Illustrate the cover design


Step 3:
Take a clean paper towel and wipe off all the Foam Paint.  Keep wiping off the paint until your paper is dry. Now “polish” the crayon parts and to make them shine.

Step 3:
After children finish, ask them to partner up with their neighbor and talk a little about their Name Doodle.  Ask them to share something about their name, like who they were named after or what they like or don’t like about their name.

Creation:
Part One - Book Assembly

 4 Steps to book creation















Part Two - Writing Exercise
Now let’s do a writing exercise which will give you ideas for your book.  I’d like you to think of nice things about yourself, things you feel good about. Think of ways you behave that make you proud of yourself.  Think of what you like your friends to notice about you - For example do your friends say that you are smart, funny, or thoughtful.  Write down some of these good qualities and turn them into “I am” statements. For example you might write down I am smart, I am funny, or I am thoughtful. 

Take a paper and a crayon or marker and number your paper from 1-5.  Then write “I am” in front of each number. Then go back and write down 5 things about yourself that you really like.  Some examples might be:  I am caring, I am strong, I am creative, I am honest, I am funny, I am smart, I am a poet, I am a dancer, I am a singer, I am a baseball player, I am a soccer player, I am helpful, I am an artist, I am happy, I am mad, I am strong, I am silly, I am funny, I am a fast learner, I am full of good ideas, I am good friend.   

  1. I am  _________________________
  2. I am  _________________________
  3. I am  _________________________
  4. I am ___________________________
  5. I am ___________________________
Part Three - Write and Illustrate Book
Now transfer your ideas onto the pages of your book, writing one “I am” statement on each page.  (Save the cover design until the end)  Put a separate I am statement on each of the 5 pages in your book.  Write with crayons or markers. Use crayons to illustrate your ideas and add color, pressing hard to lay down lots of wax.  Take your time and be creative with each page, using lots of different crayon colors.  When you are happy with the design, it’s time to add foam paint on top.  Follow the same steps you learned in the Name Doodle warm up:  Cover your designs with foam paint, rubbing it on and off with paper towels.  Each paper becomes a statement about who you are.

Note that several of the pages have "pockets" where secret messages or hidden treasure can be kept.  When you open up the book you can lift up one side of the page (the side that contains the bottom of the bag) and write messages that will stay hidden there.  If time permits, take a moment and show the children where each of the pockets and hidden spaces can be found in the book.

Part Two - Cover Design
Save the cover for last, you can draw a shape, picture, or doodle that represents you, using a bold colored crayon. If you like you can also write your name or a title for your book on the cover. Cover with the Foam Paint like you did on the other pages.

Closing Circle:
After the children finish their books, ask them to partner up with a neighbor and share their books with each other, page by page.  Ask for volunteers and see if anyone would like to share their book with the whole group.
Row.txt_description: This workshop will teach the children about using a new and fun material while empowering them to think about positive sides of themselves. The books created can be an expression of themselves plus the hidden pockets can be used to save private messages or store special things.
Row.txt_tips: You can use the Foam Paint in many different ways.  For example you can tell the children more about how Michaelangelo spent four years painting the Sistine Chapel upside down.  Then tape a piece of paper underneath a desk (for each child in the group) and ask the children to create their very own masterpiece upside down!

Row.txt_code:
About This Workshop:







This workshop came about when another support group leader in the Haven House program (Marcia Young) approached me with a request for some colored markers.  Her support group participants were asking for name tents (folded paper name signs) to help them learn each other’s names.  She thought about offering them stickers or small pictures to decorate the Name Tents.  After we talked about it and tried it out in both of our support groups we came up with this workshop.  The participants were very excited with this project and put a lot of effort into making the name tents reflect who they were, what they liked, what they wanted the other group members to know about them.







Objectives:
To give each support group participant an opportunity to focus on and express her own identity by creating a “Name Tent.”  To build sharing and connection among the group members and help them learn each others names.

Materials:
Heavy card stock paper-size  8”x11” either colored or white paper
(I find that in the finished project, colors look better than white.)
Glue sticks and scissors
Markers
Small words/pictures cut from magazines
Relaxing music
Optional: glitter glue markers, stickers, etc.

Preparation:
Make the blank Name Tents by cutting the card stock in half (widthwise). Fold each half in half again—you can get two name tents out of each piece of card stock.

Introduction:
Explain that these Name Tents will be used in support group to help them learn each other’s names.  The collages on the tents will help the other group members to learn some important things about them.  When living in domestic violence situations they often loose sight of who they are and what is important to them.  This workshop will give them a chance to identify who they are and express what they like in a safe, non-judging atmosphere. 




Name Tents lined up on the table for a photo.




Step 1
Distribute Supplies:
Pass out Name Tents, scissors, glue sticks.  Make markers and magazine pieces available to all participants.

Step 2
Relaxation:
Using relaxing music, lead participants through a simple deep breathing exercise. Emphasize that this is to help them focus on the activity at hand, honoring their own unique identity. 

Step 3
Creation of Name Tents:
Have participants write their first names (no last names) on their Name Tents.  This allows them more room to collage while making the name large enough to be easily seen. Encourage the participants to choose pictures and words to collage onto the Name Tents.  These words and pictures should describe who they are, what they like, and what they want the others in the group to know about them, focusing on the positive. 





Shar’s Name Tent with colorful flowers.



As you can see by some of the pictures included, some participants chose to collage on both sides of the Name Tent. 

However they may need to be reminded not to cover up their names in their enthusiasm!

Closing:
Encourage everyone to share their Name Tents with each other. Focus on the positive words and images of each artist, the unique qualities and the similarities.




Chris’s Name Tent with keywords about faith and balance.




Further Use:
I keep the Name Tents in our group room so they can be used in each support group.

I have the materials handy at the beginning of support group (on a small table in the room) so as new members join the group they can create their own Name Tent.  To make this as non-threatening as possible (especially since my support group has some members that don’t attend the art program), I have them start by only putting their name on the tent.  I encourage them to add pictures/words as they become more comfortable with the group.  Other group members often add to/change their Name Tents as time goes by.

This is a new project for our groups, so we are finding new ways to utilize the Name Tents—our parenting program leader is adapting this idea for her classes as well. 

This workshop is a unique way of utilizing Art Empowerment in other areas of your domestic violence program!  I would enjoy hearing about your experiences with this workshop and any changes or modifications you find that work for you and your group.




Lynn’s Name Tent with flowers, stars, and words of confidence.
Row.txt_description: Gives each participant an opportunity to focus on and express her own identity by creating "name tents" that build sharing and connection among the group members and helps them learn each others names.

Row.txt_code:
“Recovery from the Heart and Living by
Spiritual Practices...” — Kimberly Lyon
 
  
Objective:
To give participants an opportunity to recognize what they treasure in themselves and their life by exploring their blessings, dreams, beliefs, friendships, hopes, and and creating a treasure boxes to hold them and keep them safe.

Materials:
Boxes (1 per participant—I recommend the small wooden boxes you can get at Michael’s for $1 each or paper mache boxes work well too.)
Paper and pens for writing
Paper towels
Newspaper to cover table
Painting supplies: acrylic paints, paper plates, small brushes, water cups
Specialty pens: metallic, gel-roller, or opaque paint pens
Collage supplies: photo stock books, magazines, stickers, scissors, glue sticks
Mirror paper (Mirror surfaced paper is available in the poster board section at Michaels.  One sheet can be cut to fill many boxes.)


 
 
 Blank wooden boxes from Michaels,
ready to be made into Treasure Boxes.
  

Introduction:
“Today we will each be making a Treasure Box. When you picture a Treasure Box, what do you imagine? Pirates, jewels, gold coins?  Treasure Boxes were built to protect valuable things. They were made to be strong on the outside and filled with precious things on the inside. As we make our Treasure Boxes today, we will be taking time to slow down and notice the things within us and in our lives that are most precious and worth protecting: our selves, our strengths, our blessings, our dreams, our hopes, our beliefs.

To explore the treasures within ourselves, we will start by doing a visualization or guided meditation. Try not to worry about what you are going to create on your box. Try to trust that whatever comes to your mind through the visualization will be just right. This is a chance to treasure whatever happens. There is no right or wrong. Your Treasure Box can be whatever it becomes.”    

  


Painted and collaged box with view inside.
 
  
Opening Circle:
“Let’s start by each sharing thoughts about what we treasure—whatever comes to mind is fine:  what’s one thing you treasure in yourself or in your life?”  

Technical Info:
“Before we begin the visualization, I’ll share a little about the supplies we have. You can use them and combine them any way you want. We have a few different things for you to use:  There are paints, pens, and collage supplies.  (Demonstrate each technique as needed.) Feel free to decorate the inside and outside of your box. Feel free to make parts of your box blank and open, or fill them with all sorts of shapes and images. Feel free to create little notes or messages to put on the inside of your box. What you create is up to you. Take a box and place it in front of you. Open it and close it. Notice all the sides of it.  It is your blank canvas upon which to create.  Ready for the visualization?”    

Visualization/Guided Mediation:

 
 
 “I tried to include all of life’s experiences inside my box
such as friends, family, material things I ‘treasure,’
painful experiences, etc.” —Anonymous
  
In a calm, gentle, clear voice share the following...
“Get comfortable in your chair. If it feels safe, let your eyes gently close or set your gaze downward. Make sure your feet are settled on the floor and notice how the chair is holding you. Now take a deep breath in…  and let it go… Notice your breath going in and out. No need to change it, simply notice the breath as it enters your nose, fills your chest. Notice the exhalation, the letting go. Allow each breath out to be a release of tensions, of thoughts, of any stress that holds you back from being fully present.  Take a few moments to let the awareness of breathing in and out calm and relax you.  Allow your mind to rest.  

“In this clear space, we will be taking some time to notice what we treasure. There is no right or wrong way, simply try to follow your own experience without judgment.  

“Imagine yourself walking on a beautiful beach. Breathe in the fresh air. Feel the ocean breeze on your face and notice the gentle warmth of the sun on your arms.  

“What sounds do you hear?  Can you hear the waves?  Can you see the colors in each wave as it rises and falls?  Do you see any birds soaring over the water?  As you walk, feel the sand beneath your feet, between your toes, wonderful and warm. 

  


“My Treasure Box means so much to me.  I
named it ‘my treasures’ because my life is
what I treasure today, and that’s what I did
on it.  My life today is free of abuse.”
   —Laura Nelson
 
  
“As you walk, you notice something shining in the sand up ahead. It looks small, like a piece of metal. As you kneel down and brush away the sand, you find that it is a beautiful box. Notice the color of it. Notice the details of decoration.  As you hold it somehow you know that it is safe and welcoming, and meant for you.  As you lift the lid, you see your favorite colors. And you see thing you treasure. What do you see?  Notice whatever things come to mind.  What do you find in your box? [Pause…]  

“As you reach further into your box you find photographs. There are pictures of people, places, times you have treasured in your life.  Who do you see?  Notice their warmth and love for you.  What do they want you to know about yourself? [Pause…]  

“As you reach further into your box, you see notes and you recognize the words. They are the helpful things people have said to you— things that have stayed in the back of your mind and helped you through your life. What are the messages you see? [Pause…]   

“At the very bottom of your box you find one more thing. It is a beautiful mirror.  As you pull it out and look into it, you see yourself, but you see yourself in a way you’ve never seen. In this mirror, you see clearly all the things that are precious and wonderful about you. You see your strengths, you see your courage, you see your spirit, you see your caring, you see what a good person you are, what a treasure.  

“With the sun on your back keeping you warm and relaxed, you know you can take as much time as you need with your box. When you are ready,come back into this safe and special room. Here, you will be creating your own box, using whatever colors, shapes and thoughts you want to from that treasure box in your mind’s eye.


 
 
 “Look inside.  People tend to work on the
outside and then not have enough time or
energy for the inside, but my Treasure Box is
filled with work...”  —Loretta Pearce
  
“With your eyes still closed, take your time, slowly feel and wiggle your fingers and toes.  Find yourself present in this room. When you are ready, open your eyes and begin to create your treasure box.”

Creation Time:
“As you begin to create your Treasure Box, remember there is no right or wrong. You can just trust whatever comes to your mind. Try to give yourself complete freedom, freedom to explore, freedom to make a play. You can work on the inside, the outside, you can make things to put inside. It’s up to you."

Closing Circle:
Give each participant an opportunity to share their Treasure Box and what it means to them.
Row.txt_description: In this workshop, participants have the opportunity to recognize what they treasure in themselves and their life by exploring their blessings, dreams, beliefs, friendships, hopes, and and creating a treasure boxes to hold them and keep them safe.
Row.txt_notes: children’s manual pg. 43

Row.txt_code:
Crayon Feelings drawing: “So much going on, but I’m
finding my own center...”



About this Workshop:
This is a very simple and direct workshop—about as simple as you can get—but quite powerful.  It requires practically no set-up or preparation.  The supplies are very inexpensive and accessible.  

At AVDVC, our workshops are only one hour long, so we need projects that can be accomplished in an hour, including enough time for sharing.  This is an excellent workshop in a short time-frame.  If you have longer, it allows even more time for sharing, which is great!  

This workshop is a great one for clients who don’t want to participate.  They can just take all their grumbling and resistance and put it on the paper.  

This workshop is also effective with teen groups I lead.

Objectives:





Basket of crayons for
Crayon Feelings workshop.



To put feelings into shapes and color.  To experience a completely free, no-pressure, expressive process— free from worrying about creating a product or what it will look like.  To discover and explore how our feelings can change through the process of expressing them.

Materials:
White copier paper (enough for plenty of sheets per participant)
Crayons—in big shoe boxes (or baskets)
Optional: journals for the writing part of the workshop.  (It’s also fine to write on the copier paper)
Pens
Relaxing music




Simply supplies: crayons and paper.




Setup:
Place the paper, pens, and crayons in the center of the table.  Get your music ready, and you’re all set!

Timeframe:
Total:  1 1/2 hours
10 minutes    Introduction
10 minutes    Relaxation
15 minutes     Drawing
20 minutes     Writing
30 minutes    Sharing


Opening:
“Today we will be drawing our feelings in shapes and colors—no pictures—just whatever shapes express how we’re feeling.  It’s fine if you’re mad, tired, or don’t want to be here.  Whatever you’re feeling, that’s what you get to put on the paper in shapes and colors.  Remember, we’re not going to be making pictures—no drawings of things.  Just use the colors and shapes to represent what you’re feeling.  Don’t worry about what you’re going to make, or what colors you want to choose.  I’ll be leading a relaxation, and you can just see what comes to mind during that.  Take some white paper.  Take a few sheets in case you need more than one.  I’ll lead a relaxation and then we’ll dive in.”





Crayon Feelings drawing: “Letting out the anger and finding
tenderness surrounds me...”



Relaxation:
“Get comfortable in you chair and take a deep breath in.  Let your eyes close if you feel comfortable closing them.  Take another deep breath in.  As you let it go, try to let go of any tension in your body.  Let any tension out with your breath.  And take another wonderful, deep breath in.  And then let it go, breathing out any tension.  Take a few more nice deep breaths and notice yourself relaxing more and more with each one.”  (pause)   

“As you keep enjoying your relaxing breaths, picture yourself in a place where you feel safe and find beauty.  Are you inside or outside?  Notice your beautiful place.  Take some more deep breaths as you sit in your beautiful place...  (pause)  When you’re ready, notice how you are feeling.  Notice what colors come to mind.  Are you feeling blue?  Red?  Lavender?  Yellow?  Green?  What colors come to mind?  And what shapes?  Spirals?  Straight lines?  Swirls?  Scribbles?  Whenever you are ready, you can open your eyes and begin drawing in shapes and colors, however you’re feeling.”  




Crayon Feelings drawing: “Running into the
tough spots and finding joy too...”




Drawing:
As people draw, encourage them to keep trusting whatever comes to mind.  Encourage them to fill the whole page, and encourage them to use as much paper as they need.  

Allow them to continue drawing for about 12 minutes.  Then let them know “You’ve got about 3 minutes left, so start getting your thoughts together for writing.”  Then give another reminder when they have a minute or so left.

Writing:
“Now we’re going to take about 15 minutes for writing (in your journal or on a piece of paper). Write down how you feel now, and write about how you felt when we first started.”

Again, give everyone a 3-minute warning near the end, and then a 1-minute warning, etc.

Closing Circle:
Give each participant a chance to share anything she wants to about what she drew, wrote, or experienced.  Let them know it’s fine to pass if they aren’t comfortable sharing.  When you’ve gone all the way around the circle, come back to those who passed and give them a chance to share if they’ve changed their minds.
Row.txt_description: A chance to put feelings into shapes and color while experiencing a completely free, no-pressure, expressive process - free from worrying about creating a product or what it will look like.

Row.str_author_location: Sexual Assault Crisis Agency, Long Beach, California
Row.txt_code:
< /tr>


 Christina Curtis
  
Objectives:
To give the clients an opportunity to explore feelings and issues and gain self-awareness by creating a brick wall to represent the emotional walls they have built in order to survive.  To notice what shows to the world and what stays hidden inside.  To explore the positive and negative aspects of having the wall, and consider what it might be like to take it down.     

Materials:
Clay or Supersculpey
Pens, needles, or something sharp for writing into the clay
Newspaper to cover the table (if you’re using messy clay)

Relaxation:
Guide the participants through a relaxation exercise that leads them to identify things they hide from others.  

Creation:
Tell clients that they are going to make a brick wall, where each brick they create will have writing on it.  The brick that will be placed on the bottom of the stack will symbolize the things they hide from the outside world.  The brick on top of the stack will symbolize what the outside world sees.  They are free to make as many bricks as possible to create their wall.  

Sharing:
At the end, ask if they would like to share.  Encourage them to express whatever they discovered about themselves and their issues through making their wall.    Encourage them to smash down their wall, if they wish.  

Note:  The poem below by an anonymous survivor illustrates one woman’s exploration and experience of the walls she created to survive.  Remember that everyone’s wall will be unique.  There is no right or wrong.  There are positive things and negative things about having walls.  There are reasons why we built them as we did. 

 

 

The Wall: Freedom in Three Parts

Part I
It took six months to build the wall

The first brick was laid when I decided that instead of being “again” in a never ending hell, this time would mark the beginning of a change.

The second brick was laid the very next day when I broke through the silence of shame and told a friend what had happened.

More bricks were added later that week when I raised the courage to call the Family Violence Project.


 
 
  

The next week I began a new weekly routine. Tuesday morning I walked to work, went in the back door, out the front door, got on the bus and ducked when it passed our street and rode for an hour to group.  It was worth it.  Every Tuesday I returned with an armload of bricks.

In the evenings I began to take my daughter out of the house and back to my office, our hideout, where she could play in peace and I could hear the clink, clink, clink of bricks sliding into place.

When the yelling started at home and my body ached from the blows, I would leave.  I would pull inside of myself and retreat to the wall.  Just feeling its coolness, its roughness, its solidness gave me hope.

One night, when the pain was too much to bear, I wrenched my heart out of my chest and buried it in the path of the wall, laying bricks over it and marking it with a pebble.  The pain had been holding me back.  Without it I could focus on building the wall.

As the wall grew I found I could push some of the chaos behind it.  When the chaos could not touch me, I grew stronger.

It took an attorney, a restraining order, four cops and more support than I ever thought possible to push the last few bricks into place.  When the wall was complete, the chaos was gone.  The silence was deafening, the peacefulness overwhelming. 
I could finally rest.  I had escaped.  I was free.

Part II
The wall in my soul is four feet thick

It contains thousands of bricks.

It has stood for a year.

Behind the wall is chaos.  Behind the wall is the screaming voice, the raised hand, the cold gray eyes.  Behind the wall is every assault, every insult, every coercion, every degradation. Behind the wall is the power that controlled me.

The wall protects me.  It is stronger than the power on the other side.  The wall is stronger than any one person because it is held together with the experiences and understanding of many women.  I add my experiences to the mix and make it stronger.  By making bricks and passing them on to other women, I strengthen myself.

The wall is cool.  It contains the heat.  The wall is strong.  It has withstood the violence of hurricanes raging on the other side.  The wall is high.  It shelters me as I grow stronger.  The wall is solid.  It protects me.

The wall has saved my life.

The safety of the wall is my freedom now.  With it, I am able to live each day.  For now, that is enough.

Part III
The wall will not stand forever

The wall that keeps me safe also restricts me.  It gives me room to breathe but not to move.  Sometimes I wish that the wall were gone, that I could stretch my arms all the way out.  Sometimes I wish I could hear music.  Sometimes I wish I could dance.

The wall separates me from the person I was “before.”  I don’t know her anymore.  In pictures, she looks like a stranger.  I can’t get close to her because the wall is in the way.

But the wall is only temporary. 
It will not stand forever. It cannot stand forever, because my heart is buried beneath it, healing in the cool dampness of the earth.

When I am stronger than the power on the other side of the wall, the wall will no longer be necessary.  I don’t know when or how, all at once or piece by piece, but the wall will come down.  And when it comes down, I will see the power on the other side of the wall reduced to ashes blowing in the wind, no more significant than crumpled bits of leaves I can kick out of my way.

When the wall comes down,
I will stretch.  I will dance. 
I will reach out and embrace the person I used to be.  When the wall comes down, I will find the place where my heart is buried and dig it up.  I know it will still hold pain, but I will be stronger than the pain.

When I reclaim my heart, I will be whole again.  I will be able to trust, to feel, to love.

When the wall comes down,
I will finally be free.

—anonymous survivor


Extra Workshop: Rules
Note: This project was adapted from a book called A Practical Guide to Art Therapy Groups by Diane Fausek.

Objectives:
To allow clients to examine the rules in their lives.  This activity is perfect for survivors who are in shelter.  They are suddenly living in an environment where there are a lot of rules that they have to follow. 

Materials:
Pastels and Construction paper

Activity:
1.  Begin a discussion about rules.  What kind of rules are there?  There are internal rules (morals) and external rules (“Stop at the red light”).  How do rules make you feel?  How does breaking the rules feel?  Ask each client to define her feelings about rules.

2.  Ask the clients to choose a color and pattern that reflects their feelings regarding rules and cover the entire paper.

3.  Now ask the clients what breaking the rules feels like.  Ask them to create the feeling of “no rules” over the existing picture.  Do not cover the original picture completely. 

4.  After they are done, ask the clients how rules or lack thereof coexist together.
Row.txt_description: Clients are given the opportunity to explore feelings and issues and gain self-awareness by creating a brick wall to represent the emotional walls they have built in order to survive.

Row.str_author_location: Based on O Magazine article 'After Great Pain' (Sept. 2002, pg. 121)
Row.txt_code:
Helping Hands artwork on these pages
by Olivia Tamayo and Cathy Salser
 
  
Objective:
To give participants an opportunity to reflect on the events of September 11th in an atmosphere of safety and support.  To explore what it takes to emerge from great pain and trauma such as this by creating a “helping hand.”  To notice the deep significance and impact of giving and receiving help.

Non-9/11 Note:
This workshop can easily be shifted
to focus on the importance of giving and receiving help, with no reference to 9/11.  Only focus on 9/11 if you feel it would be useful for your group.

Materials:
Heavy paper
Scissors
Markers, colored pencils, collage supplies, glitter, watercolors
Hole punch and thread/string

Timeframe:
Total:         2 hours
10 min:   Introduction
20 min:   Opening circle
10 min:   Relaxation
50 min:   Creation
30 min:   Sharing


 
 
  

Introduction:
“With September here, I know we have had the 11th on our minds.    This workshop, ‘Helping Hands,’ will be a chance to explore our feelings about what has happened and give ourselves and each other a helping hand in coping and moving forward.  It is a chance to trace our hands, draw, and write as a way of finding strength and clarity together.

“There are so many different ways to find strength and clarity.  Can you think of some?  Letting the pain out is an important part of recovering.  Looking for the positive can also be an important part of healing.  There’s an article about this in the September O Magazine.  It talks about how people who have survived some of the worst situations in history - even torture and imprisonment - survived best by focusing on positive things like making a difference in the lives of those around them.  The author shares:

“Perhaps the most difficult part of recovery is squeezing the good out of the horror.  Since we’re stuck with September 11, we should try to learn from it.  We should live more fully in the present tense because we have been reminded how fragile our lives really are.   We should remember the many cell-phone calls from the buildings and planes that were about to go down, and how much that repetitive cliché of three words meant to all the people who heard ‘I love you’ before the final moment...”

“So today as we create our Helping Hands, we will notice not only the hard things but also the good things.  The ways we have seen people helping each other so bravely and boldly in the face of this tragedy.  The ways we have seen people reach out to each other.  The ways we can all make a difference in the lives of those around us. 

Opening Circle:
“Share one thing you lost and one thing you gained because of 9/11.”  (Alternative non-9/11 opening: Share one time you remember being helped by someone, and one time you helped someone else.)

  


  

Technical Info:
“Thanks so much for sharing all your thoughts and feelings.  As we create our Helping Hands today, I want you to know you can trust whatever comes to your mind.  We’ll be doing a relaxation and then diving in.  Remember that whatever you create is just fine.  There’s no right or wrong.  You can trace, cut, draw, and write.  You could make your hand two-sided or work on just one side.  Your hand could be a place to let out all the pain, worries, and fears.  It could be a place where you count your blessings and look at what you are thankful for and want to remember because of 9/11.  It could be a place where you write and draw all the help you noticed, and the ways you’d like to be a help in creating a violence-free future.  Whatever you create, let it be a Helping Hand for you, helping to carry you through these rough times of so much change and uncertainty.  You don’t need to plan it out.  Just trust whatever comes to you.”  (Show the supplies - paper, scissors, pens, glue, etc. so that after the relaxation everyone will be able to just dive in.)

Relaxation:
“Get comfortable in your chair.  Let your eyes close if you feel comfortable closing them.  And take a nice deep breath in...  And let it go...  Good.  And now take another deep breath in...   And let it go.  As you breathe in, imagine pure relaxation is coming into your body, washing through you and draining all the tension away.  And take another nice deep breath in...  And let it go...  Good.  Now with your eyes still closed, put your hands together gently.  Put them together any way you like.  Move them together, noticing the warmth and comfort hands can give.  Imagine someone giving you a helping hand when you need it... a comforting hand.  Take a deep breath in and appreciate that comfort...  And now imagine how it feels when you give someone else a hand of comfort and help, and you know it is making a difference.   Take a nice deep breath and notice the strength and caring that come from your hands.  And now imagine how it feels when you are gentle and comforting with yourself.  Take another nice deep breath in and notice how wonderful and important it is - that comfort and help from yourself.   You can keep your eyes closed as long as you want.  As you breathe deeply, just drink in all these kinds of helping hands.  Take your time.  And when you are ready, open you eyes and begin creating your Helping Hand.”

Creation:
As the group creates, encourage them to trust whatever comes to them and not criticize it.  Let them know when there are 15 minutes left, 10 minutes, 5 minutes, etc.  For those who finish early, encourage them to write about what they have created and/or create another Helping Hand to give someone else. 

Sharing:
Give everyone an opportunity to share their creations, what they means to them, and anything they discovered in the process.

Closure:
It is important to take special care to end the workshop on a positive and hopeful note, especially since this is such a deeply difficult subject.  If you think it would help, have a final closing circle after the sharing of the artwork.  Ask each participant:  What is one positive thing you take with you from this workshop?

You might want to end with a celebration of hanging all of the hands in the shelter.
Row.txt_description: Give participants an opportunity to reflect on traumatic events (i.e. September 11th) in an atmosphere of safety and support, exploring what it takes to emerge from great pain and trauma such as this by creating a "helping hand."
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Objective:
This workshop was created with the intention of bringing forth the essence of the power of boundaries.  The group had been working on creating and maintaining personal boundaries, and I wanted to offer an opportunity to touch on the strength of power, not force.

Materials:
Large paper bags (brown grocery bags)
Cray-Pas oil pastels
Watercolors (Prang makes good strong colors)
Large container of warm water
Tea candles with containers

Timeframe:
Total:         1 1/2hours
20 min:   Visualization
50 min:   Activity
20 min:   Closing Circle

Setup/Prep:
It is optimal to have an open area that has plenty of space for movement, yet is near the area they will be working.  Place one of each item from the materials list for each participant. Place the tea candles too, but don't light them yet.  Have the container of water near by, but in a location separate from the working table, so spills don't occur where the work is being done.

Visualization:
We did this standing and with the eyes closed.  If a participant is too uncomfortable with eyes closed, perhaps they could stand near you or with their back to the wall and the exit door near them.  They may choose to do this with eyes open.


 
 
 Step 1:  Cut the paper bag to the
shape you desire.
  
 
 Step 2:  Draw an image of yourself.
  
 
 Step 5:  Paint with water colors
(after folded & wet).
  

“First it is important to feel centered in your body.  Find the center of the balls of your feet.  Find the center of your heels.  Rest in that place.  Find where your hips are square and comfortable.  Find where your shoulders are set and balanced.  Find where your head rests evenly on your neck.  Stay here for a moment.  This is a good time to thank your body for what it does for you.  In front of you, imagine there are four balls of energy: one blue, one green, one violet and one white. In a way that is most comfortable for you, bend, fold, twist or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the blue ball.  This ball holds the question for you ‘What am I made of?’ Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball. In a way that is most comfortable for you, fold, bend, twist or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the green ball. This ball holds the question ‘Where did I come from?’  Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball.  In a way that is most comfortable for you, fold, bend, twist or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the violet ball.  This ball holds the question ‘Who am I?’  Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball.  In a way that is most comfortable for you, fold, bend, twist or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the white ball.  This ball holds the question ‘What is my essence?’ Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball.  Now find and gather all the balls you have stored.  With the greatest care and with all the power you can muster, bring these balls together and merge them into one singular flame.  Remember to use your power, not force.  Rest with this flame.

(At this time you may want to go around and light the tea candles at each participants place.  Another option is to light the candles after they sit down. If you light them while they are still resting with their flame, be sure to let them know you will be moving about the room.)

For children:  You can use the same visualization, however, the questions can be adapted to the appropriate age levels.  For example:  for children in the 4-8 year range, the questions might be more concrete, such as “Who is in my family?” “Who are my friends?” “What makes me special?” “What makes me strong?”

For 9-12 year range, perhaps “What are my hopes and dreams?” “What makes me special?” “How am I strong?” “What feelings are in me that help me to understand myself?”


 
 
 Step 3:  Crumple, fold, or bend.
  
 
 Step 4:  Immerse in water.
  
 
 Step 4:  Take out of water to begin painting.
  

Introduction:
I did this workshop without giving an introduction to the participants.  I did not explain to them the intended process or possible outcome.  The reason for this was that they requested a workshop that had to do with boundaries and it was my intent to allow them an individual expression of the idea and experience.  It allowed them to bring together the multitude of sensations and experiences in their lives under one umbrella of “power.” The formulation was entirely their own and was not contrived for them.

For children, youth, and adults who may not be able to grasp without guidance, introduce the workshop as an opportunity to discover that power is a root of boundaries.  Force does not make happen what you want to happen.  Power is all around and in you and comes from our pain.

Awesome Essence Making:

Step 1.  Cut the paper bag into the size and shape you desire. You may need to show younger children how to get into the paper bag and cut the bottom off so it lays flat.

Step 2.  Ask the participants to use the Cray-Pas to draw an image of themselves. I let them know they are not bound to making a body. Often the image is of abstract shape rather than an identifiable object. What ever the image is, is fine.

Step 3.  “Crumple, fold, or bend the image and the paper bag. This is often hard to do because we don't like to mess up our art!!! This portion may also be representative of the pains we have endured, times we have felt folded, crumpled or otherwise “mutilated.” The more the fold lines are accentuated (by pressing harder) the more vibrant the paint will appear on those lines.”  Note:  You should experiment with this part prior to doing the workshop.

Step 4.  “Immerse the crumpled piece into the water.  You may hold it there for about 15 seconds or more, swish it around, squeeze it, whatever.” (This part allows the paper to absorb moisture, thus allowing the watercolors to do their job.  The more moisture in the paper allows the paint to fuse across the paper.)

Step 5.  “Open the paper flat and begin painting with the water colors. This process is much like the healing process. Washing our experiences, our perceptions of ourselves with what we believe to be helping us heal. The areas covered by the Cray-Pas will repel the water colors, while the mist area will absorb the colors.”  (It is best to use Prang Professional water colors, as the pigment is more dense and shows better on the darker paper.)

Closing:
I like to allow enough time for participants to express their sensations about the process as well as what the piece expresses.  I ask “What did I notice in my body as I worked through each portion of this process?” “What were my struggles and what were my joys?” “Was there a cathartic moment while I worked?”

I ask if that individual wants to hear feedback from the other participants. If they do, I ask others to give their sensations about that persons piece, not an artistic critique.  

I ask them to ask themselves “What sensations or feelings come alive in me when I
I observe your work?”

   


Awesome Essence drawing before the
 water and paint.
 Awesome Essence drawing after the
water and paint.
Row.txt_description: Brings forth the essence of the power of boundaries by offering an opportunity to touch on the strength of power, not force.
