Row.txt_code:
Many leaders have created wonderful workshops focused on hearts.  In your reports, we’ve noticed that these heart workshops seem to always be your favorites (and the client’s favorites)!  Here we share some of these ideas, so everyone can enjoy them!

See also:  “Affirmation Hearts” project by Rose Curtis in the August 2000 Leader’s Update.

  



 
  
Objective:
To give participants a chance to explore their hearts and notice the many layers—inside, outside, hurt, hopeful, strong, vulnerable, beautiful, and healing.  To give them a chance to express all these layers and notice that their heart is beautiful as a whole.

Materials:
See variations below and decide which materials your group would like best: 
    1. Watercolor
    2. Collage
    3. Drawing 
    4. Heart Ornaments 
    5. Lamination 
Or come up with your own supplies and process!

Timeframe:
Total:         1 1/2hours
20 min:   Relaxation
50 min:   Heart-making
20 min:   Closing

Introduction:
“Today will be a special time for us to listen to our hearts.  As you listen to your heart today you might hear difficult things, and you might also hear wonderful things.  You might hear pain, strength, brokeness, hope, courage...  Today is a special time to practice having tenderness and compassion for all that our hearts hold.  This is a special time to care for ourselves and our hearts.” 

Opening Circle:
Begin with a “heart circle” check-in giving each participant an opportunity to share how her heart is feeling today:  light?  heavy?  foggy?  clear? 

Relaxation:
Before you lead the relaxation, be sure to explain the art supplies and technical aspects of the heart-making.  This way, when the relaxation is over, the group can dive right in a create without any further instruction.

“Get yourself comfortable in your chair and gently place both your hands over your heart.  Let your eyes close if you feel like closing them, and take a deep breath in.  As you let it go, picture letting go of any tension in your body... and take another nice deep breath in... and let it go.  As you breathe deeply, notice your hands resting on your heart.  Notice that this is a special time to care for your heart—all the good things, all the difficult things, all that your heart carries inside...  This is a time to protect and thank your heart.  And this is a time to listen to it.  Whenever you are ready, you can open your eyes and begin to create what your heart tells you.”

 
 
 “Shadows , darkness, and light... 
Falling apart...”
  
 
 “Nurturing, growth, beauty.”
  
 
 “My heart can be beautiful again with
patience and time.”
  

Heart-making:
1. Watercolor
Healing Hearts
from Kori Taylor, The Abbie

Materials:  Watercolor paper (three small pieces per person), watercolor sets, brushes, water cups, paper towels, relaxing music, pens and paper for writing.

Process:  Have the group use the watercolors to paint three pictures of their heart on its journey of healing.  Watercolors are a wonderful way to explore and express what’s happened to our hearts and then how our hearts are healing.  The way the colors move and blend can express so much.  (See illustrations this page.)

2. Collage
What’s in My Heart?
from Silvio Velasco, YWCA Wings

Materials:  Heart outlines copied onto colored paper (see enclosed outline), glue sticks, scissors, and magazines.

Process:  This is a very simple project.  Hand out copied colored paper with outlines of hearts and have the participants collage onto the paper to show what is in their heart.  (It’s fine if they don’t stay within the outline of the heart.)  They can make it however they wish in order to show what’s in their heart.  (See samples this page.)
Comments:  “The supplies are simple and familiar, so the participants really like it and feel comfortable with it.  It was not too hard for them and at the end of the group, everyone shared.”

3. Drawing
Both Sides of the Heart
from Jeanne Anderson and Caroline Castleforte, Good Shepherd Shelter

Materials: Markers, construction paper, pens, pencils

Process:  This project uses two sides of the paper to show two different sides of the heart.  Have them use the two sides to show their heart felt before they came into the shelter, and their heart now that they are here in the shelter.  (Note: Variation 4 also builds on this theme.)

Comments:  “Participants were able to recognize feelings that they help deep within.  They were able to see that their heart was beautiful as a whole.  One of them shared, ‘Sometimes I try to hide what is inside my heart, because I think it’s bad, or someone will take advantage of me.’”

    




“Remembering my children who are not
with me...  These pictures signify how
much I love them and wish to have them
with me very soon.”
  “I pray for things to get better for myself.
I put everything on the table.  I feel free,
standing strong today.”
    

4. Heart Ornaments
How Does My Heart Look? 
from Cecilia Bendimez, WomenShelter of Long Beach

Materials:  Hearts copied onto white paper (two per participant—see enclosed master or make your own), markers, colored pencils, beads, yarn, scissors and glue.

Note: It can also be helpful to have a chart of different colors and what they can mean in terms of emotions.

Project: Talk about how different colors can convey different emotions.  (You can use a color chart, or just discuss various feelings and what colors might convey those feelings.  Remember, there is not a right or wrong answer.  Different colors can convey different things for different people.)  Give them each two hearts and ask them to use colors on one heart to show how their heart looked when they were in the domestic violence relationship.  Ask them to use colors on the other heart to show how their heart feels now that they are in the shelter.  They can then cut out their hearts and glue them back to back with yarn in between so they can hang it and see both sides.  Encourage them to share the differences and the reasons.

Comments:  “It really worked well.  They ladies enjoyed it and at the end, they really opened up.  And their hearts were amazing.  You could see the transition they were making in their lives. 

5. Laminated Mixed-Media
Hearts of Soul
from Obbie Brown, Valley Oasis

Materials:  Construction paper, scissors, edger scissors, markers, craypas, glitter glue, contact paper or lamination equipment, yarn and hole puncher.

  



 

 
Hearts from the “Affirmation Hearts”
workshop (August 2000 Update)
 
Process:  This workshop is the same as the Affirmation Hearts project (August 2000 Leader’s Update).  Each participant creates five cut-out hearts, decorates them, and writes something on each one that she would want said to her to help uplift her soul when she’s feeling down.  When all the hearts are made and laminated, they put them all into a bag, mix them up, and then pick 5 without looking.  Then each participant can string the five hearts she picked on yarn and hang them in her room as a reminder.  This way each woman will have something that speaks to her soul during those tough times when she might feel like going back to her abuser.  The heart messages come from deep inside your soul. 

Comments:  “This has to be one of the best projects that I’ve done.  The group sure loved it.  The sharing of the hearts reminded them of the saying ‘treat others as you want to be treated.’  They liked that they could give someone else a piece of a good part of their soul.”  (See samples this page.)

Closing:
Close with a special “heart circle.”  Give each participant an opportunity to share what she is carrying in her heart from the workshop.
Row.txt_description: A collection of heart themed workshops by different leaders, always favorites!
Row.txt_notes: ER TO DO: Get heart patterns photographed and entered.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give participants a chance to experience total artistic freedom. To allow the creative juices to really flow without any boundaries and at the end have a tangible symbol of that freedom and awareness. This workshop will allow the ladies to explore their feelings, instincts, talents, dreams, hopes, fears, likes and dislikes.

Materials:
Shrinky Dinks paper (Frosted Ruff N’Ready type – for use with colored pencils)
Permanent fine point markers
Colored pencils
Scissors
Magazines/stock books/coloring books, etc (for tracing)
Hole puncher
String
Doll template (click here for template master copy)
Grocery paper bags

Opening Circle:
Share how you feel about trusting your intuition.

Introduction:
Share the project with the group (see Instructions, page 3) so they will be ready to begin after the relaxation. It will help a lot if you have a sample already made to share.

  


  

Relaxation:
Dim down the lights and put a candle in the middle of the table. “Take three deep breaths. (If you feel comfortable close your eyes. If not, look into the middle of the table at the candle.) Now, take another deep breath and hold it for three seconds... and release your breath. Now, do this two more times. In your mind’s eye go to a place where you feel safe and calm and happy. This place can be a real place (a favorite beach, park, chair) or an imaginary place. Be there. Think of the sounds, smells, etc. of that place. Feel how comfortable and safe and happy you are. (This place can also be a place in your past where you were safe/happy.) Now become aware of the wonderful energy around you. (You can visualize energy as anything you want: light, small spheres, etc). Imagine you being aware now of all this positive energy around you and being willing to allow it to come inside you. In your mind’s eye see and feel it coming through your skin into you. Feel the warmth of it. Welcome it in – invite it in!”

 
 
 Martha Contreras holds three
intuition dolls.
  

“Now, when you are ready you are going to slowly open your eyes and you will remember the energy being inside you to guide you in this project and imagine yourself being in that safe/special place in your mind. Allow the energy in!

Instructions:
“Trace your doll template with a permanent fine point marker on the smooth side of your shrinky dinks plastic. This will be a guide only. You can alter the template as you are drawing it to make long hair, ponytails, a short dress, pant suit, etc. Anything you want your doll to be and/or have (hat, jewelry, etc). Once you have this outline (on the smooth side) turn the paper around to the "rough" frosted side and draw and/or trace (from magazines, coloring books, etc.) whatever comes into your mind with color pencils. Be creative, let yourself go, allow that energy that is inside guide you now! Even if you just use colors to signify different emotions, etc., your dolls will look great – that’s a guarantee!”

Once you are done coloring and drawing/tracing, you can cut out your doll. Think about how you are going to use your doll – a holiday ornament, earrings, pin, magnet, necklace, etc. If you are using your doll as an ornament or earrings, then your doll is going to need a hole on the top of her head for you to put a string through it. The hole needs to be done PRIOR to baking. If you are using your dolls as a pin or magnet, then no hole is needed. If you are using your doll as part of a necklace where more dolls are going to be “united,” then you want to put a hole on both of her hands so you can later unite the dolls by their hands with string or a “mini” paper fastener (these work very well).

  


Intuition doll sample before
baking and shrinking.
 
  

Now you are ready to bake! Follow the instructions on the package. Place a piece of the paper bag to line the toaster oven tray, plus make a small “handle” by tipping up one of the corners – this way you won’t get your hands burned. Most dolls will be “done” in 3 minutes. Be patient. Let the doll do her transformation and “lie down flat” before you take her out of the oven. Once you take her out, quickly put a book on top of her and press down hard for 15 seconds.

Technical Note to Leaders:
If the doll gets “stuck” within itself and does not want to “lie flat” at all even after 4 minutes, take her out while she still hot and soft and unstick her and put her back into the oven and see if that helps the process.

One of the dolls got her hands stuck when she was baking (like she was praying). We tried to unstick her hands twice and she kept putting her hands together. Well, after the second time around we decided to leave the doll be. Sometimes art has to be let be! The participant later on said that she will always remember the determination of her doll to be herself!

Closing:
Give the group an opportunity to share how they felt about the process of making their doll(s). It is okay if someone does not want to share, for these dolls can be VERY PERSONAL!


 
 
 Intuition dolls samples after baking and shrinking.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants a chance to experience total artistic freedom. Allows the creative juices to really flow without any boundaries and at the end have a tangible symbol of that freedom and awareness.

Amazon.com's Best of 2001
The Blueprint may be Jay Z's most captivating record since Reasonable Doubt, but its predictably detached mood reflects the master hustler's superior ability to trick out lackluster subject matter with lyrical complexity and brief flashes of manufactured introspection. The Blueprint, a solid mix of preprogrammed radio hits ("Izzo," "Girls, Girls, Girls") and better-than-average mid-tempo compositions ("Never Change," "Song Cry"), confirms the Brooklyn rapper's legendary status. Blistering flames of the Queensbridge/Jay Z feud fan high with "Takeover," a direct attack on Nas, set over the Doors' rock & roll burner, "5 to 1." "Renegade" provides the album's only full-on guest appearance. Jay and Eminem take this opportunity to address haters (within the industry and in the general population) who don't understand the mind of an artist. Jigga spells it out on the title track: "Reasonable Doubt--classic, shoulda went triple." The Blueprint might not be quite on par with Reasonable Doubt but it is reasonably good. --Rebecca Levine

Row.str_author_location: Windows Leader, Laura's House MFT Intern
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
The purpose of this project is for each person to create a personal drinking glass or cup.  This glass can be used for self-empowerment, spiritual renewal or just to create a quiet time for self-soothing. By drinking from this glass each woman ca n “fill her self up with the power of her own life and nourish herself with positive reflection”.
  


 
Hand-painted glasses completed at the
“Taste of Life” leader’s workshop in June.
  

Materials:
Porcelaine paints (can order from Dick Blick)
Outliner pens.
Rinse cups (two per person)
Paint brushes
Paper towels
Q-Tips for wiping off drips
Popsicle sticks to dip into paint
Paint palettes
Glasses (packages of 4 juice glasses are at Big Lots for $1.29 to $1.79).
Plain coffee mugs (Big Lots $.59 to $.99)
Tiles form Home Depot are about .79 a piece and the tiles could be uses as trivets, paper weights or hanging pictures.

Introduction:
Drinking glasses have for centuries (as early as 2000 BC) been used symbolically. Whether to seal a bargain, signal allegiance, perform a spiritual ritual or simply enjoy nourishment, drinking from a glass has represented empowerment, commitment and determination.

Relaxation:
Because of the fact that all art projects have to be conducted in the kitchen at the dining room table, it is often impossible to do guided relaxation because of the distraction of people walking in and out. So, we normally just do some stretching and deep breathing. It helps the women to relax and lightens the mood of group.
  

 
Working on a “stained glass” effect.

  

Opening Circle:
Can you remember a time in your life when drinking from a glass held some symbolism for you? Have you ever had a time when you sat down with a friend or relative and shared deep feelings over a glass of iced tea or lemonade or even cold water? Have you ever just taken a break from a stressful day to sit by yourself and sip some form of nourishment to revive? Or, do you have memories of a feeling of spiritual renewal after a religious ceremony concerned with the power of sipping from a cup or glass?


Introduction:
Today we will be making our very own personal drinking glass. Take a minute to think about the things that are important to you. Think about the changes that have happened in your life and the lives of your children since you had the courage to enter a domestic violence shelter. Give yourself permission to be proud of those changes. Picture the power you are creating for you and your children as you find the strength to change your life.

Remember that change does not come with out challenge. There will be times when you feel doubtful and afraid. The glass you will be painting today will symbolize your strengths and the things in life that make you strong. Whether it’s your love for your children, your hope for a new future, or your desire to discover a new way of life, I want you to think about your ‘powers’ as you paint your glass. Visualize your energy. Go to that quiet place in your heart that holds the power of your spirit. And when you feel ready, start to paint.

It’s important to know that it does not matter what you paint. It can be a summer day at the beach or an image of your future or just colors and shapes and swirls. It doesn’t matter if the paint runs (you can always wash it off and start over!!) or if it doesn’t look like what you thought it would. The only thing that matters is that you hold the image of your own personal power in your mind as you paint you glass.
  
 

“Mi Casa” glass.
  

Process:
Each of you has one glass, two rinse waters and some paper towels in front of you. Make sure to take a few sizes of brushes, being sure to include extra small to medium in size. The glasses are small so smaller brushes work best.

There are several colors of paint. Paint with one color at a time. Pick you color, shake the jar and remove the cap. There is a little cup inside the cap top. You will be using the cap as a palette. (You can also use a popcicle stick to dab a bit onto a tile or palette instead of using the lids.)  This helps to keep your brush from getting too much paint on it and makes it easier to apply to the glass When you are finished using your chosen color, replace the cap, rinse your brush, dry your brush off with the paper towels and get another color.

You will also notice that there are some squeeze tubes (outliner pens) of various colors on the table. These are used to outline shapes. They can also be used to write names or encouraging words that mean something to you personally. It’s best to practice on the paper towel in front of you first. These tubes have to be squeezed very gently for maximum usage.

When the glasses are done, you are encouraged to share your thoughts and meanings with the other participants. I have been using this project for years and I have never seen an ugly glass! So don’t worry. Just the paint alone makes the glass pretty.
  


Participant painting flowers onto her glass.
 
  
  

Tips:
No water in the Brush:  Use a dry brush to apply the paint.  After you rinse your brush, be sure to dry the water off completely before dipping into the paint again.  Water in the brush will make the paint too runny.

Wiping off the paint:  You can use a paper towel or Q-Tips to wipe off the paint if it drips or if you don’t like what you painted.

Layers:  You can put many thin layers of color on for a beautiful layered effect.  The thin layers dry quickly and don’t drip.

Where to paint:  Don’t paint inside the glass or too close to the rim.  The paints are not intended to be in contact with your drink. 

Baking the glasses:  Let the glasses dry for 24 hours. After that drying period, the glasses are baked at 300 degrees for 30 minutes. After that, the paint is set and the glasses can be washed (hand washed preferred) without washing off the paint.

Closing Circle:
Give each woman an opportunity to share about her glass and what it means to her.  (Sometimes it helps to put a paper towel in the glass when sharing so the design can be seen by everyone in the circle.) 
  
 

Using the glass paints on tiles.
  

Variations:
Hand painted tiles can be hung on the wall for inspiration. Coffee mugs can be used for coffee, tea and other hot drinks. Also flower vases, teapots, kitchen storage jars and any number of other glass or ceramic items suitable for painting. The purpose will vary with the project; Vases – flowers can symbolize beauty and hope and serve as a reminder of spring and new beginnings. Storage jars – this can represent saving for the future and planning for family needs.
Row.txt_description: The purpose of this workshop is for each person to create a personal drinking glass or cup. This glass can be used for self-empowerment, spiritual renewal, or just to create a quiet time for self-soothing. By drinking from this glass, each participant can "fill herself up" with the power of her own life and nourish herself with positive reflection.

Row.str_title: New Beginnings Workshop Series for Adults
Row.txt_code:
The New Year symbolizes a time for resolutions, new beginnings, and a fresh start! This time also encourages us to look back at the past year and all that you have accomplished or are ready to leave behind, where you are today and where you want to go, literally and figuratively. These workshops can offer participants an opportunity to listen to their hearts desire, notice their power and resilience and envision a future of their own choosing.

If you are doing any of these workshops as a new year activity, begin by first asking  participants to think about the New Year and what it symbolically means to them, if anything. Let them know you will be sharing a variety of workshops in the next sessions that will invite them to notice their power in getting to choose what they want and how they want to create it. To prepare your group to work together please consider trying an an embodied art activity, such as The Wind Takes Away that explores the many ways we are connected to each other or try one of the workshop offerings using the body as the creative medium.

Finally, remind participant to try to take these creative 'windows of time" to explore a future created by them: "What do you want?" "What are your goals?", and "What steps will you need to take to get to where you want to go?" No matter what the New Year means to them, encourage participants to take hold of their own power by embracing the potential and promise this new year holds!

Leader Hat Reminder: Keep in mind as you try these workshops that we encourage you to adapt the material to suit your needs and leadership style. If you like the theme or objective of one workshop but would rather try it using other art mediums - please do! And as always let us know how it goes!

 
 
   
Permission Canvases — This workshop will empowers participants to give themselves permission to do something they have been longing to do, to change a habit, or let go of something.

2000 Wishes  — Gives participants opportunity to reflect on their goals in relation to the coming year. The end product are special treasure boxes decorated to express each participant's personal wishes for the year ahead.

Building Resilience Workshop — Through the process of guided imagery, watercolor painting, and dimensional putty, this workshop can help participants learn simple self-regulation techniques by creating a flower painting, which can then serve as a calming image, a personal symbol of strength and reminder of our individual resilience.

 
 
 

 "My seeds of intention are new beginnings, family,
hope, faith and strength."
— Participant

 
   
 
 "The women are really embracing this window of time where they can reflect on where they have been and are beginning to appreciate the new path of where they have the potential to go."
— AWBW Leader

 
   
A New Year Journal — Engages participants in an opportunity to visualize and create a journal with unique resolutions for each month in the coming year. This allows them to create a path of healing and growth for themselves throughout the new year and encourages them to check in each month on following through with these goals.

New Year's Garden — Offers participants the opportunity to think about and explore their past, present, and future by creating a New Year's Garden.

Spirit Candles — The Spirit Candles workshop gives participants the opportunity to search for the strength and energy or light that nurtures and guides our spirit as we prepare for new beginnings. We will decorate candles by collaging onto them our biggest dreams and deepest hopes.

New Year's Wish Marker — Gives each participant a relaxing opportunity to think positively about the year ahead, and to create a vision in collage that they can carry with them into the year.

Flying Out Beautiful — This workshop gives participants a creative way to view how all of the challenges that they went through in the past have helped them gain strengths and tools to become the beautiful creature they are, or are becoming, with confidence.

New Year Wishing Well — This workshop uses the soothing and often cathartic exercise of working with Sculpey clay to create stones for a new year's Wishing Well, which they will also create!


"It was rewarding for the the women to have the opportunity to look into their future to determine what they want, and what they need to do to get there. It's a new year and most importantly a new start in their life for themselves and their children. Women loved this outlook and having the ability to plan and see a clear, happier future."
- Embracing Your Future workshop, AWBW Leader
Row.txt_description: The workshops featured in this series present creative ways to reflect on the past and imagine a new future through art! These workshops offer participant an opportunity to listen to their hearts desire, notice their power and resilience and envision a future of their own choosing.

Row.txt_code:
This Protective Shield includes "Family, Friends, Myself, Music."
  
Objective:
To give the children the opportunity to visually express valuable aspects in their life they wish to protect when they feel a sense of danger. To explore what it means to feel protected or safe and create something tangible that helps them feel secure.

Materials:
Poster board (Could precut out to the shape of a shield. It’s nice to have life-sized - about 27” tall and 18” wide.)
Glue sticks
Cray-Pas (Permanent markers optional)
Aluminum foil
Magazines and scissors
(Could precut images for younger children)

Timeframe:
  


 Protective Shield underway at Women's and Children's Crisis Shelter brings big smiles.
  

Total Time

1 1/2 hours
Opening Circle
 15 min
Activity
 45 min
Closing Circle
 30 min

Age Range / Ratio:
This activity is best suited for children 5 years and older. Recommended ratio is 1 adult for every 4 children.

Preparation:
There are two ways you can go about making a Personal Shield. You can have it as an individual project or a group project. The shield can be a collage or a drawing, whatever you feel the children will be most comfortable working with. You can precut the poster board into a shield shape or have the children cut their own desired shape. For younger children, be sure to precut the shields. Have them use the Cray-Pas and no foil. Even for older children, it can help to precut the shields and even the foil. Cut out long sheets of aluminum foil so those can also be ready for the children to cover the poster board with. Set up Cray-Pas, scissors and glue sticks for each participant. Finally, lay out magazines in the middle of the table for everyone to share.
  

 
Participant working on Protective Shield.

  

Introduction:
Some children may not know the history of shield in the medieval times. A brief history of the shield can be told in order to have the children more or less understand the shield concept:

Shields were once used as a main source of personal protection in war during the early ages. They were carried in one hand or on the arm to ward off enemy shots. Shields were not only for protection in battle, but also to identify its owner. The shields varied in size, shapes, and design. Can you think of a time when you felt you wanted to protect someone or something when you felt they were in danger? What kind of things do you wish to protect in your life? Why do you think you wish to protect them?

Opening Circle:
I feel it is important for the children to do a brief introduction of themselves. In this way everyone knows everyone’s name and it helps to break the ice if there are any new participants. They can also share their thoughts about protection.

The “Art Rule”:
We stress the importance of the “art rule.” The “art rule” at our shelter states, “There’s no wrong way to do art because we are all different. We cannot make fun of other peoples’ art.”

Activity:
“We’re going to start by wrapping the front sides of our protective shields with aluminum foil. Let’s try and get it on as smooth as possible and to put enough glue on the poster board before setting the aluminum on. Now divide your shield into 4 parts by using the Cray-Pas. Each section can be as big or little as you want. Each divided section can express a different valuable part of your life that you want to protect. You can select a title for each section and then begin to look through the magazines or precut pictures to present your valuables in a collage form.

Closing:
After the children are all done making their own shield or group shield, have them talk about why they chose that certain someone or something to protect. Encourage each to share, but make sure no one feels forced. They need to feel secure that no one will ridicule them in order to open up. Hopefully each child gets more than one opportunity to do the art workshops, bond with the other children and learn to trust the art facilitators.

You can also talk about how important it is to keep away from their parents’ fighting because they can get hurt. Discuss other means of protection such as calling the police when there is an emergency or talking to a teacher or friend as a form of protection and help.

Submitted by:
Rosalba Gonzales
Children’s Windows Leader for Women’s and Children’s Crisis Shelter (WCCS)

About this Workshop:
I am submitting this workshop to honor the legacy of Dolores Sosa, former
Children’s Windows leader at the Women’s and Children’s Crisis Shelter.
She has been promoted to be the new legal advocate for our agency, so
she will no longer be leading Children’s Windows. This is a workshop
she developed with a group of high school students at Santa Fe High
School who were working on their senior projects. I wanted to submit
this workshop to thank Dolores for the great legacy she left in the
Children’s Program at our agency. She began working as a Child Care
Aide for W.C.C.S. in 1999 and later got promoted to the position of
Children’s Advocate. I worked along side her for two years and have
never met anyone with such a strong work ethic. Dolores truly went
beond the call of duty and genuinely cared for the children.

Dolores’ idea for this workshop was to get the children thinking about things or people that they want to protect. As Dolores says, “I’ve always heard
children say ‘I’m going to protect my mommy’ when they speak about the
problems they have experienced at home. I’ve always wondered if their
mothers knew their children felt that way. Usually when parents are
fighting, children often get in the middle of the fight to try and stop
the fighting. Of course this is not a safe way for children to express
their feelings by getting involved because they could very well get
hurt. I believe if children are given the tools and time to create a
wonderful visual piece that represents what valuable things are
important to them, it could do wonders! Is also gives the mother a
chance to have an opportunity to speak to the child and have his/her
feelings validated.”

The group of students that Dolores did work with enjoyed it very much and put a lot of themselves into making it.

Special thanks to:
Diane Sanchez, Lupita Sosa, and
Joey Chavira at Santa Fe High.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives the children the opportunity to visually express valuable aspects in their life they wish to protect when they feel a sense of danger. To explore what it means to feel protected or safe and create something tangible that helps them feel secure.
Row.txt_tips: Be sure to have an example ready so the children understand the concept.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop supports children and teens in sharing their hearts and stories through art. The workshop gives them an opportunity to listen to their hearts, value the stories within them, and know that others want to hear them too.

Materials: 
 Timeframe: 
 Age Range:
Oil pastels (Cray-Pas preferred)
Thick white paper or watercolor paper
Brushes
Watercolors
Cups with water (2 per person)
Paper towels
Optional:
Paper for placemats
Music
 1 hour
Intro: 5 minutes
Warm-up: 10 minutes
Demo/Creation: 35 minutes
Closing: 5 minutes
6 and up
Note: There are two versions of the intro/warm-up to suit a range of age levels.


















  
  
  
Introduction:
Today our project is called Heart Stories. It’s a chance to notice what’s in our hearts, a chance to notice what our hearts would say if they could talk.

“This workshop is a window of time for you—a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you do or say is voluntary. I'll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there’s no right or wrong. It doesn’t matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this window of time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. Since this space is your window of time, everything you do or say is voluntary.  Please ask for what you need, and know that I'm here in support of you.”

Option 1: Heart Talk Warm-up:
This is an interview-style warm-up that participants can do in pairs. Pick 1-3 questions from the list below or create your own. Consider the age level of your group when you choose the question(s). If you are working with an old enough group, pick three questions and write them up to show the group.

Option 2: Confetti Heart Questions:
Print several copies of the questions you have selected for your group on colored paper and cut out each question separately. Scatter questions in the center of the table. Encourage participants to pick a question at random or to pick one that they like. Invite participants to each share a short answer to the question they picked.

Possible Heart Talk Questions:
  • What is something that made your heart happy this week?
  • If your heart was a color today, what color would it be and why?
  • What makes your heart laugh?
  • If your heart could do something fun, what would it do?
  • If your heart could do something it’s never done before, what would it do?
  • What’s something your heart is proud of about you or your family?
  • What makes your heart feel safe?
  • What makes your heart feel scared?
  • What makes your heart strong?
  • What makes your heart beat faster?
  • What makes your heart happy?
  • How do you look when your heart is sad?
  • How do you look when your heart is happy?

 "My heart feels glad because
I am thankful. 
There is no wrong way to do art."
 
 
"Tomorrow we’re leaving, so my heart
is sad and crying. It is drying its eyes
with a towel."
 

Option 3: Embodied Warm-up — Happy Hearts/Sad Hearts:

This embodied warm-up can work well with younger participants. This can also be a stand alone workshop - meaning you can choose to only embody the heart stories and omit the visual art portion.

“During this exercise, I'm going to ask you some questions, if you feel comfortable following along, that's great! If you feel more comfortable just listening and watching, that's great too!

"Today we get to listen to our hearts and notice what helps our hearts feel safe and happy. Does anyone know where your heart is? Can you show me? (You can guide everyone to put their hands on their hearts) Good! What does your heart do? (ex. pump your blood around your body, bring oxygen to your whole self, tell you how you’re feeling, beat fast when you’re excited or nervous, etc.) Can you feel it beating? Your heart is right in the center of you. Sometimes you can feel feelings in your heart. Has anyone ever felt happiness in their heart? Or sadness, like your heart is breaking? When our hearts are feeling different ways, our whole body knows it.

"When you have a sad heart what does your body do? (ex. Does it curl up? Look down? Cry? Does you body react at all?) Let’s all be sad hearts with our whole body. Notice how it feels in your whole body when you are sad. It’s okay to be sad sometimes and let it out with our whole bodies. Remember that sadness can look and feel different for each person. However sadness looks for you is OK. Now take a deep breath in and breath all the sadness out with your breath. Good.

"Now let’s think about when we have happy hearts. What does your body do then? (ex. Does it smile? Jump up and down? Dance?) Let’s all be happy hearts with our whole bodies. Wonderful! Take a deep breath in and feel your heart filling up with happiness. Good! Hearts need a lot of love. And they need to be taken care of and listened to. Today will be a chance to listen to our hearts and take care of them.”

Demonstration:
"Today, we are going to make Heart Stories paintings to share the different feelings we have in our hearts. We each get to think about what our hearts would say if they could talk, and what color they’d be inside and outside. Remember, it is okay if it doesn't look like anyone else's, we are all unique and we all feel are feelings different.

 Step One: Draw Your Heart
"First let’s use oil pastels to draw a heart.Your heart doesn't have to look like other hearts you see. It can look like anything you want. What shape should I use? What colors should I use? (Use all the colors they say.) You can keep adding colors as long as they give ideas of what to add."
Step Two: Add Color
"Now let's add paint on top of the oil pastels. What colors should we use? If we use lots of water, the Cray-Pas show through. If we use thick paints, the Cray-Pas get covered up. Fill in all the paper so there's none showing!"
 
 Step Three: Add Words
"Now let’s notice if there are any words that go with our heart. We can write down the story that this heart wants to share."
 


Closing:
At the end of the workshop, have a Heart Circle where everyone has a chance to share their Heart Stories. If the group seems sad at the end, be sure to leave things on a positive note by having each person share something positive. For example, they could each share a way they want to take good care of their heart. Or they could say something they like about the person on their left – in order to put a nice feeling into everyone’s hearts.
Row.txt_description: This workshop supports children and teens in sharing their hearts and stories through art. The workshop gives them an opportunity to listen to their hearts, value the stories within them, and know that others want to hear them too.
Row.txt_tips:
• You can invite participants to continue writing their Heart Story on the back of their artwork.
  • It is very important that you and any other Leaders, staff, or volunteers in the room participate along with the group. By modeling your enthusiasm and willingness to participate, you help build trust, bonding, and make it safer for other people to play and share vulnerable experiences.

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.str_author_location: Women’s and Children’s Windows Leader Haven House
Row.txt_code:
“Mix Tape” and “My World, My Life, My Dreams”
   
About this Workshop:
I am really excited about this workshop! There are a lot of ways you can use this idea and if you have access to computers with your youth, you could actually create real CD’s for them too! There are so many possibilities to have this workshop be continued for their whole stay if they have access to a computer at your shelter. Sometimes staff have concerns about youth using computers, especially being able to go online, so if it is possible, have them work on the CD in session with you in your office. For shelters that have teens for longer periods of time, this workshop could be never ending! Here are just a few ideas for future workshops utilizing the computer and youth creating a real CD; they could write journal entries on the computer and then store it on their own CD, download pictures…create clipart collages, write poetry, write rap or other kinds of music, create computer generated art, and…of course download or copy their favorite music.

Objective:
For youth to create something about themselves…a CD jewel case insert for their debut album!

Materials:
Insert/Booklets (precut to fit in CD jewel cases)
CD jewel cases
Markers, gel pens, pencils
Glue sticks
Collage material
A few examples of CD inserts
Instant cameras
Scissors
Music
handout (click here for template)

Preparation:
It’s best to have the jewel case inserts already precut and stapled. You can use an insert from a purchased CD as a pattern. You will need a booklet stapler to staple the pages together.
Note: If you don’t have a booklet stapler, here’s a trick. It takes more time, but makes it possible without a special stapler:
>Open up the stapler completely
>Position the booklet on a pile of cardboard
>Staple it (the staples will go straight into the cardboard)
>Pull it off the cardboard
>Bend the staples by hand using a spoon

  


"My World, My Life, My Dreams" Inside Cover
 
  

 
“Mix Tape” and “My World, My Life, My Dreams”
 
  

Timeframe:
This workshop could easily be divided into two sessions or it can give them something to work on more on their own, which for teens in a shelter can be a great boredom reliever! It is good to set a goal of at least finishing the front cover in the first session.

Total Time: 1 to 2 hours
Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Photography for front cover…can be time consuming, especially if they want to go outside!
10 to 30 minutes
Creation: 45 minutes to hours…
(if they want to finish everything on the list!)
Closing Circle: 15 minutes


Introduction:
“Today we are going to find out more about ourselves and create a CD insert for our debut CD. Usually when an artist releases their first CD the insert tells the world something about them and their music. The insert sometimes has a photograph of the artist or some kind of symbol that will forever be linked with that particular artist. As you create your insert, think about what you want to say about you. Think about how you would pose if you were using a photograph, (you will be able to have an actual picture taken today), or think about a symbol or image that represents either yourself or the information you are willing to share with people about who you are. Remember that symbols can be codes about who you are or what you believe in.”

Opening Circle:
If this is a small group open with a circle, having each person share what kind of music they like and where they like to sing…in the shower etc.! (When I facilitate groups at schools I usually skip the opening circle for lack of time, unless it is an ongoing group.)

It’s easier if you already have supplies laid out but if that’s not possible begin to pass them out now. Have participants take a look at a few different CD inserts. (Try to only have ones that represent positive stuff… no drugs etc.) Some ideas are Norah Jones, “Come Away With Me,” & Christina Aguilera, “Stripped.”
Talk about the main topics that most CD inserts have:
1. Front cover
2. Track list…song titles + sometimes the words to songs are included
3. Thank you info: Every artist thanks someone in their life who inspired them to create the music or supported them through the process
4. Credits… CD mastered by…, Art Direction & Graphic Design by…, Photography by…, Art by…,etc
5. Dedications

Because there is a lot to remember I created a handout (see attached) to go along with the workshop so if a youth does not finish in the allotted time, they will have a reference of what else goes in the jewel case insert!

Relaxation:
I like to have at least a short relaxation even though they may giggle or squirm through out it!
It’s important to tell them that relaxing can feel uncomfortable but that it assists us in going within and centering ourselves. I also explain why I play “weird music” by saying that it filters out noise that can interrupt our creativity. I also explain that the music doesn’t have words because words can influence and even change the direction of our own art. The Golden Ball relaxation in the children’s manual is short and sweet but very powerful. Have it lead them into creating the front cover.

Creation:
Keep the music playing while everyone works on creating his or her front cover. You can offer assistance with the instant camera (or if you have a digital camera…they have even more options). Pass out the handout so that those who get their cover done quickly can continue working.

  


 Important people in my life
(my little sister, and older brother).
My life, my world.
  

Closing:
Encourage each participant to share his or her CD insert and talk about how it felt to create, or anything else about the process.
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps youth make a statement about themselves by making a CD jewel case insert for their debut album!
Row.txt_tips: If you or your clients need resources to help address Teen Dating Violence issues use the Teen Dating Violence Resource Page.

Row.txt_code:
“Mi Vida Loca” by Dianna
  
Objective:
To help teens to find a creative way to explore and express their feelings and thoughts on grief (as well as other feelings of sorrow, joy and pain) that would usually find outlet in the form of tears.

Materials:
Yarn - assorted colors
“Golden books” - (4”X5” cardboard rectangles to wrap yarn around)
Fabric (as many colors, solids and prints as possible)
Dress pattern (click here for template)
Beads, sequins, “gems”
Old jewelry, buttons, charms
Fishing line or wire
Feathers
3-4” sheer drawstring bags (make your own, or check bridal supply)
Mini marbles, or clear beads
Scissors
Jewelry pliers and wire cutters
Paper and pens
Tacky glue
8” x 10” wire picture frame, or wooden frame with glass removed
Clear wide tape (kind used for packing) if using wooden frame
Old towels to cut for “quilted” layer if using wooden frame
Handout for writing warm-up (click here for handout)

Timeframe:
Total Time: 1 1/2 to 2 hours
10 minutes-Introduction and opening check-in
10 minutes-Creative writing Warm-up
15-20 minutes-Make doll
15 minutes-Make clothing
10-20 minutes-Decorate with beads, jewels, feathers...
15 minutes-Fill bag of tears and attach doll to stand
10 minutes-Closing Check-out
  
“Happy” by Rocio
 
  

Introduction:
“We all owe it to ourselves to respect our feelings, especially our pain, fear and grief over losses and love in our lives. Grieving takes us to the very heart of life itself. We only grieve for that which we have loved. Love and loss are intimately connected. All of us experience some level of loss in our everyday lives, from minor situations to major losses such as the loss of a loved one, a job, a relationship, or a dream. To grieve means to bear a heavy burden. And so you will be creating your own tear catcher doll which will hold a bag of your “tears” which are your own words and symbols representing your thoughts and feelings.”


Creative Writing Warm-up:
Without judging, simply start to write your thoughts for each prompt and continue without stopping until you finish. (See attached worksheet.)

I lost...
I am sad that...
I am mad that...
I am glad that...
I really want to know why...
One thing that really scares me is...
One thing I know for sure is...
I hope...
I love...
I am...
My tears are...

Now underline the three most meaningful sentences.
Pick three colors that best represent your feelings.

  

 
 
  
 
  
 
  
  
Step 1
Making the Doll:
Now using the writing exercise and your color choices, we will make the Tear Catcher Dolls (see Intuition Dolls from Women’s Windows Update, Feb. 1999, page 4)
Technical Info:
1. Wrap yarn around long side of the “Golden Book” about 25-50 times
2. At top of book, slip single strand of yarn under all loops. Tie knot.
3. Slip yarn off book.
4. Tie at “neck.” Use single yarn, pull tight, tie knot, clip close or tie bow on top of knot. This makes the doll's “head.”
5. For “arms” wrap yarn around short side of book. Slip off book. Tie at
“wrist.” Clip and trim loops to create “hands.”
6. Insert “arms” through middle (chest area) of yarn loops. Push up close to
“neck joint.” Tie tightly at “waist.”
7. Make “legs” if desired, by dividing “skirt” in half.
Tie at “ankle.” Trim and shape “feet.”
8. Doll is ready for clothing and adornment.

Step 2
Adorning the Doll:
Doll Clothes
1. Use pattern (see attached) to cut clothing.
2. Cut fringe if you wish.
3. Cut small neck hole. (You can trim it a little if it’s too small, but you can’t add any back on if it’s too big!)
4. Slide clothing over head. Use yarn to tie around waist. Adjust gathers if necessary.
5. To make “pants” make a cut up the center of the “skirt,” adjusting length of cut according to the legs of the doll. Then tie each “pants” leg together at the “ankle” with a small strip of the same fabric.
6. Final touches: Add “hair,” beads, feathers, etc.

Step 3
Tear Catcher Bags:
1. Select three mini-marbles or clear beads to represent your three most meaningful “tears.”
2. Cut your three most meaningful answers to the writing exercise (or more if desired) and roll them up tightly and secure with ribbon or yarn, and put them inside the bag.
3. Choose any other items to place in bag and pull the drawstring tight to close the bag securely.

Step 4
Attaching Stand:
1. Use metal wire to attach the bag to the doll’s “hand.”
2. Use metal wire to attach the doll to the wire frame. Use wire in several locations on the doll and bag to distribute weight evenly.
If using a wooden frame:
1. Cut a piece of old towel 8” x 10” for “quilted” filling.
2. Cut a piece of fabric 8 1/2” x 10 1/2” for background to fill the frame.
3. Place the towel on the backing of the frame, then place the fabric on top.
4. Put the frame cover back in place and on the back side of the frame, tape down the overhanging extra fabric.
5. Next use safety pins to attach the doll and bag to the fabric frame.

  

  
  

Closing Check-out:
Give each person a chance to share as much or as little as they would like to about their doll, or anything they want to share about the group. Suggestions would be to share the three most meaningful sentences from their writing exercise and what their doll means to them. Validate the unique creativity of each person and their courage to explore their loss and love. Encourage everyone to listen as well as share. If time permits, use “echoing” after each person shares. One by one, have each member in the circle echo one word or phrase that they remember immediately following what each person shares.
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps teens find a creative way to explore and express their feelings and thoughts on grief (as well as other feelings of sorrow, joy and pain) that would usually find an outlet in the form of tears.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide a creative opportunity to explore our journey toward growth and transformation by using the butterfly as a powerful symbol for our hopes, dreams and freedom.
  
  
  Table set-up
  


  Journey Butterfly
  
  
  "Dare to Dream" Journey Butterfly

Materials:
Shrinky-Dink plastic (Ruff-N-Ready type)
Colored pencils
Individual pencil sharpeners
Small paper plates for shavings
Permanent markers
Scissors
Hole punchers
Craft wire
Wire cutters/pliers
Assorted beads
Assorted findings (fishhook earrings, key chains, jump rings)
Assorted ribbon
Toaster oven
CD player
CD's of relaxing music
Butterfly templates
Additional Butterfly Templates (click here for templates)
Moth Template
creative writing warmup handout (click here for handout)
The Butterfly Story - Spanish Translation

Preparation:
You'll need to make enough photocopies of the various butterfly templates and Creative Writing Warm-Up sheets for all the participants. Pre-cut the Shrinky Dink into 3 1/2"x4" and 2"x2" squares. (Smaller squares are used for earring-sized butterflies.) Make sure all colored pencils are pre-sharpened. It's good to have all the materials set up prior to beginning the workshop.

It’s important to try this project in advance so you have some samples to share, and also so you can get a feel for how the Shrinky-Dinks cook. It’s very exciting to see!

Timeframe:
1 1/2 to 2 hours

Introduction:
Version 1: for teens
“Welcome! Butterflies are very special and beautiful creatures, even though they don't start out that way. Like each one of us, they grow and change. In fact, butterflies go through four stages during their lifetime. Their whole life is about transformation. Butterflies are sometimes used in art as a symbol for this. Traditionally, they represent new life, hopes, dreams and freedom. I feel that butterflies are symbolic of the inside of a woman’s soul ready to take flight. So today, you are going to create your very own journey butterflies. You may make more than one to decorate with beads and wire to hang on your wall, or keychains, or earrings. Each butterfly will be as unique and special as each one of you. Relax and enjoy your special creative journey during this art workshop to explore and express your colorful soul.”

Version 2: for ages 5-12
Here are 2 different options to use in the introduction. For smaller children you may read Eric Carle's The Hungry Caterpillar. Have the children act out the 4 stages of a butterfly's life through the story. Young children will enjoy being a part of the workshop in a dramatic way.
"This workshop is about all of the hard stuff that we go through in life that make us strong. Butterflies are beautiful but they don't start out that way! They go through a lot of changes in their life. To help us understand these changes a little better, we are going to read Eric Carle's The Very Hungry Caterpillar to see what happens..."
Read the story in a fun, animated, and engaging voice! "Now that we know and have seen the changes of a butterfly, let's act it out!" (Use the description below).

Another way to engage the children is to have them stand up and physically go through the 4 life stages of a butterfly: first, a tiny egg, so very small; second, a hungry caterpillar, searching for food; next, finding a dry safe place to build a comfortable cocoon; and finally, emerging as a beautiful butterfly, spreading its wings and flying for the first time. Ask the beautiful butterflies fly back to their seats to begin the activity!

Creative Writing Warm-up for Teens:
Hand out a worksheet with the following questions:
1) Can you share something beautiful about yourself?
2) What is something that you want to change in your life?
3) If your butterfly could fly anywhere, where would it go and why?
4) What colors does your butterfly have?
5) What is your favorite flower?
  
  
   Drawing the butterfly
  
  
  Cooked Butterflies (in hands) ready for beading.
  
  
  Beading

Check-in:
Depending upon the size of the group, check in by asking participants to share names and one or two of their answers to the writing warm-up.

Creation:
Choose one of the butterfly templates in front of you. Start by tracing your butterfly. You may choose any of the colors on the table. Begin to color and create the design that will fill in your butterfly. (Be sure to draw on the rough side of the plastic.) When you are finished coloring, decide whether you want to add wire and beads to your butterfly. Cut out your butterfly with scissors. At this time you will need to use the hole punch to place holes for wiring and beads. Look at the examples of butterflies showing different decorating ideas. If you need help, please ask for it. Now the butterflies are ready for baking. Place the Shrinky-Dink on a flat metal tray and place inside the toaster oven. Bake at 300 degrees until Shrinky-Dink has completely flattened (about one minute). Watch the amazing transformation! Remove your Shrinky-Dink and allow it to cool. For curves in the wings, you can manipulate the shape while it's still warm. Now your butterfly is ready for decorating with wire and beads if you wish. Repeat this process as time permits.

Closing: "Share finished butterflies and say a few words about your favorite pieces.
OR Share how the butterfly is unique and special like you."
Row.txt_description: This workshop provides participants a creative opportunity to explore their journey toward growth and transformation by using the butterfly as a powerful symbol for our hopes, dreams, and freedom.
Row.txt_tips:
You can make wonderful flowers out of watercolored coffee filters for Mothers' Day or Spring. Pipe cleaners, stem, and leafs are good additional media.

Reading the story The Very Hungry Caterpillar, by Eric Carle, may help the kids understand and appreciate the workshop more.

When working with younger children, they may need you to cut out their butterflies for them to prevent the paper from tearing.

It also may be helpful to tape the butterfly templates to the Shrinky-Dink material to make it easier for the kids to trace the butterflies.

This story has become a favorite of the women and children's program when doing any butterfly workshop.
The Butterfly
Author Unknown

One day, a man was walking and found a butterfly still inside of its cocoon. He looked closer and saw that the butterfly was working very hard to fit its body through a tiny, tiny hole in the cocoon so it could get out and fly around. The man decided to help the butterfly. He used scissors to cut a bigger hole in the cocoon.

The butterfly was free from the cocoon and the man thought it would fly away quickly. But the butterfly could not fly. Its body was too swollen and its wings were too shriveled for flying. It was out of its cocoon, but this butterfly would never be able to fly.

Although the man was trying to help by cutting the cocoon, he didn’t realize one very important thing about butterflies. Even though it is very hard work, pushing its body through that tiny, tiny hole in the cocoon it helps make the butterfly strong enough to fly. All that hard work makes its body trim and its wings big and strong. The challenge of fitting though that tiny, tiny hold makes the butterfly able to fly.

We’re a lot like butterflies sometimes too. We need to work hard to get through challenges we face. And, like the butterfly, once we work through them, we’re stronger too. If we didn’t have those challenges, we would never get any stronger.

I asked for Strength…and was given
Challenges to make me stronger.
I asked for Love…and was given
People to help with Kindness.
I asked for Riches…and was given
Brain and Brawn to work.
I asked for Wisdom…and was given
Problems to Solve.

Row.txt_code:
Cloth flame with pipe cleaner decorations.
 
  
Objective:
This workshop was created to enhance self-esteem. The goal is to have the children imagine themselves as a candle and visualize the light that stays on inside of them, even on the worst of days when they might feel sad.  The workshop gives them a chance to notice they can always have a light within themselves to guide them to their goals, wishes, or dreams.
 
Groundrules:
—Be respectful towards others and their work.
—Listen — do not talk when other are sharing.
—Have respect for the materials.
—Communicate your needs.
—Ask for assistance if needed.

  
 Decorating the candle.
  
Materials:
Paper towel rolls / or any size cardboard tubing
Acrylic paint (Note - this is permanent, so be sure the kids are wearing “art” clothes.)
Hair dryer (to help dry the paint)
Glitter
Glue
Pipe cleaners (multi color, metallic)
Construction paper
Multi-color tissue paper
Yarn and fabric
Foil
Brushes (2 sizes, if possible)
Paper plates
Paper towels
Newspaper
Quiet CD and player
Optional:  Glue gun and cardboard squares (to add bases)

Timeframe:
Time frame: 1 - 1 1/2 hours
Age Range
5 yrs. and up (teens too!)

Set-up:
Place newspaper on table tops.  For each setting, place a cup of water, paint brushes (2 sizes) and paper plates (paint pallette). Cut strips of construction paper to place as a “bridge” at the end of the tubes.  This will be the way you can attach the pipe cleaner “flame” (see illustrations).  For paper towel  rolls, the size for the bridge piece is about 1/2 inch wide and 3 inches long.  Cut enough for all the candles, and cut a slit in the middle of each one.  This will be where the flame goes.  Place the construction paper, paper towel rolls, glue, and other materials on a separate table where the children can choose their materials after the warm up.  Be sure to make a candle in advance, so you are comfortable with the project and can better assist the kids.
  

Mary’s candle with pipe cleaner pointsettia.
 
  

Introduction:
“Today we will find out what kind of light we carry inside of ourselves, and we are going to create candles.


“Even on the worst of days when we may feel sad, we still have a little light within ourselves to guide us to our goals, wishes or dreams. The light is there, as long as we keep it inside of us and remember to notice it.  


“Today, you will get to notice what kind of candle you have inside of you and what it means to you.  You’ll get to notice what your light means—it could be happiness, warmth, sadness, fear, anger, loneliness, confusion, peace, celebration, or whatever you think of.


“No matter what kind of light we each have inside of us, we all have feelings and our feelings are important!  


“My inner light is a guide to cheer me up, to light my way, to make me feel special, beautiful, strong and courageous. This is my way to shine!”

Warm-up
“To begin, let’s get into a circle and share about our candles.  How does a candle look?  Can you stand like a candle?  And what do you have on top?  That’s right - it’s a flame!  Let’s see you burning bright!”

—What kind of candle are you?
—Short candle or tall candle?
—Does your candle have an aroma? If yes, what does your candle smell like?
—What color is your candle?
—What size will you light be?
—Big or small?
—How will you use your light?

Have the children sit in a circle and share something special about themselves.

For older children:  Have them do a writing exercise using some of the questions above.
  

 Close-up of pointsettia.
  

Creation:
Step One: Preparing the “bridge”
Before the children begin to create their candles have them glue each end of the construction paper onto the inside of their paper towel roll.
It should form a bridge across the opening that will allow them to attach their flame to the center of their candle later on.  They may need some assistance doing this.  If this seems too complicated, you can prepare the tubes in advance, or you can have the kids create their flames by pulling fabric through their tube (see illustration, page 4).

Step Two:  Decorating the candle
Once the bridge is complete they can decorate their candle any way they choose.  They can paint their candle colors, add glue and glitter, or add pipe cleaners, etc.  Encourage them to do whatever expresses what their light means to them.  

Step Three:  Adding the flame
Once the candle is decorated, the children can add their flame.  They can form the pipe cleaners and insert into the slit in their bridge.  (If this is too difficult, fabric, pulled through the tube, can make a wonderful flame.)

Step Four:  Adding the base
This is optional, and works best with a glue gun.  By attaching a piece of cardboard to the base of the tube, you can make the candle stand up more steadily.
  

 
“My Inner Light” candles.


Closing:
Give the children the opportunity to share their work with the group, and share a few words about their special candle.
Row.txt_description: This workshop was created to enhance self esteem. Children imagine themselves as a candle and visualize the light that stays on inside of them, even on the worst of days. This gives the children a chance to notice the light within themselves to guide them to their goals, wishes, or dreams.

Row.str_title: Take a Walk in My Shoes
Row.txt_code:
The road that I walked in abuse was a very rough
roa d.  The road I walk in happiness is also at times
a rough one.  The memories of abuse have not
faded.  This is the reason for the rough texture. 
— Age 70,  43 years of abuse.

  
About this Workshop:
This project was on display in Wausau, Wisconsin during April, Sexual Assault Awareness Month in conjunction with The Clothesline Project, and a healing vigil. Judy welcomed survivors in her agency’s outreach program and crisis shelter to participate.

Feel free to adapt to Domestic Violence Awareness Month activities in October. Be sure to plan ahead so you have enough time for the creation and exhibit prep.

Objective:
To give participants the opportunity to express their feelings of surviving abuse and to help others understand how it feels to “walk in their shoes.”

  
 

Victim No More:  These were the shoes I wore the
day we married, the day I now think of as the first day of my former life.  We were children when we committed our lifetimes to each other.  You were charming and unwittingly persuasive...
  

Materials:
Shoes (I announce the
project ahead of time so the women have time to find and bring in their
own shoe. I also have a variety of shoes available the day we start the
project in case someone didn’t bring one from home.)
Puffy paint or acrylic paints
Assorted glues (glue sticks, glue guns, E6000, etc.)
Ribbons and string
Stick-on letters or felt letters
(I found some at Michael’s)
Assorted decorations (e.g. feathers, beads, artificial flowers, stickers, shells, rocks, pipe-cleaners, puzzle pieces, etc.)
  


  

 
  

 
Words to go with the above series of shoes:

Sexual abuse has affected my entire life; my entire being; my entire existence.  Some say, that is the past, get over it. or what is the big deal? IT IS A BIG DEAL!


I never had a chance to just be.  I never had a chance to enjoy my childhood or to live a so-called ‘normal’ life.  Early on I was always reacting in my life in context to what happened to me...


It took me a very long time to figure out who I really was.  Who I really wanted to be when I grew up.  It took me a very long time to even begin to LIKE myself.

Now, I am healing.  I am continuously growing as a person.  I am continuously figuring out who I am. I am trying to be gentle with myself.  I am learning to be my own best friend.  This is me...
 
  

Time-Frame:
We completed this
project with 3 sessions (1 1/2 hours per session). Some participants
took their shoes home to work on them between sessions.

Introduction:
Many of us are not able to talk about sexual/domestic abuse and the profound
affect it has had on us. My hope is for all of you to express
yourselves in a different way, one that may feel safer to you. The
project we are doing is called “Take a Walk in My Shoes.” Most people
have heard, “take a walk in my moccasins” and understand its meaning.
Everyone wants to be understood so as not to feel alone. Make this shoe
that you have chosen speak for you. There are no limits, so use
whatever you need to tell your story of bravery and courage. Feel free
to try all the materials to see which work for you.

Opening:
Let's take a few deep breaths as you prepare to start your project. While breathing slowly, begin to look at the shoe you have chosen. If you like, hold it in your hands. Ask yourself why you chose that particular shoe? What does it tell you? Where has it been with you? Allow any thoughts to come to you and try to not judge them. Although some memories are difficult or painful they are part of the journey you've traveled. Be patient with yourself and take your time. Honor the difficult memories and allow your shoes to guide you through the healing path you've began. Several happy memories might also come up as you think about the person you are now and the unique experiences you have had. Only you and your shoes know where you have been. Don't forget to continue breathing as you explore.

Creation:
When you're ready, gather the materials you want to use on your shoe and fire away. Let your imagination guide you as you create. Remember to let your shoe speak to you and consider what you would like for it to tell others about your story. There is never a right or wrong way of doing it. Enjoy the process and honor your own timing.

Closing:At the close of each session, if time permits, ask each person to share how it felt working on her shoe. I find that they are always surprised how the shoe seemed to create itself. Encourage their creativity.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives participants the opportunity to express their feelings of surviving abuse, and to help others understand how it feels to “walk in their shoes.”

Row.txt_code:
Anna showing her completed boxes
Thanks to Anna Reyner for this fabulous workshop!
Anna is a nationally recognized arts advocate who is dedicated to helping people get in touch with their own creativity. Anna has conducted over 500 national and international hands-on art workshops and is a registered art therapist and licensed marriage and family therapist. Anna is the Director of Training and Special Markets for Discount School Supply and we thank her for these special techniques and workshop.

Objective:
This month's workshop is designed to engage teens in a creative exercise to identify the things about them that are strong. They will create symbols that help represent the source of their own personal strength, so that they will be able to more quickly and readily understand their strengths and access them when needed.

Materials:
Colorations Smooth & Silky Art Sticks
BioColor Paint (4 colors plus silver and gold = 6 total colors)
Nancy Paint Bottles Twist Tops (optional)
Balloons - one per person
Small paper plates - one per person
White Cardboard Pencil Box - one per person (from Discount School Supply)
White heavy weight construction paper (for warm-up and handmade stencils)
Paper towels for cleanup
Colorations Make it Glitter (optional)
Brushes – one small & one large
Glue
Cups with water 

Timeframe:
Art Material Demo and Warm-up #1, Balloon Printing: 15 minutes
Art Material Demo Warm-up #2, Silky Sticks, 15 minutes
Warm-up: Source of My Strength: 15 minutes
Creation, Part 1, Inside of Box: 20 minutes
Creation, Part 2, Outside of Box: 15 minutes
Closing & Share: 10 minutes
Total: 1 1/2 hours

 
Setup example
 
Prep:
Pre-fill Nancy bottles with BioColor, filling 4 bottles with standard BioColor and one each of gold and silver, for a total of 6 Nancy Bottles full of BioColor per small group of participants. Fill one Nancy bottle with Make it Glitter paint for every 4 people. (You can use the paint straight from the original paint bottle if you prefer).
Try out each warm-up application before the workshop. Make yourself a sample of the Source of Our Strength Box to familiarize yourself with each stage, and so you will be confident leading the session. Create your sample box from your own voice as a healer, someone who provides healing, compassion and positive solutions for children.

Setup
1.) In the middle of the table place: 4 standard and two metallic BioColors in Nancy Bottles, one Nancy bottle of Make it Glitter paint, one set of Silky Sticks, and stack the pencil boxes in the middle, to make room for the warm-ups. Place an extra small stack of white construction paper for warm ups.
2.) In front of each seat, place 2 sheets construction paper, 1 balloon and one paper plate.

Demonstration:
Note: During the demo/warm-up, it is useful to first do a demonstration of each step and then give participants a turn.
Art Material Demo and Warm-up #1: Balloon Printing with BioColor
 
 
Step 1: Using 4 standard colors of BioColor, plus silver and gold, place quarter-sized dots of paint in center of plate.
Step 2: Blow up balloons, not too big, so they fit into your fist or grasp (2"- 3"). 
STEP 3: Firmly press balloon straight down into paint palette, then "print" paint onto paper. Bounce/print balloon all over.
STEP 4: Create stencil patterns. Using thick, white construction paper, tear stencils by folding the paper in half and tearing out images as if you were making a snowflake. Position stencil, and balloon print on top. Remove stencil to see pattern surface. Repeat. Overlap stencils and repeat with a variety of colors to create a pleasing design.

Art Material Warm Up #2: Intro to Silky Sticks
 
 
Step 1: Dry Application: Take a few different Silky Stick colors and make a simple doodle to experience the materials, pressing hard to lay down bright pigments. Don't think about it too much, take this time to "loosen up" and leave your critical voice behind.
Step 2: Wet Application: Dip Silky Sticks into water before making another doodle. Experience the difference in wet and dry applications.
Step 3: Wet Application with Paintbrushes: Take your larger paintbrush and dip it into water. Apply your wet brush to your original dry doodle, creating a "flow-release" effect as it releases the colored pigment into a dilution of color, like a watercolor. Next take your smaller "detail" brush and dip it into water, making more detailed flow effects. You can also use your wet brush, or finger, directly on your Silky Stick as if it were a dry watercolor cake, and use your finger or brush directly onto your paper.

Set aside all the warm up creations to make room for the activity.

Introduction & Relaxation:
 
 Leaders warming up to their source. 
Ask the participants to try to relax, put down their art materials, and if they wish, to close their eyes for a few minutes while you guide them through a brief period of self-reflection. Continue with this dialogue (or change the concept to your own voice): Today's workshop is meant to to focus on our strengths, so that we can increase our sense of safety and well-being. We will remind ourselves today that we are each strong enough not only to survive, but to overcome and rise above what has happened to us in the past. Today is about living in the present moment of strength, community, healing and support. Our artwork will help us focus on what it is that makes us strong and keeps us strong. With that in mind, try to relax and reflect upon where it is that you find your own personal strength. In times of need, do you call upon your faith to give you strength? Or do you think of your mother, your brothers or sisters, your friends, or something else to makes you feel strong?  When you ask for help, who listens? What is the source of your strength? (Give people a short quiet time to reflect on this question). Now, open your eyes and take your Silky Sticks and a fresh piece of paper, and DRAW A SYMBOL that represents the SOURCE OF MY STRENGTH.

Your symbol can be made up of one image, or a combination of images.  Just do what comes naturally. There is no right or wrong way to create a visual symbol. The easiest way is to simply get started and see what happens!

Creation:
 
 A leader creating her source inside.
 
Part 1: Inside of box
Take your SOURCE OF MY STRENGTH drawing and re-create it on the inside of your pencil box, using the Silky Sticks. Consider your original warm-up sketch as a starting point, and re-create the image in a more finished form on the inside of your box, adding details and embellishing it however feels right. Don't over think it, just let it flow without being critical of how it looks or what it means. As you create your visual symbol of strength on the inside of your box, imagine you are creating this image from your source.  Whatever comes of this experience will be the "right" image of strength for you today.

 
Balloon printing on the outside.
 
Part 2: Outside of box
Now comes the time to decorate the outside of your box more playfully, by balloon printing the outside with BioColor and your own handmade paper stencils. Add "Make it Glitter" paint if you want to add sparkle. Create a design of your choice, so that when you place it on a shelf or dresser table where you live, you will be reminded of a pleasant time spent with creativity and community. No one but you will know that inside this box lay very important symbols, symbols that represent the source of your strength and the inner resources you call upon.

Closing:

 
 Leaders Annie Kelly of Good Shepherd and
Anna Sanchez of Rainbow Services
sharing their strengths.

Have participants share their boxes with a partner, or with the group.  If they share with a partner reinforce the importance of being a good listener (i.e. paying attention and not interrupting).
Encourage the teens to look inside their "Strong Box" whenever they need to be reminded of their personal strength.
Row.txt_description: This month's workshop is designed to engage teens in a creative exercise to identify the things about them that are strong. They will create symbols that help represent the source of their own personal strength, so that they will be able to more quickly and readily understand their strengths and access them when needed.access their core strength when needed.
Row.txt_tips: When selecting boxes to decorate, be sure to purchase ones that have an unfinished surface, similar to the one from Discount School Supply. A slick, or glossy surface will not allow the paint to stick.

Row.str_author_location: Women’s and Children’s Windows Leader Haven House
Row.txt_code:
“Mix Tape” and “My World, My Life, My Dreams”
  
About this Workshop:
I am really excited about this workshop! There are a lot of ways you can use this idea and if you have access to computers with your clients, you could actually create real CD’s for them too! There are so many possibilities to have this workshop be continued for their whole stay if they have access to a computer at your shelter. Sometimes staff have concerns about youth using computers, especially being able to go online, so if it is possible, have them work on the CD in session with you in your office. For shelters that have clients for longer periods of time, this workshop could be never ending! Here are just a few ideas for future workshops utilizing the computer and clients creating a real CD; they could write journal entries on the computer and then store it on their own CD, download pictures…create clipart collages, write poetry, or other kinds of music, create computer generated art, and…of course download or copy their favorite music.
  

 
"My World, My Life, My Dreams" Inside Cover 
 
  
  
  
  
  

Objective:
This workshop is for clients to create something about themselves…a CD jewel case insert for their debut album!

Materials:
