Insert/Booklets (precut to fit in CD jewel cases)
CD jewel cases
Markers, gel pens, pencils
Glue sticks
Collage material
A few examples of CD inserts
Instant cameras
Scissors
Music
handout (click here for template)

Preparation:
It’s best to have the jewel case inserts already precut and stapled. You can use an insert from a purchased CD as a pattern. You will need a booklet stapler to staple the pages together.

Note: If you don’t have a booklet stapler, here’s a trick. It takes more time, but makes it possible without a special stapler:
>Open up the stapler completely
>Position the booklet on a pile of cardboard
>Staple it (the staples will go straight into the cardboard)
>Pull it off the cardboard
>Bend the staples by hand using a spoon

Timeframe:
This workshop could easily be divided into two sessions or it can give them something to work on, on their own, which for clients in a shelter can be a great boredom reliever! It is good to set a goal of at least finishing the front cover in the first session.
  
 

“Mix Tape” contents: 21 Questions, Come Over, #1...
  

Total Time: 1 to 2 hours

Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Photography for front cover…can be time consuming, especially if they want to go outside!
10 to 30 minutes

Creation: 45 minutes to hours…
(if they want to finish everything on the list!)

Closing Circle: 15 minutes

Introduction:
“Today we are going to find out more about ourselves and create a CD insert for our debut CD. Usually when an artist releases their first CD the insert tells the world something about them and their music. The insert sometimes has a photograph of the artist or some kind of symbol that will forever be linked with that particular artist. As you create your insert, think about what you want to say about you. Think about how you would pose if you were using a photograph, (you will be able to have an actual picture taken today), or think about a symbol or image that represents either yourself or the information you are willing to share with people about who you are. Remember that symbols can be codes about who you are or what you believe in.”
  


Important people in my life (my little sister, and older brother).
My life, my world.
 
  

Opening Circle:
If this is a small group open with a circle, having each person share what kind of music they like and where they like to sing…in the shower etc.! (When I facilitate groups at schools I usually skip the opening circle for lack of time, unless it is an ongoing group.)

It’s easier if you already have supplies laid out but if that’s not possible begin to pass them out now. Have participants take a look at a few different CD inserts. (Try to only have ones that represent positive stuff.) Some ideas are Norah Jones, “Come Away With Me,” & Christina Aguilera, “Stripped.”

Talk about the main topics that most CD inserts have:
1. Front cover
2. Track list…song titles + sometimes the words to songs are included
3. Thank you info: Every artist thanks someone in their life who inspired them to create the music or supported them through the process
4. Credits… CD mastered by…, Art Direction & Graphic Design by…, Photography by…, Art by…,etc
5. Dedications

Because there is a lot to remember I created a handout (see attached) to go along with the workshop so if a client does not finish in the allotted time, they will have a reference of what else goes in the jewel case insert!

Relaxation:
I like to have at least a short relaxation even though they may giggle or squirm through out it! It’s important to tell them that relaxing can feel uncomfortable but that it assists us in going within and centering ourselves. I also explain why I play “weird music” by saying that it filters out noise that can interrupt our creativity. I also explain that the music doesn’t have words because words can influence and even change the direction of our own art.

Creation:
Keep the music playing while everyone works on creating his or her front cover. You can offer assistance with the instant camera (or if you have a digital camera…they have even more options). Pass out the handout so that those who get their cover done quickly can continue working.

Closing:
Encourage each participant to share his or her CD insert and talk about how it felt to create, or anything else about the process.
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps participants make a statement about themselves by making a CD jewel case insert for their debut album!

Row.str_author_location: Women’s Windows Leader, Haven House Pasadena
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
For participants to think in definite terms about where they are on the journey to Self-Love.
     
  
 

 Self-Love Map detail
 
   

Materials:
Xeroxed “Self-Love” Maps (one per participant, Click here for Map1 Map2, Map3, Map4)
Lists of Characteristics & Traits of Self-Love (spanish too)
(click here for list)
Blank strips of paper
Magazines
Scissors
Glue
Fine-point markers
Music

Preparation:
You’ll need to xerox the Self-Love maps and words, so there are enough for each participant. It’s good to have the materials all ready but to only pass out the Self-Love Map. The rest of the materials may go in the middle of the table to be accessed when the participants are ready.

Timeframe:
This is definitely a one-and-a-half-hour to two-hour workshop.

Introduction:
“Self-Love makes it possible to nurture ourselves and to feel good about setting and reaching goals. Yet often we just don’t know how to nurture ourselves. To be able to nurture ourselves, it must be done as a result of feeling loving toward ourselves. This workshop will be an opportunity to explore where we each are on our journey to Self-Love.”

Opening Circle:
Check in by asking participants to share names and one act of self-nurturing behavior they can think of. It could be something they’d like to do for themselves, or something they already do. Then, go around the table again and have participants state one act of nurturing they would do for someone else. Usually there is a difference in the time it takes to think of nurturing acts between herself and someone else. Then have each participant affirm “I will nurture myself with the same love I nurture others.”

Body of Presentation:
 
  Detail: Reaching Self-Love
(Presented on large board)
What are the childhood experiences that lead to low-self esteem? Ask participants to write an answer on the board/paper. What are the childhood experiences that lead to high self-esteem? Ask participants to write their answer on the board/paper.

Take the good experience list and ask the group to recall what each of these things FELT like. That feeling is the feeling of nurturing. We learn how to treat ourselves from the way our parents/caretakers treated us. The difference is that now we are our own caretakers. Self-Love is the result of all the good things on the list being done to us.

Creation:
Pass out the list of characteristics and read them as a group, commenting on what they mean.

Show the Self-Love Map and point out that it is their choice to change where it says on the map “you are here.” They may be anywhere on it but they are ON it. Self-Love is the destination. Using the characteristics as street names, what streets do they still have to cross to reach the destination of Self-Love? Ask them to draw a line between where they decide they are and Self-Love. It may be direct, jagged, etc. Then using the words create the path from where they are to the end.

Using the magazines cut out two pictures; one picture to put in the “I am here” spot illustrating how they see themselves now. Use the other cut-out to show what Self-Love will look like when they get here. If time permits, a picture for the mid-point is good.

  
 Overall Self-Love Map (template)
 
When it is complete, laminating makes it perfect.

Closing:
Each participant holds up her map and shares whatever she would like to about it. It is a time of affirming each participant.

Each participant is asked again what she would do to nurture herself. The answers are different in quality if not in type.

It’s nice to ask everyone to share what she chose as her last step before Self-Love (nice to see if there’s a synchronicity in what each person chose).
Row.txt_description: This workshop lets participants think in definite terms about where they are on the journey to Self-Love.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give children a way to create a recipe of the good feelings and things they want in their life (like trust, joy, fun etc.), and give them the opportunity to keep them in a safe and fun place.  They will combine t hose ingredients to create  a "Happy Healthy Cuppie Cake."  This workshop is perfect for Valentine's Day, but can also be done at other times of the year.  For Valentine's Day you can use heart shapes and ribbon in shades of pink and red colors.

  
 Using supplies for Valentine's Day Cuppie Cake
 
 
Supplies for the Happy Healthy Cuppie Cake
 
Materials:
Beads - a variety of colors
Colored sand - a variety of colors
Glitter - a variety of colors
Buttons
Ribbon
Shredded colored paper
Foam shapes
Small pom poms
Clear plastic cup
Paper cupcake liner
Clear plastic wrap or baggy
Rubber bands (one for each Cuppie Cake)
Cotton balls
White glue
Ribbon
White paper
Construction paper
Markers

Time Frame:
Approximately 1 hour

Age Range:
5 to 14 years

Set Up:
You will need a variety of materials for this workshop.You will assign a quality to each material.  For example, gold glitter can mean forgiveness, red sand can mean love, white beads can be hugs etc. Prepare each of the supplies you would like to use by placing them in individual cups, bowls or plates and place a sign by each to tell the participants what each one means. Ideally, you should have about 15 ingredients.  You might also want to pre-make recipe cards, especially for younger children.   This is made by gluing a piece of white paper onto a larger piece of construction paper with a heading that says "My Happy Healthy Cuppie Cake".

Warm Up:
We are going to imagine what it is like to make a cupcake.  Ask the children to stand up and pretend they are mixing a big bowl of cup cake batter. Ask them to think about the things that they really want for themselves, like joy, hugs, fun and friendship and add those ingredients.  Have them stir in big round circles and pretend to pour in ingredients with big physical swoops of their arms. Now ask them to imagine that they are in a warm oven - feeling the warmth from their toes to the top of their head.  Finally, imagine what they feel like as they all bake together and end with giving themselves a hug.

 
 Finished Cuppie Cakes and recipe card 
Introduction: Today we are going to make a special cup cake that has all the ingredients of the special things that we want for ourselves.  Especially around Valentine's Day we want to love and appreciate ourselves and loved ones.  These cup cakes will help you decide what you really want.  You can pick any of the ingredients and add as much of each as you like.  Notice that each item on the table has a meaning.  So you can choose if you want love, trust, hugs, support, warmth, peace, safety, kindness, happiness, respect, guidance, forgiveness, joy, encouragement etc.  These will fill your cup to make your very own cup cake.

Opening Circle:
Explain to your group that each of the supplies on the table will be available to them to create their Cuppie Cake, and that each of those supplies will become special ingredients.  Ask for their help to identify what those ingredients are or you can present them with a list of qualities (above) and go around the circle and have each child assign a word to an ingredient.

 
  Adding clear beads
 
  Adding colored sand
 
  Covering the top and adding a ribbon
 
  Adding the cotton ball (frosting) top
Creation:
When we create our Cuppie Cake we will also be creating a special recipe card.  As we start to select each ingredient we will write them down on the recipe card.  To make an ingredient card you will glue a piece of white paper onto a larger piece of construction paper and title it with the words that say "My Happy Healthy Cuppie Cake."

Step One:
Place a paper cupcake pan liner in the bottom of your clear plastic cup to use as a base.
As you add ingredients the paper cup will partially disappear.

Step Two:
Ask each child to think about each of the things that they want in their life by looking at the table with all the ingredients that have been labeled.  They can select those qualities by selecting the ingredients they want to use.

Step Three:
Begin to pour or place each one of those things into the cup. The ingredients will overflow the paper liner.

Step Four:
Ask the children to write down each of those things as they are selected. (Some of the children will need some help with this.) This will create a special recipe card for your Cuppie Cake.

Step Five:
Cover the top with a layer of clear plastic wrap or a baggy that you have cut to be a clear square, place a rubber band around the top to hold it in place and tie a ribbon around it to cover the rubber band.

Step Six:
Take a bunch of cotton balls and glue them together.  Place them on top of the plastic covered cup.  You can add a heart or sprinkle glitter on top.

Closing Circle:
Ask all the children to walk around the table to see each person's Cuppie Cake.  After all the Cuppie Cakes have been seen, ask them what they would like to share about making them.  How did they feel about selecting their own special ingredients, they may want to tell you why they selected what they did.  Remind them that having the recipe card will help them to remember what it is they wanted to have in their life.
Row.txt_description: To give children a way to create a recipe of the good feelings they want in their life (like trust, joy, fun etc.), and give them the opportunity to keep them in a safe and fun place. They will combine those ingredients to create a "Happy Healthy Cuppie Cake." This workshop is perfect for Valentine's Day, but can also be done at other times of the year. For Valentine's Day you can use heart shapes and ribbon in shades of pink and red colors.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To empower participants to make healthy choices in relationships. This is a great workshop that can be integrated into DV101 courses to discuss relationship boundaries.

Materials:
 
  Sample materials
Pens and paper for writing
Writing Template (click here )
Shrinky Dink paper
Mini Heart and Circle templates (click here for hearts /circles )
Permanent Markers (Sharpies)
Colored pencils and sharpeners
Scissors
Hole puncher and pliers
Ribbon or beading wire for necklaces and bracelets
One grocery bag
Toaster oven
Music


 
Sample Charm
 
Prep:
Cut a rectangle the size of your toaster oven cookie sheet out of a brown grocery bag and turn one corner up. The turned up corner will make it easy to remove from tray or cookie sheet after baking. Have toaster oven ready and make sure you have a working outlet.  Lay out materials and have templates copied and cut for participants to use.
Timeframe:
1-1 1/2 hours (beware: sometimes it's hard to get participants to stop once they start making Shrinky Dinks.)

Introduction/Relaxation:
Today we are going to be focusing on our future, and more specifically what we want in a  relationship.  Let's take a moment to think about this and focus on this moment, this time for ourselves, as I lead a relaxation. 

If you feel comfortable, close your eyes.  Let's be still and listen to that little voice of love deep down inside.  Before we take in a deep breath of peace and relaxation, let's exhale everything we want to let go of today.  Go ahead and think about all those things you
  
  Charm Bracelet
want to leave outside this room, your schedules, housing issues, to do lists, anything and everything that is preventing you from taking this time for you. Now  exhale these things.  Exhale completely and release any anxieties, worries, concerns, until you have no more breath.  Now inhale peace.  Completely inhale and fill yourself with peace, calm, hope and love.  Now let's sit, be still, and listen to what your heart is telling you.

Think to yourself, how have your relationships been unhealthy?  Have you ever changed to meet your partner’s standards?  Have you ever cared so much for your partner that you neglected yourself and your needs? Now lets think about some actions, thoughts or beliefs that we can change to make healthier decisions in the future. 

What are some things that come to mind when we think about healthy relationships?  Maybe you're thinking about respecting individuality, embracing differences, and allowing each other to be yourselves.  Let's continue to focus on these actions, thoughts and beliefs as we open our eyes. 

(optional) Now, if you like, take some time to journal about any thoughts or ideas that came up during the relaxation.  Feel free to use the prompt in front of you or write whatever you would like.  Whatever flows from your fingers is perfect.  Remember, there is no wrong way to do this, as long as you are allowing your inner voice to speak without censorship, you're doing great!  We're going to take 3 minutes to journal.

When time is up bring everyone back together and ask if someone would like to be the first to share.  Ask everyone to share one unhealthy thing they want to leave behind in their past relationships and one thing they want to have in a future healthy relationship.

 Finished Necklace
Creation:
Have each person create Shrinky Dinks to represent healthy aspects they want in a relationship. 
If you haven't used Shrinky Dinks with your group before you may want to demonstrate how to color on the rough side with the color pencils for the background, how to use darker colors for the words and explain that the plastic will shrink to a third of it's size after baking. You may want to show a sample or print out this workshop so they can see pictures.

  
  Creating a Loving Relationship Charm
Step 1:
Start by tracing your heart(s) or circle(s) template onto the Shrinky Dinks or you may choose to create the design that will fill in your template (be sure to draw on the rough side of the plastic). Remember the words we thought about? Use those words to write kind and loving messages to yourself on each of the charms. It can be one-word reminders or entire sentences. These charms will serve as reminders of the relationship you want in your future.

Step 2:
When you are finished coloring, cut out your charm(s) with scissors.


 
 Shrinky Dinks about to get baked
 
Step 3:
Use the hole punch to place a hole at the top of each charm so that you can use it on your necklace or bracelet. If you need help, please ask for it.

Step 4:
Now the charms are ready for baking. Place the Shrinky Dink pieces, colored side up, on the brown paper and place paper on a tray or cookie sheet.

Step 5:
Put in a 300 degree preheated oven for 1-3 minutes and watch as your Shrinky Dink shrinks! After pieces lie flat, allow an additional 30 seconds of baking time to complete the process.

Step 6:
Remove paper from tray or cookie sheet and let Shrinky Dinks cool.

 
  Andrea with her finished necklace
Step 7:
Using ribbon or plastic thread you can make a necklace that hangs low underneath your clothing that no one sees, or something beautiful you wear for all to see.  You can use craft wire and use it to attach the charms so that they hang off the necklace.  Simply thread the wire through the charm, cut the wire to your desired length and twist the two ends of the wire together around the necklace where you want the charm to hang.  You can attach the charms so they hang at various lengths. 

Closing:
Have each participant share about their Loving Relationship Charms and what they will remind them.
Row.txt_description: This workshop empowers participants to make healthy choices in relationships. This is a great workshop that can be integrated into DV101 courses to discuss relationship boundaries.

Row.txt_code:
Project Overview:
This project started as AWBW’s Unmasking Me/Unmasking the Future multi-media project designed to enable children and teens that have witnessed or experienced domestic violence, to express themselves and educate their communities in a powerful and unique way. This is a great project for Domestic Violence Awareness Month.

Objective:
For youth to have an opportunity to have their voices heard through journaling and by creating a mask that dialogues with the abuser and themselves regarding the domestic violence they experienced and/or witnessed.

 
  Mask molds and materials
  
 
  More materials for the masks
Materials:
Plastic mask molds (set of 10 “Multi-Cultural Face Forms” can be ordered from Dick Blick)
Sculpey (approx. one -pound per person)
Various rubber stamps with letters, numbers, textures, etc.
Acrylic paints (assorted colors)
Spray paint (assorted colors) - Optional
Assorted craft wire (20 to 22 gauge)
Assorted beads (plastic, metal, wood, etc), rhinestones
Foil (to ball up into a form to place under mask while working on them and during cooking)
Feathers, Yarn
Toothpicks, or paper clips (for making holes in the face for the wire to pass through for decoration)
Popsicle sticks (for smoothing, cutting the clay, etc.)
Toaster oven/s (Due to toxic fumes from the clay, toaster oven should be one dedicated or baking the Sculpey: for non-food use)
Tongs, potholders, timer
Scissors
Markers, gel pens, pencils, sharpies
Hot-glue gun, glue sticks
Music
Pre-made Journal with questions listed (click on this link to print Journal)

Preparation:
The journals should be prepared in advance. Feel free to make copies on nicer paper to make it more special. Three hole punch and assemble with ribbon or yarn. Tip: put sculpey in the refrigerator to keep it cool before the workshop.

 
  Sample Masks shown before workshop
Time Frame:
Total Time: 2-3 hour workshop plus a break in between or 2 separate days 2 hours each
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Journaling Time: 20 minutes…depending on age of group, if you have preteens or younger teens you may choose to adapt the journal questions and talk about them as a whole group instead of writing about them; you can still give the younger youth the journal to work on with their counselor, or by themselves.
Sharing Circle: 6-10 minutes
 
  Finished mask
Creation Time: 35 to 45 minutes

45 minute brake/lunch: It’s nice to have a brake or lunch while the masks are cooking…it gives time to clean up a bit, get ready for painting and gives the youth a break from a tough topic

Cooking Time: 20 to 30 minutes (depending on how thick the mask are)
Painting Mask: 30 minutes
Sharing/Writing about mask: 15 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Pictures: 10 to 20 minutes
Times will vary!

Introduction:
We hear a lot about Domestic Violence from adults but today we want to create a safe window of time for you to express your thoughts and feelings about the violence you have lived with, experienced and witnessed in your own home. We are going to ask some tough questions but you will be choosing which questions to answer and how you answer them. The journal is to get you thinking about what you have seen, heard and experienced and the mask you will be creating will be an outlet for all those feelings and answers.

Opening Circle:
(If you are a survivor or an adult survivor of childhood abuse, it is possible to share a bit of your story to create a safe atmosphere, only do so if you can share the past and still remain in the present!)
Let’s start with checking in about how we feel about sharing out loud such personal information, if you could choose one feeling or one word about how you are feeling about this process today what would it be?

Relaxation:
Doing a simple breathing relaxation before journaling could be helpful. It will assist them in going within, getting in touch with what they are really feeling, and getting in touch with their creative power within.

Journaling:
The relaxation guides the youth into the journaling part of the workshop. Remind them that the journals are confidential. They do not have to share the journals with anyone; they won’t be expected to read them out loud, although they are welcome to. They can write or draw their answers. Remind them that the journals are a safe healing space to let the feelings out so that the feelings no longer have any power over them. They don’t have to answer all the questions, if one becomes particularly difficult they can skip it and come back to it later or even on their own on another day, or they can just totally skip it! The journals ask some hard questions but they are just for them, they are theirs to assist them in figuring stuff out!

Sharing Circle:
Have the youth share whatever they are comfortable with regarding their journaling or choose a question or two for them to pick from. You can have them share about how it felt to write about what they experienced and what feelings came up for them. So that sharing is less intimidating have them pair up with each other and share in pairs. Give each partner two minutes (use a timer) to share while the other listens, then have them switch. Let them know that when they are the Listener, they only need to listen.

Remind them that they do not have to share anything that they are not comfortable sharing. Afterwards there may be a few brave teens that want to share with the whole group.

 
  Molding the mask in the plastic mold
 
  Pressing the sculpey firmly in the mold
 
  Putting mask on foil to hold its shape
Creation:
Talk about all the materials available. Show some examples of masks that have been made free form, compare to using the plastic mask. You can show pictures of masks from history and remind them there isn’t a right or wrong way to create a mask. They don’t have to look like a human face. Before they begin creating their masks have them think about the questions, their answers, and what they might want their mask to share with others. Encourage them to pick one of their journal question answers to create the mask about. Remind them that there is no right or wrong way to create their mask.

Step 1- Molding:
Have them begin molding their masks, either with the plastic mold or free form. If they use the plastic mold they should press the sculpey firmly inside the mold to create the mask’s shape, no more than an inch thick. Warn them that if the Sculpey is too warm from handling it might stick to the molds.

Step 2 - Removing from Mold: Carefully remove the clay from the mold form. This takes some patience. They may want to rest the clay on preformed foil for support and to hold its desired shape (the foil will be left under the mask for the baking).

Step 3 - Decorating:
Textures, glitter, wire, beads, sequins and rhinestones can be added by pressing into the soft clay. Remind them if they want to add wire…they need to create some holes in their masks prior to baking, this can be done with toothpicks or straws.

Step 4 - Mask cooking time/ Lunch/or break for the day:
Set the toaster oven to 275 degrees and cook the masks for 20 minutes, depending on how thick they are. Check the masks every ten minutes and pull out any masks that are turning tan so that they don’t overcook. Make sure the toaster oven is not on toast or broil. Set the timer so you don’t forget, while you are taking a break or eating, to pull the pans out of the toaster oven!

 
  Decorating mask before it's cooked
 
  Painting mask after it's cooked
Step 5 - Painting/Decorating the Mask:
Talk a little about the painting materials available. Since the masks are clay, even though they are baked, they should not get too wet with paint – do not add water to the acrylic (you might not even want to put water on the table) – if spray painting do not saturate. Have an assistant spoon out paint so participants don’t take too much. Have an adult assist with the spray painting, which is good to do outside or in a well-ventilated spot! Feathers, rhinestones, beads, wire can all be added using a hot glue gun.

Sharing/Writing about the Mask:
Celebrate the completion of the dialoging mask with each other!
If you are planning on using the masks for an exhibit here are a couple of options for sharing and writing about the mask:

1. Have them share with the group about the process and/or anything about their mask. If the participants are comfortable you could ask if it’s ok if volunteers or other group members write down what they say when they share about the mask. This will allow you to keep track of words that go along with their masks.
Or
2. You could have them work again in partners and have one partner write while the other shares and then switch places. Have the youth figure out together what words can go with the mask when they are displayed. This also creates a unity or partnership for future sharing between the youth outside of group!

 
Finished mask
 
Closing Circle:
Have everyone hold their masks in the circle so that they can all be seen. Ask the youth to share whatever they want about the mask or about the process of creating the mask. They could also give a one-sentence title for their mask to sum up their feelings. (Have paper ready if they want to write down other/more words that can go with the mask if the masks will be exhibited).

Pictures:
You might want to take a picture of the youth with their mask so they can glue it into their journal. This will give them a visual record of the whole process and their creation.

Note to Leader:
If you are choosing to facilitate this workshop using the two separate workshops it would be best to do the journaling and the mask creation on the first day, and the mask painting/decorating and writing the words to go with mask the second day. This is a very powerful project!
Row.txt_description: For youth to have an opportunity to have their voices heard through journaling and by creating a mask that dialogues with the abuser and themselves regarding the domestic violence they experienced and/or witnessed.

Row.txt_code:
Table set-up
 
  “Dare to Dream” Journey Butterfly.
 
 
 "Change" Journey Butterfly
 
Objective:
To provide a creative opportunity to explore our journey toward growth and transformation by using the butterfly as a powerful symbol for our hopes, dreams and freedom.

Materials:
Shrinky Dink plastic (Ruff-N-Ready)
Colored pencils
Individual pencil sharpeners
Small paper plates for shavings
Permanent markers
Scissors
Hole punchers
Craft wire
Wire cutters/pliers
Assorted beads
Assorted findings (fishhook earrings, key chains, jump rings)
Assorted ribbon
Toaster oven
CD player
CD's of relaxing music
optional writing handout (click here for handout)
Butterfly template
additional templates (click here for templates)
Moth Template
The Butterfly Story (click here)
(Click here for Spanish Translation)

Preparation:
You'll need to make enough photocopies of the various butterfly templates and Creative Writing Warm-Up sheets for all the participants. Pre-cut the Shrinky Dink into 3 1/2"x4" and 2"x2" squares. (Smaller squares are used for earring-sized butterflies.) Make sure all colored pencils are pre-sharpened. It's good to have all the materials set up prior to beginning the workshop.

It’s important to try this project in advance so you have some samples to share, and also so you can get a feel for how the Shrinky Dinks cook. It’s very exciting to see!

Timeframe:
1 1/2 to 2 hours

Introduction:
“Welcome! Butterflies are very special and beautiful creatures, even though they don't start out that way. Like each one of us, they grow and change. In fact, butterflies go through four stages during their lifetime. Their whole life is about transformation. Butterflies are sometimes used in art as a symbol for this. Traditionally, they represent new life, hopes, dreams and freedom. I feel that butterflies are symbolic of the inside of a woman’s soul ready to take flight. So today, you are going to create your very own journey butterflies. You may make more than one to decorate with beads and wire to hang on your wall, or keychains, or earrings. Each butterfly will be as unique and special as each one of you. Relax and enjoy your special creative journey during this art workshop to explore and express your colorful soul.”
  
  Drawing the butterfly
  
  Cooked butterflies (in hands) ready to be beaded.
  
  
  Beading

Creative Writing Warm-up:
Hand out a worksheet with the following questions:1) Can you share something beautiful about yourself?2) What is something that you want to change in your life?3) If your butterfly could fly anywhere, where would it go and why?4) What colors does your butterfly have?5) What is your favorite flower?

Creation:
Choose one of the butterfly templates in front of you. Start by tracing your butterfly. You may choose any of the colors on the table. Begin to color and create the design that will fill in your butterfly. (Be sure to draw on the rough side of the plastic.) When you are finished coloring, decide whether you want to add wire and beads to your butterfly. Cut out your butterfly with scissors. At this time you will need to use the hole punch to place holes for wiring and beads. Look at the examples of butterflies showing different decorating ideas. If you need help, please ask for it. Now the butterflies are ready for baking. Place the Shrinky Dink on a flat metal tray and place inside the toaster oven. Bake at 300 degrees until Shrinky Dink has completely flattened (about one minute). Watch the amazing transformation! Remove your Shrinky Dink and allow it to cool. For curves in the wings, you can manipulate the shape while it's still warm. Now your butterfly is ready for decorating with wire and beads if you wish. Repeat this process as time permits.

Closing: "Share finished butterflies and say a few words about your favorite pieces"
Row.txt_description: This workshop provides participants a creative opportunity to explore their journey toward growth and transformation by using the butterfly as a powerful symbol for our hopes, dreams, and freedom.
Row.txt_tips: Some leaders have used this workshop as a way to say goodbye and wish good luck to clients that are leaving the shelter. Participants can then create nice loving gifts for those who are leaving.

Row.str_author_location: Women’s Windows Liaison at Angel Step Too
Row.txt_code:
“My High Power is an image of light inside of me.   He gives me strength and knowledge, finding me where I chose to go.  He shows me a path in which to follow.  The most important quality of my god is; he accepts me for whom I am.  And, he guides me to the person I hope to be.  My god is all about the love in my life.  The love he has given to me.  Amen.”

  
  
  
  
About this Workshop:
This workshop comes out of the 12-step tradition. It was developed by Robin Haskins, AWBW art leader at Angel Step Too, a transitional shelter that supports women dealing with both substance abuse and domestic violence. Following the 12-step model, Angel Step Too encourages their clients to focus on the role of their higher power in their growth and healing journeys.
Robin noticed that many women come to Angel Step Too feeling scared of the higher power they grew up with or feeling like they don’t have one. Through this art project, she created a supportive way for them to consider what they believe and freshly identify what the concept of a higher power means to them.

With this workshop, Robin welcomes each participant’s beliefs. She found that for some, their higher power is the traditional one they grew up with. For others, it is different. Sometimes a client will come up with a female image as their higher power. She encourages them to know this is fine.

A Note of Caution:
Think about the religious beliefs of your clients, as you plan this workshop. For clients of some religious backgrounds, it may feel difficult or threatening to explore non-traditional beliefs. Also for other clients who do not think religiously, it may feel strange to be asked to do so. In this case, you could encourage them to explore their own beliefs and spirituality in whatever ways make sense to them.
  
 

“My Higher Power is awesome.  He is loving, caring, and forgiving...”
  
 
 “This workshop has been great.  This has helped me express how I feel and helped me tell how I feel inside and my higher power today, since this was my first workshop.  I’m looking forward to coming to more!”
  

Materials:
Colored paper
Pastels
Pens
Crayons
Relaxing music

Timeframe:
Total time: 2 hours
Introduction: 5 min
Opening Circle: 15 min
Relaxation: 10 min
Drawing: 60 min
Closing Circle: 30 min

Introduction:
“Today, we will be exploring the concept of our higher power. I know for some of us, we might not feel like we have a higher power. For others, we might feel scared of the image of God that we were taught when we were little.
“Each of us in this circle may have come from different traditions and have different beliefs about God or the concept of a higher power. This group today is a safe place to share and explore these traditions and beliefs.

“This workshop will be a chance to explore and identify your own higher power that you believe in. You might find that the higher power you believe in is the traditional one you grew up with, or maybe it is different.”

Opening Circle:
“Let’s start with our Opening Circle. Share one thing about what you grew up believing and one thing about your beliefs now.”
Relaxation:
“Before we start the project, we’ll begin with a relaxation. Then after the relaxation, you’ll each have a chance to write down any words that describe your higher power. You don’t have to think about it now. You can just see what comes to mind as you go. After the writing, we’ll start drawing. Again, don’t worry about the drawing now. You can just see what comes to you when we get there.

“So for the relaxation, get yourself comfortable in your chair. If you feel safe closing your eyes, then let them close. (Begin the relaxing music.)

“Breathe in… And breathe out… Feel the air go through your whole body as you breathe in… As you take another deep breath, imagine that you are breathing in peace. And as you breathe out, imagine that you are exhaling tension and letting it all go… As you take another deep breath in, visualize colors in the air around you. Imagine that you are breathing in green… green for cool, calming, peace… And as you exhale, picture that you are breathing out red, red for any tension and anger from the day. Let it all come out with your breath as red... Again, breath in peaceful colors… Imagine them swirling through your body, bringing you peace… And as you breathe out, imagine releasing all the tension and anger… As you take another deep breath in, visualize a place where you feel safe. It could be outside, or it could be inside, or it could be on a cloud… Wherever you feel safe, just picture yourself there, where it’s completely calm and peaceful and you’re safe with you. When you’re ready, begin to visualize your own higher power. Would your higher power be friendly? Would it be jealous? Would it be loving? Forgiving? What qualities would you need in a higher power of your very own? Notice what comes to mind. Do any colors or shapes come to mind? Would your higher power have a name? Just notice whatever comes to mind and when you are ready take one last deep breath, come back to the room, and begin writing.”
  

 
“I’m just beginning to have a concept of a higher power.  I don’t see my higher power as male or female, but more in the beauty of the world.  I see my higher power in the sky, in the wind, in the tree, and when I hear a baby giggle.  Spirituality is very new to me, but this is how I see my higher power now.”

  
  

Writing:
“Write whatever characteristics and qualities you would want in a higher power… When you feel done writing, you can begin to draw your higher power.”


Drawing:
“Use whatever colors and drawing materials you like. Remember that it does not matter what your drawing looks like. It can just be shapes and colors. It’s your own. It can be different from everybody else’s.”


Closing Circle:
After everyone is done drawing, give each participant an opportunity to share about her higher power. It’s important to encourage each person to know that it’s okay if her god is different than the others.
Row.txt_description: This workshop encourages the participants to focus on the role of their higher power in their growth and healing journeys.

Row.str_author_location: Women’s Windows Liaison at Laurel House, PA
Row.txt_code:
“Scared” Feelings Collage.
 
  

 
“Angry, Betrayed, Sad” Feelings Collage.
 
  
  
  
About this Workshop:
This workshop is the first in a “Creative Scrapbook” series created by Carolyn Coleman Manns of Laurel House in Pennsylvania. AWBW will be publishing each workshop in the series during the coming months. In this update, we provide an overview of the entire “Creative Scrapbook,” and share the first project, “Feelings Collage.”

Series of Workshops:
During the next several months, we will be sharing the following workshops (They’re in the order Carolyn has found most useful in leader her groups):

1. Feelings Collages
2. Power and Control Wheel
3. Letter to My Abuser
4. The Funeral of I Can’t’s
5. Mask of Abuse
6. Safe Place
7. Life Line
8. Loving Hands

Creative Scrapbook:
By mounting all of the projects into a creative scrapbook format, Carolyn’s projects give participants a record of their journey that they can use as a reference and source of support.

Carolyn got scrapbook pages donated (they tend to be pricey). You can use large black construction paper. When you punch the holes to bind it, you might want to use clear contact paper, tape, or reinforcements so the holes won’t tear.

Creating their scrapbook assists survivors in exploring domestic violence information in a very personal way. The art projects give clients the opportunity to create their own personalized Power and Control Wheel, write a letter to their abuser, and say goodbye to negative messages and insecurities with the Funeral of the “I Can’t”s project. They provide a way for participants to think deeply about the course of their lives with the Life Line project, and explore the masks they wore in order to survive. Each and every project in Carolyn’s series validates the tremendous power and courage of each survivor and assists each to set up a plan to eliminate violence from their lives, care for themselves, and make healthy choices.

Three Feelings Collages:
When Carolyn leads the projects, she has the women create three different collages during the process—beginning, middle, and end.
  
 

Collage #1: “It’s Time”

Collage #1: The first collage gives clients a chance to notice how they were feeling when they first arrived at the shelter and/or how felt when they left their abuser. It can be a chance to express the final incident that caused them to make their break. (This first collage often becomes the cover of their scrapbook).



  


Collage #2: “Very Good Reasons to Get the Most.”
 
  

Collage #2: The second collage is created during the middle of their stay. It gives participants a chance to express feelings and thoughts of how they are doing now, after having had some time to settle in, reflect on things, feel a sense of support, and recover from the trauma.










  
 

Collage #3: “Be Free.  Be You.”


Collage #3: The final collage is created at the end of the client’s stay in the shelter as they begin to envision their future lives. In this final collage, Carolyn asks each participant to create a collage expressing where she wants her life to be in ten years.






Note: If you are working with a group, and have women entering and leaving the group at different times, the three collages give a way to lead a group with women at different stages in their process. For example, one woman might have just arrived and be working on her first collage, and another may be creating her final collage.

Creating their three collages, clients gain a reflection and validation of the dramatic transformations that are occurring in their lives.

Objective:
To give participants a chance to focus on the ordeal they have experienced that brought them into the shelter, and create a collage that can serve as a reminder of their strength and courage, and a reminder of why they left.
  


“Peace” collage, illustrating where the artist wants her life to be in ten years.
 
  
  

Materials:
Heavy construction paper (Black is great!)
Magazines (Especially culturally diversified)
Paint
Paint brushes
Glitter, glitter paint
Glue sticks
Scissors
Laminator (optional)
Relaxing Music

Introduction:
Today we will be making a collage. This collage will describe your emotions and feelings you had when you entered the shelter. This collage will also describe your feelings and emotions during the last incident that brought you into the shelter.

As we create our collages today, we will reflect on the courageous choice you made to come into the shelter. This is a reminder of where you have been, and where you are headed. This will also be a piece of art that you can look at from time to time to remind you of why you left. This will validate why you left and why you are willing to start over.

Creation:
Choose whatever images and feelings and emotions you can. Create a picture in your mind of where you have come from. Think about the difficult situation you left. You can use words, letters, pictures, colors, and images to create your collage. This will become part of the scrapbook you will be putting together. It will remind you of where you came from and where you are headed.

Relaxation:
Use relaxation music to create a calm atmosphere. Deep breathing exercises will help create the mood. Encourage them to relax and emphasize that this will help them to get to the place they need to be. This will help them to think clearly, and to put their feelings into their creation.

Closing:
Give each woman the opportunity to share her collage and the domestic violence story she wants to share with the group. Make each individual aware that her experiences are important. Validate the women’s courage and the strength it took to get this far in their transition.
Row.txt_description: This workshop was designed to give the participants a chance to focus on the ordeal they experienced which brought them into the shelter. To create a collage that can serve as a reminder of their strength and courage, and to be used as a reminder of why they left.

Row.str_author_location: Women’s Windows Liaison at Laurel House, PA
Row.txt_code:
Power and Control Wheel, with glitter words.

  
About this Workshop:
This workshop is based on the Duluth Power and Control Wheel. It is the second in the “Creative Scrapbook” series created by Carolyn Coleman Manns of Laurel House in Pennsylvania.

Objective:
To help each woman understand the cycle of violence and the dynamics of the power and control wheel. To give each participant the opportunity to tell their own story of abuse by writing, drawing and collaging into a blank power and control wheel.





Note: When I lead the Power and Control Wheel section, I like to start by discussing the “Six Phases in the Cycle of Abuse.” It is also beneficial to include this project in a sequence in the same week with groups on:
—red flags of an abuser
—why women return
—creating a safety plan to avoid future violence (Unfortunately some women return and this exercise alerts them to the dangers and to put a safety plan together if they end up returning.)
  


  


Materials:
Blank Duluth Power & Control Wheel (click here for template)
Duluth Equality wheel (click here for handout)
Duluth Power and Control Wheel (click here for handout)
Construction paper (large)
Markers and Colored Pencils
Paint and brushes
Glue
Glitter
Optional: Collage materials (in case participants want to collage as well as draw and write their wheel)

Timeframe: 2 hrs
Intro and Sharing: 30 min
Creation: 60 min
Sharing: 30 min

Introduction:
“Today we are going to discuss the power and control wheel. You can go around in a circle with each individual one by one sharing a section of the wheel and how it relates to her experience.

Sharing these experiences gives each person a chance to think about what she has gone through and also how other women have handled their abusive situations and how they were not alone in experiencing violence in their lives. They get a chance to vent, cry, to comfort each other and to definitely bond together.
  

 
Sample completed Power and Control Wheel.

  
  
  
  

Creation:
Step One: Each person is given a blank power and control wheel. They are encouraged to fill in each section of the wheel. The group leader should make the group aware that everyone’s story will be different and not all of the sections of the wheel will be filled. (Allow twenty minutes for participants to fill in the wheel.)

Step Two: Participants glue their wheels on large pieces of construction paper.

They are given the opportunity to use pictures, words, paint, glitter, etc. to describe how their story of violence affected them.

They can put whatever they are feeling on the construction paper or on the blank side of the power and control wheel.

Closing:
Each woman shares how the exercise has affected her. Encourage each to share how she plans to stay safe and to take care of herself.

The group leader should encourage each individual to give her statement of what she feels is a healthy relationship.

Each person is encouraged to write up a safety plan and what methods she will use to stay free of violence in her life. (This may relate to groups later in the week.)
Row.txt_description: The workshop was created to help each woman understand the cycle of violence and the dynamics of the power and control wheel. To give each person an opportunity to tell their own story of abuse by writing, drawing and collaging into a blank power and control wheel.
Row.txt_tips: It is also powerful to have participants create a Power and Control Wheel as a group, in addition to creating one individually. This is great for cohesion building. It can then be hung somewhere in the shelter which brings a great sense of accomplishment to the participants.

Row.str_author_location: Women’s Window Liaison at Laurel House, PA
Row.txt_code:
Sample of a “Letter to My Abuser” with glitter pen writing surrounding the letter, mounted onto the scrapbook page.
 
About this Workshop:
This workshop is the third in the “Creative Scrapbook” series created by Carolyn Coleman Manns of Laurel House in Pennsylvania. Through this series, Carolyn powerfully links creative expression to the shelter’s basic DV curriculum.

Objective:
To express what you could not say in person and to express how the abuse made you feel. To express how you feel about him after leaving him. This exercise officially puts closure on the relationship.
 

 

Sample of a “Letter to My Abuser.”
  






Materials:
Large writing paper (beige or white)
Large black construction paper
Pens
Glitter pens
Glitter (optional)
Staple gun
Glitter paint (optional)
Scissors
Markers
Music
White-out pens

Timeframe:
2.15 hrs
Introduction: 15 min.
Sharing: 30 min.
Creation: 60 min.
Closing: 30 min.

Preparations:
Staple gun needed to staple the letter on to the large black construction paper. Some of the women wrote the foul names their abuser called them or the woman can write their feelings on the construction paper circling the letter.

Introduction:
“Today you will have an opportunity to write a letter to your abuser. It won’t be the kind of letter you send. It will be a safe place to get everything out onto paper, express how the abuse made you feel, and say the things you could not say. It will be a chance to talk about your feelings and emotions during your abusive relationship.”
 

Sample of a “Letter to My Abuser.”
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Opening Sharing:
“Share about the feelings you dealt with during the relationship and share about your self-esteem during the relationship.” (The group can be encouraged to talk about the methods they used to express how they felt during an incident or an argument or a physical altercation. Some of these women were unable to express verbally how they felt. Their abuser may have seriously injured them.)

Creation:
“Now we will begin our letters. There is paper to write on, and then there’s black paper to mount the letter on, and add shapes, colors and words around it. Notice any feelings, words, or thoughts that come to your mind when you are writing your letter. These words or thoughts can surround your letter in any fashion. You can use a gel pen, white-out pen, glitter and glue stick. Write the words with glue and shake the glitter on the glue.”

Closing:
Save time to allow each woman to share her letter and how this activity made her feel. Try and get the women to express if this has empowered them in any way.
Row.txt_description: This letter-writing workshop was designed to help the participants officially put closure on their abusive relationship after leaving by expressing how they they felt about their abuser and how the abuse made them feel.

Row.str_author_location: Children’s Liaison, Haven House, Pasadena, CA
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To support children to notice things that they are proud of about themselves, and create a tangible reminder of their pride that they can wear and enjoy.

  

 This Pride Medallion says,
“I’m proud I know how to play basketball.”
  
Materials:
Shrinky Dink rough and ready type pre-cut circles or (4x4 squares)
Color pencils
Hole punchers
Ribbon / yarn
Toaster oven
Scissors
Pencils sharpener
Small paper plates (to collect pencil shavings)
Pride Medallions Shrinky Dink templates
Circle shape / stencil different sizes (plates, cups, etc. ranging in diameter from 3” to 4”. Note: anything smaller than 3” will be difficult to read or see due to shrinkage of the material when it cooks.)
Paper to cover tables

Timeframe:
Time frame: 1 - 1 1/4 hours

Age Range:
3 yrs. and up.
  

 
Pride Medallion table in action.

  
Set-up:
Younger children (under age 5) may have difficulty cutting on their own medallion circles, so depending on the age levels in your group, you will probably need to pre-cut circles. Cut them into circles varying in size from 3” to 4” in diameter. Older children will probably be able to trace and cut their own circles from 4”X4” squares of Shrinky Dinks (some may still need assistance.) Cover tables with butcher/newspaper. Set out the materials: color pencils, sharpeners, small plates (for pencils shavings) pre-cut circles and/or 4x4 squares for children to trace and cut.

Introduction:
You could begin by asking if anyone knows what a medallion is. You can use the Olympic Gold, Silver and Bronze Medals for the winning athletes, or the Medal of Honor for heroic deeds as examples.

Have the children imagine how it would feel to be awarded such a medal for something they have accomplished. Talk about different types of feelings we all have. Has anyone ever felt happy about something they did for themselves or someone else? If so, what was it? Have they ever felt excited about something they have done at home or school? Are they kind to others? Did they ever help another person? Did they want to help that person? If so what did they do? Did they show a new person around? Did they pick up after themselves and feel really good about it?

Explain that today they are going to make their very own medallions to honor themselves. They will be able to decorate their medallions with colors and symbols and then thread them with ribbons to wear around their neck to represent their pride in their accomplishments.

  

 Pride Medallions, after cooking.
They are ready to wear!
  
Creation:
Encourage the children as they begin work on their own medallions. Encourage the younger children to select their circle. Have the older children trace their circles or the shape they chose from the Shrinky Dink templates. Next, they can trim the circles with scissors and begin to decorate using colored pencils and markers.
Be sure to hole punch for ribbons before baking the Shrinky Dink material.

Bake Shrinky Dink in the toaster oven at 300 degrees for about 30 seconds to 1 minute until Shrinky Dink has completely flattened.

Remove immediately to avoid scorching or bubbling. Allow medallions to cool about 1 minute before letting children handle.

String medallions with ribbons or yarn cut to approximately 28” long. Knot the ends and they are ready to wear.

There is plenty of time and material for each child to make more than one medallion.
  

This Pride Medallion reads,“I am proud to have a family.”
This picture was taken before cooking the medallion.
 
  

Closing:
Once you have finished making and baking medallions have all the children share one at a time, at least one of their pride medallions and what it represents to them.
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps children notice things that they are proud of about themselves, by creating a tangible reminder of their pride that they can wear and enjoy.

Row.txt_code:
Ready to create Guardian Jars,
with all supplies laid out.
  
Objective:
To find a place to store fears and worries so the children can have a sense of letting them go.

Materials:
Tennis ball cans – remove outer label
White glue (such as Elmer’s)
Paint brushes
Colored Tissue Paper
Small pieces of writing paper
Pencils

Timeframe:
30 to 45 minutes

Age Range:
4 years and up (This project can be adapted to children of all ages. Younger children will need help writing down their troubles.)

Set-up:
Mix the glue with water and stir ‘til it becomes very liquidy (about 3 parts glue to 1 part water). Give each child a small bowl or cup of the mixture. Rip the tissue paper into irregular size and shapes.

Introduction:
This is a very simple activity yet it can be used in many different ways. Talk to the children about things they worry about or discuss the times they feel scared. Often when someone is troubled by worries or fears they tend to dwell on them and think about them all day long. This workshop gives the children an opportunity to write down what is bothering them and put those thoughts away in a jar for safe keeping.
  

Adding the glue.
 
  

 
Adding the tissue, piece by piece.
 
  

 
Completing the tissue.
 
  

 
Writing the worries.
 
  

Creation:
Step One:
Dip the brush in the glue solution and apply to a small area of the Tennis Ball can. (Make certain that the outer wrapper has been removed.) Once the glue is applied you can start to layer the colored tissue paper onto the can. Layer each piece with a slight overlapping of the one underneath. You can use the glue on the brush to help smooth out wrinkles. As you continue you may choose to apply the glue on top of the tissue paper as well. The color on the tissue paper should bleed and the overall affect is that of a stained glass window. The outside will be colorful; slightly shiney and you will not be able to see what is inside. Cover the entire outside of the can with the pieces of tissue paper and allow to dry. Take care not to use too much of the glue solution so the jar doesn’t take too long to dry.

Step Two:
While the container dries have the children think about the things that are on their minds and troubling them. You can help them to write their comments on the slips of paper. It can be any way they want it expressed – just a word or two may be enough. Or they may wish to write a whole story, dream or memory. After that is done fold the pieces of paper up and each child can place them in the jar. You can talk about what it feels like to release these thoughts and how they can store them away for a later date.

Older children may want to add additional problems to the jar in the days and weeks to come.

Step Three (for later):
Take the jars out after some time has passed and read about the things that once were so worrisome. (These can be read out loud or privately.) Often people find that those particular issues have passed or that they are no longer scary or troubling. It is a good experience to show that sometimes time can make a difference. Even if the issues are still present sometimes we are able to look at them differently as time passes.
  


 Completed Guardian Jars drying.
  

Closing:
Assure the children that everyone has fears and worries and that sometimes expressing them out loud or writing them down on paper can be away of letting them go.

Variations:
The Guardian Jar can be used to hold joys and happy memories and children can look inside when they are feeling sad and be reminded of happy times.
You can also use these containers for children to write something positive either about themselves or about each of the other children in the group, or the other members of their family. Now each child will have their own jar filled with positive messages.

Special Thanks:
AWBW sends special thanks to Laura Slakey of Haven Hills, who shared the idea of making Guardian Jars at a 2002 training, and to Elda Unger, of Free Arts for Abused Children, who gave AWBW hundreds of tennis ball cans in 2004 and shared the similar project called “Worry Jars.”
Row.txt_description: This workshop was created to give the participant a place to store fears and worries so he or she can have a sense of letting them go.
Row.txt_tips: Depending on how many jars and much time is available, kids could make a positive dream or wish jar in addition to their guardian jars.

Row.str_author_location: Children’s Windows Liaison, Haven House, Pasadena, CA
Row.txt_code:
< td style="vertical-align: top"> 

 
The Very Hungry Caterpillar, The Butterfly Kiss, and The Caterpillar & the Tadpole are wonderful for focusing
on transformational changing and growth.

 
  
  
  
  
About this Workshop:
AWBW leader Melissa Falco facilitated a wonderful workshop at AWBW’s Venice studio, introducing her favorite projects for working with pre-school aged children. She shared how central reading and movement warm-ups are to her work with young children. In this workshop, we share her favorite story books and CDs, as well as how she integrates them into her art group.

To see Melissa’s three favorite workshops for young children check out Roller Derby Painting, Bugs and 'Mud' Workshops for Toddlers.

About Working with Young Ones:
I have worked with children at Haven House since 1989, and it has been the most rewarding work that I could have chosen for myself. I have also worked in the pre-school setting which was a great joy and extremely rewarding. Children are my favorite population to work with and I have applied a lot of my creative ideas from this period of my life to the art workshops. The children are open to learning new things and even when they’re unhappy and not quite ready to play, they still respond to my silliness, let loose and begin to enjoy just being kids. In watching them during Windows time, I have come to learn that the simple act of being a child is just a vague memory for some of the children---and for others, not a memory at all.

My own personal process in having a successful Windows Workshop is to take the time before I start the workshop to ask myself key questions:
— “What do the children want or need from me today?”
— “What kind of day are the children having?”
— “Do they want or need extra attention, maybe starting with a big hug?
— “Do I need to be a good listener?
— “Do they need an affirmation of their self-worth?

I never approach the workshop with the question
— “What do I want from them”?

The children trust me and know that the time they will spend in the workshop will be enjoyable. They will have the freedom to express themselves as kids and enjoy who they are and, more importantly, they know that it is a “safe place.” This becomes obvious when I occasionally see the children between the workshops and see their excitement and anticipation for the next workshop.

In every workshop, I start by getting on the floor with the children (which happens to be my favorite position). Just by physically lowering myself to the children’s level helps me in setting the tone for them to begin to relax and begin to rid themselves of any outside pressures and stress.

Here are some of the ways I have incorporated what I have learned from my Windows training, and some of my own ideas on Warm-ups.
  
 

 

Reading Warm-ups:
Reading is one of key missing components in the children who live at the shelter. It doesn’t matter if they are too young to read or are able to read by themselves. Reading is a vital part of childhood development and they just don’t get enough, generally due to living in a household in constant crisis. I have found that reading is a very powerful tool in helping the children to calm down and focus. It is also a great stress-reliever, especially when the story has a message pertaining to real-life issues. Further, reading to the children helps to increase the bond you will quickly establish with them.

The book titles I have listed are some of my favorites. I put them in categories to help you choose a book to match the mood of the children. Many of our children are exposed to terrible situations that are beyond their understanding. By reading and discussing stories about different point of views and cultures or familiar issues and concerns, they find a certain sense of relief and understanding. Reading is a valuable tool in getting their imaginative juices flowing and helps in opening up on some deeper anxieties. By taking the time to read slowly, showing the illustrations (also very important in choosing new books), I engage them in the story. I endeavor to make it inter-active by asking what they think of the pictures or story line and then listen to them. I always value their involvement in our reading time.

If the children seem to particularly enjoy the reading, you may want to have a couple of books handy to prolong the warm-ups at their request. Stories should be engaging, enriching and have a message. Imagination picture books are best for children between 3 – 8 years old. Board books and hard covers work well for toddlers. I have listed below a few book titles in connection with certain projects, themes, and messages. Very importantly, these are only my suggestions and you may have your own favorites. So, please feel free to choose a book based on what you think would most benefit your particular children’s group.
  


Tough Boris, Owl Babies, and Mama, Do You Love Me?, are
great for exploring separation anxieties and feelings.
 
  

 
Amazing Grace, William’s Doll, and Happy to be Nappy are
wonderful for dealing with stereotypes.
 
  

 
Caps for Sale and The Hat are great
project books for Hat Workshops.
 
  
  

Reading List:
Transformational Changing and Growth Titles:
—Butterfly Kiss, Marcial Boo (Author), Tim Vyner (Illustrator)
—The Very Hungry Caterpillar, Eric Carle
(Great story to go with “Water Color Journey Butterflies”)
—The Caterpillar & the Tadpole, Jack Kent

Separation Anxieties & Feelings:
—Owl Babies, Martin Waddell, Patrick Benson
—Mama, Do You Love Me?, Barbara M. Joosse
—Tough Boris, Mem Fox

Dealing With Stereotypes:
—William’s Doll, Charlotte Zolotow
—Happy to be Nappy, Bell Hooks
—Amazing Grace, Mary Hoffman

Enhancing Self-Esteem:
—I Like Me, Nancy Carlson
—Chicka, Chicka, Boom Boom, A,B,C (Fun Book), John Archambault
—Yoko, Rosemary Wells

Divorce:
Whenever children question a divorce with their parents, this is an excellent book to share:
—Dinosaurs Divorce, Laurene Kransy Brown, Mark Brown

Project books for Hat Workshops:
—Caps for Sale, Esphyr Slobodkina
—The Hat, Jan Brett

Dance Warm-ups:
Music is therapy in itself. How many times have we heard a song playing and start to move and sway or sing along to the music? It makes you feel lighter and happier. As an example, at my son’s school, they play music up and down the halls over the intercoms in the morning. It starts the day with a little pep and a sort of “Good Morning” to the kids and it works. The kids start walking a little faster, and become more animated. While I still use some soft music for the workshops as they are in progress, I love to utilize some terrific energizing children’s music for warm-ups. Depending on the mood of the children, I may combine Reading Warm-ups with Dance Warm-ups.

In Dance Warm-ups, I cannot stress enough how gratifying it is for me to watch the children open up and bloom like flowers, becoming joyful just by being able to jump up and down, wave their arms and legs, and use their energies in dancing and singing, often pretending to be animals with noisy sounds. In my experience, spending 5 - 10 minutes dancing and singing has a calming effect, not a nervous effect, on the children. I have listed below some of my favorite children’s music as well as different cultural music. These varied choices are invaluable in opening up the world of music for the children and teaching them respect for people’s diversity.
  
 

Getting to Know Myself, by Hap Palmer.
  
 
 We All Live Together, by Greg and Steve.
  
 
 Big Fun, by Greg and Steve.
  
 
 Samples of multi-cultural music from Putumayo:  Mexico, African Playground, and World Playground.
  

Dance & Music List:
Interactive and Background music:
—Getting to Know Myself, by Hap Palmer (Feelings music)
—Dream Land, by Putumayo (Relaxing music)
—Chant, Religious chanting very soothing for nap time

Dance and Warm-up music:
—Big Fun, by Greg and Steve (Loud dance music for warm-up)
—We All Live Together Vol 1,
by Greg & Steve (Great movement music with good morning song for A.M. workshops)
—The Amazing Adventures of Kid Astro (Fun, fast CD)
—The Kids Yoga Deck, by Annie Buckley (Yoga is wonderful for stretching warm-up)

Multi-Cultural Music:
Putumayo is the music publisher under the title “World’s Playground.” Types of music you might look for are:
—Mexico
—African
—Armenian
—Russian
—Celtic
—Cuban
—Irish/Scottish
—Australian
—Island Music
—Native American
—Reggae
—Any other multicultural music appropriate for young children

Popular Artists:
—Carole King
—Hap Palmer
—Ella Jenkins
—Raffi
—Greg & Steve

While, I have so many other ideas that I can go on and on, but these will surely make a difference with the children. Remember, just have fun and be a KID!

I’m looking forward to sharing some of my favorite Children’s Workshops in the next few months ahead.
Row.txt_description: This is an introduction to the use of story, music and dance as warm-ups for the Windows groups with children ages 3-8. Reading is used to help calm and focus the children. Stories are used as a catalyst for discussions. Dance is used as a stress reliever and has a calming effect for the kids.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.str_title: Magic Reindeer - Holidays with HeART Series
Row.txt_code:
To help participants find art in the holidays. A series of workshops with holiday themes including Ginger Bread Houses, Decorated cookies, Snowflakes and Magic Reindeer. The idea is to create something special to show loved ones that we care and perhaps even begin new family traditions.  Creating with art during the holidays as a family can be a relaxing way to connect, bond and celebrate.

Objective:
Participants make reindeer faces using the outlines of their hands and feet.

Opening:
As you begin this workshop, take the opportunity to talk about the significance of the holidays and how it is a time to celebrate yourself and those you care for. It can also be a time to begin thinking about goals and visions for the new year.

Materials:
Construction Paper
Glue Sticks
Scissors
Felt
Markers
Googley Eyes
Pom-pom balls (optional)

 
 Magic Reindeer Sample
Creation:
Magic reindeer are a fun way to decorate the shelter with holiday spirit. Using each child’s own hands and feet, these reindeer also make special gifts for mom. (Or you could involve the whole family in creating reindeer families!!) The children can work in pairs to help each other. Have each child trace one foot on the construction paper. Next, using another color, each person will trace both hands. Cut the tracings out. Glue the handprints behind the wider part of the foot (toe area). Add eyes and nose to complete the reindeer.
Row.txt_description: Participants make reindeer faces using the outlines of their hands and feet.

Row.txt_code:
Windows participant models her new hat.
  
 
 “I feel like a cool dude in my best hat!”
Objective:
Encourage young children to celebrate themselves by exploring the world of hats and their many meanings and uses. Explain that each hat has its own special purpose. Encourage the children to imagine and create their own special hat that reflects who they are and what makes them special.

Materials:
Newspaper
Masking tape
Acrylic paints (dries faster)
Markers
Crayons
Brushes
Hair dryer (aide for drying the wet paint)
Pipe cleaners
Collage materials (glitter, gems, ribbons, feathers, etc.)
Tacky Glue
Stapler (to fasten loose edges at the rim of the hat) for leader only
Pictures or cut-outs of different hats

Timeframe:
1 hour - 1 1/2 depending on the size of the group and their ages

Age Range:
Children 3 yrs. old and up
This activity requires some assistants if the group is larger than 4 children.

Set-up/Prep:
Create a sample hat in advance. Cover the tabletops and have everything in the center of each table. Position an area for the newspaper, unfold the full sheets and stack them at the end of each table. Place masking tape next to the newspaper. You may need an assistant for each table where children will be working. No more than 4 children per table.
  


Windows group decorating their hats. 
  
  

Introduction:
“Today you are going to create your own special hat, a special hat just for you to wear. Your hat needs to be special just like each one of you. Your hat can be a fun hat or a silly hat, a work hat or a serious hat. When you are done creating your special hat we will show them off for everyone to see just how special they really are.”
(You may want to display real hats or cut-outs showing different types of hats along with your sample: cowboy, derby, bonnet, athletes, rescue personnel etc.)

Warm up/ Opening Circle:
Have the children close their eyes and imagine what their hat will look like? What shape will it have? How about the color? Will their hat be big or will it be small? Once you have asked the children these questions, have them open up their eyes and one by one share one of their feelings about their very special hat that they will wear. It may be nice to photograph the children (with permission) wearing their special hat at the end of the group.
  
 

Step 1: Putting newspaper on the head.
  
 
 Step 2: Circling with a band of tape.
  
 
 Step 2: Ready for rolling the brim.
  
 
 
Step 3: Rolling the brim.
  
 
 Step 4: Decorating!
  

Creation:

Now it's time for the children to create their special hat. Have the
children line up with the assistant at their table. (There should be no
more than 4 children to each table).

Step 1: Preparing the Newspaper: Layer 3 sheets of newspaper before placing it on the top of the child's head. You want to rotate the corners so the top and bottom piece are exactly the same. The middle sheet should be the only one shifted with the corners hanging out. Explain to the child that their face will be covered for only a few moments; if the child is uncomfortable you may ask them if it is ok to ask another child to assist them with this part. Once you have their permission to cover their head, place the 3 layers of newspaper on top of their head.

Step 2: Masking Tape: Holding the newspaper down with your hand, use the other hand and begin to roll the tape around outside of the newspaper in the center of the forehead area, do this about 3-4 times to create the inside dome for the hat to sit comfortably. Once you have completed this step remove the paper from the child's head have them return to their seats.

Step 3: Rolling the Brim: You will instruct the children to then begin to roll the ends of the newspaper creating a brim. When the children have finished rolling the brim the leader may have to go around and staple any loose ends that won't stay put. Once this is complete the children are ready to decorate their hats.

Step 4: Decorating: Have the children use glue and paint only on the outside of the hat. If the children are painting you may want to have a hair dryer handy to speed up the process. For really small children you may want to use markers or crayons to cover the outside of the hat. You can have the children color the top sheet of newspaper before you place it on their heads and tape around their forehead. This process takes less time and is great for really young children who just want to color.

Closing:
Have the children share with each other their special hat. It may even be nice to parade the children in a circle with music and let them celebrate being special and unique.
You may want to play some cheerful dancing music for the end parade.
Row.txt_description: This workshop encourages young children to create their own special hat that reflects who they are and what makes them special.
Row.txt_tips:
Have a lot of help for young children. Have kids lie down and think about why they are special and what makes them different from everybody else. Why are they loved?

Have students make hat that reflect who they are.

It may be helpful to bring in a variety of different hats for the children to try on or bring a book about hats to read to the kids.

Row.str_author_location: Women’s Window Liaison at Laurel House, PA
Row.txt_code:
Sample from “Funeral of ‘I Cant’s.”

  
About this Workshop:
This workshop is the fourth in the “Creative Scrapbook” series created by Carolyn Coleman Manns of Laurel House in Pennsylvania. Through this series, Carolyn powerfully links creative expression to the shelter’s basic DV curriculum.

Objective:
To help each woman realize how much strength it took to leave her abuser and come into the shelter. To affirm that she took the power with her when she left. To say “goodbye” to her “I Cant’s” — the fears she faces as she thinks about building a new life (I can’t drive, I can’t get a job, I can’t find a place to live, etc.)
  
 

“I can’t live without him... I can’t leave him. I can’t make it on my own... No more abuse!”
  

Materials:
Paper Shredding Machine (Some shred into confetti, some into strips. Check to see what kind you have. Either works for this workshop - they just look different.)
Off-colored writing paper (Beige, grey, off-white)
Construction paper (assorted colors)
Scissors
Glue sticks
Glitter or glitter paint
Bright paints and brushes
Markers
Popsicle sticks (Optional)
Music

Timeframe: 2 hrs
Intro & Writing: 30 min
Sharing & Shredding: 30 min
Creation: 45 min
Sharing: 15 min

Introduction:
