For young children - one adult for every three children is recommended. This activity is best for children over 5. If you have a mixture of age-levels, the older children can help the younger children.

 
 Example of a finished Speak Out Mask
Set-up / Prep:
Pour glue into a bowl and add water slowly, stirring as you go. Consistency should not be too thin. Prepare pieces of tissue paper in various colors by cutting into thick strips. Prepare wet paper towels (or wipes) for hand cleaning during the project. Cover the tables or workstation with newspaper. For younger children, pre-wrap the tin foil over the mask. It is a good idea to have one or two made for examples. Expect a pleasant mess!

Introduction:
Masks provide a wonderful way to express feelings, fears and emotions that are hidden or suppressed. This activity gives an opportunity for the words to pour out of the mouth of the mask! Identifying feelings is a critical step in awareness of the things that we fear and are angry about. In time for Domestic Violence Awareness Month, Speak-Out Masks are a great vehicle for self-expression.

Opening Circle:
Take this time to talk about things the children fear or are afraid to say out loud. Explain that the Speak Out Masks can speak for them - show an example and help them to understand that the mask is a safe way to express themselves and that everyone has fears and anger – they are not alone with their feelings.

 
  Glue can be applied with fingers or a brush
Creation:
Part One:
Begin by wrapping the tin foil over the face of the mask mold. Older children may need a little help with this and as mentioned, you may want to provide pre-wrapped molds for the younger children. Before you begin to add the colors, encourage the children to think about how they want their masks to look. The tissue can be applied to the masks in several different ways – here are 2 suggestions, feel free to explore new techniques. 1. The glue mixture can be applied to the tin foil first and the paper can be layed on top. You can continue to layer by using a brush or your fingers dipped in the glue mixture. 2. You can place the tissue on the foil and apply the glue with the brush over the tissue, and continue to layer in this fashion.
The paper can be applied in clumps or strips and the features of the face can be built up by using thick layers or you can leave the surface of the mask as it is on the mold – just make certain to have enough layers of tissue paper to cover the foil. Encourage the children to explore and experiment. Allow the mask to dry.

Part Two:
Once the mask is completely dry carefully lift the foil with the tissue from the mold. Each mask can be left as it is or the features, such as the eyes or mouth, can be enhanced by cutting them out.
You can have your mask “say words” by attaching a pipe cleaner or wire that has been wrapped around a finger to make a spiral – insert one end in the mouth and glue a piece of paper with words on the other end.
       
 
     
  Apply tissue to the tin foil
  Curl pipe cleaners around a finger
  Attach words to the mask
 

Part Three:
Carefully glue the mask to the Matte Board. Younger children will definitely need help with this and older children may need supervision if using a hot glue gun. If desired, additional words can be added to the surrounding Matte Board.

 
 
  Sample Speak Out Mask
 
   
Closing:
This is a very powerful workshop. Try to allow enough time for sharing the finished masks with the group. Encourage participants to discuss what their masks have to say. Celebrate and validate the uniqueness and creativity of each piece of work. Be sure to have release forms available so the participants can give permission to display their work. Make certain to write the title of the work and the words that go with it.
Row.txt_description: This is designed to allow participants to speak out about and against domestic violence, as well as to express personal stories for the purpose of creating awareness.
Row.txt_tips:
Silence about Domestic Violence is part of the problem. Speaking out is part of the solution.
As a warm-up you might ask participants the following questions or use them as directives for journaling time:
Have you ever seen someone hurt somebody else?
How did it make you feel?
What did you say or want to say to the person doing the hurting?
What did you say or want to say to the person who got hurt?
If you could be someone else or something else to better protect yourself or someone what would you look like?
If you had a message to make the world more peaceful or safe, what would it be?

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give participants the opportunity to reflect on their identity and at the same time, encourage them to make connections with each other by noticing and celebrating their similarities and differences.


 
 APWC's We Are Quilt
 
Materials:
Pen
Paper
"I am" Poem (in English/Spanish, in Vietnamese, in Korean)
Button & loop quilt fabric squares (Discount School Supply only $9.35 for 12 squares!!)
Fabric markers
Fabric glitter paints and/or Puffy paints
Stamps and stamp pads
Fabric scraps (optional)
Fabric glue (optional)
Embellishments to glue on (optional)

Preparation:
Have a pen and piece of paper at each place setting. Set up all of the supplies so they are readily accessible to all participants. Don't forget to print the poem prompts!

Introduction:
Today you are each going to create a fabric square that illustrates and celebrates who you are and what is most important to you! All of the squares will be joined together to create one magnificent "We Are Quilt" that will celebrate our similarities and differences.  Before beginning the Opening Circle be sure to demonstrate how to use the materials provided.

Opening Circle:
Turn on some light music and hand out the "I am" poem to each participant. Explain to them that they can use the prompt hand out or they can just write their own “I am” poem.  As they are finishing up, ask them to read over their poem and to notice that they are in a safe place and that what they have written is valued by you and the group. When each person has completed their poem, have them go around the room and share their “I am” poem, and how it felt to write it.

 
  APWC participant creating her "I Am"
Creation:
Give each participant a quilt square.  Ask each participant to pick a statement made in their poem and write it with a fabric pen or to draw onto their quilt square an illustration that represents the statement using colors, symbols and/or pictures with the materials provided. If they need some encouragement, you can suggest participants trace their hands and decorate the square with words they identify with or that are important to them or they could just re-write their poem onto the square.

Closing:
Encourage the participants to share about what they have made individually and as a group. What does their individual quilt square mean or say to them? As each person shares their square (if they are dry), have them pass their quilt square to the next person to link their square to their neighbors. By the end of the sharing circle, the "We Are Quilt" will be complete.
After the quilt is complete, have everyone gather in a circle. Holding hands ask them to swing their arms back and forth and say the chant, "We are. . . we are . . . _______ (insert something special that everyone is)”  For example, everyone says "We are... we are... and the first person says 'strong!' Then everyone repeats, "We are... We are.... and the next person says, "courageous!" and the circle continues until everyone says something.
     
 
 
 
  I Hope to Find Peace
  Family
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives participants an opportunity to reflect on their identity by creating a quilt square of who they are and what is important to them. Then, the workshop encourages the group to make connections with each other by noticing and celebrating their similarities and differences. The quilt is made using button & loop fabric squares. So putting the quilt together is quick, easy and requires no sewing!

Row.txt_code:
Alaskan leaders, Reynold Okitkun, Michelle Woods, Debbie Hewitt, and Lillian Shavings, standing in front of their Team-Building porject ideas.
About these workshops:
One of the most magical parts of every new leader's training is hearing the sharing of ideas and energy among the group. In Bethel, Alaska, the leaders shared many wonderful ideas for team-building. All these projects are ways to help the kids validate each other and focus on the positive things they see in each other and in themselves.



Objective:
To build team spirit among the children and create a playful, structured way for them to practice appreciating and validating each other.


AWBW staff trying out the "Drawing Me Out" project.
Special thanks to AWBW interns Pamela Almeida and Kelley Crane.

Age Range:
These projects work best with kids old enough to express themselves by writing. Younger children can participate with a helper.

Opening:
“Have you ever had someone say something nice about you? How does it feel? And have you ever said something nice about someone else? When we appreciate each other, we are giving special gifts to each other. Today we get to practice!”

Creation:
Here are 4 different team-building project possibilities. Choose whichever seems to be the best fit for your group and circumstances. Feel free to adapt and change the workshop as needed. Enjoy!

Appreciation Envelopes
From Michelle Woods

Materials:
Colored construction paper
Scissors and staplers
Markers and/or CrayPas

Project:
This project is not just one session. It's actually and ongoing process that happens all week long. We start by having each person decorate an envelope with their name on it. It could be a simple manila envelope, or you can use construction paper, markers and scissors to make special shapes (see samples this page). Once everyone's special envelope is made we hang them all up in the room. Then every day we take a special "appreciation time" when each student writes down an "atta-boy" or "atta-girl" for every other person. Everyone puts their messages in the envelopes each day. At the end of the week, all the kids look into their envelopes and there is lots of good stuff in there. When we do this project, it creates a fun atmosphere where everyone is noticing what they like about each other.

Snap Shots
From Lillian Shavings

Materials:
Polaroid camera and film
colored construction paper
markers

Project:
We take a photo of each group participant and post it on paper on the wall. Then everyone writes positive things on it about the person in the photo. When we did that in a group I was in, it meant alot to me and I've still got my photo and all the words everyone wrote.

Positively Me
From Reynold Okitkun

Materials:
presentation pen and markers

Project:
At our program, we use presentation pad sheets and give each participant one sheet. Everyone starts by writing their name and something positive about themselves on their page. Then we all walk around the room and everyone adds to all the other sheets something positive about that person. At the end, each person shares what is on their page and how it feels to notice all these positive things.

Drawing Me Out
From Debbie Hewitt

Materials:
newsprint
markers
timer

Project:
We use a timer and roll newsprint out on the tables. Each person sits down at one spot and has two minutes to draw a picture of him or herself (no need to be "realistic"). Then after the two minutes are done, everyone shifts their seat down to the next spot, for the next two minutes, and thinks about how they see that person. It could be a word, a scribble of color, anything that expresses something positive about that person. After two minutes, everyone shifts to the next seat, and so on around the room. When we get all the way back around, we have a sharing circle where each person describes what they see.
Row.txt_description: To build team spirit among the children and create a playful, structured way for them to practice appreciating and validating each other. Here are 4 different team-building project possibilities. Choose whichever seems to be the best fit for your group and circumstances. Feel free to adapt and change the workshop as needed. Enjoy!

Row.str_title: Out with the Old and In with the New
Row.txt_code:
Workshop participants share their "Out with the Old and in with the New" Sugar Scrub jars.
Objective:
To give the women an opportunity to explore feelings in a symbolic way and have a tangible product that they can keep with them.

Note:
Children 5 and older can do this activity with hands-on help

Materials:
White cane sugar or brown sugar
Glycerin oil or vegetable oil
Aloe gel (also found in the suntan lotion section of your store)
Essential oils for scent (I found good varieties and prices on ebay)
Ground hibiscus for color (if wanted)
Small canning jars or Tupperware (donated canning jars are great)
Magazines, scissors, and glue
Paintbrushes and decoupage (you can make this with glue and water)
Markers and journals

Workshop participant decorating her "Out with the Old and in with the New" Sugar Scrub jar. 
  
Timeframe:
Opening: 5 minutes
Warm-up: 5 minutes
Demonstration: 5-10 minutes without collaging the jar
Creation: 35 minutes
Sharing/closing: 10-20 minutes

Space setup:
Tables should be covered with a tablecloth or newspaper. The sugar should be put in buckets on the table to share. (I put two old cool whip containers of sugar on each table.) The oils should be put in squeeze bottles or smaller containers and put in the center of the table. There should be one canning jar and journal at every person’s place setting. Markers, magazines, paint brushes, scissors, pens and decoupage can be put on the table for sharing.

Opening:
Today we are going to be doing a workshop called "out with the old and in with the new." This workshop will be using symbolism to represent things that you would like to get rid of and what you would like to leave behind. Sugar scrubs use course sugars that act as an exfoliant. The sugar should represent what you want to get rid of. For every scoop of sugar you can identify thoughts, feelings, items that you want to “wash away.” Examples may include, “I want to get rid of the pain I feel” or “I want to get rid of the dependency I have on my partner.” You should journal how you feel and what the sugar represents for you. The oils and the gels will be symbolic of what you want have in your life. Examples may be “I want to feel self-sufficient” or “I want to secure a safe place to live.” Journal what thoughts, feelings or things that you want to leave behind. Your jars will be representative of a safe place to keep these feelings or thoughts. You should decorate or collage them however you feel inspired. Journaling your thoughts will be helpful in reflecting on this exercise in the future. This is your time, and you can use this however you would like. There is no right or wrong way to do this.

 Essential oils — a little goes a long way.
  
 
 Sample of collaging on a jar.
  
 
 Collages can be very simple & powerful.
Warm-up:
We did a stretch-and-relax warm-up. You can use any warm-up exercise you choose.

Technical Demonstration:
The group facilitator will take a jar and add scoops of sugar. Try to identify what your scoops of sugar represent—the things you want to wash away. You should have about half the jar filled with sugar. Then add small amounts of oils, identifying what you would like to stay in your life. The vegetable or glycerin oil will be the base. Once you reach a consistency that you like, you can add a squirt of aloe gel and 1 or 2 drops of essential oils. These too will be symbolic of what you want to remain in your life. (You should have about half sugar and half oil) Mix it all up. If you are near a sink you can put a small amount in the women’s hands. Ask them to think about all of the things that they want to get rid of. Have them rub their hands for about 30 seconds to a minute. Use hot water to wash away the sugar scrub and point out that the soft, clean feeling that they have is representative of what is left behind and the fresh start they have.

Creation:
Now it is the women’s turn. Music should be used. We used holiday music, but anything soothing will do. They can decorate their jars how they would like. After about 20 minutes, you can have them think about adding the sugar to their jar and journal what the sugar represents. Then have them add the oils and journal what the oils and gel represent. Note: When we did this workshop, it was helpful for the facilitator to add the essential oils because the the women added much more than a drop or two. The essentail oils are expensive, but when used in moderation should last several sessions.

Sharing:
If the women feel comfortable, they can share their jars and what they represent.

Closing:
The facilitator should thank the women for sharing and participating in the activity. As a treat to the women, the facilitator should clean the room if you have staff available.
Row.txt_description: By creating home-made "sugar scrubs," this workshop gives participants a chance to explore what they would like to get rid of and what they would like to keep in their lives.

Row.txt_code:
Sample cover of 2006 Calendar.
Objective:
The beginning of a new year is a great time to make your own personal calendar. It can help you track all the special days to look forward to – birthdays, holidays, fun activities etc. You can decorate and bind the calendar in a variety of ways and you can even use it as a scrapbook by adding photos and other fun memorabilia.

Materials:
Construction Paper (Optional - for the cover)
White copy paper for 12 months
Markers, crayons CrayPas or paint for the cover
Binding materials – hole punch, ribbon or brads
Calendar page (click on this link for template)
Calendar cover page (click on this link for template)

Decorating Calendar Cover.
 
  

 
July page of Calendar. 
Time Frame:
1 hour

Age range:
Age 5 and older. (This project can really be adapted to children of all ages)

Set Up:
Make 12 copies of the calendar page for each child, if there is time you can fill in the month and days for the younger children. Older can set up their own pages. This activity can help with reading counting, writing and construction skills.

Note:
This rhyme can help you remember how many days are in each month: "Thirty days has September, April, June, and November. All the rest have thirty-one, Excepting February alone, and it has twenty-eight days time, but in leap years, February has twenty-nine."

Introduction:
Sometimes the day-to-day life experiences are very difficult, but this is a good opportunity to talk about goals and plans for the New Year. Children can begin to plan things they want to accomplish as well as indicate times to celebrate or look forward to. Explaining the concept of a calendar will be necessary for the younger children.

 Lindsey working on her calendar.
Creation:
Spend as much time as you can on decorating the cover – using markers for the younger children. Older children may also want to decorate the pages – and use a theme for each month – you can discuss what is special about each month – ie. Valentine's Day, Mother’s Day, Birthdays etc. Before binding the 12 pages and cover, you may want to insert a blank for each month to allow for more room for photos or drawing. Save some time to bind the book. You can punch holes and use yarn or ribbon, simply staple or use brads. This calendar book can be used and treasured all year long.

Closing:
Talk about plans for the year focusing on all the positive things to look forward to in 2006.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives participants a special opportunity to talk about goals for the New Year, plan things they want to accomplish, and mark times to celebrate or look forward to, by creating their own calendar.

Row.txt_code:
Intern Lindsey shares her "What is Love?" doll.
  
 
 Decorating the "What is Love?" doll.
About this Workshop:
This workshop is based on the children’s book by Etan Boritzer, "What is Love?"

Objective:
To give the children an opportunity to sort out the complex feelings of love, begin to define what love means to them, and explore how sharing love can help to spread love around the world.

Materials:
People shapes
CrayPas
Wiggly eyes
Markers
Construction paper   
Color tissue paper  
Foam heart shapes   
Glitter glue
Glue sticks
Yarn
Glue sticks                  
Scissors
Stickers (for earth decorating)
Large sheet of butcher paper about 36 inches in diameter (or as big as you want for your earth)

Time Frame:
Approximately one hour (Could be divided into two sessions to create the earth together.)

Age Range:
Age range 5 and older – this project can be adapted to all ages.

Set Up:
Cut or draw a large circle out of butcher paper or poster board (36 inches in diameter) This will represent the Earth. Figure out a location to hang the circle, with enough space around it to add the people at the end of the workshop. Don't forget to put supplies near Earth location so that the first group is not disrupted as the children get up to decorate the world.

If you think it would be helpful to the children to see a sample, create one or two sample people with different kinds of love in their hearts.



Completed "What is Love Doll?" with black tissue paper skirt.
 
Introduction:
Today we are going to talk about love. Love can mean different things to different people. And it can even mean different things at different times, like when we're happy and when we're mad. Have your ever been mad at someone you love? Does it mean you didn't love them? Of course not, sometimes we feel angry at those we love.

Warm Up:
Select and read a part of the book, What is Love? out loud to the group (call AWBW we may have copies available). We recommend reading pages that start with -  Love is like rainbow, or But sometimes you may feel angry, or if your friend starts to feel.

In addition, you could ask questions and have someone write the answers onto your Earth, a heart shape large sheet of paper or simply draw a heart on a black board to write in.

“What do you love?” - Answers could be one or two words - “my mom” or “ice cream”
“How do you show love?” - "I smile" or “I say please and thank you”
“How do you give love?” - “I help with chores” “I share my toys " or "I say I love you"
“How can my love help the world?” - “I don’t waste supplies” or “I help to recycle”


 Illustration from the end of the "What is Love?" book.
 Here is a way to draw a circle any size you want - by using a string tied to a pencil (like a compass).  Hold one end of the string in the middle of the circle and draw with the other end, stretching the string tight as you go around in a circle.
  
or "I'm nice to others"

(As you talk about this last question, you might want to share the page in the "What is Love?" book that shows the world with all the different people around it. (Image on right.)

You could talk about the ways their love might touch each other, and the ways their love makes a difference around the world.)

Take the time to write down all the words and discuss all the different ideas and similar ideas that come up when talking about love. Validate each one by saying each answer out loud and noting the importance of all the different kinds of love.

Creation:
Have each child choose a cutout form of a person to represent themselves and hearts to decorate. Take care to help each participant write words, thoughts, and feelings about their love onto the hearts they selected and glue their heart on their person hey have decorated.

As they finish, any one who would like can go to the large circle and help decorate the world with markers, CrayPas, stickers etc. (The younger children will need help with this).

  
  
 
 AWBW people sharing their love
  
  



Closing:
Gather the children back to the table. Ask each child to come up to the world and share their decorated person. Encourage each child to share what is in their heart. When they are finished have them tape their person to or around the world and thank them for sharing their love and making the world a better place.
Row.txt_description: By creating a paper wall mural of the earth, this workshop gives participants an opportunity to sort out the complex feelings of love, begin to define what love means to them, and explore how sharing love can help to spread love around the world.

Row.txt_code:
Intern Lindsey shares her "What is Love?" doll.
  
 
 Decorating the "What is Love?" doll.
About this Workshop:
This workshop was inspired by the children’s book by Etan Boritzer, "What is Love?" The focus of this book is on love’s ability to hold all kinds of feelings, even contradictory ones. The book expands on the concept that sharing or giving love is one of the best ways to create more love in this world.
 
Objective:
To give participants an opportunity to sort out the complex feelings of love, begin to define what love means to them, and explore how sharing love can help to spread love around the world.

Materials:
People shapes
CrayPas
Construction paper
Color tissue paper
Markers
Foam heart shapes
Glitter glue
Glue sticks
Yarn
Wiggly eyes
Scissors
Large sheet of butcher paper about 36 inches in diameter (or as big as you want for your earth)
Optional supplies:
Collage Materials (for making the earth)
Stickers
Large paper or blackboard for taking notes

Time Frame:
Approximately 2 hours including set up.

Set Up:
Cut or draw a large circle out of butcher paper or poster board (36 inches in diameter) This will represent the Earth. Figure out a location to hang the circle, with enough space around it to add the people at the end of the workshop.  Don't forget to put supplies near Earth location so that the first group is not disrupted as participants decorate their world.



Completed "What is Love Doll?" with black tissue paper skirt.
 
Introduction:
In this workshop you will have the opportunity to notice the love you hold in your heart and to see how sharing this love can make the world a more loving place for all.  Sharing love is like practicing a random act of kindness.  Has anybody ever experienced what it feels like to have some do something kind/loving for you for no particular reason?  Sometimes even that simplest act of kindness like smiling warmly at someone can makes us feel loved. 

Warm Up:
Today we are going to practice sharing love by writing a group letter filled with kind thoughts and loving feelings to an anonymous person in the room. You may want to think of it in terms of what you would say to a woman or all women in the world to create a more loving and kind world for all of us to enjoy.

Warm-up creation:  You will need to have one piece of paper per participant (maybe cut pieces of different color paper into heart shapes).  Have participants address their letter in anyway they wish (i.e. Dear Amazing woman), on the top of the page.  Let them know they will have five minutes to write their lette. Play some soft background music and begin (to mind time, let them know when they have one minute left). Once everyone is done, put all the letters in a basket and pass them around until everybody takes one. Give the ladies a minute to read the letters to themselves. Ask particpants to volunteer to share their letters and to say a few words of how it felt to receive it. When everyone who wanted to share has had the opportunity to do so you make take a minute to notice and validate the loving advice and kind words that were shared.

Demonstration: To transition to the people making part of this workshop you may choose to show a sample(s). Or just point out the supplies you have laid out and remind them of the love they shared and received is in their heart.



 Illustration from the end of the "What is Love?" book.
 Here is a way to draw a circle any size you want - by using a string tied to a pencil (like a compass).  Hold one end of the string in the middle of the circle and draw with the other end, stretching the string tight as you go around in a circle.
  
Creation:
Have the participants choose a cutout form of a person that will represent themselves. Remind them that this is an opportunity to notice the love they have to give.  Have each participant choose a heart and write words, thoughts, and feelings about their love onto the hearts.

Allow them time to decorate their person and add their heart. As they finish, have the women decorate the Earth with words, symbols etcetera to represent what a world with more love would look like.  Give them a five-minute countdown to finish decorating the earth and to return to their seats.

Closing:
Tell the women to hold their little doll and look into their heart. Ask them to notice how special each of their hearts is and to notice how much love they have to give.  Encourage each person to share their creations.  Once the Earth is completed add each participants person to encircle the earth.
Row.txt_description: By creating a paper wall mural of the earth, this workshop gives participants an opportunity to sort out the complex feelings of love, begin to define what love means to them, and explore how sharing love can help to spread love around the world.
Row.txt_tips: You may want to use the warm-up as a stand alone workshop and allow participants more time to decorate their cards.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To understand that people can express themselves in different ways, as well as to learn to look at yourself from the inside. A portrait can be any way we wish it to be and hopefully this workshop will help participants feel comfortable with materials and not be intimated by the thought of having the portrait look like a specific person.

 
    Intern Lindsey, designing her portrait
Materials:
CrayPas
Colored pencils
Markers
Watercolors
Brushes
Cups for water
Paper towels
White paper 8 1/2 x 11
Large construction paper 12 x 18 (or any size  larger than 8 1/2 x 11)
Glue sticks
Small journals (optional)
White copy paper

Time Frame:
Approximately one hour

Age Range:
Age range - Teens
Could be adapted for younger children

Note to leaders:
  • Teens learn about relationships from the adults they live with, the media, the Internet and their friends. As adults we have the responsibility to be open to discussing relationships with teens, to hear their questions with respect and give them real answers. Being honest without judgment, no matter what they share with us, goes a long way to making you a child or teen's "safe adult".
  • To help establish boundaries with the teens you may want to create Ground Rules as a group. 
  • While you may feel like you can't be a friend and advocate to the teens you serve for a myriad of reasons, keep in mind that all you need to be is their trusted adult.
  • For more tips and information about working with teens please visit the FAQ section of AWBW's website

Set Up:
If possible collect a variety of portraits, to show the wide range of techniques. These can be collected from a book, slides or the Internet. Try to include a range of styles from realistic to abstract, noting that all portraits don’t have to actually look like a person but instead can reflect how the person is feeling. (See examples on last page).

Introduction:
The idea of a self-portrait can be intimidating. This workshop will teach us how to look into ourselves and express what or how we feel on the inside as opposed to how we look on the outside. This helps us to understand that people can express themselves in different ways, keeping in mind that art is an external expression of internal feelings.

Warm-Up:
If you are able to, hand each participant a small sketchbook.  If that is not available you can use clean white copy paper. The warm-up is designed to help people feel more comfortable with seeing how we look on the inside. You can move through them rather quickly (giving 2 or 3 minutes for each) and begin each one with a small stretch or deep breathing exercise to help focus on the project.
Select as many as you have time for and experiment with the different materials:
  •  Use colors and shapes to reflect how you are feeling at this moment – red circles, green clouds, pink swirls, grey tornado etc.
  •  If you could see yourself as an animal what would you draw – a dog on a leash, a bird flying high in the sky, a lion in a cage, a cat sleeping
  •  Draw something that makes you happy or that you like doing – swimming, running, singing, laughing
  •  See what it is like to draw a body in motion – you can use stick figures or long oval

     Simple shapes can make a figure!
    shapes – dancing, running, playing sports
  •  Use the whole piece of paper to draw a face
  •  Use the whole paper to draw an abstract face
A second warm up can be leader or peer run interviews to help participants get accustomed to thinking about themselves. You can use the following suggested questions:
  •  Three words that describe me are ...
  •  My favorite song is ...
  •  The quality I like best about myself is ...
  •  My favorite movie is ...
  •  Three of my favorite foods are ...
  •  My favorite thing to do on the weekend is ...
  •  People may be surprised to know that I ...
Feel free to use either warm-up or a combination of the two.

Creation:
Now that we are warmed up and are comfortable with some of the materials we will take the time to think about how we feel and how we think we look to others. The portraits will be drawn without mirrors or the use of erasers. They are to be a form of true inner self-expression. There is no wrong way especially when the focus is on how we feel not how we look. Use of color, shapes and a variety of materials will help a free flow of expression.
As they work, have each person hold the work up at a distance away to see their creation from different point of view.
After each person is done they can select a piece of colored paper to mount/frame their portrait.

   
 
 
 
 Picture of Me
  Abstract Me
  Picture of Me



Closing:
The closing circle can be a discussion of what we now think a portrait is, to notice how we are all different and that what we feel inside is worth expressing.




Here are some examples of portraits by famous artists


  
 Salvador Dali


 
 Pablo Picasso


 
 Amedeo Modigliani
  
 Pablo Picasso


  
 Gustav Klimt


 
 Diego Rivera
     
 Rene Magritte


 
 Juan Gris


 
 Vincent Van Gogh
Row.txt_description: This self-portrait workshop teaches how to look inside and express how we feel rather than how we look on the outside.
Row.txt_tips: If you or your clients need resources to help address Teen Dating Violence issues use the Teen Dating Violence Resource Page.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Artists have been painting portraits of themselves for many centuries. This workshop gives women the opportunity to examine not only their faces, but also their identity. It also allows women to paint their selves the way t hey want to be portrayed. The project helps the women realize that they, themselves, are works of art – unique and valuable in every way.



 Leader, Ivy holding
Self-nurture Portraits
Materials:
Thick white paper or Canvas
Paint brushes
Acrylic paints
Paper plates (To use as palettes)
Water cups
Paper towels
Pencils (for sketching before painting)
Small mirror for each woman to help paint themselves
(can ask the women to bring their own mirror for the workshop)
Various samples of portraits by other artists

Introduction:
Explain that each of us looks in the mirror probably every day, but that each of us may not always take the time to see how special they are. We may not realize how unique, precious, and wonderful each of us is. Just as we have the power to create the way we want most of our days to turn out, we have the most valuable power of creating who we are and how we end up. We have the power to choose to be positive and loving. We have the power to choose non-violence. We have the power to transform and create ourselves into someone we love and value.

Opening Circle:
What is one thing you value about yourself? It could be anything. Or what is one thing you want to enhance or strengthen about yourself?

Relaxation:
Get relaxed in your chair and close your eyes. Imagine yourself walking into a large artist’s studio. You head towards a comfortable chair in the middle of the studio. You can see all around you portrait paintings of people you recognize – famous people. You also begin to see portraits of people you don’t recognize, but the paintings are all wonderful and intriguing. The studio is owned by a brilliant painter who is known for her work with portraits. Today, you are the subject of her painting. And today, that brilliant painter is
  


 Participants painting portraits
you. You will be painting your own portrait.

Think about looking into a mirror. Look into your eyes. Those eyes have seen a lot. What kind of things would you like to see more of? What kind of things would you like to see less of? Think about your nose. Think of the beautiful smells that have wafted up your nose. Think of the comforting smells like food, candles, flowers, or rain. Now, think about your mouth. Think about the things you’ve said. Have you said hurtful things before? How did that make you feel? How do you feel when you say nice things? How does it feel to smile and laugh? Also think about your mouth and the numerous taste buds on your tongue. What kind of foods have you enjoyed eating? Is it a juicy, savory steak or a rich, chocolate brownie or a ripe, fragrant peach? Think of the foods you eat that help comfort you. Now, start thinking about your ears. Do you think they’re too big, maybe too small, or just perfect? Now think about what your ears have heard. Think of all the sounds that have entered your ears and mind: car horns, whispers, music, silence, yelling, arguing, birds chirping, babies crying, children laughing, the ocean, being told you are loved. Think about how you feel when you hear these things.

Finally, think about your face and your skin. Our skin is the largest organ in our body. Think about what your skin has felt – pain and joy. What were the touches you enjoyed the most: A kiss on the cheek, putting your head on a pillow, wrapping yourself in a warm cozy blanket, a foot massage, a big warm hug? Now think of all the different ways our bodies can feel and take in different stimuli and the many different ways we react and feel about all the different things in the world. Our minds and bodies are complex. We are all intricate inside and out. We are all precious and unique. When you open your eyes and look into the mirror, remember how complex and beautiful you are. Celebrate that beauty inside and outside of you by creating your self-portrait.

Technical Info:
It’s a good idea to have participants sketch their faces with pencil before using paints. Have them look in the mirror and notice the unique details of their eyes, nose, mouth, and hair. They will also notice that their eyes are about halfway between the top of their head and the bottom of their chin. Participants should also note that their eyes are about one eye length between each other. It is good to bring a few samples (colored printouts are nice) of self-portraits to show variety and give some ideas. It’s also great to include portraits from the various styles like impressionism, modern, abstract, etc.

Here are some examples of portraits by famous artists:

 
 Salvador Dali

 
 Pablo Picasso



 
 Amedeo Modigliani
 Pablo Picasso

 
 Gustav Klimt



 
 Diego Rivera
 
 Rene Magritte

 
 Juan Gris



 
 Vincent Van Gogh
  



























There may be some women who don’t feel comfortable painting themselves. Remind them that this is their "window of time" and that they can choose what their creation will look like. Encourage them to paint something symbolic, abstract or maybe even just one feature on their face. Remind them that they can be a butterfly, shapes or just a color. The important thing is that it shows what they value in themselves or their lives.

 
 
 
 Picture of Me
  Abstract Me
  Picture of Me

Closing:
The closing circle can be a discussion of what we now think a portrait is, to notice how we are all different and that what we feel inside is worth expressing. Ask each woman to share her painting and how she felt drawing her own self.
Row.txt_description: Artists have been painting portraits of themselves for many centuries. This workshop gives women the opportunity to examine not only their faces, but also their identity. It also allows women to paint their selves the way they want to be portrayed. The project helps the women realize that they, themselves, are works of art – unique and valuable in every way.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Puzzle Piece Paper D oll Template
Objective:
Allows children and youth to name and identify feelings and notice where they hold feelings in their own body. This can be an opportunity to help normalize the myriad of emotions youth and children are feeling and give them a way to begin to process them.

Materials:
Colored markers and pencils - for coloring
Permanent markers - for writing words
Handout of paper doll made up of puzzle pieces - 1 or 2 for each participant
- click here for Person Outline Template
Handout with various emotions that the child can refer to - click here for Emotions Handout
Music- something upbeat, such as "Putamayo World Beats"

Note: If your intention is to use this workshop to address anger, it is important to begin by having a discussion on "What is Anger?" Please click here to see the entire Processing Anger Series.

   
Example by teen age boy   
Timeframe:
Intro: 10 minutes
Warm Up: 10 minutes
Creation: 25 minutes
Closing: 15 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour

Age Range: 3 and up.

Set Up:
Lay out colored markers and pencils around the table. Make sure that there is a person outline template and emotions handout for each child. These can be placed where the child will be sitting or handed out to them after the warm-up exercise.

Introduction:
Today we are going to talk about how we feel. Each of us have feelings or emotions. Sometimes emotions makes us feel good or bad, but there are actually no right or wrong feelings. Sometimes we may feel lots of different feelings at once; we can feel confused or overwhelmed by not knowing how we really feel. This is part of being human, and there are ways to learn how to understand our feelings and even how to get through ones that feel hard.

Lets start by thinking about the different kinds of feelings we have. Can you think of different kinds of feelings? Has anyone ever felt more than one feeling at the same time?

Encourage participants to think of a feeling or feelings that they have in this very moment. (You may even want to use a warm like Feelings Target for older kids or Feeling Faces for younger feelings to start this workshop.)

 
  Close-up of feelings in the present
  
 
  Close-up of feelings wanted in the future
Warm Up:
Do an exercise with the children with music to shake their feelings out. Have them dance around the room and ask them to make a face that they make when they feel a certain emotion.

What face do you make when you feel happy? Now shake it out! What face do you make when you feel sad? Now shake it out! What face do you make when you feel angry, tired, excited? Repeat and shake it out!

Then have them dance their way back to their seats!

Now, let's take a moment and breathe with our eyes closed, if that feels good to you, or keep your eyes open and focus them on an object in the room. Notice your breath as it enters and leaves your body. Let them do this for 3 breaths.

Now see if you feel any feelings in your body. How do you feel right now? Where do you feel that feeling? Is it in you shoulders, stomach, neck?

For example, if you are nervous, does your stomach feel funny or is your heart racing? Are any parts of your body stiffening up? If you are happy, do you feel it in your face or a tingling in your stomach? Take a moment and notice your feelings. As you notice how you feel, ask yourself, would that feeling have a certain color? Do different feelings or groups of feelings have different colors or shades?

Creation:
Show the children the person outline template that they will be writing and coloring their feelings on. You may want to show them an example of one that you created or explain that they can use color or words to show where they feel different feelings. Remind them that just like there are no right or wrong emotions, there is no right or wrong way of creating their art.

Have the children write inside each puzzle piece a word that describes a feeling that they have right now or feelings that they had sometime today. You will have to help the younger children write these words on their puzzle pieces if they want words, but it's not necessary. You can encourage the older children to think of where in their body they might feel their different feelings; they can then write that feeling in the place that they feel it.

After the puzzle pieces are filled with the words of emotions, then have the children color in each puzzle piece with a color that portrays each feeling. There is no right or wrong color for different feelings. We all share the same feelings like sad, mad, happy or fear but it feels and may look different for each person.

Older children may want to create two feeling puzzles in one workshop; one to represent their feelings in the present moment and one to represent what they want their feelings to be in the future. This leaves them with an empowered feeling of "putting themselves back together" with the feelings they want to have!

Closing Circle:
At the end, give all the children a chance to share their creation. For children who chose to create a second feeling puzzle, ask if they want to share how it felt to notice the feelings they wish to feel in the future. This can be an empowering process! If they don't want to share, be sure to let them know that it's okay. Remind them to respect each others art and feelings while they share. Have them notice how many different feelings and colors there are on everyone's creation. Even though each creation is different and unique, they all share similar feelings. At the end, congratulate them for such wonderful work and for sharing their feelings!
Row.txt_description: Allows children and youth to name and identify feelings and notice where they hold feelings in their own body. This can be an opportunity to help normalize the myriad of emotions youth and children are feeling and give them a way to begin to process them.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Note About Timing
This workshop can also be done at two different intervals; the first time at the beginning of the child's arrival to the program, and the second time during the last few days before they leave. This can help them see how their feelings have changed over time!

Note About Anger Workshops
We recommend that you start anger workshops with a discussion; don't be afraid to talk to the children about their anger. Anger is nothing to be ashamed of; it is important to look at and talk about it to try to understand it.

Some anger prompts that we like are:
What is Anger? What does it look like and what does it sound like?
What was the trigger to your anger?
What did you think about it?
How did it make you feel?
How did you act?
What effect did it have on you and those around you?

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give children and opportunity to learn basic printmaking skills which will allow them to duplicate a design for gifts or framing. The project can teach the value of your art, by having the ability to preserve and replicate an image.






Supplies for printmaking
Materials:
Styrofoam plates or take out cartons (Must have a smooth bottom without any previous design) – Can be round, square or rectangle
Ball point pens
Scissors
Brayers/rubber rollers – Sponges can work instead
(Sponge rollers can be purchased at craft stores like Michaels or at Discount School Supply)
White thick paper – larger than the size of the Styrofoam
Paper to practice drawings
Thick paint like acrylic, tempera is possible or inks if you have them
Paper towels
Brushes
Extra paper plates to roll out the paint (a large flat piece of plexiglass or a cookie sheet works great!!)
Construction Paper to use for frames or cards


Drawing the design
Time Frame:
Approximately one hour

Age Range:
Age range – 6 and older

Set Up:
Cover the tables with paper or newspaper. This project can be messy unless you really control the paint area. We suggest limiting the colors available to 3 or 4. If room permits it is good to have a separate table for applying the paint. Each participant can come up when they are done drawing their design to roll their paint.
We suggest practicing with this process before you teach the group.

Introduction:
You can start by asking if anyone knows what printmaking is. The first prints go all the way back to cave carvings and there was a time when printing was done on cloth before paper was invented. There are many types of printmaking, which involve engraving or carving a design. Engravings have been done on a variety of surfaces such as metal, stone, and wood. It is a way to make art and duplicate the same design again and again. Today we will use something as simple as a paper plate to do our carvings!












Applying the paint with a roller



Applying the paint with a sponge



Press the plate firmly onto the paper








Creation:
  1. Each participant will draw a design on the flat side of a Styrofoam plate. (Practice designs can be done on plain white paper). The drawing should be done with a ballpoint pen and the pressure should be firm with clean lines. Take care not to apply so much pressure that it punctures the plate. The initial design should be simple, more intricate work can be done after the printing process is learned.
  2. Once the plate is ready have the child select a color to apply. You can use either tempera or acrylic paint – pour a small amount on a flat service and either roll with a foam/rubber brayer, use a sponge or brush to apply the paint to the plate, Taking care not to let the paint fill in the lines that have been dawn.
  3. Once the plate is covered with paint turn it over and press onto a piece of thick white paper. Press firmly, trying not to wiggle or move the plate once it has made contact with the paper. Carefully lift the plate off the paper and you will see your image printed!
This process can be repeated and colors can be added. The finished project can be used for a card or gift. Perfect for Mother’s day next month!


Carefully lift the plate




The plate can be used again by cleaning
and reapplying the paint










Closing:
Lead a discussion on how it felt to see the artwork transferred from a plate to a piece of nice paper. If time permits you can mount the work on colored construction paper or make it into cards
Row.txt_description: To give children an opportunity to learn basic printmaking skills which will allow them to duplicate a design for gifts or framing. The project can teach the value of your art, by having the ability to preserve and replicate.

Row.str_author_location: Madera County Community Action Agency, Inc.
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To allow victims of domestic violence to begin to see themselves as survivors of domestic violence.  To create a visual aid and symbolic reminder commemorating their courage and representing how they are breaking with the past to a positive new future.

Note:  This workshop honors survivors in the tradition of old-fashioned silhouette portraiture.   By cutting out and turning Polaroid pictures to their black side for mounting, this workshop offers an easy way to create poignant portraits that honor the courage of survivors while protecting their anonymity.  It can also be a powerful group or family project in a multi-window frame (see variation below).

 
 Silhouette Sample
Materials:
Polaroid camera
Scissors
Poster board
Glue sticks
Markers
Glitter
Sequins
Collage materials
Miscellaneous scrap booking materials
Optional: Small inexpensive frames

Introduction:
You could begin by reading a poem such as Believing in Yourself and Your Special Dreams by Deanna Beisser, a domestic violence survivor (for an alternate poem see workshop tips online).

Believing in Yourself and Your Special Dreams

There may be days when you get up in the morning
and things aren't the way you had hoped they would be.
That's when you have to tell yourself that things will get better.
There are times when people disappoint you and let you down,
but those are the times when you must remind yourself
to trust your own judgements and opinions,
to keep your life focused on believing in yourself
and all the that you are capable of . . .

There will be challenges to face and changes to make in your life,
and it is up to you to accept them.
Constantly keep yourself headed in the right direction for you.
It may not be easy at times, but in those times of struggle
you will find a stronger sense of who you are
and you will also see yourself developing into the person
you have always wanted to be.

Life is a journey through time, filled with many choices:
each of us will experience life in our own special way.
So when the days come that are filled with frustration
and unexpected responsibilities, remember to believe in yourself
and all you want your life to be,
because the challenges and changes
will only help you to find the dreams that you know
are meant to come true for you.

Explain that today they are going to create a symbolic badge of courage using their own image.  Remind them that though they were victims of a crime, they are now survivors.
Ask them to think about their courage and strength and to focus on today as the beginning of a new life.  This new life can hold what ever they most desire.

Opening Circle:
Use soothing music, have the women share by doing a check-in circle using one-word to describe one thing they appreciate about themselves.



 Cutting Polaroid
Demo:
First demonstrate by having a Polaroid picture ready to cut out. Cut it out and turn it over, revealing the black silhouette that is created.  Explain that they will only be using the black side of their picture.  Then demonstrate how to glue it to poster board.  Encourage them to use any of the supplies provided to decorate their silhouette portrait.
(You may want to have a completed simple example.)

Creation:
Begin by having each participant come up one at time to take her picture. Have the group help and encourage each other verbally as they create their profile and chose their position of hands and head.  Take their picture using their profile from their waist up to their head. Welcome them to make a hand gesture or to position their head in a way that best shows their pride and courage.  

Once everyone's picture is taken turn on soothing music and encourage the participants to begin cutting and mounting their portraits.

Remind them along the way to chase negative thoughts away and to honor themselves for being there today.

  
 
 Sample Drawing
   Sample Collage

Closing:
Once they have finished you may want to have a closing circle allowing them to share their creation and anything that they enjoyed or discovered as they were creating.

Variations:
Leaders may want to present this project as a group portrait, or as a family portrait using a multi-window frame.  See example below:



 Silhouettes of DV Survivors
Row.txt_description: To allow victims of domestic violence to begin to see themselves as survivors of domestic violence. To create a visual aid and symbolic reminder commemorating their courage and representing how they are breaking with the past to a positive new future.
Row.txt_tips:
My Journey to Recovery
Poem by domestic Violence Survivor

 In the beginning,
    I wondered if I would
    ever make it through.
    There were periods of anger,
    sadness, pain, and grief;
    times I wondered,
    "Why me?"

    But one day,
    there was a glimpse of light,
    and then another.

    The Clouds began to break apart,
    and I started to see beyond them.

    The times when I felt happy and safe
    began to outnumber the times
    when I felt sad and frightened.
    New friendships were formed;
    feelings of trust and resolution
    began to replace past feelings
    of hopelessness and self doubt.
    I seemed to emerge from the darkness
    into the light with anew sense of empowerment.

    I now realize that there are things
    about my past that I cannot change,
    but I can stop them from controlling
    my life and my happiness.

    I know that this part of my life
    will never go away entirely,
    but it has begun to take a less
    prominent place in my existence.
    I have begun to allow other thoughts
    to enter my mind,
    and have a better understanding of myself-
    my strengths and weaknesses.
    I am not afraid to set limits
    I have begun to enjoy life again
    and to think about the future.
    I can now look back on this time for
    what it was -
    a period of growth,
    self-discovery,
    and healing.

Mi viaje a la recuperación
Por:
Una sobreviviente de la violencia domestica

Al principio,
No sabia si podía sobrevivir.
Había etapas de enojo, tristeza, dolor, y duelo
Pensaba, "porque yo?"

Pero un día
Yo vi un poquito de luz
Y otro día aun mas

Las nubes empezaron a despejar
Y podía ver mas allá

Los tiempos en que me sentía segura y contenta
Empezaron a superar en numero a los
Tiempos en que me sentía triste y tenia miedo
Nuevas amistades se formaron,
Los sentimientos de confianza y resolución
Empezaron a reemplazar a los de desesperanza y duda
Parecía que estaba saliendo de la oscuridad
Hacia la luz del poder

Ahora me doy cuenta de que hay cosas
En mi pasado que no puedo cambiar,
Pero si puedo controlar el papel que hacen
En mi vida y en mi alegría

Yo se que esta parte de me vida
Nunca se ira totalmente,
Pero esta ocupando ahora menos
En mi mente y en mi energía
Ahora permito que otros pensamientos
Tomen su espacio en mi mente

Ahora tengo mejor sentido de quien soy yo,
En mi fortaleza y mi debilidad
No tengo miedo de mis limites
Otra vez, disfruto de mi vida, y puedo pensar en el futuro
Puedo ver mas claramente a mi pasado
Y reconocerlo como era:
Un periodo de crecimiento, de auto-conocimiento,
De auto-descubrimiento, y de curación.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To bring the participants’ awareness toward themselves. Often, when survivors enter the shelter, they have lost all sense of themselves. Instead, they are the “mother” the “wife” or “partner,” or a shell of a body they have had to dissociate from. By creating this Self Box, they get to “see” who they are on the inside, as well as who they are on the outside. They will also get a chance to visualize how they want to be on the top of the box. In abusive relationships, most of the attention is focused on the abuser. Participants will usually focus on themselves only in light of their victimization and pain. This project will give them a more empowered focus on who they are, and who they see themselves becoming.

 
 Materials for Self Box   
Materials:
Shoe boxes or other small carboard boxes
Magazines
Collage materials
Glue
Scissors
Paper
Pens

Time Frame:
Allow an hour and a half for this assignment. It is very important to allow them time to engage in the art making as well as the group sharing. Thirty to forty minutes for the introduction and art making should be sufficient. The rest of the time can be left for whatever sharing they choose to do. The sharing is a very important part of this exercise.



 Outside of Self Box
Introduction and Creation:
Each participant is given a box. “The box is symbolic of you and your life. Decorate the outside of the box as who you are to the world. You might want to have each side represent a different aspect of your life. For instance, one side could be how you show yourself at work, one side could be as a mother or partner, and maybe one side can be your family of origin. Be creative and follow where your heart is leading."



 Inside of Self Box
  
 
 Top of Self Box
“For the inside of the box, decorate as your own private inner world. Symbolize your thoughts, feelings, hopes, and fears. Put things in there that you like about yourself."

“On the top of the box, create images that represent how you want to be seen, and how you want to see yourself."

“When you are finished with the box, write yourself a letter or poem. Title it ‘Who am I?’ Write another page for ‘Who I want to be,’ and be sure to include those wonderful things you already are, or that you know are within you waiting to come out. Put these inside your box."

“Tonight, or sometime soon, write down some of your hopes and fears. Then put this list in your box, and symbolically turn it over to that wise part inside of you to take care of.”

Closing:
After participants finish, allow time for each of them to talk about their box. This has healing potential in that they will be “seen” for who they are through the sharing.

 
 Finished Self Box

"Who am I?" by Shara Stevens (this can be shared with the group):
I am a woman. I am an artist. I am a student. I am a waitress. I am a friend. I am a daughter. I am strong, some people call me controlling and selfish. So be it. I am an accumulation of everything I’ve experienced and felt... every tear I’ve cried... every trauma I’ve survived. I am becoming... changing and growing and realizing just who I am with each passing moment... For eleven years, off and on, I’ve been in therapy, self-help groups, weekend workshops, reading self-help books, discussing life with friends, writing faithfully in my journal, etc., etc... I have come to one conclusion: “I am” is always changing. Nothing stays exactly the same. Some of my diehard character defects, I.E. my “control issues”, they even change. I still have them, but hey, I am aware of them. That makes it Okay. Another constant in my life is me. I am the only one I can be absolutely sure of that will stick by me ‘til the day I die. So, my most important relationship is the one I have with myself. For years I struggled with learning how to love myself. Learning how to forgive myself. Those are the most valuable gifts I’ve received in my whole life time. The rest was just a part of the journey... a journey to myself. Of which I still don’t really know, but it keeps unfolding.
Row.txt_description: Participants create a Self Box which allows them to “see” who they are one the inside, as well as who they are on the outside. This project will give them a more empowered focus on who they are, and who they see themselves becoming.

Row.str_author_location: Free Arts For Abused Children, CA
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Provides participants with the opportunity to design and create their own t-shirts or pillow cases.

 
 
Child drawing out design for her shirt
at FAAC workshop
Materials Needed:
White t-shirts or white pillow cases (one per person).
Sandpaper (medium grade - 2 per person)
Crayons (Crayola works best)
Irons (2)
Scratch paper
Pencils
Black permanent markers
Rulers
Masking tape
Scissors
Butcher paper
Shirt-shaped cardboard covered with aluminium foil

Volunteers Needed:
2 volunteers to iron designs on the shirts
1 volunteer for every 3 children (to hand out sandpaper & provide guidance)

Prep Time Tasks:
Heat irons
Divide shirts by sizes
Open sandpaper
Cover tables with butcher paper
Spread crayons, scratch paper & pencils on tables
Create a prototype and hang on wall for reference

Instructions:
Show children prototype. Tell them that they will be creating their own designs for their t-shirts. Have them sit and sketch some ideas on the scratch paper. Explain that sandpaper is costly and they have to come up with their idea before they put it on the sand paper. Names and words need to be written backward in order for the image to be correct when it is ironed on the shirt. One way to do this is to have them write what they want to say on scratch paper with a black marker. Turn the paper over and have them follow the backward writing when they put it on sand paper. When they are ready, pass out one sheet of sand paper per person. When they are coloring their designs on the sandpaper, be sure that they make them as dark as possible, so the image is clear on the shirt. When working with really young children, you may need to darken their designs for them. When the designs are ready, each child gets in line to have their decoration ironed on the shirt. Ironers should ask where the person wants their design placed (back, front, sleeve, center, right, left, etc.) Clean up is relatively easy for this project. Be sure to let the irons cool before packing them.

 
 Child creating design for her shirt at FAAC workshop

Reminder:
Encourage kids to create their own designs -- do not draw for them. Be patient. If a child appears stuck, help them by having them identify a favorite color or encourage them to use the whole piece of paper and do something abstract or geometric. The shirts and pillow cases are for the facility staff and children, not for the volunteers.
Row.txt_description: Provides participants with the opportunity to design and create their own t-shirts or pillow cases.

Row.str_author_location: Free Arts For Abused Children, CA
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide children with the opportunity to use their imaginations to create their very own Spirit Puppet.  A spirit of the child’s choice enters into the puppet when it is placed into the ground, hence, “spirit puppet.”

 
 Creating a Spirit Puppet at a FAAC workshop
Materials:
Quick dry plaster bandages (cut into long strips)
Tree branches (1 - 3 feet, not too thick)
Large bowls / salted warm water
Newspaper
Fabric scraps and bric-a-brac
Assorted acrylic paints
Glitter, feathers, yarn, beads, buttons
Paint brushes
Scissors
Elmers Glue
Hot Glue Guns and Refills
String
Butcher Paper
Masking Tape
Salt

Volunteers Needed:
1 volunteer per child

Set Up:
Cover tables with Butcher Paper
Unwrap bandages and cut into long strips
Lay sticks out by size
Set up work station with fabric, paints and embellishments
Communicate myth of “Spirit Puppet” to volunteers
Create a prototype sample

 
 Finsihed Spirit Puppets at a FAAC workshop
Instructions:
Show children prototype. Establish that a “spirit puppet” is a unique and personal creation that can take any form or shape. A spirit of the child's choice enters into the puppet when it is planted into the ground, hence, "spirit puppet." Ask the child what he/she would like to create, then choose a branch to work with as a base. S/he may take another branch and, using masking tape, adhere them together to form a cross-shape. The volunteer can hold the branches while the child tapes. Dip a long strip of plaster into the warm, salted water (the salt helps the plaster dry quickly) and squeeze out the excess water between two fingers. Wrap the plaster around the taped area. Layer 2 or 3 times until sturdy. To make a head, crumple newspaper into a ball. Use masking tape to help the paper hold its round shape and to attach it to the stick. Again, the volunteer can hold the figure while the child tapes. Use plaster strips to attach head to figure and over the paper so the head is layers of plaster. Smooth out wrinkles with warm water and fingers. While plaster dries, choose fabric to dress -- it may be tied, strung, glued or draped onto the puppet. Paint, glitter, and decorate accordingly. Plant into ground.

Reminders:
Encourage children to use their imaginations-- they don't have to follow the same "T-figure" format. The spirit can have multi heads or no head at all, arms or no arms. It does not have to be human-like or even animal-like. Individuality is the purpose and the key.
Row.txt_description: Provides participants with the opportunity to use their imaginations to create their very own Spirit Puppet. A spirit of the child’s choice enters into the puppet when it is placed into the ground, hence, “spirit puppet.”

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
The purpose of this workshop is for children to create a treasure box of their own in which they can store things that are valuable to them in order to keep them safe. These can be actual items, notes, or symbolic reminders.

Materials:
Required:
Assorted boxes (shoe, cigar, etc.)
Options:
Magazines or pre-cut pictures
Assorted paper to cover boxes
Paper, found objects and other items to create symbolic reminders of people, places or things that are meaningful or important, including drawings, notes, letters, etc.
Jewelry pieces, sequins and/or glitter
Glue and/or decoupage
Scissors
Assorted markers or Permanent Markers (if using with any liquid including glue)
Paint
Photographs of special people (optional)

Time Frame:
10-15 minutes: Introduction/Opening Circle
35-45 minutes: Creation
10-15 minutes: Closing Circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children; 1 adult for 2 young children

Space set-up:
Have cushions or pieces of rug available to sit on for the opening circle and tables for the activity.

Introduction:
When we hear treasure, we may imagine pirates, precious gems or gold. Today our treasures our simply what is important, valuable, or meaningful to each of us that we want to keep safe or protected. Explain to the children/youth that they will have the opportunity to create a special private box where they can keep whatever is valuable or important to them.

Share with participants that what is important to each person will be different and unique and so will each creation. For some people, their dreams and wishes are what is most important, for others it is memories of people, places or a time that is special in their mind, and for others it may be very specific things like a diary or a keepsake. It could be all of these thing and none of these things. This box can be decorated to represent those important things or can be decorated with favorite colors or cool images, and then filled with things that are important, special or valuable. It's up to each person how and what their treasure box looks like.

Opening Circle:
Have the children/youth share one thing that is important to them that they want to keep protected or safe. This could be their dreams, a special relationship or a favorite thing that they treasure. After everyone who wants to has shared something they treasure, invite them to notice the supplies provided by you and allow them to ask question about the materials. For any specialized materials, you may want to give brief demonstrations of how to use them in their box creation. 

Creation:
Turn on light and fun music to set the tone for creation and exploration. Participants can get very absorbed in this process and loose track of time easily, be sure to do regular time checks to be sure they know how much time they have. Allow amble time for the participants to decorate and to personalize their boxes. Give reminders that each treasure box is meant to reflect their own special and important treasure and that there is no right or wrong way to create this project. What is most important is that they fill it with whatever reminders they may need of what is most important to them, that they want to keep safe.

Closing Circle:
Allow the children time to write or to talk about how their treasures boxes are significant to them and how they felt creating a safe and private place of their own. If they choose, they can share how they intend to use their treasure boxes. Be sure to explain to the mothers the importance of keeping the treasure boxes private for the children. (See Sample Letter to Parents, in Appendix).

Variations for age levels:
With younger children, pre-cut pictures facilitate this workshop. It is important to have more leaders or helpers with this activity, especially if the children are painting their boxes. This is a great activity for younger children because they have the gross motor skills to do the artwork.
Row.txt_description: The purpose of this workshop is for children to create a treasure box of their own in which they can store things that are valuable to them in order to keep them safe. These can be actual items, notes, or symbolic reminders.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop gives participants the opportunity to connect to their
feelings as they envision their dreams. By using this fun and mysterious transfer process they are able to discover and capture the images that make their visions possible. The Dream Prints workshop allows participants to see the potential for their dreams to become a reality as they come to life on paper.

Materials:
Smooth cover stock paper
Magazines and/or photo stock books
Scissors
Matte Acrylic Medium or Mod Podge
Thick paintbrushes
Cups with water
Paper towels (This is a messy workshop)
Hand lotion (water based preferably) to highlight sections
Hair Blow-drier (Optional - to dry the print faster, it helps!)
Example prints -One print that is dried and not yet finished to use as an example of how to uncover the final image, and a finished print.

Note on Materials:
If the participants choose pictures from photo stock books, it will take longer to uncover their picture because the paper is thicker to rub off. The result is still very amazing. Make sure that they rub off all the paper until the image shows through.
 Time Frame:
Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Intro: 5 minutes
Warm Up and Writing: 10 minutes
Technical Info. & Practice Print: 10 minutes
Creation: 45 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Total: 1 1/2 hour
 
Tenderness and curiosity for life can take you places!   

  
 
  Apply a moderate amount of Matte medium
  
 
  Place the side covered with Matt medium
on the paper and press firmly
  
 
  Wet the tip of your fingers and rub off
the top layer of the magazine very gently
Opening Circle:
Go around the room and have each participant share their name, how they are feeling today, and/or a word that has to do with a dream or vision that they would like to carry with them today through the workshop.

Introduction:
It is believed that we process our emotions and deal with our present feelings in our daily dreams. We can envision the possibilities that capture our feelings and the wishes that are important in our journey as we dream at night or lose ourselves in our daydreams.

Through the Dream Prints workshop, we will visualize what we hope for in our lives and we will translate them into subtle images. We will not try to make our Dream Prints perfect as we uncover them on our paper. Just like our actual dreams, they don't have to be clear and they don't have to make any sense. Our visions are ours and only we know how they connect to us on a very deep level.

Technical Info/ Demo:
In order for the participants to feel comfortable with this process, start by having each participant create a practice print. Have them choose any picture they find, it doesn't have to be one they like. This one is just for the first trial.

With a thick brush apply matte medium or Mod Podge to the entire area you want to transfer onto paper. They will need to completely cover the actual image. It is a little scary, but that is why we suggest using a random picture the first time. Use a moderate amount of matte medium. Too much matte medium will take longer to dry and will leave random wet spots, and too little will not allow the paper to grab the ink of your picture.

Now, place the side covered with matte medium on the cover stock paper and press firmly. You are actually "gluing" that image to the paper. The end result will be a mirror image of the original picture. When you're done with the first part, let the paper dry. After the paper feels dry, the picture is ready to be uncovered.

Now, demonstrate the rubbing off process using a sample print. Wet the tip of your fingers and rub off the top layer of the magazine doing it very gently. You will notice that as the top layer starts pealing off the image you chose starts to peek through. You will continue rubbing the paper off until your entire picture is uncovered.

If you are finding that some of their creations are not coming through as clearly (especially with photo stock images), they can use a little bit of lotion to highlight some areas. Have them apply the lotion with the tip of their fingers and work it through like they did with the water. The lotion allows the image to become clearer. They can also leave areas faint or uncovered. It is up to them what they want their image to become.

It is okay if the image is not "perfect." It is not meant to be. As with our dreams, these images are fuzzy and blurry. You are never sure how they will turn out. Remember to be patient and wait until the matte medium is dry before you begin peeling off the paper. You need to give the paper enough time to absorb the ink of the picture to allow it to stay. Think of it as your dream taking time to materialize.

Relaxation:

 
As one picture dries, look for others to transfer
Take a few deep breaths to cleanse your lungs and relax your body. As you begin breathing in and out, notice the space you're in. How does it feel to be in that place? If you like, close your eyes and allow that present feeling to carry you over to other places where you're usually safe. With your constant breathing, try to envision possibilities and a dream you would like to come true. Observe everything around you and allow yourself to explore. It is okay if your imagination takes you to a completely different place. Let yourself be guided by your visions.

Keeping your eyes closed imagine using your hands. With your fingers, follow the images and colors that appear before you. How does it feel to touch them? Let those sensations spread to your arms and to your body. Let them be within you and take as long as you need to be present with them. When you feel ready, open your eyes and begin.


A finished print, Princesa del Cafe ~ Coffee Princess
Beauty, myth and power!

 
Creation:
Reflect on the warm-up exercise and begin to look for the pictures that call to you. How can your feelings and wishes be materialized in these images? Once you have selected your pictures, you can cut or tear them in different shapes or leave them in their original shape.

Follow the same process you did in your first trial to begin the transfer process. Remember again to apply a moderate amount of matte medium to the picture and allow it to dry entirely before pealing the paper off. As one picture dries, you can look for others to transfer. Practice rubbing the paper off of your sample dream print before moving on to uncovering the others. Once you feel comfortable with the process, continue by exploring and creating new prints.
