Be patient as you rub off the paper. It is always amazing to see how things turn out. If you feel frustrated, it's okay. It is all part of the process.

Closing:
Lets each share a few words about what the experience was like, what might have come up, and what dreams and visions surfaced. Maybe the images took a life of their own and became what they needed to become. Acknowledge what they did and the process they followed. After each woman has shared thank them for sharing and compliment them on how they dared to imagine the possibilities!
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives participants the opportunity to connect to their feelings as they envision their dreams. By using this fun and mysterious transfer process they are able to discover and capture the images that make their visions possible. The Dream Prints workshop allows participants to see the potential for their dreams to become a reality as they come to life on paper.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To help children get in touch with their feelings and express them in a safe way. This workshop can really help children understand the feelings they keep inside and the feelings they show on the outside through collaging them in various parts of their tunnel book.

 
 Tunnel Book by a Joyful Heart Foundation's participant.
Materials:
Picture frame mats, 8 1/2" x 11", 5 to each person
Construction paper (2 pieces per tunnel book)
Magazines to cut out
Paper for free-hand drawing
Markers
Glue
Scissors

Time Frame:
10 minutes: opening circle
40 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 2 younger children; 1 adult for 3 older children. (This workshop is not suitable for children under age 5 as the concept and construction is complicated.)

Space Set-up:
Arrange work stations with the picture frame mats, construction papers, and magazines.

Opening Circle:
Begin with the It's so Hard Reaching Out, and Get Off My Back series of exercises. When the children are seated in a circle, explain the project to them as well as introduce the idea of feelings we hide and feelings we show. Talk about safety - that when we feel safe we can show our feelings. Explain that the tunnel books are going to help keep their feelings safe because they are in charge of opening up their “books” and closing them just like they can do with their feelings.

 
 Creating their Tunnel Books.
Activity:
While children are looking through the magazines for images that represent their feelings, fold the construction paper like an accordion. The tunnel book will be constructed as follows:

1. Glue the five picture frame mats at equal intervals to two pieces of folded construction paper on each side to make a tunnel with the construction paper forming the sides of the tunnel. Arrange the mats at sufficient intervals so that there is enough space between them and they can be pushed back and forth like a concertina (small accordion). You now have a tunnel-like construction and should be able to see directly through the mat frames.

2. Have the child arrange their cut-out images so that the hidden feelings will go to the back and the feelings they show are in the front. These images will be pasted along the mat frames, from front to back, giving a three-dimensional look.

3. Make sure the back image is large enough to fill in the space of the mat frame, like a picture in a frame.

Children may need more time, in which case let this be a two-part workshop. Sometimes children need a lot of help processing their different feelings and deciding which images to pick. Make sure you have magazines that give them a broad selection.

 
Sharing their Tunnel Books.
 
Time Saver:
To allow yourself more time to help the children during the activity, fold the construction paper ahead of time. You may also want to cut out some images ahead of time to help the younger children.

Note:
The construction is easier than it appears. This project is very worthwhile; children find it rewarding and are proud of their product.

Closing Circle:
Children gather around to show their tunnel books. If children are comfortable, they can share one feeling that they hold inside. Remind children that this is a safe place to share feelings and all feelings are OK.
Row.txt_description: To help children get in touch with their feelings and express them in a safe way. This workshop can really help children understand the feelings they keep inside and the feelings they show on the outside through collaging them in various parts of their tunnel book.
Row.txt_tips:
This workshop works great for kids ages seven and up.

It may allow more time for creating if pictures from the magazines are cut out before the workshop begins.  Be sure that there is enough of a variety of magazines for everyone.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop gives women the opportunity to express what they feel and believe is a "good mother." The goal is for each woman to see themselves in their creation and help inspire themselves and others to become a better parent.



 Materials
Materials:
12x18 Large construction paper (various colors)
Poster board (for group project)
Precut 1—2 inch pieces of construction paper (assorted shapes)
Sharpies or markers
Glue sticks
Scissors
Stencil of a woman (template provided)
or Paper Doll form from Discount School Supply

Time Frame:
Intro: 5 mins.
Opening Circle: 10 mins.
Relaxation: 5 mins.
Creation: 30 mins.
Closing: 10 mins.

Introduction:


 Example of good mother qualities

Begin by discussing what each woman's idea of being a "good mother" was or currently is.  Ask questions about what our society's ideas and standards of being a mom are like today compared their mother's generation.  This may be a good opportunity to discuss the challenges of being a good mother in a domestic violence home and/or in the shelter.

Opening Circle:
Turn the lights down and begin with a meditation where the women focus on taking deep breaths. Ask them to take a deep breath for themselves while reassuring them that they should consider themselves good mothers because they have brought themselves and their children to a safe place.  Ask them to take a deep breath for each of their children because they are now safe.

Remind them that this is a window of time for them to notice their vision for a better life.  Ask them to think about what they are proud of and what their goals are as mothers.



Woman Stencil
 
Creation:
This workshop can be done as a group activity or individually.

Step I
Individual Creation:  Have each women choose one piece of the large construction paper in a color that makes them feel good, nurturing, strong and loving. Have them write "A Good Mother is..." somewhere on the margin of their paper. Then ask them to use the stencil or freehand draw the shape of a woman onto construction paper.

Group Creation: Prior to the workshop put an image of a woman on a large Poster Board. You may choose to cover it with butcher paper.

Step II
The next step is to write down the qualities that describe a good mother on the small pieces of paper (one thought per piece). Turn on some music and ask them to add as many thoughts of what a good mother is to their creation.

Throughout the workshop continue to encourage them to think about what type of mom they are to their children, about their own mother or mother figure, about how they want their child to see them, and about other mother-like role models, grandmothers, godmother, aunts, cousins, etc that touched their lives.

Step III

 
Intern Kelly with Good Mother Creation
 
Individual Creation:  Finish the session by inviting each participant to stand up and share with the rest of the group by reading out loud what they wrote or the leader can read it out loud for the participant (this is optional). 

Group creation:  At this point the women can glue their good mother notes anywhere on the poster board. 

Closing Circle: Have each woman share how doing the workshop made them feel about themselves as a mother and what they learned from others.

 



  
 Group Creation
 Individual Creation
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives women the opportunity to express what they feel and believe is a "good mother." The goal is for each woman to see themselves in their creation and help inspire themselves and others to become a better parent.

Row.str_title: Hugs and Bubbles Workshops for Toddlers
Row.txt_code:
Hugs - Toddler Workshop

Objective:
To create a caring and nurturing environment for young children and expand the creative process by providing the freedom to explore their artistic imagination through the use of art and story.

  
Haven House Leader, Melissa Falco reads as part of her warm up.
 
Materials:
Tempera Paints / Bio Colors
(for painting hand-prints)
Brushes / cut sponges
White paper plates
Yarn or ribbon
Hole-punch
Markers (big Crayola or chunky markers, crayons or sidewalk chalk for easy gripping)
Newspaper to cover tables
Special toys optional - stuffed animals for small children to hold

Suggested Books:
HUG, by: Jez Alborough, Mommy Hugs by: Karen Katz, Mama Do You Love Me? by: Barbara M. Joosse, Please, Baby, Please by: Spike Lee . Or feel free to use any picture books that are colorful and have very few words to accommodate young childrens' attention spans. This is also a great time to introduce books about healthy affection, love and nurturing.

Suggested Music:
Raffi, Greg & Steve, Marlo Thomas, Ella Jenkins, Dan Zanes, Putumayo etc.
Circle time music, rhythm and movement works best to engage young children 2-5 years, in the structured activity clapping, dancing and singing.  Choose songs that are toddler friendly and easy to catch on to through the chorus.

Time Frame:
Circle: 15 ninutes
Creation: 20-45 minutes (including final handprints and ribbon)
Closing: 15 minutes
Total Time: 50 to 75 minutes


Set-up/Prep:
Cover tables with newspaper and set materials out. For best results for young children it’s recommended to use larger size art supplies for easy gripping. Place chunky crayons, markers or sidewalk chalk out across the table. Lay out one paper plate for every child. You may want to punch holes in the plates before the children begin. This is the last step; the handprints will be applied on each child’s paper plate, by the leader towards the end of the workshop. Attach the yarn or ribbon so they may hang their hugs on the wall. Have paints mixed and have brushes or sponges ready to go.

I

 Windows Leader Marilyn making her "Hugs" 
ntroduction:
Begin by having the children gather for special story time on a rug or designated area. Talk with children to get them excited about the story and the art that will follow. You may want to have a few choices of books and have them decide which one to read first. Make the story time interactive ask questions about the story. You can also express the different emotions that may be taking place in the book; example, “ The mama bear gave the baby bear a great big hug!” Ask the children to give themselves a great big hug.  You can demonstrate using your arms and giving yourself a big hug. After reading stories you will be ready for them to move to the tables. Explain they will be creating a special hug to take home and share with their family. After the decorating the plate, have the children choose a color for their hand–prints, they may want more than one and that’s okay too. Suggestion: you may want to designate a special area for the children who finish first to play in until the other children have completed their work.


 Decorating the plate.
 Apply paint to the hand
with a brush or sponge.
 Firmly press painted hand
on to the plate.
 

Optional: Warm up or Opening Circle
Along with the story you may also want to incorporate some toddler friendly music that is fun for singing and dancing.

Creation:
Using the materials on tables have the children begin to color the paper plates. Once they have gone through each of the mediums (crayons, markers, chalks or which ever they choose) they will be ready to apply the final touch, their handprints. Once they are done, the art is complete.  Attach the ribbon to the plate for display once it has dried. This workshop may not require all the time that’s suggested, and depending on the ages of children and the amount of materials used the workshop may only last an hour. Adapt the workshop to meet your needs and incorporate your favorite books, music and supplies.

Closing:
  

   Plate ready to hang with
ribbon.

Have the children gather on the rug in a circle and share who is it they would like to give their hug to. You can also close with a story, song or special dance. Creating this special window of time will enrich the relationships we form with young children and their families.

Additional Suggestions:
Mother’s Day is approaching. This workshop would be great for young children to create for their mothers, the following poem can be attached to the back of the paper plates and given as a gift for Moms.




Mother’s Day Poem

Children Are A Special Gift of Joy
 
 Finished Plate. 
  
 Finished Plate.
 


Sometimes you get discouraged
Because I am so small
And always leave my fingerprints
On furniture and walls.

But everyday I’m growing—
I’ll be grown up someday
And all those tiny hand-prints
Will surely fade away.

So here’s a final hand print
Just so you can recall
Exactly how my fingers looked
When I was very small.

Love,
Melissa



Bubble Fun Prints - Toddler Workshop

Objective:
To encourage a relaxed and playful atmosphere for young children and to expand the abilities of imaginative play in a safe and healthy environment.

Materials:
 
 Windows Leader, Belinda blows the bubbles up high!
 

Bubble solution (store bought or homemade)
Food color (few drops to add color to the bubbles)
Bubble wands, cotton string, (or any objects that can be used to blow bubbles)
Straws
Small bowls/pie tins
White construction paper (or roll of butcher paper for larger pieces)
Aprons or smocks
Newspaper (cover tables and lay on the floors to prevent slips…)
Music (fun and happy)
Paper towels (clean up)
Books (picture books; about children playing out doors, balloons, bubbles, fun etc.)

Books & Music:
Clifford Counts Bubbles by: Norman Bridewell
Bubble Bath Baby by: Libby Ellis
You may want to choose books with related themes or books that are appealing to your listeners.
Upbeat and playful music may work best.

Bubble Solution Recipe (Optional)
1-cup water
4 tbsp. liquid dish washing soap (preferably a clear formula)
2 tbsp. clear syrup (corn syrup like Karo syrup works well)
Food coloring
Mix ingredients together. Children may use straws to blow bubbles.

Another recipe uses more basic ingredients, although the bubbles don't last as long:

1 cup water
1/2 cup dish detergent (preferably a clear formula)
1 tbsp. cooking oil (as a stabilizer)

Timeframe:
One hour 15 minutes

Age Range /Adult to Child Ratio:
2 yrs. and up
One adult to every 2-3 children

Set-up/Prep:
  

   Placing the paper on top of the bubbles.
 

Prepare mixture or use store bought solution; add the food coloring to a portion of the bubble solution and pour each color into individual containers, have enough for each child to share. 
Remember to cover any space that will be used for the workshop (tables, floor, or outdoor area etc.)
If making journals, (see additional steps, below) it’s best to have extra sheets of construction paper for each child. You may want to demonstrate the process for the children and show them how to use the bubble blowing tools, i.e. wands, hands, straws.
It is best to do a test before working with the children.




  Placing the paper over the
bubbles.
 
Introduction:
Today we are going to make bubble art. Start by blowing a few bubbles. Demonstrate how to blow bubbles with a straw into the bubble solution. You may want to show examples.

Creation:
For the Bubble Prints, have the children sit or stand at a table and pour solution into pie tins and use straws to blow outward creating hundreds of tiny bubbles. Let the bubbles rise to about 4-5” and lay white construction paper gently across the top to create the prints, repeat withthe same or different colors until desired effect.


Optional: Warm up or Opening Circle:
Open with a story and have the children participate in the story by asking questions that pertain to the book. Talk with them about the ground rules and respecting others and their space. Make certain the rules are age appropriate and the children understand. The object is to create a fun and safe space for the group.

  
 Bubble printed paper.
 Bubble printed paper.
 

Closing:
Have a closing circle ask the children to share their prints with the group. Depending on age ask them what they enjoyed most about today.

Additional Steps or Miscellaneous:
If you have children 5 yrs. and up it would be a great time to make journals with them. Some children enjoy writing or drawing pictures - encourage the children to express themselves in their hand made books. Use the decorative bubble prints to create the cover of the journal. Add paper to the center use a hole punch to place holes on the edge to bind the journal. Thread yarn through (chain stitch) along the edge and tie off at the end. (This is a g reat little book for short stories, words, collage and self–expression).

Children may also want to blow the food colored bubbles with a wand and have the bubbles drop onto the paper directly.
Row.txt_description: Workshops designed for very young children, which allows them to be free, to be messy and to have fun in a safe and creative environment.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To help children get in touch with who they are and to strengthen their self-expression. It is both solidifying and satisfying for children to make an image of themselves.

Materials:
Sculpey (masks can also be made out of clay, dried and painted, or out of papier mache)
Acrylic paints
Feathers, sequins, raffia, or yarn for decorating
Garlic press to make thin threads of sculpey for hair
Aluminum foil
Newspaper

Note about size:
Sculpey is expensive, so explain to children that the masks will be smaller than the size of their faces. Give each child a piece of sculpy to work with in creating the mask so that you have enough sculpey to go around without it being too costly.

You may wish to consider a less expensive material in order to make larger masks.

Time Frame:
10 minutes: opening circle
30 minutes: activity
15 minutes: oven baking time
30 minutes to 1 hour: painting and decorating mask

Suggestion:
This activity can be done in two parts to allow for sufficient painting time.

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 younger children; 1 adult for 5 older children

Space Set-up:
Divide sculpey into individual size pieces and arrange them at the tables. Crumple up pieces of newspaper for supporting the sculpey. Dispense small amounts of acrylic paints into cups and set aside.

Opening Circle:
Do the Focusing Breath followed by the Get Off My Back. Discuss the procedure of making the mask, including the baking and allowing it to cool before painting. You may want to show pictures of different masks from magazines or a book from the library to give children an understanding of how important masks have been to people all over the world.

Activity:
Each child gets a piece of sculpey to sculpt a mask. Use crumpled newspaper in a ball to help them mold the mask in the form of a face. They may need help with the different features. The sculpey should not be too thick - 1/4 inch is ideal.

Place the masks on a cookie sheet and bake in the oven following instructions on the packet of sculpey. You can use aluminum foil to support the shapes while baking.

Painting:
Give each child small portions of different acrylic colors to prevent wastage and mixing of colors in the jars. The masks may be varnished afterwards. Children can add feathers, raffia or sequins for added effects.

Irridescent acrylic paints can give a wonderfully rewarding effect very quickly and easily.
Row.txt_description: A basic mask workshop to help children get in touch with who they are and to strengthen their self-expression. It is both solidifying and satisfying for children to make an image of themselves.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Without any discussion of emotions or deep expressions, each woman can gain a great deal of release through simply playing with the colors, blending various combinations, and making a series of cards. To simply introduce the technique of smearing the chalk within the masked surface, and then removing the tape, can be quite enough for a rich, engaging workshop session.

Materials:
Alpha-color pastels (A wide assortment, including fluorescent colors is desirable.)
Colored Construction Paper- cut into sizes usable for cards (Colored pastel paper can be nicer.)
Masking tape (Drafting tape, magic removable tape, or blue painter's tape are all easier to remove without ripping the paper, but are more expensive.)
Colored Ribbons (And any other decorations that may be used by the women.)
Metallic Pens
Scissors (To cut the cards to custom sizes.)
Exacto knife and metal straight edge (Optional- can be helpful in cutting the cards.)
Glue Sticks for attaching ribbons and other decorations (They tend to buckle the paper less than white glue and are cleaner to handle.)

Opening:
With a playful, non-focused exercise, you may choose to begin without any formal introduction or sharing circle. When you are conducting a workshop in a shelter, you may not have everyone together at the beginning of the session. The women may filter in as their children fall asleep and chores are finished. If this is the case, it can be helpful to pursue the same information as you would in an opening circle, but without the formality. As women join the group, you can casually ask them how they are feeling and how they feel about art. In how you speak with each woman, you can informally set the tone. This is a totally voluntary activity and a "window of time" for each woman to practice respecting her own feelings, needs, and visions. (To conduct a more structured introduction and circle, see "General Workshop Format")

Demonstration:
Say to the group: "Pastels are one of the most beautiful and simplest materials to use. It is incredible what you can do with them. I'd like to demonstrate some of the things that are possible. (Begin by folding the paper in half, and then taping it down- masking the edges) Can anyone guess why I'm taping the edges down?.. (yes, to hold it still... yes, so that I can use both hands to draw... and yes, so that it will have a beautiful edge)" Begin to fill the page with color and smear it to fill the entire 'window'. Show how beautifully the colors can blend on top of each other. Show how crisp the edge looks when the tape is removed.

Warm-Up:
Say to the group: "We're going to try a practice one -- a warm-up. This is a drawing that is as free (and ugly) as can be. (There's no need to worry about making it look good!) Try covering the entire page with a single color or chalk. See what it feels like to smear it with your hands, draw another color on top of that. See what it's like to smear that with a single decisive sweep of your fingers...."

Creation:
Say to the group: "Now go ahead and tape more paper down, and begin to create as many cards as you like." Like the opening of this exercise, this can be as unstructured or structured as fits the group and atmosphere. For a more structured approach, you may wish to lead a relaxation (see "Relaxation Techniques") and have the women imagine colors and shapes in their mind's eye to put onto the paper.

Closing Circle:
Say to the group: "We have about ten (or whatever) more minutes to draw. Go ahead and finish up whatever cards you're working on, and take some time to write any words that go with the shapes and colors. We have gold and silver pens, and you can write on the front of the drawing, or on the inside of the card, or even on the very back, where you can put the date and signature and any important words. Ribbons can also be added to the cards if you like." (The women finish up.) "How did that feel?" (Responses: If they are mostly positive responses, ask if there were any negative feelings, and vice-versa. If they were all negative, ask if it was relaxing and positive for anyone.) "Let's take a few moments to go around the circle and see what everyone has made. You don't have to share anything, but if you want to, let us know what you created, and what it felt like to do."

Variations:
Card Making: This exercise may be deepened as is appropriate, by having a structured relaxation precede the card-making. In such a relaxation, each woman could begin to envision the card as a gift for herself -- an acknowledgment to herself of the journey she has made. Or she may begin to envision a series of cards representing the journey in shapes and colors: where she has come from, where she is now, and where she is going to. Cards can also be cut into pop-up book forms, materials can be collaged onto them, and writing exercises can be combined with them to enrich the card making as a focused exercise.
Row.txt_description: Without any discussion of emotions or deep expressions, each woman can gain a great deal of release through simply playing with the colors, blending various combinations, and making a series of cards.
Row.txt_notes: In Woman's Manual under "Materials and Techniques: Chalk Pastel"

Row.txt_code:
Inside/Outside Sample with
Pocket Holder
About this Project:
Karen Akamine, who was trained at the Armory Center for the Arts in Pasadena, wrote this project. The concept was adapted into this workshop by the AWBW staff.

Objective:
To explore and notice the self that you let people see on the outside and the self that is on the inside or underneath.

Materials:
9"X12" Colored construction paper
Chalk pastels
Paper towels
Pens and writing paper
(Option: participants could use their journals)
independent project handout (for individual workshop) (click here for handout)
Alternative variations: This workshop can be done using collage instead of pastels. If you use collaging, you can do it on boxes or paper bags instead of construction paper.

Time frame:
Total Time: 1 hr
Intro: 5 min
Opening Circle: 10 min
Journal Writing: 10 min
Creation: 30 min
Closing Circle: 10 min

 
 Door Fold 

Triangle Fold 

Diamond Fold Open ... and Closed 
 
Double Door Fold 








Here are some examples of ways to fold the paper so there’s an inside and an outside. Encourage the teens to be creative in their folding.

Space Setup:
It helps things to go smoothly when you have the supplies prepared and set up in advance. Try various folds (see illustrations below) so it will be easy to show the participants some possibilities. Use the pastels to make an example yourself. That way, you can make sure the supplies are ready and you’ll notice if there’s anything else needed.

Introduction:
“This art time is a special ‘window of time’ for each of you. The project we are doing is called Inside/Outside. It is a chance to explore the ‘you’ that people see on the outside, and the ‘you’ that only you know is on the inside. We will be using folded paper and pastels to create our inside and outside selves in shapes and colors. (Optional show samples.)

Opening Circle:
Make sure that you take the time to welcome everyone and to let them know that their presence is really appreciated. “Before we start the art, we’ll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art.” This is a time to reassure anyone who’s scared of art that it's ok to be scared and that if they "hate" it, it is fine too. Remind them that they don’t have to do the project. They can just watch if they want to. If they are given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in even if they say they’re just going to watch. If they don’t want to say anything for “check-in,” let them know it is fine.

  

 
 Sample — Outside Detail
 



 
 Sample — Inside Detail
   












Journaling Warm-up:
"Let’s start with a journaling warm-up. Divide a paper into two columns. On one side, write ‘Inside’ and on the other side, write ‘Outside.’ Fill the first side of the page with any words that describe how you feel on the inside, and on the other side of the page write any words that describe the ‘you’ that people see on the outside. Try not to think so much as you write. Allow the words to flow naturally. If you get stuck in one column move on to the next and you can return to the first one later. After you are done, take a moment to observe the words that you wrote without any judgement. Just acknowledge them and take them in as part of yourself. Those words will guide you in your creation process."

Creation:
"Now pick a piece of construction paper and fold it so it has an inside and an outside. Begin to create the outside of your paper as you think about colors, shapes and textures that might describe you on the outside.. You can always refer back to your writing. Are you bright or dark, sharp or soft, foggy or clear?

When you are ready, open up your paper and begin to think about how you are on the inside. Are you bright or dark, soft or rough? Are you one or many colors? Use pastels or the collaging method to decorate the inside and outside of your paper.

When you are finished, take some time to write any words that go with your drawing." You might want to encourage the participants to take a moment after they finish to think about how they might want to take care of themselves on the inside and on the outside.

Closing Circle:
Give each woman an opportunity to share what she created and talk about what it means and how it felt to make. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever comes out.

Inside/Outside Sample with Pocket Holder
Row.txt_description: To explore and notice the self that you let people see on the outside and the self that is on the inside or underneath.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This is a three-part project that will help women reflect on the gifts and strengths they bring from their past, the resources they now have in the present, and the importance of
acknowledging such gifts for the future.

 
 AWBW Intern with finished Traveling Drum
Materials:
Six-sided box or Oatmeal carton (it looks like a drum)
Acrylic paint
Different fabrics
Cut-ups from magazines
Glitter
Beads
Wire (different colors)
Color pencils
Markers
Glue
Note: This is a project to inspire the women to create without restriction. They are free to express themselves with whatever material they choose. What provides structure is the box/drum itself.



 Cutting Oatmeal carton to make a
smaller drum

Preparation:
Make sure a wide variety of materials are taken out so that the women feel they have options. Try to arrange it so that the mixture of colors and materials is appealing.

Time Frame:
The entire project is meant to be done in five or six sessions of 1 and 15 minutes each. The first part of the project might take two sessions because it needs an introduction and the preliminary visualization. The other two could also take two sessions, depending on the size and unique needs of the group. Women are intended to have enough time to create as well as to express themselves verbally.

Introduction:
"This has been part of an ongoing journey to 'self-sufficiency.' We are going to create a
six-sided drum that contains our life experiences. During the first part we will construct
the inside of the box using the gifts and strengths that have been passed on to us by our
ancestors. Let's think about the wonderful contributions they have given to us in order to
be who we are today. In the second part, we will decorate the outside of the box thinking
about our present. What are the gifts, resources, people, places, etc…that will assist us
in our self-recovery? The last part, the lid of the box, will focus on the future. We are
going to illustrate our journey. Where are we going? What are we taking with us?"

Opening Circle:
Each session will start with a general check in. Where are we today? Any feelings or thoughts that might surface, just allow them to come. As the project progresses, reflect
on what has changed, if anything, from the last time the group created together. Bring in elements of their daily lives and how they are doing at this moment.

Guided Meditation:
1st Part: "Think that we are taking a trip back in time. We are looking for our ancestors.
Once we find them, see where they are. Check the surroundings, what is the weather
like? Notice any colors, smells, feelings that come to you. What gifts are your
ancestors offering you? Are they telling you anything?"

2nd Part: "How does it feel now? What are the smells, feelings, imagery, colors that
surround you? What and who do we have that support us today?"

3rd Part: Verbal exercise. "We have arrived here with a wide variety of resources. Now
lets look into the future. Give a quick response to the following phrase. Don’t think;
just say whatever comes to your mind. 'I am going…' 'When I get there will…' 'Who
will be there with me is…' Think about people, places, colors, feelings, and smells. It
will come to you if you allow it."



 Decorating the inside of the drum

Creation:
1st Part: After guided meditation, illustrate the gifts and strengths women found in their ancestry. "What does that look like? With a wide variety of materials, decorate the inside of the box. This is our past."




Decorating the outside of the drum
 



2nd Part: Following meditation, decorate the outside of the box. Encourage women to use different materials. They should feel free to experiment. "This is the present. What are the resources we have now? How do we see them?"




 Decorating the top of the drum
3rd Part: "After the verbal exercise, let's think about what we have now that will take us into the future. How can we embody our future journey? Now we will work on the lid for the drum." As with the other parts, allow the women to be free in their material choices, they need to find what works for them.

Closing:
Each session should end with a closing circle. How
was the experience? What did they like or not like?
Say a few words about each one’s artwork. Allow them to share
what it represented to them. Relate past, present, and future. Has there been any
transformation? How can this “traveling drum” remind them of their journey to self-
sufficiency and self-recovery?




Finished Traveling Drum
 Examples of 6-sided box & Oatmeal carton drum

Miscellaneous:
Sometimes it helps if the leader also takes the journey alongside the women. It makes
them feel more comfortable knowing that they are not being “watched” or judged. But
it also depends on each individual group.
Row.txt_description: This is a three-part project that will help women reflect on the gifts and strengths they bring from their past, the resources they now have in the present, and the importance of acknowledging such gifts for the future. This is done by creating a “traveling drum” to remind them of their journey to self-sufficiency and self-recovery.

Row.str_title: Roller Derby Painting, Bugs and 'Mud' Workshops for Toddlers
Row.txt_code:
“Roller Derby Painting”
Objective:
Fun, Fast and Cool ART!
This workshop is a great way to incorporate the use of toys with art. The two seem to go side by side when it comes to having fun! Children will enjoy being creative. An introduction to a new experience can be very rewarding and increase self–esteem for any young person.
Be aware this workshop can get Messy!



 Cars and trucks for painting.
 
Materials:
- Hot Wheels/ Match Box Cars (any small or medium size cars that can be washed off and have no sharp edges)
- Tempera paints/ Bio Color paints
- Paper plates (for the paint)
- Newspaper (cover the table tops)
- Masking tape (tape the paper onto the tables)
- Construction paper (white or light colors for painting and use black, yellow or red to mount the paintings after they dry)

Music: Music for children can be found at Lakeshore Learning Store, Angel’s Teaching Supply or Barnes and Noble.com.
Favorite Artists: Raffi, Greg & Steve, Marlo Thomas, Ella Jenkins, Dan Zanes, Hap Palmer, Alan Goodman and Putumayo Multi Cultural Music from across the World.



 Painting with wheels!
 
Timeframe:
1 hour and 15 minutes
Circle:        15 minutes
Creation:     20-30 minutes
Clean up:    15 minutes
Closing:       15 minutes

Age Range /Adult to Child Ratio:
2yrs. and up
One adult to every 1-4 children

Set-up/Prep:
Cover tables and floor surrounding tables since this workshop can get messy. Lay out all materials, cars, trucks and paint. Place the paint in flat trays or on small paper plates. Place the car wheels in the different color paint. Put 3-4 choices of colors throughout the center of the table. This will make things easier for sharing. If you are going to use more than one table please have someone assist you. Set aside a separate area for the clean up. Use utility tubs to hold water. Allow the children to wash the cars (if time permits).



 Washing the cars can be fun too!
 
They will enjoy playing in the water and helping toward cleanup. Be sure to have supervision when the children are near water. You may want to have paper towels, rags, or a hand towel ready for the children to dry their hands and an empty container to place the cars when they are finished. After the children leave, you may also need to wash cars a second time to keep the paint from sticking to the wheels.

Introduction:
The introduction can be done during the opening warm up. You may explain they will be painting with cars today… show examples of cars or toys you have chosen. Ask the children about the different sounds of transportation. Display different types of vehicles that have different types of responsibilities, example; a fire truck has a siren, can you make this sound? What do fire trucks do? There are construction vehicles that build houses and tear down buildings, rescue vehicles that save lives, cars that take us places, even airplanes have wheels.  Ask interactive questions. Show pictures in books and toys as models.

Warm Up or Opening Circle:(Optional)
Today you are going to pretend to be automobiles on an amazing journey.  Have the children shout out the places their transportation will take them. Maybe the vehicle has a special job. Have the children act out sounds, movement and mechanicals of their vehicle. (Great song is the Wheels on the Bus) try not to make the warm up too technical. Simple is best especially when the children are very young. The workshops work best when the leader adapts them to fit their needs and levels of comfort.

 
 
 Painting with wheels!
 Painting with wheels!
 

Creation:
Time to create racing stripes! Let the children experience the freedom of art with little direction. You can set some guidelines and restrictions to ensure safety for the group.

Guidelines and Rules:    
  • No throwing the cars or toys
  • You must keep the cars and toys on the tables
  • Share
Closing:
Should be a winding down time. After the clean-up have all the children sit for a short story, song (Wheels on the Bus) or a sharing circle.


“BUGS”
Objective:
Creepy crawly critters give children a chance to explore the world of bugs.  Bugs can be a fun and creative adventure for children of all ages. Summer is quickly approaching and it’s a great time to take the children outdoors on a bug hunt. The children will learn to respect nature and its creatures big and small. Take every opportunity to make this a fun, learning experience for everyone.


 
 
 


 Assembling a "bug" with egg carton sections.
Materials:
Egg cartons (lots of cartons)
Pipe cleaners
Tempera paints
Brushes
Scissors
Markers
Wiggle eyes (all sizes)
Pom pom balls (large)
Tacky glue
Construction paper
Crayons (to write bugs story)
Glue gun (for adult use only)
Exacto knife (adult use only)




 
 


 Painting a bug.
 
Children’s Books:
“Bed Bugs” by David Carter
“BUGS!” by: David Greenberg
“Leo the Lightening Bug” by: Eric Drachman
“Miss Spider’s Tea Party” by: David Kirk
“Miss Spider’s ABC” by: David Kirk
“Miss Spider’s Family Album” by: David Kirk
“The Very Hungry Caterpillar” by: Eric Carle
“The Very Busy Spider” by: Eric Carle
“Caterpillar Spring, Butterfly Summer” by: Susan Hood
“Anansi the Spider” Gerald McDermott

MUSIC:
“Raffi’s Box of Sunshine (multi- CD pack)
There is tons of music to explore for children!

Songs:
The Ants Go Marching  - (Traditional action song)
The ants go marching one by one,
Hurrah, hurrah.
The ants go marching one by one,
Hurrah, hurrah.
The ants go marching one by one,
The little one stops to suck his thumb,
And they all go marching down
Into the ground to get out of the rain,
BOOM!  BOOM!  BOOM!
Two...tie his shoe...
Three...climb a tree...
Four...shut the door...
Five...take a dive...
Six...pick up sticks...

 Leader, Penelope painting her bug. 
Seven...pray to heaven...
Eight...shut the gate...
Nine...check the time...
Ten...say "THE END"

Eency Weency Spider – (A classic finger play )
The eency weency spider
Went up the water spout,
fingers imitate a moving spider
Down came the rain and washed the spider out
fingers imitate falling rain
Out came the sun and dried up all the rain
arms make a large circle
And the eency weency spider went up the spout again
fingers imitate a moving spider

Timeframe:
1 hour
     Bumble Bee and Caterpillar bugs.

Age Range /Adult to Child Ratio:
2 yrs. & up
One Adult to every 1-6 children

When working with children ages five and under, the adult to child ratio can be reduced, one adult to every 1-4 children

Set-up/Prep:
Cover table with newspaper; precut all the egg cartons into 1,2 & 3 sections sizes to make up the different critters. Precut small slits using an exacto knife into the sides of the egg carton cones for the pipe cleaners to go through, for legs and antennas. (If the slits are too big the pipe cleaners will not stay put)
The single cone section can be used for spiders, ladybugs and rollie pollies (a.k.a. weevils)
2 cones can be used for the ant, bumblebees, grass hoppers, butterflies and flies
3 cones or longer will be for the caterpillars.






  Decorating the bug.
 
Introduction:
Talk about BUGS! Today we are going to create some bugs of our own. We are going to begin by reading some stories about bugs. Has anyone ever seen a spider or ladybug? What color was it? Get them involved, make the story and sharing circle interactive.
 
Warm Up or Opening Circle Size: (Optional)
Choose books geared towards the ages you will be working with, with the subject line of BUGS… Colorful picture books, lively music and a positive attitude will get this activity going! If you would like the children to act like little bugs, create an open space for flying, crawling, hopping, jumping or wiggling and have a great time.

Creation:
You want to begin the group by going step by step with the children. It may be a good idea to have a few examples of the different types of bugs. Everything should be precut (egg cartons and pipe cleaners in different sizes). When the children put the legs on, bend the pipe cleaner from the inside. This will keep it from falling out.



 Two part bug.
  Three part bug.
 


Useful Activity Tips:
This is a wonderful activity to create a nature mural or a wall garden and include the Watercolor Butterfly Journeys (May 2005), large flowers and trees.

Closing:
Have a sharing circle and allow the children show off their wonderful work.


“Mud on My Fingers”
Objective:
To allow young children to relax and feel comfortable by getting messy within a positive and controlled environment. This workshop encourages the use of a child’s fine and gross motor
skills and will let them experience the art through a more tactile
approach.  Expanding the imagination of a small child is very important. Art can be a significant factor in the lives of children of all ages. It is very important to respect a child’s decision whether to create or not. Giving them a choice can be very empowering, for both the child and the leader. Hands on art can be a great introduction to any small child and is a wonderful way for children to experience social and emotional growth.


   "Mud" finger painting.
 
Materials:
- *Finger Paints (purchased or homemade) See below for 2 recipes for this activity
Finger paint should be made the day before the activity unless you want to include older children in the preparation process (3-5 yr. olds)
- Paint - recipes below
- Construction paper (white or light color paper)
- Utility tubs (for water)
- Paper towels
- Markers
- Aprons, smocks or large old t-shirts
- Plastic spoons
- Gloves (if the children are resistant to their hands getting dirty, also gives them a choice)
- Newspaper 
- Empty plastic trash bags
- Masking tape
- Small bowls (recycled containers, yogurt cups, margarine tubs with lids etc.)
- Story Books (ages 2 & up) – Suggestion - Harry the Dirty Dog
- Music

*This Project is great out doors, but can be done anywhere depending on the space, the number of participants, assistants and most importantly patience. Remember the focus is getting messy; it’s the process not the overall product. This activity should feel good, not stressful to both the leader and the child participating.

Ground Rules are very important and may work best by having the children participate in what the rules will be. Example: Touching, ask the question, “Is it okay to touch someone or some thing if you have paint on your hands?”  You may want to ask the same about the room, furniture or walls, etc. Explain the rule to fit the ages you are working with. For example do not use big words that very young children may not understand, or give very lengthy dialogue because young children will not remember everything.


 "Mud" finger painting. 
Having young children participate in the clean up process can be very rewarding especially to their self-esteem. Children will respond to positive reinforcement, especially when role modeled by a caring adult.

Timeframe:
1 hour & 30 minutes (depending on clean up)

Age Range /Adult to Child Ratio:
2 years & up (mixed ages 2-3 yrs. / 4-6yrs.)
1 adult to 1-6 children (recommended)

This activity is meant to be fun, please approach with an open mind for anything to happen (paint on the floors, walls, each other, etc.)  The point is to control the mess with boundaries and secure the areas with your own level of comfort.

Set-up/Prep:
Cover tables with newspaper. You may use trash bags over the chairs (optional). Place one sheet of the construction paper at each table setting; tape the corners of the paper to the covered table to prevent the paper from sliding around. Create another area strictly for the “wash tubs.” Fill them a quarter to half way with warm water; place used towels or newspaper underneath to absorb any water that is splashed around. Have paper towels, napkins or hand towels available for drying hands. Place individual paint bowls with a variety of colors in the center of the table. Use plastic spoons for scooping out colors. (The children can usually do this themselves but may require your supervision or assistance.)

Introduction:
This is how leaders may introduce the workshop..."Today we are going to make art with our fingers!" (Including excitement in your explanation will possibly encourage the children’s participation). Have the children gather in a small circle.  You may begin by talking with them about what they will be doing today. "Today we are going to create with our fingers," have the children hold up their fingers and wiggle them around. “Our fingers may get a little messy." Ask the children if they would like to create art using their fingers. "In this workshop we are going to wear a special cover to protect our clothes." You may want to show them some of the protective gear they will be wearing for this messy workshop.  Be sure to inform the parents about the messy workshop so you don’t surprise them. You can be creative by having an assistant come out and show the children what they will be wearing, (a trash bag, an apron, smock or old clothing). Can we eat the paint? Do we paint on the walls, floor, each other etc.?


  Melissa Falco reading to the group.
 
Warm Up or Opening Circle: (Optional)
Suggestions for Books: Harry the Dirty Dog, Gene Zion

Have the children gather in a half circle for a story or two. Choose books that are appealing to the age level you are working with. (Picture books that are very colorful and have very few words can accommodate young children’s attention spans and may work best for groups (2-5 years). You can creatively capture their attention when the story becomes interactive. Pictures, plots and characters can link young children to their imagination and enhance their future problem solving skills.   This is also a great time to introduce books about healthy affection, love and nurturing as well as other feelings.

Creation:
Begin by covering the children with protective clothing (smocks, t-shirts etc.) Have the children choose which colors they like. Now they may begin to paint using their hands. This is also a great time to demonstrate the process. You can start by showing them what they will be doing, moving the paint around on the paper and creating different texture and patterns. Remember the focus is getting messy; it’s the process not the overall product. Allow structured freedom and encourage the use of color. Play child-friendly music, sing and have fun.

Clean–Up:
You can include the children in the clean-up process. Have them wash their hands and help put the paint away, take paper off the tables and hand them wet paper towels, rags or sponges to help wipe off the tables and chairs. They will enjoy helping you and it will build their self-confidence and encourage their independence.

Closing:
You may end by having the children share their paintings. The paintings may still be wet. If so lay the art out on a table or on the floor and have the children walk around and share their paintings this way.   This is also a good time to praise the children for all their hard work creating such wonderful artwork and helping with the clean up. 


Finger Paint Recipes

Version One (Using food coloring)
1/4 cup cornstarch
2 cups water
Liquid food coloring

Mix cornstarch and water in a saucepan. Boil until mixture thickens. Allow to cool, then add food coloring. Pour in airtight container.

Version Two  (Using tempera paint)
1/4-cup cornstarch
2 cups water
Dry tempera paint

Mix all ingredients in a saucepan. Boil until mixture thickens. Allow to cool, and then pour in airtight container.

Version Three  (Textured Finger Paint)  
This paint, made from only the most basic ingredients, is not your typical smooth finger-paint; however, young students seem to enjoy the grainy mixture, and they also like the feel of the finished product.

1 cup flour
1/2 cup salt
3/4 cup water
Food coloring OR tempera paint

Mix flour and salt, then add water. Mix until all three ingredients are thoroughly blended. Add a few drops of liquid food coloring or tempera paint (dry or liquid) until desired color is reached. If necessary, you may add additional flour and salt in the following proportions: two teaspoons of flour, followed by one teaspoon of salt; alternate until desired consistency is reached.
Row.txt_description: This workshop is a great way to incorporate the use of toys with art. The two seem to go side by side when it comes to having fun! Children will enjoy being creative. An introduction to a new experience can be very rewarding and increase self–esteem for any young person.

Row.str_title: Bracelet Making - Holidays with HeART Series
Row.txt_code:
To help children find art in the holidays. A series of workshops with holiday themes including Holiday Cards, Shrinky Dink Blessing Charms and Bracelet making. The idea is to create something special to show loved ones that we care and perhaps even begin new family traditions. Creating with art during the holidays as a family can be a relaxing way to connect, bond and celebrate.

Objective:
To help children find art in the holidays, they will make special bracelets to show loved ones that we care and perhaps even begin new family traditions.

Opening:
If you are beginning these workshops in November, you can take this opportunity to talk about what the holidays mean and discuss things to be thankful for. Also note, these workshops can be adapted to any time of the year - not just for the holidays.

Materials:
Beads
“Home Made Beads” out of sculpey or rolled magazine paper triangles
Elastic Sting or Ribbon

 
  For sculpey beads colors can be
swirled together
 
  Use a toothpick to create holes
before baking.
Creation:
Beaded bracelets make a special gift. They can be as simple or detailed as you like. You can string regular beads or you can make your own beads. Here are 2 methods: roll small pieces of sculpey, mixing colors if you like, make a hole all the way through and bake for 10 minutes. (Feel free to experiment with the size and shape of the bead). You can also make beads from paper by cutting long narrow triangle shapes from color magazine pages. Roll the shape starting from the widest end and glue the narrow end to the rolled paper. This is an inexpensive and colorful way to make a unique beaded bracelet or necklace.




To create paper beads, cut magazine pictures into triangular strips,
wrap around a toothpick and glue at the end.
Row.txt_description: To help children find art in the holidays, they will make special bracelets to show loved ones that we care and perhaps even begin new family traditions.

Row.txt_code:
Instructor Rachal Ballon teaching the
Writing from the Heart workshop.
 
Objective:
This workshop was designed to use writing as healing tool using the Fast Flow Writing technique. This process can allow teens
to go deep within and connect to their inner selves, dormant
feelings, and powerful memories. 

This
process can allow teens to get in touch with feelings they have had a
hard time expressing verbally. Writing from the heart, they
can get in touch with their creative inner spirit and unleash their own
creativity. 

Materials:
Journals
Pens/pencils

Timeframe:
15 minutes: Introduction
 5 minutes:  Relaxation Exercise
10 minutes: Guided Imagery and Visualization
15 minutes: Fast Flow Writing Exercise
10 minutes: Sharing and Processing
20 minutes: Participants Reading

Age Range:
13 years and up
 
Set-up/Prep:
CD Player and relaxing instrumental music playing.
Quiet room with no interruptions or noises (whenever possible)
Journals and pens distributed to each participant before workshop begins.
 
Introduction:
Putting pen to paper is a
powerful way of creating new behaviors and transforming stories. 
Writing from the heart allows one to let go of past hurts, rage on the page
and rewrite sad stories into happy ones.  The pen can dig up all the
blocks that can keep people from being as they were meant to be -
unique, creative, special one-of-a-kind.
 




 Leaders at the Writing from the Heart workshop.
 

Warm up or Opening Circle:
Optional (recommended)  Go around the room and have each participant say their name, how they're feeling, and what they want/need from this workshop.
 
Using
relaxing music, begin a relaxation meditation using deep breathing and
visualization. Select a theme for the meditation, such as "my safe
place" or "I am." (See the Children's Manual or Teen Possibilities for
additional meditation suggestions.)



Set yourself in a
comfortable position and begin to take a few deep breaths.  As you
breathe, notice the tense parts in your body and direct the breath to
those areas. 

One way to focus your breathing is to breathe in for a count of 5 seconds, hold it for 3 seconds and exhale for 7 seconds.



With each breath, you have the opportunity to release the
tension in your muscles.  Continue to breathe slowly, in and out as
long as you feel necessary.  Scan all throughout your body for tense
areas.  Allow your mind to be present as you relax.  

Creation:
If there is anything in particular you want to explore, use
this safe window of time to visualize what you need at this particular
time and day.  Every time you practice this writing exercise, you can
focus on different parts of your journey.  If at any moment you can't
think of anything more to write and/or feel stuck, just write
about how you're feeling "in the moment" or write an autobiography.

When
beginning Fast Flow writing remember that there are NO RULES.  You
don't have to worry about spelling, grammar, sentence structure,
punctuation, etc.  This is not a writing class and if it were, you all have an automatic A+.

These are the Fast Flow guideliness that can help you write freely.
When writing, use first person (I) present tense
(am).  Write as fast as possible without stopping.  Try not to take the pen
from the page and don't stop writing until the allotted time is
reached.  (Approximately 15 minutes.) Also, try not to rewrite, reread, or edit
the work.  If you can't think of anything more to write, just write
about how you're feeling , an autobiography or anything at all that comes up.

Finally,
try to use all of your 5 senses - touch, taste, sound, smell, and
sight. Again, be sure to write as fast as you can and don't worry about
whether what you're writing is good or bad--Just write and enjoy the freedom of letting go!  It is not often that
we allow ourselves to say the things we really want to say.

If
time permits, you can decorate the journal with paint, collage, or
cover it with fabrics - you can have a second workshop to decorate the
journals.




 Decorating the journal with words.
 Decorating the journal with water colors
and words.
 

Closing:
Remind
the group that it is important and can be empowering to hear your words so you
can honor your feelings. If the participants feel they would like to
read out loud, encourage them to read loudly and slowly honoring each sentence.

If
they prefer,
you can have the group share in pairs or share with a trusted friend or
family member when they feel ready.  After this process is
completed, close the session by going around the room and having
participants say in one word what they're feeling after the workshop.
Some may feel relaxed and some may feel anxious; there are no
judgments; all feelings are valid.

 Participants writing in their journal.
Row.txt_description: Writing from the Heart allows the particpant to use the pen on a sheet of paper as a powerful way of creating new behaviors and transforming our stories.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give children a safe place express and store their feelings. The Feelings Friend will help children define how they are feeling and also give them the ability to display to others how they feel if they do not wish to talk about
it.




 The Feeling Friend gets to show how she feels
 
Materials:
White construction paper or other heavy weight white paper- 2 pieces for each participant
Crayons, markers or colored pencils
Scissors
Tape or stapler
Long stripes of paper (one strip for each feeling) (template provided)
/awbw/uploads/1151692686_1409152328.pdf
Stencil of figure(template provided)
/awbw/uploads/1151692758_1360146406.pdf

Note: If using this workshop to help children release or process anger it is important to begin by having a discussion on "What is Anger?" Please click here to see the entire Processing Anger Series.

Timeframe:
1 hour

Set-up/Prep:
For younger children you may want to precut the strips for the feelings. If the children need help writing, you may need to assist them in recording their feelings on the strips. Some children may also need assistance in cutting the figure out, so you may want to have the figures precut.

Introduction:
Sometimes we have trouble expressing the way that we are feeling. We don't want
to get other people down, so sometimes we hide our emotions when we feel
sad. Even when we are mad. Sometime we may not tell anybody what we are thinking or feeling. We may hold it all inside and keep it to ourselves, or we may show it through negative behaviors. If we hold too many of our feelings inside and don't let them out, these feelings will build and build and finally they become too much for us to handle.


Warm Up or Opening Circle:
Start a conversation about feelings we hold inside. Ask the children if they ever feel afraid to say how they feel or if they don't know how to express their feelings. Talk about the many ways we can get our feelings out and have the children think about ideas. Give them time to give their responses.
Suggested ways are: Have you ever talked to a friend or loved one about your feelings? (someone who we know cares about us and is willing to listen). Writing is an excellent way to release emotions. Have you ever tried to write a letter or poem - what about writing in a journal?
  • Sometimes an activity helps release emotions, like playing your favorite sport, running or dancing.
  • Sometimes making sounds help to release feelings like singing, screaming into a pillow or crying.

 Write all your feelings down on strips of paper
 
Ask the children to list all the feelings they can think of. After each one is mentioned, have the children talk about how they would deal with that feeling, or what they would do if they were feeling that way. Of all the ways we listed to get our feelings out or deal with them, which one would they choose?


Creation:
Today we are going to make a Feelings Friend! This friend will have A LOT of feelings inside of him (just like each one of us) but each day our friend will show one or more of those feelings depending on how YOU are feeling. While you may show feelings by acting differently or speaking differently, our friend will show these feelings by holding them out in front of him or her. You will be able to use your Feelings Friend to show the way that you are feeling each day. When you wake up in the morning you can ask yourself "How do I feel today?" Then, take that feeling out of your friend and place it in his or her hands. Your friend will show how YOU are feeling that day. If you come home from school or work later in the day and you are not feeling the same way, you can put that feeling back inside your friend and take out the one that better suits how you are feeling at the time. Your feelings friend will help you define how you are feeling and even be able to show others how you feel, if you do not wish to talk about it.


 
 Draw the Feeling Friend front
 Draw the Feeling Friend back
  

Ask the children to trace the friend on 2 pieces of paper or hand them 2 preprinted or 2 precut friends. Then have the them color their Feelings Friend - front and back and cut it out (if it wasn't already precut for them).
Carefully tape the bottom and sides together - leaving the top of the head open enough to put the feelings inside. (You can also staple the front to the back if you prefer).
After the friend is completed the children can start writing feelings in the individual strips of paper. Each strip can also be decorated, if time permits.
When the feeling strips are finished, children can stuff them inside their friend. Then each child should think about how they are feeling, chose a strip from inside their Friend and place the strip in his or her arms.

Closing:
Have the children sit in a circle and tell about their Feeling Friends. What feeling is he or she holding and why? How do you feel about having a friend that will always show your feelings? Does this make it easier for you to show your feelings? How does it feel to have a safe place to put your feelings?
 
 Feeling Friend front pattern
 Feeling Friend front pattern Feeling strip pattern
  

Alternate Closing:
Brainstorm a "Safety Plan" with the children to help them process their anger. Some helpful tips include:
Talk to a friend you can trust
Count to 10
Take out art supplies and draw a picture of your anger
Journal about your anger
Take deep breaths
Listen to music
Walk away
Dance or exercise
Row.txt_description: This activity creates a safe place to hold, store and express feelings.
Row.txt_tips:
We recommend that you start anger workshops with a discussion; don't be afraid to talk to the children about their anger. Anger is nothing to be ashamed of, it is important to look at and talk about it to try to understand it.

Some anger prompts that we like are:
What is Anger? What does it look like and what does it sound like?
What was the trigger to your anger?
What did you think about it?
How did it make you feel?
How did you act?
What effect did it have on you and those around you?

Row.str_title: How I Broke the Cycle for Teens Variation
Row.txt_code:
Key Topic: Teen Dating Violence: Intervention and Prevention
This Workshop Falls Under the Theme of Teen Dating Violence
Since 2010, we have been developing this program to serve the teens in our community and in our programs. This curriculum is offered to and is useful for BOTH women's and children's leaders as most agencies work with this population in some capacity. This workshop is a variation of "How I Broke the Cycle" with new handouts, additional shrinky templates, and accompanied power point presentation that may be used as a guide in your Teen Dating Violence Outreach presentations. A HUGE thank you to Giovanna Martinez and WomenShelter of Long Beach for generously providing the beautifully laid out and powerful, comprehensive presentation on the background of and resources for Teen Dating Violence.
  
  Leaders Creating  
Note: This workshop can be presented in two ways, depending on where you want your focus to be. It can used as a prevention tool, where you are educating teens on what the cycle of violence looks like to them (in their own lives, community, and the media); or as a intervention tool, where you reflect on how the teens have experienced or witnessed violence themselves.

Objective:
For teens to learn and take part in a discussion and create a piece of art to reflect their own experiences with domestic violence and more specifically the "Cycle of Violence."

  
  How I Broke the Cycle Shrinky Key Ring 
Materials:
Pens and paper for writing
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Option 1 (Journaling):
The Cycle of Violence handout
The Cycle of Violence journaling page
Option 2 (Discussion):
Dating/Cycle of Violence Basics: Cycle of Violence handout
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Shrinky Templates 1 (optional)
Shrinky Templates 2 (optional)
Shrinky Templates 3 (optional)
Shrinky Dinks material (Ruff-N-Ready)
Permanent markers
Colored pencils and sharpeners
Scissors
Hole Punchers
Toaster Oven
Ribbon or Craft Wire
Beads (Optional)
Key Chain Ring (Optional)
Jump Rings (Optional)
Teen Dating Violence Power Point Presentation (compliments of WomenShelter of Long Beach)

Timeframe:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 15 minutes
Journaling/Discussion: 20 minutes
Creation: 40 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour 30 minutes

Prep:
Set up the table with the all of the supplies except the worksheet, Shrinky Dinks material and templates.

Introduction: 
Today we are going to learn about and discuss the Cycle of Violence. Afterwards, we will reflect on our own impressions and experiences with the cycle and create art to represent it.

Opening Circle:
Have each participant share one sentence (or one word) about how they view the Cycle of Violence or how it has impacted their life.

Journaling/Discussion
Keep in mind that these are simply two models of what the Cycle of Violence might look like and that it can be different for every person.

  
   
Option 1 (Journaling):
Pass out the Cycle of Violence handout and briefly introduce the Cycle to the teens. Give them a few minutes to review the handout and ask questions. Once they are comfortable with the concept, pass out the Cycle of Violence journaling page and ask them to write about their personal experiences related to the Cycle of Violence. This could be violence they have witnessed in their homes, violence they have personally experienced, or maybe violence a friend told them about. Ask them to write whatever comes to mind. Remind them not to worry about grammar or spelling, and to try not to censor themselves as they do not have to share about what they wrote.

After participants appear to have completed their writing, ask if a few of them would be willing to share their experience with the group.

  
   Discussion About the Cycle of Violence 
Option 2 (Discussion):
Pass out the Dating/Cycle of Violence Basics: Cycle of Violence handout. Read and review the handout together and discuss the different stages of the Cycle of Violence. Give examples and reflections for each stage either from personal experiences, the community, or from the media.

Some important things to note about the Cycle of Violence:
o    The cycle can happen hundreds of times in an abusive relationship and can take anywhere from a few hours to a year or more to complete. Each stage lasts a different amount of time and can be different for each person.
o    It is important to remember that not all domestic violence relationships fit the "Cycle". Often, as time goes on, the 'Honeymoon' stage disappears.
o    The heavy weight of abuse weighs upon you a little bit more each time you travel around the Cycle, until you are physically, mentally, emotionally and spiritually drained.
o    Emotional abuse is present in all three stages.
o    Domestic violence increases in frequency and severity.  It is never an isolated incident or a one-time occurrence.

 
  Creating without a template
 
  Creating using a template
 
  Cutting out the Shrinky Dink
 
  Don't forget to punch a hole!
Creation:
"Now that you have learned about the Cycle of Violence, it is time to create a Shrinky Dink. Option 1: Have participants create one or more shrinky dinks as a means to reflect on their personal experience of the cycle of violence. Option 2: Reflect on each of the three stages and create a shrinky dink to visually represent each stage using symbols, words or imagery.

Creation Steps:
Step One:
When creating the Shrinky Dinks invite them to use the templates provided or create their own designs. Remind them to color on the rough side of the Shrinky Dink if using colored pencils; they can use permanent markers on both sides. Ask them to fill the Shrinky Dinks with colors, shapes, words or even doodles.

Step Two:
When they are finished coloring, they may use scissors to cut their Shrinky Dink into a shape.  Then they will use the hole punch to cut a hole in the Shrinky Dink. Remind them to be sure not to punch the hole too close to the edge of the Shrinky Dink paper (as it will not be sturdy enough to support the weight of the Shrinky Dink and key ring).

Step Three:
Once the group members are done coloring, cutting, and punching a hole into their Shrinky Dink, they are ready for baking. Place the Shrinky Dink on a flat metal tray and place inside the toaster oven. We have found it is best to place a piece of a paper bag inside the oven with a corner turned up to make it easier to handle. Bake at 300 degrees until Shrinky Dink has completely flattened (this will take about one minute). Watch the amazing transformation! Remove the Shrinky Dink and allow it to cool.

Step Four:
Now the Shrinky Dink is ready for decorating with wire and beads, and attached to a key ring (if you like). Thread either wire or ribbon through the hole and add beads. Next take the ribbon or wire and attach it to the key ring or place the jump ring through the Shrinky Dink hole and attach it to the key ring. If you do not have access to key chain rings you can just have the clients string the Shrinky Dinks from ribbon, wire, embroidery thread, or yarn. 

Closing Circle:
If time allows, have each of the teens share about their Shrinky Dink and anything they discovered or learned in group about the Cycle of Violence. Encourage them to keep their artwork as a reminder of what their learning means to them and how they can use this awareness in their future.
  
 
 Creating One Shrinky for Each Stage of the Cycle  Adding Beads to Create the Key Ring
Row.txt_description: For teens to learn and take part in a discussion and create a piece of art to reflect their own experiences with domestic violence and more specifically the "Cycle of Violence."

Row.txt_code:
Instructor Rachel Ballon teaching the
Writing from the Heart workshop.
 
Objective:
This workshop was designed to use writing as healing tool using the Fast Flow Writing technique. This process can allow participants
to go deep within and connect to their inner selves, dormant
feelings, and powerful memories. 

This
process can allow the women to get in touch with feelings they have had a
hard time expressing verbally. Writing from the heart, they
can get in touch with their creative inner spirit and unleash their own
creativity. 

Materials:
Journals
Pens/pencils

Timeframe:
15 minutes: Introduction
 5 minutes: Relaxation Exercise
10 minutes: Guided Imagery and Visualization
20 minutes: Fast Flow Writing Exercise
10 minutes: Sharing and Processing
20 minutes: Participants Reading

Set-up/Prep:
CD Player and relaxing instrumental music playing.
Quiet room with no interruptions or noises (whenever possible)
Journals and pens distributed to each participant before workshop begins.
Decorating materials for journals (optional)

Introduction:
Putting pen to paper is a
powerful way of creating new behaviors and transforming stories. 
Writing from the heart allows one to let go of past hurts, rage on the page
and rewrite sad stories into happy ones.  The pen can dig up all the
blocks that can keep people from being as they were meant to be -
unique, creative, special one-of-a-kind.
 
   
   


 Leaders at the Writing from the Heart workshop.
 

Warm up or Opening Circle: Optional (recommended)
Go around the room and have each participant say their name, how they're feeling, and what they want/need from this workshop.
 
Using relaxing music, begin a relaxation meditation using deep breathing and
visualization. Select a theme for the meditation, such as "my safe place" or "I am." (See the Women's Manual or Teen Possibilities for
additional meditation suggestions.)

Set yourself in a
comfortable position and begin to take a few deep breaths.  As you
breathe, notice the tense parts in your body and direct the breath to
those areas. 
One way to focus your breathing is to breathe in for a count of 5 seconds, hold it for 3 seconds and exhale for 7 seconds.

With each breath, you have the opportunity to release the
tension in your muscles.  Continue to breathe slowly, in and out as
long as you feel necessary.  Scan all throughout your body for tense
areas.  Allow your mind to be present as you relax.  

Creation:
If there is anything in particular you want to explore, use
this safe window of time to visualize what you need at this particular
time and day.  Every time you practice this writing exercise, you can
focus on different parts of your journey.  If at any moment you can't
think of anything more to write and/or feel stuck, just write
about how you're feeling "in the moment" or write an autobiography.

When
beginning Fast Flow writing remember that there are NO RULES.  You
don't have to worry about spelling, grammar, sentence structure,
punctuation, etc.

These are the Fast Flow guideliness to help you write freely.
When writing, use first person (I) present tense
(am).  Write as fast as possible without stopping.  Try not to take the pen
from the page and don't stop writing until the allotted time is
reached.  (Approximately 15 minutes.) Also, try not to rewrite, reread, or edit
the work.  If you can't think of anything more to write, just write
about how you're feeling , an autobiography or anything at all that comes up.

Finally, try to use all of your 5 senses - touch, taste, sound, smell, and sight. Again, be sure to write as fast as you can and don't worry about whether what you're writing is good or bad. Just
write and enjoy the freedom of letting go!  It is not often that we
allow ourselves to say the things we really want to say.

If
time permits, you can decorate the journal with paint, collage, or
cover it with fabrics - you can have a second workshop to decorate the
journals.




 Decorating the journal with words.
 Decorating the journal with water colors
and words.
 

Closing:
Remind
the group that it is important and can be empowering to hear your words so you
can honor your feelings. If the participants feel they would like to
read out loud, encourage them to read loudly and slowly honoring each sentence.

If they prefer,
you can have the group share in pairs or share with a trusted friend or family member when they feel ready.  After this process is
completed, close the session by going around the room and having
participants say in one word what they're feeling after the workshop.
Some may feel relaxed and some may feel anxious; there are no
judgments; all feelings are valid.

 Participants writing in their journal.
Row.txt_description: This workshops allows participants to go deep within and reconnect to their inner selves, their dormant feelings, and their powerful memories. They also have the opportunity to get in touch with their creative inner spirit unleashing their own creativity.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
The Story Tree workshop gives children an opportunity to explore their strength and growth.  Using the tree as a symbol of life and courage, participants are free to play and let their imaginations run wild as they discover what kind of tree they want to be.

 
 Sample set up during a Story Tree Workshop
Materials:
Scratch paper for writing or pre-sketching
Pens/pencils
Markers
CrayPas
Paint - Acrylic or Bio Colors
Feathers (optional)
Glitter (optional)
Foam Shapes (optional)
Card stock paper or white construction paper
Paintbrushes
Sample photos of trees
Story Tree Reflections questions (optional)

Age Range:
6 years and up
 
  


 Sample material set up
Set-up/Prep:
Cover the tables with paper
You may consider hanging some of the following questions around the room to get the children thinking about their tree.
If you were a tree, what would you be? 
If you were a tree, Would you be tall or small? 
If you were a tree, Would you have colorful fruits? 
If you were a tree, Would you have big roots? 
If you were a tree, Would you be smiling in the sun?  Would you be having fun? 
If you were a tree, Would you have a swing to play?   Would your tree have something
If you were a tree, special to say? 

 
    

     Story Tree — created with color pencil
Introduction:
Did you know there are over 20,000 types of trees growing around the world and that they live anywhere from a few years to thousands of years, but they never stop growing. Most trees are strong and have deep sturdy roots. Trees can give shelter and protection with the shade they provide.  They also nourish us with the fruits they grow. Notice how trees look different in the summer from what they look like in the winter and even though many trees live through extremely cold winters and very hot summers they still grow stronger and bigger each year. Today we are going to be creating a painting of ourselves as a tree. 

Warm up:
Ask the children to stand up, take a deep breath and stretch their "tree limbs" way up to the sky as they reach higher and higher.  Have them  spread all their fingers as far as they can and take another deep breathe in and breathe out as they shake their "leaves" and flutter in the breeze.
