Walk around the room as trees that sway and stretch as they move.

NOTE: For older children, you may want skip the warm up and instead do the above introduction as a discussion. 

Opening Circle
If you were a tree, would you be palm tree on a deserted island, a fruit tree in a farm,  a big strong tree that others could climb or maybe a Pine Tree in a forest?  Maybe your tree is an imaginary tree where hearts or candy come from?

If you were a tree what kind of a tree would you be, why?

  
  Story Tree — created with paint and glitter
Creation:
Think about what kind of tree you would be and about what story your tree would tell you if it could talk. Think about what helps your tree grow, what your trunk looks like, what kind of leaves do you have, what is growing from your tree - is it fruit or maybe flowers?  Picture the tree in your mind and paint it or draw it on the paper.

Closing:
Ask the children what their tree had to say!

For older children, you can ask them to share about their story or, if they do not feel comfortable sharing out loud, you can invite the participants to journal their reflections using the Story Tree Reflections questions.
Row.txt_description: The Story Tree workshop gives children an opportunity to explore their strength and growth. Using the tree as a symbol of life and courage, participants are free to play and let their imaginations run wild as they discover what kind of tree they want to be.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop provides participants a creative opportunity to explore their stories of survival, change and growth. Using the tree as a symbol of life, participants can express uncover and express the stories of their life.

Materials:
Note on materials: Feel free to use some or all of the suggested materials. This workshop works well with simple materials or mixed-media. It can be done with any size paper.
           
Scratch paper or journal
Heavy white cardstock
Watercolor paper
Acrylic paints
Puffy paints
Watercolors
Paintbrushes
Thread
Yarn
Fabric
Glitter
         Rafia
Artificial flowers
Sticks
Dried Leaves
Stickers
Stamps
Glue
Family pictures
Significant documents
Collaging materials
Journaling reflection page

 
                         
 Sample material set-up
                         












Opening Circle:
Do a quick check-in circle even if it's just one word on how participants are feeling in the moment.
Remember that allowing the women to check-in allows them to notice how the are feeling and to voice any insecurities about their creative abilities.



     
 Sample inspiration question
      
Introduction:
Today’s workshop is called Story Trees. During this workshop we want to remind you that there are no
expectations. Using a tree as a symbol of life we will explore who we are, where we have been and where we are going in our lives.

(At this point you can hand out the following questions or you could print out each question and hang them around the room for the women to use for inspiration.)

Remember, you don’t have to answer all the questions. Trust your intuition and see what calls out to you.
    
Sample Story Tree
    

What kind of tree are you, or what kind of tree do you want to be?
What nurtures your tree?
How does your tree adapt to changes?
What kind of seeds is your tree housing?
Who provides your tree with light, water, nutrients, and caring?
How would you describe the fruit you offer?
Where do your roots extend?
Where or what is the core of your tree?
What is your tree made of?
What is your trees story?
What kind of transformations has your tree gone or will go through?
How does your tree find strength?
What is the texture of your roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits?
What colors fill the individual shapes of your trees?
Does your tree talk? What does it tell you?

Choose on of the following options:
Option 1: Warm up:
Get comfortable, take off your shoes and make sure your feet are touching the floor. Breathe in and as you release your breath spread out your toes. Feel that your toes are breathing and expanding onto the floor like roots reaching down, grounding you. Focus all your attention on your feet and allow them to sense the floor as if they were your hands. Continue to breathe deeper and deeper until your breath reaches your feet. As you breathe out imagine that your toes are releasing any tension, letting it flow down into the floor, into the earth as you breathe and relax. Remember that our feet have traveled far and need some loving too. Repeat the breathing and expanding your toes as many times as you feel necessary.



 Story Tree created by anonymous survivor
Option 2: Relaxation:
Remember that this is a special window of time for you. There is no right or wrong in the creative process. Take a moment to relax and release some of the tension your body carries. Close your eyes if it feels comfortable. Breathe in and out thinking of your heartbeat. Try to follow this beat as you let this subtle rhythm spread throughout your legs, hips, belly, chest, throat, and forehead and back down to your arms and hands. Breathe slowly and don't force the beat. Just let it happen. Open your eyes when you are ready.

Option 3: Read Story to Participants:

Sketching Exercise:
Consider the following story, as you get ready to begin.

In the uncertainty of a thunderstorm, I feel the rain falling over my head.
I see a young girl standing in a puddle of water.
Something draws me to this girl and makes me want to protect her.
I notice a lightning approaching her in slow motion.
I extend my arms and push her to the side.
I fall on the water and become this young girl.


 Sample Story Tree sketch
I know the lightning will reach me soon.
I try to stand, but I can’t.
Unexpectedly, I see a hand.
A tree extends its arm and draws me close to its trunk.
With one arm it picks me up, with the other it takes in the full force of the lightning.
As the tree holds me close to its core, I feel the urge to caress its contours.
I can perceive its texture and the energy that flows within its being.
All my senses are awakened.
My arms feel the intensity of the tree as it battles the lightning.
My body connects to it deeply.
The feeling is so vivid.

At that moment I realize that the young girl, the tree and I are only one being.
I am the tree that rescues me.

Sketching Exercise:
Today we are going to get ready to make our trees by exploring the different materials that will work best with the
evolution of your tree.
I'm going to turn on some music and we are going to take about 10 minutes to sketch.

Without much thinking begin to play with your materials. Use scratch paper with the different kinds of paints or drawing materials. Let these sketches flow naturally. It doesn't matter if the lines, colors or shapes don't "look" like anything at all. These initial images are meant to allow you to explore the ideas and colors that come to your mind.
Encourage participants to play with different shapes and sizes without limitation. Create as many trees as you want and be free!



 Sample Story Tree in watercolor
Creation:
Now we are going to begin our story trees.

You can use your sketches as part of your artwork or to take a moment to reflect. Maybe during the warm up exercise or sketching process you were surprised by certain images or feelings? Allow yourself to be present in your thoughts and respect what you are feeling. Whether you create a seed in a field or a 4000 year old oak, let your tree become alive as you
envision your own possibilities. Let your hands be free as you
continue to create.
Let your tree come alive as you envision your own possibilities.

Just like trees we gather nutrients from our environment but also must
withstand its different seasons and unpredictability. Notice how your
story relates to this process. Think about what your tree would like
to tell you or tell others and begin to create.

As you finish up, take a moment again to notice how your tree evolved.
Did it connect to your beginning sketches? Or did it take a life of its own?

Closing:
As the workshop comes to an end, ask participant to acknowledge the different feelings and
thoughts that were present throughout the creative process. Even if the participants aren't all finished with their work, it is very important to have a closing circle of sharing. After such a journey into the unpredictable territory of intuition, it is particularly valuable to take time for each participant to sit back and look at her work from a distance, to share what they see in it. If they do not feel comfortable sharing out loud, you can invite the participants to journal their reflections using the Story Tree Reflections questions.
Row.txt_description: This workshop provides participants a creative opportunity to explore their stories of survival, change and growth. Using the tree as a symbol of life, participants can explore and uncover the stories of their life.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways.  Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
A woman in Nicaragua revealing her beauty and future in her mask.
  
 
  Unmasking the beauty within.
Objective:
This workshop was created by Judy Brodjeski, a Windows leader from The Women's Community, WI. She developed and led this powerful workshop in Nicaragua with women who are taking an active role in their communities as leaders of social change. We are grateful for the amazing work that she has done to bring healing art workshops to Central America and transform lives beyond borders!

This workshop provides participants with an empowering opportunity to create a mask that represents the person they dream of becoming. By focusing on their dreams as well as the beauty they already hold within, one can reveal their power, strength and beauty in a way that transforms them.

Materials:
Pre-made mask forms - paper mache or plastic
Acrylic paints
Brushes
Scissors
Glue gun
Tacky glue
Tissue and decorative paper
Embellishments such as beads, feathers, ribbon, yarn, pipe cleaners, glitter, and other found objects

Note: Prior to the workshop, you may want to encourage participants to bring in any found objects or items that would make their mask a personal statement of the wonder of who they are.

Time Frame:
Intro: 5 minutes
Relaxation: 10 minues
Creation: 30 minutes - 1 hour
Closing Circle: 15 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour - 1 hour and 30 minutes

 
"For me my mask expresses that I needed much love."
 
  
 
A sample mask that portrays how beauty is a part of you
that can never be lost.
 
  
Introduction:
A mask is a powerful communication medium that can conceal and protect as well as reveal and enlighten. We may have hidden behind a mask all of our lives. Now is the time to discover our true potential. Now is the time to "dare to dream." Now is the time to reveal our beauty, strength, and power.

For this workshop we will make a mask that represents the person that you dream of becoming. Our dreams are vitally important and we must think big for them to come into being. This mask should be glorious. It will show your heart, beauty, and loveliness. It will allow you to go deep inside yourself and find that special place of goodness and love that is always there within you. Maybe you were told that you were ugly, or bad, or no one else would want you. This is NOT the truth. The real truth of your beauty is that part of you that can never be lost or go away. With this mask, you can find it again and remember it forever.

Opening Circle:
Lets start by doing a visualization to help us begin to envision the mask we will be creating today. Get comfortable in your chair and take a deep breath in. As you breathe out let go of any tension that you may be holding in your body. Imagine your heart filling you with love from deep within. Begin to "dare to dream," and start to notice the beauty, strength, and power you hold deep within you. Even if you are unaware of your inner strength and beauty, it is always a part of you. It is right there within you.

Now, start to imagine all that you dream to have and hold within you. Listen to yourself with an open heart, mind and spirit. Start to picture what shapes and colors might represent your deep inner strength and glorious self. Let them take shape in your imagination. Respect what arises from within you. Think of how you might like to create your mask, what the eyes might look like, the lips, the hair, the qualities it holds deep within, its strength and beauty. When you are ready, you can open your eyes and begin to create a mask revealing all of the beauty you hold within and how you dream to see yourself in the future.

Creation:
Step 1: Choose a mask form that calls out to you.

Step 2: Paint your mask with colors, shapes, and images that represent your deep inner beauty and the person you dream of becoming.

Step 3: Add embellishments such as beads, feathers, ribbon, yarn, pipe cleaners, glitter, and other found objects. Use your imagination and be bold. Take risks, make a statement, reveal your beauty!

Closing Circle:
Go around in a circle, and give each woman an opportunity to share their masks and how it felt to create their masks. Congratulate them on revealing their beauty and daring to dream their future self into reality!
Row.txt_description: This workshop provides participants with an empowering opportunity to create a mask that represents the person they dream of becoming. By focusing on their dreams as well as the beauty they already hold within, one can reveal their power, strength and beauty in a way that transforms them.

Row.txt_code:
Example of finished bag with new positive bagga
Objective:
This workshop gives participants an opportunity to reflect on what kind of "baggage" we carry and how it is possible to change it. By changing the focus to the qualities that empower us we can begin to create the life we wish to experience. 

This is done by decorating a canvas bag, which represents the new "baggage" we want to carry, with symbols and words that represent the foundation of the life we are creating and filling it with our dreams, visions and desires.

Materials:
Canvas bags
Permanent Markers
Glitter glue
Pencils
Erasers
Crayons or Craypas
Cards or small pieces of paper 


Timeframe:
1 - 1 1/2 hours


 
 


Close-up of positive qualities and symbols
 
Introduction:
Introduce the workshop by talking about the "baggage" we carry throughout our lives: shame, fear, self-judgement, etc.  Speak with the woman about legacy and how it is passed down generations. Discuss how our needs, wants and life experiences are affected by womanhood, culture, tradition and society.  

Talk about how we can choose NOW to change and make the choice to carry only those qualities that will empower us and help us to create the life we want to experience.  By creating a bag, that represents the baggage we want to carry, we give ourselves a visual affirmation to remind us to release our focus and energy from the negative to the positive.  As we carry with us our symbolic new "baggage" we can use it to remind ourselves that if it's not on the bag it doesn't deserve our energy because it is not part of the new life we are creating.

 



 A finished bag with new positive baggage
Opening Circle and Warm-up:

After checking in with the participants have them take three slow deep breaths to allow them to begin to relax. Then begin by engaging them in a centering warm-up of "I am " affirmations (see below). Ask them to repeat the "I am" affirmations silently to themselves, or if you'd rather you can have them speak these afirmations out loud.

Examples of affirmations:

I am a valuable, beautiful creation!

I belong and am necessary for and in this world!

I am a joyful and blossoming expression of love and power!


Creation:
Give the participants about 30 minutes to decorate the outside of their bags with words, symbols, images, and affirmations that represent the foundation of the world/life they are creating and wish to live.  They may also tell stories on the bag showing what they've conquered and where they are going.

 

 



 Monica Woodfox holding the beautiful finished products
After the outside of the bag has been decorated give the participants some time to think about any and all possible dreams, visions, desires, tangible or non-tangible, such as education, career, relationships or self-care.  Then gently ask them them to think about any thoughts, feelings, or behaviors that they wish to release. When they are ready ask them to add these thoughts and wishes to the cards provided by using words or pictures.  These cards can serve as sybmolic "seeds" that will need to be nurtured to grow within ourselves as we create a new life. 


Closing:
Once the participants have finished creating and filling their bags, or if the workshop time has come to an end, let the participants know that this workshop can be ongoing allowing them to add to the bag throughout their shelter stay. End the workshop by giving thanks for the time you have spent together and encourage the participants to trust that all that came up for them in the workshop was meant to be.
Row.txt_description:
This workshop gives participants an opportunity to reflect on what kind of "baggage" we carry and how it is possible to change it. By changing the focus to the qualities that empower us we can begin to create the life we wish to experience.
This is done by decorating a canvas bag, which represents the new "baggage" we want to carry, with symbols and words that represent the foundation of the life we are creating and filling it with our dreams, visions and desires.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Participants will be provided with an opportunity to discuss the meaning of a safe home and what goes inside and around it to make it feel that way. They will be invited to make specific commitments to creating that safety in their own homes.

 
Setting the table for Our Safe Home
 
Materials:
Construction paper
White Elmer's Glue
Glue sticks
Glitter glue
Puffy paint
Assorted ribbon and yarn
Pipe cleaners
Assorted flowers
Foam shapes
Scissors
Hole punchers
Markers & Pens
Personal photos
Optional:
Large pieces of felt
Fabric

Time Frame:
Introduction and Discussion: 10 minutes
Creation: 40 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Total: One Hour (more if time permits)

Workshop Preparation:
It could be helpful if you have time to prepare the house cut-outs and questions before the workshop. If possible have all materials spread out and ready for use. Be sure to remind participants that this is a safe space for them to express and create their own vision of what goes inside and outside of a safe home.

Note: You might consider calling this workshop Happy Home if you feel this will allow the children and/or families to focus in that way.
Introduction:
Today we will be talking about what safety and a safe home means to you. You will then create a book about and decorate your very own safe home! You will be able to decorate your new home whatever way you want. And you will also be able to make commitments and decisions about the safe home you will create in the future. We will also take some time for you share what a safe home looks, feels, and sounds like.

To get started let's think about what having a safe home might mean.

What does a safe home look like?  Maybe it is full of pictures from the good and happy times? Maybe it is full of smiling faces? Maybe it is full of people or it just has the people you want there?

What does a safe home feel like? Maybe it is a place you are happy to return to at the end of the day. Maybe it is warm and cozy. Maybe you can freely share your feelings, hopes and dreams there. Maybe it is a place where you feel happy, loved, and relaxed.

What does a safe home sound like? Maybe there are no loud voices or bad words. Maybe people are happy and laughing. Maybe it is quiet and peaceful or maybe music is playing and everyone is singing.

Something else to ask yourself is, how do you want to be treated and treat others in your home? How can your family work together to make it a safe home?


 
Cutting the folded lines
 
 
Discussion Questions
 
Creation:
If it was up to you what would a safe or happy home look like?

Step 1
Create a house shape to use as a template for the project. Begin by folding a sheet of construction paper, length-wise, in half. Then fold both corners over to the centerfold. Cut along these corner fold lines. Now you have a template to create the rest of pages in your Safe Home.

Step 2
Use your template to trace and cut 5 more “Home” shapes. Next write down the following questions (1 per page) at the top of each house shape and leave one house page blank. The blank page will be the front of your book, it will be the house you will decorate later. Be sure to take the time to brainstorm and discuss the questions as a family before writing down your answers to each question:

Page 1- Keep this page blank to decorate later!
Page 2 - What does a safe home look like?
Page 3 - What does a safe home feel like?
Page 4 - What does a safe home sound like?
Page 5 - How do we treat each other inside our home?
Page 6 - How are we going to work together to create Our Safe Home?

When this is completed, line these shapes up and punch holes along the left-hand side. Make sure to put that blank page at the front, it will be the cover of your book.

Step 3
Lace a ribbon, yarn, or a pipe cleaner through the holes and tie them to create binding. An alternative is to forsake hole-punching and simply staple construction papers together.

 
Binding the Safe Home book together
 

Step 4
Have fun decorating the cover of your book with shapes, images, words, and design materials that you imagine your Safe Home to have on the outside. When doing this, remember to think about what makes you feel safe!


Closing:
If the participants feel comfortable, have them gather around in a circle and share. Give each person an opportunity to share about their home and how it felt to create this safe home.

If working with families, remind them that if they work together, they can create this safe home in their future. Thank them for sharing and for working together to create their safe home!
 
 
  Our beautiful Safe Home!
Row.txt_description: Participants will be provided with an opportunity to discuss the meaning of a safe home and what goes inside and around it to make it feel that way. They will be invited to make specific commitments to creating that safety in their own homes.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This w orkshop can built teamwork and trust amongst participants. Participants will be invited to explore the idea of sharing ideas and allow others the freedom to do the same. The end result can serve as a reflection of the group dynamic and be a strong point for meaningful conversation about team building, trust and support.

Materials:
Large poster board or large piece of butcher paper
Various types of paint (acrylic, puff paint, glitter paint, tempera)
Paint trays or small plates
Brushes
Sponges
Water and containers to rinse brushes
Music
Optional:
Markers
Smocks (You can use trash bags with holes cut for head and arms.)

Age Range:
6 years and up
    Timeframe:
1 hour
Introduction and Warm up – 10 min
Creation - 30-40 min
Sharing – 10 min
 
                  







 
  Setting the table for Pass the Painting
Set-up/Prep:
Have all the paint poured out for easy access and distribute accordingly. The painting participants should total no more than 12 - too many participants will make the process too slow. You can divide the group in 2 circles if necessary. (If doing multiple groups have a few paint trays per group).

Lay out paper and give each participant a brush or painting tool (they can switch with each other if they would like to, although with younger kids it may be easier to keep them focused on one tool).

You may want to have a small sample of a painting you and another staff created as an example. You may also want to have a timer so you can call when it is time to switch to a new artist.

Introduction:
"Today I want you to think about sharing with others. Is it easy, difficult, fun, annoying etc.? What kind of things do you share? Could it be toys, art supplies, food, clothes? How about ideas?

"We are going to be sharing some ideas with each other today. The project we are going to do is called Pass the Painting. We will be creating one piece of art that we create together. Each of you will get the change to add your unique drawing and pass it along to the next person. Try not to think too much about what you're drawing, just let your paintbrush flow and trust whatever comes us. There is no wrong way to do this.

We're going to begin by picking a person to start and simply pass the paper on until the time is up. Towards the end you will try to fill your whole paper. Remember there is no wrong way to draw your part."

  
  Each person adds their drawing.
  
  
  
  
 The paper is passed and the next person takes a turn.
  
  
  
  
  The collaborative painting begins to take shape.
  
  
  
  
 Finished painting
  
  
Warm up:
"Let's start by doing a warm-up that builds teamwork in a similar way, by combining our movements and sounds to create something. Just like how we are each going to take turns in passing the painting and adding to it, in this warm-up we are each going to take turns by adding a new movement and sound to create one "giant machine." We will start by having one person volunteer to start the machine by making any sound and movement they want. Then we will have each of you one by one add to the machine by standing near each other while making different sounds and movements until we have created one large machine! In the end it will be a giant machine full of movements and sounds that are as different and unique as each of us!"

Opening Circle:
Let's review some of the guidelines for Pass the Painting:
  • We will share the supplies.
  • We will wait for our turn.
  • We cannot write words on the paper.
  • We may not overlap or cover up another person's work.
  • We will keep circling until we cover the whole paper or all decide when the artwork is complete.
Creation:
Each group will have one person start by making a mark or shape on the page. The only rule is that they not cover up any mark that others have made or change the colors that the others have used. Support participants through the process by reminding them this is about teamwork and sharing ideas supportively. If the group ends early you can have some paper ready so the participants can journal about the experience and how it felt to share the creativity.

Closing:
It is important that each person get a chance to share about how this process made them feel and what things came up for them while doing the painting. How did they overcome those feelings or deal with them? In the end make a statement about how important teamwork can be as well as how support can be helpful to smooth out any feeling that can arise during the process. The participants will notice how they had to respect the boundaries of the other participants as well as trust that their work will be preserved, learning that each part of the work is equally important.
Row.txt_description: This workshop can built teamwork and trust amongst participants. Participants will be invited to explore the idea of sharing ideas and allow others the freedom to do the same. The end result can serve as a reflection of the group dynamic and be a strong point for meaningful conversation about team building, trust and support.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop offers participants an opportunity to give themselves empathy as they notice how they are feeling with the approaching holiday season.

This workshop also allows the participants to enjoy creating sculpey ornaments filled with hopes, prayers or wishes as reminders of the positive changes they are making for themselves and their family.

 
Ornament created by Window's Staff
 
Materials:
Sculpey (One 8-pound box for a group of 10 will be more than enough.) See sculpey.com for ordering info or local arts/crafts stores.
Various rubber stamps with letters, numbers, textures, etc. (Available at local arts and craft stores)
Acrylic paints (assorted colors)
Spray or paint-on sealer in matte or gloss to protect the painted sculpey (such as Plastercraft acrylic spray finish in matte or glossy)
Assorted cookie cutters
Assorted craft wire (18 only if pliable, 20 to 22 gauge, any thicker will be difficult to bend and the sculpey will break. Note: an easier alternative to wire is to use ribbon.
Assorted beads
Assorted ribbon (on the thin side for hanging ornaments if desired)
Rolling pin (Full soda cans or aerosol cans work too!)

Tools for working with the sculpey:
Toothpicks or straws (for making holes for the ribbon or wire to pass through)
Popsicle sticks (for smoothing, cutting the clay, etc.)

For baking the sculpey:
Toaster oven(s) (Due to toxic fumes from the clay, toaster oven should be one dedicated for non-food use)
Tongs or potholders

 
For painting the sculpey:
Paint brushes in various sizes from small detail to larger widths
Paint trays to collect desired colors of paint
Water cups
Paper towels
Cup or container to collect desired beads
For working wire, beads, ribbon:
Pliers/wire cutters
Scissors
ZipLock plastic bags for each artist to store gathered beads and parts for each ornament for the next session (if more than 1 session)
Permanent marker to mark each artist's name on the bags

Timeframe:
Total: Two 1-2-hr session
Intro & Sharing: 30 minutes
Creation: 60 minutes
Closing: 30 minutes

Advance Prep Tips:
If you have less than two hours for this project, it can help speed things along if assorted ornaments are pre-made and baked ahead of time for the participants to use.

Introduction:
The holiday season is full of meaning and traditions. For many of us it brings up certain expectations and strong emotions for and from ourselves and others. It can be difficult to sort through the conflicting emotions that come up. We may feel grief or loss, loneliness or sadness or joy and hope.

Through these stressful times we'll take a moment to acknowledge our feelings and recognize the pressures we carry. It is also important to notice our feelings as we validate our need to feel loved, secure, peaceful and safe. During these difficult times of change and growth, remember that you have the power to make healthy choices toward peace, security, hope and joy. After all isn't that what the holidays are suppose to be about.

 
 Ornament created by Window's staff
Demonstration:
You want to take a few minutes to explain the process. Make a sample ornament by having a balled up piece of sculpey, then flatten it out a bit using a rolling pin. Cut out the ornament by pressing down into the clay.

Explain that they will need to put holes where ever they want to hang beads and a larger hole if they wish to hang their ornament. These holes should be placed about 1/4" from the edge, not too close or the sculpey will break. Pass the toothpick or straw through from front to back and make sure the hole is clear of debris and smooth on the back side.

Next explain that the sculpey needs to bake before it can be painted. Show a sample piece that is baked. Remind the participants that they will need to place holes in the pieces to hang them or add beads later on.

Opening Circle:
To start this workshop I'm going to ask you all to take a few deep breaths, check-in with yourself and then share with the group three words to describe how you are feeling as the holidays approach. We will not be having an open discussion right away, but we will have more time to elaborate and process your feelings in the journaling portion of the workshop and during the closing circle. At this moment I just want you to notice how you are feeling and see if you can share it with the group.

Journaling:
Many of us forget to ask ourselves what it is we really need during the holiday season, and instead get caught up in what we think is expected of us. It's important to remember that we are in control of our lives and our future and that our choices determine our fulfillment.

We are going to take five minutes to write. You may write about your three words and how it felt to hear the group's feelings or if you may choose to write your hopes and wishes for future holidays. As you write be gentle with yourself and try to challenge yourself to think about who you are and what is important and meaningful to you.

As the participants finish up, ask them to close their journals and thank them for taking the time to notice their feelings.

 
 Gail, Windows intern with her ornament of change
Relaxation:
Before we get started we are going to take another minute to do some deep breathing as we honor ourselves for the changes we are making for a better future for ourselves an our family. Take a deep breath in and as you breathe out see if you can let go of some of the stress or anxiety you are carrying in your body. Let the breaths help you to cleanse your lungs and release tension. For the next breath, I want you breathe deeply and slowly as you allow yourself to imagine a new and better future. Hold it, and release it into the universe. With a final breath, now try to envision joy, peace and safety as a tradition in your holiday season.

Creation:
After the relaxation, play some soft music and welcome them to start creating. Remind the ladies that these ornaments should serve as reminders for the positive changes they are making for the future.
NOTE: Throughout the workshop, try to encourage the participants to chase away discouraging thoughts. Remind them that the changes they are making will change their future and destiny.


Using cookie cutters

Part 1: Making sculpey ornaments
Have the participants start creating their ornaments by choosing a cookie cutter that reminds them of a positive change they have made or that want to to make for the future. If they choose to do so they may try free forming the clay, using stamps for words or textures, etc.
NOTE: color sculpey can be used to lessen time for decoration or to ease any participant that is afraid of painting.

Part 2: Baking the sculpey.
Start to collect finished sculpey pieces as they're available, checking frequently for those who have more pieces ready for baking. Bake in toaster oven at 300 degrees for appox. 7-10 minutes based on thickness of clay. Allow pieces to cool completely before painting. (About 10 minutes)

 
 Painted sample with beads
Part 3: Painting the sculpey.
Next, the baked sculpey ornament can be painted using acrylic paint. When the paint is dry, spray with a sealer according to manufacturer directions.

Part 4: Wiring and beading
While the ornaments are drying, have each woman choose wire and select beads or other decorations, such as charms, bits of chain, etc. If using wire, keep in mind that there are many different and creative ways to use it. Cut the wire a little longer than needed to allow for wrapping and coiling. To avoid frustration, show the participants the basic way to loop the wire end through the hole and twist it around itself about 3 or 4 times to secure. They may choose to hide this part by sliding a bead over it, or to simply let it show. They may wish to curl the excess wire with a wire tool instead of cutting it off. They may also use ribbon in the ornament's top to hang it, or they may use wire. Encourage them to try their own creative solutions too. Remember to tell the participants to not twist the wire too tightly against the sculpey or it might break or rub off the paint.

Closing:
Have each woman share her ornament(s) and what it will remind them of in future holidays.
Row.txt_description:
This workshop offers participants an opportunity to give themselves empathy as they notice how they are feeling with the approaching holiday season.
This workshop also allows the participants to enjoy creating sculpey ornaments filled with hopes, prayers or wishes as reminders of the positive changes they are making for themselves and their family.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To have the children reflect on the many things in life that they are thankful for by creating Giving Thanks Placemats that they can then use or give as gifts for the holidays!

 
  Supplies for the Giving Thanks Placemats
Materials:
9 x 12 Construction paper or larger, in holiday colors
Ruler
Pencils
Laminating sheets (can be purchased from any office supply store) or clear contact tape
Markers, crayons or CrayPas (oil pastels)

Time Frame:
Approximately one hour

Age Range:
Age range – 6 and older

Set Up:
Draw a one-inch border all around a piece of construction paper. Fold the paper in half and hold vertically - pre-draw lines an inch apart. If your children are young you may want to also pre-cut the lines you just drew.

   

Draw a border around the edges of the
construction paper
 Fold the paper in half



Cut strips of construction paper (1 inch wide by 9 inches long) in assorted holiday colors. You might want to make a sample to show what the weaving will look like on the completed placemat.

 

Pre-draw the lines
  Pre-cut the lines

You can do this project for any occasion – just change the colors of the paper!

Introduction:
Talk about the many things we all have to be thankful for… laughter, playing with friends, things that make you happy, things that make you smile. Tell the children that today they will be creating Giving Thanks Placemats that can be decorated with things that they are thankful for. They can keep and use their placemats when they are done or give them as a gift!

Warm Up:
Have the children sit in a circle (they can hold hands) and go around the room asking each to name one thing they are thankful for. Keep going around the circle until the children have run out of things to say.

   
  Weaving the strips
 
Creation:
Have the children start by picking 9 paper strips and a piece of the construction paper you have prepared for them. Let the children know that they can put the colors in any order that they like, there is no right or wrong way to do it. Show the children, with an example placemat, how they will weave each paper strip in one by one by going under and over the paper strips that are on the whole sheet of construction paper. This may be a challenge for some of the younger children and they might need your help, especially with the last strip to be placed into the mat.

Once the children have finished weaving in their last strip tell them to think again about the things that they are thankful for. Have them draw or write these things on their placemat and around the border if they choose. They can use any of the colored markers, crayons or oil pastels on the table. Remind them that this is their time to do their art and have fun with it!

   
  Peel back the laminating sheet
 
When a child finishes decorating their placemat you can then laminate it for them. Do this by peeling off the clear side of the laminating material or contact tape and then gently laying the placemat directly onto the sticky part of the sheet pressing as you adhere the placemat. Do this to both the front and back. Now their mats are done!

Closing:
When everyone has finished their placemat have them share with each other what they discovered they are thankful for.

 
  The finished placemat!
Row.txt_description: To have children reflect on the many things in life to be thankful for by creating Giving Thanks Placemats that they can then use or give as gifts for the hollidays.

Row.txt_code:
Opening:
If you are beginning these workshops in November, you can take this opportunity to talk about what the holidays mean and discuss things to be thankful for. Also note, these workshops can be adapted to any time of the year - not just for the holidays.

Creation:
In this update we are sharing three activities - you can choose one each week. Feel free to adapt, change or modify to fit your group.

 
 
Holiday Card Making
Making and giving a personal home made card is a wonderful way to make someone feel special. To start, have each person draw a name of someone else in the group, Then make a card for that person, once that is done each participant can make additional cards for family and friends. You can add materials to make the card more detailed, such as magazines for collage, doillies, vellum papers and ribbons. (You could also skip the drawing names and just have everyone make cards for people they love!)

Materials:
Construction Paper
Colored Pencils
Markers
Craypas (especially great for getting bright colors on colored paper)
Glitter Glue or Paint
Scissors


Shrinky Dink Blessing Charms
Taking the time to think about what is good in your life and what you are grateful for is a powerful exercise especially at this time of year. You could open with a circle of blessing-sharing and then make Shrinky Dink charms. These charms can be used to hang in the window or on a tree. They can even be made into jewelry – such as a necklace, pendant, or earring.

Materials:
Shrinky Dink Material
Permanent Markers and/or Color Pencils
Scissors
Ribbon or Yarn
Beads (Optional)
Toaster Oven

(Feel free to call for more details if you’ve never used Shrinky Dinks before. They are fabulous!)

 
  For sculpey beads colors can be
swirled together
 
  Use a toothpick to create holes
before baking.
Bracelet Making
Beaded bracelets make a special a gift. They can be as simple or detailed as you like. You can string regular beads or you can make your own beads. Here are 2 methods: roll small pieces of scuply, mixing colors if you like, make a hole all the way through and bake for 10 minutes. (Feel free to experiment with the size and shape of the bead). You can also make beads from paper by cutting long narrow triangle shapes from color magazine pages. Roll the shape starting from the widest end and glue the narrow end to the rolled paper. This is an inexpensive and colorful way to make a unique beaded bracelet or necklace.

Materials:
Beads
“Home Made Beads” out of sculpey or rolled magazine paper triangles
Elastic Sting or Ribbon



To create paper beads, cut magazine pictures into triangular strips,
wrap around a toothpick and glue at the end.
Row.txt_description: This is a series of workshops with holiday themes including Holiday Cards, Shrinky Dink Blessing Charms and Bracelet making to help women find art in the holidays. The idea is to create something special to show loved ones that we care and perhaps even begin new family traditions. Creating with art during the holidays as a family can be a relaxing way to connect, bond and celebrate.

Row.txt_code:
Opening:
As you begin these workshops, take the opportunity to talk about the significance of the holidays and how it is a time to celebrate yourself and those you care for. It can also a time to begin thinking about goals/visions for the new year.

< span class="TextHeader2">Creation:
In this update we are sharing four activities – you can choose one each week. Feel free to adapt, change or modify to fit your specific group. Have fun!

 
 Magic Raindeer Sample
Magic Reindeers
Magic reindeers are a fun way to decorate the shelter with holiday spirit. Using each child’s own hands and feet, these reindeers also make special gifts for mom. (Or you could involve the whole family in creating reindeer families!!) The children can work in pairs to help each other. Have each child trace one foot on the construction paper. Next, using another color, each person will trace both hands. Cut the tracings out. Glue the handprints behind the wider part of the foot (toe area). Add eyes and nose to complete the reindeer.

Materials:
Construction Paper
Glue Sticks
Scissors
Felt
Markers
Googley Eyes
Pom-pom balls (optional)


 
Fold square paper in
half diagonally. Fold
in half again. Keep
folding into a
wedge		 
Snowflakes
Snowflakes are a fun and magical way to celebrate the winter holidays across traditions and religions. They can be made by folding almost any type of paper (see steps bellow). The more folds the more complex the design. The snowflakes can be decorated with markers or glitter and they can be attached to make a holiday card. After you have several snowflakes cut out you may want to hang them up in the window, string them out on a garland or hang them from a rod as a snowflake mobile. You can tape thread to them and make ornaments or decorate packages by taping them on the wrapping.

Materials:
Plain White Paper (cut into squares)
Scissors
Ribbon
Markers
Glitter or Glitter Glue (optional)

 
 
Begin to cut shapes at
the edges of your
folded wedge.		 Cutting the top of the
wedge creates the
outside shape of the
snowflake.
 Unfold to see your
beautiful snowflake.













 
 Decorated Cookie Samples
Decorated Cookies
Hand-decorated cookies can be a wonderful and delicious tradition that an entire family can enjoy together. Be sure to make enough to eat while you create!!

Materials:
Pre-baked cookies are available
at major grocery stores
Icing
Sprinkles
Gum Drops

If you want to make your own gingerbread, see at the end in workshop tips for recipe.


 
Ginger House Sample
 
Gingerbread Houses
This is an excellent group project that can teach sharing and cooperation. Many people can work on one house together and it can be as simple of elaborate as you wish. Great patience is need and houses can be completed over several days if necessary.

Materials:
Pre-made Gingerbread House Kits are available to purchase at many local retailers such as Trader Joe’s, Bed Bath and Beyond, Linens and Things or Michael’s. They usually come complete with the icing and candy decorations. Or you can bake your own (see following recipe).

The idea is to create something special to show loved ones that we care and perhaps even begin new family traditions. Creating with art during the holidays as a family can be a relaxing way to connect, bond and celebrate.

Row.txt_code:
Tree of Empowerment decorated by the Hands of Hope
created at People Against Violent Environments (PAVE), IL.
Objective:
This workshop is a great way for the participants to inspire hope with their empowering messages. These Hands of Hope can then be hung together on a tree to evoke a powerful Tree of Empowerment that represents the combined woman's hopes, strengths, dreams and encouraging words for those fleeing abuse to have hope in a better tomorrow.

Materials:
Cardstock
Watercolors
Brushes
Glitter Paint
Cups for water
Scissors
Paper for journaling
Permanent Markers
Magazines
Glue and/or glue sticks
Inspirational quotes on kindness

Time Frame: Total 1 1/2 Hours
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 15 minutes
Creation: 45 minutes
Closing: 25 minutes
Note: To save time, you can have hands precut and have journaling paper availible.

Introduction:
Today we will be reflecting on inspiring words and phrases that were, or could have been, helpful in freeing ourselves from abuse and violence in our homes. We will then begin cutting, pasting, and painting messages of hope and journaling our thoughts on our creations. We will put our messages in our hands to share with other participants. These hands can then be hung on a community holiday tree to encourage all those fleeing abuse to have hope in a better tomorrow.

Opening Circle:
Take a moment to acknowledge everyone's presence and check in with the participants. Ask them to think of hopeful words that allow them to relax. They don't have to elaborate, but they can carry those words with them throughout the creation of their hands. You may even ask them to share what words came to them.

Pass out a handout with the quotes for this workshop to inspire them. Give the participants time to read and reflect on these quotes of hope. Then have the participants journal for 10 minutes, reflecting on their own hopeful words and messages that they may like to share with others as inspiration. When this time has ended let them know that they can continue to do more journaling during the project as well.

 
  A Hand of Hope and inspiration created at
People Against Violent Environments (PAVE), IL.
Creation:
The hand shapes can be created by placing your hand in the cardstock and tracing its shape. Cut after you're done. When using watercolors for decoration, you will have two cups of water. One cup is for dipping the clean brush and the other is to clean out the brush between colors. There are magazines available for making collages as well as inspirational quotes. You can also write your own quotes if you choose to. Sharpies make good pens for lettering and you can use glitter paint to sparkle up your "hand of hope." Leave some time to journal on separate pieces of paper. These little pieces can be cut up and glued to the back of your "hands." Remeber that these hands are gifts of knowledge you give to other survivors. There is no right or wrong way to create them, just many possibilities.

Closing:
When the participants have finished creating and decorating their hands give them the opportunity to share how this experience of creation was for them. Share with them how powerful their Hands of Hope are and how they, with their own hands, are changing the world by bringing greater hope and inspiration to others.

 
 
More inspirational Hands of Hope
created at People Against Violent Environments (PAVE), IL.
Row.txt_description: This workshop is a great way for the participants to inspire hope with their empowering messages. These Hands of Hope can then be hung together on a tree to evoke a powerful Tree of Empowerment that represents the combined woman's hopes, strengths, dreams and encouraging words for those fleeing abuse to have hope in a better tomorrow. This is also a great group activity!

Row.txt_code:
Conversation Heart Shrinky Dinks
 
Objective:
To give children the words to express loving feelings. It is a reminder of how special they are and how much others appreciate them.

Materials:
Shrinky Dinks (rough and ready type) Pre-cut hearts/templates
Color pencils
Hole punchers
Ribbon / yarn
Toaster oven
Scissors
Pencils sharpener
Permanent markers
Small paper plates (to collect pencil shavings)
Heart shapes should be about 4”. Note: anything smaller than 3” will be difficult to read or see due to shrinkage of the material when it cooks.
Click here to see template

Timeframe:
Time frame: 1 - 1 1/4 hours

Age Range:
3 yrs. and up.

Set-up:
Younger children (under age 5) may have difficulty cutting their own heart, so depending on the age levels in your group, you will probably need to pre-cut the shapes and pre-hole-punch each heart. Make enough for each child to make 3 or more.

 
 
Drawing the hearts from templates
  Cutting the hearts
  Hole punching the heart before baking



Introduction:
Today we are going to celebrate love in a special and magical way. We will be making Shrinky Dinks to share the nicest feelings and kindest words that we would like to hear. We wil use words and feelings that make us feel good and cared for.

Can you think of the nicest things a friend has ever said to you? Maybe it was:
"You are special" or "You are nice" or "You are my friend" or "You are cool" or "I like you"

Explain that today they are going to make their very own hearts that send messages to those we care about. They will be able to decorate their Shrinky Dink hearts and after they are baked they will share them with the rest of the group.

If you haven't used the Shrink Dink material with your group before you may want to demonstrate how to color them with the color pencils for the background and how to use darker colors for the words. You can show a sample of the size they become after they shrink in the oven.
   
  Shrinky Dink hearts with messages before baking
 

Creation:
Explain to the children that they will be making 3 to 6 Shrink Dink hearts that will be given away. Let them know in advance that today they will be giving away and receiving hearts. The children will not know who will receive their heart so the message should include kind words or messages appropriate for anyone in the group. Younger children might need help writing the messages.

When the hearts are ready for baking, make sure to hole punch them for ribbons.

Bake the Shrinky Dinks in a preheated toaster oven at 325 degrees. Cut a rectangle shape out of a brown grocery bag and turn one corner up. (The turned up corner will make it easy to remove from tray or cookie sheet.) Place Shrinky Dink pieces, colored side up, on the brown paper and place paper on the tray or on a cookie sheet. Put into preheated oven. Watch as your Shrinky Dink shrinks. Bake approximately 1 to 3 minutes. After pieces lie flat, allow an additional 30 seconds of baking time to complete the process.
Remove paper from tray or cookie sheet and lightly press flat with a pad of paper or magazine until the pieces have cooled – approximately 15 seconds.

Place all the hearts in a basket.

Pass the basket around the room and have each child pick one. Continue to pass the basket until each child has selected the same number of hearts that they created.

If the children want to they can string their hearts with ribbons or yarn (cut approximately 28” long). Knot the ends and they are ready to wear.
   
  Candy conversation
hearts!
 


Closing Circle:
Have the children discuss how it felt to make the special hearts for others and how it felt to receive the positive messages from others in the group.
Row.txt_description: To give children the words to express loving feelings and a reminder of how special they are and how much others appreciate them.

Row.txt_code:
An example of a Peace Wreath
Objective:
To have the children contribute to the holiday decorations by creating a personal Peace Wreath made from their own hand shapes. This activity leads the children to think about what creates peace and in what ways they can use their own hands to create a more peaceful world.


Materials:
Lots of green construction paper
Red construction paper
(one for each participant) or red ribbon
One paper plate for each participant
Pencils
Scissors
Glue
Glitter glue (optional)
 
  Tracing hands to create the wreath
Quotes on Kindness

Age Range:
3 years and up

Timeframe:
Under an hour

Set-up/Prep:
This is a very easy activity with no real set up or prep except for laying out the supplies. The younger children will need help tracing and cutting their hand from the construction paper.

Introduction:
Talk about the many ways we can share something special for the holidays. Ask the children what they have to share – is it a smile, helping their mom, or could it be decorating their room? Today we are making decorations for the holidays that we can share with our friends and family. When you are kind to others it not only changes you, it changes the world. What acts of kindness can each of us do to change the world to create a more peaceful place to live...

"Don't wait for people to be kind, show them how." Unknown

Opening Circle:
Begin the workshop by having the children share what they think they can do to create more peace in the world. Speak with them about how in their own way they can bring peace into the world through...showing love, sharing, kindness, smiling, forgiveness, being nice to someone who is having a bad day, etc.

It is optional to then share with the children a song about kindess and then have them sing it with you.

Song (to the tune of "Are You Sleeping?):
Kindness matters, kindess maters
Every day, in every way
Share with one another
Care for one another
Let us all, be kind today.

Another option is to read some inspiring quotes on kindness to the children. Click here for the link to quotes on kindness.

 
Cutting out and glueing hands to wreath
 
 
Putting the wreath together
 
 
Creation:
Trace the child’s hand on a piece of green construction paper. Cut the hand out and then trace the cut hand 9 more time on the green paper. Cut all the hands.
Glue the hand cut-outs together, using the plate as a base, in a wreath shape. Glue the wrists so that they are overlapping a little creating the center of the wreath. The fingers then flar out at the edges and look like leaves!
Make a large red bow, either from construction paper or the ribbon, and glue it to the bottom of the wreath.
Remind the children that their hands can create a more peaceful world and have them write on the wreath some of their ideas of how they can create peace. They can then use the glitter glue to decorate the hands.

Closing:
Ask the children if they would like to talk about their creation and ask where they would like to hang their holiday wreath. They can even think about what they can do today to create more peace in the world. Or share who they might want to give their wreath to as a gesture of peace and love.
Row.txt_description: To have the children contribute to the holiday decorations by creating a personal Peace Wreath made from their own hand shapes. This activity leads the children to think about what creates peace and in what ways they can use their own hands to create a more peaceful world.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give children the opportunity to appreciate someone who has made a difference in their lives.

 
Certificate of Appreciation with lace trim
 
Materials:
Watercolor paper
Watercolors
Gel pens
Ribbon / yarn (optional)
Glue sticks (optional)
Scissors (optional)

Paper to cover tables

Timeframe:
Time frame: 45 minutes to 1 hour

Age Range:
6 yrs. and up

 
Painting and decorating the certificate
 
Set-up:
Lay out watercolor paper and watercolor paints. If more decorations are wanted you can also add ribbon or yarn with glue sticks. Younger children might need help writing the words of appreciation.

Introduction:
Have the children imagine how it would feel to be awarded a certificate for something they have accomplished or for kindness they have exhibited. Talk about different types of accomplishments. Accomplishments can be big or small, they can be things we do to help or support ourselves or others, it can be kind words, help or even smiles.

Explain that today they are going to make certificates to honor, or give a formal expression of thanks to someone who has made a difference in their lives; someone who has been kind, generous or supportive. A certificate is a fun way to show that special person how much they are appreciated. Discuss who those people could be -- is it your mom or other family member, a teacher maybe a friend? The children can decorate their certificates with watercolors and can add ribbons or yarn to the borders.

Creation:
Encourage the children as they begin work on their certificates. Have them think of the special words of appreciation for each certificate they wish to create. Offer to assist them if they need help writing the words. Leave a space in the center of the paper to inset the persons name.

 
Three certificates
 

Closing Circle:
Talk about how it feels to appreciate someone special and what it will feel like to give the certificate to that person.
Row.txt_description: To give children the opportunity to appreciate someone who has made a difference in their lives.

Row.txt_code:
Tree of Empowerment decorated by the Hands of Hope
created at People Against Violent Environments (PAVE), IL.
Objective:
This workshop gives the children the ability to create cut-outs of their own hands and decorate them with color, images, and words that inspire hope. These Hands of Hope can then be hung together on a community holiday tree to evoke a powerful Tree of Empowerment that represents the combined hopes, strengths, and dreams to inspire others to have hope in a better tomorrow.

Materials:
Cardstock
Watercolors
Brushes
Glitter Paint
Cups for water
Scissors
Paper for journaling
Permanent Markers
Magazines
Glue and/or glue sticks
Inspirational quotes on kindness

Time Frame: Total 1 1/2 Hours
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 15 minutes
Creation: 45 minutes
Closing: 25 minutes
Note: To save time, you can have hands precut and have journaling paper availible.

Introduction:
Today we will be reflecting on inspiring words and phrases that were, or could have been, helpful in freeing ourselves from abuse and violence in our homes. We will then begin cutting, pasting, and painting messages of hope and journaling our thoughts on our creations. We will put our messages in our hands to share with others. These hands can then be hung on a community holiday tree to encourage all who aww it to have hope in a better tomorrow.

Opening Circle:
Take a moment to acknowledge everyone's presence and check in with the children. Ask them to think of hopeful words that allow them to relax. They don't have to elaborate, but they can carry those words with them throughout the creation of their hands. You may even ask them to share what words came to them.

Pass out a handout with the quotes for this workshop to inspire them. Give the children time to read and reflect on these quotes of hope. Then have them journal for 10 minutes, reflecting on their own hopeful words and messages that they may like to share with others as inspiration. When this time has ended let them know that they can continue to do more journaling during the project as well.

 
  A Hand of Hope and inspiration created at
People Against Violent Environments (PAVE), IL.
Creation:
The hand shapes can be created by placing your hand in the cardstock and tracing its shape. Cut after you're done. When using watercolors for decoration, you will have two cups of water. One cup is for dipping the clean brush and the other is to clean out the brush between colors. There are magazines available for making collages as well as inspirational quotes. You can also write your own quotes if you choose to. Sharpies make good pens for lettering and you can use glitter paint to sparkle up your "hand of hope." Leave some time to journal on separate pieces of paper. These little pieces can be cut up and glued to the back of your "hands." Remember that these hands are gifts of knowledge you give to other survivors. There is no right or wrong way to create them, just many possibilities.

Closing:
When the children have finished creating and decorating their hands give them the opportunity to share how this experience of creation was for them. Share with them how powerful their Hands of Hope are and how they, with their own hands, are changing the world by bringing greater hope and inspiration to others.

 
 
More inspirational Hands of Hope
created at People Against Violent Environments (PAVE), IL.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives the children the ability to create cut-outs of their own hands and decorate them with color, images, and words that inspire hope. These Hands of Hope can then be hung together on a community holiday tree to evoke a powerful Tree of Empowerment that represents the combined hopes, strengths, and dreams to inspire others to have hope in a better tomorrow.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To think about & quot;mistakes" and what we can learn from them, using Native American traditions.

Materials:
Native American Circles or Wheels handout
Solid colored fabrics, preferably canvas, muslin or suede-like materials
Yarn, ribbons or suede laces
Different colored feathers
Beads
Round hoops or rings (if available - embroidery hoops work well) or heavy cardboard rounds
Hole punchers
Scissors
Pens and/or puffy paints
Extra fine tip permanent markers
Have something on hand to trace a smaller inner circle
Rulers
Example of a finished product
Native American music
Note: (AWBW can provide you with FREE Native American music by Carlos Reynosa if you request it!)

Time Frame:
Total: 1 1/2 - 2 hours

Set-up and Environment:
Lay out a variety of different colored beads, suede, feathers, pens and/or puffy paints, and any other materials that you think the participants would enjoy using for this project. To set the mood for the workshop use Native American music in the background while the participants work on their projects. Try to keep your supplies in an assortment of natural colors.

 
Center Section of Mistake Wheel
 
Introduction:
Today we will be exploring the concept of mistakes and self-acceptance by creating a decorative "mistake wheel." Teaching everything in terms of circles or wheels is a Native American spiritual tradition. The "mistake wheel" is a new perspective on the medicine wheel, which is part of the Sweet Medicine Path, and shares the keys to self-acceptance and acceptance of the universe. The five sections of the disk hold five messages about "mistakes," leading us to reflect on what we can learn from them and how we can accept them.

We are going to create this wheel to learn a different perspective regarding mistakes in life and so that we can have a final product that can be a reminder to us that we can perceive all circumstances fruitfully and as a learning process.

Opening Circle:
Begin the workshop by passing out the handout, Native American Circles or Wheels, before the creation so that the participants can start to think about the 5 messages about mistakes.

Briefly discuss each of the meanings of each of the messages.

Lead the participants through a relaxation. Have them focus on their breathing, taking long deep inhales and equally long exhales, as they relax their whole body and spirit. Let the participants sit in this place of peace and stillness for a few minutes. As they finish the relaxation, let the participants know that just as all Native American wheels are sacred, the work that they will be doing for themselves today is sacred as well.

 
  North Section of Mistake Wheel
Creation:
Have the participants pick out their circle or ring and fabric to be the foundation of the wheel that they will decorate according to the five messages about mistakes. If the participants are using rings and fabric, give them time to wrap the fabric around the ring making certain to secure it by punching holes in the fabric and then fastening the fabric to the ring by stringing pieces of suede laces, ribbon or yarn through the holes and tying them tightly. Have them do this on all sides to secure the fabric around the ring. Once the fabric is secured to the ring, you are ready to begin decorating.

First, trace a circle in the center of your wheel then use a ruler to divide four equal sections. Label each section with one direction - North, East, South and West.

Once the participants have the foundation for their wheels you can introduce the North part of the wheel.

 
  East Section
In the North part of the wheel, the message reads:
"Learning from our own mistakes"

Give the participants 2 minutes each to share in pairs what they have learned from their own mistakes. Or you may generate a larger timed discussion on this with the group as a whole. Do whichever you think may be more appropriate for your group. After they have discussed, let the participants have 10-15 minutes to decorate this part of their wheel with words and images that have to do with this message; they can even write the very message itself in this section.

In the east portion, the message reads:

"Learning from the mistakes of our teachers"

Give the participants time to discuss, in pairs or as a group, what they have learned from the mistakes of their teachers. Then give them 10-15 minutes to decorate this part of their wheel with words and images that have to do with this message.

And, in the South segment, the message reads:

"Being willing to make as many mistakes as it takes"

 
  South Section
Then give the participants time to discuss with each other, in pairs or as a group, what being willing to make as many mistakes as it takes means to them. Then give them 10-15 minutes to decorate this part of their wheel with words and images that have to do with this message.

In the West part, the message reads:
"Learning from the mistakes of others"

Give the participants time to discuss, in pairs or as a group, what they have learned from the mistakes of others. Then, as before, give them 10-15 minutes to decorate this part of their wheel with words and images that have to do with this message.

Finally in the center of this Mistake Wheel, a portion which represents the essence of the teaching, the following is written:

"Learning that there is no such thing as a mistake"

 
  West Section
Give the participants time to discuss with each other this message and what it means to them. Then give them 10-15 minutes to decorate the center of their wheel with any words and images that have to do with this message and that might encourage them to remember this teaching in the future.

Give the participants a few more minutes to finish their wheel by adding any final touches, such as hanging beads and feathers from the bottom

Closing Circle:
Give the participants time to share their art piece with the group or how the experience as a whole was for them. After the participants have shared, you can share with them that: "If we open ourselves to the possibilities that all we encounter and opportunities for joy and learning, then we can make all circumstances useful and fruitful."

Share with the participants before they leave that we each have our own wisdom and medicine to share with the world. What we have experienced and what we have learned from our so called "mistakes" can become this wise medicine that we have to share. This wheel can become a reminder of this for them.
Row.txt_description: Teaching everything in terms of circles or wheels is a Native American spiritual tradition. The "mistake wheel" is a new perspective on the medicine wheel and shares the keys to self-acceptance and acceptance of the universe. The five sections of the disk hold five messages about "mistakes," leading us to reflect on what we can learn from them and how we can accept them.

Row.txt_code:
An example of a Peace Wreath
Objective:
To have the participants contribute to the holiday decorations by creating a personal Peace Wreath made from their own hand shapes. This activity motivates the participants to think about what creates peace in their lives and in the world and in what ways they can use their own hands to create a more peaceful world.

This is a great workshop for community building or as a family activity!

Materials:
Lots of green construction paper
Red construction paper
(one for each participant) or red ribbon
One paper plate for each participant
Pencils
Scissors
Glue
 
  Tracing hands to create the wreath
Glitter glue (optional)
Quotes on kindness

Timeframe:
Under an hour

Set-up/Prep:
This is a very easy activity with no real set up or prep except for laying out the supplies!

Introduction:
Speak with the participants about the many ways we can share something special with others for the holidays. Today we are making decorations for the holidays that we can share with our friends and family as a way to promote peace during the holidays. When you are kind to others it not only changes you, it changes the world. What acts of kindness can each of us do to change the world to create a more peaceful place to live?

"Don't wait for people to be kind, show them how." Unknown

Opening Circle:
Begin the workshop by having the participants share what they think they can do to create more peace in the world. Pass out a handout of quotes on kindness and have this spark conversation of how all of us can bring peace into the world even through small gestures. Things such as showing love, kindness, smiling, forgiveness, reaching out to others, being nice to someone who is having a bad day, etc. always have an impact on others and the world.

As Archbishop Desmond Tutu states, "Do your little bit of good where you are; it's those little bits of good put together that overwhelm the world."

 
Cutting out and glueing hands to wreath
 
 
Putting the wreath together
 
 
Creation:
Have the participants trace one of their hands on a piece of green construction paper. Then have them cut the hand out and trace the cut hand 9 more time on the green paper. Once this is done they can cut-out the rest of the hands.
Next have them glue the hand cut-outs together, using the plate as a base, in a wreath shape. Tell them to glue the wrists so that they are overlapping a little creating the center of the wreath. The fingers then flar out at the edges and look like leaves!
Make a large red bow, either from construction paper or the ribbon, and glue it to the bottom of the wreath.
Speak with the participants again about how their hands can create a more peaceful world and have them write on the wreath some of their ideas of how they can create peace. They can then use the glitter glue to decorate the hands further.

Closing:
Check in with the participants and ask them if they would like to talk about their creation and what might have come up for them during the creative process. After they have shared you can further motivate them to think about what they can do today to create more peace in the world, or have them share who they might want to give their wreath to as a gesture of peace and love during the holidays.
Row.txt_description: To have the participants contribute to the holiday decorations by creating a personal Peace Wreath made from their own hand shapes. This activity motivates the participants to think about what creates peace in their lives and in the world and in what ways they can use their own hands to create a more peaceful world. This is a great workshop for community building or as a family activity!
Row.txt_tips: This is a great workshop for community building or as a family activity!

Row.txt_code:
This workshop was inspired by two of AWBW's
friends and supporters, Karalee Hayes and
Lina Paredes.
 
  Sample Spirit Candle and Materials
Objective:
The Spirit Candles workshop gives participants the opportunity to search for the strength and energy or light that nurtures and guides our spirit as we prepare for new begginings. We will decorate candles by collaging onto them our biggest dreams and deepest hopes.

Materials:
Glass candles (glass should be clear for decorations)
Photostock books
Magazines
Colored tissue paper (non-bleeding)
Scissors
Mod Podge
Brushes
Paper and pen for journaling
Note: The glass candles can be any shape and size you choose. A great place to purchase this kind of candle is at local discount stores such as The .99 Store.

Opening Circle:
Have the participants share their name a happy dream they had growing up.

Introduction:
As we prepare for the beginning of a new life and all it's possibilities, we go through a winding down period, which is meant to release what we no longer need and to collect and gather the energy to face our new experiences. During these quiet times, we dream and imagine what is to come. We will honor these wishes by creating a tangible reminder of the will that allows us to make these dreams a reality.

Candles have different uses all throughout the world, but at their most basic, they are meant to bring forth light. In this case they will also assist us in honoring the fire within us, our inner spirit. With our collages we bring to life the hopeful and strong spirit that gives us the strength to face change. In order to connect to the emerging light in our lives, we will be decorating candles. We hope you will light these candles to celebrate new beginnings.

Note: If there is a policy against using candles within the shelter stay, you may want to encourage the participants to keep it for the future.

 
Painting with Mod Podge
 
Warm Up:
Let's begin by taking a few deep breaths. With every slow breath, allow your body to relax. Try to be patient with yourself as you become centered. Continue to breathe in and out and when you're ready, begin to think about the new stages in your life. How do you feel about them? How are you preparing for them? What hopes emerge with this new beginning? What fears might be blocking your way?

Now let's consider this new year. What visions do you have? What do you imagine for your life? What experiences would you like to have? As you consider and process these questions, you may want to journal.

Timeframe:
Total: 2 hrs per workshop
10 min. Opening circle
10 min. Introduction
10 min. Relaxation
60 min. Mask-making
(or Painting in the second workshop)
30 min. Closing circle

 
  Finished Spirit Candle Samples
Creation:
Step one
If you purchase candles that already have stickers and images you can remove them by soaking with warm soapy water for about one hour.
Step two
Participants can use tissue paper to cover glass and/or to prevent the back of the images from showing through when the candle is lit.
Step three
Gather images and words.
Step four
Paste images and words by using a medium brush to spread the Mod Podge evenly on the glass to ues as glue and then directly over the pictures to protect and provide a clear glossy finish.
Caution: Do not to apply too much Mod Podge as the ink may run.

Let the images dry and your Spirit Candle is ready.

Closing:
Ask the participants to share their creations and how they think they will feel when they light them.
Row.txt_description: The Spirit Candles workshop gives participants the opportunity to search for the strength and energy or light that nurtures and guides our spirit as we prepare for new beginnings. We will decorate candles by collaging onto them our biggest dreams and deepest hopes.

Row.txt_code:
"Sometimes I am sad or happy but
I am always beautiful and strong."
 

Masks are a very powerful technique for self-expression. We were so excited at AWBW when Sandra Mueller shared this new mask-making process with these plastic molds and tissue paper. This project was designed to provide a simple, accessible, inexpensive way to create life-sized masks.

Objective:
To allow participants to speak out about and against Domestic Violence, as well as express personal stories, for the purpose of creating awareness.


Materials:
Part 1:
Plastic mask molds
(set of 10 “Multi-Cultural Face Forms” can be ordered for $6.69 from Dick Blick:


 Example of a Speak Out Mask with the eyes cut out

1-800-447-8192)
Elmer’s glue or white glue
Tin foil
Bowls
Paintbrushes
Non-bleeding colored tissue paper – all
colors, including skin tones
Paper towels
Newspaper

Part 2:
Matte board 1 for each participant
– cut 8 1/2 x11
Tape
Wire
Scissors
Crayons or markers
Construction paper
Hot glue gun
Pipe cleaners and/or wire
Paper clips

Timeframe:
Plan for at least 2 hours. While the glue/water solution and tissue paper dry, work can be done on the framing. (Or, you may want to consider this a 2 day activity).

 
 Example of a finished Speak Out Mask
  
Set-up / Prep:
Pour glue into a bowl and add water slowly, stirring as you go. Consistency should not be too thin. Prepare pieces of tissue paper in various colors by cutting into thick strips. Prepare wet paper towels (or wipes) for hand cleaning during the project. Cover the tables or workstation with newspaper.
