Objective:
This workshop teaches the children to create a charm bracelet or necklace that encourages them to notice their positive qualities and how to link them creating a brighter, more optimistic world for themselves.

Materials:
 Pens
Writing paper
Scissors
Flexi-foam shapes
String
Yarn
Ribbon
Construction paper
Colored cotton balls
 Markers
Hole puncher
Pipe cleaners
Felt
Wire
Faux gems
Buttons
Glue
Stapler











Note to Leader: To make the bracelet or necklace more durable and wearable you may want to use jewelry making materials and beads. Shrinky dinks with words can also be added to create charms.

Age Range:
6-16 years old
 		 
  
Time Frame:
Relaxation:
Introduction:
Warm-up:
Creation:
Closing:
Total Time:

5 minutes
10 minutes
15 minutes
40 minutes
5 minutes
1 hour, 15 minutes








Balloon Relaxation:
We are going to pretend you are blowing up balloons with positive words and as we let them go they will fill the room with all of these positive things like love, happiness or peace. Let's take the first breath together. Ready? I want you to close your eyes, take a deep breath in, think of a positive word and then as you breathe out imagine your breathing your word into a balloon. Now imagine the balloon floating up into the air. Let's take another deep breath in, thinking of something you like about someone in the room and breathe that word into the balloon. Visualize the balloon floating up into the air. Now I want you to take a moment to think of your favorite thing about yourself and put it into a word or words, take a deep breath in and imagine breathing it into your balloon.


Sample bracelet with positive qualities and strengths
 
Another sample bracelet with different materials
Introduction:
Today we are going to do a workshop called "Words are Like Charms."

Charms can be reminders of things that are important to you. We will have a chance to create our own charms using positive words that best describe the positive things about ourselves. Did you know that our words are very powerful and just repeating a positive sentence helps your confidence and self-esteem?

A wonderful thing happens when we take time to notice how special we are, it can help us shape our goals and who we will be in the future.

Warm-up:
Before we start creating we are going to think about our own unique and positive qualities, strengths, and talents.

Begin by asking each child to take a piece of paper and a pen and write a list of words that reflects their positive qualities, strengths, and talents. Remind them that even something as simple as having a nice smile or being a good friend are important qualities that will continue to shape the person they become in the future.

When they are finished, have the children make a list of the goals they want to achieve in the future, such as being a non-violent person, going to college, or becoming an artist or a teacher.

Once the individual lists of strengths and goals are finished, ask each child to share one of their positive qualities, strengths, or talents from the warm-up and one goal for the future. If we tie our positive qualities, strengths and talents together along with our goals, the words become sources of tremendous inspiration, hope, and strength--just like the charms on a charm bracelet or necklace.

 
  Sample charms
Creation:
Now you get to design a bracelet or necklace and add “charms” to it.

Step 1: Use paper, wire, pipe cleaners, beads, ribbon, or string—anything you like--to create your bracelet or necklace.

Step 2: Next step will be to create your charms. You may choose to design a “charm” using foam shapes, paper or buttons and write words on them or the “charms” can simply represent your positive qualities, strengths, or talents or goals.

Step 3: Attach your charms with ribbon or string.

As they create, remind them to focus on the good in them and all they will accomplish.

Closing:
Once the children are finished with their necklace or bracelet, have them think about the words they used to describe themselves and the goals they've thought about. Ask them to notice throughout the week how focusing on 'the positive' feels. Have them think about the “charms” they created which describe their strengths. Remind them that each day they focus on these "charms" and goals, the more these positive thoughts and words will help bring magic into their lives!
Row.txt_description: This workshop teaches the children to create a charm bracelet or necklace that encourages them to notice their positive qualities and how to link them creating a brighter, more optimistic world for themselves.

Row.txt_code:
Monster in Me example
Objective:
To provide participants with the opportunity to reflect on their own personal experiences with domestic violence, explore difficult emotions in a safe and fun way, and give voice to the feelings that may be hidden inside by creating artwork that represents the “monster” within.

Materials:
Craypas
Thick white paper (twice as much as the number of participants)
Watercolor sets
Watercolor brushes
Cups for water - 1 per particpant
Hand mirrors

Note: If using this workshop to help the participants release or process anger, it is important to begin by having a discussion on "What is Anger?" Please click here to see the entire Processing Anger Workshop Series.

   
Monster in Me examples,
in their various forms and environments
   
Time Frame:
Warm Up: 15 minutes
Intro. and Technical Demo: 10 minutes
Creation: 50 minutes
Closing Circle: 15 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour and 30 minutes



Warm Up:
We are going to begin today's workshop with a warm up that will help the each of us relax our bodies, get in touch with our feelings and the way we express ourselves, and prepare and inspire us for when we sit down to create. Let's begin by standing up and forming a circle.

We will start by reaching our right arm up as far as it will extend.

Now reach your left arm up as far as it will extend.

Stretch your face into a big yawn and breathe out a sigh and then let go.

Now squish your face as tight as a prune and then let go.

 
  A Windows leader creating
  
 
 Another Windows leader creating her monster
  
Begin chewing as if there were a huge wad of gum in your mouth – chewing on the right side of the mouth and then moving it to the left side of the mouth.

Reach both arms up and then bring them down in a hanging position by folding from the waist.

Stand back up vertebrae by vertebrae until you are standing up straight.

Now... All together!
Everybody make a sound that expresses silliness...

Make a sound that expresses anger.

Make a sound that expresses fear.

Make a sound that expresses sadness.

Make a sound that expresses relief.

Now let's sit down at our seats, and we will get started.
(For an extended version of this warm up see "variations.")

Intro and Technical Demo :
There is a side of us we don't show to other people unless we feel certain emotions. For example, when we feel sad, sometimes we try to put on a happy face, and it's like we have another person inside that we don't want to show. Today we are creating a drawing that exposes that person inside and the name of the workshop is called the Monster in Me.

We are going to start by looking at the materials we'll be using to create our monsters. I'm going to show you how to use them by starting to create my monster and then I will let you know when you can begin creating your own. Now remember that no two monsters will be the same because we show our emotions and experiences in different ways. Everyone feels angry, sad, happy, afraid... but it can look very different on different people.

(Walk around while doing the demonstration it helps to keep peoples attention.)

The first material is like a crayon and is called an oil pastel. My monster is going to have a face and I'm going to use this oil pastel to create the shape of a face. I'm going to draw a shape... (draw a shape). You can use the whole page to create your monster. You can make the body fill up the whole page, or it's face, or it could be in an environment. There are lots of different ways that your monster can take its shape.

Next I'm going to use these watercolors... First I'm going to get the brush really wet then I'll pick my color. (Demonstrate how the oil pastels holds the color inside the shape.
Add some other shape with an oil pastel and show them how to clean their brush then show them how using the watercolor over the "crayon" resists the color.)

   
A monster taking shape
   
    
   
A close-up of another Monster in Me
   
What do you see on the table that we didn't talk about? Mirrors. Pick up the mirror in front of you and look at yourself. Notice how your face changes when you make different expressions, when you make a frown, squint your eyes, smile, look at your teeth.

Now I want you to look in the mirror and I want you to look deep inside and see if you can see your monster inside. How does your monster feel? What does she look like? Does your Monster look happy, sad, angry, afraid?

You don't have to answer these questions with words, we are going to expose these monsters on paper and let them express themselves. When you're ready put down your mirror and begin to create.



Creation:
As you create remember that this is a safe place for you. You don't have to know who your monster is or what they look like when you begin, they will appear and take their own shape as you create.

Closing Circle:
Give each participant an opportunity to share their monster. You can have the participants share in pairs or as a group (whichever way you feel would be best for your particular group). If the participants share in pairs have them decide who will share first and who will practice listening, sharing one at a time for 3 minutes each. You can let them know when to switch.

You can encourage the participants to share with questions like: “What does your monster feel like? What is it thinking?” Ask the participants to think about what their monster needs, to feel better. Does it need to be loved? Does it need to be understood? Sometimes monsters have important things to say if you listen to what they need in order to feel better.

Thank the participants for sharing and for being brave by exposing their monsters within.

Alternate Closing:
Brainstorm a "Safety Plan" with the participants to help them process their anger. Some helpful tips include:
Talk to a friend you can trust
Count to 10
Take out art supplies and draw a picture of your anger
Journal about your anger
Take deep breaths
Listen to music
Walk away
Dance or exercise
Row.txt_description: Using a simple technique with oil pastels and watercolors, each person will have the opportunity to reflect on their own personal experiences with domestic violence, explore difficult emotions in a safe and fun way, and give voice to the feelings that may be hidden inside by creating artwork that represents the “monster” within.
Row.txt_tips:
If you'd like to include journaling in this workshop, here is a journaling handout that you can distribute to the participants.

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways.  Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Note About Anger Workshops
We recommend that you start anger workshops with a discussion; don't be afraid to talk to the participants about their anger. Anger is nothing to be ashamed of, it is important to look at and talk about it to try to understand it.

Some anger prompts that we like are:
What is Anger? What does it look like and what does it sound like?
What was the trigger to your anger?
What did you think about it?
How did it make you feel?
How did you act?
What effect did it have on you and those around you?

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide participants with an opportunity to create a Vision Board to help them bring to life their vision for a future filled with what they want and need in their life.

Materials:
   
  A beautiful, inspirational guide to your future
 
   
   
  Creating a path to your dreams using
a game board as your foundation.
 
Poster boards or old game boards if available
Magazines - a wide variety, for collage
Colored tissue paper
White Elmer's Glue or Matte Medium
Foam brushes
Glue sticks
Markers, Pens, Color Pencils, Crayons
Paper for writing
Acrylic paint
Pastels
Embellishments: feathers, beads, buttons, alphabet letters, gamepieces
(use hot glue gun or stronger glue for these)
Paper towels
Assorted ribbon & yarn
Scissors
Personal photos (Optional)
CD player and relaxing music

Time Frame:
Introduction and Warm up: 10 minutes
Creation: 40 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Total: One Hour (more if time permits)

Age Range: Teens to Adults

Workshop Preparation:
This workshop can be created on actual game boards if you can find them at thrift shops, garage sales or donations. If they are not available you can have precut poster board available in rectangular or square shapes. Size approximately 18 inches by 18 inches.

Have three or four magazines with a variety of topics within reach of each participant. You can also have the tissue paper and embellishment objects on that table or set them up on a separate counter or table depending on your workspace. The same applies to the paints.

If you will be using game boards it is helpful for each person to select their game board before the breathing relaxation so once they open their eyes they can start right into working on their Vision Boards.

Introduction:
In today's workshop we will be creating Vision Boards to help us envision our dreams and wishes for the future. When you choose to focus on more of what you want in your life you begin to take conscious and meaningful steps towards fulfilling that which you desire. Your Vision Board can become a visual reminder of what you want in your life, something you can continue to be inspired by with each day, something you can look at when you need a reminder of where you want your life path to take you.

 
  Begin to explore using materials that represent
where you see yourself in the future.
Relaxation/ Warm Up:
Ask everyone to close their eyes and get comfortable. Get them to notice how their feet feel connecting with the floor, where their shoulders are in relation to their neck. Have them take a couple of deep breaths in and out saying "Breathing in I feel calm, breathing out I smile." Then slowly repeat just the words “in, out" and “calm, smile.” With their eyes still closed, have them notice that this is a time just for them. It's a quiet, peaceful time for them to be aware of their gut feelings. After a minute or two ask them to open their eyes and begin writing four or five “I am” words or statements of how they wish to see themselves in the future. (You can share with them that stating their wishes in "I am" form, as if they already exist, can help their wishes feel and become real sooner. It helps to bring them to life. You can even share with them "I am" statements of your own, such as "I am strong," "I am curious," "I am courageous," "I am a good friend," etc.)

Opening Circle:
Ask each participant to share their name and one word describing how they are feeling in an “I am” statement. For example, “I am Mary and I am tired.” Then go around a second time and ask them to share a word or two about what they want in their life, such as “I am Mary and I want to be happy.” You can go around the circle as many times as you wish. Notice that the more you circle the more wishes and dreams will surface. The words can then become stepping stones to lead them to the future.


 
Include whatever words & images that inspire you to take hold of your dreams
 
Creation:
Search the materials and magazines to find images of what you want in your life. Think about what your heart's deepest desires may be, where you want to be in the future, how you may want to feel when you're there, who you want to be surrounded by, what you see yourself doing in your future life, how you wish to be in the world. This can be as literal or symbolic as you wish. Try to envision all the details and feelings associated with whatever it is you desire. This collage will be a vision of how you want your future life to be. As you create, don't worry about making it perfect. This is about expressing your hopes, wishes and dreams and allowing you hands, eyes and intuition to guide you.

Cut or rip the images into desired shapes adding colored tissue paper and any of the embellishments available. As you lay the images down let the images speak to you and the possibilities of your future take form. Know that you can create your future any way you wish.

Closing:
By sharing in a closing circle the participants can better see what they want to create in their lives. Have each of the participants share their Vision Boards and how it felt to create them. Remind them that they can look at it every day to keep inspired and focused on their goals. The Vision Board can help them feel as if they are getting ready to live their dream life right now by watching it daily. It can be a powerful way to visualize the future!

    
Create wonders with basic materials
     Another fabulous example of a Vision Board
Row.txt_description: To provide participants with an opportunity to create a Vision Board to help them bring to life their vision for a future filled with what they want and need in their life.
Row.txt_tips:
Note to Leader:
If you prefer you can focus the vision to - what makes you happy or what gives you a peaceful mind.

Row.txt_code:
Example of a A New Year Journal:
"Step By Step: A Fabulous New Year of Growth"
  
Objective:
Engages participants in an opportunity to visualize and create a journal with unique resolutions for each month in the coming year. This allows them to create a path of healing and growth for themselves throughout the new year and encourages them to check in each month on following through with these goals.

Materials:
Colored Construction Paper
Writing Paper
Scissors
Markers/Colored Pencils
Glue Sticks
Yarn/Ribbon
Stickers
Magazines
Glitter Pens
Hole Punchers
Staplers
Pens (to write with)
Foam Cut-Outs
 
  Prep materials to create an inviting atmosphere.
Various Fabrics (optional)
Spiral-Bound Notebooks (optional journaling alternative)

Age Range:
Teen to Adult

Time Frame:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Relaxation: 5 minutes
Creation: 40 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Total: One Hour (more if time permits)

Workshop Preparation:
If possible have all materials spread out and ready for use. Be sure to remind participants that this is a safe space for them to express and create their own vision for this brand new year. You may want to pre-bind the journals prior to the session. This way the only thing the participants have to do is concentrate on decorating the journals.

Introduction:
Today we will be talking about what nurturing goals and resolutions you would like to create for yourself as you embark on your personal journey through this new year. This is an opportunity for you to explore what goals you would like to create for yourself, map out a timeline, and have a visual reminder to check in with yourself each month about how far you have come and where you would like to go next. You will then create and decorate your very own journal for this new year in your life! You will be able to decorate it whatever way you want, and you will also be able to make commitments and decisions about nurturing resolutions you would like to keep in the future.

Relaxation:
To get started let's begin with a relaxation. If you are comfortable close your eyes, and if you don't want to, that is fine too. Now begin by focusing on your breath: take a deep breath in and then slowly out. Let go of any tension and stress you are holding with each out breath. Now continue to focus on your breath, breathing in and out slowly, and begin to think about what a brand to new year means to you.

 
An example of a resolution to nurture yourself:
"This month I resolve to take control of my BODY & MIND"
 
Start to envision what you want this year to look like. What things you would like to do for yourself? How would you like to take care of yourself this year? Think of nurturing things that give you happiness and joy. You could take a bubble bath, a long walk, read a book just for fun, treat yourself to some of your favorite food. What would nurture your heart and soul?

Now think about some places you imagine yourself going? Maybe this place is a special place only you know about. Maybe it is outdoors, or maybe it is in different weather. Maybe it is far away, or maybe it is right around the corner. What makes you want to go there? What does this place look like, smell like, feel like?

 
  Fill your New Year Journal with all of your dreams:
"This month I resolve to get in touch with the NATURE around us"
Who are the people you would like to see alongside you? Maybe they are a good friend whom you trust. Maybe they are someone you care for. Maybe they are a family member or maybe a favorite pet. Take a few more deep breaths and think about all of the many things you want to do, places you want to go, and people you want to be with in this year ahead.

What are the self-nurturing things you want to do for yourself and the goals you want to achieve over the next 12 months? Remember that you can be patient and loving with yourself if they do not happen right away. Maybe you will ask others for help. You can also keep your journal nearby as a continuous gentile reminder and inspiration to guide you through the year.

How do you think you might keep all of these promises to nurture yourself, what will inspire you to do so?

Creation:
When you are ready open your eyes. You can begin to journal about your ideas for the new year. Different months may have different significance, such as celebrating your birthday when that time comes, Valentine's Day in February, Mother's Day in May, the beginning of Summer in June, Halloween in October--whatever inspires you!

 
 Creating the binding for A New Year Journal.
Step 1:
Stack one sheet of 8 1/2" x 11" colored construction paper (or card stock) and seven 8 1/2" x 11" sheets of copy paper (colored or white) in a single pile.

Step 2:
Fold in half, then staple along the crease.

Step 3:
On opposite side, punch a single hole (center).


 
Another example of how you might design monthly goals:
"This month I resolve to treat myself to FUN ADVENTURES"
 
Step 4:
Now open up your journal, and begin by writing down the month and then any nurturing activities, goals, or hopes that you envision for yourself in that month. Include any images that might correspond with what you've journaled, you can draw, paint, or cut out images from magazines/books. These are all creative ways that serve as reminders of how you might nourish yourself over the next year.

Step 5:
Now decorate the cover. It is entirely up to you to fill the pages in your journal with whatever your heart desires for the year. You can use this part of your New Year Journal as a visual reminder towards creating a path for yourself to set foot in a nurturing direction.

 
 Putting the finishing touches on A New Year Journal

Step 6:
Finally, lace a ribbon or piece of string through the punched hole. Tie a bow to put the finishing touch on your New Year Journal. Now you can open and close it as you desire.

Closing:
Remind yourself that this journal functions as a continuously evolving art project. It is your choice when you feel comfortable enough to create in it.

Take a few minutes to absorb what you've just put in your New Year Journal. When you're ready, take a deep breath in. Then go ahead and let it out slowly, surely. Whatever your goals are, let this be a manifestation of just that.

Be sure to check in with yourself each month and truly take this year to nurture yourself!
Row.txt_description: Engages participants in an opportunity to visualize and create a journal with unique resolutions for each month in the coming year. This allows them to create a path of healing and growth for themselves throughout the new year and encourages them to check in each month on following through with these goals.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To use new techniques of working with Polymer Clay (Sculpey) and to learn to identify and express our range of feelings to begin a healing process. The faces created can help to connect to our feelings and expressions of thos e feelings.


 
Sample set-up using optional tools to create.
 
 
Sample Expression Face.
 
Materials:
Sculpey (Polymer Clay) in assorted colors
Wooden skewers or tooth picks
Clay tools or plastic knives
Drinking straws
Scissors
Finger paint paper or clean surface to work on
Toaster ovens
Timer for timing the baking of the faces
Telephone wire (Optional)
Acrylic rollers/brayers (Optional)
Magnets or pin backs (Optional)

Age Range:
7 years old to Adult

Time Frame:
1 hour and 30 minutes

Workshop Preparation:
Set the table with all the supplies and preheat toaster ovens to 265 degrees using a calibrator or oven thermometer.

Introduction:
Today we are going to be changing the look of our faces by using clay. Expressions can change depending on our mood and feelings. Expressions can change from frowns to smiles, from anger to joy, from bored to excited. Sometimes our feelings can change while we are being creative working with the clay, as we may release difficult thoughts and feelings.

Warm Up:
Pick up a piece of the clay to begin to condition it for easier use, by warming it up in our hands. Start by rolling the clay into a ball, then into a long thin snake. Fold the snake in half and reshape it into a ball, then again into a snake. Keep rolling, twisting and kneading until the clay is soft and pliable, but still has stretch to it when pulled.

Now, close your eyes, if you feel comfortable, and try to imagine a face inside the clay that is waiting to come out. Think about what the face looks like and how the face can show what you are feeling. Sometimes we can feel more than one way at a time!

Open your eyes when you are ready and select colors that you like - remember that the face we will create is a product of our imaginations. We can create a face for each of the feelings we are experiencing or put all of our feelings into one face.

   
 Blending clay technique to create swirls or
marbling effect.		 
   
   
  Twirling wire around a pen to create curling effect. 
   
   
  Poking wire into face to add hair. 
   
Creation:
You will be using various techniques to create different effects with the clay. Before we begin creating our faces let's discuss some of these techniques. The first of these techniques is swirling the clay. For example, take a pea size of red and white. Stretch out each color into a 2 inch snake shape. Then warp the colors around each other so they swirl together (like a barber pole or candy cane). The more you twirl, the finer the design. If you keep twisting and rolling eventually the colors will blend to form a new color -- pink! Or you can use the clay stripped.

The next technique is layering the clay. Notice how the clay has the ability to stick to itself. Take one piece of clay, set it on top of another one and push in using a tool or your fingers. The layers will melt together in the baking process.

Step 1:
To form a simple face, roll a 2 inch round ball of clay and flatten to about 1/4 inch then reshape into an oval or any other shape that expresses the feeling(s) you want to express.

Step 2:
Next we will add the features. The eyes can be little balls of clay placed in the face and flattened with the round end of a paint brush or your fingers. Eyebrows, noses, mouths etc, can be added in the same way. Talk about different expressions and what they look like on our faces. For example, lips can curl up for a smile or down for a frown.

Step 3:
Decorations such as beads, sequins and colored wires for crazy wild hair can be added by pushing it in so that the clay comes up around it. You may even need to add more clay and sort of sandwich the wire decoration to make sure they are secured onto the piece. Another way to attach wire etc. to the mask is to poke holes using straws and add after the baking process is done.


Step 4:
Place the faces on a tray for baking at 265 degrees for 17 minutes.

Step 5 (optional):
Add pin backs or magnets to the back of the faces.

Closing:
Ask each participant to share their work and talk about what feelings show on their Expression Faces.
Row.txt_description: To use new techniques of working with Polymer Clay (sculpey) and to learn to identify and express our range of feelings to begin a healing process. The faces created can help to connect to our feelings and expressions of those feelings.
Row.txt_tips:
Each oven will vary - you may want to do a test sample of the sculpey and time it in the oven you will be using or use an oven thermometer. The thinner pieces will cook faster and might burn.

The clay may feel slightly undercooked when it comes out of the oven but if you wait 10 minutes it will harden more. It is possible to rebake the sculpey if necessary.
   
   
   Expression Faces

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop supports participants through a process that builds self-compassion through the creation of a shrinky-dink suncatcher.

Sample of a finished suncatcher
 
Materials:
  • Clear shrinky dinks (at least 5 per participant)
  • Heart template (download)
  • Permanent markers
  • Color pencils
  • Pencil sharpeners
  • Plain white paper plates
  • Hole punchers
  • Scissors
  • Ribbon or yarn
  • Beads
  • Toaster oven
  • Brown paper bag (for easy removal of shrinky dinks from toaster oven). See Instructions for Baking Shrinky Dinks in the Creation section below.
Age Range:
5 years and up

Time Frame:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Relaxation: 5 minutes
Creation: 1 hour and 15 minutes
Closing Circle: 5 minutes

Total Time: 1 hour and 30 minutes

Tip: If you’re short on time in your workshops, you can shorten this workshop by having participants create fewer shrinky dinks or you can break up the workshop into multiple sessions. You could also have the entire group make a single suncatcher together.

  
  Setting the table
  
Workshop Preparation:
 Set up table with all the materials. Have enough shrinky dinks for each participant to create five or more.

Younger children may have difficulty cutting or hole-punching their own shrinky dinks, so depending on the age levels in your group, you may need to pre-hole-punch the shrinky dinks. You could also pre-cut some shrinky dink hearts or eliminate the template/cutting all together, inviting participants to create any shapes that speak to their own heart.

Ideally, the center of the plates should also be pre-cut and divided in three for the base of the suncatcher. You may also need to help the younger participants to punch the holes around the inside edge of the plate and add a hole on both sides at the top for a way to hang the finished suncatcher.

Optional: Watch this short example video of the warm-up exercise before you lead the workshop to get an idea of how it can look.

Introduction:                                                                                                          "Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you. This means that this is a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you do or say is voluntary. I'll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there's no right or wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. Please ask for what you need, and know that I'm here in support of you. If you can't think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just play with the materials.

"Today we are going to take this time to remember the things that make us special, and send loving messages to our hearts. We are going to make suncatchers made of shrinky dinks with nurturing words and symbols that can catch the sunlight when we hang them in a window. These loving messages can become like the sunlight shining, warming our lives and bringing light into each day, especially when we need it most."                                

Materials Demonstration:
"Before we start with a warm-up, I want to show you the supplies so that you can begin creating right after the warm-up."
 
  Loving words and images for your heart
  
  Cutting the plate into thirds
  
  Punching holes for the suncatcher
  
  Tying the ribbons for the suncatcher

Step 1: 
 "Create your shrinky dinks! If you want to use a template, start by tracing it onto the shrinky dink (or use the pre-cut shrinky dinks, if they are available)."

Optional Material Explanation:
If your participants have never created shrinky dinks before or need a reminder, demonstrate how to use colored pencils on the rough side or markers on either side of the shrinky dink. It can also be helpful to have a pre-shrunk sample so that participants can see how small the material will get. In addition, let them know to do any cutting or hole-punching before putting their shrinky dinks in the oven.

Step 2:
"When you are finished coloring, you can cut out your shapes with scissors (if the shrinky dinks were not pre-cut the way you want them)."

Step 3:
"Use the hole punch to place a hole at the top of each shrinky dink so that you can hang it to create your suncatcher."
Step 4:
"Then we’ll bake your shrinky dinks!"
Step 5:
"Use the hole puncher to punch holes around the inside edge of the cut-out paper plate (punch as many holes as shrinky dinks you want to hang). Add a hole on both sides at the top for a way to hang the finished suncatcher. Hang your shrinky dinks from the suncatcher with ribbon or yarn, and add beads if desired. Add another ribbon to the top two holes to create a way to hang your suncatcher. I’m here to help at any point if you need or want it."

Warm-Up:
 "Since we’re going to be making suncatchers with messages to our hearts today, we’re going to start with a warm-up that involves feeling the sun and listening to our hearts. In this warm-up, I’ll make suggestions for you to try simple movements to go with your imaginations, but each person is different so please do whatever feels best for you. If what feels good to you is just to sit and listen, that is absolutely fine."

As you share the following warm-up, remember to speak slowly and take significant pauses so that participants can feel into the experience. (You can view an example video of this warm-up here.)

  
Wiggling toes against the ground
in a safe place
 
  
  
 Welcoming the sunbeam
 

"You can close your eyes or keep them open, whatever will best help you to connect to yourself. Start by imagining yourself in a safe place outdoors. Wiggle your toes against the ground and imagine what it feels like in your safe place. Is it sand under your feet? Dirt? Sidewalk? Something else?

"Slowly, you begin to feel the sun warming the top of your head. Take a deep breath in and imagine the sunbeam coming in with your breath through the top of your head and flowing out through your heart as you breathe out. In through the top of your head, and out through your heart.

"As you keep breathing, you notice that the sun feels so nice on the top of your head that you begin to tilt your head up to face the sun. Welcome the sunbeam onto your face, and as you breathe, let it flow in through your cheeks and out through your heart. In through your cheeks and out through your heart.

"As you keep breathing, you notice that the sun feels so nice on your cheeks that you begin to stand up so you can feel the sun on your chest. As you breathe in, raise your arms to welcome the sun. This time, breathe in through the tips of your fingers and out through your heart. In through the tips of your fingers and out through your heart.

"Keep breathing and feeling the sun. When you’re ready, reach up to the sunbeams and pull them down to your heart. With your hands on your heart, remind yourself that this is a special time just for you. 

  
 Listening to the heart,
surrounded by
loving messages
 

"Think about what your heart would tell you if it could speak. Can you hear any special message your heart has?

"Think about the many things that make you special, the things that you love about who you are. It could be something simple or something deep. Have compassion for yourself if you can't think of something right away, it will come. Think about the loving and nurturing things you could tell your heart. What would it like to hear? Imagine your heart surrounded by loving messages. Those messages could be words or symbols or colors or any combination. Think about all of the loving messages you can tell yourself and imagine them shining within you.”


Creation:
"Whenever you’re ready, you can bring your attention back to this room and begin to create shrinky dinks for your suncatcher. Let me know how I can support you."

Give participants time to create their suncatchers, and help out as needed.

 
  
  
  
  
  

Instructions for Baking Shrinky Dinks:
A toaster oven is ideal for baking shrinky dinks. However, a regular oven will "shrink" the art just as well. Do not microwave the shrinky dinks!

Step 1: Cut a rectangular shape out of a brown paper grocery bag and turn one corner up. (The turned up corner will make the bag and shrinky dink easy to remove from the tray after baking.)

Step 2: Place the shrinky dinks, colored sides up, on the brown paper and place paper on a tray or cookie sheet. Be sure to punch any holes before baking. 

Step 3: Bake the shrinky dinks at 300" until the art has completely flattened (about 1-3 minutes). After the pieces lie flat, allow an additional 30 seconds of baking time to complete the process. Note: participants generally really enjoy watching their art shrink.

Step 4: Remove paper from tray and let the shrinky dinks cool.

  
Closing:
Give each participant an opportunity to share their loving heart suncatcher and/or to talk about the process of making it. Remind participants that it's always okay to pass.

Appreciate the group for taking this window of time to let the sun shine into their hearts.
Row.txt_description: This workshop supports participants through a process that builds self-compassion through the creation of a shrinky-dink suncatcher.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Hanging the Suncatchers
After the closing, think about taking some time for a ceremony where everyone chooses a spot to hang their suncatcher. During the ceremony, everyone can walk around to see all of the special spots that were chosen.

Indoors, suncatchers look especially nice hung in windows, where they can catch the sunlight coming in and remind participants of the loving messages in their hearts.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To create your very own clock that will show how we want to fill our days so we can have the life we want.

   
  Mixed up numbers on the clock
 
   
   
  A clock with no numbers at all 
Materials:
White or light color construction paper
Colored pencils
Pencil sharpeners
Markers

Time Frame:
This workshop takes approximately 1 hour

Age Range:
Age 6 through teen

Opening Circle:
Have everyone think about and discuss all the important things they spend their time doing everyday - sleeping, going to school, chores, homework etc. Then share some fun things they would like to do with their time, that they might not get to do often - like go to the beach, play games, watch TV, eat ice cream, go to the movies etc.

Introduction:
There are all kinds of clocks - ask if anyone can name some? - What about a grandfather clock, a cuckoo clock, a wrist watch, or a clock radio? Can anyone name any other kind of clock?

Today we are going to make our own special clock that will have just the things we want to spend our time doing. Things that will give us the right mix of fun and things that will help us build our future.

We will be drawing a clock, and on the face of the clock we will be able to draw whatever we want that will represent how we want to live our lives, it could be numbers or words, small pictures, symbols or designs.

Relaxation:
(Speaking slowly with a calm voice)

Before we start we are going to close our eyes and try to imagine a very special clock. What makes it special is that it can look any way you want it to look. So just take a deep breath and then gently let all the air out. If you are sitting, it’s good to sit with your back straight, your feet flat on the floor, and your hands lying loosely in your lap. And if it feels safe for you, you can gently close your eyes. As you concentrate on your breathing, realize this is a time for you.

   
  Floating numbers
 
   
   
   
  Filling the day with things that matter 
   
   
   
  Making time for all the important things 
   
Breathing in, you start to feel your body become more and more relaxed. Start to imagine a clock. Notice the shape of your clock. Is it a tall clock like a grandfather clock? Maybe your clock is just a large round wall clock. Or maybe it looks like a wrist watch. Try to imagine the details of your clock.

Breathing in and out you notice your body becoming more deeply relaxed and the shape of your clock is becoming more and more clear.

Now picture the face of the clock and picture all the numbers slowly flying away and notice that now this is your own clock and your own time. Begin to picture exactly what you want in your life on the face of your clock. Maybe there are words or certain colors or shapes that you picture.

Gently open your eyes and begin to draw the clock you just pictured in your mind, or start the process and see where your creativity wants to go.

Creation:
You can use the markers or colored pencils in front of you to draw your very own clock with things you want in your day that will help you create a life that feels good in your body, mind and heart. The most important this to remember as you make your clock is that you get to choose how you spend your time, and, what your clock looks like is also totally up to you!

Remember some important things about planning your time. If you spend the whole day eating sweets, it may seem like fun but you likely feel sick after or may have a hard time focusing. And if you spend the day only watching cartoons on TV you won't get to learn things or get your body strong. It is important to plan things on your clock that will be fun and also the things that help you have the life you want when grow up. Can you think of what those things might be? - what about music, sports, school, art, dancing, learning, playing, exercise, helping others, chores or fun time with friends and family. All these things will help us to have our days be filled with a good mixture and something that we call balance. This balance will help us to have the life we want.

Closing Circle:
Ask participants to share about their clocks and welcome them to share how it felt to make up how they spend time!
Row.txt_description: To create your very own clock that will show how we want to fill our days so we can have the life we want.

Row.str_title: Helping Hands, Healing Hands - Community Mandala Project
Row.txt_code:
About This Workshop:
Helping Hands, Healing Hands is a community art project created by Lori Rothfus, a healing artist and AWBW Leader in New York.

It began as Lori thought about finding a way to allow the community to participate in the creation of a simple work of art. The key to this project is a focus on “community.” Lori wanted a range of people from the community to make art that reflected what a healthy, safe and inspiring community “looks like.” She used the line “give a hand to our community” to illustrate each individuals vision of a healthy community and/or ways that they could contribute. It is significant for the participants in group to feel like they can move beyond the defined “group” and become part of something bigger for the community.


Helping Hands Healing Hands Community Mandala Project from the Salvation Army, Jamestown NY


Objective:
To give participants an opportunity to think about what a “healthy and safe” community, home, or group looks like by making a hand collage to explore this question. These collage hands will become part of a larger hands mandala to inspire the greater community that together our hands can help and heal.

Materials:
Large Masonite board or canvas board or poster board (depending on how sturdy or permanent you want the project. Large enough to accommodate the number of hands you wish to include - Original project was 4 ft x 4ft)
Colored card stock
Scissors
Glue sticks
Elmers glue
Q-tips and/or small cheap brushes or toothpicks to apply glue (optional)
Magazines (We recommend local magazines that have inspirational images or words)
Markers
Pens
Pencils
Glitter and assorted embellishments (optional)
Mod Podge and brush applicator (this is used once the final large project is put together to glue down the pieces and then to paint over the hands as a sealer which protects it and also offers a shine to the project)
Optional: Copies of pages from a mandala coloring book to illustrate the concept of a mandala or use as centerpiece.

 
Sample collaged hand
 
Time Frame:
Introduction: 15 minutes
Meditation: 10 minutes
Creation: 1 - 1 ½ hours
Closing circle: 30 minutes
Total time: 2 – 2 ½ hours

Note: The project may be longer lasting with several groups or individuals making hands over time until you have the amount you wish to have to make the mandala.

Introduction and Opening circle:
Today we will be working on a project called “Helping Hands, Healing Hands - Community Mandala Project.” This is a collage project where we will be finding images and words in magazines to create our own unique hand print that will illustrate what we envision as a healthy, safe and inspiring community to live in. The possibilities are endless of the ways that you can create your hand and what you might express.

Once we have made our hands they will be placed in this basket with other hands that have been created and will be created. Once we have enough hands, we will be arranging them together on this board into a Community Mandala.

A mandala is an ancient art form that has been used as a meditative and healing tool. Mandalas, such as the Tibetan Sand Mandalas, are well rooted in symbolic language, spiritual meaning and cultural story telling. These mandalas are often geometric and predetermined. Today mandalas are being made in many forms including organic and intuitive images that are contained within a circle but reflect the basic nature of the mandala – that the circle is a container or symbol of the world, inclusive and representing the Whole....or wholeness that we can attain.


 
Another powerful collaged hand 
I would like us to begin by picking out a piece of colored card stock and tracing your hand print and then cutting it out. This way, we can hold our hand that we will be creating while we do the relaxation and then begin to create.

When we do our relaxation I am going to ask you to think about specific things that you believe are necessary in order for a community to be considered safe, healthy and inspiring - things like love and respect, or safe playgrounds. Your helping hand might focus on just one aspect that would uplift a community or it might contain many ideas and a larger vision of what a healthy community looks like to you. You may also make your hand about the ways in which YOU personally contribute to the community. Perhaps you don't litter, or you volunteer, or perhaps just by finding ways to stop violence in your own life you are helping to create a safe and healthy world.

Relaxation:
Get comfortable in your seat. Take your healing/helping hand in your hands.....do this lovingly and gently. Do it tenderly and compassionately ....hold your hand realizing it is a unique expression of who you are and how you contribute to the world in your own special way.

If you are comfortable, close your eyes. Allow yourself to feel supported in your chair and in this room. Know you have chosen to come here and given yourself a window of creative and social time for your own well being. Let us all allow our minds, bodies and spirits some time to heal, relax and be inspired.

Allow yourself to notice your breathing...the gentle flow in and out of the air we breathe. Allow your shoulders to drop down from your ears and feel your body grow heavier; your back supported by the chair...your feet on the floor grounded to the earth. Inhale peace....and exhale any tensions or worries........for now you can let them go. Feel your body relax more deeply with each breath you take.......

Now I want you to bring your attention to your healing hand.....think about the many hands involved in building a community. Hands can be the source of great creations. Using your imagination and bring to mind your vision of a safe and healthy community. What is happening? What does it look like? Who is there? What is there? What are the things that seem most important to you and your family? What have you appreciated most about being part of a community? Just become aware of the ideas as they come to you. Don't try to force it... What are the qualities and conditions that make something healthy and safe? What unique ways can each person lend a hand? What is your gift or interest or talent that makes your contribution unique? Trust whatever comes to you....don't question it but allow the voice of your inner wisdom to guide you.

Creation:
Allowing yourself to remain relaxed and clear about your ideas, I want you to gently open your eyes....and on the back of your hand, I would like you to write down a few things that you saw in your relaxation. You may just jot down a few words, or write a poem or prayer or a paragraph about what a healthy community is to you. Once you have that done, turn your hand over and begin to cut out images and words for your collage and begin to create.

Play relaxing music while they create.

If someone does not want to make a hand, they can color in a mandala. Mandala images can be found as coloring books or online. When the final project is put together you may want to use one of the colored mandalas as the center piece. Remind participants who may be struggling looking for a specific image, that they can find a symbol of it or use words. They can also choose to just draw or color their hand.

As the participants finish their hands have each woman cut out inspiring words that you can surround the final mandala with, so that it forms a large circle. You may also want to add words around the outside marking the four corner directions or paint words, such as "Helping hands, lend a hand, healing hand....," to form the outside circle of the mandala.

 
  Sharing finished hands
  
 
  Final Community Hands Mandala!
Closing Circle:
Give each participant an opportunity to talk about the hand they created. You may have her pass her hand around the circle for everyone to see before they begin to share their story. Once everyone has shared you may wish to have them put all their hands in the center together to look at them collectively...noticing how all the hands together add to a larger vision.

The leader can arrange the final art work, or allow the group to partake in a cooperative exercise to make the final piece. You may also have the group arrange their hands in a creative way on a poster board and photograph the final project so each woman gets a copy. Give any final direction as to when the final mandala will be constructed and when and where it will be displayed.

Thank them for participating and sharing their visions!

Final note on including the larger community:
You may chose to find ways to include other community groups on the project. Include children or family members. Someone can always make a hand at home and drop it off. You may get other social service organizations to participate. This could be used as a project during an art exhibit or during Domestic Violence Awareness Month etc. This project can be adapted to be as large or as small as you like. You can display your mandala publicly for all to see at a library, city hall, local window display that is available or even at a mall. Participants can be kept anonymous.
Row.txt_description: To give participants an opportunity to think about what a “healthy and safe” community, home, or group looks like by making a hand collage to explore this question. These collage hands will become part of a larger hands mandala to inspire the greater community that together our hands can help and heal.

Row.txt_code:
My Coat of Arms
 
   
   
   
   
   
   
  Drawing the Coat of Arms
 
Objective:
To provide each participant with an opportunity to create a Coat of Arms with special symbols that represent who they are. This allows the children to explore how they are unique and special and how that makes them strong.

Materials:
Coat of Arms templates for each participant
Markers/Cray Pas
Pencils/erasers
Colored pencils/pencil sharpeners
Crayons

Optional: Family pictures, glitter glue, beads, feathers yarn scissors and glue

Introduction:
Today, you will be creating a Coat of Arms to represent you. Coat of Arms were used many years ago. They were made to show what people stand for, what is important to them, where they were from, and who they were. These Coat of Arms were passed down through generations of families. Some people still have their family’s Coat of Arms today. Native American tribes also use symbols to represent their different tribes and families. Today you are going to make your own Coat of Arms to tell others about you and why you are strong.

Opening Circle:
Before you begin to create lets begin to think of what makes you special and what makes you strong. Maybe you are kind and loving or maybe you like to study and learn. Maybe you are a good friend or are loving to your family. After you have thought of the things about you that are special we will list some symbols that you would use to represent those things. Maybe the symbols are shapes or colors or designs. So if you are kind and loving you might draw a heart to represent you - or if you if you like to study and learning you might draw a school or some books. You could select animals or flowers. Think about your favorite colors, shapes, animals. Think about how would you describe yourself and those you want to include in your Coat of Arms.

   
  Part 1 What represents my family?
 
   
  Part 2 My favorite thing to do
 
   
  Part 3 People in my family
 
   
  Part 4 What makes me feel safe?
 
Creation:
You can use the Coat of Arms templates provided as a basis for your creation, or create one from their imagination.

Begin by dividing the Coat of Arms into 4 sections. Then use markers, crayons, or colored pencils to draw the following:

In the upper left box: Pick and draw an thing animal, shape, or color to represent your family (examples: flags, fish, lions or a combination of a few).

In the upper right box: Draw a symbol of your favorite thing to do. An activity that makes you happy or that makes you feel special. (examples: swimming, dancing, favorite family outing, a holiday or going to the beach)

In the lower left box: Draw people who you consider your family (example: this could include siblings, grandparents, cousins, etc.). If you have a photo of your family, you can include that here.

In the lower right box: Draw what makes you feel safe. Draw people, places, or things that help you stay safe and feel strong. (examples: a hug from your mom or dad, going to school or your favorite stuffed animal)

Once the Coat of Arms is finished cut it out and add any additional decorations with glitter glue, beads, feathers, buttons, stickers and yarn to make it just as unique and special as you.

Closing Circle:
Have each person share their new Coat of Arms with the group. Point out the uniqueness. These Coat of Arms are a powerful symbol of how strong, unique and special each person is.
Row.txt_description: To provide each participant with an opportunity to create a Coat of Arms with special symbols that represent who they are. This allows the children to explore how they are unique and special and how that makes them strong.

Row.txt_code:
A sample Stained Glas s Window, by anonymous artist
"Being abused leaves you feeling like you're
broken into pieces. Just like broken glass."
Objective:
To give participants an opportunity to look at their strengths and identify ways they have coped in the past when faced with loss and trauma. By creating a Stained Glass Window, one can piece together parts of their lives that feel shattered and begin to create something beautiful, letting the light shine through.

Materials:
White paper (poster size or 8 1/2 X 11)
Colored markers
Paint
Pastels
Brushes
Scissors
Construction paper (for the borders)

Timeframe:
Intro: 15 minutes
Relaxation: 10 minutes
Poem Making: 20 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes - 1 hour
Closing Cirlce: 15 minutes
Total Time: 1 1/2 - 2 hours (depending on how big you create the stained glass windows)

  
Creating beauty out of the broken pieces
  
Introduction:
Today we will be creating Stained Glass Windows, while looking at our lives, our strengths, and what has helped us take steps forward in our lives during challenging times. Take a moment to think about loss, the different losses you have experienced in the past or are currently experiencing. What does it feel like? When you experience Domestic Violence it can often leave you feeling shattered, like you have been broken into pieces, just like broken glass. It's encouraging to know that you can take those pieces and put them back together in a new way, a way that makes you feel empowered, strong, and beautiful. Think about a glass bottle when it falls and shatters into pieces; now imagine a skilled artist taking those shattered pieces of glass and creating something beautiful. That is what we will be doing today, taking the pieces of our lives and putting them back together in a way that brings beauty into our lives.


  
Taking the pieces of your life and letting the
light shine through
  
Have you ever seen a stained glass window? (Have some pictures of stained glass to share with them).

The art of stained glass dates back to the Middle Ages. “Stained glass” refers to the material of colored glass or to the art and craft of working with it. Stained glass is formed when metallic salt is added to glass during its manufacture. Small pieces of colored glass are arranged to form patterns and pictures which are held together by strips of lead and supported by a frame. In the tradition of this thousand year old art form, today I’d like us to create our own “stained glass windows” with construction paper and magic markers or paints.

Relaxation:
We will begin by doing a relaxation to help us let go of any tension we may be holding in our body. Sit comfortably, and if you feel comfortable doing so, close your eyes. If you want to keep your eyes open that is fine too. Now bring your attention to your belly and feel it rise and expand as you take a deep breath in. Then feel it relax as you breath out. Continue to take deep breaths in, and as you breathe them out imagine that you are letting go of all of the tension in your body. Feel your whole body relax and feel nurtured by focusing on your breath. Every time you notice your mind has wandered off your breath, notice what it was that took you away and gently bring your attention back to your breath. Think of each breath as healing, as a way for you to care for yourself and bring peace into your body and into your mind, as a way for you to heal your spirit.

 
  A group poem created by Arctic Women In Crisis'
Women's Empowerment Group
Poem Making:
When a Women’s Empowerment Group at Arctic Women In Crisis did this project, they began by creating a group poem about loss and healing. The group chose to create a poem with the title “Broken Glass.” The first member’s line was “Broken bones shatter,” and so it began, with each person then taking turns to add to the poem:

“Broken bones shatter.
Emotional scars are yet to heal.
Tears pour down my face.
How will I be tomorrow?
Do I need to hide my face?
My life has been shattered like broken glass.
I need peace.
I take the shards of glass and create
a stained glass window.
Light shines through, and I begin to heal.”

Lets take a moment to think about the loss, healing and strength in our own lives. If shattered glass represents loss, consider the impact of loss on you and your family. What are some ways you have dealt with loss? What are some options for dealing with your grief? How can you take the pieces of shattered glass in your life and create beautiful stained glass windows so that the light can shine through? See what words come to you, and together, or individually, we can begin to weave a healing poem of our own with heart-felt words.

(Check in with the group to see if they would prefer to do this together as a collaborative group poem, or individually. If they decide to create a group poem it can be written on a large piece of poster board and decorated with a border of stained glass, to be hung somewhere within the shelter. You could also have the poem writing be optional, and instead share reflection questions about loss and the impact of loss with the participants. You can have them reflect on the idea of a bottle breaking into pieces—what can one do with broken glass?)

 
 
Letting the light shine through as one takes a stand
against violence. This Stained Glass Window includes
the words "Violence is a Crime".
Creation:
Now we will be creating our own beautiful “windows,” using colored markers, paint and construction paper in place of glass. The windows you are creating will be made up of all of these shattered pieces of glass, pieces of your life that you are putting together in a new way.

You can begin by choosing either markers or paint to create your window. First decide on the shape of your window, and then draw or paint an outline for it on the white paper provided. Next, begin to draw or paint various shapes and colors to resemble the glass that makes up your window. You can even include a symbol in your window if you wish (such as one that represents strength, beauty, or transformation). You can create your window in any way you like, with whatever colors you like, in any shape you like. This window can become a metaphor for your life and how you would like to recreate it.

As you create your window, think of the following: The windows you are creating with the shattered glass represent where you would like to be in terms of dealing with loss and grief. What can you do to get to that place? How can you reconstruct something beautiful out the of chaos of broken glass? From reflecting on your strength and all of the possibilities before you, you can take the pieces of your life and put them back together in a way that brings beauty into your life.

One woman stated, "Things were dark, and I lived in the shadows. When I was able to leave him, light began to shine on me and show me all my beautiful colors." Let her words inspire you!

Play soothing music. Have the participants chose either markers or paint and begin to create their windows. When they are done, they can use the construction paper to create a border around their window to give it a framed look.

Closing Circle:
Encourage the participants to go around in a circle and describe their windows. What feelings do they hold? What have they learned about themselves from doing this activity? How can they apply what they’ve learned to their journey?

These windows can represent the "light" peace and non-violence bring into their lives. You can even exhibit the windows and let the light shine through to inspire others!
Row.txt_description: To give participants an opportunity to look at their strengths and identify ways they have coped in the past when faced with loss and trauma. By creating a Stained Glass Window, one can piece together parts of their lives that feel shattered and begin to create something beautiful, letting the light shine through.
Row.txt_tips: Leader Mary Claire Yanga of Pacific Clinics has participants use colored tissue paper for their stained glass.

Row.txt_code:
A butterfly's transformation represents the possibility of our ow n!
Objective:
To give participants a creative way to view how each of us can work through the challenges in our lives to transform ourselves, just as a caterpillar works to transform itself into a butterfly. By looking at our life in this way, we can see how the challenges that we have gone through in our life help us gain strengths and tools to become the beautiful creature we are, or are becoming, with confidence and empowerment.

Materials:
Markers
Pencils
Glue
Glitter
Scissors
Cotton balls
Large paper or poster board
Your choice of paint (optional)
Butterfly templates (optional: for inspiration)

Time Frame:
Intro: 5 minutes
Journaling: 5 minutes
Creation: 60 minutes
Closing Circle: 20 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour and 30 minutes

  
A closeup of a butterfly's transformation.
  
Introduction:
Today, we will be thinking about our strength and ability to transform ourselves and our lives. We will create a drawing of a caterpillar as it goes through the different stages in its life to become a butterfly. Butterflies are amazing creatures that have to go through many different stages before they get their wings, their beautiful colors, and begin to fly. Just as a caterpillar works to transform itself into a butterfly, we work through the challenges in our lives to transform ourselves.


  
Looking at the past and the challenges that have
made us stronger.
  
   
Journaling:
We are going to start by taking some time to journal. Sometimes the difficult things we face in life can be chances for us to learn and grow in positive ways. Begin by writing about something hard that you’ve been through in your life and one way that it has helped you to grow. Reflect on what tools or positive things have you gained from these challenges.

You can write a list, you can write stream of consciousness, use this time to write in whatever way works best for you. This is your time. Whatever you write will be just for you.

 
  
 
  Beautiful samples created at Angel Step Too.
Creation:
Step 1:
Using the colored pencils and markers you will draw a caterpillar at the bottom of the page to represent your past. The caterpillar that you are going to draw will represent the trials, challenges, situations, issues, and feelings that you feel have held you back or hurt you in your life. Within or around this caterpillar write these challenges and feelings from the past.

Step 2:
Above the caterpillar you will create a cocoon using the colored pens, pencils, and cotton balls. This cocoon represents a place for you to grow and change. Within or around the cocoon write the different positive ways you have grown and the helpful tools you have gained to transform your life. Think of all the many wonderful things in your life that help you grow. They can be things you have changed in your life, positive people, feelings, or thoughts in your life that have helped you.

Step 3:
At the top of your paper you will draw a butterfly (or glue and then color in a butterfly template) to represent your transformation in overcoming domestic violence. Think about how the strengths and tools you have gained through the challenges you have faced in your life have helped you become the beautiful creature you are, or are becoming, with confidence and empowerment!

As they create, encourage them to trust their gut feelings about what colors and words they choose. There is no right or wrong way. Encourage them to give themselves the freedom to explore and trust whatever expresses itself.

Closing Circle:
Make sure to have time at the end to allow each participant to share what she created and what it means to her. Encourage each participant to be proud of themselves and their transformation as they work to be free of the domestic violence of their past. Congratulate them for being brave, and for working like a butterfly to transform their lives!
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives participants a creative way to view how all of the challenges that they went through in the past have helped them gain strengths and tools to become the beautiful creature they are, or are becoming, with confidence.
