Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Allows participants to create a visual representation of their life story. The goal is to empower the participants to change or re-write the next phase of their lives by being news reporters telling their own stories.

 
  Life Story sample
Materials:
Scissors
Magazines (Newsweek, Oprah and National Geographic have good headlines)
Markers
Colored pencils
Large black construction paper
Plain white writing paper cut into columns
Glue Sticks
Silver or white gel pens
List of positive words and quotes
Example Newspapers

Time frame: 1 hour
Intro: 10min
Relaxation: 5min
Creation: 25min
Closing: 20min

Set-up/Prep
Cut out inspirational words and pictures that you would see in a newspaper. (e.g. "Headlines", news clippings, "Classifieds", "Letter to the Editor"  etc.) You may also allow the participants to find their own pictures and words using donated news magazines such as "Newsweek" or "Times".  Cut columns of white paper for the participants to write their story.  Cut long, thin strips of paper to use as headlines.

  
Don't forget real newspaper examples
 
Introduction:
Today's project is called Life Story Newspaper. We will take time to reflect on our own lives as if they were stories featured in a newspaper.  Your Life Story can have any headlines you choose including but not limited to: current events, classified, entertainment, or breaking news. Feel free to be as detailed or as private as you would like. Remember there is no right or wrong way to create your Life Story, just trust your instincts and let your creative juices flow.  During the relaxation I will invite you to think about your life as a section of the newspaper.  Begin to think about what section of the newspaper would contain your life story.  Pay close attention to where your thoughts take you as they will guide your creation.

Relaxation:
Use calm music as background to invoke a sense of calm and peace.  Now you are going to lead the participants in a guided exercise which focuses on visualizing a newspaper laid out on the table.  Begin the relaxation by asking the participants to make themselves comfortable, and if it feels safe for them, close their eyes. Take three deep breaths. As you take your deep breaks, inhale for a count of three, pause briefly, exhale to a count of six, and pause again.  Repeat your deep breaths and as you take a moment to pause after inhaling, feel how centered, content, and still you are. Take another deep breath in and exhale. Begin to visualize a newspaper in front of you. Which section would you start reading first? What does it say? What news do you want to report on? (Pause) Is it Current Events...Classified...Obituaries... Cover Story? (Pause) Think about your Life Story. (Pause)  When you feel that you have your story, you may open your eyes and begin to write. Take as much time as you need to create your Life Story Newspaper.

 Creating the Life Story Newspaper
Creation:
Have participants choose columns of white paper to begin writing their news story. Pass out the long, thin strips of paper to use as headlines, and advise the participants that making headlines may assist them with focusing on the aspects of their lives they want to include in their Life Story.  Let
  
  Cover Story
them know it's okay to re-write the negative parts of their story and make them positive.  For example they may have relapsed or went back to an abuser in the past.  This is their opportunity to re-define what they consider possible and change the newspaper to reflect what they would like to change or what they would have done differently.  Encourage the participants to think about what they need from certain sections of their Life Story (for example, in the Classified section the participant may need a safe place to live).  Also advise the participants to reflect on what each section of the newspaper says about their current life situation. Participants can be as detailed as they'd like to about where they are right now and where they'd like to be in the future. This is a time to recognize the negative aspects of our past and use the knowledge we gained from those difficult situations to envision change and a better life.  After the participants have completed their news stories have them begin to create their Life Story Newspaper. Have participants arrange magazine cut outs or phrases and positive words and quotes to help tell their story.

Closing:
Encourage the participants to share whatever aspects of their newspapers they feel comfortable sharing one at a time.  If the group members do not know what to say about their project advise them to focus on one particular section of their Life Story newspaper and what it says about their lives.
Row.txt_description: This workshop allows participants to create a visual representation of their life story. The goal is to empower the participants by giving them the courage to change or re-write the next phase of their lives. Giving group members the opportunity to tell their own stories as if they were reporting on the news will ideally allow them to regain control over their lives and redefine what they consider possible.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
The workshop allows the children to use different parts of their body to create a fun work of art that represents well know Halloween images.

 
 
  Setting up the supplies
 
Materials:
Paint (Black and white plus any accent colors you like)
Crayons
Color pencils
Wiggly eyes
Large bucket of water (to have for children to rinse off the paint from their hands and feet)
Black and white construction paper
Paint brushes
Old towels or rags
Paper towels
Scissors
White glue
Paper plates

Time Frame:
  Age Range: 
 
 About 1 hour              
 5 to 12 years old
For children under 4 years old:
one adult per child
 






Set Up:
This workshop is best done in a room with open spaces and a non-carpeted floor.
Lay newspapers on the floor and work area.   Pour black paint on one paper plate and white paint on another plate. Fill a large bucket with at least 4 inches of water and lay a towel next to the bucket.  It is recommended that you make a sample first to see how much paint it takes to make the images.
 
 
 
  Place foot on the plate with white paint to create the ghost
  Place hand on the plate with black paint to create the spider
 

Introduction:
Halloween is a holiday that is based on ancient traditions, myths, religion and customs.  Today Halloween is celebrated based on its spooky history of using symbols that are still common today, like skeletons, ghosts, spiders, masks and black cats.  These symbols are sometimes used as decorations to help create a fun and playful mood to celebrate the holiday.

Today we are going to create some of these symbols by using our hands and feet in a positive and fun way!

Warm Up:
Have the children sit in a circle and ask them...if your feet could take you anywhere this Halloween, where would they go and why? Ask for a child to volunteer to share  their answer first and then go around in a circle until each child has had an opportunity to share.

Opening Circle:
Today we are going to make ghosts and spiders for Halloween! The best part of this is that we are going to use our own hands and feet to create them!  Explain to the children that we will put paint on our hands and feet to create our ghosts and spiders and then we will wash them off in the buckets of water when done.

  
  Ghost created from
foot print
 
Creation:
  • To make the ghost give each of the children a piece of black construction paper.  Have the children come up to the paint table, one at a time.  Then help them to place their foot in the white paint, which you have put on a paper plate o n the floor.  Have the black paper right here on the ground so the child can step down and press their foot on the paper. After the image is created, place the child's foot in the bucket of water to rinse off the paint - be sure to have the towel ready!
  • To make the spider give each child a piece of white construction paper and have them go over to the paint station again and place their hand on the paper plate with the black paint.  Help the children place one hand on the paper keeping their thumb off the paper, and then place it again facing the other way - overlapping the palms so you can create a solid center section with the fingers on either side.  Next have the children go to the "wash Bucket" to rinse their hands and dry them on the towel.
   
  Spider created from 2 hand prints
 
After the paint dries the children can add wiggly eyes and faces to their ghosts and spiders.  The ghosts and spiders can be cut out and hung around the room or they can be left on the paper.

Closing Circle:
Talk to the children about their ghosts and spiders and how they would like to share them with their friends and family to celebrate Halloween.  If time permits have the children make up a short story about their ghosts and spiders such as where they came from and what they will do for the holiday.
Row.txt_description: The workshop allows the children to use different parts of their body to create a fun work of art that represents well know Halloween images.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
The goal for this workshop is to empower families to share their story of surviving domestic violence by illustrating their journey through the metaphor of a tree. In creating their trees, families will be asked to reflect on where they came from, how they escaped, and the kind of future that they envision for themselves.

Materials:

 Materials Sample Set-up
Assortment of acrylic paints (Biocolors)
Scissors
Glue
18 x 24 flat canvas pieces
Brushes
Oil pastels
Watercolors
Various collage materials. 
 
We'd love your help making sure each family's expression is unique in size, shape, color, etc. Feel free to add any supplies that you would like to include.

Note on Materials:
Instead of limiting everyone to a uniform size canvas and selection of materials, we realize it would be much stronger to have individually unique pieces.  We are very fortunate to have a gallery where we will be able to display a range of pieces. 

To help make each family's experience different we want to invite you to supplement this project with materials based on your unique expertise on materials for the workshops you will be co-facilitating.

 
 
Introduction:
Thank the family for being willing to create with you and help them feel comfortable. Begin to share with them what this project is about.  Inform the family that their tree can be completely anonymous to ensure they feel comfortable to create without censoring themselves. 

Create, discuss and review any Ground Rules.  Make sure to include a statement about the importance of confidentiality.  It is also important to let the family know they may not like or agree with what the other participants say and create, which is just fine.  However, no one is allowed to critique or censor anyone.  Talk about trees in general and how they survive many things in their lives including drought, floods, fires, lightening, and even abuse from humans. Explain how the family can use this tree to represent their journey through domestic violence. For example, the roots might represent where they have come from and thus the foundation that allowed them to become the person they are today.  The trunk could represent where they are now, the  branches reaching out for help, and the leaves and blossoms, new growth or what they want to have in the future. The environment can also help illustrate the families’ story. For example, falling leaves, dead branches on the ground or roots buried underground could symbolize the bad memories or experiences they want to leave in their past.

It is important to share with the family that you hope this project helps to create more open communication between family members as they reflect and discuss their own unique experience so that they can begin to heal as individuals and as a family. Also, you will need to inform the family that as they tell about their journey out of domestic violence that it important that they explore and share all of the experiences and feelings in their story.  Including what they've been through at home, in the shelter, how they escaped, what they left behind (fear, sadness, anger, Dad, home, etc.) & what they're moving toward (safety, love, growth, rebuilding family together, etc.)  Leaders may consider asking the families to bring family pictures and significant documents to include in their piece.

Explain that sometimes when there is domestic violence in the home, parents and their children don't discuss what happened, what each person experienced, and the differences between each person’s point of view, feelings, and memories. Talking about it may seem scary and counterproductive, but it actually ends up taking the power away from the pain to talk about it together.  Moreover, sharing our pain with others helps us heal and let go. Remind everyone how courageous and important it is to talk about the pain and the abuse.  Expressing feelings, both negative and positive alike, in a healthy manner, takes practice and today we will all experience how it feels to open up lines of communication.    

 
  Stand Up Version of Tree
Warm Up/Opening Circle:
Option 1: (For mixed age groups or younger participants)
Using a tree and leaves, set up a tree form in the middle of the each family's table. Give at least two foam leaves to each person to hold. Have the participants close their eyes if it feels safe for them and ask them to think about their journey through domestic violence, (pause) and ask them to think about a word that represents their past, (pause). Then ask them to think about their future (pause) and what they want in their future.

Ask everyone to open their eyes and put a word or words or even a drawing on a leaf for their past.  Give them time to do this. Then ask them to put a word or symbol on the other leaf to represent what they want in their future.  If the younger ones are struggling with this task encourage the parent to assist their children.  Pass the tree and two adhesive dots to the person who volunteers to share their leaves first.   Have the person share their name and whatever they feel comfortable sharing about their leaves.  Then instruct that person to attach the leaves to any part of the tree (including underneath).  Then pass the tree to the next family member who wants to share and repeat the process until everyone has had a chance to share their leaves and attach them to the tree.  After everyone has shared let them know that this tree represents letting go of the past and celebrating the future. Encourage the family to clap and cheer to recognize the significance of opening up about the past and looking to the future!


 
  
Option 2: (For more advance participant or families with older children)
First do a brief demonstration of the materials they will use for the warm-up (participants will be using watercolor crayons, water, and 5 x 7 pieces of paper). Explain to the family that during this warm-up you will be asking them some questions and giving them directions for putting marks on their paper.  If they don’t feel comfortable with the warm-up they can simply use the watercolor crayons to see how they work.

“We are going to try a very loose, quick warm-up. We're going to move quickly, so that nobody has time to think too much, and you can practice focusing on the thoughts that first come to mind without having time to criticize them."

If it feels safe for you, close your eyes and picture yourself as a tree.  Now look beyond the tree and see what color the sky and background are.  Is it night?  Is it morning?  (pause) Is there blue a sky? Sunshine?  Rain? Or a glowing sunset?  Open your eyes and choose the color that you just saw and cover your entire page with that color. (pause)  

Now think about the bark of your tree… What color is the bark?  What shape comes to mind for the bark? Is it rough or smooth?  Curly? Bent?  Or straight?  Go ahead and put on your page the first thought you had for the bark.  (pause)  Now think about the leaves of your tree. What colors and what shapes come to mind for the leaves? Choose a color and draw a leaf. (pause)  Does your tree have flowers or seeds? What color and what shapes come to mind for your flowers or seeds? Go ahead and put your first thoughts on the page. (pause)  Now think about how many branches your tree might have...Does your tree have lots of branches?  Are they little branches or big branches? Make a mark for the color and shape that come to mind.  (pause)   Is your tree an angry tree?  What color and shape come to mind for anger?  Make a mark on your page for anger.  (pause)   Now think about if your tree is happy.  What color and shape come to mind for happy?  Make a mark on your page if your tree is happy.  (pause)   Now think about if your tree is sad.  What color, and what shape come to mind for sad?  When you’re ready, make a mark on your page if your tree is sad. (pause)  Now think about if your tree is peaceful.  What color and shape comes to mind for peaceful.  Make a mark on your page if your tree is peaceful.    Now begin to think about if your family is part of your tree.  What shapes and colors would they be?  Think of your mom.  What shape and color comes to mind?  Make a mark on your tree for your mom.   Now think of your dad.  What shape and color comes to mind for your dad?  Make a mark on the page for your dad.  Now think about any brothers and sisters you have.  What shape and colors would they be?  Make a mark on your page for them.  And now think of yourself.  What color would you be?  What shape?  Make a mark on your tree for yourself...Now think about the future you envision and wish for your tree - think of a color or shape for your wish, and make a mark on your page for the future."

Have everyone take a minute to share their name and anything they would like to share about their tree.

 
Option 3: (for participants that respond to visualizations)
(Speaking slowly with a calm voice) Before we start our project I am going to guide you through a relaxation. All you have to do is sit comfortably with your hands on your lap, close your eyes, and imagine you are sitting in a very special tree.  Picture yourself swinging back and forth on a very comfortable swing on one of the branches.

As you are swinging back and forth begin to look around….glance up through the tree branches and notice the sky ….Is your sky bright or dark?  Are there fluffy clouds, or do you just see a blue sky?  Perhaps you see a rainy sky.  Maybe it’s night time.  Keep breathing deep breathes as your body relaxes more and more. Now turn your attention to the branches of your tree (pause)… feel sunshine bouncing warmly off the leaves, notice the color and shape of your leaves….Are they a dark color or a light color?  Are they all the same or are some leaves different? Now take another deep breath and notice if your tree has a special scent…can you smell flowers or maybe even pine needles?  Keep breathing and imagining your tree. Now begin to notice if your tree has lots of branches or just a few. Are the branches on your tree reaching up or down… are they chunky branches or skinny branches? And lastly while you are still swinging on your special swing notice the bark on your tree …is it wrinkly or smooth…. notice the color of the bark on your tree…Is the bark only one color or lots of colors?… Just keep swinging and imaging your tree...  
          
Whenever you are ready you may open your eyes and create a drawing of what you saw in your imagination using construction paper and colored pencils.


 "Family" Proudly Displaying Their Tree
Option 4: (simple relaxation)
Have everyone take off their shoes and gather the participants in a circle. Ask the family to begin to imagine if they could be any kind of tree, what kind of tree would they choose.  Then recite the following relaxation: Ok everyone let’s breathe in a deep breath and as you release your breath, let’s stretch up towards the ceiling and let out your big breath! Ok now let’s spread out a little and begin to pretend you are a tree. Look at your feet and spread all your toes out.  Feel your toes breathing and expanding into the floor.  Focus all your attention on your feet and allow them to feel the floor as if they were the roots of a tree and you are taking hold of the ground. Now bend down, and then slowly run your hands up your calves and thighs and imagine that those parts of your body are your trunk. Feel the bark - is it rough or smooth?  Now stretch your arms up as if they were branches reaching towards the sun. Feel the warmth of the sun nurturing your leaves, your branches and your bark! Now position yourself as a stationary tree, remember to keep breathing.  Begin to envision the shape of your trunk (pause) and your branches (pause).  What do they look like?  Are they reaching up towards the sky, across the room?   Are some sloping down? Imagine you are now a tree growing in a very safe forest filled with trees just like you ... A forest where you are taken care of, protected and loved. Just stand for a moment and hear the peaceful silence of the forest. (Pause)  Now give your tree a big hug (everyone hugs themselves) and give your tree and nice squeeze.  Take another deep breathe in. As you let your breath out slowly begin to bring yourself back to the room and begin to create your Family Tree.

Technical Demonstration:
Now begin the transition to each family working together on their tree. Give the family a tour of all the supplies along with a few options or possibilities of what they may create. If appropriate you may give each family only one option.

Give a demonstration on how to use all the materials. Never assume the family knows how to use a material. Some may have never used a paint brush or even a crayon.


  
 Planning Sheet 1
  
   
   
 Planning Sheet 2
  
   
Creation Possibilities:
Depending on family size and the ages of the children, there are different options for what to do next!  Share the creation process with the families based on the artist and leaders plan.  Have the parent direct the family to reach a consensus on how they will create their tree.  Be sure to reinforce that the parent is the lead designer, or creative supervisor for the project.

Here are some new possibilities to consider:
  • You may start by giving the parent a planning sheet (provided).
  • Different materials (watercolor, acrylics, assemblage, textiles, pastels...)
  • Different shapes and size canvas or paper (it may even be cool to have some mini-trees!!)
  • Creating a dyptych (i.e. dark & light, mother & child) or triptych(i.e. past, present & future)
  • Focus on one part of the tree(i.e. just the leaves, or the roots rather than creating a whole tree).
  • Selection of a color palette (i.e. a monochromatic tree or black and white tree).
  • A Mosaic tile tree.
  • A tree made out of words
As they consider the different options you may want to keep the following age related family dynamics issues in mind:
• Teens: Some teens might want to just create their own tree or section to add onto the bigger tree, that is fine! They may not be used to having mom/dad in charge or they may just be vying for independence as teens typically do.   Try to channel their energy in a positive direction. Sometimes teens just want to know they have choices, and they like attention just like we do!

• Very active children/or a family that can't seem to work together: For this family it might be easier for each participant to have their own separate piece to work with such as: leaves, flowers, trunk, or branches.  They can write, paint, or collage on them.   Then give the family the option to have mom/dad piece it all back together.  You can make a ceremony out of each person gluing their creation on the tree which will enable the family to put their separate creations together to form one family tree!

• Toddlers (under 3) and younger: The hand print option will probably be the easiest for this age! Don't forget footprints work too! Or a combination of the two.

Closing:
Have the family gather around their project (in whatever stage of completion) and let them just absorb its magnificence!  Give everyone an opportunity to share what they experienced…  Encourage each participant to share about the part they created, and how it felt.  You can prompt their responces by asking:  what was hard for you, what was easy, what did you let go of, and what did you like best?  We suggest that you begin with having the kids share first.  Remind the participants that they do not have to share if they don’t want to.  It will be important to have a closing circle after each Family Tree creation session.  The closing circle will give them a safe to place to process what they are going through and provide closure on that days work.

  
 Family Tree Example
 
About Reconvening:
Before you leave be sure to schedule follow-up sessions(s) if it is necessary to complete the tree.  Each time you regroup to work on the Family Tree it will be important to have some sort of Opening Circle or Warm-up to create safety and establish the  “window of time” for creativity and expression. 

 
Day 2

Opening Circle:
You can begin by asking the family to share their answer to the following question: If you were part of a tree, what part of the tree would you be and why? Are you the roots, the trunk or a beautiful flower? 

*After the check-in circle feel free to use any Warm-up from Day 1.

Creation:
Using the plan the families created continue to create the Family Tree.


 "Family" showing off their completed tree
Closing:
At the final gathering it is important to gather words about the family’s journey out of domestic violence and about what their tree represents.  Each family member may have a different story.  Gathering words usually works best through dictation, rather than having the family try to write it themselves. For younger children, it will be especially helpful for you to ask them questions and write down their answers. This can be helpful for participants of all ages. It is also good to read their words back to them so they can change their mind and/or add to it!

Prompts: (no special order, pick and choose or use all of them!)
If your tree could talk what would it say?
If your tree was hurt what would it say?
If the leaves could share secrets what would they share?
If the blooms, flowers, or fruit on your tree had feelings what would they feel?
If the bark on your tree could tell you what it has seen what would it tell you?
If your tree could grant wishes what would you ask for?
If your tree could see into the future what does your future look like?
What does your tree need for the future?
If you wanted to help others experiencing the same thing what would you tell them?
What feeds your tree?

Be sure the words share some description of the family’s journey out of domestic violence and some description of the future they want to create.  If those things don’t come out in answering the above questions, you can ask more direct questions. Most likely, these questions are for the parent to answer, but if it seems like the children have something to add, please welcome them:

What do you want others to know about your family’s journey out of domestic violence?  
What was the hardest part of your journey?
What are you most proud of?
What kind of future are you building together?
How does your tree show your journey?
Did you discover anything about your family while creating your Family Tree?
Row.txt_description: The goal for this workshop is to empower families to share their story of surviving domestic violence by illustrating their journey through the metaphor of a tree. In creating their trees, families will be asked to reflect on where they have come from, how they escaped, and the kind of future that they envision for themselves.
Row.txt_tips:
Letter to Parents (the letter is located in the Family Trees Manual):
Review the letter with the parent and discuss any questions, concerns, suggestions or emotions that arise. 

Optional Pre-workshops:
You may choose to do a pre-workshop with the family if they have never done a workshop before.  You can use one of your favorite workshops or choose one of the following suggestions (or the Letter from Parent to Children):
Monster in Me
Journey Butterfly
My Footprints
 
Letter From Parent to Children:
This pre-workshop was created to prepare the parent to guide and support their children through the art process.

Using paper cut in the shape of leaves, have the parent write a letter to his/her children (they can write to each individually or one collectively).  The letter can reflect the thoughts and feelings they have as a result of reading the Letter to Parents.  The letter can also focus on the wishes she/he has for their children (or family) in the future.  Allow the parent to take the letter in any direction she/he sees fit.  Ideally the letter (or letters) should be written on paper shaped like a leaf or piece of fruit to tie in the Family Tree theme.  The parent can also decorate their letter.  Advise the parent that they have the option to keep, destroy, or give the letter to their children.  The choice is theirs!

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide participants with the opportunity to think of their old leaves (past) and turn it over, transforming it into a new leaf, and a new life.
Keep in mind this workshop can be done in one or two sessions. Doi ng this workshop in one session requires prep time.

Materials:
One Session Only:
Medium to Large leaves, pre-cut from posterboard and painted with Acrylic iridescent paint
 
  Completed New Leaf with poem

  
  Close up of medallions
Craypas
Pens
Markers
Relaxing Music

Optional Materials:
Puff paints/ Glitter glue
Scissors
Magazines
Sequins/Medallions
Fall themed scrapbooking accessories

Two Sessions:
Large and Medium Size posterboard pieces
Acrylic iridescent paint
Paint brushes
Paint Palettes or plates/bowls
Puff paints/ Glitter glue
Scissors
Magazines
Sequins/Medallions
Fall themed scrapbooking accessories

Time Frame:
Intro: 5 minutes
Opening: 15 minutes
Relaxation: 5 minutes
Creation: 30-45 minutes
Total Time: up to 70 minutes (add 30-60 minutes for prep time if doing only One Session)

Workshop Preparation:
In order to make this a one session workshop, you must cut out large scale leaves of varying shapes and sizes on poster board and paint them various colors. Paint all leaves with one side green and opposite side shades of either orange, purple, yellow or red.

If you cannot do any preparation, this would be a two session workshop. Give each participant a piece of poster board and ask them to draw the shape of their leaf, and then cut it out. Session One: Create old side of leaf. Session Two: Create new side of leaf.

  
 Completed New Leaf
 
Introduction:
Each fall, leaves turn breathtaking shades of orange, purple, red, yellow and brown in a fantastic show of nature's glory. But why do leaves change color? Although Jack Frost gets most of the credit, the scientific reason for our beautiful fall foliage is a process called photoperiodism. As the sun moves further south, the hours of daylight shorten and the temperatures fall. This causes leaves to cease production of chlorophyll, the chemical that colors the leaves green. As the chlorophyll disappears, the underlying colors of the leaves are unmasked. The next strongest pigment becomes dominant giving the leaves a "new" color.
While we are in abusive relationships we are not able to be the person we want to be, spend our time how we want or design our lives.  After we leave our abusive partners, we are able to begin a new season (chapter) in our lives and allow our true colors to shine.  As we shed the colors of our past we are able to re-establish who we are, and what we want in our lives.  Today we will decorate one side of a leaf to represent our past and then "turn over a new leaf" and decorate the opposite side to represent our new life free from violence.  

Opening Circle:
When leaves change their color they are transformed into a range of colors such as Dark Crimson, Pale Brown, Scarlet, Yellow or Pink. Go around the room and have everyone share what color they see when they "turn over a new leaf," a color that YOU choose to represent your violence free present and future.

Relaxation:
Have everyone sit in their chairs with feet on the floor and hands to their sides.
If you feel comfortable you may close your eyes. Take in a deep breath and let it out. Take in another deep breath and imagine you are taking in the fall wind, as you exhale, pretend you are the fall wind blowing away all the old leaves still left on the tree. Continue to take in deep fall wind breaths and blow away the leaves. Now pretend you are a leaf still on the tree, shake your head, your shoulders, your arms, your hips, your legs, and your feet. Shake your old self and your old leaves off the tree. Shake off all the old, all the past. Now as
 
  Completed Old Leaf
your old leaf falls to the floor, imagine yourself changing colors. Imagine your new color, are you Brown, Clear Yellow, Brilliant Red, Glossy Green, Burnt Orange? What does your color mean? What does it represent? As you are turning over your old leaf, what does your new leaf, your new life look like?
Continue to imagine your new life, your new colors. When you feel relaxed and ready you can open your eyes and begin to create your new leaf.

Creation:
Ensure that each participant has their leaf and ask them to think back to their abusive relationship.  What colors, shapes, symbols, words and images come to mind?  Now, keeping those thoughts in mind, decorate one side of your leaf to reflect your life when you were experiencing domestic violence.  After you have completed the old side of your leaf that represents your past, you may then turn over your leaf, and begin to picture, in your minds eye, all of the colors, shapes, symbols, words and images that represent your new life, free from abuse.  Be bold and allow your mind to open up to the infinite amount of possibilities that your future holds.  Whenever you are ready you may begin to create your new leaf that reflects all of the wonderful things you just envisioned for your abuse free present and future.

Closing:
Give time for everyone to share something about their leaf and what they experienced during the workshop.  You may also ask how it felt to reflect on their past, examine their present life, look to their future, and turn over a new leaf.  If no one wants to share it's always easy to ask how the experience creating their leaf was for them.
Row.txt_description: This workshop allows participants to turn over a new leaf when they let go of the power and control their abusive partner had on their past and allow themselves to re-design their life and re-define who they are.

Row.txt_code:
Objective
Facilitate a discussion about different types of fear the participants experience and how to effectively cope with the fear.


 
 Supplies to make Fear Ghost Busters
 
Materials:
Styrofoam Balls (you can also use wood, rubber or any other type of ball you can write on)
White fabric
Ribbon/yarn
Pens
Markers (fabric markers are preferred, but all kinds of markers will work)
Scissors
Glue
Wiggly eyes

Time Frame
Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Creation: 40 minutes
Closing Circle:10 minutes


 
 Monsters are something we are afraid of!
 
  
  
 Tying the bow around the neck of the ghost
 
  
  
 Happy words bust the fears
 
Opening Circle
Gather the participants and have them sit in a circle.  Begin the discussion by asking if anyone can define the word fear.  Then add to the definition by telling the group that fear is a feeling that makes us aware that something may be wrong. For example, we feel fear or get scared when we think someone or something is dangerous (or bad).  We may be fearful because we feel scared, anxious, afraid, threatened or because something is new and we don't know what to expect.  Offer examples to clarify the definition such as "when you can't find your favorite toy," "when you first came to the shelter" or "when your mom leaves you with a babysitter" as examples of times they may have felt fear.  You can also give Halloween themed examples such as "when you see someone in a scary costume" or "when you see a scary movie."  Then have each of the children think of a time they felt fear, and go around the circle and have each share one example.  Some of the participants may not want to share which is fine, just tell them to keep their fears in mind for the project.

Creation:
Pass out one ball and something that will write with on the ball (pens work for rubber, wood and Styrofoam balls) to each participant.  Instruct the children to write their fears or a picture or symbol to represent their fears on the ball.  Then talk about how in this project they will bust or get the fear out of their ghost.  You can ask the children how they deal with their fear, and then follow up with your ideas on fear busting.  For example "when you feel scared or fearful, it may be helpful, to tell a safe grown up how you feel."  Sometimes the things we are afraid of aren't really scary at all and people we love can help us to bust out our fears.  Sometimes just talking about the scary stuff helps to bust our fear, because when we keep our fears (the scary stuff) hidden they get bigger.

Tell the children that happy words and happy things are also great fear busters.  Ask the group to share one thing that makes them happy.  You can then facilitate a discussion about how we can bust our fears by throwing out the bad stuff (fear, anxiety) and replacing it with good stuff (affirmations, positive words and thoughts). 

Give each participant a piece of white fabric and markers (preferably fabric markers, but all types of markers work also). Instruct the group to write as many happy words or symbols they can think of on their piece of fabric.  Give each participant a piece of ribbon and tell the group that they are now going to bust their fears!  Demonstrate covering the ball with the fabric and tying the ribbon to secure the ball in place.  During the demonstration tell the group that their happy thoughts are now going to cover up or bust their fears to create their very own Fear Ghost Busters.  Assist each participant with gluing the wiggly eyes on their ghost. 

Closing Circle:
Congratulate the group for being brave and talking about their fears (you may also want to remind them of the importance of sharing their fears with a safe person).  Encourage the participants to use their Fear Ghost Buster to take out (disarm) any fearful or scary things they encounter in the future.  Ask the group to each take turns sharing something about their Fear Ghost Buster.  Encourage them to speak about the words and symbols they used.  You can also ask each participant how they can use their Fear Ghost Buster to fight fear in the future.  Be sure to take notes on the things they say and share them with windows!
 
   
  Finished Fear Ghost Buster with all it's words!
Row.txt_description: Facilitate a discussion about different types of fear the participants experience and how to effectively cope with the fear.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To get children thinking about what they are thankful for.  Although many of the children may come from difficult situations, this activity allows them to focus on the simple things we are thankful for.  The children can use pens, crayons, or markers to draw pictures or write the things they are thankful for.  The activity also has a strong focus on teamwork, because Tom the Thankful Turkey is not complete until each child has added his or her feather or feathers.  Once completed, Tom becomes a very special turkey who holds all that everyone is thankful for.

 
 
  Supplies for Tom the Thankful Turkey
 
   
   
   
   
   
   
   
   
   
  Cutting out the pieces
 
   
   
  Adding the face to Tom
 
   
   
  Gluing all the pieces together - each child
will add one feather at a time
 
   
  Tom is complete!
 
Materials:
Red, brown, green, orange and yellow construction paper.
Scissors
Markers, pens or crayons
Glue sticks or tape
Googly eyes (Optional)
Feather Template
Tom the Turkey Template
(Thanks to Enchanted Learning www.enchantedlearning.com)

Time Frame:
Approximately 1 hour

Age Range:
Children 4 years old and older. One adult for every 6 children is recommended for children aged 4-7.

Set Up:
Take the time to cut out all the individual feathers before the workshop or draw the templates onto red, orange, green and yellow paper for the children to cut out. (See the templates)  Also prepare Tom the Turkey without his feathers and have him hanging on the wall ahead of class time. You can use the template provided or create your own larger turkey. Depending on the size of your group, you may want to make a larger body in order to accommodate a large amount of feathers.


Introduction:
Begin by discussing Thanksgiving.  Explain that Thanksgiving is a holiday that gives us an opportunity to think about what we have in our lives to be thankful for.

Warm Up:
Ask the children to stand in a circle. Have them turn to the left and slowly walk around in the circle. You will ask them to sing and make sounds or movements to go with the song as they walk in the circle.
Sing to the tune of "This Old Man"
Little Turkeys walking by
They can move from side to side
With a ........here and a .....there
Here a........there a........
They can .......everywhere
Little turkeys making sounds
They can ........as they move around
With a ........here and a .....there
Here a........there a........
They can .......everywhere
You can insert the words like goobble, wooble, wiggle, hop, jiggle -  feel free to add anything else you might like.

Opening Circle:
Ask the children to think about and discuss all the things they do or have in their daily lives.  Then narrow the list down to include only the positive things they have and explain how Tom will be used as a way to share all the ideas they have.

Creation:
Have the children select "feathers" choosing whatever color they like.  (If you have time you may want to write on each feather  "I am thankful for_______" ). They can then either write or draw one thing they are thankful for on each feather.  One by one each child can come up to Tom and glue or tape the feathers around Tom's body.

Closing Circle:
Tom will be complete because everyone has added their feathers!  Ask each child to share what he or she likes best about Tom.
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps children think about the things they are thankful for and work together to create "Tom the Thankful Turkey".

Row.txt_code:
Helping Hands and Feet Turkey
 
Objective:
To create a simple fun way to show how our hands and feet can be used to think about the holidays and how we can help others.  This workshop idea is from Enchanted Learning  - www.enchantedlearning.com

Materials:
Red, yellow, orange and brown construction paper
pencils
Scissors
Glue
Googly eyes (optional)
Markers or Crayons

Time Frame:
45 minutes to an hour
                   
    Age Range:
Children 4 years old and older. One adult for every 4 children is recommended for children aged 4-7. Help will be needed for the tracing of the hands and feet
 




Set Up:
Have the colored paper set out and have help available to trace the hands and feet.  Older children can also help the younger children.

Warm Up:
Ask the children to stand in a circle. Have them turn to the left and slowly walk around in the circle.  You will ask them to sing and make sounds or movements to go with the song as they walk in the circle.  Add as many verses as you like.

Sing to the tune of the Hokey Pokey

You put your right foot in,
You put your right foot out;
You put your right foot in,
And you shake it all about.
You do the Hokey-Pokey,
And you turn yourself around.
That's what it's all about!		 You put your tail feathers in,
You put your tail feathers out;
You put your tail feathers in,
And you shake it all about.
You do the Hokey-Pokey,
And you turn yourself around.
That's what it's all about!

   
  Trace the children's feet
 
   
  Trace and cut the shape of the children's hands
 
   
  Attach the feet and add the face
 
   
  Add words to the "feathers"
 
Introduction:
Talk about Thanksgiving and how we all have things to be thankful for.  Today we are going to think about 6 people who have helped you in your life like a teacher, a brother or sister, or your mom. You can ask the children to think about 6 ways they have helped others during the year. Examples for the children might be, helping with chores, helping a friend with homework, or making a gift for someone you care for.

Creation:
Step One:
Ask each child to stand on a piece of brown construction paper and help them to trace the outline of their feet on the paper to create a turkey body. The children will then trace the outline of their hands, making 2 red, 2 yellow and 2 orange.  These pieces will be the turkey's feathers. Younger children will need assistance.

Step Two:
Cut out the hands and feet. Once again, younger children will need help.

Step Three:
Glue the 2 feet together to make the turkey body. The head will be the two heels overlapping.

Step Four:
Cut out a red wattle and an orange beak.  Glue the beak on top of the wattle and googly eyes (or paper eyes) above the beak, to the turkey's head.

Step Five:
On each hand (feather), write or draw one of the 6 things that were discussed in the opening (6 people who have helped you or the 6 good deeds you have done).

Closing Circle:
Ask  the children to show their turkey and talk about their 6 accomplishments. Each child creates their own turkey that can be used for a great decoration during the holidays.
Row.txt_description: To create a simple fun way to show how our hands and feel can be used to think about the holidays and how we can help others.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give the participants a tangible reminder to treat one another with love and kindness, as they are two positive things that we will never run out of.   This important message will be conveyed via a fairy tale about corrup tion and the power of love.  

Materials
 
  Materials needed to create Warm Fuzzy
:
Yarn (yarn that is very thick and fuzzy works best)
Small paper plates (cardboard also works)
Circular object (with the circumference approximately the size of the circle your fingers make when you touch the tips of your thumb and index fingers together)   
Circular object (with a circumference approximately the size of the circle your fingers make when you make the ok sign)
Pen
Scissors
Copy of the Warm Fuzzy Tale by: Claude Steiner
Copy of the Warm Fuzzy Tale in Spanish
Click here to access the Warm Fuzzy Tale in other languages
 

 
 Two paper plate donuts
 
Time Frame:
Introduction and Story:  15 minutes
Discussion: 10 minutes
Creation: 20 minutes
Closing: 15 minutes
Total: One Hour

Workshop Preparation:
It is helpful to have a warm fuzzy to use as an example for the group.  If you feel the group would benefit, make copies of the tale to pass out to the group.  To create the circles that you will wrap the yarn around place the larger circular object in the middle of a paper plate and trace it with a marker.  Place the smaller circular object in the middle of the circle you just traced, and then trace it.  Put two paper plates together, cut out the circle in the middle of the plate and the outside of the plate (so you are left with two paper plates that look like donuts).   It is helpful to have two of the paper plate donuts for each of the participants.

Introduction:
Today I am going to read you a great story called the Warm Fuzzy Tale!  After we finish the story each of you are going to create your very own warm fuzzy!  You may want to pass out copies of the story to participants who would like to read along as you tell the story.  Then read the warm fuzzy tale out loud to the group.  You can also encourage them to take the story home to share with other people!

Discussion:

 Yarn wrapped around the donut
If time permits you can ask the group what they think the message was behind the story.  Take this opportunity to reinforce the importance of being kind and loving to one another.  Just as the story suggests we have an infinite amount to love and positive energy, which goes to waste if we don’t give it to others.  Spreading love and kindness is not only fun but also free!  When we give love and kindness to others, we are more likely to get the same in return.         


Creation:
Step 1: Pass out a variety of different types of yarn, allow each participant to select the color (or colors) they would like to use.  Then give each participant two paper plate donuts and a pair of scissors.

Step 2: Take two paper plate donuts and lay them on top of one another (so the holes in the middle of the donuts are lined up). Show each of the participants how to wrap the yarn around the inside and outside of the donut so it covers the entire circle (so you are unable
 
  Cutting the yarn around the donut
to see the paper plate).

Step 3: Pull the two paper plate donuts apart so you have enough room to cut.  Cut the yarn that lies in between the donuts, the entire outer-circumference of the donut.

Step 4: Cut a piece of yarn and wrap it around the yarn that remains in the middle of the
  
 Tightly knotting the yarn
 
two donuts. Tightly knot that same piece of yarn in the middle of the donuts.  This will connect the middle of the project together.

Step 5:  Remove the paper plate donuts, fluff, trim off any excess yarn, and enjoy your warm fuzzy!
 
For Younger Children:
Step 1: Have the children hold three of their fingers together.  Wrap the yarn around their fingers (approximately 65 times).

Step 2: Cut the end of the yarn.  Take a new piece of yarn, weave it through the middle of the circle of yarn,  and tie it in a tight knot.

Step 3: Fluff out the yarn, and trim off any excess yarn if necessary.

 
  Three completed warm fuzzys
Closing:
If time permits you can ask each of the participants why they chose the particular color (or colors) that they made their warm fuzzy.  You may also ask where they plan to keep their warm fuzzy or if they plan to give it away.
Row.txt_description: This project was created by the arts and crafts staff at the Rowdy Ridge Gang Camp. The project is centered around the classic Warm Fuzzy Tale by Claude Steiner about the importance of spreading love and kindness. Participants will create their own warm fuzzy.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To facilitate a discussion about the act of screaming based on the famous Edvard Munch painting called The Scream.  After the discussion the participants will create their own version of Edvard’s painting, which can then be transferred onto canvas bags.

  
 The Scream by Evard Munch
 
Materials:
Click here for a copy of The Scream
Markers
Cray-Pas
Black and white paper
Scanner
Iron-on paper (available at any office supply store) Iron
Canvas Bags (white or light colored work best) - many options are available from Discount School Supply
*you can iron the images onto any type of fabric

Note: If using this workshop to help children release or process anger it is important to begin by having a discussion on "What is Anger?" Please click here to see the entire Processing Anger Series.

Time Frame:
Opening Screaming Circle: 20 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing: 20 minutes
Scanning, Printing and Iron-on transfer process: 5 minutes per bag

Workshop Prep: 
If you decide to put the images on canvas bags, this workshop can be time consuming and expensive, as it requires scanning the participant’s creation into a computer, printing it out on iron-on paper, and then ironing it onto a canvas bag.  However, the project is just as effective if you omit transferring the images onto bags.

Introduction:
Show a copy of the painting, The Scream, to the group (you may also want to pass a copy around the room) and briefly explain that it is a very famous painting by Edvard Munch.  Today we are all going to release our screams and put them on paper.  Your creation does not have to look like Edvard Munch’s painting, just think about how you feel when you scream, or when you want to scream but you feel you can't, and put those feelings on the paper.  There is no right or wrong way to make your scream, just trust your instincts and let your creative juices flow!  

   
  Art by Monabel Contreras  
Opening Screaming Circle:
Begin a discussion about screaming.  You can ask the following questions to start the conversation; how did it feel to scream, who screams in your house, when and why do you (or other people) scream, what about happy screams, or scared screams?  You can also ask the children when is it ok to scream and when it is not ok?  Be sure to reinforce that screaming is an important way to stay safe. If you have a place where it's acceptable to be noisy, a fun and effective way to begin the project is to take the participants to that location and ask everyone to take turns screaming.  It may be helpful for the leader to go first so you can set the tone and let the participants know it’s ok to let go, and release their deepest and loudest scream.  Make sure to encourage each participant as they scream.          

Technical Demonstration:
First demonstrate how to draw with the Cray-Pas, how to smear the color with your fingers, and the different ways they look on either the black or white paper.  Encourage the group to blend the colors together and fill up the entire paper with their creation.


 
 Example of a happy scream
 
Creation: 
Allow the participants to select either the black or white paper to use to create their version of The Scream.  Make sure the participants have a variety of different colored Cray-Pas at their disposal.  Remind the children that if they don’t want to draw a picture, they can use colors, words, or symbols to represent their scream.  Happy screams, sad screams and angry screams are all welcome; there is no wrong or right way to create. Begin the creative portion by telling the participants “now take a deep breath, and release your scream onto your paper.” 
  
Closing:
Give each of the group members a chance to share their art.  You can also ask the participants to give their artwork a title, and write the title, their name, and the date on the back of their project.  If the participant does not feel comfortable sharing in a group, encourage them to share their project with a safe person later.  If it’s appropriate you can also ask questions that allow the participants to open up about their project such as:  Why did you choose that colored paper, why did you choose that color, shape, word, or symbol, how did it feel to make your artwork?  If you plan on transferring the projects onto canvas bags, ask each participant what color bag they would like (white or light colored canvas bags work best) and write that color on the back of their project (to remind you of their color choice later).  Then make sure to collect the projects and tell the participants you will return their projects with their very own screaming bag!

Alternate Closing:
Brainstorm a "Safety Plan" with the children to help them process their anger. Some helpful tips include:
Talk to a friend you can trust
Count to 10
Take out art supplies and draw a picture of your anger
Journal about your anger
Take deep breaths
Listen to music
Walk away
Dance or exercise

 
 
 Completed Screaming Bag
 
Iron-on process:
Step 1: Scan the artwork into your computer
Step 2: Load the iron-on paper into your printer
Step 3: Print the artwork on the iron-on paper
Step 4: Follow the directions for the particular type of iron-on paper you used, to iron the picture onto the canvas bag (usually the packaging for the paper will offer instructions).  Click here for more information.
Step 5: Give each participant their artwork and their very own Screaming Bag!
Row.txt_description: To facilitate a discussion about the act of screaming based on the famous Edvard Munch painting called The Scream. After the discussion the participants will create their own version of Edvard’s painting, which can then be transferred onto canvas bags.
Row.txt_tips:
We recommend that you start anger workshops with a discussion; don't be afraid to talk to the children about their anger.  Anger is nothing to be ashamed of, it is important to look at and talk about it to try to understand it.

Some anger prompts that we like are:
What is Anger? What does it look like and what does it sound like?
What was the trigger to your anger?
What did you think about it?
How did it make you feel?
How did you act?
What effect did it have on you and those around you?

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide children with the opportunity to think of their old leaves (past) and turn it over, transforming it into a new leaf, and a new life.
Keep in mind this is a workshop can be done in one or two sessions. Do ing this workshop in one session requires prep time.

Materials:
One Session Only:
Medium to Large leaves, pre-cut from posterboard and painted with Acrylic iridescent paint
 
  Completed New Leaf with poem

  
  Close up of medallions

Craypas
Pens
Markers
Relaxing Music

Optional Materials:
Puff paints/ Glitter glue
Scissors
Magazines
Sequins/Medallions
Fall themed scrapbooking accessories

Two Sessions:
Large and Medium Size posterboard pieces
Acrylic iridescent paint
Paint brushes
Paint Palettes or plates/bowls
Puff paints/ Glitter glue
Scissors
Magazines
Sequins/Medallions
Fall themed scrapbooking accessories

Time Frame:
Intro: 5 minutes
Opening: 15 minutes
Relaxation: 5 minutes
Creation: 30-45 minutes
Total Time: up to 70 minutes (add 30-60 minutes for prep time if doing only One Session)

Workshop Preparation:
In order to make this a one session workshop, you must cut out large scale leaves of varying shapes and sizes on poster board and paint them various colors. Paint all leaves with one side green and opposite side shades of either orange, purple, yellow or red.

If you cannot do any preparation, this would be a two session workshop. Give each participant a piece of poster board and ask them to draw the shape of their leaf, and then cut it out. Session One: Create old side of leaf. Session Two: Create new side of leaf.

  
 Completed New Leaf
 
Introduction:
Each fall, leaves turn breathtaking shades of orange, purple, red, yellow and brown in a fantastic show of nature's glory. But why do leaves change color? Although Jack Frost gets most of the credit, the scientific reason for our beautiful fall foliage is a process called photoperiodism. As the sun moves further south, the hours of daylight shorten and the temperatures fall. This causes leaves to cease production of chlorophyll, the chemical that colors the leaves green. As the chlorophyll disappears, the underlying colors of the leaves are unmasked. The next strongest pigment becomes dominant giving the leaves a "new" color.
As we shed the colors of our past we are able to re-establish who we are, and what we want in our lives.  Today we will decorate one side of a leaf to represent our past and then "turn over a new leaf" and decorate the opposite side to represent our new life free from violence.  

Warm Up:
Have everyone stand up like a tall tree. Take in a deep breath and let it out. Take in another deep breath and imagine you are taking in the fall wind, as you exhale, pretend you are the fall wind blowing away all the old leaves still left on the tree. Continue to take in deep fall wind breaths and blow away the leaves. Now pretend you are a leaf still on the tree, shake your head, your shoulders, your arms, your hips, your legs, and your feet. Shake your old self and your old leaves off the tree. Shake off all the old, all the past. Now as
 
  Completed Old Leaf
your old leaf falls to the floor, imagine yourself changing colors. Imagine your new color, are you Brown, Clear Yellow, Brilliant Red, Glossy Green, Burnt Orange? Have children shout out what color their leaf is.

Creation:
Ensure that each child has picked a leaf and ask them to create one side of their leaf to represent their past and to turn it over and create their new leaf.

Closing:
Give time for everyone to share something about their leaf.
Row.txt_description: To provide children with the opportunity to think of their old leaves (past) and turn it over, transforming it into a new leaf, and a new life. Keep in mind this is a workshop can be done in one or two sessions. Doing this workshop in one session requires prep time.

Row.txt_code:
Workshop Objective:
To provide the children an opportunity to and express their own wishes and hopes for the holidays and the New Year. In this workshop we learn how to create holiday wish lists that will express those wishes and hopes.  

< table border="0" align="right">     Set the table with the supplies to make
Holiday Wish Lists
 Materials:
White card stock, cut to size desired (4x6 or 5x7 works well)
Masking tape
Cray-Pas
Toothpicks or any fine tipped scrapping tool

Time Frame:
Total Time:    60 minutes
10 min        Opening Circle
    
 30 min        Creation Time
10 min        Demonstration  10 min        Closing Circle

About Holiday Diversity:
To effectively address holiday issues, it is important to be aware of the cultural and religious backgrounds of those in your group.  You may need to work on this ahead of time to find out who celebrates Chanukah, Kwanzaa, Christmas, etc.  If there is someone in your group who is in the minority in terms of what they celebrate, it can help if you do some research into the meaning of their traditions and share a bit with the group.  This can be wonderful for the whole group.  (However, don’t put them on the spot by asking them to be the one to explain their traditions in front of the group, unless they want to).
 
 
 
  Sample of Holiday Wishes  Sample of Holiday Wishes 

Opening Circle:
Ask the children to share about how they are feeling about the holiday season. Sometimes during the holidays you can have all kinds of feelings, for example you might be excited and sad at the same time.

Then ask them to share one wish or hope they might have for either the holidays or for the New Year.  You can explain that it could be something they would like to change in the New Year or something they would like to be different. Ask the children to think of "things" that cannot be bought, maybe it is a special wish they might have for their family or something that would they want for their family to do together in the New Year.  It’s important to encourage the sharing of thoughts and ideas even though they may be difficult.  By sharing the tough stuff, they can see that many if us have similar feelings and maybe even similar wishes.

Demonstration:
Demonstrate the steps. it will help make the children comfortable with the materials.  As you demonstrate, be sure to stress that each participant can use the supplies however they want.  There is no right or wrong way.  Let them know they can make many lists and as they do that they will get more used to the Cray-Pas if they haven't used them before.

Step 1: Taping
Select the size of your paper and tape around the edges to the table.  This will create a clean looking border around the image.  Younger children will need help with this.  

   
  Use light color Craypas all over the paper
 
   
   
  Add dark colors over the light colors
 
   
   
  Scratch words through the layers of color
 
   
   
   
  Decorate the borders 
Step 2: Light Colors
Add a layer of light colors.  These will be the colors underneath your drawing—the colors you will be able to find when you scratch through your drawing with a toothpick!  Explain that they can press hard with the Cray-Pas and encourage them to cover the card with color.   Lighter colors could be yellow, pink, orange, white...

Step 3: Darker Colors
Next, add a layer of darker colors.  Add whatever colors you like to color over all the light colors you just colored on the card.  You could use blue, purple, green or black. Just remember to work light to dark.  It’s hard to put light colors over dark ones..

Step 4: Scratching
Next, you get to scratch through the darker colors which will show the light ones underneath.  You can create all kinds of beautiful detail with your scratching. Your scratches can be the words you thought of about the things you would wish or hope for the holidays and New Year.  You can write lists of words, draw pictures or write a poem.  It is up to you.
 
Step 5: Remove Tape
When you are ready, gently remove the tape.  If you pull too quickly, it may tear the paper, so be careful!   



Step 6: Borders
After you remove the tape, you may wish to draw designs into the border.  Enjoy!
 
Creation:
After the demonstration, welcome everyone to begin.  Remind them that they get to just “play around” with the colors.  They can experiment with the Cray-Pas and make as many lists as they wish.  If anyone is hesitant to begin, encourage them to start with a practice card one where they just try to make a “mess.”  Sometimes making messes leads to the very best discoveries.  

Closing:
Have all participants share what they created, and what they want to remember to take with them into the holiday season.
Row.txt_description: To provide the children an opportunity to and express their own wishes and hopes for the holidays and the New Year. In this workshop we learn how to create holiday cards that will express those wishes and hopes.
Row.txt_tips: This technique could be used any time of the year - not just for the holidays.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop gives participants the opportunity to create a postcard from themselves five years in the future, using drawing, collage and a sensory visualization. This process supports participants to focus on future goals and celebrates possibilities.

 
  Table set-up
  
Materials:
  • Magazines and photostock books
  • 8 ½” x 11” card stock (cut in half to create two large postcards that are 8.5”x5.5”) or large blank index cards
  • Glue sticks
  • Scissors
  • Colorful pens, pencils, and/or fine point markers
  • Optional Materials (if using collage): Mod Podge or glue solution (1 part water to 3 parts white craft glue, like Elmer's glue), to create a protective coating
Time Frame:
Preparation: 10 mins.
Introduction: 5 mins.
Relaxation: 15 mins.
Creation: 45 mins.
Closing: 15 mins.

Total: 90 mins.

Introduction:
"Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you. This means that this is a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, needs and visions. Since this space is your window of time, everything you do or say is voluntary. I'll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there's no right or wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. Please ask for what you need, and know that I'm here in support of you. If you can't think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just play with the materials.

“Today we will create postcards from our future self, five years in the future. You will have the opportunity to acknowledge anything that has happened in those five years, from new discoveries you've made about yourself, ideas you’ve come up with or things you’ve accomplished. You will create a picture of your life in the next five years on one side and on the other side write yourself a letter from your future self. Remember that no idea is too big to be possible or too small to matter. Trust yourself throughout this whole workshop.

“Let’s begin the creative process with a guided meditation. If you have never done guided meditation before, it is a relaxation process designed to reduce tension and anxiety and to increase awareness. 

“During this process of relaxation you may find your mind wandering or recall a worrisome moment from earlier today or in the past. That is normal. Simply acknowledge it and bring yourself back to your quiet, meditative place. For now give yourself permission to let go of all else, remember this is your special window of time. As with everything in this workshop, it’s your choice how to participate. If you’d like to follow my suggestions exactly, that’s just fine. If you’d like to ignore me and follow your own meditation, that’s okay, too.”

Relaxation:
"As you share this relaxation, take your time so that participants can slowly notice their bodies and respond to your suggestions.

“To begin, let your body sink back into your chair. Notice your entire body. What areas feel calm and relaxed? What parts feel tight or tense? Notice your breathing – feel your lungs expand and your chest rise and fall. Now, take a deep breath – in through your nose, out through your mouth. 

“Focus on your feet, how do they feel? Tighten the muscles in your feet and then release. Now focus on your calves. How do they feel? Tense them for a moment and then relax. Notice your hips and lower back and release any tension resting there. 
Travel up to your chest. How does it feel? Take another deep breath and let it out slowly. Now notice any sensations in your shoulders and neck. Push your shoulder blades firmly together and then release them. Now concentrate on your neck, turn your head gently from side to side to stretch your neck muscles. 
“Now take one more deep breath to prepare yourself for a mental journey to a safe, warm, and sunny beach. 
“Begin the journey by seeing yourself standing next to a beautiful palm tree on a seashore enjoying the sand, water, and sun. You hear the waves on the beach and the gentle call of the seagulls overhead. Take a moment to observe your surroundings. Incredibly, you are the ONLY one present, and it is a glorious day.

“Begin to walk along the beautiful seashore and enjoy what lies ahead. What kind of shoreline do you see? Is it grassy, rocky or open and spacious? What color is the water? Green, brilliant blue or a combination? Take a moment to breathe deeply in and out. 
“Continue your walk and keep noticing what you see around you. Are there seashells in the sand? Are there any you would like to take with you? If so, pick up the seashells and put them in your pocket and keep them to use as memories of this lovely day. 
“See the sun shimmering on the water and on the waves. Do you see any ocean life in the water?

“As you continue your walk, you suddenly see a reflection in the sand on the beach just ahead of you.  As you walk toward it, you bend down and find a bottle. And inside the bottle is what appears to be a note of some kind. 
“You clean the sand off the bottle and take the cork out and shake the note out of the bottle.  The note is from a stranger talking about glorious adventures and far away places. As you read you begin to wonder what glorious adventures and far away places might await you in the future. 

“Think for a moment about what you imagine your life will be like 5 years in the future. (pause) What will you accomplish? (pause) What new places and things will you experience? (pause) What WILL you do with your grand and glorious life?

“Release any hesitation or worry about HOW you will achieve what you desire. Know that it is already yours – you just have to ask. 

“Now take a moment to focus on your surroundings once more. Take one last look at the beach and appreciate the beauty of nature as you prepare to leave. Begin to make your way back along the beach until you reach the palm tree where you started. Know that as you walk you are taking the feelings of wonderment and curiosity about the future with you. 

“Now, take a deep breath and focus on the room where you are sitting. Notice how your muscles feel. Are any muscles more relaxed than before?

“And when you are ready, you may slowly bring yourself back to the room, open your eyes and begin to create your Postcard from the Future."

Creation:
On one side of their postcard, participants can write a letter to themselves as if it were five years in the future, appreciating any new perspective they’ve gained and acknowledging all the things that have gone well for them in those five years.

On the other side, participants can create a picture by collage or drawing (images, words, or symbols) that represents where they want to be in five years.

  
   
  
   
Closing:
"Now that you are finished with your project let's take a moment to honor your futures and any feelings that may have surfaced while creating your postcard." Invite each participant to share about their future and how the process of creating their postcard was for them. Remind participants that it is okay to pass.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives participants the opportunity to create a postcard from themselves five years in the future, using drawing, collage and a sensory visualization. This process supports participants to focus on future goals and celebrates possibilities.
Row.txt_tips: We encourage you to experiment with materials for this workshop including scrap booking supplies! Scrapbook, decorative, and card making paper; gift tags; punches; ribbons; etc. would make beautiful additions to this workshop.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
"Queen of the World" offers the chance to notice ones potential as empowered participants. The project encourages the participants to make choices and imagine their potential. As Queen of their World participants get to imagine and create a world in which they are in charge. Making this project in the form of the crown is a tangible commitment to self. This project also, provides a chance for the group to support each others dreams.


Materials:
  
 blank Discount School Supply crown
Card stock crowns (Discount School Supplies) click here for link - or make your own!
Scissors
Glue
Magazines
Stickers
Markers
Colored pencils
Sequins
Poem by Beatrice Schenk de Regniers "Queen of the World" click here for poem
Music (Women of Spirit by Putumayo World Music is reccommended)

Timeframe:
Intro: 5min
Relaxation: 10min
Creation: 45min
Closing: 5-15 min
Total Time: 65-70 minutes

Introduction:
Today we are going to imagine we are the queen of our world. Each one of us has a vision of what our world would be like if we were in charge. During this time each of you will have the opportunity to develop ideas that you can incorporate into your life. These ideas represent the best life for you. We are going to read a poem called "Queen of the World", meditate, and create a crown with the words, pictures and colors that represent your new world.


 
Relaxation:
We are going to take a few minutes to center ourselves in the moment. Close your eyes if you feel comfortable doing so, put your feet flat on the floor, and start to notice your breathing. While you are in this moment, I will read the poem......Now think about being the Queen of your world. What would that look like (pause)...Take a deep breath in/out...How does it feel ... what would your world sound like...Take a deep breath in/out. What words or pictures come to mind? Now go to your perfect world and begin to create it and being to visualize who you are as the queen of this world. What values, beliefs, responsibilities, are important to you? Breath in/breathe out/ relax deeply. Quiet...when you are ready to come back to the room you may open your eyes.

Creation:
Play music. These are the crowns and you can decorate them however you wish. The supplies are on the table. If there is any other art supply you would like to add let me know. Now let us begin to create our crown representing the power to create the life we love.

 Carly's finished crown
Closing:
Have everyone start by completing this sentence: "If I were queen of the world..."
Encourage everyone to share their crowns and how the process of creating them felt.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives participants the opportunity to be queen for a day by creating their own crown.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop is inspired by the words of wisdom and illustrations from "A Woman with Wings" by Patricia Varga.  A unique approach to journaling, this workshop shows the power of keeping a journal or sketchbook – the perspective i t provides on fear, negative programming, the life you can create and the healing it provides. 
 
  Art from A Woman With Wings

Materials:
A journal or sketchbook with lots of blank pages
A pen, special pens that the participants can keep is a great idea! (Such as Faber-Castell Artist Pens)
An open mind and heart
Relaxing music
A Woman with Wings intention quotes click here  OR A Woman with Wings Quote Card packets:
Gratitude Cards
Inspiration Cards
Leadership Cards
Passion Cards
Wisdom Cards
A basket or bowl for the intention quotes
A candle, preferably soy (optional)
Journaling Tips to give to participants (optional) click here

Time Frame:
Intro: 2 minutes
Power of Prayer Meditation/Journaling: 20-25 min.
Up A Flight of Stairs Meditation/Journaling: 20-25 min.
Finding your Genius Seed Meditation/Journaling: 20-25 min.
Intention quotes/Journaling: 20-25 min.
Total time: 60-90 minutes
Note: Please read the Tips section at the end of this workshop before getting started.

Introduction:
Patricia Varga created "A Woman with Wings" from a journaling exercise in July of 1993. She says, "I wrote my name a 1,000 times a day, even if I couldn’t write anything else – the act of selecting a pen and connecting with paper became a meditation that allowed me to connect with "The Divine" within – once I trusted this connection and allowed for my own abilities to come through, I found my voice, my place, my ability to create and heal."

"Once you trust this connection, (some call it "God", some call it "The Divine", some call it the "Goddess of Creativity", some call it "Self", some call it nothing at all,) the creativity and ultimate healing is limitless."

Today we will be exploring this connection through journaling.
 
 
  Sample set up
 
Creation:
As the participants sit quietly and comfortably, light a candle and say a few words of inspiration, a mantra or prayer. You may also read: "Surrender to the beauty, surrender to the light, rest, restore, reunite." which is Patricia's own prayer.

The Power of Prayer, and Meditation:
Have each participant go around the room and say one word to describe what they intend to get out of this workshop.  It could be peace, comfort, strength - each person will have their own word.

Start playing soft and gentle music, preferably with no words and encourage participants to begin to journal by taking your one word intention from the introductions, write it down and allow other words to tumble onto the page. Keep your hand flowing, even if you write the same word over and over. If you feel you want to develop your own prayer through this process do so. We'll take about 10 minutes to do this.

Ask a few participants to read what they wrote. As they share thank them for their willingness to share or courage to change.

  
 workshop participants during meditation
Guided Meditation #1: Up a Flight of Stairs
To begin the creative process, say or read the following:

If you are comfortable, close your eyes, and breathe, just breathe, for breath is like magic…
Your breath holds the knowledge of your pleasure; it holds the knowledge of your pain.
