Move your thoughts to your mind... knowing you can relax your mind just like a muscle ... take a deep breathe and go deep within and begin to meet your inner-self. What colors come to mind for your inner-self? What shapes or images arise as you meet your inner-self, are they large or small, round or heart? Is your inner-self male or female, are they young or old, is your image clear or foggy?

Greet your inner self, and ask him or her what they need from you... maybe a hug?.. maybe they just need you to sit and listen... take a moment and just spend some time getting to know and loving your inner-self.

Take a deep breath in and let it out, continue breathing comfortably and know that you can return to talk and share with your inner-self any time you want, reassure her/him you will be back! Hold onto all the images you saw and felt... now bring yourself back to the room  slowly open your eyes... and begin to create a portrait of your inner-self, selecting one of the techniques.

 
 Participants diligently working on their Inner Self Portraits!
 
Creation:
Remind participants that it doesn't have to look like anything in particular. Remember that is doesn't matter what it looks like, we offer three technique options to choose from. Ask the participants to follow their intuition and see what comes out.  Have fun! There are so many materials that it is good to give the participants time warnings.

Closing Circle:
Ask everyone to share their portrait and what it means to them. What did they discover? Are they pleased to meet their inner self. Were they surprised by who they found? What was most important for them to share about the experience or their art.
Row.txt_description: This workshop will assist the participant in going within and discovering more about their inner-self! This workshop gives us an opportunity to go to a deep level and expose, explore, celebrate and get more in touch with our inner-self... our inner most being. This workshop offers 3 different techniques to allow the participant to fully express their inner-selves. This is also a great project for an exhibit.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways.  Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
all photos courtesy of pinwheelsfo rpeace.com
 
Description: This workshop was taken from the Pinwheels for Peace website and adapted by AWBW staff. The Pinwheels for Peace art installation project started in 2005 by two Art teachers, Ann Ayers and Ellen McMillan, who teach at Monarch High School in Coconut Creek, Florida. Ann and Ellen started this project as a way for their students to express their feelings about what’s going on in the world and in their lives. The project was quickly embraced by their students and the entire school community and by millions of art teachers, teachers, parents, children and adults who desire peace in our world.

In this workshop everyone will create  pinwheels of all shapes and sizes on International Day of Peace, Sept. 21st as a public statement and art exhibit. The spinning of the pinwheels in the wind will spread thoughts and feelings about peace throughout the country and the world!

For more info, please visit: www.pinwheelsforpeace.com

 
  A girl creating her pinwheel from
pinwheelsforpeace.com
Materials:
Pinwheel templates (enough for each participant plus a few more in case people want to make another)
Peace symbols for the pinwheel center
Pencil with eraser
Markers, Crayons or colored pencils
Collage materials including glue (optional)
Scissors
Glue
Straight Pin (one per participant)

Preparation:
Make sure to create an example, or at least buy a pinwheel to show.

  
 Kids putting their pinwheels in the ground
from PinwheelsforPeace.com
 
Introduction:
"Everyday, we are bombarded with television images, video games, music, and magazine articles/newspapers that give importance to conflict and war. Violence has become commonplace and accepted as part of our society and, for some, it is a way of life. It is our hope that through the Pinwheels for Peace project, we can make a public visual statement about our feelings about war/ peace/ tolerance/ cooperation/ harmony/ unity and, in some way, maybe, awaken the public and let them know what we are thinking." (from pinwheelsforpeace.com) And for some us violence is part of our daily life, part of our home. We've seen it as commonplace, but also as a secret, something we have to hide and keep within our home.

 
 Creating Peace! from pinwheelsforpeace.org
 
The Pinwheels for Peace project believes the idea of peace "is not political. Peace doesn’t necessarily have to be associated with the conflict of war, it can be related to violence/intolerance in our daily lives, to peace of mind.  To each of us, peace can take on a different meaning, but, in the end, it all comes down to a simple definition: a state of calm and serenity, with no anxiety, the absence of violence, freedom from conflict or disagreement among people or groups of people."

Today we are going to create pinwheels for peace, writing about our feelings about peace on one side and on the other we will visually express our feelings.

Technical Demonstration:
Following the creation steps, show the participants how to create the pinwheel.

Warm Up (optional):
Have a brief discussion about what peace means, you may want to go around the room having each person talk about what peace means to them.

You also may want to read the book What is Peace? by Etan Boritzer to the children.

Creation:

 
 A pinwheel from the pinwheelsforpeace.com gallery
 
Getting Started
1) Cut the pinwheel square out from the template
2) On one side of the paper, write down your feelings about war/peace/tolerance/living in harmony. On the other side of the paper, use markers, colored pencils, paint, or other art media to visually express your feelings.
3)Following the lines on the template, cut in from all four corners, leaving about 2 inches of center uncut.

Creating the Pinwheel
1) Gently bend (don't fold) one of the cut corners to the center point.
2) Skip the next corner, and bend the next one.
3) Skip and bend until the four points meet in the center.
4) Then stick the straight pin through all four points AND the back of the pinwheel.
5) Stick the pin into the pencil eraser.
6) Use wind or your breathe to test our the pinwheel

For a video on how to create a pinwheel, go here.

Closing:
Have each person share their pinwheel. Remind them that the spinning of the pinwheels in the wind will spread thoughts and feelings about peace throughout the country, the world!

"On International Day of Peace, Sept. 21, 2009, "plant" the pinwheels outside as a public statement and art exhibit/installation. The spinning of the pinwheels in the wind will spread thoughts and feelings about peace throughout the country, the world!"

 A great installation example from the
Pinwheels for Peace gallery

Extra Bonus: Join the Pinwheels for Peace Project and see the 2 million Pinwheel locations across the nation and world!
Row.txt_description: In this workshop everyone will create pinwheels of all shapes and sizes on International Day of Peace, Sept. 21st as a public statement and art exhibit. The spinning of the pinwheels in the wind will spread thoughts and feelings about peace throughout the country, the world!

"Everyday, we are bombarded with television images, video games, music, and magazine articles/newspapers that give importance to conflict and war. Violence has become commonplace and accepted as part of our society and, for some, it is a way of life.

Following the creation steps, show the participants how to create the pinwheel.

Warm Up (optional):
Have each person talk about what peace means to them.

Creation:

 
 A pinwheel from the pinwheelsforpeace.com gallery
 
Getting Started
1) Cut the pinwheel square out from the template
2) On one side of the paper, write down your feelings about war/peace/tolerance/living in harmony. On the other side of the paper, use markers, colored pencils, paint, or other materials to visually express your feelings.
3)Following the lines on the template, cut in from all four corners, leaving about 2 inches of the center uncut.

Creating the Pinwheel
1) Gently bend (don't fold) one of the cut corners to the center point.
2) Skip the next corner, and bend the next one.
3) Skip and bend until the four points meet in the center.
4) Then stick the straight pin through all four points AND the back of the pinwheel.
5) Stick the pin into the pencil eraser.
6) Use wind or your breath to test out the pinwheel

For a video on how to create a pinwheel, go here.

Closing:
Have each person share about their pinwheel. Remind them that the spinning of the pinwheels in the wind will spread their thoughts and feelings about peace throughout the country and the world!

"On International Day of Peace, Sept. 21, 2009, "plant" the pinwheels outside as a public statement and art exhibit/installation. The spinning of the pinwheels in the wind will spread thoughts and feelings about peace."

 A great installation example from the
Pinwheels for Peace gallery

Extra Bonus: Join the Pinwheels for Peace Project and see the 2 million Pinwheel locations across the nation and world!
Row.txt_description: Participants get to create pinwheels of all shapes and sizes on International Day of Peace, Sept. 21st as a public statement and art exhibit. The spinning of the pinwheels in the wind will spread thoughts and feelings about peace throughout the country, the world!

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop utilizes our past experience with domestic violence to prevent us from being victims in the future.  We will learn how to identify red flags, or warning signs, of a potentially abusive relationship.  Participants will have an opportunity to discuss the red flags their batterer displayed and create an art project to help identify potentially abusive partners in the future. 
A personal Red Flag Banner
 
  "Never underestimate a woman's intuition."
 
  "It's a relationship that makes
your eyes sparkle"
Materials:
Red paper (cardstock works best)
Large flag template
Small flag templates
Glue
Scissors
Beads (optional)
Collage materials (Oprah magazine works best)
Permanent markers (dark colors and metallics)
3 to 5 yards of twine, string or clothesline
3 foot pieces of ribbon or yarn
Red Flags of Abusive Relationships Handout
Healthy Relationship Journaling Page
Pens

Time Frame:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 20 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing Circle: 20 minutes
Total: 1 hour, 15 minutes

 
Cutting out your Group Project Template
 
  
 
Cutting out your Individual Project Template 
Preparation:
First decide if you will create this project as a team project, individual project or both. For the team project we recommend using the large template and the smaller template for individual projects.
Print or copy flag template(s) onto red paper or hand out multiple templates and allow participants to trace. You may also want to pre-cut the flags in order to reduce the length of the workshop.
Print out copies of the Red Flag handout and Journaling handout for each participant.  To save time you may want to read through the Red Flag handout and highlight the bullet points you want to cover.  You may also choose to do this workshop in two sessions.

Outreach Program Note: 
Participants who are living with their abusive partners may not be able to take the flags home with them because of safety issues. You may present group project, which can be hung to serve as a reminder of the red flags of an abusive relationship. This will allow the participants to revisit their red flags every time they come to group.

Introduction:  
Have you ever thought, “I saw all the red flags and looked the other way”?  Red flags are intuitive warnings that let us know something is wrong.  All too often we silence that little voice inside of ourselves that warns us of a potential danger.  Abusive people are skilled at manipulating us into believing them and doubting ourselves.  Over time, abusers may convince us to automatically defer to what they think and want and to disregard our own needs, wants and opinions.  Today we are going to take a look back at the red flags from past abusive relationships, and then create our own red flags to honor and allow our inner voice, needs and desires to be heard. We can save ourselves a lot of frustration and pain in the future by practicing identifying our red flags. During this workshop you will also have an opportunity to notice the things your want in your future relationships.

Opening Circle:
Begin by passing out the Red Flags of Abusive Relationships handout and go over it as a group. Ask the participants to share about the red flags the saw in their relationship and how they reacted. 
 
 Writing out the Red Flags
 
 Creating a background image for the collage
 
 Gluing the inside of the flag together
 
  Tying a knot between each flag
For example, “I knew something was off when he said that all of his ex-girlfriends were crazy, but I rationalized that he was right because he was such a great guy and convinced myself I was being paranoid”.  Start the circle by asking someone to volunteer to go first and then have the rest of the group share one at a time.

Creation:
Now that we have identified some of our red flags, we are going to create a banner made of “red flags”. On one side we will simply write down the warning signs we have experienced in our past relationships as a reminder to not overlook or ignore the red flags of unhealthy relationships.  Encourage the clients to make more than one flag of time allows. Be sure to show a sample as a reminder of the two steps of the project. Allow about 10 minutes for everyone to write on one side of the flag.

After everyone has completed the first part of the project, hand out the Healthy Relationships Journaling page.  If you have time you may want to discuss the characteristics of healthy relationships, otherwise simply turn on some light music and give participants a few minutes to fill out their journaling page.  After most of the participants have finished journaling, lower the music and ask the participants to use the collage materials and markers to create a vision of the most important things they wish to have in future relationships on the other side of their red flag(s).  

If everyone is doing individual red flag banners, explain that they can begin to put their banner together by looping the first flag over the ribbon or string, gluing the insides together and then tying a knot or adding a bead between each flag. They can then take it home and hang it up as a reminder!

Closing:
Ask a volunteer start the closing circle by sharing something about the red flags they missed or ignored in past relationships and something about their future relationship collage.  If you are doing this as a group project, after each person shares, have them loop their flag over the clothesline or ribbon and glue the sides together. Then add either a knot or a bead before the next flag. Once everyone has put their flag on the line, ask for some one to volunteer to help you to hang the red flag banner! Thank everyone for sharing, participating and for creating an important reminder to pay attention to the red flags and break the cycle of violence!  End by reminding the participants that they deserve and are worthy of a healthy relationship.
Row.txt_description: In this workshop participants can learn how to identify red flags, or warning signs of a potentially abusive relationship. Participants will have an opportunity to identify the red flags they missed or ignored in past relationships and to notice the qualities they want in future relationships.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To teach children a new way to look at what they are currently thankful for and to imagine what they might be thankful for in their future.


 
 Supplies for Leaves of Thanks
 
Materials:
Green, orange, brown, yellow, red construction paper or card stock if available
Markers or crayons
Scissors
Glue sticks
Leaf template

 Time Frame:      
 Age Range: 
 30 to 45 minutes   3 to 12 year old
 




Preparation:
For younger children you might want to have the leaves precut.  If the children are able to cut for themselves you can have the leaves drawn on the paper ahead of time.


 
 Tracing the leaf image 
  
 Writing the words on the leaves 
  
Warm Up:
Ask the children to sit quietly and think about the things they experience in their life that they might feel thankful for.  Remind them that we often forget about the small things that happen, which we really are most grateful for. Things like a good meal, or a friend to laugh with, or learning something new at school or being able to play outside.  Have the children call out those things. If you like, you can write those things on a large piece of paper in the front of the room.  After they are done ask them to think about the kinds of things they might be thankful for in the future. It might be having a pet, or living in a safe place, going to college or getting a good job. Let their imagine go wild as they call out all the things they might have or be in their lives in the future.  These can also be written on the large paper.

Creation:
Using the leaf templates have the children cut out the leaves that they will write on.  If the children are young you might want to precut all the leaves, if the children are older you might want to pre draw the leaves for them to cut for them and if the children are old enough - they can trace, draw and cut on their own.

Step 1:
Set out the leaves and ask the children to write or draw messages or words on each remembering the things they said during the warm up.  Each leaf can have a word or sentence of each thing the child is grateful for.
Step 2:
Repeat this for the things that they think they will be grateful for in the future.
Step 3:
The leaves can be used to decorate the table for holiday dinners, or they could be hung on the wall or they can be used to create a wreath filled with things to be thankful for!

Closing Circle:
Talk about how it felt to be able to think about and then call out things they were thankful for, realizing that there are many things. Then you can ask the children what it was like to  think about their future and imagine what there will be to be grateful for.

  
 
  Leaves of Thanks centerpiece for the holidays
  Leaves of Thanks wreath
Row.txt_description: To teach children a new way to look at what they are thankful for now and what they might be thankful for in their future.
