Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give the clients an opportunity to focus on the good things and people they have in their lives and recognize those things they are grateful for, especially themselves and the positive choices they have made so far in their journey.
  
 Window's Intern Bree's Thank you card to herself
 

Materials:
Warm-up Handout
Cardstock or blank greeting cards
Envelopes (same size as cards)
Scrapbook paper
Pens (it's fun to have pretty pens too, like gels pens and glitter pens)
Glue sticks
Glitter or Glitter Pens
Fine point sharpies (optional)
Colored Pencils (optional)

Introduction:
Very often, we get caught up focusing about what we think is wrong,  what we don’t have, or what we want to be different.  Of course, there is nothing wrong with this since it is part of human nature.  However, when we tend to focus on the negative, we begin to forget the things we are grateful about, such as what is going right or what we do have and wouldn't change.

Gratitude is such a powerful and rewarding emotion.  It cannot be manufactured, but has to come on its own.  Sometimes it is there, but can go unrecognized for so long.  The activity for today is meant to give us an opportunity to sit and focus on what is good in our lives, and to give us a chance to acknowledge all of those people or things for which we are deeply thankful. 

It is very easy to thank others for their kindness and support, however, let us not forget to thank ourselves.  We have always been our own constant companions through our personal journeys of healing.  Today, let us remember and thank ourselves for all of the good things that we bring to our own lives for example healthy decisions, strength and love.

 
 "I'm so grateful for your perseverance..."
 

Warm-Up:
Pass out handout and play soft music. Let the clients know that they will have about 5 minutes to do the warm-up.

If clients seem to need more than 5 minutes, feel free to let them keep going, but give them a 1 minute warning before ending this exercise.

Once the time is up, let them know they will start a relaxation and then create a card to thank themselves.

Relaxation:
“Sit in a comfortable position.  Close your eyes.  Take a few deep breaths, and fill your lungs completely with air.  Feel the breath right down to your tailbone.  Let your mind quiet down.  Let go of all thoughts and focus on your breath.

Bring your attention to the middle of your chest, your heart space.  Imagine a ray of sunshine beaming its way to this space.  Fill the entire area with golden warmth.  Breathe in an feel this warmth deeply inside your chest, in a circle that encompasses the entire area including your actual physical heart.

Take a few moments to focus on how this golden warmth feels.  Bask in it.

After a few more breaths, inhale and draw this golden warmth up to the place right between your eyes.  Sit for a few moments and feel the warmth spread across your forehead.”

“With your attention on the warm golden glow on your brow, say thank you, quietly to yourself or out loud, for five things you are grateful to yourself for today.  For each thing you are grateful for, you can say:

            Thank you, (state your own name), I am grateful for __________.”

After listening to what you are thankful for, sit quietly and notice any feelings that have come up for you.  Take a few more long breaths, and feel again the golden warmth across your forehead and in your heart space.

Slowly open your eyes and re-enter the outside world.  Remember any feelings that you just experienced and carry these over into your creations today.”

(Adapted from Joy-Filled Living, Copyright 2006)

 
Bree's Thank Me Card- Reach for the Stars!
 

Creation:
Ask the clients to start their creation by choosing a card and beginning to write a letter to themselves, recognizing all the positive things they have in their lives and the positive choices they've made. If they feel stuck, have them refer back to the handout.

After writing their letter, they can jump right in to decorating their card(s)!  Welcome them to add extra pages to their card or to make multiple cards.

Don't forget this time is for you to relax and love yourself, to respect your own thoughts and feelings and anything that comes up today!

Closing:
Have the participants close the workshop by sharing their card, what they are most grateful for and one positive word about themselves.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives participants the opportunity to look at the things they are grateful for in their lives and appreciate themselves by creating a thank you card to themselves.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This project is great for all ages and enables the children to create a festive centerpiece to proudly display on their Thanksgiving dinner table.  While creating their Grateful Gobbler the children focus on what they are thankful for, and an optional exercise is included that allows the children’s family to share all of the things they are thankful for as well. 

  
The Grateful Gobbler
 
Materials:

Paper Plates (optional)

Orange liquid watercolor (to paint the plates orange) from Discount School Supply

Thick paintbrushes (to paint the paper plates orange)

Construction paper (red, brown, orange, yellow, and green)

Glue stick

Markers or crayons (to write on "feathers")

Scissors

Stapler

Wiggly Eyes

Grateful Gobbler face, feet and feathers templates

Grateful Gobbler body template


Time Frame:

1 hour total

Opening Circle: 20 minutes

Creation: 30 minutes

Closing: 10 minutes


Age Range:
Children 4 years old and older. One adult for every 6 children is recommended for children aged 4-7.


  
Assembling the Grateful Gobbler
 
Workshop Prep:
When working with younger children it is helpful to pre-cut all of the template pieces to make the creation process easier.  You can make the body with either construction paper (using the template) or a paper plate. 

If you decide to use paper plates it is helpful to have the children paint the paper plates with liquid watercolor. 
To paint with the liquid watercolor you can place the watercolor in a spray bottle that allows the children to spray the color onto the plate.  Another option is to put the liquid watercolor on a paint pallet and allow the children to paint their paper plate using a thick paintbrush.  The thick paintbrush will allow the children to cover their plate with paint faster. We suggest that you use liquid watercolor paint because it dries much faster than tempera paint and will allow the children to complete this project in one session.

Introduction:
How many of you have ever heard of the Grateful Gobbler?  Wow, I’m surprised that you haven’t heard of him!  He is a super happy bird that only comes around during the month of November because that is the one time of year where all of us take time to notice who or what we are grateful for.  The Grateful Gobbler is one of the happiest creatures in the world because his only job is to spread the love and appreciation we feel for the people, places and things that we are grateful for!  So you might be wondering just how he does this? Well every year the Grateful Gobbler waits until someone talks or draws about something they are grateful for, once that happens it is his job to deliver that message of gratitude to the person who the message is about (much like the owls from the Harry Potter books who deliver messages all over the world).  As you can imagine the Grateful Gobbler is VERY busy and can use our help, so today we are going to make our very own Grateful Gobblers to deliver our messages of gratitude to the people and things we are grateful to have in our lives.   

Opening Circle:
To get us started, I would like for each of you to think about one person, place or thing that you are super thankful for to have in your life?  Who or what has helped you this year?  It can be anything such as, I am thankful that I am not sick anymore, I am thankful for music, the beach, my mom.  Go around the room and have each child share one thing they are thankful for.
  
  
 Words on the feathers
 

 
Fold the short sides for the basket
 
  
 Folding the longer sides to create the basket
 
  
 Creating the corner of the Turkey "basket"
 
Creation: 
Begin by either painting your paper plate or tracing the template on a piece of orange construction paper.  Then cut it out, including the four slits on the template.  Cut out the template pieces, then trace onto the construction paper and have the children cut the pieces out.  Write words or messages about what you are thankful for on each of the feathers (you can make as many feathers as you like).   If they choose, the children can start each feather by writing “I am thankful  for…”  

To make the basket, begin by folding in the two small center sections, then fold the area between the slits.  Then overlap the two larger sections and staple them to the small section.  Repeat this process on both sides until the basket shape is formed.  Now, glue or staple the feathers to the back of the basket.  Glue the feet to the bottom, and glue the eyes, gobble, and beak to the face.  Finally glue the face to the front of the basket.    

Closing:
Be sure to affirm each child as you go around the room and ask each child to share something about their Grateful Gobbler.  After the children have shared, remind them that in order to help the grateful gobbler we all need to make sure to tell all of the people we are grateful for how much we love and appreciate them.  So if you put that you are grateful for your mom, make sure to tell her how you feel, it will make her feel good and save the Grateful Gobbler a trip!  You can also help recruit more people to help the Grateful Gobbler by sharing your project with family and friends at Thanksgiving dinner! Just have them share about what they are grateful for, write it on a piece of paper, and then place it in the Grateful Gobbler!  On behalf of the Grateful Gobbler I want to say thanks!  He is grateful for you!
Row.txt_description:
This project is great for all ages and enables the children to create a festive centerpiece to proudly display on their Thanksgiving dinner table. While creating their Grateful Gobbler the children focus on what they are thankful for, and an optional exercise is included that allows the children’
s family to share all of the things they are thankful for as well.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give participants time to reflect on the things they are grateful for in their past, present and future and to create beautiful leaves representing these things.

 
 Completed Leaves of Thanksgiving made into a centerpiece
Materials:
Writing paper
Pens
Leaf template printed on cardstock in fall colors (1 page per participant)
Tissue paper in fall colors
Scissors
Permanent markers
Mod Podge or water-glue solution (3 parts glue for 1 part water)
Sponge brushes or extra large bristle brushes
Timer
Samples

Prep:
Print the leaf template onto cardstock in fall colors. Each participant will need 3 leaves.

It's a good idea to create samples of the different ways to use the tissue paper ahead of time.

 
Don't forget to prepare your space, make sure you have enough supplies and lay out the templates, markers, etc. in an inviting way.

Time Frame:
Prep: 10 mins — 45 mins
Intro: 3 mins
Warm Up: 6 mins
Creation: 30 — 60 mins
Closing: 10 — 20 mins
Total: 60 mins — 1hr 20mins


Introduction:
Today we're going to take some time to reflect on our past, our present and our dreams about future possibilities. We're going to have some time to reflect on these times in our life and the things we are thankful for. We're also going to get a chance to create beautiful leaves to represent our gratitude and serve as reminders of the good things in our lives.

Journaling or Paired Sharing Warm-Up:
To begin, choose if you would like participants to have 3 short listening times or 3 short journaling times. Then, tell participants that you will provide them with 3 topics to discuss or journal. Tell them that you will keep time, and ask them to keep sharing or journaling until you say stop. Either way, make sure you let them know in advance how much time they will have to share with their partner or to journal on the topic. Have a timer ready.

For the first prompt, ask them to share or write for 2 minutes about things that have happened to them in the past that were unwelcome challenges or struggles, but for which they are now grateful.

For the second prompt, ask participants to share or write about people (including themselves) in their life, for whom they are thankful for at the present moment.

Finally, let the participants know that this will be their last prompt. Ask them to share or write about what they hope to be thankful for five years from now. Have fun, be creative, and dream big for your future!

Using the Mod Podge as a top coat
Different fall leaves
Rolled tissue, to create texture

Creation:
Tell the participants they can choose any three leaves they would like. They will create one leave to represent something they are grateful for in their past, one leaf to represent something they are grateful for currently in their lives, and one leaf for their future!

Explain to participants how to use Mod Podge or the glue solution.
  • Mod Podge dries clear
  • It can be used as glue to stick the tissue to the leaf or applied as a top coat/sealer to give it a more finished look
  • The tissue can be layered using the Mod Podge or the glue solution.
  • Another option is to dip the tissue in the glue and manipulate it to create different textures.
Have participants decorate with tissue and write words onto the leaves. Using the permanent markers, they can write directly onto the leaf or onto the tissue paper.

Closing:
Ask participants to share their creations and how it felt to notice what they have that they are thankful for. For example, "I am thankful that I can dream and that I can have a future that I want!"
Row.txt_description: This workshop give participants time to reflect on the things they are grateful for in their past, present and future and time to create beautiful leaves representing these things.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
The goal for this workshop is to empower survivors to appreciate their inner child, that strong, powerful little girl who holds their secrets, protects them, likes to eat pancakes for dinner, loves pink ribbons, and is always there!

Materials:
Scrapbook Journaling Page - printed on pretty paper
 
 Celebrating Rosie, by Rose Curtis
A childhood photo or image for each participant
12 x 12 decorative paper or scrapbook paper and cardstock
Collage materials of all sorts
Glue sticks
Fabric
Stickers
Glitter
Ribbon and/or lace
StazOn ink pads
Stamps
Scissors
Chipboard letters
Stapler
Relaxing Music

Prep:
Make sure to ask participants ahead of time to bring a picture of themselves as a child or image to represent themselves.

It's always great to have an example on hand to show participants.

Time Frame:
Intro: 5 minutes
Opening: 10 minutes
Technical info: 5 minutes
Creation: 70 minutes
Closing Circle: 15 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour and 10 minutes

 
In My World by Karen
When I was young I would hide in a closet and
create & imagine beautiful things in my mind.
Pretty safe and loving places in my mind.  		 
Introduction:
Within each of us there exists an amazing inner child, someone who may not have ever been celebrated! She's a darling, caring, powerful little girl who has been waiting for us to acknowledge her, to applaud her, and to sing her praises! This workshop gives the participant the opportunity to do all of that!

Opening:
Have the group members share the photo or image they brought to create their page about and share something they appreciate about the little girl in the photo!

Journaling:
Pass out Journaling page and give participants at least 10 minutes to journal.

Relaxation:
During the relaxation, it's good to sit with your feet flat on the floor, your hands lying loosely in your lap, and begin to feel your chair holding you very comfortably and safely! If it feels safe for you, close your eyes and begin to picture in your mind... the photo of yourself as a little girl, ... take a deep breath and let it go... breath deeply and begin to feel your body intuitively relaxing... wiggle your toes, feel the calves of your legs relaxing... keep breathing deeply, letting out any stress your body might be holding, move your breath up to your thighs and feel them relaxing. Breath in deeply...let it go... and focus on your stomach... release any fear you might have about loving this little girl ... feel the fear melting, and unconditional love taking its place! Move up to your shoulders and wiggle them around... feel your body intuitively relaxing more, roll your head around allowing all the stress to leave your neck. Breathing deeply, begin to relax your jaws, your mouth, wiggle your eyebrows and just feel totally relaxed. Taking another deep breath, allow your mind to just relax and let go of everything else for right now...
Picture in your mind what your inner child looks like... see her hair, her face, her nose, take a look into her eyes, notice everything about her from her chin, to her knees, to her toes... ... see yourself as a child...and remember your strengths, ... think about some of your likes as a little girl,  some of your favorite toys or favorite games to play... let happy memories of childhood come back to you.
Now slowly and gently begin to bring yourself back to the room, holding on to all the images you saw in your mind; slowly open your eyes and begin to create your inner child's scrapbook page.

 
 Precious Baby
by Rose Curtis
"When I see you, I see someone so sweet and innocent
Someone who is still able to see the good in life
despite the evilness that hurt you in your past.
I love your sweet innocence that hides your
inner fierceness!"
Creation:
Begin to transform your inner child scrapbook page.  If negative feelings start to come up for you, know that you are ready to handle them and you can always stop and take some time to journal about them. This journaling can be included on the front of your page as part or the page or mounted on the back of your scrapbook page, for only you to see

Closing:
Give time for everyone to share what they experienced. Encourage each participant to share their page, and share the special qualities their inner child brings to them.
Row.txt_description: Some people believe that the holidays are for the children. The goal of this sweet and powerful scrap booking workshop is to empower survivors to appreciate their inner child, that strong powerful little girl who holds their secrets, protects them, likes to eat pancakes for dinner, loves pink ribbons and is always there!

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To help the clients redirect any negative holidays feelings and focus on the positive changes they are making.

 
Materials:
Clear Glass Ornaments- 3 per person (Try dollar store-3pks for .99)
Rubbing Alcohol
Funnel or spray bottle
Cups (2 per person)
Acrylic Paint- lots of small bottles is best (even the cheap stuff works)
Blank Christmas/Holiday Cards
Pens
Newspaper for tables

Time Frame:
Total Time: 1hour

Prep:
Cover the tables in newspaper and put the paints in the center of the table. Put two cups at each person's place setting.

Keep the ornaments aside until it is time to start dropping paint into them...build the anticipation of holiday cheer!

Introduction:
Negative feelings or thoughts may feel particularly intense during the holidays, so today we will be creating affirmation ornaments. These ornaments can be a reminder of your resolve, your will, and your road to self-love, a reminder that you deserve peaceful holidays, filled with joy and love. 

Relaxation:
Ask everyone to get comfortable in their chair, and if it feels safe, they may close their eyes. Ask the participants to wrap their arms around themselves as if they were giving themselves a hug. Ask the participants to notice their breathing. Take a deep breath in and let it out, continue to breath comfortably, inhale and exhale, and complete this sentence silently to yourself: "I am proud of myself because..."(pause). Take a loving breath for this affirmation. Breathing comfortably, inhale and exhale, and notice your breathing. Complete this sentence silently to yourself: "I deserve..."(pause). Don't censor yourself, let your imagination run wild. You are a beautiful person who deserves to chase and embrace your
joy...(pause). Still breathing comfortably, take a loving breath for this affirmation. Think to yourself and complete this sentence silently: "I will..."; if can be something small or something big. Breathe in positivity and breathe out negativity. Take a breath in for your "I will..." statement. Take a deep and loving breath for all of these affirmations.

 
  
 
  
 
  
 
Creation:
Start by asking participants to choose a color, or as many colors as they want to represents all the positive changes they've made in their life. Then, bring out the ornaments and bask in the holiday excitement you will hear and see all around! Give participants 3 ornaments each.

Demonstrate how to create the ornaments using the steps below.  Ask participant to use their first ornament as a way to practice using this method and to play with the colors. 

Steps:
1.    Show everyone how to pull the hanger and cap out of the glass ornament; remind them to be careful, as the ornaments are delicate.
2.    Rinse the bulb by spraying or dripping a tiny bit of rubbing alcohol through the funnel into the bulb and swish it around. Pour out any excess alcohol into the cups.  Make sure to allow the ornaments to dry thoroughly.
3.    Drip paint inside the glass bulbs using the colors you chose.  Allow the paint to drip down the inside of the ornament and start slowly turning it around inside the ornaments. Participants can keep adding colors and swirling the bulb. If it is cold in the room, the paint will flow slowly. You can water down the paint a little in the bottle if you wish, or tell the participants to let the bulb lay on its side and turn it every 5 minutes or so. If you wish, you may use small beads and drop them into the bulb to help swirl the paint.
4.    Drain the excess paint into the cup.
5.    Dry the ornaments by resting them in the ornament box it came in, an egg carton, or paper cup. It may take a few days to dry completely. Once the bulbs are dry, replace the hanger and hang as decoration or on a Christmas tree.
If time allows, let the clients create two or more ornaments.

Closing:
Participants may close by creating their holiday card to themselves. Or you may go around the circle and have participants share their ornaments and one word describing how they are feeling.
Row.txt_description: Leader Shelley Huff created this workshop to help clients redirect any negative holidays feelings to focusing on the positive changes they are making.
Row.txt_tips:
While the ornaments are drying:
·      Give the participants the opportunity to write a holiday card that they give to themselves.
·      Serve cookies and something warm (hot chocolate, coffee or cider).
·      If you choose to play holiday music please ask permission from participants, as it may trigger sad, nostalgic or traumatic feelings.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop provides children an opportunity to notice the people who are special in their lives during the holiday season. The children will create felt gingerbread people as a reminder of the people who have had a positive influence on them or have been supportive to them. This is especially important because the holidays can be a difficult time and this workshop helps the children focus on the positive in their lives.


 
 Felt gingerbread people set up
 
  
  
  
  
  Felt Gingerbread people 
Materials:
Skin tone color felt
Gingerbread people template 
Scissors
Tacky Glue
Tape
Popsicle Sticks
Yarn
Buttons
Ribbon, Trim
Novelty papers
Construction paper
Wiggly eyes

Time Frame:
        
 Age Range:
 1 – 1 ¼ hours  Ages 6-13




Preparation:
For younger children you might want to have the gingerbread people cutout ahead of time.
If the children are able to cut for themselves you can have the gingerbread people shapes drawn on the felt ahead of time.
Note: this workshop can also be done with paper people - see the tips below.

Introduction:
Special people help us feel safe and happy, they are people who are on our side and support us through good times and bad times.  A special person can be someone we have known our whole lives, someone we have known for a few years, or a person we just met. These people can be family members, friends, or teachers. They can be older or younger than you. The holidays are a great time to remember and celebrate the people who are special to us. During our project today, you will decorate gingerbread people that represent you and the special people in your life. Then, you will tie your gingerbread people together to show how you are all connected.

  
 Making a small slit at the end of the hands
 
  
 Threading the yarn to tie the gingerbread
people together
 
  
 Tying the people together with a bow
 
  
 Taping a Popsicle stick to the back
 
Opening Circle:
Ask the children to sit in a circle. Have them bring a paper and pencil. If they feel safe doing so, ask them to close their eyes, and think about all the people that are special to them. You may want to ask the children to think of someone who makes them feel safe when they are scared, or is there someone that can always make them laugh when they are sad? Instruct the children to write down the names of the people who are special to them.

Creation:
Step One
Begin by asking the children to create a gingerbread person that represents them. Using the template the children can trace and then cut out a gingerbread body, then decorate the cutout any way they like. They can add clothing, hair and accessories, if they like.

Step Two
Next ask the children to follow the same steps to create gingerbread people representing the rest of the special people on their list.

Step Three
When all the people are created, help the children cut a small slit at the end of each hand. Then use an 8-inch piece of yarn or ribbon to string the gingerbread people together, making a bow at each hole to keep the people in place.

Step Four
Tape a Popsicle stick to the back of each person to keep them from flopping over. The children may need help with this also.

Step Five
Tie a loop on first and last person so you can hang all the people on a wall.

Closing:
At the end of the workshop, ask the children to think about one of the people they created and what it is that made that person special to them. Allow each child an opportunity to share about that person with the group if they want to.

Ask the children to hold up their connected people and remind them that each of those people represents someone who is special in their life. Suggest that they might want to show their project to one of the special people in their life and tell them just how special they are.  You can also help the children (or show them how to) hang their gingerbread people on a wall by using the loops you created one the end of the first and last gingerbread person.



          
   
  Tying the gingerbread people together and hanging on a wall
Row.txt_description: This workshop provides children an opportunity to notice the people who are special in their lives during the holiday season. The children will create felt gingerbread people as a reminder of the people who have had a positive influence on them or have been supportive to them. This is especially important because the holidays can be a difficult time and this workshop helps the children focus on the positive in their lives.
Row.txt_tips: If you already have paper people you can create the gingerbread people using those as the forms.

Row.txt_code:
Ornament painted on the inside
 
Ornament filled with beads
 
Objective:
To create a holiday ornament that helps the children redirect any negative feelings about the holidays and focus on the many ways they are special. 

Materials:
Clear plastic ornaments - approximately 3 per person
(Discount School Supply (DSS) has 3 different shapes - 12 for $6.95 minus your AWBW discount)
Acrylic paint or BioColor paint (DSS)
Ribbon in various colors
Brushes
Newspaper for tables
Optional Additional Supplies:
Make it Glitter or Make it Shimmer Paint Additive (DSS)
Glitter, Pom poms, feathers, colored sand

Time Frame:
Total Time: 1 hour

Age Range:
6 - 16

Prep:
Cover the tables in newspaper and put the paints and embellishments in the center of the table. The decorating does not take a very long time so you might want to have up to 3 ornaments available for each participant. Since the children will be working with acrylic paint, you may want to provide smocks or oversized t-shirts to protect their clothing.  Making a mess is half the fun!

Note: We are using clear plastic ornaments, but if you have older children or teens you might want to use the clear glass type.

Introduction:
Sad feelings or thoughts may happen during the holidays. It's okay to feel sad for what you have lost or wish you had. When we're feeling sad it helps to think about what makes us happy too. Today we will be creating our very own joy ornaments. These ornaments can be remind you of your special qualities and special happy memories that you have or hope to have.

Opening Circle:
We are going to make this holiday season extra special by thinking about all the ways you are special. Each of you are special in your own way, so as we go around the room please say one thing about yourself that makes you the special person that you are.  It could be that you are special because you help your sister or brother, or maybe you are special because you are nice to the other children, or maybe you have a nice smile...there are many things that make you special!  Today we are going to make ornaments to remind us about all the ways we are special and each ornament can represent one of those special things.

 
 Empty clear ornaments
 
 
 Pouring paint inside
 
 
 Swirl the paint
 
Demonstration:
Have the ornaments on the table ready for the children to choose from. Explain to the children that they will be decorating the ornaments from the inside out.  There are several ways to decorate the inside so ask the to  pay close attention and watch what how you do it first.

Steps:
1. Add a few drops of BioColor paint or other acrylic paint to the ornament. If you have the Make it Shimmer or Make it Glitter by BioColor, you can add a few drops to get a shimmery effect. If you don't have it, you could also use regular glitter.
2. Simply swirl or lightly shake the ornament and the paint will create a fun marble like effect inside.

Another option if you don't have paint is to paint (or swirl) the inside of the ornament with a mixture of glue and water; then sprinkle in glitter, colored sand, beads, colored rice or confetti - you can even add pom poms or feathers!

Creation:
Ask the children to choose one ornament to represent a special thing about themselves. The children can select special things they like or favorite colors so the ornament is a person reflection of themselves. As they finish the first ornament, welcome them to take another one that represents a special memory or something or someone that makes them happy. For the third ornament, ask them to to fill it with wishes for the future.

Closing:
When the ornaments are completed you may go around the circle and have the children share their ornaments and one thing that makes them special.
Row.txt_description: To create a holiday ornament that helps the children redirect any negative feelings about the holidays and focus on the many ways they are special.
Row.txt_tips:
WARNING: CHOKING HAZARD - Small parts. Not for children under 3 yrs.

 WARNING: CHOKING HAZARD - Toy contains a small ball. Not for children under 3 yrs.

 WARNING: CHOKING HAZARD - Toy contains a marble. Not for children under 3 yrs.

 WARNING: CHOKING HAZARD - This toy is a marble. Not for children under 3 yrs.

 WARNING: CHOKING HAZARD - This toy is a small ball. Not for children under 3 yrs.

 WARNING: CHOKING HAZARD - Children under 8 yrs. can choke or suffocate on uninflated or broken balloons. Adult supervision required. Keep uninflated balloons from children. Discard broken balloons at once.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To help children make resolutions for the new year by deciding what they would wish for in their lives (other than material things) and creating a personal wishing well.

 
 Wishing Wells
Materials:
Basic Supplies:
Paper drinking cups (one for each participant)
Colored tissue paper (Be sure to have earth tone colors in the mix)
Mod Podge or make your own with a solution of 1/2 water 1/2 white glue
Thick paint brushes for Mod Podge
Paper towels
Pipe cleaners
Scissors
Hole punch
Permanent markers
Small stones (available at building supply/garden stores/in nature)
Paper and Pens
Optional Supplies:
Glitter
Sequins
Yarn
Embellishments of your choice


  
  Gathering Rocks
Time Frame:
45 minutes — 1-hour

Age Range:
7 — 13 year old


Workshop Prep:
You might want to collect stones ahead of time by going on a nature walk with the kids, or if you like, you can create your own stones by using sculpey (see tips). 

Introduction:
Today we are going to start making plans for the New Year.  Sometimes you hear grown-ups making something called "a new years resolution", a resolution is a decision that you make to change something or make it better in your own life. For example, my resolution is to exercise more to keep me healthy; your resolution could be to get better grades.

All resolutions start with having a wish to do something.  You can make many of your wishes come true by working hard and never giving up. Today, we are going to think about those wishes and make our very own wishing well.  Remember the wishes we are making today are not for things you want from other people, these are wishes you want for yourself.

 
 Decorating the rocks
Warm Up:
Before we start this project, I want us to let go of any disappointments we had last year. We are going to write down any things we wish we hadn't
happened.

Opening Circle:
Ask the children to think about what they would wish for if they could.  Encourage them to think about something other than things you can buy, like toys or candy.  You might want to suggest some things like - more time to play, or learning how to swim, or someone to teach them to play an instrument. You may want to help the younger children to write down their wishes, and the older children can write them down themselves.

Creation: 
Ask each child to select any 3 stones and write one wish on each of the stones.  Set the stones aside while they create the wishing well.

Each child gets a cup and they can decorate it anyway they choose, using the tissue paper and Mod Podge.  You can have them cut or rip shapes and pieces of the tissue paper and use the Mod Podge to help stick the pieces all the way around the cup.  If you like you can add glitter, ribbons, foam stickers, pom poms and any embellishments you would like to use. 

Punch two holes across from each other near the top of the cup and attach the pipe cleaners for the handle; you can loop the pipe cleaner around the hole to get it to stand up on top of the cup.

 
 Inside side view of a Wishing Well
Place blue crumpled up tissue inside the cup, to look like water.  Place the stones inside.

Closing:
Ask the children to show their wishing wells and if they like, they can talk about the 3 wishes they placed inside.
Row.txt_description: To help children make resolutions for the new year by deciding what they would wish for in their lives (other than material things) and creating a personal wishing well.
Row.txt_tips:
Materials:
Super Sculpey Polymer Clay
Toaster Oven
The older children might have fun creating their own rocks for this project.  Sculpey works well for this. You might want to demonstrate how to make swirly Sculpey rocks first.

 
1. Snakes of each color wrapped like
a candy cane		 2. Roll up the snakes into a ball

  
3. Making a snake out of the ball and
twist again		 4. Flatten the ball to become
the rock

Step One: Choose at least two colors.

Step Two: Roll each color into a snake.

Step Three: Wrap each snake around each other like a candy-cane and roll together.

Step Four: Twist each little section of the roll until the colors are blended just the way you want them.

Step Five: Roll the snakes into a ball, and if you want, repeat step Four & Five to create more swirlies. Once you have rolled just the right amount of swirlies, flatten the ball to be stone.

Step Six: Bake the Sculpey at 275 degrees for 15 minutes for each ¼ inch of clay thickness. You can use a thick piece of paper grocery bag to line the tray in your toaster oven or in a conventional oven, you can use foil lined cookie sheet. Always allow the clay to cool completely before handling it.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To help participants dream about the new year, a new life free of violence, full of hopes and wishes.

 
 Two Wishing Wells, Inside & Out!
 
Materials:
Basic Supplies:
Super Sculpey Polymer Clay
Toaster Oven
Scissors
Hole punch
Paper drinking cups (one for each participant)
Pipe cleaners
Colored tissue paper (Be sure to have earth tone colors in the mix)
Mod Podge or make your own with a solution of 1/2 water 1/2 white glue
Thick paint brushes
Paper towels
Permanent markers
Optional Supplies:
Glitter
Sequins
Yarn
Embellishments of your choice

Time Frame:
45 minutes - 1 hour

Prep:
It's great to make a sample Wishing Well for participants to view.
To make it easier for the participants to choose colors, you may want to break up the pieces of Sculpey.

Introduction:
Did you know January comes form the Latin word meaning "the door to the year." Today we get to think of this door, and what we want to open the new year to. Today we are going to think about the next steps we are taking in our lives in a fun and creative way, by making a New Year Wishing Well. Take this opportunity to open the door to a hopeful new year and  new life free of violence.

Demonstration:
 
 Making snakes and a candy cane.
 
 
 Rolling up the snakes.
 
 
 Making a snake out of the ball...and twisting again.
 
 
 Squishing to ball of clay to be a stone.
 
 
 A finished wishing stone!
 
It's great to demonstrate how to make swirly or marbled stones out of Sculpey before the relaxation so that they can jump right in.
Demonstrate using the following steps:
Step One: Choose at least two colors.Use no more than a pinch of each color to make the appropriate size stones.
Step Two: Roll each color into a "snake".
Step Three: Wrap each "snake" around each other like a candy-cane and twist together.
Step Four: Twist each little section of the roll until the colors are blended just the way you want them.
Step Five: Roll the "snakes" into a ball. If you want, repeat steps 4 and 5 to create a more marbled effect.
Step Six: Flatten the ball to be stone.
Step Seven: Use a thick piece of paper or grocery bag to line the toaster oven tray. In a conventional oven you can use a foil lined cookie sheet. Bake the Sculpey at 275 degrees for 15 minutes (for each ¼ inch of clay thickness). Always allow the clay to cool completely before handling it.

Warm Up/Relaxation:
We're going to start this workshop by choosing a piece of clay, but before we begin, I'm going to ask each of you to take a minute to think about your wishes or hopes for your new life.

Be creative. Try to wish for something you  can't buy in a store.  You could wish for more time with your children, the courage to apply for a Restraining Order, or to love yourself more.

Once you're ready, I'm going to ask you to choose the clay in a color that represents one of your wishes. As you take the clay, begin to warm and play with it, squish it in your hand over and over.

If you feel safe, go ahead and close your eyes with your feet on the floor. Let's start by taking a deep breath in, a deep positive and loving breath for your whole body. Now exhale that breathe all the way from the bottom of your feet. Let's take a moment to think about wishes and all of your hopes for the future.

Think about the door to the new year opening to a realm of possibilities, possibilities for a new life. Take a deep breath in as you see the door opening to your new year, and exhale that deep breath. As you look through the door, feel a comforting new you embracing you into this new year. Your wishes may be as fun, simple or elaborate as you want.  Wish whatever crazy thing you want for your life. Take a deep breath in for that first wish you thought of, and exhale a deep love for that wish.

Now begin to think about the other wishes you have for your new year.  Feel free to take as much time as you need to sit in the moment and listen to wishes from your heart.

Creation: 
Ask participants to decide what wishes are most important to them and to begin creating their wish stones. Have them start with two and remind them to choose colors that represent those wishes. It may be a good idea to remind them that a pinch of each color is all they will need to create each stone.

Once participants are done creating their wishing well stones, begin to bake. While the stones are baking, participants will create their well.

Using the tissue paper and Mod Podge, give each participant a cup to decorate any way they choose.  Participants can cut, rip or tear shapes and pieces of the tissue paper and use the Mod Podge to help layer the pieces all the way around the cup.  If participants choose, they can add glitter, ribbons, foam stickers, pom poms and any embellishments provided.

After decorating, participants will punch two holes across from each other near the top of the cup and attach the pipe cleaners for the handle by looping the pipe cleaner.

For the last portion of the wishing well, have the participants place blue crumpled up tissue inside the cup to look like water to keep their wishing stones.

Closing:
Ask the participants to share their creations, and if they like, they can talk about the 3 wishes they placed inside.
Row.txt_description: This workshop uses the soothing and often cathartic exercise of working with Sculpey clay to create stones for a new year's Wishing Well, which they will also create!

Row.txt_code:
Objective
To give children the opportunity to build or recreate a friend.  This friend can represent a friend that they had in the past and maybe lost touch with after moving from one place to another. Or, if the child hasn't really had a close friend before, they can create one with the characteristics that they would like their true friend to have.

 
 
  Workshop supplies
 
Materials
Shape of a person (people paper pad)
Scissors
Glue sticks
Tissue paper
Construction or novelty paper
Colored pencils
Permanent markers
Transparency sheets
Magazines to collage (optional)
Laminating sheets (optional)
Dearest Friend Template (click here if needed)
The Word Friend Template (click here is needed)

Time Frame
1 to 1 1/2 hours

  
 
  Pre-cutting may be necessary
 
   
  Words from the Word Friend Template
 
Age Range
6 and older

Setup
Lay out the people paper with all the college materials.  Make certain there are enough "people" for each child to make one. You can purchase precut people or cut them from the template provided. Younger children will need help to cut the border out on the people paper.

Warm-up
Print out the Word Friend Template provided and cut out the words.  Sprinkle the words all over the table (like confetti).
As the participants enter the room instruct them to choose whichever version of the word friend they like.  Tell the children they can use any colors, designs, etc. that remind them of a friend, then decorate their word.

Next go around the room and have each child share what the word friend means to them, or they can say some words that describe good friends - such as honest, fun, trust worthy, kind, caring or anything else that comes to mind when they hear the word friend.

Introduction
In today's workshop we will create a friend. This friend will be created in honor of a special person that has always been there for you and that you consider your dearest friend. Give examples of places and ages where these friends might have been.  If you prefer, you can create a whole new friend, someone that has all the qualities you ever wanted in a friend.

Creation
Ask the children to sit comfortably and relax.  Ask them to think back to a time when they had a special friend, someone who was always there for them.  Someone they could talk to, someone to play with, someone who liked to do some of the same things they liked to do. Maybe this friend was very special to them a long time ago, but they lost touch with them for one reason or another. Ask them to think about the good times they had and the adventures they shared together as they recreate their friend. 

If someone shares that they have never had a friend you can tell them to imagine what a friend would be like and the qualities that special friend would have.  Maybe the friend would be a good listener, or someone who liked to laugh or maybe someone they could trust with secrets.  When thinking about what they would like from a friend, ask them to think about how they can be a good friend to someone else too.

Steps:
   
  Writing words about your friend
 
   
   
Step One:
Use either pre-made people shapes or the template provided, each child can pick one.
Step Two:
Cut a border around the entire people shape and glue a transparency sheet behind then cut out the transparency just out side the border.
Step Three:
Decorate the friend in any way you like using the supplies available.  You can make clothes out of tissue paper, construction paper or any novelty paper. Or, you can simply write words, shapes or pictures that remind you of your dearest friend.

Step Four:
If you like, you can hang the friend in a window by punching a hole at the top and putting a ribbon or yarn looped through the hole, and let the light shine through.

Ask each child to create their own friend, as they would like.  When working with younger children offer to help them with either cutting or writing words.

Closing Circle
Give everyone the opportunity to share what it was like to create his or her dearest friend.  What memory did they have of this friend?  Who was this special friend?  Do they still keep in touch?  Or, what was it like to imagine what specific qualities you would like from a friend. Talk a little about how wonderful it is to have a good friend and how special it is to be a good friend.

   
 
  Outline of your fiend with
transparency behind
 
 My Dearest Friend
Row.txt_description: To give children the opportunity to build or recreate a friend. This friend can represent a friend that they have had in the past and maybe lost touch with after moving from one place to another. Or, if the child hasn't really had a close friend before, they can create one with the characteristics that they would like their true friend to have.
Row.txt_tips:
My Dearest Friend can be constructed by collaging or writing directly on the people paper without cutting out the border using the transparency sheet behind, as shown in these photos.  You can then laminate the friend if you like using laminating sheets that are available at any office supply s tore.
   
 
  My Dearest Friend "Beatris"
done with collage
  My Dearest Friend "Edgar"
done using words

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To allow participants to identify positive affirmations through different forms of meditation. Participants will meditate through a listening style called Lectio Divina and and create a beautiful Shrinky Dink Mandala.
 
Materials:
Affirmation Quote Page English/ Spanish (cut into strips)
Affirmation Poem (1 per participant)
Mandala Template / Blank Mandala Template
 Pens
Color pencils
Pencil sharpener
Permanent markers
Shrinky Dink paper
Scissors
Hole punch
Key rings or ribbon
Toaster oven

Prep:
Prep time will take about 10 minutes, but it's very important to make sure your toaster oven is working. Print copies of the Affirmation Poem to place at each seat. Print the Affirmation Quote Page and cut the affirmations into strips and sprinkle them all over the table for the participants.

Intro:
Today we are going to focus on an affirmation for our life, while creating a mandala on a Shrinky Dink that we can keep to remind us of that affirmation. We'll do this through different types of meditation. Before we get started though, does anyone know what an affirmation is? (You may want to get a couple people to explain what they think an affirmation is) Put simply, an affirmation is a wish you say as if it were already true. Affirmations can help us to change our attitudes and in turn, change our habits and our life!

Relaxation:
For our relaxation I am going to read a poem out loud entitled "Affirmation". I will be doing this in an ancient style of meditation used in monasteries called Lectio-Divina (pronounced Lectio - LEK-tsea-oh Divina - di-VEEN-ah). To do this, I will read the poem out loud three times. The first time I read you will just sit and listen. The second time I read, you will listen for a word or phrase that touches your heart or resonates with you. The third time I read, you will ponder or think about why this word or phrase is for you, and during the fourth reading, you will ask what it is you are to do, with this new knowledge.

Before we begin, I'm going to ask that if you feel safe you close your eyes and start to get comfortable in your chair and breathe deeply as I read for the first time. Now, remember this is for to just listen to the poem. (Make sure as a leader you do not put any emphasis on any part of what you read, read slow and clear).

 
 
 
 

Read Lectio Divina:
"I celebrate my courage in coming here.
I was lone, but now I am not alone.
I was victimized but I am no longer a victim.
I name the violence in my life - and declare it wrong.
I name that  I need help, and that  I am willing  to give help.
Nothing I do provokes the violence.
Nothing about me causes the violence.
Nothing gives one person the right to abuse another person.
My abuser can change themself; I cannot change them.
Nothing I can do will change my past.
Everything I do changes my future."

Pause.

For the second reading, remember to listen for anything that sticks out to you, anything that touches your heart .

Repeat Lectio-Divina

I'm going to read for the third time. As you are listening, think about why this word or phrase is important to you.

Repeat Lectio-Divina

For the last reading, as you are listening, ask yourself what it is that you are to do with this phrase or word, think about what action will you take from this.
Repeat Lectio-Divina

Creation:
Today you will get to take the affirmation you identified with during Lectio Divina or from the affirmation quotes provided, and create a beautiful mandala on a Shrinky Dink. Once you have chosen your affirmation, feel free to choose a template, or a blank circle to begin your mandala. A mandala is just a form of meditation using a circle, we'll use this form of meditation to focus on our affirmation while coloring the circular Shrinky Dink. You can choose any colors or shapes that you would like to remind yourself of the word or phrase that touched your heart.

For those participants that have not created Shrinky Dinks before, you may want to remind them of the steps to make Shrinky Dinks.

 
 
 
 
 Affirmation Mandala Shrinky Dink
Step 1:
Start by tracing a mandala template onto the rough side of the Shrinky Dink paper. Feel free to create any design to reflect your chosen affirmation.

Step 2:
With the pencils or markers, fill in your Shrinky Dink using any colors, symbols, words or shapes.

Step 3:
When you are finished creating, you may cut your Mandala out with scissors.

Step 4:
Participants may choose to punch a hole at the top of their Mandala to attach a key ring or ribbon. Remind participants to not punch the hole too close to the edge to make the hole sturdy.

Step 5:
Now the Mandala's are ready for baking. Place the Shrinky Dink pieces, colored side up, on brown paper and place the paper on a tray or cookie sheet.

Step 6:
Put Shrinkies in a 325 degree preheated oven for 1-3 minutes and watch as your Shrinky Dink shrinks! After pieces lie flat, allow an additional 30 seconds of baking time to complete the process.

Step 7:
Remove paper from tray or cookie sheet and let Shrinky Dinks cool.

Step 8:
Participants may keep their Affirmation Mandala Shrinky Dink as a pocket charm or attach it to a key ring or ribbon.


Closing:
Traditionally with Lectio Divina, you apply what you have learned to your life by sharing your Lectio experience with others. Ask participants to share what they have learned from this experience about themselves and what they would like to remember.
Row.txt_description: This workshop allows participants to identify positive affirmations through different forms of meditation. Participants will meditate through a listening style called Lectio Divina and then create a beautiful Shrinky Dink Mandala.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Children will create a dancing monster and experience the joy and freedom of letting themselves go in the monster dance. A perfect workshop for Halloween (and all year round), this promotes the playful and fun side of monsters! 
   
  Dancing Monster
 

Materials:
White card stock
Markers, color pencils, crayons
Paint (watercolors, Biocolors, etc.)
Brushes
Water cups
Paper towels
Scissors
18x12 construction paper
Scotch tape
Stapler
Ribbon
Craft sticks
Feet/hand template
Head template (optional)
Music that makes you want to dance!

Time Frame:
Intro: 5 minutes
Warm up: 15 minutes
Creation: 20 minutes
Monster Dance: 15 minutes
Closing: 5 minutes
Total: 1 hour

Age Range:
3-12

Set-Up/Prep:
This is a perfect Halloween workshop (and all year round), and can serve to calm children's fear about scary monsters, by making monsters playful and fun! It's also a great "movement" workshop, allowing the kids to be silly and free during the Monster Dance!

If you have time before the workshop, create your own monster...make sure you give it a name. That way you can demonstrate (and participate in) the monster dance with the children. As a role model, you set the tone for the workshop, and can inspire the children to be really free! 

For younger children, you may want to cut out the heads, hands and feet beforehand (templates are provided). Make enough hands and feet so each person has at least 2. Have some extras available to be used as needed. Older children may want to create their own shapes. 

Pre-cut 1" strips of construction paper for the monster's legs and arms. It's fun if you use a lot of different colors! Participants can make the arms and legs as long as they want by stapling  or taping 2 or more strips together. (Note: 18" strips when folded will reduce to 5". If you want a 10" arm, put 2 strips together). Have a lot of extra strips available if children get really creative and want their monsters to have 3 or more arms and legs!

Find up-tempo music that will inspire the children to have fun, be creative and dance! You can play upbeat music throughout the creative process, and save the best for the monster dance. Some examples are Putumayo's African Playground, Caribbean Playground and Animal Playground. Monsters also like Boogie Woogie music!

Introduction:
Today we're going to make a happy monster! We're going to be silly and dance with them too! Sometimes the things we are afraid of aren't really scary at all!

Warm up:
Remind children that monsters can be happy and fun! To set the tone, you can start by reading a book about happy monsters. Examples are: Where the Wild Things Are by Maurice Sendak, My Monster Mama Loves Me So by Laura Leuck, or Go Away Green Monster by. If you have time, you can make it interactive by asking what the children what think about the pictures and story.

Note: Reading helps to get children's imaginations flowing. It's always helpful if you take time to research books that are appropriate for your group (age range, language, etc)...online or at a local library or bookstore. 

Creation:
Draw the shape of the monster head (if not pre-made) and cut it out. Use your imagination and create a fun, wacky shape. It can be large or small, any shape at all. Paint your monster with fun and bright colors. Create the eyes, they can be really big or little, there can be one or many, even one as big as a pie...you decide! You can add stripes or dots to make you monster pop!

   
 
  Cutting the Monster head
  Cutting the Monster feet
 

Now we're going to make the bouncy legs. Start with 2 long strips. They can be the same color or different colors. Staple one on top of each other in an "L" shape. Fold the bottom strip across the top strip to create a new "L" shape. Keep doing this until the entire paper is folded. Gently pull the ends of the strip so you can see the bouncy shape. Do the same for both legs. Create arms in the same way by using the shorter strips.

 
 
 
 Starting the folded limbs by securing with a stapler
 Start by folding one piece over the other
  Keep folding the 2 strips

Staple the hands and feet onto the flat end of the each leg or arm. Then, staple the arms to the front of the body and the legs to the back. Your monster is almost done! Punch holes around the top of the body, and tie on ribbon to make hair.

 
 
 
 You can make the arms or legs longer
by adding more strips
 Attach the hands and feet to the end
of the strip
 

To hang your monster, punch a hole on the top of the head and tie a ribbon to it (at least 12"). Attach a craft stick to the other of the ribbon so the child can hold their monster and make it dance!

Give your monster a silly name like, "Ugalah Boogalah" or "Octavia, the Spotted Monster from Planet Nublia." You can help children write the name on the back of their monster, so they can remember it.

Towards the end of the workshop, ask the children to think about how their happy monster would dance. Would it wiggle? Would it move from side to side? Would it jump up and down? Would it spin in circles?

Monster Dance:

 
 
   
   

Gather the kids together with their monsters. Let them know, "now we're going to have fun and do the happy monster dance!"

First, show the children how your monster likes to dance. Have fun, and be creative! This gives the children permission to be really free. You can make silly monster noises, and have your monster jump, wiggle and twirl. Note: This is a perfect workshop for helping children overcome shyness and come out of their shells. The sillier you are, the more involved they will be! 

Play upbeat music, and have the children dance around the room with their monsters. Happy monsters love to dance! Remind the children it's okay to be silly and make funny monster noises. Encourage them to let go and have fun!

If you have space, you can have a Monster Boogie Parade and march your monsters around the room (or up and down the hall, or even outside). Ask if there's a child who's feeling extra silly who wants to lead the group, or have the children take turns!

Closing:
Go around the circle and ask the children what their monster's name is, and how it felt to do the happy monster dance. Remind them that its okay to be silly and have fun!
Row.txt_description: Children will create a dancing monster and experience the joy and freedom of letting themselves go in the monster dance. A perfect workshop for Halloween (and all year round), this promotes the playful and fun side of monsters!
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For mor e about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Note About Older Children
For older children, you can get really creative with your monsters. Monsters can have 3 heads or a separate head and body. You can supply more sophisticated materials: yarn, glitter, etc. You can create monster "rap" songs. Or the kids can write about their monsters and have a monster performance. The possibilities are endless!

Note About Family Workshops
This can also be a fun Family Workshop. Engage the moms and kids together in making dancing monster families: a mommy monster and kiddy monsters. Let them know, "the family that dances together stays together!"

Row.txt_code:
A Loving Lily
Objective:
To give participants an opportunity to recognize what they like about and appreciate in themselves.  It also gives them an opportunity to share a lily with a loved one -even if they are that person!

Materials:
Pipe cleaners: 1 yellow, 3 green per person
Green masking tape
Tape
Scissors  
Cray Pas, crayon, pencil or marker
White heavy construction paper (or pastel colors)
Yellow construction paper cut into strips for flower center (optional)
Pencil (optional to curl fingers)

 
 Creating a Loving Lily
 
Introduction:
It is a generous and loving custom to receive flowers from people, but why should we wait for other people to make us feel special?  Today we are all going to make flowers for ourselves!  This flower is called a Lily, and we will have the opportunity to fill each petal on the Lily with positive things about ourselves.  

Opening Circle:
Go around the room and have each participant share one thing that they love or appreciate about themselves.  It can be anything, from something big such as, "I love that I have the courage to make big changes in my life," or something small such as, "I am a good singer!"  If the participant is unable to think of something, you can assist by affirming them.  It can be a short phrase or a whole sentence; there is no wrong way.

 
  Cut out your hand shape and write loving words
 
  Create pipe cleaner leaves
 
  Add the leaves to the stem
 
  Loving Lilies bouquet
Creation:
Step One:
Have each participant trace their hand onto the white paper with a crayon or pencil.  Have them cut out as many as they want for the lily blooms.

Step Two:
Remind participants to keep in mind some of the things they said in the opening circle; ask them to write at least one positive thing about themselves on each of the fingers.  You can say, "remember, you can write anything you like, as long as it celebrates you!"  If they so choose, have the participants decorate their hand using Cray Pas and/or markers.  There is no right or wrong way to decorate the lily.  Encourage the participants to feel free to go wild and decorate their lily in any way they like.

Step Three:
Roll the hand print vertically to form a funnel shape, and secure the side with clear tape. 

Step Four- the Lily:
Roll each finger down to form the curls of each bloom. You can wrap the fingers around a pencil or scrape against the side of a pair of scissors to create the curls.

Step Five- stamens: 
Loosely curve the yellow pipe cleaner to form a ‘U' shape.  Wrap the top of a green pipe cleaner at the center of the ‘U'. Curl the ends of the yellow pipe cleaner to form the center of the bloom.
If you prefer you can also use strips of yellow construction paper and curl them using scissors.  (see A Loving Lily Photo above)

Step Six- stem:
Insert the completed green stem into the center of the bloom and pull through.

Step Seven- leaves:
Use the green tape to secure the stem onto the Lily and add another green pipe cleaner to create the leaves.  An easy technique you can use to make the leaves is to attach each end of the pipe cleaner together to create a circle, then pull the circle from opposite sides to make the circle look like an oval, then pinch the middle of the oval shape, and wrap it around the stem to create two leaves.

Step Eight- bouquet:
If time allows, have the participants make more lilies for themselves or for their loved ones.

Closing Circle:
Have each participant share their lily and some positive things about themselves.  After everyone has shared, remind the participants that it is important for them to recognize and appreciate all of the wonderful things that make them who they are.
Row.txt_description: The workshop will give participants an opportunity to recognize what they like about and appreciate about themselves.

Row.txt_code:
Images courtesy of TVPP
 
This workshop comes from The Valentine Peace Project. The Valentine Peace Project is serious about peace and works to promote the UN International Day of Peace (21 September - internationaldayofpeace.org). TVPP also promotes international Fair Trade all year.
TVPP is a collective of schools, programs and artists developing actions and images to move forward the conversation of Peace.
To find out more about The Valentine Peace Project, visit their website at www.thevalentinepeaceproject.org.

Objective:
To re-imagine Valentine's Day as a day of community, connection and peace. Participants create their own poems and/or Valentine's Day peace cards and distribute them (if possible attached to flowers) within their community during Valentine's Day.

  
 Images courtesy of TVPP
  
Materials:
Peace Quotes Page
Pens, pencils or markers
Peace Poem Template or pieces of blank paper (2 per person)
Peace poem examples
Carnations or other long stemmed flowers
Ribbon or string

Setup:
Make sure to print enough copies of both the Peace Poem Template and the Peace Quotes Page. You'll also need to allot for some time to cut the quotes into stripes and the template in half.

Intro:
Imagine receiving a poem or message of peace or love from someone in your community or somewhere else in the world...

Through poetry and reflection, The Valentine Peace Project encourages actions on Peace leading up to and on the worldwide holiday of Love. The Valentine Peace Project is a growing initiative developing community thoughts, hopes and images on Peace and the many faces of Love.

On and around February 14, poems will be shared or performed in different cities and communities - some then wrapped around stems of local and international flowers to give out.

Today we are going to re-imagine Valentine's Day and create our own poems.

Warm-up:
Pass around the individual quotes and have each person take one.

Once everyone has a quote, ask each person to read their quote out loud.

Creation:
Today we're going to use these quotes as inspiration to write our own poem about peace. Everyone has a template for the poem on the table, and once we're done, we're going to wrap these around a flower stem and give them to people in our community. The poem can say anything you want about peace, and remember this poem is intended for someone in our community as a random act of kindness.

 
Images courtesy of TVPP
 
If you need further inspiration, I placed peace poem examples on the table as well.

Closing:
As a closing, participants can give these poems to people in their community. Remind them to be bold and give them to anyone they see in their community. If you would like, participants can read their poems out loud to the group members. Remember to encourage each participant by thanking them for their poem of peace.
Row.txt_description: The aim of the Valentine Peace Project is to re-imagine Valentine's Day as a day of community, connection and peace. Participants create their own poems and/or Valentine's Day peace cards and distribute them (if possible attached to flowers) within their community during Valentine's Day.

Row.txt_code:
An Aggressive Crayon example 
Objective:
To allow the children to release some of their feelings and/or energy onto a piece of paper.

Materials:
Crayons or Cray Pas
Paper

Note: If using this workshop to help children release or process anger it is important to begin by having a discussion on "What is Anger?" Please click here to see the entire Processing Anger Series.

Prep:
Put out a large piece of paper, and have the children take out several crayons of their choosing.  You can instruct them to choose colors that represent how they are feeling that day.

 
Micala of United Methodist Youthville
warming up!
 
Warm-up:
Have the children scribble as hard and fast as they can to get a mess of color.  You can instruct them to choose colors that represent how they are feeling that day. Encourage the children to keep scribbling until they feel satisfied that they have gotten that feeling out, and then switch colors.  You may want to use music to set the pace - fast upbeat music to start and switch to slower music to calm things down at the end.

Follow this warm-up with a workshop about discovering feelings, dealing with anger, etc using the "Emotional Theme" search tool on the AWBW website.
Row.txt_description: A great warm up that will allow the children to release some of their feelings and/or energy onto a piece of paper.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Note About Anger Workshops
We recommend that you start anger workshops with a discussion; don't be afraid to talk to the children about their anger.  Anger is nothing to be ashamed of, it is important to look at and talk about it to try to understand it.

Some anger prompts that we like are:
What is Anger? What does it look like and what does it sound like?
What was the trigger to your anger?
What did you think about it?
How did it make you feel?
How did you act?
What effect did it have on you and those around you?

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To get the children moving and reinforce the power of positivity.

Materials:
Paper
Scissors
A parachute or sheet (you may want to borrow this from your children's program; for an example of a parachute, click here)
Affirmation confetti words click here

Prep:
Make a list of positive or affirmation words (using different fonts and sizes is ideal), or use the above template and cut out each word. 

Introduction:
Let the children know that today we're going to have fun.  Remind them to try their hardest to just enjoy this time and take each affirmation they hear to heart.

Warm-up:
1. Place the affirmation in the middle of the parachute.

2. Lay the parachute (so it is open completely) on the ground.  Have the children sit around the edges of the parachute so there is equal distance between people.   

3. Have the children grab the edge of the parachute with both hands.

4. Have the children stand up and lift the parachute up to their waist.

5. Ask the children to move their arms up and down (while keeping them straight and extended in front of their body) at a quick pace over and over again, so the parachute and affirmation words dance in the air.

6.  One at a time, have the children grab a word from the parachute and say it out loud.

7.  To add a discussion to the warm-up, have then children share about a time when they felt the feeling they just read out loud.

8.  Follow this warm-up with a workshop that focuses on the positive attribute of the children.  Do this by doing a find for workshops using the Emotional Theme (e.g. self-care, self-esteem,discovering my feelings, etc.) search tool.
Row.txt_description: The warm-up gets the children moving, but also reinforces the power of positivity.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To help capture the inner childlike voice of the participants, and bring out their playfulness.  The movement releases stress and gives permission to be silly and carefree.

Materials:
Assorted scarfs or pieces of sheer, flowing fabrics
Upbeat music

Warm-up:
Have each person select a piece of fabric and form a circle.  You can have soft music playing at first as the children walk slowly in the circle gently swaying the fabrics - gradually increase the pace and the beat of the music, walk a little faster and have the leader call out things to do with the fabric.  Encourage the participants to be carefree, playful and free to move and dance around the room.

Here are some suggestions of scarf movements:
Swing over your head
Bend over and dust your shoes
Wave it up in the air
Hold it over your head with two hands and sway side to side
Dust off your knees
Dust off the person to your lefts feet
Pretend you are an animal like a butterfly or a bird
Make it become an elephant trunk by swinging up and down
Cover your face (and play peek a boo)
Throw it up in the air and catch it
Wrap yourself in it and give yourself a hug
This warm-up is great to use with a playful workshop such as those found using the search tool on AWBW's website (including My Body, Self-care and Self-esteem workshops).
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps to capture the inner childlike voice of the participants and is a way to bring out playfulness. The movement releases stress and gives permission to be silly and carefree.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.
