  Tying the ribbons for the suncatcher
"Before we start with a warm-up, I want to show you the supplies so that you can begin creating right after the warm-up."

Step 1: 
 "Create your shrinky dinks! If you want to use a template, start by tracing it onto the shrinky dink (or use the pre-cut shrinky dinks, if they are available)."

Optional Material Explanation:
If your participants have never created shrinky dinks before or need a reminder, demonstrate how to use colored pencils on the rough side or markers on either side of the shrinky dink. It can also be helpful to have a pre-shrunk sample so that participants can see how small the material will get. In addition, let them know to do any cutting or hole-punching before putting their shrinky dinks in the oven.

Step 2:
"When you are finished coloring, you can cut out your shapes with scissors (if the shrinky dinks were not pre-cut the way you want them)."

Step 3:
"Use the hole punch to place a hole at the top of each shrinky dink so that you can hang it to create your suncatcher."
Step 4:
"Then we’ll bake your shrinky dinks!"
Step 5:
"Use the hole puncher to punch holes around the inside edge of the cut-out paper plate (punch as many holes as shrinky dinks you want to hang). Add a hole on both sides at the top for a way to hang the finished suncatcher. Hang your shrinky dinks from the suncatcher with ribbon or yarn, and add beads if desired. Add another ribbon to the top two holes to create a way to hang your suncatcher. I’m here to help at any point if you need or want it."f

Warm-Up:
 "Since we’re going to be making suncatchers with messages to our hearts today, we’re going to start with a warm-up that involves feeling the sun and listening to our hearts. In this warm-up, I’ll make suggestions for you to try simple movements to go with your imaginations, but each person is different so please do whatever feels best for you. If what feels good to you is just to sit and listen, that is absolutely fine."

As you share the following warm-up, remember to speak slowly and take significant pauses so that participants can feel into the experience. (You can view an example video of this warm-up here.)

  
Wiggling toes against the ground
in a safe place
 
  
  
 Welcoming the sunbeam
 

"You can close your eyes or keep them open, whatever will best help you to connect to yourself. Start by imagining yourself in a safe place outdoors. Wiggle your toes against the ground and imagine what it feels like in your safe place. Is it sand under your feet? Dirt? Sidewalk? Something else?

"Slowly, you begin to feel the sun warming the top of your head. Take a deep breath in and imagine the sunbeam coming in with your breath through the top of your head and flowing out through your heart as you breathe out. In through the top of your head, and out through your heart.

"As you keep breathing, you notice that the sun feels so nice on the top of your head that you begin to tilt your head up to face the sun. Welcome the sunbeam onto your face, and as you breathe, let it flow in through your cheeks and out through your heart. In through your cheeks and out through your heart.

"As you keep breathing, you notice that the sun feels so nice on your cheeks that you begin to stand up so you can feel the sun on your chest. As you breathe in, raise your arms to welcome the sun. This time, breathe in through the tips of your fingers and out through your heart. In through the tips of your fingers and out through your heart.

"Keep breathing and feeling the sun. When you’re ready, reach up to the sunbeams and pull them down to your heart. With your hands on your heart, remind yourself that this is a special time just for you. 

  
 Listening to the heart,
surrounded by
loving messages
 

"Think about what your heart would tell you if it could speak. Can you hear any special message your heart has?

"Think about the many things that make you special, the things that you love about who you are. It could be something simple or something deep. Have compassion for yourself if you can't think of something right away, it will come. Think about the loving and nurturing things you could tell your heart. What would it like to hear? Imagine your heart surrounded by loving messages. Those messages could be words or symbols or colors or any combination. Think about all of the loving messages you can tell yourself and imagine them shining within you.”


Creation:
"Whenever you’re ready, you can bring your attention back to this room and begin to create shrinky dinks for your suncatcher. Let me know how I can support you."

Give participants time to create their suncatchers, and help out as needed.

 
  
  
  
  
  

Instructions for Baking Shrinky Dinks:
A toaster oven is ideal for baking shrinky dinks. However, a regular oven will "shrink" the art just as well. Do not microwave the shrinky dinks!

Step 1: Cut a rectangular shape out of a brown paper grocery bag and turn one corner up. (The turned up corner will make the bag and shrinky dink easy to remove from the tray after baking.)

Step 2: Place the shrinky dinks, colored sides up, on the brown paper and place paper on a tray or cookie sheet. Be sure to punch any holes before baking. 

Step 3: Bake the shrinky dinks at 300" until the art has completely flattened (about 1-3 minutes). After the pieces lie flat, allow an additional 30 seconds of baking time to complete the process. Note: participants generally really enjoy watching their art shrink.

Step 4: Remove paper from tray and let the shrinky dinks cool.

  
Closing:
Give each participant an opportunity to share their loving heart suncatcher and/or to talk about the process of making it. Remind participants that it's always okay to pass.

Appreciate the group for taking this window of time to let the sun shine into their hearts.
Row.txt_description: This workshop supports participants through a process that builds self-compassion through the creation of a shrinky-dink suncatcher.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Hanging the Suncatchers
After the closing, think about taking some time for a ceremony where everyone chooses a spot to hang their suncatcher. During the ceremony, everyone can walk around to see all of the special spots that were chosen.

Indoors, suncatchers look especially nice hung in windows, where they can catch the sunlight coming in and remind participants of the loving messages in their hearts.

Row.txt_code:
Mary Ann, Prison Teacher
 Harlem Renaissance Women
 
Inspired by the Harlem Renaissance, leader Pam Albers of Crescent House Healing Center in New Orleans, LA created hats for her group at Orleans Parish Prison to decorate. With lots of giggles and smiles, her workshop was a success. We've used Pam's idea as the basis for this empowering workshop. 

Pam created hats using the McCall's pattern below. To make this workshop more accessible, AWBW's fabulous new Program Assistant, Sheli experimented and created a hat without a pattern. Much like Sheli, we're sure you'll encounter some giggles, smiles and discoveries during your workshop!

Objective:
To explore the many metaphorical hats we wear as survivors and discuss the hats worn during abusive relationships and the new hats we will choose to wear.

 
  A hat with a felt flower.
 
  A hat with embellishments.
Materials:
36x36" pieces of felt in multiple colors (or by the yard) (1 per person)
Embroidery thread in multiple colors
Embroidery/tapestry needles (1 per person)
Fabric tape measure or string (1 per person)
Scissors
Markers
Hot glue gun and extra glue sticks or strong fabric glue
Optional but recommended supplies
Ribbon or trim
Embellishments of your choice
Stapler
Various buttons
Straight pins
McCalls M55641 or Vogue v8405 sewing pattern
Flower petal template printed on cardstock (1 per person)

Timeframe:
1-2 hours

Set-up/Prep:
Create a sample hat in advance, this is essential for this workshop. You may want to try the different techniques, hot gluing the hat together, sewing the hat or using the stapler, as in the sample below.  All three techniques work for this project, but the sewing technique is the most meditative and permanent.

Introduction:
As survivors we wear so many hats in just one day. Whether it be at home, work, or school we are constantly changing the hats we wear. No matter our culture, socioeconomic background, political party or religion, we all wear different hats, and change them very frequently. Not only do we wear different hats during our day to day activities, but we were also forced or sometimes needed to wear certain hats in our abusive relationships. For example, instead of simply wearing the hat of wife or partner, batterers often force us to wear the hat of caretaker, cook, maid, and often hostage. Today, we're going to have a discussion about the hats we wore before our abusive relationship, the hats we had to wear during our relationship, and hats we will choose to wear in our violence free future. And, we'll also get to create a survivor hat, to celebrate and remind us that we are free to choose the hats we wear.

Warm up/ Opening Circle:
Because this workshop is quite long, you'll want to facilitate only a short discussion or opening circle before jumping into creating.

Begin a loose discussion or have each person name a hat they wore before being in an abusive relationship (example Athlete- you used to love to work out, but once you began dating he didn't want you keep going to the gym). After everyone has shared, ask the participants to name a hat they wore during an abusive relationship (example Storyteller- I lied all the time to myself, strangers, my family, everyone. I lied to cover the abuse). For the last hat, have everyone name a hat they are choosing to wear now (example Student- He always told me I wasn't smart enough to graduate, I've now put on the student hat I wasn't allowed to wear before), or want to wear in the future (example, a graduation hat).

 
  Cutting, after tracing
 
  Sewing the three pieces together
 
  Voila! And the hat is finished
Creation:
(Please note these are approximate measurements, if you want to make exact measurements, please use the pattern listed in the materials. Measurements are also estimated a little larger to account for stitching)

Ask the participants to choose a color to make their hat out of.

Step 1 — Top of hat: To start, each person will begin by tracing the top of their hat. Ask each person to get a partner to help them measure the top of their head where the hat will sit. Another way to measure this is by having each person place their hand flat on the felt with their fingers spread apart and tracing a circle around their hand. A person's head is usually about the size of their hand with outstretched fingers. Add about an inch all the way around to account for stitching.
To make an exact circle, you may provide bowls in different sizes to trace around.

Step 2 — Band of hat: Before cutting the top of the hat, participants will measure 4" from edge of the top circle all the way around, and then trace another larger circle. Now there will be two circles.
Alternatively, cut out a long strip that is 4" wide by the circumference of the top of the hat. Therefore, if your head is 19" around at the very top, your band would be 4"X19". Participants can use a string to go around the circle they have traced onto the felt and stretch it out against a ruler to find out how long to make the band.

Step 3 — Brim of hat: To create the brim, participants will follow step two again. This time, on their large sheet of felt, there will be one large circle (the brim) with two circles inside (the band and top).
The brim can be as wide or thin as participants would like.

Step 4 —Finishing hat: Have participants cut out all three pieces. Remind participants to cut just inside the traced line so that there are no marks on the finished piece.
Once all pieces are cut out, participants can begin gluing, stitching or stapling all three pieces together starting with the top and band.

 
 Tracing the flower template
 
 
 Putting all the flower layers together
 
 
 A finished flower with a button center!!
 
Step 5 (optional) — Creating a felt flower: To create a Peony flower, have each participant cut out a template. Using the flower templates, pin each one to the color felt of their choice. Trace and cut the flower petal out. Once all petals have been cut, participants may start layering the petals as displayed on the template page. Using the hot glue gun put a dot of glue in between each layer as you stack large to small or with a needle and thread, once the stack is finished push the needle through all layers, from the underneath to the top, loop through a button and then back through all the layers finishing with a knot.

You could choose to create only the felt flowers for this workshop. Add the completed flower to a pin, hair clip or headband. However, make sure to have enough supplies available for participants.

Closing:
Have each woman close the group by showing off their hat, starting with "I am now choosing to wear the hat of...".
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives participants the opportunity to create a hat or hair clip to explore the many "hats" we wear as participants. During the workshop participants will explore the hats they wore during their abusive relationships and the new hats they choose to wear in the present.

Row.txt_code:
Talking Sticks
 
  
 Christy holding a completed
Talking Stick
 
Objective:
To teach children the value of sharing, listening respecting each others stories.  Talking Sticks teach us that communication can be as much about listening as it is about talking.

Materials:
Sticks (can be varied lengths & widths, although 12 inches is a good length to work with, washed and dried)
Glue
Glitter
Sequins
Yarn, ribbon, string, pipe cleaners or leather strips
Feathers
Beads
Jewels and embellishments like small shells

Time frame:
1.5 hours
Intro: 15 minutes
Opening circle: 15 minutes
Creating: 45 minutes
Closing: 15 minute

Set-up/Prep:
Gather, wash, and dry the sticks beforehand. Wait until everybody is seated and ready to begin before handing out the sticks. Remind the children that their stick is used only for Talking Stick purposes (no hitting, swinging, or throwing allowed). It's handy to make a sample Talking Stick to give the kids some ideas of how to use the materials. You can use yarn, string, or ribbon to wrap around the base of the stick for a handle, added feathers to the top, beads, jewels, glitter all over, etc.). Have all the materials spread out over the table so that children can see what is available for them.

Introduction:
Begin by showing everyone an example Talking Stick and ask if they have ever seen one before? Do they know what it is used for? Explain that a Talking Stick has special magical powers and that whoever holds it receives the respect and attention of everyone else in the circle. Talking Sticks are popular in many different cultures and they are used to help share stories. People have used some form of a Talking Stick for years to pass along information to and about family members. Let the children know that today they will have the opportunity to share a story about their family.
  
  Supplies for Talking Sticks
 
Explain that stories are powerful tools for teaching, but we have to be open to listening to them if we are to learn from them.  Stress the importance of listening and asking the children to think about how it feels when others do not listen to them when they have something they want to say.  Each of us has stories from our lives that make us who we are, and those stories have taught us important things. We can be proud of our stories, and share them with others, so that they may learn, too.

Warm-up/Opening Circle:
After practicing with the Talking Stick, we will each get to make our own. Begin by passing your sample around the circle, giving everybody the chance to just hold the stick for a few seconds. After each child has held the stick ask them if they can feel the magic. The next time they pass the stick ask each child to share their name and three favorite things. "I am Susan and I like the beach, ice cream and dancing." They next time they pass the stick ask each child to share a personal story that is important or special to them. The story could be about a family experience, it could be a memory of another time, maybe a story about school, a favorite pet or a grandparent. You might want to suggest they begin by saying "I remember when..." Any short story the child would like to share will be great. Make sure to emphasize that only the person holding the Talking Stick is allowed to speak, everyone else's job is to listen carefully. 

   
  Gluing the ends
 
   
  Wrapping ribbon & yarn
 
   
  Adding feathers
 
Creation:
Begin by handing out the sticks to each child (TIP: handing them out usually works better than giving them a choice because it cuts down on arguing over sticks. After assigning each child a stick, you can give them the option to trade if they would like).
After each child has a stick, reiterate the rules (no hitting, banging, throwing etc…)  Tell the children they can use anything on the table to decorate their stick in anyway they like.
The string, ribbon or yarn can be used to wrap around the base of the stick to make a comfortable grip for your hand. Beads can be added by threading through the yarn,  pipe cleaners can be added for extra texture.  Feathers can be glued or wrapped into the yarn at the top or any where on the stick.

Closing:
Once everyone has finished their stick, go around the circle and have everyone who would like to, share their Talking Stick with the group. As they hold their stick ask them to say something special they learned about someone in the group.
You might like to end the Talking Stick workshop with a ceremony of the Talking Sticks. The ceremony is to enact the silencing power of the Talking Stick, and to give its owner the strength to share their story. The leader/leaders may go around the table, chanting and shaking the “sample” Talking Stick over each of the childrens’ sticks. Finish by holding all the sticks together in the middle, and all chant together. (The children have gotten really excited about the ceremony - no matter how you do it, it adds meaning and importance).
Row.txt_description: To teach children the value of sharing, listening respecting each others stories. Talking Sticks teach us that communication can be as much about listening as it is about talking.

Row.txt_code:
Meghan's group's Talking Sticks
 
  
Objective:
To reinforce the value of sharing, listening and respecting each others point of view through creating a Talking Stick. To also aid in communication among close friends, family or groups or people.

Materials:
Sticks (of various sizes)
What Medicine do you need? handout
Glue
Glitter
Leather lanyard, yarn or ribbon
Feathers
Beads
Jewels & embellishments
Small shells

Time frame:
Intro: 5 minutes
Opening circle: 10 minutes
Creating: 45 minutes
Closing: 15 minute
Total: 1 1/4 hours

 
Various supplies for the Talking Sticks
 
Set-up/Prep:
It is handy to have an example to give the participants some ideas of how to use the materials. Have the materials spread out over the table so the participants can see what is available to them.

Introduction:
Begin by showing everyone an example of a Talking Stick and ask if they have ever seen one before? If they know what it is used for? Explain that in some Native American tribes, Talking Sticks are used as a means for just and impartial hearing, as well designating who has the right to speak. It allows all members of the conversation to present their "Sacred Point of View". The Talking Stick is sometimes accompanied by an Answering Feather, both carry respect for free speech and assures the speaker they have the freedom and power to say what is in their heart, without fear of reprisal or humiliation. When the stick is passed on to the next person to speak, that person must repeat the essence of what the previous speaker said before her turn, similar to echoing which is used in other AWBW workshops. A Talking Stick does not ensure we will all agree, but rather that we are bound by our personal honor to allow everyone their "Sacred Point of View".

 
 Christy with her Talking Stick
Warm-up/Opening Circle:
If you have a sample Talking Stick you can use it for the opening circle. Begin by passing it around the circle, giving everybody the chance to share something they have, or are beginning to heal from. Remind everyone that only the person holding the Talking Stick is allowed to speak, everyone else listens and the person the Talking Stick is passed onto will summarize what the previous speaker said before sharing their own story. (It's okay if participants applaud others healing!)

Creation:
In the Native American tradition, each piece of material used in the Talking Stick speaks of the personal "Medicine" of the stick owner. Native traditions refer to trees as "Standing People" and each "Standing Person" brings specific "Medicine". (Hand out the page of descriptions and go over a few) White Pine is the Peace Tree, Birch symbolizes truth, Evergreens represent the continued growth of all things. Cedar symbolizes cleansing. Aspen is the symbol for seeing clearly since there are many eye shapes on the bark. Remind participants when they get to create their own Talking Sticks they can refer to their handout for more descriptions. Each person making a Talking Stick must decide which type of "Standing Person" (Tree) will assist their needs and add needed medicine to the Councils or in our case, conversations or family meetings held.

  
  Gluing the ends
  
  Wrapping ribbon & yarn
  
  Adding feathers
Ornaments used to decorate the Talking Sticks also have meaning. In the Lakotah Tradition, red is for life, yellow is for knowledge, blue is for prayer and wisdom, white is for spirit and purple is for healing. For further color meanings, participants can refer to the handout. In other native traditions, a shell is used as it is iridescent and ever changing, it reminds the speaker that all creation changes -- the days, the seasons, the years -- and people and situations change, too.

The type of feathers and hide used on a Talking Stick are very important. The "Answering Feather" is usually an Eagle Feather, which represents high ideals, truth as viewed from the expansive eye of the eagle, and the freedom that comes from speaking total truth to the best of one's ability. The "Answering Feather" can also be the feather of other birds, further descriptions can be found on the handout.

Although there are many different Native American symbols presented, when we create our own Talking Stick we don't have to use any of these, the only thing we must do with our Talking Stick, is make it our own, using symbols or items that have meaning to us.

Participants may begin by choosing a stick to decorate using all the materials on the table. Choosing just the right "medicine" for their own personal or family or "councils". Remind participants they may use the handout for direction, but are not limited to it.

Closing:
Once everyone has finished their stick, you could tell the group that you hope it will serve as a reminder of the importance of respect in healthy communication. Then, have everyone share their Talking Stick, what it means to them and how they will use it in the future.
Alternative Closing:
You may ask each participant to share what "Medicine" they need for their conversations and what "Councils" they will use their new Talking Stick in.
Row.txt_description: This workshops reinforces the value of sharing, listening and respecting each others point of view through creating a Talking Stick. Talking Sticks teach us that healthy communication can be as much about listening as it is about talking.
Row.txt_tips: The talking sticks can also be used in group or house meetings in the shelter.

Row.txt_code:
Anna showing her co mpleted box
Thanks to Anna Reyner for this fabulous workshop!
Anna is a nationally recognized arts advocate who is dedicated to helping people get in touch with their own creativity. Anna has conducted over 500 national and international hands-on art workshops and is a registered art therapist and licensed marriage and family therapist. Anna is the Director of Training and Special Markets for Discount School Supply and she maintains an active art studio in her Los Angeles home where she lives with her husband and two children.

Objective:
To engage the participants in a creative exercise to identify and strengthen their sense of personal power, so that they will be able to more quickly and readily access their core strength when needed.

Materials:
 
Colorations Smooth & Silky Art Sticks
BioColor Paint (4 colors plus silver and gold = 6 total colors)
Nancy Paint Bottles Twist Tops (optional)
Balloons - one per person
Small paper plates - one per person
White Cardboard Pencil Box - one per person (from Discount School Supply)
White heavy weight construction paper (for warm-up and handmade stencils)
Paper towels for clean up
Colorations Make it Glitter (optional)
Brushes – one small & one large
Glue
Cups with water 

Timeframe:
Art Material Demo and Warm-up #1, Balloon Printing: 15 minutes
Art Material Demo Warm-up #2, Silky Sticks, 15 minutes
Warm-up: Source of My Strength: 15 minutes
Creation, Part 1, Inside of Box: 20 minutes
Creation, Part 2, Outside of Box: 15 minutes
Closing & Share: 10 minutes
Total: 1 1/2 hours

 
Set-up example
 
Prep:
Pre-fill Nancy bottles with BioColor, filling 4 bottles with standard BioColor and one each of gold and silver, for a total of 6 Nancy bottles full of BioColor per small group of participants. Fill one Nancy bottle with Make it Glitter paint for every 4 people. (You can use the paint straight from the original paint bottle if you prefer).

Try out each warm-up application before the workshop. Make yourself a sample of the Source of Our Strength box to familiarize yourself with each stage, and so you will be confident leading the session. Create your sample box from your own voice as a healer, someone who provides healing, compassion and positive solutions for survivors.

Setup
1) In the middle of the table, place 4 standard & two metallic BioColors in Nancy bottles, one Nancy bottle of Make it Glitter, one set of Silky Sticks, and stack pencil boxes in the middle for now, to make room for the warm-ups. Place an extra small stack of white construction paper for warm-ups.
2) In front of each seat, place 2 sheets of construction paper, 1 balloon, and 1 paper plate.

 
 
Demonstration/Warm-Up:
Note: During the demo/warm-up, it is useful to first do a demonstration of each step and then give participants a turn.
Art Material Demo and Warm-up #1: Balloon Printing with BioColor
Step 1: Using 4 standard colors of BioColor, plus silver and gold, place quarter-sized dots of paint in center of plate.
Step 2: Blow up balloons, not too big, so they fit into your fist or grasp (2"- 4"). 
STEP 3: Firmly press balloon straight down into paint palette, then "print" paint onto paper. Bounce/print balloon all over.
STEP 4: Create stencil patterns. Using thick, white construction paper, tear stencils by folding the paper in half and tearing out images as if you were making a snowflake. Position stencil, and balloon print on top. Remove stencil to see pattern surface. Repeat. Overlap stencils and repeat with a variety of colors to create a pleasing design.

 
 
Art Material Demo and Warm-up #2: Intro to Silky Sticks
Step 1: Take a few different Silky Stick colors and make a simple doodle to experience the materials, pressing hard to lay down bright pigments. Don't think about it too much, take this time to "loosen up" and leave your critical voice behind.
Step 2: Dip Silky Sticks into water before drawing with them. Experience the difference in wet and dry applications.
Step 3: Take your larger paintbrush and dip it into water. Apply your wet brush to your original dry doodle, creating a flow-release effect as it releases the colored pigment into a dilution of color, like a watercolor. Next take your smaller "detail" brush and dip it into water, making more detailed flow effects. You can also use your wet brush, or finger, directly on your Silky Stick as if it were a dry watercolor cake, and use your finger or brush directly onto your paper.

Introduction & Relaxation:
 
 Leaders warming up to their source.
 
This introduction gives participants the chance to get into the mood of the exercise: Source of My Strength. Have participants relax, put down their art materials and pencils, and close their eyes for a few minutes while you guide them through a brief period of self reflection. Continue with this dialogue (or change the concept to your own voice): "We have gathered here today to focus on our strengths, so that we can increase our sense of safety and well being. We will remind ourselves today that we are each strong enough not only to survive, but to overcome and rise above what has happened to us in the past.
Today is about living in the present moment of strength, community, healing and support. Our artwork will help us focus on what it is that makes us strong and keeps us strong. With that in mind, try to relax and reflect upon where it is that you find your own personal strength. In times of need, do you call upon your faith to give you strength? Or do you think of your parents, your children, your belief in something larger than yourself that makes you feel strong? What is the source of your own personal strength, when you go deep inside and search your soul for relief or answers? When you ask for help, who listens? Each of us has a unique combination of people, faith and beliefs that we call upon when we need to rise up and overcome challenges. What is the source of your strength? (Give participants a short quiet time to reflect on this question). Now, open your eyes and take your Silky Sticks and a fresh piece of paper, and DRAW A SYMBOL that represents the SOURCE OF YOUR STRENGTH. This is your initial "sketch" so you have time here to work out the details, it is a brainstorming time for you so think of this stage as a "work in progress". Your symbol can be made up of one image, or a combination of images. For example, you could focus exclusively on your spiritual faith, or you could choose to create an image that combines your love of nature, your family, and your belief in the goodness of mankind. Maybe you were born with an innate "positive outlook" on life, and if so, what would that look like as a visual symbol? Don't over-think this exercise, just do what comes naturally. There is no right or wrong way to approach visual symbol making, but the easiest way is to simply get started and see what happens. Experiment with your Silky Stick and let your inner strength and instincts guide you!

 
 A leader creating her source inside.
 
Creation:
Part 1: Inside of box
Take your SOURCE OF MY STRENGTH drawing and re-create it on the inside of your pencil box, using the Silky Sticks. Consider your original warm-up sketch as a starting point, and re-create the image in a more finished form on the inside of your box, adding details and embellishing it however feels right. Don't overthink it, just let it flow without being critical of how it looks or what it means. As you create your visual symbol of strength on the inside of your box, imagine you are creating this image from your source. Try to feel, or "be" in a state of balance and inner strength in the present moment, and let your imagination flow from there. Whatever comes of this experience will be the "right" image of strength for you today.

 
Balloon printing on the outside.
 
Part 2: Outside of box
Now comes the time to decorate the outside of your box more playfully, by balloon printing the outside with BioColor and your own handmade paper stencils. Add "Make it Glitter" paint if you want to add some sparkle. Create a pleasing design on the top and sides of your box, so that when you place it on a shelf or dresser table where you live, you will be reminded of a pleasant time spent with creativity and community. With a pleasing cover design, no one but you will know that inside this box lies a very important symbol, the symbols that represent the source of your strength and the inner resources you have to call upon whenever you need to.

 
 Leaders Annie Kelly of Good Shepherd and
Anna Sanchez of Rainbow Services
sharing their strengths
Closing:
Have people share their boxes with a partner, or with the group. If sharing with
a partner remind participants this is a great time to practice the listening and caring parts of ourselves by listening only and then repeating back to their partner what they heard them say.

Remind participants, we leave here today with a tangible reminder of the fact that we are each strong individuals and that we are made stronger by our community of survivors who join us on a path towards recovery. Be sure to place your "Strong Box" somewhere that you will see it as you go about your daily routine.
Row.txt_description: This workshop engages participants by painting in a new way. Participants strengthen their sense of personal power through creating visual symbols that help each person differentiate the source of their own personal strength.
Row.txt_tips: When selecting boxes to decorate, be sure to purchase ones that have an unfinished surface, similar to the one from Discount School Supply. A slick, or glossy surface will not allow the paint to stick.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To celebrate children by having them make a Fish Wind Sock that acknowledges their strengths and and how special they are.

   
   
   
   
 
 
  Colorful Flying Fish
 
Materials:
One sheet of heavy white or yellow construction paper (11” x 17”)
Markers, crayons, Craypas or Silky Sticks
Pipe cleaners 12” in length
Masking tape
Clear tape
45” of string or colorful ribbon
Fish template click here -  Head and Tail

Optional:
Glitter & glue
Paint & brushes or sponges
A 36” dowel, ¼” diameter or yardstick.

Timeframe/Age Range:
One Hour/ Children 5 and older.  Note that younger children will need help assembling the fish.

Set-up/Prep:
It is good to have a finished sample pre-made for the children to view before they begin. Make enough copies of the template so each child has two fish heads and a fish tails.

Introduction:
Japanese people have celebrated something called "Children's Day" for a long, long time. On this day a windsock that looks like a fish is flown outside the house for each child in the family. The fish used most often is a carp because it is a symbol of courage, strength and success in life. We can create any fish that we choose.

Although there is an actual day that celebrates children - called Children's Day, we think children should be celebrated everyday! So today we will each create our very own windsocks that celebrates our special qualities.

Warm-up/Opening Circle:
We are all used to celebrating certain occasions like Mother's Day, Father's Day, and Birthdays. Today we are going to acknowledge and celebrate children by making a strong and courageous Fish Windsock in honor of all the wonderful children in the world - and especially each of YOU.

We will begin with a fish warm-up exercise done while standing in a circle.  Once all the children have found a place in the circle ask the following questions and have the children act out the answers: how does the mouth of a fish look, how does the mouth of the fish move, how does a fish move their body to swim through the water?

A fish breathes by moving the gills on the sides of its body. Let's bend our arms at the elbow and move our arms in and out doing our own fish breaths.

While remaining in a circle ask everyone to sit and start a discuss about how every fish is different and each one has something special about it just like people. Ask each child share one of their special personal qualities with the group.  Some ideas might be: I get good grades in school, I like to help my mom, I love animals, I like to read, I have a creative mind, I love math, I am kind, I am good at sharing things.

Creation:
  
 Cutting the 2 fish halves
 
Step One:
Print fish template and tape the Head of the Fish Template to the Tail of the Fish Template at the dotted line to make one full fish shape.
Step Two:
Using the template provided, trace the shape of the fish, including the eyes, onto one sheet of 11x17  construction paper or tape 2 smaller pieces together to get the correct size. If possible, cut two identical fish shapes at the same time. If a child would like to draw their own fish shape, encourage them to use the entire length of their paper and cut two.
Step Three:
Cut out both of the fish shapes.
Step Four:
Lay both sides of the fish together with tails touching. Mark the inside of each fish by making a symbol or line so you will know which side of each cut out to decorate. Decorate each of the outer sides of the fish, (the sides without the mark you just made).
Step Five:
Lay decorated sides down, eyes at the top. Securely tape two or three pipe cleaners on the tummy part of the fish vertically, with equal lengths extending out from the top and bottom. Making sure to have the eyes across from one another, decorated sides facing outward, twist the top pipe cleaners together and tuck them in toward the middle to suggest a fuller stomach on each side, then twist the bottom two pipe cleaners together. Shape these pipe cleaners to make a full looking stomach toward to bottom. At the mouth, fold 1" of paper into the mouth of the fish. Insert the pipe cleaner inside the fold with the excess length on the top and bottom. Tape the paper firmly in place (inside the mouth) with the pipe cleaner laying as close to the fold as possible. To form the mouth into a circle, twist the pipe cleaner ends together and shape. Tuck ends of pipe cleaner inside the mouth.

 
  
 
  Decorate both sides of the fish
  Adding the pipe cleaners
 Lining up the top and bottom
 

Step Six:
Tape the top and bottom edge of the entire fish closed using clear tape, leave tail open.
Attach the ribbons at the mouth by wrapping the ribbon around the pipe cleaner and tying a knot. Also, you can tie the ribbon to a dowel to hang. You might want to have the children hang their fish on trees outside or they can catch the wind by having the children run with the fish behind them.

 
 
 
 
  Twisting the pipe cleaner on the sides to make the Fish body fuller
  Making the Fish mouth
  Adding ribbons to hang the Fish
 

Closing:
This is the time for each child to show their creative fish windsock (and it's name if they wish).  Also ask the children share how they liked making their windsock and how it felt to pick something special about themselves for their fish to represent.  Remind them that their fish is meant to celebrate how special they are!
Row.txt_description: This workshop celebrates our children by having them make a Fish Wind Sock that acknowledges who they are and how important they are.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give participants a chance to focus on the love they have for themselves and a way to remind themselves on a daily basis.

 
Materials:
Paper Mache recipe box (can be found for $1-$3 at Michael's)
4X6 index cards
4X6 index card dividers
List of affirmations (english /spanish )
"How to Write your Own Affirmation" handout (1 per person)
Collage materials- magazines, embellishments, patterned paper, etc.
Markers & fine tip markers
Mod Podge (or make your own with a solution of 1/2 water, 1/2 white glue)
Large paint or sponge brushes

Timeframe: 1 1/2 hrs

Prep:
If you have a larger group, you may want to divide the bottle of mod podge into bowls for participants to share.  At each place setting, set out one recipe box, 4 dividers and a stack of index cards. Spread collage materials and affirmations across the table.

 
 Intern Kelsey's personal recipe box.
 
Intro:
Today we're going to create a special recipe box. This box will hold recipes for your heart and soul. We'll be decorating the outside of our box with images, words and embellishments that evoke positive feelings and filling the inside with affirmations. Affirmations are words or phrases that gently remind us to love and accept ourselves. Affirmations help us feel more hopeful and positive.
We're going to create a recipe box of affirmations to give you the ingredients you need to help pick you up when you're feeling down.

Relaxation:
Begin to relax, find a comfortable position and start to let the tension leave your body.
Imagine that you are at the top of a stairway. At the bottom of the stairway is a state of peace, calm, and relaxation.
Take note of how you are feeling right now, at the top of the stairway.
Imagine taking a step down the stairway... a single step closer to relaxation. As you take this step, feel your arms relaxing. Becoming heavy. Limp... loose... relaxed.
Further descend the stairway, going down toward relaxation..... down.... down.... to a state of calm and relaxation. Feel your legs relaxing and becoming limp. Your legs are feeling very heavy.... so heavy... feel your legs sinking down, the heaviness pulling your legs down into relaxation.
Feel the heaviness in your arms and legs.... your arms are so warm and so heavy.... feel gravity pull on your arms gently, pulling your shoulders down into a relaxed position.
Take another step down.... and another.... more deeply relaxed with each step. Feel your neck and back relaxing. Feeling warm, loose... relaxed.
The closer you get to the bottom, the heavier and more relaxed you feel. You're almost there. Your body is so heavy.... but at the same time feels light, as if floating. It is an unusual feeling, but pleasant. So peaceful. Take the last few steps down to the bottom of the stairway..... sinking into relaxation.
Reaching the bottom now.... a state of calm. You are now feeling peaceful.
Now I'll repeat some affirmations. You don't even have to listen or pay attention, you can simply relax while I talk.
You are a worthwhile person.
You are capable of achieving many things.
You deserve to be happy. You can be happy even through difficult circumstances.
You can handle all the problems that come your way.
You are a strong person... while understanding that no one needs to be strong all the time.
You are perfectly alright, just the way you are.
Accept yourself.
Be kind to yourself.
You are okay the way you are.
(pause)
Continue to allow your mind to drift. Allow these affirmations to be true for you, repeating them silently in your mind if you want to, or simply taking them in.
I am a worthwhile person.
I deserve to be happy. I deserve good things.
I am unique, and I appreciate my uniqueness.
I feel good about myself.
I have many good qualities.
I do some things wrong and many things right.
I learn from my mistakes, and forgive myself when I make them.
I take time for myself. I deserve this time, and need this time.
I accept help, support, and love from others.
I am confident.
I like myself.
I am not perfect, and that is okay.
I accept myself.
(pause)
Continue allowing your mind to drift. Let the affirmations become true for you, filling you with a sense of confidence and self-assurance.
You are capable of making positive changes.... capable of increasing your self-esteem.... and of nurturing your self-esteem.
Notice what it is like to feel good about yourself. Allow yourself to feel calm and confident.
(pause)
(Relaxation excerpt adapted from InnerHealthStudio.com)

 
 
 
 
Creation:
Step One: Decorate the outside of your recipe box.
Remind participants to use any images they find positive or affirming on the outside of this box.

When adding the Mod Podge, remind participants to let their box dry with the lid open so that it doesn't glue together.

Step Two: Create the individual dividers.
Ask participants to make a divider by either writing and/or collaging on it. The dividers will help you organize your personal affirmations based on themes like "Joy", "Love", "Patience", "Gentleness" etc. This way, when you're in need of more reminders to love yourself in specific ways, you can go to your box.

Step Three: Make your affirmation cards.
While the Mod Podge dries on the box and dividers, ask participants to write affirmations on the provided index cards. Participants can choose from the affirmations provided, or write their own personal reminder to themselves of the positive messages about themselves, their life and the future. Participants can feel free to use the handout if needed.

Closing:
Ask participants share their affirmations with a neighbor. When they are finished sharing, have a few participants share what they heard.

Negative thoughts will surface in your head, they may be triggered by you, your batterer, or someone close to you. Just because these negative thoughts enter your head, it doesn't mean that you have to entertain them. You decide what thoughts you give your attention to. The next time a negative thought comes, take an affirmation card out of your recipe box and use it to send the bad thought out of your head and replace it with something uplifting and positive, you can even carry your affirmation with you throughout the day.  Remember, negative thoughts will come knocking at your door, but YOU decide whether or not you will entertain them.
Row.txt_description: In this workshop, participants get to decorate a traditional recipe box to hold their personalized affirmations.
Row.txt_tips: If you have a hard time finding inexpensive recipe boxes, a coupon organizer will work great too, however, because of the slick plastic surface, participants will not be able to collage over it.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop provides a window of time for each child to think of messages that are positive and encouraging about themselves and others.  These words will be added to hearts, which will become a fun and beautiful reminder of how special they are.

 
 
  Supplies for Feel Good Hearts
 
Materials:
Scissors and/or fancy edge scissors
Construction paper
Collaging materials
Glue sticks
Markers or gel pens
Ribbon, string, or yarn
Hole punch
Small basket or bag
Relaxing music
Optional: Laminator (or clear Avery brand laminating sheets)
Heart Template

Timeframe/Age Range:
One hour/ 10 and older
Introduction:         5 minutes
Opening Circle:      5 minutes
Demonstration:      5 minutes
Relaxation:            5 minutes
Creation:              25 minutes
Closing:                15 minutes
Total Time:           1 hour

Set-up/Prep:
Print and cut enough heart templates so that everyone in the group can have one.  It might be helpful to make a few finished hearts ahead of time for yourself to share with your group. You can pass the hearts around to show what the finished hearts will look like. If you are working with younger children, you might want to precut all the hearts for each child - you will need 5 hearts per person. Older children might want to laminate the hearts, so have the sheets ready.

Your your hearts should be approximately 3 1/2 by 3 1/2 inches, so you can fit at least three hearts on the laminating sheet.  Note: you can also have the hearts laminated at a copy center or use clear contact paper.
 
 
   
 Placing the heart on the
lamination sheet
 Covering the heart with the
lamination sheet
 Trimming the lamination around
the heart leaving a small clear
border all the way around
 

Introduction:
Today we are going to create special reminders that will make our hearts feel good (show your demo or create one with the group as you share about the project).  We will be making two positive message hearts for ourselves and three hearts to share with each person in the group!  That means that at the end of the workshop you will have a total of five hearts. These hearts will remind you how special you are and help pick you up whenever you are feeling down.
 
   
 
  Feel Good Heart garland
  Feel Good Heart book
 

Opening Circle:
Begin by asking each participant to share phrases or messages that sound encouraging or hopeful—anything that they would like to hear when they are having a bad day.  You might say things like: "I know I am strong, even if sometimes I don't feel strong", or "Sometimes I feel lonely, but I know that I am a good friend", "Even if today is a sad day, I will remember the happy days I have had"...

Relaxation:
Play relaxing music and speak softly and lovingly.

Tell the children that you are going to ask them to use their imaginations while they are seated in their chairs.  Ask them to close their eyes, if they feel comfortable doing that, and to listen to your words as you tell them different things to imagine, reminding them that all they need to do is sit back, listen and relax. 

In a calm, slow and soothing tone say:
Please sit with your feet flat, your back straight and your hands just lying loosely in your lap (If you have a silly group, it may be easier to ask them to put their head down). Try to picture what I am saying in your mind! Take a deep breath until your stomach feels full of air and as you slowly let it out, see yourself surrounded by peaceful blue balloons the color of the sky, notice as they float around in the air.  Feel yourself calmly breathing in and out. Imagine your worries flying away with the balloons. (Pause) Now picture yourself floating on a soft pink fluffy cloud, while you hear beautiful music all around you. You feel very light, almost like cotton candy.  Try to keep breathing peacefully and in a calm and relaxed way.  Now think about  the bright yellow sunshine gently warming your body.  Try to let your arms and legs and your head and neck just relax.  Take a deep breath, fill your lungs and as you let all the air out, picture how nice, warm and safe the sun feels on your body.  Now pretend that you are outside and you can smell the wonderful smell of fresh cut green grass and notice a nice cool breeze of sweet smelling air.

Now take a deep breath and think positive things about yourself  - remember how strong you are, how absolutely wonderful you are, how special you are... just soak these positive thoughts up, holding onto them...  knowing that they are all true.

When you are ready you can open your eyes and begin to create our beautiful positive messages on the hearts.  Make sure to create two hearts for yourself and three more hearts to share with each person in the group.

Creation:
   
  Cutting the heart with fancy scissors
 
   
  Punching a center hole on the heart
 
   
  Decorating with a hole punch
 
   
  Decorating the heart
 
   
  Weaving  the yarn to hang the heart
 
Step One:
Pass out the heart templates and draw the heart shapes on paper, the children can select colors of paper to use to cut their hearts, using regular or fancy scissors.  Then they can collage with scraps of paper or draw designs with the markers or gel pens.  Next ask them to write positive messages on the hearts like the ones you suggested in the introduction.  Encourage or help the children to write words or phrases that feel good to them. Remind them that they are creating 2 hearts to keep for themselves and the other 3 will be shared with everyone else so 2 of the hearts may have more personal messages and the other 3  are more general, uplifting positive messages.  If the children get stuck on what to write for the general messages you might ask them to think of what makes them feel better when they are down?

Step Two:
Have everyone choose which hearts they are keeping and then put the other three in a basket or bag. Then pass the basket or bag around the circle.  Have each participant pick one at a time until they are all gone.  If they pick their own, give them the choice to keep it or pick again.

Step Three:
You have the option to laminate before or after this process depending on time and supplies. Younger children will need help with this step. If you do laminate, remember to cut the shape slightly larger leaving a small clear border around the edge of the heart.

Step Four:
Punch a hole at the top/center of the heart.  (Note: If you wish to create a garland with the 5 hearts you will need to punch 2 holes at the top and weave the yarn through.)
Participants can string them together creating book of hearts, a heart garland, or they can tie a ribbon on each heart separately to make an ornament or a bookmark.

Closing:
Go around the room and ask each child to share their favorite heart message.  Ask them to talk about what it felt like to make their two positive personal messages and then to receive three other messages from other people.  You can ask "How did it feel to make those extra messages knowing other people would receive them?"
Row.txt_description: This workshop provides a window of time for each child to think of messages that are positive and encouraging about themselves and others. These words will be added to hearts, which will become a fun and beautiful reminder of how special they are.

Row.str_author_firstname: Coalition of Womens' Groups in Cape Cod, MA
Row.txt_code:
Virginia Tech's Clothesline Project (photo courtesy of Google images)
 
  A Clothesline Project example. (Photo courtesy of theclotheslineproject.org)
Project History:
"According to the Men's Rape Prevention Project in Washington DC, "58,000 soldiers died in the Vietnam war. During that same period of time, 51,000 women were killed mostly by men who supposedly loved them.
In the summer of 1990, this statistic became the catalyst for a coalition of women's groups in Cape Cod, Massachusetts to consciously develop a program that would educate, break the silence and bear witness to one issue - violence against women.

This small, core group of women, many of whom had experienced some form of personal violence, wanted to find a unique way to take staggering, mind-numbing statistics and turn them into a provocative, "in-your-face" educational and healing tool."

The Clothesline Project (CLP) is a vehicle for women affected by violence to express their emotions by decorating a shirt. "They then hang the shirt on a clothesline to be viewed by others as testimony to the problem of violence against women. The clothesline is commonly used on college campuses during Sexual Assault Awareness month and Domestic Violence Awareness month." History taken from theclotheslineproject.org. For a more detailed background, visit the history page of The Clothesline Project's official website.

Objective:
To give each woman an opportunity to tell her unique story using words and artwork to decorate a shirt. To raise awareness about domestic and sexual violence.

Materials:
T-shirts (one per participant)
Permanent Markers
Acrylic paints
Paint brushes
Water bowls
Writing paper
Pens
T-shirt board or cardboard(optional, but useful)
Clothesline (optional)
Clothespins (optional)
The Clothesline Project flyer (optional)

*Puff paint, white glue and fabric paint do not dry well and can cause the shirts to stick together. They are not recommended for this project.

 
The Utah Capitol Rotuda Clothesline Project display.
(photo courtesy of Google images)		 
Preparation:
Lay out t-shirts on tables (insert card board or t-shirt boards in the shirts). Arrange markers, paints, paper and pens neatly around workspace.

You may want to mark each shirt with a code or secret marking to confidentially identify the shirts.



Timeframe:
Warm-up/Participant Preparation:  15 minutes
Creation:   45 minutes  to 1 hour
Closing:  20 minutes
Total:  1 hour and 20 minutes or longer

Introduction:
Begin by explaining the origins of The Clothesline Project. You may use the following short description or the entire history at theclotheslineproject.org:
"A coalition of women’s groups in Massachusetts banded together in the summer of 1990 to develop a project that would increase awareness of violence against women, and empower survivors and families of victims to break the silence and tell their stories. Inspired by the harrowing statistics of all types of violence against women, these women wanted to create a program that could educate and heal. Drawing from the AIDS quilts concept, the women thought of using a clothesline because it represents the notion of traditional women’s work and the social bonds formed while chatting with neighborhood friends while clothes hung out on the line. The clothesline allows each woman’s unique story to be told, while powerfully demonstrating the community of women survivors and victims."

Talk about how each woman can use her shirt to tell her own story, using whatever words and artwork she feels best tell it. These shirts can serve as a way for us to walk away from the violence of the past, and come together as survivors.

(If you will be collecting and displaying the t-shirts, make sure to let the participants know in advance.)

Technical Info:
The Clothesline Project uses different color shirts to represent different types of abuse, and whether the victim survived the abuse. It's up to you and your clients if you want use the color coding or allow the survivors to choose a color that is significant to them. The color-coding used TCP is as follows:
    White: Women murdered due to sexual or domestic violence
    Yellow/Beige: Domestic violence women
    Red, Pink, Orange: Rape and sexual assault survivors
    Blue, Green: Incest and sexual abuse survivors
    Purple, Lavender: Attacked due to sexual orientation
    Black: Designation of your choice

 
 A Clothesline Project display at UCLA.
(photo courtesy of Google images)
Warm-Up:
If you are creating a display, have participants think about what words, symbols and messages represent their stories. What do they want their shirts to convey to those who view it? How can sharing our stories help us heal?  If you are not using it as part of a TCP display, simply generate a discussion about the statistic shared in this workshop and have the participants share their reactions.

 
Haven Hills 2008 Clothesline Project
 
Creation Process:
Suggest to the participants that it can be help to begin by sketching ideas and messages on paper before decorating their shirts. This is also helpful to get a feel for the paints and markers, and to get comfortable with the process.

Start by saying "there is no right
 
Haven Hills 2008 Clothesline Project
 
or wrong way to decorate your shirt! Use the paints and markers however you choose in order to tell your story. But, since this is a clothesline project it's important to decorate both sides of your shirt."

Suggest that each participant include a written story to accompany their shirt. The stories may be attached to the shirts or simply kept together.

Once a shirt is complete, and has had some time to dry, it may be hung on a clothesline. You can set up a clothesline in your workspace, or create an event. (See Tips below.)

If you do hang the shirts, try hanging them in blocks of color, and alternating dark and light colored shirts in order to highlight each shirt and the impact of the story represented.

Closing:
If you are not using a clothesline, encourage each woman hold up her shirt and share her story. What message has she conveyed? How does each participant feel about the shirts as a group of stories?
If using a clothesline, encourage participants to walk around the clothesline and take the time to absorb the message of each shirt. Invite discussion and communication among the participants.

Click here for the official site of The Clothesline Project!
Row.txt_description: The Clothesline Project is a vehicle for adults affected by violence to express their emotions by decorating a shirt. The shirts are used to raise public awareness about the issue of domestic and sexual violence.

Row.str_title: Pearls of Wisdom:End the Violence Workshop Draft-For Participating Programs Only
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop is designed to help participants and their chil dren recognize their personal strength, and uses the metaphor of "pearls" as treasures that form inside an oyster in response to an irritant. Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence.

Materials:
Collage materials (different kinds of tissue and natural fiber papers work well)
Magazines for images or words (use sparingly)
Watercolors, Acrylic or Biocolors
Biocolor Shimmer paint additive for pearlized look
Water cups
Paint brushes
Paint palettes
Sandpaper(provided in toolkit)
Color pencils
Yarn, string, buttons
Scraping tools (paper clips, toothpicks,screwdrivers, spoon, knives etc)
Tacky glue
Mod Podge and thick brushes
Hand wipes
Images of Kim Abeles Pearl Disc Samples:
1. Braille Collage / Safe Place Carving Image
2. Pencil Drawing and Woven Words
3. Woven Collage and Iridescent Paint
4. Paint and Collage with Nylon Stocking
5. Simple Layering Technique

Timeframe:
Plan for this workshop to take between 1 and 3 hours.


 
Project Background:
Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence is a two year community project organized by A Window Between Worlds in collaboration with artist Kim Abeles and AWBW Community Art Advocate Sandra Mueller. 

The Pearls of Wisdom project will culminate with an exhibition, online blog, catalogue and related events commemorating A Window Between Worlds’ 20th Anniversary at the Korean Cultural Center in March 2011. As the only national organization using art to help end domestic violence, this project affirms AWBW’s pioneering work in bridging the realms of art and social change.

About Kim Abeles: Kim Abeles has been described by Artscene’s, Orville O. Clarke as “one of the most acute observers of the state of our region's body and soul.”  Abeles’ art crosses disciplines and media to explore and map the urban environment and chronicle broad social issues.  Her body of work gives the community a voice to address social issues in a positive, constructive way.  Both her personal experience as a survivor and her broad experience with large scale collaborative installation work position her well to conceive and implement this statewide collaboration weaving the voices of survivors and community members around the issue of domestic violence.

To see Kim talk more about her background and this project, click here.

 
Preparation/Set-up: 
We are offering several options for warm-ups and creation. As always we want you to make this workshop your own. Feel free to use some or all of the different options presented to facilitate this project.  Each step will have an approximate timeframe to help you plan.

If you would like, you could do this workshop in stages. For example, you could spend the first session exploring the process of 'becoming a pearl' as it relates to each survivor using the journaling exercises suggested below. In the second session you could choose to offer a relaxation and/or opening circle of revelations or discoveries from the first session and create your pearl. 

We encourage and welcome all workshop Leaders to create their own “Pearl” and explore the creative process of this project. Leaders who do create a Pearl are asked to submit their creation for inclusion in the final exhibition.

After you decide how you will present this workshop, collect the materials you would like to offer and create an art supply buffet table or different supply stations with material laid out by supply type.
 

 
Workshop Introduction:
A pearl is a wonderful metaphor for the survivor’s journey. Do you know how a pearl is formed? Basically, it starts with an irritant that enters an oyster; protective layers transform that mollusk and create a pearl. Throughout our lives, we all have challenges and difficulties (irritants). There are lessons to be learned in all these challenges (pearls).

Sharing your story as a survivor, from pain to wisdom, can empower and inspire an individual or even a community to help end the violence perpetrated against our innocence, our hearts, our souls and our bodies. What you’ve experienced and the ways you survived are valuable and essential in helping to end the cycle of violence.

As you reflect and create your pearls, notice your strength, beauty and wisdom. Embrace the ways you are transforming and growing. Thank you for being here to share your story.

Opening Circle:

 Basket of "irritants"
Provide small objects in the middle of the table (or pass around a basket) that the group can pick from to represent their irritant. Found objects such as symbolic items, charms, stickers or images, Mexican Loteria cards and other knick-knacks. If possible you may want to welcome participants to bring a personal object that represents a significant irritant in their lives (i.e. letter, photo, etc.). 

Choose one:
A. Have participants share why they chose their object(s). How did this irritant/challenge affect your journey?
B. Ask participants to say the first thing that comes to mind about what they would say to a friend or complete stranger, right now, about getting out of a DV relationship or staying safe.
C. Go straight to journaling and share after.

 
 Oyster Journal
Demonstration:
Before the creation process on the pearl disc, share about the materials you provided for your workshop and the different techniques that can be used for their creations.   As you share, pass around the workshop sample images. If you haven't already done so and it's feasible, this might be a good time to share the dvd created by Kim Abeles that goes with this project.  After the demonstration suggest that it is important to make a commitment to one idea for their pearl project. Let the art become their voice.

 

Journaling (using the journals provided):
You may want to offer several journaling times (about 5 minutes each) to help participants reflect through the irritant on the process of transforming it into a pearl. They can use words, phrases, or draw symbols, whatever they feel like doing.

A. Using the mirror paper, have participants write about the irritants that have affected their journey to today.  They can write about why they chose the object during the opening circle or write about the people or experiences that affected their journey.  

B.Using the bandage paper, participants can reflect the ways they are healing or what has helped them through difficult experiences in their lives.

C. The extra sheets can be used at any time as a place to put thoughts, write personal notes or continue the creative process. 

Relaxation(optional):  
Have participants hold the unsanded pearl in their hands during the meditation and with their eyes closed. Begin...This is your window of time. This is a time to honor yourself as a wise and strong survivor. Get comfortable in your chair and if it feels safe, let your eyes close.  (Read slowly) Now, notice your breath (pause). With each breath notice that your breath has been with you in pain and in joy. Your breath and you are one. Your breath is your life force. Continue to breathe and connect with how you are feeling right now.  Notice how strong and courageous you are to be sitting in this room.  Give yourself permission to feel whatever you may be feeling.  Notice that you are safe, that you are taking important steps to heal the parts of you that are hurt and to honor the parts of you that are strong, courageous and authentically you. Take a few deep breaths and when you are ready open your eyes.     

 
Creation:
Start in any of the ways described above. Have participants select a plaster disc.  Invite them to choose the material they will need and tell them how much time they will have to create.

Explain that they will now sand their disks as their 'Pearl' begins to take shape. After sanding they will begin to create using the materials provided. 
With sand paper provided welcome participants to sand the disc/pearl’s jagged edges and/or rough surface or if they prefer they may leave it rough. 
(They could use this opportunity to think of this process as symbolic of letting go of their irritants, the challenges, the pain and struggles. Remind them that it is okay not feel ready to take this step at this time and that they can just notice how it feels to sand the rough edges.  It is also important to remind them that it is okay to leave it rough. What is most important is that they trust what feels right.)

When they have complete the sanding process they are ready to create.

Throughout the creative process, remind participants that their is no wrong way to create their story of survival and wisdom. The messages on their pearls of wisdom are meant to inspire, educate and encourage others in their healing journey.

Toward the end of the creating time, start to encourage participants to think about their pearls of wisdom. Ask them to look back at the process of creating, what they learned today and what they may want to share as part of this exhibit. 
      
Closing Circle:

Option A: Share about your pearl and the wisdom your represented on it.

Option B: What would they tell themselves today or what would they share with a younger friend who might be going through something similar?

Option C: If the participants have good relationships with one another, have them share with a partner.  Then, when we go around the circle - the partner speaks the 'wisdom' she heard and vice versa.  It makes it more of a 'wisdom circle'. 

Submit Pearls to AWBW:
Using release form have them share their words of wisdom to go with their pearl.
Pack the Pearls using the Pearls Handling Instructions provided in your toolkit.

Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence.

Row.str_title: Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence Workshop (Paper Version)
Row.str_author_firstname: AWBW Staff - Adapted from Pearls of Wisdom Project by Kim Abeles
Row.txt_code:
I have the power to chose how I see myself. Claiming one’s self worth is empowering and life changing. This helped me crystalize what I have learned from my experiences.
Objective:
This workshop is designed to help women and their children recognize their personal strength, and uses the metaphor of "pearls" as treasures that form inside an oyster in response to an irritant. Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength and wisdom as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence.

Project Background:
Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence is a two year community project organized by A Window Between Worlds in collaboration with artist Kim Abeles and AWBW Community Art Advocate Sandra Mueller. 

The Pearls of Wisdom project will culminate with an exhibition, online blog, catalogue and related events commemorating A Window Between Worlds’ 20th Anniversary at the Korean Cultural Center in March 2011. As the only national organization using art to help end domestic violence, this project affirms AWBW’s pioneering work in bridging the realms of art and social change.

About Kim Abeles: Abeles’ art crosses disciplines and media to explore and map the urban environment and chronicle broad social issues.  Her body of work gives the community a voice to address social issues in a positive, constructive way.  Both her personal experience as a survivor and her broad experience with large scale collaborative installation work position her well to conceive and implement this statewide collaboration weaving the voices of survivors and community members around the issue of domestic violence.

To see Kim talk more about her background and this project, click here.

  
  Love should never hurt!  Keep moving forward, beautiful, INSPIRE, resilient
Timeframe:
1 hour to 1 1/2 half hour

Materials:
Collage materials including different kinds of paper-doilies, tissue and natural fiber papers work well.
Magazines for images or words (use sparingly)
Scissors
Glues Sticks
Mod Podge and thick brushes
Acrylic or Biocolors paint
Make it Shimmer by Biocolor(this is an additive for a pearlized look)
Paint brushes
Paint palettes
Water cups
Paper towels
Colored pencils
Permanent Markers
Found objects (see Preparation/Set-up for details)
White card stock or watercolor paper 
Circle to trace 5-inch diameter or larger (Bowls, cds etc. work well)

Preparation/Set-up: 
We encourage and welcome all workshop Leaders to create their own “Pearl” and explore the creative process of this project. Leaders who do create a Pearl of Wisdom are encouraged to submit their creation for inclusion in the final exhibition. Provide small objects in the middle of the table (or pass around a basket) that the group can pick from to represent their irritant. Found objects such as symbolic items, charms, stickers, keys or images, Mexican Loteria cards and other knick-knacks. If possible you may want to welcome participants to bring a personal object that represents a significant irritant in their lives (i.e. letter, photo, etc.) prior to the workshop. 

Our story, our journey is not over.
Forgive to reclaim your power.
Workshop Introduction:
A pearl is a wonderful metaphor for the survivor’s journey. Do you know how a pearl is formed? Basically, it starts with an irritant that enters an oyster; protective layers transform that mollusk and create a pearl. Throughout our lives, we all have challenges and difficulties (irritants). There are lessons to be learned in all these challenges(pearls).

Sharing your story as a survivor, from pain to wisdom, can empower and inspire an individual or even a community to help end the violence perpetrated against our innocence, our hearts, our souls and our bodies.  What you’ve experienced (these difficulties and challenges) and the ways you survived are valuable and essential in helping to end the cycle of violence.

As you reflect and create your pearls, notice your strength, beauty and wisdom. Embrace the ways you are transforming and growing. Thank you for being here to share your story.

Demonstration:
Share about the materials you provided for this workshop and the different techniques that can be used for their creations.  As you share, pass around the workshop sample images. If you haven't already done so and it's feasible, this might be a good time to share the dvd created by Kim Abeles that goes with this project.  After the demonstration suggest that it is important to make a commitment to one idea for their Pearl.  Let the art become their voice.

Opening Circle:
  
Ask participants to choose a symbol of their "irritant" from the found objects provided. Ask why they  chose that object to represent their irritant.

Journaling:
From an irritant a beautiful pearl emerges. We are now going to take some time now to journal about your pearls of wisdom. 

A. How did the irritant affect your journey?
B. What has helped you through tough times? What helped you survive? What gave you strength?
C. What advice would you give your younger self?
D. What advice would you share with another person to give them strength?  It can be very practical things, a simple idea, or something more philosophical

E. In an oyster, a beautiful pearl emerges from an irritant. From the irritant you find a treasure.  From difficulties we gain so much wisdom. That wisdom is something you can share to help others get through their own issues. What wisdom would want to share?

 
 Journey through pain towards hope and serenity. Love Yourself.
Relaxation(optional):
Begin...This is your window of time. This is a time to honor yourself as a wise and strong survivor. Get comfortable in your chair and if it feels safe, let your eyes close.  (Read slowly) Now, notice your breath (pause). With each breath notice that your breath has been with you in pain and in joy. Your breath and you are one. Your breath is your life force. Continue to breathe and connect with how you are feeling right now.  Notice how strong and courageous you are to be sitting in this room.  Give yourself permission to feel whatever you may be feeling.  Notice that you are safe, that you are taking important steps to heal the parts of you that are hurt and to honor the parts of you that are strong, courageous and authentically you. Take a few deep breaths and when you are ready open your eyes.     

 
 I am breaking the cycle 
Creation:
Create artwork that shares your pearl of wisdom. As you create, remember to illustrate your message in any way that feels right. You can create an image, use words or both.

Throughout the creative process, remind participants that there is no wrong way to create their story of survival and wisdom.

Toward the end of the creating time start to encourage participants to think about their pearls of wisdom. Ask them to look back at the process of creating, what they learned today and what they may want to share.
      
Closing Circle:
 
  
Option A: Share about your pearl and the wisdom you represented on it.

Option B: What would you tell yourself today or what would you share with a younger friend who may be going through something similar. 

Option C: If the participants have good relationships with one another, have them share with a partner.  After sharing in pairs, go around the circle and have the listener speak the 'wisdom' from her partner and vice versa.  It makes it more of a 'wisdom circle'. 

Submit Pearls to AWBW:
Submit your pearls through AWBW's blog by clicking here . If you prefer you may send original artwork or a high resolution image with releases to AWBW for inclusion in the Pearls of Wisdom blog.
Row.txt_description: This workshop is designed to help survivors recognize their personal strength, and uses the metaphor of a "pearl" as a treasure that form inside an oyster in response to an irritant. Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength and wisdom as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence.
