Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop gives participants an opportunity to look at the thoughts, feelings or experiences they want to leave behind, and to express what they want to move towards in their life.

  ;
 Supplies for My Window
Materials:
Scratch Art Boards (can be purchased at Discount School Supply or Oriental Trading Company )
Toothpicks, pencils, or any object that can be used to scratch off the black layer of the art board
Tablecloth or newspaper (to cover the table as the Scratch Art Boards can be very messy)
Glue stick
Hole punch
Ribbon (assorted colors)
Scissors
Paper cutter (optional)

Note: If using this workshop to help the survivors release or process anger, it is important to begin by having a discussion on "What is Anger?" Please click here to see the entire Processing Anger Workshop Series.

Framing options:
Option 1. Glass: 2" x 2" Memory Glass purchased at Ranger
                Frame: 2" x 2" Memory Frame purchased at Ranger

Option 2: Laminating sheets, Contact paper or laminator cut into 3"x3" squares.

Preparation:   Be sure to lay out newspaper on top of the table the participants will use when they create to catch the black scrapings (they can be messy and/or stain).  Since you cannot purchase 2"x 2" Scratch Art Boards, you will need to cut them to size.  You will also need to cut the laminating sheets into 3" x 3" squares, if you are using the laminating sheets.  It is helpful to use a paper cutter to get the exact size. 

Time Frame:  1 hour
Introduction: 5 min
Opening Circle: 15 min
Creation: 25 min
Closing Circle: 15 min

Introduction:
Today we are going to create a window that expresses the things we want to leave behind and what we want to create more of in our life. We'll start by reflecting on what you'd like to let go of. Then, I'm going to ask you to be brave and think about what you REALLY want to move towards, now and in your future.
  Using a toothpick to scratch images on the board
Opening Circle:
Have each participant share a word, or sentence, about one thing they want to let go of or leave behind.

Creation:
Pass out two Scratch Art Boards and a scratch tool to each participant.

Part 1: We'll start by reflecting on what you'd like to let go of or leave behind. Maybe it's something weighing you down or holding you back in someway. On the first board, using the scratch tool, scratch through words, shapes, symbols, images or doodles that represent the thoughts, feelings or experiences you want to let go of or leave behind.  For example, if you want to leave tears behind, you can scratch a rain cloud into your board. Give the participants ten minutes to complete part 1.

Part 2: Now that we've looked at what we want to let go of, let's look at what we want to move towards. Be brave, be daring, and think about what you REALLY want more of in your life. Have each participant share a word, or sentence, about one thing they want to go towards. On the second board, scratch through words, shapes, or images that represent the positive things you want now and in your future. For example, you can scratch through a sun and ocean to represent that tropical vacation you've always wanted to take, or a heart to represent love. Let you're imagination run wild! The future is wide open, and only you know what you want it to look like! Give the participants ten minutes to complete part 2.

Part 3: Once you are done scratching through, glue the backsides (white sides) of your boards together using a glue stick.


 
 
 Framing Option 1: Placing the Memory Glass.
  Inserting glass into Memory Frame
 
    
  
 
 Framing Option 2: Peeling lamination sheet.
  Sticking the two laminating sheets together.
 

Framing:
Option 1 - Frames:  Place the boards in between two pieces of Memory Glass.  Cut off any parts of the board that are not covered by the glass.  Place the Memory Glass pieces into the Memory Frame and close the frame using the latch.

Option 2 - Lamination: Cover the entire board using the pre-cut 3" x 3" self-laminating sheets or contact paper on both sides. Cut off any excess laminating material (leave at least 1/4" on all sides). Note: If you are using a laminator, be careful, as lamination sheets can be tricky and unforgiving. Then, use a hole punch near the top of the board to create a place for the ribbon to go.  Be sure you don't punch the hole too close to the edge of the board.

 
  Completed My Windows into what they are leaving behind.
 (framed version on the left / Laminated version on the right)
To finish your window string ribbon through the hole at the top of your board or frame.

Closing Circle:
Ask each participant to share what they created on their window, and what they want to remember and keep in their hearts from today.  Remind the participants that it is important to keep in mind that we have the power to let go of the past and create the future WE want! We are very powerful, and identifying what we want is the first step in embracing our futures!

Alternate Closing:
Brainstorm a "Safety Plan" with the participants to help them process their anger. Some helpful tips include:
Talk to a friend you can trust
Count to 10
Take out art supplies and draw a picture of your anger
Journal about your anger
Take deep breaths
Listen to music
Walk away
Dance or exercise
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives participants an opportunity to look at the thoughts, feelings or experiences they want to leave behind, and to express what they want to move towards in their life.
Row.txt_tips:
We recommend that you start anger workshops with a discussion; don't be afraid to talk to the survivors about their anger. Anger is nothing to be ashamed of, it is important to look at and talk about it to try to understand it.

Some anger prompts that we like are:
What is Anger? What does it look like and what does it sound like?
What was the trigger to your anger?
What did you think about it?
How did it make you feel?
How did you act?
What effect did it have on you and those around you?

Row.txt_code:
Corn husk dolls/figures created by Refuge House, Inc.
Spanish Support group members & leaders (Tallahassee, Florida).
Background:
Corn husks are an interesting and fun material to use during the month of November as we celebrate and decorate for Thanksgiving. They can be crunched or stretched in a variety of ways. They can be made round, ruffled, tied, braided or curled. You can also leave them in their natural color or they can be painted or dyed.

Objective:
To look at the things that help the children to grow into strong, healthy adults while creatively using simple, natural materials.

Materials:
   
  Cornhusks
 
Dry corn husks (at least 5 per participant). These are available in most grocery stores or craft stores.
Large water bowl to soak the husks in.
Paper towels at each station to soak the water from the corn husk when they are first pulled out of the water bowl.
Raffia, twine, or pipe cleaners.
Scissors
Step by step Handout
Optional:
Paint
Paint brushes
Cups of water

Note: Some suggestions may require additional materials.You may also use fresh corn husk leaves. If you want to save them until you are ready to do the workshop store them to dry.

 Age Range:        
 Timeframe:
 Ages 6 - 16
 One hour.  If you choose to paint the body or create
clothing you can do this is a separate session.





 Preparation:
You may want to start soaking the corn husks in warm water prior to the group session so they are ready when your group arrives. You can dry them by laying them out on a folded paper towel.

Introduction:
Corn husk dolls have been around for centuries are seen in most all cultures that harvest and use corn.  Native Americans produced dolls of varying styles to look like members of their tribe. Later, European settlers learned from the natives and made corn husk dolls for their children too.  Corn also plays an essential role in Mexican culture, using different parts of the plant for medicine, food and crafts, like the corn husk dolls. Some cultures use the dolls in ceremonies to help heal people who are ill or to help stop evil dreams.

Corn husks dolls are perfect to make during this time of year since corn is a traditional food for Thanksgiving and the husks can make beautiful and creative decorations.

Today we are going to create a corn husk doll that can tell our story of growth.

  
 
Corn Husk dolls from
El Salvador
  Corn Husk doll from
Mexico		  Native American
Corn Husk doll

Warm-up/Relaxation:
To begin this meditation have the participants sit straight and as comfortable as possible. Ask them to close their eyes if this is comfortable to them. Ask them to put their hands in their laps and to begin taking a few even breaths to settle down.

Say, "Breathe in for 3 counts; hold 3 counts, breathe out 4 counts." (You can count along out loud). Do this several times until the room feels still and quiet. Then say, " Think about what corn needs to grow big and tall and healthy - like water and sunlight, now think about all the things that will help you to grow into a strong, healthy and happy adult. Breathe in 3 counts; hold 3 counts, breathe out 4 counts. It could be a family member who loves and supports you, close friends you can trust, a special teacher that encourages you to learn and explore new things, or someone who believes that you can do anything you try to do. Try to picture all the different ways people can help you as you grow up. Breathe in 3 counts; hold 3 counts, breathe out 4 counts. Think about the things in your life that make you feel proud. Breathe in 3 counts; hold 3 counts, breathe out 4 counts. Notice how good it feels to take a few minutes to think about the ways you can grow and learn and develop. Breathe in 3 counts; hold 3 counts, breathe out 4 counts.

Creation Process:
Create a doll that represents the person you would like to become when you grow up, remembering some of the positive influences on your life that you were just thinking of.

1) Layer 4 corn husks on top of each other.

2) Join the upper inch of the husks and tie tightly with raffia or twine.  Note, if it is easier for the younger children you can use pipe cleaners and twist around to tighten.

3) Take 2 leaves on each side and pull over covering the knot, reversing the outside in.

4) To make a head, draw a string around approximately one inch below the top view of the folded back husks which should then envelop the knot hidden underneath. The raffia, string, bow or pipe cleaner makes the doll's neck.

 
   
1
  2  3  4
5) To make the arms, fold a new sheet in half lengthwise, coiled (corn leaves work better if you roll with the grain of the leaf rather than against the grain). Tie each end. You can also braid the leaves for the arms.

6) Place the arms between the two sets of corn husks into the body of leaves. Slide your arms as high as they will rise up towards the neck loop.

7) With a string of raffia (or pipe cleaner), tie a belt under their arms. Tie it tightly enough to hold your arms firmly in place.


 
 
 5  6  7

Optional:
-Make a doll/figure with braids using 3 strings of raffia tied at each end.
-Make a doll/figure in pants rather than a skirt by tying each side off at the ankle.
-Make a doll/figure by painting the body by creating clothing.

Closing:
Go around and ask the participants to share their corn husk dolls and how these dolls represent the things they want for themselves in their future as they grow into healthy strong adults.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives participants the opportunity to look at the things that help them to grow into strong, healthy adults while creatively using simple natural materials.
Row.txt_tips: Keep in mind: Make every knot with the twine or raffia on the same side for a more finished look. All knots can be cut at the end, just make sure you double tie knots before each crop.

To help participants find art in the holidays. A series of workshops with holiday themes including Ginger Bread Houses, Decorated cookies, Snowflakes and Magic Reindeer. The idea is to create something special to show loved ones that we care and perhaps even begin new family traditions.  Creating with art during the holidays as a family can be a relaxing way to connect, bond and celebrate.

Objective:
Participants make unique snowflakes to celebrate the winter holidays and their own individuality.

Opening:
As you begin these workshops, take the opportunity to talk about the significance of the holidays and how it is a time to celebrate yourself and those you care for. It can also be a time to begin thinking about goals and visions for the new year.


 
Fold square paper in
half diagonally. Fold
in half again. Keep
folding into a
wedge		 
Creation:
Snowflakes are a fun and magical way to celebrate the winter holidays across traditions and religions. They can be made by folding almost any type of paper (see steps bellow). The more folds the more complex the design. The snowflakes can be decorated with markers or glitter and they can be attached to make a holiday card. After you have several snowflakes cut out you may want to hang them up in the window, string them out on a garland or hang them from a rod as a snowflake mobile. You can tape thread to them and make ornaments or decorate packages by taping them on the wrapping.

Materials:
Plain White Paper (cut into squares)
Scissors
Ribbon
Markers
Glitter or Glitter Glue (optional)

 
 
Begin to cut shapes at
the edges of your
folded wedge.		 Cutting the top of the
wedge creates the
outside shape of the
snowflake.
 Unfold to see your
beautiful snowflake.

Pre-made Gingerbread House Kits are available to purchase at many local retailers such as Trader Joe’s, Bed Bath and Beyond, Linens and Things or Michael’s. They usually come complete with the icing and candy decorations. Or you can bake your own (see following recipe).

Row.txt_code:
To help participants find art in the holidays. A series of workshops with holiday themes including Ginger Bread Houses, Deco rated cookies, Snowflakes and Magic Reindeer. Creating with art during the holidays as a family can be a relaxing way to connect, bond and celebrate.

Objective:
In this workshop, participants make charms out of Shrinky Dinks that represent what they are grateful for and how they are blessed.

Materials:
Shrinky Dink Material
Permanent Markers and/or Color Pencils
Scissors
Ribbon or Yarn
Beads (Optional)
Toaster Oven

(Feel free to call for more details if you’ve never used Shrinky Dinks before. They are fabulous!)

Creation:
Taking the time to think about what is good in your life and what you are grateful for is a powerful exercise especially at this time of year. You could open with a circle of blessing-sharing and then make Shrinky Dink charms. These charms can be used to hang in the window or on a tree. They can even be made into jewelry – such as a necklace, pendant, or earring.

Row.str_title: Holiday Card Making - Holidays with HeART Series
Row.txt_code:
To help participants find art in the holidays. A series of workshops with holiday themes including Ginger Bread Houses, Decorated cookies, Snowflakes and Magic Reindeer. Objective:
This workshop gives participants an opportunity to create and receive home made holiday cards.

Opening:
If you are beginning these workshops in November, you can take this opportunity to talk about what the holidays mean and discuss things to be thankful for. Also note, these workshops can be adapted to any time of the year - not just for the holidays.

Materials:
Construction Paper
Colored Pencils
Markers
Craypas (especially great for getting bright colors on colored paper)
Glitter Glue or Paint
Scissors

 
 
Creation:
Making and giving a personal home made card is a wonderful way to make someone feel special. To start, have each person draw a name of someone else in the group, Then make a card for that person, once that is done each participant can make additional cards for family and friends. You can add materials to make the card more detailed, such as magazines for collage, doilies, vellum papers and ribbons. (You could also skip the drawing names and just have everyone make cards for people they love!)

Row.str_title: Flower Angel Ornaments - Holiday Decorating Series
Row.txt_code:
This workshop is part of Windows' Holiday Decorating Series: Use this and other simple workshops during your holiday parties and festivities, to decorate your shelter, or just to help the adults and children feel surrounded by loving, hopeful feelings, especially during this particularly difficult time for those living in the shelter.

 
  Flower Angel Ornament
Objective:
To help participants get in touch with their inner child. To remember when they were children and think of happy thoughts associated with fairies or magical creatures, while exploring their own innocence.

Materials:
Artificial flowers (large roses are recommended)
Pipe cleaners
Large wooden doll head (with or without the face painted on) available at craft stores i.e. Micheal's or orientaltrading.com
Yarn of different colors
Beads
Hook or key chain ring
Hot glue gun and glue sticks
Embellishments such as gemstones, ribbons, glitter, sequins, feathers etc.

Timeframe:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Warm-up: 5-10 minutes
Creation: 40-45 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Total time: 60 minutes

Preparation:
 
    Materials set-up
For this workshop make sure to create a sample so that you can confidently walk the participants through each step of the creation process.

Play fun holiday music, such as Putamayo or make a CD of various holiday songs. You may also want to create that special "holiday smell" by bringing in fresh cinnamon pine cones, candles or even bake gingerbread cookies for your group.

Introduction:
Today we are going to create holiday fairy/angel decorations to fill the shelter (or our homes) with hope, strength, courage, beauty, creativity, warmth and love. With this workshop, we're going to get in touch with our inner child and create these beautiful flower fairies, or angels to remind us of our hopes and dreams.

Warm-up:
Have everyone go around the circle and share their favorite holiday song, food, story, memory or movie, whatever they choose is fine.  Remind participants that what's important during this warm-up is they think of anything that brings them joy. If they have a difficult time thinking of something, encourage them to share their hopes and dreams for future holidays.

Creation Process:
Step 1 - Hair:
First select a yarn for the color of hair you want. Wrap it around four fingers until you get the amount of hair you want, about ten rotations around your hand. Secure the center with a pipe cleaner and connect the hook or ring to the center of the pipe cleaner, then cut the ends of the yarn to create the hair.
 Wrap yarn around hand Attach pipe cleaner & add ring Cut ends of yarn for hair

Step 2 - Body:
Use the wooden doll head with the flat side and the hole in the center to glue the flower to the bead. Add enough glue to the hole of the bead and fit the stem of the flower into the glued hole. Then glue the center of the hair to the top of the head.
 
 
   Hot glue wood bead to flower steam  Hot glue hair to head 

Step 3 - Arms and Wings:
Wrap another pipe cleaner around the neck so that the two sides on either end are even, for the arms. Fold the ends of the arms to create small oval hands.  Create wings by adding a glittery pipe cleaner to the back of the neck by securing to the other pipe cleaner. Bend into a wing shape and attach to the middle.

  Wrap pipe cleaner around neck  Fold ends to make oval hands  Bend arm to look more realistic

Step 4 - Decorating:
Using a permanent marker, draw a face. Using the hot glue gun, hang the ribbon from the hook or ring, then add beads and embellishments.

  Hot glue decorations on flower  Hot glue decorations on wings  Add ribbon and beads to hook

After you've shown the participants how to create their fairy or angel, and they begin the creation process, remind them to focus on their hopes and dreams.

Closing:
It's important to have the participants do a closing of the workshop. Have each woman share what their fairy or angel means to them and how their inner child feels in this moment.

To end on a hopeful note, remind participants that you hope they will hold onto their ornament as a reminder that they need to care for their inner child and to nurture their joy.  Thank all participants for taking a window of time to create with you.
Row.txt_description: By creating flower angel ornaments, participants get in touch with their inner child by remembering when they were children and thinking of happy thoughts associated with fairies or magical creatures, while exploring their own innocence.

Row.txt_code:
This workshop is part of Windows' Holiday Decorating Series: Use this and other simple workshops during your holiday parties and festivities, to decorate your shelter, or just to help the children feel surrounded by loving, hopeful feel ings, especially during this particularly difficult time for those living in the shelter.

Objective:
To educate the participants about the power of words by giving them an opportunity to say loving things to one another and then create a Shrinky Dink ornament to serve as a reminder of all the positive words and feelings they heard and felt.  Includes an interactive warm-up that helps build the participants self-esteem and allows them to bond.

  
  Holiday templates for Shrinky ornaments
Materials:
Shrinky Dink material (Ruff-N-Ready)
Permanent markers
Colored pencils and sharpeners
Scissors
Hole puncher
Toaster oven
Ribbon or craft wire
Holiday Template (shapes)
Holiday Template (characters)
Beads (optional)
CD Player & holiday themed music (optional)

Timeframe:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Warm-up:     20 minutes
Creation:      30 minutes
Closing:        5 minutes
Total Time:   60 minutes

Preparation:
During this workshop, make sure to play fun holiday music, Putamayo is great resource for various holiday songs. You may also want to create that "holiday smell" by bringing in fresh cinnamon pine cones, candles or even bake gingerbread cookies for your group.

You'll need to make enough photocopies of the various templates for all the participants. Pre-cut the Shrinky Dink into 3 1/2"x4" squares to fit the size of our template (AWBW sells pre-cut Shrinky Dink material, $5 for 100 sheets). Make sure all colored pencils are pre-sharpened. It's good to have all the materials set up prior to beginning the workshop.

It’s important to try this project in advance so you have some samples to share. If you have never used the Shrinky Dink materials you will also want to get a feel for how the Shrinky Dinks cook. It’s very exciting to watch!

Introduction:
Today we are going to create Shrinky Dink ornaments as a reminder of all of the positive qualities you each have and fill the shelter (or our homes) with happiness and love.

Warm-up:
One at at time, have each person share one positive thing about the person sitting next to them (you can have them say the positive thing about the person to the right or left of them, or if time permits, have each person say something nice to every person in the group).  It can be anything you think will make that person feel good.  You can say something you like about them, something they are good at, or something that makes them special or unique.  We will do this so that you can hear all of the loving, awesome things people say about you to remind you of just how special and valued you are.

Creation:
If you haven't used Shrinky Dinks with your group before, be sure to review the following steps before the begin.  Demonstrate how to color on the rough side with the color pencils for the background, how to use darker colors for the words and explain that the plastic will shrink to a third of it's size after baking. You may also want to show a finished sample.

 
  Tracing the design
 
  3 Holiday Shrinkys
 
  Baking the Shrinkys
Step 1:
Choose one of the holiday templates in front of you. Start by tracing the template on the rough side of the Shrinky Dink. Keeping in mind all of the nice things you just heard from the group, write words, colors, shapes, or scribbles on the Shrinky Dink to help you remember all of the good feelings you had and words that were said about you.  Begin to color and create the design that will fill in the shape of your template. (Be sure to draw on the rough side of the plastic.)

Step 2:
When you are finished coloring, cut out your ornament with scissors.

Step 3:
Use the hole punch to place a hole on each ornament in order to hang it up.  Make sure you don't punch your hole too close to the edge of your ornament. 

Step 4:
Now the ornaments are ready for baking. Place the Shrinky Dink pieces, colored side up, on a small, cut out piece of a brown paper bag and place paper on a tray or cookie sheet.

Step 5:
Put the tray of Shrinky Dinks in the oven at 300 degrees for 1-3 minutes and watch as your Shrinky Dink shrinks! After pieces lie flat, allow an additional 15 seconds of baking time to complete the process.  If you pull it out prematurely you may put it back in the oven.

Step 6:
Remove paper from tray or cookie sheet and let Shrinky Dinks cool.

Step 7:
Use ribbon, plastic thread or wire to make a loop to hang your ornament. You can also add beads to the wire or ribbon.

Closing:
Ask each of the participants to share something about the Shrinky Dink ornament they made and one loving word they heard today they want to remember.  Ask the participants how it felt to hear positive words from their fellow group members.  Remind the participants that they don't have to wait until they are in the art group to say nice things to one another.  Generate a brief discussion about the awesome power of saying kind things.  You can speak about the great power words have, and that they can choose to use that power everyday to spread love.
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps to educate the participants about the power of words by giving them an opportunity to say loving things to one another and then create a Shrinky Dink ornament to serve as a reminder of all the positive words and feelings they heard and felt. Includes an interactive warm up that helps build the participants' self-esteem and allows them to bond.

Objective:

Materials:

Permanent markers
Colored pencils and sharpeners
Scissors
Hole puncher
Toaster oven
Ribbon or craft wire
Parachute (Large round table cloth, or piece of fabric for warm up)
Beads (optional)
CD Player/holiday themed music (optional)
Holiday template (shapes)
Holiday template (characters)

Age Range:
 
 3-18 years old 
 
  Timeframe:
 
   Introduction: 5 minutes
Warm-up:     20 minutes
Creation:      30 minutes
Closing:        5 minutes
Total Time:   60 minutes		 








   
  Holiday templates for Shrinky ornaments 
Preparation:
During this workshop, make sure to play fun holiday music, Putamayo is great resource for various holiday songs. You may also want to create that "holiday smell" by bringing in fresh cinnamon, pine cones, candles or even bake gingerbread cookies for your group.

You'll need to make enough photocopies of the various templates for all the participants. Pre-cut the Shrinky Dink into 3 1/2"x4" squares to fit the size of our template (AWBW sells pre-cut Shrinky Dink material, $5 for 100 sheets). Make sure all colored pencils are pre-sharpened. It's good to have all the materials set up prior to beginning the workshop.

It’s important to try this project in advance so you have some samples to share. If you have never used the Shrinky Dink materials you will also want to get a feel for how the Shrinky Dinks cook. It’s very exciting to watch!

Introduction:
Today we are going to create Shrinky Dink Ornaments as a reminder of all of the positive qualities you each have and fill the shelter (or our homes) with happiness and love.

Warm Up:
Parachute of Love

o   If you don’t have a parachute this can be done with any type of cloth, fabric, or even plastic tablecloths.  You can use ones that are square in shape but the round tablecloths work best.

o   Tell the children that they are going to use the parachute to trap all of the nice things they say about each other.  “I am going to have each of you sit under the Parachute of Love, one at a time, while each of us goes around the circle and says nice things about you!  We will do this so that all of the loving, awesome things people say about you can circle around and stick to you."

o   Tell the children that you will be calling out instructions about when to raise and lower the parachute, so pay close attention. 

o   "Each of you will take turns sitting under the Parachute of Love. We will go around in a circle and one at a time, have each of you say something nice about the person under the parachute.  It can be anything you think will make that person feel good.  You can say something you like about them, something they are good at, or something that makes them special or unique.  Remember this will only work if we say nice things!"

o   Ask if there is anyone who doesn’t feel comfortable sitting under the parachute. 

o   If yes, simply have them sit on top of the parachute, right in the middle while the other children (who are sitting around the parachute, holding the edge with both hands) lift the parachute up and down to create a wave like effect while they say loving things about the child in the middle.

o   Lay the parachute (so it is open completely) on the ground.  Have the children sit around the edges of the parachute so there is equal distance between people.    

o   Have the children grab the edge of the parachute with both hands.

o   Ask if there is anyone who wants to go first.  Once you know who will go first have them stand up and remove themselves from the circle.  Have the other children move to fill in the empty space. 

o   Tell the child to wait until you say go, and once you do, instruct him/her to run under the parachute (after completing the next bullet point), which should be in the air.

o   When everyone is ready, have the children grab the sheet with both hands and stand up, lifting the parachute as high as they can. Then have the first child run under the parachute and sit in the middle.  Have the children lower the parachute so it sits above the child’s head as they sit in the middle.  Have the children move their hands up and down (while keeping their arms extended out straight in front of their body) at a quick pace over and over again, so the parachute dances above the child’s head.  If the child in the middle feels like the parachute is too close, have them lay down.

o   Begin by having one child say something nice about the child in the middle.  Then continue around the circle until each child has had an opportunity to speak. 

o   Once everyone has said an affirmation to the child in the middle have the next child go under the parachute and repeat the process until each child has taken a turn.  

Creation:
If you haven't used Shrinky Dinks with your group before, be sure to review the following steps before the begin.  Demonstrate how to color on the rough side with the color pencils for the background, how to use darker colors for the words and explain that the plastic will shrink to a third of it's size after baking. You may want to show a finished sample.

 
 
  Tracing the design 
   
   3 Holiday Shrinkys 
   
  Baking the Shrinkys 
   
   
Choose one of the holiday templates in front of you. Start by tracing the template on the rough side of the Shrinky Dink. Keeping in mind all of the nice things you just heard from the group, write words, colors, shapes, or scribbles on the Shrinky Dink to help you remember all of the good feelings you had and words that were said about you while you were in the middle of the Parachute of Love. If you need help with the words or writing please ask.  Begin to color and create the design that will fill in the shape of your template. (Be sure to draw on the rough side of the plastic.) When you are finished coloring, decide whether you want to add wire or ribbons and beads to your ornament. If you like, you can cut out your ornament with scissors. At this time you will need to use the hole punch to place holes for wiring or ribbons and beads. If you need help with this, please ask for it.  Make sure you don't punch your hole too close to the edge of your ornament.   

Now the Shrinkys are ready for baking. We will place the Shrinky Dink on a flat metal tray and place inside the toaster oven. We will bake at 300 degrees until the Shrinky Dink has completely flattened (this will take about one minute). Watch the amazing transformation! Remove your Shrinky Dink and allow it to cool. Now your Shrinky Dink is ready for decorating with wire or ribbons and beads if you wish.

Closing:
Ask each of the children to share something about the Shrinky Dink ornaments they made and one loving word they heard today they want to remember.  Ask the children how it felt to be in the Parachute of Love.  Tell the children that they don't have to wait until they have the Parachute of Love to say nice things to one another.  Generate a brief discussion about the awesome power of saying kind things.  You can speak about the great power words have, and that they can choose to use that power everyday to spread love.
Row.txt_description: To educate the participants about the power of words by giving them an opportunity to say loving things to one another and then create a Shrinky Dink ornament to serve as a reminder of all the positive words and feelings they heard and felt. Includes an interactive warm up that helps build the childrens' self-esteem and allows them to bond.

Row.str_title: Helping Hand Sculpey Ornaments - Holiday Decorating Series
Row.txt_code:
This workshop is part of Windows' Holiday Decorating Series: Use this and other simple workshops during your holiday parties and festivities, to decorate your shelter, or just to help the adults and children feel surrounded by loving, hopeful feelings, especially during this particularly difficult time for those living in the shelter.

Objective:
The holidays represent a time for family and friends to get together and share meals, gifts, and kindness with each other. One way we can do that is by using our hands in ways that are loving and helpful. This workshop helps to reinforce that we have the ability to help stop the cycle of violence and and choose to use our hands to help, not hurt.  Participants will create a Helping Hand Ornament to remind them of all the helpful and and loving things they can do with their hands.
 
  Finished Sculpey Ornament

Materials:
Super Sculpey Polymer Clay
Toaster Oven
Cookie cutters (hand shapes or any holiday shapes available)
Small coffee straws or skewers
Ribbon, craft wire or yarn
Beads (optional)
Sharpie markers

Timeframe:
60 minutes

 
 Materials
 
Preparation:
Prepare several Sculpey balls, in various holiday colors, enough for each person.
During this workshop, make sure to play fun holiday music, Putamayo is great resource for various holiday cds. You may also want to create that "holiday smell" by bringing in fresh cinnamon pine cones, candles or even bake gingerbread cookies for your group.

Introduction: 
The holidays represent a time for family and friends to get together and share meals, gifts, and kindness with each other. One way we can do that is by using our hands in ways that are loving and helpful.
As survivors of domestic violence we all know from experience the devastating and far reaching effects of using your hands to hit or hurt others.  We don't have to repeat the cycle of violence.  We can choose to use our hands in helpful and loving ways.  Today, we are going to think about how we can use our hands to help others.  You can use your hands to help pick someone up when they’ve fallen down.  You can also put your hand on someone’s shoulder to let them know everything will be okay.  All of these are examples of how we can use our hands to help.  Today each of you will make your very own Helping Hand Ornament to remind you about all the good things you can do with your hands!

Warm Up:
We’re going to begin by giving each of us a chance to share about how someone helped you or about someone you have helped. It could be someone in your family, or someone far away. It could be something from today, or it could be something from a long time ago.  For example, "I comforted my friend when she was upset by holding her hand."

 
  Sculpey "snake" using 3 colors
 
  Twisting Sculpey colors
 
  Rolling Sculpey in a ball
 
  Flatten Sculpey
 
  Roll Sculpey to about 1/4 of an inch
 
  Cut Sculpey with a cookie cutter
 
  Make a hole to hang the ornament
Creation:
It is a great idea to demonstrate how to make swirly or marbled shapes out of Sculpey before the workshop so that they can jump right in.

Demonstrate using the following steps:
Step One:
To blend the clay, choose at least two colors. Use no more than a pinch of each color.

Step Two:
Roll each color into a "snake".

Step Three:
Wrap each "snake" around each other like a candy-cane and twist together.

Step Four:
Twist each little section of the roll until the colors are blended just the way you want them.

Step Five:
Roll the "snakes" into a ball. If you want, repeat steps 4 and 5 several times to create a more marbled effect.

Step Six:
Using a pen or a marker roll the ball flat to be about 1/4 inch thick. Use a cookies cutter of a hand shape (or any shape you choose.)  Use the coffee straw or skewer to make a hole at the top so you can hang the ornament after it bakes.

Step Seven:
In a conventional oven you can use a foil lined cookie sheet. Bake the Sculpey at 275 degrees for 15 minutes (for each ¼ inch of clay thickness). Always allow the clay to cool completely before handling it.

Step Eight:
Write one word, shape, symbol or color on your ornament that reminds you of the way you can use your hands in productive rather than destructive ways.

Once you've shown the participants how to create their Helping Hand Ornament, and they begin the creation process, ask them each to share with the group a word of encouragement that someone once shared with them that has helped them along the way?

Step Nine:
Encourage the participants to use ribbon and wire to hang their helping hand and use beads to decorate.
 
Closing:
Ask each of the participants to share something about what they wrote on their hand (i.e. what the words, shapes, colors they choose represent).  If they are hesitant to share let the participants know that they don’t have to share anything they don’t want to and that there is no right or wrong way to share.  Be sure to thank them for being so creative and for sharing about what they made!  Reinforce that what they use their hands for is their choice.  They are the only ones with the power to choose to use their hands to help others and themselves!  Also let them know that they can look at their Helping Hand Ornament anytime they need a reminder of all the ways they can use their hands to help.
Row.txt_description: This workshop reinforces that we have the ability to stop the cycle of violence and and choose to use our hands to help, not hurt. Participants will create a Helping Hand Ornament to remind them of all the helpful and and loving things they can do with their hands.

Row.str_title: Whimiscal Wood Creation - Holiday Decorating Series
Row.txt_code:
This workshop is part of Windows' Holiday Decorating Series: Use this and other simple workshops during your holiday parties and festivities, to decorate your shelter, or just to help the women and children feel surrounded by loving, hopeful feelings, especially during this particularly difficult time for those living in the shelter.

Objective:
  
 
   Popsicle Stick Ornaments
 
To help children experience the joys of childhood by noticing their hopes and dreams through their creations of fun and cheerful holiday decorations.

Materials:
Popsicle sticks and tongue depressors
Hot glue or tacky glue
Yarn, ribbon or string
Markers or paint pens
Construction paper
Glitter
Gold or silver string, ribbons or pipe cleaners
Paint and/or puffy paint (optional)
Embellishments (optional)

Timeframe:
       
 Age Range:
 
 60 minutes   3-12 




Preparation:
 
 
   
During this workshop, make sure to play fun holiday music, Putamayo is great resource for various holiday songs. You may also want to create that "holiday smell" by bringing in fresh cinnamon, pine cones, candles or even bake gingerbread cookies for your group.

Introduction:
Today we are going to create holiday decorations to fill the shelter (or our homes) with hope, strength, courage, beauty, creativity, warmth and love. These fun wooden/flower angels decorations will help our creative juices flow and remind us our hopes and dreams

Warm Up:
Have everyone go around the circle and share their favorite holiday song, food, story, memory or movie, whatever they choose is fine.  Remind participants that what's important during this warm-up is they think of anything that brings them joy. If they have a difficult time thinking of something, encourage them to share their hopes and dreams for future holidays.

Creation:
Popsicle (craft stick) ornaments are fun and easy.  You will need to use tacky glue or hot glue to adhere all the parts, and decorate!  You can use a silver or gold string for a hanger.

 

  Star of David
 Star Reindeer



 		 
 
 Reindeer   
 Snowman 

Closing:
It's important to have the teens do a closing of the workshop. Have each person share what their fairy or angel means to them and talk about how they feel in this moment.

To end on a hopeful note, remind participants that you hope they will hold onto their ornament as a reminder that they need to care for themselves nurture their joy.  Thank all participants for taking a window of time to create with you.
Row.txt_description: To help children experience the joys of childhood by noticing their hopes and dreams through their creations of fun and cheerful holiday decorations.

Row.str_title: Revealing Power and Control for Teens
Row.txt_code:
Key Topic: Teen Dating Violence: Intervention and Prevention
This Workshop Falls Under the Theme of Teen Dating Violence
Since 2010, we have been developing this program to serve the teens in our community and in our programs. This curriculum is offered to and is useful for BOTH Adult's and children's leaders as most agencies work with this population in some capacity. A HUGE thank you to Giovanna Martinez of WomenShelter of Long Beach for enhancing our Teen Dating Violence curriculum.

Power and Control Wheels, Scratch Art Board, and Toothpick

About this Workshop:
Based on the Duluth Power and Control Wheel this workshop gives teens the opportunity to identify different forms of dating violence.

Objective:
This workshop helps teens understand the cycle of violence and the dynamics of the teen power and control wheel. Using Scratch Art, participants explore different forms of Teen Dating Violence and identify what a healthy relationship means to them.

Materials:
Blank Teen Power & Control Wheel (click here for template )
Teen Equality wheel (click here for handout )
Teen Power and Control Wheel (click here for handout )
Scratch Art Boards (can be purchased at discountschoolsupply.com or Oriental Trading Company)
Toothpicks, pencils, or any object that can be used to scratch off the black layer on the art board
Pens
Tablecloth or newspaper (to cover the table as the Scratch Art Boards can be very messy)

Preparation:
Please be aware that the black scraps that come off the art board when you scratch through are very messy and stain easily.  You may want to lay out newspaper on top of the table the teens will use the Scratch Art Board on.  Make sure to print out enough Handouts for each participant.

Timeframe: 1 hr 20 min
Intro and Sharing: 20 min
Creation: 40 min
Sharing: 20 min

Introduction:
Today we are going to discuss the Teen Power and Control Wheel.  Pass out the Teen Power and Control Wheel and have each teen share one by one their thoughts about a section of the wheel, and if they have witnessed or are aware of any examples of these types of abuse.  If the group is reluctant to share, reinforce that they do not have to reveal who they are talking about, and can talk about examples they have seen in the media.  For example you can ask the group what they have heard about Rihanna and Chris Brown.  That is an example of physical abuse (he hit her in a car) and isolation (it is rumored that he was upset she was communicating with a male friend on her cell phone).  Moreover, like many victims, she returned to the relationship even after the abuse became public.  You can also explain the cycle of violence by saying that the abuse didn't begin that infamous night.  Abuse is a slow pattern of controlling behavior that starts off with verbal, emotional and psychological abuse and leads to more obvious forms of abuse such as physical.

Sharing these experiences gives each person a chance to think about what they know about teen dating violence, debunk myths and stereotypes, and to learn from their peers as well.  This is also an effective way to show that they were not alone in experiencing violence in their lives. This workshop is an opportunity for the teens to vent, cry, to comfort each other and bond.
  
 
Filling out the blank Power and Control Wheel.

  
Creation Process:
Step One: Give each teen a blank Teen Power and Control Wheel. Have the teens fill in each section of the wheel with examples of that particular type of abuse.  They can fill the wheel in with their own experiences, with examples that were just shared in the group, or with general ideas about each type of abuse.  Make sure the group is aware that everyone’s story will be different, and encourage the teens to write at least one example in each section of the wheel.


 
 Scratching through to reveal abuse.
Step Two: Speak to the teens about how domestic violence is usually kept secret, hidden just below the surface waiting to come out.  Reinforce that speaking about the abuse takes away some of the power it has over you, and is the only way to get help.  Using the Scratch Art Boards, have each teen scratch words or phrases on the black layer to reveal their own experiences with abuse.  If a participant says that they have never experienced any abuse, have them scratch words or phrases that represent the types of abuse mentioned in the group discussion (like Rihanna and Chris Brown).  As they begin, remind the teens that they don't have to share anything about what they are scratching to the group.  Scratching is intended to reveal their experience with abuse for their own knowledge.     
 
  Scratching through the symbols of equality.
Step Three: Pass out the Teen Equality Wheel and start a discussion about healthy relationships.  Ask each teen to share a shape or symbol that represents an aspect of a relationship based on equality.  For example, you can scratch a t-shirt to remind you to never let your partner dictate what you can and cannot wear.  It may be helpful to write all the symbols shared by the group members on a list to use as a reference for the final aspect of the creation process. 

Inform the teens that they have the power to move forward and not repeat unhealthy patterns or allow abusive behavior in their relationships.  Then say, "to remind ourselves that we can overcome the past and have equality in our relationships, we will now scratch symbols and shapes that represent the healthy things we want in our future relationships.  You will scratch right on top of the words written in step two of the creation process."  

Closing:
Ask each participant to share something that they learned or will take from the group today.  Encourage each to share how they plan to make sure they have healthy and violence free relationships in the future.  For example, "I will never let my boy/girlfriend tell me what to wear."
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps teens understand the cycle of violence and the dynamics of the teen power and control wheel. Using Scratch Art, participants explore different forms of Teen Dating Violence and identify what a healthy relationship means to them.

This curriculum is offered to and is useful for BOTH Adult's and children's leaders as most agencies work with this population in some capacity. A HUGE thank you to Giovanna Martinez of WomenShelter of Long Beach for enhancing our Teen Dating Violence curriculum.
 
 Leader's defining and revealing their boundaries.
Objective:
To introduce participants to the concept of boundaries and having healthy levels of independence in their intimate relationships.

Materials:
Relationship Boundaries handout
Scratch Art Boards (can be purchased at discountschoolsupply.com or Oriental Trading Company)
Toothpicks, pencils, or any object that can be used to scratch off the black layer off the art board
Pens
Scratch paper
Tablecloth or newspaper (to cover the table as the Scratch Art Boards can be very messy)

Preparation:
Please be aware that the black scraps that come off the art board when you scratch through are very messy and stain easily. You may want to lay out newspaper on top of the table the participants will use when they create. Make sure to print out enough handouts for each participant.

 
A participant's boundaries revealed
 

Timeframe:
Introduction: 10 min
Opening Circle: 20 min
Creation: 20 min
Closing: 20 min

Total: 1 hr 10 min

Introduction:
Today we are going to focus on boundaries and having healthy levels of independence in your intimate relationships. Ask the group, "does anyone know what a boundary is?" After hearing the group's thoughts, if necessary, give an example such as a fence. A boundary is an invisible fence that protects us. There are various types of boundaries. The most obvious type of boundary is a physical boundary. To demonstrate this concept ask one of the group members to join you at the front of the room and stand facing you, approximately ten feet away. Tell them that you're going to start walking towards them and it is their job to stop you when you get to the point where they would feel uncomfortable if you got any closer. Once they stop you, tell the group that exercise just revealed the volunteers physical boundary. Then speak to the group about the importance of identifying and honoring not only your physical, but also your emotional boundaries in your relationships. While emotional boundaries may be less obvious than physical boundaries, it's necessary to be aware of them.  It's up to each and every one of us to decide what is and what isn't okay in an intimate (dating) relationship and to make sure our partner is aware of and respects those boundaries.

Warm Up:
Give each person a piece of scratch paper and a pen. Ask the group to use circles to represent two people in a relationship. Have them position two circles on a piece of paper to show what a healthy relationship looks like, and then position two more circles to show what an unhealthy relationship looks like. In each example, are the circles far away from each other, close together, overlapping or touching? If the participants have difficulty doing this on their own, you can make it a group activity and have them instruct you as you draw the circles in front of the group. Then pass the Relationship Boundaries handout to the participants. Read through and generate a discussion about the information on the handout, and their ideas about healthy and unhealthy relationship boundaries. Be sure to talk about the importance of maintaining a healthy level of independence within a relationship. In fact one "red flag" of an abusive relationship is being completely immersed in your partner's life and detaching from your friends, hobbies, and the activities that are not connected to your significant other.

 
Revealing boundaries
 

Creation Process:
Pass out the Scratch Art Boards and a scratch tool. Keeping in mind everything we have just discussed, I want you to think about what boundaries you want to create in your intimate/dating relationships. What do you want to share with your partner? What do you want to keep just for yourself? Now using your Scratch Art Board reveal your relationship boundaries. Scratch words, shapes, symbols or even pictures onto your Scratch Art Board to represent what you will and will not allow in your relationship to maintain healthy boundaries.   

Share examples such as:
-Write the name of a friend or family member to remind you not to lose touch with people who are close to you (other than your partner).
-Draw a mouth to remind you to be open, and honest, and that you have a voice and the right to speak up for yourself.
-Draw two shapes that are the same size to symbolize how you and your partner are equal and have mutual respect for one another.

Keep in mind that what you create doesn't have to make sense to anyone but you. Try not to censor yourself when you create; your project should serve as a reminder of what you want in your intimate/dating relationships. If you are open and honest with yourself about what you want and don't want in your relationship, you will be able to talk to your partner about it and work together to make it happen!  

 

Closing:
Ask each participant to share anything they want about their creation, and what knowledge they will take with them from today. You may also ask participants what steps they will take to implement these boundaries in their current or future relationships, or where they will display or keep their project and why. Thank the participants for jumping into this complex, yet very important topic of boundaries, and encourage them to keep their project as a reminder to make sure they feel safe, comfortable and happy in their relationships.
Row.txt_description: This workshop introduces participants to the concept of boundaries and having healthy levels of independence in their intimate relationships.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Supplies for Bookmark to the Future
 
Objective: This workshop is about noticing what you want to leave behind and go toward.

Materials:
Scratch Art materials (can be purchased at Discount School Supply or Oriental Trading Company )
Toothpicks, pencils, or any object that can be used to scratch off the black layer off the art board
Tablecloth or newspaper (to cover the table as the Scratch Art Boards can be very messy)
Glue stick
Laminating sheets, Contact paper or laminator (optional)
Hole punch
Ribbon
Scissors

Preparation:
Please be aware that the black scraps that come off the art board when you scratch through are very messy and stain easily. You may want to lay out newspaper on top of the table the participants will use when they create. Make sure to print enough handouts for each participant.

 Time Frame:    
Age Range:
Introduction: 5 min
Opening Circle: 15 min
Creation: 25 min
Closing Circle: 15 min
Total: 1 hour
 6-18 years old



 






Introduction:
Today we are going to create a bookmark all about the things we want to let go of and move towards.  We'll start by reflecting on what you'd like to let go of, leave behind...maybe it 's something weighing you down or you holding you back in someway. Then I'm going to ask you to be brave, be daring and think about what you REALLY want, what you want to go toward.

 
 
  Bookmarks letting go and moving towards
 

Opening Circle:
Have each participant share one word, or sentence about what they want to let go of or leave behind.

Creation:
Pass out the Scratch Art Boards and a scratch tool.

Part 1: We'll start by reflecting on what you'd like to let go of, leave behind.  Maybe it 's something weighing you down or you holding you back in someway. Using the scratch tools, instruct the participants to scratch through words, shapes, symbols, images, doodles, etc. about what they want to let go of or leave behind on one Scratch Art Bookmark.  For example, if you want to leave tears behind you can scratch a rain cloud into your bookmark. Give the participants ten minutes to scratch through what they want to leave behind.

 
 
  Bookmark that represents something you would like to let go of
 

Part 2: Now that we've looked at what we want to let go of, now lets look at what we want to move towards. Be brave, be daring ,and think about what you REALLY want, what you want to go toward. If time permits you can have each participant share a word or sentence about what they want to go toward.  Ask the participants to scratch words, shapes, or images into another Scratch Art Bookmark that represent what they want to move towards in the future. For example, you can scratch through a sun and ocean to represent that tropical vacation you've always wanted to take or a heart to represent love. Let you're imagination run wild! The future is wide open and only you know what you want to move towards in your future.  Give the participants ten minutes to scratch through what they want to move toward.

   
  Bookmark that represents something you would like to move towards
 

Part 3: Once you are done scratching through glue the backside (white side) of your bookmarks together. Cover the entire bookmark using self-laminating sheets or contact paper on both sides. Cut off any excess laminating material and voila...they look great and last longer! If you are using a laminator, the leader will most likely need to do the laminating, as lamination sheets can be tricky and unforgiving when you make a mistake.

   
  Laminate and add ribbon
 

Then use a hole punch to punch through the circular area at the top of the bookmark (where the laminating sheet covered the area where the ribbon will go). Then have the participants choose what color of ribbon they want and loop it through the hole at the top of the bookmark.

Closing Circle:
Ask each participant to share what they created on their bookmark and what they want to remember and keep in their heart from today. Remind the participants that it is important to keep our imaginations active and remember that we have the power to let go of the past and create the future WE want! Our minds are very powerful and identifying what we want is the first step in making our dreams come true!
Row.txt_description: This workshop is about noticing what you want to leave behind and go toward.
