Row.txt_code:
Objective: This workshop gives participants an opportunity to look at the thoughts, feelings or experiences they want to leave behind, and to express what they want to move towards in their life.
 
 Supplies for Bookmark to the Future

Materials:
Scratch Art Bookmarks (can be purchased at Discount School Supply or Oriental Trading Company )
Toothpicks, pencils, or any object that can be used to scratch off the black layer of the art board
Tablecloth or newspaper (to cover the table as the Scratch Art Boards can be very messy)
Glue stick
Laminating sheets, Contact paper or laminator (optional)
Hole punch
Ribbon (assorted colors)
Scissors

Preparation:
Please be aware that the black scrapes that come off the art board when you scratch through are very messy and stain easily. You may want to lay out newspaper on top of the table the participants will use when they create.  

Time Frame: 1hr
Introduction: 5 min
Opening Circle: 15 min
Creation: 25 min
Closing Circle: 15 min

Introduction:
Today we are going to create a bookmark that expresses the things we want to leave behind and what we want to create more of in our life. We'll start by reflecting on what you'd like to let go of. Then, I'm going to ask you to be brave and think about what you REALLY want to move towards, now and in your future.

  Bookmarks letting go and moving towards

Opening Circle:
Have each participant share a word, or sentence, about one thing they want to let go of or leave behind.

Creation:
Pass out two Scratch Art bookmarks and a scratch tool to each participant.

Part 1: We'll start by reflecting on what you'd like to let go of or leave behind. Maybe it's something weighing you down or holding you back in someway. On the first bookmark, using the scratch tool, scratch through words, shapes, symbols, images or doodles that represent the thoughts, feelings or experiences you want to let go of or leave behind.  For example, if you want to leave tears behind, you can scratch a rain cloud into your bookmark. Give the participants ten minutes to complete part 1.


 Bookmark that represents something you would like to let go of

Part 2: Now that we've looked at what we want to let go of, let's look at what we want to move towards. Be brave, be daring, and think about what you REALLY want more of in your life. Have each participant share a word, or sentence, about one thing they want to go towards. On the second bookmark, scratch through words, shapes, or images that represent the positive things you want now and in your future. For example, you can scratch through a sun and ocean to represent that tropical vacation you've always wanted to take, or a heart to represent love. Let you're imagination run wild! The future is wide open, and only you know what you want it to look like! Give the participants ten minutes to complete part two.


Bookmark that represents something you would like to
move towards

Part 3: Once you are done scratching through, glue the backsides (white sides) of your bookmarks together using a glue stick. Cover the entire bookmark using self-laminating sheets or contact paper on both sides. Cut off any excess laminating material (leave at least 1/4" on all sides). Note: If you are using a laminator, be careful, as lamination sheets can be tricky and unforgiving. 

 
  Laminate and add ribbon

To finish your bookmark, use a hole punch near the top to make a place for the ribbon to go. 

Closing Circle:
Ask each participant to share what they created on their bookmark, and what they want to remember and keep in their hearts from today.

Remind the participants that it is important to keep in mind that we have the power to let go of the past and create the future WE want! We are very powerful, and identifying what we want is the first step in embracing our futures!
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives participants an opportunity to reflect on what they want to leave behind, and what they want to move towards in their life. The bookmark they create will serve as a positive visual reminder.

Row.txt_code:
Setup for "Revealing What I Want"
 
Objective:
This purpose of this workshop is to help children gain awareness about things they don't want in their lives by making either a door hanger or a bookmark that reveals what they actually want.


 

 

Materials:
Scratch Art Materials (can be purchased at Discount School Supply or Oriental Trading Company)
Toothpicks, pencils, or any object that can be used to scratch off the black layer off the art board
Tablecloth or newspaper (to cover the table as the Scratch Art Boards can be very messy) 
 Paper (copy paper will work)
Pen
For the Bookmarks:
Laminating sheets, contact paper or laminator
Hole punch 
Ribbon
Scissors

Preparation:
Be aware that the black scraps that come off the scratch art board when you scratch through are very messy and stain easily. You may want to lie out newspaper on top of the table before the children begin to create.

If possible play music while the children are writing, as it will help them focus on the task.

If the children decide to make the bookmark, you will need to help them laminate it so it doesn't smear.

Time Frame:
    
Age Range:
Intro: 10 min
Journaling Warm-Up: 10 minutes
Creation: 20 min
Closing: 20 min
Total: 1 hour
 8 to 18





 

 

 

 

Introduction:
It is important to think about what sorts of things you don't want in your life to help you know what you do want in your life. What we don't want can be actual things like not wanting violence in your home, or thoughts like thinking or saying mean things about your siblings or friends, or even feelings like being afraid of someone or angry at something. 

Once you take time to notice what you don't want, what you do want is easier to see. For example, once you realize that you don't want violence in your future you can picture having a peaceful home. When you realize that you don't want meanness in your life you may decide to try to always be a good friend even to your siblings.  Or you may notice that you don't like feeling mad and afraid so you will work hard to live your life in a way that makes you feel happy and strong.  By clearly defining what we do want in our lives, we can begin to picture what it would be like to really have those things, thoughts or feelings.

 
 Using the words on the list to create a door hanger!

Journaling Exercise:
This exercise can help you to start thinking about what you want. We will begin with a piece of paper and fold it in half vertically.

On the left half of your paper, start by making a list using words or pictures of the things you don't want in your life.  If you like, you can write, "What I Don't Want" at the top left hand side of your paper.  

Give the children two to five minutes to create the list of what they don't want in their lives. Be sure to explain that they don't need to worry about spelling, grammar, and they don't even need to write complete sentences or words. The most important thing is that they don't stop their thoughts; just let them flow onto your paper however they come out.  When the time is up have the children read over their list.  Ask each child to share at least one thing from their list.

On the top of the right side of the paper you can write the words "What I Do Want" giving the children another 2 - 5 minutes they can write all the things they Do want in their life. When finished, you can ask them to share one thing from this list.

 
Reminders of what we want in our life!
 
  

Creation:
Pass out the Scratch Art Door Hangers or Bookmarks and scratch tools. Looking back at the things they don't want ask the children to now think about what their life will look like and feel like if they don't have any of those things.  Using their scratch through boards ask the children to write a letter, words, shapes, pictures, doodles or symbols to reflect and remind them of the things they do want in their life.

At the end of the workshop walk around the room with a wastebasket and suggest to the children that they crumble up their "don't want" list or drawing and throw them in the trash. Tell the children that the reason to do this is so that they can focus on the positive things they represented on their artwork. This can give the children an opportunity to get rid of all of the negatives. Finally, ask them to write today's date somewhere on their artwork so they can look back at their project in the future and see how they are doing on getting all they things they want.

As a final step, you will need to laminate the bookmark. If you don't cover it, it will smear eventually.  Cover the entire board using self-laminating sheets or contact paper on both sides. Cut off excess laminating material making all sides even for a neater look. Be aware if you are using a laminator it can be tricky and unforgiving if you make a mistake.

   
 Laminate and add ribbon
to the bookmark
 
Have each child choose a color ribbon. Then use a hole punch to punch a hole near the top of the bookmark and loop the ribbon through the hole.

Closing Circle:
Have each participant share about what they created, what they discovered during the journaling, and what they will take with them from this workshop.

After the closing circle, you may want to share an some encouraging words with the children. Ask them to close their eyes if it feels safe, and wrap their arms as if they were giving themselves a hug. Then have them say, "I deserve the life I want. In my future, I can choose the life I want ."
Row.txt_description: This workshop was designed to help children gain awareness about things they don't want in their lives by making either a door hanger or a bookmark that reveals what they actually want.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To help participants think about what they want in their lives, and where their personal boundaries lie. The Scratch Art Door Hanger will serve as a reminder of what they expect, and will allow into their life, home, and hearts.
 
  Setup for Reveal Your Artistic Self...from Scratch! Series

Materials:
Scratch Art materials (can be purchased at Discount School Supply or Oriental Trading Company )
Toothpicks, pencils, or any object that can be used to scratch off the black layer of the art board
Tablecloth or newspaper (to cover the table as the Scratch Art Boards can be very messy)
Paper for journaling
Pen

Preparation:
Please be aware that the black scrapes that come off the art board when you scratch through are very messy and stain easily. You may want to lay out newspaper on top of the table the participants will use when they create.  

Time Frame: 1 hour
Intro: 10 min
Journaling Warm-Up: 10-15 min
Creation: 20 min
Closing: 20 min

Introduction:
What is the purpose of a door hanger? Sometimes door hangers say: "Do Not Enter," and allow people to protect their worlds and keep them private.  

Today, we will be looking at what we want, and the experiences we wish to invite into our lives. We all get to decide what our personal boundaries are and how we want to be treated. The Scratch Art Door Hanger will serve as a positive reminder of what we expect. We are saying, "if you enter here, you will treat me the way I expect to be treated; you will respect my values, my principles and what is important to me." 

 
  Participant transforming her journaling into a door hanger!

Journaling Warm-Up:
In the journaling exercise, participants will first look at the thoughts, feelings or experiences they do not want in their lives, and then "flip" them around so they can gain understanding of what they do want, and where their personal boundaries lie.   

Have each participant select a piece of paper and fold it in half vertically.

Part 1: We will begin by making a list of the things you don't want in your life on the left half of your paper. You can write, "What I don't want" on the top left. Give the participants five minutes to create this list. Let them know that they don't have to write complete sentences; they can just write words or phrases such as "negativity" or "no more abuse." The most important thing is that they don't censor themselves, and just allow their thoughts to flow onto the paper. If possible, play music while the participants are writing, as it will help them focus on the task.   

Part 2: Now we are going to take a few minutes and make another list that takes an opposite view of the list we just made. We're going to turn those negatives into the positive things we want in our lives. Look at your list and think about the experiences you really want in your life. You can use one word, several words or a phrase to reframe the negative words. For example, if what you don't want is "abuse," you might want to add "kindness" and "respect" on your list. Start the music again and give the participants five minutes to write their "What I do want" list.  Participants may need more time to create the second list; adjust time accordingly by checking in towards the end of the exercise.


 
Revealing reminders of what we want to enter our life!
 

Creation Process:
Before starting, have the participants cut or tear off the "What I don't want" list and crumple it up. You could even walk around the room with a wastebasket to let them dispose of it. This will represent the letting go of negative things in their life. 

Pass out the Scratch Art door hangers and scratch tools. Ask participants to reflect on the thoughts, feelings and experiences they do want in their life, and scratch through words, shapes, pictures, doodles or symbols that represent them.

Closing Circle:
Have each participant share about what they created, what they discovered during the journaling, and what they will take with them from this workshop.

After the closing circle, you may want to share an affirmation with the participants. Ask them to close their eyes if it feels safe, and wrap their arms as if they were giving themselves a hug. Then have them say, "I'm worthy of having the life I want. Going forward, I will decide what thoughts, feeling and experiences I will invite into my life." Encourage the participants to use their Do-Enter Door Hanger as a reminder of the things they want in their lives, and the positive boundaries they have created.
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps participants think about what they want in their lives, and where their personal boundaries lie. The Scratch Art Door Hanger will serve as a reminder of what they expect, and will allow into their life, home, and hearts.

Row.txt_code:
Objective: This workshop is intended to help children feel a sense of their own power by guiding them to create their very own Safe Place.

Materials:
Colored pencils
Construction paper

Time frame: 40 minutes
Introduction: 10 minutes
Relaxation: 5 minutes
Creation: 15 minutes
Closing Circle: 10 minutes

Introduction:
Today we are going to make a drawing of our safe place.  This safe place can be real or imaginary; it's totally up to you. Who can tell me what it means to feel safe? (What are some feelings you feel when you feel relaxed and free?) Those are all wonderful ways of being safe.  Now if it feels safe for you, I'd like you to close your eyes (cue music) and get comfortable in your chair.

Relaxation:
Now, think of something quiet: You may be floating on a cloud. Swinging on a swing, surrounded by your friends or lying on bunches of soft cushy pillows. Choose any special place where you feel quiet and safe.  Think about what that place looks like? What does it smell like? Who is there? What does it feel like?  Is it a place you have never been before? Is it in your imagination? Once you can picture it in your mind, notice what it feels like to be in your special place and...When you are ready open your eyes and begin to draw your safe place. Remember there is no right or wrong. Trust your vision.  It can be a place, words, scribbles or just colors. 

Creation:
Instruct the participants to choose which color of construction paper they will create on. Using the colored pencils have the participants draw their safe place.

Closing Circle:
Please share something about your Safe Place and what you want to remember from today's workshop.  How did it make you feel to create your Safe Place?  What do you like about your project?  What does it mean to you?  Where will you put it?

Variations: Give the participants magazines and instead of drawing, collage their Safe Place.
Row.txt_description: This workshop is intended to help children feel a sense of their own power by guiding them to create their very own Safe Place.

Row.txt_code:
Background:
Lisa Morgan of Harmony Place in Front R oyal, Virginia created this workshop. Iris folding is a technique that originated in Holland. Color coordinated strips of folded paper are taped into place over a pattern, creating a spiraling design that resembles the iris of an eye or camera. Originally, Dutch crafters would cut their strips from envelopes with patterned interiors, but now it is common to use lightweight papers including those used for origami to create iris folded designs. Lisa's participants have stated, "I can't believe I made something so beautiful!" and "This is so relaxing! I could do it every day!" 

Objective:
To realize that we are putting the pieces of our life, our spirit, our family and our emotions back together, and these pieces make us a beautiful masterpiece!

 
 Necessary materials for Iris Folding
Materials:
Wrapping paper or thin scrapbooking paper, five different patterns, pre-cut into 1½ inch strips
Shiny or solid paper, for center of design
Heavy card stock, in various colors, at least 1 per participant 
Scissors
Clear Tape
Pencils
Temporary Tape such as painters tape
Frame (optional)
Iris Folding Templates:
Heart Shape Template
Butterfly Shape Template
Flower Shape Template

 
 Lisa's finished Iris Folding project!
Timeframe:
Preparation: 30 min
Introduction: 5-10 min
Demonstration: 5 min
Relaxation: 4 min
Creation: 30 min
Closing: 15-25 min
Total: 1½ - 2hrs

Preparation:
It's essential to try the project first. A finished sample for your participants to view is necessary because of the intricate pattern-work involved! You may also want to create an example for each step.

Print more than twice as many templates as there are participants. 
Cut the patterned paper into 1½ inch strips beforehand.
For your demo, have the strips of paper ready, and your chosen template already cut out.

Introduction:
Today we're going to talk about how our past trauma's can tear away little pieces of who we are. We will then put these pieces together, revealing a beautiful masterpiece!

Discuss the ways in which past traumas can "tear away little pieces" of who we are. You may want to illustrate this concept by holding up a piece of paper and tearing after each example you share. For example, every time he hit you, it took away a little piece of who you are (tear off a piece of the paper). Every time he told you how stupid you are, it took away a little piece of who you are (tears off another piece of paper), and so on. Feel free to ask the participants to join in an give examples of past traumas. These can also include, "I no longer felt safe in any intimate situation with another male" or "I no longer felt like a little girl," etc. Once the paper has been torn to pieces, ask the participants to share some things they have, or can use, to help put the pieces back together; for example, self-esteem, courage, strength, faith, etc.

 
  Step 1
 
  Step 2
 
  Step 3
 
  Step 4
 
  Step 5
 
  Step 6
 
  Step 7
Demonstration:
This workshop may seem overwhelming at first so it can be helpful to demonstrate how to Iris Fold. Also show the sample(s) you made to give a visual reference. Reinforce that the project is simpler than it looks, and once the participants get started, they'll love it!

For your demo, follow the steps listed below in the creation process. You don't need to complete the design. Simply show enough so the participants can understand the steps. 

Relaxation:
Play soft music in the background, such as Lifescapes, Pure Relaxation or Relaxing Piano.

As you read this relaxation have participants hold each movement for five seconds. Let them know that today they'll being doing an "active relaxation" to notice each part of their body, when they get to their face, their entire body will be free to tension.

"If you feel comfortable, put both feet on the floor, leave your arms to your side or resting on the table, and close your eyes. Take a deep breath in, and exhale any tension you're feeling. Scrunch up your toes and feet, curling them toward our arches (let five seconds pass before moving them onto releasing this movement). Note the feeling of tension there and then relax your feet and toes. Now focus on your legs, tense your shins and calf muscles, holding them for five seconds, and then release those muscles. Straighten your legs, flexing your thigh muscles and hold. Feel that tension in your thighs, now release it and let your legs relax with your knees bent and the floor supporting your legs. Squeeze your butt (wait five seconds) and release, feeling how loose your legs are. Tense your stomach, make it feel tight like a ball, (wait five seconds) feeling all those muscles tight, relax your stomach. Now squeeze your shoulder blades together, pretend your holding a pencil between your shoulder blades (wait five seconds), slowly loosen your shoulders, letting them fall to your side. Make fists with both hands, squeezing as tight as you can (wait five seconds), now open your hands letting all the tension flow out. Squeeze your arms into your sides, tightening each muscle in your arms, hold this for five seconds, now release your arms and let them dangle at your side. Raise your shoulders to your ears, feel how each muscle in your neck is holding your arms up (hold for five seconds), now slowly let each of those muscles drop your shoulders down, completely relaxed. Now focusing on our face, squint your eyes and wrinkle your nose, bringing them together (hold for five seconds). Now let your nose and eyes feel the tension leaving them. Pull your lips in as tight as you can and hold for five seconds, let your lips relax to a beautiful smile. Now open your mouth as wide as you can, making a huge oval (hold for five seconds), and then let all the tension come out of your mouth as you slowly bring your lips back together. As we begin to bring ourselves back to the present, raise your eyebrows as high as you can and hold them there for five seconds, now feel the warmth of relaxation come over your face, releasing your eyebrows and open your eyes."

 
Step 8
 
 
 The big reveal! 
Creation Process:
Have participants choose an Iris Folding template, and the patterned paper they will be using. Depending on the template they choose, participants will need to take anywhere from 3-5 different patterns. They will also need a small piece of solid or shiny paper for the center. 

Step 1: Cut out the template you selected. Place the pattern guide to the side, as you will be using it in Step 6.

Step 2: Trace the template onto the card stock (in the center).

Step 3:  Cut out the template shape from the card stock. Start by puncturing the center, and then cutting around the traced line. 

Step 4: Place the template in the opening (face down). Secure using the temporary tape, because you're going to remove it for the big reveal!

Step 5: Turn the card stock over so you can see the numbers through the opening. Using the temporary tape, tape the card stock to your workspace. 

Step 6: Fold the strips of patterned paper in ½ lengthwise. Separate into piles and decide which pattern will be A, which will be B, and so on.

Following the pattern guide, start with the area labeled #1 on your template. Position the first strip (pattern A) so it completely covers the area, and the folded edge faces the center. Using the clear tape, tape both ends of the strip to the back of the card stock. Trim any excess paper that extends way beyond the covered area. 

Step 7: Using the second strip (pattern B), follow the same instructions for area #2. Repeat all the way around your shape, working inwards and following the numbers sequentially. Stop when you have completed the last number.

Step 8: To finish the center, attach a piece of shiny or solid paper, just bigger than the space left to fill. Don't turn your design over yet! We'll reveal it in the closing circle.
Note: Don't worry if the back looks messy. You'll be surprised how beautiful your design will turn out!

Important: As the participants create, ask them to think about all the ways they are growing, and putting the pieces of their life, their spirit, their family and their emotions back together. They may want to reflect on a positive step they have taken, or a quality they appreciate about themselves, as they apply each paper strip. Or they can simply take in a deep breath of appreciation. Remind them, that just like their creations, they are becoming a beautiful masterpiece themselves!

Closing:
To close, go around the circle and have each participant gently peel up their creations for the big reveal (they've been taped face down to the table during the creation process). Have each person share their thoughts on creating their piece. You may want to ask them to share how it feels to be putting all the pieces back together in their lives, and becoming a beautiful masterpiece!
Row.txt_description: Participants reveal the beautiful masterpiece, themselves, through the technique of Iris Folding.
Row.txt_tips: Note: Sometimes the Iris Folding doesn't turn out perfectly, but that's okay. Tell participants that imperfections are a part of life, and we are all still masterpieces!

Row.txt_code:
To Leader: A circle is a very powerful symbol and when we put ourselves at the center of our World, we can only expect powerful changes to happen in our lives. As you lead this workshop, I hope you are truly inspired to support the children in boldly creating their Worlds.

Objective:
This workshop is an opportunity for the children to focus on putting themselves at the center of their World.  Each child's vision of what this would mean to him/her unfolds during the workshop and becomes clear and tangible throughout the collaging process.
 
Materials:
 
 
  At the Center of My World!
 
Collage material (magazines)
Glue sticks
Scissors
Construction Paper or Card Stock 
Plate or circle cut to 8 inches in diameter (or larger), to be used as a template 

Age Range: 6 and up

Timeframe:  1 hour
10 minutes - Introduction and demonstration
5 minutes - Relaxation
30 minutes - Creation Process
15 minutes - Closing circle

Prep:
Cut enough circles for each participants.
Find appropriate magazines and cut images ahead of time (if possible).  Note: select images that will peak children's imaginations, and get them excited about the World they are creating.  Examples: children playing, families together, pets, vacations, etc. You can also include positive words and phrases like: happy, I am strong, etc.  Make sure there are a lot of expressive pictures of children that can be used for the center image.

Introduction:
"This is a window of time to think about what exactly you want in your World.  You will get to put yourself in the center, and decide how you want it to look.  What sort of things, experiences or people are around you in the World you get to create?  Do you want a puppy? Do you want to play sports with your friends?  Do you want more hugs from mom?  As you create your World, it's important to remember that you get to decide what it will look like. Be bold and feel free, and see all your dreams coming true!" 

Demonstration:
Demonstrate collage techniques to the children using scissors, or by tearing images out of magazines.  "First, select an image that represents you.  Using a glue stick, place that picture in the center of the circle provided.  Arrange the other pictures or words around it." Be sure to show an example of layering pictures (see below).  Explain to the children that it is perfectly fine to overlap the pictures.  

 
   
 
 Large image used as
a background
 Layered images over
background image
 Top images over solid
background image
 

Relaxation: 
Speak slowly, softly and very lovingly. "Make yourself comfortable.  It is good to be sitting with your back straight, your feet flat on the floor and your hands lying loosely in your lap. 

Take a deep breath in and let it out slowly... and if it feels safe for you, you may close your eyes.  Or if you would rather, rest your head on the table.  Keep feeling how good it feels as your breath fills your tummy, and how your body feels as the air goes out.
 
This is a special time just for you... to breathe in love and breathe out any worries. 

In your imagination, see yourself strong and brave at the center of your world.  (pause) What do you want in your world?  (pause)  What does it look like? (pause) How does it sound? (pause) What does it have in it?  (pause)  What are the things you like to do? (pause) Who is there with you?  (pause)  What have you done that you're proud of? (pause)  How does it feel to know that you have the power to create your own world? (pause)

Keep these pictures in your mind as you gently open your eyes, and begin to create a collage of your World with you in the center."

Collage Activity:
 
 
Remind the children, "What we will be doing today is creating exactly what we want in our World.  Each of you is going to create a circle and add a picture in the center that represents you, because YOU have the power to create you own World!  You will then add pictures all around you that remind you of the things, experiences or people you want in your life."

Closing Circle:
Ask the children to share their collage and how they feel about creating their World.
Row.txt_description: This workshop is an opportunity for the children to focus on putting themselves at the center of their World. Each child's vision of what this would mean to him/her unfolds during the workshop and becomes clear and tangible throughout the collaging process.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To take responsibility for our own health, happiness and safety, by paying attention to (and honoring) our physical, emotional and spiritual needs.

 
 Paying Attention to ME! supplies
 
Materials:
Scupley III (variety of colors) - 2 contrasting colors per person
Band-aid color Sculpey – 2-inch ball (1 per person)
Manilla Folders (will serve as work surface; don’t work directly on the table)
Handiwipes
Something to roll out the clay (ex. small rolling pin, jar, bottle )
Sharp knife/blade
Rulers
Copy paper for journaling (different colors) & Pens
Toothpicks/Thin Skewers
Cookie sheet (covered with paper, like from a grocery bag)
3" jewelry head pins (from a craft or bead store)
Small beads
Pliers (needle-nose work well)
Jump ring (small size works well)
Ribbon (optional)

Timeframe: 
Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Journaling: 10 minutes
Explanation/prep: 15 minutes 
Creation: 45 minutes
Baking: Time varies: 275 degrees for aprox. 15 minutes
Assembling: 10 minutes
Closing Circle: 15 minutes
Total: 2 hours (can be longer)


 
 Leaders preparing their "cane"
 
  
Prep:
There are many steps in creating the “Paying Attention to ME” person.  The activity may seem intimidating at first.  It’s helpful if you make a sample before the workshop; that way you will understand all the creation steps, and can easily explain it to the participants.

It is also helpful to preheat the oven before you begin creating; that way the oven is nice and hot when it's time to bake the clay.  An oven thermometer to accurately maintain the correct temperature is helpful.

Introduction:
Most of us are very good at taking care of other people’s needs.  We readily make ourselves available when someone else needs us …our friends, our children, etc.  But we often forget to acknowledge and honor our own needs.  It can be such a blind spot for us, we are often not even aware of it!

Today we are going to talk about our needs, and putting our needs first.  We all have needs and when we nurture and take care of these needs, we are healthier, happier and feel safe.

Opening Circle:
Today we are focusing on identifying what each of us needs to lead a safe, happy, and healthy life.  Taking time to pay attention to our needs is very important; when we are feeling nurtured and fulfilled, we are more loving and honoring to ourselves and we have more love to give to others!

We are going to start by having each person think about what they want or need in order to feel safe, happy and healthy.  Have each participant share one word about what they need right now.  Share the first word that comes to mind.

After all the participants have shared, ask them to notice the similarities and/or differences in all of their needs.  Thank them for sharing and acknowledge that all of these needs are important!

  
 Leaders journaling their needs
 
Journaling/Warm up:
We are going to journal about 3 different types of needs we all have: the needs of our body, our mind and our spirit.  Ask each participant to take a piece of paper (choose a color that makes them feel comfortable and safe, or even strong and hopeful).  Fold that paper into thirds lengthwise.  On the top of the first column, write the word Physical, on the second Emotional, and on the third Spiritual. 

I'm going to talk a little bit about each of these three needs and give you two minutes after each one to write and reflect on this need for yourself.  Keep in mind that there is no right or wrong way to do this journaling exercise.  You can write sentences, words, lists, draw symbols, shapes, or anything else you like.  The most important thing is that you don't censor yourself.  Just allow your thoughts to flow onto your paper without judgment.  What you write does not have to make sense to anyone but you!  (You might want to play soft background music during this journaling portion).

Physical needs are what we usually think about first.  What are your physical needs in order to be safe, happy and healthy?  For example:  We need to be free from harm.  We need shelter and a safe place to live.  We need good nutrition: healthy food and clean water.  We need exercise - keeping our bodies healthy and strong.  We need rest, giving us energy to do what we need to do, like succeeding at work or going to school.  In the first column, begin writing words, sentences, symbols or shapes to represent your physical needs (allow two minutes for this).

Another need that may be a little harder to think about, but just as important, are our emotional needs.  What are your emotional needs in order to feel safe, happy and healthy?  Examples are: feeling understood, feeling accepted and heard.  Knowing we are loved and appreciated also gives us the feeling of having emotional support.  Relaxation, fun and friendship help us to find emotional balance.  Having boundaries, realistic expectations and a positive attitude are other ways of supporting our emotional health.  Now in the second column, begin journaling about your emotional needs (allow two minutes for this).

Finally, we will address our spiritual needs.  What does your spirit need to give you peace?  Is it the ability to forgive, have patience or acceptance of others?  Do you need quiet time to reflect or pray?  Do you need to do good deeds or help others feel uplifted?  In the third column write words, sentences, shapes, or symbols to reflect your spiritual needs (allow two minutes for this).

Thank each participant for taking the time to reflect on (and honor) their own personal needs. Remind them they are worth it!

Project Explanation:
Today we’re going to create a “Pay Attention to ME” person.  We’re going to use a technique called “cane work.”  This is the same technique that is used to do glass beadwork in Italy.  The first step is to make the “cane”  which will become the foundation of our creation. A cane is a cylinder of clay that has a design running through the middle of it.  When the cane is sliced at any point, the design will be revealed.


 
 Sculpey cane with straight seam
 
In this workshop, we will be using a “jelly roll” design for the cane. (When sliced, it will resemble an old-fashioned cake that is rolled with jelly in the middle of it). The “jelly roll” is one of the simplest cane designs; there are many other beautiful cane designs that can be made!

Creation:
Look back at your journaling exercise and reflect on the needs you identified.  Decide what you want your clay person to be.  You can choose to represent one aspect of your needs (physical, spiritual or emotional), or focus on one specific need (such as eight hours of sleep).  Or, your clay person can be a reminder to pay attention to all of your needs!

First, we will need to condition the clay.  When you first open the package of Sculpey, the clay will feel stiff and hard.  In order to soften and easily work with it, you will need to warm it up first.  We will be each using the band-aid color and two contrasting colors that you can select.

Starting with the band-aid colored clay, you can begin to manipulate and play with it.  Break it apart into smaller pieces.  Squeeze it.  Stretch it.  As you continue handling it, you’ll start to feel it getting softer.  Keep working with it, rolling it, kneading it and stretching it.  Join the pieces back together.  When it’s soft, roll it up into a ball.  Once the band-aid color is softened and made into a 2" ball, do the same with the 2 contrasting colors.  You will end up with 3 balls of clay.

Note: Some colors (especially red) may bleed onto your hands.  Don’t worry. You can use a handiwipe to clean your hands when you’re done.

Perspective reminder: After each step, remind participants that this is their window of time to notice and respect their needs.

Tell your group that you will be walking them through the entire creation process. There are 17 steps to creating your Pay Attention to ME person and it is made up of 3 parts: a head, arms (upper body), and legs (lower body).  Making the “jelly roll” cane is the most important step; it will become the foundation of your whole project!  Are you ready to start making your “jelly roll” cane?

Making the “Jelly Roll” Cane:
For this part you will be using the two contrasting colored balls you made earlier. Put the band-aid colored ball aside to rest, as we will be using it later (in Step 6).

  
Rolling out the layers of contrasting
colors for the cane 
 
Step 1: After you condition each color, you’ll need to turn each one into a rectangular sheet.  Start with the first color.  Using all the clay, begin to pinch and pull your shape into a rough rectangular slab.  You can flatten it more by using your rolling pin.  You’re going to end up with a shape that is 3” wide by 5” long.  It doesn’t have to be exact.  There are rulers on the table if you want to measure it.  You can also use the side of the blade to “push in” and straighten the sides.  As you finish with one of the colors, do the same with the other one.  Both rectangles should end up being the same size.

  
Slicing the edge at a slant for easier rolling
to create the cane
 
  
 Rolling the Sculpey
 
  
 Stretching the cane to 12 inches
 
  
 Slicing the cane
 
  
Make small band-aid color balls and
thinly slice the cane		 
  
 Cover the ball with the slices 
  
 Roll the ball so it is seamless 
  
 Cut the cane in 2" pieces and share colors
 
  
 Explore by mixing colors
 
Step 2: Layer one colored rectangle on top of the other one.  Once you’ve done this, gently press them together so there are no air bubbles.  On one side of the rectangles, use your blade to create a slanted edge. This will make it easier to roll the clay.

Step 3: Starting with the slanted side, gently roll one color inside the other one.

Step 4: Reduce the cane in size by rolling it between the palms of both hands and the work surface (pressing gently to make it smaller).  Make sure to distribute the pressure evenly along the cane.  You can also gently pull at both ends to stretch it.  Your goal is to end up with a cane that is approximately 12” in length.  Make certain that the seam created, from the roll, is straight. Don’t worry if the ends get distorted. 

Step 5: Once your cane is approximately 12” long, take your blade and make a cut/slice in the middle.  You can now see your jelly roll!  Put both pieces aside (you will use them in Steps 7 & 10).

Tips for Cutting/Slicing
Use a sharp knife/blade to cut your cane, so the shape will become less distorted. Getting a nice clay cane slice can sometimes be trickier than it looks, especially if the clay is too soft.  Clay is easier to slice when it is on the cooler side.  If you have time (and a refrigerator close by), you can refrigerate it for 5 to 10 minutes to firm up.  If not, don’t worry; you’ll still achieve a beautiful effect!

If the cane is soft, roll it at the same time you are cutting it.  This will help to keep it round, and not flatten.
 
Step 6: Take the band-aid colored ball you made earlier.  This will be used to make the insides of the beads.  Cut it in quarters, you will end up with 4 pieces.  Roll each piece into a ball.

Step 7: Next take one half of the cane you cut in Step 5 (6-inch length).  We’re going to cut off a dozen thin slices (approx. 1/8” thick). You can make more if needed later.  The slices may come out a little more oval than round, that’s okay!

Step 8: Next you’re going to cover one of the band-aid color balls (made in Step 6) with the thin slices you just cut.  Place the slices next to each other, with all of the edges touching (like putting pieces of a puzzle together).  Cover the whole ball with the tiny slices.  If you need more slices, cut them off the cane (only cut the amount you need).  Put the leftover cane aside - it can be used later to make beautiful beads!

Step 9: After the ball is completely covered, roll it gently in the palms of your hands to blend the design together.  As you continue to roll it, you’ll see that all the seams will disappear.  That is what you want to achieve.  If any of the band-aid color is exposed, you can move around the slices around to cover it.

Step 10: Take the other half of the cane you cut in Step 5 (6-inch length).  We’re now going to make the cane a little thinner for another design variation.  We’re going to stretch this 6-inch piece into approx. 14 inches (to compensate for the distorted ends).  Just as you did in Step 4, (keeping the seam straight), you can gently pul the ends.

Step 11: From the cane you just made, cut off approximately 1 inch to remove the distorted end.  If you don’t see the jelly roll, cut off another 1/2 inch.  Now we’re going to share your colors with other participants in the workshop.  Cut 2” pieces of your cane, and give each person a piece.  You’ll still have the original color you chose; now you’ll also have other colors to work with! 

Step 12: You are now going to cover 2 more band-aid colored balls (from Step 6) with tiny slices.  (Note: we will only be using 3 “covered” balls for our clay person: the 2 made here, and the one made in Steps 8 & 9). You will have one band-aid ball left over.

You have many options. You can use the same colored cane for each ball (your original color or a color you just received).  Or you can mix and match colors.  You can also mix the large and small designs.  You can make all 3 balls the same, or all different - whatever you like!  Tell participants to choose the colors/designs that nurture their needs!

To cover the balls, use the technique in Steps 8 and 9.

Creating Body Parts: Head, Arms & Legs
Step 13: We’re going to start with the head.  Decide which ball/color you want to use.  Using a toothpick, you’re going to make a hole that goes completely through the ball.  This is going to be used to attach the body parts later.

Tip: The best way to make a hole is to put the ball on the table.  Slowly punch though the ball with the toothpick until you feel it hitting the table.  Pick up the ball; push the toothpick all the way through and pull it out the other side. If the ball distorts a little, you can use you fingers to reshape it.  Next, run the toothpick all the way through the ball, the opposite way, to make a clean hole! Don’t use anything wider than a toothpick.  We want the hole to be as small as possible!
 
 
 
  Piercing the head with a tooth pick
  Piercing legs and arms with tooth pick
 

Step 14: Next we’re going to make the arms.  Decide which ball/color you want to use for the arms.  Using your hands, you’re going to roll the ball into a hotdog-like shape.  You can pull the ends slightly to stretch it to the desired length.  Make the ends rounded or squared off, whatever you like.  Decide how you want the arms to look.  You can have both arms go out straight.  Or, you can bend both arms slightly, by creating a “u” shape.  Or, you can make one arm look like it’s waving by creating an “s” shape.  Once your shape is done, use the technique (in Step 13) to create a hole in the middle of the “u” or “s” curve. 

Remember: This is your “Paying Attention to ME” clay person, and it will serve as a reminder to take care of and honor your own personal needs.  You get to decide how you want it to look! 

Step 15: Now, we’re going to make the legs.  Take the last colored ball and roll it into a hotdog-like shape.  You can keep the ends round, or flatten them off.  Gently bend the shape in the middle to make a “v” shape, or to create a “u” curve.  Whatever feels right to you!  Using the same technique in Step 13, create a hole using a toothpick.  The hole will go right in the middle of the bend.

Keep in mind that after baking, the arms and legs will stay exactly as you positioned them.  For the arms, you can face the “u” up or down.  Manipulate the legs to be open or closed, or bend them how you see fit.  

If you have time, you can make small individual beads from the cane that is leftover by cutting 1/4 inch or thinner slices.  Use your fingers to shape the slices into cubes or disks.  Make a hole where you want it; you can make the hole slightly bigger than before to accommodate a ribbon.

Baking the Clay
  
 Lining up the parts before baking
 
Step 16. Next we’re going to bake the head, arms and legs.  Slide each body parts on a skewer.  Make sure the pieces aren’t touching each other, or they will stick together during cooking.  Place the clay-filled skewers on a baking sheet covered with paper from a bag.

Cooking instructions will vary depending on the thickness of clay. Baking directions are listed on each Sculpey package.  Generally, you will be baking at 275 degrees for approx. 17 minutes. It is helpful to use an oven thermometer to accurately maintain even baking temperatures.

Listening Exercise (optional way to fill the time while clay is baking):
While the clay is baking, you can have the participants do a listening exercise.  “How we listen to each other is very important and creates safety for the person who is sharing.  As we practice listening, we’re going to practice making it very safe and supportive for each other.  We are giving the other person a special ‘window of time’ to share about their thoughts and feelings, or whatever is on their mind.”

Explain to participants, “We all have places inside where we have been hurt.  In a way, these are like ‘ice-cubes’ - when we run into them, they are cold and hard.  Sometimes we think that in order to heal, we need to chisel away at the ice-cubes and break that ice.  But actually, if we let them out (and share about these hurts) with the warmth of someone listening, the ice begins to melt.”

Ask the each participant to choose a partner.  Give the first person 2 minutes to share about their needs, and anything that has come up so far in this workshop.  Let them know if they run into any “ice-cubes” or if tears come up, that is okay.

While the first person is sharing, the other person will practice listening.  Supportive ways to listen include: warm and caring facial expressions, making good eye contact – but it’s most important to maintain silence.  If the person sharing runs out of things to say, the listener can ask a question like, “What are you needs right now?”  They should simply encourage the person to speak, and not make it into a conversation.  After 2 minutes are up, let the partners know that it’s time to switch.

When both partners are done, ask a few members of the group to share about how it felt to “listen” or be “listened to.”

Assembling your “Pay Attention to ME” person:
  
Finished "Paying Attention to ME doll"
hanging from a beaded necklace.
 
Step 17: Make sure your clay pieces have cooled down before assembling (about 10 minutes).  Take a 3” Head Pin; string one bead on the pin (the “head” of the pin should be facing down, so it holds the bead).  Next slide the legs of your clay person down the pin; then place another bead on top of the legs.  Next slide the arms down the pin; then place another bead on top of the arms (this will become the neck).  Slide the bead that serves as the head on top of the neck bead.  Place another bead on top of the head.  Using pliers, bend the head pin so it forms a closed circle around a jump ring.  Finally you can string a piece of ribbon through the jump ring to hang the clay person (and add any additional beads you created).    

Your “Paying Attention to ME” person can be worn as a necklace or hung by your bedside, in your car, etc.  It will remind you of how valuable you are, and to take care of and honor your personal needs!

Closing Circle:
Ask each participant to share about their “Paying Attention to ME” person and anything they learned about their needs from this workshop.  After each person has shared, remind participants to use their clay person as a tangible reminder to take responsibility for identifying and honoring their own needs. 

Remind participants, that by nurturing themselves and by taking care of their needs, they are filling up their own “cup.”  This will give them more vitality, more power, more peace of mind, and they will also have more energy to help and support others!

Encourage participants to continue the journaling exercise at home, in their own time, and to keep identifying more of their physical, emotional and spiritual needs.  They are worth it!  Remember: Noticing what we need to feel safe, happy and healthy in our lives is one of the most important jobs we will ever have, and one job that no one else can do for us!
Row.txt_description: To take responsibility for our own health, happiness and safety, by paying attention to (and honoring) our physical, emotional and spiritual needs.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give participants an opportunity to reflect on what they are leaving in the past, and what they'd like to move towards in their future.

Materials:

 
 Completed Stepping Stones
 
Super Sculpey Polymer Clay
Toaster Oven
Sharpie markers (metallic Sharpies work best)

Preparation:
Prepare the Sculpey Clay by breaking up the blocks into in various colored balls of clay. Make sure to have enough clay for each person to make two stones.  If you only have a short amount of time to do the workshop, use real rocks or pre-baked Sculpey rocks.

Timeframe:
40 minutes

Introduction: 
Today we are going to create our very own Stepping Stones to give us a chance to reflect on where the path of life has taken us and where we want it to lead us in the future.  We are all on a path, always growing.  When you give yourself a window of time to practice respecting yourself, your feelings, your visions, it is very powerful. It has an impact on you. You are not the same person at the end as you were at the beginning which is why today we are going to look at what we are walking away from and what we are walking towards in our path of life.

 
  Sculpey "snake" using 3 colors
 
  Twisting Sculpey colors
 
  Rolling Sculpey in a ball
 
  Flatten Sculpey into a rock shape
Technical Info/Demonstration:
Step One:
To blend the clay, choose at least two colors. Use no more than a pinch of each color.

Step Two:
Roll each color into a "snake".

Step Three:
Wrap each "snake" around each other like a candy-cane and twist together.

Step Four:
Twist each little section of the roll until the colors are blended just the way you want them.

Step Five:
Roll the "snakes" into a ball. If you want, repeat steps 4 and 5 several times to create a more marbled effect.

Step Six:
Using a pen or a marker roll the ball into a rock shape.

Creation Process:
Remind each person to make two rocks for themselves and to use as many colors as they want.

Lay out all the rocks on a cookie sheet. Bake the Sculpey at 275 degrees for 15 minutes-for each ¼inch of thickness. Always allow the clay to cool completely before handling it.

After each person rock has been baked, play some music. You can now guide participants to write on their baked rocks. "I'd like you to relax, and take a moment and think about what your walking away from.  Think about one thing you'd like to leave behind (is it stress?  Is it worries?  Is it self-consciousness?  What would you like to let go of?)  Think of a word, shape or symbol for what you'd like to leave behind, and using a Sharpie write it on one stone. I'll give you few minutes to decide what you want to write and then write it on your rock."

"On your other rock, write something you'd like to go towards in your life.  What would you like to learn?  How would you like to grow?  What would you like to find?  Think of one word, shape or symbol to represent what you want to go toward and write in on your other stone."

Closing:
Ask each of the participants to share something about what they wrote on their Stepping Stone (i.e. what the words, shapes, colors they choose represent).  If they are hesitant to share let the participants know that they don’t have to share anything they don’t want to and that there is no right or wrong way to share. 

Be sure to thank participants for being so creative and for sharing about what they made!  Reinforce that what they walk towards in their future is their choice, "remember, these are your Stepping Stones.  As you walk through life, keep these with you, in your pocket, in your purse.  They are yours to carry with you as a reminder of where you are going."  You can also encourage participants to get rid of the stone that represents their past if they so choose.  Some options include burying their past stone in a garden, putting it in the trash, or throwing it into the ocean.
Row.txt_description: Participants write words, shapes, symbols on stones to remind them of what they are walking away from and walking toward in their lives.

Row.txt_code:
Objective: 
To enhance the family dynamic by celebrating positive family moments, both big and small. Families can reflect on the bond they share, and look forward to building a happy future!
 
Materials:
Feeling face template (multiple expressions)
8 1/2 x 11 Printable Brave/Scared Face Template
8 1/2 x 11 Printable Calm/Mad Face Template
8 1/2 x 11 Printable Happy/Sad Face Template
8 1/2 x 11 Printable Proud/Shy Face Template
8 1/2 x 11 Printable Loving Face Template
Paper plates (optional)
Pennies or small sandbag
Timer (optional)
Construction paper or card stock, various colors
Ice cream cone template
Ice cream scoop template
Copy Paper & Pens (for making lists)
Markers or Crayons
Scissors
Glue

 Age Range:    Timeframe:   
5 and older        
Introduction: 5 minutes
Warm-Up: 20 minutes
Opening Circle: 5 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing Discussion: 15 minutes
Total 1 hour 15 minutes		 









  
   
Set-Up/Prep for the Warm Up:
Using the templates provided, print out the feelings faces.  Print out one set (if you are doing this as a large group exercise), or create a set for each family.  You can cut the circles out and glue them onto paper plates, or you can use them as they are.  Before the warm-up, group the faces together on the floor.


   
 Prepare multi color ice cream scoops
from the template
 
Set-Up/Prep for the Workshop:
On different colored paper, print out the ice cream scoops and the cone.  You will need one cone per family.  You will want to make enough ice cream scoops so that each family has 10 or more.  For the scoops, use a variety of colors so the finished cones are fun and colorful!

Depending on the number of participants and their ages, you may decide to cut out the individual scoops beforehand.  It may be helpful to create an ice cream cone sample to display so that everyone knows what to expect during the workshop.

Introduction:
Sometimes when we have experienced challenges in our lives, we have a hard time remembering the happy times.  Today we’re going to take a special window of time with our families to have fun, and reflect on the positive things we’ve shared!  You will first have the opportunity to bond doing a warm-up exercise that helps us notice and talk about our feelings.  Then you will have the chance to play together and create a “Life is Sweet” ice cream cone!

Opening Circle: 
Today we’re going to reflect on the positive things we have done as a family.  Sometimes we forget to value the time we spend together and how precious it is.  When we take time to think abut the happy times we share, life is so much sweeter!

First, we will create a list of all the things we like to do together as a family.  Give some examples like: “My family and I love to have breakfast together on Sunday morning.”  Or, “We love to bake cookies together.”  Or, “We like to give each other hugs.”  They might choose to use one word responses like movies, games, art or picnics.  Either way is fine.

Next, each person will then write one idea or activity on an individual ice cream scoop, and glue them onto a cone.  The more things each person thinks of, the more scoops they get!

Warm Up:
   
This warm-up helps participants notice and express their feelings, and encourages group bonding.  You can have each family do this activity on their own.  Or you can do it in a large group with all the workshop participants.

“Today we’re going to play a game where you will each have a chance to share about your feelings. When we talk about our feelings, whether they are ones we like or ones that are difficult for us, it gives us the freedom to be ourselves and notice what's alive for us!”

Let participants know that we all have many different feelings, and even sometimes we feel all of these emotions simultaneously. In one day, we can feel joyful, upset, angry, and proud. Remember that while many of these feelings may seem uncomfortable, strange, challenging, or frustrating, it is useful to acknowledge each and every one of them! 
Have the first participant stand a few feet away from the plates and toss a penny/sandbag towards them. If the penny/sandbag lands on a face, the participant will share a story about the last time (or any time) they felt that particular feeling. For example, if the penny lands on the “happy” face, the participant will share about the last time (or anytime) they felt happy.  Depending on the size of the group, allow the participants to talk for at least one minute. If the penny/sandbag lands between two feelings, the participant can talk about either one of the feelings (move the penny/sandbag on top of the feeling the participant will be talking about). The other participants can practice listening as each person shares. Make sure everyone has an opportunity to take a turn or pass. If there’s time, you can go around a second or third time.

You can also incorporate more embodied art into the warm-up by giving participants the option to make a statue of the feeling instead of sharing verbally. For example, you might say, "Another option is that instead of talking, you can show us an image (statue) of that emotion. For example, here's what I look like when I'm nervous." Create a statue with your body, perhaps by hiding your face behind your hands and crouching down. 

You might also give the participants an opportunity to practice making images together by saying, "Let's do a demo. Everyone show what you look like when you're feeling excited in 3-2-1-FREEZE." Count slowly, and give participants an opportunity to notice how many different ways there are to show excitement. 

If it’s feasible, you can also do this warm up outside!


Creation:
   
  Adding words/phrases to each scoop
 
   
  Cutting out the cone
 
   
  Gluing the scoops on top of each other
 
   
   
  Two scoops!
 
We want to support a positive family experience, and encourage each person to be part of the creation process.  You can give the families one minute to assign responsibilities (assignments may include one person who cuts, one person who writes, one person who glues, etc).  The Moms can take on a leadership role, or family members can decide together.

Go around the circle and have each family member share one thing they like to do with their family.  As each person shares, add their ideas to the list.  Go around the circle 2-3 times, and encourage each person to share.  The more things the family can come up with the better!

When the families have created a significant list, transfer the ideas onto the ice cream scoops (one idea per scoop).  They can glue their scoops on the cone as they finish writing each one, or they can wait until they are done and glue them all at once. 

Note: If children or families cannot come up with things that they’ve done as a family, have them list things that they would like to do as a family when they leave the shelter.  They can focus on the positive changes they wish to experience once they are living a life that is free from violence.   

Closing Circle:
Encourage family members to share what it felt like to do this activity together.  
 
You can ask questions such as, “How many of you didn’t know that you and your family did so much together?  Where can we display these ice cream cones so we are always reminded of this activity and what it meant for us?  Did anyone think of some activities that their family hasn’t done yet, but would like to try in the future?  Does anyone have any ideas on how you can plan out how your family is going to do some of these activities once you leave the shelter?
 
Encourage families to display their ice cream cones as a reminder of the positive experiences they’ve shared together.  Remind them how much sweeter life is when they are spending time with each other and having fun!
Row.txt_description: To enhance the family dynamic by celebrating positive family moments, both big and small. Families can reflect on the bond they share, and look forward to building a happy future!
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.
