Row.str_title: I Can: Requiem for I Can't Pilot workshop
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop is about confronting the things we feel we cannot do in out lives so we can move towards recognizing we can.  We are going to help start a movement of survivors coming together and collectively letting go of our I Cant's and embracing our I Cans. 
  
 

“I can’t live without him... I can’t leave him. I can’t make it on my own... No more abuse!”
  

Materials:
White card stock for writing
Multi-colored pens (optional)
Colored paper for scrolls
Paper Shredding Machine (Some shred into confetti, some into strips. Check to see what kind you have. Either works for this workshop - they just look different.)
Small ziploc bags
Shrinky Dink paper
Shrinky templates
Colored pencils
Hole punch
Scissors
Toaster oven
Ribbon
Copper wire
Beads
Music (suggested: Miles Davis Kind of Blue for I Can't journaling and heavenly for I Can Creation)
Timer
I Can Introduction Video
Digital camera
Audio Release form
Art/Photography Release forms (including contact info for exhibit invite)

Timeframe: 2 hours
Opening Circle: 15 min
Intro & Video: 15 min
Writing: 15 min
Sharing & Shredding: 30 min
Shrinky Creation: 30 min
Closing: 15 min

Opening Circle:
Go around the room and have each person share their name and how they're feeling right now.

Introduction:
Lynn introduces us and the I Can: Requiem for I Can't video.  Briefly explains who is in the video and what they are doing for the exhibit, and warns that there is a part that may be disturbing to some viewers.  Play introduction video.  Then introduce Christy who will run the workshop.

This workshop is about confronting the things we feel we cannot do in out lives so we can move towards recognizing we can.  While the trauma we experienced may be the most powerful thing that has ever happened to us, it is also the source of our power.  During this workshop you will have the opportunity to write and then shred all of the things you believe you can't do once and for all!  Our shredded I cant's will then be given to Barbara and Nina who will transform them into ash by burning them.  Barbara and Nina will then combine all of the I can't ashes and use them in an art exhibit you will all be invited to.  The exhibit will raise awareness about domestic violence and celebrate our collective strength. After we shred our I cant's we will then focus on all of the things we can do.  First by writing the I can(s) you want to share with the world on a colorful scroll that will also be used in the exhibit. Then by creating an I Can shrinky dink to serve as a reminder that anything is possible as we can do anything we put our minds to! 

This workshop is an opportunity for you to practice noticing your feelings and respect what needs to come out. Every part of this is voluntary and everyone in the room supports you.  Notice you are safe and among friends.  Each creation will be different, as our challenges are unique.
  

 
“Rest Peacefully I Cant’s.”

  
  
Writing I Cant's:
Place a variety of colored card stock on the table for the participants to choose from.  As we grow fears and insecurities may come up.  Our inner and outer critics, the stress of our everyday lives makes us feel as though we can't get what we want...Today will be a chance to release these I cants.  To begin we are going to do some writing.  Pick a color paper for your I cants... take a second to think... are your I cant's yellow, red, green...just a pick color  (meanwhile cue music)... I'm going to turn on some music and we are going to take 5 minutes to write all the I cant's that come up.

Keep in mind that there is no right or wrong way to do this writing exercise. You can write sentences, words, lists, draw symbols, shapes, or anything else you like. The most important thing is that you don't censor yourself. Don't worry about spelling or grammar, just allow your thoughts to flow onto your paper without judgment.  What you write is just for you and thus does not have to make sense to anyone but you!

You can begin by writing the words I can't on the top of your paper.  Try to keep writing until time is up.  If you feel powerful today have no I cants to speak of .... Think of a time when you did and just keep writing.  As you write keep trusting whatever comes to mind, it doesn't have to make sense, it's okay if you repeat one I can't over and over again. It's okay.  Give five minutes to write.

In the last minute remind them - keep trusting what comes to mind.  We have about one more minute. As you finish up read over your thoughts and really take a look at what you wrote...Cue music off.

Ask the participants to look over their writing and circle all of the I cant's that stand out.  Then Pass out the Art/Photography Release form and instruct the participants to write the one or two I can't they want to share with others.

Sharing & Shredding:
Christy stands at the front of the room.  Think about how this felt?  Was it really powerful, scary or freeing... now were going to ask a few people to be brave and to come up here with me and share your I cants and then shred them. Remember this is a chance to let go of your I cants. Ask: "Does anyone else want to share some or all of their I cant's with the group?"  As each person comes up tell them its okay to take their time and notice how brave they are.  Thank everyone who shared. Invite others to come shred.  Continue until each woman, one by one, has had an opportunity to share her list (which is optional) and finally shred it. One by one, each woman shreds her "I cant's" and places the shredded paper in a small zip loc bag to send to AWBW.  The shredded I can'ts will then be given to Nina and Barbara who will first burn them and then use them in an upcoming art exhibition you will all be invited to! 

I Can Circle:
Discuss how we are all like Cathy, Barabra, and Nina in that we overcame great challenges and as a result gained great strength and knowledge.  Now that we have had a funeral for our I Cant's, were going to take this opportunity to celebrate our strength and notice what we can do.  Keeping that in mind, I want us to stand up, gather in a circle, hold hands and each share one thing we've overcome in our lives that make us stronger.  Something significant in your life that you thought you couldn't do, but you did.  If your having a hard time thinking of something, one thing that you did was come to this group. There is no right or wrong way to share and you don't have to share anything you don't want.  After each person has shared have the participants sit back down and begin the I Can scroll writing portion of the workshop. 

I Can Scrolls:
Now that we have released and gotten rid of all of our I cant's we are ready to focus on all of the things we can do.  Now, instead of journaling were going to write our I Can(s) that we want to share on strips of paper and then we will create reminders to carry with us.  Now I want you to think about all of your I cans...what comes to mind when you think about all of the things you want to do in your future...be bold...you can do anything you put your mind to! 

Pick a color paper for your I cans... take a second to think... are your I cans purple, green, pink...just a pick color (meanwhile cue music)...

Ask the participants to think about I cans that stand out, the ones they want to carry with them. Pass out the scroll paper, have the participants choose a color to represent their I can, and then write their I can(s) on the paper.  If they so choose the participants can make more than one colorful I can scroll.  Tell the participants that we are going to gather all of the I can scrolls from everyone who does the project and use them in the exhibit, then collect the I Can's they just wrote.

Creating Shrinky Dink:
Now we are going to create an I Can shrinky dink to remind us of the I Can's we chose to embrace today! 

Step 1:
Start by tracing the template on the rough side of the Shrinky Dink (you don't have to use a template). Keeping in mind all of the things you can do, using colored pencils, write words, colors, shapes, or scribbles on the Shrinky Dink to help you remember your I Can's.  Begin to color and create the design that will fill in your shrinky dink. (Be sure to draw on the rough side of the plastic.)

Step 2:
When you are finished coloring, if you like, cut out your I Can shrinky with scissors.  Make sure to punch a hole in the shrinky dink so it can be hang around your neck.

Step 3:
Now the I Can shrinkys are ready for baking. Place the Shrinky Dink pieces, colored side up, on a small piece of a brown paper bag and then place the paper on a tray or cookie sheet.

Step 4:
While the shrinkies are cooking have the participants complete the Art/Photography Release.  Make sure they leave contact info to invite to exhibit.  Put the tray of Shrinky Dinks in the oven at 300 degrees for 1-3 minutes and watch as your Shrinky Dink shrinks! After pieces lie flat, allow an additional 15 seconds of baking time to complete the process.  If you pull it out prematurely you may put it back in the oven.

Step 5:
Remove paper from tray or cookie sheet and let Shrinky Dinks cool.  If you like you can add ribbon or wire so you can hang your I Can shrinky.  You can also add beads if you so choose.

Photograph the shrinky dink for exhibit.

Thank the participants for creating their I Can shrinky and reiterate that while the trauma we experienced may be the most powerful thing that has ever happened to us, it is also the source of our power.  Use your I can shrinky as a reminder that you have the power to overcome any obstacle and that you can do anything!

Closing:
Have a each participant share anything they want about their experience writing their I cant's and what they created on their I Can shrinky. 

Reinforce the importance of putting their contact info on the art release so that we can stay in touch as the participants may discover an I Can in the future and we want to hear about it!  This workshop is just the beginning of us recognizing our potential and we want to hear about all of the new things you come to find you can do in the future!

Exhibit paperwork:
Pass out Art/Photo release and complete it.
Row.txt_description: This workshop is about inspiring us to have the courage to uncover all of the things we believe we cannot do and then transform them into a tangible that we can accomplish the positive things we would like to do. Confronting the things we feel we cannot do in our lives is the first step towards recognizing we can. Participants express and then shred all of the things they feel they cannot do to enable them to refocus and embrace their I Can's.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
 To help break down barriers between family members by engaging them in messy art activities that enable them to build more positive connections.  Starting with crayons and continuing with foam paints and soft clay putty, family members are immersed in sensory explorations that activate their emotions and encourage closeness.

Materials:
White construction paper (18 x 24) or Butcher paper (for larger families)
Crayons (the cheaper and more waxy works best)
Colorations® No-Drip Foam Paint  (variety of colors)Discount School Supply
Soft white paper towels
Colorations® Super Lightweight Air-Dry Putty - White  Discount School Supply
(1/2 pack of putty per person)
9” Paper plates – good quality plates without coating, such as Chinette
Tacky Glue
Handi wipes
Hole punch
Ribbon (assorted colors)
Paint Brushes (optional)
Sharpies (optional)

   
  Fun Foam Paint!
 
Set Up:
Make sure you cover tables with a tablecloth and/or paper place mats.  While the foam paint is easy to clean up, working with it can be messy!

On a paper plate, squirt a dollop/blob of each color of the foam paint.  You will need one plate per family.  Squirt a small amount at first… a little paint goes a long way!   Replenish as needed.  Note: It works best if the can is upright when you squirt out the paint.  You can hold the plate on an angle or upside down since the paint doesn’t drip.

Time Frame:
Introduction
Opening 
Warm Up - Scribble Chase
Demonstration
Creation:
•    Finding Symbol / Sharing                
•    Making Symbol out of Air Putty
•    Create the Family Unity Symbol on paper plate
Closing Circle:
   
5 minutes
5 minutes
15 minutes
10 minutes
40 minutes



15 minutes
TOTAL
 1 hour 30 minutes

           
                          
                
                   
                                      





Introduction:
Today we are going to use art materials to work together as a family and create our Family Unity Symbol.

Opening Circle:
Today we’ll explore our senses with colorful paints, magical clay putty, and simple crayons.  We will be learning new ways of working together as families.  These exercises give us permission to be messy and lose control with art materials.  Working together to create art not only builds connections on paper, it helps us find courage to try new things, believe in ourselves, express our feelings, and feel closer and more connected.

As you do the exercises today, remember there is no right or wrong way to experience them, just jump right in.  It’s okay to be silly!  It’s ART, so just go for it! 

Warm Up:
Step One: Scribble Chase
  
  Follow the leader Scribble Chase
 
   
   
  Patting the Foam Paint onto the paper
 
   
  
 Covering the whole paper with Foam Paint
 
   
   
   
   
  Looking for the symbol
 
   
We’re going to start by doing an exercise called the “Scribble Chase.” Each family will be able to do this exercise, together.

Have each family member select different colored crayons.  Decide who will be the leader and who will be the follower(s).  The first person “leads” by drawing on the paper with their crayon, while the others “follow” (chases) with their crayons.  Make sure to have each person in the family participate in the Scribble Chase.  The "leader" can scribble in whatever way he/she chooses and all the “followers” will chase.

Press hard and put a lot of wax down with the crayons.  Larger families can use butcher paper so they have enough space for their designs.  Keep layering on top of the same drawing, until the whole page is filled with scribbles.  In the end you should have one very layered design with lots of lines, shapes and colors.

Step Two: Add Foam Paint to Your Scribble Chase
Foam Paint:
Swish and Pitter Patter Demonstration
I’m going to show you two techniques that you can use with the foam paint: Swish and Pitter Patter.  We will be using a paper towel instead of a paintbrush.  Crumple up a small piece of paper towel in your hand to use as your “paint dabber.”  Touch your dabber lightly onto several colors of paint. 
•    For the Swish technique: SWISH your dabber over the paper and make a rainbow of color, texture, and color designs.  POLISH to dry by blotting/rubbing with a clean paper towel.
•    For the Pitter Patter Technique:  DAB the paper towel in up and down motions with the dabber (like rain). POLISH to dry by blotting/rubbing with a clean paper towel.
Show participants how to get their whole body into their art, not just their wrist, so they can have the full, fun experience.

Crayon Resist
Now we will cover the Scribble Chase paper with foam paint.  The waxy crayon will “resist” the painted surface, and the image will "pop" though.  Try using foam paint colors that contrast with the crayon colors (for example: warm colors such as red, yellow, and orange contrast with cool colors such as blue, green, and purple).  The contrast will make the images stand out.

Using Foam Paint (and the Swish or Pitter Patter technique), work together as a family to cover the entire paper with color.  Everyone can take turns applying and wiping off the foam paint to reveal the crayon designs.  Make sure all the family members get involved.  Use a clean paper towel to wipe off excess paint and “polish” off the remaining residue.  The wax in the crayon will “resist” the paint and your symbols will stand out.

Creation
Step 1: Find Your Personal Symbol/Image
   
  Covering the Putty symbol with color
 
   
   
  Creating and coloring the symbol
 
   
As a family, study your scribble chase design.  Have each person look and find one personal symbol that stands out.  You can feel free to turn the paper in different directions to find your image.  Your symbol can be simple, like a heart, a bird or a butterfly.

Hints to finding your symbol:  Think about looking up at the clouds to find images or symbols in them.  In this same way, try to find a simple symbol in your scribbles.  

Once you find your symbol, reinforce it with crayon so it stands out on the page.  You can choose a contrasting color to outline it and fill the symbol in.

Step 2: Make Your Own Symbol Out of Air Putty

Demonstration: Air-Dry Putty

The material we are using is spongy and sticks to itself.  It also starts to harden within one hour after it has been opened.  Take a piece of air-dry putty in your hand and play with the material.  Swish it, smell it, and think about how it feels.  Take a small piece, and roll out a small snake shape.  Make it into a coil like a snail.  If you prefer, you can also substitute the putty for play doh or sculpey, which needs to be baked.

Important note about Air-Dry Putty: Do not open up the package of putty until you are ready to use it.  It completely dries and hardens in 24 hours, but it will begin to dry within one hour of opening the package.

Creation: Have each family open a packet of Air-Dry Putty, take a minute or two to get familiar with the material.
Now you will each create your individual Scribble Chase symbol out of the Air-Dry Putty.  This will require some creative thinking as you adapt your crayon design into putty.  There is no right or wrong way to do this, just trust the process!  You can mix Foam Paint into the clay, or paint on top using any of the techniques we learned today.

Family Sharing:  Have each family share about their symbol and why they chose it.  What does the symbol mean to you?  Is there a message?  It’s okay if emotions come up as family members talk about their symbols.  Encourage family members to practice listening and being there for each other.  As a family, discuss how all your symbols can work together into one design.  What do they have in common?  How do they relate?  How can you combine them for an interesting or meaningful effect?
   
  Completed project
 

Step 3: Decorate your Paper Plate

Decorate the plate to coordinate with the symbol(s) as it will serve as the background for your Family Unity Symbol. Using crayons, add lines, shapes and colors to embellish your paper plate.  Remember to make bold shapes with the crayons for a dramatic “resist” effect.  Make sure everyone in the family participates.  Using paper towel “dabbers” and the swish/pitter patter techniques, apply foam paint to the entire paper plate.  Wipe off excess foam paint with clean rag and polish to finish.  If paintbrushes are available, you can use them for more detail. Or you can use markers to add accents. 

Step 4: Create the Family Unity Symbol

Combine all the Air-Putty symbols together into one design by gluing them on the paper plate. 

Punch a hole at the top of the plate and add ribbon so you can hang the Family Unity Symbol later.

Closing:
Today, we’ve worked together as a family to create a symbol of unity.

How did it feel to do this as a family together?  What did you notice about yourself or each other?  What can you take with you that you learned today?

Hang your Family Unity Symbol in a place where family members can view it often.  It can serve as a reminder of your fun creation!
Row.txt_description: To help break down barriers between family members by engaging them in messy art activities that enable them to build more positive connections. Starting with crayons and continuing with foam paints and soft clay putty, family members are immersed in sensory explorations that activate their emotions and help encourage closeness.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Objective: 
In creating a time capsule that represents them and holds their
secrets, hopes or dreams; this activity allows participants to honor who
they are now in their lives, and where they wish to be.

Materials:
   
  Time Capsule Supplies
 
Empty containers with lids (examples: Potato chip cans, formula canisters, etc.)
Paint - Acrylic or Biocolor Paint from DSS
Rhinestones, glitter, and other embellishments
Paintbrushes
Construction paper
Glue
Scissors
Markers or colorful pens
Found objects that may haves symbolic meaning for participants
Photos (whenever possible)

Optional Materials:
Magazines for cut-outs
Patterned paper or tissue paper (for a more polished look)
Mod podge (or make your own with a solution of 1/2 water, 1/2 white glue)

Timeframe: 
Introduction: 5 minutes
Creation: 45 minutes
Closing Circle: 10 minutes
Total: 60 minutes

   
  Time Capsule Supplies
 
Set-Up/Prep:
This is a great project when funding is low; you can get really creative when finding materials.  This is also a recycling project.  Yeah-go green!!!!

Note: It is helpful if you take all the labels, paper and glue off the containers before the workshop.

If you are using magazine cut-outs, cut images ahead of time (if possible).  Be sure to select images that will inspire participant's hopes and dreams.  You can also include positive words, quotes or affirmations and phrases like: happy, free, etc.

In addition, gather small objects to represent the participants, including what their wishes, hopes, and dreams might be (examples: coins, charms, magazine images, etc.).  Or, you can ask each group member to bring pictures or special trinkets that represent special things they want in their lives.

Warm-up (Optional)
This warm up will help to focus participants on where they are in their present journey:

Stepping Stones:
You can gather stones outside, purchase them at a garden store, or make them out of sculpey or other clay.  Bring enough so that each person has two.  Start by having each participant pick two stones.  Remind participants that we are all growing and taking steps towards a richer and happier future.  Every experience we go through, even the challenging ones, are stepping-stones in our lives. 
   
  Stepping Stones
 

Turn on some music and have participants take a minute to think about what they want to let go of or leave in their past.   On the first stone, write a word or symbol that represents what they want to move away from.  Next, let the participants take a minute to think about what they want to move towards.  On the second stone, write a word or symbol that represents something they want for themselves.  Let participants know they can carry these stones with them on their life’s journey, as a reminder of the steps they are taking in their life.

Introduction:
   
  Time Capsule Lid
 
   
  Time Capsule decorated outside
 
   
  Time Capsule inside collage
 
   
  Placing the message in the capsule
 
You can start by asking if any of the participants have ever made a time capsule at school or when they were younger.  Explain that usually time capsules are created to hold information that reflects who you are at the present time, so you can look back on it someday.  Let the participants know they will be making a time capsule that represents them and holds the secrets, hopes or dreams that they have now. 

Encourage the participants to be playful and feel free as they are creating their time capsule.  Even though this may feel like a childlike activity, remind participants that it is important to get in touch with their playful and creative sides as they envision their hopes and dreams.  This activity is meant to honor participants where they are now in their lives, and where they wish to be.

Creation:
Give the participants 10-15 minutes to decorate the outside of the container using colorful paper, paint, glitter, rhinestones, or whatever makes them feel happy and hopeful.  They can also add words, pictures, or make drawings and symbols that have a special meaning to them.

Next, ask the participants to think about their hopes, dreams or goals in this moment. Encourage participants to be free and not to judge what they are dreaming about, or worry about whether it will come true or not.  They can write or draw personal messages (a letter to themselves, etc.) on pieces of paper and place them inside the container.  They can also place pictures or trinkets in the time capsule to represent special things they want in their lives.  If you did the stepping stone warm-up they can add both stones, or the one that expresses what they are moving towards.

Thank participants for giving themselves permission to play, create and dream!

Towards the end of the workshop, encourage them to reflect on why they placed particular items or messages in the time capsule.  Also, ask them to select a date in the future when they will open it.

Closing Circle:
Go around the circle and have participants share about one thing they placed in their time capsule, and why it has a special meaning for them.

Remind participants to tuck their time capsule away in a secret place.  Encourage them to open it after a lapsed time to reflect on their personal messages, and to remember who they were when they created it and the hopes and dreams that they expressed today.
Row.txt_description: In creating a time capsule that represents them and holds their secrets, hopes or dreams; this activity allows participants to honor who they are now in their lives, and where they wish to be.

Row.txt_code:
Objective: 
The children/teens will create a time capsule to represent who they are.

   
Materials:
Empty containers with lids (examples: Lays/Pringle potato chip cans, coffee canisters, Lysol/baby wipes containers, etc.)
Paint - Acrylic or BioColors
Paintbrushes
Construction paper
Glue
Rhinestones, glitter, etc.
Markers
Magazines cut-outs

Optional Collage Materials:
Magazines cut-outs
Patterned paper or tissue paper,
Scissors
Mod Podge (or make your own with a solution of 1/2 water, 1/2 white glue)

Timeframe:
Warm-Up/Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Creation: 40 minutes
Closing Circle: 10 minutes
Total: 60 minutes

   
Set-Up/Prep:
This is a great project when funding is low; you can get really creative when finding materials.  This is also a recycling project. Yeah-go green!!!!

Gather up the containers; it is helpful if you take all the labels, paper and glue off before the workshop.

If you are using magazine cutouts, cut images ahead of time (if possible).  Be sure to select images that the children can relate to like pictures of families, homes, vacation locations, sports etc. You can also include positive words and phrases. You can also gather up a basket of small objects to represent children's favorite activities and things they may want. 

Warm-up (Optional)
For this workshop we recommend the Affirmation Confetti Warm Up, that we presented March 2010, which celebrates positive qualities in ourselves and others.
 
Introduction/Opening Circle:
A Time Capsule is a fun way to think about what's important to you now.  This could include your favorite things such as, colors, songs, places or food! Or it can include the names or pictures of family or friends that are special or important to you.

 
 
   
   
   
Creation:
Give the children 10 - 15 minutes to decorate the outside of the container using colorful paper, paint, glitter, rhinestones, etc., whatever best represents them.  They can add words, pictures, or make drawings or symbols that only have are special to them!

Next, ask the children to think about what sorts of things are really important to them, such as family, friends, music, dancing, safety, school etc. and then ask them to fill their capsule with things that represent those things.  Encourage the children to be free and not judge what they select.  If they like, they can write or draw personal messages (a letter to themselves, etc.) on pieces of paper and place them inside the container.  They can also place pictures or trinkets of things that represent what they love to do or play with in the Time Capsule.

Towards the end of the workshop encourage them to think about why they placed particular items or messages in the Time Capsule.  Ask the children to select a date in the future when they will all open it and the date to the outside of the container as a reminder.

Closing Circle:
Go around the circle and ask the children to each share about one thing they placed in their Time Capsule, and why they chose it. Remind them to tuck their Time Capsule away in a safe and secret place.  Encourage them to open it after the designated time has lapsed, so that they can then reflect on their personal messages and to remember who they were when they created it!
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives children/teens the opportunity to create a Time Capsule to represent who they are.

Row.txt_code:
The finished Lotus Flower 
   
   
  Workshop set-up 
  
 
   
   
   Cutting the 3 different layers 
   
Objective:
To assist participants in seeing and believing that out of a murky and dark environment, something beautiful can be created and they can rise above. 

Materials:
Lotus flower templates
Small
Medium
Large
Heavy paper (construction paper or cardstock)
Watercolor paper
Watercolors
Paintbrushes
Glue
Lotus Flower meditation handout (optional)

Timeframe:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Warm-Up: 10 minutes
Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Creation: 25 minutes
Closing Discussion: 10 minutes
1 hour

Set-Up/Prep:
On heavy paper, print one set of the lotus flower templates (3 sizes). Cut the 3 shapes out. You will be using these to trace the shapes onto the watercolor paper.

On the watercolor paper, trace the 3 shapes. Prepare and cut out enough shapes so each participant has one set of all 3.

If you do not have time to cut the watercolor paper in advance, be sure to have enough of the templates printed on heavy paper for the group to share.

   
  Real Lotus flower floating in a pond 
Introduction:
Introduce the lotus flower; share how the flower grows and blooms and what it represents. The lotus flower, which is considered sacred to many Asian cultures, is believed to represent innocence, rebirth, growth and potential. Rooted firmly in the mud, the lotus flower grows in murky waters. With a long stem and petals sprouting from it, the flower always rises above the water's surface, and opens with the light of the morning sun.

A core Buddhist value says: "Like a lotus flower that grows out of the mud and blossoms above the muddy water surface, we can rise above our defilements and sufferings of life." Just like the lotus flower, we can grow to be strong, beautiful and healthy no matter what surrounds us!

Window of Time
"Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you - a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you do or say is voluntary. I'll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there's no right or wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this window of time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. Please ask for what you need, and know that I'm here in support of you."

You can take this time in whatever way feels good and right for you. If you can't think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just play with the materials."

Warm Up:
Read the lotus flower meditation:

Imagine that you are a lotus seed buried beneath a muddy lotus pond. There is mud all around you.  Above you, above this muddy pool, are sunshine and air. You are not disheartened as you begin your journey towards the surface.

With a determined heart, you begin to wiggle in the earth. You grow roots deep, deep into the mud. Your little stem grows up slowly.  Suddenly, "pop" you are out of the mud! Your stem grows higher and higher, taller and taller.  You rise up slowly, fighting against the muddy water.  All of a sudden, you are out of the muddy pond! You reach up towards the warm sun, shining down on you.

Your lotus bud begins to grow on top of your stem. It expands and grows larger and larger, finally bursting into full bloom.  You stand beautifully above the muddy water, not dirtied by the mud from which you grow.  You are fragrant and beautiful.

Everyone who saw you marveled at your beauty! Your determination to grow out of the muddy pond reminds them of the Buddha and his journey towards Enlightenment. The Buddha, like a lotus, is determined to grow out of the muddy surroundings that are the pain and sufferings of life. He has done all that is to be done and he is showing us that we can all do it too.  We may have pain but we all have the potential of growing out of our sufferings and achieving wisdom, like the Buddha.

You are a beautiful lotus flower, and your role is to remind people to rise above their pain and sufferings, just as you are rising above the muddy water and not dirtied by the mud from which you grow.

Adapted from "Lotus Meditation" BuddhaNet's Guided Meditation for Primary Students.

Opening Circle:
Ask the participants, "After hearing the background of a lotus flower, think of one thing that you have grown out of or through. We will go around in a circle and everyone may share one thing about how they relate to the lotus flower."

Note: If participants are reluctant to share, and if you feel comfortable as the leader, share a personal story about how you grew out of a dark or difficult time.

Creation:
With the three different size cutouts of the lotus flower in front of them, ask participants to use the watercolors to paint each layer. They can paint each layer differently or they can all be the same.
 
   
 
  Painting the layers.
  Rolling the edges.
  Gluing the layers together.
 

"Beginning with the largest shape, use the watercolors with your fingers or a brush to lightly cover the petals. Then take each petal and roll it gently inwards until it curls (you can use a paintbrush or pencil to help with the rolling method). Follow the same process with the two smaller shapes." Once all three layers are dry, have the participants glue them together with a small amount of glue on the bottom/center of each layer.

As they are creating, remind participants that we all are like lotus flowers.

At the end of the workshop, have the participants notice that they have created something beautiful...and they are beautiful too!

Closing:
Ask participants how it felt to create the lotus flower. They can share how they are like a lotus flower, and how it felt to create something beautiful.

Encourage the participants to keep their lotus flower visible, as a memento that something beautiful can come out of a painful situation. Remind them, "whenever we are feeling sad or frustrated about the muck that we have to work through, we too can grow and rise above!
Row.txt_description: To assist participants in seeing and believing that out of a murky and dark environment, something beautiful can be created and they can rise above.
Row.txt_tips:
If you want to deepen the participant's experience, you may want to add this to the closing: With music playing in the background ("Baby Blue" by Carlos Reynosa is a great suggestion), ask participants to take the last 10 minutes to journal (provide journal and pen) about their creation and its meaning. If they want to share their writing, go around the room and have each participant share any discoveries that they made.

Another great tip, from leader Laura Maldonado at South Gate Police Department, is to create a lily pad for the lotus flower to lay on! This creates a beautiful color contrast and shows the full representation of the flower.
   
  Lotus Flowers on lily pads
