Row.str_title: I Can: Requiem for I Can't
Row.txt_code:
Shredded I Cant's

  
Objective:
This workshop is about confronting the things we feel we cannot do in our lives, allowing us recognize and embrace that we can do anything!  By participating in this workshop you will be part of a movement of survivors coming together and collectively letting go of our I Cant's and embracing our I Cans.
  
 
 Completed I can shrinky

Materials:
White card stock for I Can't journaling
Pens/Multi-colored pens (optional)
Colored paper for I Can statements
Paper Shredding Machine (Some shred into confetti, some into strips.  Either works for this workshop.)
Shrinky Dink paper
Shrinky templates
Colored pencils
Permanent Markers (Sharpies)
Hole punch
Scissors
Toaster oven
Ribbon
Beads
Music (suggested: Baby Blue by Carlos Reynosa for I Can't journaling and Heavenly for I Can statement and shrinky creation)
Timer
I Can Introduction Video
2012 Art/Photography Release forms (including contact info for exhibit invite)
Women's Windows Participant Evaluation

Timeframe: 2 hours 25 minutes
Opening Circle: 15 min
Intro & Video: 20 min
Writing: 15 min
Sharing & Shredding: 20 min
I Can Circle: 15 min
I Can Statement Creation: 15 min
Shrinky Creation: 20 min
Closing: 15 min
Exhibit paperwork: 10 min

Note: The children's version of this workshop is in the Variation at the bottom of the page.

Opening Circle:
Go around the room and have each person share their name and how they're feeling right now.

Introduction:
Introduce AWBW and the I Can: Requiem for I Can't video.  Briefly explain who is in the video and what their plans are for the exhibit.  For example, Barbra T. Smith will do a performance art piece at the exhibit and Nina Jun will use video to enhance our creations.  Warn the participants that there is a part of the video that may be disturbing to some viewers.  Play I Can introduction video.

This workshop is about inspiring us to have the courage to release all of the things we think we cannot do.  Confronting the things we feel we cannot do in our lives is the first step towards recognizing that we can. By allowing ourselves to go through this process and sharing it through the exhibit, we are coming together to collectively let go of our I Cant's and embracing our I Cans.

We will begin by writing and then shredding our I Cant's (all the things we think we cannot do).  Next we will focus on all of the things we can do by writing an I Can statement you want to share with the world. Finally you will create an I Can shrinky dink to serve as a reminder that anything is possible and we can do anything we put our minds to!

This workshop is an opportunity for you to practice noticing your feelings and respect what needs to come out. Every part of this is voluntary and everyone in the room supports you.  Notice you are safe and among friends.
  
 
Completed I Can shrinky

  
Writing I Can'ts:
We are going to begin by identifying and releasing our I cant's during ten minutes of journaling with an "I Can't" prompt. Provide a piece of white card stock (Note: we chose white paper for our I Cant's as it represents death and burials in Nina Jun's, Installation Artist,  Korean culture) for each of the participants. 

We're going to take about ten minutes to write all the I cant's that come up. Optional: you can use a colored pen to write your I cant's... take a second to think... are your I can'ts yellow, red, green...just pick a color.

Keep in mind that there is no right or wrong way to do this writing exercise. You can write sentences, words, lists or draw symbols, shapes. The most important thing is that you don't censor yourself and that you don't stop writing during the whole ten minutes. Don't worry about spelling or grammar, just allow your thoughts to flow onto your paper without judgment.  What you write is just for you and does not have to make sense to anyone but you!

You can begin by writing the words "I Can't" on the top of your paper.  Try to keep writing until time is up.  Note: If you have a client who has difficulty identifying an I can't you can say, "If you feel powerful today and have no I can'ts to speak of, think of a time when you did and just keep writing."  As you write keep trusting whatever comes to mind; it doesn't have to make sense. It's okay if you repeat one I can't over and over again. Now, I'm going to turn on some music and we are going to take ten minutes to write all the I can'ts that come up...Cue music on.

In the last minute remind them - keep trusting what comes to mind.  We have about one more minute. As you finish up, read over your thoughts and notice what stands out...Cue music off.

Sharing & Shredding:
Now I'm going to ask each of you to come up, one at a time, share your I Can'ts with the group, and destroy them by either shredding or tearing them.  Remember, this is voluntary, and you don't have to share anything you don't want to.  Even if you don't want to share what you wrote, I will ask each of you to come up and shred your I Cant's.  This is your opportunity to let go of your I Can'ts. 

Do I have a brave volunteer who would like to come up here with me and share your I Can'ts and then shred them?  Standing at the front of the room, next to the shredder(s), invite others to come shred. As each person comes up tell them its okay to take their time and notice how brave they are.  Continue until each participant has had an opportunity to share their I Can'ts and shred or tear them.

Note: If this is a bilingual group, do not translate simultaneously while the participant shares as it may be disruptive.  We ask that you wait until after the participant has shared and shredded.

I Can Circle:
Discuss how we are all like Cathy, Barbara, and Nina in that we overcame great challenges and as a result have gained great strength and knowledge.  Now that we have let go of our I Cant's, we're going to take this opportunity to notice and celebrate our strength.  I want us to stand up, gather in a circle, hold hands and each share something significant in your life that you thought you couldn't do, but you did and it made you stronger. There is no right or wrong way to share, and you don't have to share anything you don't want. 

Note: If your client is having a hard time thinking of something you can say, "one thing that you did was come to this group. By coming to group you are saying, I can take care of myself." After each person has shared, have the participants sit back down and begin the I Can statement writing portion of the workshop. 

 
 I Can statement created by a child
 

I Can Statements:
Now that we have let go of our I Can'ts and noticed our strength, we are ready to focus on our I Can's. Think about all of the things that you can do, and choose one that really stands out. Pick a color to represent your I Can...take a second to think... is your I Can purple, green, pink?  Then write your I Can statement on the paper provided by AWBW (cue music on). If they choose, the participants can make more than one colorful I Can statement.  Tell the participants that we are going to gather all of their I Can statements and use them in the exhibit.  Give ten minutes for the I Can statement writing. Cue music off.

 
  I Can statement created by an adult
 

I Can Shrinky Dink:
Now we are going to create an I Can shrinky dink to remind us of the I Cans we chose to embrace today! Don't worry if your I Can seems impossible. Be bold!  Never underestimate the power of putting our I Cans out into the world!  Cathy thought her idea of sharing art with others was crazy too; now look at what she has created as a result! 

Note: Play music during the entire I Can creation portion.

Step 1:
Keeping in mind all of the things you can do, use colored pencils and/or permanent markers, write words, colors, shapes, or scribbles on the Shrinky Dink to help you remember your I Can(s).  You can color with permanent markers on both sides of the Shrinky Dink, but can only use colored pencils on the rough side. 

If you'd like to use a template, choose the one that best represents your I Can (remind participants that using a template is optional). Then trace the template or draw on the Shrinky Dink. Add color to fill in your design.

Step 2:
When you are finished coloring, if you like, cut out your I Can shrinky with scissors.  Make sure to punch a hole in the shrinky dink so it can be hung.  Make sure your don't punch your hole too close to the edge of the shrinky paper, as it may break after cooking.

Step 3:
Now the I Can shrinkys are ready for baking. Place the shrinky dink, colored side up, on either a small piece of a brown paper bag, or a metal tray, or a piece of aluminum foil; then place the paper, tray, or foil in the toaster oven.

Step 4:
Cook the shrinkys at 300 degrees for 1-3 minutes.  Watch as your shrinky dink shrinks!  After the shrinky lies flat, allow an additional 15 seconds of baking time to complete the process.  If you pull the shrinkys out prematurely, it is okay to put them back in the oven.

While the shrinkys are cooking have the participants complete the 2012 Art/Photography Release.  Make sure they leave their contact info so they can be invited to the exhibit.

Step 5:
Remove paper, tray, or foil and let Shrinky Dinks cool.  If you like, you can add ribbon so you can hang your I Can shrinky.  You can also add beads if you choose.

Closing:
Have a each participant share anything they want about their experience writing their I Cant's, and the I Can(s) they represented on their I Can statement and shrinky. 

Thank the participants and suggest they use their I Can shrinky as a reminder that they can do anything!

Reinforce the importance of putting their contact info on the art release so that we can stay in touch!  Everyone at AWBW hopes to see you at the I Can: Requiem for I Can't exhibit next march!

Exhibit paperwork:
Pass out the the Women's Windows Workshop Evaluation and have each participant complete it.  Make sure the client completes the 2012 Exhibit Art/Photography release and collect them.  Using the manila envelope provided by AWBW, follow the Handling Instructions: mail back the I Can't shreds, the I Can statements, the 2012 Exhibit Art/Photography Releases and the Women's Windows Workshop Evaluations back to AWBW.
Row.txt_description: This workshop is about confronting the things we feel we cannot do in our lives, allowing us recognize and embrace that we can do anything! By participating in this workshop you will be part of a movement of survivors coming together and collectively letting go of our I Cant's and embracing our I Cans.

Row.txt_code:
Completed Permission Canvas
Objective:
This workshop can give participants permission to do something they have been longing to do, to change a habit, or let go of something.

Materials:
Canvas (see Blick - we recommend 6x6 inch pieces)
Paint & Brushes
Mod Podge
Cake doilies
Scrapbook paper
White glue
Magazines                              Pre-cut or pre-typed words
Sponges etc. to make texture in paint
Foam brushes or Brayers
Bubble wrap
Sharpies (ultra fine & regular)
Scissors
Stamps & ink pads
Writing Paper
Journaling Questions
Paper Dolls Template

 
 
  Art supply materials
 
Preparation:
Print words and phrases that can be collaged onto the canvases by the participants. (For example: They gave themselves permission to; They decided to; They let ______ go). Try using interesting fonts (the text can be around size 36 pt. depending on font used).

Print out body templates for all the participants. Also, print and arrange journaling questions and pens at each place setting.

Timeframe:
Introduction: 10 minutes
Journaling: 20 minutes
Group Sharing: 15 minutes
Technical Information: 5 minutes
Creation: 60 minutes
Closing Circle: 15 minutes
Total: 1 1/2 to 2 1/2 hours

Introduction:
"New Years is a time of the year that symbolizes renewal and rebirth. It's a time to bid farewell to the concerns and problems of the past year, and prepare for a new and healthy beginning. We can focus on the things that we want more of in our lives, and look forward to the coming months with more hope, enthusiasm, and an open heart!

This workshop will give you the opportunity to transition into the New Year in a positive way. We will notice how it would feel to let go of something or someone who is holding you back in your life or a habit you wish to break.

Afterwards, we are going to give ourselves permission to think about something we really want to accomplish or a healthy habit we would like to take on. Through journaling and painting, we will create a canvas that gives us the affirming permission to do whatever we choose in the future!"

Journal Questions:
Play some relaxing music and invite the participants to answer the journal questions. Reassure them that their writing is for themselves and they won't be reading their answers out loud, unless they want to. Remind them that they can skip questions that don't work for them, but ask them to try to look at each question with curiosity. This is their 'window of time' to be present to whatever surfaces and let go of any blame or shame that comes up!

Encourage participants to take special care in coming up with their permission phrase(s) and creating a positive focus for the New Year. This expression can be something as simple as giving themselves permission to just breathe or as significant as changing jobs or starting a new relationship. Some ideas for their canvases are, "They gave themselves permission to let love in" or "They decided to go back to school."

Note: For a gentler approach, we have chosen to create the permission phrases in the third person, using the word "they" instead of "I." Sometimes, when we speak from the viewpoint of another person, it is easier and more comfortable to embrace a vision beyond ourselves. We understand that change may be challenging for some but we can all appreciate some gentleness from time to time!

Group Sharing: 
Have each participant pick one of their answers to the journal questions to share with the whole group. They can also share what it would feel like to let go of a thought, a person or a habit that no longer supports them. Or they can share one of their permission phrases and why it would be important to embrace this... whatever they like!

   
  Paint, brayer or sponge brush then roll
the paint on bubble wrap. Stamp bubble wrap
to your canvas to give an artsy background!		 
Technical Info:
Demonstrate how to use the materials to create textures and unique effects. Show how to use a foam brush, sponge or brayer for blending and layering paint on bubble wrap and then transfer to canvas to create a polka dot effect.

Also, show how to use materials to create textures, shapes and tone on tone effects, by using a light dabbing motion.

Explain how mod podge can be used as glue for collaging, or as a coating to finish their art.

   
  Tear the magazines for a unique collage finish
 
   
  Use mod podge to glue on mixed media materials
 
Creation:
Let participants dive in and start creating! Suggest that they paint the background of their canvas first, and then think about their permission phrase while the paint dries. Since this is a "mixed media" project, they can blend a variety of techniques when creating their art: paint, stamping, and/or collage.

"Give yourself permission to create your canvas in whatever way that you wish! You can collage, paint, or simply have an abstract background.

You might want to add a person as a focal point of your art. You can use the doll template as a guide, and collage to create clothing from different scrapbook patterns. You can also draw your person freehand or find a magazine image that represents the future you want to create... whatever you wish!

"Choose the permission phrase that is most meaningful to you. Are you giving permission to take more time out for yourself in the future? Maybe you are deciding to spend more quality time with your children? Or perhaps you want to finally tackle that dream or goal you have not yet gotten around to? You fill in the blank! Once you decide, you can collage the statement onto the background or you can paint to write your phrase directly on the canvas. Since the canvas is focusing on the future that you want, try to keep your wording optimistic and affirmative!"

If some of the participants finish earlier than others, invite them to look back at their journaling questions. They can answer questions they did not answer previously, or they can journal about their creation.

Closing Circle:
Have the participants share their canvases with the group and anything they discovered about themselves while creating.

They can also share their permission phrase out loud. If there's time, try using "echo listening" where the other group members repeat the phrase back to them. Echo listening is a form of listening which is structured to be completely non-judgmental. After listening to participants read her piece, everyone in the room simply repeats at least one thing they remember the person saying, word for word, so that they hear the entire room "echo" her their words to them, rather than judging them. It is one structured way to use supportive listening and ground the vision of the participant.

Suggest that everyone display their canvas somewhere that they will be able to see it everyday, as encouragement and inspiration to look towards the New Year with and hope!

   
 
 Completed Permission Canvas
 Completed Permission Canvas
Row.txt_description: This workshop can give participants permission to do something they have been longing to do, to change a habit, or let go of something.
Row.txt_tips:
Another variation, if the leader cannot purchase the canvases, is to use thick watercolor paper or thick poster board.

For more information and ideas about making paper dolls, and to find other free templates, a great resource is: http://www.theenchantedgallery.com/paperdolls.html.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide children an opportunity to create a plan for what they want and need in the coming year.

< td> 

 
  Supplies for your New Year Canvas
 
Materials:
Canvas (see Blick - we recommend 6x6 inch pieces)
Magazines - a wide variety, for collage
Scissors
Glue Sticks
Mod Podge (available in both a gloss and a matte finish)
Thick brushes
Glitter
Markers
Yarn/Ribbon
Foam Cut-Outs
Jewels & Other Embellishments
Paint (Optional)
Brushes / Foam Brushes (Optional)
Glitter glue (Optional)

Age Range:
3 and up





   
Time Frame:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Relaxation: 5 minutes
Creation: 45 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Total: 1 1/4 Hours (more if time permits)








Workshop Preparation:
 When ever possible cut out the magazine images ahead of time. Make sure to pick images that will inspire the children to boldly think about their future, and what they want to create in the New Year (ex. family time, a happy home, friendships, pets, travel, etc.). You can also include positive words and phrases.

   
  Painting the canvas
 
   
  Collaging on the canvas
 
   
  Ripping instead of cutting the words from magazines
 
   
   
  Close up detail of collage
 
Introduction:
January is the perfect time to look at all the things we did not like about last year, and to think about how to make this year better, happier and more fun! 

We will start by talking about the things and people we would like to surround us. Then we will create our visions on a canvas so that we will have a visual reminder of all our wishes for the New Year. You will be able to decorate it any way you want.

Your canvas can become something you can continue to look at each day, and remember the things and people that are important to you.

Opening Circle:
Ask each child to share about one or two of their favorite things to do, or the people and/or activities they want to surround themselves with in the New Year.

Relaxation:
Let's begin with a relaxation. If you want close your eyes or put your head down. If you don't want to, that is fine too! Now, begin by focusing on your breath: take a deep breath in and then slowly let it out.  Now do this at least three times. Breathing in and out slowly, try to see yourself doing the things you want to do this year.

Start to picture what you want this year to look and feel like. What activities do you really like to do? What are the things you enjoy most? Who are the people you like to be with? What would your most favorite day feel like?  Be sure to leave out the things you don't want.

Now think about some places you imagine yourself going. Maybe this is a special place that only you know about. Maybe it is outdoors, or maybe it is in different weather. Maybe it is far away, or maybe it is right around the corner. What makes you want to go there? What does this place look like, smell like, feel like?

Who are the people you would like to see alongside you? Maybe they are good friends whom you trust. Maybe they are someone you really care about. Maybe they are a family member, a favorite teacher or a special pet. Take a few more deep breaths and think about all the many things you want to do, the places you want to go, and the people you want to be with during the coming year.

When you are ready, open your eyes. Continue to think about your ideas for the New Year. Can you imagine all of these things being a part of your life in the year ahead?

Creation:
You will get to make decisions about what you would like to keep and what you would like to change in the New Year. Remind children that this is a safe place for them to express and create their own vision for this brand new year; so be bold and brave!

Introduce any new materials such as the Mod Podge by doing a simple demonstration. Mod Podge is an all-in-one glue, sealer and finish that dries clear in less than 10 minutes. Show the children how to brush it on over the images they selected. This process is called decoupage.

The children can decorate, paint, decoupage or draw on the canvas anyway they wish. You might suggest that they pick some magazine images and/or words of the special things they want to create in their life, and the places they want to go. Or, they can dive right in with the paint, glitter and ribbon.

Remind the children, as they think more about what they want in their life, they can start taking steps towards creating a happy future!

Closing:
Ask the children to share their canvas, and how it felt to create their vision for the New Year. They can share their favorite wish for the future, and/or who they want to be with.  Suggest that they keep their canvas in a place where they can look at it every day, and be inspired to have a better and happy future! 

 
   

 
 Canvas BEFORE Mod Podge  dries completely
 Canvas AFTER Mod Podge dries completely
Row.txt_description: Using an exciting combination of materials including Mod Podge, this workshop can provide children an opportunity to focus on their hopes for the future by creating a canvas vision board of what they want and need in the coming year.
Row.txt_tips:
This activity would be great to use to create a display for the shelter as a reminder of the hopes and wishes for the year.

Use thick watercolor paper or thick poster board if the canvases are not available.

Make your own Mod Podge using a 1/2 white glue and 1/2 water.

Row.str_title: Losses Altars inspired by Dia de Los Muertos
Row.txt_code:
Display of the Losses Altar
 
Objective:
To honor those parts of ourselves that we feel we have lost or have "died" due to the Domestic Violence in our relationships.

Materials:
Paper / Pens for Journaling
Boxes: cigar box, shoebox (top and bottom) (one per participant)
Paints/brushes
Glitter
Collage materials: buttons, scrabble pieces, jewels, etc.
Magazines
Scissors
Glue
Optional additional items to celebrate Dia de Los Muertos: candles, flowers, etc. (see set-up below)

Timeframe:
Introduction: 15 minutes
Journaling: 15 minutes
Creation: 45 minutes
Closing Circle: 15 minutes
Total: 1½ hours

Set-Up/Prep:
The preparation time can vary, depending on your budget, and how much you want to embody the Día de los Muertos theme. Collect boxes that will be used for the altars.

You can create the atmosphere of Día de los Muertos through the décor of the room, the music, and maybe even food/snacks like Pan Dulce (Mexican sweet bread) and coffee to represent the special day. It is also fun to have the room set up with skulls or with yellow chrysanthemums, which are also symbolic of the day.

You can also gather items for participants to use in their displays or in the group display.
• Small flower vases (or small bottles to be used as vases)
• Flowers (fake or real)
• Candles (being safe, of course)
• Candies or other sweet foods

Music with a Latin flavor will support the theme! An option for music is the Buena Vista Social Club. During the journaling portion, it works best to play music without words.

If you have time, you may want to cut out magazine images ahead of time. When choosing magazines, be sure to include expressive pictures of participants (or men if there are male participants). Also, images that represent things the participants may have lost. Examples: families together, pets, pretty clothes, etc. You can also include positive words like: happy, strong, etc.

Prepare the participants prior to the group. You can ask them to bring photos of themselves, as well as special keepsakes to honor what they have lost. They can also bring any religious images or symbols that are meaningful to them.

If you have space, have a table ready to display all the finished altars at the end of the workshop. Dress it up with a pretty tablecloth! You could also use it as a DV Awareness exhibit!

Introduction:
Begin by asking the clients if any of them has heard of Dia de los Muertos, or if they have participated in a "Day of the Dead" event. Ask one or two people to share with the group what they know about the holiday and tradition.

If no one has an experience to share, briefly explain the history of the holiday and its tradition. If applicable, include a personal anecdote about the "Day of the Dead." Typically, to celebrate Dia de los Muertos, families will create altars to deceased family members or loved ones and light candles, offer flowers and sometimes their favorite food and drink. Participants may also take time to talk about those whom have passed and tell them how much they miss them and honor their spirit.

Explain to the participants that today, we are going to celebrate this tradition in a special and different way. We are going to honor the most precious loved one, "ourselves." This is an opportunity for them to acknowledge the parts of themselves they have lost, feel have "died," or the person that they think they no longer are as a result of DV.

Journaling:
Ask the participants to think about things they have stopped doing and parts of themselves that they have repressed since being involved in a DV relationship. What parts of themselves have "died" because of their involvement with their batterer? Were there things that they liked about themselves that they no longer express or show or even think about anymore?

Give some examples like "some of us worked and had good jobs with good futures but our partners didn't want us to work anymore so we quit." Or "going to school was not an option" or "he told me what clothes I had to wear."

Ask the participants to write words or draw pictures to express what they have lost. They can write single words, phrases or complete sentences, draw symbols, or even a letter to themselves; whatever they wish.

   
  Gluing box for collage
 
   
  Collaging materials
 
   
  Losses Altar side view
 

Creation:
Let participants know, that even though these parts of ourselves have been dormant or forgotten, they are still part of who we are. Remind them that they are not "dead."

Start by selecting the box you want to use for your altar. You might want to select a special picture (or create a collage) to serve as the backdrop, and glue it to the back of the box. Decorate your box in any way you wish, with paint, glitter, jewels, or any materials that are available.

Tell participants that they can include the words they wrote in the journaling portion, if they wish. They can also add magazine words to express their sentiments. Once you have finished decorating your box, arrange the other objects that are meaningful to you: photos, keepsakes, flowers, candles, etc.

After about 40 minutes, invite the participants to put the finishing touches on their altars, and place them on the display table. As a group, you can decorate the table, by adding flowers, food, candles, etc. Have the participants take a few minutes to look at each altar and celebrate the group members as well as themselves!

Closing:
Ask the participants to share anything that they want to about their altar. They can talk about how it felt to create it, or celebrate the parts of themselves that they've lost. During the sharing, participants can drink coffee and eat Pan Dulce as a finishing touch.

Encourage the participants to take their altars home and display them in a special place. Remind them to honor what they lost and the spirit of who they are!
Row.txt_description: To honor those parts of ourselves that we feel we have lost or have “died” due to the Domestic Violence in our relationships.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop gives us an opportunity to look at our family in a positive way; to be grateful for each family member, and the strength we have as we stand together.

 
 
  Totem pole materials
 
Materials:
Lined or blank white paper (or any scratch paper)
Card stock or construction paper (light colors preferred)
Markers
Crayons
Colored pencils
Scissors
Ruler
Glue or tape
Feathers
Yarn
Beads
Wings Template (1 set of wings per child)
Totem Pole images

Time Frame:
Intro: 5 minutes
Warm Up: 15 minutes
Creation: 25 minutes
Totem Pole Ceremony/Closing: 15 minutes
Total: 1 hour

Age Range:
5 and up

Set-Up/Prep:
Print out wings template. Copy onto card stock or construction paper (for sturdiness). For younger groups, you might want to cut out the wings prior to the workshop.

If you have time, prepare a totem pole sample. You can use this to demonstrate the thought process involved in your creation.

Introduction:
Thanksgiving is usually a time for family gatherings when we think about the things we are grateful for. Today we will create a Family Totem Pole that will tell the story of our entire family. We will look for the value in each family member, and see how each person makes the family stronger as they stand together on the totem pole created.

   
  Totem family descriptions
 
Warm up:
You can start by briefly telling the children what a totem pole represents and how important it is in Native American cultures (in Northwest United States). Show the totem pole images, and mention how each one has a different look.

Totem poles were originally carved out of giant trees, and were sometimes 60 feet high. That's over 60 times as big as the ones we are making today! The symbols on these totem poles represented a tribe, a family, or a person. Some totem poles told about events that happened to a family, and some honored special people. The meanings on totem poles were as varied as the people who made them. Having a totem pole was a source of pride, and it stood tall for everyone to see!

Point out to the children, that all families are different, just like these totem poles. Give examples of different types of families to bring children into the present (e.g., single-parent homes, large families, small families, grandparents as parents, etc.). Today, you're going to honor your unique family!

We're going to start by looking at each family member and what makes them special to us. It might make their jobs easier to first write down the names of the family members they want to include on their totem pole. Reinforce that it's okay if there are some family members they don't want to add. Think about each person and one thing that you like best about them. For example, does your mom give you big hugs, or is she a good cook? Does your aunt help you with your homework?

Give the children some time to think about or write down their feelings about each family member. If there are siblings in the group, this would be a great time for them to sit together as they may want to collaborate.

     
  Draw line with a ruler across paper
  Cut out wings from template
 
 
 
  Drawings to tell family story
 
   
  Decorate the totem pole wings
 
   
  Glue totem pole base and wings together
 

Creation:
We are now going to express our thoughts about each family member on our totem poles and tell our family story. Each family member is special to us, and when we all stand together we are stronger!

You can set the tone by showing your totem pole and sharing the thoughts you had in creating it. For example, you can say, "I remember that a totem pole tells the story of a family. How can I draw my mom? I want to give my mom a place of honor so maybe I can make her bigger than everyone else to show that. Or... She likes to cook so maybe I can draw a fork and spoon!"

Have the children cut out one set of wings (2), if it has not been done already. Younger children may need help with this. Put them aside for later.

On the card stock or construction paper, ask the children to use a ruler and draw a line down the length of the paper (1/2 inch from the edge). Let them know that their drawing should not go past this line, as this 1/2 inch area will be covered up when the totem pole is rolled up and glued.

Have each child come up with their own drawings or symbols to tell their family story. They can do this in anyway they choose. They might want to draw a picture of each family member, or create a symbol to represent what they like about them. There is no wrong or right way! Make sure they add something about each person as well as themselves. They can also add positive words or phrases. Once their totem pole is done, roll it into a tube (use the line they drew as the marker for the overlap). Fasten with glue or tape. Take some care with this; if the bottom is even, the totem pole can stand up.

Next, they can create wings for their totem pole. They might want to add the family members names and/or a positive word about them. Or any design that they choose. To attach the wings, fold the tabs back and glue them near the top of the totem pole.

They can decorate their totem pole with yarn, beads, and feathers to complete the look. This will also give a Native American feel!

Towards the end of the creation portion, remind the children to think about how each family member has a special quality, and this helps to make the family strong!

   
  Completed totem pole
 

Totem Pole Ceremony/Closing:
Give each child a few minutes to share about their totem pole and their family story. Did they learn anything new about their family today? How did it feel to see the strength of their family together? If you have a shy group, you can share your totem pole first. Children can come up with their siblings if they choose. After each story has been told, display the poles altogether and allow the children free time to explore the totem poles.

Remind the children, that even though we've had struggles, we can be grateful for each family member, and the strength our family has when we all stand together!

Encourage the children to share their totem poles with their families and let each family member know what they appreciate about them.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives us an opportunity to look at our family in a positive way; to be grateful for each family member, and the strength we have as we stand together.

Row.str_title: Home is Where the Heart Is Aprons
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To encourage the participants that they can create their own "Home Sweet Home" and family unit no matter where they live.

   
  Apron and decoration materials. 
Materials:
Blank aprons (under $5.00 each at Wal-Mart)
Fabric Paints and/or Puff Paints
Craft embellishments: rhinestone letters (iron-on), ribbon, jewels, etc.
Glitter glue
Multi-colored fabric squares
Iron (optional)
Glue

Timeframe:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Relaxation: 10 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing Circle: 15 minutes
Total: 1 Hour

Set-Up/Prep:
It may be helpful to plan this project ahead of time, so you can secure apron donations and inexpensive art materials.

Note: This workshop recommends fabric paint, so that the aprons are functional and washable. Fabric paint can be purchased at Discount School Supplies and most craft stores (Michael's, Jo-Ann Fabrics, etc.). You can also use other kinds of paint for this project, but keep in mind that the aprons may or may not be washable.

If you choose to use fabric squares, it helps if you cut the material beforehand into small squares as opposed to having large pieces of material. Set up the iron and iron board before you start the project.

Introduction:
You can begin by talking to the participants about how difficult it can be to live in a shelter or far away from their traditional home. Remind them that "wherever we are, we have the power to create our own 'Home Sweet Home' no matter where we live. We still can love our children, laugh, have fun, be happy, make good choices, be strong, be positive role models and, continue to live life to the fullest. Home is where the heart is; it lives within us and is whatever we choose to make of it.

"We will be using the popular and meaningful phrase, 'Home is Where the Heart Is' to create beautiful, comforting and functional aprons."

 
 
  Blank apron 
   
  Puff paint to create images 
   
  Glue craft embellishments 
   
  Completed "Home is Where the Heart is" apron 
Relaxation:
A short meditation will help participants connect with the feelings of home inside.

"If you are comfortable, close your eyes and picture a warm and comforting setting at home... maybe a holiday dinner with everyone sitting around a table, laughing and eating; or a mother in the kitchen baking cookies with her children. Bring to mind whatever reflects a relaxing home atmosphere for you. Picture your home in your mind and imagine yourself in your favorite place there. Do you hear the sounds of children playing together or the voices of happy family members telling stories? Are your favorite smells coming from the kitchen? Maybe you are enjoying a meal that only Mom knows how to make with tender, loving care. What makes your home so warm and inviting? How do you feel being in this safe and secure place? Perhaps you are wrapped in the cozy hugs of family or lying in the grass with your kids in the backyard. Do you play a part in making that environment loving and welcoming? Whenever you are ready, open your eyes, and begin creating your apron."

Creation:
"Keeping this vision of what home feels like, smells like, etc., decorate your apron in any way that is meaningful to you. You can write names, add pictures, words, or symbols that represent home and reflect what you want for your family or for your life. You can also write words of encouragement for yourself; whatever you like. Use any of the craft embellishments or fabric squares to add a special touch!

"As you are creating, think about what home really means to you, and the things that make you feel happy, strong, and peaceful inside. Remember, home does not have to be a house. It can be any place in your mind or simply a loving feeling that you have. Whenever you wear your apron, no matter where you are, it can remind you of the positive qualities that you hold in your heart!"

Closing:
Share aprons, and what each creation means to the participants. "How did it feel to reflect on your feelings about home?"

Remind participants that "you truly can determine your own happiness and balance in life, no matter what the circumstances are and no matter where you live. A home is not made up of walls and fences, it lives within us all. It is about keeping our head above water and focusing on what is really important: family, safety, comfort, health, well-being, and taking care of each other and ourselves. Home begins with you; you hold the keys to a safe and happy life!"


 
 
  "Love and Hope" and "Heart and Soul" aprons
Row.txt_description: To encourage the participants that they can create their own "Home Sweet Home" and family unit no matter where they live.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Participants will be provided with an opportunity to discuss the meaning of a safe home and what goes inside and around it to make it feel that way. They will be invited to make specific commitments to creating that safety in their own homes.

Materials:
  • Construction paper
  • White liquid glue
  • Glue sticks
  • Glitter glue
  • Puffy paint
  • Assorted ribbon and yarn
  • Pipe cleaners
  • Assorted flowers
  • Foam shapes
  • Scissors
  • Tape
  • Hole punchers
  • Markers, pens, pencils
  • Personal photos
  • Radio/CD player
  • Relaxing music
Optional:
  • Large pieces of felt
  • Fabric
Time Frame:                         Age Range:
1 hour                                          3 and up
Introduction: 2 mins.
Opening Activity: 8 mins.
Creation: 40 mins.
Closing: 10 mins.


Table setting
 

Workshop Preparation:
If you're working with younger children, it could be helpful if you have time to prepare the house cut-outs and write the questions on each page before the workshop. If possible have all materials spread out and ready for use.

Note: For younger children, you might consider calling this workshop Happy Home if you feel this will allow the participants to focus in that way.

Introduction:
"Today we will be talking about safety and what it means to us. We'll be doing this by talking about safety in our homes - what safety looks like, what it sounds like, and even what it smells like! I'm going to invite you to create a book that shows all of these different things. You'll be able to add words and drawings that say and show all of the things that make up your safe home and we'll even talk about ways we can make that happen in the future."

Opening Activity:
"To get started, let's take some time to think about what a safe home means to you. In a minute, I'm going to ask you a few questions and all I want you to do is to think. I want you to just think about what the questions are asking. There are no right or wrong answers to these questions and whatever pops into your mind, thoughts, feelings, pictures or anything, I want them to just float around up there and get comfortable because you're going to use all of those things to make your book. Any questions before we get started?"

Begin by inviting participants to close their eyes if they feel comfortable enough to do so. With their feet planted on the ground, ask them to begin thinking about the questions you're about to ask. Gently ask each question with a generous amount of time in between for them to think and/or visualize. Soft background music can aid in this process.

"What does a safe home look like? Maybe it is full of pictures from the good and happy times. Maybe it is full of smiling faces. Maybe it is full of people or it just has the people you want there. Think about who those people might be."

"What does a safe home feel like? Maybe it is a place you are happy to return to at the end of the day. Maybe it is warm and cozy. Maybe you can freely share your feelings, hopes and dreams there. Maybe it is a place where you feel happy, loved, and relaxed."

"What does a safe home sound like? Maybe there are no loud voices or bad words. Maybe people are happy and laughing. Maybe it is quiet and peaceful or maybe music is playing and everyone is singing. Think about what you would like to hear in your safe home.

"How do you want to be treated and treat others in your home? Maybe you'd like a hug when you get home from a long day of school. Maybe it's important to you for everyone to say please and thank you. Also think about what you could do to help treat others they way they'd like to be treated in your home, too."

"How can your family work together to a safe home? What small steps can you take to work toward making your home feel safe to you?  Making little changes over time can help make these changes a little easier."

Creation:
"Now that you've had some time to think about these questions, I'm going to invite you to create a big book that will be full of drawings and words that show and tell all about your safe home. But before we do that, we'll need to put our books together and I'm going to show you exactly how to do that."

Note: If participants aren't interested in creating a book, give them some alternative ways to express their safe homes. Here are some possibilities:
  • Younger children: Give them a piece of construction paper and ask them to draw their safe home with all of the things that make them happy, both inside and outside of the home. Guide them by asking questions like, "What kinds of things would make you feel safe in your bedroom?" "What people would you like to see in your safe home?" "What can you draw outside of your home to make you feel safe?"
  • Teens: Using graphing paper, pencils, and rulers, ask teens to create a floor plan of their safe home and invite them to label all of the different aspects of the home (people, things, sounds, etc.) that make them feel safe. Encourage them to share with the group or journal about their experience. A possible journal prompt might be, "What steps can you take to make your home feel safe?"
  • Families: Give each family member big piece of construction paper. Give each family member the task of creating the "My Safe Room." This can be their personal bedroom, the living room, the kitchen, or anywhere else in their house where they like to spend their time. When they're done, encourage the family to talk about their creations.

Note: When working with individuals and families in homeless or DV shelter settings, you might want to use this opportunity to help create hope for a future safe home.


  
 
 After folding, cut on the folded lines
to create a house shape.
  
  
Step 1: Create a House-shaped Stencil
Create a house shape to use as a template for the project. Begin by folding a sheet of construction paper, length-wise, in half. Then fold both corners over to the centerfold, just like you would when creating a paper airplane. Cut along these corner fold lines. Now you have a stencil to create the rest of your pages.

Step 2: Create Additional Pages
Use your stencil to trace and cut 5 more house shapes. You can choose different colors for each page, or you can keep them all the same. You're going to have 6 different houses when you're done.

  
   Write discussion questions on the
top of each page.
Step 3: Write Questions on Pages
Write down the following questions (1 per page) at the top of each house shape and leave one house page blank. The blank page will be the front of your book, it will be the house you will decorate later.

Note: If you're working with younger children, writing these questions for them beforehand will help save time. If you're working with families, you might want to ask the parent(s)/guardian(s) to help out with this process. They can give each sibling a page or they can write each page, one-by-one, together as a family. Make sure to leave room for more writing on the main part of the page.

Page 1 - Keep this page blank to decorate later.
Page 2 - What does a safe home look like?
Page 3 - What does a safe home feel like?
Page 4 - What does a safe home sound like?
Page 5 - How can we treat each other inside our home?
Page 6 - How can we work together to create our safe home?

When this is completed, line these shapes up and punch holes along the left-hand side. Make sure to put that blank page at the front, it will be the cover of your book.

Note: Be sure to take the time to brainstorm and discuss the questions with the group before writing down your answers to each question. If you're working with families, give the families time to discuss together.

 
   Our safe home smells like...
Step 5: Answer the Questions
This is where you'll want participants to spend most of their time. Invite them to answer the questions on each page by writing words, short sentences, and/or drawings. Remind them that whatever comes up is just fine.

Note: You'll want to have participants do this before they bind the pages together just in case they need to be separate for drying purposes or in the sense of working with families, divided up between family members to work on. It might be a good idea to have younger children of the family (the ones who can't yet write) focus on drawing.

  
   Bind the book together with ribbon or yarn.
Step 4: Punching Holes and Binding the Book
Punch about three holes on the left-hand-side of each page. Lace a ribbon, yarn, or a pipe cleaner through the holes and tie them to bind them together. If you're pressed for time, stapling the pages together is a quick solution. Keep in mind that this process can take up a lot of time so plan accordingly.

Step 5:
Have fun decorating the cover of your book with shapes, images, words, and design materials that you imagine your safe home to have on the outside. When doing this, remember to think about what makes you feel safe!

 
  Our Safe Home
Closing:
If the participants feel comfortable to do so, invite them gather around in a circle. Give each individual or family an opportunity to share about their home and how it felt to create it. Ask the group how they will share this home with their families and how they can help create what they wrote and/or drew in their books in their real homes.

If you're working with families, remind them that if they work together, they can create this safe home in their future.

Thank everyone for sharing and for working together to create their safe home!
Row.txt_description: Participants will be provided with an opportunity to discuss the meaning of a safe home and what goes inside and around it to make it feel that way. They will be invited to make specific commitments to creating that safety in their own homes.

Row.str_title: I Can: Requiem for I Can't
Row.txt_code:
Note: This variation was developed for children ages 12 and under but can be used with older clients.
 
Shredded I Cant's

  
Objective:
This workshop is about getting rid of the things we think we can't do and realize that we can! 
  
 
 Completed I Can Shrinky Dink

Materials:
White card stock for I Can't journaling
Pens/Multi-colored pens (optional)
Colored paper for I Can statements
Shrinky Dink paper
Shrinky templates
Colored pencils
Hole punch
Blunt Scissors
Toaster oven
Ribbon
Beads
Music (suggested: Baby Blue by Carlos Reynosa for I Can't journaling and Heavenly for I Can statement and shrinky creation)
Timer
2012 Art/Photography Release forms for parent to complete.

Timeframe: 1 hour 30 minutes
Opening Circle: 5 min
Intro: 5 min
Writing/Drawing: 10 min
Sharing & Tearing: 20 min
I Can Statement Creation: 15 min
Shrinky Creation: 20 min
Closing: 15 min

Opening Circle:
Go around the room and have each child share their name and how they're feeling right now.

Introduction:
Explain to the children that some of what they will be creating today will be turned in and used in an art exhibit. Explain to them that an exhibit is a collection of art that other people can see and learn from. 

This workshop is about getting rid of the things we think we can't do and realize that we can!  Confronting the things we feel we cannot do in our lives is the first step towards recognizing that we can. By allowing ourselves to go through this process and sharing it through the exhibit, we are coming together to collectively let go of our I Cant's and celebrate our I Cans. 

We will begin by writing and drawing our I Cant's and then we will destroy them! 
Then, we will focus on all of the things we can do. Finally you will create an I Can shrinky dink to remind you that anything possible!

  
 
Completed I Can shrinky

  
Writing I Can'ts:
We are going to begin by taking 5-10 minutes to write about or draw a picture of anything or things that you think you can't do. You can use a pen or pencils to write your I cant's or draw pictures.Keep in mind that there is no right or wrong way to do this exercise.

Give a piece of white card stock paper to each child.  You can write sentences, words, lists or draw symbols, shapes. The most important thing is that you that you keep writing or creating for the whole ten minutes. Don't worry about spelling or grammar.  What you write is just for you and does not have to make sense to anyone but you!

You can begin by writing the words "I Can't" on the top of your paper.  Try to keep writing until time is up.  Note: If you have a child who has difficulty identifying an I can't you can say, "If you feel powerful today and have no I can'ts to speak of, think of a time when you did and just keep writing."  As you write keep trusting whatever comes to mind; it doesn't have to make sense. It's okay if you repeat one I can't over and over again. Now, I'm going to turn on some music and we are going to take ten minutes to write all the I can'ts that come up...Cue music on.

Sharing & Tearing:
Now we are going get into a circle. Ask each child to share their I Can'ts with the group, destroy them by tearing them, and put them in the center of the circle.  Remember to tell them, "this is voluntary, and you don't have to share anything you don't want to."  Even if you don't want to share, I will ask each of you to tear your I Can't and add it to the pile. 
Continue until each child has had a turn.  Then have all the children walk into the middle of the circle and stomp on the I can't pile.

Tell the children, "now that you have destroyed your I can'ts I want you to remember that you are strong and capable and you can do anything!"  Before we go back to our seat I want each child to say out loud something that they "can" do but thought they couldn't do. Give examples, such as, "If you thought that you couldn't get good grades, I want you to say 'I can get good grades!' After you say your I can, you may sit down."

After each person has shared, have the participants sit back down and begin the I Can portion of this workshop. 

 
 I Can statement created by a child
 

I Can Statements/Drawings:
We are ready to focus on our I Can's. I don't want to hear any more "I can'ts", those were left in the pile.  Remember, you are strong and capable! 
Tell the children that we are going to gather all of their I Can statements/drawings and use them in the exhibit but they will get to create something for themselves too! Ask them to think about all of the things that they  can do, and choose one that is really important to them. Ask them to pick a color paper to represent this "I Can"... is your I Can purple, green, pink?  Then write or draw a picture of your "I Can" (turn happy music on).   Give ten minutes for the I Can statement writing/draing. Cue music off.

 
  I Can statement created by an adult
 

I Can Shrinky Dink:
Now we are going to create an I Can shrinky dink to remind us that WE CAN! Don't worry if your I Can seems impossible. Be brave! (Cue music back on.)

Step 1:
Keeping in mind all of the things you can do, use colored pencils to write words, colors, shapes, or scribbles on the Shrinky Dink to help you remember that YOU CAN! 

You can use a template or draw on the Shrinky Dink. Add color to fill in your design.

Step 2:
When you are finished coloring, if you like, cut out your I Can shrinky with scissors.  Make sure to punch a hole in the shrinky dink so it can be hung.  Make sure your don't punch your hole too close to the edge of the shrinky paper, as it may break after cooking.

Step 3:
Now the I Can shrinkys are ready for baking. Place the shrinky dink, colored side up, on either a small piece of a brown paper bag, or a metal tray, or a piece of aluminum foil; then place the paper, tray, or foil in the toaster oven.

Step 4:
Cook the shrinkys at 300 degrees for 1-3 minutes.  Watch as your shrinky dink shrinks!  After the shrinky lies flat, allow an additional 15 seconds of baking time to complete the process.  If you pull the shrinkys out prematurely, it is okay to put them back in the oven.

While the shrinkys are cooking have the participants complete the 2012 Art/Photography Release.  Make sure they leave their contact info so they can be invited to the exhibit.

Step 5:
Remove paper, tray, or foil and let Shrinky Dinks cool.  If you like, you can add ribbon so you can hang your I Can shrinky.  You can also add beads if you choose.

Closing:
Have each child share how it felt to destroy their "I Can'ts" and/or create their "I Cans."

Thank the participants and remind then to look at their I Can shrinky dink as a reminder that they can do anything!
Row.txt_description: This workshop is about getting rid of the things we think we can't do and realize that we can!

Row.str_title: Stuff Your Stockings Full of Joy
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide a way for participants to express their love and connection to their children and families during the holiday season.

    
    Workshop set up
 
M aterials:
Felt in a variety of colors
Glue gun and/or tacky glue
Buttons, bows, bells and Ribbons
Glitter/glitter glue
Sequins
Beads and pearls
Large-eye sewing needles
Yarn
Fabric Pens, Gel pens
Scissors
Heavy construction paper or Cardstock
Holiday or regular stationary
Index cards
Stocking/Cuff/Symbols Template

Timeframe: 
Introduction: 5 minutes
Warm-up: 15 minutes
Creation: 1 hour
Closing: 10 minutes
Total: 1 hour 30 minutes

  
  Trace the cuff on felt
 
   
  Trace the stocking on felt
 
Set up/Prep:
To save time during the workshop, you may want to make the stockings ahead of time. This is a great project for all of your Christmas volunteers! If you prefer to have the participants enjoy the sewing experience, be sure to build enough time into the workshop to complete the decorating and letter writing portions.

Using the template, cut out the stocking shapes and cuffs. You can use felt in traditional holiday colors (red, green, white, or blue) or try non-traditional holiday colors like yellow or purple. Sewing makes the stockings look really special, but tacky glue also works well (be sure to place the glue around the edges of the stocking so the opening is as big as possible).

Sewing Instructions (can be done as a part of the preparation or can be completed by the participants): Thread a large-eye sewing needle with yarn, and use a simple "whip" stitch to sew the back and front of the stocking together. Use contrasting colored yarn for a fun, festive look! You may want to glue the pieces together first with tacky glue to secure the pieces in place. You can glue or sew the cuff on. Once the stocking pieces are cut out the stitching takes less than 5 minutes. 
 
Lay out the embellishments, scissors, and trims in an attractive manner. Find a safe place to set up the glue guns that is away from the general work area for safety. Set up a “glitter station” and ask the participants to use glitter at the glitter station; this will also help with clean up at the end of the workshop. Lay out the holiday stationary; set out gel pens to write the letters and ribbons to tie them. 

Introduction:
"The holidays are a special time to remember and celebrate our family and loved ones. When we take time to think about the people who are special to us and reflect on what we appreciate about them, it fills us with joy. Even if someone we care about is far away and we miss being with them, it makes us happy to remember them with love.

"This project is called Stuff Your Stockings Full of Joy. This window of time is just for you to reflect on the meaning of the holidays... to remember your family and loved ones and tell them how you feel. You will be creating a holiday stocking, and have the opportunity to fill the stocking with heartfelt letters to them."

Warm Up:
"Take a few minutes and reflect on the special, loving, things that you don’t always have the time or opportunity to tell your children and loved ones. You can include people you see everyday, or even those who are far away. What makes you happy when you think of each person? How has he or she had a positive impact on your life? What special qualities does each person have that perhaps you have not acknowledged lately? Are you especially proud of that person? Why? Now take about 5 minutes to write the positive feelings, love, admiration, etc. that you feel on an index card."

Creation:
  
  Stitch the stocking with yarn
 
   
  Whip stitch around enter stocking
 
   
  Add on decorations and embellishments
 
   
  Write a letter to a loved one
 
   
 Insert rolled up letters into the
finished stocking
 
Step One: Creating Holiday Stockings (if not done prior to the workshop)
"First, you are welcome to glue or sew together your stocking pieces to create it! You can either place glue along the rim of the stocking and stick them together OR use a "whip" stitch to sew along the edges of the stocking pieces together."

Step Two: Decorating Holiday Stockings
"After the stocking pieces are securely in place, take a piece of heavy paper and fold it in half long ways. Place this paper inside the stocking. This will prevent any glue from soaking through and causing your stocking to be glued together.

"We want to make these stockings really festive and special. Maybe you want to design your stocking with a holiday theme. Are there images that come to mind like snowmen, candy canes, snowflakes, gingerbread men, or stars? Maybe you want to add words that express the meaning of the holidays or the feeling you have when you think of your loved ones, like joy, hope, or peace? Then you can select embellishments and glue the pieces down. Keep in mind that drying time can take at least 24 hours."

Step Three: Writing holiday letters
"Gather your thoughts and feelings about your family members and loved ones. If you wish, you can refer back to the index card that you wrote earlier. Using the stationary, write a letter to each person that expresses your heartfelt sentiments, or what you love and appreciate about them. This is your opportunity to write positive words and affirmations and express your holiday spirit! Finish the letters by rolling them up tightly, like a scroll, and tying a pretty ribbon around them. You can write as many letters as there is time for and put them inside of the stocking.

"As you place each letter in the stocking, take a moment to reflect on the joy that you feel as you remember and celebrate these special people in your life."

Closing:
"Thank you for taking the time today to remember the special things about your children and loved ones. We do not always get to or make time to express our feelings of love and gratitude.

If you feel comfortable, share your stocking and how it felt to think about the special people in your life. If you want to read one of your letters to the group, you can feel free to do so!"

Encourage participants to hang their stocking as a lasting memory of the special people in their lives. They may want to give the letters to their loved ones on a special day or on Christmas day. The participants may also want to keep the letters for themselves. Throughout the holidays they can add more letters, and continue to fill their stockings (and hearts) with joy and appreciation!
Row.txt_description: To provide a way for participants to express their love and connection to their children and families during the holiday season.

Row.str_title: Stuff Your Stockings Full of Joy
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide a way for children to express their love and feel connected to the people they care about during the holiday season.

   
   Workshop set up
 
Materials:
Heavy construction paper
Tacky glue
Glitter/glitter glue
Sequins
Buttons
Ribbon
Markers
Scissors
Holiday stationary
Gel pens in nice colors
Felt Fabric (optional)
Yarn and large-eyed needle for felt stockings (optional)
Fabric Pens (optional)
Heavier embellishments: beads, bells, etc. (optional)
Glue gun (optional)
Stocking/Cuff/Symbols Template

 Timeframe:  Age Range:
 
Introduction: 5 minutes
Warm-up: 15 minutes
Creation: 1 hour
Closing Circle: 10 minutes
Total: 1 1/2 hours		   
3 and up 




 





  
 Trace the cuff
on construction paper or felt
 
   
 Trace the stocking
on construction paper or felt
 

Set-Up/Prep:
You may want to cut out/glue the stockings and cuffs beforehand. This way, the children can spend more time decorating their stockings and writing their letters during the workshop. You can use construction paper in traditional holiday colors (red, green, white, or blue) or try non-traditional holiday colors like yellow or purple.

Set up a "glitter station" and ask the children to only use glitter at this station. This will help with clean up at the end of the day. Have gel pens and stationary laid out for the letter writing.

Note: For an extra special Holiday touch, try making the stockings/cuffs out of felt instead of construction paper. You can use tacky glue to attach the front, back and cuff or sew with a contrasting colored yarn for a festive look (use a large-eyed sewing needle and a simple "whip" stitch). If you are making felt stockings, take a piece of heavy paper and fold it in half long ways. Place this piece of paper inside each stocking; this will prevent any glue from soaking through and causing the stocking to be glued together. Glue guns work well for heavier embellishments like buttons and beads. If you are using a glue gun, make sure you find a safe place to set it up that is away from the general work area and there is adequate supervision.

Introduction:
The Holidays are a special time to remember and celebrate the people we care about. Whenever we think about our loved ones and what each person means to us, it brings us joy. Even if someone we care about is far away and we miss them, we can feel better by remembering positive things about them and what we appreciate about them. 

Today we will be creating a Holiday stocking, and filling it with letters that we will write to the special people in our lives. It makes us feel good to remember the special people in our lives and let them know how much we love and care about them!

Opening Circle:
"Think of someone that you want to remember and celebrate today. It can be anyone you really care about - maybe someone you see everyday (your mom, your brother or sister) or someone who is not with you (Grandma, your best friend or favorite teacher). What makes them special to you? What are the loving things they have done for you that make you feel happy? Maybe more than one person comes to mind that you want remember today. That's okay!"

Go around the circle and have each child share something special about the person(s) they are celebrating today.

Creation:

  
  Glue around the edge of the stocking
 
   
  Glue the cuff to the top of the stocking
 
   
  Add on decorations and embellishments
 
   
  Write a letter to a loved one
 
   
  Roll letter tightly and secure with ribbon
 
   
 Place rolled up letters into
the finished stocking
 

Step One: Decorate stockings
"First, we're going to decorate our holiday stocking. We want to make it really special to hold the letters we will write to the people who we care about in our heart."

You may want to suggest that the children use a holiday theme. You can ask, "What are the special images that come to mind when you think of the holidays? Do you think about candy canes, snowflakes, stars or gingerbread men? Or, when you think of being with your family or loved ones is there a special feeling that you have? Is there a word that describes this feeling, like joy?"

The children can decorate their stockings with holiday images, words, and/or any materials that they choose.

Step Two: Write/draw holiday letters.
"Think about a person(s) who is really special to you. Is there something nice you want to say to them, maybe something that you haven't told them lately? Did they do something that made you feel good, like bake cookies with you or give you a big hug? Maybe they are far away, and you just want to tell them that you love and appreciate them. When you are ready, write a letter and let the person know why they are special to you."

Letters can be written to more than one person... whatever they feel in their heart! Be prepared to assist them with the letter writing as needed.

If younger children aren't able to write yet, they can draw a picture that expresses their feelings about each person. If they wish, you can help them write the name of the person on the drawing and/or some special words that they want to share.

Finish each letter/drawing by rolling it up tightly and tying it with a pretty ribbon. Place it in the stocking. 

Thank the children for taking this special time to remember the people they care about. We don't always get to share our feelings of love and gratitude!

Closing:
Have the children share their stockings and how it felt to write letters to the people they care about. If they want to share one of their letters/drawings, encourage them to do so!

Encourage the children to hang their stocking as a reminder of the special people in their lives. They may want to give the letters to their loved ones or keep them for themselves. Throughout the holidays they can add more letters, and continue to fill their stockings with joy. Remind them how big their heart is and how much love they have to give!
Row.txt_description: To provide a way for children to express their love and feel connected to the people they care about during the holiday season.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give the participants an opportunity to create something unique and beautiful that can be given to friends and/or family. It also allows them to experience the holiday spirit and the gift of giving.

Materials:
  
  Crystals from the Heart
 
Glass beads and/or other assorted beads
Craft wire 
Craft wire cutters
Craft long-nosed pliers
Small plastic cups
Ribbon
Scissors
Tissue paper, gift wrap and/or small gift bags
Holiday gift tags
Scotch tape
Small suction cups (optional, if participants want to make the ornaments into sun catchers).

Timeframe:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Creation: 35 minutes
Closing: 10
Total: 1 hour

Set-Up/Prep:
It will save time during the workshop if you pre-cut the wire beforehand. Cut wire pieces in a variety of sizes ranging from 8-12 inches so that there is plenty of wire to work with. Have enough wire cut so the participants can make more than one ornament; they may be able to complete 2-3 during the hour.

Set up a table with beads, ribbon, pre-cut wire, pliers and wire cutters. Also, artfully lay out the gift-wrapping supplies.

Introduction:
For many of us, the holidays are a magical time. They represent family celebrations, holiday treats, music, colorful decorations, twinkling lights, etc. It is a special time of year to create lasting memories with our families and friends through holiday traditions, old and new.

The holidays can also be an emotional time. Sometimes we feel sad, lonely, or only focus on the things that bring us stress in our life.

When we give a gift from our heart, though, it always lifts our spirit. Whether it be a physical gift or simply the gift of ourselves (volunteering, helping a neighbor, etc.), our problems seem to melt away and we are filled with joy! There is no better way to celebrate the spirit of the holidays than by sharing our hearts and love. So today, we are going to create a beautiful gift that we can give to the special people in our lives.

Opening Circle:
Ask the participants to think about what makes the holidays magical to them. Have each person share about their favorite holiday memory. "What is a favorite tradition that you do with your friends or family only during the holiday time? Or the first time you saw snow? It can be a time that really touched your heart and/or just made you giggle...whatever brought you joy!"

If someone can't recall a favorite holiday memory, encourage them to share their hopes and dreams and what they wish their holiday to be.

Creation:
Before the participants start the creation portion, you can demonstrate how the crystal is made. Show how to "string" the beads onto the wire, and the different ways to shape and finish off the ends (coiling the wire, creating swirls, etc.). You can ask if any of the participants has a unique way of wire-shaping to share.

  
 Beading the wire
  Twisting the wire end
  Different ways to finish the wire



"Think about the people in your life that you want to create a magical gift for...your children, your siblings, or your best friend. Don't forget to include the most important person...yourself!"

Ask the participants to select the beads that they would like to use to create their ornaments (they can place them in a plastic cup and take them to their work table). They are welcome to create their crystals in anyway they choose. They can use the wire cutters to cut off excess wire, depending on the finished length. They can also add ribbon to enhance the beauty of their creation and give a special touch!

   
Once everyone is finished making their crystals, you can offer small gift bags, tissue paper, etc. to wrap their gifts, and small gift cards if they want to write a personal message.

Closing:
Go around the table and and have each participant share their crystal(s). They can talk about why they chose certain colors, who they plan to give it to, or how it felt to create a gift for someone special.

Remind participants that just like the ornaments they created; they are magical too! Encourage them to do something really special for themselves during the holidays. Through the spirit of giving, these crystals, like icicles will melt their worries into warm smiles, bright laughter, and joy!
Row.txt_description: To give the participants an opportunity to create something unique and beautiful that can be given to friends and/or family. It also allows them to experience the holiday spirit and the gift of giving.
