Row.str_title: How I Broke the Cycle for Teens Variation
Row.txt_code:
Key Topic: Teen Dating Violence: Intervention and Prevention
This Workshop Falls Under the Theme of Teen Dating Violence
Since 2010, we have been developing this program to serve the teens in our community and in our programs. This curriculum is offered to and is useful for BOTH Adult's and children's leaders as most agencies work with this population in some capacity. This workshop is a variation of "How I Broke the Cycle" with new handouts, additional shrinky templates, and accompanied power point presentation that may be used as a guide in your Teen Dating Violence Outreach presentations. A HUGE thank you to Giovanna Martinez and WomenShelter of Long Beach for generously providing the beautifully laid out and powerful, comprehensive presentation on the background of and resources for Teen Dating Violence.
   
  Leaders Creating
 
Note: This workshop can be presented in two ways, depending on where you want your focus to be. It can used as a prevention tool, where you are educating teens on what the cycle of violence looks like to them (in their own lives, community, and the media); or as a intervention tool, where you reflect on how the teens have experienced or witnessed violence themselves.

Objective:
For teens to learn and take part in a discussion and create a piece of art to reflect their own experiences with domestic violence and more specifically the "Cycle of Violence."

Materials:
 
 How I Broke the Cycle Shrinky Key Ring
Pens and paper for writing
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Option 1 (Journaling):
The Cycle of Violence handout
The Cycle of Violence journaling page
Option 2 (Discussion):
Dating/Cycle of Violence Basics: Cycle of Violence handout
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Shrinky Templates (optional)
Shrinky Templates 2 (optional)
Shrinky Templates 3 (optional)
Shrinky Dinks material (Ruff-N-Ready)
Permanent markers
Colored pencils and sharpeners
Scissors
Hole Punchers
Toaster Oven
Ribbon or Craft Wire
Beads (Optional)
Key Chain Ring (Optional)
Jump Rings (Optional)
Teen Dating Violence Power Point Presentation (compliments of WomenShelter of Long Beach)

Timeframe:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 15 minutes
Journaling/Discussion: 20 minutes
Creation: 40 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour 30 minutes

Prep:
Set up the table with the all of the supplies except the worksheet, Shrinky Dinks material and templates.

Introduction: 
Today we are going to learn about and discuss the Cycle of Violence. Afterwards, we will reflect on our own impressions and experiences with the cycle and create art to represent it.

Opening Circle:
Have each participant share one sentence (or one word) about how they view the Cycle of Violence or how it has impacted their life.

Journaling/Discussion
Keep in mind that these are simply two models of what the Cycle of Violence might look like and that it can be different for every person.

 
 
  How I Broke the Cycle Journaling
 
Option 1 (Journaling):
Pass out the Cycle of Violence handout and briefly introduce the Cycle to the teens. Give them a few minutes to review the handout and ask questions. Once they are comfortable with the concept, pass out the Cycle of Violence journaling page and ask them to write about their personal experiences related to the Cycle of Violence. This could be violence they have witnessed in their homes, violence they have personally experienced, or maybe violence a friend told them about. Ask them to write whatever comes to mind. Remind them not to worry about grammar or spelling, and to try not to censor themselves as they do not have to share about what they wrote.

After participants appear to have completed their writing, ask if a few of them would be willing to share their experience with the group.

   
  Discussion About the Cycle of Violence
 
Option 2 (Discussion):
Pass out the Dating/Cycle of Violence Basics: Cycle of Violence handout. Read and review the handout together and discuss the different stages of the Cycle of Violence. Give examples and reflections for each stage either from personal experiences, the community, or from the media.

Some important things to note about the Cycle of Violence:
o    The cycle can happen hundreds of times in an abusive relationship and can take anywhere from a few hours to a year or more to complete. Each stage lasts a different amount of time and can be different for each person.
o    It is important to remember that not all domestic violence relationships fit the "Cycle". Often, as time goes on, the 'Honeymoon' stage disappears.
o    The heavy weight of abuse weighs upon you a little bit more each time you travel around the Cycle, until you are physically, mentally, emotionally and spiritually drained.
o    Emotional abuse is present in all three stages.
o    Domestic violence increases in frequency and severity.  It is never an isolated incident or a one-time occurrence.

 
  Creating without a template
 
  Creating using a template
 
  Cutting out the Shrinky Dink
 
  Don't forget to punch a hole!
Creation:
"Now that you have learned about the Cycle of Violence, it is time to create a Shrinky Dink. Option 1: Have participants create one or more shrinky dinks as a means to reflect on their personal experience of the cycle of violence. Option 2: Reflect on each of the three stages and create a shrinky dink to visually represent each stage using symbols, words or imagery.

Creation Steps:
Step One:
When creating the Shrinky Dinks invite them to use the templates provided or create their own designs. Remind them to color on the rough side of the Shrinky Dink if using colored pencils; they can use permanent markers on both sides.

Step Two:
When they are finished coloring, they may use scissors to cut their Shrinky Dink into a shape.  Then they will use the hole punch to cut a hole in the Shrinky Dink. Remind them to be sure not to punch the hole too close to the edge of the Shrinky Dink paper (as it will not be sturdy enough to support the weight of the Shrinky Dink and key ring).

Step Three:
Once the group members are done coloring, cutting, and punching a hole into their Shrinky Dink, they are ready for baking. Place the Shrinky Dink on a flat metal tray and place inside the toaster oven. We have found it is best to place a piece of a paper bag inside the oven with a corner turned up to make it easier to handle. Bake at 300 degrees until Shrinky Dink has completely flattened (this will take about one minute ). Watch the amazing transformation! Remove the Shrinky Dink and allow it to cool.

Step Four:
Now the Shrinky Dink is ready for decorating with wire and beads, and attached to a key ring (if you like). Thread either wire or ribbon through the hole and add beads. Next take the ribbon or wire and attach it to the key ring or place the jump ring through the Shrinky Dink hole and attach it to the key ring. If you do not have access to key chain rings you can just have the clients string the Shrinky Dinks from ribbon, wire, embroidery thread, or yarn. 

Closing Circle:
If time allows, have each of the teens share about their Shrinky Dink and anything they discovered or learned in group about the Cycle of Violence. Encourage them to keep their artwork as a reminder of what their learning means to them and how they can use this awareness in their future.

   
 
 Creating One Shrinky for Each Stage of the Cycle
 Adding Beads to Create the Key Ring
Row.txt_description: For teens to learn and take part in a discussion and create a piece of art to reflect their own experiences with domestic violence and more specifically the "Cycle of Violence."

Row.txt_code:
Creating Safety Series for Children

"One young boy was talking with a child new to the shelter. The newcomer was crying and scared; the slightly older boy was trying to comfort him and said,
‘Just wait ‘til Friday when we have Windows. Everything will be all right then.’"

 
 
  Our Safe House
 
Let's take a moment to think about how we offer art as a unique zone of safety that the children can look forward to and count on. What are our favorite ways to do this?  How can we do this better?  Creating a safe environment for the children is one of the principle philosophies of Windows because this safety is the gateway to healing. It is also be the path we will follow in all the other themes we will discuss later this year... so in many ways it is the most fundamental.

If children feel safe in their group and safe to talk openly with their Windows leader and peers, then they are able to express their feelings, fears, anxieties and doubts. Once they can express those things freely, they can finally begin the healing process because they will have tools to process many of the challenging issues in their lives. It is essential for the children to understand their feelings and know that they can feel many things at one time. Most importantly, they should know that all feelings are acceptable.

Here are some areas to consider:

Non-Judgmental Listening — Remember that the Windows group might be the first time (and place) that the children find the safety to share something they have never shared before!  This will be a place to build safety that will allow the child to have a voice and to know that they are in the presence of an adult, who will listen to them.

 "These workshops help build relationships
with children who have been taught about
the dangers of trust.  It is so amazing to
form successful and healthy connections
with these kids - they are such warriors -
they never give up on hope."
 
  Leader Quote
 
   
It is essential that the child feels the adult understands if they are having a difficult time and knows that they will not, under any circumstances, be judged. You are that person! Art can become the vehicle for them to find their voice and courage, art is the path to take them from fear to healing, and art gives them the freedom to find themselves.

Ground Rules — Each agency and leader develops their own way of setting art-time ground rules with the children.  Take a moment to think about how you establish ground rules in your group.  Is it fun?  Does it motivate the kids?  Do you set the rules yourself or have the children participate in the creation of rules?  Having the children sign the rules helps give them a sense of ownership to the process.  Please see our Children's Training Manual pages 14 - 15 for more information on emotional (and physical) safety.  Do you have tips to share on how you establish ground rules for safety with the children?

Consider Developmental Stages of the Children — Think about how you meet the children where they are in the their healing and developmental stage. The most direct way may be to solicit the children's opinion of the given topic. You might ask a direct question such as, "What does it mean to feel safe?" With younger children we suggest reading an age appropriate book that relates to your topic then engage the children in a discussion.

For additional suggestions on creating safety such as 'Keep reinforcing that there is no right or wrong way to do the art,' please see our FAQs #19 How do you create safety in the group? 
  "My safe place is an island
and I am the only one I can
trust to keep me safe (for now)."		 
   Participant Quote 

After working on safety with the children, you might want to offer each child a special large envelope (10x13) - or large box - where the children can keep the art they created about safety. This will provide them with a great reminder that they can have some things in their lives that feel safe.

To see how the art helped the children find their "safe places" please click on these Leader Spotlights A Window of Change and Creating a Safe Place

And this special Art Page that was created by the stories and art that one of our leaders submitted based on the workshop Creating a Safe Place.

Below we will revisit several workshops from past years and look at them as a guide to creating safety.

Creating a Safe Place - Children can focus on the meaning of what safety feels like and create images as a reminder.

Attitude Journals - Children can create a journal about what safety means to them providing them with a place to collect their thoughts.

 
 
  God's Eyes
 

God's Eyes - This workshop gives the children an opportunity to create a symbol for safety.

Our Safe Home - Children get to discuss what the things are that they would like to have in their home to make it a safe space.

Safe Rocks - Children can create something that they can keep with them to help keep them safe by providing comfort.

Note: To see the workshops, you must be a registered online leader, and log in with your password. If you are not registered, or need help, contact Cheryl.

 "A 3-year-old asked me, ‘Did you know
that my dad hits me?’  I told him that
I didn’t know that.  He then said,
‘I learned in Windows that it was okay
for me to tell you.’"		 
   Leader Quote

Row.str_title: Safety and Self-Awareness Workshop Series for Adults
Row.txt_code:
Safety and Self-Awareness Workshop Series for Adults

"Wow I didn't realize how hard it would be to know what it is I really need."
"Personal Needs Flower" Participa nt, Life Center for Growth and Healing
"Awareness is the first step of the twelve step programs. Awareness is the goal of many meditation practices. Awareness is the beginning process leading to choice." - Shara Stevens 

Looking back at our very first Leader's Update that featured amazing Windows leader and groundbreaker, Shara Stevens, we were inspired to share this essential series of workshops with you all. Shara, an experienced MFT and survivor herself, found that facilitating art workshops was the perfect path toward realizing and then addressing her needs. Put simply, Shara attributes the art as a force that empowers survivors through bringing awareness. Guided by her words and the Window's philosophy of nurturing and healing, we will focus on creating awareness by noticing our needs.

In order for this awareness and healing to begin, one must be in (or create for themselves) a safe place. Oftentimes, this place is created during the Windows group when the participants can use "a window of time" to feel and be whatever they want. However, survivors cannot always turn to the Windows group for safety and must also rely on themselves and their own resources. Retreating into oneself through art can be a wonderful way to find that safe place anytime.

 "I have found that by abandoning myself to the creative process, without the focus being on the end result, that somehow a seed within me has been watered. Through cognitive education coupled with creative expression, the body, mind and spirit can come together and begin a healing process." - Shara Stevens

We recommend facilitating a series of workshops with the participants that they can use to build self-awareness by noticing their own needs, and can carry forward as a "safe place" for themselves beyond the Windows group setting. This culmination of workshops will be bound through "A Safe Place Journal" with the participants! In this, they can write their private thoughts and feelings, tap into their awareness, and create art. This journal provides a safe environment symbolically, assists participants in finding a safe place mentally, and allows them to recreate that place on the cover of the journal through drawing, collaging, or painting.

Participants will use their Safe Place journals as a place both to create and journal. The first workshop we recommend for this special book is "I Am (timed writing)." This spontaneous and instinctual exercise helps the participants truly focus in on who and what they are without judgment, insecurity, and inhibitions. The echo listening exercise shows the participants what it is like to be heard without judgment. This exposure of oneself, which can only be explored in safety, fits perfectly as an introduction for the first page of the journal. 

As the workshop series progresses, the participants are introduced to art projects that allow them to explore feelings and personal issues, gain self-awareness, and realize how unique and valuable they are. Their art will reinforce for them that what they feel inside is worth expressing. In addition, by taking responsibility for themselves and recognizing their own physical, emotional, and spiritual needs, they are empowering themselves. To complete the series, we recommend the following workshops:

 
 
  Inner-self Portraits
 

Brick Wall - The participants have an opportunity to realize and acknowledge the emotional walls that they have built up and explore the possibility of taking that barrier down.

Self-nurture Portraits or Inner-self Portraits - These portrait workshops will help participants focus on and portray their inner selves and identities.

Paying Attention to ME or Personal Needs Flower - Two great workshops that delve into the physical, emotional, spiritual, and personal needs and represent them artistically.

Journey Butterflies - Participants can use this workshop to explore their journey of awareness and can use their butterfly as a bookmark for their journals.

"I feel I need safety and I feel safe here at the shelter." 
"Paying Attention to ME" Participant, Rainbow Services

Note: To see the workshops, you must be a registered online leader, and log in with your password. If you are not registered, or need help, contact Cheryl.

See the Recovering a Sense of Safety testimonial to read how the art creates a safe haven free from rejection, judgment, and criticism.

To read related Highlight Stories click here: Art Transcends All Barriers and Painting Past the Pain: A Self Portrait of Transformation

For further information on safety, please read FAQ #19 answering "How do I create safety in the group?" (i.e. Explain that every aspect of the workshop is voluntary, including sharing with other participants. Tell the participants that the workshop is a window of time for them to express and explore their feelings, thus they do not have to do anything they don't want to.)

Row.str_title: Creating a Safe Place (Do Not Use)
Row.txt_code:
Description:
Through exploring images of safety, this workshop can help participants feel a sense of their own power by inviting them to create a safe place within themselves.

Materials:
Colored pencil
Pencil sharpeners
Construction paper (various colors)
Envelopes (10" x 13") or paper to protect artwork (optional)
Relaxing music for Guided Imagery (optional)

Timeframe: 
  Age Range:                    
1 hour
Intro: 5 minutes
Embodied Art Activity: 10 minutes
Guided Imagery: 5 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes		    
 6 and up




                   









Set-up/prep:
 
Creating a Safe Place Table Set-up
Prepare the art supplies on the table for easy transition during the group. If you are using music, cue the song that you will be using. An open space for the Opening Circle and/or Guided Imagery can be helpful but is not necessary. If an open space is not available, the activities can be done at the table.

Intro:
"During this workshop, we will be talking about safety and what it means to you. We will be doing three activities that will help you create a safe place. We will have opportunities to be creative and use our bodies, our minds, and a drawing on paper.

"Since this is your time to think about your safe place you get to choose what that looks like. Throughout this workshop, you are invited to participate, which means you always have the option to pass. Passing can look like you sitting back and watching what goes on or it can look like you participating in only a few activities that you feel comfortable with or use the paper to take time to journal, or write a letter, about what safety means to you - it's totally up to you. "

Embodied Art Activity: What Makes You Feel Safe?
Invite participants to gather and stand in a circle. Ask them to space themselves so that they're able to move around without bumping into the person next to them. If you're doing this activity at the table, each person can sit or stand to create their image when it's their turn.

"We are going to start our workshop off by using our bodies. I'm going to start off by asking a question, and we're going to think of how we can answer this question by using our bodies.

"The question is: 'What makes you feel safe?' I'm going to give you a minute to think about what makes you feel safe.

"When I think of what makes me feel safe, I think of hugs. Hugs make me feel safe, so my image might look like this." Wrap your arms around yourself and say "hugs." Ask the participants to repeat your movement and word after you. "But for you, hugs may not be safe, so your image might look like this." Hold your arms straight out in front of you as if you're motioning to stop and say, "Stay away!" Ask the participants to repeat after you again.
 
 Embodied Art Activity at the Table:
"Hugs" (modest)
  Embodied Art Activity at the Table:
"Hugs" (exaggerated)

 
 Embodied Art Activity in a Circle:
 "Stay Away" (modest)
  Embodied Art Activity in a Circle:
 "Stay Away" (exaggerated)

Invite someone to start sharing their image and word/phrase, and remind the group to repeat both parts.

NOTE: You can also show the possible range of images from a small, modest statue to a large, exaggerated image.

Guided Imagery: What Is Your Safe Place?
"For our next activity, we're going to relax and use our imagination to picture our safe place in our minds. After we use our imagination, you'll get a chance to create your safe place on paper with any of the art supplies you see here. Remember: there is no wrong way to imagine or create your safe place!

"Before we start, I'm going to invite you to find a place in the room where you feel most comfortable. This can look like you sitting in a chair, sitting or lying on the floor, standing, or anything in between. Once you get to your comfortable place, feel free to close your eyes if you feel comfortable doing so."

During the guided imagery use a slow, calm voice. It will give the participants time to create the images in their minds.

The guided imagery can sound something like this: "Start by taking a deep breath in and slowly letting it out. Now feel your feet and give them a squeeze and let go. Feel your knees, give them a shake and pause. Feel your shoulders, move them up and move them down. Up and back down again. Notice your arms and wiggle them around and pause. How about your hands? Squeeze your hands tightly and let go. Squeeze them tightly and let go.

"Take a deep breath, and begin to envision your safe place." Continue by asking any or all of the following questions to aid participants in visualizing their safe place:
  • What does your safe place look like?
  • What colors do you see?
  • What does your safe place feel like?
  • What does your safe place sound like?
  • Is it quiet in your safe place?
  • What do you hear?
  • Are you alone in your safe place?
  • If you're not alone, who's with you?
  • What are you doing in your safe place?
  • Did you bring something with you to your safe place?
  • What did you leave behind?
  • Is your safe place somewhere you've been before or a place you've made up?
  • How does your safe place make you feel?
Slowly bring the group back to the room by asking, "When you're ready, open your eyes, move slowly back to your seat, and begin to create your safe place on paper."



 
The group creating their safe place.

Creation:
As the participants create, be available but non-intrusive to support participants if they have any questions or need any supplies. You may wish to give time reminders as well.

Closing Circle:
If you have a separate space for the closing circle, invite the participants to find a place that is most comfortable for them, whether it be on a

A Safe Place

chair or on the floor.

As you begin the closing, let the participants know that this time is for "heart talk." It's a time when they can talk about their art and each participant chooses how they want to talk about their creation. They have the option to participate however they'd like, from sharing their story to being a witness and listening to the other stories.

After each participant has a chance to share, give them a "special envelope" or a piece of paper to save their art and keep it protected from other people's eyes and judgements - a safe place for their safe place.

Optional closing question: "Now that you've created your safe place, what will you do with it?"
Row.txt_description: Through exploring images of safety, this workshop can help participants feel a sense of their own power by inviting them to create a safe place within themselves.
Row.txt_tips:
• It is very important that you and any other Leaders, staff, or volunteers in the room participate along with the group. By modeling your enthusiasm and willingness to participate, you help build trust, bonding, and make it safer for other people to play and share vulnerab le experiences.
  • As an additional strategy, you may want to ask the group about examining their different safety strategies. You can ask questions like, "Which safety strategies have been helpful in the past?" "Which safety strategies aren't serving you anymore?"
  • Support your participants in understanding that because of trauma it's completely normal not to feel safe all the time and that part of healing from trauma can be opening up the possibility for safety. Being gentle and patient, with what can be a slow process, can be helpful.
  • Let the participants define for themselves their visions of safety and their journey to feeling safe. 
  • If "violent" images come up as safety strategies, having a non-judgmental approach and encouraging other participants to do the same will help create safety in the group. It's okay if someone uses a strategy that you or the other participants wouldn't use.
  • It's okay if participants can't envision a safe place. They can try something out to see if it feels safe and notice what feelings come up for them. They can just play with the supplies, breathe with their hand over their heart, or use this time to write in a journal.
  • Remember that it's not your job as facilitator to problem-solve, find a safe place for your participants, or protect them from feelings they find uncomfortable. Instead, consider seeing your role as providing the space for the participants to acknowledge their feelings and experiences and for you to validate whatever comes up.

Row.str_title: Processing Anger Workshop Series for Adults
Row.txt_code:
"Processing Anger" Workshop Series for Adults


 
When arriving at a domestic violence shelter, a survivor might feel a whole range of different emotions. Sometimes, even all in one given day! These different feelings will ebb and flow, increase and lessen in intensity over time and with healing. It is extremely important to remember that while many of these feelings may seem uncomfortable, strange, challenging, depressing or frustrating, it is essential to acknowledge each and every one of them!

Anger is often viewed and treated as a problem that must be controlled. Of course, "out of control" and violent expressions of anger are problematic, but anger itself is not a shameful or "bad" emotion. Abuse, especially in Domestic Violence, is never the result of a lack of self-control. Domestic Violence is a deliberate choice by the abuser for the sole purpose of controlling another human being. Feeling anger does not make one a bad person or a batterer, nor should one feel badly about feeling angry. Suppressing our emotions, especially anger, only leads to inner-self tumult and an eventual explosion. Disarming anger can only be achieved when it is discussed openly without judgment and when it is seen as an important and normal part of each of us.

The Windows curriculum offers a variety of different workshops to encourage the participants to understand their own anger, examine that of other aggressors, and approach it in a healthy way when it arises. The art workshops provide the participants with a gentle and safe avenue to express anger. This process will look different for each and every one of us, but is essential to identify, work through, and develop coping skills for these feelings. Moreover, our anger can be used as a way to look at any needs that are not being met and empower survivors to make positive choices in their lives.

  
  
  
 "I have hope...
I worked on a small slice of my whole anger pie."
Participant, Anger Sequence: Before and After Workshop
The workshops featured in this series are meant to address ways of processing anger and uncovering new coping methods through art. A great, and even fun, way to start this process is through the Aggressive Crayon warm-up. Using simple scribbling, participants use their heated energy in a productive manner. Through vigorous and spontaneous drawing, they are able to release pent-up anger and connect with their buried feelings inside. We recommend following this cathartic warm-up with workshops that help participants understand their own anger. It is essential to know where our anger comes from, how we feel it in our minds and bodies, and how we choose to express it.

Anger Sequence Before and After is a new variation of a very popular workshop, Putting Myself Back Together. This workshop gives participants an opportunity to examine and understand their own anger by asking the following questions: What are my past and current triggers of anger? What thoughts come up when I am angry? How does my anger feel? Where do I feel my anger? How do I react and behave when I am angry? And, what effect does my anger have? By creating an anger sequence, participants can begin to have a clearer understanding of how their anger expresses itself. Note: The second creation part in this workshop focuses on how we want to process anger in the future and can be a great way to end an anger workshop series with your groups.

Befriending Your Feelings offers the clients a deeper of understanding of how all feelings are acceptable, and to notice what their own relationship to their own current feelings are. Accepting anger as an essential part of ourselves is the first step in showing us our freedom to choose.

   
  Aggressive Crayon warm-up
 
Another beneficial, and often times loud, activity that the participants can participate in to freely unleash their emotions and notice their power over their own behavior is the Screaming Bags workshop. This workshop allows the participants to explore when is it okay to scream and when it is not okay. This workshop gives the participants permission to liberate their inner turmoil and, at the same time, learn that they have the freedom to control and decide when and how to express themselves.

  
  The Monster in Me 
One of our most popular workshops, The Monster in Me allows participants to explore their difficult emotions and give voice to the feelings that may be hidden inside by creating artwork that represents the “monster” within. By putting our monsters "on the table" we can take an earnest look at what is behind our own anger... sorrow, hurt, or feelings of frustration. With this awareness, participants can connect with the true feelings behind the anger as well as the work that needs to be done in order to release it and embrace their own needs.

Putting Myself Back Together - This is a two-part workshop that gives the participants an opportunity to notice how feelings "feel" in our bodies and how they can feel fragmented and confused by their conflicting emotions. Through nurturing and loving themselves, they can begin to transform old feelings and start fostering the feelings that they wish to have. This workshop is a great reminder to have compassion for the times that they feel broken or lost in their emotions.

"Anger seems to be a difficult emotion to talk about and work through. Two group members complained about having to ‘talk about anger today.’ Acknowledging and validating how scary anger can feel, I was able to help the women get more involved in the activity."
Leader, That Anger Workshop

That Anger - This workshop also allows participants to safely let out their anger through journaling and drawings in addition to taking the opportunity to learn about their feelings through the creation process. This simple activity can facilitate a process of letting that anger out, and noticing that it is there to teach them something.

Expression Masks - This workshop gives the survivors a powerful visual representation of the anger, hate, frustration, that they are feeling as a result of abuse. The masks can express what is inside of them and/or what their mask says about abusive relationships.

 
 
Letting Go - By discarding what it is they want to let go of, the survivors are able to free themselves of the harmful and painful feelings that are holding them back. This workshop also features a second variation: "I love you, I forgive you, I let you go."

My Window - A simple way to create what they want to leave behind and what they want to move towards, the survivors are able to put their "out of control" feelings behind them and move towards their healthy and controlled feelings instead.

See the "Releasing Anger" testimonial and read how the art allowed these survivors a "breath of healing" to express their emotions and transform their lives.

Note: To see the workshops, you must be a registered online leader, and log in with your password. If you are not registered, or need help, contact Cheryl.

Feelings of anger are often rooted in what we feel we are lacking and can help us identify
what we are not fulfilling in our lives. See "Safety and Self-Awareness" Workshop Series for more workshop ideas.

Additional resources to support you and your clients in further processing anger:
The Dance of Anger: A Woman's Guide to Changing the Patterns of Intimate Relationships by Dr. Harriet Lerner - "Anger is a signal and one worth listening to," writes Dr. Harriet Lerner, in her renowned classic that has transformed the lives of millions of readers. While anger deserves our attention and respect, women still learn to silence our anger, to deny it entirely, or to vent it in a way that leaves us feeling helpless and powerless. In this engaging and eminently wise book, Dr. Lerner teaches women to identify the true sources of our anger and to use anger as a powerful vehicle for creating lasting change. (Amazon)

Anger Management: Tips and Techniques for Getting Anger Under Control  The website helpguide.org features ways of understanding, processing, and coping with anger. It also explores some common misconceptions in the myths and facts section!

 
Taking Charge of Anger: http://kidshealth.org/kid/feeling/emotion/anger.html. While this article is written for kids, the steps and skills it covers and the discussion it facilitates can be helpful for anyone at any age.
 
 This information was provided by KidsHealth®, one of the largest resources online for medically reviewed health information written for parents, kids, and teens. For more articles like this, visit KidsHealth.org or TeensHealth.org. © 1995- 2012 . The Nemours Foundation/KidsHealth®. All rights reserved.

For further help with managing anger and other strong emotions, see FAQ #38, "How Do You 'Deal' with Emotional Clients?"
Row.txt_description: The workshops featured in this series are meant to address ways of processing anger and uncovering new coping methods through art.

Row.txt_code:
Purpose:
To start a journal by collaging the cover. To make this journal a safe place to write or collage thoughts and feelings anytime.

Materials:
Journals (you could use spiral-bound notebooks, or create journals with a comb binder. For low budgets, a three-hole-punch and twine can work.)
Magazines/ photostock books
Glue sticks
Scissors
Clear Contact Paper or Clear Packing Tape (to protect the cover once it's done)
independent project handout (for individual workshop) (click here for handout)

Set-up:
Set out the supplies, with a journal, glue stick, and scissors at each place. Spread out the magazines for easy access.

Welcome and Ground Rules:
It can help create a safe environment if you take time to individually welcome each teen, connect with them, and let them know you are glad they are there. Introduce the project and the philosophy of Windows time: "This is a special "window of time" for each of you. For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? Are there any other Ground Rules you'd like to add?" At this time you can mention any pre-established ground rules you have.

Check-In:
Check-in is a brief opportunity for everyone to share their names, how they're feeling, and any apprehensions they may have about doing art. A good example of an appropriate check-in would be: "Before we start the art, we'll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art." This is a time to reassure anyone who's scared of art that it's fine, and to tell anyone who "hates" art that's fine too. Remind them that they don't have to do it, that they can just watch if they want to. When given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in even if they say they're just going to watch. Let them know that it's fine if they don't want to say anything for "check-in", too.

Project Suggestion:
"In this workshop, you will have a chance to begin a journal for yourself by collaging the cover. To create your collage, select images from the magazines and photostock books. Choose whatever images you feel drawn to. You don't have to understand why you choose them, just rip or cut out whatever pictures seem important to you or catch your attention. When you are ready, begin to collage them onto your journal. It helps if you start by covering the whole front of your journal with soem images or a big image to be your background. Then it's easier to add pictures on top. When you are done, take some time to begin writing in your journal. You could start with writing about what you'd like your journal to be. At the end, use clear contact paper or clear packing tape in strips to protect the cover of your journal. Wrap it around the edges of your collage."

Optional Feedback Exercise:
Ten minutes before the workshop ends, pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You could even take them to copy and return them the next week, so that the teens can add them to their journals.

Closure and Validation:
At the end of the project, a Closing Circle can be a way to give each teen an opportunity to share what she or he has created and talk about what it means to them and how it felt to make it. Just like the check-in circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.
Row.txt_description: Give participants a chance to start a journal by collaging the cover and making the journal a safe place to write or collage thoughts.

Row.txt_code:
This Month's Theme - Processing Anger for Children

"Before the Monster in Me project, physically I felt calm but mentally all the anger and pressure surfaced in my mind. My monster is an angry demon who feels suffering within. She doesn't feel completely understood or happy. She wants to strangle and bite and just fly away. After drawing my monster I see the demon I wish didn't exist. I see the monster within that shouldn't be this way and was just simply happy like a butterfly.
T his demon/monster is me!"
  
 Anger Vo lcano erupting!
 

The topic for this month is Processing Anger. Everyone has angry thoughts and feelings; it is a part of life. Sometimes children cannot find the words for their anger. In their struggle to express themselves, they can explode with frustration and behave in a manner that is not acceptable to adults or often to themselves. When this happens, children often say and do things they really do not mean and carry feelings of guilt and even shame. The question is how to express that anger in a way that does not hurt themselves or others?

 

Art is an extremely effective tool that you can use to help children express and find a voice for what they are feeling. It provides a non-judgmental platform for the children to relax their anger triggers for a moment, and release some of the fears and stresses that are causing these feelings and the volatile behavior that may result. Through the art the children can see their anger in a new way and hopefully understand that the anger is trying to tell them something that is important for them to know.  Once they are able to recognize that their anger is a warning signal, that something may be wrong or that they may feel threatened in someway, they can begin to safely navigate those feelings  

Here are some useful tips to consider using for support of your anger curriculum:


 "My dad explodes like a volcano and the fire comes out hitting!" 
Participant Quote		 

Non-Judgmental Listening — The children we work with have many reasons and circumstances that trigger their angry feelings. They might feel frightened about what will happen to them, or feel upset that they had to leave their home; they could be missing their friends, or be confused about what happened to their family. Looking at where their anger is coming from and talking about it in an open way can help them see that it is nothing to be ashamed of. The art gives them the opportunity to voice the feelings that have not been expressed before. This can be the first step in releasing all those hard feelings in a healthy and constructive way.

Row.txt_code:
Puzzle Piece Paper Doll Template
Objective:
The participants will create an anger sequence processing the triggers, thoughts, feelings, behaviors, and effects of their anger. They will create their past and future anger sequences on two "Putting Myself Back Together" dolls. By writing and coloring emotions on a paper doll made up of puzzle pieces participants are able to reflect on their current emotions and where they feel these emotions in their body. Through journaling and reflecting on their present emotions and envisioning what they wish to feel in the future they will begin to transform their way of expressing anger in a healthy manner.

Materials:
Colored markers - for coloring
Pencils - for coloring
Permanent markers - for writing words
Blank paper for journaling
Handout of paper doll made up of puzzle pieces - 2 for each participant
- click here for Paper Doll Template
Relaxing music

Note: If using this workshop to help the survivors release or process anger, it is important to begin by having a discussion on "What is Anger?" Please click here to see the entire Processing Anger Workshop Series.

 
  Materials for "Anger Sequence Before and After"
Timeframe:
Intro: 5 minutes
Journaling: 15 minutes
Creation, Part 1: 15 minutes
Creation, Part 2: 15 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour

Set Up:
Lay out blank paper, colored markers, pens, and pencils around the table. Make sure that there are two paper doll handouts at each seat, or you can hand them out at the beginning. Have relaxing music ready to be played during their journaling time.

Introduction:
"Today we are going to use these paper dolls to represent the causes of our anger, how we act and feel about them, and where we hold these emotions within our body. When we become angry, our minds might start racing, maybe your face gets hot and red, your hands may shake, and your heart could start beating rapidly. Sometimes we are able to act in a healthy way when we feel angry and talk to someone calmly or walk away. Other times though, we lose control and we behave in a way that makes us feel guilty afterwards. When we stop to pay attention to what is happening in our bodies, we notice that we may tend to hold that anger in different places physically. Maybe a tightening in our chest, or a pit in our stomach, or a vice around our heart. Each time we feel angry may even have a different intensity and manifest itself in a different place in our body. At times we may feel really angry, or we may feel mad, guilty, sad, and confused all at once. Sometimes we may not even know what we are feeling and why we are feeling it, and that is okay too.

"By really noticing our anger and how our body holds it and reacts to it, we can begin to process the feeling and express it in a healthy way. Through the creation of a sequence to understand what our anger looks, feels, and thinks like, we can eventually transform our mindset about it and the the way that we act. We will journal about our five part anger sequence that will take us through our triggers, thoughts, feelings, behaviors, and effects from anger. Through nurturing, loving, and empowering ourselves, we can begin to transform our past ways of expressing anger and start fostering healthy ways of expressing our anger we wish to have and use in the future."

Journaling:
"Through journaling, we will be expressing where our anger comes from and the order that it surfaces in. We will examine our anger by asking ourselves questions about what our anger looks, feels, and acts like and the ways that we express it. Know that this process will look different for each and every one of us but it is essential to identify, work through, and develop coping skills for these feelings.

"We will take fifteen minutes to think about and write the five elements of our anger sequence. For the first part of the sequence, think about, 'what are my past and current triggers of anger'? Write any triggers that have come up for you in the past or currently make you angry. Now contemplate 'what thoughts come up when I am angry?' Write down what goes through your mind when you feel angry. Next concentrate on 'how does my anger feel?' Journal about what it feels like for you to be angry. For the next part of the sequence, reflect on 'how do I react and behave when I am angry?' Write down different behaviors and actions that you show when you are mad. Lastly, consider 'what effect does my anger have?' Journal about how your anger effects not only you but also with others. Remember while you are writing that it is essential to know where our anger comes from, where we feel it in our minds and bodies, and how we choose to express it."

Creation, Part 1:
"Now that we have processed through our anger sequence and looked at all of these feelings that come up, we will think about and depict where we feel our anger. Using the first doll template, you can write a word or sentence or draw a symbol or picture inside each puzzle piece to represent the different parts of the anger sequence. Think of where in your body you might feel the triggers for your anger; where you feel the thoughts you have when you are angry; the places that you feel your anger; what parts of your body react from anger; and where the effect of your anger manifests itself in you physically. You might feel these elements of anger in more than one place in your body or even feel it outside of yourself! You can then write that feeling or feelings in the place or places that you feel it. Just remember to represent 'where do I feel my anger?'

"After you have filled in the puzzle pieces with the words or symbols to represent your anger, you can then color in each puzzle piece with a color that portrays each feeling and where it is felt."

Creation, Part 2:
"Now, we can create a second doll to represent how you want to express your anger and how you will choose to represent that anger in the future. With nurturing and loving feeling words and colors, we will see that through creating a second doll, we are actually taking a step to create this transformation in our lives! By envisioning how we can express our anger in the future in a healthy manner when it arises, we are beginning to foster the feelings and actions that we wish to have."

Closing Circle:
At the end, the participants can reflect on why they put certain words in certain places, what the different colors meant to them and how it feels to look at their doll made up of all of their present emotions and future goals. Give all of the participants a chance to share their paper dolls. If they do not want to share, be sure to let them know that that is okay.

After the participants have shared encourage them to see how strong they are and to have compassion for the times that they feel angry. This is perfectly normal and it is so important that they are doing the work here to create healthy ways of expressing anger in the future! Congratulate them for doing such wonderful work and sharing their feelings!

Alternate Closing:
Brainstorm a "Safety Plan" with the participants to help them process their anger. Some helpful tips include:
Talk to a friend you can trust
Count to 10
Take out art supplies and draw a picture of your anger
Journal about your anger
Take deep breaths
Listen to music
Walk away
Dance or exercise

They will create their past and future anger sequences on two "Putting Myself Back Together" dolls. By writing and coloring emotions on a paper doll made up of puzzle pieces participants are able to reflect on their current emotions and where they feel these emotions in their body. Through journaling and reflecting on their present emotions and envisioning what they wish to feel in the future they will begin to transform their way of expressing anger in a healthy manner.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways.  Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Note About Anger Workshops
We recommend that you start anger workshops with a discussion; don't be afraid to talk to the survivors about their anger. Anger is nothing to be ashamed of, it is important to look at and talk about it to try to understand it.

Some anger prompts that we like are:
What is Anger? What does it look like and what does it sound like?
What was the trigger to your anger?
What did you think about it?
How did it make you feel?
How did you act?
What effect did it have on you and those around you?

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To facilitate a discussion about the act of screaming based on the famous Edvard Munch painting called The Scream.  After the discussion the participants will create their own version of Edvard’s painting, which can then be transferred onto canvas bags.

  
 The Scream by Evard Munch
 
Materials:
Click here for a copy of The Scream
Markers
Cray-Pas
Black and white paper
Scanner
Iron-on paper (available at any office supply store) Iron
Canvas Bags (white or light colored work best) - many options are available from Discount School Supply
*you can iron the images onto any type of fabric

Note: If using this workshop to help the survivors release or process anger, it is important to begin by having a discussion on "What is Anger?" Please click here to see the entire Processing Anger Workshop Series.

Time Frame:
Opening Screaming Circle: 20 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing: 20 minutes
Scanning, Printing and Iron-on transfer process: 5 minutes per bag

Workshop Prep: 
If you decide to put the images on canvas bags, this workshop can be time consuming and expensive, as it requires scanning the participant’s creation into a computer, printing it out on iron-on paper, and then ironing it onto a canvas bag.  However, the project is just as effective if you omit transferring the images onto bags.

Introduction:
Show a copy of the painting, The Scream, to the group (you may also want to pass a copy around the room) and briefly explain that it is a very famous painting by Edvard Munch.  Today we are all going to release our screams and put them on paper.  Your creation does not have to look like Edvard Munch’s painting, just think about how you feel when you scream, or when you want to scream but you feel you can't, and put those feelings on the paper.  There is no right or wrong way to make your scream, just trust your instincts and let your creative juices flow!  

   
  Art by Monabel Contreras  
Opening Screaming Circle:
Begin a discussion about screaming. You can ask the following questions to start the conversation; how did it feel to scream, who screams in your house, when and why do you (or other people) scream, what about happy screams, or scared screams? You can also ask the participants "when is it ok to scream and when it is not ok?" Be sure to reinforce that screaming is an important way to stay safe. If you have a place where it's acceptable to be noisy, a fun and effective way to begin the project is to take the participants to that location and ask everyone to take turns screaming. It may be helpful for the leader to go first so you can set the tone and let the participants know it’s ok to let go, and release their deepest and loudest scream. Make sure to encourage each participant as they scream.          

Technical Demonstration:
First demonstrate how to draw with the Cray-Pas, how to smear the color with your fingers, and the different ways they look on either the black or white paper. Encourage the group to blend the colors together and fill up the entire paper with their creation.


 
 Example of a happy scream
 
Creation: 
Allow the participants to select either the black or white paper to use to create their version of The Scream. Make sure the participants have a variety of different colored Cray-Pas at their disposal. Remind the participants that if they don’t want to draw a picture, they can use colors, words, or symbols to represent their scream. Happy screams, sad screams and angry screams are all welcome; there is no wrong or right way to create. Begin the creative portion by telling the participants, “now take a deep breath, and release your scream onto your paper.” 
  
Closing:
Give each of the group members a chance to share their art. You can also ask the participants to give their artwork a title, and write the title, their name, and the date on the back of their project.  If the participant does not feel comfortable sharing in a group, encourage them to share their project with a safe person later. If it is appropriate, you can also ask questions that allow the participants to open up about their project such as: Why did you choose that colored paper; why did you choose that color, shape, word, or symbol; how did it feel to make your artwork? If you plan on transferring the projects onto canvas bags, ask each participant what color bag they would like (white or light colored canvas bags work best) and write that color on the back of their project (to remind you of their color choice later). Then make sure to collect the projects and tell the participants you will return their projects with their very own screaming bag!

Alternate Closing:
Brainstorm a "Safety Plan" with the participants to help them process their anger. Some helpful tips include:
Talk to a friend you can trust
Count to 10
Take out art supplies and draw a picture of your anger
Journal about your anger
Take deep breaths
Listen to music
Walk away
Dance or exercise

 
 
 Completed Screaming Bag
 
Iron-on process:
Step 1: Scan the artwork into your computer
Step 2: Load the iron-on paper into your printer
Step 3: Print the artwork on the iron-on paper
Step 4: Follow the directions for the particular type of iron-on paper you used, to iron the picture onto the canvas bag (usually the packaging for the paper will offer instructions).  Click here for more information.
Step 5: Give each participant their artwork and their very own Screaming Bag!

Row.txt_code:
This Month's Theme - Processing Anger for Children

"Before the Monster in Me project, physically I felt calm but mentally all the anger and pressure surfaced in my mind. My monster is an angry demon wh o feels suffering within. She doesn't feel completely understood or happy. She wants to strangle and bite and just fly away. After drawing my monster I see the demon I wish didn't exist. I see the monster within that shouldn't be this way and was just simply happy like a butterfly.
This demon/monster is me!"

  
  Aggressive Crayon warm-up 
Everyone has angry thoughts and feelings; it is a part of life. Sometimes children cannot find the words for their anger. In their struggle to express themselves, they can explode with frustration and behave in a manner that is not acceptable to adults or often to themselves. When this happens, children often say and do things they really do not mean and carry feelings of guilt and even shame. The question is how to express that anger in a way that does not hurt themselves or others?

Art is an extremely effective tool that you can use to help children express and find a voice for what they are feeling. It provides a non-judgmental platform for the children to release some of the fears and stresses that are causing these feelings and the volatile behaviors that may result. Through the art, the children can see their anger in a new way and come to understand that their anger is trying to tell them something that is important for them to know. Once they are able to recognize that their anger is a warning signal, that something may be wrong or they may feel threatened in someway, they can begin to safely navigate those feelings.

Here are some useful tips to consider when using your anger curriculum:

 My dad explodes like a volcano
and the fire comes out hitting!
 
  Participant Quote
 

Non-Judgmental Listening - The children we work with have many reasons and circumstances that trigger their angry feelings. They might feel frightened about what will happen to them, or feel upset that they had to leave their home; they could be missing their friends, or be confused about what happened to their family. Looking at where their anger is coming from and talking about it in an open way can help them see that it is nothing to be ashamed of. The art gives them the opportunity to voice the feelings that have not been expressed before. This can be the first step in releasing all those hard feelings in a healthy and constructive way.

Talking About Anger - If it's useful, don't be afraid to open up your workshops with a discussion about anger. You can ask the children, "What made you angry today?" or "What goes through your mind when you get angry?" or "How does getting angry make you feel?" or "Can you think of a time you were angry, and how did you behave?" As you learn to express anger with others or yourself, not only will you feel better but you are more likely to get you needs met.

 
 

Consider Developmental Stages of the Children - It is important to understand that children's ability to process thoughts and feelings about anger changes as they develop emotionally. As you define what anger is, keep it simple and ask questions that are inclusive and relevant to all developmental stages. For example, "Do only bad people get angry?" or "Are you a bad person because you behaved poorly?" Explaining how everyone has angry thoughts, feelings or actions at some point will be important for the child to know they are not "bad" or alone in those behaviors. Relieving the shame a child may feel about their anger is another step toward helping them cope with their confused emotions. Simply asking them to create art that represents their anger, what it looks like or how if feels, can gently guide the children in noticing and expressing their inner feelings.

Below are several workshops from past years that you can use to help children recognize their feelings and process their anger. 

 
 
   

Aggressive Crayon  A fun, fast exercise that allows children to release some of their feelings and pent-up energy onto a piece of paper. Using simple scribbling, the children can release and connect with their buried feelings inside. We recommend following this cathartic warm-up with workshops that help participants understand their own anger.

Anger Sequence Before and After  A new workshop variation of Putting Myself Back Together walks youth through the path that anger usually takes from trigger to the effects of behavior. Explaining to children that anger is a process that all people experience can be comforting and useful in learning how to cope with anger when it feels overwhelming. This workshop allows the children to be a detective of their own anger sequence. It helps them look at how their expression of anger is affecting their lives and their relationships. 


  Anger Volcano erupting!  

Anger Volcanoes   Children can understand the cycle of violence through the creation of a volcano and then experience its three stages - the tension-building, the explosion, and the cooling-off period. This workshop can also be used as a starting point for a discussion about what triggers our angry behavior (the tension-building phase).

Letter to the Fathers  Unexpressed feelings about fathers are a common source of anger and confusion for children. Composing a letter (whether it gets mailed or not), helps to provide a safe place and release for children/teen's thoughts and feelings for and about their father, and to notice why they have those feelings. 

Screaming Bags  Helps encourage a discussion about screaming and exploring the differences between healthy/happy screams and angry screams. This workshop gives the children permission to liberate their inner turmoil and, at the same time, learn that they have the freedom to control and decide when and how to express themselves.

 
 

The Monster in Me  Gives children an opportunity to explore and examine some of the more difficult emotions that they experience and usually hide. Through this exercise, the children take time to notice if their monsters have important things to say. Exposing those feelings can help them to determine what they need to feel better.

Putting Myself Back Together  This workshop fosters awareness of the many and often conflicting feelings the children hold inside. They learn to identify and name each feeling while noticing how and where they feel it in their body. Click on this link to read a heartwarming story about a boy who used this workshop Changing Words to Feelings.

Feeling Friends Creating a "feeling friend" helps the children create a safe place to express the feelings we hold inside. This workshop explains how if we hold too many of our feelings inside and don't let them out, these feelings will build and build and finally they become too much for us to handle.

Note: To see the workshops, you must be a registered online leader, and log in with your password. If you are not registered, or need help, contact Cheryl.

  "The children learned new
ways to express their anger,
feelings and emotions in a
creative, nonviolent way".		 

Share Your Thoughts - As we continue to develop these themes we would love to hear your thoughts related to the topics. Please send us your insights, quotes, comments, stories, successes, challenges, etc. so we can continue to support you. Click here to submit your stories! We know each of you have tailored the workshops to fit the needs of your clients...we would love for you to share those variations also!!

To see how the art workshops have helped some children process their anger, please click on these Leader Spotlights: The Power of Art and His Monster Put a Face to His Anger

Also, this special Art Page was created by the stories and art that one of our leaders submitted based on the workshop The Monster in Me.

Row.txt_code:
"Re-examining Broken Relationships" Workshop Series for Adults

In life, we encounter countless relationships. Whether this relationship is simply that of acquaintance with our mailman, the deep re lationship we share with our partner, or the relationship that we have with ourselves. All of these relationships, no matter how minute they may seem, are significant and have a role in our lives. While we may act differently and play different parts in each of our relationships, it is essential that these relationships are healthy.

In order for a relationship, and both parties in the relationship, to coexist in a healthy way, there must be solid relationship fundamentals. These stipulations will look different for everyone but they must be present as the foundation for this bond. The "Relationship Fundamentals" that help to make relationships strong are:
Communication - having open, honest communication that allows both parties to freely express themselves and their feelings without judgment. (this includes not only verbal communication but communicating with body language as well through eye contact, touch, etc.)
Support - showing and giving genuine care and interest to the other person despite the challenges that the relationship faces.
Trust/Honesty - having faith in the other person, being able to depend on the other person when you need them, and vice versa, and the ability to reveal one's true self.
Mutual Respect - appreciating and honoring the other person for who they are without judgment or condescension.
Equality - knowing that both people are proportionately important and that both roles played in the relationship are vital.
Safety - being able to be vulnerable and secure with sharing intimate thoughts, feelings, and physical protection.
Happiness - sharing joy, laughter, bonding, and a positive and loving connection.
Through the generation of a discussion or a journaling exercise, ask the participants if these are elements that they have in their relationships!

...Boundaries Chart...

"Call To Action." Now that we know what our relationships look like, what can we do about them? What do we need to have a healthy relationship with ourselves and others? How do we advocate for what we need in our relationships? How can we continue to meet these needs in our future relationships?

Re-examining Broken Relationships

My Relationship Boundaries...Revealed!

Healthy Relationship Collage

Losses Altars inspired by Dia de los Muertos

Red Flag Banners

See the "Releasing Anger" testimonial and read how the art allowed these survivors a "breath of healing" to express their emotions and transform their lives.

Feelings of anger are often rooted in what we feel we are lacking and can help us identify
what we are not fulfilling in our lives. See "Re-examining Broken Relationships Workshop Series" for more workshop ideas.
