Row.txt_description: This workshop series is designed to help participants take another look at their relationships, including the one that they have with themselves, and to move forward from there.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give the children/teens an opportunity to look at one relationship in their lives (siblings, parents, friends etc.) and to better understand that relationship.

  
  Relationship Collage
 
Materials:
Cray-Pas (or crayons)
Patterned papers
Glue sticks
Pipe cleaners
Scissors
Markers
White 12x18 inch paper (at least 2 per participant)
Large head template
Small head template
Child head template
Cardstock (for head templates)
Optional - have some other template shapes/symbols or stencils (cloud, arrows, hands...etc.)

 Time Frame:    Age Range:  
Introduction: 5 minutes
Warm-up: 10 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing: 15 minutes
Total: 1 hours		      
6 - 18 years old
 




 

 
 
  Workshop table set-up 

Set-Up/Prep:
Cut out enough templates to allow children to express a variety of relationships or to best meet the needs of your group. These will serve as "stencil" templates for use during the workshop.

Introduction:
Introduce the activity by guiding discussion of difficult relationships. "In life, we encounter all types of  relationships. Whether this relationship is casual like with the person who serves us food at a restaurant, the deeper relationship we share with our siblings, or have you ever thought about the relationship that you have with you? All of these relationships are significant and have a role in our lives. While we may act differently and play different parts in each of our relationships, it is important that these relationships are healthy.

Sometimes relationships between parents and their children are conflicted, sometimes we have conflicts with our brothers or sisters - or our friends. It may even be that we have more than one relationship within our family that is conflicted or difficult.

Relationships can be challenging and wonderful for many reasons. It is important that we take the time to deeply look at the relationships in our lives and look at what they mean to us, why they look the way they do, and why we are in them. We all have had at least one relationship within our family or life that is conflicted or painful and sometimes the most challenging and conflicted relationship in life is the one that we have with ourselves. Whether these strained relationships are past or current, all of your other relationships can be affected. 

In this workshop, rather than thinking we have to change the conflict relationships, we will just be looking at them. We might even find that sometimes the only way to "fix" a broken relationship is letting it (or that person) go. We might also notice that there are relationships that are important to work on and heal in order to be happy and healthy. Today, we will take the time to pick ONE conflicted relationship we would like to work on.
  
   "Scribble warm-up" exercise 


Warm Up:
This warm up can help to bring the children/teens into the present moment and gain access to their sensory memories. Announce that today we are going to do a "scribble warm-up." Ask participants to pick up a Cray-Pas (or crayon) and begin making large circular scribbles on their 12 x 18 paper. Encourage them to try to not think about what they draw and experience the simple motion of their hands and arms making random circular scribbles on their paper. Allow the participants to do this for half a minute or so until you feel that everyone is focusing on the scribble motion and becoming more present. Encourage the children to add to their scribble by picking up another color and using the same motions.

Next, direct participants to turn their paper over. Now we will user use lines, shapes and colors to represent how they feel. Simplify this by reviewing a list of commonly shared feelings. For example, start with "ANGRY." Ask them to select a color that represents ANGER to them, and show "How I feel when I'm angry" - that is, how would my anger look as a line or shape using Cray-Pas or crayons on the paper. Ask participants to "doodle" a line or shape that represents how those feelings would look to them.

You can use these feelings as prompts for the feelings warm-up:

ANGRY
SAD
AFRAID
CONFUSED
JEALOUS
NERVOUS/ANXIOUS

Address at least 3 of these emotions but continue to give feeling prompts until you sense that the participants are ready to move on to the main exercise.

Creation:
STEP 1:
Now, we will select one relationship in our lives to focus on today. Through the collage creating process, we are representing a relationship between ourselves and another person(s) that is in conflict or a relationship that is not the way you want it to be. We all have people in our lives who we would like to change our relationship with. This constantly changes; maybe you were feeling great about your relationship with your mother last week but today you are really mad at her. Pick a relationship that comes to mind.

  
   Silhouettes representing the relationship dynamic
 
   
   
   Creating the collage 
   
   
    Coloring the collage 
STEP 2:
Select two colored or patterned papers; one to represent YOU in your relationship and a second to represent the OTHER PERSON or one side of you versus another side of you. Use your head template(s) to trace profile heads on to colored or patterned papers. After tracing the template, cut out each head. Now you have two or more heads representing the roles in the relationships! The heads are in profile so that you can make them look at each other or look away from each other or relating (or not relating) in some way to the other. 

Hold up the heads at the same time and demonstrate a few of the variety of ways that the heads can face to represent the relationship.

STEP 3:
Glue down the heads in a way that shows how the relationship feels.  The possibilities for where you place these heads are endless and how it demonstrates your relationship is totally unique because the feelings that we have about the people in our lives are different for each of us.

STEP 4:
Using the materials provided, represent the conflict relationship. You may want to create symbols of yourself and the other person(s). Do not over think this exercise, simply select materials and glue them down without asking yourself 'why' you are choosing this particular material. Feel free to cut, glue, scribble, and draw out anything that feels right at this moment.

Closing Circle:
Each of you has bravely taken the opportunity to try to uncover painful feelings that you may not feel comfortable expressing or sharing. We will have a closing circle that will give everyone the opportunity to express any feelings that came up during this workshop. 


  
 
 Relationship collage with many heads
  Relationship collage with opposite facing heads
 

Time Permitting: If you want to further examine and understand the strained relationship with the hopes of moving forward, encourage the children to think and journal, on the back of their creations, about the next steps in moving forward!

We suggest that you end the exercise by handing out these prayers or mantras. This may offer the participants some peace, calm, and strength to move forward in their lives.

The Serenity Prayer
God grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot change, courage to change the things I can, and wisdom to know the difference. - Reinhold Neibuhr, 1934

The Gestalt Prayer
I am I, and you are you. I do my thing, and you do your thing.
I am not in this world to live up to your expectations, and you are not in this world to live up to mine. If by chance we meet, it's beautiful. If not, it can't be helped. - Fritz Perls, M.D.
Row.txt_description: To give the children/teens an opportunity to look at one relationship in their lives (siblings, parents, friends etc.) and to better understand that relationship.

Row.txt_code:
Examining Broken Relationships Collage
 
Objective:
The participants will take the time to deeply look at the relationships in their lives and notice what they mean to them, why they look the way they do, and why they are in them. By exploring a strained relationship, they will examine and gain a better understanding of the dynamic taking place.

Materials:
Cray-Pas (or crayons)
White paper 12 x 18 (at least 2 per participant)
Patterned papers
Glue Sticks
Pipe cleaners
Scissors
Markers
 
 
  Workshop table set-up
 
Large head template
Small head template
Child head template
Card stock (for head templates)

Timeframe:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Warm-up: 10 minutes
Creation: 45 minutes
Closing: 30 minutes

Total: 1 1/2 hours

Set-Up/Prep:
Cut out enough templates to allow participants to express a variety of relationships or to best meet the needs of your group. These will serve as "stencil" templates for use during the workshop.

Introduction:
"In life, we encounter countless relationships; whether the relationship is simply that of acquaintance with our mailman, the deep relationship we share with our family or friends, or the relationship that we have with ourselves. All of these relationships are significant and have a role in our lives. While we may act differently and play different parts in each of our relationships, it is essential that these relationships are healthy.

"Relationships can be challenging and wonderful for various reasons. It is important that we take the time to deeply look at the relationships in our lives and re-examine what they mean to us, why they look the way they do, and why we are in them.

"In domestic violence, a batterer often uses destructive behaviors that can negatively impact relationships on many levels. Abuse can make trust, communication, joy, safety, and shared dreams with anyone seem impossible and unattainable. Even in non-violent relationships there can be chaos and conflict. Then again, sometimes the most challenging and conflicted relationship in life is the one that we have with ourselves. We all have had at least one relationship, past or current, that is conflicted or painful.  

"The idea of looking at these relationships can be intimidating and challenging. It can be difficult to make the time or space to allow ourselves to do this. In this workshop, rather than jumping to 'repair' strained or broken relationships, we will be examining them. In doing so, we might find that sometimes the only way to "fix" a broken relationship is letting it (or that person) go. We might also notice that there are relationships that are important to mend and heal in order to be happy and healthy. Today, we will take the time to pick ONE conflicted relationship we would like to work on."

   
  "Scribble warm-up" exercise
 

Warm-Up:
"Before we start with the creation process, sometimes it is helpful to move your body because we store many of our emotions there. Sometimes these emotions become so suppressed and repressed that we don't even have access to them anymore because they are so deeply buried."

Ask participants to pick up any Cray-Pas (or crayon) color and begin making large circular scribbles on their 12 x 18 paper. Encourage them to experience the simple motion of using their hands and arms by engaging their shoulder to slowly make random circular scribbles.  This will help them to try and "get out of their heads" and quiet their internal chatter or self-talk. Allow participants to do this for half a minute or so until you feel that everyone is focusing on the scribble motion and becoming more present. Next, instruct them to add to their scribble by picking up another color and using their non-dominant hand to make fast and angular motions. Then, using both hands together, make either angular or circular motions using the two colors next to each other.

 
 
  Representing feelings with lines and shapes
 

Next, direct participants to use lines, shapes and colors to represent their feelings so that the line serves as a metaphor. We recommend that you start with common emotions like "anger" or "sadness," and then transition to more complex feelings like "jealousy."

Ask participants to select a color that represents ANGER to them, and show "how I feel when I'm angry" - that is, how would my anger look as a line or shape using Cray-Pas on the paper. Ask participants to turn their papers over and "doodle" a line or shape that represents how those feelings would look to them.

Some sample feelings to use in this warm-ups are: ANGRY, SAD, AFRAID, CONFUSED, JEALOUS, NERVOUS/ANXIOUS, etc. Continue to give feeling prompts until you sense that they are ready to move on to the main exercise.

Creation:
STEP 1:
"Now, we will select one relationship in our lives to focus on today. Through the collage creating process, we are representing a relationship between ourselves and another person(s) that is in conflict or a relationship that is not the way you want it to be. We all have people in our lives who we would like to change our relationship with. This constantly changes; maybe you were feeling great about your relationship with your mother last week but today you are really mad at her. This relationship might be one that ebbs and flows - maybe you think, "I love my daughter, but whenever we talk about money, we have an argument." Pick a relationship that comes to mind that you would like to work on examining today.

 
 
  Silhouettes representing the relationship dynamic 

STEP 2:
"Select two colored or patterned papers; one to represent YOU in your broken relationship and a second to represent the OTHER PERSON (or one side of yourself versus the other). Use your head template(s) to trace profile heads on to colored or patterned papers. After tracing the template, cut out each head. Now you have two or more heads representing the roles in the relationships!" Explain that the head templates are in profile so that they can choose to place them looking at each other or looking away from each other or relating (or not relating) in some way to one another. Hold up the heads at the same time and demonstrate a few of the variety of ways that the heads can face. The direction they are facing and their placement on the paper can represents the conflict.

 

   
  Creating Collage
 
   
   Coloring Collage 

STEP 3:
"Decide how you will glue down your heads in a way that reflects the current relationship. Place them in a way that represents the relationship dynamic (i.e. facing each other, turning away from each other, one facing the other and the other turning away, etc.) The possibilities for where you place these heads are endless. How you choose to demonstrate your relationship is totally unique to the reality of it in your life."

STEP 4:
"Using the materials provided, represent the conflict relationship. You may want to add symbols of your relationship. Try to select materials and glue them down without asking yourself 'why' you are choosing these particular materials. Work 'from your instincts' and cut, glue, scribble, and draw out anything that feels right at this moment."

Closing Circle:
"Each of you has bravely taken the opportunity to try to uncover painful feelings that you may not feel comfortable expressing or sharing. We will give everyone the opportunity to express any feelings that this exercise evoked."

Ask the participants to share: how the Examining Relationships Collage helped them to better understand their relationship? What did they notice or learn from taking a deeper look at their relationship? 

Remember to thank them for bravely taking this window of time to notice their relationships that have been significant to them and for sharing!

 
 
   
  Examining Broken Relationship Collages
 


Time Permitting: If you want to further examine and understand the strained relationship with the hopes of moving forward, encourage the participants to think and journal, on the back of their creations, about the next steps in moving forward! (If you would like to generate a discussion with the participants to further process as a group, see the "Tips" section).

We suggest that you end the exercise by handing out these prayers or mantras. This may offer the participants some peace, calm, and strength to move forward in their lives.

The Serenity Prayer
God grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot change, courage to change the things I can, and wisdom to know the difference. - Reinhold Neibuhr, 1934

The Gestalt Prayer
I am I, and you are you. I do my thing, and you do your thing.
I am not in this world to live up to your expectations, and you are not in this world to live up to mine. If by chance we meet, it's beautiful. If not, it can't be helped. - Fritz Perls, M.D.
Row.txt_description: The participants will take the time to deeply look at the relationships in their lives and notice what they mean to them, why they look the way they do, and why they are in them. By exploring a strained relationship, the participants will examine the dynamic and how the relationship and roles function.
Row.txt_tips:
Discussion: "Now that we have examined our relationships, we can start to think about what can we do about them? What do we need to have a healthy relationship with ourselves and others? How do we advocate for what we need in our relationships? How can we continue to meet these needs in our future relationships? Is it possible that this is a relationship that you need to let go?" Generate a discussion with the participants about what the next step is or encourage them to use this "call to action" as homework! To help facilitate this conversation, refer to the handouts provided.

Relationship Boundaries handout

Row.str_title: Moving Forward Workshop Series for Adults, Part 1
Row.txt_code:
"I am lovable, with all my flaws, and my history."

The art has a gentle, but surprising way of bringing the participant's inner world to the surface. With the deeper, more expressive workshops, the participants can consciously explore new territories of emotion and thought through the power of creation. Workshops such as  Funeral of I Can'ts or Miniature Mask Making often bring up deep emotions, thoughts and discoveries about buried memories and hurts. Even lighter, more playful workshops such as Heart Workshops and Loving Relationship Charms can have a profound and empowering effect on how the survivors see themselves.


Art workshops allow for the freedom of choice and safety of each woman as she can decide for herself how to guide her own process. Through exploring forgiving, accepting, and understanding oneself, one can find clarity and move forward. Throughout the series, the participants will be learning about their inner world and how they relate to their outer world. We have created a two-step process to guide them through this journey. The participants will start by looking inside themselves to uncover their essence and gain perspective.
 
Workshops for Exploring and Understanding Our Inner World:
Through these workshops, the participants can make connections to their beliefs, feelings, history, and perspective. Connecting to oneself is the first step in moving forward.

 
I Am (timed writing) - This journaling workshop taps into a woman’s creative and expressive self. It cuts through the sense of pressure, the doubts, and the self-criticism that blocks creative expression. It gives each woman the opportunity to create something deep and powerful.
Writing From The Heart - This journaling workshop allows participants to go deep within and reconnect to their inner selves, their dormant feelings, and their powerful memories. They also have the opportunity to get in touch with their creative inner spirit, unleashing their own creativity.
Inner Child Page - The goal of this endearing and powerful scrap-booking workshop is to empower survivors to appreciate their inner child, that strong powerful child who holds their secrets, protects them, is playful, and is always there!
Losses Altars - To honor those parts of ourselves that we feel we have lost or have “died” due to the Domestic Violence in our relationships.
Inspirational Scrolls - This workshop helps
 
"It’s time to wake up!
My heart is in the middle but it’s trying to have clear thoughts.
Time to remember dreams, look at the truth, to have quiet times,
to play, to leap and to soar."
 
participants access their deepest feelings through the use of writing and Liquid Watercolors to create an Inspirational Scroll.
Life Clocks - You Decide - Gives the participants a chance to decide how they want to fill their time by drawing the face of a clock and substituting words and/or images (instead of numbers) of how they want to spend their lives.

Workshops to Gain Perspective and Clarity:
As Windows Leaders we offer the survivors a window of time not only to reflect, but to practice respecting their thoughts, feelings, and visions. Once we have an understanding of our inner world, the participants can move toward the second step in the series. These workshops can help them relate to their outer world with perspective and clarity.

 
 
   
Examining Relationships - The participants will take the time to deeply look at the relationships in their lives and notice what they mean to them, why they look the way they do, and why they are in them. By exploring a strained relationship, the participants will examine the dynamic and how the relationship and roles function.
Native American Mistake Wheel - The "mistake wheel" (a Native American spiritual tradition) is a new perspective on the medicine wheel and shares the keys to self-acceptance and acceptance of the universe. The five sections of the disk hold five messages about "mistakes," leading us to reflect on what we can learn from them and how we can accept them.
"When I left my abuser,
I started my path towards balance in my life.
This doll is a representation of me
and she is harvesting love and slowly
but surely healing from all the abuse
of the past." 
Thoughtstoppers - Provides participants with positive images to focus on, when finding themselves overwhelmed with negative thoughts and feelings. The end product are framed images - gentle reminders of the ability to redirect negative thoughts to positive thoughts with visualization.
Eagles in a Storm - Gives participants an opportunity to identify the "storms" faced in their lives and choose the perspective they would like to hold through them. The end product is a beautiful visual reminder to rise above the "storms."
Corn Husk Dolls - This workshop reinforces that the participants have made the right decision to leave their abusive situation. Corn husk dolls serve as an important reminder that the participants are taking steps to harvest goodness in their lives.
Self-Box - Participants create a Self-Box which allows them to “see” who they are on the inside, as well as who they are on the outside. This project will give them a more empowered focus on who they are and who they see themselves becoming.

"This made me feel good about myself. More powerful about myself.
Helped me find out more about myself, and it's all about me."

Note: To see the workshops, you must be a registered online leader, and log in with your password. If you are not registered, or need help, contact Cheryl.

Share Your Thoughts: As we continue to develop these themes, we would love to hear your thoughts related to the topics. Please send us your insights, quotes, comments, stories, successes, challenges etc. so we can continue to support you. Click here to submit your stories! We know each of you have tailored the workshops to fit the needs of your clients...we would love for you to share those variations also!!

To read related Highlight Stories click here: Survivors Discovering Their Inner Artist

Note about Family Workshops:
Since relationships with family members are so important to how we see ourselves and our world, it can be helpful to add a family workshop from our Family Windows curriculum. Try our Family Windows curriculum by using the "Family Windows" Workshop search tool.

Note about Intimate Partner Relationships:
Examining relationships with intimate partners can be powerful and impactful, especially if violence has been involved. To help sort through these reflections, you might find the Dating Violence Curriculum helpful! Search for "Dating Violence for Teens" workshops under the Strength category in the Workshop search tool.

Row.str_title: Compassionate Creation: Trauma-Informed Care Through Art
Row.txt_code:
“Every day I take this class I feel
stronger in my life to go forward.
Thanks for helping me.”
Adult Windows Participant
There is a lot of enthusiasm in the Domestic Violence movement centered around the Trauma-Informed Care protocols and best practices. Recently, AWBW invited Windows' Leader and Trauma-Informed Care expert trainer, Tiombe Preston, to explain the Trauma-Informed Care model and how the Windows Program accomplishes the goals of this approach. To download the PowerPoint presentation click here: Compassionate Creation: Trauma Informed and Art; to view the engaging and powerful video, click here.

Would it surprise you to know that Windows has been trauma informed for 21 years?
The Windows Program philosophy overlaps with the trauma-informed model of providing care. To be trauma informed is to place trauma at the center of our understanding of survivors. In our roles as Windows Leaders and helpers, we can reasonably assume that the people we serve are survivors of trauma. Windows honors each person as the expert of their own experiences and supports their healing in an atmosphere of safety and creativity. From this perspective, we attempt to offer a "window of time" for each individual to understand, process, and heal in an atmosphere of safety and creativity.

This key topic highlights many of the ways in which the Windows program, philosophy, and practices complement Trauma-Informed Care.

 Windows was founded on the idea that art provides survivors a window of safety, freedom and creativity; a place where they can honor and respect their feelings, thoughts and visions without judgment. For women emerging from domestic violence, art becomes an ideal resource. The creative sessions offer a private, non-threatening avenue through which the women can begin to communicate with themselves; sometimes for the first time.
Why art? As art therapist Anna Reyner writes, after experiencing trauma, "our reality is tainted, our trust is shattered, and emotions are unpredictable." Through art, the survivors are able to reconnect parts of the brain and heal trauma. Read more about how non-verbal expression helps foster healing through a trauma-informed model in Anna Reyner's article "Healing from Trauma - Art and the Brain."

Through their creations, participants are granted an opportunity to explore their own sense of possibility and identity of who they can be, what they dream of, and inspire and instill hope for what lives they want to create and cultivate for themselves.
"A Windows Between Worlds is a great place for me to feel safe and
express myself." 
I Can: Requiem for I Can't Workshop
 
Since creating art expresses our own truth and tells our own narrative, the power is the hands of the survivors (literally and figuratively) as they are in charge of their own creative self-exploration. We further empower participants through affirmations and encouragement that they can take leadership in their own lives. Rather than being placed under the control of another, their batterer, society, rules, and restrictions, participants have a powerful opportunity to reclaim their own sense freedom to decide what they want to create.

What is my role as a Windows facilitator? As AWBW Leaders, we serve as supportive friends and compassionate witnesses for the participants. As you prepare yourself to lead a Windows group, from a perspective of compassionate observer, there are simple but empowering ways to create safety and to facilitate recovery, resilience, and healing. By introducing yourself and explaining the significance and value of the art to you, it creates an immediate sense of trust and understanding. By affirming and validating, rather than diagnosing or explaining, we listen supportively to the participants and serve as a compassionate witness to their creative expression and their experience. As a partner in their healing, you can educate each individual by understanding and communicating knowledge about trauma and trauma responses. (For more information about Domestic Violence, trauma, and trauma responses, watch Tiombe's Video and use AWBW's DV 101 curriculum.)

I appreciate the opportunity
this group provides for safe expression in a supportive, understanding, non-judgmental environment."
The Garden of New Beginnings Workshop


Leaders reported that 96% of the time, workshops helped the adults
to deal constructively
with feelings,
such as releasing
anger and pain.
 
How am I creating safety?
When guiding an empowerment art group, creating a safe and calming environment is of utmost importance to help survivors to begin and continue the healing process. Knowing what the participants need in order to be and feel safe is vital to the collaborative and supportive nature of the group. It is also key to hold the group in a private, safe place that is a closed setting from others to foster the mentality that "what happens in the room, stays in the room." This sanctuary facilitates a space for "me time" and a sense of expression and self-discovery. Even if this means people are not participating or are "acting out," our role is to respect where they are (emotionally, physically, mentally, spiritually, etc.) and how they are choosing to meet their needs. Click here to read a survivor's powerful story of finding her safety through being given the choice to participate.

It is also essential to remind participants, as often as necessary, of our philosophy. Give them the permission to take a window of time for themselves in whatever capacity best supports them. Remind them that every aspect of the program is voluntary. If a participant needs to take a break, opt out of any aspect of the project, or ask for some support, encourage them to do so and remind them that part of your role is to be there for each participant. Empower participants to respect whatever comes up throughout the creation process, and challenge them to imagine without judgment. Throughout the creation process, remind them to be gentle with themselves and honor their experience.

  
 
The art medium provides me the
safety and freedom to unearth that
which was buried.
How do I get the group to be focused and supportive of each other?
Establishing guidelines with the group, that the participants  are responsible for creating and modifying, fosters predictability and consistency in a flexible environment that is crucial for safety. (See the related Impact Spotlight "Letting the Participants Choose" for ideas and insight!)

Begin every workshop with a group check in. An opening circle can give the participants an opportunity to reflect and think about themselves, their feelings, and each other. This is also a wonderful opportunity for the Leader to gauge their attitudes and emotions to better respond to their needs. In addition, it brings everyone's voice into the room and allows for connection and trust. Follow the check-in with a centering exercise such as a relaxation or journaling exercise. These warm-up activities promote introspection, reflection, and regrouping.

It is essential to hold weekly Windows workshops to foster consistency and to instill a sense of security and comfort that participants can grow to expect and become accustomed to. This truly enables them to have the opportunity to relax and regroup their energies, take the time as a revitalization period, and notice what they need to be present to, without the distractions and responsibilities of their every day lives.

Once participants have finished their creations, all Windows workshops include a closing circle to encourage voluntary sharing by posing questions in a supportive way. Questions such as, how did you feel during the session? what did you create? how do you feel about your creation? what did you discover? create an opportunity for validation of their experience. This time also allows participants to process their creation, their feelings, and the project experience as a whole and enables a space for discussion and debriefing, if necessary.

93% of the leaders reported that
the art program was highly effective
in helping participants to clarify
present needs and future goals,
and the majority found it to be
MORE effective than
ANY OTHER service in this regard. 

 "It is rewarding providing clients
with a safe environment
to process their feelings
and experiences in others ways
than traditional talk therapy."
Windows Leader 
How do I prepare myself for leadership? It is important to modify and accommodate your leadership style, materials, topics, and workshops according to the needs and requests of the participants in the group. Identify what the triggers of the group are or might be and incorporate what and how you will plan accordingly. Flexibility is crucial as so many circumstances are subject to change! Be ready for a wide range of emotions and feelings to emerge. Remind yourself that it is normal for trauma survivors to express all sorts or emotional reactions, including emotional outbursts or the desire to withdraw. Remind yourself and participants that these reactions are simply a manifestation of the trauma they have endured.
 
"One important take away I learned from attending the Windows Leadership Training was to suspend your judgment about how the workshop is going and whether or not it is being received or is meaningful and enjoyable. All any of us can do is to offer and invite. As we plant seeds, some will take and others will not, but there are many seeds within each workshop and the ones that will take root are those that the soil is ready for. Everyone is journeying at their own pace, in their own way. I smiled inside remembering this when one woman rolled her eyes and made a snarly face at me as I was reading the relaxation. This same young woman made it clear that she hated art and was not one bit happy about being there wasting her time. She did not participate in anything until it was time to create the cards and she was the first one to jump right into it! It made me giggle inside." - Windows Leader
 

After each workshop facilitated, the participants are asked to complete a Participant Evaluation based on their experience with the workshop. The participants only complete the evaluations if they choose to and the form asks for their opinion and feelings about self-expression, taking decisive steps to break the cycle of domestic violence, and making healthy decisions for the future through the art in a way that supports them. These forms are a helpful tool to use when planning future workshops, addressing certain topics, and gauging the feelings of the participants.

99% of the leaders
found the Women's Program
succeeded in helping
participants develop the confidence/self-esteem
they need to break with the past and start new lives.
 "The ‘uglier’ the artwork gets,
the more it tells me those participants are feeling safe enough in the group
to face their fears and pain.
I enjoy quietly witnessing
the courage the women show,
and I cheer them on
silently in my heart."
AWBW Leader

Participant Favorite Workshops
By providing a collaborative opportunity for survivors to choose workshops, themes, or discussion topics that speak to their interests and needs, you empower and promote partnership with the survivor. Based on our participant evaluations, survivors participating in the Program have chosen these workshops as some of their favorites.

   
The Lotus Flower - To assist participants in seeing and believing that out of a murky and dark environment, something beautiful can be created and they can rise above. Participants create an analogy between their story of abuse and the meaning and origins of the lotus flower.
Tunnel Books - Helps to create chapters of identities in the participant's lives and shows past, present, and future identities. Allows participants to get in touch with their inner feelings and express them in a safe way and can truly help them understand the feelings they keep inside and the feelings they show on the outside.
 
 
What Makes Me Shine - Participants are giving the opportunity to think about and see themselves through their own eyes, by creating a sun full of rays with the words, images, and color that make them who they are.
Vision Masks - Through the creation of masks, participants will think of a small, do-able step to take as they boldly envision how they want to create their future. Using the No Limits process, by following their dreams and setting goals, participants will discover their own vision.
   
The Butterfly - Helps each participant find patience, compassion, and trust in facing the struggles and difficulties of her life's path. The end product is a reminder that even through struggle and pain, we can gain growth and perspective.
Self-Love Maps - This workshop allows participants think in definite and concrete terms about where they are and want to go on their journey to Self-Love.
   
Source of my Strength - This workshop engages participants by painting in a new way that activates kinesthetic movement. Participants strengthen their sense of personal power through creating visual symbols that help each person differentiate the source of their own personal strength.
Story Trees - This workshop provides participants a creative opportunity to explore their stories of survival, change, and growth. Using the tree as a symbol of life, participants can explore and uncover the stories of their life.
 
 
Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence Workshop (Paper Version) This workshop is designed to help survivors recognize their personal strengths and uses the metaphor of a "pearl" as a treasure that forms inside an oyster in response to an irritant. Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength and wisdom as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence.
Eagles in A Storm - Gives participants an opportunity to identify the "storms" faced in their lives and choose the perspective they would like to hold through them. Their compassionate creation is a beautiful visual reminder to rise above the "storms."
   
   
Safe Place - This workshop is designed to support participants in creating a safe place where they can go to in their minds when facing stressful situations. Through identifying ways to build safety and security in their lives, this project can complement the creation of a domestic violence safety plan.
A Journey Within - This workshop takes the participant on their own journey of creativity, where the product is their own wisdom. The journal or sketchbook becomes a point of reference for their lives and lends perspective on their fears and challenges, joys and enthusiasm, and every emotion and feeling in between.

In addition to these featured workshops, please also refer to our Workshop Series that delve into key topics of compassionate creation and empowerment. Safety and Self-Awareness Workshop Series for Adults, Processing Anger Workshop Series for Adults, Moving Forward Workshop Series for Adults, Part 1, Moving Forward Workshop Series for Adults, Part 2, Opening Up and Expressing Emotions Series for Adults, and Exhibit Planning Workshop Series for Adults).

See the "Finding Support for Change" testimonial and read how gaining creative expression as a coping skill is a powerful and transformative experience for survivors. Art helps survivors to realize the strength and possibility they carry within themselves to change their lives.

Share Your Thoughts: As we continue to develop these themes, we would love to hear your thoughts related to the topics. Please send us your insights, quotes, comments, stories, successes, challenges etc. so we can continue to support you. Click here to submit your stories! We know each of you have tailored the workshops to fit the needs of your clients... We would love for you to share those variations, too!

To read related Impact Spotlights click here: A Special Time for Special Souls, The Art Helped Her Stay..., and Facing Challenges in a Creative Way.
Row.txt_description: In this series, we will explore what it means to serve as a compassionate witness as Windows Leaders in recognizing that each person is an expert on their own experience. We will use the Windows philosophy and workshop curriculum to look at the way the participants cope and survive their trauma with curiosity, rather than judgment.

Row.str_author_firstname: Janet Shlesman with contributions by AWBW Staff
Row.txt_code:
Completed Vision Mask 
Objective:
Through the creation of masks, the participants will think of a small, do-able step to take as they boldly envision how they want to create their future. Using the No Limits process, by following their dreams and setting goals, participants will discover their own vision.

Materials:
Polymer Clay (Sculpey Clay) in an assortment of colors
Plastic rolling pins
Rulers
Paper mask template
Scissors and/or plastic knives
Sequins
Small glass beads
Markers or colored pencils
Wooden skewers
24-gauge wire - Optional
Finger paint paper - Optional

Time Frame:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 15 minutes
Creation: 50 minutes
(Baking: about 17 minutes per baking tray)
Closing: 10 minutes
Total: 1 1/2 hours

 
 		 
  Vision Masks materials and set-up 

Set-Up/Prep:
Prior to the workshop, cut Sculpey cubes in half and provide enough so each person has 3 different colors. Use Finger Paint Paper for a smooth, nonstick surface that can be helpful when working the Sculpey. Print or purchase mask template and supply one for each person.

Prior to the workshop be sure to test  the consistency of the clay. The clay should be malleable and not crumbly.

Line baking sheets with brown craft paper to prevent the masks from sticking to the surface.
Note: We recommend having a volunteer to assist with the baking process.

Introduction:
"Forty years ago, the artist Betsy Damon observed that other women artists were struggling to make a living from their art. The result was that many were losing hope and giving up on their dreams of being an artist. To encourage them not to give up, Betsy created the No Limits process.

"In this process, a network of women artists would come together to put forth their greatest visions for what they wanted in their future. They supported one another as they struggled to make their aspirations come to fruition. After sharing their greatest intention, the participants would come up with the very next step (a small, incremental step) that they would take to make their vision a reality. Betsy asked them to focus on small, do-able steps so the participants could see a path to making and seeing their dream come true.

AWBW was founded, in large part, thanks to Betsy's idea! It was practicing the No Limits process that Cathy shared her greatest vision. Her dream was to create a place like A Window Between Worlds and bring art as a healing tool to others, just as it had been a form of safety and a voice for her in the midst of Domestic Violence in her home. At the time, she thought this was a crazy and impossible goal but, with a little encouragement from the other artists and her friends, she took the first step... and we are still here 20 years later!

"We must remember to never underestimate the power of small steps and boldly imagining our own personal visions."

Opening Sharing Circle:
"Today, we will be creating an art workshop designed to help us think of a small, do-able step we can take to create our future. Remember that this future should reflect your own personal vision of what you want in your life, not that of your batterer, children or anyone else.

"I will begin by sharing a poem to help encourage us to think boldly and envision our future called Our Deepest Fear by Marianne Williamson from A Return To Love: Reflections on the Principles of A Course in Miracles.
'Our deepest fear is not that we are inadequate. Our deepest fear is that we are powerful beyond measure. It is our light, not our darkness that most frightens us. We ask ourselves, Who am I to be brilliant, gorgeous, talented, fabulous? Actually, who are you not to be? You are a child of God. Your playing small does not serve the world. There is nothing enlightened about shrinking so that other people won't feel insecure around you. We are all meant to shine, as children do. We were born to make manifest the glory of God that is within us. It's not just in some of us; it's in everyone. And as we let our own light shine, we unconsciously give other people permission to do the same. As we are liberated from our own fear, our presence automatically liberates others.'

"Now, if you feel comfortable enough to do so, please close your eyes and take a minute to breathe and think about or imagine your greatest vision for what you want in your life. Try to picture it in your mind however it comes to you, as an image, a place or a list of things you truly want."

Keeping your vision and the poem in mind, be bold! Cathy thought her vision for A Window Between Worlds could only come true in her wildest dreams and now the organization reaches 65,000 people per year, including you!"

Demonstration:
Ask participants to refrain from working with the materials set out for them until you have demonstrated the entire mask-making project.

"Using three Sculpey colors, we will create a mask that will help to remind us that what we imagine for ourselves and our lives can come true!" You can chose your colors to represent you, your dreams or just colors that you love.

Show a mask sample and demonstrate how to use materials.
STEP 1:
"Start by taking the first color of Sculpey and soften it in your hands. As it softens, begin to roll it between your open hands to make an 8-inch long snake-like shape. You will then do the same with the other two colors that you choose. Then, begin to wrap each 'snake' around each other like a candy cane and gradually twist those colors together. As the 'snake' grows long, bend it in half and twist again. Continue to bend, twist, and roll the Sculpey until the colors are blended together in the way that best supports your vision. Note: If you marble the Sculpey too much, it will over blend the colors together."
   

   Roll Sculpey into 8-inch "snakes"
   Twist the Sculpey to create a "candy cane"
 Fold the "candy cane" in half and twist and roll it again

STEP 2:
"Next, take the clay and lay it flat on the Finger Paint paper and roll it out so it is about 1/8 inch thick. Continue to roll the clay until it is the full dimension of the mask template and trace the mask template onto the Sculpey. Cut out the traced mask shape using scissors or a knife. Also cut the area for the eyes and the two small holes on the sides if you would like to hang the mask after it is baked."
  
  
Roll Sculpey candy cane 1/8 inch thick
  Use rolling pin to flatten Sculpey
  Trace and cut out mask from the Sculpey
STEP 3:
"Decorate the mask with symbols, beads, wire, and/or sequins to represent your greatest and boldest vision. Be sure to firmly press the decorations into the mask so that the embellishments do not come out during baking."
 
 
  Decorate Sculpey with beads, sequins, etc.
 

STEP 4:
Bake the Sculpey masks at 275 degrees for 17 minutes. 

Creation:
"We will be creating our vision masks in two steps. First, we will represent our greatest hope for the future by using colors and symbols to create a mask. We will then bake our creations and after, add the first step we can take toward our vision using markers.
   
 
 
  Group creating Vision Masks 

"To start, create a mask using at least three colors that represent your vision of what you want in your future. For example, if your intention is to have a healthy partner, you could use purple clay to represent DV awareness. Keep in mind that your vision can be your greatest hopes and dreams."

When participants are finished creating their masks, collect them on a baking sheet (make sure that those who would like to hang their masks have placed holes on the sides) and have an assistant bake and monitor them according to the instructions.

While the clay is baking, ask the participants: "Does anyone feel comfortable sharing the greatest vision that you represented on your mask?" After a few participants have shared, you may say something like this, "Thank you for being bold and bravely sharing! Now, I would like for us to take a moment to reflect on what small step you can take to make your dream come true." After a minute or so, ask, "Do you feel you have captured what that step may be?"

If time permits to hold a sharing circle ask participants, "If you feel comfortable, please share your next step. If time is limited try paired sharing. "Choose a partner who you feel safe to share your vision with. Now, using a timer, I will give each person 2 minutes to share both their greatest vision and the next step that they will take. Please try your best to listen quietly to allow the 'sharer' to reflect out loud and support her without making the sharing a conversation."

After the clay has cooked and cooled, and the participants have shared their first step, give each participant their Vision Mask to add the final step.

"Windows was founded because Cathy made sure to think of small, do-able steps to take in order to make her vision come to life. Now, it is your turn to think of the next steps that you need to take in order to begin the process of making your dreams a reality. This is an essential part of the process because it is this very task that enables us to move forward with attaining these visions that might seem impossible!

You can add words, shapes, symbols, doodles, or colors on the inside of the mask by using permanent markers or etching into the clay. These symbols can serve as a reminder of the next step that you can take to see your aspirations come to life!"

STEP 6:
Add wire or ribbon to the small holes at the top so you can hang your mask or add any final touches (i.e. glue on embellishments that cannot be baked).

Closing:
Remember that no matter what anyone says or believes, you can have the future you want! Now you have your vision mask to remind you of your vision and the steps you can take to bring it to light! You can choose to share your mask with others or you can keep it as a special and private reminder for yourself to be bold, follow your heart, and create your future in your own vision!
Row.txt_description: Through the creation of masks, the participants will think of a small, do-able step to take as they boldly envision how they want to create their future. Using the No Limits process, by following their dreams and setting goals, participants will discover their own vision.

Row.str_title: Moving Forward Workshop Series for Children, Part 1
Row.txt_code:
" I'm slowly working through it to come out
a better person. I do not feel like I'm in
bondage anymore. I'm starting to live a
happy and enjoyable life. My past doesn't
have to hold me back from all the
opportunities I'll have in the future."
 
The art has a gentle, but surprising way of bringing the children's inner world to the surface. Some workshops such as Looking at Relationships or Unmasking Me/Unmasking the Future have a deeper focus and can bring up strong feelings. When this happens the children don't always have the language or tools to communicate or understand those feelings. This workshop series offers the children an opportunity to connect with and explore their inner world. This can help them begin to understand their stories and the feelings, beliefs and hopes that go with them. By allowing the children to share about what is on the inside, they can develop a deeper connection with themselves so they can start to move forward.

The first step in empowering children is to help them figure out what their feelings are. Throughout this workshop series, create a discussion with the children/teens about how important it is to understand and share their feelings. Let them know that even if they are scared that others won’t understand or like what they think or feel, an important part of the process of understanding what they need or want is being able to share their story and be heard.
 
 
  

Explain to the children that when sharing how they feel, the other person does not have to agree with them to understand what they are trying to say. It is important to remember that sharing what you feel can be helpful for both the person sharing and the person being shared with, no matter what the feelings are. Also, it can be comforting to know that you are not alone in your feelings and that you don't have to solve every problem on your own. When people start to understand each other, they can help and support each other better.


We also suggest that you pair workshops with some helpful discussion questions we have provided which can help the children further process what they are feeling. For example:
What did your art make you think of?
How did your art make you feel?
Were you surprised by your feelings or reactions?
How did it feel to look at your art and talk about it?

Workshops for Exploring and Understanding Our Inner Worlds:
 "I drew a mountain because it is where
me and my dad always went.
It makes me feel happy and
I have good memories of it.
I want to tell him that I miss him."
 
Inside Me/Outside Me - This workshop provides an opportunity for children to gain insight into the feelings they hide to protect themselves and the feelings they show to the public. This workshop helps children express what they are feeling as opposed to what others say they are feeling.
Scroll: Losses and Hopes - This workshop provides a tangible outlet where participants can express their feelings of grief and vulnerability while acknowledging the gains of leaving the violence and their hopes for the future.
Puppet Fun - This workshop is designed to help children of all ages voice feelings, emotions, fears and inner thoughts through puppetry.
  
  
Looking At Relationships - This collage project gives children and teens an opportunity to look at one relationship in their lives and try to better understand that relationship and how they feel about it.
Letters to the Fathers - Provides a safe place for children to release their emotions and feelings for their father or absent parent.
Inner Self Portraits - This workshop will assist older children and teens to look inside and discover more about their inner-self. We are used to looking at our outer selves, our looks, our clothes, our appearance, the image we try to portray. This workshop gives us an opportunity to go to a deeper level and get more in touch with our inner-self.

Workshops to Share Our Story:
To start this series you might try starting and ending with a group bonding workshop. Creating emotional safety and a sense of shared purpose. We recommend starting with Talking Sticks and ending with I Am Strong Because...
Talking Sticks - To teach children the value of sharing, listening and respecting each others' stories. Talking Sticks teach us that communication can be as much about listening as it is about talking.
Take a Walk in My Shoes - This workshop gives participants an opportunity to communicate what it is like to walk in their shoes and tell the story of their experience.
Story Trees - The Story Tree workshop gives children an opportunity to explore their strength and growth. Using the tree as a symbol of life and courage, participants are free to let their imaginations run wild as they discover what kind of tree they want to be.
   
Unmasking Me/Unmasking the Future - This workshop is for youth to have an opportunity to have their voices be heard first through journaling. Then by creating a mask that dialogues with the abuser and themselves regarding the domestic violence they experienced and/or witnessed.
Speak Out Masks - This workshop is designed to allow participants to speak out about and against domestic violence, as well as to express personal stories for the purpose of creating awareness.
Debut CD - This workshop helps youth make a statement about themselves by making a CD jewel case insert for their debut album!
I Am Strong Because... -  Offers the chance to build a sense of pride in oneself as well as a sense of cohesion within the group about the obstacles and hard times that they have been through. The finished artwork serves as a pride badge and reminder to not give up.

Note: To see the workshops, you must be a registered online leader, and log in with your password. If you are not registered, or need help, contact Cheryl.

Share Your Thoughts: As we continue to develop these themes, we would love to hear your thoughts related to the topics. Please send us your insights, quotes, comments, stories, successes, challenges etc. so we can continue to support you. Click here to submit your stories! We know each of you have tailored the workshops to fit the needs of your clients...we would love for you to share those variations also!!

A Window Opens by Stacy Kahn

Note about Family Workshops:
Since relationships with family members are so important to how we see ourselves and our world, it can be helpful to add a family workshop from our Family Windows curriculum. Try our Family Windows curriculum by using the "Family Windows" Workshop search tool.
Row.txt_description: This workshop series offers the children an opportunity to connect with and explore their inner world. This can help them begin to understand their stories and related feelings, beliefs and hopes. By allowing the children to share about what is on the inside, they can develop a deeper connection with themselves and start to move forward.

Row.str_author_firstname: Janet Shlesman with contributions by AWBW Staff
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Today, we will be creating a mask that will help us see what our lives can be like when we are older. We will choose steps to take to help us see that what we imagine can come true.

  
    Vision Masks materials and set-up 
Materials:
Sculpey Clay (Polymer Clay) in an assortment of colors
Plastic rolling pins
Rulers
Paper mask template
Scissors and/or plastic knives
Sequins
Small glass beads
Markers or colored pencils
Writing paper
Wooden skewers
24-gauge wire - Optional
Finger paint paper - Optional

Time Frame:    Age Range:  
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 15 minutes
Creation: 50 minutes
(Baking: about 17 minutes per baking tray)
Closing: 10 minutes
Total: 1 1/2 hours		      
5-18 years old
Children 5-10 will need extra help with the cutting and decorating
 



 

 
 

Set-Up/Prep:
Before the workshop, cut enough Sculpey (polymer clay) cubes in half so each person can have 3 different colored halves. Working with the Sculpey on Finger Paint Paper provides a smooth, nonstick surface that can be helpful.

Prior to the workshop, be sure to test the consistency of the clay. The clay should be malleable and not crumbly.

Line baking sheets with brown craft paper to prevent the masks from sticking to the surface.

Print or purchase 1 mask template per person.

Note: Children under the age of 7 will need assistance with Step 3. Tracing and cutting the mask can be challenging.

Introduction:
"Today we are making vision masks (show an example that you made or a picture from this workshop). You may be wondering why we call them 'vision' masks. Do you think they will give you better vision like a pair of reading glasses? Nooo...

"We call them 'vision' masks because they can help you see your future. Can anyone tell me what this means? (pause) The future is any time after right now, right? The future can be tomorrow, next week or when we are older.

"How will these magical masks let you see your future? Today we are making these masks by thinking about how we wish or want our future to look like or be. First, we will think about our biggest wishes for when we grow up. Then we will think about what other wishes or steps we might need to come true first, so we can get what we really want in our future.

"How do we get from one place to another? We have to take steps, right? Steps to go upstairs, steps to walk on a crosswalk, etc. Steps take us where we want and need to go! We can also think of steps as things that we need to get from where we are to where we want to be. Thinking of steps to make your wishes come true can help to make it happen!"

Give the children an example such as this: "When I was your age, what I wished for was to be a teacher and a mother. I also wished to live in a place by the beach and to have nice friends. To have all of those things, I thought about what steps I would need to make them happen. First, I worked hard in school so I could become a teacher, then I looked carefully to find a nice person to marry, and I only became friends with the nicest people. Then because I wished to be close to the beach, I worked hard to save my money and buy a house in California."

Warm up:
"I'm going to give you a few minutes to write, draw or just sit and think about the things you really want for your future."

Give the children some drawing paper, pens, and colored paper to put their "vision" on paper. Ask the children,"Take a minute to write or think… what do you wish for your life in the future?"

Creation:
STEP 1: Pick colors for wishes
"To make our masks we are going to first pretend that we found a Genie (like the one in the movie Aladdin) that will grant us 3 wishes for our future. Think of 3 wishes for what you want in your life when you are older. Once you have 3 wishes in your mind, pick 1 color to represent each of your wishes.

"For example, I have 3 colors (show cut Sculpey bars). The blue is to represent my wish for living by the beach, the yellow is to represent my nice friends and family and the green is for my children because it reminds me of when we go to the park.

"Okay, it's your turn, pick out 3 colors for your 3 wishes.

"Now I need your full attention. Put your clay down and look at me. Remember the vision masks I told you about?" Show the picture. "Now that you have thought about your vision and wishes for your future, we are going to create our own vision masks so that we don't forget what our wishes are today."

STEP 2: Combine wishes to make your Vision Mask
Take the first color of Sculpey and soften it in your hands. As it softens, start to roll it between your open hands to make a long snake-like shape. Do the same with the other two colors. Continue to roll until each snake is about 8 inches long. Now begin to wrap each snake around each other like a candy cane and gradually twist those colors together. As  the snake grows long, bend it in half and twist again. Continue to do this until the colors are blended together just the way you like them. Try not to over-blend the colors.
    
 
 Roll out Sculpey into 8-inch snakes Twist the Sculpey to
make a "candy cane"		 Fold the Sculpey
snake and roll again
 
STEP 3: Trace, cut, and decorate (decorating is optional: This step is best suited for older children with the dexterity to embellish the clay)
Take the blended clay and lay it flat on the paper. Roll it out so it is about 1/8 inch thick.  Continue to roll the clay until it is the full dimension of the mask template.

Trace the mask template onto the Sculpey. Cut the traced shape using scissors or a knife.  Also cut the area for the eyes and the two small holes on either side for hanging the mask after it is baked.
  
 
 
  Use rolling pin to flatten Sculpey  Roll Scupley to fit the mask form
 Trace and cut out Sculpey mask
 
Decorate the mask with symbols, beads, wire, and/or sequins to represent what you imagine your life to be like when you are older. This can include some of the wishes you just thought about. Be sure to firmly push the decorations into the mask so they will not pop out during the baking but do not push too hard or they will come out through the back side of the clay.

 
 
  Decorate Sculpey with beads, sequins
and extra Sculpey		 
   
STEP 4: Bake
Bake the Sculpey masks at 275 degrees for 17 minutes.

STEP 5: Preparing the mask to hang
Add wire or ribbon to the small holes at the top so you can hang your mask.

STEP 6: Steps to making our wishes come true
During the baking, go in a circle and have the children share one of their wishes, the color they made it, and why.

When the circle is finished, begin to explain the second part of this workshop.
It can go something like this: "Remember I told you that because I wanted to be a teacher I had to work hard at school? Wishes are a good first step in knowing what you really want, but what do we need to do to make those wishes come true? We could try to find a Genie but that probably won't happen. Can anyone tell me what we need to do if we want to make our wishes come true?

"Now, I want you to think of all the things you need to do to make your wishes come true for your future. If one of your wishes is to go to college, then you will need to do all your homework. If your wish is to be an athlete you need to take care of your body and practice. Right? On your vision masks, I want you to use the markers to write words or shapes on the inside of the mask where only you can see it. Write or draw about the things you need to do starting today or tomorrow to make your wishes come true. If you get stuck, we can talk about it and figure out a plan.

Closing:
"Always remember that no matter what anyone tells you or thinks, you can be anyone you want to be in the future. Now, you have your mask to see what you imagine more clearly and to remind you what you can do to make your wishes come true! Even if you forget, need a little help remembering or want to show someone that your wishes are real, you now have your beautiful mask to prove it. You are the only one that can see what you imagine through your mask and you can keep it with you always!"
  
  Completed Vision Mask
Row.txt_description: We will create a mask that will help the children see what their life can be like when they are older. They will choose steps to take to help them see that what they imagine can come true.

Row.str_title: Moving Forward Workshop Series for Children, Part 2
Row.txt_code:
Sometimes it can be challenging to imagine what we want for our future. Part 1 of this series was designed to help the children connect with their feelings and better understand their personal stories. In this part of the series we will help the children look toward their future.

Understanding what it is that we imagine for our future can help us build the steps needed to achieve our dreams. The art can help make those transitions and visions happen in a relaxed and empowering way.

Some workshops that can help this process are:
Vision Masks — To create a mask that will help the children see what their life can be like when they are older. They will choose steps to take to help them to see that what they imagine can come true.
   
   

Three Wishes — This workshop allows a window of time where the children can express their wishes for the past, present or future. Depending on which age group you are working with, you can modify the complexity of your direction and focus.

Turning Over a New Leaf — To provide children with the opportunity to use the symbol of turning over a new leaf. This process allows the children to think of their past and turn it over, transforming it into a new life.

My Footprints — This allows children to validate and express feelings about their unique journey, creating collages about where they have been, what they are learning, and where they want to go in their lives.

Vision Boards — To provide the children with an opportunity to create a Vision Board to help them see a future filled with what they want and need. The Vision Board can help them feel as if they are getting ready to live their dream life right now by watching it daily.

"I don't want my children to
grow up in a house of violence,
I want it to be peaceful." 

 
"I have the right to be safe,
I have the right to ask for help,
I have the right to speak up.
Say NO, get away and tell."

"I want a house. Not a big one,
just one I can be happy in."
 

Create Your Own Calendar! — This workshop gives participants a special opportunity to talk about goals for the year, plan things they want to accomplish, and mark times to celebrate or look forward to, by creating their own calendar.

A Dream House — This family workshop provides the  children with an opportunity to explore with their family a vision of the future they can have, free from domestic violence. Working together as one, in creating a representation of their future home, they can bond and look forward with a shared vision.

 
 
Note: To see the workshops, you must be a registered online leader, and log in with your password. If you are not registered, or need help, contact Cheryl.

Row.txt_description: By imagining what they want in the future, children are taking the first steps needed to achieve their dreams. This workshop series allows children to see where they want to go in their lives and begin to explore this vision for themselves and their families.

Row.str_title: Moving Forward Workshop Series for Adults, Part 2
Row.txt_code:
"I've really been thinking a lot about the art project we made last week.
It helped me to realize I want to move forward. When I was doing it, I was just kind of thinking 'this is fun arts and crafts' and I wanted to make it look pretty.
But I really want the things I put on there -- empowerment; to feel beautiful.
I think I am going to go back home and see where I put it. I am going to look at it again. Maybe I will take it with me and look at it whenever I need to."
- Inner Self Portrait Participant

  
In the first part of the series, Moving Forward Workshop Series for Adults, Part 1, the participants explored their inner and outer world in order to gain perspective and clarity to move forward. As the survivors find clarity to move forward, they begin to envision a world created by them. This final part of the series will help the participants to both envision and create their own future through tangible steps. It is important to remind the survivors that everyone takes their own time to explore, reflect, and utilize their window of time to create a vision for the future. Through the art process, participants have the opportunity to explore their vision for the near and distant future and discover how their present life is supporting that vision. Once we have the awareness of that vision, all that we can do is remain true to ourselves.

Workshops for Letting Go of the Past and Welcoming the Future:
Stepping Stones — Participants write words, shapes, symbols on stones they create to remind them of what they are walking away from and walking toward in their lives.

Journey Footprints — Participants create collages that validate their unique journey past, present and future through domestic violence using the outline of their own feet.

Turning Over a New Leaf — To provide participants with the opportunity to think of their old leaves (past) and turn it over, transforming it into a new leaf, and a new life.

Changing Our 'Baggage' - This workshop gives participants an opportunity to reflect on what kind of "baggage" we carry and how it is possible to change it. By changing the focus to the qualities that empower us, we can begin to create the life we wish to experience.

The Garden of New Beginnings — As we grow, each person has the opportunity to create the future that they want for themselves. This workshop helps promote the visualization of a new beginning by planting seeds for what they want in their lives and hope for the future.

 "I feel like I've wasted a lot of years in my life not moving forward, although I don't regret anything I've been through. I just feel now is the time to move forward healthily and follow my dreams." 
 
 

Permission Canvases — This workshop will give the participants permission to do something they have been longing to do, to change a habit, or let go of something.

Workshops for Envisioning and Creating our Future:
In order to envision the new beginning that we wish to move towards, it is important to visually create that future for ourselves. By putting our minds to something and working to build a life for ourselves, we have the power to turn that vision into a reality.

Spirit Candles - The Spirit Candles workshop gives participants the opportunity to search for the strength and energy or light that nurtures and guides our spirit as we prepare for new beginnings. The participants can decorate candles by collaging their greatest dreams and deepest hopes onto them.

Pastel Windows — This workshop allows the participants to create a window with the chalk into the world of present feelings and needs, and then another window into the world of visions and hopes for the future.

 
Notes From The Future — This workshop encourages participants to think positively about their future by creating a postcard from their future self. This is a great workshop for those that feel stuck in their present situation.

Center of My Universe - Participants can take the time to focus on placing themselves at the center of their universe. Each participant's vision of what it means to put themselves as a priority unfolds throughout the collaging creation process.

Vision Masks - Through the creation of masks, the participants will think of a small, do-able step to take as they boldly envision how they want to create their future. Using the No Limits process, by following their dreams and setting goals, participants will discover their own vision.


Vision Boards - To provide participants with an opportunity to create a Vision Board to help them bring to life their vision for a future filled with what they want and need in their life.

Collage Pins (Vision Pins) - This workshop allows participants to see their creative potential and express their emotions and dreams. The pin is a reminder to relax, and to take time out of the day to unwind. 

Note: To see the workshops, you must be a registered online leader, and log in with your password. If you are not registered, or need help, contact Cheryl.

See the Developing a Positive Vision for the Future testimonial and read how the art can positively impact future decision choices, relationships, and goals.
