Row.str_title: Opening Up and Expressing Emotions Series for Adults
Row.txt_code:
"My art opens me up to my feelings!"
- Adult Windows Participant


 
As humans, we are constantly feeling! From the time that we wake up, until we fall asleep, our minds, bodies, and spirits experience countless different emotions. Even while we are sleeping, our subconscious is fast at work sorting through different moods. While it can be very easy to feel many ways, it is much harder to find the courage, strength, and honesty to express what that is.

The concept of opening up can be challenging for anyone. This task becomes especially difficult after a batterer has told a survivor that what he or she thinks does not matter. Through this negative reinforcement, it becomes even harder to believe that how one feels is not only worth sharing, but that it is essential to do so to heal. As a survivor, the participants now have the freedom to express their emotions without judgment. The experience of expressing feelings in a safe space, sometimes for the first time, empowers survivors with a valuable tool for their future. It is through opening up that we are able to express not only our deepest emotions but also our deepest selves.

  "I love to share my opinions with others...
  It just makes me feel a lot better about myself
and it makes my emotions open up more."
 - Adult Windows Participant
This series of workshops offers many opportunities for the participants to gently explore what is below the surface through creation. With the variety of mediums and techniques offered, the
survivors can express themselves artistically through their art projects while acknowledging and revealing their feelings. Since revealing emotions, especially after trauma, can be so difficult, it is important to be patient and understanding of the process. This journey through art can help the survivors heal and can bring up surprising and intense emotions (for more ideas, refer to the Processing Anger Series for Adults). Through the safety of art and the window of time provided to them, it is essential to encourage the participants to not censor themselves and to freely share at their own pace.

 
 
Feelings Target —  This warm-up workshop can serve as an ice-breaker for the participants to identify and express their feelings. The participants can share about their emotions in a playful manner while listening to others and recognizing that we all experience a myriad of feelings.

Crayon Feelings — This expressive workshop gives participants a chance to put their feelings into shapes and colors while experiencing a completely free, no-pressure, expressive process - free from worrying about what it will look like and if it will be judged.

Mini-Workshops — Through several short workshops ideas, participants can enjoy the freedom of expressing their feelings using drawing and painting. These workshops are simple in materials and concept but can quickly serve to help draw out emotions.

Feelings Collages — This workshop was designed to give the participants a chance to focus on the ordeal they experienced which brought them into the shelter and their feelings related to this transition. Participants create a collage that can serve as a reminder of their strength and courage and can be used as a reminder of why they left.

Befriending Your Feelings — Allows participants an opportunity to explore and understand their feelings, know that all feelings are acceptable, and notice what their relationship to their feelings is like today.Through a series of quick, intuitive drawings, the focus is placed on tapping into the different emotions.

     "The ladies were able to open up and share parts
of themselves that they had buried down deep
and didn't want people to see."
- Adult Windows Leader
      




Journaling — Writing in a fluid and non-stop manner helps participants acknowledge and express their feelings without putting intense thought into the process.

 Inside/Outside — To explore and notice the feelings that you exhibit on the outside and the emotions that you feel deeply on the inside or underneath.

Sides of Myself —  This workshop gives participants an opportunity to notice and accept different sides of themselves and the feelings associated with them by creating two contrasting CrayPas drawings.

 
 
  Miniature Mask-Making workshop
 
Miniature Mask-Making — This workshop allows participants to express their feelings and identify their emotions. The participants have a chance to look at their own profound reflections and thoughts through their creation.

Sculpey Expression Faces — To learn to identify and express our range of feelings to begin a healing process through various techniques. The faces created can help to connect to our feelings and expressions of those feelings.

"It's like opening up a water faucet and allowing ourselves to be nourished with our own feelings, hopes and strengths." - Adult Windows Leader

Heart Workshops — A collection of heart themed workshops by different leaders help the participants to identify different feelings held within their hearts.

   
  Treasure Box workshop
 
My Treasure Box — Gives each participant the opportunity to recognize what he or she feels. The creation of the treasure box allows the participants to cherish these emotions and acknowledge their blessings, dreams, beliefs, friendships, hopes, and to hold and protect them in a safe place, just like their feelings.

Personal Needs Flower — Provides an opportunity for participants to tune into their own personal needs by creating a flower where each petal represents one need and emotions. They begin to see the many layers of needs and feelings and to honor them.
See the Paying Attention to ME warm up Variation for a deeper focus on the needs and emotions associated with one's Physical, Emotional, and Spiritual self.

   
  Me Dolls workshop 
Me Dolls — This workshop allows the participants to create a doll that they feel represents a version of themselves. Each artist can reach within their emotions and create a "me" that perhaps no one has heard or seen before. This doll can express the feelings of the participant and celebrate their strengths.

   "This is the first time I opened up to people about me."
                        - Adult Windows participant

Row.str_title: Opening Up and Expressing Emotions Series for Children
Row.txt_code:
Most of us find it difficult to identify, express, and share our feelings. Children who have experienced trauma have a particularly difficult time sorting through and coping with their emotions. All the emotions they feel at one time can be very confusing, especially when some of these emotions might be totally opposite from each other, such as... a child might be mad about leaving home but, on some level, they might also feel relieved.

This workshop series is designed to help children express themselves through the use of specific art activities to identify, explore and share their feelings. The children will learn to notice and gently explore what can be difficult to express and find a variety of ways of expressing themselves through the art. Through the safety of art and the window of time provided to them, the children can begin to share and release some of their emotions.

It is important to explain to the children that by not telling someone if they are feeling sad, worried, scared or upset, it can make it harder on them. If they don't share these emotions, then they are all alone with these difficult feelings. Sometimes keeping all or these feelings inside can make them feel sick or depressed or even be the reason for violent behaviors. The workshops listed below can be used to help the children express their feelings, manage their anger, and cope with stress. For more ideas, refer to the Processing Anger Series for Children. The goal is to help the children cope with their overwhelming experiences and emotions and heal.

We recommend the following:
 
 
Feelings Faces — Offers time to learn about feelings, identify with them, and express them as art. The Feeling Faces can be helpful and fun reminders of what the children have learned.

Children Throughout The World Are Victims Too — Offers a chance to educate, discuss and have children share their feelings about being in a family with domestic violence. While doing the workshop, children learn that children all over the world have experienced domestic violence issues.

A Book About Me — This workshop assists young children in exploring feelings about their stay in the shelter.

Tear Catcher Dolls — This workshop helps teens find a creative way to explore and express their feelings and thoughts on grief (as well as other feelings of sorrow, joy and pain) that would usually find an outlet in the form of tears.

 I am happy in the shelter
because I don't have to be
afraid anymore.
 
Feelings Target — This activity is a playful way to allow the children to share about a time they felt a feeling in a group setting. This workshop helps the children to notice the spectrum of feelings and that all children feel all of the different emotions. This warm-up can stand alone as a workshop or can be used to support other workshops.

   
Paying Attention to ME — Feelings and needs are intrinsically tied together. This workshop helps the children to focus on identifying their own personal needs to feel happy and healthy, as well as serve as a reminder that they each have unique needs.

Tunnel Books — This workshop helps children get in touch with their feelings and express them in a safe way. It can really help children understand the feelings they keep inside and the feelings they show on the outside.

Heart Stories — This workshop supports children and teens in sharing their hearts and stories through art. The workshop gives them an opportunity to listen to their hearts, value the stories within them, and know that others want to hear them too.

Expressing Feelings with Watercolor — Allows the children time to express their feelings without criticism. Gives the opportunity to experience the magic and beauty of seeing something invisible become visible.
 I am going to wear my art
as a necklace to remind me
that it's OK to love.		 
   

Sculpey Expression Faces — To use new techniques of working with Polymer Clay (sculpey), and learn to identify and express our range of feelings to begin a healing process. The faces created can help us connect to our feelings and expressions of those feelings.

As children express a wide variety of feelings that need to come out, it is essential to their healing process to give them opportunities to feel hope, joy and recognize their worth.

These workshops are recommended for help in expressing those positive emotions:

   
My Happy Self — This workshop gives young children an opportunity to express happiness through their art. It helps them focus on themselves and share their feelings with others. The end result will create a “People Rainbow” of happiness for all to see.

Loving Lilies — This workshop will give participants an opportunity to recognize what they like and appreciate about themselves. It also gives them an opportunity to share a lily with a loved one, even if they are that person!

 This is my path with the
Important things for me:
lots of love, friends,
be self-confident, be
cool, be able to share
emotion.		 
What Makes Me Shine — Offers children the opportunity to see themselves through their own eyes and notice the things that make them shine by creating a sun full of rays with the words, images, and colors that make them special.

Feel Good Hearts — This workshop provides a window of time for each child to think of messages that are positive and encouraging about themselves and others. These words will be shared and added to heart books, which will become a fun and beautiful reminder of how special they are.


 
My Dancing Monster — Children will create a dancing monster and experience the joy and freedom of letting themselves go in the monster dance.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop warm-up helps participants notice and express their feelings, and encourages group bonding.

Materials:
Feeling face template (multiple expressions)
8 1/2 x 11 Printable Brave/Scared Face Template
8 1/2 x 11 Printable Calm/Mad Face Template
8 1/2 x 11 Printable Happy/Sad Face Template
8 1/2 x 11 Printable Proud/Shy Face Template
8 1/2 x 11 Printable Loving Face Template
Paper plates (optional)
Pennies or small sandbag
Timer (optional)
Note: This warm-up can stand alone as workshop or can be used to support other workshops.

Set-up:
Using the templates provided, print out the feelings faces. You might want to print more than one set. You can cut the circles out and glue them onto paper plates, or you can use them as they are.  Before the warm-up, group the faces together on the floor.

Workshop Warm-up:
“Today we’re going to play a game where you will each have a chance to share about your feelings. When we talk about our feelings, whether they are ones we like or ones that are difficult for us, it gives us the freedom to be ourselves and notice what's alive for us!”

Let participants know that we all have many different feelings, and even sometimes we feel all of these emotions simultaneously. In one day, we can feel joyful, upset, angry, and proud. Remember that while many of these feelings may seem uncomfortable, strange, challenging, or frustrating, it is useful to acknowledge each and every one of them! 
Have the first participant stand a few feet away from the plates and toss a penny/sandbag towards them. If the penny/sandbag lands on a face, the participant will share a story about the last time (or any time) they felt that particular feeling. For example, if the penny lands on the “happy” face, the participant will share about the last time (or anytime) they felt happy.  Depending on the size of the group, allow the participants to talk for at least one minute. If the penny/sandbag lands between two feelings, the participant can talk about either one of the feelings (move the penny/sandbag on top of the feeling the participant will be talking about). The other participants can practice listening as each person shares. Make sure everyone has an opportunity to take a turn or pass. If there’s time, you can go around a second or third time.

You can also incorporate more embodied art into the warm-up by giving participants the option to make a statue of the feeling instead of sharing verbally. For example, you might say, "Another option is that instead of talking, you can show us an image (statue) of that emotion. For example, here's what I look like when I'm nervous." Create a statue with your body, perhaps by hiding your face behind your hands and crouching down. 

You might also give the participants an opportunity to practice making images together by saying, "Let's do a demo. Everyone show what you look like when you're feeling excited in 3-2-1-FREEZE." Count slowly, and give participants an opportunity to notice how many different ways there are to show excitement. 

If it’s feasible, you can also do this warm up outside!
Row.txt_description: This activity is a playful way to allow participants to share about a time they felt a feeling in a group setting. This workshop helps the children to notice the spectrum of feelings and that all children feel all of the different emotions. This warm-up can stand alone as workshop or can be used to support other workshops.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_description: This activity is a playful way to allow the participants to share about emotions. This workshop helps them to notice the spectrum of feelings and realize that all people feel a variety of different emotions. This warm-up can stand alone as workshop or can be used to support other workshops.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways.  Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To use new techniques of working with Polymer Clay (Sculpey) and to learn to identify and express our range of feelings to begin a healing process. The faces created can help to connect to our feelings and expressions of thos e feelings.


 
Sample set-up using optional tools to create.
 
 
Sample Expression Face.
 
Materials:
Sculpey (Polymer Clay) in assorted colors
Wooden skewers or tooth picks
Clay tools or plastic knives
Drinking straws
Scissors
Finger paint paper or clean surface to work on
Toaster ovens
Timer for timing the baking of the faces
Telephone wire (Optional)
Acrylic rollers/brayers (Optional)
Magnets or pin backs (Optional)

Age Range:
7 years old to Adult

Time Frame:
1 hour and 30 minutes

Workshop Preparation:
Set the table with all the supplies and preheat toaster ovens to 265 degrees using a calibrator or oven thermometer.

Introduction:
Today we are going to be changing the look of our faces by using clay. Expressions can change depending on our mood and feelings. Expressions can change from frowns to smiles, from anger to joy, from bored to excited. Sometimes our feelings can change while we are being creative working with the clay, as we may release difficult thoughts and feelings.

Warm Up:
Pick up a piece of the clay to begin to condition it for easier use, by warming it up in our hands. Start by rolling the clay into a ball, then into a long thin snake. Fold the snake in half and reshape it into a ball, then again into a snake. Keep rolling, twisting and kneading until the clay is soft and pliable, but still has stretch to it when pulled.

Now, close your eyes, if you feel comfortable, and try to imagine a face inside the clay that is waiting to come out. Think about what the face looks like and how the face can show what you are feeling. Sometimes we can feel more than one way at a time!

Open your eyes when you are ready and select colors that you like - remember that the face we will create is a product of our imaginations. We can create a face for each of the feelings we are experiencing or put all of our feelings into one face.

   
 Blending clay technique to create swirls or
marbling effect.		 
   
   
  Twirling wire around a pen to create curling effect. 
   
   
  Poking wire into face to add hair. 
   
Creation:
You will be using various techniques to create different effects with the clay. Before we begin creating our faces let's discuss some of these techniques. The first of these techniques is swirling the clay. For example, take a pea size of red and white. Stretch out each color into a 2 inch snake shape. Then warp the colors around each other so they swirl together (like a barber pole or candy cane). The more you twirl, the finer the design. If you keep twisting and rolling eventually the colors will blend to form a new color -- pink! Or you can use the clay stripped.

The next technique is layering the clay. Notice how the clay has the ability to stick to itself. Take one piece of clay, set it on top of another one and push in using a tool or your fingers. The layers will melt together in the baking process.

Step 1:
To form a simple face, roll a 2 inch round ball of clay and flatten to about 1/4 inch then reshape into an oval or any other shape that expresses the feeling(s) you want to express.

Step 2:
Next we will add the features. The eyes can be little balls of clay placed in the face and flattened with the round end of a paint brush or your fingers. Eyebrows, noses, mouths etc, can be added in the same way. Talk about different expressions and what they look like on our faces. For example, lips can curl up for a smile or down for a frown.

Step 3:
Decorations such as beads, sequins and colored wires for crazy wild hair can be added by pushing it in so that the clay comes up around it. You may even need to add more clay and sort of sandwich the wire decoration to make sure they are secured onto the piece. Another way to attach wire etc. to the mask is to poke holes using straws and add after the baking process is done.


Step 4:
Place the faces on a tray for baking at 265 degrees for 17 minutes.

Step 5 (optional):
Add pin backs or magnets to the back of the faces.

Closing:
Ask each participant to share their work and talk about what feelings show on their Expression Faces.
Row.txt_description: To use new techniques of working with Polymer Clay (sculpey) and to learn to identify and express our range of feelings to begin a healing process. The faces created can help to connect to our feelings and expressions of those feelings.

Row.txt_code:
Oak of Mercy by Lori Minick created for the
Story Tree Exhibit		 
What is the Impact of an Art Exhibit?
Art exhibitions are a powerful way to break the silence that allows domestic violence to continue in our communities.

Statistics of Domestic Violence are staggering. An estimated 1.3 million women are victims of physical assault by an intimate partner each year and on average, more than three women and one man are murdered by their intimate partners in this country every day!  An Art Exhibit can educate the community and help survivors be heard.

"The exhibit increased understanding about shame and
other barriers survivors experience as well as the healing power of art."
SAN-South Asian Network - Sunoh! Tell Me Sister March 2011

A Window Between Worlds Art Exhibition HIstory
   
Since 1992, AWBW has facilitated almost 200 exhibitions in 19 states with our network of shelter partners. Exhibit sites have ranged from museums and art centers to colleges, department stores and even the US Senate Building in Washington D.C.

Our most recently completed work, Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence, a collaborative art project led by internationally acclaimed L.A. artist and survivor Kim Abeles, engaged over 800 survivors and 425 dedicated community members in 80 hands-on workshops. With an initial audience of 2,281 at the Korean Cultural Center Los Angeles, it then received a curatorial invitation to appear at the Skirball Cultural Center, where an estimated 400,000 visitors viewed the exhibit September '11 - May '12. Click here: Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence Workshop (Paper Version) created by AWBW Staff and adapted from Pearls of Wisdom Project by Kim Abelesto lead your own Exhibit.

 
 
Many exhibits have included hands-on participatory components that invite viewers to join in the creation process and raise their own voices to bring an end to the violence. In 2012 the community engaged art project, I CAN: Requiem for I Can't, takes the voices of survivors to a new level of visibility. In collaboration with internationally recognized artist and educator, Suzanne Lacy; renowned performance artist Barbara T. Smith; post graduate artists in residency from Otis College of Art and Design's MFA Public Practice Program, Neda Moridpour and Teresa Flores; and shelter partners throughout Los Angeles we are building on the high level of visibility of Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence. This collaborative art project offers tools to mobilize social change on a wide spectrum, from the deeply personal and familial levels to the collective and communal and illuminates the relationship between these diverse levels of social change.

To plan your own Exhibit, please refer to AWBW's Leader's Exhibit Guide:

Why Hold an Exhibit?
An exhibit of survivors art is an important tool that raises awareness and helps to break the silence of domestic violence. They help to amplify the voices of survivors in a safe way that protects their privacy yet spark public dialogue and build momentum to end domestic violence. In addition, hosting an Exhibit:
— Empowers clients and builds pride in their work
— Gives a public, yet confidential and safe voice to the survivors
— Helps clients' self-esteem and builds pride in their work
— Creates awareness and support for your agency
— Educates the public about domestic violence and sexual assault
— Raises awareness and helps to break the silence of domestic violence
— Creates opportunities for community engagement
— Sparks dialogue on the subject of Domestic Violence
— AWBW can provide funding opportunities to support you

"The exhibit impacted the community in a very positive way.
Not only did it get our group out but it also helped bring awareness
to all types of abuse issues."
Sexual Assault/Domestic Violence Center

Building a support community through art and exhibit.

"This was such an inspiring and positive month. The theme of giving thanks and being grateful really got to the children. It was amazing to see some of their attitudes and behaviors change this month." 
 
Thanksgiving is the perfect time to help children notice the good that exists in their lives. When children feel anxious, sad or loss due to the circumstances that bring them to the Windows Program, it may be challenging for them to understand how gratitude is useful or even relevant in their lives. Now that Thanksgiving is almost here, we want to show how gratitude can not only make children feel happy and hopeful, but it can be practiced in meaningful ways - not just during the holidays but everyday!

Creating an "attitude of gratitude" is something we have heard about, but how can this be achieved? Here are some small, but impactful ways to "teach" or practice gratitude with children:
 "I am thankful that today
we can make our art and
get along; it's like it brought
peace to us today."
 
Encourage a child to write thank you notes or letters to special people in their lives as an acknowledgment for some kind deed or help that was given by that person. This teaches children that thanking someone is about more than when something material has been given, and helps them feel supported and cared for by the  people in their lives.

 "I am thankful for
my heart, that I am
able to love!"		 
Help the children create a "Gratitude Journal." It can be a place for the child to write or draw about something that happened during the day that they were glad or happy about. These things can be simple, like "the weather was good today, not too hot and not too cold." "We played a fun game at recess" or, "I had a yummy snack after school today." This teaches children that expressing gratitude doesn't have to be about big events and that many small, good things can happen in a day.

 "It was great to direct the
children to focus on the
positive aspects of their
lives and the things they
are thankful for."
 
Create a "Happiness Jar." Ask the children to write or draw on a card something that makes them happy. These can be simple things. For example, one card can say, "I am happy at the beach." Another can say, "I like to bake cookies" or "I enjoy drawing pictures for my friends." Collect these cards in a clear jar for each child. When the child is feeling overwhelmed by a specific situation or is unhappy, they can select a card as a reminder of the things that have made them happy in the past. This teaches children that there is always something that you can be thankful for.

An art activity is a powerful way to remind a child of the things in their lives that are positive and worth celebrating. The following workshops focus on gratitude and help us to show and express gratitude for each other and ourselves during the holidays and beyond.

   
  Three Warm Fuzzies
 
Warm Fuzzy
This workshop gives participants a tangible reminder to treat one another with love and kindness, as they are two positive things that we will never run out of. This important message will be conveyed via a fairy tale about corruption and the power of love. Participants will create their own warm fuzzy.

Shrinky Dink Blessing Charms - Holidays with HeART Series
In this workshop, participants make charms out of Shrinky Dinks that represent what they are grateful for and how they are blessed.
 
 
 
 "I am grateful for all of my
friends and family."		 "I am grateful for having
a place to live."		 

 
 
  Leaves of Thanks
 
Leaves of Thanks
To teach children a new way to look at what they are thankful for now and what they might be thankful for in their future.  

 "I am thankful for having a roof over my head
and a great family that is always there for
me. I am also grateful for having a healthy life."
 





  
The Grateful Gobbler 
The Grateful Gobbler
This project is great for all ages and enables the children to create a festive centerpiece to proudly display on their Thanksgiving dinner table. While creating their Grateful Gobbler the children focus on what they are thankful for, and an optional exercise is included that allows the children's family to share all of the things they are thankful for as well.

Giving Thanks Placemats
To have children reflect on the many things in life to be thankful for by creating Giving Thanks Placemats that they can then use or give as gifts for the holidays.

   
   Tom the Thankful Turkey 
Tom the Thankful Turkey
This workshop helps children think about the things they are thankful for and work together to create "Tom the Thankful Turkey".

 "It is always great to hear that children are grateful, not only for the material things in their lives, but for the people in it too."  

 

 
Fall Workshops: Show Me your Tail Feathers; Let Bad Feelings Fall
Two workshops that provide a wonderful way to take the themes of the Fall season and use them to explore emotions; what we are proud of as well as letting go of bad feelings.

   
 
  Show Me your Tail Feathers
  Let Bad Feelings Fall Away
 

Helping Hands and Feet Turkey
To create a simple fun way to show how our hands and feet can be used to think about the holidays and how we can help others.

    
 Helping Hands and
Feet Turkey		   
 "It was rewarding listening to the girls speak excitedly about all the things they are thankful for. After speaking about how they are thankful for music, we started to dance and sing as a group. It was super silly fabulous fun! It made me, the facilitator, feel like a kid again."

We know each of you have tailored the workshops to fit the needs of your clients... We would love for you to share those variations, too!

Row.txt_description: These workshops help the children to notice the good in their lives and be thankful. They can focus on gratitude and help us to show and express gratitude in meaningful ways for each other and ourselves during the holidays and everyday.

Row.txt_code:
"I am thankful for this program
that has helped me to transform
and believe in myself."
- AWBW Participant,
Leaves of Thanksgiving
  
 
It's wonderful when we can take a window of time to reflect on all of life's gifts and what we are thankful about! Sometimes our heart just feels too full of other emotions to notice what we are happy about. Even during the times that it may feel challenging to appreciate the things that make us smile, it is so important to give ourselves the space to do so. In the spirit of Thanksgiving, the participants can take the time to notice the things in their lives that they feel are going well or on their way. This workshop series provides an opportunity for the survivors to nurture and connect to their hearts. As they create, participants can express gratitude through art that they can use during the holiday season, and carry with them throughout the year.
   
  Gratitude Journals
 
A helpful and useful tool to inspire and instill a positive perspective is for the participants (and Leaders as well) to create a Gratitude Journal! This journal can be a special place to write or draw about the people or experiences that they are thankful for and all the different ways their hearts have been touched. By noticing and reflecting on what they are grateful for, these journal can become a reference to go back to when they need a little inspiration to feel their gratitude. By decorating the journals in their own unique way, they will also have a beautiful place to go that holds their thankful thoughts and will be more encouraged to continue to write or draw in it, even on a daily basis.

"Thank you, this was a fun
and simple yet challenging exercise.
I thought of a lot of stuff
that I was grateful for
and I am very grateful for myself."
- AWBW Participant,
Thank Me Card
Beginning the group with an opening circle and simply asking the participants, "what does gratitude mean to you?" or "when do you feel thankful?" allows people to check-in with themselves and offers an open ended opportunity to reflect and notice where they are at in terms of thankfulness. Gratitude can come from the past, present, or the hope for the future! For all of us it could be a wonderful opportunity to try to get back in touch with that emotion and what it feels like. By checking in with themselves and noticing what they are grateful for, they have the opportunity to consider and honor the feelings that come up for themselves and others. Sharing in a group setting can further increase the sense of unity and help participants to uncover that are grateful for one another, the group, their window of time or even the art itself. Even when times get tough and we feel emotionally overwhelmed we can remind ourselves and each other that we can there is something or someone to be grateful for. We can gently encourage others to illustrate this state of being too!
 
 "I am thankful to be here at this workshop and be able to express
my feelings and things I want to accomplish in life."
- AWBW Participant,
Funeral of "I Can'ts"
 
Our journals and thankfulness can be carried with us whenever and wherever we go and we can encourage our friends and family to embody this way of thinking as well. These workshops are a fun and beautiful way of connecting to ourselves, each other and the holiday season. For the holidays, we can try to hold on to the spirit of Thanksgiving and make it last not only on the day or month of, but all year long!

These workshops focus on gratitude and can help us to show and express gratitude for each other and ourselves.
   
Thank me card - This workshop gives participants the opportunity to look at the things they are grateful for in their lives and appreciate themselves by creating a thank you card to themselves.

Leaves of Thanksgiving - This workshop give participants time to reflect on the things they are grateful for in their past, present, and future and time to create beautiful leaves representing these things.
  "Just being able to take a closer look at themselves and express what they feel
allowed them to see what they have and where they are today. They realized they have a lot to be grateful for; for life itself and even just being able to smile again."
- AWBW Leader,
Leaves of Thanksgiving
 
 
 
Gratitude Mandalas - Gives participants an opportunity to reflect on different aspects of themselves (body, heart, mind, and spirit) and notice their gratitude for gifts and blessings associated with each of these aspects.
Gratitude Journals - Gives participants time to reflect on the good and positive aspects of her life. The end products are individualized, personalized journals, expressions of those positive aspects and a place to record daily gratitude lists and strengths.
 "I am grateful for the art of life and learning how to deal with my emotions through it."
- AWBW Participant,
Stuff Your Stockings Full of Joy
 
Holiday Inspiration Cards - Provides an opportunity for participants to explore and express their own personal, positive perspective for the holiday season by choosing their own message of inspiration, and creating holiday cards which reflect this message.
Holiday Feeling Collages - Helps participants identify and explore feelings about the approaching holidays. Helps each person find creative ways to be thoughtful and loving toward herself during the holidays.
   
Affirmation Gems - Provides participants with a beautiful, tangible tool to help focus on affirming that which is positive and growth-promoting within themselves. The Affirmation Gems can be displayed in a bowl also created during the workshop.
The Reasons We Smile - Helps to remind the participants that even though life can be hard, there are daily overlooked reasons for us to smile.
 "I am very grateful for this workshop.
It has helped me talk about much of the things
I keep bottled up inside."
- AWBW Participant,
Women's Windows Workshop
 

 
 
Facilitating these workshops is a meaningful way to reach the participants during this holiday season, especially if any challenging feelings come up for them. Encourage the participants to think about what they are happy for and feel good about in their lives through providing them with a window of time to safely express themselves! Through facilitating four workshops (gratitude, Holidays with HeART series or other) or more during the months of November and December, you will receive a special Holidays with HeART incentive so that we can show our gratitude to YOU for all of the wonderful work you do!

Please send us your insights, quotes, comments, stories, successes, challenges etc. so we can continue to support you. Click here to submit your stories! We know each of you have tailored the workshops to fit the needs of the participants you work with... We would love for you to share those variations, too!

Oak of Mercy by Lori Minick created for the
Story Tree Exhibit		 
Statistics of Domestic Violence are staggering. An estimated 1.3 million women are victims of physical assault by an intimate partner each year and on average, more than three women and one man are murdered by their intimate partners in this country every day. Art exhibitions are a powerful way to break the silence that allows domestic violence to continue in our communities.

A Window Between Worlds Art Exhibition History

Since 1992, AWBW has facilitated almost 200 exhibitions in 19 states with our network of shelter partners. Exhibit sites have ranged from DV Conferences and shelter events at local libraries and colleges,  police departments and even the US Senate Building in Washington D.C.

Our most recent and successful completed work, Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence, a collaborative art project led by internationally acclaimed L.A. artist and survivor Kim Abeles, engaged over 800 survivors in AWBW programs and 425 dedicated community members and an estimated 400,000 visitors viewed the exhibit.

While we encourage partners to reach for their greatest exhibit vision we realize resources are limited. We aim to make the process as easy as possible by providing our Program Leaders with planning aids, workshop ideas, consultation and funding.  To lead your own Pearls of Wisdom exhibit click here (link) or see below for other powerful (and feasible!) exhibition ideas.
To lead your own Pearls of Wisdom exhibit click here (link).

Refer to:
 - this Guide. Link PDF version of entire Guide

What is the impact of a Survivors Art Exhibit?
An exhibit of survivors art is an important tool that raises awareness and helps to break the silence of domestic violence.  The specific reasons are as follows:
Helps clients to build self-esteem and pride in their work
Gives a public, yet confidential and safe voice to the survivors
Creates awareness and support for your agency, including potential funding
Sparks dialogue on the subject of Domestic Violence in the community
Educates the public about domestic violence and sexual assault
Raises awareness and helps to break the silence inherent in domestic violence

 
 
     
In what ways do survivors feel empowered by exhibiting their artwork?
Seeing your personal creations exhibited can create a sense of pride and self worth than can be empowering in ways that are hard to imagine. Some of those ways are:
Affirms and validates their story of survival
Confirms that they have wisdom to share with others and educate the community
Builds a community of support in discovering that they are not alone
Gives survivors feel a sense of purpose when giving back
By sharing their individual experience through their unique voice, myths and stereotypes can be broken and free the survivors to create their life in they're in own vision
Through sharing their art and stories the women and children role model to other survivors to break the silence
When is the best time to hold a survivor art Exhibit?
Anytime is right to host an art exhibit, but if you are looking to create more of an impact you might want to tie it into one the following events:
February - Teen Dating Violence Awareness Month and V-Day
March - Women's History Month
April - Sexual Assault, Child Abuse Awareness Month, and Denim Day
October - Domestic Violence Awareness Month & Bullying Prevention Awareness Month
Where to hold an Exhibit?
There are many venues that work well for an art exhibition and many locations are happy to host the work, you might want to consider one of the following:

 Your DV Agency
An Office Building
During Your Open House
Fund Raising

Row.txt_description: This workshop will serve as a resource, tool, and guide for Leaders looking to plan and host an Exhibit featuring artwork created by survivors of Domestic Violence and/or Sexual Assault. These tips, suggestions, and guidelines will help to simplify the Exhibit process and prepare Leaders in time for Domestic Violence Awareness Month.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Using the tree as a symbol of life, participants will have the opportunity to express their stories and share their hopes and visions for a violence-free future. Through images of roots, bark, branches, leaves, fruits, and s ky, participants will join together to create a special tree embodying their community commitment against domestic violence.

   
  AWBW Community Story Tree
 
Materials:
Note on materials: Feel free to use some or all of the suggested materials. This workshop works well with simple materials or mixed-media.
         
Square Canvas tiles (one per participant) (see dickblick.com for inexpensive pre-stretched canvas of various sizes) We used tiles that are 12 inches X 12 inches.
AWBW Community Story Tree Grid (Color version included) or Blank Grid  
Acrylic paints
Paintbrushes (various sizes)
Sponge Brushes
Puffy paints
Cray-pas
Embroidery thread
Yarn
Tissue paper
Fabric
Glitter
Sponges
Markers/Sharpies
       Rafia
Artificial flowers
Sticks
Dried Leaves
Stamps
Glue / Tacky glue
Collaging materials
Mod Podge
Paper plates (to be used as paint palettes)
Water cups
Wall putty - 4 pieces per tile (optional)
Level for hanging (optional)









Other Options for Story Tree grid:
Footprint Tree Grid (Color version included)
Footprint Heart-Tree Grid (Color version included)
Leaf Tree Grid (Color version included)
Crescent House Community Story Tree Grid 

   
  AWBW Community Story Tree Grid
 
   
  AWBW Community Story Tree
Color Version
 
Set-Up/Prep:
Whether you use the AWBW Community Story Tree Grid (72 squares) or you create your own tree on the Blank Grid provided you will need to either use a transparency and projector or a capable artist to sketch out the design directly onto the canvas tiles.

If you choose to create your own tree, start by creating a sketch on the blank grid provided or onto a similar grid that fits the proportions of the space and size of tiles you will be using.

Be sure to have a color version of the overall tree available, so participants will have a rough guide for the color scheme of their tile.

Note: It's helpful if you mark the back of each canvas tile with a number that corresponds with the position of the tile on the grid, such as A1, A2. That way the participants can refer to the chart to see where their tile is located on the overall tree. Also, it's helpful that you put an arrow on the back of each tile pointing to the top, to ensure that participants are creating with the correct side up.

Warm-up:
Ask the participants to stand up, take a deep breath and stretch their "tree limbs" way up to the sky as they reach higher and higher. Have them spread all their fingers as far as they can and take another deep breath in and breathe out as they shake their "leaves" and flutter in the breeze (repeat as necessary). In addition, or alternately, have participants walk around the room (or standing in one place) as they to sway and stretch their "branches" and "roots" while continuing to breathe.

Introduction:
Your voice is important in helping to create a future free from domestic violence. Using  images of roots, bark, branches, leaves, and fruit I welcome you to express your own experiences, hopes, dreams, and commitment toward ending domestic violence in our communities. You may choose to delve into your past to share your personal stories of pain and triumph. Or you may reflect on the wishes, hopes, and dreams you have for the future. Each artist will use this creative opportunity to explore the issue of domestic violence in any way that is most meaningful for you.

Creation:
Start the process by explaining to the group that each person will be creating one tile from the overall design. Explain that once they have selected their tile, they will need to note the section number on the back of their canvas and refer to the "color" chart to see where their tile is located on the overall tree.

Introduce the project by saying something like,"We are all part of ending domestic violence. What words, shapes, symbols, or images represent or tell your story? How does your story speak out about domestic violence? What story would your root, bark, or leaves tell? How do you hope to affect the future? What story or wisdom does your heart want to share?"

"Feel free to be creative as you express yourself. For example, is your bark made up of loving hands? Is your sky filled with faces taking deep, soothing breaths? Do your words reveal the new directions you are taking in your life or your hopes for a better future? Maybe there are creatures in your branches. Maybe there is someone peeking out of a hole in your bark! Maybe your leaf is splitting open to show a road into your hopes and dreams. How does your story speak out against domestic violence? Feel free to play...and let your voice be heard!"

 
 
 
 
    Community Story Tree tiles
   

Welcome participants to be creative with the materials. "Feel free to paint, collage, draw, or use mixed media. It will be powerful to see a tree created with many diverse art styles. Don't be afraid to layer colors/materials. Puffy paints are a great way to add dimension. You can smudge cray-pas with your fingers to make a blended effect. You can use Mod Podge as a glue or to create a glossy finish for your piece."

Welcome artists to include words in their art. Let them know, "it would be okay if a piece of the tree could be entirely covered with words or it could include just a few. It's fine to hide the words, make them tiny, almost invisible, or large and bold. Please think of a title for your piece and include the words somewhere on your square. You can also add quotes, inspirational words, or personal reflections...whatever expresses the story you want to tell."

Remind them along the way to "use the colored sketch as a 'rough' guide for their color scheme. Doing this will help to give the overall tree a sense of cohesiveness. But please feel free to play. The 'fruits' were left white like a blank canvas. If you have fruit in your square, invent your own way to represent what you want to say. Be sure you cover all parts of the tile with color so no parts of the canvas are left white."

Another important reminder will be to "try to stay 'within' the lines provided, so that each piece will fit with the surrounding pieces like a puzzle."

As participants complete their individual tiles, have them assemble them into the tree. We recommend using a level to evenly hang the tiles and Wall Putty, if available, to secure the tree tiles in place. Hang the tree for all to see and to represent a community statement.

Note: This can be simply a group bonding project or you may welcome the entire community, shelter staff, board members, friends, and family members to join survivors and express their stories and share their hopes and visions for a future free from domestic violence.

When completed, this project lends itself to become a powerful and beautiful exhibit. To view the AWBW's Community Story Tree, click here. To view Community Story Trees Across the Country, click here. The Community Story Tree will be made of up of a series 'tiles' each telling its own unique story about the journey toward creating a violence-free future (see design at left). Together, the tiles will create a mosaic of commitment to ending violence.

Closing:
As the workshop comes to an end, even if the participants aren't all finished with their work, it is very important to have a closing circle of sharing. After such a deep creative process, it is particularly valuable to take time for each participant to sit back and look at his or her work from a distance, to share what he or she sees in it. Ask participants to acknowledge the different feelings and thoughts that were present throughout the creative process.

Invite the participants to take a step back and admire the tree as a whole. Ask them to acknowledge their stand in the community against domestic violence, for sharing their journey, and the impact and commitment they have made together.

Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Note About Exhibiting Community Story Trees
Collaborating agencies such as Pacific Clinics - Bonita Family Center in Los Angeles have created their own Community Story Tree to remain as a permanent installation to show their community's commitment to end domestic violence.

Row.str_title: Compassionate Creation: Trauma-Informed Care Through Art for Children
Row.txt_code:
Would it surprise you to know that Windows has been practicing a trauma informed principals for 21 years? In our roles as Windows Leaders and helpers, we can reasonably assume that the people we serve are survivors of trauma. From this perspective we attempt to offer a "window of time&quo t; for each individual, as the expert of their own experiences, to understand, process and heal in an atmosphere of safety and creativity.

In October of 2012, AWBW invited Windows' Leader and Trauma-Informed Care expert trainer, Tiombe Preston, to explain the Trauma-Informed Care model and how the Windows Program accomplishes the goals of this approach. To download the PowerPoint presentation click here: Compassionate Creation: Trauma Informed and Art; to view the engaging and powerful video, click here.

  
  


This key workshop topic highlights many of the ways in which the Windows Program, philosophy, and approach use suggested best practices of the Trauma-Informed Care model with children.

 

  “It is rewarding hearing about all of the children’s safe places and the peaceful tone in their voices when they share. It is like creating this place through art makes them believe that this safe place does exist.”
Creating a Safe Place Workshop 
Why art?
In the Windows groups, children have opportunities to work through their trauma and increase their self-esteem. Art projects stimulate their creativity and accelerate the healing process. The process of making art is a wonderful way for children to work through the issues in a safe, non-verbal, and non-confronting manner.

At Windows, we share art with the children as a tool for their own self-exploration and instead of interpreting what they create or offering any sort of diagnosis, we listen. Listening supportively to the experience of the process
of creating is incredibly valuable, keeps the roles clear, and reinforces the reality that the power is in the children's hands. 

What is my role as a Windows facilitator?
As AWBW Leaders, we serve as supportive and compassionate witnesses for the children. When trauma responses occur for the children, it is essential to see their panic, "acting out," anger, fear and anxiety as normal responses for someone in a traumatic state. It is important to keep in mind that the traumatic experience manifesting in front of us could be only one in a long line of traumas that child has experienced in their life. Educate yourself in trauma responses by doing research and attending trainings about the subject. You can start by watching the video included in this key workshop topic.

  Leaders reported that 97% of the workshops were effective in establishing a sense of freedom from judgment and ridicule.

As you prepare yourself to lead a Windows group,
from a perspective of compassionate observer, there are simple but empowering ways to create safety and to facilitate recovery, resilience, and healing. It is important to modify and accommodate your leadership style, materials, topics, and workshops according to the needs and requests of the participants in the group. Flexibility is crucial as so many circumstances are subject to change! Be ready for a wide range of emotions and feelings to emerge. To help you address related feelings, thoughts and discussion topics, search through our curriculum of workshops using the Emotional Theme category. 

 
 “It was rewarding seeing the child's eyes
light up as she was able to fully express herself and explore her own creativity without judgment or reprisals.”
My Gingerbread People Workshop
 
How do I create safety?
When we train AWBW Leaders, we start by talking about ways to establish safety, both emotionally and physically, for the children to create freely. The art offers a private and non-threatening avenue through which the children begin to explore and express themselves without fear or ridicule or disapproval. Through their creative expression, the children can learn to trust themselves and rely on their own inner resources. They can begin to notice the power of their own thoughts, feelings and creations. Assure them you are not there to judge them and that their Windows time is for them to express themselves through their art. Share with them that during Windows there is no wrong way to express themselves and that their creations will be valued, not judged.

For more ideas on how to create safety and workshops that speak to this theme we recommend the Creating Safety Series for Children. In this workshop series, we offer suggestions for serving as a compassionate witness through non-judgmental listening, creating collaborative ground-rules, and how to address the different developmental stages of the children.

How do I prepare my group?
At AWBW trainings we always start by noticing and brainstorming together about what the children are experiencing in the groups. Emotions range from relief to fear and from anxiety to hopelessness from the trauma they experienced in the DV situation. In addition, the children have often left a parent, their home and life as they know it, adding a huge sense of loss and feelings of grief. Through the art, the youth can gently explore what can be difficult to express and find a variety of ways of expressing it. The Opening Up and Expressing Emotions Series for Children provides a window of time and the safety of art to begin to share and release some of their emotions.

Any aspect of the workshop may be triggering for the children. Notice what the triggers are or might be for the children and be ready to respond. Speak to the children honestly, clearly and concisely about trauma responses they could be experiencing. Even though

 99% of Windows Leaders found that the art sessions helped to reduce children's depression, anxiety and fear levels.  

they may recognize they have been through a lot, they may not know that feeling sad, frightened, lonely and angry is normal. No one is superman or superwoman, so tell the children it's okay to let themselves feel their feelings and that it is okay to express themselves through their art and to only talk about it when they are ready. Let them know that their feelings and behaviors are normal responses to trauma.

Help the children to process their feelings while reminding them to take their time and only do what they feel ready to do in the moment. The Processing Anger Series for Children can help the children express and find a voice for what they are feeling. Once they are able to recognize that their anger is a warning signal, that something may be wrong, they can begin to safely navigate those feelings. If you are dealing with a specific manifestation of normal trauma responses you will want to search
 
 
“I have never felt safe talking about my real feelings. Just knowing that I can write down honest things in this journal, and that I can keep it here, makes me feel free.”
Child,age 13, Attitude Journals
for workshops that attend to that need and help the children find comfort. For example, children often have difficulty sleeping so you will want to try workshops such as Dream Catchers or Fear Ghost Busters to give the children an opportunity to notice and process that response.

For older kids especially, it is important to teach them about healthy and unhealthy ways of coping. For example, talk to them about using drugs, alcohol or sex as a distraction or to escape from their feelings. Share with them the pitfalls of coping in that way and that it will not will not change what is making them upset. Instead, doing these things could most likely create more problems in the long run. Tell them you understand that they want to feel better and that they are in a lot of pain. Comfort them and encourage them by reminding and reassuring them that they have a future and that new hopes and dreams can replace old ones. Great workshops for this are withing the Moving Forward Workshop Series for Children, Part 1 and Part 2.

How do I get the group to be focused and supportive of each other?
Establishing guidelines with the group that the youth are responsible for creating and modifying fosters the predictability, consistency, and flexibility that are
“I had an 8-year-old boy tell the group, ‘This is a place where you can express your
feelings through art, and there is no wrong art.'"
 
crucial for emotional safety. Essential components to include in the guidelines are ground rules about privacy, confidentiality, mutual- and self-respect. Remind them that Window's art "rule" is that there is no wrong way to create. It is also important to express in these guidelines that each youth has the power and freedom to respect themselves by choosing in what manner, when and how much they participate.

How do I know the group is meeting their needs?
Begin every workshop with a group check-in. An opening circle can give the participants an opportunity to reflect and think about themselves, their feelings about being in the group, and each other. This is also a wonderful opportunity for the Leader to gauge their attitudes and emotions to better respond to their needs. In addition, it brings everyone's voice into the room and allows for connection and trust. Follow the check-in with a centering exercise such as a warm-up or journaling exercise.

It is essential to hold weekly Windows workshops to foster consistency and to instill a sense of security and comfort that the youth can grow to expect and become accustomed to. This truly enables the children to have the opportunity to relax and commit some time to focus and connect to themselves, their feelings and their hopes and dreams.

Once the youth have finished their creations, all Windows workshops include a closing circle to encourage sharing by posing questions in a voluntary and supportive way. Questions such as, how did you feel during the session? what did you create? how do you feel about your creation? what did you discover? create an opportunity for validation of their experience. This time also allows the youth to process their creation, their feelings, and the project experience as a whole and enables a space for discussion and debriefing, if necessary.

Your Thoughts: As we continue to develop these themes, we would love to hear your thoughts related to the topics. Please send us your insights, quotes, comments, stories, successes, challenges etc. so we can continue to support you. Click here to submit your stories! We know each of you have tailored the workshops to fit the needs of your clients... We would love for you to share those variations, too!

Row.txt_description: In this series, we will explore what it means to serve as a compassionate witness as Windows Leaders in recognizing that each person is an expert on their own experience. We will use the Windows philosophy and workshop curriculum to look at the way the participants cope and survive their trauma with curiosity, rather than judgment.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Using the tree as a symbol of life, participants will have the opportunity to express their stories and share their hopes and visions for a violence-free future. Through images of roots, bark, branches, leaves, fruits, and sky, participants will join together to create a special tree embodying their community commitment against domestic violence.

   
  AWBW Community Story Tree
 
Materials:
Note on materials: Feel free to use some or all of the suggested materials. This workshop works well with simple materials or mixed-media.
         
Square Canvas tiles (one per participant) (see dickblick.com for inexpensive pre-stretched canvas of various sizes) We used tiles that are 12 inches X 12 inches.
AWBW Community Story Tree Grid (Color version included) or Blank Grid  
Acrylic paints
Paintbrushes (various sizes)
Sponge Brushes
Puffy paints
Cray-pas
Embroidery thread
Yarn
Tissue paper
Fabric
Glitter
Sponges
Markers/Sharpies
       Rafia
Artificial flowers
Sticks
Dried Leaves
Stamps
Glue / Tacky glue
Collaging materials
Mod Podge
Paper plates (to be used as paint palettes)
Water cups
Wall putty - 4 pieces per tile (optional)
Level for hanging (optional)









Other Options for Story Tree grid:
Footprint Tree Grid (Color version included)
Footprint Heart-Tree Grid (Color version included)
Leaf Tree Grid (Color version included)
Crescent House Community Story Tree Grid 

   
  AWBW Community Story Tree Grid
 
   
  AWBW Community Story Tree
Color Version
 
Set-Up/Prep:
Whether you use the AWBW Community Story Tree Grid (72 squares) or you create your own tree on the Blank Grid provided you will need to either use a transparency and projector or a capable artist to sketch out the design directly onto the canvas tiles.

If you choose to create your own tree, start by creating a sketch on the blank grid provided or onto a similar grid that fits the proportions of the space and size of tiles you will be using.

Be sure to have a color version of the overall tree available, so participants will have a rough guide for the color scheme of their tile.

Note: It's helpful if you mark the back of each canvas tile with a number that corresponds with the position of the tile on the grid, such as A1, A2. That way the participants can refer to the chart to see where their tile is located on the overall tree. Also, it's helpful that you put an arrow on the back of each tile pointing to the top, to ensure that participants are creating with the correct side up.

Warm-up:
Ask the participants to stand up, take a deep breath and stretch their "tree limbs" way up to the sky as they reach higher and higher. Have them spread all their fingers as far as they can and take another deep breath in and breathe out as they shake their "leaves" and flutter in the breeze (repeat as necessary). In addition, or alternately, have participants walk around the room (or standing in one place) as they to sway and stretch their "branches" and "roots" while continuing to breathe.

Introduction:
Your voice is important in helping to create a future free from domestic violence. Using  images of roots, bark, branches, leaves, and fruit I welcome you to express your own experiences, hopes, dreams, and commitment toward ending domestic violence in our communities. You may choose to delve into your past to share your personal stories of pain and triumph. Or you may reflect on the wishes, hopes, and dreams you have for the future. Each artist will use this creative opportunity to explore the issue of domestic violence in any way that is most meaningful for you.

Creation:
Start the process by explaining to the group that each person will be creating one tile from the overall design. Explain that once they have selected their tile, they will need to note the section number on the back of their canvas and refer to the "color" chart to see where their tile is located on the overall tree.

Introduce the project by saying something like,"We are all part of ending domestic violence. What words, shapes, symbols, or images represent or tell your story? How does your story speak out about domestic violence? What story would your root, bark, or leaves tell? How do you hope to affect the future? What story or wisdom does your heart want to share?"

"Feel free to be creative as you express yourself. For example, is your bark made up of loving hands? Is your sky filled with faces taking deep, soothing breaths? Do your words reveal the new directions you are taking in your life or your hopes for a better future? Maybe there are creatures in your branches. Maybe there is someone peeking out of a hole in your bark! Maybe your leaf is splitting open to show a road into your hopes and dreams. How does your story speak out against domestic violence? Feel free to play...and let your voice be heard!"

 
 
 
 
    Community Story Tree tiles
   

Welcome participants to be creative with the materials. "Feel free to paint, collage, draw, or use mixed media. It will be powerful to see a tree created with many diverse art styles. Don't be afraid to layer colors/materials. Puffy paints are a great way to add dimension. You can smudge cray-pas with your fingers to make a blended effect. You can use Mod Podge as a glue or to create a glossy finish for your piece."

Welcome artists to include words in their art. Let them know, "it would be okay if a piece of the tree could be entirely covered with words or it could include just a few. It's fine to hide the words, make them tiny, almost invisible, or large and bold. Please think of a title for your piece and include the words somewhere on your square. You can also add quotes, inspirational words, or personal reflections...whatever expresses the story you want to tell."

Remind them along the way to "use the colored sketch as a 'rough' guide for their color scheme. Doing this will help to give the overall tree a sense of cohesiveness. But please feel free to play. The 'fruits' were left white like a blank canvas. If you have fruit in your square, invent your own way to represent what you want to say. Be sure you cover all parts of the tile with color so no parts of the canvas are left white."

Another important reminder will be to "try to stay 'within' the lines provided, so that each piece will fit with the surrounding pieces like a puzzle."

As participants complete their individual tiles, have them assemble them into the tree. We recommend using a level to evenly hang the tiles and Wall Putty, if available, to secure the tree tiles in place. Hang the tree for all to see and to represent a community statement.

Note: This can be simply a group bonding project or you may welcome the entire community, shelter staff, board members, friends, and family members to join survivors and express their stories and share their hopes and visions for a future free from domestic violence.

When completed, this project lends itself to become a powerful and beautiful exhibit. To view the AWBW's Community Story Tree, click here. To view Community Story Trees Across the Country, click here. The Community Story Tree will be made of up of a series 'tiles' each telling its own unique story about the journey toward creating a violence-free future (see design at left). Together, the tiles will create a mosaic of commitment to ending violence.

Closing:
As the workshop comes to an end, even if the participants aren't all finished with their work, it is very important to have a closing circle of sharing. After such a deep creative process, it is particularly valuable to take time for each participant to sit back and look at his or her work from a distance, to share what he or she sees in it. Ask participants to acknowledge the different feelings and thoughts that were present throughout the creative process.

Invite the participants to take a step back and admire the tree as a whole. Ask them to acknowledge their stand in the community against domestic violence, for sharing their journey, and the impact and commitment they have made together.
