Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Note About Exhibiting Community Story Trees
Collaborating agencies such as Pacific Clinics - Bonita Family Center in Los Angeles have created their own Community Story Tree to remain as a permanent installation to show their community's commitment to end domestic violence.

Row.str_title: Exhibit Planning Workshop Series for Children
Row.txt_code:
Oak of Mercy by Lori Minick created for the
Story Tree Exhibit
 
Statistics of domestic violence are staggering! An estimated 1.3 million women are victims of physical assault by an intimate partner each year and on average, more than three women and one man are murdered by their intimate partners in this country every day. Art exhibitions are a powerful way to break the silence that allows domestic violence to continue in our communities.


Since 1992, AWBW has facilitated almost 200 exhibitions in 19 states with our network of shelter partners. Exhibit sites have ranged from DV Conferences and shelter events, local libraries and colleges, police departments and even the U.S. Senate Building in Washington D.C.

   

Our most recent and successful completed work, Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence, a collaborative art project led by internationally acclaimed L.A. artist and survivor Kim Abeles, engaged over 800 survivors in AWBW programs and 425 dedicated community members. An estimated 400,000 visitors viewed the exhibit. 


While we encourage our AWBW partners to reach for their greatest exhibit vision, we also realize resources may be limited. We aim to make the process as easy as possible by providing our Program Leaders with planning aids, workshop ideas, consultation and funding. To lead your own Pearls of Wisdom exhibit click here or see below for other powerful (and feasible!) exhibition ideas.


To plan your own Exhibit, please refer to AWBW's Leader's Exhibit Guide .

What is the impact of a Survivor's Art Exhibit?
An exhibit of survivors' art is an important tool that raises awareness and helps to break the silence inherent in domestic violence and sexual assault. It is impactful in the following ways:

 "It was rewarding to
see the excitement
in the children's faces.
They were so proud
their artwork was
going to be for an
exhibit!"
 
- Helps clients to build self-esteem and pride in their work.
- Gives a public, yet confidential and safe voice to the survivors.
- Creates awareness and support for your agency, including potential funding opportunities.
- Educates the public and sparks a dialogue on the subject of Domestic Violence in the community.
 
 
   Children's and Women's
Monster in Me Exhibit
  

In what ways do Survivors feel empowered by exhibiting their artwork?
Seeing their personal creations exhibited can create a sense of pride and self-worth that can be empowering in ways that are hard to imagine. Some of these ways are:
- Affirms and validates of their story of survival.
-
 
 "THANK YOU for this
exhibit! SO much silence
stifled my son's growth.
Participating in this project
gave him a voice: and a
listening audience. This
exhibit gave our whole
family room to breathe.
We are strong.
We see it now!"
 
   
Confirms that they have wisdom to share with others and educate the community.
- Builds a community of support in discovering that they are not alone.
- Provides a sense of purpose when giving back.
- By sharing their individual experience and unique voice, myths and stereotypes can be broken and free survivors to create their life in their own vision.
- Through sharing their art and stories, women and children role model to other survivors to break the silence.
When is the best time to hold a Survivor's Art Exhibit?
An art exhibit can be held at any time, but if you are looking to create a stronger impact you might want to tie your exhibit into one the following events:
February - Teen Dating Violence Awareness Month, and V-Day
March - Women's History Month
April - Sexual Assault, Child Abuse Awareness Month, and Denim Day
October - Domestic Violence Awareness Month, and Bullying Prevention Awareness Month

Where can I hold an Art Exhibit?
There are many venues that work well for an exhibit and many locations are happy to host the work. You might want to consider one of the following:

 Your DV Agency
An Office Building
During your Open House
Fundraising Events
Local Libraries 		 Police Departments
Community Centers
Schools
Chamber of Commerce
Banks		 Restaurants
Bookstores
Coffee Shops
Senior Centers
Churches
 


  
 
 Viewing an exhibit at a Library Viewing an exhibit at a Fundraising Event
 Viewing an exhibit at an
Art Gallery

Who benefits from an Art Exhibit?
Everyone can benefit from the experience of witnessing survivor art. You may choose to hold an intimate gathering for the participants themselves with staff and board members, share a modest display at an event or local public venue or seek a larger arena with funding support.


How does AWBW support Collaborating Agencies to hold an Art Exhibit?
AWBW provides you with a comprehensive Leaders Exhibit Guide that includes the following:

- An Exhibit Planning Worksheet to formulate your vision and goals.
- Windows Exhibit Planning Tips for successful planning/implementation.
- An opportunity to apply for a $300 Exhibit Scholarship (per exhibit).
The scholarship can be used for exhibit expenses including art supplies, framing/mounting costs, site fees, and up to $100 for reception and printing of exhibit announcement materials.
- Ongoing one-on-one consultation with AWBW Program Staff.
- Inspiration and ideas through a diverse selection of Windows workshops that can be featured as an Exhibit.
- An opportunity to post your Exhibit on the AWBW website, along with other featured Exhibits (selected Exhibits are also available to travel to assist communities in breaking the silence).

"Exhibit Recommended" workshops can be found on the website using the Workshop Search Tool (Strength category). Some of AWBW's workshops that we recommend featuring in an Exhibit can be found below:

Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence Workshop (Paper Version) thanks to AWBW Staff - Adapted from Pearls of Wisdom Project by Kim Abeles                                      

  
  

This workshop is designed to help survivors recognize their personal strength and uses the metaphor of a "pearl" as a treasure that form inside an oyster in response to an irritant. Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength and wisdom as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence. Link to the AWBW version of the Exhibit here.

Inner Self Portraits thanks to Rose Curtis                                                                          

  

This workshop will assist older children and teens to look inside and discover more about their inner-selves! Many people are used to looking at their outer selves, their looks, their clothes, their appearance, and the image they are trying to portray. This workshop gives youth an opportunity to go to a deeper level and get more in touch with the feelings they have inside.



Family Trees thanks to AWBW Staff                                                                                  
The goal for this workshop is to empower families to share their story of surviving domestic violence by illustrating their journey through the metaphor of a tree. The project is designed to enable survivors and their families to rebuild a sense of connection with each other by telling their stories through art. In creating their trees, families will be asked to reflect on where they have come from, how they escaped, and the kind of future that they envision for themselves. Link to the AWBW version of the Exhibit here.

Take a Walk in My Shoes thanks to Micala Rush                                                                  

  

This workshop gives participants an opportunity to communicate what it is like to be them and take a walk in their shoes as they tell the story of their experience. Exhibit viewers are then able to better understand the life and experience of the survivors and have more empathy for the survivors themselves. Link to the AWBW version of the Exhibit here.


Unmasking Me / Unmasking the Future thanks to AWBW Staff & Rose Curtis                       


 


This workshop allows youth to have their voices heard through journaling and by creating a mask that dialogues with the abuser and themselves regarding the domestic violence they experienced and/or witnessed. Survivors have the opportunity to share personal stories and reflect on who they want to be in future relationships for the purpose of creating awareness and educating their communities in a powerful and unique way. Link to the AWBW version of the Exhibit here.

 

Story Trees thanks to Pamela Almeida                                                                               The Story Tree workshop gives children an opportunity to explore their strength and growth through their journey of survival. Using the tree as a symbol of life and courage, participants are free to play and let their imaginations run wild as they discover what kind of tree they want to be. Link to the AWBW version of the Exhibit here.

Community Story Tree thanks to Pamela Almedia                                               
Through images of roots, bark, branches, leaves, fruits, and sky, individuals from the community can raise awareness about an issue that has a profound and painful impact on our community. Joining together, their tiles and voices create this special tree embodying their community commitment against domestic violence.

Speak Out Masks thanks to AWBW Staff                                                                             


 

This workshop allows participants to speak out about and against domestic violence, as well as to express personal stories for the purpose of creating awareness. The creation process gives survivors an opportunity to create and watch the words of their feelings, fears, and emotions pour out of the mouth of the mask.

 

 

Heart Stories thanks to AWBW Staff                                                                                   This workshop supports children and teens in sharing their hearts and stories through art. The workshop gives them an opportunity to listen to their hearts, value the stories within them, and discover and know that others want to hear them too. Link to the AWBW version of the Exhibit here.

Expression Masks thanks to Rose Curtis                                                                             

  

This mask process allows youth to think about teen dating violence in a visual way. The masks demonstrate how people look when they are in abusive relationships and are experiencing a combination of complex emotions.

 

 

The Monster in Me thanks to Cathy Salser                                                                       

  

Gives children an opportunity to be playful in exploring some of the more difficult emotions they experience. This process offers a safe way to explore some of the feelings that result from living with abuse and create a "monster" that can look bold and powerful. Releasing this monster and having others view it can be rewarding and satisfying for the children. Link to the AWBW version of the Exhibit here.

 

For Exhibits created by other Children's Windows leaders like you, click here.
Monster in Me, Unmasking Me/Unmasking the Future, Heart Stories, and Children's Windows Quilts.

Please send us your insights, quotes, comments, stories, successes, challenges etc. so we can continue to support you. Click here to submit your stories! These tips, suggestions, and guidelines will help to simplify the Exhibit process and prepare Leaders in time for Domestic Violence Awareness Month.

- An Exhibit Planning Worksheet to formulate your vision and goals.
- Windows Exhibit Planning Tips for successful planning/implementation.
- An opportunity to apply for a $300 Exhibit Scholarship (per exhibit).
The scholarship can be used for exhibit expenses including art supplies, framing/mounting costs, site fees, and up to $100 for reception and printing of exhibit announcement materials.
- Ongoing one-on-one consultation with AWBW Program Staff.
- Inspiration and ideas through a diverse selection of Windows workshops that can be featured as an Exhibit.
- An opportunity to post your Exhibit on the AWBW website, along with other featured Exhibits (selected Exhibits are also available to travel to assist communities in breaking the silence).

 "This exhibit was displaying empowerment and transformation,
which was very strong and beautiful. In a way, there are NO ‘victims' in this show."
Pearls of Wisdom: KCCLA End the Violence Exhibit
Opening Reception March 2011

"Exhibit Recommended" workshops can be found on the website using the Workshop Search Tool (Strength category). Some of AWBW's workshops that we recommend featuring in an Exhibit can be found below:

Losses Altars inspired by Dia de Los Muertos thanks to Emma Guerrero-Pavich                    Through the creation of an altar in homage to what has been lost in the wake of domestic violence, survivors are able to honor those parts of themselves that they feel have "died" or are gone due to the Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault in relationships.

Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence Workshop (Paper Version) thanks to AWBW Staff - Adapted from Pearls of Wisdom Project by Kim Abeles                                                      

 
  

This workshop is designed to help survivors recognize their personal strength and uses the metaphor of a "pearl" as a treasure that form inside an oyster in response to an irritant. Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength and wisdom as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence. Link to the AWBW version of the Exhibit here.

The Clothesline Project thanks to Coalition of Womens' Groups in Cape Cod, MA                
The Clothesline Project is a vehicle for survivors affected by violence to express their emotions by decorating a shirt or other article of clothing. The shirts or clothing articles are used to tell the stories of the survivors and raise public awareness about the issue of domestic and sexual violence.

Inner Self Portraits thanks to Rose Curtis                                                                          

 

This workshop will assist the participants in going within themselves and discovering more about their inner-selves! This workshop gives us an opportunity to go to a deep, internal and emotional level and expose, explore, celebrate to get more in touch with their inner-selves... their inner most beings. This workshop offers 3 different techniques to allow the participants to fully express their inner-selves. This is also a great project for an exhibit. Link to the Haven Hills Outreach version of the Exhibit, entitled "The Forgotten Goddess" here.


My Traveling Story thanks to Judy Brodjeski & Rose Curtis                                                  Each life is a journey. We travel from place to place both physically and emotionally. On this journey there are things we want to take with us and things we want to leave behind. This workshop allows survivors of abuse to use transform a suitcase as a means for expressing their journey, including their unique experience of survival. This art experience is meant to be a source of healing, with an emphasis on the creative process. Link to the AWBW version of the Traveling Stories Exhibit here.

Family Trees thanks to AWBW Staff                                                                                   The goal for this workshop is to empower families to share their story of surviving domestic violence by illustrating their journey through the metaphor of a tree. The project is designed to enable survivors and their children to rebuild a sense of connection with each other by telling their stories through art. In creating their trees, families will be asked to reflect on where they have come from, how they escaped, and the kind of future that they envision for themselves. Link to the AWBW version of the Exhibit here.

Helping Hands, Healing Hands - Community Mandala Project thanks to Lori Rothfus            To give participants an opportunity to think about what a "healthy and safe" community, home, or group looks like by making a hand collage to explore this question. These collage hands will become part of a larger hands mandala to inspire the greater community that together our hands can help and heal.

The Monster in Me thanks to Joanne Webb, Melissa Falco-Williams, and AWBW Staff          


 

The "monsters" are created using a simple technique with oil pastels and watercolors, each person will have the opportunity to reflect on their own personal experiences with domestic violence. Participants can explore difficult emotions in a safe and fun way, and give voice to the feelings that may be hidden inside by creating artwork that represents the "monster" within. Link to the AWBW version of the Monster in Me Exhibit here.

Unmasking Me / Unmasking the Future thanks to AWBW Staff & Rose Curtis                       

 

Through a combination of journaling and mask making this workshop gives participants an opportunity to explore their feelings about the abuse they have experienced and think about who they want to be in future relationships. This workshop offers the opportunity for survivors to share personal stories for the purpose of creating awareness and educating their communities in a powerful and unique way. Link to the AWBW version of the Exhibit here.


Story Trees thanks to Pamela Almeida                                                                               Using the tree as a symbol of life, participants can let their imaginations run wild to find out the kind of tree they were as they explored their journey of survival. This workshop provides survivors with a creative opportunity to explore their stories of survival, change, growth, and life. Link to the AWBW version of the Exhibit here.


 
  

Community Story Tree thanks to Pamela Almeida              
Through images of roots, bark, branches, leaves, fruits, and sky individuals from the community can raise awareness about an issue that has a profound and painful impact on our community. Joining together, their tiles and voices create this special tree embodying our community commitment against domestic violence.

Speak Out Masks thanks to AWBW Staff                                                                            
This self-expression project is designed to allow participants to speak out about and against domestic violence, as well as to express personal stories for the purpose of creating awareness. The creation process gives survivors an opportunity to create and watch the words of their feelings, fears, and emotions to pour out of the mouth of the mask.

Me Dolls thanks to Lori Minick Melissa Falco-Williams                                                     

  

Me Dolls give voice to the messages of survival and healing that make each survivor's journey unique. This workshop is designed to explore the different messages and themes within each woman's experience. Each artist can reach within and create a doll that is all about the "me" that perhaps no one has heard or seen before; a doll that will reach out with humor and whim to celebrate her strengths and claim a violence-free future. Link to the AWBW version of the Exhibit here.



Take a Walk in My Shoes thanks to Judy Van Brodjeski                                                       
 

"Take a Walk in My Shoes" tells the stories of the many survivors who are not able to talk about domestic abuse and the profound effect it has had on them. This workshop gives participants the opportunity to express their feelings of surviving abuse, and to help others understand how it feels to "walk in their shoes." Link to the AWBW version of the Exhibit here.

 

Windows into Our Future - Part 1 and Part 2 thanks to Cathy Salser                              
Through the creation of a "window" participants are provided with an opportunity to think about and look into their violence-free futures using various Cray-Pas techniques. Participants take the time necessary for each to envision what their future free of domestic violence will look like for them personally. Link to the AWBW version of the Windows Into Our Future I Exhibit here and the Windows Into Our Future II Exhibit here.

"I can see by this mask that she is a woman who won't let anything bring her down."
Viewer, CPAF 33rd Anniversary Garden Party Exhibit September 2011

For Exhibits created by other Women's Windows leaders like you, click here: Dawson County Domestic Violence Program - Masks of Violence, Dawson County Domestic Violence Shelter Me Doll Exhibit, Unmasking our Pain, Revealing our Power - Masks from Nicaragua and Wisconsin.

Share Your Thoughts: As we continue to develop these themes, we would love to hear your thoughts related to the topics. Please send us your insights, quotes, comments, stories, successes, challenges etc. so we can continue to support you. Click here to submit your stories! We know each of you have tailored the workshops to fit the needs of your clients...we would love for you to share those variations also!!

To read related Impact Spotlight click here: Dear Wonderful Leaders, Faces of Domestic Violence, Just Try It!, and Windows Opening Beyond Borders.
Row.txt_description: This workshop will serve as a resource, tool, and guide for Leaders looking to plan and host an Exhibit featuring artwork created by survivors of Domestic Violence and/or Sexual Assault. These tips, suggestions, and guidelines will help to simplify the Exhibit process and prepare Leaders in time for Domestic Violence Awareness Month.

Row.txt_code:
Oak of Merc y by Lori Minick created for the
Story Tree Exhibit		 
What is the Impact of an Art Exhibit?
Art exhibitions are a powerful way to break the silence that allows domestic violence to continue in our communities.

Statistics of Domestic Violence are staggering. An estimated 1.3 million women are victims of physical assault by an intimate partner each year and on average, more than three women and one man are murdered by their intimate partners in this country every day!  An Art Exhibit can educate the community and help survivors be heard.


A Window Between Worlds Art Exhibition HIstory
   
Since 1992, AWBW has facilitated almost 200 exhibitions in 19 states with our network of shelter partners. Exhibit sites have ranged from museums and art centers to colleges, department stores and even the US Senate Building in Washington D.C.

Our most recently completed work, Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence, a collaborative art project led by internationally acclaimed L.A. artist and survivor Kim Abeles, engaged over 800 survivors and 425 dedicated community members in 80 hands-on workshops. With an initial audience of 2,281 at the Korean Cultural Center Los Angeles, it then received a curatorial invitation to appear at the Skirball Cultural Center, where an estimated 400,000 visitors.  To lead your own Pearls of Wisdom exhibit click here (link).

 
 
Many exhibits have included hands-on participatory components that invite viewers to join in the creation process and raise their own voices to bring an end to the violence. In 2012 the community engaged art project, I CAN: Requiem for I Can't, takes the voices of survivors to a new level of visibility. In collaboration with internationally recognized artist and educator, Suzanne Lacy; renowned performance artist Barbara T. Smith; post graduate artists in residency from Otis College of Art and Design's MFA Public Practice Program, Neda Moridpour and Teresa Flores; and shelter partners throughout Los Angeles we are building on the high level of visibility of Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence. This collaborative art project offers tools to mobilize social change on a wide spectrum, from the deeply personal and familial levels to the collective and communal and illuminates the relationship between these diverse levels of social change.

Refer to:
 - this Guide. Link PDF version of entire Guide

Why Hold an Exhibit?
An exhibit of survivors art is an important tool that raises awareness and helps to break the silence of domestic violence.  The specific reasons are among the following:
Helps clients' self-esteem and builds pride in their work
Creates awareness and support for your agency
Sparks dialogue on the subject of Domestic Violence
Gives a public, yet confidential and safe voice to the survivors
Can provide funding opportunities
Educates the public about domestic violence and sexual assault
Raises awareness and helps to break the silence of domestic violence

 
 
     

Whose Work do you Feature in an Exhibit?
Hosting an Exhibit featuring the artwork of survivors of domestic violence and sexual assault empowers the participants whose voices can be heard!
What is it like for the clients?
Affirmation and support from exterior source
Building a support community through art and exhibit.
They will receive this packet, 300 dollars and one-on-one support to make it a successful exhibit. If you don't need extra funding but would like to hold an exhibit please still let Annie know. Either way we would love to help you or at least hear about your exhibit.
Be sure to complete Release forms for the artists' work. Link Windows Art and Photo Registry forms.


Who do you Feature in an Art Exhibit?
Hosting an Exhibit featuring the artwork of survivors of domestic violence and sexual assault empowers the participants whose voices can be heard!


When do you Host an Exhibit?
Anytime is right to host an art exhibit, but if you are looking to create more of an impact you might want to tie it into one the following events:
February — Teen Dating Violence Awareness Month and V-Day
March — Women's History Month
April — Sexual Assault, Child Abuse Awareness Month, and Denim Day
October — Domestic Violence Awareness Month & Bullying Prevention Awareness Month
Where do  Exhibit?
There are so many venues that work well for an art exhibition and many locations are happy to host the work, you might want to consider one of the following:

 Local Libraries
Community Centers
Schools
Coffee Shops
Banks
                   
Restaurants
Bookstores
Chamber of Commerce
Senior Centers
Churches
