Row.str_title: Creative Holiday Workshop Series for Children
Row.txt_code:
The holiday season can have a different definition for each person or family; each with their own meaning or tradition for what they want the holiday to be. For many of us it can bring up expectations and emotions for and from ourselves and others. For some, it can be a time of finding peace within, for some it might be about all the bright and festive decorations, and for others it can be about connecting with people who are special to them.

Art workshops offer opportunities to understand that the holidays don't only have to be about material, store-bought gifts, but about something that comes from the heart which can be deeper and more meaningful. To help get into the holiday spirit, these workshops focus on the joy of giving, sharing, and creating hopes and wishes during the holiday season and beyond.

We are presenting this workshop series to help us notice what we need to feel the spirit of the holidays, and to inspire each person to create positive experiences that can lead the way to dreams and wishes for a better future. 
     
 "I wish everybody could do
one so we all can live
together in peace."		   

Peace Wreath
This workshop encourages the children to contribute to the holiday decorations by creating a personal Peace Wreath made from their own hand shapes. This activity leads the children to think about what creates peace and in what ways they can use their own hands to create a more peaceful world. This workshop can be done to create a family wreath, a group wreath or an individual wreath.



   
 "My hands can hold many things;
even things I can't see,
like hopes and dreams."
 
Hands of Hope/Tree of Empowerment
This workshop gives the children the ability to create cut-outs of their own hands and decorate them with color, images, and words that inspire hope. These Hands of Hope can then be hung together on a community holiday tree to evoke a powerful Tree of Empowerment that represents the combined hopes, strengths, and dreams to inspire others to have hope in a better tomorrow.

Helping Hands Ornaments - Holiday Decorating Series
To reinforce that we have the ability to help stop the cycle of violence and choose to use our hands to help, not hurt. Participants will create a Helping Hand Ornament to remind them of all the helpful and loving things they can do with their hands.

   

Stuff Your Stockings Full of Joy
This workshop provides a tools for children to express their love and feel connected to the people they care about during the holiday season. Even if someone we care about is far away and we miss them, we can feel better by remembering positive things about them and what we appreciate about them.



   
  "My heart is exploding with the
love I have for my mom and
sisters. We have peace and are
free from fighting."		 
   
   
Heart Stories
This workshop supports children and teens in sharing their hearts and stories through art. The workshop gives them an opportunity to listen to their hearts, value the stories within them, and know that others want to hear them too.

Crystals from the Heart  
To give the children an opportunity to create something unique and beautiful that can be given to friends and/or family. It also allows them to experience the holiday spirit and the gift of giving.

Shrinky Ornaments! - Holiday Decorating Series
To educate the participants about the power of words by giving them an opportunity to say loving things to one another and then create a Shrinky Dink ornament to serve as a reminder of all the positive words and feelings they heard and felt. Includes an interactive warm up that helps build the childrens' self-esteem and allows them to bond.

 
 
   
   
   
   
Whimiscal Wood Creation - Holiday Decorating Series
To help children experience the joys of childhood by noticing their hopes and dreams through their creations of fun and cheerful holiday decorations.

 
 
Flower Angel Ornament for Teens - Holiday Decorating Series    
To help teens notice their hopes and dreams. Their creations, of angels or fairies, can become a reminder and the guardians of their dreams and hopes for their future.

My Special Ornament    
To create a holiday ornament that helps the children redirect any negative feelings about the holidays and focus on the many ways they are special.

   
Holiday Card Making - Holidays with HeART Series
This workshop gives participants an opportunity to create and receive homemade holiday cards.

Holiday Wish List
To provide the children an opportunity to express their own wishes and hopes for the holidays and the New Year. In this workshop we learn how to create holiday cards that will express those wishes and hopes.


 "My butterfly wants to live life
peacefully and unafraid to fly
far away from abuse and shame."		 
Stained Glass Butterflies
Gives the children the opportunity to try new materials that give rewarding visual effects and make beautiful butterflies. Encourages them to think about the changes they are experiencing by thinking about how caterpillars change into butterflies.

   
My Gingerbread People
This workshop provides children an opportunity to notice the people who are special in their lives during the holiday season. The children will create felt gingerbread people as a reminder of the people who have had a positive influence on them or have been supportive to them. This is especially important because the holidays can be a difficult time and this workshop helps the children focus on the positive in their lives.
Row.txt_description: By building positive experiences through workshops that focus on dreams and wishes for a better future, we are presenting the children with an opportunity to help sort through their emotions and expectations of the holiday season.

Row.txt_code:
Objective: To remind participants that even th ough life can bring us challenges, there are always reasons for us to smile.

Materials:
Sheet of white paper
Markers
Crayons
Colored Pencils

Timeframe:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Warm-Up: 10 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing Circle: 15 minutes
Total: 1 Hour

Set-Up/Prep:
To prepare your materials beforehand, we suggest that you set out a stack of white paper, a box of crayons, colored pencils, and markers on each table.

Introduction:
"In our daily lives, sometimes we can become so consumed with the reasons that make us frown that we forget we have plenty of things to smile for. As adults, we might focus on all the stressors that have us feeling like we are being held down. When we are feeling flooded or overwhelmed, it can be easy to overlook the little things that truly matter like the laughter of our children, the roof over our head, the food on our table, etc. Today, we're going to take a window of time to appreciate the things (big and small) that make us smile."

Warm-up:
"If you feel comfortable and safe, please close your eyes and think about a typical day in your life. Rather than focusing your thoughts on everyday worries like the bills that need to be paid, the responsibilities you have to take care of, or thinking you might be in a different place than where you thought you might be... try to clear your mind and center yourself in the present. Now place your focus on the simple joys.. perhaps the child that unexpectedly gave you a hug only to feel their arms around you and your warmth...imagine the butterfly that landed on the flower next to you...the smile and wave that you shared with a stranger. Think of all the little things that happen throughout the day that are worthy of the biggest smile you can give. Take a few more minutes to imagine all of those wonderful moments (big and small) we experience, even in one day, that make us smile. And when you feel ready, please open your eyes."

Creation:
"After you have given yourself enough time to think about the reasons you smile, we will draw a smile as large as you want and full of teeth. Within these teeth, we will fill each one in with words, shapes, symbols, thoughts that bring you a smile! No matter how little or insignificant you might feel the reason for the smile is, you can label each tooth in your mouth with a reason."
 
   
  The Reasons We Smile creation
   The Reasons We Smile creation 
Closing:
"If you are ready and would like to share, we will show our smiles to the group. You can choose to simply share your picture or share your picture as well as the reasons you smile." Thank everyone for sharing and being bold, creative, and thoughtful in thinking about the reasons they smile.
 
 
   The Reasons We Smile creation 
"Remember that you are the only one who can see, feel, and appreciate the reasons you have for smiling. Those reasons are all unique, special, and wonderful. It is perfectly normal to  feel like frowning sometimes. Try to shake it off and remember that there are things in our lives all around us that can make us smile, if only we slow down and try to appreciate them!"
Row.txt_description: Helps to remind the participants that even though life can bring us challenges, there are always reasons for us to smile.

Row.str_title: Creative Holiday Workshop Series for Adults
Row.txt_code:
For some, the holidays represent a time of peace, joy, and happy celebration. This might mean decorating, craft-making, cooking and baking, and expressing love for themselves and others and fostering positive feelings. For others, especially survivors of domestic violence who might be far away from their families, homes, and usual holiday traditions, the time of year can feel challenging and seem like a painful reminder of the past. Whatever emotions and expectations come up and however we think or feel about the holidays, it is important to recognize what we are feeling. These workshops offer tools to help notice and express emotions present during the holiday season and keep the spirit and joy of the holidays alive within our hearts.

Since the holidays can mean different things and look different to each person, it is important to check in with the participants and allow them to reflect on the feelings and experiences this time of year brings. Encourage the participants to think about: What do the holidays mean to you? What are some holidays memories you have? What does it smell like? feel like? taste like?, etc. Facilitating an open and safe discussion, even paired with holiday music and themed food, can help the participants to get back in touch with the meaning and delight that the holidays can spark!

Use these workshops to ignite the festive feeling and holiday spirit and inspire hope and love throughout the season and your life! The creative projects can create new traditions, gifts, and a sense of magic and connection for the participants and their families to share.
 "Because of the holidays, we really tried to let the ladies dictate the mood
for the workshops. Many came to group looking sad and depressed but
left with smiles on their faces." - AWBW Leader
 
   
 
 
Stuff Your Stockings Full of Joy - To provide a way for participants to express their love and connection to their children and families during the holiday season.

Shrinky Ornaments! - Holiday Decorating Series - This workshop helps to educate the participants about the power of words by giving them an opportunity to say loving things to one another and then create a Shrinky Dink ornament to serve as a reminder of all the positive words and feelings they heard and felt. Includes an interactive warm up that helps build the participants' self-esteem and allows them to bond.

 
 
Crystals from the Heart - To give the participants an opportunity to create something unique and beautiful that can be given to friends and/or family. It also allows them to experience the holiday spirit and the gift of giving.
 "All women participated, even those who insisted they are ‘not crafty.' Some of the women who were most resistant at first didn't want to leave. They made beautiful earrings and necklaces and gave each other a lot of support. One woman gave the earrings she made to another woman who admired them."
- AWBW Leader, Crystals from the Heart
 

 

   
Home is Where the Heart Is Aprons - To encourage the participants that they can create their own "Home Sweet Home" and family unit no matter where they live.
 "I thought I had to wait for my ‘sweet home.'
Now I know I can create one."
- AWBW Participant, Home is Where the Heart Is
 




Holiday Card Making - Holidays with HeART Series - To help participants find art in the holidays. A series of workshops with holiday themes including Holiday Cards, Shrinky Dink Blessing Charms and Bracelet making. The idea is to create something special to show loved ones that we care and perhaps even begin new family traditions. Creating with art during the holidays as a family can be a relaxing way to connect, bond and celebrate.

Peace Wreath - To have the participants contribute to the holiday decorations by creating a personal Peace Wreath made from their own hand shapes. This activity motivates the participants to think about what creates peace in their lives and in the world and in what ways they can use their own hands to create a more peaceful world. This is a great workshop for community building or as a family activity!
 "We need to learn to use our mouths
and not our hands to create peace.
Violence does not help make peace."
- AWBW Participant, Peace Wreath
 

Turning Point Ornaments - Participants create unique ornaments which they can save and see each year as a reminder of this particularly special holiday: this turning point in their lives.
 "This is the first ornament of my own that I have,
and that is a turning point for me;
knowing I can have something of my own
to share with my children."
- AWBW Participant, Turning Point Ornament
  
    







Holiday Inspiration Cards - Provides an opportunity for participants to explore and express their own personal, positive perspective for the holiday season by choosing their own message of inspiration, and creating holiday cards which reflect this message.

 
 
Affirmation Ornaments - Helps clients redirect any negative holidays feelings to focusing on the positive changes they are making.







 
 
Decorated Cookies - Holidays with HeART Series - Participants decorate holiday cookies together.
 "The holidays should be fun, loving, and domestic violence-free,
and this activity helped me remember that."
- AWBW Participant, Decorated Cookies- Holidays with HeART Series
 
Ornaments of Change - This workshop offers participants an opportunity to give themselves empathy as they notice how they are feeling with the approaching holiday season. This workshop also allows the participants to enjoy creating sculpey ornaments filled with hopes, prayers or wishes as reminders of the positive changes they are making for themselves and their family.
Row.txt_description: However we think or feel about the holidays, it is important to recognize what we are feeling. These workshops offer tools to help the participants notice and express emotions present during the holiday season and keep the spirit and joy of the holidays alive within their hearts.

Row.str_title: New Beginnings Workshop Series for Children & Youth
Row.txt_code:
Each new year can present us with opportunities to notice what we want in the year ahead. The art workshops can help inspire youth to notice what's most important to them so that they can make decisions about how to create a new start for themselves.

Starting a journal or calendar to plan ahead can help the children stay on task, of their own choosing. Other workshops will help the children notice what they want as they think about their hopes and wishes for their future. Having these type of activity can help start the new year in a positive and fun way while allowing the children to experience the power they hold in their own lives.

If you are doing this workshop as a new year activity, begin by first asking participants to think about the New Year and what it symbolically means to them, if anything. Let them know you will be sharing a variety of workshops in the next sessions that will invite them to see their power in getting to choose what they want and how they want to create it. Encourage them to this time to explore a future created by them: "What do you want?" "What are your goals?", and "What steps will you need to take to get to where you want to go?"

The following art workshops can create a path of growth, hope and healing for the children and youth: 

"The children felt safe and comfortable expressing what their dreams for the
future were and realizing that if they believe in themselves they can do anything."		 

           
 
 
A New Year Journal — Engages participants in an opportunity to visualize and create a journal with unique resolutions for each month in the coming year. This allows them to create a path of healing and growth for themselves throughout the new year and encourages them to check in each month on following through with these goals.

Vision Boards — To provide participants with an opportunity to create a Vision Board to help them bring to life their vision for a future filled with what they want and need in their life.

 
 "I want love, hope, and dreams
for the New Year!"
 
New Year Canvases — Using an exciting combination of materials including Mod Podge, this workshop can provide children an opportunity to focus on their hopes for the future by creating a canvas vision board of what they want and need in the coming year. 

Create Your Own Calendar! — This workshop gives participants a special opportunity to talk about goals for the New Year, plan things they want to accomplish, and mark times to celebrate or look forward to, by creating their own calendar.

  
 

My Wishing Well — To help children make resolutions for the New Year by deciding what they would wish for in their lives (other than material things) and creating a personal wishing well.

"It was rewarding to see the children have
an opportunity to express their wants,
dreams, and hopes, and see
themselves with a positive future."

My Time — To create a clock that will help the children notice how the children want to fill their days to have the life we want.
 

 
Happy Healthy Cuppie Cake — To give children a way to create a recipe of the good feelings they want in their life (like trust, joy, fun etc.), and give them the opportunity to keep them in a safe and fun place. They will combine those ingredients to create a "Happy Healthy Cuppie Cake."

  
  "I would like my feet to
carry me to a place where
there is peace and love ."
My Footprints — Allows children to validate and express feelings about their unique journey, what they are learning and where they want to go in their lives, by creating drawings or collages using outlines of their own feet. 

 
 
Words are Like Charms — This workshop teaches the children to create a charm bracelet or necklace that encourages them to notice their positive qualities and how to link them creating a brighter, more optimistic world for themselves.
Row.txt_description: The workshops shared in this series offer children and youth an opportunity to creatively reflect on their future. Each workshop can support participants to recognize their own power and resilience and to create dreams and wishes based on what they want and need most to be happy and whole.
Row.txt_tips: Search for more New Years workshops ideas by using the advance search tool - Holidays!

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Using their own hand as a canvas, each participant in this workshop w ill take a creative window of time to notice the possibility and power that lies within them, and then make a pledge to claim one I CAN to end violence in their lives. By participating in the workshop, participants will join a movement and a community that supports their vision and those of others t aking steps to end violence in our communities.

  
AWBW wants to support Leaders throughout the country to take an additional step of using the I CAN WE CAN workshop to engage their community. Using art to move your community towards change is a powerful and inviting Community Engagement strategy. We encourage you to include members of the broader community in this project (volunteers, board, staff, personal friends), as it truly takes all of us to create change. Documenting the art created by survivors and non-survivors you share this project with via photography is an essential step in using art to engage your community through this project. The details of the Community Engagement aspects of this project are outlined throughout this workshop in italics. 

Pre-workshop Planning:
The first step in leading this workshop is to take a moment to consider when, where, how, and with whom you will gather to create.

You will also need to decide in advance if you have the capacity to offer this workshop as a Community Engagement opportunity. Through documenting the workshop and uploading your artwork to the AWBW I CAN WE CAN website, you can share your agency's online gallery through social media or as a link.

Leaders not able to take this additional step are still encouraged to use this workshop with survivors, staff, and in their communities. This project offers a creative window of time to notice what we all can do to end violence and welcome them to join by adding their name to our anonymous online pledge.

 
  
To help you prepare to facilitate this workshop please consider the following:
Prepare yourself: Be sure to try out the project yourself, in advance, from beginning to end. This is very important and will give you an idea of what your participants will be experiencing during the workshop and how you want to organize your supply layout and timeline.

Make arrangements to offer your group ample time for check-ins, creation, processing, and a closing circle (and photography). You may even consider creating an outline of how you will manage your workshop time and share it with the group to help them pace their creation process.

To get an idea of what the I CAN WE CAN workshop is like, watch this short video of an AWBW community workshop: click here. 

Prepare your supplies: You might be surprised by the materials and how they feel as you use your hand as a canvas. Becoming familiar with the supplies and the creation process yourself will make it much easier to support those you are leading and also identify any supplies you would like to include or omit. The list below is simply a suggested list of supplies; we welcome you to be bold, get creative and add any supplies you like such as Henna or cosmetic make-up. Anything goes!

Prepare your group: Some people may have preconceived notions about art. You may want to begin by asking your group, “Who is scared of art? Who has not done art since grade school?” After they reply, it is a wonderful opportunity to assuage any apprehension by assuring the participants that there is no wrong way to do this project. "During Windows time we have the opportunity to focus on enjoying the process and allowing your authentic expression to come out."

Final Note to facilitator: When guiding an empowerment art group of any size, creating a safe and calming environment is of utmost importance. To help you “set the stage” for your I CAN WE CAN group, we have included a welcome that promotes empowerment using AWBW’s philosophy of creating a window of safety, freedom, creativity, and respect. You will also want to add your intention for this workshop and what your role will be in the group. Explain in advance if you plan to participate or be in the room as a compassionate observer to support and document their I CAN WE CAN pledge.

If necessary, remember to establish guidelines with input from group members. Guidelines should include mutual respect for one another, acceptance of all feelings and expressions, and an agreement of confidentiality.

 
  
Timeframe:
1-2 hour(s) to facilitate the I CAN WE CAN workshop only.
2-3 hours to facilitate workshop and document it for the community engagement project and online exhibit. Add an additional hour to make this workshop part of AWBW's Community Engagement Project and have a personalized gallery created of your groups artwork on AWBW's I CAN WE CAN website.

Additional Set-Up/Prep Instructions for Community Engagement:
Set aside 2 hours of uninterrupted space and time to lead this workshop with a group. The 2-hour time frame is recommended to provide enough time for check-ins, creation, processing, a closing circle, and photography.

You may want to designate a wall space or use a poster board or other blank wall or material to use as the background for the photos to be taken in front of. This is especially important because when working indoors, space is limited. Lighting should also be taken into consideration to ensure the photos are of high quality and representative of the participants' creations. We also encourage you to first practice using the camera that you will use during the workshop so that you are comfortable photographing the creations.

To expedite the photograph taking process, it is helpful to have the Art/Media Releases available for the participants to complete at the beginning of the workshop. Ask the participants to bring their Art/Media Release with their name written legibly on it when you take their photographs. This is very important since it will allow you to match the artwork to necessary releases, prior to uploading them to the I CAN WE CAN gallery.

Additional supplies:
Camera
Art/Media Release for each participant
Art/Media Release for each participant - Spanish

 
  
Materials:
Face paint, makeup, washable markers - anything washable to write on skin
Eyeliner pencils
White-out pens
Paint brushes and/or sponges to apply face paint
Pens
Copy paper for journaling and sketching
Non-bleeding tissue paper and permanent markers (you can write on the paper and then apply it to your hand using water!)
Scissors
Spray bottle for water
Water
Baby wipes or make-up remover and cotton balls
Music
See I CAN WE CAN gallery for more supply ideas!
Pledge Sheet Sign-in



 
I CAN WE CAN Workshop Steps:
Step 1: Welcome
"This is 'a window of time' to practice respecting your thoughts, feelings, needs, and vision. This workshop is designed to enable us to re-focus our energy from the things we think we cannot do, to what each of us is capable of doing to end violence in our lives and in those around us!  Be gentle with yourself and honor all that has come before this moment. Embrace and notice that today you are safe and free to choose I CAN.

"As you notice your power and the possibility that lies within you, know that whether what comes to you seems 'too small' to be important or seems 'too big' to be possible, please try to trust that your ideas are just right. When you truly honor your heart, you can create a change that ripples out from you to those around you and to the community at large, as part of a global change. Your I CAN, no matter how small or big is part of changing the world. If you need to take a break or opt out of any aspect of the project, please do so. If you need some support, let me know, as part of my role here today is to be here for each of you."


 
Step 2: Check-in:
Take a moment to check-in with the group by asking each person to share their name and a word or a sentence about how they are feeling in this moment. "Are you feeling nervous, excited, afraid, or happy? Please know that today is about you and you are safe and encouraged to do, say, and feel whatever is your unique expression.

"Who would like to start the opening circle sharing your name and how you feel about being here today?"

The check-in is important since it brings everyone's voice into the room and allows for connection and trust.

Step 3: Warm-up:
"Many of us have heard all of all our lives that we can’t have or be who or do what we really want, whether it was someone in our family, friends, society, our community, or even our own thoughts. Maybe one of the things you have been told is that 'it is not possible to live free from violence' or that 'it is selfish to get what you want or you feel you deserve.'

"We are going to take a moment to release those doubts and 'I Can't' thoughts and notice the power we already have inside. Pick a partner to share for one minute about something that you thought could not do, or were told you could not do, but you did and it made you stronger as a result. It can be anything you would like to share. We will take turns sharing for the full minute so that each person can share one at a time. I will help you take turns by timing a minute and letting you know when it is time to switch speakers."

After everyone has shared: Validate the group by thanking them for taking the time to notice that they have the power to do what they want.

 
Step 4: Introduction to the Creation Process:
"The I CAN WE CAN project is about the difference we can ALL make in ending all forms of abuse by taking a moment, a creative 'window of time,' to notice our own personal vision and commitment to end violence using our own hands.

"Today each of us will make a personal commitment or pledge for ending violence in our own lives. Please remember that there is no wrong way to participate in this project and every aspect of this workshop is voluntary. Please honor your feelings, thoughts, and ideas about how you want to create your expression for ending violence."

Step 5: Releasing "I Can’ts" (Optional step):
  
  
 
In preparing to move the threshold of what we can do to help end violence, it can be quite powerful to take some time looking closely at any "I Can'ts" we carry. Be aware that acknowledging what we feel we can’t do can bring up intense feelings in participants. This is a step that is done with the intention of unburdening participants from perceived limitations and negative thoughts.

If you choose to do this exercise, be sure to allow 5 to 10 minutes for participants to free-write or journal without stopping and editing, about any "I Can'ts" they can think of. Next, ask them to share what came up for them with a partner or with the group (allow for at least 5 min. per participant). Lastly, you can provide some way to encourage the participants to let go of their "I Can’ts," whether it is by literally destroying them or creating a ceremony to unburden themselves of their "I Cant's."

Step 6: I CAN Reading (Optional step)
Reading an inspirational poem or even a quotation can be a powerful and a quick way to prepare your group. Below, we have included a reading by Marianne Williamson that one of our Leaders has found to be useful in facilitating this workshop. After doing a reading, you might try a brief relaxation to help participants get centered before beginning the creation process. Feel free to share another poem, story, or quote that you find inspiring and pertinent to this project.

"Before we begin creating, I want to share a reading called Our Deepest Fear by Marianne Williamson to help encourage us to think boldly and envision what I CAN we want to embrace today.”

“Our deepest fear is not that we are inadequate. Our deepest fear is that we are powerful beyond measure. It is our light, not our darkness that most frightens us. We ask ourselves, 'Who am I to be brilliant, gorgeous, talented, fabulous?'' Actually, who are you not to be? You are a child of God. Your playing small does not serve the world. There is nothing enlightened about shrinking so that other people won't feel insecure around you. We are all meant to shine, as children do. We were born to make manifest the glory of God that is within us. It's not just in some of us; it's in everyone. And as we let our own light shine, we unconsciously give other people permission to do the same. As we are liberated from our own fear, our presence automatically liberates others.”

  
Step 7: Brief Relaxation
 "Now, if you feel comfortable enough to do so, please close your eyes or just sit quietly. Take a minute to breathe and think about or imagine your vision for your I CAN. Try to picture it in your mind, however it comes to you, as an image, a place, or a list of things you truly want. Notice how it feels in your body to make this pledge to yourself and share it with the world. Do you feel joy, power, peace? Take as long as you need but remember that your I CAN might be something simple and personal or it can be your greatest vision.   Keeping your vision and the poem in mind, be bold when creating your I CAN hand! "

Step 8: I CAN Creation:
"Now, think about being part of a circle of people around the globe committed to ending violence. If each of us notices a new step we want to claim and act on, we can move the world. What I CAN do you want to claim today? Again, no idea is too small or too large. Just notice what resonates in your heart as most meaningful for you. When you are ready, begin to create your I CAN hand using your hand as your canvas. Place your I CAN message on it however you like. Your I CAN expression can be painted on, glued on or placed on paper and held in the palm of your hand. Anything goes! We will create art that represents the I CAN each of our hearts is telling us to reach for and we will using our own hand as a canvas for that expression. "

 
Step 9:  Documenting I CAN Pledge Hands:
You may want to have a camera ready and encourage the participants to have you take their picture once they are done creating. This can streamline the photography process since people will finish creating at different times.

"Taking a photo of your I CAN hand is part of the creative process so be as creative as you like with it. Your I CAN hand could be against whatever background you wish, a color of paper, your face, blades of grass, or torn/shredded I Can'ts--whatever most powerfully expresses your I CAN!"
 
Step 10:  Closing Sharing Circle:
You may want to end by giving each participant an opportunity to share anything they want with the group about their experience with the workshop. After each person is done creating you can say, “Now I would like to give everyone an opportunity to share something about their experience here today. We will go around the room and each take turns sharing anything you want about your I CAN pledge, what you created, and your overall experience with the workshop.”

Step 11:  Participant Evaluations and Workshop Closing
Pass out participant evaluations and thank all participants for taking a window of time to notice their strength and what they CAN do to end abuse! Share with them that by creating their I CAN pledge they are joining other survivors and non-survivors coming together to end abuse. If possible, provide the participants the pledge sheet sign-in to add their names (or pseudonyms) and join the I CAN WE CAN movement. After the workshop, you will need to go the I CAN WE CAN website to add the names from the pledge sign-in by clicking "Join Us."

  
Step 12: Submit I CAN WE CAN Pledge Hands for Customized Online Exhibit
Let the group know that you will be adding their voices to the I CAN WE CAN project by uploading a photo of their creation to the I CAN WE CAN website. Or, when appropriate, you could ask the participants to upload their photo themselves and sign the I CAN WE CAN pledge online. To keep your groups' pledge hands together, be sure to enter them using your program name. If possible share the online gallery with participants and let them know that their artwork and pledge will help inspire others to do what they can to end abuse in their own lives and their communities. Finally, be sure to share your online gallery or own pledge hand with your community using the tools provided in the I CAN WE CAN website.
Row.txt_description: Using their own hand as a canvas, each participant in this workshop will take a creative window of time to notice the possibility and power that lies within them, and then make a pledge to claim one I CAN to end violence in their lives. By participating in the workshop participants will be joining a movement and a community that supports their vision and those of others taking steps to end violence in our communities.
Row.txt_tips:
Supply tips for participants:
  • Feel free to plan and gather all materials you will need create you hand before you start working, since using only one hand will make it more difficult to work.
  • Washable markers on tissue paper may run and stain when wet, so be sure to cover your work surface and clothing. The colored tissue paper may also run and stain your hands. Tissue squares will run.
  • When you wet the paper, the washable markers will run, so use only permanent markers with the tissue paper.
  • Even washable markers may not wash off right away, so you may have your I CAN with you all day (depending on the number of times you wash your hands).
  • Be mindful of the amount of face paint you are taking; a little goes a long way and you can always come back for more.
  • Be gentle when writing on tissue paper with permanent markers and/or white out pens since they may rip the paper.
  • Sharpies and other permanent markers will stain your hand for several days.
  • Use scratch paper if you wish to sketch your design prior to creating.

Row.txt_code:
Introduction to Embodied Art 
At Windows, we often say that art empowers survivors to transform how they view themselves, allowing them to see past the abusive messages they learned to rebuild their self-confidence. Embodied art (theatre, d ance, and other types of movement or body awareness) also provides survivors the opportunity to heal, rediscover a sense of hope, and take charge of their lives.

Reclaiming one’s body for oneself through embodied art can be profoundly healing, allowing survivors to re-connect with their bodies and repair the mind-body connection that is so often disrupted in abusive relationships. Furthermore, there's a strong connection between how we hold or move our bodies and how we feel about ourselves.

      

 As researcher Amy Cuddy explains, standing like a superhero for just two minutes—as silly as it seems—actually changes your brain’s chemistry, leading you to feel less stressed and more confident. In other words, simply embodying a superhero pose, no matter how ridiculous you feel while you’re doing it, makes you feel more like a superhero! Click here to watch a video of her TED talk.      

As with Windows visual arts workshops, there is no right or wrong way to participate in embodied art. Just as a participant in a visual arts workshop might need to scribble furiously or even rip their paper up, a participant in an embodied workshop gets to use their body in whatever way makes sense to them, whether that’s tensing up completely, relaxing by putting their head down, or jumping up and down. For one person, the perfect embodied experience might look like sitting still, with a hand over their heart, and paying attention to what’s present for them, what parts of their body are tense and what parts are calm. For another person, it might look like exercise or a playful game. For others, it could be theatrical techniques, relaxation exercises, or dancing. Embodied workshops operate in the same way as visual art workshops, allowing participants to honor whatever emerges.

Many Windows workshops have embodied elements, and we invite you to lead one (or more!) of them and notice how movement or body awareness affects your participants. See below for a list of workshops, many of which might be familiar to you already. It's up to you to decide which workshops to lead and in what order. You can also lead any workshop using embodied art and let us know by sending us this form!

We encourage you to share with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. You might say to them, “Today, I’m going to invite you to take this window of time to connect to yourself—to your thoughts, to your feelings, and to your body. Some of you might feel scared. Some of you might feel proud. Know that any thoughts, feelings, or sensations that come up are just fine. This is your window of time, and you get to claim it for yourself, while noticing that you’re not alone. For many survivors, bodies can be reminders of the past. Today, I’m inviting you to let your body be a reminder that you are here, in this room, with this incredible, strong group.”


AWBW staff and partners participate in an embodied art exercise.

14 Windows Workshops Featuring Embodied Art
Expressive Crayon Warm-Up - In this simple yet powerful warm-up, participants can safely express any emotions they have been holding inside by scribbling freely.

The Wind Takes Away - This workshop promotes group bonding by playfully showing connections and shared experiences through an engaging and active embodied art activity.

Image of the Hours - In this embodied art workshop, participants get to explore their "typical" day and their ideal day nonverbally. In this "rehearsal for real life" process, they have the opportunity to better understand their experiences, needs, and visions.

River Stories - Through visual art (drawing) and embodied art (movement), participants are invited to use the metaphor of a river to acknowledge their past, notice their resilience, and honor their present strength.

Feelings Target Warm Up - This activity is a playful way to allow the participants to share about a time they felt a certain way in a group setting. This workshop helps the participants to notice the spectrum of feelings and realize that all people feel a variety of different emotions. This warm-up can stand alone as workshop or can be used to support other workshops.

  
  Three different statues of excitement from the Feelings Target Warm Up.
Anger Sequence Before and After - The participants  will create an anger sequence processing the triggers, thoughts, feelings, behaviors, and effects of their anger. They will create their past and future anger sequences on two "Putting Myself Back Together" dolls. By writing and coloring emotions on a paper doll made up of puzzle pieces participants are able to reflect on their current emotions and where they feel these emotions in their body. Through journaling and reflecting on their present emotions and envisioning what they wish to feel in the future they will begin to transform their way of expressing anger in a healthy manner.

Inner Self Portraits - This workshop will assist the participant in going within and discovering more about their inner-self! This workshop gives us an opportunity to go to a deep level and expose, explore, celebrate and get more in touch with our inner-self... our inner most being. This workshop offers 3 different techniques to allow the participant to fully express their inner-selves. This is also a great project for an exhibit.

The Monster in Me - Using a simple technique with oil pastels and watercolors, each person will have the opportunity to reflect on their own personal experiences with domestic violence, explore difficult emotions in a safe and fun way, and give voice to the feelings that may be hidden inside by creating artwork that represents the “monster” within.


 
 A participant connects with her body through a guided relaxation.
 
Our Body Relationship - Gives survivors a way of renewing their relationships with their bodies after possibly managing their abuse through disassociation or addiction. Offers another option in which to experience and relate to their bodies.

Personal Needs Flower - Provides an opportunity for participants to tune into their own personal needs by creating a flower where each petal represents one need. They begin to see the many layers of needs, and to honor all these layers.

Putting Myself Back Together - By writing and coloring emotions on a paper doll made up of puzzle pieces the survivors are able to reflect on their current emotions (or needs) and where they feel these emotions (or needs) in their body.

Seeing Me - Participants are offered a chance to see the beauty within themselves and to know how others view them. The goal of the project is for participants self-esteem to be raised each time they look at the art they create in this workshop.
 
Sleep Collages - Gives participants a time to relax and take a nap, followed by the creation of a collage filled with relaxing images that can help them sleep better during this difficult time in their lives. There are several variations to this sleep workshop: sleep rocks, nap goggles, etc.


  
A participant explores facial expressions in The Monster in Me workshop.

Story Trees - This workshop provides participants a creative opportunity to explore their stories of survival, change and growth. Using the tree as a symbol of life, participants can explore and uncover the stories of their life.

For publicly available sample Embodied Art workshops, click here: The Wind Takes Away or River Stories.
Row.txt_description: When survivors reclaim their bodies for themselves through embodied art (theatre, dance, and other types of movement or body awareness), they gain the opportunity to heal, rediscover a sense of hope, and take charge of their lives. Through these popular Windows workshops participants can re-connect with their bodies and repair the mind-body connection that is so often disrupted in abusive relationships.

Row.txt_code:
Embodied Art
Have you ever noticed how eager most children are to move and explore the world with their bodies? Or perhaps you've notice that it can be challenging for your group to sit still for an art workshop. One reason is that chi ldren naturally learn and heal through movement and embodied play, from babies putting objects in their mouths to older children playing "pretend" or tag. One way to support children's natural interest in movement and their bodies is through workshops that feature embodied art (theatre games, movement warm-ups, dance, etc.).

Embodied art allows children who have experienced or witnessed violence to re-connect with their bodies and repair the mind-body connection that is so often disrupted in abusive situations. Reclaiming one's body for oneself through embodied art can be profoundly healing. Furthermore, there's a strong connection between how we hold or move our bodies and how we feel about ourselves.

      

 As researcher Amy Cuddy explains, standing like a superhero for just two minutes—as silly as it seems—actually changes your brain’s chemistry, leading you to feel less stressed and more confident. In other words, simply embodying a superhero pose, no matter how ridiculous you feel while you’re doing it, makes you feel more like a superhero! Click here to watch a video of her TED talk.      

As with Windows visual arts workshops, there is no right or wrong way to participate in embodied art. Just as a child in a visual arts workshop might need to scribble furiously or even rip their paper up, a child in an embodied workshop gets to use their body in whatever way makes sense to them, whether that's tensing up completely, relaxing by putting their head down, or jumping up and down. For one child, the perfect embodied experience might look like sitting still, with a hand over their heart, and paying attention to what's present for them, what parts of their body are tense and what parts are calm. For another child, it might look like exercise or a playful game. For others, it could be theatrical techniques, relaxation exercises, or dancing. Embodied workshops operate in the same way as visual art workshops, allowing participants to honor whatever emerges.

"I think that movement helps to ground and center us into our workshops,
so I can only see this as enhancing the healing."— AWBW Windows Leader

We also encourage you to share with your group the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. You might want to share the many was our bodies are amazing at helping us to know ourselves better. Butterflies in our stomach, energy in our legs or arms, and tension on our foreheads are all messages from our bodies telling us about our personal needs or wants. At the same time, how we move or don't move our bodies can be an expression of what we want for ourselves. Moving our bodies can even cause our brains to release chemicals that make us feel happy.

Even something as simple as how we move our breath in and out of our body sends messages to our brain about what is going on with us in that moment. Think about a time you felt happy or excited. How did you move your body? Did you jump up and down? Did you stand taller? Did you have a huge smile on your face?

Now think about a time when you felt sad or disappointed. How did you move your body then? Did your shoulders slump down or get tense? Did you move slowly?

It makes sense that our bodies sometimes don't want to sit still and other times don't want to move.

You might engage the children by saying to them in a light tone, "Raise your hand if you like to play. Raise your hand if you like to run around. Raise your hand if you're tired of adults telling you to sit still. Raise your hand if you like getting a hug. There are many ways we can use our bodies in fun and safe ways, and different people like to move their bodies in different ways. For example, I like to __________ (dance, nap, run etc.). What are some fun and safe ways you like to use your body?" As they offer ideas, you can let the other children raise their hands if that way is true for them as well. You might need to remind them that there's no right or wrong answer, and that it's okay if not everyone likes all the same activities.

Many Windows workshops have embodied elements, and we invite you to lead one (or more!) of them and notice how movement or body awareness affects your group. See below for a list of workshops, many of which might be familiar to you already. It's up to you to decide which workshops to lead and in what order. You can also lead any workshop using embodied art and let us know by sending us this form!


AWBW staff and volunteers do the Monster Dance from The Monster in Me workshop.

17 Windows Workshops Featuring Embodied Art
Expressive Crayon Warm-Up - Ages 4 and Older
This warm-up allows participants to safely explore and express emotions.

The Wind Takes Away - Ages 7 and Older
This workshop promotes group bonding by playfully showing connections and shared experiences through an engaging and active embodied art activity.

My Day, My Way, (Image of the Hours) - Ages 7 and Older
In this embodied art workshop, participants playfully act out their daily reality. Then in a "rehearsal for real life," they get to imagine and create their perfect day.

River Stories - Ages 12 and Older
Through visual art (drawing) and embodied art (movement), participants are invited to use the metaphor of a river to acknowledge their past, notice their resilience, and honor their present strength.

Feelings Target (warm-up) - Ages 3 and Older
This activity is a playful way to allow the children to share about a time they felt a feeling in a group setting. This workshop helps the children to notice the spectrum of feelings and that all children feel all of the different emotions. This warm-up can stand alone as workshop or can be used to support other workshops.

 
   Three different statues of excitement from the Feelings Target (warm-up) workshop.
Body Tracing (Celebrating My Body) - Ages 3-12 (For teens, use the Women's Windows version called Our Body Relationship.)

This is a supplement to "Celebrating My Body," a workshop in the Children's Windows Manual. Shares in detail the words and tone of Binah Taylor when working with young children; how she engages them in the process and specifically how she talks them through being traced.

Feelings Birds - Ages 3-12
Allows time for exploration of feelings through colors and motion, the end result, "Feeling Birds," are finger puppets.

Feelings Shakers - Ages 3-12
This workshop is designed by Ellen Denninger and is intended to let mothers and children create a very simple musical instrument with which to express and identify feelings concretely using movement and rhythm. Their physical action and sound vibration can help release blocked energy, which becomes more available for creative use in present awareness.

Happy Healthy Cuppie Cake - Ages 5-14
To give children a way to create a recipe of the good feelings they want in their life (like trust, joy, fun etc.), and give them the opportunity to keep them in a safe and fun place. They will combine those ingredients to create a "Happy Healthy Cuppie Cake." This workshop is perfect for Valentine's Day, but can also be done at other times of the year. For Valentine's Day you can use heart shapes and ribbon in shades of pink and red colors.


 
 Mixing joy into cupcake batter in the Happy Healthy Cuppie Cake workshop.
 
Inner Self Portraits - Ages 6 and Older

This workshop will assist older children and teens to look inside and discovering more about their inner-self! We are used to looking at our outer selves, our looks, our clothes, our appearance, the image we try to portray! This workshop gives us an opportunity to go to a deeper level and get more in touch with our inner-self. You will have 3 options of material to work with, you can mix them up if you prefer.

The Monster in Me - Ages 3 and Older

Gives children an opportunity to be playful in exploring some of the more difficult emotions they experience. Offers a process that will look bold and powerful, and be rewarding and satisfying for the children.


My Dancing Monster - Ages 3-12

Children will create a dancing monster and experience the joy and freedom of letting themselves go in the monster dance. A perfect workshop for Halloween (and all year round), this promotes the playful and fun side of monsters!

My Footprints - Ages 6-12
Allows children to validate and express feelings about their unique journey, what they are learning and where they want to go in their lives, by creating drawings or collages using outlines of their own feet.

Putting Myself Back Together - Ages 3 and Older

Allows children to look at and discover the many feelings they have inside themselves as they color and name emotions on a paper doll made up of puzzle pieces.

 
  Participants play a mirroring game in the Seeing Me workshop.
Seeing Me - 
Ages 6 and Older
Gives children a chance to see the beauty within themselves and insight into how their peers view them. The goal of the project is for the kids' self-esteem to be raised each time they look at the art they create in this workshop.

Story Trees - Ages 6 and Older
The Story Tree workshop gives children an opportunity to explore their strength and growth. Using the tree as a symbol of life and courage, participants are free to play and let their imaginations run wild as they discover what kind of tree they want to be.

Summer Wind Catchers - Ages 3 and Older
Gives children an opportunity to explore and creating their own sense of peacefulness and beauty through the wind inside (their breath) and outside of them. The end product are breezy strips of finger painted art, ready to hang outside or in.

To see publicly available sample Embodied Art workshops click here: The Wind Takes Away or River Stories.
Row.txt_description: Youth re-connect with their bodies and repair the mind-body connection through embodied art. Using popular Windows workshops, participants can experience how holding or moving their bodies can help them uncover and express who they are or want to be.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Participants will create I CAN art to help raise awareness, support others, and get support for themselves.

Materials:
Shrinky Dinks
Hand templates
Colored pencils
Permanent markers
Ribbon
Beads
Toaster or conventional oven
Brown paper bag
Cardstock
Hole puncher

Note: You can do this project with any supplies at all (e.g. paper, scratch art, clay, etc.). You can even participate in Find Your I CAN virtually by going to the online gallery at icanwecan.awbw.org and using the social media buttons to comment and share artwork and stories!

Time Frame:
1 hour
Intro: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Creation: 40 minutes
Closing: 5 minutes

Age range:
5 and up

Set-up/Prep:
Prior to the workshop, print out a variety of hand templates for participants to use. Provide an example of what the Shrinky Dink paper looks like with permanent marker and colored pencils after the shrinking process. Create a finished I CAN with a statement and a message for participants to see.

Introduction:
Let's take about ten minutes to reflect on what we can do to help end violence in our own lives. If you feel comfortable, you can close your eyes and relax as you take this time for yourself. As you're reflecting, remember that any I CAN that comes to mind is great and don't worry if it seems too small to be important or too big to be possible.

Opening Circle:
We are going to take about 10 minutes and share our ideas with one another. This is a perfect time for us to share our ideas with a partner and get some feedback. If you're having trouble coming up with ideas, this is a good time to talk with your partner and work with them. Try to come up with an I CAN statement such as "I CAN speak up." as well as a short explanation like, "I CAN speak up when someone is in trouble."

Creation:

Step 1: Create Your I CAN Statement

  1. Now that you've chosen your I CAN statement, think about how your want to represent it on your Shrinky Dink. What colors do you want to use? How do you want to design it?
  2. On the shrinkable plastic, draw your I CAN (e.g. "I CAN Listen," "I CAN Speak Up," "I CAN_______"), making sure that your I CAN statement is large and clearly readable (this will help make sure that people can find your uploaded photo). You can either use colored pencils on the rough side or permanent markers on either side of the shrinkable plastic. Feel free to embellish your I CAN statement by tracing one of the provided hand templates or adding other drawings or doodles.
  3. Punch a hole at the top of your artwork so you can attach the tag during Step 4. Leave at least a 1/4" between the edge of the plastic and your hole.

If you would like to keep your I CAN creation for yourself as well as put one into the community, create a duplicate I CAN statement by tracing your artwork before shrinking it. To make the tracing easier, temporarily tape the two shrinkable plastic sheets together.


Step 2: Shrink Your Artwork

  1. Preheat an oven (toaster or conventional is fine) to 300˚F.
  2. Bake your shrink art in the oven for a couple of minutes. Your artwork will curl up then flatten. After it flattens, take it out to cool.

Tip: Place your shrink art on a paper bag cut-out for easy removal.


Step 3: Wear and Share your I CAN

  1. Make a necklace, bracelet or something you can wear
  2. Wear your I CAN shrink art .
  3. Share your I CAN with someone. If someone asks about what you're wearing and tell them about your I CAN and your experience with the movement.

 ADD PHOTO OF NECKLACE/BRACELET

 
   
   
   
Closing Circle:
Bring the group back to a circle and invite each participant to share about their experience. You can offer some of these prompts to start a conversation:
  • How did this process make you feel?
  • How will you use your I CAN to reach people?
  • Who would you like to share I CAN with?
  • How do you see your I CAN changing in the future?

Row.txt_code:
Pre-workshop Planning:

The first step in hosting a peer group workshop is to take a moment to consider when, where, how and with whom you will gather to create. To help you prepare you will also need to consider the following:

  1. Prepare yourself: Be sure to try out the project yourself in advance, from beginning to end. This is very important and will give you an idea of what your participants will be experiencing during the workshop and how you want to organize your supply layout and timeline.

To get an idea of what a facilitated workshop looks like click here to watch AWBW’s I CAN Community Workshop video 

  1. Prepare your supplies: You might be surprised by the materials and how they feel as you use your hand as a canvas. Becoming familiar with the supplies and the creation process yourself will make it much easier to support those you're leading and also identify any supplies you’d like to include or omit. The list below is just a suggested list of supplies; we welcome you to be bold, get creative and add any supplies you like such as Henna or cosmetic make-up. Anything goes!
  1. Prepare your group: Some people may have preconceived notions about art. You may want to begin by asking your group, “Who’s scared of art?  Who hasn’t done art since grade school?” After they reply, it is a wonderful opportunity to assuage any apprehension by assuring the participants that there is no wrong way to do this project. During Windows time it is all about enjoying the process and allowing your authentic expression to come out.

Suggested Materials:

Suggested Materials
  • Pens and paper
  • Scissors
  • Face paint, makeup, washable markers—anything washable to write on skin 
  • Tissue paper and permanent markers (you can write on the paper and then apply it to your hand using water!)
  • Paint Brushes
  • Water
  • Baby wipes or make-up remover and cotton balls
  • Music (you may want to play something jazzy during the I Can’t journaling portion and relaxing or soothing music during the I CAN creation portion)
  • Camera
  • Consider planning a backdrop (for photographing your hand)

Time and Space:

Set aside 2 hours of uninterrupted space and time to lead a group. The 2-hour time frame is recommended to give ample time for check-ins, creation, processing, a closing circle and photography. Create an outline of how you will manage your time and share it with the group to help them pace their creation process.

Note to Peer Group Host:

When guiding an empowerment art group of any size, creating a safe and calming environment is of utmost importance. To help you “set the stage” for your I CAN WE CAN group, we have included a welcome that promotes empowerment using AWBW’s philosophy of creating a window of safety, freedom, creativity and respect.

Feel free to add your intention for this workshop and what your role will be in the group. Explain in advance if you plan to participate or be in the room as a compassionate observer to support and document their I CAN WE CAN pledge.

You will need to establish guidelines with input from group members. Guidelines should include mutual respect for one another, acceptance of all feelings and expressions, and an agreement of confidentiality.

I CAN WE CAN Workshop Steps:

I. Welcome
Three survivors standing in unison.

"This project is about noticing what YOU can do to end interpersonal violence in all its forms (physical, emotional, psychological, and spiritual). Your I CAN expression is a personal commitment, or pledge to yourself, of taking a step in creating your vision of what WE can accomplish if we all say 'I CAN end violence.' There are many ways of getting to this place inside yourself.

"If you need to take a break or opt out of any aspect of the project, please do so. If you need some support, let me know as part of my role here today is to be here for each of you. We encourage you to respect whatever comes up and allow it to flow without judgment.

"This is 'a window of time' to practice respecting your thoughts, feelings, needs and vision. Be gentle with yourself and honor all that has come before this moment. Embrace and notice that today you are safe and free to chose I CAN.


"Whether what comes to you seems 'too small' to be important or seems 'too big' to be possible, please try to trust that your ideas are just right.  When you truly honor your heart, you can create a change that ripples out from you to those around you and to the community at large, as part of a global change. Your I CAN, no matter how small or big, is part of changing the world."

About One Billion Rising:

AWBW is proud to kick off the I CAN WE CAN project in support of One Billion Rising, a global movement to end violence against women and girls. One Billion Rising is the latest project of playwright and activist Eve Ensler. Ms. Ensler created the Vagina Monologues and V-Day to help end violence against women. One Billion Rising is a global movement created to bring awareness and respond to the fact that:

ONE IN THREE WOMEN ON THE PLANET WILL BE RAPED OR BEATEN IN HER LIFETIME. ONE BILLION WOMEN VIOLATED IS AN ATROCITY.

This project is inviting ONE BILLION women and those who love them to WALK OUT, DANCE, RISE UP, and DEMAND an end to this violence. ONE BILLION RISING will move the earth, activating women and men across every country. V-Day wants the world to see our collective strength, our numbers, our solidarity across borders. A Window Between Worlds is contributing to this project by adding voices of support through the I CAN WE CAN project. By participating in I CAN WE CAN you are standing up and being counted as one of the billion people rising to end violence against women. AWBW’s goal is to add 20,000 voices to this project and we thank you for being an important part of helping us reach our goal!

II. Check-in:

Take a moment to check-in with the group by asking everyone to share a word or a sentence about why they are attending this workshop. The check-in is important as it brings everyone's voice into the room and allows for connection and trust.

III. Introduction to the creation process:

"The I CAN WE CAN project is about the difference we can ALL make in ending all forms of abuse by taking a moment, a creative 'window of time' to notice your personal vision and commitment to end violence using you own hands. Today each of us will embrace a personal commitment for ending violence through creative expression. Please know that there is no wrong way to participate in this project and every aspect of this workshop is voluntary. Please honor your feelings, thoughts and ideas about how you want to create your expression for ending violence. Whether what comes to you seems 'too small' to be important or seems 'too big' to be possible, please try to trust that your ideas are just right. When you truly honor your heart, you can create a change that ripples out from you to those around you, to the community at large as part of a global change. Your I CAN, no matter how small or big, is part of changing the world."

IV. Releasing "I Can’ts" (Optional step):

"In preparing to move the threshold of what we can do to help end violence, it can be quite powerful to take some time looking closely at any "I Can'ts" we carry. Be aware that acknowledging what we feel we can’t do can bring up intense feelings in participants. This is a step that is done with the intention of unburdening participants from perceived limitations and negative thoughts. Be mindful of your group's needs when choosing one of the choices below.

Writing her I-Cant's

Option 1: "I Can't" Journaling

If you choose to do this exercise, be sure to allow 5 to 10 minutes for participants to free-write or journal without stopping and editing, about any I Can'ts they can think of. Next, ask them to share what came up for them with a partner or with the group (allow for at least 5 min. per participant). Lastly, you can provide some way to let go of their I Can’ts whether it’s by literally destroying them or creating a ceremony to unburden themselves.

Before you begin this exercise, remind participants that every aspect of the workshop is voluntary, that they are in a safe space and their expression is welcome. Allow each participant to share without interruption and remember to validate each person as they share (or choose not to share) by acknowledging them with gratitude for respecting what may have come up.

Note: If you do the I Can’t journaling, we encourage you to do the I CAN circle immediately after to help the participants transition from Can’t to Can.

 

 

Participating in the Circle

Option 2: I CAN Circle

"Let's start by taking a moment to notice our past victories over things that seemed impossible. I’m going to ask each of you to share about one thing you thought you couldn’t do, but did, and it made you stronger. What is an "I Can't" that you have overcome? It can be something simple or something monumental; there is no right or wrong way to share. If you don’t feel comfortable sharing, just say pass when it is your turn to share.”

You may want to do this with everyone standing in a unified circle, holding hands or by allowing peers to share with a partner during a timed sharing exercise. This can help create a feeling of intimacy. After everyone has shared, validate the group and each person by acknowledging that all of us have done things we thought we couldn’t do. 

 

Option 3: I CAN Reading with Brief Relaxation

Reading an inspirational poem or even a quotation can be a powerful, and a quick way to prepare your group. Below we are offering a reading by Marianne Williamson that one of our leaders has found to be useful. Feel free to share another poem, story or quote that you find inspiring. If you have the capacity, you might consider projecting AWBW’s Virtual Meditation Room for the participant to view (the full meditation slide show is 7 minutes.) 

After doing a reading, you might try a brief relaxation to help participants get centered before beginning the creation process.

"Before we begin creating, I want to share a reading called Our Deepest Fear by Marianne Williamson to help encourage us to think boldly and envision what I CAN we want to embrace today.”

“Our deepest fear is not that we are inadequate. Our deepest fear is that we are powerful beyond measure. It is our light, not our darkness that most frightens us. We ask ourselves, 'Who am I to be brilliant, gorgeous, talented, fabulous?'' Actually, who are you not to be? You are a child of God. Your playing small does not serve the world. There is nothing enlightened about shrinking so that other people won't feel insecure around you. We are all meant to shine, as children do. We were born to make manifest the glory of God that is within us. It's not just in some of us; it's in everyone. And as we let our own light shine, we unconsciously give other people permission to do the same. As we are liberated from our own fear, our presence automatically liberates others.”


"Now, if you feel comfortable enough to do so, please close your eyes or just sit quietly. Take a minute to breathe and think about or imagine your vision for your I CAN. Try to picture it in your mind however it comes to you, as an image, a place, or a list of things you truly want. Notice how it feels in your body to make this pledge to yourself and share it with the world. Do you feel joy, power, peace? Take as long as you need but remember your I CAN can be something simple and personal or it can be your greatest vision.

"Keeping your vision and the poem in mind, be bold when creating your I CAN hand! The founder of A Window Between Worlds, Cathy Salser thought her vision for using art in a way that would make a difference could only come true in her wildest dreams and now the organization reaches 65,000 people per year, including you!"

 

  


 
V. I CAN Creation  
Drawing letters on her hand

"Now think about being part of a circle of people around the globe committed to ending violence against women. If each of us notices a new step we want to claim and act on, we can move the world. What I CAN do you want to claim today?  Again, no idea is too small or too large. Just notice what resonates in your heart as most meaningful for you. When you're ready, begin to create your I CAN hand using your hand as your canvas. Place your I CAN message on it however you like. Your I CAN expression can be painted on, glued on or placed on paper and held in the palm of your hand. Anything goes!  

Supply tips for participants:

  1. Washable markers on tissue paper may run and stain when wet, so take care to cover your work surface and clothing. The colored tissue paper may also run and stain your hands.
  2. Some types of face paint are more difficult to get off so you may be required to provide a sink with soap and water, make-up remover or even rubbing alcohol.
  3. Be gentle when writing on tissue paper with permanent markers and/or white out pens since they may rip the paper.
  4. Sharpies and other permanent markers will stain your hand for several days.
  5. Provide scratch paper for people who may want to sketch their design prior to creating.
  6. Suggest to participants that they create and gather all components they will need create their hand before they start working, as it will be more difficult to work using only one hand.
  7. You may want to encourage the participants to be mindful of the background they will use when photographing their hands.
VI. Documenting I CAN Pledge Hands:
Documenting the hands

You may want to have a camera ready and encourage the participants to have you take their picture once they are done creating. This can streamline the photography process, as people will finish creating at different times.

"Taking a photo of your I CAN hand is part of the creative process, so be as creative as you like with it. Your I CAN hand could be against whatever background you wish, a color of paper, your face, blades of grass, or torn/shredded I Can'ts. Whatever most powerfully expresses your I CAN!"

 

VII. Closing Circle:

You may want to end by giving each participant an opportunity to share anything they want with the group about their experience with the workshop. After each person is done creating you can say, “Now I’d like to give everyone an opportunity to share something about their experience here today. We will go around the room and each take turns sharing anything you want about your I CAN, what you created, your overall experience with the workshop, anything you like.”

VIII. Join WE CAN

Let the group know that you’ll be adding their voice to the I CAN WE CAN project by uploading a photo of their creation to the I CAN WE CAN website. Or you can ask the participants to upload their photo themselves and sign the I CAN WE CAN pledge online.

Thank participants for adding their I CAN pledge hand to the online gallery where it will be counted as they join the ripple of hands across the country that are rising up as part of One Billion Rising. Encourage them to go to icanwecan.awbw.org to join our online community and share their pledge via social media.

Encourage participants to consider how they might wish to be visible on 2-14-13 as part of One Billion Rising. Their action could fall anywhere on the spectrum from a solo action (like simply writing their I CAN on their hand that day), to an open dialog with those around them throughout the day, to a large group action (like coordinating a performance piece). Click here for instructions on reenacting an I CAN performance art piece by performance art legend, Barbara T. Smith.

Thank you for taking a window of time to notice your strength and broadening your ideas about what you CAN do to end abuse! And thank you for helping AWBW start a movement of people coming together to collectively embrace I CAN!
