"Don't forget to write a couple of messages for yourself and slip them into your slot as well. It's always nice to say good things about ourselves. By the time we're done with this workshop our pigs' bellies will be full of positive notes for you to read!"

Closing Circle:
"Taking a look around at all of these plump pigs, I'm so glad to see that you have lots of uplifting things to say about one another. Let's take a moment to reach into the coin slots of our pigs and take out one message. We're going to take a moment for ourselves to read a message that we received. As you read it, I want you to think about what it says and really take it in and realize that you are an awesome person!"

"As we go around in the circle, I'm going to give you an opportunity to read your message out loud for the whole group to hear. If you've received a special drawing, show us! As always, you have the opportunity to 'pass' because this moment belongs to you and you can choose to share it or keep it to yourself."

"As we finish up our workshop and take our pigs home, keep them in a safe place. When you're feeling down, or just need a little boost, head on over to that safe place and take a moment for yourself, take a strip of paper out and read it. You'll quickly be reminded of how special you are and will always be."
Row.txt_description: Participants are invited to explore positivity and the uplifting effects it can have on themselves and others.

Row.txt_code:
Objective: Using the concepts and images in the picture book Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs, participants can identify, express, and work through their feelings about separation, anxiety, grief, and loss. Participants can develop positive coping strategies to maintain their sense of connection and well-being even when loves ones are not physically present. Using creativity in a gentle, encouraging, and supportive environment can help to build resilience.

 
 
  Workshop set-up
 
   
  Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs
 
Materials:
BioColor Foam paint
(preferably 4 or 5 different colors)
 - Can be purchased at www.discountschoolsupply.com.
 - Remember to use the source code AWBW to receive your 17% discount.
Paper plates
Paper towels
Sponges
Brushes
Baby wipes
Cray-Pas
Watercolor paper (9x12 or 4x6 depending on your group needs)
Spray bottle for water
Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs by Susan Bernardo and Courtenay Fletcher
- You can purchase a copy of this book on Amazon.com OR you can request a free copy by ordering from us directly. One book per AWBW Program while supplies last!

Timeframe:
Introduction: 15 minutes
Warm-up: 15 minutes
Technical Information: 5 minutes
Reading: 15 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing: 15 minutes
Time frame: 1 hour 45 minutes

Set-Up/Prep:
Prepare paint palettes, 1 palette (paper plates) for every two participants. Squirt a small “mound” of foam paint (about 3-5 colors in total) onto a paper plate. Keep in mind that a little bit goes a long way! You can replenish colors later if needed.

Introduction:
Engage the group in a discussion by asking questions about feelings of loss. "Has anyone ever missed someone or something before? What does it feel like to miss someone? What do you do when you miss someone or something? Whether the person you miss moved far away or died or if you just saw them a few hours ago, this feeling of loss and separation can be really hard! Even when you miss someone, there are ways to feel connected to and be reminded of them. Together, we will read Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs which explores ways to maintain connection, even when those we love are not physically present."

Warm-up:
Prepare the group for creation through a short discussion. "We are going to take a few minutes to reflect and share about who or what you may be missing. Take a moment to think of someone or something you miss sometimes or even right now. Notice how that separation makes you feel. You can simply think about and sit with these emotions or you can create symbols and drawings to go with your reflections." Give participants a moment to reflect and notice who or what they miss.

"Can you think of an object or symbol or is there something in nature that represents or reminds you of the person or thing you miss? Notice why it's special to you. What does it say about how you feel about that person or thing? If you would like to represent this object or symbol, you can create it using the cray pas or if you would just like to think about what that might be and look like, that is OK, too." Give participants another moment to think about their response.

"It is okay if you cannot think of anything specific! You will have the opportunity to explore this concept more through workshop. You might also find that something may emerge once you get home or even later this week.

"When you are ready and if you feel comfortable, I invite you to share by naming who or what you miss and what object or symbol came up for you and why. If you created a drawing, you are welcome to share that, as well. For example, 'I miss my Dad because he lives across the country. When ever I see the moon, I think of him because it is our favorite part of nature and he gave me a lunar calendar.'" After participants have shared, "thank you for looking into your hearts and sharing about the loved ones you miss. Remember that this love you have for those you care about is inside yourselves and you can feel and share it in all kinds of ways!

Technical Info:
Demonstrate resist technique with the art materials. "Before we read the book today, I will demonstrate how to use the supplies to create. We will be using a crayon resist technique with the materials at your place setting; including a watercolor paper, oil pastels, and foam paint."
Steps for creating:
   
  Creating drawing using oil pastels
 
Step 1: "Using the oil pastel, you may want to create a representation of yourself on one side and a representation of what or whom you are missing on the other side." You can create a simple drawing and show it to the group OR consider asking the group to participate together in creating a sample drawing (encouraging them to share who or what they are missing, etc. to create the sample with you.)
Step 2: "Using symbols in nature, from your imagination, symbols or concepts from the story, or anything that is significant to you, we will create a drawing to represent how you can feel connected even if you are apart." Add to the drawing by representing the connection and encourage the participants to share their ideas. Explain and demonstrate that the white crayon draws on invisible but stands out against the paint.
Step 3: "When you are ready to begin painting, raise your hand to signal that you need the spray bottle to lightly wet your paper. The water helps the color to spread more easily and allows the crayon resist technique to really pop through the paint. You can use the foam paint with a paint brush, as you would watercolors, to resist the oil pastels. Feel free to use your fingers, too, but be aware that your hands may be stained for a little while afterward. You can also use sponges to apply the paint and add texture. Keep in mind that a little paint goes a long way!" (Demonstrate how to add paint and the final effect of crayon resist, how they white shows up invisible, etc.)

 
  Painting with foam paint
using a sponge		 Painting with foam paint
using a paintbrush
 Finger painting with
foam paint

Reading:
Depending on the wants, needs, and expectations of your group, ask the participants to follow along and read the story with you, invite them to close their eyes and simply listen to the story, OR encourage them to gather around you and engage in the words and pictures in the book Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs together.
After reading the story, ask the participants if they saw something in the book that they connected to. If so, invite them to share.
Time permitting: Invite the participants to share how or what in nature can help them feel connected to the people they love and sometimes miss.

Creation:
"This is your 'window of time' to practice respecting and connecting to your thoughts, feelings, visions, and anything else that comes up for you. There is no wrong way create; simply notice your needs and honor your expression. If this means just sitting and noticing what your heart is feeling or if you need to put your head down that is okay, too.
 
 
  Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs creations
 

When you are ready, you can begin to create a drawing to represent you and the person or thing you miss. Just like in the book, you can connect the two figures using the feelings in your heart, ideas from your imagination, images from the book, something in nature (sunshine rays, a tree, rainbow) or something that you have to remind you of this special person or thing."

Closing: "If you feel comfortable, please share your art and anything that may have come up for you during the discussion, reading, or creation process." After everyone who wanted to share has had a turn, ask the participants, "'who or what can you look to in nature or is there a special object to comfort you and remind you of the person or thing you miss?' Thank you all for creating and sharing so deeply! Remember that, if we look for it, there are always ways for us to connect to and share our embodiment of love with those we feel far away from. Your creations are a wonderful reminder of how close our loved ones and prized possessions can actually be!"
Row.txt_description: Using the concepts and images in the picture book Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs, participants can identify, express, and work through their feelings about separation, anxiety, grief, and loss. Participants can develop positive coping strategies to maintain their sense of connection and well-being even when loves ones are not physically present. Using creativity in a gentle, encouraging, and supportive environment can help to build resilience.

Row.txt_code:
Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs
 
Objective:
To use the concepts and images in the picture book "Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs," to help children learn to identify and express their feelings about separation/loss and develop ways to maintain their sense of connection, comfort and well-being even when loved ones are not physically present.

Materials:
BioColor Foam paint (preferably 4 or 5 colors)
Can be purchased at www.discountschoolsupply.com    
Remember to use the source code AWBW to receive your 17% discount.
Paper plates
Paper towels
Sponges
Brushes
Baby wipes
Cray-Pas
Watercolor paper (9x12)
Spray bottle for water
The book, "Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs" by Susan Bernardo and Courtenay Fletcher
You can request a FREE copy of this book by notifying AWBW (one per program, while supplies last!) OR you can purchase a copy of this book on Amazon.com.

   
  Workshop set-up
 
   
  Foam Paint
 
Timeframe:
Warm-up: 5 Minutes
Opening Circle: 10 Minutes
Demonstration: 5 Minutes
Reading: 5 Minutes
Creation: 25 Minutes
Closing: 10 Minutes
Approximately 1 Hour Total

Age Range:
3-15

Set-Up/Prep:
Prepare paint palettes (paper plates): 1 palette for every two children. Spray small “mounds” of foam paint onto plates (3-5 different colors on each). Use about 1/4 to 1/2 cup of each color, but don’t measure, just estimate. You can replenish colors later if needed. Light and bright colors work best.

Warm-up:
Guide children through an embodied warm-up to create a personal connection and center them.

Let children know that love can be found everywhere! It is inside each of us; it is also all around us, in this room and in the world. All you have to do is look and see! Invite the children to stand up in a circle if they feel comfortable. Using your body, act out different symbols of love to show how easy it is for us to see and find; as you do so, invite the children to follow along. Take your time with each movement so children can connect with the love that is inside and around them.

You can first ask the children to put their hand on the hearts to see if they can feel their heartbeat and the love they have inside!

Some symbols that you can act out (you may want to ask the children if they can think of others):

A heart is a symbol for love!
- Create a little heart with your fingers and hands.
- Hold the heart up to your eyes and look through it at others in the room.

"X" is a symbol for a kiss!
- Make a little "X" with your fingers or hands.
- Create a big "X" with your body; stretch your arms wide and reach up to the sky to create a big "V." Then, spread their legs wide to create and upside-down "V."

"O" is a symbol for a hug!
- Make a little "O" with your fingers or hands.
- Reach your arms over your head in a curved shape to create a big "O."
- Slowly move your arms (in the "O" shape) in front of you, then cross your arms and wrap them around your body to give yourself a big hug!

Opening Circle:
"Let's take a moment and see if you can you think of someone or something you miss sometimes. Try to reflect and notice who or what you miss and how it makes you feel. Now, try to think about if you have personal item, or if there is something in nature that reminds you of the person or thing you miss? Notice why it's special to you."

If they are comfortable, invite children to share by naming who or what they miss, what object or symbol they came up with and why. Reassure participants that it is okay if they can't think of anything specific at this time and that they will get to explore this more during the workshop. Model the sharing in a few words so that it doesn't run too long. For example, "I miss my sister because she and her family live across the country. Whenever I see pink flowers I think of her because they are her favorite."

Demonstration:
Before we read the book today, we will demonstrate how to use the special supplies. We will be using a crayon "resist" technique with the materials at your place setting; including watercolor paper, Cray-Pas (oil pastels), water, brushes, sponges, and foam paint.

   
  Drawing with oil pastels 
Step 1 Explain that oil pastels are like fancy crayons! When making your drawing with the Cray-Pas, it's important to press hard. That way the color will be strong enough to show through when you put the foam paint over it. If you color with white it will look invisible on the paper, but when you add the paint something special will happen... the image will appear!

You may want to create a representation of yourself on one side of the paper and, on the other side, a representation of what or whom you are missing.

Step 2 In your drawing, add a symbol to represent how you are connected even if you are apart. You may borrow symbols or concepts from the book we will read, use symbols in nature, in your imagination... anything that is significant to you and the person/thing you miss.

Step 3 Raise your hand to signal that you are done with the drawing; this is when you will need the spray bottle to lightly wet your paper. You will use the foam paint as you would watercolors to "resist" the oil pastels. There are sponges and brushes on the table to apply the paint. You can also use your fingers but be aware that your finger may be stained for a little while. A little paint goes a long way! (Demonstrate ways to add the foam paint and the final effect of the resist technique; also, show how the white appears after the paint is added).

   
 
 
  Painting with foam paint
using a sponge		  Painting with foam paint
using a paintbrush		   Finger painting with
foam paint		 

"Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs" Reading:
Explain to the children that they are about to hear a story called Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs. It’s a story about love and how love is all around us – and that even when someone you love goes away, you can still feel connected to them.
 
Depending on the wants, needs, and expectations of your group, ask the children to follow along and read the story with you, or invite them to close their eyes and simply listen.  After reading the story, ask the children if they heard or saw something in the book that they connected to or if they can think of times when someone they love can’t be with them. If so, invite them to share.
 
Time permitting: Invite the participants to share how or what in nature can help them feel connected to the people they love and sometimes miss.

NOTE: Children can seek and find “love” in the illustrations – there is at least one hidden heart, “X” or “O” on every page of the book! If time permits you can give the children an opportunity to find some of these hidden images.

   
   
Creation:
Start by reminding the children that this is a window of time for them to notice what their heart is feeling and to honor whatever comes up. There is no wrong way to create. If this means just sitting and putting their head down that is okay, too.

Remind the children, "even though you may miss a special person/thing and  they are not with you, you can bring them into your heart anytime! By thinking about something that reminds that you of them, it will help you to connect to them, even if they are far away!"

"When you are ready, you can begin to create your Cray-Pas drawing that represents you and the person or thing you miss. You can connect the two figures using ideas from the book or your imagination. This can be something in nature (sunshine rays, a tree, a rainbow), X's, O's, hearts, or something that reminds you of this special person or thing. Finish your drawing by using the foam paint."

Closing Circle:
Invite everyone who is comfortable to share by showing their art and anything that may have came up for them during any part of this activity. Invite them to also share how or what they will look to in nature or elsewhere to comfort them.

Remember that, if we look for it, there are always ways for us to connect to those we feel far away from. Your creations are a wonderful reminder of how close our loved ones and prized possessions can actually be!
Row.txt_description: To use the concepts and images in the picture book "Sun Kisses, Moon Hugs," to help children learn to identify and express their feelings about separation/loss and develop ways to maintain their sense of connection, comfort and well-being even when loved ones are not physically present.

Row.str_title: Self-Esteem: What Kind of Person Do You See Yourself As?
Row.txt_code:
Objective: The participants have an opportunity to think about the kind of people they see themselves as and reflect on the way their experience with abuse has affected that.

Materials:
Figure template on tri-folded legal-size paper
Drawing supplie s and/or collage supplies
Journaling Page

Time Frame:
Introduction - 2 minutes
Relaxation - 5 minutes
Technical Information - 1 minute
Journaling - 12 minutes
Creation - 20 minutes
Closing Circle - 20 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour

Introduction: We often think of "self-esteem" as something that is high or low - we either feel good about ourselves or we don't - but it is really more complicated than that. "Esteem" means "to consider as a certain type; to regard," so self-esteem is really about how we think about ourselves and the type of person we consider ourselves to be. In this workshop, we are going to take time to think about the kind of person you see yourself as and the way your experience with abuse has affected that.

Relaxation: If you feel comfortable, close your eyes or find a focal point so you can concentrate on your thoughts and limit distractions. Take a few deep breaths to give your body oxygen and to let go of any tension that your muscles might be holding.

Try to picture yourself in your mind's eye. When you think of you, who do you think of? What do you look like? Act like? How do you present yourself? It is okay if your image is not the same thing as your reflection in the mirror! Our self is so much more than what is visible to others. Continue to reflect on this image and how it makes you feel.

We will start by identifying some of the ways that we regard ourselves - considering who we were, how we perceive ourselves to be today, and how we would like to be in the future. We will do this first with a short written exercise and then through creating a series of paper-figure cutouts. The three connected figures are designed to represent the past, current, and future self. They could also represent how you think about yourself, how other people think about you, and how you want to regard yourself or any other creation that is true to your journey and experience! You can decorate the figures with any words, colors, or images that reflect how you regard - how you esteem - each manifestation of your self. Notice how, though each figure is independent and unique, they are also joined together and one becomes the next.

Technical Information: Fold a piece of legal-size paper into thirds. Trace the template/draw the figure of a person making sure that the figure touches both edges/folds of the folded page. Cut out the figure. Unfold the paper to reveal three, distinct figures joined at the folds. Decorate each of the figures, one for each different life phase.

Journaling:

Creation: 

Closing Circle: If anyone would like to share a piece of their experience - the art they created, a feeling or thought or insight they had in making the art - this is an opportunity to do that. There is no pressure to share and it is equally important to honor the decision not to share anything if that feels best.

Again, if you feel comfortable, close your eyes and try to picture yourself in your mind's eye. Is the image you see of yourself the same as the image you saw in the first relaxation? Take a moment to notice how they are the same or different. In what ways do they look or feel similar or separate? Notice that there is beauty and strength in each image. We are constantly evolving and changing so giving yourself permission to be different is okay. As you reflect on and work towards developing positive self-esteem, remember that to do that means changing how you think about yourself.

Perhaps this means seeing and hearing the messages others have sent you about who you are or what you are capable of with curiosity. Maybe you will choose to recognize that despite what others say, think, or feel, you are the responsible for how you carry and hold yourself. You may consider changing or reframing specific facets of the different pieces that compile you. Or you might start reminding yourself of the parts of you that make you smile. Adapting an affirmative mantra could become a part of your routine. Whatever you decide to do, if anything, and how you decide to it is entirely your choice to make!

Sometimes, it helps to break down the overall goal of enhancing your self-esteem into smaller, concrete, and tangible steps. Whether you want to try new things, make a significant impact on your community, volunteer, become involved in a government cause, or even start each morning by looking in the mirror and telling yourself you are beautiful. With time and practice, changing the things you do changes the way you see yourself! When you esteem yourself differently, your self-esteem will be different, too.
Row.txt_description: The participants have an opportunity to think about the kind of people they see themselves as and reflect on the way their experience with abuse has affected that.

Row.txt_code:
Objective: To remind participants that even though life can bring us challenges, there are always reasons for us to smile.

Materials:
Sheet of white paper
Markers
Crayons
Colored Pencils

Timeframe:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Warm-Up: 10 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing Circle: 15 minutes
Total: 1 Hour

Set-Up/Prep:
To prepare your materials beforehand, we suggest that you set out a stack of white paper, a box of crayons, colored pencils, and markers on each table.

Introduction:
Sometimes people have an easier time saying what they are unhappy about, then talking about the things that make them happy. For example people say the things that displease them or make them sad all the time like: I don't want to do my homework, or I don't want to wear the clothes my mom wants me too, or I don't like to eat vegetables or I hate to go to sleep at bedtime or, so easily say things like I'm hungry, tired, bored, hot or cold. 

Every day it seems so easy to notice the reasons that make us frown that we often forget that we have plenty of things to smile for. Today, we're going to take time to appreciate the things (big and small) that make us smile.

Warm-up:
If you feel comfortable and safe, please close your eyes and think about a typical day in your life. Rather than focusing your thoughts on everyday worries like the ones just mentioned... try to clear your mind place your focus on simple joys... maybe a friend told you something nice or gave you a surprise treat...maybe you remember when you saw a beautiful butterfly land on a flower right next to you...maybe you got a good grade on a test and you feel proud. Think of all the little things that happen throughout the day that are worthy of the biggest smile you can give. Take a few more minutes to imagine all of those wonderful moments (big and small) we experience, even in one day, that make us smile. And when you feel ready, please open your eyes.

Creation:
After you have given yourself enough time to think about the reasons you smile, we will take a piece of white paper and draw a smile, full of big white teeth. Feel free to make the mouth with teeth as large as you want. We will fill each tooth with words, shapes, symbols, thoughts that bring you a smile! No matter how little you might feel the reason for the smile is, you can label each tooth in your mouth with a reason.

 
   
  The Reasons We Smile creation
   The Reasons We Smile creation 
Closing:
If you are ready and would like to share, you can  show our smiles to the group. You can choose to simply share your picture or share your picture as well as the reasons you smile.Thank everyone for sharing and being bold, creative, and thoughtful in thinking about the reasons they smile.
 
 
   
Remember that you are the only one who can see, feel, and appreciate the reasons you have for smiling. Those reasons are all unique, special, and wonderful. It is perfectly normal to  feel like frowning sometimes. Try to shake it off and remember that there are things in our lives all around us that can make us smile, if only we slow down and try to appreciate them!"
Row.txt_description: Helps to remind the participants that even though life can bring us challenges, there are always reasons for us to smile.

Row.txt_code:
Theatre of the Oppressed
Developed in Brazil in the 1960s, Theatre of the Oppressed (T.O.) has been successfully used worldwide to support people in transforming themselves and their communities. In this context, "oppressed" does not mean "downtro dden" or "hopeless," but rather represents awareness that there is an issue affecting the community and shared responsibility for creating change. T.O. is a rehearsal for real life, using theatre to help people move from passive objects of oppression to active agents in creating their own futures.

   

Windows Theatre of the Oppressed
Windows Theatre of the Oppressed combines the trauma-informed programs of A Window Between Worlds and the techniques of Theatre of the Oppressed, emphasizing the overlapping principles of both:
  • The belief that artistic creation is a human right that belongs at the center of strategies for change.
  • The confidence in each person's inherent ability to heal from violence.
  • The commitment to sharing tools that are accessible-not requiring therapists to lead.  
  • The dedication to changing the circumstances that produce violence.
  • The belief in collaboration-more hands and minds working together on issues of abuse and violence builds deeper understanding, stronger community strategies, and greater safety for everyone.

For information about why Windows Theatre of the Oppressed is especially effective for survivors of trauma, click here to download our flyer.

If you'd like to know more about this powerful type of healing art and the Windows T.O. program, contact Julianne at jgale@awbw.org or 310-396-0317 x213.
Row.txt_description: Windows Theatre of the Oppressed is a trauma-informed theatrical and movement-based tool for individual and community transformation.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To promote group bonding by playfully showing connections and shared experiences.
 
 
  Create a Circle of Chairs for Everyone but One Person
 

Materials:
Provide enough chairs and space for every participant, including the leader, to sit in a circle around an empty center space. (Optionally, if there aren't enough chairs or space, you can modify this workshop to use post-it notes or tape on the floor to mark spaces to sit or stand. However, the chair version is the clearest and most effective version). You will also need at least four participants to play, but the game works best with six or more people.

Timeframe:
10 minutes - 1 hour, depending on interest level and whether the activity will stand alone or be the warm-up or closing to another workshop. 20-40 minutes is usually ideal.

Age range:
7 years old and above

Set up/prep:
Arrange all chairs in a circle so that everyone has a chair and there are no extra chairs. Clear the space in the center of the circle so people can move from one chair to another without tripping.

   
  Welcome Group and Introduce the Game
 

Introduction:
Invite the participants to find a seat and welcome them warmly. Let them know that today is an opportunity to explore the many ways we are connected to each other. Remind them that this workshop is their window of time to practice respecting their feelings, thoughts, and needs, and they will always have the invitation to participate and the option to pass.

Warm-up:
(Optional) Invite each participant to say their name and answer the question, "Who is your community or who are 'your people'/those you most connect to?" You might want to give some examples or go first to set the tone. For example, "I am in a community of people who like to dance, people who like animals, and people who love to read books," or "My community includes people who are students, family members, and teenagers." This is an opportunity for participants to share the communities where they feel most connected and notice that they belong to multiple groups.

   
   
   
  The Wind Takes Away Anyone Who.....
 
   
   
   
   Those Who Identify with the Statement Change Seats!
 
   
  Race to get the Available Chair!
 
   

Game Play:
Let the participants know that the game they'll be playing is called, "The Wind Takes Away," and that it is a little like musical chairs, except that no one ever gets "out" and there are no winners or losers. Because they may be moving around and switching chairs, ask the participants to place any personal items under or behind the chairs so that they don't damaged in the movement. Explain that the phrase everyone will be repeating over and over is, "The wind takes away anyone who..." Invite the group to practice saying that phrase with you a few times, until they get comfortable with it.

Remove your chair from the circle and explain that whoever is in the center without a chair (like you are now) will share something that is true about themselves by saying the sentence: "The wind takes away anyone who is ____________." Explain that you'll start so everyone will get the idea. Start with a silly example, such as: "The wind takes away anyone who is wearing socks. I can say that because I'm someone wearing socks; that's something that's true about me.

"Who knows what 'identify with' means? It's like being the same or a part of a group that is like you. So if I say, I love the color pink, and you identify yourself as someone who loves the color pink - then together we a group/community who loves pink.  So if I say 'I love pink,' who identifies with my statement? If any of you who are sitting in the circle can identify with my statement, identify with loving pink, and are feeling safe enough to share that about yourself, please stand up.

"Notice that each person gets to decide for themselves if they want to identify with the statement. It's not up to anyone else to say ‘but you love pink, stand up!' Now that everyone who feels comfortable identifying themselves has stood up, let's take a moment to acknowledge the awesome pink-loving community we have right here by giving each other a psychic high five." Put your hand up and turn around as if you're giving a high five to the whole group, without actually touching them. "Now, when I say GO, everyone who is currently standing will try to find a new seat, and I'll try to find a seat for myself. Then there will be someone new in the center to say, ‘The wind takes away anyone who ___________.' As we get the idea, I may give additional instructions, but for now, you can share any basic fact about yourself that you'd like, if you're the one in the center. Okay, GO!"

   
  Symbolic High Fives
 

Take a new seat and let all the standing participants try to find an empty chair. Whoever is left standing begins the next round by saying, "The wind takes away anyone who _____________" (is wearing something red, has brown hair, took the bus to get here, etc.). After people stand up, take a moment to acknowledge the ___________ (red-wearing, brunette, bus-riding, etc.) community and give each other the symbolic high fives. Then the person in the center says, "GO!" Once everyone except one has found a seat, the game continues with the next round.

Once the group is getting the hang of the game, you can invite particular types of statements. For example, after 3-5 rounds, you might say, "You can still share basic facts about yourself, or you can choose to share likes and dislikes. For example, ‘The wind takes away anyone who loves to read' or the ‘The wind takes away anyone who doesn't like homework.'"

After another 3-5 rounds, you can add another category by saying something like, "You can still share basic facts about yourself, likes and dislikes, or you can share about a challenge you've faced."

It's helpful to work up to more personal topics. Here's one suggested sequence:

  1. Basic facts (e.g. "anyone who is wearing jeans")
  2. Likes and dislikes (e.g. "anyone who likes ice cream")
  3. Challenges you've faced (e.g. "anyone who was ever scared of the dark")
  4. Accomplishments (e.g. "anyone who has ever sung a song in public")
  5. Visions, hopes, or goals for the future (e.g. "anyone who wants to go to college")
   
  Celebrate by Creating a Heart Shape
 

Also, if the group enjoys the high fives and/or if they share things that may be inappropriate to celebrate with a high five, you can invite the center person to create a new solidarity gesture for the group to repeat instead of the high five. For example, you might say, "If a high five doesn't feel like an appropriate response to what you shared, you can make up a new movement for the group to repeat, such as putting your hand on your heart and taking a deep breath."

Closing:
Bring your chair back into the circle and give each participant a chance to share what they thought about this game. For example, you can offer one of the following prompts:

  • What did you like about playing this game?
  • What did you notice when you played this game?
  • Share how you feel now and if anything is different from before you played the game.
  • Share one thing you appreciate (about yourself, about the group, and/or about this workshop).

Note:
If this workshop is used in combination with another Windows activity, it may make more sense to have a single closing circle at the end of the entire workshop. If this workshop is the only activity for the group, then a closing circle can help participants feel a sense of completion.
Row.txt_description: This workshop promotes group bonding by playfully showing connections and shared experiences through an engaging and active embodied art activity.
Row.txt_tips:
• It is very important that you and any other Leaders, staff, or volunteers in the room participate along with the group. By modeling your enthusiasm and willingness to participate, you help build trust, bonding, and make it safer for other people to play and share vulnerable experiences.
  • It can help some participants if the phrase, "The wind takes away anyone who..." is written and posted on the wall so that the person standing does not have to worry about remembering the words.
  • If you find that a few people are frequently in the center while other people have not had a turn, you can pause the game to say, "I want to make sure that everyone who would like to have the opportunity to be in the middle gets a chance to do so. So please raise your hand if you have not had a turn yet but you would like to." Then invite the person who is currently in the center (but has gone more than once) to choose one of the people whose hands are raised to go next.
  • If someone says something and no one else stands up, you can say, "Even though there is only one person in this group for whom that is true, notice that we still have someone in this community who ___________(whatever the person shared)." Ask the person in the center to create a movement anyway and invite the whole group to show their support of that person by repeating the movement in solidarity (while staying seated). Then the person in the center can offer another statement to the group or can choose a new person to be in the center.
  • You may want to wait until someone who is more comfortable is in the center to offer new directions or topics.
  • Give one new direction at a time. For example, add a new category or invite a new solidarity gesture, but not in the same round.
  • Try to end on an affirmative statement, ideally one that every participant or most participants feel safe enough to identify with and stand up for.
  • Be flexible about the group's interests and comfort level. For example, if the group seems reluctant to create and repeat movements even with your encouragement, feel free to play the game without those solidarity movements. It is also perfectly fine if the group chooses to stay with "safe" or "superficial" topics like, "The wind takes away anyone who is wearing something red" for the entire game. No matter what people share, the participants are getting the opportunity to share something about themselves, engage playfully and physically, and notice that they are not alone.

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Timeframe: 10 minutes - 1 hour, depending on interest level and whether the activity will stand alone or be the warm-up or closing to another workshop. On average, the activity can take 20-40 minutes.

Set up/prep: Arrange all chairs in a circle so that everyone has a chair and there are no extra chairs. Clear the space in the center of the circle so people can move from one chair to another without tripping.

Introduction:
"Please find a seat around the circle. Today, we are going to participate in an embodied art activity and take the opportunity to explore the many ways we are connected to each other. Remember that, even though we are using our bodies to participate rather than creating visual art, this workshop is your window of time to practice respecting your feelings, thoughts, and needs. Please know that you will always have the invitation to participate and the option to pass."

Warm-up:
"Before we begin, if you feel comfortable, please share your name and your answer to the question, 'Who is your community or who are "your people"?'" You might want to give some examples or go first to set the tone. "For example, 'My communities are dancers, tea-drinkers, and people who love to read children's books aloud,' or 'My communities are survivors, teachers, and people of color.' This is an opportunity for us to share the communities we feel most connected to and notice that we can feel a part of multiple groups."

   
  Introducing the game
 

Game Play:
"We will be playing a game called 'The Wind Takes Away!' It is similar to musical chairs, except that no one ever gets 'out' and there are no winners or losers. Since you may be getting up and switching chairs, you might want to place any personal items under or behind your seats so that they do not get damaged in the movement. The phrase we will be repeating over and over is, 'The wind takes away anyone who...' Let's practice saying that phrase a few times, until we get comfortable with it." Support the group in repeating the phrase all together a few times.

"I am going to remove my chair from the circle and whoever is in the center of the circle without a chair, like I am now, will share something that is true about themselves by saying the sentence, 'The wind takes away anyone who is ____________.' I will start so that everyone can get the idea."

Start with a silly example, such as: "'The wind takes away anyone who is wearing socks. I can say that because I am someone wearing socks; that is something that is true about me. Now, if any of you who are sitting in the circle identify with my statement, if you are someone who agrees that you are part of the group who is wearing socks and are feeling safe enough to share that about yourself, please stand up.

 
 
  Identifying community with a solidarity heart symbol
 

"Notice that each person gets to decide for themselves if they want to identify with the statement, if they want to say that it is true for them, too. It is not up to anyone else to say, ‘but you're wearing socks, stand up!' This activity is completely voluntary and it is your choice whether or not you want to participate and in what capacity you choose to do so.

"Now that everyone who feels comfortable identifying themselves has stood up, let's take a moment to acknowledge the awesome sock-wearing community we have right here by giving each other a psychic high five or a solidarity heart symbol. You can put your hand up and turn around as if you're giving a high five to the whole group (without actually touching the group) or hold your hands in the shape of a heart or do anything that feels right to you in acknowledging your solidarity. Now, when I say 'GO,' everyone who is currently standing will try to find a new seat, and I will also try to find a seat for myself. Then there will be someone new in the center to say, ‘The wind takes away anyone who ___________.' As we get the idea, I may give additional instructions, but for now, you can share any basic fact about yourself that you would like if you are the one in the center.

   
  Running to a new seat
 
   
  Someone is left without a chair
 

"Okay, sock-wearing community, GO!" Take a new seat and let all the standing participants try to find an empty chair. Whoever is left standing begins the next round by saying, "The wind takes away anyone who _____________" (is wearing something red, has brown hair, took the bus to get here, etc.). After people stand up, take a moment to acknowledge the ___________ (red-wearing, brunette, bus-riding, etc.) community and give each other a solidarity symbol. Then, the person in the center says, "GO!" Once everyone except one has found a seat, the game continues with the next round.

Once the group is getting the hang of the game, after 3-5 rounds, you can invite particular types of statements. You might say, "You can still share basic facts about yourself or you can choose to share likes and dislikes. For example, ‘The wind takes away anyone who loves to read' or ‘The wind takes away anyone who does not like to sing in public.'"

After another 3-5 rounds, you can add an additional category by saying something like, "You can still share basic facts about yourself, likes and dislikes, or you can share about a challenge you have faced."

It might be helpful to work up to more personal topics. Here is one suggested sequence to follow when introducing new rounds:

  1. Basic facts (e.g. "anyone who is wearing jeans")
  2. Likes and dislikes (e.g. "anyone who likes ice cream")
  3. Challenges you've faced (e.g. "anyone who was ever scared of the dark")
  4. Accomplishments (e.g. "anyone who has ever sung a song in public")
  5. Visions, hopes, or goals for the future (e.g. "anyone who wants to go back to school")



Also, if the group shares things that might not feel appropriate to celebrate with a high five or solidarity heart, you can invite the center person to create a new solidarity gesture for the group to repeat instead. For example, you might say, "If a high five does not feel like an appropriate response to what you shared, you can make up a new solidarity movement for the group to repeat, such as putting your hand on your heart and taking a deep breath."

Closing:
Bring your chair back into the circle (so that everyone has a place to sit) and invite the group to share what came up for them during the game. You could also offer one of the following questions:

  • What did you like about playing this game?
  • What did you notice when you played this game?
  • Share how you feel now and if anything is different from before you played the game.
  • Share one thing you appreciate (about yourself, about the group, and/or about this workshop)."

Note: If this workshop is used in combination with another Windows activity, it may make more sense to have a single closing circle at the end of the entire workshop. If this workshop is the only activity for the group, then a closing circle can help participants feels a sense of completion.

  • It can help some participants if the phrase, "The wind takes away anyone who..." is written and posted on the wall so that the person standing does not have to worry about remembering the words.
  • If you find that a few people are frequently in the center while other people have not had a turn, you can pause the game to say, "I want to make sure that everyone who would like to have the opportunity to be in the middle gets a chance to do so. So please raise your hand if you have not had a turn yet but you would like to." Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways.  Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones.
