Row.txt_code:
Objective:
  
  "Good for 10 'Me' Hugs" Coupon
 
Gives participants an opportunity to create gifts for themselves that they do not need to buy that satisfy their heart and soul. These coupons can help them notice how important they are and that they deserve to be treasured and treat themselves.

Note:
In leading this workshop, it is very rewarding to witness the partcipants actually realizing that the most important gifts are those they do not need to buy. And, sometimes, the most important gifts they can give, are to give themselves self-care. It may be challenging but important to help them face the reality that they may not have enough money for many of the things they want (and maybe even some of what they need at times). Giving themselves precious alone, reflective, or exercise time might even end up being what they need the most.

   
  Workshop Set-up
 
Materials:
Construction paper
Markers
Scissors (if you have “edger scissors,” it’s nice to give a special edge to the coupons)
Glue sticks
Glitter, stickers, etc.

Timeframe:
Opening: 5 minutes   
Discussion: 5 minutes  
Creation: 20 minutes   
Closing: 10 minutes  

Feelings Discussion:
“Raise your hand if you like to receive gifts! (Acknowledge the raised hands or nodding within the group). Great. Why do you like to receive gifts? How do they make you feel? What makes them important to you?" Invite the participants to answer these questions and share their feelings about gifts. Let them know that they are welcome to pass if they do not feel comfortable or ready to share. "Gifts often make us feel good, appreciated, and loved. It is wonderful when others recognize and acknowledge us through gift giving but we can also always give ourselves gifts! This might seem impossible because you are always rushing from one thing to the next, in a big hurry and unable to take time for yourself. Maybe you cannot afford to treat yourself to a manicure. Perhaps you are too busy taking care of others; your children, your pets, your friends, to take care of yourself. What are some ways that you can give and show love to yourself?" Invite the participants to share ideas for self-care that they do now or would like to do.

   
   
Creation:
“Today, we are going to make heart and soul self-care 'gift coupons.' You have this opportunity to take all of your wonderful self-care ideas and create them on coupons to give to yourself when you really need them or anytime you want!

“You can make ‘gift coupons’ for anything that your heart, soul, body, and spirit desires! This is a chance to think about something that will make you happy, something that you can give yourself and that you do not need to buy.  It could be a break from cooking dinner, a bath, free T.V. time, a long chat with a girlfriend, or quiet time to yourself... anything you will enjoy.

"When you are ready, you can start creating your coupons.

Closing:
“If you feel comfortable, please share your coupon(s) and something you learned about yourself from doing this project. How do you feel about using these coupons for yourself?”
   
  Empathy - Self-Care Coupon
 
Variations:
This workshop can be adapted to focus on giving at any time of year.  Any day is a special day to give someone you love a gift, and a Gift Coupon is one way that the participants can express their caring for themselves or others.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants an opportunity to create gifts for themselves that they do not need to buy that satisfy their heart and soul. These coupons can help them notice how important they are and that they deserve to be treasured and treat themselves.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Participants will explore, uncover, and identify the source of their joy through a variety of creative exercises including guided imagery, painting, music, and movement.

   
  Creating Joy table set up
 
Materials:
Tambourine kits - can be purchased at Discount School Supply
Confetti paint
Tissue circles or squares
Non bleeding tissue paper
Glitter paint
Paper plates for paint
Chubby brushes
Cups for water
Scissors
Feathers
Ribbons 1/8 inch
Pony beads
Glue sticks
Tacky glue
1/4 sheets of heavy white construction paper for warm-up
Paper towels
Clippings and images on joy
Any other embellishments - optional

Timeframe:
Introduction/Discussion of Joy (large group): 10 minutes
Tambourine Assembly/Continue discussion of joy (small group): 15 minutes
Introduction to Materials & Warm Up: 15 minutes
Opening Circle & Guided Imagery Relaxation: 15 minutes
Creation: 25 minutes
Closing/Music & Movement with Tambourines: 10 minutes
Total: 1.5 hours

Preparation Before the Workshop:
1) We recommend that you make a sample tambourine so you will have confidence in teaching it. The instructions provided in the kit are easy to follow, but stringing the bells takes a little time and practice. The kits do NOT include beads but it's fun to string beads along with the bells for a fancier result. Any beads with large holes will work, but pony beads work especially well. The kits do NOT include ribbons but a variety of thin colored ribbons are also a nice addition. In Renaissance Festivals, tambourines are a popular instrument and ribbons often trail from their sides to emphasize movement and add color.

2) Select Rhythmic Music: Pick a CD or a song with a good upbeat rhythm to play at the end of the workshop. Participants can shake their tambourines to the music in unison as closure.

 
 
  Creating Joy collage materials
 
   
  Creating Joy place setting
 

Workshop Set-up:
Set up materials on paper plates for easy distribution and clean up. For every two people, prep one plate of stringing materials and one plate of paints.

1) Stringing materials: Set up the following materials (to be shared by two people) on one plate: two tambourine blanks, 2 cords, 12 bells and a small handful of pony beads (at least 12 per plate but does not have to be exact).

2) Paint palettes: Squirt 4 colors of washable glitter paint onto different plates. You do not need a lot of paint, it will be used as a thin glaze to secure tissue paper and collage. Estimate 2-3 tablespoons of each color per plate. Set out brushes.

3) Collage materials: Place clip art quotes, markers, tissue paper shapes, torn tissue paper, lightweight collage and feathers in middle of table at easy reach. Use bowls or trays (whatever is convenient).

4) Practice paper: Provide ¼ sheets of heavy white construction paper for practice after the art materials demo.

5) Finishing ribbons: Cut ribbons in 2' strands (allowing 3-5 different colored ribbons per person). The ribbons will be doubled over to 1' lengths in the attaching process, so 3 ribbon strands of 2' each will make 6 ribbon strands when doubled and attached. 5 ribbon strands will make 10 ribbon trails, etc. Prep ribbons, but wait until the final 10 minutes of workshop to set them out (they will be attached after painting and decorating are completely dry). Putting the ribbons out later will avoid confusion and avoid getting wet paint on the ribbons.

   
  Joy clip art inside tambourine
 
   
  Stringing tambourine with beads
 
   
  Warm-up creation
 

Introduction/Discussion of Joy:
"Joy is the theme of the day. Today, you are invited to leave your cares behind and live in the here and now of music, art, friendship and community. Today, we actively set our intentions on joy, on experiencing gratitude, hope, and a renewal of faith in all that is good in ourselves and in our world."

"You will find quotes on your table, find one quote that speaks to you on a personal level, one that strikes a positive cord within you and brings you joy. Take that one quote and glue it down on the inside or outside of your tambourine."

Tambourine assembly: Demonstrate how to string your tambourine from what you learned from the instruction sheet when you made your sample. As they string their tambourines, invite participants to continue their discussion of  what brings them joy in their small group.

Introduction to Materials & Warm-up:
Demonstrate how to use the glitter paint as a glaze or clear glue for the tissue paper circles, squares, and torn shapes. Using a "chubby" or bigger brush, apply a thin layer of silver glitter paint colored onto the tambourine top. Set circles and squares of tissue paper on top of paint, and brush a very light layer of silver paint on top of the tissue paper. Begin to layer more tissue shapes adding different colors of glitter paint and tissue, if you wish. Add feathers and other light collage materials on top, using glitter paint/glue sticks as a lightweight glue to adhere collage items. Use tacky glue to adhere heavier items to the tambourine.

Warm-up using practice paper(optional):
Invite the participants to practice applying paint and tissue paper onto their practice paper (¼ sheets of heavy white construction paper) so they become comfortable with the materials.

Opening Circle & Guided Imagery Relaxation:
This guided imagery relaxation sets the tone for an inward journey to experience relaxation and strive to connect with the inner experience of safety, peace, and joy.

"I invite you to relax, put down your art materials, and if you wish, close your eyes for a few minutes while I guide you through a brief period of self-reflection. Today's workshop is meant to focus on our inner experience of safety, peace, and joy. Today we will make an effort to get in touch with gratitude for all that life has offered us, in spite of its challenges and difficulties. Our artwork will help us focus on the source of our strength and give us the time and place we need to nurture ourselves and experience peace and joy and safety for this moment in time - this hour, this day. We can come here together to explore our own personal joy that is our birthright as human beings. Today, we pause together for a time of healing, to join in fellowship and support each other. Here our inner voice tells us we can be truly understood, we can be seen. Here we can reveal our secrets if we choose to, and be accepted unconditionally. Here there is no shame, we can feel safe and cared for. Here we can find solution and work with others towards wholeness, inner peace and feelings of joy."

"If you feel comfortable, close your eyes and relax your body, letting go of muscle tightness in your shoulders, your jaw, and in the muscles in your face. Drop your shoulders even lower, letting go of all the tension. Do a mental 'body check' and loosen any areas of tightness that you find in your legs, arms, fingers or forehead. Breathe slowly and deeply."

"Now, you find yourself lying down on a grassy field with a bright sun shining overhead. The grass is cool and soft and welcoming and the sun is just the right temperature on your skin. You feel relaxed and safe and become aware of the sounds of nature all around you. What do you hear?"

"Slowly, you begin to realize you are lying near a forest and you look over at a group of trees nearby at the entrance to the forest. You stand up and find a path in the grass that takes you right to the edge of this lush green forest. The sounds of the leaves rustling in the gentle breeze are inviting, and the forest appears to be a safe and nurturing haven that awakens your curiosity. You decide to enter this inviting forest and see where the path takes you. You continue to breathe slowly and deeply and your heart is open. You feel safe and at peace. You are meant to be here in this moment. You sense that a gift is waiting in the forest, but you don't know yet what it is. You feel eager and open to experience the life within."

"As you continue to walk into the forest, you hear a small mountain stream and notice that the path takes you right alongside this beautiful source of water. The sunlight peeks through the trees and glistens on the water as it bubbles over colorful rocks and continues deeper into the forest. You wonder where this lovely clear water is coming from, and you follow it deeper into the forest in search of its source. As you follow the stream and the path, listen to the sounds of the forest. What do you hear? What are you wearing? Are you comfortable and relaxed? Can you let go of all that concerned you before  and experience this moment in time as if it were real? Can you make it real? Continue to relax and breathe and let go."

"Continue down the path until you reach the stream's original source, the wellspring from which it all began. You find yourself at a deep clear pool of water, and you realize this is your perfect resting place, both the end of your journey and a new beginning. Here is a place you can feel safe, you are finally home. Here there is comfort and rest. Here there can be joy and peace and calm. Notice the beauty all around you and sit down on a large stone to rest. Feel the water, how does it feel on your skin? Remember to breathe slowly and deeply."

"Now slowly come back to the room, making sure to relax the tension in your shoulders, dropping them down. Relaxing any tightness in your jaw, your stomach, your chest, your fingers, and your forehead. Reviewing your body for signs of tension and letting those tension points go. Staying in the moment and continuing to experience the gift of this day and the gifts of joy and peace, and the gift of willingness to let go."

 
 
  Decorate inside of tambourine
 

Creation:
Part 1: Inside of Box/My Inner Joy
"Starting with the inside of your tambourine, use the paint and collage materials to express the colors and feelings of your guided journey. Don't over-think this part, simply start playing with the art materials and see what happens. Think of what was most important about your experience in the forest and at the source of your stream and create a design that contains elements of your experience. There is no right or wrong way to express these feelings with the art materials. Use the shapes and colors of the art materials to inspire you."

 
   
  Decorate outside of tambourine
  Using embellishments
 

Part 2: Outside of Box/My Outer Joy
"Use the same materials, paint the outside of your tambourine. Select colors that bring you joy. This is a purely abstract exercise and there is no right or wrong way to paint. Personalize the outside of your tambourine and imagine hanging it on a wall where you live, to remind you of your experience today; that joy that is your birthright."

   
  Stringing ribbons on tambourine
 

Part 3: Ribbons
"Cluster a small group of ribbons together, double them over, and tie them as a cluster onto one part of your tambourine string. They will wave colorfully when you shake your tambourine."

Closing Circle:
"Thank you all for tapping into your own joy and creating to represent what that feels like to you. I invite you to share your tambourines with a partner or with the group. I encourage you to talk about your experience on the guided imagery journey and how that experience translated into your artwork."

  
  Creating Joy tambourines
 

After everyone who wanted to do so has shared their tambourines with their partners, play music so participants can shake their tambourines together in unison to a rhythmic song as closure.

Optional Closing: "We are going to do an embodied exercise with our creating joy tambourines! To align with the theme of this workshop, if you feel comfortable, we will each share one word to describe something that brings us joy and create a movement to go with that word."

"For example, my word is 'dancing' (do movement). Dancing brings me joy and I can think about that word, movement, and my tambourine when I'm feeling joyful or need to remind myself to see the joy in things."

"Take a moment to think about that one word that you will share. You can hold your tambourine as your inspiration. When you feel ready to share, I would like you to stand up, and we will form a large circle around the room. Everyone who would like to do so can take a turn to share their joy word and after each person shares, everyone will mimic the word and movement in acknowledgment and solidarity! Keep in mind that your tambourines might be wet and, if so, you might not be able to use it with your movement!"

 
 
  Creating Joy embodied movement
 

"I will share my example again and afterward, I invite all of you to repeat and mimic the word and motion. 'Dancing' (mime dancing) and gesture to group to repeat and mime 'dancing.' Who would like to start?"

 
 
  Group Creating Joy tambourines
 

After each participant has shared, invite everyone to say "joy" and mimic their joy word movement at the same time.
Row.txt_description: Participants will explore, uncover, and identify the source of their joy through a variety of creative exercises including guided imagery, painting, music, and movement.

Row.txt_code:
Materials 
Materials:
Super Sculpey Polymer Clay (have multiple colors available)
Toaster Oven
Hand shaped cookie cutter
Small coffee straws or skewers
Ribbon, yarn, embroidery thread or craft wire
Beads (optional)
Permanent markers (metallic colors look great on dark colored clay)
White-out pens

Pre-workshop prep:
Prepare several Sculpey balls, enough for each person, in various colors. It is a great idea to demonstrate how to make swirly or marbled shapes out of Sculpey.

 
 
  Sculpey "snake" using 3 colors 
   
  Twisting Sculpey colors 
   
  Flatten Sculpey 
   
  Roll Sculpey to about 1/4 of an inch 
   
  Cut Sculpey with a cookie cutter 
   
  Make a hole to hang the hand 
Creation:
Step One:
To blend the clay, choose at least two colors. Use no more than a pinch of each color. When choosing your clay, you may want to choose colors that feel powerful to you - any colors that come to mind when you think, "I CAN."

Step Two:
Roll each color into a "snake".

Step Three:
Wrap each "snake" around each other like a candy-cane and twist together.
Tip: Use at least three different colors of clay when blending them together. It also looks great when the colors complement each other.

Step Four:
Twist each little section of the roll until the colors are blended just the way you want them.
Tip: Be careful not to over blend the colors as they can start to look muddy.

Step Five:
Roll the "snakes" into a ball. If you want, repeat steps 4 and 5 several times to create a more marbled effect.

Step Six:
Using a pen or a marker roll the ball flat to be about 1/4 inch thick. Use a hand shaped cookie cutter to cut the clay into the shape of a hand. Use a coffee straw, skewer or pencil to make a hole at the top so you can hang the hand after it bakes.
Tips:
1) Before using the cookie cutter, pIck-up and flip the clay periodically so it doesn't stick to the paper/surface you are working on.  
2) It's important to make sure that the clay is at least 1/4 of an inch thick, as if they clay is any thinner the hand will easily break.
3) If the clay is sticking to to the cookie cutter it is helpful to put the clay (after the balls have been flattened) in the refrigerator and the use the cookie cutter after the clay is cold.
4) When making the hole in the hand, make sure it is not too close to the edge (to prevent it from breaking).

Step Seven:
Using a foil lined tray, place the clay hand in the oven. Bake the Sculpey at 275 degrees for 15 minutes (for each ¼ inch of clay thickness). Always allow the clay to cool completely before handling it.
Tip: If the clay hands are dark in color, metallic permanent markers work great to make sure the color stands out.

Step Eight:
"Now that you have identified an I CAN, it is time to create on your I CAN clay hand to serve as a tangible reminder of your I CAN. Place your I CAN message on the clay hand using the permanent markers and/or white out pens however you like. Your I CAN expression can be words, swirls, colors, shapes! Anything goes!  You are all incredibly powerful individuals and I invite you to be bold, let go of judgment, and allow your creative juices to flow!"

Step Nine:
Encourage the participants to use ribbon, yarn, embroidery thread or wire to hang their I CAN hand and use beads to decorate.
Tip: If you offer beads, keep in mind that will add a lot of time to your participants creation.

   
  I CAN Spread Awareness finished clay creation
Row.txt_description: Sculpey clay hands are a wonderful way to give participants a quick yet meaningful way to experience the I CAN WE CAN workshop.

Row.txt_code:
Be a part of the I CAN WE CAN action by creating your own I CAN art to raise awareness, support others, and get support for yourself! You can create your own art or lead a group in this project. The directions below give you detailed instructions for participating in Find Your I CAN using shrinka ble plastic ("shrinky-dinks"), but you can do this project with any supplies at all (e.g. paper, scratch art, clay, etc.). You can even participate in Find Your I CAN virtually by going to the online gallery at icanwecan.awbw.org and using the social media buttons to comment and share artwork and stories!

Step 1: Create Your I CAN Statement

  1. Take a moment to reflect on what you can do to help end violence in your own life or in your community. Don't worry if the I CAN that comes to you seems too small to be important or too big to be possible.
  2. On the shrinkable plastic, draw your I CAN (e.g. "I CAN Listen," "I CAN Speak Up," "I CAN_______"), making sure that your I CAN statement is large and clearly readable (this will help make sure that people can find your uploaded photo). You can either use colored pencils on the rough side or permanent markers on either side of the shrinkable plastic. Feel free to embellish your I CAN statement by tracing one of the provided hand templates or adding other drawings or doodles.
  3. Punch a hole at the top of your artwork so you can attach the tag during Step 4. Leave at least a 1/4" between the edge of the plastic and your hole.

Optional Variation: If you would like to keep your I CAN creation for yourself as well as put one into the community, create a duplicate I CAN statement by tracing your artwork before shrinking it. To make the tracing easier, temporarily tape the two shrinkable plastic sheets together.





Step 2: Shrink Your Artwork

  1. Preheat an oven (toaster or conventional is fine) to 300˚F.
  2. Bake your shrink art in the oven for a couple of minutes. Your artwork will curl up then flatten. After it flattens, take it out to cool.

Tip: Place your shrink art on a paper bag cut-out for easy removal.


Step 3: Upload Your Artwork

  1. Take a photo of your I CAN shrink art.
  2. Go to icanwecan.awbw.org/upload.
  3. In the text box where it says "Title," type in the words exactly as they are written on your I CAN shrink art. (This will help people to find your I CAN artwork.)
  4. In the text box where it says "Artist name (as you want it displayed)," you can type your name, a psuedonym, or leave it blank.
  5. In the text that says "Organization/Company name," you can type in your agency, company, or organization name, or leave it blank.
  6. Upload your photo by clicking on the "Browse..." button to locate the image on your computer.
  7. In the text box that says "Words to accompany this piece," write any additional words or explanation you'd like to go with your artwork.
  8. Click the "SAVE" button.

 

 

Step 4: Attach the I CAN WE CAN Tag

  1. Attach the tag to your artwork with a ribbon or string so people will know what to do with your art when they find it. If you want to print your own tags, here is a double-sided version and a single-sided version. You'll need to cut out the tags and punch a hole in each one. Tip: Printing on cardstock makes the tags more durable.
  2. If you'd like, you can also add beads or multiple colors of ribbon. Tip: If you're using ribbon, cut it on an angle so that it's easier to pass through the holes.

Step 5: Put Your I CAN Out in the World

  1. Choose a location to leave your I CAN for others to find. It could be hanging on a fence post, in a bowl of other I CAN art pieces to be given out as party favors, pinned up on a bulletin board, or in any place that feels exciting to you!
  2. On or before the Day of Action, put your I CAN out in the world in your chosen location so people can find it and respond to it.

Step 6: Check for Support

  1. Check the photo of your I CAN shrink art to see if anyone has found it and left you a comment of support or solidarity by visiting this link: icanwecan.awbw.org/find.
  2. Type your title (or artist name, if you used one) in the box that says "Search words."
  3. Click on the blue "SEARCH" button.
  4. You will see a list of I CAN artworks that match your search. Click on your artwork.
  5. Read the comments at the bottom of the page and respond if you wish!
Row.txt_description: Find Your I CAN

Row.str_title: I CAN WE CAN Unite to End Abuse Community Engagement Workshop Variation
Row.txt_code:
About I CAN WE CAN Unite to End Abuse:
This ongoing participatory art project invites participants to create art as a symbol of solidarity, a commitment to doing what they can to help end abuse. Our shared vision is a world in which art is used to forge a sense of personal connection and shared responsibility to say WE CAN create a violence-free future.

Objective: Participants will take a creative window of time to find the "I CAN" that gives voice to their personal commitment to end abuse and share it in the community via the I CAN WE CAN Unite To End Abuse online community. This community engagement version of the project aims to break the silence and start a conversation during Domestic Violence Awareness Month. Artwork created can be used for art exhibits and community engagement events.

To help you prepare to facilitate this workshop please consider the following:
Prepare yourself: Be sure to try out the project yourself, in advance, from beginning to end. This is very important and will give you an idea of what your participants will be experiencing during the workshop and how you want to organize your supply layout and timeline.

Make arrangements to offer your group ample time for check-ins, creation, processing, and a closing circle (and photography in case you plan on adding it to the I CAN WE CAN website). You may even consider creating an outline of how you will manage your workshop time and share it with the group to help them pace their creation process.

To get an idea of what the I CAN WE CAN workshop is like, watch this short video of an AWBW community workshop: click here. 

Prepare your supplies: Gather supplies from the chosen art type. Try to give participants a variety of choices to express themselves. Use the ideas below to guide you in gathering materials. The list below is just a suggested list of supplies; we welcome you to be bold, get creative and add any supplies you feel will work for your group.

Prepare your group: Some people may have preconceived notions about art. You may want to begin by asking your group, “Who is scared of art? Who has not done art since grade school?” After they reply, it is a wonderful opportunity to assuage any apprehension by assuring the participants that there is no wrong way to do this project. During Windows time we have the opportunity to focus on enjoying the process and allowing your authentic expression to come out.

Time Frame:
1-2 hour(s)
We have provided four I CAN WE CAN variations and we welcome you to introduce all or some of these variations to your participants. As always, we also welcome you to use your own judgement and provide variations and materials that your participants will feel most comfortable with. We want you and your participants to be confident with this process and to create from the heart.

 
 Hand Art
 Shrink Art

 
 Clay Art
 Paper Art

Materials:
Hand Art:
Face paint, makeup, washable markers - anything washable to write on skin
Eyeliner pencils
White-out pens
Paint brushes and/or sponges to apply face paint
Pens
Copy paper for journaling and sketching
Non-bleeding tissue paper and permanent markers (you can write on the paper and then apply it to your hand using water!)
Scissors
Spray bottle for water
Water
Baby wipes or make-up remover and cotton balls
Music
See I CAN WE CAN gallery for more supply ideas!

Shrink Art:
Plastic shrink paper
Templates
Permanent markers
Colored pencils
Paper towels
Toaster oven
Hole puncher
Ribbon
Beads		Clay Art:
Sculpey clay
Paint
Permanent markers
Metallic markers
Clay tools
Conventional oven
Ribbon
Beads
Paper Art:
Construction paper
Markers
Colored pencils
Crayons
Watercolors
Paint
Scissors
Glue
Magazines

We encourage you to join the movement and do what you can to create awareness and engage your community through the I CAN WE CAN project. To help you develop your plan, download the I CAN WE CAN Community Engagement & Exhibit Planning Guide and Tips.

Welcome:

 
  
I CAN WE CAN Workshop Steps:
Step 1: Welcome & Check-in
"This is 'a window of time' to find the 'I CAN' that gives voice to your personal commitment to end abuse, and share it in the community as part of Domestic Violence Awareness month and in the I CAN WE CAN Unite To End Abuse online community.

 

Take a moment to check-in with the group by asking each person to share their name and a word or a sentence about how they are feeling in this moment. "Are you feeling nervous, excited, afraid, or happy? Please know that today is about you and you are safe and encouraged to do, say, and feel whatever is your unique expression.

"Who would like to start the opening circle sharing your name and how you feel about being here today?"

The check-in is important since it brings everyone's voice into the room and allows for connection and trust.


Step 2: Workshop Demo
Share about the supplies provided and techniques about how to use the materials.

Supply Tips for Participants:

For Hand Art:

  1. Washable markers on tissue paper may run and stain when wet, so take care to cover your work surface and clothing. The colored tissue paper may also run and stain your hands.
  2. Some types of face paint are more difficult to get off, so you may be required to provide a sink with soap and water, make-up remover or even rubbing alcohol.
  3. Be gentle when writing on tissue paper with permanent markers and/or white out pens since they may rip the paper.
  4. Sharpies and other permanent markers may stain your hand for several days, but alcohol will remove them.
  5. Provide scratch paper for people who may want to sketch their design prior to creating.
  6. Suggest to participants that they gather all components they will need to create their hand before they start working, as it will be more difficult to work using only one hand.

Shrink Art:

  1. Create an example of what the shrink art looks like using colored pencils and permanent markers. Each of them has a slightly different look.
  2. Remind participants that if they choose to punch a hole in their artwork, they need to be mindful of where their words go.
  3. Remind the participants that shrink paper can be very fragile and to be very careful when cutting.

Clay Art:

  1. Clay art will usually take more time considering the baking process. 
  2. Provide examples of different techniques such as marbling and shaping.
  3. Metallic markers usually show up the best on marbled clay.

Paper Art:

  1. Prepare a variety of paper materials for participants.
  2. Magazines can be a good way for participants to find and cut out images that help them convey their message.
  3. Glue sticks usually work better than craft glue because they help create cleaner edges with less bubbling.
  4. If providing watercolors or paint, use watercolor paper if possible.
Step 3: Warm-up:
"Many of us have heard all of all our lives that we can’t have or be who or do what we really want, whether it was someone in our family, friends, society, our community, or even our own thoughts. Maybe one of the things you have been told is that 'it is not possible to live free from violence' or that 'it is selfish to get what you want or you feel you deserve.'

"We are going to take a moment to release those doubts and 'I Can't' thoughts and notice the power we already have inside. Pick a partner to share for one minute about something that you thought could not do, or were told you could not do, but you did do it and it made you stronger as a result. It can be anything you would like to share. We will take turns sharing for the full minute so that each person can share one at a time. I will help you take turns by timing a minute and letting you know when it is time to switch speakers."

After everyone has shared: Validate the group by thanking them for taking the time to notice that they have the power to do what they want.

 
Step 4: Introduction to the Creation Process:
"The I CAN WE CAN project is about the difference we can ALL make in ending all forms of abuse by taking a moment, a creative 'window of time,' to notice our own personal vision and commitment to end violence using our own hands.

"Today each of us will make a personal commitment or pledge for ending violence in our own lives. Please remember that there is no wrong way to participate in this project and every aspect of this workshop is voluntary. Please honor your feelings, thoughts, and ideas about how you want to create your expression for ending violence."

Step 5: Releasing "I Can’ts" (Optional step):
  
  
 Free-writing during warm-up
In preparing to move the threshold of what we can do to help end violence, it can be quite powerful to take some time looking closely at any "I Can'ts" we carry. Be aware that acknowledging what we feel we can’t do can bring up intense feelings in participants. This is a step that is done with the intention of unburdening participants from perceived limitations and negative thoughts.

If you choose to do this exercise, be sure to allow 5 to 10 minutes for participants to free-write or journal without stopping and editing, about any "I Can'ts" they can think of. Next, ask them to share what came up for them with a partner or with the group (allow for at least 5 min. per participant). Lastly, you can provide some way to encourage the participants to let go of their "I Can’ts," whether it is by literally destroying them or creating a ceremony to unburden themselves of their "I Cant's."

  
Step 6: Brief Relaxation
 "Now, if you feel comfortable enough to do so, please close your eyes or just sit quietly. Take a minute to breathe and think about or imagine your vision for your I CAN. Try to picture it in your mind, however it comes to you, as an image, a place, or a list of things you truly want. Notice how it feels in your body to make this pledge to yourself and share it with the world. Do you feel joy, power, peace? Take as long as you need but remember that your I CAN might be something simple and personal or it can be your greatest vision.   Keeping your vision in mind, be bold when creating your I CAN hand!"

Step 8: I CAN Creation:
"Now, think about being part of a circle of people around the globe committed to ending violence. If each of us notices a new step we want to claim and act on, we can move the world. What I CAN do you want to claim today? Just notice what resonates in your heart as most meaningful for you.

"As you notice your power and the possibility that lies within your I CAN, know that whether what comes to you seems 'too small' to be important or seems 'too big' to be possible, please try to trust that your ideas are just right. When you truly honor your heart, you can create a change that ripples out from you to those around you and to the community at large, as part of a global change. Your I CAN, no matter how small or big is part of changing the world. If you need to take a break or opt out of any aspect of the project, please do so. If you need some support, let me know, as part of my role here today is to be here for each of you."

 
Step 9:  Closing Sharing Circle:
You may want to end by giving each participant an opportunity to share anything they want with the group about their experience with the workshop. After each person is done creating you can say, “Now I would like to give everyone an opportunity to share something about their experience here today. We will go around the room and each take turns sharing anything you want about your I CAN pledge, what you created, and your overall experience with the workshop."

Step 11:  Participant Evaluations and Workshop Closing
Pass out participant evaluations and thank all participants for taking a window of time to notice their strength and what they CAN do to end abuse! Share with them that by creating their I CAN they are joining other survivors and non-survivors coming together to end abuse. If you or they want to share their I CAN artwork, click here to upload photos and words to the I CAN WE CAN online gallery.
Row.txt_description: Participants will take a creative window of time to find the "I CAN" that gives voice to their personal commitment to end abuse and share it in the community via the I CAN WE CAN Unite To End Abuse online community. This community engagement version of the project aims to break the silence and start a conversation during Domestic Violence Awareness Month. Artwork created can be used for art exhibits and community engagement events.

Row.str_title: I CAN WE CAN: Finding Your Voice
Row.txt_code:
About I CAN WE CAN:
This ongoing participatory art project invites participants to create art as a symbol of solidarity, a commitment to doing what they can to help end abuse. Our shared vision is a world in which art is used to forge a sense of personal connection and shared responsibility to say WE CAN create a violence-free future.

Objective:
Participants will take a creative window of time  to find the "I CAN" within them. Through their art, participants can give a voice to their commitment to end abuse and learn about Domestic Violence Awareness Month, and join the ongoing efforts to increase awareness.

To help you prepare to facilitate this workshop, please consider the following:
 
Prepare Yourself: Be sure to try out the project yourself in advance, from beginning to end. This will give you an idea of what your participants will be experiencing during the workshop and how you may want to organize your supply layout and timeline.

Make arrangements to offer your group ample time for check-ins, creation, processing, and closing circle. You may even consider creating an outline of how you will manage your workshop time and share it with the group to help them pace their creation process.

Prepare Your Supplies:  Gather supplies from the chosen art type. Try to give participants a variety of choices to express themselves. Use the ideas below to guide you in gathering materials. The list below is just a suggested list of supplies; we welcome you to be bold, get creative and add any supplies you feel will work for your group.

Prepare Your Group: Some people may have preconceived notions about art. You may want to begin by asking your group, “Who’s scared of art or thinks they are not good at it?"  After they reply, it is a wonderful opportunity to relieve any apprehension by assuring the participants that there is no wrong way to do this project. During Windows time it is all about enjoying the process and allowing your unique voice to come out.

If necessary, remember to establish guidelines with input from your group. Guidelines should include respect for one another, acceptance of all feelings and expressions, and an agreement of confidentiality.

Timeframe:
1-2 hour(s)
We have provided four I CAN WE CAN variations and we welcome you to introduce all or some of these variations to your participants. As always, we also welcome you to use your own judgement and provide variations and materials that your participants will feel most comfortable with. We want you and your participants to be confident with this process and to create from the heart.

We encourage you to join the movement and do what you can to create awareness and engage your community through the I CAN WE CAN project. To help you develop your plan, download the I CAN WE CAN Community Engagement & Exhibit Planning Guide and Tips.

Welcome:
"I CAN WE CAN is a project where people of all ages are coming together hand-in-hand, to say no more hurting, no more pain, no more fear. Each of us can make a pledge to end abuse by saying or showing what we can do to make our world safer, kinder, and more peaceful. This is one of the best times to join the I CAN WE CAN movement because October is Domestic Violence Awareness Month (DVAM). DVAM was created by the National Coalition Against Domestic Violence has been working hard for over 30 years to bring awareness to domestic violence. They have been helping people understand what you've gone through and they try to educate people to help end domestic violence. Through your participation today, you get the chance to become one of those people who helps change the world!"

"If you need my help, let me know. My role today is to be here for each of you."

Introduction:
"The workshop we are doing today is called I CAN WE CAN: Finding Your Voice. This project is about the power in all of us as unique people realizing what we can do to create peace in our own lives! Today is about respecting and honoring what you believe you can do and be to end domestic violence in your own lives, and sharing it with others. You might say, 'I'm just a kid what can I do?' There are many things you can be, do and say to help end abuse."

"In a bit, we will do a warm-up to get us thinking about what we can each do and then we will make an artistic pledge of one I CAN we want to make come true in our own lives."

Workshop Demo:
Share about the supplies provided and techniques about how to use the materials.

Supply Tips for Participants:

For Hand Art:

  1. Washable markers on tissue paper may run and stain when wet, so take care to cover your work surface and clothing. The colored tissue paper may also run and stain your hands.
  2. Some types of face paint are more difficult to get off, so you may be required to provide a sink with soap and water, make-up remover or even rubbing alcohol.
  3. Be gentle when writing on tissue paper with permanent markers and/or white out pens since they may rip the paper.
  4. Sharpies and other permanent markers may stain your hand for several days unless you use alcohol to remove them.
  5. Provide scratch paper for people who may want to sketch their design prior to creating.
  6. Suggest to participants that they gather all components they will need to create their hand before they start working, as it will be more difficult to work using only one hand.

Shrink Art:

  1. Create an example of what the shrink art looks like using colored pencils and permanent markers. Each of them have slightly different looks to them.
  2. Remind participants that if they choose to punch a hole in their artwork, they need to be mindful of where their words go.
  3. Remind the participants that shrink paper can be very fragile and to be very careful when cutting.

Clay Art:

  1. Clay art will usually take more time considering the baking process. 
  2. Provide examples of different techniques such as marbling and shaping.
  3. Metallic markers usually show up the best on marbled clay.

Paper Art:

  1. Prepare a variety of paper materials for participants.
  2. Magazines can be a good way for participants to find and cut out images that help them convey their message.
  3. Glue sticks usually work better than craft glue because they help create cleaner edges with less bubbling.
  4. If providing watercolors or paint, use watercolor paper if possible.

Warm-up:
Refer to the following lists to start the conversation:

  
  
  

Start by asking participants to call out ways they CAN BE to create a world free from abuse.

I CAN BE gentle, helpful, peaceful, kind, courteous, patient, forgiving, trustworthy, free, truthful, a friend, original, unique, different, positive, powerful, me, brave...

Next ask the youth to call out ways they CAN CREATE a world free from abuse.

I CAN learn, forgive, love, respect, help, think, apologize, tell the truth, share, dream, care, hope, believe in myself, make a difference, stand up for myself, stand up for others...

Next ask the youth to call out what they CAN SAY to create a world free from abuse.

I CAN SAY... No! That's not okay, Stop, I don't like that, I forgive you, I'm sorry, Thank you, You are special, I love you, I CAN, WE CAN....

Additional or Alternate Warm-up:
"Let's start by taking a moment to notice our past victories over things that seemed impossible." You may want to do this with everyone standing in a unified circle, holding hands, or by allowing peers to share with a partner during a timed sharing exercise. This can help create a feeling of intimacy. "Share about a time when someone told you or you thought you couldn't do something, but then you tried and you did it!" Remind the group that every accomplishment counts and there is not a wrong answer to this question!

After everyone has shared, validate the group and each person by acknowledging that all of us have done things we thought we couldn't do but did it anyway. Ask them to notice that it is possible to do things they think they can do and that they have the power inside of themselves!

"Now, we will take some time to think about what we can do to end abuse and create a world that is more peaceful, joyful, and safe."

I CAN Creation Process
"Now think about being part of a circle of people around the world committed to ending abuse. If each of each of us did what we could to help end abuse, what would you do, say or change? Just notice what you feel in your heart that is most meaningful for you and give it a voice by creating your artistic pledge. This pledge is for you and should reflect your unique expression. We all must do what we can to end violence in our lives and in our world. When you're ready, begin to create your I CAN artwork. Place your I CAN message on it however you like. Anything goes!"

Closing Sharing Circle:
You may want to end by giving each participant an opportunity to share anything they want with the group. After each person is done creating you can say, "Now I would like to give everyone a chance to share their I CAN. We will go around the room and each take turns sharing anything you want about your I CAN pledge, what you created, and any feelings you have about the workshop."

After the workshop is over, if you or they want to share their I CAN artwork, click here to upload photos and words to the I CAN WE CAN online gallery. Remember to follow your agency's protocol for photographs and other media.
Row.txt_description: This workshop will take a creative window of time to for participants to find the "I CAN" within them. Through their art, participants can give a voice to their commitment to end abuse.

Row.txt_code:
Balance 
   
   
  Breathe 
   
Objective:
To create a mantra themed bracelet which can be worn as a reminder of what you can manifest/celebrate in your life. A mantra is a sound, word, or phrase that is repeated by someone who is praying or meditating, or it can be a word or phrase that is repeated often or over and over to expresses someone's basic beliefs. By creating your own mantra you can acknowledge what you want in your life as well as celebrate your journey towards healing.

Materials:
Beads, assorted including alphabetical letter beads if available
Elasticated bead thread ( approximately 10 inches per bracelet)
Beads made of Sculpey (additional/ or alternative)
Charms or personal item that can be strung on bracelet (additional/ or alternative)
Scissors
Writing paper and pen
Example list of empowering affirmations and mantras – (try to encourage participants to choose one or create one that would be meaningful to them.)

Time Frame:
Introduction - 5min
Opening Circle/Warm up - - 10 minutes
Meditation – Breathing exercise – 10 to 15 minutes
Creation - 1 Hour (but can be longer if participants wish to make more!)
Total  - 1 hour 30 minutes

Set-up/Prep:
Before your group, ask participants to bring a personal item, like  a charm or something small and meaningful to them that can be threaded on the elastic thread. You might also want to print out the example mantra list from the materials list above if participants need help in thinking of mantras.
Optional: If possible make create Scupley beads ahead of time from left over clay if there is no time to have bead making class.

   
  I Am Safe
 
   
   
  Let It Be
 
   
   
  There Is Only Now
 
   
   
Introduction:
Ask the participants if they know what a mantra is. After everyone has had a chance to share their thoughts you can tell them that a mantra can be a sound, word, or phrase that is repeated by someone who is praying or meditating, or it can be a word or phrase that is repeated often or over and over to expresses someone's basic beliefs.

The word/concept of a mantra comes from Sanskrit (the classical ancient literary language of India) meaning a “sacred message,  text, charm, or spell". Your mantra can be something like  "I am learning how to trust" or I choose to believe in me" or "I can follow my dreams"

Opening Circle/Warm Up:
Ask the participants to think about what they would like to manifest in their lives or if they have things in their lives they wish to celebrate.
Remind the participants that it could be simple things like making the time each day to go for a 30 minute walk or it could be more tangible thing like a creating a safe place to live or having a satisfying job. It could be "I am proud of myself" or I know I continue to grow".
Give the participants time to write down these visions in a list.  Once they complete the list ask them to select one they would like to create a mantra for. The words or thoughts that they would like to use can become daily reminders. It could be phrases like "I will walk everyday" or "one day I will have a safe home of my own"  or "I will have my dream job".  Or it could be just a one word reminder of what they want or are proud of in their life such as "grateful" "family" "friendship" or  "balance".


Meditation:
To begin, let your body sink back into your chair. Notice your entire body. Notice your breathing - feel your lungs expand and your chest rise and fall. Are there areas that feel tense or tight?  Maybe a tightness in the shoulders, just notice this and then come back to the breath, feel your chest rise and fall.
Now take a deep breath - in through the nose and out through the mouth.
Focus on your feet, how do they feel? Tighten the muscles of your feet and then release.
Now focus on your calves, are they tight or tired?
Notice your hips and lower back, do they feel tight? As you breathe, try to visualize breathing into those areas of tension, as if we are creating space to help ease the muscles to relax.
Put your hand on your belly and as you breathe in try to expand the abdomen - feel the pressure against your hand, as you breathe out, pull the stomach in and notice the pressure decrease between your hand and stomach.
Let's breathe in this time to a count of 8 while expanding your belly, if this is uncomfortable to you, then breathe as you normally do.
Pause a second
Now breathe out to a count of 4 as you pull your belly in
Pause a second and this time breathe in to a count of 7, again letting the belly expand
Pause
Breathe out to a count of 4
Pause
Breathe in to a count of 6
Pause
Breathe out to a count of 4
Pause
Breathe in to a count of 5
Pause
Breathe out to a count of 4
Pause
Breathe in to a count of 4
Pause
Breathe out to a count of 4
Pause
Breathe in to a count of 3
Pause
Breathe out to a count of 4
Pause
Breathe in to a count of 2
Pause
Breathe out to a count of 4
Pause
Breathe in to a count of 1
Pause
Breathe out to a count of 4
Pause and simply allow yourself a moment to experience how do you feel right now?
Take a deep breath, in through the nose and out through the mouth. Remove your hand from your belly and make a fist with both hands, as tight as you can, then slowly release.
Take another deep breath and let it out slowly.
Notice any tightness in your shoulders and neck.
On an inhale, lift your shoulders up as high as you can towards your ears, hold as long as you can, as you release, breath out.
Lets do this one more time.
Take one more deep inhale through the nose and out through the mouth.
Take a moment to feel connected to your body and when you are ready, slowly open your eyes.

Creation:
Have the participants select the beads or charms that are symbolic of their vision, if you have the letter beads they can also use the beads to spell out their mantra. Remind them that a color or colors can be selected to be symbolic or representational of their vision. Cut elastic thread approx 10'' long and start threading beads. Finish the bracelet with a knot or a bead and a knot at the end. (making certain that the length of bracelet is enough to go around the wrist.

Closing Circle:
Ask each participant to share their mantra, what it means to them and why they chose to focus on this one today. Ask how these bracelets can become daily reminders of all that is possible for their future.
Row.txt_description: To create a mantra themed bracelet which can be worn as a reminder of what you can manifest/celebrate in your life.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop promotes self-awareness and a healthy understanding of our thoughts, feelings, and actions.

Materials:               &n bsp;                                                                                               Optional Print-outs and Templates for Workshops:                                                            The Two Wolves Story Handout                                                                                       Shrinky Dink Template                                                                                             Watercolor and Collage Template

Shrinky Dink Method                           Shrinky Dink paper                               Permanent markers
Colored pencils
Pens or pencils
Hole punchers
Thin ribbon or string
Scissors
Toaster oven or conventional oven
Journals or paper
Radio/CD player for music
Watercolor Method
Watercolors
Cups
Water for cups
Watercolor paper (optional)
Paint brushes
Markers
Colored pencils
Pens or pencils
Journals or paper
Radio/CD player for music
 
Collage Method
Magazines
Scissors
Glue sticks
Markers
Colored Pencils
Pens or Pencils
Journals or paper
Radio/CD player for music

 

 

Timeframe: 
  Age Range:                    
1 hour 30 minutes
Intro: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 25 minutes
Creation: 50 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes		    
 10 and up




                   

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Set-Up/Prep:

  • Set-up tables according to the chosen artistic method(s)
  • Select a space to do the Opening Circle
  • Print story handouts and templates
  • Prepare and shrink a sample Shrinky Dink with colored pencil and marker to show how each each shows up after the shrinking process
  • Select relaxing music to play during the workshop
  • Prepare additional activities for participants who finish early (e.g., journal prompts, coloring pages, extra paper for drawing or painting)

Introduction:
"How many of you think you know yourself pretty well? Can you think of three words to describe yourself? If you were to ask one of your friends to think of three words to describe you, what would they be? Do these words match with yours?"

"Sometimes, how we feel on the inside doesn't match what we show on the outside. What only we know is that inside of us, there is a lot going on. There are thoughts and feelings that we don't necessarily share with anyone. Maybe we're afraid to share them, we don't know how to share them, or we were told not to share them. Sometimes our feelings turn into actions that we aren't always proud of. For example, when we get into an argument with someone, we may say or do something that we look back on and disapprove of."

"Today, we are going to take a look at some of the things than can go on inside of us and how we can manage or make choices about the actions that happen on the outside."

"All of the activities that we do today are completely optional. You have the freedom to pass altogether or participate in any or all of the activities as you see fit. From asking many questions to sitting back and observing, any form of participation is welcomed. Only you know what you are comfortable with so please take the time to notice your boundaries and respect them. If you feel uncomfortable doing any part of this project including the sharing, it's okay to pass. I'll also ask that everyone in the group shows respect for one another and everything that is said in this group, stays here and is never shared with anyone. We are all safe here and in order to keep this a safe place for all of us, these guidelines should be followed."

Opening Circle:                                                                                                    Embodied Art Activity: I Like To Think of Myself As...  

Invite participants to gather and stand in a circle. "Today we are going to start our workshop off with an embodied art activity. What this means is that we are going to use our bodies to create images and expressions. Just like we create images on a piece of paper by drawing them, we are going to be using our bodies as we would a pencil, crayon, or marker to create a moving image. Does that sound like fun?  As I mentioned, I'm going to invite you to participate, but you always have the option to pass. Keep in mind your physical limitations and respect them. If you have a sore back or an injured knee, please notice them and take care of yourself."

"The name of this activity is called 'I Like To Think of Myself As...' We will have a chance to share a little about ourselves and get to know the other people in the group as well. Here's what we're going to do: One by one, each person who wants to participate will take a giant step into the circle and introduce themselves in a statement that sounds something like this: "My name is Chris and I like to think of myself as silly!" But that's not all, when you say your statement, you're going to pair it with a movement. For example (while waving your arms in the air) you can say, "My name is Chris and I like to think of myself as silly." After each person goes, the rest of the group is going to reflect back by repeating, "Silly Chris" while waving their arms in the air. Does everyone understand? To get us started, I'm going to go first so we have a chance to practice before I ask for my first volunteer."

Tip: For a smaller groups, you may want to repeat each phrase and movement three times to build a stronger connection.

Have the group transition over to a table or have them sit to listen to the story. You can also choose to have the participants take turns reading a sentence or two.

The Two Wolves

     An elder Cherokee Native American was teaching his grandchildren about life. He said to  them, "A fight is going on inside me. It is a terrible fight, and it is between two wolves. One wolf represents fear, anger, envy, sorrow, regret, greed, arrogance, self-pity, guilt, resentment, inferiority, lies, pride, and superiority. The other wolf stands for joy, peace, love, hope, sharing, serenity, humility, kindness, benevolence, friendship, empathy, generosity, truth, compassion, and faith. The same fight is going on inside of you and every other person too." The children thought about it for a minute and then one child asked his grandfather, "Which wolf will win?" The old Cherokee simply replied: "The one I feed."

Tip: For younger participants, use this time to define some of the harder words associated with the wolves.

You can pose any of the following questions after the story:

  • What are some of the thoughts that came to your mind?
  • What do the wolves represent? 
  • What is the grandfather trying to teach the children?
  • Have you heard a story like this before?
  • Do you think everyone has this conflict?
As the discussion goes on, write key words and phrases on a display board for participants to refer to during the creation process. Invite the group to journal about what this story means to them. They can write sentences, words, images, or doodle to express themselves. Offer more questions from the list above or below that can be used as journaling prompts or discussion topics.
  • Are you aware of the wolves inside of you and how they affect your life?
  • Have any of your experiences caused a change in your wolves?
  • What are some ways you feed the wolves within you?
  • Being aware of the wolves within you, which one will you choose to nurture more or pay more attention to?
  • How have your actions been affected by your wolves?

This is a good opportunity to validate and normalize feelings for the participants. Share with them that this is a struggle we all deal with and what is most important is notice and be aware of our feelings and the actions associated with them. When we take a moment to notice what we're are feeling, we come from a more insightful place and can make better decisions about our actions.

When the discussion is over, ask the participants to choose the wolf inside themselves that they will choose to nurture or pay attention to. You can ask them to choose a few attributes from one of the wolves to focus on. For example, a participant might want to focus on peace and hope. Ask them how they will focus on peace and hope. What kinds of actions might they change or start taking?

If participants choose attributes that are more difficult to deal with, encourage them to think about where those feelings are coming from. How can they find ways to help themselves or alleviate some of those feelings? For example, they may say, "A lot of the time I feel angry and it's all I think about." You can ask them about where they think might come from. Encourage them to talk about their feelings and some of the needs that they can focus on the next time they are feeling this way. When they are ready they can create a wolf that represents how they will care for themselves or a reminder of what they want to do next time they are feeling that way. Remind the participants that there is no wrong way to create their art. Ask them to honor this process and respect what comes out.

Creation:                                                                                                                        "We are going to create an artistic representation using colors, words, and images of the wolf within ourselves that we have chosen to nurture." Chose any of the following creation methods or choose one of your own that best suits your participants' needs.

Shrinky Dink Method

  
1) Tape the template and Shrinky Dink to the table.
 2) Outline the template for easier coloring.
  
3) After adding coloring and adding words, cut the template out and punch a hole at the top before shrinking process. Using a conventional or toaster oven, place the cut outs on a clean cookie sheet with the colored side facing up. Ensure that the Shrinky Dinks don't touch each other on the pan. Bake the cut outs at between 300 and 325 °F for approximately 3 minutes.4) After the shrinking process, add beads and other embellishments to create a beautiful keepsake. Participants may want to put their creations on display or wear them as a reminder of this process.

Watercolor Method

  
1) Add colors that represent your dedication to nurturing your chosen wolf.
 2) Feel free to use painting methods that fully express your feelings.
  
 3) Add words and other images.
4) When they're done, participants may want to put their creations on display or wear them as a reminder of this process.

Collage Method

  
1) Cut out images and text that represent how you will nurture your chosen wolf.
 2) Glue the cut-outs to the paper.
  
3) Add words and other images.
4) When they're done, participants may want to put their creations on display or wear them as a reminder of this process.

Closing Circle:
Giving each participant a chance to share their artwork, encourage the conversation by asking questions like, "How does your art show how you will nurture your chosen wolf?" "What were some of your thoughts when you were making your art?" "How will your actions change after this workshop?" "Did you notice anything about yourself when you were creating your art?" If the participants are too shy to share their artwork, welcome them to journal and use these questions as writing prompts/suggestions. You can also offer them sentence frames such as, "After this workshop, I will..." "The one thing I learned about myself is..." "The people in my life that can help me nurture my chosen wolf are..." When all willing participants share, thank them for taking the time to create with you and share their thoughts and feelings. Welcome participants to take their artwork and display it or wear it as a reminder of their journey.
Row.txt_description: This workshop promotes self-awareness and a healthy understanding of our thoughts, feelings, and actions.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Objective:
Participants will take a moment to think about what the holidays mean to them and create a keepsake symbol to remind them of this special time.
 
 
   

Materials:
Various colors of felt
Paper for patterns                       Pencils                                         Markers                                      Rulers                                        Scissors
Tacky glue

Optional Embellishments:
Ribbon or rick-rack
Buttons
Sequins
Trim
Glitter
Puffy paint
Embroidery needles                                                                                                       Thread                                                                                                                            Yarn

Timeframe: 
 Age Range:   
1 hour 15 minutes
Intro: 5 minutes
Opening Circle (Visualization): 15 minutes
Creation: 45 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes		    
5 and up




  

 

 

 

 

 

Set-Up/Prep:

Introduction:
"What do the holidays mean to you? When you think of this time of year, what comes to mind? Today, we're going to be talking about the holidays, what they mean to you. We're going to start off with a visualization, and then we're going to create something that reminds you of how the holidays are or how special you would like them to be today and in the future."

Opening Circle:                                                                                                  Visualization Exercise: 15 minutes

Intro/Explanation (3 minutes):
"We are going to start off with a visualization exercise. What this means is that we're going to take a few minutes to think about and imagine all of the different things that come to mind when I ask you a few questions. Just like all of our activities, you have the option to pass and the invitation to join in the exercise however you feel comfortable."

"When this time of year comes around, lots of different things happen. We are going to take a moment to relax ourselves and get ready to visualize. Before we begin, find a comfortable position and let all of the tension go from your neck, back, legs, and anywhere else you feel it. During the visualization, I'll be asking different questions that you'll think about in your mind. If your feel comfortable to do so, I'm going to invite you to close your eyes when we start. Again, however you'd like to go through this process is totally OK and welcomed. The only rule is that we remain quiet to respect the thought process of the other people in the group. If at any point you need to sit, stand, or move your body in any way, you are welcomed to do so."

"Now, that you're comfortable, I welcome you to close your eyes and listen to the following questions. Let you mind go wherever it needs to go. Recognizing any of the feelings that come up along the way."

Visualization (7 minutes):                                                                                                  Ask the any of the following suggested questions in a slow, calm, voice. Remind participants to embrace any thoughts and images that come up for them during this process. Use soothing music to help the participants relax. Give about 5 minutes for participants and gently guide them out of the visualization.

"We are going to think of the holidays. Listen to the following questions and notice what comes up for you." Choose a few of the following questions to ask.

Questions for Younger Children:
  • What happens during the holidays?
  • Do you do anything special?
  • What do you see?
  • What do you hear?
  • Who do you smell?
  • What do you eat?
  • Do you visit people?
  • Who would you like to visit?
  • What's your favorite part of the holidays?
  • How do you feel during the holidays?
Questions for Teens:
  • What changes do you start to see around you?
  • What do you start to hear?
  • What do you start to smell?
  • What do you start to feel?
  • How does TV change?
  • How does the Internet change?
  • How does your family change?
  • How do you change?
  • Do you celebrate the holidays? If so, how?
  • Do you have any traditions?
  • Would you like to start a tradition?
  • Who do you see?
  • Who would you like to see?

Discussion (5 minutes):                                                                                                    "How was that for everyone? Would anyone like to share what came up for them? What are some of the feelings that came up for you? Have you ever had a chance to sit back and think about the holidays in this way?"

Creation:
"Now that we've had a chance to think about the holidays, I want us to focus on one image that really stood out in your mind as you were going through the visualization. The image can be anything; it can be a color, a sound, a smell or it can be a person, place, a thing and anything and everything in between. We are going to transform that image into a symbol that will remind us of our thoughts and feelings about the holidays. For example, when I was visualizing, I kept thinking of the music that is always playing during the holidays. It plays on the radio, in stores, and even at the homes I visit. So, with that image of me hearing holiday music, my symbol is going to be a radio. This symbol will remind me that I love to hear holiday music."

Before you begin the creation process, do an art supply run-through to familiarize the participants with the art supplies they have available to them.

"Before we start, think about what kind of symbol you would like to create. You can create a flat symbol or a more three dimensional puffy pillow.

 
 
  Color the pig any color you like
 
   
  Cut out both sides of the pig
 
   
  Cut out the slot 
   
  Create the pipe cleaner tail 
   
  Glue the sides together
 
   
  Create positive messages
 
   
   

Step 1: Draw the shape that you want your symbol to be on a piece of paper to create a pattern.

Step 2: Depending on your chosen design, choose one or two pieces of felt and use your pattern as a stencil. Trace the pattern on the felt with a marker.

Step 4: Using scissors, cut the patters from the felt.

Step 4: Using a needle and thread, thread the two shapes together to create a pocket. You can also use tacky glue to secure both pieces of felt together.

Step 5: If you're making a pillow, fill the pocket with cotton to create a pillow

Step 6: Decorate your symbol with colors, words, and symbols. Use different embellishments such as ribbon, sequins, puffy paint, glitter, etc. as desired.

Closing Circle:
Row.txt_description: Participants will take a moment to think about what the holidays mean to them and create a keepsake symbol to remind them of this special time.

Row.txt_code:
Objective: This workshop helps participants focus on themselves and what they want the winter holiday season to represent by creating decorations that have a special meaning for them.

Materials:                                                                                                                    Various colors of felt
White paper to create patterns (optional)
Markers
Scissors
Tacky Glue
Stuffing material

Optional Embellishments:                                                                                             Ribbon or rick-rack                                                                                                      Buttons                                                                                                                       Sequins                                                                                                                            Trim                                                                                                                           Markers                                                                                                                      Glitter                                                                                                                            Puffy Paint (8 and up)                                                                                               Embroidery needles                                                                                                             Cotton balls                                                                                                        Thread                                                                                                                            Yarn                                                                                                                                    

Timeframe: 
  Age Range:   
1 hour 15 minutes
Intro: 5 minutes
Opening Circle/Warm-up: 15 minutes
Creation: 45 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes		    
 5 and up




  

 

 

 

 

 

Set-Up/Prep:


Table set-up

Prior to the workshop, set up your table with different types of felt, paper, markers, embellishments, and any other materials you'd like your participants to use.

Introduction:
“Today we are going to create winter holiday decorations that celebrate what each of us wants the holidays to represent. Using symbols, words, colors or a combination of all of these you can make a memento, or reminder, of what is important and special to you about the holidays."

"Your Celebration Symbol can be hung each holiday to remind you of what you want this season to really be about for you. You can also keep it on your bed, or carry it with you. You can add wishes, hopes or happy memories that you want to make in the future."

"One thing to remember about your creation, is that you get to choose what is important to you during this holiday season. Maybe it is the things you already like about the holidays or maybe you want things to be different for you and your family. Either way, you get to decide what you want to celebrate."

Opening Circle & Warm-up:
"Share one thing that makes you feel good or that you like about the holidays, and why it special to you." Give all participants an opportunity to share, but remind them that sharing is optional. It is also important to consider that many participants have experienced traumatic experiences, scarcity, and disappointment during this season so they may not have a happy memory to share or recall about the holiday season.

End with yourself, and share an example that crosses many cultural traditions, that is accessible to those in the group and that models attaching special meaning to a symbol. For example, “I like the lights. When I see the lights I feel happy and joyful. I think I’ll make a candle and write the word joy on it to remind me that no matter what, I always want to feel joy during the winter holidays."

Once all those who wanted to have shared and you’ve shared your example, determine if it is appropriate to ask the group to notice the similarities and differences in their shares. Point out how special it is to celebrate in all of sorts of different ways and what things we have in common.

Demonstration:


Create a pattern
Trace your pattern
  
Sew felt pieces together
 Leave a pocket for stuffing
 
Stuff cotton into the pocket
Decorate your symbol
 
House
Christmas Tree
 
Buttons
 Words and embellishments

"Today you will create a symbol of what you want your winter holidays to represent using felt and the materials laid out on the table."

The instructions are simple:

  1. Decide if you want to make your creation into a pillow or flat decoration
  2. Using a marker, draw a symbol or shape that represents what you want the holidays to be about on a piece of felt – this can be anything, a house, a circle, a heart or anything at all. Another option for this step is to create a pattern on paper and then use it to trace the image/drawing onto the felt.
  3. Cut it out. If you are making a pillow or want to make your creation thicker or layered you will need to use your cutout as a template to make two identical shapes.
  4. If you're creating a pillow, sew the two pieces of felt together to create a pocket.
  5. After the pocket is complete, stuff it with cotton balls and sew the two pieces completely together.
  6. Using the glue and embellishments, decorate your celebration symbol.
  7. If you'll be hanging your creation, use ribbon and glue to make a loop on the back.
  8. Create different variations, both big and small.

Creation:

As you invite participants to create, remind them that this isn’t about what they “want" for someone to give them, but rather that they get to focus more on what makes or would make them happy in their heart and to create a reminder of that. Invite them to put  today’s date somewhere on their creation so they can remember this special moment.

Closing Circle:                           
"Tell the group about your creation and what it means to you. Who do you want to share your creation with?"
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps participants to focus on themselves and what they want the winter holiday season to represent by creating decorations that have a special meaning for them.
