Row.txt_code:
Description:
Through exploring images of safety, this workshop can help participants feel a sense of their own power by inviting them to create a safe place within themselves.

   
  Creating a Safe Place Table Set-up 
   
   
Materials:
Colored pencils
Pencil sharpeners
Construction paper (various colors)
Envelopes (10" x 13") or paper to protect artwork (optional)
Relaxing music for Guided Imagery (optional)

Time Frame:
1 hour
Intro: 5 minutes
Embodied Art Activity: 10 minutes
Guided Imagery: 5 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes

Set-up/prep:
Prepare the art supplies on the table for easy transition during the group. If you are using music, cue the song that you will be using. An open space for the Opening Circle and/or Guided Imagery can be helpful but is not necessary. If an open space is not available, the activities can be done at the table.

Intro:
"During this workshop, we will be talking about safety and what it means to you. We will be doing three activities that will help you create your safe place. We will have the option to creatively use our bodies, our minds, and drawing something on paper. At the end of the workshop session what is most important is that you trust your own needs to connect to what safety means to you.

"Throughout this workshop, you are invited to participate, which means you always have the option to pass. Passing can look like you sitting back and watching what goes on or it can look like you participating in only a few activities that you feel comfortable with - it's up to you."

Embodied Art Activity: What Makes You Feel Safe?
Invite participants to gather and stand in a circle. Ask them to space themselves so that they're able to move around without bumping into the person next to them. If you're doing this activity at the table, each person can sit or stand to create their image when it's their turn.

"We are going to start our workshop off by using our bodies. I'm going to start off by asking a question, and we're going to think of how we can answer this question by using our bodies."

"The question is: 'What makes you feel safe?' I'm going to give you a minute to think about what makes you feel safe.

"When I think of what makes me feel safe, I think of hugs. Hugs make me feel safe, so my image might look like this." Wrap your arms around yourself and say "hugs." Ask the participants to repeat your movement and word after you. "But for you, hugs may not be safe, so your image might look like this." Hold your arms straight out in front of you as if you're motioning to stop and say, "Stay away!" Ask the participants to repeat after you again.
 
 
 
   Embodied Art Activity at the Table:
"Hugs" (modest)		    Embodied Art Activity at the Table:
"Hugs" (exaggerated)		 
     
   Embodied Art Activity in a Circle:
 "Stay Away!" (modest)		   Embodied Art Activity in a Circle:
 "Stay Away!" (exaggerated)		 

Invite someone to start sharing their image and word/phrase, and remind the group to repeat both parts.

NOTE: You can also show the possible range of images from a small, modest statue to a large, exaggerated image.

Guided Imagery: What Is Your Safe Place?
"For our next activity, we're going to relax and use our imagination to picture our safe place in our minds. After we use our imagination, you'll get a chance to create your safe place on paper with any of the art supplies you see here. Remember: there is no wrong way to imagine or create your safe place!

"Before we start, I'm going to invite you to find a place in the room where you feel most comfortable. This can look like you sitting in a chair, sitting or lying on the floor, standing, or anything in between. Once you get to your comfortable place, feel free to close your eyes if you feel comfortable doing so."

During the guided imagery use a slow, calm voice. It will give the participants time to create the images in their minds.

The guided imagery can sound something like this: "Start by taking a deep breath in and slowly letting it out. Now feel your feet and give them a squeeze and let go. Feel your knees, give them a shake and pause. Feel your shoulders, move them up and move them down several times. Notice your arms and wiggle them around and pause. How about your hands? Squeeze your hands tightly and let go, repeat several times."

"Take a deep breath, and begin to envision your safe place." Continue by asking any or all of the following questions to aid participants in visualizing their safe place:
  • What does your safe place look like?
  • What colors do you see?
  • What does your safe place feel like?
  • What does your safe place sound like?
  • Is it quiet in your safe place?
  • What do you hear?
  • Are you alone in your safe place?
  • If you're not alone, who's with you?
  • What are you doing in your safe place?
  • Did you bring something with you to your safe place?
  • What did you leave behind?
  • Is your safe place somewhere you've been before or a place you've made up?
  • How does your safe place make you feel?
Slowly bring the group back to the room by asking, "When you're ready, open your eyes, move slowly back to your seat, and begin to create your safe place on paper."

 
 
  Creating a Safe Place
 
   
   
  Creating a Safe Place 
  
 
Creation:
As the participants create, be available to support participants if they have any questions or need any supplies. You may wish to give time reminders, if necessary.

Closing Circle:
As you begin the closing, let the participants know that this time is for "heart talk." It's a time when they can talk about their art and each participant chooses how they want to talk about their creation. They have the option to participate however they'd like, from sharing their story to being a witness and listening to the other stories.

After each participant has a chance to share, offer them a "special envelope" or a piece of paper to save their art and keep it protected from other people's eyes and judgements - a safe place for their safe place.

Optional closing question: "Now that you've created your safe place, what will you do with it?"
Row.txt_description: Through exploring images of safety, this workshop can help participants feel a sense of their own power by inviting them to create a safe place within themselves.
Row.txt_tips:
• It is very important that you and any other Leaders, staff, or volunteers in the room participate along with the group. By modeling your enthusiasm and willingness to participate, you help build trust, bonding, and make it safer for other people to play and share vulnerable experiences.
  • As an additional strategy, you may want to ask the group about examining their different safety strategies. You can ask questions like, "Which safety strategies have been helpful in the past?" "Which safety strategies aren't serving you anymore?"
  • Support your participants in understanding that because of trauma it's completely normal not to feel safe all the time and that part of healing from trauma can be opening up the possibility for safety. Being gentle and patient, with what can be a slow process, can be helpful.
  • Let the participants define for themselves their visions of safety and their journey to feeling safe. 
  • If "violent" images come up as safety strategies, having a non-judgmental approach and encouraging other participants to do the same will help create safety in the group. It's okay if someone uses a strategy that you or the other participants wouldn't use.
  • It's okay if participants can't envision a safe place. They can try something out to see if it feels safe and notice what feelings come up for them. They can just play with the supplies, breathe with their hand over their heart, or use this time to write in a journal.
  • Remember that it's not your job as facilitator to problem-solve, find a safe place for your participants, or protect them from feelings they find uncomfortable. Instead, consider seeing your role as providing the space for the participants to acknowledge their feelings and experiences and for you to validate whatever comes up.

 

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
My objective is to give children an opportunity to have a voice and to feel safe. This workshop gives them a chance to be with a grown-up who provides an environment where that safety can happen, a grown-up who can sa y “I know what’s been happening in your life and it’s safe to talk about it here.” The aim is also for the children to know they have the capacity inside of them to create healing images.

 
  
Materials:
Safety Picture-Making (for children under seven):
Non-toxic marker
Construction paper (white, lavender, light grey, light brown)
Permanent marker (for name writing)
Large envelopes for the artwork to go home in
Clear contact paper (optional)

Collage-Making (for children over seven):
Glue stick (one for each child)
 
 Materials
Appropriate magazines
Construction paper
Scissors (one for each child)
Large envelopes
Clear contact paper (optional)

Time Format:
15 minutes: Opening circle
15 minutes: Relaxation and focus time
30 minutes: Creation time
20 minutes: Closing circle
10 minutes: Clean-up time, goodbyes

Total time: 1 1/2 hours

Space Set-up:
For the Opening Circle and Relaxation, it is ideal for each child to be on the floor on their own mat or piece of carpet. This way they have a defined space, a boundary for their body in which to relax and feel safe. The creating should take place at a table nearby. All materials should be set up and ready to go before the children arrive at a table or some place away from your opening circle so they aren’t at the table and they aren’t tempted to play with the art supplies before creation time. After the relaxation, the children can move right to the table to begin creating.

Opening Circle:
Introduce the theme - what does it mean to feel safe? “We’re going to talk about being safe. How do you feel safe? Everyone will get a turn to talk. It’s OK if you don’t feel like saying anything because sometimes that doesn’t feel safe.” As the children speak in a circle, let them go as fast as they want. The circle usually goes much quicker than it would with adults.

Dream Pillows:
For young children it can be helpful if they have something to hold on to as they imagine their safe place. They need something to do with their hands. It’s too difficult to focus for and just listen for a long time, especially for kids who have been abused.

You can use stuffed animals but I like to make “dream pillows” that they can keep. Dream pillows are small bean bags I make and fill with rice. All the pillows are exactly the same size, shape, and color. I scent them with geranium and lavender essence oil. I explain at the beginning that they get to take their dream pillow with them when they go. It is helpful to carry something nurturing with them, a reminder of having that safe time. The dream pillow is the reminder they can carry with them.



 Photograph from Children of Many Lands
Relaxation and Focus:
1. Pass out the dream pillows
2. Help each child choose a place to rest
3. Wiggle down exercise
Facilitator begins:
a: Wiggle your toes, now take a deep breath, then relax those toes
b. Wiggle your legs, now take a deep breath, then relax those legs
c. Wiggle your bottom, now take a deep breath, then relax your bottom
d. Wiggle your tummy, now take a deep breath and relax your tummy
e. Wiggle your shoulders, now take a deep breath and relax your shoulders
f. Wiggle your arms and hands, now take a deep breath, then relax them
g. Last one now, wiggle your eyes, now take a deep breath, then relax your eyes (eye closing is optional, it might not feel safe for some kids)
4. If you don’t have any pillows, you could begin with, “Now let’s start by giving ourselves a nice warm hug...” and continue, "Now think of something quiet. You might be floating on a cloud or swimming in the sea or walking in a beautiful forest or lying on bunches of soft pillows or moving your body. Any special place you feel quiet and safe. Think about what that place looks like. What does it smell like? Who is there? What does it feel like? Is it a place you have never been before? Is it in your imagination? It can be special and safe just for you. You make it safe, you make all the magic and power in this safe place. When you are ready, quietly go to the table and make your safe picture. When you are doing your drawing, this is a no-talking time.”



 Child drawing her Safe Place

 
 Child drawing their Safe Place
Creation:
Children ages seven and under draw their safe place using colors that feel safe. Children ages seven and up will create a safe place collage.
For older kids you can use this handout, “Safe Place” Handout (optional - click here for handout)

Closing Circle:
This is the time children can talk about their drawings/collages. Some children may choose not to talk about their work. That is okay because it is very important that each child gets to choose what they want to say about their creation. It can be a very private thing and needs to be respected by adults. After each child has their turn, give them a "special envelope" in which they can save their art and keep it private and safe.

As each child has a turn to share (or not) it is important to phrase what you say very carefully. When adults make judgments or labels about children's art work, they learn not to trust art. It could be a deep blow to their self-esteem and damage how they feel about themselves and their art.
 
 Part of a child's Safe Place

Most importantly, use a pleasant voice tone and be authentic when you respond to each child! Children know when adults are not being true to their feelings, especially children who have been a part of domestic violence. These children have a special radar that makes them hyper-sensitive to adults. This is a defensive tactic that may have kept them safe in the past. Now we have a window of time with them to show that adults can be safe and authentic.

Also, be aware of what other children say. They may need verbal support from you in order not to crush another child's work. Remember some of these kids may not be used to hearing praise or non-judgmental comments before now. For example:

Do not say inappropriate statements like:
--What's that supposed to be?
--Is that a dog, tree, cat, etc.?
--That's a nice, pretty, ugly, little, dark, bright, etc.
--I like that (you could not like it too)
--Is that all, you could have done better.
--Do it over or try again later, or that was not the assignment, etc.

Do say appropriate comments to children like:
--Tell me about your safe picture/collage
--Did you choose colors that make you feel safe?
--I really see how hard, diligently, long, you worked on your creation.
--Wow! (smile)
--Oh my! (smile)
--Awesome, brilliant, fantastic! (if you choose these adjectives, be fair and careful to say it
to every child).

Clean-up/Goodbyes!
Row.txt_description: My objective is to give children an opportunity to have a voice and to feel safe. This workshop gives them a chance to be with a grown-up who provides an environment where that safety can happen, a grown-up who can say “I know what’s been happening in your life and it’s safe to talk about it here.” The aim is also for the children to know they have the capacity inside of them to create healing images.

Row.txt_code:
Description:
Through embodied and applied art, participants are invited to use the metaphor of a river to acknowledge their past, notice their resilience, and honor their present strength.

Materials:
Colored pencils
Crayons
Markers
Pencil sharpeners
Journaling page
Construction paper or card stock (various colors)

Optional Materials
Metallic markers
White-out pens
Objects to pass around during Fill the Space warm-up
Relaxing music for visualization

Timeframe: 
 Age Range:                
1 hour 30 minutes
Intro: 5 minutes
Warm-Ups: Fill the Space: 5 minutes
                 Expressive Crayon: 5 minutes
Visualization: 5 minutes
Creation and Journaling Page: 30 minutes
Sharing Our River Stories: 30 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes		 12 and up




               











Set-up/prep:
 
River Stories Table Set-up
  • Prepare the art supplies on the table, including one journaling page for each participant.
  • If you will be using the Fill the Space and Walk the River exercises, determine how you will transition into the space.
  • If music will be used during this workshop, cuing it to the song/playlist will help ease transition.
Intro:
"How many of you have seen a river before either in real life or on TV? Today, we're going to be talking all about rivers and how they connect to telling the story of our our lives so far. Throughout this workshop, we'll be using our bodies and the art supplies you see here. Just like every workshop, you will be invited to participate in any way you'd like to. I ask that you respect your thoughts, feelings, and anything else that comes up and know that whatever comes out is OK. I will also ask that you do the same for the other people in the group as well because together, we create this safe place to explore and learn."

Warm-Ups: Fill the Space and Expressive Crayon
NOTE: Depending on time, you can use one, both, or any of your own warm-ups for this workshop.

Fill the Space:
Ask the participants spread out throughout the space. Start by having them walk around the space to get in touch with their bodies. Using the following prompts, and/or any of your own, can help participants connect with one another. If you'll be introducing objects for the participants to pass around, prepare them so you can easily access them.

NOTE: Remind participants to respect their bodies and notice any physical limitations.

  
 Participants fill the space in the room.
 
With the following prompts, or some of your own, encourage interaction between participants. You can make it as playful as you'd like.
  • Make eye contact with one another
  • Notice the space between people
  • Say hello to someone
  • Take up a lot of space
  • Take up very little space
  • Smile at someone
  • Wave at someone
  • Act like your favorite animal

Passing objects: if you choose to pass objects around, start by announcing that objects will be floating around and that someone who gets an object has the option to "gift" it to someone else.

 

Expressive Crayon depicting anger.
 

Expressive Crayon depicting happiness.
 
   

Expressive Crayon:                               "This warm-up is all about the feelings we don't usually get to express because something or someone has held us back. I want you to think about a feeling or emotion that you don't normally show for whatever reason. Think about some of the times where you held back from letting all of those feelings fly out of your body. Today, you're going to get the chance to let them fly out of you and onto a piece of paper! So take a moment to think of that feeling and choose one or more crayons and a piece of paper that you think best fit the colors of that emotion.

When we start, you're going to scribble, doodle, or anything you feel like doing that best fits that emotion. Don't be afraid of breaking crayons or ripping the paper, just let the feelings flow. I invite you to use your body to show those feelings."

Visualization: Imagine Your Life as a River

 

Participants start their river on their birthday
and end with today's date.
 		 
Before the visualization starts, ask participants to choose a piece of paper that they will draw their river on. Invite them to start with their birth date on one end of the paper (the beginning of their river) and end with today's date (the end of their river). They can choose to write this any way they'd like to.
Ask participants to make themselves comfortable and invite them to close their eyes if they feel comfortable enough to do so. If you're using music, start the music."

"As you begin to relax, notice a part of your body that you don't really pay much attention to, like the space between your toes, the space between your shoulders, or the bends in your joints. Slowly breath in and out and imagine that your breath is slowly filling up a hot air balloon that you are about to get on. Each slow breath makes your balloon grow bigger and bigger and bigger. Breathe in and out. In and out. Now that you're balloon is full, it's time to get on. As you get on, feel your body rising with the balloon as you look down. As you move higher and higher, feel the wind on your face as you see everything below you get smaller. As you float along, notice that there's a river below you. Imagine that this river is your life. Notice all of the twists and turns that the river makes. Where is your river shallow? Where is it deep? Where is the water fast? Where is it slow? What do the banks of the river look like? Take a moment to take your river in and notice all of its beauty. As you take a few more deep breaths, slowly bring your hot air balloon back to the ground. When you're ready, open your eyes and take what you saw and create it on your paper."

Creation:

Ask the participants to open their eyes (if they're closed) and think about the images that came to mind when you were looking down on your river. They can think about all of the moments in their lives where their rivers twisted and turned. 

When they're ready, they can begin creating their rivers. They can create their river by using symbols, dates, ages, words, or anything else to represent important times in their lives. Participants might want to create their rivers in a timeline form.

NOTE: Giving gentle time prompts like, "We have about ten minutes to finish up our artwork" can help participants manage their time.
 Participants create their River Stories.
 
Preparing to Share
In a moment, you're going to be invited to share three key moments that you'd like bring to the room today to honor or acknowledge.
To get you ready to share, the journaling page can help you gather your thoughts.

Sharing Our River Stories:
  
  Completed River Story
"We're going to be sharing our stories in a special way today. In a moment, I'm going to invite you to share your story with your body, your words, or both."



Walking the River
Preparing the space:

Here are the steps for Walking the River. See links to video demonstrations and examples below.
  1. In groups of two or three, participants can stand together, facing the rest of the group, in a line, side by side.
  2. One by one, each person will take a step forward, share the beginning of their river, beginning with their birth date, birth month, or any other way they'd like to share. For example a statement can sound like this, "March 15, 2001, I was born." or "On March 15, I was born." Remind participants that they can use their body, words, or both to share their significant moments.
  3. Taking turns, each person shares the beginning of their river. Each step of the river will follow this routine: take one step, share, and the next person goes. A share can sound like, "October 3, 2006, I learned how to read." or "October 3, 2006, something big happened!"
  4. After each of the three significant moments, the last step will end with this phrase "(Today's date) I am here, in this room, with you."
  5. The rest of the group affirms by saying, "We see you." after each person finishes their last step.
  6. At the end of each group's share session, you can acknowledge their bravery by clapping or snapping your fingers.
Video Demonstrations
Intro and Demo
Walking the River: Sample 1
Walking the River: Sample 2
Walking the River: Sample 3
Walking the River: Sample 4
 




Methods of sharing with limited space:
  1. Table Share: participants can share at the table, one at a time, choosing to sit or stand at their seat when presenting.
  2. Mini Art Gallery: participants who wish to share can leave their artwork and River Story journaling page at their place at the table and everyone can walk around and view the "art gallery."
  3. Paired Sharing: participants partner up and share their River Stories with one another.
Closing Circle:
"Today we imagined our lives as a river and we talked about three big things in our lives that were a part of our river."

Optional closing questions:
  • What came up for you during the this exercise?
  • Looking back at your river, what did you notice?
  • How have you handled some of the twists and turns in your river?
  • How do you'll handle changes in your river in the future?
  • Where would you like your river to go from today on?
Row.txt_description: Through embodied and applied art, participants are invited to use the metaphor of a river to acknowledge their past, notice their resilience, and honor their present strength.
Row.txt_tips:
• It is very important that you and any other Leaders, staff, or volunteers in the room participate along with the group. By modeling your enthusiasm and willingness to participate, you help build trust, bonding, and make it safer for other people to play and share vulnerable experiences.

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Description:
Through visual art (drawing) and embodied art (movement), participants are invited to use the metaphor of a river to acknowledge their past, notice their resilience, and honor their present strength.

Materials:
  • Colored pencils and/or markers
  • Pencil sharpeners (if using colored pencils)
  • Construction paper or card stock (various colors)
  • River Stories worksheet (pdf or doc, one copy per person)
  • Pens (one per person)
  • OPTIONAL: Metallic markers, white colored pencils, or whiteout pens (shows up better on dark paper)
  • OPTIONAL: Relaxing music for Visualization and Creation (Stars of the Lid is one possibility)
Timeframe: 
1 hour 20 minutes
Intro: 5 minutes
Visualization: 5 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Sharing Our River Stories: 30 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes









Set-up/prep:
 
River Stories Table Set-up
Prepare the art supplies on the table for easy transition during the group. If you are using music for the visualization and creation portions, cue the song that you will be using.

An open space for the sharing portion is helpful but not necessary. If you have limited space, please look at the "workshop tips" below for more info.

IMPORTANT NOTES:
  • If you are re-arranging your usual room to allow for more movement space, you might invite the participants to help you or do it in front of them, so that the transition is not jarring.
  • It might be helpful for you to create your river art and worksheet ahead of time, so that you can be prepared to demonstrate the sharing process or be a buddy for someone sharing (so that they don't have to share alone).
  • It can be helpful to have the date and the phrase "I am here, in this room, with you." written in large letters on a poster or a whiteboard as a "prompt" so that when participants share they can look up and see the words (instead of just reading them from the River Stories worksheet).
Video Samples: Because the sharing part of this workshop has more steps than usual, we recommend watching one or more of the sample videos below so that you can more easily understand the process. We suggest that you let the group have their own experience (instead of sharing the videos with them). In watching the videos, you will notice how participants have chosen to share in slightly different ways (e.g. using body movements, expressing emotions, using more or less words, etc.). We have included all of these samples, so you see some of the variety that can occur in this workshop.
  • River Stories Intro and Demo
  • River Stories Sample 1
  • River Stories Sample 2
  • River Stories Sample 3
  • River Stories Sample 4
Intro:
"Today we're going to think of our lives as a river. Just like a river, our lives can have twists and turns. We're going to have the chance to notice what we've been through in our past and how we got to be here today. We will be doing this by creating art on paper, then physically with our bodies. As always, this is your window of time to practice noticing your thoughts, feelings, and needs, and to respect whatever comes up.

"This workshop is all about noticing how you got here and giving others a chance to see you and acknowledge your journey. It's a big deal that we all get to be in this room together today. Let's start by going around and anyone who would like to can share one thing that they experienced today that led up to this moment. For example, you might say, 'I got on the bus to come here' or 'I has having a really hard day, and I came to this workshop anyway!'"

Give the participants the opportunity to speak or pass.

   
 Participants start their river on their birth date
and end with today's date.		 
Visualization: Imagine Your Life as a River
Before the visualization starts, ask participants to choose a piece of colored paper that they will use to draw their river. Invite them to start with their birth date on one end of the paper (the beginning of their river) and end with today's date (the end of their river). They can choose to write this any way they'd like to.

"I'm going to offer a visualization next, and first I invite you to make yourself comfortable. That could be sitting in your chair, standing behind it, sitting on the floor, eyes open or eyes closed, whatever will best help you connect to yourself and your experiences."

If you're using music, start the music. Speak slowly and gently, with lots of pauses for participants to consider your questions and come up with their own answers silently.

"Imagine your life as a river. You might picture yourself floating above your river and looking down at it or walking along side of it. What does it look like? What does the beginning of the river look like? Where does your river flow quickly and where does it flow slowly? Where is your river deep? And where is it shallow? Does your river have any twists, turns or bends? Where is it narrow and where is it wide? What do the banks of your river look like? Does the water in your river have a color? Can you see where your river is going?

"When you're ready, you can open your eyes (if they're closed), come back to the table (if you've moved somewhere else), and begin to create your river on paper."

Creation:
 




  Participants create their River Stories.
"As you create, you might consider the times or events that have shaped your life. Remember that the river you are creating on paper can look like what you saw in your mind during the visualization or it could be something new. You can use symbols, words, dates, ages, or anything else you'd like to represent the times in your life you'd like to honor today. There is no right or wrong way to create your river - it may not even look like a river, and that's just fine."

As the participants create, you can make yourself available to answer any questions or get any additional supplies, if needed.

If anyone finishes early, they can journal freely on the back of their river art, take time to sit quietly with their experience, begin to work on their River Stories worksheet to get ready for the sharing portion, or anything else that works for them, you, and the group.

NOTE: Giving gentle time prompts like, "We have about ten minutes to finish up our artwork" can help participants be aware of their time.

Sharing Our River Stories, Step 1: Worksheet
"We're going to be sharing our stories in a special way today, so to get ready for that, each person can pick three moments from their life that they'd like to acknowledge or honor today. You can be very specific (such as 'age 26: we moved to a new home and it was hard') or very general ('age 26: something new'). You get to decide what you want to share and how you want to share it. Here's a worksheet to help get us ready for the sharing."

Pass out the River Stories worksheet, and invite participants to fill it out.

Sharing Our River Stories, Step 2: Walking the River
Once everyone who wants to has completed their River Stories worksheet, invite the group to bring their creations with their worksheets and sit together, facing the same direction.

It's helpful for participants to see a physical demonstration of the sharing process, and for the Leader to be the first person in the first group to share. Stand up in front of the group, facing them but a few steps back, to show what you mean. If possible, have another 1-2 people stand up with you so they can demonstrate with you. (NOTE: The River Stories intro and demo video above  will show you one version of this intro and demonstration.)

Introduction:
"In a moment, I'm going to invite you to share your story with your body, your words, or both.

"How many of you have ever felt like something happened to you but it wasn't seen, heard, or acknowledged the way you would have liked? Today, we will each have the option to share our river with the group, and the group's job is to really see, hear, and acknowledge the person, without any judgment - to really honor each journey.

"You get to choose if you want to share, and no one will share alone unless you want to. The basic structure is that a few people will stand up here together, facing the group but a few steps back. It's your choice if you want to show the your river art as you do this."

   
 The beginning of the river.
 
River Beginning:
"Now those of us who are standing here are going to imagine that our river is stretched out in front of us, that we are standing at the beginning, at our place of birth, and that the river flows towards the rest of the group. One by one, each person standing up will start by saying their birthday and 'I was born.' For example, the first person might say 'August 17, 1985: I was born,' then the second person would say, 'June 15, 1971: I was born.'"

Sharing First Event
"After all the people standing up here have shared their birth date, the first person will take a step forward and say the first event from their river that they want to honor today. As a reminder, you get to decide how much you want to share with us either with your words or with your body. For example, you could say 'Age 8: My teacher yelled at me in front of the class or' '1989: I felt embarrassed,' or '4th grade: People looked at me,' or '4th grade' while silently making a movement. You can demonstrate this last option by covering your face in an embarrassed way while saying '4th grade.'

"Then the second person will take a step forward and share their first event, then the third person, and so on."

   
  One by one, the group shares their second events.
 
Sharing Second Event
"Once everyone has shared their first event, the first person will take another step forward and share their second event. One at a time, the other people standing will take their steps forward and share their second events."


Sharing Third Event
"Once everyone has shared their second event, then each person up here will take a third step and share their third event, one at a time."

River Ending/Group Acknowledgement
"Once everyone has shared their third event, then each person will step forward one at a time, and say today's date and the sentence 'I am here, in this room, with you.' We say this because in addition to honoring everything we've gone through, we also get to come to this present moment in time and space and notice that we're not alone.

 
 
  The group reaches the end of their rivers.
 
"After each person says 'I am here in this room with you,' the rest of the group says, 'We see you,' all together in response, showing the community of support that we have here. Let's practice. Say today's date and 'I am here, in this room, with you,' and give the group a chance to repeat 'We see you.'"

NOTE: With this workshop, it can be very helpful to set up the expectation of confidentiality ahead of time. It can be safer for participants to share if they know that not only will nothing be shared but that they don't have to answer any questions about their experiences. You might say, "Before we begin, can we make the agreement that we will keep whatever anyone shares confidential? That way, we can each share exactly what we want to, and know that no one, even people in this room, will ever mention it to us unless we bring it up again first."

After the explanation, invite participants to begin sharing their river stories. After each set of sharing finishes, you can invite the group to acknowledge the courage of the sharers by snapping their fingers.

Closing:
"Thank you all for taking this window of time to honor yourself, your journey, and the journeys of others." Invite a group to take a breath or two together. "Let's take a moment to share anything that came up for you during this workshop. You can share your art, your feelings, your thoughts, or anything that was meaningful about your experience today."

Optional closing questions (for groups that are shy and/or if there's more time for discussion):
  • Looking back at your river, what did you notice?
  • What made your river twist and turn?
  • How did it feel to share your river?
  • How did it feel to be acknowledged?
  • Where did you notice your strength or resilience today?
  • Where would you like your river to go from today on?
Row.txt_description: Through visual art (drawing) and embodied art (movement), participants are invited to use the metaphor of a river to acknowledge their past, notice their resilience, and honor their present strength.
Row.txt_tips:
• It is very important that you and any other Leaders, staff, or volunteers in the room participate along with the group. By modeling your enthusiasm and willingness to participate, you help build trust, bonding, and make it safer for other people to play and share vulnerable experiences.

  • If you have limited space, you can encourage participants to make very tiny steps when they walk their river so that the participants still get the experience of moving forward towards the group.

  • If you end up with one person left who wants to share but everyone else has shared already, you or another participant can share your river again so that the one person does not feel alone walking their river. Of course, it's great to also honor the choice of any participants who request to walk their river alone.

  • If anyone in your group feels uncomfortable sharing their birth date, they do not need to share their birth year or age. They can just share the day and month or say whatever feels comfortable to them (for example, "a long time ago" or "at one point in the not too distant past").

  • In case anyone expresses concern, you can let them know that it's okay if different people's rivers don't line up when they share together. For example, one person's river might be in 1990 while another's river is in 2007 even though they are standing side by side. The reasons to share rivers with buddies is so that we can feel support or connection while we share.

  • If you like, you can invite participants to add a sentence or phrase along with "I was born." For example: "August 17, 1985: I was born and welcomed into the world."

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways.  Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Description
In this simple yet powerful warm-up, participants can safely express any emotions they have been holding inside by scribbling freely.

Materials:
Crayons              
Paper



  Time frame:
Introduction                         3 min
Preparation (optional)          5 min
Creation                               2 min
Closing                               10 min
  
                     Total Time: 15-20 min
  

Set Up
Place crayons and paper on the table so that they are easily accessible to participants.

Introduction 
Welcome participants and remind them that this is their window of time to practice honoring their feelings, needs, and thoughts. Let them know that they get to choose what their participation looks like. For example, participation might mean sitting quietly with their head down, just playing with the supplies, trying out all the suggestions you give, or anything else that feels right to them.

Start by asking each participant to share one or two words of how they are feeling right now. (Remind them that "I don't know" or "pass" are perfectly acceptable answers.)

Preparation (optional)
 
 
 Circular Doodles
 
   
 Angular Scribbles on Top
of Circular Doodles
 
"We're going to begin by warming up our bodies and getting comfortable with the supplies. So I invite you to take a piece of paper and any crayon you like and just begin doodling by making random circular motions. Don't worry if you break the crayon or about what your doodle looks like--see if you can just let yourself feel the movement of your arm without judging it." Give the participants 30-60 seconds to draw circular scribbles.

NOTE: It can be helpful if you participate with your group, so that they can see you being playful and relaxed with your scribbles and doodles.

"Now add to your scribble by picking a new crayon and with your other hand, make fast and angular motions." Give the participants 30-60 seconds to draw angular scribbles.

"Finally, using both hands together, make either angular or circular motions using the two colors together." Give the participants 30-60 seconds to create, and invite them to find a pausing place.

Offer participants a moment to share anything they'd like to about their experience, and then ask them to take a new piece of paper or flip their current piece of paper over.

Creation
   
 Expressive Crayon depicting anger. 
   
 Expressive Crayon depicting happiness. 
"Choose any emotion you like. I invite you to pick one that you feel like you haven't had permission to feel. For some of you that may be anger, for others it may be grief, aggression, confidence, love, or something else.

"So go ahead and choose an emotion and crayon to represent that emotion. Consider going with your first thought--you can always change the emotion or the color later if you like.

"In a moment, I'm going to invite you to express that emotion on the paper in front of you for two minutes. When we start, I want to use your crayon to express that emotion on the paper. Think about how you might move your arm to express that emotion. This can look like scribbling or tapping, moving slowly or quickly, or anything else that you feel like doing." It can be helpful to give examples in the air with a crayon and your own body movements as you say this.

"Don't worry about what it looks like, or even ripping the paper or breaking the crayons--just take this activity where you need it to go. Is everyone ready?"

Give participants two minutes to explore their chosen emotion. When two minutes are up, you can say, "Find a pausing place so we can take a moment to reflect on what that was like."

Closing
Give the participants an opportunity to share anything they like about their scribbles, their chosen feeling, or whatever they noticed by participating. It can also be helpful to remind participants that they are welcome to pass if they don't feel like sharing and that each person's representation of an emotion could be different, and that is okay.

End by validating each person's experience and their taking a window of time to honor themselves.
Row.txt_description: In this simple yet powerful warm-up, participants can safely express any emotions they have been holding inside by scribbling freely.
Row.txt_tips:
• This warm-up often works best without music so that participants can connect to their own experiences and different participants can work on different emotions simultaneously without being influenced by the music.
  • If your group has a hard time thinking of emotion words, you can brainstorm words with them ahead of time or have them start with emotions you suggest (like anger, confusion, joy, etc.) and then end with an emotion of their choice.
  • This warm-up works well with emotion-focused workshops or workshops that use crayons.
  • If you have extra time, participants can do additional emotions.

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways.  Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Description:
Through visual art (drawing) and embodied art (movement), participants are invited to use the metaphor of a river to acknowledge their past, notice their resilience, and honor their present strength.

Materials:
  • Colored pencils and/or markers
  • Pencil sharpeners (if using colored pencils)
  • Construction paper or card stock (various colors)
  • River Stories worksheet (pdf or doc, one copy per person)
  • Pens (one per person)
  • OPTIONAL: Metallic markers, white colored pencils, or whiteout pens (shows up better on dark paper)
  • OPTIONAL: Relaxing music for Visualization and Creation (Stars of the Lid is one possibility)
Timeframe: 
 Ages:             
1 hour 20 minutes
Intro: 5 minutes
Visualization: 5 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Sharing Our River Stories: 30 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes		 12 and up
             









Set-up/prep:
 
River Stories Table Set-up
Prepare the art supplies on the table for easy transition during the group. If you are using music for the visualization and creation portions, cue the song that you will be using.

An open space for the sharing portion is helpful but not necessary. If you have limited space, please look at the "workshop tips" below for more info.

IMPORTANT NOTES:
  • If you are re-arranging your usual room to allow for more movement space, you might invite the participants to help you or do it in front of them, so that the transition is not jarring.
  • It might be helpful for you to create your river art and worksheet ahead of time, so that you can be prepared to demonstrate the sharing process or be a buddy for someone sharing (so that they don't have to share alone).
  • It can be helpful to have the date and the phrase "I am here, in this room, with you." written in large letters on a poster or a whiteboard as a "prompt" so that when participants share they can look up and see the words (instead of just reading them from the River Stories worksheet).
Video Samples: Because the sharing part of this workshop has more steps than usual, we recommend watching one or more of the sample videos below so that you can more easily understand the process. We suggest that you let the group have their own experience (instead of sharing the videos with them). In watching the videos, you will notice how participants have chosen to share in slightly different ways (e.g. using body movements, expressing emotions, using more or less words, etc.). We have included all of these samples, so you see some of the variety that can occur in this workshop.
  • River Stories Intro and Demo
  • River Stories Sample 1
  • River Stories Sample 2
  • River Stories Sample 3
  • River Stories Sample 4
Intro:
"Today we're going to think of our lives as a river. Just like a river, our lives can have twists and turns. We're going to have the chance to notice what we've been through in our past and how we got to be here today. We will be doing this by creating art on paper, then physically with our bodies. As always, this is your window of time to practice noticing your thoughts, feelings, and needs, and to respect whatever comes up.

"This workshop is all about noticing how you got here and giving others a chance to see you and acknowledge your journey. It's a big deal that we all get to be in this room together today. Let's start by going around and anyone who would like to can share one thing that they experienced today that led up to this moment. For example, you might say, 'I got on the bus to come here' or 'my mom drove me here.'"

Give the participants the opportunity to speak or pass.

   
 Participants start their river on their birth date
and end with today's date.		 
Visualization: Imagine Your Life as a River
Before the visualization starts, ask participants to choose a piece of colored paper that they will draw their river on. Invite them to start with their birth date on one end of the paper (the beginning of their river) and end with today's date (the end of their river). They can choose to write this any way they'd like to.

"I'm going to offer a visualization next, and first I invite you to make yourself comfortable. That could be sitting in your chair, standing behind it, sitting on the floor, eyes open or eyes closed, whatever will best help you connect to yourself and your experiences."

If you're using music, start the music. Speak slowly and gently, with lots of pauses for participants to consider your questions and come up with their own answers silently.

"Imagine your life as a river. You might picture yourself floating above your river and looking down at it or walking along side of it. What does it look like? What does the beginning of the river look like? Where does your river flow quickly and where does it flow slowly? Where is your river deep? And where is it shallow? Does your river have any twists, turns or bends? Where is it narrow and where is it wide? What do the banks of your river look like? Does the water in your river have a color? Can you see where your river is going?

"When you're ready, you can open your eyes (if they're closed), come back to the table (if you've moved somewhere else), and begin to create your river on paper."

Creation:
 




  Participants create their River Stories.
"As you create, you might consider the times or events that have shaped your life. Remember that the river you are creating on paper can look like what you saw in your mind during the visualization or it could be something new. You can use symbols, words, dates, ages, or anything else you'd like to represent the times in your life you'd like to honor today. There is no right or wrong way to create your river - it may not even look like a river, and that's just fine."

As the participants create, you can make yourself available to answer any questions or get any additional supplies, if needed.

If anyone finishes early, they can journal freely on the back of their river art, take time to sit quietly with their experience, begin to work on their River Stories worksheet to get ready for the sharing portion, or anything else that works for them, you, and the group.

NOTE: Giving gentle time prompts like, "We have about ten minutes to finish up our artwork" can help participants be aware of their time.

Sharing Our River Stories, Step 1: Worksheet
"We're going to be sharing our stories in a special way today, so to get ready for that, each person can pick three moments from their life that they'd like to acknowledge or honor today. You can be very specific (such as 'age 5: we moved to a new home and it was scary') or very general ('age 5: something new'). You get to decide what you want to share and how you want to share it. Here's a worksheet to help get us ready for the sharing."

Pass out the River Stories worksheet, and invite participants to fill it out.

Sharing Our River Stories, Step 2: Walking the River
Once everyone who wants to has completed their River Stories worksheet, invite the group to bring their creations with their worksheets and sit together, facing the same direction.

It's helpful for participants to see a physical demonstration of the sharing process, and for the Leader to be the first person in the first group to share. Stand up in front of the group, facing them but a few steps back, to show what you mean. If possible, have another 1-2 people stand up with you so they can demonstrate with you. (NOTE: The River Stories intro and demo video above  will show you one version of this intro and demonstration.)

Introduction:
"In a moment, I'm going to invite you to share your story with your body, your words, or both.

"How many of you have ever felt like something happened to you but it wasn't seen, heard, or acknowledged the way you would have liked? Today, we will each have the option to share our river with the group, and the group's job is to really see, hear, and acknowledge the person, without any judgment - to really honor each journey.

"You get to choose if you want to share, and no one will share alone unless you want to. The basic structure is that a few people will stand up here together, facing the group but a few steps back. It's your choice if you want to show the your river art as you do this."

   
 The beginning of the river.
 
River Beginning:
"Now those of us who are standing here are going to imagine that our river is stretched out in front of us, that we are standing at the beginning, at our place of birth, and that the river flows towards the rest of the group. One by one, each person standing up will start by saying their birthday and 'I was born.' For example, the first person might say 'August 17, 1985: I was born,' then the second person would say, 'June 15, 2001: I was born.'"

Sharing First Event
"After all the people standing up here have shared their birth date, the first person will take a step forward and say the first event from their river that they want to honor today. As a reminder, you get to decide how much you want to share with us either with your words or with your body. For example, you could say 'Age 8: My teacher yelled at me in front of the class or' '2009: I felt embarrassed,' or '4th grade: People looked at me,' or '4th grade' while silently making a movement. You can demonstrate this last option by covering your face in an embarrassed way while saying '4th grade.'

"Then the second person will take a step forward and share their first event, then the third person, and so on."

   
  One by one, the group shares their second events.
 
Sharing Second Event
"Once everyone has shared their first event, the first person will take another step forward and share their second event. One at a time, the other people standing will take their steps forward and share their second events."


Sharing Third Event
"Once everyone has shared their second event, then each person up here will take a third step and share their third event, one at a time."

River Ending/Group Acknowledgement
"Once everyone has shared their third event, then each person will step forward one at a time, and say today's date and the sentence 'I am here, in this room, with you.' We say this because in addition to honoring everything we've gone through, we also get to come to this present moment in time and space and notice that we're not alone.

 
 
  The group reaches the end of their rivers.
 
"After each person says 'I am here in this room with you,' the rest of the group says, 'We see you,' all together in response, showing the community of support that we have here. Let's practice. Say today's date and 'I am here, in this room, with you,' and give the group a chance to repeat 'We see you.'"

NOTE: With this workshop, it can be very helpful to set up the expectation of confidentiality ahead of time. It can be safer for participants to share if they know that not only will nothing be shared but that they don't have to answer any questions about their experiences. You might say, "Before we begin, can we make the agreement that we will keep whatever anyone shares confidential? That way, we can each share exactly what we want to, and know that no one, even people in this room, will ever mention it to us unless we bring it up again first."

After the explanation, invite participants to begin sharing their river stories. After each set of sharing finishes, you can invite the group to acknowledge the courage of the sharers by snapping their fingers.

Closing:
"Thank you all for taking this window of time to honor yourself, your journey, and the journeys of others." Invite a group to take a breath or two together. "Let's take a moment to share anything that came up for you during this workshop. You can share your art, your feelings, your thoughts, or anything that was meaningful about your experience today."

Optional closing questions (for groups that are shy and/or if there's more time for discussion):
  • Looking back at your river, what did you notice?
  • What made your river twist and turn?
  • How did it feel to share your river?
  • How did it feel to be acknowledged?
  • Where did you notice your strength or resilience today?
  • Where would you like your river to go from today on?

• It is very important that you and any other Leaders, staff, or volunteers in the room participate along with the group. By modeling your enthusiasm and willingness to participate, you help build trust, bonding, and make it safer for other people to play and share vulnerable experiences.

  • If you have limited space, you can encourage participants to make very tiny steps when they walk their river so that the participants still get the experience of moving forward towards the group.

  • If you end up with one person left who wants to share but everyone else has shared already, you or another participant can share your river again so that the one person does not feel alone walking their river. Of course, it's great to also honor the choice of any participants who request to walk their river alone.

  • If anyone in your group feels uncomfortable sharing their birth date, they do not need to share their birth year or age. They can just share the day and month or say whatever feels comfortable to them (for example, "a long time ago" or "at one point in the not too distant past").

  • In case anyone expresses concern, you can let them know that it's okay if different people's rivers don't line up when they share together. For example, one person's river might be in 1990 while another's river is in 2007 even though they are standing side by side. The reasons to share rivers with buddies is so that we can feel support or connection while we share.

  • If you like, you can invite participants to add a sentence or phrase along with "I was born." For example: "August 17, 1985: I was born and welcomed into the world."

 

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Through the process of guided imagery, watercolor painting, and dimensional putty, this workshop can help participants learn simple self-regulation techniques by creating a flower painting, which can then serve as a calming image, a personal symbol of strength and reminder of our individual resilience.
   
Materials: 
  • Fresh cut flowers
  • 11 x 17 white card stock
  • Colorations® Liquid watercolors (can be purchased at Discount School Supply)
  • Air Dry Putty (can be purchased at Discount School Supply)
  • Washable markers
  • Bingo Bottles (to be filled with liquid watercolors) (can be purchased at Discount School Supply)
  • Rulers
  • Pencils
  • Erasers
  • Scissors
  • Tacky glue pens

Optional:

  • Paper for placemats
  • Additional card stock for materials demo
  • Colorations® Liquid Watercolor - gold and silver (can be purchased at Discount School Supply)
 Time frame:
 
Total time: 1 hour, 30 minutes
Intro: 5 minutes
Materials Demo/Explaining Resilience: 10 mins.
Warm-up/Relaxation: 10 mins.
Drawing a Border: 5 mins.
Breathing Techniques & Mindful Meditation: 5 mins.
Creation: 50 mins.
Closing: 5 minutes

Age Range: 6 and up




  • Small brush for accenting
  • Magnifying glass
  • White crayons
 







 
 Building Resilience Set-up
Preparation/Set-up:
Before you begin this workshop, you might want to think of how you'd like to gather the fresh flowers. You can take participants on a nature walk, in or around your agency to allow them to make a connection with nature and to find a flower that really speaks to them. If this isn't possible, you can bring in various flowers of your own and have children choose. You can also substitute flowers with fresh herbs.
 
At each place setting, set out all materials for each participant to easily access during the demo and creation portion of the workshop, including fresh flowers to use during the Opening Circle. If you're using Bingo Bottles, they may need to be filled prior to the workshop as they may take some time to fill up. If Bingo Bottles are new to you, take some time to explore them for yourself so you can be better prepared to introduce them to your group.

Note: If you'll be using Air Dry Putty, make sure to keep the packages sealed until you will be using them to create. This will help insure freshness and avoid any drying of the putty.

Introduction:
"Today we're going to be talking about something that is inside all of us. It's something that some of us may notice inside ourselves more than others but once we notice it and really understand it, it can be really helpful.

"The topic of today is resilience. What does this word mean? Well, resilience is a process that allows a person to bounce back after difficult things happen. Resilience is not a trait that some people have and others not, resilience is an ability that we can all learn and develop.

Let me give you an example: When Emma was learning to ride her bike, she fell many times, but she kept getting back up until she finally learned to ride without falling. Even though it hurt to fall so many times, Emma was able to keep trying and learned to ride her bike. It took some work for Emma to keep trying - she had to believe in herself, she had to try new ways of balancing and eventually, she did it!

Here's another example: John was upset that he had to move out of his old home. This meant that he also had to move to a new school, too. He was so angry and he told his mom that he would never go to school again. But, after a few weeks of being scared and going to his new school, he started to make friends and slowly, he started to enjoy it.

With these two examples, how were these two children showing that they were resilient? Can you think of a time when something happened in your life where you were resilient? What did you do to get through your difficult situation? Did you ask for help? Did stay positive? Did you find a way to solve a problem? Did you make a plan? What did you do? Think about this for a moment and remember throughout today that you are strong and capable of getting through things that are difficult.

As we create paintings today we will solve problems, trust ourselves and our creativity, learn new things and learn something new about ourselves - we all have the power to be resilient.

Materials Demo/Explaining Resilience:
"We will be using different art materials to draw and paint a flower that can represent our resilience. During this workshop, I will be giving you directions that you can follow completely or you can choose which parts you would like to follow. You can even choose to create something different. This is your window of time and you can use it however you'd like, even if it's sitting back and observing; as long as you're honoring your thoughts and feelings, you are doing a great job!

"To start us off, I'm going to be showing you the art materials that we're going to use. While I'm doing this, we're going to talk a little more about resilience."

 
  Liquid Watercolors
Liquid Watercolors: Continue the conversation by moving into the watercolor demonstration. If you're using Bingo Bottles, briefly demonstrate how to apply watercolor onto the paper by gently squeezing. Show the participants how they can also make dots and blend colors.

"As we begin to explore the watercolors, choose some colors and put them onto your paper. Notice how the colors begin to soak into the paper and spread around. If you'd like, choose different types of colors and see what happens when you blend them together. When we're working with watercolors, we can also think about how we're able to handle the things in our lives that we can't control. Just like the watercolors soak into the paper and blend into one another, we usually can't control the difficult things that happen to us. All we can do is work with what is given to us and and figure out the healthy ways to deal with it. We will learn some of these skills today. How have you been able to make the best out of a difficult situation?"

  
    Air Dry Putty
Air Dry Putty: Before you begin, open up the packages of the Air Dry Putty and ask participants to grab a small chunk of any color they'd like.

"As you get to know the Air Dry Putty, let's talk a little more about resilience. Take a piece of the putty into your hands and take a moment to feel it. Move it around and squeeze it with one hand, try squeezing it with two hands. How does it feel? If you'd like, smell the putty. What does it smell like?

"When we talked earlier about resilience we said that it's a person's ability to "bounce back" after difficult things happen to them. Let's see if we can make a round ball out of the putty (give participants some time to create their balls). Now, imagine that these round balls are us. We're going to twist, turn, break apart these balls (pause and allow time for this). Let's imagine that this twisting, turning, and breaking apart can be all of the difficult things that can happen in our lives. What kinds of difficult things have you faced?

"Now let's shape our putty back into a ball (pause and let participants gather their putty). For some of you with more pieces to pick up, it took a little more time to gather and mold back into place. This is also true about our lives. Let's take a look around and notice that everyone is back to the same ball that they once started with. Inside of all of us, we have the ability to pick up all of the pieces and put ourselves back together again. As we sit here, notice that everything that we have gone through in our past is behind us and it's a big deal to be here today. Maybe you're going through something difficult right now and you feel like it will never get better. I hope this can give you a sense of comfort knowing that you are resilient. Resilience is inside of you."

Gold and Silver Watercolor (optional): The gold and silver watercolors can be added as a last step of the art project to add accents. Briefly demonstrate how to apply the paint with a small paintbrush.

Warm-up/Relaxation:
"I invite you to find a comfortable position in your chair. Take a deep breath and look around you. Breathe in some fresh, clean air. You are in a safe place and this is your window of time to notice your thoughts, feelings, and your needs.

 
Meet your flower and notice its details.
 
Make Friends: "Look at the people at your table. We all have a lot in common and we are not alone. If you're comfortable enough, look at each person and make eye contact with them and give them a gentle nod or smile. Let's support each other and build a creative and helpful community here. Relax and settle in for some fun!"

Meet Your Flowers: "Now pick up the flower that you chose. This is your special flower for today's art activity.

"Take a good, slow look at all of its colors and shapes. What do you see? Notice the details in the flower. If you'd like, get a closer look by bringing it closer to your face or by using a magnifying glass. What new things did you notice about your flower after looking closer? I also invite you to smell your flower. What kind of smell does it have? What do you think about when you smell it? Does it remind you of anything?

"As you take the time to notice all of the great things about your flower, think about why you chose the flower you did. Think about all of the ways your flower is unique. Is it strong? Delicate? Colorful? What do you see in the flower that is the same in you?

  
   Draw a border around the edges of the paper.
Drawing a Border: "Let's begin by taking our pencils and rulers to draw a border around our papers. You can measure the width of the ruler to space your border all around the page. This will create a built-in frame. Leave the border white for now and we'll have a chance to come back to write something inside of it."

Breathing Techniques & Mindful Meditation:                                         "Before we draw our flowers, we are going to learn some breathing exercises that you can do when you are going through a difficult time. Breathing exercises can help us calm ourselves down and relax. Whenever you get upset, remember to take three deep breaths. Taking these breaths can help us think more clearly and build resilience."

Before you begin the breathing exercises and meditation, remind participants that they get to choose how they'd like to participate."

Note: Gently guide the participants through each breath so they don't rush through and they have a chance to experience them in their bodies.

 
  Standing Breaths
  
  Sitting Breaths
Standing Breaths
  1. Stand up with your feet placed apart for balance.
  2. Make sure the person next to you is more than an arm's length apart from you.
  3. Take three deep breaths while raising your arms up and down at each breath (in a slow, flying motion).
Sitting Breaths                                 
  1. Find a comfortable position in your chair.
  2. Cross the fingers of both hands together and place them lightly on your belly.
  3. Rest your elbows comfortably along your body.
  4. Relax and drop your shoulders.
  5. If you feel comfortable enough to do so, close your eyes and take three deep breaths.
  6. Feel your belly as you breathe in and out.   
Flower Meditation (to continuously flow from sitting/standing breaths): In a soft, gentle voice, you can use some of the prompts below. Leaving plenty of silent space in between these prompts allows participants to take in each of them with tenderness. Invite participants to close their eyes if they feel comfortable enough to do so.

"Stay focused on your breathing and keep your body relaxed. Listen to the sounds of the room. Now think about your flower growing tall and strong. Imagine your flower reaching toward the sun. Think of a gentle rain refreshing your flower. Think of all you have in common with your flower. Just like this flower, you are born into this world fresh and pure. You are loving and loveable. Now think about all of the different qualities of your flower and how you are just like it. No matter what is going on around you or happening to you, deep inside you there is always this calm, safe place that you can always find, today and always."

  
 Draw a flower on your paper.
 
  
 Add color to your drawing.
 
  
 Add accents with watercolor and/or putty
to highlight certain parts of your painting.
 
  
  Write affirmations to remind you of your strength. 
Creation:
Draw a Flower: "Now that you're calm and collected, take your flower in your hand again and look at it as you draw it on your paper. If you want, you can draw the flower very large on your page so you can really focus on the details. Don't worry if your drawing doesn't look just like your special flower, remember that whatever comes out is just right."

Adding Color: "Using the watercolors, let's add color to our flowers. You can follow the color(s) of your flower or you can come up with new colors. There is no wrong way to add color. If you choose not to add any color, adding more detail to your drawing can be something you might want to try out. Take a look at your flower again and see if you can add some details that you may have missed."

Adding Accents: "You can use the Air Dry Putty to add accents to your painting. Adding a fun border or details to your flower might be something to consider. You can use the glue to stick the putty on.

"Using the gold and silver watercolors, can add shimmer to your flower. You can use these colors to highlight any features or parts of the flower that you really want to stand out."

Writing Affirmations: "Let's add some positive and calming words to your drawing. I'm going to invite you to write some affirmations or words of encouragement that can help you get through difficult times. You can write the following words exactly as you hear and see them or you can write some positive words of your own."


You can say and write these words down for the participants to easily refer to:
  • At the very top, you can write: I am as fresh as a flower.
  • On the left side, you can write: I take 3 deep breaths to calm myself.
  • On the right side, you can write: I am loving and loveable.
  • On the bottom, you can write and finish this sentence: I am ___________.

  
  Fresh as a flower!
Closing:
"As we close, let's do three more deep sitting breaths. Cross your fingers and place them lightly on your belly. Rest your elbows comfortably along your body. Relax and drop your shoulders. If you feel comfortable enough to do so, I invite you to close your eyes. Take three deep breaths, feeling your belly as you breathe in and out."

Optional Closing Questions:
  • What did you discover about yourself?
  • What's one new thing that you learned?
  • What is one way you can calm yourself down when you're upset?
  • Why is it important to calm yourself when you're upset?
  • How are you resilient?
  • How have you been resilient in the past?

"Take a look around and remember, we are not alone. We have a lot in common and we all go through difficult times and we are learning to support ourselves and each other each time we come here."
Row.txt_description: Through the process of guided imagery, watercolor painting, and dimensional putty, this workshop can help participants learn simple self-regulation techniques by creating a flower painting, which can then serve as a calming image, a personal symbol of strength and reminder of our individual resilience.
Row.txt_tips:
• It is very important that you and any other Leaders, staff, or volunteers in the room participate along with the group. By modeling your enthusiasm and willingness to participate, you help build trust, bonding, and make it safer for other people to play and share vulnerable experiences.

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
“Depressed, Sad”
“Nice, Happy”

  
Objective:
To support children and teens in sharing their hearts and stories through art. To give them an opportunity to listen to their hearts, value the stories within them, and know that others want to hear them too.

Materials:
Cray-Pas
Thick white paper 5 1/2” X 7” (cover stock)
Brushes
Water cups / paper towels
Watercolors, tempera paints, or puffy paints:
Note: Watercolors work best for having the Cray-Pas show through.
Acrylic paints or puffy paints have the most bright and cool colors (but they stain clothes)
Tempera paints are good because they are washable (but they crack and get dull when they dry)

  

Heart Story in the shape of a tree.
 
  
  
  
  
  

Age Range / Ratio:
Here are two versions of the intro/warm-up to suit a range of age levels. Have a look at both and see what you think will work best with your group.

Introduction:
Today our project is called Heart Stories. It’s a chance to notice what’s in our hearts, a chance to notice what our hearts would say if they could talk.

Heart Talk Warm-up (for older children):
This is an interview-style warm-up the kids can do in pairs. Pick 1-3 questions from the list below (or make up your own questions). Consider the age level of your group when you choose the question(s). If you are working with an old enough group, pick three questions and write them up to show the group.

Possible Heart Talk Questions:
—What’s something your heart is proud of about you or your family?
—Share something that made your heart happy this week
—If your heart was a color today, what color would it be and why?
—What makes your heart laugh?
—If your heart could do something fun, what would it do?
—If your heart could do something it’s never done before, what would it do?
—What makes your heart feel safe?
—What makes your heart feel scared?
—What makes your heart strong?
—What makes your heart beat faster?
—What makes your heart happy?
—How do you look when your heart is sad?
—How do you look when your heart is happy?
After the kids interview each other, have them think about what their partner shared. Then go around in a circle and have them each share something they like about their partner’s heart.

Happy Hearts/Sad Hearts Warm-up
(for younger children):
“Today we get to listen to our hearts and notice what helps our hearts feel safe and happy. Does anyone know where your heart is? Can you show me? (Everyone puts their hands on their hearts) Good! What does your heart do? (Pump your blood around your body, bring oxygen to your whole self, tell you how you’re feeling, beat fast when you’re excited or nervous, etc.) Can you feel it beating? Your heart is right in the center of you. Sometimes you can feel feelings in your heart. Has anyone ever felt happiness in their heart? Or sadness, like your heart is breaking? When our hearts are feeling different ways, our whole body knows it.

"When you have a sad heart what does your body do? (curl up, look down, cry, etc.) Let’s all be sad hearts with our whole body. Notice how it feels in your whole body when you are sad. It’s okay to be sad sometimes and let it out with our whole bodies. Now take a deep breath in and breath all the sadness out with your breath. Good.

"And now let’s think about when we have happy hearts. What does your body do then? (smile, jump up and down, dance, etc.) Let’s all be happy hearts with our whole bodies. Wonderful! Take a deep breath in and feel your heart filling up with happiness. Good! Hearts need a lot of love. And they need to be taken care of and listened to. Today will be a chance to listen to our hearts and take care of them.”

Technical Info:
"Today, we are going to make Heart Stories paintings to share the different feelings we have in our hearts.
