We each get to think about what our hearts would say if they could talk, and what color they’d be inside and outside. Does anyone remember the Windows rule? Remember, there’s no right or wrong way. We’ll just explore some steps you could try."

Step One: Cray-Pas
"First let’s use Cray-Pas to draw a heart. Let’s do a sad heart. What colors should I use? (Use all the colors they say.) You can keep adding colors as long as they give ideas of what to add."

Step Two: Paint
"Now let's add paint on top of the Cray-Pas. What colors should we use? If we use lots of water, the Cray-Pas show through. If we use thick paints, the Cray-Pas get covered up. Fill in all the paper so there's none showing!"

Step Three: Words
"Now let’s notice if there are any words that go with our heart. We can write down the story that this heart wants to share."

Closing:
At the end of the workshop, have a Heart Circle where everyone has a chance to share their Heart Stories. If the group seems sad at the end, be sure to leave things on a positive note by having each person share something positive. For example, they could each share a way they want to take good care of their heart. Or they could say something they like about the person on their left – in order to put a nice feeling into everyone’s hearts.
Row.txt_description: This workshop supports children and teens in sharing their hearts and stories through art. The workshop gives them an opportunity to listen to their hearts, value the stories within them, and know that others want to hear them too.
Row.txt_tips: Some kids may want to write stories to go along with their hearts.

Row.txt_code:
Personal Needs Flower< /td> 
Objective:
This workshop provides an opportunity for participants to notice their personal needs by creating a flower where each petal represents one need. They will begin to see the many layers of needs—physical, emotional and spiritual—and to honor all these layers. To notice that our needs are deeply linked to who we are as a unique and special person.




 Materials:
Colored journaling paper
Pens
Colored construction paper 
CrayPas
Sharpies
Glue sticks
Timer
Blank envelopes (optional)

          
Time frame:
Total Time: 1 hour 15 minutes
Introduction           5 min
Opening Circle      10 min
Demonstration        5 min
Journaling             10 min
Creation                30 min
Closing Circle         15 min


 












   
  Set up of supplies
 
Set-up / Prep:
Lay out all the materials in the center of the table so that each person will be able to reach all the colors. Prepare a sample so that your demonstration can go quickly and leave plenty of time for creating.

Introduction:
"Many of us are willing to give SO MUCH of ourselves to our families, our friends, our coworkers, etc. We're often willing to sacrifice so much for others, that we forget to acknowledge and honor our own needs. Sometimes we don't even take time to breathe. It can be such a blind spot for us and we are often not even aware of it!

"This workshop is called Personal Needs Flower. Today, we're going to take a window of time to notice and honor our needs... what we want more of in our lives, or what might be out of balance and need our attention. Tending to our needs (physical, emotional and spiritual) is a vital part of self-care and one of the most important jobs we have. It is not only important, it is necessary for each of us to respect and honor our needs so we can recharge our batteries and be there in greater ways for ourselves and others.

Opening Circle:
"We are going to start by thinking about what each of us wants or needs in order to feel safe, happy, and healthy. I am going to ask anyone who wants to, to share one word about a need that is coming to mind as we start this workshop. Is there some need that's asking for attention right now? First thoughts are fine!"

After participants have shared: "Thank you for sharing and acknowledging that your needs are valid and important!"

Demonstration:
“Before we create our Personal Needs Flower, we will start with a journaling exercise to help us notice our needs. I’ll demonstrate the materials and creation process now, so that at the end of the journaling process, you can dive right in. As I demonstrate the steps, remember that more than anything else, this is your special time to listen to and trust your own needs. There is no right or wrong to what you create. Just listen to the voice inside of you as you go. Whatever emerges is fine!

"Today, we're going to try something new, and 'tear' the paper to create our flower. This is an opportunity to let go and enjoy the freedom that tearing allows. Allowing ourselves to be curious and playful can help us discover needs we might not even be aware of!

"I am going to be demonstrating a flower, but your creation can be anything you like. It does not even have to look like a flower. For example, you could create a deck of cards, where each card represents a specific need."


  
 
 
 Step One: Tearing the center circle.
 
   
 
 
 Adding a face to represent the peaceful,
nurturing part of you.
 
   
  
 Step Two: Drawing/writing on petals.
 
1.  Creating the Center
The first step is creating the center of your flower. (Hold up a sample or demonstrate by making one). With the colored paper, tear a circle as small or as large as you like. You can create this center to represent you. You might want to draw a face that represents the peaceful, nurturing, supportive part of yourself that is here to help you. Whatever you choose is up to you.

2.  Creating the Petals
The next step is creating the petals, each one representing one of your needs. To make each petal, choose the paper and tear it into whatever shape or size you want. You may want to vary the size of the petals to illustrate the importance of each need. For example, one of your greatest needs might be "peace," so you can choose to tear a large piece to represent that and a smaller need of yours might be "entertainment" so you could use a smaller petal for that.

Then you’ll go ahead and draw a symbol or use words to represent each need. Use your imagination to create colorful representations of all you discover. Place each petal, adding layer upon layer to the flower-like shape.

3.  Completing your Flower
"The final step is deciding how you want to finish your flower. Using a glue stick you can attach your petals together or glue them onto a larger piece of construction paper or collect them into a pile that can travel with you. If you are going to keep your petals loose, you might want to decorate an envelope to keep them in. 

"You can finish your flower whichever way will best support you not only in being reminded of the needs you noticed today, but also in the ongoing process of discovering more of your needs. (You could even make some extra petals without anything on them yet so you can add more needs as you discover them).

“Any questions? Remember it is very special to take this window of time for ourselves—a need most of us never acknowledge. Ready for the relaxation?” 

   
  Journal page, showing flower construction
 
  
   Journal page, showing flower construction 
   
   Journal page, showing flower construction 
   
Journaling/Warm up:
First, pick a color paper that speaks to you or makes you feel strong or hopeful.

We are going to journal about 3 different types of needs we all have: the needs of our body, our mind and our spirit. You can fold that paper into thirds lengthwise (show example). On the top of the first column, write the word Physical, on the second Emotional, and on the third Spiritual.

I'm going to talk a little bit about each of these three needs and give you two minutes after each one to reflect on/write about this need for yourself. There is no right or wrong way to do this journaling exercise. You can write sentences, words, lists, draw symbols, shapes, or anything else you like. Just allow your thoughts to flow onto your paper without judgment. What you write does not have to make sense to anyone but you! It is also fine to just sit quietly and notice what comes up. Remember this is your window of time to connect with yourself and what's meaningful for you.

Physical needs are what we usually think about first. What are your physical needs in order to be safe, happy, and healthy? (Ex. We need to be free from harm. We need shelter and a safe place to live. We need good nutrition: healthy food and clean water. We need exercise - keeping our bodies healthy and strong. We need rest, giving us energy to do what we need to do, like succeeding at work or going to school).

In the first column, begin writing words, sentences, symbols or shapes to represent your physical needs. (Give participants two minutes to write).

Another need is our emotional needs. What are your emotional needs in order to feel safe, happy, and healthy? (Ex. Feeling understood, accepted, and heard. Knowing that we are loved and appreciated also gives us the feeling of having emotional support. Relaxation, fun, and friendship help us to find emotional balance. Having boundaries, realistic expectations, and a positive attitude are other ways of supporting our emotional health).

Now in the second column, begin journaling about your emotional needs. (Give participants two minutes to write).

Finally, we will address our spiritual needs. What does your spirit need to give you peace? (Ex. The ability to forgive, have patience or acceptance of others? Do you need quiet time to reflect, meditate, or pray? Do you need to do good deeds or help others feel uplifted? Do you need "me" time to care for your soul?)

In the third column write words, begin journaling about your spiritual needs. (Give participants two minutes to write).

Creation:
As the participants create their flowers, gently remind them that there is no right or wrong way. The only important thing to keep noticing and honoring their own needs. Encourage them to keep asking the question, What are my needs?

Be sure to leave time for sharing at the end. Encourage each person to decide how they want to finish their flower. Do they want to glue it together? Do they want to create any extra petals to carry with them to add more needs as they are discovered?
  
 
 
   Keep your petals in a pile to carry with you
 Or glue your flower together 

Closing:
Give everyone an opportunity to share about their Personal Needs Flower, and any discoveries they made as they took time to notice their needs.

Remind participants: "This process does not end today; you can reflect back on it anytime, however it best serves you. Noticing what we need to feel safe, happy and healthy in our lives is one of the most important jobs we will ever have, and one job that no one else can do for us!"

Encourage participants to continue the journaling exercise at home and to keep identifying more of their physical, emotional and spiritual needs. They are worth it!
Row.txt_description: This workshop provides an opportunity for participants to notice their personal needs by creating a flower where each petal represents one need. They will begin to see the many layers of needs—physical, emotional and spiritual—and to honor all these layers.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Conflicting Needs:
Sometimes a person might notice that their different needs seem to be in conflict with each other. (For example, the need to have more quiet alone time and the need to spend more playful, fun time with her children). This is okay. The purpose of this workshop is to reveal the many needs that can be seen as part of our entire makeup. It is okay not to be problem-solving at this time, but rather supporting participants as they reveal and learn to accept themselves at this creative stage, seeing not only the needs that can be fulfilled, but also those that seem far from resolution. By putting all the needs around a single circle, we allow our conscious mind to see how they all can coexist and we can begin to find safer and more creative ways to embrace and move through any conflicts.

Row.txt_code:
Description
This warm-up allows participants to safely explore and express emotions.

Materials:
Crayons              
Paper

  Time frame:
Introduction                         8 min
Creation                               2 min
Closing                               10 min
  Ages:
4 and up
(for teens, see
variation below)
                          Total Time: 20 min
   

Set Up
Place crayons and paper on the table so that they are easily accessible to participants.

Introduction
Begin by brainstorming emotions with the group. You can ask, "What are some feeling words?" As they share some answers, validate their responses and invite the group to show what they look like when they feel that emotion. For example, if someone says "happy," you can say, "Show me what 'happy' looks like to you in 3-2-1, go!"

NOTE: During the brainstorm, it can be helpful to remind the group that there's no wrong way to show a feeling (as long as you're not hurting anyone else), and that there are many ways to show each feeling.

After the group has brainstormed a number of feeling words, validate them for sharing and introduce the creation part of this exercise: "Today, we're going to get to not only show on our faces what those feelings look like but also we're going to get to show them on paper with crayons! Pick a feeling word. It can be a feeling word that you heard already today or it could be a new one. It's okay if your feeling word is the same or different than another person's in this group." Pause for a moment for each person to choose an emotion.

Creation
   
 Expressive Crayon depicting anger. 
   
 Expressive Crayon depicting happiness. 
"In a moment, each of us will choose a crayon color that reminds us of that emotion and for two minutes we're going to scribble on our papers, drawing as if we were experiencing that feeling right now. You can scribble fast or slow, big or small, whatever feels best to you. It's okay if the crayon breaks or you rip the paper. No need to worry about what it looks like, we're just going to try out how it feels. Ready? Choose your color. Go!"

Give participants two minutes to explore their chosen feeling.

After two minutes, you can say, "Find a pausing place on your artwork so that anyone who wants can get a chance to share."

Closing
Give the participants an opportunity to share anything they like about their scribbles, their chosen feeling, or whatever they noticed by participating. It can also be helpful to remind participants that they can pass if they don't feel like sharing and that each person's experience of an emotion could be different, and that is okay. Validate each person's experience and their taking a window of time to explore feelings.
Row.txt_description: This warm-up allows participants to safely explore and express emotions.
Row.txt_tips:
• This warm-up often works best without music so that participants can connect to their own experiences and different participants can work on different emotions simultaneously without being influenced by the music.
  • If your group has a hard time choosing emotion words, you can have them start with emotions you suggest (like anger, confusion, joy, etc.) and then end with an emotion of their choice. Or you could have participants take turns suggesting emotions for the whole group to work on.
  • This warm-up works well with other emotion-focused workshops or workshops that use crayons.
  • If you have extra time, participants can do additional emotions.

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Personal Needs Flower 
Objective:
This workshop provides an opportunity for children to notice their own personal needs by creating a flower where each petal represents one need. They will see that we have many kinds of needs: physical, emotional and more! They will begin to understand how important it is to take care of their needs in order to have a healthy, happy and safe life.





Materials:
Colored construction paper
CrayPas
Glue stick


 Time frame:
Introduction         5 min
Opening Circle      5 min
Relaxation            5 min
Creation               30 min
Closing Circle       30 min
  
  Total Time: 1 hour 15 minutes
  

   
Set-up / Prep:
Lay out the materials in the center of the table so that each person will be able to reach all the colors. You may wish to prepare a sample so that your demonstration can go quickly and leave plenty of time for creating.

Introduction:
Many of us are very good at taking care of other people’s needs - we help our siblings when they need support with their homework, we help when our mom needs chores done, sometimes our friends need us to listen to them, and even our teachers might need help. We readily make ourselves available when someone else needs us. However, we often forget to acknowledge and take care of our own needs.

Today, we are going to talk about our needs and putting those needs first. We all have needs and when we nurture and take care of these needs, we are healthier, happier, and feel safe.

Some of our needs might be to eat better and exercise so we can be healthy. Maybe we need to study hard so we can be prepared for school or go to bed early because we are tired. Maybe we need time with friends to play and laugh. We have all kinds of needs!

Some of our needs are more hidden needs. They are harder to sense, like our needs for comfort, safety, security, or our need to feel loved and supported.

Some of our needs are conflicting needs such as needing two things at the same time that might be opposite, such as needing to go to sleep early because you had a long day and you are very tired AND needing to stay up so you can finish your homework! Or needing to be loyal to a friend but needing to tell them something that might be hurtful.

Looking at all our needs can help us to sort through what is important to us and what we can change to help us have a more peaceful and happy life.

Opening Circle:
"We are going to start by thinking about what each of us needs in order to feel safe, happy, and healthy. I am going to ask everyone to share one word or thought about a need of yours that is coming to mind as we start this workshop. Is there some need that’s asking for attention right now? First thoughts are fine!” (Encourage everyone to share).

After all the participants have shared… "Thank you for sharing and acknowledging that all of our needs are valid and important! Now I want everyone to take a minute to notice the similarities and/or differences in all of your needs ...give examples like I heard a lot of 'I need time to play or be with friends!' It could be interesting to point out our similarities.

Relaxation:
"Before we create our Personal Needs Flower, we will start with a relaxation to help us begin to listen to our needs.
 
"If you feel comfortable closing your eyes, please do so and nestle into your seat. Wiggle about until you feel cozy and comfortable. Tune into your body from the top of your head, scanning slowly through to the tips of your toes. As you move your attention gracefully down your body, I’m going to be asking you some questions. Let the questions in and allow the answers to surface in whatever way your particular senses want to speak. For some of you, it might mean hearing an answer in your mind. For others, it could be that you see images in front of your closed eyes. The body also can speak to us through physical sensations. Whatever languages your body speaks in today, note the responses and trust whatever comes to you as I share these questions.

Speaking slowly...
"Can you notice what your needs are?
Do you have any physical needs?
Are you comfortable or do you need to shift your weight?
Are you too warm or cool? Do you need the temperature changed?
Are you breathing?
Do you need to slow down your breathing by taking a deep inhale and exhale?
Are you thirsty? Are you tired? Are you hungry?
Are you aware of any emotional needs you have right now?
Do you have a need for comfort? Security? Safety?
Do you need to have someone safe to talk to?  Are you keeping a secret that you don't feel safe or comfortable to talk about.

Take time to notice any hidden needs that you have. Tune in to your belly, to your heart, to the senses in your torso. Allow an impression of something to arise and bubble-up as a thought, image or sensation. Pay attention to pictures, colors and memories that may appear. Just relax and take your time as you ask yourself, “What are my needs?”

With these thoughts and images stirred in your mind, begin to think about your flower.  What color comes to mind for the center? Can you picture a face that represents the peaceful, nurturing, supportive part of yourself that is here to help you and notice your needs? Whenever you are ready, you can open your eyes and begin to create your flower.


 
 Torn flower center
 
 Adding a face to represent the peaceful,
nurturing part of you.

  
  
  
 Drawing on the petals
 
 Keep your petals in a pile like a special deck of cards
to carry with you in a special envelope
  
  
  Or glue your flower together
Creation:
As the participants create their flowers, gently remind them that there is no right or wrong way. The only important thing is that they keep noticing and honoring their own needs. Encourage them to keep asking the question, "What are my needs?"

Encourage each person to decide how they want to finish their flower. Do they want to glue it together? Or keep it in a pile like a very special deck of cards? Do they want to create any extra petals to carry with them so they can add more needs as they discover them?

1. Creating the Center
The first step is creating the center of your flower. (Hold up a sample or demonstrate by making one). With the colored paper, you’ll tear a circle as small or as large as you would like. Tearing will allow you to be freer and not worry about being perfect! You can create this center to represent you. You might want to draw a face that represents the peaceful, nurturing, supportive part of yourself that is here to help you. Whatever you choose is up to you!

2. Creating the Petals
The next step is creating the petals, each one representing one of your needs. To make each petal, choose a piece of colored paper and tear it into whatever shape or size you want. If you like, you can use the size and shape of the petal to represent the importance of each need. For example, one of your greatest needs might be “having fun,” so you can choose to tear a large petal to represent that need, and a smaller petal to represent a less important need.

Then you’ll draw a symbol or you can use words on each petal to represent each need. Use your imagination to create a colorful representation of all that you discover. Place each need petal around the circle, adding layer upon layer to the flower-like shape until it spills out all around you.

3.  Completing your Flower
"The final step is deciding how you want to finish your flower. You could use a glue stick to attach your petals together, and glue them onto a larger piece of construction paper. Or, you could collect them in a pile that can travel with you in your purse or a secret, special compartment. If you are going to keep your petals loose, you might want to decorate an envelope later on to keep them in. 

"You can finish your flower whichever way will best support you and your needs, not only in being reminded of the needs you noticed today, but also in the ongoing process of discovering more of your needs in the future. You could even make some extra petals without anything on them yet so you can add more needs as you discover them.

“Any questions? Remember, it means something very special to take this kind of time—a need most of us never give credence to. It means something to be curious and playful—two more needs many of us have forgotten about. This is your special time to be curious and playful and listen to your needs! Ready to create?” 

Closing:
Give everyone an opportunity to share about their Personal Needs Flower. Encourage them to share any discoveries that came to them as they took time to notice their needs.

Encourage the participants to continue noticing their needs after the workshop is over. They are worth it! Remind them that noticing what we need to feel safe, happy and healthy in our lives is one of the most important jobs we will ever have!
Row.txt_description: This workshop provides an opportunity for children to notice their own personal needs by creating a flower where each petal represents one need. They will see that we have many kinds of needs: physical, emotional and more! They will begin to understand how important it is to take care of their needs in order to have a healthy, happy and safe life.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Conflicting Needs:
Sometimes a person might notice that their different needs seem to be in conflict with each other (for example, the need to have more quiet alone time and the need to spend more playful, fun time with friends). This is okay. The purpose of this workshop is to reveal the many needs – even conflicting ones that can be seen as part of our entire unique personality. By placing all the needs around a circle to create a flower, we see them all together.

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.str_title: Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence (self-led workshop)
Row.txt_code:
Pearls of Wisdom
Objective: This workshop uses the metaphor of a "pearl" as a treasure that forms inside an oyster in response to an irrit ant. Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength and wisdom as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence.  Each participant in this workshop will take a creative window of time to notice what Pearl of Wisdom they want to share to create awareness about domestic violence later in life.

Participants' creations will be included in an exhibition during the 2015 City of Los Angeles Domestic Violence Task Force Day of Action on October 9th at L.A. City Hall.

Materials:
Clear round glass stones
Card stock cut into circles
Permanent Markers
Clear tacky glue
Paper Towels or Wipes
Art/Media Release

 Workshop Flow:
Introduction
Information About How to Create Your Pearl of Wisdom
Reflection Time
Creation
Complete Art/Media Release
Photographing Your Pearl of Wisdom
Sending Photographs and Artwork to AWBW
 

 

 
 Table set-up









Introduction: A pearl is a wonderful metaphor for the survivor’s journey. Do you know how a pearl is formed? Basically, it starts with an irritant that enters an oyster; protective layers transform that mollusk and create a pearl. Throughout our lives, we all have challenges and difficulties (irritants). There are lessons to be learned in all these challenges (pearls).

Sharing your story of what you have learned, witnessed or experienced as an advocate or a survivor, experiencing or bearing witness to the transition from pain to wisdom, can empower and inspire an individual or even a community to help end the violence.  What you’ve experienced (these difficulties and challenges) and the ways you survived, or witnessed someone survive, are valuable and essential in helping to end the cycle of violence.

Window of Time
Before you begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you - a safe space to notice your thoughts and feelings. There's no right or wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this window of time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out.

  
 Draw or write words or images to represent the Pearl of Wisdom you want to share
  
 Add a pea-sized amount of the glue
on top of your drawing/words.
  
  Place your stone on top of the glue and press down. Wipe off any extra glue and let it dry.
Information About How to Create Your Pearl of Wisdom:
  1. Using permanent markers and/or colored pencils, write words, create images, symbols, or use colors to represent the Pearl of Wisdom you'd like to share on the shiny side of the circular paper.
  2. After you're done creating, add a pea-sized amount of the clear tacky glue on top of your creation.
  3. Place the flat side of your clear glass stone on top of the glue and press down.
  4. Wipe off any extra glue and let it dry.
Reflection time: Take a few deep breaths and reflect on what you've learned about domestic violence. What Pearl of Wisdom would you like to share to help create awareness about this issue?  In particular, to create awareness about domestic violence later in life. To help inspire survivors and motivate others to get involved in the movement to end domestic violence later in life.

Take a deep breath and come back to this moment with the intention of bringing back with you any thoughts, feelings, colors or images that represent your Pearl of Wisdom. When you are ready, begin to create.

Creation: Create artwork that shares your Pearl of Wisdom. As you create, remember to illustrate your message in any way that feels right to you. You can create an image or symbol, use colors or words, or any combination of the four. Keep in mind there is no wrong way to create.

Complete Art/Media Release: Fill out the Art/Media Release completely. Please note that we must have releases for each piece of art in order to include it in the exhibit.

Photographing Your Pearl of Wisdom: Taking a photo of your pearl is part of the creative process so be as creative as you like with it. Your pearl could be against whatever background you wish, holding it in your hand, on a colored piece of paper, holding it in front of your face, on blades of grass, or whatever most powerfully expresses your pearl!

Take at least two photographs of your creation: one with the Art/Media Release (with the name of the artist visible so that the correct artist name can be matched with the artwork) and one without (we encourage you to take several pictures without the release).

Sending photographs and artwork to AWBW: For each creation, email all photos and completed Art/Media Release(s) to Christy at cturek@awbw.org no later than August 15th.

*For City of Los Angeles Mayor and Councilmembers Only: Please contact Christy to arrange sending your completed Pearl of Wisdom back to AWBW as we are planning to include photos and your actual artwork in the exhibit.
Row.txt_description:
This workshop uses the metaphor of a "pearl" as a treasure that forms inside an oyster in response to an irritant. Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength and wisdom as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence. Each participant in this workshop will take a creative window of time to notice what Pearl of Wisdom they want to share to create awareness about domestic violence later in life.
Participants' creations will be included in an exhibition during the 2015 Los Angeles City Domestic Violence Task Force Day of Action on October 9th at L.A. City Hall.

Row.txt_code:
Puzzle Piece Paper Doll Template
Objective:
By writing and coloring emotions on a paper doll made up of puzzle pieces participants are able to reflect on their current emotions and where they feel these emotions in their body. Through journaling and reflecting on their present emotions and envisioning what they wish to feel in the future they will begin to deepen the process of "putting themselves back together" after all that they have been through.

Materials:
Colored markers - for coloring
Pencils - for coloring
Permanent markers - for writing words
Blank paper for journaling
Handout of paper doll made up of puzzle pieces - 2 for each participant
- click here for Paper Doll Template
Relaxing music

Note: If using this workshop to help the women release or process anger, it is important to begin by having a discussion on "What is Anger?" Please click here to see the entire Processing Anger Workshop Series.

 
&nXbsp; Materials for "Putting Myself Back Together"
Timeframe:
(feel free to break this workshop into two sessions if needed)
Intro: 5 minutes
Relaxation: 5 minutes
Creation, Part 1: 10 minutes
Journaling: 15 minutes
Creation, Part 2: 10 minutes
Closing: 15 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour

Set Up:
Lay out blank paper, colored markers, pens, and pencils around the table. Make sure that there are two paper doll handouts at each seat, or you can to hand them out at the beginning. Have relaxing music ready to be played during their relaxation and journaling time.

Introduction:
Today we are going to use these paper dolls to get in touch with the emotions we hold within our body. We often go through each day without slowing down to really feel how our body feels, to notice what emotions may be surfacing, and to listen to what our body may be telling us. When we stop to listen we notice that we may tend to hold certain emotions in different places in our body. Maybe in our chest, or our stomach, or our heart. Each feeling may even have a different intensity. At times we may feel one feeling really strongly, or we may feel lots of feelings all at once. Sometimes we may not even know what we are feeling, and that is okay too.

By really noticing our feelings and how our body holds them we can begin to work with them. We can begin to feel and process each emotion and eventually transform them. Sometimes we may feel both happy and sad at the same time. It can be confusing to have so many varying emotions at once, yet we may find that it can be a large part of being human. We all have feelings, and these feelings change with each day and each experience. Through nurturing and loving ourselves we can begin to transform old feelings and start fostering the feelings we wish to have.

 
Writing feelings where we may feel them 
  
 
Connecting colors with feelings
 
  
 
Reflecting on the process
 
Relaxation:
Put on relaxing music silently in the background and begin to lead the women through relaxation...

"Set yourself in a comfortable position and begin to take a few deep breaths. You can close your eyes or keep them open, do whatever is going to make to feel relaxed. We rarely slow down and focus on ourselves, so know that this time is for you. Bring yourself into this present moment and feel your breath move in and out. Send the message to your entire body to relax. Focus your attention on your breath, not seeking to change it in any way but simply become aware of your in-breath and your out-breath. With each breath allow your body to relax further. Begin to focus on how your body feels. What feelings do you have in the present moment? Become aware of them. Notice if you feel different feelings in certain places in your body. Maybe there is a certain feeling in your chest or your heart or your stomach. Breathe into those places and simply notice how your body feels. Are there certain colors that come to you when you feel each emotion? See what comes to your mind naturally with each breath. Continue to breathe slowly, in and out. Remember that it is safe to feel these feelings, that you are in a safe place. Begin to breathe in love and compassion for yourself, and know that you are surrounded by love and support. Now when you are ready you can slowly open your eyes if you closed them."

Creation, Part 1:
Have the women begin by reflecting on what feelings and colors came up for them in the relaxation. Inside each puzzle piece they can write a word that describes a feeling that they have right now or even a feeling that they have had sometime today. Encourage them to think of where in their body they might feel these different feelings, they can then write that feeling in the place that they feel it.

After the puzzle pieces are filled with the words of their emotions they can then color in each puzzle piece with a color that portrays each feeling.

Journaling:
After the women have created their dolls they can move on to journaling about how to process and look at all of these feelings that came up for them. They can reflect on why they put certain words in certain places, what the different colors meant to them, what came up for them in the relaxation, and how it feels to look at their doll made up of all of their present emotions.

They can reflect on how to make peace with conflicting emotions. For example how for some of the women in their heart they may still feel love for their batterer, but everything else is telling them to run.

 
  Close-up of feelings in the present
  
 
  Close-up of feelings wanted in the future
Share with them how these dolls help us see that all human beings can feel fragmented at times. That at some point in our lives all human beings experience brokenness and are left to rediscover their sense of self and sense of the world again. If they are feeling fragmented and broken how can they, and how do they want to, put themselves back together again? Have them reflect on what this next step would be for them. What feelings do they want to replace other feelings with. What do they want to replace fear with? What do they want to replace loneliness and sadness with, etc?

What kind of nurturing self-loving things can they begin to do to piece themselves back together? What would help them create a more empowered sense of self?

Creation, Part 2:
Once the women have journaled they can create a second doll to "put themselves back together" with nurturing and loving feeling words and colors. Encourage them to see this as actually taking a step to create this transformation in their lives! Through nurturing and loving themselves they can begin to transform old feelings and start fostering the feelings that they wish to have.

Closing Circle:
At the end, give all of the women a chance to share their paper doll. If they don't want to share be sure to let them know that that's okay.

After the women have shared encourage them to see how strong they are and to have compassion for the times that they feel broken or lost in their emotions. They are doing the work here and now to "piece themselves back together again" in loving and empowered ways! Congratulate them for doing such wonderful work and sharing their feelings!

Alternate Closing:
Brainstorm a "Safety Plan" with the women to help them process their anger. Some helpful tips include:
Talk to a friend you can trust
Count to 10
Take out art supplies and draw a picture of your anger
Journal about your anger
Take deep breaths
Listen to music
Walk away
Dance or exercise

Variation:
Lupe Diaz & Debi Barrett of WomenShelter of Long Beach had participants write, color and cut the pieces before gluing the pieces on construction paper. They felt that doing this had a demonstrated how difficult it is to put your life back together after a traumatic event, however with great care and patience it can be done.
Row.txt_description: OLD OBJECTIVE: By writing and coloring emotions on a paper doll made up of puzzle pieces the women are able to reflect on their current emotions, where they feel theses emotions in their body, and how they envision themselves "putting themselves back together" after all that they have been through.
Row.txt_tips:
Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

We recommend that you start anger workshops with a discussion; don't be afraid to talk to the women about their anger. Anger is nothing to be ashamed of, it is important to look at and talk about it to try to understand it.

Some anger prompts that we like are:
What is Anger? What does it look like and what does it sound like?
What was the trigger to your anger?
What did you think about it?
How did it make you feel?
How did you act?
What effect did it have on you and those around you?

Row.txt_code:
Puzzle Piece Paper D oll Template
Objective:
Allows children to look at and discover the many feelings they have inside themselves as they color and name emotions on a paper doll made up of puzzle pieces.

Materials:
Colored markers and pencils- for coloring
Permanent markers- for writing words
Handout of paper doll made up of puzzle pieces - 1 or 2 for each participant
- click here for Paper Doll Template
Handout with various emotions that the child can refer to - click here for Emotions Handout
Music- something upbeat, such as "Putamayo World Beats"

Note: If using this workshop to help children release or process anger it is important to begin by having a discussion on "What is Anger?" Please click here to see the entire Processing Anger Series.

   
Example by teen age boy   
Timeframe:
Intro: 10 minutes
Warm Up: 10 minutes
Creation: 25 minutes
Closing: 15 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour

Age Range: 3 and up.

Set Up:
Lay out colored markers and pencils around the table. Make sure that there is a paper doll handout and emotions handout for each child. These can be placed where the child will be sitting or handed out to them after the warm-up exercise.

Introduction:
Today we are going to talk about how we feel. Each of us have feelings, and sometimes we may feel lots of different feelings at once. Sometimes you can even be happy and sad at the same time. Lets think about what different kinds of feelings we can have. What kinds of feelings can you think of? What kinds of feelings do you have today?

You may have each child share what they are feeling right now, if they are comfortable. They may feel one feeling really strongly, or they may feel lots of feelings all at once, or they may not know what they are feeling.

Encourage them to think of a few feelings that they have in that very moment. Have them think of where they might feel these feelings inside their body. Do they feel it in their chest? Do they feel it in their heart? Do they feel it in their stomach? Would that feeling have a certain color? What color would happiness be for them? What color would sadness be? What color would love be?

 
  Close-up of feelings in the present
  
 
  Close-up of feelings wanted in the future
Warm Up:
Do an exercise with the children with music to shake their feelings out. Have them dance around the room and ask them to make the faces that they make when they feel a certain emotion.

What face do you make when you feel happy? What face do you make when you feel sad? What face do you make when you feel angry, tired, excited? Etc...
Then have them dance their way back to their seats!

Creation:
Show the children the paper doll that they will be writing and coloring their feelings on. You may want to show them an example of one that you created.

Have the children write inside each puzzle piece a word that describes a feeling that they have right now or a feeling that they had sometime today. You will have to help the younger children write these words on their paper doll. You can encourage the older children to think of where in their body they might feel their different feelings, they can then write that feeling in the place that they feel it.

After the puzzle pieces are filled with the words of emotions then have the children color in each puzzle piece with a color that portrays each feeling. You can ask them to think of what colors come to their mind when they think of each emotion. They can be any color. Their color for happiness or sadness may be a different color than the person sitting next to them chose for happiness or sadness. Each person's paper doll will turn out different!

Older children may want to create two dolls in one workshop; one to represent their feelings in the present moment and one to represent what they want their feelings to become in the future. This leaves them with an empowered feeling of "putting themselves back together" with the feelings they want to have!

Closing Circle:
At the end, give all the children a chance to share their paper doll. The older children can share what it felt like for them to create their second doll, what it felt like for them to chose the feelings they wish to feel in the future. This can be an empowering process! If they don't want to share be sure to let them know that it's okay. Remind them to respect each others art and feelings while they share. Have them notice how many different feelings and colors there are on everyone's dolls. Even though each doll is different and unique, they all share similar feelings! At the end congratulate them for such wonderful work and for sharing their feelings!

Alternate Closing:
Brainstorm a "Safety Plan" with the children to help them process their anger. Some helpful tips include:
Talk to a friend you can trust
Count to 10
Take out art supplies and draw a picture of your anger
Journal about your anger
Take deep breaths
Listen to music
Walk away
Dance or exercise
Row.txt_description: Allows children to look at and discover the many feelings they have inside themselves as they color and name emotions on a paper doll made up of puzzle pieces.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Through the process of guided imagery, watercolor painting, and dimensional putty, this workshop can help participants learn simple self-regulation techniques by creating a flower painting, which can then serve as a calming image, a personal symbol of strength and reminder of our individual resilience.
   
Materials: 
  • Fresh cut flowers
  • 11 x 17 white card stock
  • Colorations® Liquid watercolors (can be purchased at Discount School Supply)
  • Air Dry Putty (can be purchased at Discount School Supply)
  • Washable markers
  • Bingo bottles (to be filled with liquid watercolors) (can be purchased at Discount School Supply)
  • Rulers
  • Pencils
  • Erasers
  • Scissors
  • Tacky glue pens

Optional:

  • Paper for placemats
  • Additional card stock for materials demo
  • Colorations® Liquid Watercolor - gold and silver (can be purchased at Discount School Supply)
 Time frame: 

Total Time: 1 hour, 30 minutes
Intro: 5 minutes
Materials Demo/Explaining Resilience: 10 mins.
Warm-up/Relaxation: 10 mins.
Drawing a Border: 5 mins.
Breathing Techniques & Mindful Meditation: 5 mins.
Creation: 50 mins.
Closing: 5 minutes

Age Range:
 6 and up



  • Small brush for accenting
  • Magnifying glass
  • White crayons









 
 
 Building Resilience Set-up
 
Preparation/Set-up:
Before you begin this workshop, you might want to think of how you'd like to gather the fresh flowers. You can take participants on a nature walk, in or around your agency to allow them to make a connection with nature and to find a flower that really speaks to them. If this isn't possible, you can bring in various flowers of your own. You can also substitute flowers with fresh herbs.
 
At each place setting, set out all materials for each participant to easily access during the demo and creation portion of the workshop, including the fresh flowers. If you're using Bingo bottles, you may want to fill them prior to the workshop as they take some time to fill up. If Bingo bottles are new to you, take some time to explore them for yourself so you can be better prepared to introduce them to your group.

Note: If you'll be using Air Dry Putty, make sure to keep the packages sealed until you will be using them to create. This will help insure freshness and avoid any drying of the putty.

Introduction:
"Today we're going to be talking about something that is inside all of us. It's something that some of us may notice inside ourselves more than others but once we notice it and really understand it, it can be really helpful.

"The topic of today is resilience. What does this word mean? Well, resilience is a process that allows a person to bounce back after difficult things happen. Resilience is not a trait that some people have and others not, resilience is an ability that we can all learn and develop.
Can you think of things that have happened in your life where you were resilient? Something that happened to you that was really hard to deal with but you made it through anyway? What helped you get through that situation? Was it turning to someone to get support or did you go inside your self to find a solution to a particular problem? Did you find ways to calm down or stay safe? Any of those ways of are examples of resiliency.

"We will be taking steps to create artwork about how each of us is strong in our own, unique way. We will also learn some easy techniques that we all can do when we are faced with  difficult moments or problems to help us be able to move through it."

Materials Demo/Explaining Resilience:
"We will be using different art materials to draw and paint a flower that can represent our resilience. During this workshop, I will be giving you directions that you can follow completely or you can choose which parts you would like to follow. You can even choose to create something different. This is your window of time and you can use it however you'd like, even if it's sitting back and observing; as long as you're honoring your thoughts and feelings, you are doing a great job!

"To start us off, I'm going to be showing you the art materials that we're going to use. While I'm doing this, we're going to talk a little more about resilience."

 
  Liquid Watercolors
Liquid Watercolors: Continue the conversation by moving into the watercolor demonstration. If you're using Bingo Bottles, briefly demonstrate how to apply watercolor onto the paper by gently squeezing. Show participants how they can make dots, spread and blend colors.

"As we begin to explore the watercolors, choose some colors and put them onto your paper. Notice how the colors begin to soak into the paper and spread around. If you'd like, choose different types of colors and see what happens when you blend them together. When we're working with watercolors, we can also think about how we're able to handle the things in our lives that we can't control. Just like the watercolors soak into the paper and blend into one another, we usually can't control the difficult things that happen to us. All we can do is work with what is given to us and and figure out the healthy ways to deal with it. We will learn some of these skills today. How have you been able to make the best out of a difficult situation?"

  
    Air Dry Putty
Air Dry Putty: Before you begin, open up the packages of the Air Dry Putty and ask participants to grab a small piece of any color they'd like.

"As you get to know the Air Dry Putty, let's talk a little more about resilience. Take a piece of the putty into your hands and take a moment to feel it. Move it around and squeeze it with one hand, try squeezing it with two hands. How does it feel? If you'd like, smell the putty. What does it smell like?

"When we talked earlier about resilience we said that it's a person's ability to "bounce back" after difficult things happen to them. Let's see if we can make a round ball out of the putty (give participants some time to create their balls). Now, imagine that these round balls are us. We're going to twist, turn, and break apart these balls (pause and allow time for this). Let's imagine that this twisting, turning, and breaking apart can be all of the difficult things that can happen in our lives. What kinds of difficult things have you faced?

"Now let's shape our putty back into a ball (pause and let participants gather their putty). For some of you, it took a little more time to gather and mold back into place. This is also true about our lives. Inside of all of us, we have the ability to pick up all of the pieces and put ourselves back together again. Resilience is inside of each of us. As we sit here, notice that everything that we have gone through in our past is behind us and it's a big deal to be here today. Maybe you're going through something difficult right now and you feel like it will never get better. I hope this can give you a sense of comfort knowing that you are resilient.

Gold and Silver Watercolor (optional): The gold and silver watercolors can be added as a last step of the art project to add accents. Briefly demonstrate how to apply the paint with a small paintbrush.

Warm-up/Relaxation:
"I invite you to find a comfortable position in your chair. Take a deep breath and look around you. Breathe in some fresh, clean air. You are in a safe place and this is your window of time to notice your thoughts, feelings, and your needs.

 
Meet your flower and notice its details.
 
Make Friends: "Look at the people at your table. We all have a lot in common and we are not alone. If you're comfortable enough, look at each person and make eye contact with them and give them a gentle nod or smile. Let's support each other and build a creative and helpful community here. Relax and settle in for some fun!"

Meet Your Flowers: "Now pick up the flower that you chose. This is your special flower for today's art activity.

"Take a good, slow look at all of its colors and shapes. What do you see? Notice the details in the flower. If you'd like, get a closer look by bringing it closer to your face or by using a magnifying glass. What new things did you notice about your flower after looking closer? I also invite you to smell your flower. What kind of smell does it have? What do you think about when you smell it? Does it remind you of anything?

"As you take the time to notice all of the great things about your flower, think about why you chose the flower you did. Think about all of the ways your flower is unique. Is it strong? Delicate? Colorful? What do you see in the flower that is the same in you?

  
   Draw a border around the edges of the paper.
Drawing a Border: "Let's begin by taking our pencils and rulers to draw a border around our papers. You can measure the width of the ruler to space your border all around the page. This will create a built-in frame. Leave the border white for now and we'll have a chance to come back to write something inside of it."

Breathing Techniques & Mindful Meditation:                                        "Before we create our flowers, we are going to learn some breathing exercises that you can do when you are going through a difficult time. Breathing exercises can help us calm ourselves down and relax. Whenever you get upset, remember to take three deep breaths. Taking these breaths can help us think more clearly and build resilience."

Before you begin the breathing exercises and meditation, remind participants that they get to choose how they'd like to participate."

Note: Gently guide the participants through each breath so they don't rush through and they have a chance to connect to their bodies.

 
  Standing Breaths
  
  Sitting Breaths
Standing Breaths
  1. Stand up with your feet placed apart for balance.
  2. Make sure the person next to you is more than an arm's length apart from you.
  3. Take three deep breaths while raising your arms up and down with each breath (in a slow, flying motion).
Sitting Breaths                                 
  1. Find a comfortable position in your chair.
  2. Cross the fingers of both hands together and place them lightly on your belly.
  3. Rest your elbows comfortably along your body.
  4. Relax and drop your shoulders.
  5. If you feel comfortable enough to do so, close your eyes and take three deep breaths.
  6. Feel your belly as you breathe in and out.   
Flower Meditation (to continuously flow from sitting/standing breaths): In a soft, gentle voice, you can use some of the prompts below. Leaving plenty of silent space in between these prompts allows participants to take in each of them with tenderness. Invite participants to close their eyes if they feel comfortable enough to do so.

"Stay focused on your breathing and keep your body relaxed. Listen to the sounds of the room. Now think about your flower growing tall and strong. Imagine your flower reaching toward the sun. Think of a gentle rain refreshing your flower. Think of all you have in common with your flower. Just like this flower, you are born into this world fresh and pure. You are loving and loveable. Now think about all of the different qualities of your flower and how you are just like it. No matter what is going on around you or happening to you, deep inside you there is always this calm, safe place that you can always find, today and always."

  
 Draw a flower on your paper.
 
  
 Add color to your drawing.
 
  
 Add accents with watercolor and/or putty
to highlight certain parts of your painting.
 
  
  Write affirmations to remind you of your strength. 
Creation:
Draw a Flower: "Now that you're calm and collected, take your flower in your hand again and look at it as you draw it on your paper. If you want, you can draw the flower very large on your page so you can really focus on the details. Don't worry if your drawing doesn't look just like your special flower, remember that whatever comes out is just right."

Adding Color: "Using the watercolors, let's add color to our flowers. You can follow the color(s) of your flower or you can come up with new colors. There is no wrong way to add color. If you choose not to add any color, adding more detail to your drawing can be something you might want to try out. Take a look at your flower again and see if you can add some details that you may have missed."

Adding Accents: "You can use the Air Dry Putty to add accents to your painting. Adding a fun border or details to your flower might be something to consider. You can use the glue to stick the putty on.

"Using the gold and silver watercolors, can add shimmer to your flower. You can use these colors to highlight any features or parts of the flower that you really want to stand out."

Writing Affirmations: "Let's add some positive and calming words to your drawing. I'm going to invite you to write some affirmations or words of encouragement that can help you get through difficult times. You can write the following words exactly as you hear and see them or you can write some positive words of your own."


You can say and write these words down for the participants to easily refer to:
  • At the very top, you can write: I am as fresh as a flower.
  • On the left side, you can write: I take 3 deep breaths to calm myself.
  • On the right side, you can write: I am loving and loveable.
  • On the bottom, you can write and finish this sentence: I am ___________.

  
  Fresh as a flower!
Closing:
"As we close, let's do three more deep sitting breaths. Cross your fingers and place them lightly on your belly. Rest your elbows comfortably along your body. Relax and drop your shoulders. If you feel comfortable enough to do so, I invite you to close your eyes. Take three deep breaths, feeling your belly as you breathe in and out."

Optional Closing Questions:
  • What did you discover about yourself?
  • What's one new thing that you learned?
  • What is one way you can calm yourself down when you're upset?
  • Why is it important to calm yourself when you're upset?
  • How are you resilient?
  • How have you been resilient in the past?

"Take a look around and remember, we are not alone. We have a lot in common and we all go through difficult times and we are learning to support ourselves and each other each time we come here."
Row.txt_description: Through the process of guided imagery, watercolor painting, and dimensional putty, this workshop can help participants learn simple self-regulation techniques by creating a flower painting, which can then serve as a calming image, a personal symbol of strength and reminder of our individual resilience.
Row.txt_tips:
• It is very important that you and any other Leaders, staff, or volunteers in the room participate along with the group. By modeling your enthusiasm and willingness to participate, you help build trust, bonding, and make it safer for other people to play and share vulnerable experiences.

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways.  Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.str_title: I CAN WE CAN for Male Victims (for WSLB and Valley Oasis Only)
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Using their ha nd as a canvas, each participant in this workshop will take a creative window of time to notice the possibility and power that lies within them, and then make a pledge to claim one I CAN to end violence in their lives. After the workshop, the participants' creations be uploaded to the gallery of the I CAN WE CAN website which will connect them to a community that supports their vision and those of others taking steps to end violence in our communities.  Their creations will also be linked to other artwork created to educate the community about male survivors during Domestic Violence Awareness Month.


Prepare yourself:
  • Decide who will participate in the workshop and make necessary arrangements. Confirm attendance a day before the workshop.
  • Gather all of the supplies necessary for your workshop. Becoming familiar with the supplies and the creation process yourself will make it much easier to support those you are leading and also identify any supplies you would like to include or omit.
  • The list below is simply a suggested list of supplies; we welcome you to be bold, get creative and add any supplies you like!
  • You may want to designate a wall space or use a poster board or other blank wall or material to use as the background for the photos to be taken in front of. Lighting should also be taken into consideration to ensure the photos are of high quality and representative of the participants' creations. We also encourage you to first practice using the camera that you will use during the workshop so that you are comfortable photographing the creations.

Prepare your group:

  • Inform participants prior to the workshop that they will be creating artwork for an on-line exhibit to create awareness and educate the public about the prevalence of and unique challenges faced by male survivors of violence.
  • Give participants ample time to create. Choose a day when participants do not have lots of things to do. We recommend a minimum of 2 hours. All participants should be informed about the amount of time needed to complete the workshop before they agree to create art for exhibition.
  • To help create safety and lessen self-censorship, be sure to tell participants that they can choose to keep their piece totally anonymous or they can even create a pseudonym or artist name that they would like to use.
  • Try to complete the art project, releases and evaluation in one session, as there is no guarantee that all participants will return for multiple sessions.
  • If time permits, it may be helpful to schedule another session where you meet with the clients individually and make additions to their captions on the Art/Media Release. 
  • Taking time to support the participants with writing words to go with their art is important as their words are what give the viewer insight into what the participant is trying to convey through their creation.

At the workshop:

  • Have the Art/Media Release forms printed (one per participant)
  • If necessary, remember to establish guidelines with input from group members. Guidelines should include mutual respect for one another, acceptance of all feelings and expressions, and an agreement of confidentiality.
  • Have Art/Media Release forms completed before each person leaves. This is very important because any artwork sent to AWBW without an accompanying release cannot be included in the online exhibit.

 

Timeframe:
Set aside at least 2 hours of uninterrupted space and time to lead this workshop with a group. The 2-hour time frame is recommended to provide enough time for check-ins, creation, processing, a closing circle, photography and filling out the Art/Media Release.

 
  
Materials:
Face paint, makeup, washable markers - anything washable to write on skin
Eyeliner pencils
White-out pens
Paint brushes and/or sponges to apply Face paint
Pens
Copy paper for sketching
Non-bleeding tissue paper and permanent markers (you can write on the paper and then apply it to your hand using water!)
Scissors
Spray bottle for water
Water
Baby wipes or make-up remover and cotton balls
Music
Camera
Art/ Media Release (one per participant)
See the I CAN WE CAN gallery for more supply ideas: http://icanwecan.awbw.org/galleries/i-can-we-can-community-wall


 
I CAN WE CAN Workshop Steps:
Step 1: Welcome
"This is 'a window of time' to practice respecting your thoughts, feelings, needs, and vision. This workshop is designed to enable us to re-focus our energy from the things we think we cannot do, to what each of us is capable of doing to end violence in our lives and in those around us!  Be gentle with yourself and honor all that has come before this moment. Embrace and notice that today you are safe and free to choose I CAN.

As you notice your power and the possibility that lies within you, know that whether what comes to you seems 'too small' to be important or seems 'too big' to be possible, please try to trust that your ideas are just right. When you truly honor your heart, you can create a change that ripples out from you to those around you and to the community at large, as part of a global change. Your I CAN, no matter how small or big is part of changing the world. If you need to take a break or opt out of any aspect of the project, please do so. If you need some support, let me know, as part of my role here today is to be here for each of you."


 
Step 2: Check-in:
Take a moment to check-in with the group by asking each person to share their name and a word or a sentence about how they are feeling in this moment. "Are you feeling nervous, excited, afraid, or happy? Please know that today is about you and you are safe and encouraged to do, say, and feel whatever is your unique expression.

"Who would like to start the opening circle sharing your name and how you feel about being here today?"

The check-in is important since it brings everyone's voice into the room and allows for connection and trust.

Step 3: Warm-up:
"Many of us have heard all of all our lives that we can’t be who we want to be or do what we really want, whether it was someone in our family, friends, society, our partner, our community, or even our own thoughts.

"We are going to take a moment to release those doubts and 'I can't' thoughts and notice the power we already have inside. Pick a partner to share for one minute about something that you thought could not do, or were told you could not do, but you did and it made you stronger as a result. It can be anything you would like to share. We will take turns sharing for the full minute so that each person can share one at a time. I will help you take turns by timing a minute and letting you know when it is time to switch speakers."

After everyone has shared: Validate the group by thanking them for taking the time to notice that they have the power to do what they want.

 
  Participants creating I CAN artwork.
Step 4: Sign top part of Art/Media Release:
Pass out the Art/Media Release and ask the participants to fill out each section of the top portion of the release including: name, signature, date and email. 

If the participants want to recieve email updates about the project, welcome them to check the box that says "YES! I am making the I CAN WE CAN pledge to help end domestic violence and sexual assault."  AWBW sends out email updates every few months so you can assure the participants we won't flood their inbox. Explain that at any point in the workshop they can fill out the bottom portion of the form. Share that their piece can be anonymous, all they need to do to make it anonymous is to leave the "Artist Name" section blank.

Step 5: Introduction to the Creation Process:
"The I CAN WE CAN project is about the difference we can ALL make in ending all forms of abuse by taking a moment, a creative 'window of time,' to notice our own personal vision and commitment to end violence using our own hands.

"Today each of us will make a personal commitment or pledge for ending violence in our own lives. Please remember that there is no wrong way to participate in this project and every aspect of this workshop is voluntary. Please honor your feelings, thoughts, and ideas about how you want to create your expression for ending violence.

  
Step 6: Brief Relaxation:
 Put on some slow, relaxing music (preferably without words) and speaking in a soft, slow and relaxed tone say: "If you feel comfortable enough to do so, I invite you to close your eyes or just sit quietly. Take a minute to breathe and think about or imagine your vision for your I CAN. And as you breathe deep, notice that you get to take this window of time as long as you like, just for you. To hear your heart, and to hear what it says to you when you ask it I CAN...notice what comes to you...I CAN...what's your wish...I CAN... Try to picture it in your mind, however it comes to you...as an image...colors...shapes... symbols...a place...or a list of things you truly want. Take as long as you need but remember that your I CAN might be something simple and personal or it can be your greatest vision.   Keeping your vision in mind, be bold when creating your I CAN hand!"

Step 7: I CAN Creation:
"Now, think about being part of a circle of people around the globe committed to ending abuse. If each of us notices a new step we want to claim and act on, we can move the world. What I CAN do you want to claim today? Again, no idea is too small or too large. Just notice what resonates in your heart as most meaningful for you. When you are ready, begin to create your I CAN hand using your hand as your canvas. Place your I CAN message on it however you like. Your I CAN expression can be painted on, glued on or placed on paper and held in the palm of your hand. Anything goes! We will create art that represents the I CAN each of our hearts is telling us to reach for and we will using our own hand as a canvas for that expression."

 
Step 8:  Photographing I CAN Hands:
Have a camera ready and encourage the participants to have you take their picture once they are done creating. This can streamline the photography process since people will finish creating at different times.

You can say to the participants: "Taking a photo of your I CAN hand is part of the creative process so be as creative as you like with it. Your I CAN hand could be against whatever background you wish, a color of paper, your face, blades of grass, or whatever most powerfully expresses your I CAN!"

Ask the participants to bring their Art/Media Release with their name written legibly on it when you take their photographs. This is very important as it will allow AWBW to match the artwork to the releases so we can upload them to the I CAN WE CAN gallery.

Take at least two photographs of each creation: one with the Art/Media Release (so that the correct artist name can be matched with the artwork) and one without. For each creation, email both photos and the completed Art/Media Release to Christy at cturek@awbw.org (see photography instructions for more info).

Step 9:  Closing Sharing Circle:
We encourage you to end by giving each participant an opportunity to share anything they want with the group about their experience with the workshop. After each person is done creating you can say, “Now I would like to give everyone an opportunity to share something about their experience here today. We will go around the room and each take turns sharing anything you want about your I CAN, what you created, and/or your overall experience with the workshop.” Remind participants that they also have the option to pass.

Step 10: Thank Participants:
Thank all participants for taking a window of time to notice their strength and what they CAN do to end abuse! Share with them that by creating their I CAN pledge they are joining other survivors and non-survivors coming together to end abuse. Remind participants that their creations are valuable and will help educate the public and create awareness about male survivors of abuse. Moreover, their creations will provide support to other male survivors by breaking any feelings of isolation and inspiring hope for the future. 

Step 11: Complete Art/Media Release:
Spend time appreciating your clients for sharing their stories and letting them know how a big part of this project is to amplify their voices in order to raise awareness, inspire others, and support other survivors in knowing they are not alone. Give extra time for each participant to finish filling out their Art/Media Release with additional words.

Here are some suggestions for encouraging words to go with their art:
  • Add questions on the back of release to get them thinking about their story.
  • Create a journaling questionnaire related to the project or simply provide paper or simple journals and encourage participant to use it before, during and after the workshop.
  • During the closing circle, participants will often open up about how the art or the art process impacted them. Ask for permission to take notes so that you can capture their wisdom and reflections.
  • If a participant has a hard time getting started sharing words for their piece, ask them to think of a title for their piece. Then ask why they chose that title.
  • If you are working on the words with them, you can reference things they spoke about during the workshop, in the closing circle or relating to their title.
  • You may ask with additional questions such as:
    • What did you notice about yourself during this workshop?
    • What does your art mean to you?
    • What do you want other people to know about domestic violence?
    • What has been most supportive to you in your healing process? What has been most challenging in your healing process?
    • Is there anything else you would like to share?
  • Encourage the participants to add their responses to the questions on the caption portion of the Art/Media Release.
  
Step 12: Submit I CAN WE CAN Hands for Customized Online Exhibit:
Let the group know that AWBW will be adding their voices to the I CAN WE CAN project by uploading a photo of their creation to the I CAN WE CAN website.

Remember to email both pictures and the Art/Media Release for each creation to Christy at cturek@awbw.org.

If possible, share the online gallery with participants and let them know that their I CAN artwork will help inspire others to do what they can to end abuse in their own lives and their communities.
Row.txt_description: Using their hand as a canvas, each participant in this workshop will take a creative window of time to notice the possibility and power that lies within them, and then make a pledge to claim one I CAN to end violence in their lives. After the workshop, the participants' creations be uploaded to the gallery of the I CAN WE CAN website which will connect them to a community that supports their vision and those of others taking steps to end violence in our communities. Their creations will also be linked to other artwork created to educate the community about male survivors during Domestic Violence Awareness Month.

Row.txt_code:
Description
In this embodied art workshop, participants get to explore their "typical" day and their ideal day nonverbally. In this "rehearsal for real life" process, they have the opportunity to better understand their experiences, needs, and visions.

Materials
No materials needed except enough space to have a "sharing"/performance area and a "witness"/audience area.

Time Frame
Creating Safety with Embodied Art: 5 min.
Name and Gesture Warm-Up: 5-10 min. (depending on group size)
Image of the Hours: 40-60 min. (depending on group size)
Closing Circle: 10-15 min. (depending on group size)
Total: 1-1.5 hours (depending on group size)

 

Creating Safety with Embodied Art

 
 
 Participants take a window of time to connect
to their bodies in their own ways.

"Many of us have consciously or unconsciously disconnected from our bodies as a way to cope with trauma. When we use our bodies to explore our inner and outer worlds, we can start to reconnect to ourselves. This process can support us in feeling more whole and integrated. When we do this in community or in a group we may not only connect to ourselves more deeply but connecting to others. Sometimes, new things can feel anywhere from exhilarating to silly or uncomfortable. Throughout today's workshop, notice how you are feeling and only do what feels right for you and your body.

"Today, we're going to take a window of time to connect with each other and ourselves by doing some movement related to how we each want to spend our time. Throughout this workshop, we'll get an opportunity to connect to our playfulness and to our bodies in a safe and supportive way--this means you get to decide what safe and supportive means to you. For example, maybe you can't wait to move around or maybe you want to challenge yourself by trying something new. Maybe you want to connect and play by watching other people experiment or sitting quietly with a hand over your heart and just breathing deeply. Know that in this window of time, you get to decide what's right for you. I will make some invitations, and you get to honor yourself and your body in whatever way feels right to you.

"To begin, let's stand together in a circle."

 

Name and Gesture Warm-Up
Stand in a circle with participants. Invite each person to share how they are feeling today with their name and a movement (for example, by saying "sleepy Ana" while yawning and stretching or shouting "excited Bobby" while jumping up and down). After each person shares, the whole group repeats the feeling, name, and movement twice, trying to match the original person's words, tone, and movement as exactly as possible, while still taking care of their bodies. Remind participants that they can always pass and take care of their bodies. For example, if someone jumps really high but you have injured knees, you can do your own version of jumping-for example, maybe that looks like raising your shoulders instead or even just thinking about jumping instead of doing it. Click here to see a short video of this warm-up.

 

Image of the Hours

  1.   
      Sharers show what they do at 4 a.m.
    Introduction: Begin by giving a preview of the process: "In this next activity, we're going to get a chance to notice and share what a typical day looks like for us and later we'll get a chance to notice and share what our ideal day would be like.
