However, instead of just talking about it, we're going to show with movement what we do during the day without using words or sounds. Half the group will have the opportunity to share while the other half will witness and reflect back silently what they saw, and then we'll switch. At the very end, after we've each had a chance to share and witness, then we'll get a chance to share what that experience was like for us. As a reminder, this is your window of time, so you get to practice honoring your thoughts, feelings, needs, and bodies--that could mean that when acting out ‘sleeping' you lie down on the floor or you could just stand and close your eyes or you could choose to pause and get a drink of water, and so on. There's no right or wrong way to participate here."

  2. Divide the group in two: Have one group be the "sharers" and the other group be the "witnesses" first. Invite all the witnesses to sit together, facing the sharing area. Welcome the sharers to the sharing area.

  3.  
      Sharers show their 8 a.m. images to witnesses.
    Creating images: "I will be calling out hours of day, such as 1 p.m., 2 p.m., etc. At each hour the sharers will silently act out whatever it is that they usually do at that time everyday. If you don't have a typical day, you can pick something that you do frequently at that time or choose a specific day like yesterday. After we've gone through the whole 24 hour day, the witnesses will reflect back 3 images that they saw and remembered. Any questions?" After answering any questions that come up, invite the sharers to start in a position of what they are doing at 4 a.m. (for many people, this would be sleeping). Begin calling out the hours of the day, with long pauses between each hour to give participants a chance to show what they do. "4 a.m. ... 5 a.m. ... 6 a.m. ... 7 a.m. ... 8 a.m. ... 9 a.m. ... 10 a.m. ... 11 a.m. ... 12-noon ... 1 p.m. ... 2 p.m. ... 3 p.m. ... 4 p.m. ... 5 p.m. ... 6 p.m. ... 7 p.m. ... 8 p.m. ... 9 p.m. ... 10 p.m. ... 11 p.m. ... 12-midnight ... 1 a.m. ... 2 a.m. ... 3 a.m. ... and all the way back to 4 a.m. ... Witnesses, give a round of applause to the sharers for their courage and creativity!"

  4.   
      Witnesses reflect back images they saw.
    Reflection: "Now, sharers take a seat, and witnesses come up to the sharing area to reflect back some of the images that you saw. This is an opportunity to let the sharers know that they were seen and that their experiences are acknowledged. You'll get an opportunity to act out three of the different things you saw. Any questions?" After answering any questions, call out "Image 1" and pause for the witnesses to show one thing they saw. Then call out "Image 2" and pause again for the witness to show something else they saw. Finally, call out "Image 3" and pause for the witnesses to show a third thing they saw. Offer an opportunity for the original sharers to give appreciative applause for their witnesses.

  5. Switch roles: Repeat steps 3 and 4 with the groups in opposite roles (the sharers become the witnesses, and the witnesses become the sharers).

  6. Discussion: Invite the group to share what they noticed and if anything surprised them. Validate the feelings and experiences that came up for participants.

  7. Transition: Ask the group if the day they showed is how they'd like their day to be in their ideal world. If they say no (as most groups do), say to them, "So let's take a window of time to imagine how we would like our days to be-how we would set up our day if we didn't have to settle for anything less than absolutely everything. In order to give our visioning a little flexibility, this time, instead of calling out specific hours, I'll be calling out general times of the day, such as ‘early morning,' and witnesses will reflect back just two of the images."

  8.  
      Sharers show their ideal evening.
    Ideal images: Invite one group to come to the sharing area and start in a position of what they are ideally doing in the early morning. Begin calling out the times of the day, with long pauses between each hour to give participants a chance to show what they do. "Early morning ... late morning ... 12-noon ... afternoon ... evening ... late night ... 12-midnight ... and back to early morning ... Witnesses, give a round of applause to the sharers for sharing their visions!"

  9. Reflection: "Now, sharers take a seat and witness get ready to reflect back some of the images you just saw. Maybe you want to try out an image because you think it might be good for your ideal day or maybe it stands out to you for another reason. Ready?" Call out "Image 1" and pause for the witnesses to show one thing they saw. Then call out "Image 2" and pause again for the witness to show something else they saw. Finally, offer an opportunity for the original sharers to give appreciative applause for their witnesses.

  10. Switch roles: Repeat steps 8 and 9 with the groups in opposite roles (the sharers become the witnesses, and the witnesses become the sharers).

  11. Discussion: Invite the group to share what they noticed and if anything surprised them. Ask what was different about their typical day and their ideal day. Validate the feelings and experiences that came up for participants.


Closing Circle
If not everyone has had an opportunity to share, invite participants to go around and share one thing they appreciated about this workshop or themselves and any final word that they'd like to say. Remind participants that they have the option to pass.


 
 Participants hold hands in
the closing circle breaths.
 
  

Thank the participants for connecting to themselves, their experiences, and the expression of their bodies. Close out the group with collective breaths: "Now we are going to take three breaths together. This first breath is for this group right here." Pause to let everyone breathe together. "The second breath is for yourself." Pause to let everyone breathe together. "The third breath is for your ideal day and all the support you can get to make it a reality." Pause to let everyone breathe together.
Row.txt_description: In this embodied art workshop, participants get to explore their "typical" day and their ideal day nonverbally. In this "rehearsal for real life" process, they have the opportunity to better understand their experiences, needs, and visions.
Row.txt_tips:
• It is very helpful if you and any other Leaders, staff, or volunteers in the room participate along with the group (when possible-if you are calling out the hours of the day, you may not be able to also participate). By modeling your enthusiasm and willingness to participate, you help build trust, bonding, and make it safer for other people to play and share vulnerable experiences.
  • Sometimes groups enjoy picking specific days of the week to share-for example, a typical Monday might look different than a typical Saturday.
  • Especially if you lead this workshop more than once with a particular group, participants might like variations on the prompt such as "your birthday," "the best day of your life," or "a rainy day." You can ask the group what they'd like to do or see.
  • If someone feels too shy to share, you could invite them to say the hours of the day while you participate.
  • Remember that at any point, participants can choose to participate actively or take care of their needs by passing. Honor them for whatever choice they make.
  • If you do this workshop with younger children or with people who find naming specific hours stressful, you can modify the prompts to be "morning, lunchtime, afternoon, dinner, night..." or whatever simpler/broader prompts would work best for your group.
  • Depending on the group, you may need to remind them not to touch or bump into each other while they are sharing, explaining that each person is sharing individually even though there is a group sharing simultaneously.
  • If you have a group that disengages easily, it can be helpful to have the witnesses stay with the process by calling out the hours with you.

 

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways.  Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.str_title: My Day, My Way (Image of the Hours)
Row.txt_code:
Description
In this embodied art workshop, participants playfully act out their daily reality. Then in a "rehearsal for real life," they get to imagine and create their perfect day.

Materials
No materials needed except enough space to have a "sharing"/performance area and a "watcher"/audience area.

Time Frame
  
    
 Age Range
Creating Safety with Embodied Art - 5 min.
Name & Gesture Warm-Up - 10 min.
My Day, My Way - 35 min.
Closing Circle - 10 min.
Total - 1 hour		      
  Ages 7 and up
(for older youth, see
Image of the Hours variation below)

Creating Safety with Embodied Art
"Raise your hand if you like to dance." Pause to let them raise their hands. "Raise your hand if you like to run." Pause to let them raise their hands. "Raise your hand if you like to play soccer." Pause to let them respond.

"These are all ways that people have fun moving their bodies. What are some other ways people have fun moving their bodies?" With each suggestion, invite the participants to raise their hands if they like moving their body in that way. If necessary, reassure participants that it's okay if different people like different things.

"There are many ways to move your body safely, just like all those ways you just shared. Whatever way you like to move your body is just fine, as long as you aren't hurting anyone! Today, we're going to play some games that let us be silly, fun and safe when moving our bodies. Throughout this our time together, you get to decide what feels right for you and your body.

"To begin, let's stand together in a circle."

 

Name & Gesture Warm-Up
Stand in a circle with participants. Invite each person to share how they are feeling today with their name and a movement (for example, by saying "sleepy Ana" while yawning and stretching or shouting "excited Bobby" while jumping up and down). After each person shares, the whole group repeats the feeling, name, and movement twice, trying to match the original person's words, tone, and movement as exactly as possible, while still taking care of their bodies. Remind participants that they can always pass and take care of their bodies. For example, if someone jumps really high but your feet are tired, you can do your own version of jumping-for example, maybe that looks like raising your shoulders instead or even just thinking about jumping instead of doing it. Click here to see a short video of this warm-up.

 

My Day, My Way

  1.   
      Sharers show what they do at 4 a.m.
    Introduction: "This game is called ‘My Day, My Way!' First, we're going to need to split into two groups. One group will share their day first and the other will watch, and then we'll switch." If necessary, have a brief discussion about what makes a good listener/watcher/audience member to prepare the group to be supportive to one another. Then divide the group into "sharers" and "watchers."

  2. Explain the sharers' role: Welcome the sharers to the sharing area. "Now, sharers, I'll be calling out times of the day, and your job will be to act out silently what you do during that time. For example, if I said lunchtime, what would you do?" Give a moment for the sharers to show they understand by pretending to eat lunch.

  3. Explain the watchers' role: Invite all the watchers to sit together, facing the sharing area, and share the importance of their role with them. "Now, watchers, you have a very important job to do. Your job is to watch the sharers very carefully, because after they share, you'll get a chance to act out something you saw."

  4.  
      Sharers show their early morning actions to witnesses.
    Daily Actions: "Are you ready? Sharers, start with what you do when it's really early in the morning." Pause to let everyone start. Begin calling out time periods, with long pauses between each one to give participants a chance to show what they do. "Early morning... Getting ready for school... Going to school... School morning... Lunchtime... Afternoon... After school... Dinnertime... After dinner... Bedtime... Nighttime... And back to early morning... Watchers, give a round of applause to the sharers for their courage and creativity! Sharers, give yourselves a pat on the back or take a bow."

  5.   
      Watchers reflect back actions they saw.
    Reflection: "Now, sharers take a seat, and watchers come up to the sharing area so that you can show the sharers two actions (two things) you saw the sharers do." Call out "Action 1" and pause for the watchers to show one thing they saw. Then call out "Action 2" and pause again for the watchers to show something else they saw. Finally, offer an opportunity for the original sharers to give appreciative applause for their watchers.

  6. Switch roles: Repeat steps 4 and 5 with the groups in opposite roles (the sharers become the watchers, and the watchers become the sharers).

  7. Discussion: Invite the group to share what they noticed and if anything surprised them. Validate the feelings and experiences that came up for participants.

  8. Transition: Ask the group if the day they showed is the best school day ever that they could imagine. If they say no (as most groups do), say to them, "So let's take some time to imagine the best day ever. What would you do in the morning? What would school be like?"

  9.  
      Sharers show their ideal "after dinner" actions.
    Best Day Ever: Invite one group to come to the sharing area and start in a position of what they are ideally doing in the early morning. Begin calling out time periods, with long pauses between each one to give participants a chance to show what they wish they did every day. "Early morning... Getting ready for school... Going to school... School morning... Lunchtime... Afternoon... After school... Dinnertime... After dinner... Bedtime... Nighttime... And back to early morning... Watchers, give a round of applause to the sharers for their courage and creativity! Sharers, give yourselves a pat on the back or take a bow."

  10. Reflection: "Now, sharers take a seat and watchers get ready to show some of the actions you just saw. Maybe you want to try out something because you think it might be good for your best day ever or maybe you remember it for another reason. Ready?" Call out "Action 1" and pause for the watchers to show one thing they saw. Then call out "Action 2" and pause again for the watchers to show something else they saw. Finally, offer an opportunity for the original sharers to give appreciative applause for their watchers.

  11. Switch roles: Repeat steps 9 and 10 with the groups in opposite roles (the sharers become the watchers, and the watchers become the sharers).

  12. Discussion: Invite the group to share what they noticed and if anything surprised them. Ask what was different about their real day and their best day ever that they could imagine. Validate the feelings and experiences that came up for participants.


Closing Circle
If not everyone has had an opportunity to share, invite participants to go around and share one thing they liked about this workshop or themselves and any final thing they want to say. Remind participants that they have the option to pass.


 
 Participants hold hands in
the closing circle breaths.
 
  

Thank the participants for sharing, watching, and moving together. Close out the group with collective breaths: "Now we are going to take three breaths together. This first breath is for this group right here." Pause to let everyone breathe together. "The second breath is for yourself." Pause to let everyone breathe together. "The third breath is for your best day day and all the ways we can support each other in making that happen." Pause to let everyone breathe together.
Row.txt_description: In this embodied art workshop, participants playfully act out their daily reality. Then in a "rehearsal for real life," they get to imagine and create their perfect day.
Row.txt_tips:
• It is very helpful if you and any other Leaders, staff, or volunteers in the room participate along with the group (when possible-if you are calling out the hours of the day, you may not be able to also participate). By modeling your enthusiasm and willingness t o participate, you help build trust, bonding, and make it safer for other people to play and share vulnerable experiences.
  • Sometimes groups enjoy picking specific days of the week to share--for example, a typical Monday might look different than a typical Saturday.
  • If you lead this workshop more than once with a particular group, they might like variations on the prompt such as "your birthday" or "a rainy day." You can ask the group what they'd like to do or see.
  • If someone feels too shy to share, you could invite them to say the times of the day while you participate.
  • Remember that at any point, participants can choose to participate actively or take care of their needs by passing. Honor them for whatever choice they make.
  • If you do this workshop with younger children or with people who find naming specific hours stressful, you can modify the prompts to be "morning, lunchtime, afternoon, dinner, night..." or whatever simpler/broader prompts would work best for your group.
  • Depending on the group, you may need to remind them not to touch or bump into each other while they are sharing, explaining that each person is sharing individually even though there is a group sharing simultaneously.
  • If you have a group that disengages easily, it can be helpful to have the witnesses stay with the process by calling out the times with you.

 

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with the youth the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways. By sharing this information with them, you empower them to feel a sense of ownership over their bodies and their expression. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Objective:
To provide Window's Leaders with a new way to support survivors and engage community through the art of storytelling utilizing digital media. A toolkit, resources and information about the benefits to survivors are included.

Background:
Since 2012, the I CAN WE CAN initiative has brought individuals and communities together to create positive change. Each I CAN pledge to end abuse has a story that it tells in our fight for peace, equality and wholeness. As a continuation of the I CAN WE CAN initiative, we are very excited to introduce a new way for you to share your stories, engage your communities and be a part of the digital storytelling community! 

Introduction:
What is digital storytelling?
Digital storytelling is the modern expression of the ancient form of storytelling. Storytelling can be regarded as one of oldest healing arts. Storytelling can enable us to communicate, teach, make meaning of experiences, to inspire and encourage, pass on wisdom and make meaningful connections to ourselves and others.

Digital media is a creative, powerful and deeply engaging way to share our stories. Through sharing their stories, survivors and allies are empowered to raise their voices, creating awareness and a ripple effect that moves people to action in their own lives and in their communities.

Materials:
With the help of Windows Leaders, AWBW has created a toolkit with tips, suggestions, and guidelines including suggested Windows Workshops to get you started!! Click here to download the toolkit.

  • Digital stories can be captured through many types of digital media including, but not limited to: computers, tablets, smart phones, digital cameras, video cameras, etc.
  • How you tell your stories has endless possibilities by combining various images and/or audio. This includes digital images such as photographs, artwork, text, clip art, video, etc. and digital audio including voice, narration, music, sounds, and sound effects.

Does AWBW offer resources and support for digital storytelling?
In addition to the comprehensive toolkit provided, AWBW offers the following resources to support your digital storytelling process:
  • Digital Storytelling Toolkit
  • Access to funding -- up to $20 per year for apps to create your story with digital media
  • Use of a dedicated YouTube channel for digital storytelling through the
    I CAN WE CAN initiative
  • iPad loan, when devices are available
  • Technical support from AWBW program staff (appointment may be necessary)
  • Inspiration and ideas through the Windows workshops and curriculum.

How will survivors feel empowered by creating a digital story?
Even while maintaining anonymity, seeing their personal art and stories shared publicly and in this innovative way can create a sense of pride and self-worth that can be empowering in many ways. Some of these ways are:

  • Affirms and validates their story of survival, wisdom and hope
  • Confirms they have wisdom to share with others and educate the community
  • Builds a community of support in discovering they are not alone
  • Provides a sense of purpose by giving back
  • By sharing individual experience and unique voice, myths and stereotypes can be broken and free survivors to create life in their own vision
  • Through sharing their art and stories, other survivors are inspired to break the silence
