Row.txt_code:
Description
In this embodied art warm-up, participants get to introduce themselves in a playful and connected way.

Materials
No materials needed, although it can be nice to have enough space for everyone to stand in a circle. (See tips section below for a possible modification if there is limited space.)

Time Frame
Total: 5-15 minutes, depending on the size of the group.

Introduction
"Today, we get to say hello to each other in a playful way with words and movement. To begin, let's stand together in a circle."

Name and Gesture Warm-Up

  
 Participants play "Name and Gesture."
Click here or on the picture to see a short
video of this warm-up. 

Stand in a circle with participants. Invite each person to share how they are feeling today with their name and a movement (for example, by saying "sleepy Ana" while yawning and stretching or shouting "excited Bobby" while jumping up and down). After each person shares, the whole group repeats the feeling, name, and movement twice, trying to match the original person's words, tone, and movement as exactly as possible, while still taking care of their bodies.

Remind participants that they can always pass and take care of their bodies. For example, if someone jumps really high but you have injured knees, you can do your own version of jumping-for example, maybe that looks like raising your shoulders instead or even just thinking about jumping instead of doing it.

Closing/Transition to Next Activity
Appreciate the participants for their explorations before going on to the next activity.
Row.txt_description: In this embodied art warm-up, participants get to introduce themselves in a playful and connected way.
Row.txt_tips:
• It is very helpful if you and any other Leaders, staff, or volunteers in the room participate along with the group. By modeling your enthusiasm and willingness to participate, you help build trust, bonding, and make it safer for other people to play and share vulnerable experiences.
  • If you do not have enough space for everyone to stand in a circle, another option is to have everyone stay seated except when sharing their name/gesture. Everyone else can repeat the name/gesture from their seats instead of standing. This allows people to be able to see each movement even if there isn't a single big circle.
  • Consider variations on the prompt, especially if you lead this warm-up frequently but would like to keep it fresh. For example, instead of having participants share a feeling word, they could share a word that describes them, something they appreciate about themselves, something that they would like to be true about themselves in the future, etc.
  • Remember that at any point, participants can choose to participate actively or take care of their needs by passing. Honor them for whatever choice they make.

Note About Introducing Embodied Art
Consider sharing with your participants the benefits of moving their bodies in playful and safe ways.  Understanding what’s meaningful about movement and body awareness can help participants feel at ease expanding their comfort zones. For more about embodied art workshops and how to introduce them in your groups, see Introduction to Embodied Art Workshops.

Row.txt_code:
Completed Permission Canvas
Objective:
This workshop will give the participants permission to do something they have been longing to do, to change a habit, or let go of something.

Materials:
Canvas (see Blick - we recommend 6x6 inch pieces)
Paint & Brushes
Mod Podge
Cake doilies
Scrapbook paper
White glue
Magazines                              Pre-cut or pre-typed words
Sponges etc. to make texture in paint
Foam brushes or Brayers
Bubble wrap
Sharpies (ultra fine & regular)
Scissors
Stamps & ink pads
Writing Paper
Journaling Questions
Paper Dolls Template

 
 
  Art supply materials
 
Preparation:
Print words and phrases that can be collaged onto the canvases by the participants. (For example: I gave myself permission to; I decided to; I let ______ go). Try using interesting fonts (the text can be around size 36 pt. depending on font used).

Print out body templates for all the participants. Also, print and arrange journaling questions and pens at each place setting.

Timeframe:
Introduction: 10 minutes
Journaling: 20 minutes
Group Sharing: 15 minutes
Technical Information: 5 minutes
Creation: 60 minutes
Closing Circle: 15 minutes
Total: 1 1/2 to 2 1/2 hours

Introduction:
The new year is a time of the year that symbolizes renewal and rebirth. It's a time to bid farewell to the concerns and problems of the past year, and prepare for a new and healthy beginning. We can focus on the things that we want more of in our lives, and look forward to the coming months with more hope, enthusiasm, and an open heart!

This workshop will give you the opportunity to transition into the New Year in a positive way. We will notice how it would feel to let go of something or someone who is holding you back in your life or a habit you wish to break.

Afterwards, we are going to give ourselves permission to think about something we really want to accomplish or a healthy habit we would like to take on. Through journaling and painting, we will create a canvas that gives us the affirming permission to do whatever we choose in the future!

Journal Questions:
Play some relaxing music and invite the participants to answer the journal questions. Reassure them that their writing is for themselves and they won't be reading their answers out loud, unless they want to. Remind them that they can skip questions that don't work for them, but ask them to try to look at each question with curiosity. This is their 'window of time' to be present to whatever surfaces and let go of any blame or shame that comes up!

Encourage participants to take special care in coming up with their permission phrase(s) and creating a positive focus for the New Year. This expression can be something as simple as giving themselves permission to just breathe or as significant as changing jobs or starting a new relationship. Some ideas for their canvases are, "I gave herself permission to let love in" or "I decided to go back to school."

Note: For a gentler approach, we have chosen to create the permission phrases in the third person, using the word "she" instead of "I." Sometimes, when we speak from the viewpoint of another person, it is easier and more comfortable to embrace a vision beyond ourselves. We understand that change may be challenging for some but we can all appreciate some gentleness from time to time!

Group Sharing: 
Have each participant pick one of their answers to the journal questions to share with the whole group. They can also share what it would feel like to let go of a thought, a person or a habit that no longer supports them. Or they can share one of their permission phrases and why it would be important to embrace this... whatever they like!

   
  Paint, brayer or sponge brush then roll
the paint on bubble wrap. Stamp bubble wrap
to your canvas to give an artsy background!		 
Technical Info:
Demonstrate how to use the materials to create textures and unique effects. Show how to use a foam brush, sponge or brayer for blending and layering paint on bubble wrap and then transfer to canvas to create a polka dot effect.

Also, show how to use materials to create textures, shapes and tone on tone effects, by using a light dabbing motion.

Explain how mod podge can be used as glue for collaging, or as a coating to finish their art.

   
  Tear the magazines for a unique collage finish
 
   
  Use mod podge to glue on mixed media materials
 
Creation:
Let the participants dive in and start creating! Suggest that they paint the background of their canvas first, and then think about their permission phrase while the paint dries. Since this is a "mixed media" project, they can blend a variety of techniques when creating their art: paint, stamping, and/or collage.

"Give yourself permission to create your canvas in whatever way that you wish! You can collage, paint, or simply have an abstract background.

"You might want to add a person as a focal point of your art. You can use the doll template as a guide, and collage to create clothing from different scrapbook patterns. You can also draw your person freehand or find a magazine image that represents the future you want to create... whatever you wish!

"Choose the permission phrase that is most meaningful to you. Are you giving permission to take more time out for yourself in the future? Maybe you are deciding to spend more quality time with your children? Or perhaps you want to finally tackle that dream or goal you have not yet gotten around to? You fill in the blank! Once you decide, you can collage the statement onto the background or you can paint to write your phrase directly on the canvas. Since the canvas is focusing on the future that you want, try to keep your wording optimistic and affirmative!"

If some of the participants finish earlier than others, invite them to look back at their journaling questions. They can answer questions they did not answer previously, or they can journal about their creation.

Closing Circle:
Have the participants share their canvases with the group and anything they discovered about themselves while creating.

They can also share their permission phrase out loud. If there's time, try using "echo listening" where the other group members repeat the phrase back to them. Echo listening is a form of listening which is structured to be completely non-judgmental. After listening to participants read their piece, everyone in the room simply repeats at least one thing they remember the person saying, word for word, so that each person hears the entire room "echo" their words to them, rather than judging them. It is one structured way to use supportive listening and ground the vision of the participants.

Suggest that everyone display their canvas somewhere that they will be able to see it everyday, as encouragement and inspiration to look towards the New Year with and hope!

   
 
 Completed Permission Canvas
 Completed Permission Canvas
Row.txt_description: This workshop can give participants permission to do something they have been longing to do, to change a habit, or let go of something.

Row.str_author_firstname: Coalition of Womens' Groups in Cape Cod, MA
Row.txt_code:
Virginia Tech's Clothesline Project
(photo courtesy of Google images)
  
 
 
 A Clothesline Project example.
(Photo courtesy of theclotheslineproject.org)
  
Project History:
"According to the Men's Rape Prevention Project in Washington DC, "58,000 soldiers died in the Vietnam war. During that same period of time, 51,000 women were killed mostly by men who supposedly loved them.
In the summer of 1990, this statistic became the catalyst for a coalition of women's groups in Cape Cod, Massachusetts to consciously develop a program that would educate, break the silence and bear witness to one issue - violence against women.

This small, core group of women, many of whom had experienced some form of personal violence, wanted to find a unique way to take staggering, mind-numbing statistics and turn them into a provocative, "in-your-face" educational and healing tool."

The Clothesline Project (CLP) is a vehicle for women affected by violence to express their emotions by decorating a shirt. "They then hang the shirt on a clothesline to be viewed by others as testimony to the problem of violence against women. The clothesline is commonly used on college campuses during Sexual Assault Awareness month and Domestic Violence Awareness month." History taken from theclotheslineproject.org. For a more detailed background, visit the history page of The Clothesline Project's official website.

Objective:
To give each participant an opportunity to tell their unique story using words and artwork to decorate a shirt. To raise awareness about domestic and sexual violence.

Materials:
T-shirts (one per participant)
Permanent Markers
Acrylic paints
Paint brushes
Water bowls
Writing paper
Pens
T-shirt board or cardboard(optional, but useful)
Clothesline (optional)
Clothespins (optional)
The Clothesline Project flyer (optional)

*Puff paint, white glue and fabric paint do not dry well and can cause the shirts to stick together. They are not recommended for this project.
  Timeframe:
1 hr. 20 mins. (or longer)
Warm-up/Participant Preparation:  15 minutes
Creation: 45 minutes /1 hr.
Closing:  20 minutes


 
The Utah Capitol Rotuda Clothesline Project display.
(photo courtesy of Google images)		 
Preparation:
Lay out t-shirts on tables (insert card board or t-shirt boards in the shirts). Arrange markers, paints, paper and pens neatly around workspace.

You may want to mark each shirt with a code or secret marking to confidentially identify the shirts.



Introduction:
Begin by explaining the origins of The Clothesline Project. You may use the following short description or the entire history at theclotheslineproject.org:
"A coalition of women’s groups in Massachusetts banded together in the summer of 1990 to develop a project that would increase awareness of violence against women, and empower survivors and families of victims to break the silence and tell their stories. Inspired by the harrowing statistics of all types of violence against women, these women wanted to create a program that could educate and heal. Drawing from the AIDS quilts concept, the women thought of using a clothesline because it represents the notion of traditional women’s work and the social bonds formed while chatting with neighborhood friends while clothes hung out on the line. The clothesline allows each woman’s unique story to be told, while powerfully demonstrating the community of women survivors and victims."

Talk about how each participant can use their shirt to tell their own story, using whatever words and artwork she feels best tell it. These shirts can serve as a way for us to walk away from the violence of the past, and come together as survivors.

(If you will be collecting and displaying the t-shirts, make sure to let the participants know in advance.)

Technical Info:
The Clothesline Project uses different color shirts to represent different types of abuse, and whether the victim survived the abuse. It's up to you and your clients if you want use the color coding or allow the participants to choose a color that is significant to them. The color-coding used TCP is as follows:
    White: Women murdered due to sexual or domestic violence
    Yellow/Beige: Domestic violence survivors
    Red, Pink, Orange: Rape and sexual assault survivors
    Blue, Green: Incest and sexual abuse survivors
    Purple, Lavender: Attacked due to sexual orientation
    Black: Designation of your choice

Warm-Up:
If you are creating a display, have participants think about what words, symbols and messages represent their stories. What do they want their shirts to convey to those who view it? How can sharing our stories help us heal?  If you are not using it as part of a TCP display, simply generate a discussion about the statistic shared in this workshop and have the participants share their reactions.

  
 A Clothesline Project display at UCLA.
(photo courtesy of Google images)		 
  
 
Haven Hills 2008 Clothesline Project
 
  
  
  Haven Hills 2008 Clothesline Project 
  
  
  
Creation Process:
Suggest to the participants that it can be help to begin by sketching ideas and messages on paper before decorating their shirts. This is also helpful to get a feel for the paints and markers, and to get comfortable with the process.

Start by saying "there is no right or wrong way to decorate your shirt! Use the paints and markers however you choose in order to tell your story. But, since this is a clothesline project it's important to decorate both sides of your shirt."way to decorate your shirt! Use the paints and markers however you choose in order to tell your story. But, since this is a clothesline project it's important to decorate both sides of your shirt."

Suggest that each participant include a written story to accompany their shirt. The stories may be attached to the shirts or simply kept together.

Once a shirt is complete, and has had some time to dry, it may be hung on a clothesline. You can set up a clothesline in your workspace, or create an event. (See Tips below.)

If you do hang the shirts, try hanging them in blocks of color, and alternating dark and light colored shirts in order to highlight each shirt and the impact of the story represented.

Closing:
If you are not using a clothesline, encourage each participant hold up their shirt and share their story. What message have they conveyed? How does each participant feel about the shirts as a group of stories?

If using a clothesline, encourage participants to walk around the clothesline and take the time to absorb the message of each shirt. Invite discussion and communication among the participants.

Click here for the official site of The Clothesline Project!
Row.txt_description: The Clothesline Project is a vehicle for participants affected by violence to express their emotions by decorating a shirt. The shirts are used to raise public awareness about the issue of domestic and sexual violence.

Row.str_title: Reclaiming Denim - A Denim Day Workshop
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To learn about the history of Denim Day, define sexual assault, and empower participants to know they can make change. This workshop also gives participants the opportunity to look at their own lives and make a personal commitment to protect themselves.

  
  Reclaiming Denim supplies
  
 
  Different pocket options
Materials:
Denim pockets or pieces of denim (two for each person)
Button backings or safety pins
Permanent markers (silver sharpies look great on denim)
Hot glue gun, with glue OR FabriTac glue
Ribbon, including rickrack
Puff paints
Foam Shapes
Assorted embellishments such as buttons, sequins, letter beads etc.
Embroidery needle (optional)
Embroidery thread (optional)
Denim Day Action kit from Peace Over Violence click here
 Scissors (fabric scissors are preferred)
Pocket template click here
 Paper (for participants to write messages on)
Pens
Glue sticks (if making pockets out of paper)

Preparation:
It is helpful to have the pockets already cut out before the group begins to expedite the creation process. 

If you do not have enough pockets you can make your own out of denim, fabric or paper.  Simply use the pocket template provided and trace it onto whatever material you have available. If you are doing paper pockets, use heavy cardstock.

Post statistics around the room or on the table for participants to use on their pockets if they choose to.

  
  Break the silence. Silent no more.
Some statistics from the Denim Day in L.A. toolkit include:
•    1 in 5 female students reported being physically and/or sexually abused by a dating partner (JAMA Vol. 286 No.5 2001)
•    Teens 16 to 19 were three and one-half times more likely than the general population to be victims of rape, attempted rape, or sexual assault. (U.S. Department of Justice, 1996)
•    In 3 out of 4 incidents of sexual assault, the offender was not a stranger. (DOJ, 1997)
•    One in 5 girls and 1 in 10 to 20 boys will be sexually abused at some point in their childhood, according to most reliable studies of child sexual abuse in the United States. (Finkelhor, 1994)
•    Only 3% of high school students who had been physically or sexually abused by a dating partner reported the abuse to an authority figure; only 6% told a family member. 61% of the respondents indicated that they told a friend and 30% indicated that they told no one at all. (The Prevention Researcher, 2000)
•    Most people know at least one person who has experienced or will experience sexual assault or rape. Everyone has a role in preventing sexual assault.

For a single page printable version of these statistics from the Denim Day in LA toolkit, click here, for a page of Common Misconceptions click here.

  
 Don't forget your prep time!
  
Time frame:
Introduction:15 minutes
Opening Circle:10-15 minutes
Creation: 45 minutes
Closing Circle: 15-20 minutes
Total: 1 hour, 20 minutes

Introduction:
Take some time to define sexual violence and rape. You may want to use the Denim Day Toolkit linked above or click here for one page of definitions.

Sexual assault is one of the most common, and most under reported forms of domestic violence. Every 2 minutes, somewhere in America, someone is sexually assaulted, and the victims often blame themselves for the attack.  Unfortunately, victims are often blamed by society for the assault and even blame themselves.

In 1998, an Italian Supreme Court decision overturned a rape conviction because the victim wore jeans, reasoning she must have helped her attacker remove them.  People all over the world were outraged.  Wearing jeans became an international symbol of protest against erroneous and destructive attitudes about sexual assault. Denim Day was created to unite against the sexual assault of girls, women, boys and men.  People who participate in Denim Day stand in support of survivors, break the silence to end sexual violence, and wear jeans as a visible sign of protest against the myths that still surround sexual assault!  Today we will create our very own pins to wear in support of, and increase awareness about Denim Day.  Denim day falls at the end of April and this year Denim Day is April 22.  To learn more
  
  
 Christy and SACA leader Ana
about Denim Day please visit denimdayinla.org. 

For further information about sexual assault, you may want to use Peace Over Violence’s curriculum and make copies of their handouts for group members. Click here for the Action Kit.

You can also show an educational video regarding sexual violence from CALCASA.org or Peace Over Violence .

Opening Circle:
Ask the participants to close their eyes and imagine that they are making a public service announcement that informs people about sexual assault (you may want to have the scratch paper and pens for them to make some notes). Ask them to think about what words, symbols, or catch phrases they would use in their commercial.  For example, "Sexual Assault is Never the Victims Fault," "Got Consent?," "No Means No," or "Rape free Zone".  Give the participants some time to create their commercial. After about 5-10 minutes, ask the participants to share about the commercial they created in their minds eye.  Ask them to focus on a quote, statement or symbol that encompasses the message behind their commercial.  

  
POV leader Isabel reclaiming a pocket
  
Creation:
Have everyone choose two pockets, one to keep for themselves and one to give another person to help educate their community about Denim Day.

Let each person know they can use any of the materials laid out before them and if they need help to ask. They may need help gluing the pinbacks. If they so choose, the participants can use the color turquoise, which represents Sexual Assault Awareness. It is also fitting for April, Sexual Assault Awareness Month.

Have each person create the first pocket for themselves. Remind the group that the purpose of their pin is to help spread awareness about sexual assault. Once they have created their pocket, have each participant write a personal commitment on a piece of paper.  The personal commitment should be related to how they will protect their bodies from abuse.  For example: "I promise to trust my instincts and leave any situation where I feel unsafe.” This
   
 
 
  My body is sacred.
 
can be a letter they write to themselves or a simple one-line statement.  The participants will then place that commitment inside their pocket to keep it close to their heart. If you are using paper pockets or one piece of denim, you can have them write this commitment on the back of the piece. Make sure each person has a way to pin the denim so they can wear their creation.

The second pocket will be a pocket to make for someone else.  Inside this pocket the participant will place a message they hope the person who receives the pin will adopt as a commitment to himself or herself to avoid abuse in their lives. For example, "firmly assert your boundaries". The pin and personal commitment are intended to not only increase awareness about denim day, but also to encourage the recipient to protect and respect their body.


 
 Different examples of Reclaimed Denim
  
  
Closing:
Ask each participant to share something about the pins they created and why they chose the particular messages they displayed on their pocket or ask participants to share about how it felt to create this project. They may also want to share who they made their second pin for and why. Encourage the group to commemorate this event yearly by wearing their pin on Denim Day and continuing to share their commitment against abuse with friends, family co-workers etc.
Row.txt_description: This workshop covers the history of Denim Day, defines sexual assault and empowers participants to know they can make change. This workshop also gives participants the opportunity to look at their own lives and make a personal commitment to protect themselves.

Row.txt_code:
Resilience Stones
Objective:
This workshop can offer participants time to notice and reflect on when they were strong during difficult or challenging times in their lives. Resilience Stones can serve as great reminders of their strength.
Materials:
Clear round glass stones
Card stock (multiple colors)
Colored pencils
Tacky glue

NOTE: you can find clear round
stones of different sizes on Amazon
by clicking here.
 Timeframe:
1 hour
Intro: 5 mins
Opening Circle: 10 mins.
Demo: 5 mins.
Creation: 30 mins.
Closing: 10 mins.
 Age Range:
6 and up 		 







 
 Table set-up
 
Preparation:
Before the workshops, cut out round paper circles by tracing one stone onto cardstock and using it as a stencil to create multiple circles. Write the word "resilience" on the board for participants to see. Consider writing the questions on a large piece of paper or a white/chalkboard for participants to see and refer to during the Opening Circle. You might also want to create a finished sample to show as well.

Table Set-up:
Arrange pre-cut paper circles, stones, colored pencils and glue for easy access for each participant.

Introduction:                                                                                     
Window of Time                                                                                                                "Before we begin our workshop, I want you remind you that this is your window of time. What this means is that you get to practice noticing your thoughts, your feelings, your dreams, and your visions. During windows time, there is no wrong way. I will be giving you some suggestions on how to create. You can follow along completely, do something totally different, or anything in between. You get to decide what is best for you and I will be here to help you out in any way you need me to.

"Today’s workshop is called Resilience Stones. Has anyone ever heard the word resilience before?"

Pause to let the participants raise their hands or share a comment. Affirm any comments and, if necessary, add, "Resilience is a person’s ability to cope with or bounce back from something hard. In other words resilience is what helps each of us get through the hard stuff that happens to us. Anything that makes us feel like we are able to do things makes us stronger to get through a difficult time. Any questions?"

Take a moment to answer any questions participants may have.

"Can you think of a time when your were going through something hard? Did you ever think that it took strength to get through it? I don’t mean the kind of strength that helps you open a jar or lift something heavy. I mean the kind of strength that comes from inside of you because of who you are, what you know. It could also be because you believed you would be okay again after the hard thing was over. Maybe it was the kind of strength you get from knowing you have someone that cares about you."

After each question you ask, pause for a moment to let participants consider their own experiences.

"Another way to look at it is each person's resilience is made up of their inner and outer strengths, memories and relationships with people or even animals that help them to get through the hard times.

"Everyone has challenges or difficulties and often times we grow and learn from valuable lessons. This is how we get stronger. Today we are going to take some time to notice our own resilience."

Opening Circle:                                                                                                         "As a reminder, this is your window of time. You get to choose what to share or not share, you also get to choose how to create your stones and do it your way. There is no wrong way to do art. Your art only needs to be what you want it to be, it doesn’t have to look like anyone else's, but if it does that’s okay to. You can take this time in whatever way feels good and right for you.

"We're going to be drawing and/or writing about our resilience. If you can’t think of anything to draw or write, it’s perfectly okay to just play with the materials and have fun."

Ask the children to share about a time when they felt happy. If they can't think of a time right now, they can share about anything that makes you feel happy. When they are done, thank them and reflect back to them that whatever they shared about their happiness. Remind them that their happy memories have a lot to do with their resilience.

"If we can think of time, a person or a place that made us happy, we know we have the ability to be happy. So when something feels hard remembering that happy thing can remind us that life is not always hard and can help us feel better and even stronger!

"Before we begin creating I want to share some more possible questions to help you think about your own personal strengths, memories, thoughts, people, animals or anything that will remind you of your own resilience."

Possible Questions to Ask. You might want to write questions on a board or paper big enough so all participants can read and refer back to them.

  • What connects you to your strength?
  • What helps you meet challenges?
  • What gives you the ability to bounce back from setbacks?
  • What gives you hope?
  • What inspires you?
  • When do you feel loved?
  
 Draw or write words or images as reminders of what helps you through the hard, challenging, or difficult times.
  
 Add a pea-sized amount of the glue
on top of your drawing/words.
  
  Place your stone on top of the glue and press down. Wipe off any extra glue and let it dry.

Demo:                                                   

"I’m going to show you how to use the materials you see to create your resilience stones.

  1. Draw or write words or images as reminders of what helps you through the hard, challenging, or difficult times.
  2. Add a pea-sized amount of the glue on top of your drawing/words.
  3. Place your stone on top of the glue and press down. Wipe off any extra glue and let it dry."

Creation:

"If you don’t want to use these questions, remember that it’s okay to play with the materials and make stones with colors, symbols or words that make you feel happy or strong. When you are ready, start creating! 

Before doing a final closing, ask participants to hold their creations in their hands and to take a moment to look at their resilience stones and the good, meaningful things that bring them happiness.

Closing:

Give participants an opportunity to share their stones and what they learned in the process about their own resilience.
Row.txt_description: This workshop can offer participants time to notice and reflect on when they were strong during difficult or challenging times in their lives. Resilience Stones can serve as great reminders of their strength.

Row.txt_code:
Resilience Stones
Objective:
This workshop allows participants to connect to their resilience, strength and power. Through creating Resilience Stones, participants will use words and images as reminders of whatever helps them through the hard moments, challenging times or difficult situations in their lives.
Materials:
Clear round glass stones
Card stock (multiple colors)
Sharpies (permanent markers only)
Colored pencils
Tacky glue or Matte Medium
Paper Towels or Wipes

NOTE: you can find clear round
stones of different sizes on Amazon
by clicking here.
 Timeframe:
65 minutes
Introduction: 5 mins.
Opening Circle: 5 mins.
Meditation/Relaxation: 5 mins.
Demonstration: 5 mins.
Creation: 30 mins.
Closing: 10 mins.
 

 







 
 Table set-up
 
Preparation:
Prior to the workshop pre-cut the cardstock circles to match the size of the glass stones. Trace one stone onto cardstock and use it as a stencil to create multiple circles. You might also want to create a finished sample to show as well.

Table Set-up:
Arrange pre-cut paper circles, stones, colored pencils and glue for easy access for each participant.

Introduction:                                                                                     
"Today's workshop is called Resilience Stones. Does anyone know what resilience is?"

Pause for a moment to allow participants to think about the question and perhaps share a comment.

Affirm any comments and, if necessary, add, "Resilience refers to a person's ability to cope with or bounce back from something (that may feel, seem or be) hard. That ability grows depending on our inner and outer resources. A resource is anything we can use to (support and) meet a need. In this case, the need is to overcome something hard that has happened by using our own inner resources. In other words, resilience grows from the feelings, experiences, relationships and thoughts that make us feel like we will be okay or that we can handle what has happened.

"Can you think of a time when your were going through something hard? Did you ever think that it took strength to get through it? I don’t mean the kind of strength that helps you open a jar or lift something heavy. I mean the kind of strength that comes from inside of you because of who you are, what you know. It could also be because you believed you would be okay again after the hard thing was over. Maybe it was the kind of strength you get from knowing you have someone that cares about you."

After each question you ask, pause for a moment to let participants consider their own experiences. Optionally, you could take time let participants share in pairs (see tips section below for listening process suggestions).

"Another way to look at it is that each person's resilience is made up of their inner and outer strengths, memories and relationships with people or even animals that help us to get through the hard times we all go through from time to time.

"No one is free from challenges or difficulties and often times we learn valuable lessons, grow and get stronger. Today we are going to take some time to notice our own resilience."

Window of Time
"Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you - a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you do or say is voluntary. I'll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there's no right or wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this window of time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. Please ask for what you need, and know that I'm here in support of you.

"You can take this time in whatever way feels good and right for you. If you can't think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just play with the materials."

Opening Circle:                                                                                                         "Before we start, we're going to do a brief opening circle to bring our awareness inside ourselves. I am going to invite everyone to share one word about how you are feeling right now. First thoughts are fine!

"As a reminder, this is your window of time. You get to choose what to share or not share, and passing is always okay."

Once participants have had a chance to share: "Thank you for sharing and acknowledging  wherever you are in this moment."

  
 Draw or write words or images as reminders of what helps you through the hard, challenging, or difficult times.
  
 Add a pea-sized amount of the glue
on top of your drawing/words.
  
  Place your stone on top of the glue and press down. Wipe off any extra glue and let it dry.
Demonstration:
"I'm going to show you how to use the materials we have available to create your Resilience Stones.
  1. Create images or write words as reminders of whatever helps you through the hard moments, challenging times, or difficult situations.
  2. Add a pea-sized amount of the glue (or matte medium) on top of your creation. Note: The glue will dry clear.
  3. Place your stone on top of the glue and press down.
  4. Wipe off any extra glue and let it dry.
Meditation/Relaxation:
"We are going to start with a short meditation to get us ready to create our Resilience Stones. When you are ready, sit comfortably in your chair, close your eyes or fix your gaze on a point in the room.

"Take a slow deep breath in and let it out. Notice how the chair holds you; notice the places your body is touching the chair; all the way down to your toes. Notice your feet touching the ground and take another deep breath in down into your belly and let it out. I want to remind you this is your window of time to connect with yourself and honor all of you thoughts, feelings, needs and visions about your own resilience.

"Now, I invite you to travel in your mind to a place where you feel still, quiet, rooted or grounded. Take in the stillness, the quiet. Notice you are safe. Take another deep breath in and notice that you have the power to be resilient in the face of challenges. You are whole and powerful just as you are and you get to express it. Take a moment to notice the ways you are already resilient and the ways you want to grow. Think of the moments, people or things that support you in feeling more resilient, and more ready to use your inner resources. Maybe you can find your resilience by asking yourself: What connects you to your strength? What helps you meet challenges? What gives you hope? What inspires you?

"Now, take a deep breath in and come back to this moment with the intention of bringing back with you any thoughts, feelings, colors or images that remind you of your resilience. And, when you are ready, begin to create."

Creation:
Halfway through the creation process, remind participants: "As you create, see if you can stay connected to your resilience, power and strength."

Before doing a final closing, ask participants to hold their creations in their hands, and to take a moment to look at their creations and see how it feels to notice the meaningful things, thoughts, or people that give them strength.

Closing:
Give everyone an opportunity to share their Resilience Stones and what they learned in the process about their own resilience.

Let participants know that they can carry their stones with them, or place them in a special place, as a reminder of their resilience, strength and power.
Row.txt_description: This workshop allows participants to connect to their resilience, strength and power. Through creating Resilience Stones, participants will use words and images as reminders of whatever helps them through the hard moments, challenging times or difficult situations in their lives.
Row.txt_tips:
Suggestions for the Listening Process
Listening and being heard can be powerful tools of resilience. In addition, the listening process can help create safety and connection in a group. Often, it can be meaningful to use timers and have pairs take turns being the person sharing and the person listening, so that each person gets an equal amount of time to be heard. It can be useful to remind the listeners that they do not need to comment or give advice, just listen with all the warmth in their hearts. Sometimes speakers need to be reminded that it's okay to sit in silence or talk about whatever comes to mind when it's their turn to speak. With new groups, starting out with just a couple minutes each can feel like plenty of time. As the safety grows in a group, longer turns can be successful as well.

When introducing the listening process or paired-sharing in a group, it can be helpful to explain the value of listening and invite concrete suggestions for how to be a supportive listener. For example: "We all have places inside where we have been hurt. They are sort of like ice cubes. Sometimes we think that to heal, we have to chisel away at those hard places to break the ice. But often, the warmth of someone's gentle, nonjudgmental listening will melt the ice without any effort at all. In the warmth of a good listener, it can feel safer to notice your feelings, to laugh, to cry, to take risks in your thinking and visioning for yourself. I'd really like this workshop to be a space where we can share safely and listen warmly to melt any ice cubes. Can anyone tell me some ways they know that someone is being a supportive listener?" People might share things like eye contact, nodding, warm facial expressions, etc. Remember that each person could have a different way they like to be supported, and, if needed, remind participants that it's okay to like different things and ask for what they need (e.g. one person might not want eye contact while another really likes it).

Row.str_title: Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence DVAM 2015
Row.txt_code:
Pearls of Wisdom
Objective:
This workshop uses the metaphor of a "pearl" as a treasure that forms inside an oyster in response to an irritant. Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength and wisdom as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence.  Each participant in this workshop will take a creative window of time to notice what pearl of wisdom they want to share to create awareness about domestic violence.

Participants' creations will be included in an exhibition at the 2015 Los Angeles City Domestic Violence Task Force Day of Action on October 9th in the city hall rotunda. Their creations will also be linked to other artwork created to educate the community during Domestic Violence Awareness Month.

Materials:
Clear round glass stones
Card stock (multiple colors)
Sharpies (permanent markers only)
Colored pencils
Tacky glue or Matte Medium
Paper Towels or Wipes


 Workshop Flow:
Introduction
Opening Circle (optional)
Meditation/Relaxation (optional)
Demonstration
Creation
Closing
Complete Art/Media Release
Photographing the Pearl
 

 

 
 Table set-up
 








Workshop Introduction:
A pearl is a wonderful metaphor for the survivor’s journey. Do you know how a pearl is formed? Basically, it starts with an irritant that enters an oyster; protective layers transform that mollusk and create a pearl. Throughout our lives, we all have challenges and difficulties (irritants). There are lessons to be learned in all these challenges(pearls).

Sharing your story of what you have learned, witnessed or experienced as a advocate or a survivor, from pain to wisdom, can empower and inspire an individual or even a community to help end the violence.  What you’ve experienced (these difficulties and challenges) and the ways you survived, or witnessed someone survive are valuable and essential in helping to end the cycle of violence.

As you reflect and create your pearls, notice your strength, beauty and wisdom. Embrace the ways you are transforming and growing. Thank you for being here to share your story.

Window of Time
"Before we begin, I want you to know that this workshop is a window of time for you - a safe space to notice your thoughts, feelings, and needs. Since this space is your window of time, everything you do or say is voluntary. I'll offer a suggested workshop idea, share about the materials we have available, and invite you to create, but there's no right or wrong way to do this. It doesn't matter what it looks like. What matters is taking this window of time to truly honor your thoughts and feelings, however they come out. Please ask for what you need, and know that I'm here in support of you.

"You can take this time in whatever way feels good and right for you. If you can't think of anything or draw a blank on what to create or write, feel free to just play with the materials."

Opening Circle:                                                                                                         "Before we start, we're going to do a brief opening circle to bring our awareness inside ourselves. I am going to invite everyone to share one word about how you are feeling right now. First thoughts are fine!

"As a reminder, this is your window of time. You get to choose what to share or not share, and passing is always okay."

Once participants have had a chance to share: "Thank you for sharing and acknowledging  wherever you are in this moment."

  
 Draw or write words or images as reminders of what helps you through the hard, challenging, or difficult times.
  
 Add a pea-sized amount of the glue
on top of your drawing/words.
  
  Place your stone on top of the glue and press down. Wipe off any extra glue and let it dry.
Demonstration:
"I'm going to show you how to use the materials we have available to create your Pearl of Wisdom.
  1. Using the permanent markers and/or colored pencils, create images, write words, symbols, or colors to represent the pearl of wisdom you'd like to share.
  2. After you're done creating, add a pea-sized amount of the glue (or matte medium) on top of your creation. Note: The glue will dry clear.
  3. Place your stone on top of the glue and press down.
  4. Wipe off any extra glue and let it dry.
Meditation/Relaxation:
"Begin...This is your window of time. This is a time to honor yourself as a wise and strong survivor. Get comfortable in your chair and if it feels safe, let your eyes close.  (Read slowly) Now, notice your breath (pause). With each breath notice that your breath has been with you in pain and in joy. Your breath and you are one. Your breath is your life force. Continue to breathe and connect with how you are feeling right now.  Notice how strong and courageous you are to be sitting in this room.  Give yourself permission to feel whatever you may be feeling.  Notice that you are safe, that you are taking important steps to heal the parts of you that are hurt and to honor the parts of you that are strong, courageous and authentically you.

Take a deep breath and come back to this moment with the intention of bringing back with you any thoughts, feelings, colors or images that represent your pearl of wisdom. And, when you are ready, begin to create."

Creation:
Create artwork that shares your pearl of wisdom. As you create, remember to illustrate your message in any way that feels right. You can create an image, use words or both.

Throughout the creative process, remind participants that there is no wrong way to create.

Toward the end of the creating time start to encourage participants to think about their pearls of wisdom. Ask them to look back at the process of creating, what they learned today and what they may want to share.

Closing:                                                                                                                         Share about your pearl and the wisdom you represented on it.

Complete Art/Media Release:                                                                 Spend time appreciating the participants for sharing their stories and letting them know how a big part of this project is to amplify their voices in order to raise awareness, inspire others, and support survivors of violence in knowing they are not alone. Pass out the Art/Media Release and give time for each participant to fill it out. Encourage the participants to fill it out completely. Please note that we must have releases for each piece of art in order to include it in the exhibit.

Photographing the Pearl:                                                                          Have a camera ready and encourage the participants to allow you take their picture once they are done creating. This can streamline the photography process since people will finish creating at different times.

You can say to the participants: "Taking a photo of your pearl is part of the creative process so be as creative as you like with it. Your pearl could be against whatever background you wish, holding it in your hand, on a colored piece of paper, holding it in front of your face, on blades of grass, or whatever most powerfully expresses your pearl!"

Ask the participants to bring their Art/Media Release with their name written legibly on it when you take their photographs. This is very important as it will allow AWBW to match the artwork to the releases.

Take at least two photographs of each creation: one with the Art/Media Release (so that the correct artist name can be matched with the artwork) and one without. For each creation, email both photos and the completed Art/Media Release to Christy at cturek@awbw.org.
Row.txt_description:
This workshop uses the metaphor of a "pearl" as a treasure that forms inside an oyster in response to an irritant. Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength and wisdom as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence. Each participant in this workshop will take a creative window of time to notice what pearl of wisdom they want to share to further the movement to domestic violence.
Participants' creations will be included in an exhibition at the 2015 Los Angeles City Domestic Violence Task Force Day of Action on October 9th in the city hall rotunda. Their creations will also be linked to other artwork created to educate the community during Domestic Violence Awareness Month.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Participants are given the opportunity to create a postcard from their future self five years in the future. This workshop allows participants to focus on future goals and celebrates possibilities.

 
  example
Materials:
Magazines and photostock books
81/2x11 Card stock, (cut in half to create two large postcards that are 81/2x51/2)
Gluesticks
Scissors
Colorful pens
Colored pencils
Fine point markers
Craypas

Optional Materials:
Modge Podge
 
    
  example    
Glitter or glitter gluesticks

Time Frame:
Preparation: 10 mins
Introduction: 5 mins
Relaxation: 15 mins
Creation: 45 mins
Closing: 15 mins
Total time: 90 Minutes

Introduction:
Today we will create postcards from our future self, five years in the future. You will have the opportunity to look back on all the things you have accomplished. You will create a picture of your life in the next five years on one side and on the other side write yourself a letter from your future self.

Let’s begin the creative process with a guided meditation. If you have never done guided meditation before it is a relaxation process designed to reduce tension and anxiety and to increase awareness.

During this process of relaxation you may find your mind wandering or recall a worrisome moment from earlier today or in the past. That is a normal event. Simply acknowledge it and bring yourself back to your quiet, meditative place.  You can always return to the unpleasant thoughts at another time if necessary. For now give yourself permission to let go of all else, remember this is your special windows of time.


 
 A folded postcard "Creation side" view
 
Relaxation:
To begin, let your body sink back into your chair.
Notice your entire body. What areas feel tight or tense?
Notice your breathing – feel your lungs expand and your chest rise and fall.
Now, take a deep breath – in through your nose, out through your mouth.
Focus on your feet, how do they feel? Tighten the muscles in your feet and then release.
Now focus on your calves? Are they tight or tired?
Tense them for a moment and then relax.
Notice your hips and lower back and release any tension resting there.
Travel up to your chest. Is it tight? Take another deep breath and let it out slowly.
Now notice any tightness in your shoulders and neck.
Push your shoulder blades firmly together and then relax them.
Now concentrate on your neck, turn your head gently from side to side to stretch your neck muscles.

Now take one more deep breath to prepare yourself for a mental journey on a warm and sunny beach.

Begin the journey by seeing yourself standing next to a beautiful palm tree on a sea shore enjoying the sand, water, and seagulls. You hear the waves on the beach and the gentle call of the seagulls overhead. Take a moment to observe your surroundings.
Now, notice the brilliant white sandy beach beckoning you to a walk along it’s beautiful shore line.

 
 
  A folded postcard "Letter side" view
Incredibly, you are the ONLY one present and it is a glorious morning. Begin your walk and enjoy what lies ahead.

What kind of shoreline do you see? Is it grassy, rocky or open and spacious?

What color is the water? Green, brilliant blue or a combination? How does the water smell? Take a moment to breathe deeply in and out.

Continue your walk and keep noticing what you see around you. Are there seashells in the sand? Take a moment to stop and look around you. Are there shells you would like to take with you?

If so, are pick up the seashells and put them in your pocket and keep them to use as memories of this lovely day.

See the sun shimmering on the water and on the waves. Do you see any ocean life in the water? If so, observe their beauty and distinct colors and shapes.

As you continue your walk you suddenly see a reflection in the sand on the beach just ahead of you.  As you walk toward it, you bend down and find a bottle. And inside the bottle is what appears to be a note of some kind.

You clean the sand off the bottle and take the cork out and shake the note out of the bottle.  The note is from a stranger talking about glorious adventures and far away places. As you read you begin to wonder what glorious adventures and far away places might await you in the future.


 
 example 
Think for a moment about what you imagine your life will be like 5 years in the future. (pause) What will you accomplish? (pause) What new places and things will you experience?(pause) What WILL you do with your grand and glorious life?

Release any hesitation or worry about HOW you will achieve what you desire. Know that it is already yours – you have to ask.

Now take a moment to focus on your surroundings one more. Take one last look at the beach and appreciate the beauty of nature as you prepare to leave.

Begin to make your way back along the beach until you reach the palm tree where you started. Know that as you walk you are taking the feelings of wonderment and curiosity about the future with you.

Now, take a deep breath and focus on the room where you are sitting. Notice how relaxed your muscles feel.

And when you are ready, you may slowly bring yourself back to the room, open your eyes and begin to create your Postcard from the Future.

Creation:
Depending on the materials used, participants have the option of choosing which side to create. Let the participants know that if they are using glitter or glitter glue they will want to
  
  "Creation Side" example
start with writing their note, and then flip the paper over to create their image.

Letter Side: Have participants write a letter to themselves as if it were five years in the future. The letter focuses on the participant  congratulating themselves for their ability to overcome abuse (and other issues they may have struggled with) and recognizing all their accomplishments and breakthroughs.

Creation Side: Have participants create a picture by drawing (pictures, words, or symbols) or collage that represents where they want to be in 5 years.

Closing:
Now that you are finished with your project let’s take a moment to honor your future accomplishments and any feelings that may have surfaced while creating your postcard. Have each participant share about their postcard and how the process of creating their postcard was for them.

You may also choose to end by doing a progressive muscle relaxation (see variation below)
It’s very simple, relaxing, and is an excellent example of a way to take care of yourself (as self-care is an important component of being able to fulfill your vision of the future). 

Process:
Sit comfortably in your chair with both feet on the floor and your arms resting comfortably in your lap. You can close your eyes if you like, but if you are not comfortable doing so feel free to leave them open.

Take two long, slow, deep breaths. Breathe in through your mouth and out through your nose. …..That’s fine.

Let yourself relax - and as you relax clench your right fist. Clench it tighter and tighter and study the tension as you do that. Keep it clenched and feel the tension in your fist, hand and forearm……now relax.

Let your fingers become loose, wiggle them, and observe the contrast in your feelings…now let go…..and try to relax all over. Once more clench your fist really tight and hold it…….notice the tension again……Now let go…..Relax.

Repeat with the left fist.

Now clench both fists together following the same routine.(repeat two times)
 
  
 example 
Straighten your arms in front of you. Reach across the room so that you feel the most tension in your upper arms and along the backs of your arms. Stretch your arms and feel the tension..…now relax. Put your arms back into a comfortable position and let the relaxation proceed on it’s own. Your arms will feel comfortably heavy as you allow them to relax.....more......and more. Try to go one step further and let your arms go completely limp.....feeling very heavy.....with no tension at all.

Now, with your eyes closed, raise your eyebrows and wrinkle your forehead. Wrinkle it tighter……now stop wrinkling. Relax and smooth it out. Picture your entire forehead and scalp becoming smoother as the relaxation increases…..and the tension fades away.

Now frown. Crease your brow and study the tension. Now let it go. Smooth out your forehead one more time. Close your eyes really tight. Feel the tension in, and around, and behind your eyes. Now relax your eyes. Keep your eyes closed and gently notice the relaxation.

Now grin broadly – from ear to ear. Feel the tension around the corners of your mouth……and now relax. Just feel the tension drain away from your face…….draining……draining…….draining.

  
 example 
Now, shrug your shoulders up as tight as you can toward your ears. Now relax. Bring them up again ……a little tighter if you can…..Now relax and feel the tension drain away from your upper back and shoulders. Let the relaxation spread deeply into your shoulders and upper back.

Now as a last step. Relax your neck and your throat...your jaw...and the rest of your face…….pure relaxation take over and grows……deeper…..even deeper.

Relax your entire body to the best of your ability and breathe two long. slow, deep breaths.

Now take two more deep breaths but this time exhale with a loud “SHEW”.
As in I am “SHEWING” my tension away.

Whenever you are ready, please bring yourself back to the room, open your eyes, and enjoy your fantastic Note From the Future.
Row.txt_description: This workshop encourages participants to think positively about their future by creating a postcard from their future self. This is a great workshop for those that feel stuck in their present situation.

Row.txt_code:
Touchstones co mmunity engagement workshop
 

What is Community Engagement?
To A Window Between Worlds (AWBW), community engagement means using the arts to bring awareness and move your community toward change, on both the individual and communal level. We encourage you to use ANY AWBW art workshop as a community engagement project. The Community Engagement project can be implemented to support the people you serve, your agency, your community, and the movement to empower and transform those impacted by violence and trauma.

Every agency can may have a different creative approach that might include focusing on community engagement through places of worship, to creating a vigil, holding an online teen exhibit campaign, displaying a student created Clothesline Project, to facilitating workshops for agency supporters and public officials, to hosting a community art project in a park in conjunction with a walk-a-thon, to collaborating with a local tattoo parlor to engage men. As always, just as these agencies have done, we encourage you to meet the needs of your community and trust your vision.

To plan your own Community Engagement event, please refer to AWBW's Community Engagement Planning Guide.

We encourage you to consider bringing AWBW's newest Community Engagement Project Touchstones, to your community!

How does AWBW support Collaborating Agencies to hold a Community Engagement event?
AWBW provides you with a comprehensive Community Engagement Planning Guide that includes the following:

  • Community Engagement Planning Tips to help guide you in holding a successful event.
  • Community Engagement Planning Worksheet to help you plan what you need and when you need it for the implementation process.
  • A $300 scholarship to be used toward community engagement expenses (can include art supplies, site fees, signage and up to $100 for reception and printing of community engagement announcement materials).
    • The Community Engagement Scholarship Application letter guidelines
    • The Community Engagement Scholarship Agreement
  • Tabling Tips and suggestions for your event
  • One-on-one support from the AWBW staff to help you every step of the way!
  • I CAN WE CAN online art gallery where you can upload images of the art, if you are creating/displaying Touchstones or I CAN WE CAN Hands, so it will live on well after your event!
  • Community Engagement Project Report Form to be completed two weeks after your Community Engagement event.
   
  
   
  
When is the best time to hold a Community Engagement Event?
A Community Engagement Event can be held at any time, but if you are looking to create a stronger impact you might want to hold your event during one of these awareness times:
February - Teen Dating Violence Awareness Month
              - V-Day
              - Black History Month
March     - Women's History Month
April       - Sexual Assault
              - Child Abuse Awareness Month
              - Denim Day
May        - Mental Health Awareness Month
June      - LGBT Pride Month
October - Domestic Violence Awareness Month
             - Bullying Prevention Awareness Month

We have had great success holding our events at local art walks and Farmer's Markets as it greatly helps to increase community attendance and awareness.

 
 
 
     

Where can I hold a Community Engagement event?
There are many venues that work well for a community engagement event and many locations are happy to host. You might want to consider one of the following:

 - Your Agency
- Open House
- Fundraising Events
- Local Libraries
 - Community Centers
- Schools
- Coffee Shops
- Banks
- Police Department
 - Chamber of Commerce
- Senior Centers
- Churches
- Restaurants
- Bookstores		 - Malls
- Art Galleries
- City Hall
- Non-profit community spaces (contact your local City Council member)
- An Office Building  		 
 
 
  

"Community Engagement Recommended" is now a strength category for the workshop search tool on the website! Consider the Community Engagement Recommended workshops below and those listed within this category for your project/event!

   

Touchstones - Participants in this workshop will take a creative window of time to create Touchstones to carry on their personal journey of transformation. The Touchstones project invites participants to carry their art as a personal and collective action for positive change, and to join a movement where art is used to support individuals and communities in their process of healing from trauma.

Clothesline Project - The Clothesline Project is a vehicle for adults affected by violence to express their emotions by decorating a shirt. The shirts are used to raise public awareness about the issue of domestic and sexual violence.

Helping Hands, Healing Hands - Community Mandala Project - To give participants an opportunity to think about what a “healthy and safe” community, home, or group looks like by making a hand collage to explore this question. These collage hands will become part of a larger hands mandala to inspire the greater community that together our hands can help and heal.

How I Broke the Cycle - This workshop combines a basic DV101 curriculum topic, the Cycle of Violence, and art as a healing tool. Participants will learn and take part in a discussion about the Cycle of Violence and will create a piece of art to reflect their own experiences with domestic violence and the Cycle.

I CAN WE CAN - Participants will take a creative window of time to find the "I CAN" that gives voice to their personal commitment to end abuse and share it in the community via the I CAN WE CAN Unite To End Abuse online community. This community engagement version of the project aims to break the silence and start a conversation during Domestic Violence Awareness Month. Artwork created can be used for art exhibits and community engagement events.

Introduction to Digital Storytelling - To provide Window's Leaders with a new way to support survivors and engage community through the art of storytelling utilizing digital media. A toolkit, resources and information about the benefits to survivors are included.The objective of this "workshop" is to provide Window's Leaders with a new way to support survivors and engage community through the art of storytelling utilizing digital media: Helping Hands Conference for Women Veterans: A Window Between Worlds Workshop and Exhibition; I hArt Teen Dating Violence Awareness Month: Workshop and Exhibition; I CAN WE CAN at One Billion Rising in Downtown Los Angeles 2015.

 
 
  I Can We Can paper hands mandala
for Santa Monica College Denim Day
 

Reclaiming Denim - A Denim Day Workshop - This workshop covers the history of Denim Day, defines sexual assault and empowers participants to know they can make change. This workshop also gives participants the opportunity to look at their own lives and make a personal commitment to protect themselves.

Red Flag Banners - In this workshop participants can learn how to identify red flags, or warning signs of a potentially abusive relationship. Participants will have an opportunity to identify the red flags they missed or ignored in past relationships and to notice the qualities they want in future relationships.

Stepping Stones - Participants write words, shapes, symbols on stones to remind them of what they are walking away from and walking toward in their lives.

Row.txt_code:
Touchstones
< span class="TextHeader2">Objective: Participants in this workshop will take a creative window of time to create Touchstones to carry on their personal journey of transformation. The Touchstones project invites participants to carry their art as a personal and collective action for positive change, and to join a movement where art is used to support individuals and communities in their process of healing from trauma.

Materials:
Minimum 3 clear round glass stones (approx.1 1/4") per participant (Stones of various sizes are available at craft stores, garden stores and online)
Card stock in various colors cut into circles in the same dimension as the stones (Circle hole punchers in various sizes are available at most craft stores)
Clear tacky glue bottles with a tip
Small sheer bags (Can be purchased at craft stores or online at Papermart.com)
Paper Towels and Wipes
Music for reflection and creative time
Options for artmaking:
Permanent Markers (Fine and/or extra fine)
Sharpie paint pens with extra fine point
Colored pencils
- white (Prismacolor brand ONLY) for dark colored paper
Ballpoint pens in various colors
Optional Journaling Pages:
Touchstones Journaling Worksheet
Touchstones Reflective Journaling Worksheet (English/Español)
  Workshop Flow/Timeframe:
Total Time: 60 minutes
Introduction:  5 min
Demonstration:  5 min
Relaxation:  5 min
Creation:  30 min
Closing Circle:  10 min
Share about online participation:  5 min
Website Gallery — See Workshop Tips for more information about how to use this workshop to connect the people you work with to the Touchstones movement.
     
      
           



































  
  
 Table set-up options 
About this project:
"Touchstones is a year-long art project created by Cathy Salser, artist, AWBW's Founder and Executive Director. This project calls upon the collective participation and co-creation of our community to create change. The art process not only includes the tangible stones themselves, but also the living, breathing, collective action of carrying our Touchstones into our lives, relationships, and community. The Touchstones workshop invites you to join A Window Between Worlds and survivors to embark upon this journey, both personally and as a part of the greater movement towards healing for survivors of trauma. The Touchstones project celebrates our collective energy and commitment to embrace this journey together to make a difference in our own lives and those of others."

Introduction:
"This workshop is an opportunity for you to notice, reflect and connect to the journey you are on or one you want to embark on. In art there are no limits; there is no right or wrong way so you are safe to explore and dream.   This is your creative window of time to create Touchstones. These Touchstones will be reminders of the intention you are setting into action. They are yours to carry with you on your own personal journey of growth or transformation (you can hand out small special bags so participants can have a place to carry the stones).

"This workshop is also part of a collective action of using art to keep us connected to our own truth, identity, strength or purpose as well as to others. By participating in this workshop you are part of an open circle of hands and hearts using art in the form of Touchstones, as a catalyst for change, both personally and collectively; a voice and intent to create safe, whole and resilient communities.

"What we are going to do today is to create Touchstones using simple symbols and words to support us on our own journeys, notice how we may want to carry them through the year ahead, and notice we are not alone in this journey. Our Touchstones can be reminders, serve as a compass or a tool for grounding and renewal. As you think about your Touchstones, please know that whatever supports you in your process and journey is what is most important to connect to. It may come up for you as a set of commitments, goals (new or old), values or principles you hold; it could be life lessons or reminders of your strengths or gifts. You determine the possibilities because these Touchstones are for you to use in your life path."
  
 Draw or write words or images to represent the Touchstone you want to share
  
 Add a pea-sized amount of the glue
on top of your drawing/words.
  
  Place your stone on top of the glue and press down. Wipe off any extra glue and let it dry.
 
Information About How to Create Your Touchstones:
  1. Using a writing utensil of your choice, write words, create images, symbols, or use colors on the circular paper to represent the Touchstone you would like to create as a marker to represent the steps in your journey.
  2. After you are done creating, add a pea-sized amount of the clear tacky glue on top of your creation.
  3. Place the flat side of your stone on top of the glue and press down.
  4. Wipe off any extra glue and let it dry.
Optional Journaling Handouts:
Print and use either of their journaling handouts provided in the material section of this workshop or create your own.

CENTER
Relaxation:
"Now, I invite you to sit comfortably in your chair with your feet placed on the floor. If you are comfortable, close your eyes or fix your gaze somewhere in the room. I will guide us as we take three relaxing breaths together. First, notice your breath as it goes in and out (– pause). Take another breath that goes down into your stomach, and let it out (- pause). And, finally take a third, deeper breath all the way down to your toes, and let it out (– pause). Feel your muscles relax and notice your heart. As you sit in this quiet space, notice that your breath holds the knowledge of your joy; it holds the knowledge of your pain. It knows what you dream of. It holds the knowledge of all your identities, your strength, you purpose. It knows all that you would like to be and how you would like to be seen and felt. And, it holds your truth. Your breath goes everywhere… it is part of everything that you are (longer pause).  
  
"Now, I invite you to join me in taking three last intentional breaths together. Breathe in and out. As you let this last breath out allow yourself to come back to the room with the intention of bringing back with you any thoughts, feelings, colors or images that represent your Touchstones that you will carry with you. When you are ready, begin to create."

CREATE
Creation Process:

  
"Create artwork that represents your Touchstone(s). As you create, remember to create your message in any way that feels right to you. You can create an image or symbol, use colors or words, or any combination you choose.
Listen to your heart - what words, shapes, colors will support you on your journey? Whether it seems too big to be possible or too small to be important, honor whatever comes to your mind. Keep in mind there is no wrong way to create."

In the last 5 minutes of the workshop, turn down the music and give a time warning. Ask for peoples attention for a moment as you invite them to consider the final piece of this workshop, and share the following, "when you are done creating, the final step will be to think about how will you use these stones, literally and figuratively, in your life. How do you want to carry them with you?"
  
  

CARRY
Closing:
Share in pairs - "How will you use these stones, literally and figuratively, in your life? How do you want to carry them with you?

"Finally, remember that the art is not just the stones themselves, but the action of using them in our lives, relationships and community. No matter where you go, these Touchstones can support you in staying connected to your intent, truth and purpose. They can be kept close at hand  - in pockets, under pillows, hanging on rear view mirrors - as reminders of your clarity, support, strength, and hope. In sharing our Touchstones, it connects us to others using their Touchstones, though our collective journeys of transformation."

CONNECT
"Who will support you on your journey? How will you get support? One option will be to share your Touchstones on a website where others are doing the same. You might find that putting them out in the world may support you and that your stones may support others on they journey." Share about website and offer opportunities to help participants add their Touchstones to the website.

The Touchstones project invites participants to carry their art as a personal and collective action for positive change, and to join a movement where art is used to support individuals and communities in their process of healing from trauma.
