&ldq uo;Possiblities for Teens” workshop participants
with their Inside/Outside creations.
 
  


About this Project:
This project was brought to us by Karen Akamine who was trained at the Armory Center for the Arts in Pasadena. The concept was adapted into this teen workshop by the AWBW staff.

Objective:
To express the self that you let people see on the outside and explore the self that is on the inside, underneath.

    




Inside/Outside creation (closed,
opening, and open all the way)
from the “Possibilities for
Teens” Leaders’ Workshop.
   
    



  


Materials:
9"X12" Colored construction paper
Chalk pastels
Paper towels
Pens and writing paper
(Option: teens could use their journals)
independent project handout (for individual workshops) (click here for handout)
Alternative variations: This workshop could be done using collage instead of pastels. Plus if you are doing collage, you could do it on boxes or paper bags instead of construction paper.

Timeframe:
Total Time: 1 hr
Intro/Ground rules: 5 min
Check-in: 10 min
Journal Writing: 5 min
Creation: 30 min
Closing Circle: 10 min

Age Range: 3 and up

Ratio:
This workshop is geared for teens, so the ratio can be whatever the leader is comfortable with.

     





Door Fold
  Triangle Fold
 
Diamond Fold Open ... and Closed

    
Here are some examples of

ways to fold the paper so

there’s an inside and an

outside. Encourage the

teens to be creative in

their folding.
     Double Door Fold

Space Setup:
It helps things go smoothly when you have the supplies prepared and set up in advance. Try various folds (see illustrations below) so it will
be easy to show the teens some possiblilities. Use the pastels to make an example yourself. That way, you can make sure the supplies are ready and you’ll notice if there’s anything else needed.

Welcome:
When possible, try to individually welcome each teen and let them know you’re glad they’re there. One-on-one contact can help them get connected and feel safe and comfortable enough to truly use their Windows time for themselves.

  



Inside/Outside created with a
diamond fold: closed (above)
and open (below).

 

 
  

Introduction:
“This art time is a special ‘window of time’ for each of you. The project we are doing is called Inside/Outside. It is a chance to explore the ‘you’ that people see on the outside, and the ‘you’ that you know is on the inside. We will be using folded paper and pastels to create our inside and outside selves in shapes and colors.” (Optional: show samples.)

Ground Rules:
“For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? (See Ground Rules for teen workshops—attached.) Are there any other Ground Rules you’d like to add?”

Check-in:
“Before we start the art, we’ll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art.” (This is a time to reassure anyone who’s scared of art that it’s fine, and to tell anyone who “hates” art that’s fine too. Remind them that they don’t have to do it. They can just watch if they want to. If they are given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in, even if they say they’re just going to watch. If they don’t want to say anything for “check-in,” let them know that’s fine too.)

Journaling Warm-up:
(Note: The journaling is optional. If you feel your group would be better off just diviing in with the project, that’s fine too.)

"Let’s start with a journaling warm-up. Divide a paper into two columns. On the left side, write ‘Inside’ and on the right side, write ‘Outside.’ Fill the left side of the page with any words that describe how you feel on the inside, and fill the right side of the page with any words that describe the ‘you’ that people see on the outside."

Creation:
"Now pick a piece of construction paper and fold it to so it has an inside and an outside. Think about the outside of you, and then start with the outside of your paper. On the outside are you bright or dark? Are you sharp or soft? Are you foggy or clear? With the pastels, use shapes and colors to draw how you are on the outside. When you are ready, move to the inside. Open up your paper and begin to think about how you are on the inside. Are you bright or dark? Are you one color or many colors? Are you soft or rough? Use pastels to draw shapes and colors that show the inside ‘you’ on the inside of your paper. When you are finished, take some time to write any words that go with your drawing." You might want to encourage the teens to take a moment after they finish to think about how they might want to take care of themselves inside and outside.


 
 
 Inside / Outside creation
with diamond fold.
  

Optional Closing Feedback Exercise:
(10 minutes before the workshop ends) Pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You can even take them to copy and return them the next week. I think you will be pleased. (AWBW would love to receive copies too!)

Closing Circle:
Give each teen an opportunity to share what she/he created and talk about what it means and how it felt to make. Just like the Check-in Circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.
Row.txt_description: Opportunity to express the self that we let people see on the outside and explore the self that is on the inside, underneath.

Row.txt_code:
Touchstones
Objective: Participants are invited to create Touchstones as their safe place for their wants and needs. They can carry these with them in their pockets, backpacks, or secret places and hold them when they need them!

Materials:
  • Minimum 3 clear round glass stones (approx.1 1/4") per participant (Stones of various sizes are available at craft stores, garden stores and online)
  • Card stock in various colors cut into circles in the same dimension as the stones (Circle hole punchers in various sizes are available at most craft stores)
  • Clear tacky glue bottles with a tip
  • Small sheer bags (Can be purchased at craft stores or online at Papermart.com)
  • Paper towels and wipes
  • Music for reflection and creative time
Options for Artmaking:
  • Permanent Markers (fine and/or extra fine)
  • Sharpie paint pens with extra fine point
  • Colored pencils - white/silver for dark colored paper
  • Ballpoint pens in various colors
Timeframe:
Introduction: 5 min
Demonstration: 5 min
Relaxation: 5 min
Creation: 35 min
Closing Circle: 10 min

Total: 1 hour		         Age Range:
6 years and up

  
  
  
 
  
  
  Table set-up options
  
Introduction:
Some of us like to keep our art in our pockets, under our pillows, in our backpacks, we may even hang it on our bedroom walls or on the fridge. During Windows art time you get to choose what you create. Today's project is called Touchstones. Touchstones are meant to be carried with you or kept in a special way. The reason we keep touchstones is because they are meant to remind us of important things and by keeping them close, they are there for us to touch when we need them.

"You could think of your Touchstones as a compass that helps to guide your way once you know where you want to go. Any questions so far?"

"You can also make Touchstones that will remind you that you are strong, special and loved. If you can remember you are strong, special and loved it can help you when you are feeling sad, mad, or frustrated, and get you back on track to the way you want to live your life."

Window of Time
"Before you start, remember that this is your Window of Time. It is a safe space just for you. This is your chance to get messy, be silly, imagine, and create whatever is in your heart. I'm going to be demonstrating how you can create your stones, but you can make yours however feels right to you. You get to choose how you want to participate."

 

     
 
   
     
  Draw or write words or images to represent the Touchstone you want to share.   
     
     
 
Add a pea-sized amount of the glue
on top of your drawing/words.		   
     
     
 Place your stone on top of the glue and press down. Wipe off any extra glue and let it dry.   
     
Demonstration:
Demonstrate each of the following steps and check for understanding along the way.
  1. Using a writing utensil of your choice, write words, create images, symbols, or use colors on the circular paper to represent the Touchstone you would like to create as a marker to represent the steps in your journey.
  2. After you are done creating, add a pea-sized amount of the clear tacky glue on top of your creation.
  3. Place the flat side of your stone on top of the glue and press down.
  4. Wipe off any extra glue and let it dry.
Relaxation:
"Before we begin I want us to take a moment for us to listen to our thoughts, feeling, dreams, and wishes. We will do this by sitting quietly and looking inside ourselves. If you'd like, I invite you to sit comfortably in your chair with your feet placed on the floor and your hands on your lap. Now close your eyes or if you prefer, put your head down or you can look at your hands. I am going to guide you as we take three long breaths together, and I'm going to ask for all us to stay quiet so we can hear our breath. Breathe in slowly and breathe out slowly. Take your first breath to the bottom of your lungs and let it out slowly. Take your next breath and try to fill your stomach with air. And take a last breath all the way down to your feet and let it out. Sit quietly and let the sound of the music calm you or notice your breath as it goes in and out of your body.

"As you sit quietly, think about the Touchstones you are about to create. How can these stones help you in your life?

"Remember, this workshop is a chance for you to think about who you are and what you need to feel happy, safe, and loved. In Windows there are no limits; there is no right or wrong way so you are free to explore and dream. What positive message can your stone share? How can this stone help you in taking steps toward your future? Whether it seems too big to be possible or too small to be important, be true to whatever comes to your mind.

 
Creation:
"On the paper circles, create artwork that shares your Touchstones. As you create, remember to show your message in any way that feels right to you. You can create an image or symbol, use colors, words, or any combination. You get to choose what your Touchstones look like because you will be the one to use and carry them."

"Once you are done creating, I encourage you to think about where you can keep this stone to remind you of your journey and all the people, places you have touched - and will continue to touch - throughout your life. How and where can you use these stones in your life?"

 

Closing:
"No matter where you go, these Touchstones can help remind you to carry the experience of your art with you.

"Whether or not you have these stones with you in your mind, or in your heart, they are an important celebration of your life!"

If participants feel comfortable enough to do so, they can share:

  • Whatever you would like about your Touchstones and how represent your life
  • How it felt to create your Touchstones
  • How you want to use your Touchstones

Note: Remind participants that they can carry their stones in a special place like their pockets or backpacks. If they choose to do so, they can hold them in their hands when they need them to help them feel safe, happy, strong, and loved.
Row.txt_description: Participants are invited to create Touchstones as their safe place for their wants and needs. They can carry these with them in their pockets, backpacks, or secret places and hold them when they need them!

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give participants the opportunity to create a Shrinky Dink sun catcher made of hearts with positive and self-nurturing words for themselves. This becomes a visual reminder of how special and loving we are and how it is so i mportant to send loving messages to our own hearts.

Sample of a finished sun catcher
Materials:
Shrinky Dink (rough and ready type)
Heart Template
Permanent Markers
Color pencils
Pencil sharpeners
Small paper plates (to collect pencil shavings)
Plain white paper plates
Hole punchers
Scissors
Ribbon or yarn
Beads
Toaster oven

Heart shapes should be about 4”. Note: anything smaller than 3” will be difficult to read or see due to shrinkage of the material when it cooks.
Click here to see template

Setting the table for Loving Heart Sun Catchers
Age Range:
5 years old to Adult

Time Frame:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Relaxation: 5 minutes
Creation: 1 hour and 15 minutes
Closing Circle: 5 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour and 30 minutes

Workshop Preparation:
Set table with all the materials. If time permits you can have the shrinky dink hearts pre-cut. Younger children may have difficulty cutting their own hearts, so depending on the age levels in your group, you will probably need to pre-cut the shapes and pre-hole-punch each heart. Make enough for each child to make 5 or more. The center of the plates should also be precut and divided in three for the base of the mobile. You will also want to help the younger clients to punch the holes around the inside edge of the plate and add a hole on both sides at the top for a way to hang the finished mobile.

Introduction:
Today we are going to take this time to nurture ourselves by thinking about the things that makes us unique and special, as well as the loving messages we can tell our hearts. We are going to make mobiles made of hearts with positive and self-nurturing words that can catch the sunlight when we hang them in a window. They can become a visual reminder of how special and loving we are and how it is so important to send loving messages to our own hearts! These loving messages can become like the sunlight shining and warming our lives and bringing light into each day, especially when we need it most.

 
Shrinky Dink hearts full of loving words
 
Relaxation:
If you are comfortable you can close your eyes and put your hands on your heart. Take a deep breath in and a deep breath out, letting your whole body relax as you breathe out. Remind yourself that this is a special time just for you.

Think about what your heart would tell you if it could speak. If you remain still can you hear any special message your heart has? If you have negative thoughts let them pass and leave room for good thoughts and words to come to you. What kind of things would your heart tell you to do to take care of yourself? How can you love and take care of your heart?

Think about the many things that make you special, the things that you love about who you are. It could be something simple like the way you make people laugh or how you care for others. Try not to judge yourself if you can't think of something right away, it will come. Think about the loving and nurturing things you could tell your heart. What would it like to hear? How can you tell your heart how much you love and appreciate it? How much you love and appreciate yourself? Imagine your heart surrounded by loving words. Think about all of the loving messages you can tell yourself and imagine them shining within you.


Decorating the shrinky dinks with loving words
Loving words and phrases for yourself and your heart
 
Cutting the edge of the plate to create the mobile
 
Punching holes for the mobile
 
Tying the ribbons for the mobile
Creation:
Now open your eyes if you had them closed and select the hearts on the table that you want to use to create your Shinky Dinks.

(If you haven't used Shrink Dinks with your group before you may want to demonstrate how to color on the rough side with the color pencils for the background and how to use darker colors for the words. You can show a sample of the size they become after they shrink in the oven).

Step 1:
Start by tracing your heart template onto the Shrinky Dink (or use the pre-cut heart Shrinky Dinks, if they are available). You may choose any of the colors on the table. Begin to create the design that will fill in your heart (be sure to draw on the rough side of the plastic). Remember the words we thought about? Use those words to write kind and loving messages to yourself on each of the hearts. It can be one-word reminders or entire sentences. They can even be secret messages that only you will know the meaning of.

Step 2:
When you are finished coloring, cut out your heart shapes with scissors (if the hearts were not pre-cut).

Step 3:
Use the hole punch to place a hole at the top of each heart so that we can hang it to create your sun catcher. If you need help, please ask for it.

Step 4:
Now the hearts are ready for baking. Place the Shrinky Dink on a flat metal tray and place inside the toaster oven. Bake at 300 degrees until Shrinky Dink has completely flattened (about one minute). Watch the amazing transformation! Remove your Shrinky Dink and allow it to cool.

Step 5:
Now your hearts are ready to be hung and decorated with ribbon or yarn. Thread the ribbon through the hole in the Shrinky Dink, and add beads if desired.

Step 6:
Now it is time to create the mobile. Use the hole puncher to punch holes around the inside edge of the cut-out paper plate, and add a hole on both sides at the top for a way to hang the finished mobile.

Add each of the ribbons and hearts to the holes on the plate by threading them through the holes. Tie a knot (or series of knots) at the top to secure the ribbon. Keep adding the ribbons, being sure to vary the length. Add another ribbon to the top two holes to create a method of hanging the mobile. Now your Loving Heart Sun Catcher will be ready to hang!

 
Hanging words on your Loving Heart Sun Catcher 
Closing:
Have the group share how it felt to create sun catchers full of loving and nurturing messages for themselves. Encourage them to hang their mobiles in a window so that they can catch the sunlight and remind them of how special and loving they are.

If we let the sun shine in we can see how beautiful and special we are. It is so important to send loving messages to our own hearts!
Row.txt_description: To give participants the opportunity to create a shrinky dink sun catcher made of hearts with positive and self nurturing words for themselves. This becomes a visual reminder of how special and loving we are and how it is so important to send loving messages to our own hearts.

Row.txt_code:
Workshop Modifications:
 
 
Creating Balance Key Tags - Participants explore how to be more in balance in their everyday lives through the creation of Shrinky Dink key-tags that act as daily reminder of items they wish to work on.

Creating a Safe Place - (Create as Touchstones variation) Through exploring images of safety, this workshop can help participants feel a sense of their own power by inviting them to create a safe place within themselves.

 
 
Journey Footprints - Participants create collages that validate their unique journey through domestic violence using the outline of their own feet as the template of the collage.

Life Clocks - You Decide - This workshop gives participants an opportunity to decide and honor what is important to them and explore how they want to spend their time by designing a clock.

   
My Footprints - Allows children to validate and express feelings about their unique journey, what they are learning and where they want to go in their lives, by creating drawings or collages using outlines of their own feet. C

My Time - To create your very own clock that will show how we want to fill our days so we can have the life we want. C
   

My Treasure Box - (Create as vessel for Touchstones) In this workshop, participants have the opportunity to recognize what they treasure in themselves and their life by exploring their blessings, dreams, beliefs, friendships, hopes, and and creating a treasure boxes to hold them and keep them safe.

   

My Wishing Well - (Create as vessel for Touchstones) To help children make resolutions for the new year by deciding what they would wish for in their lives (other than material things) and creating a personal wishing well. C

 
 

New Year Wishing Well - (Create as vessel for Touchstones) This workshop uses the soothing and often cathartic exercise of working with Sculpey clay to create stones for a new year's Wishing Well, which they will also create!

   

Pearls of Wisdom - This workshop is designed to help survivors recognize their personal strength, and uses the metaphor of a "pearl" as a treasure that form inside an oyster in response to an irritant. Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength and wisdom as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence.

   

Personal Needs Flower - (Create as Touchstones variation) This workshop provides an opportunity for participants to notice their personal needs by creating a flower where each petal represents one need. They will begin to see the many layers of needs—physical, emotional and spiritual—and to honor all these layers.

 

   

Putting Myself Back Together - Through writing and coloring emotions on a person outline made up of puzzle pieces, participants are able to reflect on their current emotions and where they feel these emotions in their body. Through journaling and reflecting on their present emotions and envisioning what they wish to feel in the future, they will begin to deepen the process of "putting themselves back together" after all that they have been through.

   

Putting Myself Back Together - Allows children and youth to name and identify feelings and notice where they hold feelings in their own body. This can be an opportunity to help normalize the myriad of emotions youth and children are feeling and give them a way to begin to process them. C

   

River Stories - (Create as Touchstones variation) Through visual art (drawing) and embodied art (movement), participants are invited to use the metaphor of a river to acknowledge their past, notice their resilience, and honor their present strength.

   

River Stories - (Create as Touchstones variation) Through visual art (drawing) and embodied art (movement), participants are invited to use the metaphor of a river to acknowledge their past, notice their resilience, and honor their present strength. C

 
 

Safe Rocks - (Create as Touchstones variation) Gives the children the chance to think about when they felt secure, and to create something solid as an expression of that safe feeling. C

 
 

Stepping Stones - Participants write words, shapes, symbols on stones to remind them of what they are walking away from and walking toward in their lives.

   
Treasure Boxes - (Create as vessel for Touchstones) The purpose of this workshop is for children to create a treasure box of their own in which they can store things that are valuable to them in order to keep them safe. These can be actual items, notes, or symbolic reminders. C

   
Wish Boxes - (Create as vessel for Touchstones) Wish Boxes are designed to guide participants and set their minds for their bright new future. It is a perfect project for before the New Year, but anytime will do.

   
Wish Boxes - (Create as vessel for Touchstones) Gives participants an opportunity to enjoy exploring their wishes as they layer colors and pictures onto their own personal box. End product is a private place to store notes and treasures with a feeling of safety. C


Self-care variation
Row.txt_description: Touchstones can lend themselves to many different variations, modifications, and additions to pre-existing workshops. Use these suggestions to create a collective piece of art that survivors can use and take with them.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give children an opportunity to express some of the rage they feel toward the batterer in a safe environment and to overcome the feelings of guilt and self-blame.

Materials:
Blank paper
Toi let paper
Crayons
Markers
Pens

Time Frame:
10 minutes: opening circle
40 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children

Space Set-up:
Have a quiet place where the children can sit comfortably on cushions or pieces of carpet, and table space for the writing part of the activity.

Have all the materials set up on the table before the group begins so that there is no distraction. If possible, space the chairs around the table so that each child can have privacy while writing his or her personal thoughts and feelings.

Opening Circle:
Play soothing music in the background and have the children do deep breathing exercises from the Breathwork section of the Children's Manual.

Guide them in focusing on their feelings now and how they felt being in the home with the batterer. Have the participants think about the things they would have liked to say to the batterer but were afraid to voice.

Some children may become very anxious or agitated with the memories. Be watchful throughout this workshop to help children process the feelings that come up.

Activity:
Once the children are ready to write, have them move to the table. On sheets of toilet paper, allow the children to write down hurtful things that were said to them and the things they would have liked to say. Begin the exercise with, “I didn’t like it when...” Be sure to tell the participants that they do not have to share these messages with anyone.

When they have finished writing, allow them to crumple up and throw away the sheets of hurtful words. They may choose to flush these messages out of their lives (the whole group may literally stand around the toilet to flush away all of the hurtful messages together). If they would like, the children can keep the sheets of what they would have liked to say, maybe to store in their treasure boxes. This can be very empowering to be able to verbalize the hurt and anger. State that this is a time when he or she can let go of the anger that goes along with the message if he or she is ready. Allow participants to share their feelings and/or messages with the group if they would like.

Closing Circle:
During the last 10 minutes, allow participants to discuss how they felt. Was the activity empowering or did it make them feel powerless? Discuss alternative methods to letting go of anger in safe ways where they do not hurt themselves or others. Discuss how everyone has the right to be safe and to live a life without fear.

Have participants stand in a circle holding hands. They can take turns saying: “I deserve to be safe.” Then the person talking should squeeze the next person’s hand to let him or her know it is his or her turn. Young children really enjoy this closing activity.

Variations for age levels:
With young children who may have difficulty working with paper, have them work with clay. Discuss what makes them angry, especially when Mom and her partner are fighting. Allow the children to pound on the clay and state that they can use their anger to be creative and make something.

Toward the end of the workshop, show the Video 10 Things to Do Instead of Hitting if your shelter has a copy (available through Sunburst Communications: 1-800-431-1934). Talk about alternatives to hitting. At a later date, the children can paint their creations.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives children an opportunity to express some of the rage they feel toward the batterer in a safe environmnet and to overcome the feelings of guilt and self-blame.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 67

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
My objective is to give children an opportunity to have a voice and to feel safe. This workshop gives them a chance to be with a grown-up who provides an environment where that safety can happen, a grown-up who can sa y “I know what’s been happening in your life and it’s safe to talk about it here.” The aim is also for the children to know they have the capacity inside of them to create healing images.

 
  
Materials:
Safety Picture-Making (for children under seven):
Non-toxic marker
Construction paper (white, lavender, light grey, light brown)
Permanent marker (for name writing)
Large envelopes for the artwork to go home in
Clear contact paper (optional)

Collage-Making (for children over seven):
Glue stick (one for each child)
 
 Materials
Appropriate magazines
Construction paper
Scissors (one for each child)
Large envelopes
Clear contact paper (optional)

Time Format:
15 minutes: Opening circle
15 minutes: Relaxation and focus time
30 minutes: Creation time
20 minutes: Closing circle
10 minutes: Clean-up time, goodbyes

Total time: 1 1/2 hours

Space Set-up:
For the Opening Circle and Relaxation, it is ideal for each child to be on the floor on their own mat or piece of carpet. This way they have a defined space, a boundary for their body in which to relax and feel safe. The creating should take place at a table nearby. All materials should be set up and ready to go before the children arrive at a table or some place away from your opening circle so they aren’t at the table and they aren’t tempted to play with the art supplies before creation time. After the relaxation, the children can move right to the table to begin creating.

Opening Circle:
Introduce the theme - what does it mean to feel safe? “We’re going to talk about being safe. How do you feel safe? Everyone will get a turn to talk. It’s OK if you don’t feel like saying anything because sometimes that doesn’t feel safe.” As the children speak in a circle, let them go as fast as they want. The circle usually goes much quicker than it would with adults.

Dream Pillows:
For young children it can be helpful if they have something to hold on to as they imagine their safe place. They need something to do with their hands. It’s too difficult to focus for and just listen for a long time, especially for kids who have been abused.

You can use stuffed animals but I like to make “dream pillows” that they can keep. Dream pillows are small bean bags I make and fill with rice. All the pillows are exactly the same size, shape, and color. I scent them with geranium and lavender essence oil. I explain at the beginning that they get to take their dream pillow with them when they go. It is helpful to carry something nurturing with them, a reminder of having that safe time. The dream pillow is the reminder they can carry with them.



 Photograph from Children of Many Lands
Relaxation and Focus:
1. Pass out the dream pillows
2. Help each child choose a place to rest
3. Wiggle down exercise
Facilitator begins:
a: Wiggle your toes, now take a deep breath, then relax those toes
b. Wiggle your legs, now take a deep breath, then relax those legs
c. Wiggle your bottom, now take a deep breath, then relax your bottom
d. Wiggle your tummy, now take a deep breath and relax your tummy
e. Wiggle your shoulders, now take a deep breath and relax your shoulders
f. Wiggle your arms and hands, now take a deep breath, then relax them
g. Last one now, wiggle your eyes, now take a deep breath, then relax your eyes (eye closing is optional, it might not feel safe for some kids)
4. If you don’t have any pillows, you could begin with, “Now let’s start by giving ourselves a nice warm hug...” and continue, "Now think of something quiet. You might be floating on a cloud or swimming in the sea or walking in a beautiful forest or lying on bunches of soft pillows or moving your body. Any special place you feel quiet and safe. Think about what that place looks like. What does it smell like? Who is there? What does it feel like? Is it a place you have never been before? Is it in your imagination? It can be special and safe just for you. You make it safe, you make all the magic and power in this safe place. When you are ready, quietly go to the table and make your safe picture. When you are doing your drawing, this is a no-talking time.”



 Child drawing her Safe Place

 
 Child drawing their Safe Place
Creation:
Children ages seven and under draw their safe place using colors that feel safe. Children ages seven and up will create a safe place collage.
For older kids you can use this handout, “Safe Place” Handout (optional - click here for handout)

Closing Circle:
This is the time children can talk about their drawings/collages. Some children may choose not to talk about their work. That is okay because it is very important that each child gets to choose what they want to say about their creation. It can be a very private thing and needs to be respected by adults. After each child has their turn, give them a "special envelope" in which they can save their art and keep it private and safe.

As each child has a turn to share (or not) it is important to phrase what you say very carefully. When adults make judgments or labels about children's art work, they learn not to trust art. It could be a deep blow to their self-esteem and damage how they feel about themselves and their art.
 
 Part of a child's Safe Place

Most importantly, use a pleasant voice tone and be authentic when you respond to each child! Children know when adults are not being true to their feelings, especially children who have been a part of domestic violence. These children have a special radar that makes them hyper-sensitive to adults. This is a defensive tactic that may have kept them safe in the past. Now we have a window of time with them to show that adults can be safe and authentic.

Also, be aware of what other children say. They may need verbal support from you in order not to crush another child's work. Remember some of these kids may not be used to hearing praise or non-judgmental comments before now. For example:

Do not say inappropriate statements like:
--What's that supposed to be?
--Is that a dog, tree, cat, etc.?
--That's a nice, pretty, ugly, little, dark, bright, etc.
--I like that (you could not like it too)
--Is that all, you could have done better.
--Do it over or try again later, or that was not the assignment, etc.

Do say appropriate comments to children like:
--Tell me about your safe picture/collage
--Did you choose colors that make you feel safe?
--I really see how hard, diligently, long, you worked on your creation.
--Wow! (smile)
--Oh my! (smile)
--Awesome, brilliant, fantastic! (if you choose these adjectives, be fair and careful to say it
to every child).

Clean-up/Goodbyes!
Row.txt_description: Offers the children a chance to know they have the capacity to create healing images. Participants focus on the meaning and feeling of safety and create images that impart this feeling on the covers of their journals.
Row.txt_notes: Children's manual pg. 41
Row.txt_tips:
Note to Facilitator:
If you have access to a laminator, it would be great to seal their art work. If not, clear contact paper works great.

Using glitter glue and stickers can also be fun for the children.

Give the option of including safe people in the picture or collage.

Row.txt_code:
Sample doll collaged to illustrate boundaries
Objective:
To help class members become aware of their personal boundaries.  Offers time to consider personal boundaries by creating collages of people with and without boundaries and focusing on framing the picture in a way that represents a healthy personal boundary.

Materials:
Cardboard
Magazines
Scissors
Glue

Process Overview:
Based on Guilford's Divergent-Productive Questioning which encourages creativity, four questions are commonly used: quantity (producing many ideas), viewpoint (role-playing to develop insight into others' views/positions), forced association (metaphoric thinking and looking for new insights by comparing unlike items) and reorganization (rearranging facts, parts, whole to see events/problems in a different way).

Session One utilizes quantity, viewpoint, and forced association. Class members are asked a succession of boundary type questions, followed by an activity and an art project.

Question:
How many different kinds of boundaries can you think of? (Quantity)

Give examples of a variety of boundaries (door frames, body, and school). Have them take two to three minutes to write their thoughts down and then split them into either pairs or triads to share their answers. The class members may be more comfortable talking amongst themselves, since a trust level has not yet been developed between the facilitators and class members. The group comes back together to share their responses. They are encouraged to produce as many examples of boundaries as possible. If personal boundaries do not come up, question the class members to elicit desired responses. Move into the next step by using a rhetorical question such as, "How might a person feel who had their boundaries invaded? Let's look at art done by people who had their boundaries ignored."

Question:
Pretend you are the artist. What do you think the artist is saying about boundaries? (Viewpoint)

Show pictures created by survivors of childhood abuse. As each picture is shown, ask for their reactions from the viewpoint of the artist. Allowing the class members to take the viewpoint of the artist presents an opportunity for the creatively-gifted to express insight that can be positively reinforced. It also encourages others to express different views not commonly shared. Follow up responses with open-ended questions. Possible areas may be: Why do we do what we do? What about the oppositional feelings of the person? How might healthy boundaries be achieved? Depending on the time and group a five to ten minute break can be taken.

Warm-up Activity:
One person stands while another person walks toward the standing person. The standing person says stop when the walking person reaches the boundary of their space.

In a mixed group, pair females with females and males with males. Have one partner stand. The other partner walks towards the standing person two separate times. A third time the person standing closes her/his eyes while their partner walks towards them. By shutting their eyes, they realize they have boundaries they cannot see. Then the partners switch. If time allows, switch to opposite sex partners and repeat the exercise. Class members are generally surprised at the variety of distances between partners and the difference in boundaries when their eyes are open or closed, and the contrast when they are matched with partners of the opposite sex. Discuss the differences, why they occur and what they might mean.

Question:
How are boundaries like lies? (Forced Association)

Shift into this question by giving examples of how boundaries are like lies (both are confining, threatening or protecting.) Forced association questions allow the creatively-gifted to think with more insight. Other class members may piggy-back on ideas generated by peers such as: "Lies keep us from others, but also keep us inside ourselves," and "Lies and boundaries are like the light-switch. You can turn them on and off." The class members have now talked about boundaries, experienced their boundaries, and internalized ideas concerning them. It is time to express boundaries.

Art Project Creation:
Each person creates a picture of how a person would feel without boundaries, or how a person who invades boundaries would feel.

Class members may choose a variety of ways to express themselves. They may do collages, drawings, paintings, or writings. It is important to offer a variety of media for expression. If a class member presents an unusual method of expressing his/her boundaries, encourage all of their ideas. Allowing each class member options develops trust and higher levels of creativity. Encouraging class members to defer judgment of their art and the process assists a truer representation of the class members' emotions and their creativity to emerge.

A frame could be used around the picture to establish a visual boundary.

If the class member finishes the first art project, have them make a second picture showing a person with healthy boundaries.

Resources:
Resources used were Guilford's Divergent-Productive Questions (Clasen 1995), Counseling the Gifted and Talented (Silverman, 1993), Multiple Intelligences in the Classroom: The Foundations of the Theory of Multiple Intelligences. (Armstrong, 1994) and Sidney Parnes' Creative Problem Solving (Maker, 1982).
Row.txt_description: Offers time to consider personal boundaries by creating collages of people with and without boundaries and focusing on framing the picture in a way that represents a healthy personal boundary.

Brings participants' awareness toward themselves, to see how they are defined on the outside and who they are on the inside. They get a chance to visualize how they would like to be, giving a more empowered focus on who they are, and who they see themselves becoming. End product is a decorated box that serves as a reminder of their different roles as well as a private place.

Row.txt_notes: Web-NO. TO DO: Rewrite T-Shirts and Pillow Cases workshop.
Web-NO. TO DO: Rewrite Spirit Puppets workshop.

Row.txt_code:
Rose Curtis with a sample Comfort Journa
Objective:
To provide participants with a window of time to think about what brings them comfort and nurturance and to collage related images onto a journal. The end product is a journal that can be used as an ongoing reference and source of comfort.

Materials:
Spiral binders or sketch books
Cover stock paper (in various colors and textures if possible)
Cardboard or poster board (for front and back of covers)
Construction paper or 20 lb copy paper (to glue onto the bound pages and then collage on top of)
Magazines (such as Home Beautiful, Arizona Highway, Sunset, Glamour, Bath and Body, Garden Botanica or Red Rose Collection)
Collage material (ribbon, scraps of fabric, greeting cards, calendar pictures, etc.)
Markers and metallic pens
Calligraphy pens
Crayons
Glue stiks
Scissors

Opening:
“This is a window of time to think about what brings comfort to you. The more we are able to nurture ourselves the easier it becomes to love ourselves. As we are guided through the relaxation try to let images of comfort flow through your mind. Scenes of peaceful places, bubbles floating through the air, scents of flowers, notes of windchimes tinkling... whatever sounds, scents or scenes comfort you, let them wash over you.”

Technical Demonstration:
“What we will be doing today is starting our own Comfort Journal. The plan is to have your cover done today and if you have time, to fill a few pages of your journal to get you started. “Comfort Journals are a way to comfort yourself when you are feeling blue, sad, lonely, and even when you are feeling good. We all need extra nurturing everyday. I hope you find working and looking through your comfort journal is like giving yourself a warm hug!”

Note: As a leader, if you feel comfortable showing examples, this can be a good idea because if your audience is new to the idea of self comfort they may need some examples just to get them started.





 
  Pages from a Comfort Journal

Guided Relaxation:
Speak slowly feeling very relaxed....

“Make yourself comfortable. If you are sitting, it is good to sit with your back straight, your feet flat on the floor and your hands lying loosely in your lap.

“Take a deep breath and exhale slowly....if it feels safe for you....close your eyes. This is a time for you to breath in love.... and breath out tension. In your mind, let comforting colors wash over you.

“Let’s start with your toes, picture them curling in soft sand....now move up to your calves and feel them gently relax....relax your thighs and feel the sun gently warming your body.

“Breathe in deeply and become aware of any holding you are doing in your body. Calmly release the tension....breathing in love.... breathing out tension....let your stomach relax....feel yourself relaxing more deeply.

“Move your awareness to your shoulders....feel the weight lifting off as if someone very kind was massaging your muscles....you feel the knots smoothing out as you smell your favorite fragrance drifting by....if there is any tension left...imagine it flowing down your arms....through your fingers.... slipping down onto the floor and seeping down into the earth.

“Relax your throat....relax your chin....relax your jaws.... breathing in love ....breathing out tension. Relax your scalp.... relax your eyelids....imagine your whole body totally relaxed.

“Now, move your awareness into a very deep place inside of you....Let images of comfort come into your mind....notice if any particular colors come to mind.... notice if any fragrance floats in.... open all your senses .....are there notes of music that relax you? ....let you mind wander....are there special places that feel safe for you? ....are there plants, flowers or perhaps tall grasses to lie in?......let yourself be whimsical.....

“Just think about what makes you feel good and start to gently bring yourself back into the room.... holding onto the peace....breath in love.....and when you are ready, gently open your eyes and begin to go through the materials in front of you....and begin to create comfort...”



 A Comfort Journal
Allow at least 30 minutes for the creation of the Comfort Journal Cover. Participants who complete their cover early may explore the first pages of their journal, filling it with whatever brings them comfort (see “Future Comfort Ideas” below).

Closing:
Ask the group to share their creations and how it felt for them to totally focus on comfort. Ask them if they are inspired to add to their journal and if they would like to share their ideas for future pages.

Future Comfort Ideas:
These are ideas of what to put inside your Comfort Journal...
Love Notes to yourself
Love Notes from others
Comfort Letters from friends
Affirmations
Inspirational Sayings
Photographs
Pressed Flowers/Leaves
Prayers
Poetry
Pictures of items that comforted you as a child i.e. teddy bears or dolls
Whatever is positive, loving, nurturing, and comforting to you, save it for your Comfort Journal!!!

Special Thanks:
I received inspiration from and give credit to The Women’s Comfort Book by Jennifer Louden.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants a window of time to think about what brings them comfort and nurturance and to collage related images onto a journal. End product is a journal that can be used as an ongoing reference and source of comfort.

Row.txt_code:
"Inner Me" Artist: Rose Curtis
 Objective:
To learn more about yourself by going within and discovering your inner self through creating a portrait!

Introduction:
This workshop will assist older children and teens to look inside and discovering more about their inner-self! We are used to looking at our outer selves, our looks, our clothes, our appearance, the image we try to portray!This workshop gives us an opportunity to go to a deeper level and get more in touch with our inner-self. You will have 3 options of materials, you can also combine them.

  Materials:   
 Timeframe:    
  Large Head & Body Template Introduction: 5 min
  Small Template Opening Circle:10 min
  11x14 Thick white paper (recommended)
 Journaling/Sharing: 20 min 
Technical: 5 min
  Journal Questions (You may want to print them on novelty paper   
Paper or Journals & Pen		 Relaxation: 5 min
Creation: 1 hour
Closing: 15 min
     













Below is a list of materials you may need  based on which medium you want to use:
 Collage
Option One
 Paper Mosaic
Option Two
 Oil Pastels Resist
Option Three
Magazines with images and words
Scissors
Glue sticks
Embellishments as wanted -
butterflies, flowers
Markers
 Novelty papers - patterns, textures, metallics
Pre-cut mosaic shapes are available at
Discount School Supply
Glue Sticks
Mod Podge with brushes
Scissors
 Oil Pastels
Watercolors         
Brushes
Cups
Spray Bottle
Water pitcher

Prep:
Have body and head templates ready, one for each participant. Print journal questions on special paper. Have samples on hand if available. If you are using watercolors, be sure to pre-moisten them with a spray bottle before the participants use them. It's great to make an example of each medium so the participants get an idea of what they can create.

 
  Pre-collage Without a background image
 
  Adding a background image
 Collaging with layers
Technical Demonstration:
Explain to the participants the materials that will be available, especially if you are giving all three options. It is important to demonstrate all of the materials you give to them.

Collage - You may want to show your participants the different effects you can get by layering. You can show them how adding a background image can add hidden meaning and also make a collage "pop"!

Another wonderful collage technique is to not use scissors. Tearing the paper creates a cool effect.

Finally, encourage participants that while choosing images they should try to follow their intuition. This process can be quite surprising and freeing.

Paper Mosaic
You may not need to show a technical demonstration of how to do a paper mosaic, but it's good to at least show an example of what a mosaic is. Participants may choose to use a pencil to outline the spaces they would like to fill with mosaic pieces. It's also important to remind them that mosaics don't necessarily have to be squares, they can do long strips for hair and use lots of shapes.

 
 Notice how the white oil pastel was used
 in the bubbles of this Inner self portrait		 
  
Oil Pastel Resist
Give a demonstration to the participants by drawing a shapes with oil pastel on card stock  then using the watercolor over pastel to show how the pastel resists the watercolor. Remind them to use a lot of water and a lot of paint on their brush to create richer color effects. Using a spray bottle is an easy way to add water to the paper to help the watercolors flow.

Opening Circle:
Remind the group that anything shared in this circle is anonymous and should not be shared with anyone outside of this room.  Have the participants introduce themselves and share one thing that others don't know about them!  Ask the clients to be brave when deciding what to share and remind them that everything that is said in group stays in group.

 
 Combination Collage and Paper Mosaic Inner-Self Portrait
Journaling & Sharing (optional): 
Have participants journal on the questions provided and then share what they feel comfortable sharing. It is sometimes helpful to give participants a time frame and play soft music to get them writing.

If you plan to use the journal questions provided, realize it takes a lot more time to write and then share. If you are doing this workshop with teens it may be a good idea to have them share in pairs. It may feel safer to share if they are not asked to share with the group. If they are not up for sharing, that is okay too. If you have the time use this step as you may notice participants tend to go to a deeper level when they write and share before they create.

Relaxation:
Feel free to adapt this relaxation to work with your group and time frame.  Ask the children/teens to close their eyes and or put their head down on the desk. If you fall asleep that is great! Just like with the art there is no right or wrong way to do the relaxation. Read slowly, pausing in between sentences to create a relaxing atmosphere. Encourage the children/teens to breath deeply and try the relaxation. Then read the following:

 
  Paper Mosaic Inner Self Portrait
“Get comfortable in your chair, it is good to sit with your feet flat and your hands just laying loosely in your lap. If it feels safe for you, you can close your eyes. Just notice your in-breath and out-breath. No need to change it, simply notice the breath as it enters your nose and fills your chest.

Move your thoughts to your mind... knowing you can relax your mind just like a muscle ... take a deep breathe and go deep within and begin to meet your inner-self. What colors come to mind for your inner-self? What shapes or images arise as you meet your inner-self, are they large or small, round or heart? Is your inner-self male or female, are they young or old, is your image clear or foggy?

Greet your inner self, and ask him or her what they need from you... maybe a hug?.. maybe they just need you to sit and listen... take a moment and just spend some time getting to know and loving your inner-self. Take a deep breath in and let it out, continue breathing comfortably and know that you can return to talk and share with your inner-self any time you want. Hold onto all the images you saw and felt, slowly open your eyes and begin to create a portrait of your inner-self, selecting one of the techniques.
  
Participants working on their Inner self portraits!
Creation:
Remind the children and teens that their portrait doesn't have to look like anything in particular, especially a person. If their inner self is just shapes and colors or even lots of words, that is okay.  Just have fun and enjoy the process! Reminder:  There are so many materials that it is good to give the participants time warnings.

Closing Circle:
Ask everyone to share their portrait and what it means to them. What did they discover?   What is important for them to share about the art.
Row.txt_description: This workshop will assist older children and teens to look inside and discovering more about their inner-self! We are used to looking at our outer selves, our looks, our clothes, our appearance, the image we try to portray! This workshop gives us an opportunity to go to a deeper level and get more in touch with our inner-self. You will have 3 options of material to work with, you can mix them up if you prefer.

Row.txt_code:
Project Overview:    
The New Year's Wish-Markers are small collages similar to book-markers, but they can vary in size and shape.  They are something that you can carry with you or keep around the house to remind you of the wishes you h ave for the upcoming year.

In this workshop we will look at the upcoming year as if has already passed.  This way, rather than seeing our wishes as something to be reached, we will let our imaginations and instincts show us these wishes as if they have already come to life and we can see even our wildest dreams come true.  We will use the wish-markers as personal reminders to affirm our power in the creation of our lives.    














Seasons of Healing
"Cada estacion del año es para sanar y recuperar cuando el fruto de Dios esta en nuestro espiritú!"
"There is a season for healing and restoration when God is the fruit of our spirit!"








Materials Needed:
Tag board to collage on (Different sizes and shapes)
Glue stick
Magazines
Scissors
Hole-Puncher
Ribbons
Pens and Paper for writing
Relaxing music
Timer
Magnets (optional)
Laminator (if you don't have one, each participant may laminate their own at Kinko's, or you could take the group's markers there in a bunch.)



















Restoration Reunification Successfulnes
"Esto es de mi futuro, esperanza en mi familía, y de prosperidad en mi vida."
"This is about my future, hope in my family and prosperity in my life."




Time Frame: 2 1/2 hrs
Introduction: 15
Opening Circle: 20
Timed Writing: 15
Technical Demonstration: 10
Collaging: 75
Closing Circle: 15

Introduction:
Remember that this workshop is a window of time for you to appreciate yourself completely, to respect all of your efforts, struggles and triumphs of the past year, and to think about the up-coming year with full respect for all of your thoughts, dreams and wishes. 

We will be creating "New Year's Wish-Markers" (show samples).  They can serve as book markers, but they can also be magnets to be placed in the kitchen, bedroom, desk or whethever you need them most.  They will mark your place in your very own wish for the upcoming year. 

You can create as many as you need.  You don't have to figure out your wishes right now.  During the relaxation and writing portions of the workshop you will have the chance to reflect on the wishes that are vital to you.
 





It's Behind Us ... A New Life
Todó se quedó atrás...Una nueva vida








Opening Circle:
Let's begin to notice that this is a safe space for each of us to respect what we are feeling by having an opening circle.  Let's start with everyone sharing your name, how you're feeling, and one thing you appreciate about yourself most during the past year.  You can also acknowledge how you feel after the holiday season ( ie. Christmas and New Year).

Technical Information:
Show all the materials that are available to work with.  Demonstrate tearing, cutting and gluing onto the marker.  Show some different sizes and shapes we have can work with and mention the possibility of using magnets.  State that there are no right or wrongs in their creations. 
 
Relaxation:
(adapted from Jennifer Louden's The Women's Comfort Book)  

Get yourself comfortable.  Take a deep breath.  Hold it for a moment, and then slowly let it go.  Inhale another deep breath.  Imagine you are breathing pure relaxation in.  Hold your breath.  Now exhale, and imagine you are breathing out all the tension of your day, your week, your life.  As you take another breath, keep noticing you are breathing in pure relaxation.  As you let it go, keep noticing that you are letting go of any tensions.  Notice your body.  Are there any areas of tension?  Inhale and send your breath curling around the knotted muscle, the stored stress.  Exhale and imagine your pure, relaxing breath melting any tension away.  


  Reflections of Fear



Writing Warm-up:
Set your timer to 15 minutes, and during that time, write without stopping, without crossing anything out, without censoring or criticizing yourself.  

Begin by writing about the past year.  Try starting with the phrase:  "2005 was the year I....  " and writing about it in a completely triumphant way.  Remember any compliments you received during the year.  Remember any new things you learned.  

If any negative thoughts come into your mind, take a deep breath and see if you can notice what was positive about each experience.  Notice the strength you showed in the face of challenges.  Notice the decisions you made.  Notice the steps you took and the insights you gained, even from your mistakes.  You deserve to be appreciated for all you have done and been during this past year.

Writing Ahead:

Now try writing about the year ahead.  Try pretending you are sitting here a year from today.  What are your wishes for the year ahead?  Write them as if they have already happened.  Begin with the phrase “2006 was the year I...”  Let your imagination run wild.  You can concentrate on the year as a whole or on each individual month.
  
As you finish your last sentence, look back at what you've written.  Circle what seems most significant to you, and see if you can choose what you'd like to focus on for your Wish-Markers.





Angels Holding Our Hearts
"Veo el futuro positivamente. La mariposa representa libertad después de la lucha y el angel representa como sostiene nuestro corazón y cuida al mundo entero."
"I see the future very positively. The butterfly represents freedom after struggle and the angel represents how they hold our hearts and watch over the whole world."






Collaging:

When you're ready to start your collage, begin to look through magazines and pull out any images, colors, textures, words that you are drawn to, or that you feel are related to your wish.   When you are ready, begin to collage them together onto the tag boards.   

Wrap-up:

As you finish up, write what each marker means to you on the back.  The words you choose are an important part of your Wish-Markers.  You will be able to read them throughout the year when you feel like you’ve lost your way or when you need to congratulate yourself on what you have been able to accomplish.

(If people are not finished with their collages, welcome them to take their images so that they can finish at home.  They can also continue to work on them during the closing circle.)



Life Is Not A Gamble


Lamination:

You can get your Wish-Marker Laminated inexpensively at a place like Kinko’s.  Lamination makes the Wish-Marker into something beautiful and strong that you can carry with you throughout the year ahead.

After lamination, holes can be added to the marker.  They can have a ribbon on top or they can be attached to one another.  The magnets can also be added at this time.

Throughout the Year:

Carry your Wish-Markers throughout the year and use them to remind you of your visions and wishes.  They can also become magnets you place around the house. Take notes throughout the year regarding your successes and challenges as you reach for your wishes.  We would love to hear your stories.
Row.txt_description: Gives each participant a relaxing opportunity to think positively about th eyear ahead, and to create a vision in collage that she can carry with her into the year.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
For survivors coming from an abusive environment, one way to manage their experience is to dissociate from their body. Instead of experiencing their reality and being fully present in body, mind, and soul, they are u sually distracting their attention away. They may use drugs, alcohol, food, denial of food, TV, or an endless list of ways to be distracted from being present in their experience. This adaptive behavior unfortunately takes them so far from the sacred vessel they inhabit, that they have become disembodied. The body map is a way of getting back in touch with the body. Awareness of the relationship that is held with the body is the goal. This exercise also gives them another option in which to experience and relate to their body.




Body Image from Group Interactive Art Therapy
by Diane Waller
Materials:
Felt tip markers
Tempera paints
Pastels
Crayons
Collage material
Magazines
Glue
A roll of butcher paper/mural paper, Newsprint in rolls, or brown packaging paper

Timeframe:
This workshop can take between 1 1/2 and 2 hours to complete depending on the size of the group and their willingness to share.

Getting the Paper:
I was able to call some of the large paper suppliers nearby and asked for a roll of paper as a tax deductible donation to the shelter. If you need to get large paper, you might try this. The shelter should have a form to give you. You may also call some of the local craft or art suppliers, or even the local health food store that has a meat department. Locally owned stores are sometimes easier to get donations from than the larger chain stores. (You may also inquire at this time about any type of collage materials that the store can spare.) If you are unable to acquire the butcher paper, then use masking tape to tape pieces of paper together that are large enough for participants to lay down on and trace their body.

Note:
This is one of those exercises that include a guided meditation, and arrangements for the children to be occupied elsewhere would be ideal. If not, they can participate in the body tracing, and then set them up with crayons while you do the guided meditation with the participants.

Introduction and Preparation for Body Map Exercise:
Pair participants up. You can be a partner if there is an odd number. Have them take turns in tracing their partner’s body. They can move their arms and legs in whatever position they like. A dark felt marker works best for this if it’s available. When they are finished, have them lay down over their traced image. Explain that, “We will be doing a guided meditation to bring awareness to the body. We will then try to replicate any feelings, energy, numbness, cold, heat, tension, etc. onto the body map using the art materials.”

Relaxation:
[To be spoken in a calm, even, and slowly paced voice. Make pauses appropriately.]

“Take a couple of slow deep breaths and relax. Now let the floor support you... sink into it... allow the gravity of the earth to pull all your tension away... just let it sink into the earth. Now we’re going to focus on specific areas of our bodies. Just notice how it feels without judgment. Just bring your awareness and make a mental note of anything you notice. Let’s start with the head... is it tight? Is it soft? What color or colors might represent the way it feels? What sound or movement could represent the energy? Just allow any free associations you might have to come to your mind. [Pause] Now move to your neck and shoulder area. Again, what colors, images, or movements could represent the feelings you are experiencing there? You may not be feeling anything. How might you represent that? Spend a moment to notice your neck and shoulders... and now move down your arms and just notice how they feel. [Pause] Move your awareness now to your torso. Does your back feel different from your front area? Spend a moment to notice the feelings. [Pause] Now move to your abdomen area... notice how your buttocks support you on the floor... Does the left side of your body feel different from the right side? Just notice your experience. [Pause] Move your attention down to your upper legs and slowly move down as you feel ready to the very tip of your toes... Take a minute to do so...[Pause] When you are ready you may open your eyes.”




Body Image from Group Interactive Art Therapy
by Diane Waller
Art Directive/Creation:
Have participants use the available material to symbolize what they noticed in their bodies. Tell them they may need to refocus on each particular area as they try to represent what they experience with color, shape, movement, texture, etc. If they are having difficulties with the art media, suggest picking a color that would work with some words to express their experience. Tell them, “Let your imagination go and do whatever you feel to do. Feel free to explore and experiment.”
Body Image from
Group Interactive Art Therapy
by Diane Waller
Sharing:
Invite participants to hang up their images and talk about them if they choose to. After they finish, suggest to them to consider journaling about, and to, the image. Write a letter to your body! Write a poem to honor the vessel that makes it possible for you to be on this earth. Suggest that they may want to continue to add to their art piece. Just as you take the time to decorate your home, decorate your body image. Give it power symbols. Bring some magic into your image. Write some positive and powerful words on it. Feel free to explore and experiment. Communicate that the purpose of this exercise is to bring awareness to their own body, and awareness about their relationship to their body.

Note to Facilitator:
As always with art, but especially with the body map, strong emotions may come up for some of the participants. Be aware of this, and notify the staff if you are concerned about someone in particular. For instance if they withdraw from the group and choose not to talk, you can be supportive of their
choice and ask if they are OK. Then alert the staff
to her reaction to the art experience. Enjoy!
Row.txt_description: Gives survivors a way of renewing their relationships with their bodies after possibly managing their abuse through disassociation or addiction. Offers another option in which to experience and relate to their bodies.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide a family, or a group of families, with an opportunity for each member to create a symbolic representation of self and place it within a commonly created family context. The aim is to facilitate individual ex pression and encourage an atmosphere of tolerance for similarities and differences. Each family member will decide where to place their decorated hand cut-out on or around the family tree trunk. As a result, they will have the freedom to choose a comfortable level of closeness or distance in relation to each other.

 
 
 
 
 


 Materials
Materials:
Large white butcher paper
8 1/2 x 11 white and colored paper
Markers
Pastels
Crayons
Colored pencils
Scissors (adult and children’s)
Glue sticks
Optional: Glitter glue, stickers, stamps and ink pads.

Time Frame:
This workshop can last between 60-90 minutes depending on the age of the children participating. It is helpful to have some simple toys available (building blocks, cars, dolls, etc.) for the younger children who might not be able to participate or who might lose interest after a short time.


A family with their finished Family Tree 
Space:
If possible, it is nice to have a separate table and chairs for each family. Otherwise have the family sit together at one end of a table or clear a space for them on the floor. There should be enough art materials so that each family has their own and doesn’t have to keep getting up to go get things they need. I have done this workshop with one family working outside at a picnic table and others inside a room. The goal is to allow each family to focus on their particular group process and not get too distracted by the activities of other families. There will be time to share as a whole group at the end of the workshop.

Introduction:
“In the next hour or so each family here will have the chance to create a picture of their family tree. The ideas and suggestions I give you are just one approach to follow, so feel free at any time to select your own method and make any changes that you wish. I have asked you to sit together as a family so that you can make decisions as a group about how you want your picture to look and so that the adults in each family can assist the younger children if they need help. If anyone does not want to participate or would prefer to work independently, that is okay too. There is no right or wrong way to do this art project. The most important thing is to let yourself by guided by how you feel and respect each others choices.



 Family tracing and decorating their hands
“The first step in making a family tree is for each family member to trace their hand on a piece of construction paper. Choose colors that are expressive of who you are and feel free to draw or write any shapes, symbols, or words on your hand that are significant and meaningful to you. After you have finished coloring or decorating your hand, cut it out. Smaller children may need help with this. If there is an infant in your family, a small hand can be made for them.



 Mother drawing the tree trunk
“The second step is for the adult in each family to draw a tree trunk on the piece of large white butcher paper. Children can make suggestions to her as she draws. Next each family member decides where they would like to place their hand on the tree and glues it down. It may be necessary to discuss with each other the exact position of your hand so that you respect each other’s boundaries and need for space. If you wish to place your hand elsewhere on the large piece of paper, that is okay too.



 Creating the Family Tree's environment
“The last step is to talk together as a famly and decide what kind of environment you would like to have around your tree. You may use any of the art materials to decorate the areas of ground and sky. It may be helpful for the adult to assign each child a space to draw within, or you may decide to let everyone draw what and where they please. Finally, if your family would like to title the completed picture, dicuss this together and write it on the front. You might like to have everyone sign their names either on the front or back of the drawing.”

Creation:
Have the families begin the art process after you have answered any questions they might have. Multi-family groups can become a little noisy and chaotic, so know that this is normal! You will probably have to repeat the directives step-by-step individually to each family because they will progress at their own pace and be involved in different stages at different times.
 
 Example of Our Family Tree






Example #2 of Our Family Tree
  Example #3 of Our Family Tree

Sharing Circle and Closing:
When all the families have completed the art directive have them come together in a large circle, if possible, and take turns holding up their picture for everyone to see. Make sure that every individual in the family is given the opportunity to speak about both the content of their drawing and the process of doing it. Always offer the option of not sharing, but if they are willing, have them discuss the significance of their hand, it’s placement, and their contribution to the tree’s environment. Even if the experience was not a positive one it is important to listen to all feelings being expressed. Closing the circle can be done with a rousing round of applause in appreciation of the efforts of everyone and families are encouraged to hang their family tree in their rooms at the shelter.

Note: Some shelters create a shelter tree with a hand from each resident. Some children make a tree that includees other relatives and ancestors. Encourage participants to take it in whatever direction they want.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants an opportunity to explore their sense of family and their place within it by using their hands to create a "family tree."
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual Pg.87 TO DO: Create varation for adults (appropriate for all ages). TO DO: Check against manual’s version of same.

Row.txt_code:
< td style="vertical-align: top">
 
  
 
  
 
 Example of series from Watercolor Windows
Overview:
This workshop offers survivors an opportunity to notice their inner and outer worlds, and to express their sense of self-transformation. The simplicity of this project allows it to work successfully within a short time frame and with participants who may never have used watercolor before. Participants may discover how beautiful and rewarding watercolor can be as a form of self expression.

Materials:
4" x 4" watercolor paper (3 pieces per participant)
Masking tape (one per participant)
Watercolor sets (one per participant)
Brushes (one medium sized brush per participant)
Cups of water (2 per participant)
Paper towels
Writing paper
Pens (one per participant)
Relaxing music

Time Frame:
This workshop will take 1 1/2 - 2 hours to complete.

Note to Leaders:
With watercolors, many beginners miss out on the beauty and ease of this material because they paint with the full strength of the pigment rather than using water washes. This workshop puts the focus directly on the water wash, having the women select the shape of the wash and define it on the page before adding any color. Once the water wash is in place, the rest flows easily and beautifully.

This workshop focuses on this single-wash process. It does not teach participants how to use multiple washes to render objects in a representational way. That sort of thing takes more time for the washes to dry in between, and takes more training than this workshop involves.

Opening Circle:
“Share your name, how you're doing, and how you feel about art. As you share, remember that this is your time to really notice yourself. As you listen to the others in the circle, remember that your listening helps to create the safety and respect in this room.”

Introduction:

1. A window of time

“This workshop is a window of time for you to practice respecting yourself and all of your thoughts and feelings. We will be using watercolors, a material which is quite wonderful and surprising. As you use the watercolors today, try not to be critical of what you do. It's fine to make a mess on the paper. It's fine to leave the paper blank. Whatever you decide to do is fine, as long as you try to keep respecting yourself instead of criticizing yourself.”

2. About watercolors

“Watercolors are a great chance to let yourself loosen up and have fun witnessing what emerges. This kind of paint can be layered in delicate washes to create incredible paintings. To do that sort of layering takes a lot of time and patience. Today, we will be using them in a more simple way. This workshop is designed to share the full beauty of the watercolor, without the frustration.”

3. Today's project

“We will each choose a simple shape to represent ourselves. It can be as simple as a circle or line or triangle. You don't have to think of the shape right now. We'll be doing a relaxation, and you can just let it come to you.

We'll be creating the shape on all three pages with water, and then adding color. The three pages can represent whatever you want them to represent. They can represent how you feel on the inside, and how the world feels around you. They can represent your transformation and healing. They can represent your different states of mind. They can represent your past, your present and your future.”



Fig.1: Taping the paper down

 

 
Fig.2: Defining your shape
with watercolor

 

 
Fig.3: Dropping color into the water
 
Technical Demonstration:
Tape down the three pieces of paper. Explain the various supplies, (fig. 1) especially the reason for the two cups of water (one is to rinse the brush, and one is a source of clear water to paint with).

To demonstrate the use of the water washes, paint a shape with pure water on all three papers (fig. 2). Use plenty of water so that the shape remains wet like a lake on the page.
Begin to drop color into the shapes (fig. 3). Notice how the beauty of watercolor comes from what the color does by itself as it is carried through the water. When the paint is dropped into it, the magic begins effortlessly.

Show what it's like to drop it near the edge. Show what it's like as the color spreads and runs into other colors (fig. 5).

Show what it's like to paint the area outside the shape with color, leaving a space of dry paper between the shape and the background (fig. 6).

Show what it's like if you join the two wet spaces. You can work the three papers at the same time, or one at a time (fig. 7).
 
 Fig.4: General set-up of materials





Distribute Supplies:
Make sure everyone has her paper taped down, and make sure each has her paints, water cups, brush, writing paper and pen ready (fig. 4).



 
Fig.5: Filling the shape with color

 
 
Fig.6: Leaving an edge of dry paper between the shape and the ground

 
 Fig.7: Bridging the dry edge,
where desired
Relaxation:
(Adapted from Jennifer Louden's The Women's Comfort Book.)

Note: relaxation is optional. If you are leading a group of participants who won't be comfortable with a guided relaxation, go ahead and skip to the creating.

“Get yourself comfortable. Take a deep breath. Hold it for a moment, and then slowly let it go. Inhale another deep breath. Imagine you are breathing pure relaxation in. Hold your breath. Now exhale, and imagine you are breathing out all the tension of your day, your week, your life. As you take another breath, keep noticing you are breathing in pure relaxation. As you let it go, keep noticing that you are letting go of any tensions. Notice your body. Are there any areas of tension? Inhale and send your breath curling around the knotted muscle, the stored stress. Exhale and imagine your pure, relaxing breath melting any tension away.

“When you feel relaxed and ready, take a moment to think about how you feel. What shape would you choose to represent yourself?

“Once you have fixed upon a shape, go ahead and open your eyes and begin to create that shape on each of your papers in pure water.

Creation:
Each participant can go ahead and create her shape in water on the three pages and then begin to add color as she wishes.

As participants begin to finish up, encourage them to write about their paintings. This gives them a way to process what they have experienced while the paint dries and the others finish up.

Closing Circle:
