When participants are finished, leave the papers taped down during the closing circle. This will give the water washes a chance to dry.

For the closing circle, encourage each woman to share what she created and what she discovered in doing her paintings.

After the circle, participants can go ahead and take the tape off. If the paint is still wet, they may want to wait longer, or use a hair dryer gently, to dry the water before taking the tape off.
Row.txt_description: Offers survivors an opportunity to notice their inner and outer worlds, and to express their sense of self-transformation through the use of watercolors. Allows participants an opportunity to work successfully with the medium in a short time with rewarding results regardless of experience.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Allows participants an opportunity to explore and understand their feelings, know that all feelings are acceptable, and notice what their relationship to their feelings is like today. Participants do a series of quick, intuitive drawings, the focus being more on their experience than on the final product.




Materials
Materials:
Paper (8 sheets per participant)
Pastels (1 set per participant)
Pens
Extra writing paper

Time Frame:
This exercise goes fast and will take up the entire hour. I encourage participants to discuss their experience, but find it best to do after you have gone through all the emotions in the experiential process. In this way they will talk about the most poignant awarenesses they came across, and it will be most conducive to your time allowance.

The introduction should be about ten minutes in length. Each feeling should get five minutes. One minute to access and express the feeling, and four minutes to write and contemplate in silence. Let them know that time will be allowed for discussion after the art experiential.

This workshop will take 1 1/2 - 2 hours to complete.

Set Up:
It helps to have a large piece of paper with the questions written on them and displayed on a wall where participants can refer to if needed. The first four questions are the important ones to include. In order, the questions keep the participants in their “here and now” body experience with the emotion, and then moves them into an intellectual understanding of the feeling and their relationship to it. So encourage them to answer the first four in order, and then draw a line and write optional for the rest of the questions, or anything else they might want to include.

Also, have the eight sheets of paper and pastels placed before each participant before you begin the introduction.

Introduction:
Part of our experience as human beings is the capacity to have emotions. They are called “feelings,” because we are supposed to feel them. It’s unfortunate that we live in a society that has marked certain feelings as acceptable, and others as not. Some feelings are only acceptable if you are a certain sex. (Everyone has probably experienced the implied message that boys are not supposed to cry, and that women are not to assert their anger).

The fact is that as a human being, regardless of our gender, we are all capable and expected to feel a full range of emotions. Love and empathy are for the purpose of connection. Fear and anger are to warn and prepare us to fight off that which threatens our survival. Grief provides a relief process when we experience loss. This physical body is like a faucet that opens up to allow the emotional waters to pour through. Emotions are meant to be fluid and move the energy of our reactions that we experience through our senses.

If we don’t allow the energy to flow by it’s natural process of emoting, then it may become stuck or turned inward. For instance, have you heard the expression that worry causes ulcers, or repressed anger turns inward into depression. These notions even carry truth in modern medicine, which is looking more towards the body/mind connection in regards to “dis-ease.” It’s very important to feel your feelings!!

“The purpose of this exercise today is to explore and understand how all feelings are acceptable, and notice what your own relationship to your feelings is like today.

“I would like to emphasize ‘explore and notice.’ To explore and notice is to take a curious look at something, noting it’s qualities. We are not here to judge or shame ourselves in regards to what we think we ‘should’ be. The simple act of awareness provides a space for change and transition to occur naturally in it’s own time and way.

“You have developed a very intricate and necessary adaptation in life in regards to your feelings. The way you relate has been the way you have needed to survive in the social setting that you grew up in and find yourself today. This information may give you some options as to how you will relate in the future. Change and new behavior seem to come too slowly at times, but remember to put it in perspective with it taking your whole life to get where you are now.

“So above all, be kind and loving and patient with yourself when it comes to learning new ways of being.”

Art Directive and Creation:
“We will do a series of drawings today. For each sheet of paper, you will take a moment to reflect on a feeling. You will then pick one color that best suits that feeling, and make a mark or series of marks that may represent the energy of the feeling. “Allow your hand to touch the paper with your chosen color and move it however it wants to move. Don’t worry about how it looks, but rather, trust that deep inside you know how to express this feeling, and to let it come out through you. Whatever you draw will be perfect, and it does not necessarily need to be a picture.

“Pay attention to how your body feels when you hold the thought of each feeling. Just notice any sensations, tensions, or numbness you may be feeling. You may notice that you don’t even seem to be in your body.

“We will take about thirty seconds to complete each emotional gesture drawing. After you finish each one, take a moment to just be with the expression. Again, just notice any thoughts, judgments, bodily sensations, or whatever goes on when you contemplate this paticular feeling. You may not feel particularly charged about it one way or another.

“On the back of the picture write:

(1) The name of the feeling.

(2) How you feel about this feeling.

(3) How do you feel in your body with this emotion?

(4) What thoughts, judgments, or messages do you have about feeling this emotion?

(Optional questions and considerations:)

“Who influenced you on these judgments (Parent, peers, society)? You may have some wishes or concerns about this feeling.

“What are your fears or hopes in regards to this feeling?

“Spend a few minutes writing what ever comes to mind. These questions are merely a jumping off place.”

Visualization:
At the beginning of this exercise, and in between each feeling, it is very important to let go of the feeling they experienced prior.

Do this by having them close their eyes and take a couple of deep breaths...

“Now imagine a waterfall that starts at the top of your head and flows through your entire body... washing the last feeling experience (or for the beginning of the session just say washing any tension...) out of your body and soaking into the earth... Let go of all tension with your out breath...

“Now think of a time when you felt (Insert feeling here. Suggested order: sad, happy, disappointed, excited, fearful, hopeful, angry, peaceful. It is important to end with a positive emotion.), allow yourself to really imagine the situation in which you experienced this... engage your senses by trying to visualize, smell, hear, or feel whatever you can about this experience... and when you are ready, open your eyes and choose a color that best suits the feeling, and make a mark or movement that best shares the energy of the feeling you are experiencing.

“When you are finished with this quick gesture drawing, be with it for a moment and really take it in... then when you are ready, turn over the paper and refer to the questions here (on the wall).”

After the first drawing, you can continue by saying, “...and when your ready, open your eyes and draw your gesture drawing, contemplate, and reflect and write on the questions as before...”

Suggested Discussion and Closing:
Open the floor for discussion on anything that comes up for participants. Remember, no right or wrong, but just reflection and consideration.

They may want to take some of their concerns into therapy. As a further exploration, they might consider taking the emotional expressions that they felt most resistant to, and to pin them up in their room somewhere where they have contact with them often. Encourage them to notice how over one week’s time the resistance and feelings towards these emotions change and shift.

You may also encourage them to write in their journal each night: one or two sentences to each of the emotions in this workshop. At the end of the week, ask them to consider any changes that they have experienced.
Row.txt_description: Allows participants an opportunity to explore and understand their feelings, know that all feelings are acceptable, and notice what their relationship to their feelings is like today. Participants do a series of quick, intuitive drawings, the focus being more on their experience than on the final product.
Row.txt_notes: ER TO DO: Rewrite!

Row.txt_code:
Designs by Sherrill Kahn, creator of
"Impress Me" rubber stamps compan
Background:
This workshop was developed for the “In Touch with Teens” Program at Monroe High School in Los Angeles County. It was inspired by the work of Sherrill Kahn, a wonderful artist who was my high school art teacher. I have adapted it here for your use in the shelters, and I hope you enjoy it!

Objective:
To provide an opportunity for participants to explore their own, violence-free definitions of love, power and identity. To guide each participant to put their own definitions into a visually powerful form that she can carry with her and use to reminder of what she stands for as she leaves the shelter.

Materials:
Shrinky Dinks paper (Frosted Ruff N’Ready type cut to 2”x2” in advance, at least 4 per person) You can order bulk online! Search for “The Magical Land of Shrinky Dinks.”
Permanent markers
Colored pencils
Hole punchers and scissors
String/ribbon/yarn
Beads
White paper
Pencil sharpener
Oven

Note: Ballpoint pens work wonderfully!

Timeframe:
This workshop takes about 2 hours to allow for participants to write, sketch and design their own definitions in visual form, and share what they come up with.

Introduction:
Perspective to share with participants, “Throughout your stay in the shelter, you have probably had a chance to look at your own definitions of love, power and personal identity. You’ve probably looked at violent forms of power, love, and identity and uncovered the ways that violent power isn’t really power at all, and violent love isn’t really love. Hopefully, you’ve had a chance to imagine what love, power and identity could be without violence.

“With so much violence all around, it can be hard to remember what these things might be without violence. It can be hard to remember what you stand for, and how you can stand against the violence.

“This workshop offers a chance to put what you have learned into a form you can remember easily. In this workshop, each person gets a chance to notice how you can personally stand for what you believe.

“By creating designs that represent your own violence-free definition of love, power and your own identity, you can take this chance to notice, explore and express what you stand for.”

As You Begin:
“Remember that this workshop is a window of time for you to respect your deepest hopes and visions. Defining violence-free power, love, relationships, and identity are no small task, but it is an important one. As you do this, make sure you respect your own thoughts. Remember that you count. Your visions count. Your actions count.”

Relaxation:
(Adapted from JenniferLouden's The Women's Comfort Book.)

“Get yourself comfortable. Take a deep breath. Hold it for a moment, and then slowly let it go. Inhale another deep breath. Imagine you are breathing pure relaxation in. Hold your breath. Now exhale, and imagine you are breathing out all the tension of your day, your week, your life. As you take another breath, keep noticing you are breathing in pure relaxation. As you let it go, keep noticing that you are letting go of any tensions. Notice your body. Are there any areas of tension? Inhale and send your breath curling around the knotted muscle, the stored stress. Exhale and imagine your pure, relaxing breath melting any tension away.”

Writing Warm-up:
“In the four corners of your page, write four concepts that you want to define, violence-free. You may choose power, love, relationships, or identity, or you may choose other concepts that are important to you.

“Once you have selected your four concepts, begin writing whatever comes to mind as a definition for each of your concepts, violence-free. As you write, remember to write without stopping, without crossing anything out, without censoring or criticizing yourself.

“When you feel done writing, move on to the sketching.”

Sketching:
“Begin to imagine shapes that express your definitions. You can sketch them out on scratch paper. Try to stay really loose and uncritical. Explore as many shapes as you can for each concept.”

Drawing:
“When you have one or more sketches that you want to use to create a final design, go ahead and put it onto a fresh piece of paper.

You may create a design for each of your four concepts, or you may create one. You might find that your one design expresses all of your ideas. Make as many or as few designs as you wish.”

Making the Shrinky Dinks:
Draw on the “rough” frosted side of the Shrinky Dink plastic. Draw and/or trace the image and/or word(s) that will remind you of what you stand for. If you want to change the shape of your plastic, use scissors to cut to the shape you want. Keep in mind that a hole will be punched on the top portion so don’t write/draw anything too crucial in that section. Once you are done coloring and drawing/tracing, punch your hole on the top so you can later put ribbon or string through it. The hole needs to be punched PRIOR to baking. (When you punch the hole, don’t punch it too close to the edge, or too far. The distance from the edge should be about a half the diameter of the hole-punch circle.)

Baking Instructions:
A toaster oven is ideal for baking Shrinky Dinks. However, your conventional oven will “shrink” your masterpieces just as well. Step 1: Pre-heat oven to 325°F (163°C). Step 2: Cut a rectangle shape out of a brown grocery bag and turn one corner up. (Turned-up corner will make it easy to remove from tray or cookie sheet). Step 3: Place Shrinky Dinks pieces, colored side up, on brown paper and place paper in tray or onto cookie sheet. Put into pre-heated oven. Step 4: Watch as your Shrinky Dinks shrink. Bake approximately 1 to 3 minutes. After pieces lay flat, allow an additional 30 seconds of baking time to complete the process. Step 5: Remove paper from tray or cookie sheet and lightly press flat with folded paper or a pad of paper (or book) until pieces have cooled. (Approximately 15 seconds.)

Using Your Creation:
Use your “What I Stand for” creation throughout the year to remind you of the definitions you take with you. Take notes throughout the year regarding your discoveries as you remember “what you stand for.”
Row.txt_description: Provides an opportunity for participants to explore their own definitions of love, power and identity and put these definitions into a visually powerful form. The end product can be carried on a key-chain or elsewhere as a reminder of what he or she believes in.
Row.txt_notes: PROG-both ER TO DO: Check scans. TO DO: Create variation for Children.

Row.txt_code:
“Story telling is the soul’s speech, and it is free to move between the realities of imagination and literal events.” -Shaun McNiff (from Art as Medicine).




Story Doll, Shara Stevens
Objective:
The importance to tell one’s story is vital to rising above the shame, secrecy, and isolation that can accompany the abusive relationship. Another important aspect is using the imagination to create a new ending to the story. By making “story dolls” we give participants a voice to explore what has happened, and what direction they can choose to take for the future. By externalizing their own story onto the doll, it becomes a safer place to explore all of this. The doll often becomes a mirror, and a way for participants to discover feelings and thoughts she may have never claimed as her own before. A powerful transformation can occur when one is given the opportunity to truly speak their truth. The doll can also be used as a way to get in touch with their inner wisdom through dialogue. By asking a question to the doll, participants actually give the answer she needs to hear. Much like when we give advice to others, it’s the very thing we need to hear ourselves. This exercise allows participants to embrace their own advice and wisdom.

Materials Needed:
Fabric or felt
Beads
Buttons
Feathers
Miscellaneous collage material
Needles and thread or embroidery supplies
Scissors
Glue
Cotton batting or toilet paper for stuffing

Note:
This workshop can tap powerful emotions. If your group has established a sense of closeness and safety it might be a good workshop to try. Fabric stores are usually good resources for donations. I also frequent garage sales and thrift stores and buy articles for a dime or quarter and use those for material scraps.

Time Frame:
Participants may get very involved in their dolls so you might want to allow forty-five minutes for the making of them. If children are sitting in on this group, you can cut out ginger bread shaped persons on paper, and give them colors or magazines to decorate their own doll. After the dolls are finished, the participants can break up in groups of two or three to tell a story. A half an hour to forty-five minutes should be enough for each participant to have a turn.

Doll Making:
The doll can simply be two gingerbread person shapes that can be sewn together by hand and then stuffed. It could also be assembled in parts (body, head, arms and legs). It could also be as simple as a single sided hanging wall piece. If there is no material to work with, you can make the doll a single sided decorated paper cutout. Glue or sew on any items that seem appropriate and meaningful. Beans and pasta found in the kitchen pantry can be used. Be creative. Pull out colored markers and paints as well.

Introduction:
“In making our dolls today, think about the part of you that holds your inner wisdom. Think about the intuitive voice that resides within. Think about your soul or spirit, the energy that gives you life and yet is bigger than your life. Try to meditate on these aspects while creating your doll. Try not to worry about how the doll looks or how well it’s stitched together, but rather trust in the process of creating, understanding that the doll will be perfect exactly how it turns out. This doll is a part of you. When you talk to it and ask it questions, the immediate response that comes to mind will be coming from your own reservoir of wisdom and intuition. Sometimes it takes something outside of us to initially hear that wisdom and to trust it. This doll can be a part of you that needs to talk and tell a story. It may be literal or it may be a fantasy or symbolic of something bigger. Most importantly, this doll can be a window to your personal journey of discovering your self."

Sharing Exercise and Closing:
After the dolls are completed have participants pair up (if they are not done with their doll, try to encourage participants to finish them as they can during the week, but to use them as is for now). Groups of two are ideal because they will have more time to tell their story to one another. Give them a time limit for each person and also announce that you will let them know when they have five minutes left before switching. Have the owner of the doll tell its story. They can begin with “Once upon a time....” Make sure they include an ending. The ending can be however they wish things to be for themselves in the future. Some participants will take off immediately in this role play. However, others will not know how to start or what to say, or just not feel motivated to do anything. As an alternative idea, I have listed some questions here that they can ask of the doll. You may want to copy this and hand out for them to do at a later time on their own, if they engage well with the story telling. These are basic questions that can access the intuitive voice within on any given issue.

Possible Questions to Ask Your Doll:
“You may want to ask these questions with your doll in front of you, and either verbalize or write out the answers. It is important not to edit what you say or write. Trust the process and express what ever comes to mind without questioning or judgment. Be open to whatever response arises and just be available to hear it out. What comes up can be the intuitive wise part of you that you are getting more in touch with. It may also be old messages that are not true for you today. The important part is to let out what needs to be said, and be with that response to see what wisdom it has for you today.”
“What is it that you need from me?

“What do I need to know about my situation right now?

“What advice do you have for me in regards to this choice I need to make right now? (Verbalize the choice.)

“How can I achieve __________ right now in my life?

“Is there anything that you want to tell me?

“What is it that you feel I need to know about myself?”

Of course all these questions are being asked of your inner wise self. The doll just makes it easier to start these conversations and to connect to that wise part of you. Remember, trust the answers and the process. Trust your inner wisdom and intuition.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants a voice to explore their abuse and what directions they can choose to take for their future. By externalizing their own story onto a doll, it becomes a safe place to explore, often becoming a way to discover feelings and thoughts never before claimed.
Row.txt_notes: ER TO DO: Get scans

Row.txt_code:
Spring 1996 Hands Comforter #8 (Won County Fair Blue Ribbon)
"Hands are not for hurting. I will not use my hands for violence!"
Background on The Project:
Quilts have always evoked visions of comfort and nostalgia. The imagery and symbolism run very deep throughout the entire quilt process. Right from the start, participants being taking scraps of fabric, piecing them together into something beautiful and functional, and creating order out of chaos. Women are literally and figuratively stitching their lives together.

At Humbolt Women for Shelter (HWS), the Children's Comfort Project began in the Spring of 1993. Initially the comfort project was done just with children during childcare and/or kids groups. When HWS opened a shelter in the summer of 1995, the project was expanded to include adults. In this article,
I share the children’s quilting process, although it can be easily be adapted to use with adults.

The comforters are as varied as the children who have worked on them. At first, the comforters did not have themes. The children could draw anything they wanted. After 3-4 quilts, we began using themes. Some of the themes groups have chosen are; Hands are not for Hurting, Alcohol and Other Drug Prevention, Friendship, the Strength of Women, and My Favorite Things.

We have used our comforters in many different ways. Four have gone home with children, two remain in the children's room where they are used for stories, naps, picnics, etc. Two comforters are used for public display and community education (the names have been covered to protect confidentiality), two comforters are in use at our shelter house and two are used in our group room at our office. Three comforters have also been made by staff members for other staff members going through difficult times. Since the project began, fifteen comforters have been completed. We currently have three comforters in progress.

In August, 1996 the kids comforter, "Hands Are Not for Hurting" was entered in the Humboldt County Fair. It won a Blue Ribbon and a Special Award. The children are so proud when they come into HWS office and see the quilt on display with the ribbons pinned on.




Detail of Moon Stone House
 Comforter #1
Objectives:
Part of healing from the cycle of domestic violence is giving children a safe space to express their thoughts and feelings. The HWS Children's Comfort Project has been a wonderful and tangible way for this to happen--children are encouraged to share their unique ideas through the supportive creative process of making a group comforter.

The Comfort Project is very good for shelter houses on many levels. It gives adults and children a chance to share their stories and all of the pain, sorrow, love, joy and laughter... the strength and courage they have all shown in their lives. It brings comfort in the making and in the use of the finished product. Whether the comforter goes home with one family or stays in the shelter house to be used by all, adults and children are literally wrapping themselves in comfort and hope. It is a project that all ages are able to work on, from adult to young child. If a child can hold a crayon and make a mark, they can make a square. The squares can be as simple or as complex as the maker desires.

The creation of a group comforter takes place over a period of time. The children get to see a process. Some children will see the entire process, while others will see only certain stages. The first stage is the creation of the squares. The final stage is, of course, the completed comforter.

This particular comforter uses the theme: "Hands are not for hurting. I will not use my hands for violence!" In addition to making a pledge of non-violence, the children get to express themselves through the creation of the square. Each child gets to decide what colors and shapes they want to use. Then they can choose what fabric they want to frame their square. There is immediate gratification in the completion of the square. They also get to see the long term process and the eventual reward of the completed group project. Each child has an important part in the creation of the comforter. The finished comforter becomes a visual reminder of the group process and the support the group has to offer. It reminds the child they have a place where they belong and where they are safe.




Detail of Moon Stone House Comforter #1
Materials:
Muslin fabric: 2-4 yards depending on size of comforter.
Pentel fabric crayons and fabric pens
Quilt batting:
45x69 for 12 square comforter,
72x90 for 20 square comforter.
Flannel or other fabric for backing
Fabric for 3" framing strips
Yarn and yarn needles
Masking tape
Basic sewing supplies
Iron and ironing board
Newsprint
Polaroid camera and film

Timeframe:
The entire group is about 90 minutes, for the children to make the quilt squares and choose the frame.
15-20 min: Snack, check-in
45-50 min: Making squares, choosing frame
15-20 min: Sharing squares, check out

(Sometimes there is enough time for the children to make more than one square. Then they can leave one for the comforter and have one to take home with them, if they want.)

Sometimes making the squares is all I have the children do. Then I take the squares home and bring back a finished comforter. Other times, I involve them in more steps along the way, depending on their interest level.

The average time that goes by from the completion of the first square to the completed comforter is about 6-12 months. Depending on how many squares I collect and what the finished size of the comforter is, it may take 1-6 months just to collect enough squares for the quilt.

Once the squares are collected it takes about 15-20 hours to complete the comforter. It takes longer if you bring the quilt back to the group for the various stages (see “Follow-up” for a list of all the stages.), if the names have to be covered, if the comforter is larger than 20 squares, or if this is your first time constructing a comforter.

If you can collect 12 squares in one group and have an eager volunteer (hopefully one who already knows how to construct a quilt) with 15-20 hours available, the comforter could be completed in a week. Usually the process takes a little longer than that.

I like to plan working on the comforter in one stage or another about one group a month for about 6-9 months. In the shelter house, adults and children get to see whatever stage is being worked on while they are at the house. If they continue coming to HWS ongoing support groups, they can see the quilt when it is finished.

There is also time spent documenting the comforters. I don't have an estimate on this as it is something I am just beginning. I have always had the adults and children tell their stories with the squares, but I haven't written them down until this most recent comforter started in the shelter house The Strength of Women. I have now started asking the women's permission to write down their story as they tell it. I want to make journals, books to stay with the comforters.

Preparation:
*Cut 25-30 8”x1/2" muslin squares (this is so you will be sure to have enough extra. Cut more if your quilt will be larger than 20 squares).

*Cut 80-100 fabric framing strips 3" x 15" from assorted fabric scraps (Lots of colors and prints are desired. The more variety the more choices available to the children.)

*Tape the muslin square to the table on all four sides. Tape in 1/2" from edge of fabric. This does three things: 1) It secures the fabric so it won't slip around while drawing on it. 2) It frames the drawing space, anything beyond the tape will probably be sewn into the seam and not show. 3) It is a chance to stretch the fabric and smooth out any wrinkles.

*Set up ironing board and newsprint. (If the children are very young or unable to contain their energy, you may want to iron the squares later for safety’s sake.)

*Notebook or journal and pen to record the stories that go with the squares. Always ask permission before writing anything down.

*Polaroid camera (to take pictures of each adult and child and their quilt square, so each person has something to keep from group, since they are leaving their squares for the comforter.)




Detail of Hands Comforter #8




Detail of Hands Comforter #8




Detail of Hands Comforter #8
Opening Activity:
I have the group start with a snack and a quick check-in. We go around a circle with the following: say your name, how you are feeling right now, and is there anything you want to talk about today? After everyone has a chance to share, I describe the project:

“Today we're going to make quilt squares. The theme (you can use this theme or you can have the group choose a theme) for this comforter is: Hands are not for hurting. I will not use my hands for violence. So, what I want you to do is to trace your hand on the square. Then you can decorate it anyway that you want to. Now, I want you to think of the positive ways you can use your hands and write one way on your square. We have lots of extra squares, so if you don't like how yours is coming out and you can't fix it, you can start again on a fresh square."

While the squares are being made, the kids are talking about the different ways that hands can be used to hurt and the ways that hands can be used to help. When they have finished drawing and writing, the tape is removed from the fabric and the square is ironed to set the crayon. Place a piece of newsprint on the ironing board, then place the square face down, then another piece of newsprint. Now iron, holding the iron in place for 10 seconds, then move it over a couple of inches and hold 10 seconds. Repeat until the entire square has been ironed. Adults can do this themselves, older children may need help, and younger children need it done for them. The ironing melts the crayon and sets it into the fabric. It is an important step. Next the framing strips are chosen. The framing strips are 3"x15" strips of fabric. Each person can choose four to frame their square. They can all be the same, or they can all be different. Have each person pin the strips on, one on each side of the square.

Closing:
For closing we sit in a circle again. Each person has the chance to say anything they want to say about the group, share their square and say anything they want to say about their square, and close by saying something they like about themselves. (I may ask a question like "Do the colors, shapes, images have any special meaning for you?" if the person is hesitant or doesn't seem to know where to begin.) Remember to ask permission to record their story in the journal, and always respect it when they say no.




1994 Comforter #4 (No Theme)
Follow-up:
There is quite a bit of follow-up involved for this project, but the end result is worth the effort! The following are 8 Basic Stages of the Comfort Project.

Stages of Comforter Construction:
1) Make squares
2) Sew frames on (volunteer)
3) Lay out quilt (group or volunteer)
4) Piece top (volunteer)
5) Tie it (group or volunteer)
6) Bind it (group or volunteer)
7) Label it (group or volunteer) Have group decide how quilt will be used. Cover names if it is to be used for public display.
8) Photograph it (volunteer) Reproduce to give photos of finished comforter to women and children who worked on comforter.

I have not included basic quilt making instructions. There are a lot of good books already written. Check your library or local Quilt Guild. Quilt Guilds are a good place to recruit volunteers for this project.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants a chance to share their stories and emotions in individual quilt squares and brings comfort in the making and in the use of the finished product, a comforter. Comforters are finished over a period of time and children will get to see some or all of the process, depending on their length of stay at the shelter.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
My objective is to address the subject of self-respect and respect for others in an engaging, powerful way through the vehicle of the ancient symbols of the circle, the ceremonial staff, and drumming. Our society has trained most of us to have difficulty saying no and drawing our boundaries (that would be considered unaccomodating and selfish!) Through this process we create some symbols of self-respect on which to focus and use as tools in our self-growth.




Cate O'Hagan drums with "Ceremonial Staff" art workshop participants in Central Oregon





Materials:
Sticks of all sizes that no longer have bark
Paints (acrylic house paint or the less expensive acrylic artist colors)
Found materials
Feathers
Brass tacks
Leather
String for wrapping and tying
Beads
Trinkets
Bones 
Brushes
Paint rags
Water containers for cleaning brushes
Small plastic cups for individuals to work from
Scissors
Larger size needles
Fast drying glue
Tape player (for drumming and relaxing music)
Optional: woodburning tools, glue-guns, etc.

Note:
If the participants are given advance notice, they may be invited to gather their own stick to work with (from 24" or so to several feet tall) and to bring their own treasures to attach to their staff, such as beads, feathers, old jewelry, etc.

Note to Facilitator:
While inspiration for the Ceremonial Staff workshop came from Native American peoples, the staff has been used as a symbol of respect in all cultures throughout time. We think of it being associated with indigenous peoples, but if you watch the opening ceremonies for the United States Senate you will see a ceremonial staff used!

I have not yet encountered resistance to this process, or any alarm that it may hint at the pagan. If this occurs, it may be neutralized by pointing to such things as flags as forms of decorated staffs that symbolize national self-respect and healthy pride.

I suggest using a drumming tape, unless you have some familiarity with fast, rhythmic, regular beat drumming. I use a "double drumming" tape by Michael Harner, which should be widely available. It is this particular type of drumming, with the fast, regular beat, that naturally puts the listener into a relaxed state. (It actually relates to the brain wave function that causes relaxation.) Over the last five years, I have experienced only one person resistant to drumming, yet they made it through this process with flying colors. Again, the drum is common to all peoples, and is used just like we would use a tape of calming music.

Introduction:
While staffs are common to all cultures, the inspiration for this particular exercise originates with the Native American Sioux. During times of battle, some of the experienced and wise warriors would feel moved to ride into the heat of a battle armed with nothing more than a decorated stick, rather than a weapon. This stick is called a "coup stick" (pronounced koo and actually a French word). The warrior would ride up to the enemy and touch him with his coup stick, (which is the origin of the term "counting coup.") The warrior would touch his enemy with the stick, rather than wound or kill him. The enemy was therefore very aware that his life had been spared, and that he had been put on notice to never cross certain boundaries again.

We can use this imagery to represent our "inner warrior," that place in us that respects our boundaries and the boundaries of others. During the guided meditation we will look for or feel symbols that we can use to decorate our staff.




Touch drawing
by Daborah Koff-Chapin
Guided Meditation:
Let participants know that any part of this exercise is elective, and invite them to sit or lay in a comfortable position, with eyes open or closed. In a soothing, evenly-paced voice suggest they take three or more deep breaths, feeling each breath as it flows through the upper body, relaxing the neck shoulders, back and chest; then on to the lower body... releasing any tension in the lower back and abdomen, letting any excess tension flow out the toes. Let the mind wander, allowing the thoughts to pass through like a breeze.

“In your mind, find yourself in a totally comforting space... whether it be on a tropical beach or snuggled in a down comforter, whatever image or feeling works for you. While in this space, we will be listening to drumming to assist your relaxation. While listening to the drumming, create images of what your very own inner warrior may look like, or sound like or feel like. We will be bringing these images with us as inspiration for creating our staffs. Remember that if you feel you are not sensing any images, that's OK. This is your time to relax. Please enjoy about ten minutes of drumming, and when I turn down the sound at the end, slowly bring yourself back and we will begin.”

Facilitator’s Note:
After the meditation, suggest that each participant select a stick that feels right to her and dive into the materials. Invite them to paint or attach anything they want. There usually is a fair amount of interaction as participants share materials and methods of attaching items. I usually make no overt efforts to draw out comments at this time, but let the process take its natural course. I usually play soothing music during this part.

Closing Circle:
This is an opportunity for all of us to stand in a circle with our Ceremonial Staffs and talk about anything we feel moved to talk about, including about our staff and our inner warrior. As we stand in a circle we can notice that it is that self-respect and respect for each other that allows us all to co-exist harmoniously within the circle. For most of us that sense of safety within our family circle has been broken, and this is a way we can practice rebuilding it, beginning with self respect. So when you talk about your own staff or inner warrior, share with the group some ways you might begin to respect yourself more.




"Ceremonial Staff" workshop participants
Row.txt_description: Addresses the subjects of boundaries, saying no, self-respect and respect for others in an engaging, powerful way through the vehicle of the ancient symbols of the circle, ceremonial staff, and drumming. The end product, the ceremonial staff acts as a symbol of self-respect on which to focus and use as a tool in self-growth.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for Children.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Offers a way of doing affirmations that focus on what participants want to believe and be, while acknowledging, challenging and learning about all the old beliefs. The project is a writing exercise geared to editing and ultimately deleting negative self-thought.

Materials:
Paper
Colored pens
Optional: Journal (to create into an "Affirmation Journal"), any other art supplies to decorate their affirmations.

Introduction:
Self-worth is an extremely important issue in dealing with survivors coming from abusive relationships. I don’t feel there are any easy ways to obtain this, but what we can do is offer some tools in order to help them move toward this goal. I think that it’s important to discuss the issue of raising self-worth as a process, rather than a point of arrival. Each small step is a victory toward this goal, and should be celebrated as such.

Sometimes it may seem like three steps forward and two steps back, but overall the general movement is toward health, healing, and gentleness and love towards oneself. It’s important to explain this to the women. Otherwise, they may be discouraged and feel “what’s the use in trying”. It is very hard to change a life time of internal messages about oneself: messages that are so ingrained that we experience them as who we are, rather than just the messages that we somehow took on and believed.

What if, as an infant, you were raised with parents who completely accepted you; they allowed you to be who you are without shame or guilt or disapproval; they encouraged you and allowed you to make mistakes and learn from them? You would have the belief system that you are OK. You are inherently lovable and perfect even with your human imperfections.

Instead, we have been raised with parents who only knew what they were taught and did only what they were capable of. Most of us grow up thinking that we are not OK, and we have this internal message ingrained into our beliefs about ourselves. Just because we believe this to be true doesn’t mean it is true. If you grew up in the other family, you would have the belief that you are OK. This analogy is important. It challenges our beliefs about ourselves by showing how we could have just as easily believed in our self-worth had we grown up in a different environment.

What we are faced with now is to unlearn and relearn. This is going to be challenging, but not impossible. This is where it’s very important to focus on celebrating small achievements as we move toward the goal of self-love.

What will be given in this art project is a way to do affirmations that affirm what you want to believe, while acknowledging, challenging and learning about all the old beliefs. These old beliefs are like a tape recorder that keeps playing the old messages over and over regardless of their validity. As an adult, we can challenge and eradicate these old beliefs.

Incorporating Art with the Affirmations:
Learning how to do the affirmations is really the main point of this exercise. In order to incorporate the art piece, I can suggest two options:

1) After participants have done the first affirmation exercise, they can write their affirmation on a piece of paper, decorate it and use it as the front page of an “Affirmation Journal;”

2) They may also simply make it into an art piece and hang it on their wall above their bed or next to the bathroom mirror.

Remember, the negative messages have been repeated by our own minds for years and years. So, it’s important to repeat the positive loving messages over and over in order to override the negative. You can learn the positive just as easily as the negative. Whatever gets repeated and given more attention will win out. It’s important to relate this to the participants. You must put some time and energy into relearning these new messages, but the end result is worth it. More importantly, you are worth it.

Affirmation Techniques:
Make two columns on a sheet of paper. On the left side, have the participants write out an affirmation (some suggestions are given below). On the right side, let them write the immediate response they have to the affirmation. Go back to the left side and write the affirmation again. Then write the immediate response again on the right side. Keep doing this until all the possible negative reactions are no longer coming to mind. Be patient, as this may take a while, but know that they will eventually stop. After they have stopped, write the affirmation on the left side of the paper twenty to thirty more times. Remember, repetition is tedious, but very necessary. The negative messages have been repeated over and over for years. So, put some time and energy into repeating the positive.

After participants have their successful affirmation, write it out on another piece of paper and decorate it with magazine pictures, positive word cut outs, drawings or whatever. Celebrate your new commitment to reinforcing the positive and challenge and dispute those old negative messages from now on. You deserve it.

Example Affirmations:
I am worthy of love from myself and others.
I deserve to be appreciated and loved.
I am worthy of being treated with gentleness and kindness.
I deserve to be happy.
I love myself.
I am gentle and nurturing towards myself.

You may have participants brainstorm with each other on other positive statements.

A Note on Wording:
Always keep affirmations in the positive rather than “I am not...” , “I cannot...”, “I don’t...”, etc. For some reason the mind does not acknowledge the “am not” part and sees it as “I am unworthy”, rather than the way you wrote it as “I am not unworthy”.

Example Exercise & Possible Reactions:
I am worthy of love         No you’re not
I am worthy of love         You are always fucking up
I am worthy of love         Not if you knew me
I am worthy of love         I want to believe it, but I don’t know how
I am worthy of love         Only if I earn it
I am worthy of love         Love doesn’t exist
I am worthy of love         Not the kind of love I am looking for
I am worthy of love         I want to be
I am worthy of love         Only if I love you first
I am worthy of love         Only if I am needed
I am worthy of love         I don’t believe you
I am worthy of love

Suggested Follow-up:
This exercise could be done everyday if possible, even twice a day if you can. You can even rip the page in half and take all the negative responses and tear them up and say good-bye to all that old conditioning and claim that this is not true for me today. I let these go. There is so much power in a simple ritual like this.
Row.txt_description: Offers a way of doing affirmations that focus on what participants want to believe and be, while acknowledging, challenging and learning about all the old beliefs. The project is a writing exercise geared to editing and ultimately deleting negative self-thought.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for Teens.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Shares a simple weaving method as a way for participants to express themselves creatively, learn about themselves and their world, and raise their self-esteem. A sketchbook/notebook is used as a loom, leading the finished product to be a woven journal cover.




Yarn
Materials:
Small-to-medium size spiral sketchbooks/notebooks
Warp yarns
A variety of weft yarns
Pencils
Crayons
Watercolors
Scissors
Waving needles

Note:  Weavings are created by interlacing threads or yarns on a loom. The "warp" is the strong set of yearn or threads which run lengthwise in the loom, while the "weft" is the yarn or threads that are used to weave back and forth across the warp. Warp yarns need to be non-stretchy; cotton works well. Weft yarns, what you weave into the warp threads, can be anything!

Timeframe:
Classes can be 1-1&1/2 hours long. For a workshop, two hours would be great.

Introduction:
I love sitting in a circle, introducing ourselves and sharing what we know about weaving.

Guided Relaxation:
“This exercise is a way to get centered and visualize a cover for your weaving journal. If you feel safe, you can close your eyes. Become aware of your breathing. Think of a place that is very special to you, a place where you feel very safe. Smell the smells, listen to the noises, feel the breezes if you are outdoors, or the sand under your feet. This is your special place and because you are safe here, you can be your most creative. Let yourself begin to imagine the kind of picture you would like to bring back from this special place: the colors, the feelings, the words. When you are ready to come back from this place, begin to become aware of your breathing again.”

I usually sense when the group has had enough and begins to get restless and I respect their timing.








Diagrams for creating weaving with sketchbook
Creation Process:
In this workshop we use the notebook as a loom. To do this we tie warp thread around it and tape it to the back. Keeping the tension even, wind the warp around the “loom,” keeping the yarns parallel but the spacing depends on personal choice. They can be wound close together, far apart, or both. It will affect the design and looseness or tightness of the woven piece. When you have as much warp on as the width of the piece you want to weave, tie off and tape at the end. Some people like to cut a small slit in the cardboard to anchor the weaving in with a knot.

Then, tie a piece of yarn (about a yard, not too long or it can tangle) to a needle or use your fingers to take the weft yarn over and under the warp threads. Leave an inch or so of the end thread hanging and weave it into the next row. To begin a new color do the same, weaving about an inch or more on either end back into the weaving. Keeping the edges straight is a new (and old) weaver’s biggest challenge.

To finish, cut the warp string down the middle of the back, 2-4 strings at a time and tie two strings at a time together. This prevents the weaving from unraveling and creates a fringe. Cut the fringe long enough so that the knots do not untie.

The sketchbook is for anything! I use mine to write in, do poetry, it's a scrapbook and a place to draw and design.

Towards the end of our time, I like to read a short story about weaving and life.

Reflection and Closing:
This time is very important and I am just learning how to incorporate this into my groups with a sharing of the work, comments on the experience and time to clean up the things they were using.

Background and Inspiration for Peace Weaving Project:
In 1991, The first Gulf War began and the first Peace Weaving was created. People from many ages, backgrounds, and beliefs have worked on these weavings. They have been sent with groups or individuals having a commitment to peace and restoration.

Iraq             -Physicians for Social Responsibility
Bosnia          -Halcyon Weavers
Haiti            -Bryan Sirchio
                   It now hangs in a hospital on a ward for
                   children with tuberculosis and AIDS.
Madison        -We are currently looking for a place to share
                   this weaving.
Israel           -There are plans to display this weaving with
                   the one for Palestine.
El Salvador    -Arcatao Sister City delegation, summer, 1996.
Burma          -In the process of being delivered to Burma.
Cuba            -Delivered to Havana, Cuba, January, 1997.
Nicaragua      -Being taken to our sister city, Managua,
                   Nicaragua, summer, 1997.
Palestine      -Current Peace Weaving.

Each weaving is a prayer or a thought of peace for a place in turmoil and pain. The hope is that each weaving will hang in a place of healing, such as hospitals, community centers, shelters, daycare centers, or homes for the elderly.

Project Variation:
Other than creating their own small weavings with the sketchbook/notebook as a loom, they can take part in creating larger Peace Weavings. Once they have the basic idea of their own looms I bring in a Navajo upright loom with a weaving in progress and I invite them to add a special color (obviously different for everyone) that feels like peace to them, or any symbolic piece they find, feathers, shells, etc. This can be worked on by, at most, four at a time. It is something they can turn to if they need a break from their project.

I choose the locations to send the Peace Weavings by my feelings. Sometimes, I am moved to send a weaving by the news, sometimes, friends have inspired me or social action groups, such as the Madison's Sister-City projects. I take my loom to family, friends, classes, churches, schools, the streets. It is a great way to open conversation and educate.
Row.txt_description: Shares a simple weaving method as a way for participants to express themselves creatively, learn about themselves and their world, and raise their self-esteem. The finished product is a woven journal cover.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide participants with a sense of safety in expressing all the negative things that have been said to them and they have thought about themselves so that they may:
-Write down anything, person or reason th at they feel has held them back, kept them     from accomplishing (eg: ugly or negative secrets, fears, negative thinking or remarks,         etc.)
-Free themselves to grow and live a productive, spiritual and empowered life.
-Take responsibility and reclaim or establish their power. To stop claiming the negatives     and allowing them to "rent" space in the head.
 -Reclaim the positives and allow them to roam freely in the growing span of their             minds.
 -Discover a tool to use when the negatives are surrounding them and trying to break         their spirit and put them down.

This exercise will help the warrior inside come out and fight the negatives and will help your “empowered self” to increase in strength.  This workshop is especially useful when we are our functioning as own worst enemy by putting ourselves down.

Materials:
Pens
Pencils
Bright markers
Paper
Bucket or garbage pail
Water (to drown the papers)
Dirt (to dig a hole)
Match (to burn papers)
Area where there is a garbage bin, open grassy area, or dirt lot (for burial)

Music:
Music with drums or songs of empowerment (eg: Tracy Chapman, Gabriel Roth, Ubaka Hillor, Agape Choir). Uplifting songs work well with this workshop. It helps to evoke the emotions for release.

Time Format:
1-2 hrs., sometimes just 20-35 minutes. It depends on what place the group is in after completing this “Labor of Love” and how much they feel like talking.

Introduction:
“This excercise is a Labor of Love for oneself. It may not feel that way in the beginning, but hopefully it will in the end. Let's do this exercise in silence so that the ultimate in concentration can occur. There will be time of sharing if you choose to do so in the end. We can all agree not to share, but if someone wants to, they can do so without judgment and in the safety of this circle or room. Please do not ask to read someone else’s paper or comment on anyone else's sharing. Let's respect each other's needs and space.

Writing:
“Thank you for participating in this process! Each of you has a writing utensil and at least two pieces of paper. Please write down everything you hate about yourself. Put down what you can remember that was said to you: anything you want to let go of, any secrets that you want to release, anything that is hateful for you. You may also write down the person who has said harmful remarks or things to you if you so choose.”

Give about 5-20 minutes to write. Gauge your time by seeing what place everyone is in. Look around the room. No rescuing if someone is crying. Please don't run with a tissue. Let them ask for what they need, respecting they'll know when they need it. After completion of the list, ask the group if anyone wants to share. If no, move into the rest of the ceremony.

Creation:
One of two things can be done.
1. Each participant can fold their papers and tear it with all their might into tiny pieces. Then throw the paper into a trash can filled with water. Explain that it is important not to reclaim what was written, it is time to work towards the positive. If they do reclaim it at a later date, complete the ceremony again until they no longer reclaim the negatives back into their lives. Go out to that garbage bin. Let each participant either take a handful of water and paper flinging it into the bin or they may each pour some into the bin. Have them cheer and clap for themselves. Now is time for the closing and relaxation.

2. If you are in a grassy area or dirt filled place, dig a hole with a shovel and bury or burn the negatives in a deep hole. Let each participant share in digging the hole and placing the shredded paper in. The last person fills the hole in with water and dirt or covers the negatives. Let them cheer for themselves. This is where the ceremony ends and the relaxation and closing begin.

3. If there is a safe place to do it, i.e. a fireplace, the negatives can simply be burnt for a very satisfying finish followed by cheering, clapping and relaxation.

Relaxation & Closing:
The relaxation is the actual closing of the group. With a voice as soft as the wind and guided with a loving flow, begin the relaxation: “Please close your eyes, if this feels safe for you. [Open-eye meditation is still possible for those who are not safe closing their eyes.] Take a deep breath and let the air flow from your mouth slowly. Again this time follow the deep breath to your abdomen. Hold it for two seconds and release. This time make a soothing sound as the breath is exhaled. Inhale again deeper this time. Now release slowly making the soothing exhaling sound: sounds like music flowing from deep within you. For your last breath, go as deep as you can inhale. Picture yourself in a place that is peaceful for you. Exhale with a breath that is so soothing you send it to the center of the room. Whoever walks in this room afterward will feel all the good vibes you have left behind. Seek peace for yourself and do this relaxation before you go to bed at night or when you awaken. This has been a Labor of Love, a celebration of self. Note: If time permits, do a “feelings check” to make sure that everyone feels safe especially leaving the safety and support of the circle. This “feelings check” can be done quickly using one to two words or a sentence from each participant.
Row.txt_description: Provides participants with a sense of safety in expressing all of the negative things that have been said to them and they have thought about themselves. Allowing for a chance to free and reclaim their empowered, "warrior" selves from negative thoughts.

Row.txt_code:
“Disarming Your Critic” is the second part of the self-esteem art directive "Affirming Self-Worth" which appeared in the September Leader’s Update of 1997. Part of unlearning and replacing negative belief systems is through positive affirm ations. Another key part in this process is “disarming the internal critic.”



 "Flight of Escape!" by Twyla Swanson
Objective:
Offers participants the opportunity to explore the voice of their inner critic and then unlearn and replace negative belief systems through positive affirmations. The finished product is a two-part collage, one part is a vision of the critic's messages, the second is an image of a rescuer or some other kind of support against the critic.

Materials:
18” x 24” sheet of paper (or as large as you can find around this size)
Magazines
Glue
Scissors
Colored markers
Pencils

Note on Leading This Workshop:
It is important to impress upon the participants that this is a learning process and to look at progress rather than perfection. Explain to them that this internal critic has been having a big part in their mind for just about their entire life, and it probably won’t go away too easily or quickly. It’s important to celebrate small victories rather than expect huge changes right away. Impress upon them to be gentle with themselves as they grow and change into a new life of self-love and respect. Just as a caterpillar goes through many stages to become a butterfly, they too must go through a lifetime of transformation toward their own “becoming.”

Introduction:
What is this inner critic anyway? The internal critic is that “parental voice” inside you that condemns and criticizes you throughout the day. These messages are either ones that you heard directly when you were growing up, or messages that you internally believed that others felt about you or your behavior. This means that they are actually an “old tape” that continually plays in your head which was formed in your childhood. It may or may not be true for you today, yet you unknowingly keep replaying the tape.

In order to feel good about yourself, it’s important to be aware of the messages you believe and tell yourself. This way, you can begin to refute them.

For the purpose of this exercise, think back to a recent time when you made a mistake or accidentally did something which you felt bad about. Once you have that memory, recreate the scenario in your mind and listen to the things you told yourself about the mistake you made. It may be messages such as: “you can’t do anything right,” “you are such a screw-up”, “you’re such a klutz,” “you’re late again; that figures,” etc., etc., etc.

In this workshop, we will be exploring these messages so you can become more conscious of them. From this awareness of your critical messages, you can begin to change the way you treat yourself when they start in on you. In this workshop, we will accomplish this with some help from an imaginary or real person of your choosing.

This is very important! Just because you made a mistake or did something wrong does not make you a horrible person. Sometimes we need to talk to ourselves the way we would a child. We need to talk to ourselves about learning from our mistakes and giving ourselves an understanding and forgiving break. Human beings are not perfect. It’s human to make mistakes. It’s human to mess up and forget. Have kindness and gentleness in your heart when dealing with yourself.

Today’s art exercise will help you do two things: First, it will help you to be aware of the things you say to yourself, and second, it will give you creative ways to tame that critic in order to feel better about yourself. Have fun and learn about yourself. Use some humor if you can in dealing with the internal critic. Humor is very healing for something so harsh and critical.

Art Project:
This workshop will take place in a two-part collage. On the first half of the page, we will create a collage of our inner critic’s messages. We will have a chance to explore all the things the critic says. On the other half, we will create a collage of an imaginary rescuer coming to support us against the critic. This will give us a chance to explore new, creative, loving ways of disarming our critic.

Part I.
The Critic’s Message:
Cut out symbols of your own “critical inner voice.” Messages or comments that you tell yourself can be written down or cut out from magazines: pictures that symbolize some part of the critical inner voice. The collage could also be about how you put “shoulds” on yourself. That is, things you feel that you should be, or should be doing, or should be doing better. Create a collage of the inner critic’s message on the left half of your page.

Part II.
Finding Support:
After the critic part of the collage is done, see if you can come up with a cartoon character who comes to the rescue. If the cartoon character doesn’t work, perhaps you can think of someone in your lifetime who seems loving, positive, and gentle. You could imagine that person coming to your rescue to deal with the inner critic.

Once you have found your “helper,” create a collage or symbol for it on the right half of the page. Add encouraging words or phrases the helper would say to you during the critic’s attack. By creating this symbol and adding these positive messages, they will more likely resurface automatically next time you begin to criticize yourself.

Note to Facilitator:
You may need to play around with ideas and help participants share with each other until each participant has a “helper” who will work with them. If they cannot come up with a person or cartoon figure, perhaps the good fairy in the Wizard of Oz or fairy godmother in Cinderella would suffice. Finding support is the main objective here.

You will probably also have to help participants brainstorm on positive messages to tell themselves. Get everyone’s input so they are personalized rather than you giving them the “answers.” However, if they are truly stuck, here are some options:

“It’s OK to make mistakes, I can learn from them.”
“I am doing the best I can with what I know.”
“I am a child of God, therefore I am valuable.”
“Silly me, I goofed up.”
“This is about a behavior and not about who I am.”
“I choose to let go of this old negative belief.”

Winding Down:
After the participants have shared with each other their artwork, ask them to sit in a comfortable position and close their eyes for a moment. Ask them to take a few long deep breaths. Then say the following:

“Now imagine yourself as you were when you were a five or six year old child, and imagine her sitting or standing in front of you. (Pause for a moment.) Imagine her innocence and magic of simply being the delightful child she is.... Now think of some of the messages you have realized today that you continually tell yourself. Think of how it would feel to this child if you told her those things. (Pause.) This is exactly what happens when you say those things to yourself. You are telling them to the five-year-old emotional child within yourself. Take a moment to understand that you actually did not realize what you were doing. But you can start watching what you say to yourself today. Forgiving yourself first and foremost, make a commitment to this five-year-old inside you. Tell the little child that you will start to lessen these critical messages as much as you can, and that you will work on being supportive and loving and forgiving to her. Love this little child, because she still lives within you. She is your soft heart and needs your continued nourishment. Treat yourself with gentleness and forgiveness, always.

Closing Circle:
Give each participant an opportunity to share one word, phrase or thought about what she takes with her from this workshop.

Further Resources:
There are many good books out there on building self-esteem. I would like to recommend the book Self-Esteem by Mathew McKay, Ph.D., & Patrick Fanning. This is a very thorough and practical guide, but may be too clinical for some. Two other very excellent books are: You Can Heal Your Life by Louise Hay and Healing The Shame That Binds You by John Bradshaw. These go beyond just self-esteem to include it in a more holistic way in your life. Bradshaw actually goes more into understanding the dysfunctional family system and its effects on the individual. This may be more appropriate and helpful for those leaving abusive situations.
Row.txt_description: Offers participants the opportunity to explore the voice of their inner critic and then unlearn and replace negative belief systems through positive affirmations. Finished product is a two-part collage, one part is a vision of the critic's messages, the second is an image of a rescuer or some other kind of support against the critic.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: See list of workshop ideas in this update that might need fleshing out as whole updates (Spirit Ornaments, Cards & Stationery Making, A Gift for Myself).

Row.txt_code:
Suzanne Karcher Rogers


About the Author:
My name is Suzanne Karcher Rogers.  I'm a survivor of domestic violence and have been a painter for fifteen years.  I've always thought of art as my home.  I decided to share this home of art experience with others last July in shelters in Ohio.  Showing others a place where they can gain clarity through their creations seems very important, or just inviting them to play with the idea of creating something seems to make a difference.  I'm not sure I'm always able to relate the home I've found in art to other people, but I come with the idea that we can all create meaningful things.  I've noticed the energy is uplifted during workshops.  If nothing else, it brings some good feelings and smiles, and sometimes more.

Objective:
To provide a space of time for survivors to think about dreams and goals for the future.  Since I've been running workshops, I've noticed that many of the adults have so many responsibilities in their lives - with children, finding new homes, and starting over - that they don't always give themselves time to think about their goals and visions.  My guess is some have long put their dreams on hold.  This is a chance to get back in touch with what they want for themselves, dreams they may have, but just forgotten.

Materials:
Plain greeting cards and envelopes
Masking tape (optional)
Oil pastels (sets can be shared)
Money saving option: assorted cattle markers or oil sticks
Pencils, Writing paper
Tape player and relaxing tapes

Note: This project can be done with any materials you have on hand, oil pastels are only one option.





Example from Dreams and
Goals Card workshop



Note to Facilitator:
Plain greeting cards are sold in packs of 10 to 20, in craft stores, card stores, or some large super stores.  They are fairly inexpensive.  Cards could also be made from various paper (cut and folded) and standard envelopes.

Cattle markers are a type of oil stick.  They are sold in feed mills and art supply stores (they are made for marking cattle, therefore are much more reasonably priced than conventional oil sticks.)

Timeframe:
20 minutes - opening circle, taping off cards, materials explanation
10 minutes - relaxation/meditation
10 minutes - timed writing
15 to 30 minutes - card front creation time
20 minutes - closing circle
Total time - 1 1/2 hours




Detail of drawing by Sandy Stallings




Introduction:
“This is a time for you to think about yourself - your dreams, visions, and goals.  While we do this we'll be making a greeting card to ourselves.  I will not be asking you to read this card aloud, so it can say anything!  First we'll do a short relaxation exercise so you will have time to think about your dreams/goals, so if nothing comes to mind right this minute that's fine.”   I think it's important to explain to people that the relaxation-meditation exercise is nothing they have to do.  I always explain that all they need to do is sit there during it - this seems to make the idea more comfortable.

“After we do the meditation, we'll do 10 minutes of timed writing for the inside of the card.  This is a time to write your most unimaginable goals for your life.  No dream is too big!  This is a time to think, ‘I can do anything.’

Timed writing is - writing your first fresh thoughts.  Don't stop writing keep your hand moving across the page.  Don't cross anything out.  Don't hesitate to write any goal or dream no matter how silly it seems.  Imagine your life exactly how you would love it to be, and write about that.  Don't hesitate - write your first thoughts.”
You could begin with one of the following phrases:

My goal for my life is -
My dream for me & my family is -
I've always dreamed of -
If I could do anything with my life, I would -

“After this writing time (10 minutes) we will make an image that represents this dream on the front of the card, or you could continue writing on front and other sheets of paper.”





Detail of drawing by Sandy Stallings



Technical Information:
“The materials available for these cards are oil sticks, oils pastels, and pencils.  Oils sticks make a greasy workable surface.  There is no wrong way to use these materials, and you may not want to use both sticks and pastels, but one way to use them is to apply the oil sticks first liberally and then work in pastels.  It's kind of a layering process, moving the paint around, changing and building the colors.  I've chosen these mediums because they are so changeable and you are not stuck with a surface.  The more you layer these paints (I think of them as paints, not crayons) the more interesting the image normally becomes.  Writing on the surface with pencil is also an option.  It creates very nice dark lines (writing) on the oil.”

Option: Taping off a square on the front of the card (with masking tape) before applying paints makes a nice crisp edge around your image.  (Show example of this.)

Relaxation:
This relaxation involves imagining colors as light or fog coming down into the room.  Some thoughts about meditation colors are included (page 4).  Feel free to copy and share these with participants.  Also, feel free to change the relaxation to better suit the needs of your particular group.

“Sit back in a relaxing position.  Take a deep breath and let it out slowly.  Think about any tension that may be in your body, and take a deep breath for that tension.  As you exhale, imagine the tension leaveing you.  (Continue taking breaths for arms, legs, stomach, neck, etc.)  Now imagine that a soft blue fog of light is coming down around you.  Breathe in the light and know that the light protects you.  Imagine violet light is coming down around you.  Breathe it in, and with this light you are free.  Imagine a soft yellow light coming down around you, and with it is your source of inner wisdom.  Imagine that a soft pink light comes down around you, and with it is an unconditional source of love.”




Detail of drawing by
Sandy Stallings




(You can continue with other light/colors if you like - I've found that passing out the Colors Meditation Thoughts tends to make people more interested in trying this relaxation technique and others.)

Lead-in to Timed Writing:
“Now start to think about dreams you have had in the past, and any that come to mind now, don't feel pressured, just let your thoughts flow through your mind.  When you're ready, open your eyes and begin writing.  Remember not to cross anything out, and don't stop writing.  Just write whatever comes to mind.  (Set timer when most of the group has begun writing.)

Painted Image:
When writing time is up (10 minutes) encourage participants to continue writing thoughts on other sheets of paper while making the card front image.

Closing Circle:
Give each person a chance to show the image on the front of their card, and share any thoughts about it.  Invite anyone to read their card,  explain there is no pressure to do so, or they could share how this experience has affected them.

Have everyone write their name on the front of a card envelope.

(Oil sticks take a few hours to dry, 2-10 hours according to the thickness applied) so the cards will not be placed in the envelopes right away.)

Keep your card to re-read occasionally!

Colors Meditation Thoughts:
This is a guide of colors you can meditate on, and the qualities known to these colors.  It is not meant to guide your art works, because the colors you choose then come from the inside of you.  I've included this because meditating with the idea of a color/light can be very relaxing, and can be done at any time.  The color is imagined, for example, as a soft blue fog or blue light coming down aroud you.  The color/light can be breathed in for a relaxed feeling of protection and faith.  Knowing as you breathe in the light you are safe and protected.

Light blue - Protection, Faith, Will
Shamrock Green - Healing, Supply
Violet - Freedom, Forgiveness, Transmutation
Light Yellow - Wisdom
Rose Pink - Love, Devotion
White - Purity
Purple - Service, Ministration
Row.txt_description: Provides a space of time for participants to think about dreams and goals for the future and to take those dreams and goals off "hold." The end product is a decorated greeting card that the participant writes to herself, reminding herself in a positive voice of her desires for the future.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for Teens.
