< br/>

Deborah Koff-Chapin


Abou t the Author:
My name is Deborah Koff-Chapin.  I discovered Touch Drawing in 1974.  I was in the print shop on my last day of art school.  As I was about to clean an inked glass, I playfully moved my hands on the back of the paper towel.  Upon lifting it, I saw that lines had been transferred to the underside through the pressure of my fingers.  I became ecstatic with the realization that lines had just come directly from the movement of my fingertips on the paper towel.  I felt in this moment that ”Touch Drawing” was not for myself alone.  My calling in life is to share this healing creative process with others.  I am honored to be presenting it to you, who are doing such important work to support healing and creativity!  

Note:  Compared to other Windows workshops these materials are fairly expensive and the process is relatively messy and requires a lot of space.   

Objective:
“This workshop provides a very safe, deep and private space to be with yourself.  You draw whatever you feel in the moment.  Each drawing takes you to a new place in yourself, which you again draw.  There is room for all feelings; from pain and darkness to playfulness and joy.  All you need to do is draw what you feel in the moment, not thinking of what it ‘looks like.’  The sense of freedom and permission to draw whatever you feel allows a deeper part of yourself to emerge.  In one session you will do a whole series of drawings.   While reflecting on the drawings after they are done, you may be surprised by the beauty, strength, and honesty that came through; you may gain insight from these images that came from the non-verbal part of yourself.  In Touch Drawing you learn to trust yourself; that the deeper part of you can guide you through even the darkest times into the light.”

Materials:
Student grade oil paints, any colors
Printmaking rollers (two people can share one)
Any smooth surface: used glass, plastic lunch trays, Formica scraps from a cabinet-maker, or marker board from a lumberyard
Plenty of paper: at least 20 sheets per person.  Many types will work; I recommend tissue paper, available in packaging supply stores, because it is so sensitive to the touch.  Freezer paper, butcher paper, typing paper, and newsprint will all work.  

Note About Materials:  Touch Drawing books, videos, and Soul Cards are available at The Center for Touch Drawing (www.touchdrawing.com).





Hands in the midst of Touch Drawing.



Timeframe:
Two hours
Opening: 15 minutes
Activity: 45 minutes
Sharing with partner: 15 – 30 minutes
Closing circle: 30 minutes

Space Set-up:
If you are working on tables that need to be kept clean, cover them with newspaper or a plastic drop cloth.  Set a drawing board at each participant’s place.  Next to it place a roller, tubes of paint, and a generous supply of paper.  Completed drawings can be piled one on top of another on the floor next to each participant’s chair.

Opening Circle:
Demonstrate Touch Drawing.  Put a little paint on the board.  Show them that they do not need as much paint as they might think.  Roll the paint smooth.  Put a sheet of paper on top of the paint.  Move your hands upon the paper.  Lift it and show how the paint only sticks to the paper where you have touched it.  (Hence the name, Touch Drawing!)

Emphasize that this will be a safe and private time to be with your own feelings, that it is okay to allow whatever feelings to come up to be valid expressions.  Show how you can draw with your eyes closed or open, with both hands or either hand.  Show how even the feeling of “not being able to draw” can be turned into a drawing.  Encourage participants to just stay with the process and honor whatever they are feeling by drawing it.  Encourage them to just trust themselves to know what to do.  Say you will give some suggestions while they are drawing, but that it is most important that they draw what they are feeling; only following the suggestions if they feel right. 




Touch Drawing by Deborah
Koff-Chapin




Activity:
Have participants each go to their own drawing board.  Invite them to take a few moments in silence to be open to the possibility of having an experience that will be most helpful, healing and fulfilling for them.

Encourage participants to begin by closing their eyes and moving their hands on the page.  Lift the paper off and put another one on the board immediately.  Occasionally, you can make suggestions such as the following:

“Bring your attention to your face.  Draw what your face feels like right now.

“Become aware of what your body feels right now.  Draw from those feelings.

“If you could do anything right now that would express how you feel, what would that be?  Imagine yourself doing that and draw yourself.

“Become aware of how your body would like to feel right now.  Draw from those feelings.

“Think of a relationship or situation in your life that you would like to change.  First draw it the way it feels to you right now.

“Next, draw the change you would like to experience.  Allow yourself to feel as if it has actually happened.  Draw from that feeling.

“Allow yourself to just be free of any thoughts.  Look at the paper.  Do you ‘see’ any drawing that has begun by itself through paint sticking to the paper, or anything that just pops into your mind’s eye as you gaze at the paper?”

A few minutes before the end of the drawing time, let the participants know they will be coming to a close soon.





Touch Drawing by Deborah
Koff-Chapin



Sharing in Partners:
When the activity time is over, encourage participants to find a partner they feel safe with.  One at a time, honor each other’s experience by looking through the drawings from the first to the last.  It is not necessary to interpret the drawings.  Just being deeply “seen” can be enough.  The participants can talk about what their experiences were while drawing.

Closing Circle:
Encourage each participant to share something about her experience.  Invite them to share a drawing or two if they would like.  This is not required.  Suggest that participants look at their drawings again in a few days.  They will be able to appreciate them more over time.  Talk about how they can take their drawing experience further by working creatively with their drawings.  This could happen as a group in another session; journal writing, storytelling, movement; whatever modes of expression you are comfortable leading the group in.   

Close the session with a moment of quiet to give thanks for each participant’s experience.  State the intention that each participant will find her own way to integrate and use this experience in a positive way.
Row.txt_description: Provides a very safe, deep and private space to draw whatever participants feel in the moment. The end product is a series of quickly done, intuitive drawings.

Row.txt_code:
Suzy Karcher with Art Festival participant



About the Author:
Suzy Karcher Rogers is an artist and survivor of domestic violence who traveled from Ohio to attend the Window’s Leadership Training in 1997.  Since then, she has launched weekly art workshops for the residents at two local Ohio shelters.  In the process, she has developed many of her own workshops, and this is the second one she has written up to share with all of us at AWBW.  

Because of staffing and childcare challenges at the shelters, Suzy has often found herself working with children and adults together.  While this situation has been less than ideal and Suzy has had her hands full, she has been able to make a success out of these situations.  Her flexibility, her willingness to prepare for the unexpected, and her relaxed delight in participants of all ages help make this possible.





Freedom Beads



Objective:
This is a fun and lively workshop.  It is also a time to think about freedom, and its importance to us.  Being in an abusive relationship, or part of a family where abuse has taken place can make it hard to remember what freedom is.  This workshop gives us a period of time to think about freedom - what it means to us personally, and how we can also allow others (including our children) to feel a sense of freedom.

Materials:
Super Sculpey
Acrylic paint
Brushes
Palette paper, or paper plates
Bead string
Scissors
Writing paper
Markers
Relaxing music
Optional: Assorted colored beads (young children are not always able to complete the process of making and painting beads to string.  It’s nice to have assorted beads for them to string along with the others).

Note:  Plastic beads can be bought in a large bag fairly inexpensively.

Less Messy Option:  Instead of using acrylic paint, buy colored Sculpey.  It‘s more expensive than plain Sculpey but can save a lot of time and mess with the paints. 





Freedom Necklace (enlarged detail)



Timeframe:
(Total time - 1 1/2 to 2 hours)
15 minutes - opening circle
30 minutes - making Super Sculpey beads
10 minutes - baking time  (This can be time spent experimenting with the paint - mixing colors on the palette.)
15 to 30 minutes - painting the beads
10 minutes - stringing beads (Children may need more time.)
10 minutes - closing circle

Note to Facilitator:  I’ve found during this workshop that adults and children really have a good time making these beads. Because they are making so many quick art works (beads), they are not bound by the idea that they all have to turn out good - as often happens when only making one thing.  The idea of making a bead necklace is just frivolous enough to take away some people’s hesitation of making “art,” and they become free to create however they want.

Working with Adults and Children:
I have had some very good workshops where both adults and children are involved, but I basically try to go with the flow of the residents.  If the group is small (3 to 5 people) it normally goes very well, but with larger groups it becomes a little hectic.  Ideally, there should be other volunteers or staff to help the children in this workshop, but it’s been my experience that volunteers are not abounding at the shelter, and staff usually have a lot of their own duties.  Still, planning ahead to have others help would certainly make the workshop run smoother.  Normally there is child care staff around and I invite them to help run the workshop.  If that is not an option, I try to arrange the group in a circle where adults and children are involved together.  Children like working with Super Sculpey, so they don’t get bored too quickly.  They can make a couple of large beads and then start stringing plastic beads while the adults are still working.  Children should be at least 3 or 4 years old to be in this workshop. 





Freedom Necklace



Opening Circle:
“We’re going to be making beads out of Super Sculpey, painting them, and stringing a ‘Freedom Necklace.’  This necklace could be worn or hung on a nail on the wall to remind us of the freedom we want for ourselves and others.  We’ll begin with a discussion of what freedom is, and how we might bring this idea to the beads we’ll be making.”  (Everyone should have a chance to talk in the circle, or feel “free” not to.  I normally start the conversation and just invite anyone else to jump in, they always do, and it takes away the pressure of those who do not feel like talking.)

Exploring Ideas of Freedom/Creating the Beads:
“Freedom may be being able to make decisions for yourself, and voice them, without fear of what others will do.  You may just want to think of a time when you have felt very free.  You could allow yourself the freedom now to make these beads any way, any size, without concern for how they might look.  Think about what shape freedom is for you.  Maybe it’s just a round bead that you don’t have to do much to.  What color is it?”

I encourage the adults to write thoughts while making beads.  In addition, when working with the children, I have a large sheet of paper beside me.  I invite them to voice their thoughts, while making beads.  I write their thoughts on our “Together List.”  When everyone is finished making the beads they can place them on their own area of the baking pan (everyone needs their own space on a baking tray to keep people’s beads separate).

Baking Time/Paint Exploration:
Beads bake quickly (about 5 minutes) because they’re small.  Large beads should be put on a different pan to begin with so they can bake longer (10 minutes).  “While the beads are baking we will experiment with the paint on palette sheets.  Let’s not settle for the colors in the tube.  That may be what you want, but let’s see what we can make first.”  (This becomes a very interesting part of the workshop.  Many people have never really mixed colors, and discovered what paint can do.  If the palette becomes interesting, I suggest they keep it as a painting, and mix for the beads on another sheet.)
 
Painting and Stringing the Beads:
One suggestion for painting beads is to paint small lines on the palette paper and just roll the beads through it.  Some may want to paint intricate paintings on the beads.  Acrylic paint dries fast (about 5 minutes).  Children will finish first, so you could take them away from the table and do some stretching games, while the beads are drying, and the adults finish painting.  Children will also need help stringing the beads.  String at a new table, and have the plastic beads there to add to the necklaces.  Older children can help the younger ones string beads also.  

Closing Circle:
Everyone should have a chance to show their necklace and talk about it.  Some participants will want to read part of what they have written.  Let them know that their writing is a valid form of art as well as the necklace, and they should keep it.  The “Together List” should be read also - children like to know that their thoughts are important.




Freedom Pin, Super Sculpey
Row.txt_description: A fun and lively workshop, giving time to think about the importance of freedom. End product is a Freedom Beads necklace or other form of wearable art.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation specifically for adults and children together.

< br/>

Fig. 1: Unusual handmade book shape


As a volunteer staff person at AWBW, I participated in a handmade book-making workshop recently led by Sherrill Kahn.  Sherrill is a dynamic artist and teacher and her energy is infectuous.  We had a great time making and sharing our books.  Since we had almost the whole day to explore book-making, Sherrill introduced a lot of techniques.  However, since shelter workshops are limited to two hours or less, I’m going to share the basics of book-making in this update.

Objective:
This workshop is a wonderful opportunity for participants to create something deeply personal, something they can keep and cherish.  A book can be whatever shape, size or color the participant wants.  They can be used as journals for art or writing or photos.  The important thing is, as Sherrill stressed, is that there is no right or wrong.  She showed us some of the different shapes, colors and cover designs of books she had made.
 
Materials:
Cover-weight paper for book covers
Paper for inside pages (try to provide a variety of colors for both cover and inside paper)
Acrylic paint (include iridescents)
Sponges cut into 1” squares
Net/mesh bath sponges (you can buy one mesh sponge, undo the metal staple at the center, cut into several pieces, and restaple, to create many mesh sponges from one)
Stapler: Long-necked (if available) or standard (if using a standard stapler, you will need corrugated cardboard and a metal table knife or spoon to hand-close the staples)
Plastic forks
Edgers (scissors that cut an interesting edge design)
Rubber stamps (optional)
Scissors (one per participant)
Glue sticks (one per participant)
Paper plates (to use as pallettes)
Paper towels
Water bucket (for rinsing sponges and rubber stamps)

Timeframe:
(Total time - 1 1/2 to 2 hours)
15 minutes - opening circle
10 minutes - demonstration
60 minutes - making books
15 minutes - closing circle

Note on Preparation:
It is helpful to have a few examples of books you have made to show at the beginning of the workshop.  It’s good to show some unconventional shapes (see Fig. 1), and let participants know they can make any shape they want.  It doesn’t need to look a certain way. 

To create the samples, I recommend that you try the following 6 steps yourself.  It will be well worth the time and will make it much easier for you to assist the participants.

Opening:
“Today, we will be making hand-made books.  As we make our books, the most important thing to remember is that there is no right or wrong.  You get to make your book any shape, size, color you think of.  Here are some examples of hand-made books (show your samples).  I’ll be demonstrating some of the steps we can use to make the books, but I want you to remember, you never have to do it like I am.  You get to do it however you want to.”  (If you want to have an opening circle, with each person sharing something about how she is feeling, go ahead and incorporate that into your opening.)

Demonstration:
To best share the book-making steps, create a demonstration example in front of the group.  That way, you can show each step hands-on, while encouraging each participant to be creative and make her book however she wants it. 

You can either do a full demonstration of the steps before the group begin their own books, or you can demonstrate each step along with them.  Use whichever way works best for you.






Fig. 2: Cutting triangular book cover

Fig. 3: Cutting round book cover



Step 1: Cover
The first step is for each participant to select her cover paper and then fold and cut it into her desired size and shape.  Books can be large, small, square, round, triangular, or any shape the participant chooses.  Encourage each person to create her own cover (see Fig. 2&3).   

Step 2: Select Pages
Next, each participant selects the paper to put inside her cover (usually about 4 sheets, folded, is enough).  Trim the pages so that they are slightly smaller than the cover.  Again, remember that creativity is welcome.  Some women may want to design their books with the paper sticking out of the cover.

Step 3: Staple Pages
Third, participants can bind their books.  They can staple along the fold using a long-neck stapler, if one is available (see Fig. 4).  Otherwise, they can use a standard stapler.  Open it up so that it is flat, and use corrugated cardboard underneath to staple into (see Fig. 5).  The book will be stapled, with the staples sticking straight into the cardboard.  You will need to pull the book off of the cardboard and then use a knife or scissors to bend the ends of the staple down (see Fig. 6).






Fig. 4: Using long-necked Stapler

Fig. 5: Using regular stapler, opened up,
pressed into corrugated cardboard








Fig. 6: Using scissor tip to close staples
by hand


Step 4: Hiding the Staples
It’s amazing what a difference it can make to disguise the staples.  They can be hidden by gluing pieces of paper down the center of the booklet and/or down the outside edge of the cover (see Fig. 7&8).  (For decorative effect, you can sponge-paint the paper before gluing it over the staples.)







Fig. 7: Covering staples on
outside of book

Fig. 8: Covering staples on inside of book



Step 5: Detailing the Edges 
Add a decorative edge to the pages either by using paper-edgers (see Fig. 9&10), or by lightly finger-painting the edges of the cover with paint (see Fig. 11).  Gold paint looks especially elegant as an edge.






Fig. 9: Using edgers on inner pages

Fig. 10: Edged cover






Fig. 11: Finger-painting




Step 6: Decorate Cover 
The surface of the covers can be decorated by stamping paint on in many ways.  Sponges, forks and rubber stamps are only a few suggestions we have included for you to demonstrate. 

Once participants get going, they may find all sorts of objects around the shelter to use to create interesting patterns.  Encourage them to experiment.





Fig. 12: Plate palette with white paint



Preparing the palette:  To use these techniques, each participant will put paint onto a plate (this will be her palette).  Then she can use the sponges, net mesh, forks, and anything else she wishes, to apply the paint from the palette to the book).  She may also want to have some scratch paper at hand to experiment with creating stamp effects (see Fig. 12).

Sponge-effect:  Dab the sponge onto the pallette until the paint is the consistency you want.  The amount of paint on the sponge makes a big difference as to how the sponge-effect will look.  Experiment on the pallette with having different amounts of paint on your sponge. 

Web-effect:  Using a web-mesh bath sponge is a quick and easy way to decorate the booklet cover.   Similar to the sponge-effect, you will dab the mesh bath sponge onto your pallette.  It may take some vigorous dabbing to distribute the paint throughout the mesh for a web-like effect (see Fig. 14).  Experiment with amounts of paint.  For a fine web, it does not take very much paint, just a lot of dabbing.





Fig. 13: Dabbing mesh into paint





Fig. 14: Creating web pattern on cover



Fig. 15: Fork pattern, white paint on black



Fork-effect:  The tip of a fork can be used to place paint onto the cover of the booklet.  The effect can be somewhat like shooting stars (see Fig. 15).  This was discovered during the workshop thanks to one of the participants.

Rubber stamps:  If you have rubber stamps available, these can provide a wonderful source of decoration for the covers.  Use sponges to dab the paint onto the rubber stamps.  Then press onto the cover.  Before stamping on your cover, you may want to experiment on scratch paper with the effects created by different amounts of paint.

Further Decorations: 
Sherrill had lots of wonderful ideas for decorative ideas for the cover.  She suggested wooden beads, charms, raffia, yarn, shells and anything else the leaders or the women come up with.  A lot of items can be sewn or glued to the book. 

Closing Circle:
Save some time for the group to share what they made, what feelings and thoughts went into their decisions.  Perhaps they will be open to sharing what they will use the book for, and perhaps the next workshop can be dedicated to creative word pieces or picture collages to put into their books.
Row.txt_description: A powerful opportunity for participants to create something deeply personal to keep and cherish. The books can be whatever shape, size or color they want and can be used as journals for art, writing, or photos.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variations for Children's and Teens.

Row.txt_code:
Rose Curtis



As an AWBW Art leader, I am forever grateful for the opportunity to lead and participate in workshops with those staying at the shelter.  I had this idea of a round, “pizza-shaped” collage for many months now, and recently Katlin, the Survivor's Art Circle Director, inspired me to lead a workshop that would become part of the Survivor's Art Letter.  I had a great time coming up with the "Center of My Universe" idea, and of course, Cathy Salser motivated me to write up the workshop formally to share it with all of you!

I believe a circle is a very powerful symbol and when we put ourselves at the center of our universe, we can only expect powerful changes to happen in our lives. As you lead and participate in this workshop, I hope you are truly inspired to boldly create your Universe.

Objective:
This workshop is an opportunity for participants to focus on placing themselves at the center of their universe.  Each person’s vision of what this would mean to her unfolds during the workshop and becomes clear and tangible throughout the collaging process.
 
Materials:
Collage material (magazines, photostock books, etc.)
Glue sticks and scissors
Round poster board, approximately 9 inches across

Timeframe:
(Total time - 1 1/2 to 2 hours)
15 minutes - opening circle
10 minutes - demonstration
5 minutes - relaxation
45 minutes - making books
15 minutes - closing circle 







Strong Medicine
1998, collage
Artist: Brigitte Bailey

This represents who
I am inside and out.
All these things: my mother, my kids, and my father... being strong and loving.

   -Brigitte Bailey


Opening:
“This is a window of time to think about what exactly you want in your world. Put yourself in the center of your universe and decide what pleases you, what makes your life work, what is absolutely necessary to thrive.

As you are guided through the relaxation, see yourself as the
most important person in your universe and visualize what you want in your world. Be bold and feel free to see all your dreams come true!”

Demonstration:
“What we will be doing today is creating exactly what we want in our Universe. We are going to create a round collage. Put an image in the center of the collage to represent you. Then surround this image with all that you want in your world. When we know firmly in our hearts and our souls what we want, and when we put out to the Universe what we want, we are most likely to receive and achieve exactly what we want.”

Relaxation: 
Speak slowly, softly and very lovingly. “Make yourself comfortable. When you are sitting it is good to be sitting with your back straight, your feet flat on the floor and your hands lying loosely in your lap.





All the words featured in this
collage have a special meaning to me.  Especially
the phrase that surrounds
the woman who represents
me.  Now is the time to
think about me.  Many of the
words are things I look
forward to in my future such
as... the perfect marriage
and baby number two.  I look
at this collage and realize all
the words on the collage are
a part of me.

    -Jennifer Galvan

The Power of Words
1998, collage
Artist: Jennifer Galvan





“Take a deep breath and if it feels safe for you, you may close your eyes. This is a special time just for you...to breathe in love and breathe out any tension.

“Take another deep breath and exhale softly... move your awareness down to your feet and gently wiggle your toes... feel the relaxation moving up your calves... gently relax your thighs and your whole pelvic area. Breathe in slowly... exhale slowly and feel your stomach muscles gently relax.

“Breathe in love... breathe out tension and feel your shoulders relax. If there's any tension left in  your shoulder area, imagine it sliding off your shoulder.
Breathe in deeply and become aware of any last holding you are doing in your body, calmly release the tension... breathing in love... breathing out tension... feel yourself relaxing more and more deeply. Imagine your entire body is now totally relaxed.

“Now move your awareness into a very deep place inside of you... let images of the world you want float into your mind. See yourself strong and daring at the center of your universe... (pause) What do you want in your Universe? Notice what you want to surround yourself with... notice what your universe is made up of... breathing in love, visualize everything you desire in your Universe.

“Keeping those images with you bring yourself gently back to the room and when you are ready, open your eyes and begin to create a collage of your world with you boldly in the center of your Universe.”

Collage Activity:
Afer the relaxation, allow the next 45 minutes for participants to create their collages.

Closing Circle:
Ask the group to share their collage and any of the feelings that came up for them while creating their Universe.

Special Thanks:
The relaxation is adapted from "Meditations" by Shakti Gawain.





For me it means getting on with
life and becoming a better
person; learning to love myself
and having another person love
me and respect me.

It means being alright with
myself, and doing the things I
like—being happy, singing,
dancing and being very
feminine.

   -M. Ebdulia Leyva

Untitled
1998, collage
Artist: M. Ebdulia Leyva
Row.txt_description: An opportunity for participants to focus on placing themselves at the center of their universe. Each participant's vision of what this would mean unfolds during the workshop and becomes clear and tangible throughout the collaging process.

Row.txt_code:
Chari Grenfell, AWBW Art Leader
  
Chari Grenfell is an artist who coordinates and teaches art workshops to survivors of domestic violence in Central Oregon. Art materials for the workshops are provided by the Central Oregon Art Association (COAA) “Art in Healing” Program.  The COAA is an organization committed to serving the community through the arts.

Objective:
In this workshop, each participant creates a mask of her face and divides it in half, painting one side to represent her feelings as a victim and the other to represent her feelings as a survivor.  This workshop allows the participants to express feelings caused by their abuse on the victim side of the mask. By acknowledging and identifying their emotions, the participants can then move on to the positive feelings of self-love and personal empowerment on the survivor side of the mask. The completed masks become a visual validation of the power of choice.

   


“Victim— Eyes are dark.  Nose is
dark.  I don’t know why.  Lips
are hot, pissed.  The neck is
pissed...  Survivor is not as
dark.  I feel strong,
proud and look to my future
goals and dreams. 

I sometimes laugh in order to
move forward.”

   
Materials:
Aluminum foil cut into face size
Acrylic paint
Brushes
Palettes or paper plates
Water cups
Paper towels
Newspaper
Writing paper creased in half vertically
Pencils

Note to Facilitators:
This is a powerful workshop, and because it summons up many buried feelings, we allow as much time as possible for the closing circle. Our art workshops are incorporated into the shelter's weekly Support Group meeting, and the time allowance reflects a group size of 12-15 women.

   


The survivor who created this mask shared:

“The eyes are black slashes because they are sqeeaed shut in terror.  The lips are a black slash because they are sealed shut—they can’t open.  The mask is painted yellow because I was a coward and was too scared to leave, and my baby could have been killed because I was a coward.” 

When asked what the blue dot under the nose was, she responded, “the tiniest smell of freedom”.

She was a young pregnant woman whose husband had just tried to kill her.  At the time of making the mask, she did not know if the unborn baby would survive.
   
Timeframe:
(Total time 1 1/2 - 2 hours)
15 minutes: opening circle
10 minutes: forming aluminum foil mask
10 minutes: relaxation
5 minutes: writing victim/survivor feelings
30 minutes: mask painting
20-40 minutes: closing circle
 
Opening:
We usually open with a seemingly silly question, such as, "If you could be a telephone, what kind would you be, and why?" Or, "What kind of animal would you like to be today, and why?" These questions not only relax the group, but also serve to get them into a creative, right-brained frame of mind. They never fail to astound me with their insightful, pertinent analogies.

Forming the Mask:
"Today, we are going to be making a mask with two sides: a victim side and a survivor side. But first, we have to make an impression of your face on the aluminum foil. Simply put it over your face and begin to pat it into shape, starting with the area around and under your nose. Don't worry about getting it perfect because it will look much different when it is painted."

Some people put a tuck in the forehead, which makes it easier to handle when wet and easier to carry home. At this time, distribute foil, water, brushes, and palettes, making sure each person has newspaper under their painting area.  Also, make sure each person has a piece of paper creased in half vertically, and a pen ready for the writing warm-up which follows the relaxation.


 
 
 “The victim side has two dark colors
and is scared and worried.  The
survivor side is scared and worried,
too.  Scared of other men and how to
cope.”
  

Relaxation: 
When everyone is finished, we start the relaxation, explaining that participation is elective, with the objective that everyone relax and be comfortable. In a soothing tone, we follow the AWBW relaxation in the book. Sometimes we have them imagine that the air they are inhaling is a beautiful, colored fog that represents calm, and they should inhale it to the farthest tips of their fingers and toes. At the same time, they are exhaling tension, and they must exhale deeply to remove it from every part of their bodies.

Writing Warm-up (Victim/Survivor Feelings):
Writing, is an excellent way to transition into painting the masks.  By writing on the right and left halves of a piece of paper, the participants can begin to identify the feelings they will be painting on the right and left sides of their mask. 

When everyone is all relaxed and breathing deeply, we gently say, "When you feel you are ready to begin, take a moment and think about the times that you've been hurt—either physically, mentally, or verbally—and think about how that made you feel. On one side of your sheet of paper, please list all the words describing your feelings.  Just write them all down nonstop as they come into your mind." (Give them a few moments.)

"Now think about the times you've really felt good about yourself. Maybe someone said something nice to you, or maybe when you've been pleased with something you've done that was hard for you to do. How did that make you feel? Please take a few minutes to list all of your positive feelings on the other side of the paper.” 

Painting the Masks:
“When you are finished writing, paint your mask in whatever way will express your feelings best.  You might want to begin with the victim side, putting all those thoughts and feelings you wrote down on one side of your mask.  Then go ahead when you are ready, to paint the survivor side of your mask.  Remember, you are the only one who will interpret your mask."

(In general, it works best if the women divide the mask vertically, like the paper was divided.  However, if a participant wants to create two masks to represent the two states, or if she wants to paint the inside and outside of the mask, I always encourage her to do it as she wishes.)

Note to Facilitators:
This workshop could also be done with collage, glitter glue, and all sorts of embellishments. It could also be done in a more diminutive form using Sculpey.

Sharing Circle:
This workshop is extremely powerful, with the survivors reliving all the painful memories of their abuse, yet the positive side of the mask serves to nullify the pain. Most of the participants are very proud of their masks, and wish to share their reasons for painting the masks the way they did, but many prefer to keep their paper list of feelings to themselves.

   



“Victim—scared, angry, hurt, tired, sick, guilty,
ashamed, terrified, sad, alone...  The victim
side of the mask is just the way it looks.  

Survivor—tired, strong, sad, lonely, angry,
hopeful, excited, scared, curious, adamant...
The survivor side of the mask is a kind of a
butterfly symbolizing metamorphosis, change,
and freedom and my Mother.”
Row.txt_description: Participants create masks of their faces, divided in half. One side of the mask represents feelings and memories of being a victim and the other as a survivor.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for Teens.

Row.txt_code:
Some of the cigar boxes recently donated
to AWBW for “2000 Wishes”


Objective:
To give participants an opportunity to reflect on goals in relation to the coming years.  To create special treasure boxes decorated to express each participant's personal wishes for the year ahead.  To give participants a place (the box) to store notes and treasures, both as reminders and encouragement towards each step they take to fulfill their goals throughout the year. 

Materials:
Cigar boxes-one per participant
Colored tissue paper
Large margarine containers
Elmer's glue
Large, soft brushes
Magazines
Scissors
Newspapers
Crayons
Writing paper
Ball-point pens
Ribbons
Glue sticks
Feathers, sequins
Beads, buttons
Paper towels

Timeframe:
Introduction:  5 min.
Opening Circle:  15 min.
Demonstration:  5 min.
Supply Distribution:  5 min.
Relaxation:  5 min.
Writing:  5 min.
Creation:  60 min.
Closing:  15 min.





Glue & water mixture, ready to dip into





Torn tissue paper, ready for gluing





Tearing magazine pictures instead of using
scissors gives a wonderful edge







Setup:
Cover table with newspaper.  Make a bowl of glue/water mixture (half glue, half water).   Rip up some tissue paper and rip out a few magazine pictures to use during your demonstration.
Note:
This worksop is titled “2000 Wishes” because it was created in preparation for the year 2000.  With the new millenium feeling so momentous, this workkshop provided an opportunity to prepare for the big new year.  Feel free to adapt it for any year.

Introduction:
"Today we are going to think about our lives and our goals for the coming year.  With only a little time to go before the new year, many people are taking special care to examine the direction of their lives.  This workshop will be a chance for us to do that.

"We will be creating special treasure boxes - boxes of dreams - expressing our wishes for this coming year.  Your 2000 Wishes box will serve as a special place to store notes, treasures, and mementos throughout the year to commemorate each step you take toward achieving your own goals.  Today, we will be decorating the boxes to define and express our goals."

During the introduction, it might be good to get a sense of how participants feel about the new year.  Have they had a chance to think about it?  If they don't seem to care personally about the new year, you can focus on how it's always helpful (at any time) for us to focus on our wishes and have a special place to honor each step we take toward making them come true.

Opening Circle:
"Share how you are feeling today and a time in your life when you made a wish or dream of your own come true.  If you can't think of one that you already made come true, share one you are working on."




Step A:  Brush glue
onto the surface





Step B:  Lay tissue paper or
picture onto glue





Step C:  Brush more glue
over the paper




Demonstration:  
(Try this process before the workshop, to familiarize yourself with it).  The following steps demonstrate how to paste onto the 2000 Wishes boxes:

1.  Choosing a box to decorate (for the demonstration, you may want to use a spare piece of cardboard instead of box).

2.  Choosing and ripping up tissue paper and/or magazine pictures that have colors or images expressing our wishes.  (Demonstrate ripping out some images and tissue paper.  Explain that scissors are available for precision cutting, but the torn edge can look especially wonderful).

3.  Pasting the torn tissue paper and magazine pieces onto the box.  (Demonstrate brushing the glue/water mixture onto the box, then applying the tissue or image to the sticky surface; followed by brushing more glue/water on the surface of the tissue or magazine image.  Demonstrate how the tissue paper can overlap and create beautiful see-through multicolored layers.)

Supply Distribution:  
Before the relaxation, have each participant select her box and some tissue paper and magazines.  Also, make sure there are brushes, scissors and a bowl of glue-water within everyone's reach.   If you are going to use the optional writing exercise, make sure everyone has paper and pen before beginning the relaxation.

Relaxation:
(Use the following example or your own favorite relaxation, and of course, include soothing music).  "Get yourself comfortable.  Take a deep breath.  Hold it for a moment, and then slowly let it go.  Take another deep breath.  Imagine you are breathing in pure relaxation.  Hold your breath for a moment.  Now exhale, and imagine you are breathing out all the tension of your day, your week, your life.  As you take a third deep breath, notice again that you are breathing in pure relaxation.  As you exhale, notice once again that you are releasing any tension.  Notice your body.  Are there any areas of remaining tension?  Inhale, and as you exhale, send your relaxing breath to those areas.  Imagine melting any tension away.

"When you feel relaxed and ready, focus your thoughts on your wishes for yourself, your wishes for your life, your wishes for your world.  Any wishes that come to mind are to be honored and respected.  Notice what surfaces and floats across your mind.  Remember, you get to honor the beauty of your wishes, as if watching the clouds cross the sky: slow and beautiful."

Writing (Optional):
After the relaxation, you might have the group do 5 minutes of peaceful, free writing; allowing any thoughts regarding their wishes to flow through their pens.  Encourage them to respect whatever wishes come to mind:  large or small, whatever they think of is important.   

If you are not going to have the group do the writing together, you might mention that paper and pens are available for those who wish to write before starting their box.

Creation:
As the group begins to tear the paper and make collages on their boxes, encourage them to hold their wishes in mind and honor them.  Encourage them to relax, to acknowledge their value, and to know that each of their wishes is a treasure to cherish and enjoy.  Assist with the technical process where needed.







Closing Circle:
As the workshop draws to a close, validate the creativity and focus of the group.  If some participants are still not finished, encourage them to continue on their own after the workshop.  Remind them that each box is a precious box of dreams, and a place to honor each step of the journey.  The boxes are a place throughout the year to keep notes and treasures and mementos of each step.

Encourage each participant to share the meaning of her box as a part of the closing circle.  After everyone has spoken, remind the group, "Every time you complete each thing towards your goal, remember to add it to your box."
Row.txt_description: Gives each participant an opportunity to reflect on her goals in relation to the coming year. The end product are special treasure boxes decorated to express each participant's personal wishes for the year ahead.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Look at (Children's) Treasure Boxes for potential variations.

Row.txt_code:
Ornament made with the Sculpey technique.


Objective:
To create unique ornaments that participants can save and see each year as a reminder of this particularly special holiday: this turning point in her life.  To bring a personal touch to the celebration of the holidays.  To gain a sense of satisfaction with the “professional” look of the finished product.   

Materials:
Glass ball ornaments (one per participant)
Acrylic paints
Sculpey clay
Paint brushes
Hot glue & glue gun    
Clear sealer gloss spray
Gold/silver spray paint
Newspaper
Wire hanger
Decorative ribbon

Note: See page 4 for project variations without sprays or without glass ball ornaments.

For Children and Teens:  While this project may be too tedious for younger children, it could be captivating for older ones.  Be sure to try the process out first so you’ll know how to explain it smoothly.





Glass ball ornaments, ready to decorate.



Timeframe:
Introduction:  5 min.
Opening circle:  10 min.
Demonstration:  10 min.
Sculpey creation:  20 min.
Cooking and Cooling:  20 min.
Painting:  20 min.
Closing:  10 min.

Note:  If you have more time, you may want to have a longer workshop or leave it open-ended with supplies available after the workshop so participants can take all the time and care they wish as they complete their ornaments.


Depth Considerations:
This workshop can be more playful or more focused depending on the tone of your group.  You can encourage the group to create traditional holiday decorations, or you can encourage them to notice the turning point that this holiday season represents in their life, and to create a more emotionally expressive design or decoration that shows the meaning of these holidays for them. 




Glass ball ornament-
maker smiles.




Introduction:
“Sometimes the holiday season can be a difficult time for people.  Feelings of sadness and stress can be strong.  Being in a shelter during the holiday season can also feel difficult.  Does anyone feel some sadness?  Some stress?  The holidays can also be a time of many positive feelings and joys.  It can be a time to notice all that we appreciate.  Appreciating the simple fact of being alive, being able to breathe, having food, warmth, other people around us and a roof over our head...  Can anyone think of something you appreciate this year during this season?  Today, we will be taking some time to celebrate what the holidays mean for us this particular year.  It’s a special year.  As you know, you’ve each taken a tremendous step in your lives just be being here, being at ________ (shelter name), and reaching out for support to make the future you want.  This holiday season is a turning point.   Today we are going to be making “Turning Point Ornaments” to celebrate the holidays in a special way.  You will be able to take your ornament with you, and use it year after year, a marker of this special holiday and this turning point in your life.”

Opening Circle:
"What’s a positive thought or turning point that this particular year’s holiday represents for you?"





Sculpey pressed directly onto the ball.



Demonstration:  
(Try this process before the workshop, to familiarize yourself with it).  Walk the group through the various steps involved in creating the ornaments.  If you can show a finished example, painted, decorated with ribbon, hook and all, that will give a sense of what’s possible.   

Creation Steps:

1. On a clean glass ball, mold sculpey into various shapes representing the holidays for you.  You may choose traditional shapes such as stars, candles, snowmen, trees, wreaths, etc...  You may also create your own designs and symbols of your holiday, or some combination of traditional and individual.

2. Bake in oven at 250 degrees - 10 minutes for every 1/4 inch thickness. (It helps to hang the ornaments from the rack.)  

3. Allow the ornaments to cool.

4. Using the glue gun, glue the ornament cap (that holds the hook) onto the ball.  Remove any glue strings.  The gluing make the ornament’s hook strong and secure.





A hanger helps hold the ornament
when you spray the ball.



5. Spray paint the entire ball with silver or gold spray paint in light, even strokes.  This will need to be done outside, or in a well-ventilated room away from the main workshop space.

6. Dry completely (may need 2-3 thin coats to cover evenly and completely).

7. Paint sculpey part (or other designs you may want) using acrylic paints.  You may wish to paint words on your ornament, and/or the year and your initials.  

8. Dry completely.

9. Use a spray sealer gloss to coat ornaments.  This gives a protective coating and a professional look.




Sculpey pressed directly onto the ball.





A ribbon adds a finishing touch




10. Hang with hook or decorative ribbon.

11. Enjoy!

Closing Circle:
Encourage participants to share the meaning of what they created.





Painting the sprayed ornament.
Row.txt_description: Participants create unique ornaments which they can save and see each year as a reminder of this particularly special holiday: this turning point in their lives.

Row.txt_code:
< br/>

Susan Reichmann, M.A., M.F.C.C.


About the Author:
AWBW art leader Susan Reichmann, M.A., M.F.C.C., is the staff art therapist at Haven House in Pasadena.  She has a private practice in Santa Monica and is also a painter and a writer.

Objective:
This workshop helps foster a sense of community, whether it is done by a group of children or by parents together with their children.  Each person has an equal amount of space in which to express her identity through the symbolism of creating her own "world."  

When the worlds are all placed together, each participant can choose to place herself in the world, both independently and in relation to the group.  Often, families or siblings place themselves near each other.  Perhaps a child who feels isolated will place herself far away from others, but during the "visiting" stage of the project, she may be pleased when another group member ventures to her world, or when she has the opportunity to reach out and visit one of her peers.  The visiting/exploring stage is a creative, enjoyable and natural way for each participant to share her world with the group and learn about another person's point of view.

For the shelter residents, both the children and adults, the opportunity to "think big" and envision their own personalized worlds can be an empowering experience.  When parents participate with their children, invariably, their children figure prominently in the worlds they make, which can be very reassuring for the children.  Also, they quite naturally are able to support their children in the creation of their "worlds" and this is precisely the role of the parent in her child's universe.





Example of world drawings connected
during“Making Your Own World” workshop.



Materials:
Butcher paper (55" x 65")*
Pre-cut round pieces of paper (14") (you could also buy pizza rounds from a restaurant supply store)**
Markers, crayons, colored pencils, pastels
Glue sticks
Masking tape
Colored tissue paper (optional)
Star stickers (optional)

*Size of background paper is to be tailored to the size of the group
**A pie tin or a compass can be used to outline the circumference of the paper

Timeframe:





Example world drawing from
Children’s Windows Workshop.



10 minutes: opening circle/introduction
30 minutes: creation of the worlds
20 minutes: closing circle/visiting each other's worlds

Note: This workshop can be expanded to a 90-minute workshop, time permitting.  The time allotments are provided as guidelines only.  It is preferable to allow the workshop to unfold naturally.  When it is time to proceed to the "visiting" stage, the leader can give the stragglers a "three more minutes" time limit so that they can finish creating their worlds.

Ratio:
One adult per four older children; one adult per two younger children.

Note:  When mothers are involved in the workshop, they supervise and help their own children.

Space Setup:
A place to sit and draw is needed for each member of the workshop.  The drawing utensils and colored tissue paper are placed on the tables beforehand.  The paper circles are handed out to each participant during the introduction to the workshop.  The glue sticks are handed out after the individual worlds are created.  The large piece of butcher paper is placed on the floor with plenty of room to walk/sit around it.   It is also an option to provide a blank wall upon which the "worlds" mural can be taped either during the "visiting" phase, or at the conclusion of the workshop.

Opening Circle:
Begin with “Golden Ball Visualization.”  (From the Children’s Windows Manual):

Invite each child to sit or lie down.  Some quiet breathing is necessary for focus.  Ask the children to close their eyes (if they want to) so they can use their imaginations.  

Guided Imagery: Ask the children to take two deep breaths, letting the air out each time with a sound.  “Imagine there is a ball of golden white light floating safely over your head.  It does not touch your head, but floats above it.  The ball of light is round and glowing full of light, love, and energy.  Now imagine that the ball is sending out rays of light that feel warm and loving and spread all over and into your body.  This golden white light surrounds and protects you.  The beams of light come into your head, shoulders, arms, chest, belly, bottom, back, legs, and feet.  Those beams of private golden white light feel safe, loving, and healing.”




Example world drawing from
Children’s Windows Workshop




Variation: “Riding the Butterfly's Wings”:

“Close your eyes.  See yourself in a beautiful park.  All around you, you see beautiful butterflies flying in the breeze.  See their colors: blues, yellows, purples... Let yourself sway gently in the breeze with the butterflies.  Now you see a special butterfly that is bigger than the others, big enough for you to hop on.  The butterfly spreads its large, beautiful wings and takes you on a ride up to the clear blue sky.  From there, you can see the world down below. Breathe in the fresh air.  Now see the butterfly slowly bringing you back to the park.  Open your eyes.  Take a couple of deep breaths.  Remember that in the world of your imagination, everything is possible.”

Introduction to the Workshop:
"Today everyone is going to make their own 'worlds.'  You can make your world however you want it to be. I will hand everyone a piece of paper.  Use the materials on the table to draw your world on this piece of paper.  When everyone is finished, we are going to join all our worlds together on a large piece of paper.  Then we will all have the chance to visit each other's worlds."





Example world drawing from
Children’s Windows Workshop



Part I
Making the Worlds:
Hand out the worlds.  Individuals make their own worlds.  Leaders help and encourage the children (and the adults) as needed.  As the children begin to finish their worlds, place the paper either on the floor or attach it to a blank wall where it is at eye level and is easily accessible to the children.

Part II  
Placing the Worlds:
Each child can place her own world where she wants it on the large group mural paper.  Teamwork can be used in deciding where the worlds will be placed.  Using glue sticks, they can glue the back of their worlds to the paper.  Older children can help the younger children, or the leaders can help the younger children.  If the mothers are participating, they can be in charge of placing their children's worlds in a constellation near their own.  Those who have finished their worlds before the rest of the group have the option of drawing stars, sky, and clouds on the background paper if they so desire.

Part III
Visiting the Worlds:
Once everyone's world has been put in place on the background paper, the group is seated in a circle around the mural.

"Now we are going to be able to visit each other's worlds.  We are going to do this by drawing our way from our own world to someone else's world.  Before you go to someone else's world, you need to ask that person whether or not you can come and visit their world.  If they say "yes," then you can take a marker and draw a line to that person's world.  You can choose the way you want to get to that person's world, you can go by plane or car or train or you can even walk there." (Time and group size permitting, the children can draw their mode of transportation onto the mural.)

The children take turns, one at a time "visiting" while the rest of the group listens.

When a child "arrives" at another child's world, this is the opportunity for the "host" child to tell the group about his world and the group sees his world come to life and learns what his world is all about.  Usually, the group unfolds in such a way that the children are aware of which worlds have not yet been visited.  Everyone gets a turn to go to a world that has not yet been seen.  If this does not occur, then the leader can ask the remaining children to tell the group about their worlds.

Variation:
Time permitting, each participant can be given the time to describe his world in more detail, and similarities and differences between the worlds can be noted.

Closing Circle:
The children stay seated around the mural for the remainder of the time.  One by one, they tell what they liked (or didn't like) about the workshop.  The leader may then make a brief summary statement about the specialness of the worlds, each one different, and all of them together in the universe.  The participants can talk a little about what it felt like to be near or far from each other on the large mural paper and what it felt like to be visited by the others.

Note to the Facilitator:
Most of the time, the children enjoy this project greatly.  When parents participate, they tend to share the same enthusiasm for the project.  Occasionally, you will have a child who does not feel a sense of attachment to his family or his peers.  At the time when the worlds are glued to the large paper, this child may place his world far away from the others as a way of expressing his sense of isolation or separateness.  Often, a child who is feeling this lack of connection to the group will express disinterest in visiting someone else's world.  Usually, another child will reach out to this child and will ask to visit his world, and in most cases, this breaks through the child's sense of isolation and brings him into the group.  This is the preferable way for this situation to be resolved, without the leader's intervention.  However, if this does not occur, the leader can reach out to the child and ask him about his world.  If a child does not want to share his world with the group, then he does not have to do so.
Row.txt_description: Fosters a sense of community within the group and allows each participant an equal amount of space in which to express her identity through the symbolism of creating her own "world."

Row.txt_code:
About the Author:





Facepainting Workshop partners



AWBW art leader Susan Reichmann, M.A., M.F.C.C., is the staff art therapist at Haven House in Pasadena.  She has a private practice in Santa Monica, and is also a painter and a writer.

Objective:
This workshop helps develop a sense of trust between the participants.  The opportunity to pair off and take turns painting each other’s faces allows the children to experience reciprocity, giving and receiving as a mutually rewarding activity.  It provides a chance for the children to communicate their wishes and to learn through the process of working towards a common goal.  In the selection of the “face” the child wants portrayed, this workshop allows the child to express, externalize, or embody his or her innermost feelings or a specific part of his/her personality in a safe, non-judgmental environment.





Facepainting Workshop materials



Materials:
Facepaints (one kit for every 2-3 participants)
Brushes
Paper/paper plates
Markers/crayons
Polaroid camera (optional but recommended)
Paper towels
Water
Handheld mirrors

Note About Materials:  These kits are available at many art supply stores, all costume supply/rental stores, (i.e., at Make Believe in Los Angeles) and can also be ordered through art supply catalogs (i.e., Leisure Crafts).  They range in price from $5 to $8, include six basic colors per kit, and while they are small, they can be used for several workshops.  (Not pictured in this article are facepaints in a crayon form, which are used by be dipping in water before being applied to the face.  These are particularly easy to manipulate for younger children and work very well for the purposes of this workshop.  The best brand is Caran D’ache Neocolor II Watersoluble Crayons.  They cost $10-20 but are worth it because they last for years even with heavy use by many kids.





Facepainting Workshop-: Parents and children



Timeframe:
10 minutes: opening circle/introduction
30-40 minutes: facepainting activity
10-20 minutes: closing circle/sharing/roleplays

Adult to Child Ratio:
One adult per three to four older children; one adult per two younger children.
(See variations for Teens.)

Example I:
In a group with 6 children, ages 8, 7, 5, and 5, the group can pair off with the two older children together requiring less supervision and the two younger children receiving more supervision.  If for some reason one of the children cannot work with another child, one of the group leaders can paint the face of that child.

(It is also possible for one of the older children to paint her own face with the help of the mirror if she is too threatened or unwilling to have anyone paint her face, although this has not been an issue.)

Example II:
In a group with one family of a parent and two children 9 and 6, a parent and two children 5 and 2, and a parent and an infant, the parent with the infant can paint the face of the 9-year-old and he can in turn paint her face. His parent paints the face of her younger child, the third parent paints the face of her 5-year-old.

Space Setup:
The leaders will have all the materials ready and set aside at the beginning of the workshop.  The children/families will sit at clean, empty tables.  The leaders will introduce the workshop and then hand each child paper to make the design of the face.  Then, the leaders will hand the facepaints, water and brushes, either to the mothers, or to the pair of children who will be working together.  The mirrors are not to be introduced until after the faces have already been painted.  Otherwise, the children can be distracted by the image and by trying to perfect it, rather than remaining present and invested in the community-building aspect of the activity.  

Opening Circle:
Begin with “Monkey Breaths,” and “Hot and Cold Breaths” (from the Children’s Windows Manual, p. 35).

Follow with “Weather Report.”  Ask participants to leave their seats and mingle with the other participants.  Tell them you will call out a kind of weather and when they hear the weather report, they are to act as if they are experiencing the weather.  To practice, ask the participant to act as if the weather is HOT.  Then call out CLOUDY, RAINY, SUNNY, BREEZY, SNOWY, FREEZING, STORMY, WINDY...




Part I: Designing the Faces




Introduction:
“Today we are going to do a facepainting workshop.  In this activity, you will have a chance to have your face painted, and a chance to paint someone else’s face, too.  You will take turns painting each other’s faces and decide as a team who will go first and who will go second.  First, I am handing out to you a piece of paper.  On this piece of paper, I have drawn a circle and some lines to represent your face, (eyes/nose/mouth).  You can use the markers and crayons on the table to draw a picture of how you want your face to be painted by your partner.  You can also use the paper while your face is being painted to keep showing your partner your idea of how you want your face to look.  It is important to keep checking in with each other and to keep asking and telling each other how you want your face to be painted.  Sometimes your face may not turn out exactly as you pictured it, but at the end you can make some changes yourself with the paints if you want to.*  And remember, some of the ways that your face/design looks different from what you had imagined might be a pleasant surprise.





Facepainting Workshop Participant





Facepainting Workshop Participants



“For some of us, the face is a very private area, so if you are not comfortable with having somebody (your friend, your brother/sister, your mom or dad) touch your face while painting it, you can choose to have your hand painted instead.  Just make an outline of your hand on the paper and show your partner how you would like your hand to be painted.  After everyone has had a chance to have his/her face painted, we will have time to talk about our faces together.”

*Note: It is up to the leaders’ discretion whether or not to allow the group the option of making changes.  This is not recommended with a group of younger children but is an option when working with a group of adolescents.

Activity Part I:
Designing the Faces
Hand out the paper with the pre-drawn circles or use paper plates (see above illustration) and allow the children (or the children and the parents) time to draw the face or hand the way they would like to see it painted.**  At the close of the group, the children will often want to keep their drawings.  Let each pair decide who will paint first and who will be painted first.  Assist in this decision-making process as needed.  For example, if the parents are participating in the group, they can each be handed a kit to work with.  The leaders can each paint the face of a child that is not immediately teamed up with a partner.  Later, two children can paint their parent’s face together, if they are able to do so amicably.  Otherwise, one of the children can paint the face of a parent who may have only one child who is too young to participate.  

**Variation:  It is possible to ask the children to practice on paper drawing the images that their partners want painted in an effort to help the children get a better understanding of what the other person wants before actually doing the face painting.

Activity Part II:
Facepainting
Remind the group of the time constraints, (i.e., there will be 15 minutes for each face) and give them a two-minute warning before switching turns.  Leaders need to be aware of the time so that everyone has a chance to take part in the activity.  Having obtained signed releases, the leader(s) may take pictures of the facepainting while it is in process, or may decide to take pictures once the work is completed.  Polaroid pictures are best because each child can be immediately given a tangible souvenir of the experience to keep long after the paints have been washed away. The children love to pose for their indiviual polaroid portraits and greatly enjoy posing for group shots as well.

Closing Circle:
The children will take turns talking about the experience of having their faces painted, both from the point of view of being the painter and the one who is painted.  Which did they prefer and why?  What did they like and not like about the exercise?  What did they learn?  What does the painted face mean to them, in other words, what part of themselves is expressed by it?  Is this a face that they would or would not want to show to the world?  How are the faces in the group similar and different in terms of color selection, theme, design?  If there is time, it is possible to do some role playing with the “characters” represented by the faces by asking the children to speak in the voice of the face, one at a time, or to ask the characters to interact in pairs before the group speaking from the point of view of the painted face that each one is inhabiting. 





Facepainting Workshop Participants



Note to Facilitator:
As always with Children’s Windows workshops, freedom from judgment and the creation of a safe space are essential in making this workshop fun and beneficial to the participants.  Each group is different, and sensitivity to the needs of the people present is very important.  If the leaders know the children somewhat, it becomes easier to know which siblings can work together and which are too competitive to cooperate and would profit from working separately during the workshop.  Also, there are children who can work more independently, versus those who really need to work with an adult throughout the process.  Respect for each other is key; children and adults both need to be encouraged throughout the process to speak up when they feel that the person painting their faces is not paying attention to their wishes or is perhaps being too rough with the brushes.  Participants can be reassured that the paints are entirely non-toxic and washable, and that they can remove them right after the workshop, or wear them proudly and gleefully around the shelter for the rest of the day if they so desire.

This workshop has been designed to be used with children of mixed ages.  See Variation for Teens.
Row.txt_description: Participants develop a sense of trust by being given the opportunity to pair off and take turns painting each other's faces. Allows time to experience reciprocity, giving and receiving as a mutually rewarding activity.

Row.txt_code:
Binah Taylor


About the Author:
Binah Taylor has been working with children in shelters for the past seven years.  She has used art extensively in this process, and in 1997, she helped to develop and pilot the AWBW Children’s Windows Program and co-authored the manual.  In response to requests from the local leaders for further information on how to work with the younger age-levels, Binah recently volunteered to lead a workshop.  The following information was adapted from her Leader’s Workshop on this issue.

Objective:
This workshop is designed to be effective with young children, ages 1 to 5 years old.  Handprints are really basic.  The children can make marks, stamp, glue, and stick.  In this project, process is more important than product.  Sometimes parents and leaders do not understand this.  They like to be able to say, “Look what Johnny did!” This workshop, however, is about the children getting to experience the joy of the process.  You can make this workshop more sophisticated or more simple as needed.  Older children can definitely also enjoy it.





Reaching for the paint.



Materials:
Table covering (newspaper)
Relaxing music
Tempera paints
Brushes
Heavy craft paper
Paper towels
Assorted stickers
Glitter
Water containers
Markers
Glue sticks

Timeframe: 1 hour
You may use the entire hour for the following warm-up, handprints activity and closing.  However, depending on your group, you may want to add additional activities (see June ‘98 Leader’s Update).  For example, you might have four different activities set up that you can move through (about 15 minutes each).  If you plan different activities, you can have a beginning, where you gather together, do your little opening circle exercise, and establish the expectations.  Then, with your room already set up, you can move the kids around to the different activities.  Young kids are going to want to move around.  They are not going to want to stay in one place and do one thing and you can’t make them.





Single handprint with sticker.



Adult to Child Ratio:
One adult to every 2-3 children.  

For working with children ages five and under, the adult to child ratio should always be one adult per 2-3 children.   To have enough art facilitators and volunteer assistants, it requires the advance work of recruiting, orienting and maintaining your volunteer force, or raising the funds for additional staff assistance.  

To effectively reach the youngest children, a shelter can start a therapeutic preschool such as the one being started at Human Options, a shelter in Orange County.  Funding is available for programs such as these.  They entail having additional experienced staff, and enable you to go beyond just doing damage control.
With this in mind, our focus is not on finding “magic tricks” for having one adult work single-handedly with ten young ones.  In creating effective art experiences for the young children, we need to make sure there really is adequate adult support, whether it be staff of volunteer.

Space Setup:
At least two spaces are needed:  a circle-area for the opening and closing, and a table-area prepared for the handprinting activity. 




Handprint design created during
Binah’s Leader’s Workshop.




Circle-area:  The circle is the place for “sit-down time” and “listen time” and “talking time”.   Such a circle can be marked with masking tape on the floor.  We have one taped on our floor, and this is like a little marker in the room that the kids sit down in.  It’s where we talk about some of the group rules and it’s where we talk about some things that are going on with the kids.  It’s also where we do some sit-down musical stuff.  It’s amazing that after one and a half weeks of being in the shelter, the kids start saying, “This is the circle, I need to be quiet here.”

Table-area:  For the set-up of the Handprinting workshop, make sure the table is covered with newspaper and all the supplies are in the center of the table, ready to distribute and use.  

If you want to set up a variety of other activities for young children, see the June ‘98 Leader’s Update.  

Opening Circle:
This is a guided imagery exercise where you gather the kids to stand in the circle and you lead them in making motions with their whole bodies and using their voices to match the motions.  The imagery flows from everyone pretending to reach for a butterfly; to pretending to dig in the dirt; to stomping feet; to wiggling like a rag doll; to taking a deep breath like a balloon.  To lead this well and get the children into it, it’s really important to model it fully and enthusiastically with your own body and voice:

“Let’s imagine there’s a butterfly.  Let’s reach and catch it.  Oooh.  Ooooh.  And look at the sun.  The sun is mine.  It’s mine, it’s mine!  (Reaching for the sun.)  Let’s see the butterflies in the air (Wiggling hands.).  Wiggle, wiggle, wiggle.  How about some sounds, come on.  Oooooh.   

“I know we all like to play in the dirt, so let’s pretend we’re in the dirt now. (Kneel down to dig and reach into the pretend earth.) Ahhhh.  Mmmmm.  But we don’t put it in our mouths, no.  Just in the hands, yeah.  And now we get to wash our hands.  So we pretend to wash them all clean.

“And some of us are feeling a bit angry, so how about we stamp our feet.  (Begin stomping loud and add some angry noises with the rhythm of the feet.) Arrrr.  Arrrr.  Arrrr.  Stomp.  Stomp.  

“And now how about if we just wiggle and pretend we’re like a Raggedy Ann doll.  (Start shaking your whole body around like a rag doll)  Let’s listen to our voices when we do that.  Ahhhhh.  And now, show me the biggest breath you can take.  Let’s make our stomachs like balloons.  You know grown ups don’t like their stomachs to be big, but it’s OK when you’re a kid...   And now let the air out.  

“Is everybody ready to go to the table?”  

You can adapt and add on to this warm-up.  Be creative.  Just remember to use your whole body and voice and enthusiasm to get the whole group into it.

Introduction:
You can decide how much of this to say as introduction, and how much to say during the activity as you go along:

“Let's go to the table and everyone sit: two kids and a grown-up to help out.  Spread out because you want lots of space for your project. Here are the paints and everyone gets paper and their very own paintbrush. I'm going to pass around the stickers and everyone can choose a color.

“You're going to paint your hand a color.  You can do your fingers another color if you want, but have the grown-up (helper) help you rinse out your brush before using another color of paint.




Painting the hand (at Leader’s Workshop).




“When you've finished painting your hand and fingers, press it down hard on the paper. If you want, you can put your sticker on your hand-print.
“Now let's make another hand-print.  Rinse the brush and your hand. Pick another sticker and paint your hand a new color.  If you want to make a cool color, just rinse the brush and paint a new color on top of the color already on your hand.

“You can paint pictures on your hand or make pictures out of the hand-prints using the stickers and the empty spaces.”

Activity:
During the workshop, as everyone is painting and being helped by the helpers, go around the table and ask “What kinds of things can we do with our hands?”  Write the suggestions down on a big piece of paper.  (At the end, for the closing circle, you can recap the list, so everyone hears their ideas again.)





Pressing to make print.



During the workshop, talk to the kids about their choice of colors and the images they are painting—on their hand or through the hand-prints on the paper.  This is a way of getting to know more about them, their experiences, or if anything is bothering them. Let them know you want them to share but ask their permission and talk to them after the workshop, perhaps in the circle area.  During the workshop, the kids will usually help each other and share.  Commend them for this as you go along.

Handling Situations:
The following are some suggestions for ways to handle common challenges or demands the children may make:

possible demand: “I want it first!”
possible response:  “Everybody wants it first.  What am I going to do?”  (Said in a pleasant and firm, loving tone)





Lifting to see print.



possible demand:  “I want the XYZ!”
possible response:  “You know what?  That’s going to be very hard for me to make everybody happy all at once.  How am I going to do that?”  (Said in a pleasant and firm, loving tone.)

possible situation:  The children start threatening to paint each other.
possible response:  “You know what?  We don’t paint each other.  We keep the paint to ourselves”

possible question:  “Can I keep my brush?”
possible response:  “No, I’m sorry.  There would be no brushes here for everyone to use.”
Closing Circle:
Wrapping up the workshop: “Everyone is doing great.  The paintings look beautiful.  For now we're going to leave them here and put them in a safe place to dry out and then you can keep them.  If you want to leave it here that's okay.  I can keep it safe for you.”





Wet Paint - ready to print.





Applying sticker.



For the close of the workshop, share the list of “Things I can do with my hands.”
Row.txt_description: Offers an experience of art that is focused more on process than product. Participants paint their hands and the prints made are then decorated with stickers and/or glitter.

Row.txt_code:
Photo from Joy of Photography


Note: This Update is a supplement to the concepts presented in the May Leader’s Update.  Remember that in order to be able to provide the range of activities and flexible responses to the children’s needs, it is necessary to have enough adult support.  The ratio Binah suggests for working with children under age 5 is a minimum of one adult for every 2-3 children.  

Supplemental Activities:
As mentioned in the May Update, with young children, you may need to provide several activities that you can move the children through during the hour.  Young children are not going to want to focus on one activity for an entire hour.  These are some of Binah’s suggestions of alternative activities you can prepare and move the children through during the hour.




Photo from Joy of Photography




Boat Warm-up:  This is a cooperative activity that you can use as a warm-up or a transition to bring the children together between other activities: we all pretend that we're in a boat together.  The kids sit on the floor and make the shape of a boat.  The kid in the front who's doing the look-out can say, "Yes, I can see the land", and all the kids rowing can go "Heave-ho. Heave-ho." So that's something that really kind of gets kids together.  They can put treasures on the boat and play an imagination game.  You can use this little warm-up exercise like stretching before the next activity.

Play Dough: With play dough, children can just touch, feel, and be able to do free-flowing things.





Photo from Joy of Photography



Quiet Corner: At our shelter, we have a quiet place where we can just kind of sit and play with them, and look at books and stuff.  

Chalk Board: We also have a big chalk board, and kids with attention deficit disorder seem to enjoy doing stuff on the chalk board.  They are drawn to that.  If the kids are having a hard time, I just let them go and do the chalk play.   

Music Circle:  I bring out the musical instruments: rhythm instruments, drums, triangles, bells, even a keyboard, if possible.
