To provide a chance for children to express their feelings about themselves and their families by creating a family of fish.  To assist the children in finding a sense of pride in creating their pictures with this beautiful, vivid process.

Materials:
Cray-Pas sets (one set per child)
Small, thick white paper (4”x4” is good)
Newsprint to cover the table
Plastic forks for scraping
Tempera paint:  three strong colors that would be good for water (blue, green, black) plus one light color (you might try white or light blue)
Tempera paint brushes (one per color)
Cups of water for rinsing the brushes
Paper towels for drying the brushes

Note: Tempera glitter paint is especially beautiful and rewarding to use.

Timeframe:
60 min—Total Time
Opening:  5 min
Fish Circle Warm-up:  5 min
Technical Demonstration:  10 min
Creation:  30 min
Closing:  10 min

Age Range: 5 and up 

Ratio:
One adult to 3 young children

Note:
Because you will be covering the entire page with Cray-Pas for this project, it’s good to have small paper.

Space Setup:
Cover the table with newspapers.  Open the Cray-Pas sets in advance.  Prepare containers of the tempera paint.  Place supplies out of reach, (if necessary, depending on the age level) to bring out when needed.

Opening:
“Today, we’re going to make a family of fish.  Have you ever seen a fish?  What did it look like?  If you were a fish, what would you look like? Would you be big?  Or small?  How would your family be?  Who would be close?  Who would be far?”

Fish Circle Warm-up:
“For our warm-up today, we’re going to make a fish circle.  Can you become a fish?  How would your face look?  (Puff up your cheeks and open and close your mouth like a fish.)  Which way do you want to swim around the circle?  (Start swimming around the circle.  It’s okay to have everyone swimming in their own directions.)  Say ‘hello’ to the other fishes!”





1. Fish colors





2. Painting on the paint





3. Making the Fish



Technical:
There are three steps.  Demonstrate them to the children, but get them involved in the demonstration.  Ask them to guide you as you go through the three steps, so you’re creating what they are telling you to make. 

1. Fish Colors:
“What colors should we make our fish?  Yellow?  Red?  Silver?  Many colors mixed together?  We’re going to cover the page with these colors.  Did I cover it all up?  (Cover all the parts of the page.  Bright colors look especially good with this technique.)  It’s important to press really hard so the page is filled with Cray-Pas.”

2. Painting on the Paint: 
“Now we’re going to cover the page with paint. Which color resembling water should we make for our fish?  (Note:  the paint color must be different from the Cray-Pas color for the scratches to show through.)  Paint over the Cray-Pas.  Try to paint as thinly as possible.  That makes it easier to scratch through.  Some colors may bead up on top of the Cray-Pas, but you can usually cover the page pretty well.”

3.  Making the Fish: 
“Now we get to make our fish.  (Scratch with a fork, so the children can see how the light colors come shining through.)  Here’s our fish.  Should we put some underwater plants around it?  Anything else?”  (Do whatever they suggest.)

Creation: 
“Now it’s your turn.  Go ahead and make your fish colors.  Be sure to fill the page and press really hard!

“When you are ready, let me know so we can add the paint.  (Go around the room as needed, with the tempera colors, assisting each child to put his water on.  For some children, you might put the paint on for them.  Others might wish to paint it themselves.)

“Now you get to make your fish family!  (Encourage each child as she creates.)  If time allows, write the children’s words about their fish family, or the title of their paintings.  Scratch the children’s names and the date at the bottom of their paintings, if they’d like
you to.”




“Fish Families” sample drawing




Closing Circle:
“Tell me about your fishes?  Which one are you?”  (Give each child an opportunity to share his or her picture.)
Row.txt_description: Provides a chance for children to express their feelings about themselves and their families by creating a family of fish. Assists them in finding a sense of pride in creating their pictures through a beautiful, vivid process.

Row.txt_code:
“A Day of Feelings” samples


“A Day of Feelings” is the fourth in a series of workshops AWBW has developed to assist your workshop participants in fully enjoying and exploring Cray-Pas.  Thanks to a generous donation from Sakura, each Children’s Windows Program has been given an ample supply of Cray-Pas for the year.  Cray-Pas are oil pastels that can be used in many diverse and fabulous ways.  The technique used here is “Cray-Pas etchings.”  This technique can be used to draw anything- landscapes, families, doodles, flowers, etc.  The “A Day of Feelings” idea is just one way of using this technique.  Enjoy, and feel free to use this technique in whatever ways you wish.   Please join us in experimenting and sharing new project ideas.

Objective:
First, to help the children identify emotions and express them with colors and a drawing. Second, to let them enjoy the element of surprise made possible with this technique.

Materials:
Cray-Pas sets (one set per child)
Small, thick white paper (4”x4” is good) - 4-6 pieces per child
Newsprint to cover the table
Pencils





“A Day of Feelings” etching sample -
sunshine and smiles



Time-Frame:
60 min—Total Time
Opening:  5 min
Warm-up:  10 min
Technical Demonstration:  10 min
Creation:  25 min
Closing:  10 min

Age Range: 3 and up 

Ratio:
One adult to 3 young children

Note:
Because you will be covering the entire page with CrayPas for this project, it’s good to have small paper.

Space Setup:
Cover the table with newspapers.  Open the Cray-Pas sets in advance.  Make sure to have the paper cut and ready.  Place supplies out of reach (if necessary, depending on the age level), to bring out when needed.

Opening:
“Today, we’re going to draw feelings.  Have you ever had a feeling you liked?  Can you name it?  If you were going to draw it, what color would you make it?  (Encourage each child to share a feeling they like and a color for it.)  Have you ever had one you didn’t like?  Can you name it? What color would you make that feeling?”  (Encourage each child to share a feeling they don’t like and a color for it.)

Feelings Warm-up:
Play easy, rhythmic music.  Ask everyone to move around the room to the rhythm, pantomiming how they are feeling at the beginning of the workshop.  Allow a few minutes.  Then gather in a circle and ask for volunteers to share what feelings they saw expressed.  Ask for volunteers to share what feelings they pantomimed. 
 





1. Feeling colors





2. Creating the etching with pencil
on top of second paper





3. Turning it over to see the etched
drawing in color


Technical:
There are three steps.  Demonstrate them to the children, but get them involved in the demonstration.  Ask them to guide you as you go through the three steps, so you’re creating what they are telling you to make.  

1. Feeling Colors:
“Let’s pick a feeling.  What feeling should I start with?  What colors would it be?  We’re going to cover the page with these colors.  Did I cover it all up?  (Cover all the parts of the page.)  It’s important to press really hard so the page is filled with the Cray-Pas.” 

2.  Etching: 
“Now we’re going to cover the page with another piece of paper, and draw on it.  I’m going to draw a picture of this feeling.  What should I draw?” 

3.  Turning it Over: 
“Now we can turn it over, and here’s our picture!”  (Show the children how the lines are etched in the Cray-Pas colors.)

Creation: 
“Now it’s your turn.  Go ahead and pick your feeling colors.  You can make more than one etching if you have more than one feeling you are trying to express.  Maybe you could pick a feeling you don’t like.  What are some feelings you don’t like?  What are some feelings you like?  Go ahead and begin with whatever feeling you want.  Be sure to fill the page and press really hard!

“When you are ready, let me know so I can give you another paper to cover your colors with.  (Go around the room as needed to give the second page.)  




“A Day of Feelings” sample - mad feelings




“Now you can draw your etching!”

Closing Circle:
“Tell me about your picture!”   (Give each child an opportunity to share his or her picture.)  Write words down to go with each picture if the child wants you to.





“A Day of Feelings”
sample - smiles
Row.txt_description: Helps children identify emotions and express them with colors and a drawing. Lets them enjoy the element of surprise made possible with this technique.

Row.txt_code:
“Fork, Knife, Spoon” sample design


Objective:
To give the children an opportunity to use materials they are familiar with (spoons, knives, and forks) in an inventive way.  To provide them an opportunity for play and discovery with the creative process.

Materials:
Black construction paper (other dark colors work too)
White tempera paint (possibly other light colors too)
Containers for the paint
Water containers to rinse brushes
Paper towels





Step One:  covering the page



Plastic forks, knives, and spoons (one of each per child)
Wide paintbrushes
Newsprint to cover the table

Timeframe:
60 min—Total Time
Opening:  5 min
Warm-up:  10 min
Technical Demonstration:  10 min
Creation:  25 min
Closing:  10 min

Age Range: 3 and up  

Ratio:







One adult to 3 young children

Note:
Be sure to test the supplies in advance, so you will be familiar with the process, and you will know the paint you have will work well on the paper.  (If the paint is too thin, it won’t work for this technique.)   

Space Setup:
You will need to set up three areas:  1) Open floor space for the warm-up.  2) Cover the table area with plenty of newsprint, and place the supplies in the center of the table.  3) A drying area, covered with newsprint, where the paintings can be left to dry.  

Opening:
“Today, we’re doing ‘Fork, Knife, Spoon.’  Do you have a favorite?  If you had to be a fork or a knife or a spoon today, what would you be?  Why?  (Encourage everyone to share.)

“Has anyone ever used a fork or knife or spoon for something besides eating?  What did you use it for?  Has anyone ever made a drawing using a fork or knife or spoon?  Today we are going to use forks and knives and spoons to make art.  Ready?”  

Fork, Knife, Spoon Warm-up:





Fork lines





Knife lines





Spoon lines



“Let’s make a circle together holding hands.  There we go - everyone holding hands.  Now let’s see how big we can make the circle, with our hands still together.  How far can we stretch?  That’s great!  Look at how big our circle is!  Now imagine this circle is a great big table.  Does it have a table cloth?  What color?  Is there food on the table?  What kind?  Are there good smells?  What do you smell?  Now let’s lay our selves down on this table and get comfortable.  As we melt into the table, let’s imagine that we are the forks on the table.  Can you be a fork?  Can you stretch your arms out?  Can you make the pointy ends of the fork?  Good job!  And how about being knives?  Can you make yourself straight and pointy like a knife.  Great knives!  And how about a spoon?  Feel yourself relaxing and melting into the curving, smooth shape of a spoon.  Beautiful spoons!  Now let yourself melt down again and this time, become a part of the table.  Let your whole self relax and melt into this big round table.”  (Rest a few moments.)  

Technical:
There are two steps to demonstrate to the children.  Get them involved as you demonstrate.

1. Covering the page with paint:
Apply paint evenly, covering the entire page.   This workshop can be done with just white paint.  It’s up to you, how many colors you want to make available.  Also, depending on the capabilities of the participants, you might want to cover their pages for them, or you might welcome them to cover their own pages.  It’s up to what you, as leader, think will work best with your group.

2. Scratching designs:  
Demonstrate how the fork can scratch lines into the paint.  Likewise, with the spoon and knife.  Encourage the children to notice how many different kinds of marks can be made.  Cover the whole page with designs.  

Creation:  
Now it’s your turn.  (Assist the children in beginning their work.)  As they complete their drawings, help them move the wet pictures to the drying area.

Closing Circle:
Each child has an opportunity to share his or her design.  You might encourage the children to share with questions like: “Who used a fork? Who used a spoon?  Who used a knife?”  The paint may take an hour to dry after the children are finished.  It depends on how thick the paint is, and how damp the weather is.
Row.txt_description: To use familiar materials to enhance discovery and the creative process.

Row.txt_code:
Cheering Frog Flag examples



Objective:
To encourage the children to never give up on their dreams.  To help them notice and remember the supportive voices in their lives—voices that have cheered them on—and give the children a way to take those cheering voices with them, as encouragement forever.

Materials:
Colored construction paper
Cray-Pas oil sticks
Glue sticks





“I love you” — Cheering Flog Flags example



Colored yarn or string
Paper towels
Newspaper to cover the table

Timeframe:
60 min—Total Time
Opening Story:  10 min
Warm-up:  5 min
Technical Demonstration:  10 min
Creation:  25 min
Closing:  10 min

Age Range: 3 and up  

Ratio:
One adult to 3 young children

Note:
Be sure to test the supplies in advance, so you will be familiar with the process.   It will also help if you have an example to show the children.  

Space Setup:
Cover the table area with plenty of newspaper, and place the supplies in the center of the table.  If you are working with younger children, pre-cut and fold the construction paper for the flags, and pre-cut the string into 1-yard lengths.  







Extra Special Prep:
Special Advance Prep:  If you have time, it makes this workshop very special if you can add to each child’s chain, a few flags created by shelter staff.  In advance of the workshop, make 3-5 flags for each child and on each one, have a staff person write some simple, encouraging thoughts to cheer on that child.  During the workshop, you can go around the group and ask each child for permission to add some special flags on to their chain.  As you do this, you can read what the staff person wrote on the flag.  This way, each child will have a special thought from some staff people at the shelter.  

Opening:
“Today, our project is called ‘Cheering Frog Flags.’  I’m going to share a story about cheering.  It’s called Two Frogs in the Woods. After I share it, I want to hear what you think it means.  Ready?”

“Two Frogs in the Woods” Story:
(Feel free to change the story into your own words, instead of reading the words here):
“A group of frogs were traveling through the woods, and two of them fell into a deep pit.  All the other frogs gathered around the pit.  When they saw how deep the pit was, they told the frogs that they could never get out.  The two frogs ignored the comments and tried to jump out of the pit with all of their might.  The other frogs kept telling them to stop.  They said:  “There’s no way you’ll ever get out of there.  You might as well stop trying!”  Finally, one of the frogs decided they were right.  He believed what all the other frogs were saying and gave up.  But the other frog continued to jump and jump and jump as hard as he could.  Once again, the crowd of frogs yelled at him.  They said he could never make it and they shook their arms at him and told him it would be better if he just gave up.  He jumped even harder and finally he made it out.  When he got out, the other frogs were amazed.  They said “Didn’t you hear us?”  The frog explained to them that he was deaf.  He couldn’t hear them, but he saw them yelling, and he thought they were encouraging him and cheering him on the entire time.
 
After sharing the story ask the children, “What does this story teach?”  Encourage them to share what they think.  Here are some possible lessons:

- When someone is encouraged and cheered, it can help lift them up so they can make it through the day.  

- When someone is told negative things, it can make them want to give up.  

- It’s important to not believe the negative things people say about you.  

- If you can remember all the good things and all the people who have cheered you on, it can help you to do great things.

- Be thoughtful of what you say to people when they are struggling.  You can be that special person for someone else.  You can be someone who encourages them, so they don’t give up.  An encouraging word can go a long way.

The Wave Warm-up:





“You’re Smart” — Cheering Flog Flags



If possible, gather a circle of chairs so everyone can sit together in a circle.  This is a cheering warm-up. “Has anyone ever had a crowd of people cheering for them?   What did it feel like?  (Encourage the children to share their stories.)  That’s what we are going to do for a Windows warm-up today:  we are going to see what it’s like to cheer for each other!  Has anyone ever seen a crowd do “the wave” at a sports event?  It’s a way people cheer for their team (if you don’t know what the wave is, be sure to ask someone who does, so you know how to teach it).  Let’s do a couple of practice rounds.  Here we go--yay!--

You can start the wave yourself by yelling ‘yay!’ and standing up and putting your arms high in the air.  Then the next person follows, and so on around the circle in a wave.  After a few rounds, once the group has gotten comfortable with it, do a round of the wave for each person in the group.  Do one round for the young person sitting next to you.  Instead of saying “yay!”, say “yay Maria!” (whatever that child’s name is).  Then do a wave for the next child, and the next and the next, until you’ve cheered for each person in the group.  






Cutting and folding flags





Applying glue across the fold





Placing the string





Sealing the flag onto the string


If doing ‘the wave’ is too confusing or difficult for your group, you could just cheer each person in the group, one at a time.  Clap, cheer and yell their name for half a minute or so.  Then cheer the next person, and so on, around the circle.  

After the warm-up, ask each person what it felt like to be cheered on.   

Introduction:  
“For the frog who jumped out of the hole, it was very important that he was thinking about having a group of other frogs cheering him on.  Even though they weren’t really cheering for him, what mattered was that he was picturing them cheering for him.  What was in his mind was most important.  Just like for the frog, it’s very important for all of us to keep in our minds thoughts of people cheering for us.  To do that, we are going to make ‘Cheering Frog Flags’ today.  We can each make our own set of flags that will remind us of people who cheer us on.”

Technical Demonstration: 
1. First, pick your string.

2. Then fold and cut out your flags. (For younger children, have the pieces of paper already cut, so it’s just a matter of picking out the colors.)  You could make a flag for each person (or animal) in your life that is a support to you.  Who do you like?  Who do you feel safe with?  Make a flag for each one of them.  They are your “cheering frog flags.”   

3. Then attach your flags to the string.  Hint: It helps to fold them first, and then put the glue on.  Then you can lay the string along the crease and fold it up easily.  

4. Then decorate your flags.  Put words and colors on them that represent people who have cheered you on.  You might want to ask for help with the writing. (If you have made some flags for each child in advance, you might let them know you’ll be asking their permission to add some extra flags to their string.)

Creation:
Now it’s your turn.  (Assist the children in beginning their work.)  As they complete their flags, help them with writing any words they want on the flags.   You might need to encourage them to think about times someone has been nice to them. 

Closing:
Gather in one final circle and give each child an opportunity to share his or her Cheering Frog Flags.  You might want to do the “wave” warm-up again, but this time, each child can be holding their flags.  Encourage the children to think about where they want to keep their Cheering Frog Flags.  Do they want to hang them next to their bed?  Do they want to wear them like a necklace?  Do they want to keep them private, in an envelope, and just take them out to look at when they want to?  (Have envelopes available for those who want them).




“I love your imagination” — example flag




Age Variations:
Depending on the ages of the children, they may need help with the words.  For younger children, the flags may be just happy colors and no words at all.  For older children, each flag could represent someone who has cheered them on.
Row.txt_description: Encourages the children to never give up on their dreams. To help them notice and remember the supportive voices in their lives - voices that have cheered them on - and give the children a way to take those cheering voices with them, as encouragement forever.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create version for adults.

< /tr>


 Silvia Gutierrez, Children’s
Windows leader at Women and
Children’s Crisis Center,
Whittier, CA..
  
In response to last month’s request for holiday-themed workshops, Silvia has contributed “My Scarecrow.” Thank you Silvia, for this beautiful and deeply meaningful workshop!

Objective:
Scarecrows have been used by farmers to frighten away intruders (crows) and keep them from eating their valuable crops. This activity can help the children focus on protection. They can make their own special scarecrow to scare off their intruders. It can also provide them with the opportunity to identify what is valuable to them. (For example: crops are valuable to farmers.) During this workshop, they can notice what, for them, needs protection.

Materials:
White paper (for watercolors)
Cray-Pas
Watercolors

 
 
 Supplies: Watercolor sets
and Cray-Pas sets
  
 
 Scarecrow in a field
  

Brushes
Spray bottle for water
Newspaper to cover tables

Timeframe:
60 min—Total Time
Warm Up: 5 minutes
Idea Circle: 5 minutes
Intro/Demo: 10 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes

Age Range: 3 and up

Ratio:
One adult for four children; one adult for two young children.

Space Setup:
Cover the table with newspapers. Open the Cray-Pas sets in advance. Open each watercolor set and spray lightly with water. The water helps soften the colors so that they will be easy to use when the children paint. Prepare the cups of water for brush rinsing. Place supplies out of reach, (if necessary, depending on the age level), and bring out when needed. Have a space for the “Monster Dance” to occur, away from the art supplies. You’ll also need a “drying area,” for the paintings to dry when the are finished.

Monster Dance Warm-up:
When the children arrive, the Monster Dance warm-up can be used to tie in the Halloween Theme:

“Let’s do a Monster Dance. First we can start by moving around in a circle being monsters. Now let’s all be scary monsters! Now let’s be happy monsters! Can you be really loud monsters? Can you be really quiet monsters?”


 
 
 Drawing the scarecrow
  
 
 Adding the paint
  
 
 Painted scarecrow
  

Idea Circle:
After the warm-up, sit together in a circle to share thoughts about:

a) What is a scarecrow? Have you ever seen one? What are they used for?

b) Why are crops important to farmers? To all of us? What is valuable to each of us?

“Sometimes things that are valuable to us need a little added protection. Today we are going to make our own special individual protection for what’s important to each of us. Today we will make our own scarecrows to keep us safe.”

Technical:
(Note: this is the same procedure as for “The Monster in Me” workshop.)

There are three steps. Demonstrate them to the children, but get them involved in the demonstration. Ask them to guide you as you go through the three steps, so you’re creating the Scarecrow they are telling you to make.

1. Drawing the Scarecrow:
“What kind of hat should I put on this scarecrow? What color straw? What kind of arms? How about legs? Anything else I should add? Notice that I’m pressing really hard to make the lines. This is important because it makes the lines strong enough for when we put the paint on.”

  


Smiling scarecrow
 
  

2. Watering the Scarecrow:
“Now we get to make the scarecrow all wet. (Spray the entire page with a spray bottle.) Did I get the whole scarecrow wet? Is there anywhere I missed? (Keep spraying until the whole surface is wet. You could call the water “Scarecrow Juice” or “Protection Juice.”)

3. Coloring the Scarecrow:
“Now we get to add the colors. Tell me what colors to use. We can just drop the colors into each space and see them spread. (Demonstrate how the watercolors spread in the water.) Isn’t that beautiful? What color should I make the hat? How about the arms? How about the space around the scarecrow?”

Creation:
“Now it’s your turn.” (Assist the children in beginning their work.) As they complete their drawings, help them move the wet pictures to the drying area.


 
 
 Scarecrow drawing
  

Closing Circle:
Each child has an opportunity to share his or her scarecrow. “What is your scarecow protecting? How does your scarecrow protect you?”
Row.txt_description: Helps children focus on protection through the metaphor of the scarecrow, used by farmers to frighten away intruders (crows) and keep them from eating their valuable crops. Also provides an opportunity to identify what is valuable to them.
Row.txt_tips: This workshop can work particularly well as a follow-up after Monster in Me.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:


 
 
  

To create an opportunity for speaking out. To offer a safe outlet for emotions of all kinds: anger, sadness, happiness, playfulness. To offer children who feel they don’t know how to express themselves through speech, a tool for exploring their own voice.

Age Range: 3 and up

Ratio:
1 adult for 6 children; 1 adult for 3 young children.

Materials:
Socks of all colors (not just white)
Tempera paint


 
 
 
 
  
 
 Wrapping pipe cleaners around your
finger makes great curls!
  

Paper towels
Brushes
Water cups
Newsprint to cover table
Wide-tip markers
Optional: materials to create hair (Fake hair can be bought in braids at craft stores, as can crimped paper shreds and pipe cleaners. Use a stapler for attaching the hair.)

Timeframe:
Total time: 60 min
Opening: 5 min
Warm-up: 5 min
Technical Demo: 5 min
Creation: 20 min
Rapping Circle: 20 min
Closing: 5 min

Space Setup:
Cover the table with newspapers. Set up the tempera paints, water and brushes in advance, and place out of reach until the creating begins.

Opening:
“Today with Rapping Puppets we are going to have a chance to express or talk or sing about any emotions we are having today or any emotions we have had in the past. Does anyone know what an emotion is? What’s an emotion you have felt? Let’s each share one.”

Warm-up:
“Let’s all take a deep breath in and let all the air out with a very long breath. (A couple of times) Let’s all stand straight up and relax our shoulders (shake and roll your shoulders a couple of times). Now let’s bend at the waist and just let our heads hang off the ends of our bodies. That’s good. Feel your head hanging there. And now let’s stand up straight again. Now imagine that all of our feelings and thoughts and voices will be taken care of by our puppets this hour. Our puppets will feel and think and sing and speak for us.”

  


  

Technical Demo:
“We will be making Rapping Puppets today, and then listening to what each puppet wants to say. We each can make our own puppet however we want it to be.”

For demonstration, put your own hand inside a sock and show how you can make a mouth by closing your hand. Have everyone pick a sock and try it out together.

Then use the paint or pens to draw eyes, a mouth, etc. You could encourage the children to tell you what to draw, and follow their lead as you demostrate.
Before diving into the creation, encourage the children to share their thoughts. “Do you know what your puppet would say or sing or express? How are you feeling today that you might let your puppet tell us about?”

Creation:
“Now it’s your turn. Go ahead and begin on your sock. If you need any help, let me know.” (Encourage the children as they create.)

     





     
Rapping Circle:
Encourage each child to take the spotlight for a turn, and have their puppet share or rap whatever it wants to. If the group is hesitant to share, you can draw them out with encouraging questions, and instead of going in a circle, everyone can respond to the questions. If you notice someone not sharing, you can draw them out playfully. Here are some questions you might explore together: What if your puppet was mad? Is there anything your puppet wants to say? Does your puppet have friends? Is your puppet happy about anything? Does your puppet have a song? Did your puppet sleep good last night? Is your puppet shy? Who has a shy puppet? Is there something it would like to share?

It is important to appreciate what is shared, and even what is not shared. You can say that it’s OK for the puppets to be shy, and that the things that they haven’t shared are very, very important.

Later, one on one, you might encourage any shy puppets to say more. With a shy puppet, it’s especially important to appreciate him/her, to help create safety.

You could ask the children to notice all the emotions that the puppets shared, and make a list together, appreciating how many feelings were voiced.













  











  




“Love” Closing Circle:
In case some dark emotions came out with the puppets, it can be wonderful to end the workshop with the emotion of love. You can lead this in any way you think would work with your particular group of children.

Possibly, they could each imagine their puppet loving them, and have their puppets say loving things about them: “Now, for our closing, I would like us all to end with a very special emotion: love. Let’s each look at our puppets and imagine that they feel nothing but love—love for us, the special person who created them. Imagine that your puppet loves you very very much, and for the closing, it gets to say one thing it loves about you. If your puppet has a hard time saying the good things, we can all help it along, and say lots of good things about you.”

An alternative is that they could each say something they love about their puppet. This might be easier than thinking of something they love about themselves. Again, if they can’t think of anything they love about their puppet, then the group could help out.
Row.txt_description: Creates an opportunity for speaking out, offering a safe outlet for emotions of all kinds and, for children who feel they don't know how to express themselves through speech, a tool for exploring their own voice.
Row.txt_tips: Make sure that the socks are the right sizes for the participants hands.

Row.txt_code:
Amy Degenfelder
 
  
About the Author:
Greetings! My name is Amy Degenfelder and I am a Children's Advocate at Humboldt Women For Shelter (H.W.S.).  My work here is challenging and quite fulfilling.  I do believe I make a difference in these children's lives, and that often keeps me going.  The highlight of my workweek is the two weekly children's support groups I co-facilitate.  We call this group "A Voice Of Their Own" and it is a special, rare time for children to share, express themselves through art, and relate to other children who have experienced domestic violence. It is heartwarming to hear the children say how much they look forward to group each week, and I feel so lucky to be a part of it! I think it is obvious I love my job!" Recently an eight-year-old girl who has been coming to group for years was asked what she wanted to be when she grew up, and she said, "I want to do what Amy does!" You can be sure I grinned from ear to ear! I had the amazing opportunity to attend AWBW training in November and highly suggest it for anyone working with children from violent homes. AWBW project ideas have been so helpful, and ideal for our groups at H. W. S. I only hope to add to the wonderfully creative ideas.

Objective:
To allow children an avenue to explore and name different feelings and to realize that we can have more than one feeling at a time. Not only will we identify possible emotions, but also have the chance to experience them.  This project is a wonderful way to express feelings of anger, and children can turn to this project at home in the future.  It combines cognitive, emotional, and physical elements, which allows true healing and change to occur. 

Age Range: 3 and up


 
 
 Example of “Emotions Target” created
at Humboldt Women for Shelter.
  

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children.

Materials:
Water balloons
Piece of cardboard (one yard by one yard)
Pens, preferably permanent or waterproof
Tacks and a hammer
A plastic bag
A paper towel
Glue sticks
Paper

Timeframe:
Total time: 1.5 hours
15 minutes-Check-In
20 minutes-Part I- Brainstorming and creating Emotions Target
20 minutes- Part II- Throw balloons! (and clean up broken bits)
20 minutes- Part III- Make collage and debrief
15 minutes- Check-Out

Space Setup:
It is necessary to have space outdoors, with a fence or wooden surface to tack the Emotion Target upon. If this space is not readily available, a walk to a nearby park is appropriate, as long as there is enough safe space away from passersby. (And then more time for Part II would be necessary.) 

Check-In:
At Humboldt Women for Shelter we always start group by having a nutritious snack while we read our group rules and have an individual Check-In. It is a good idea to have the children help create the rules when you first start a group series and post them on the wall for everyone to see. As an example, our rules are... 

1. Listen to everyone in group.

2. Don't interrupt, wait for your turn to talk (Raise your hand if you'd like a turn).

  


“Blow off STEAM, Angry, Happy...” close-up
 
  

3. No hitting, kicking, biting or any body contact that hurts. Hugs are okay if both people want them.

4. No saying mean things that can hurt feelings. No cussing, laughing at someone or whispering about people.

5. Confidentiality: That means we don't talk about group or group members to people outside of group. What is said in group stays in group.

6. No grabbing toys or art supplies. Take turns and share.

For Check-In we alternate between many questions...

—What animal (or color) describes how you are feeling today?

—Act out your emotion and we will guess how you are feeling.

—What is a rose in your life?—This is something good and desirable, like a rose.

—What is a thorn in your life?—This is something that doesn't feel very good, or even hurts like a thorn.

We try to have a question that ties into the day’s art project. For this particular activity, it may be "What do you do to release feelings of anger or frustration?"

Children come up with wonderful ideas to this question and give the others in the group more ideas to add to their own.

Children take turns one at a time to do Check-In. Then we clean up, snack, and segue into Part I of the project.


 
 
 “Venting, Angry, Happy,
Frustrated...” close-up
  

Part I:
"Okay, so in Check-In today we discussed some positive things we can do when we feel angry, to help us let our anger go.  Today we are going to show you another possible activity.  We are going to make a big “Emotions Target” together as a group, and then go outside and throw water balloons at it!" (Allow time for shouts of joy!) "Let's think about all the possible feelings we may experience while doing this activity. Anger may be one of them, but there could be many other possibilities. Let's go around the circle and name them." While brainstorming, set the large piece of cardboard on the table and begin drawing large circles to create a target.  After ideas cease, put pens on the table and let everyone draw or write words expressing each emotion mentioned.  It is good to write or draw in between the target circles, so when you throw the balloons you can aim toward an emotion you're experiencing.  After the target is complete, it is time to journey outside!

Part II:
Take the target, pre-filled water balloons, tacks, a hammer and a plastic bag outside with you. (The target needs to be hammered tightly onto your wooden surface, so the impact of the thrown balloons doesn't knock it down.) Count the balloons and explain how many each person gets to throw. Have the children look at the target and be thinking about where they will aim when it’s their turn.

Part III:
One or two people can be in charge of drying the rubber bits off with paper towels. Gather around the table again for discussion.

"How did it feel to throw the balloons?" "Would it be helpful to use this project in the future to get out your feelings?" "Which feelings?"

Hand out a piece of paper and glue stick to each child. "Now we are going to make a collage with all these broken balloon pieces. This will remind us of our project today, and this way you can each take a piece of it home with you."

Make collages. The kids can just glue the pieces on, or make them into pictures using pens.

Check Out: 
For closing circle at our Humboldt Shelter groups, we usually ask "What did you like or not like about this project?" as well as one other question that applies to the activity.  One example for this project would be "Name one emotion you felt while throwing your balloons."

If possible, send a few balloons home with each child, so they can truly turn to this project at home. Hand the balloons to the care-provider who picks the child up from group, and explain how they can be used!
Row.txt_description: Allows children an avenue to explore and name different feelings and to realize that we can have more than one feeling at a time. A wonderful way to express feelings of anger, children can turn to this project at home in the future. It combines cognitive, emotional, and physical elements which allows true healing and change to occur.

Row.txt_code:
My Home sample
  
Objective:
This workshop is intended to help children identify and verbalize what "Home" means to
them individually. Also to provide a forum where the children can express their hopes
and dreams for their future "Homes."

Materials:
Pre-made Houses for each child
Scissors
Glue
Magazines
Pre-cut images for younger children
Markers
Pens

Age Range: 3 and up

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children
1 adult for 2 younger children

   



My Home sample, with windows
and door closed
 My Home sample, with windows opened
   
Advance Prep:
Create pre-cut Houses (made from construction paper). The Houses need to be made before the workshop. They are made by using three construction papers:
1 - the front ( w/ windows and a door cut through)
2 - the back ( glue to the front - but remember to not glue the windows and door shut!)
3 - the roof

Timeframe:
10 min: Warm-up/Opening Circle
35 min: Activity
15 min: Closing Circle


 
 
 Closed window: Family
  
 
 Open window: Family
  

Space Setup:
Have a spacious environment for the children to spread out their magazines and colors. Have pre-cut houses ready.

Warm-up: Growing As a Tree
(from November 1999 Update)
Have the children gather either in a circle, or just ask them to find a favorite spot near you in the room. Ask them to make space around them because they are going to grow from small to big. Tell the children that they are going to be special trees that are going to grow big and strong.

“Now I first want you to be a small tree but with strong roots. So let’s make sure our feet are on the ground and we have good roots that will help us grow. Let’s hunker down close to the ground so we can be small trees. Now we are going to grow, little by little. First let’s put our arms up above our head and our fingers are like little leaves, wiggling about and then little bit by little bit we are going to get bigger, and bigger, and bigger [until you are standing up fully]. Now we are a strong, wise tree, upright and ready for anything. Yes, let’s keep our arms and hands straight up in the air. Now let’s imagine that a wind comes up — not too big a wind, but a wind that makes us move around and about. Be careful, we can’t move our feet, because our roots are in the ground! Let’s just move our bodies at the top just like a real tree. Can anyone show me how the wind in the trees sounds? Yes, that’s good...”

Activity:
Have the children choose a house and let them look through magazines and cut out
pictures that appeal to them as being part of their home. They can glue the pictures to the inside of their house, behind the windows and door, or to the outside of their house. They may also use markers to draw what and who is a part of their home. (If the children are too young to write, leaders and assistants might help them to place the words they may want on different parts of their home.)

 
 

 
Open window: Laughter and Smiles
 Open window: Unity and Acceptance
   
Closing Circle:
Allow participants to share their Homes. Their houses represent their hopes and dreams for their futures. They are very important. Encourage the children to share why they made their home the way they did. What do the different pictures mean to them? If they have drawn themselves in their house, ask them to share how they feel in their home. Encourage them to notice that their hopes and desires for their own home are very important.
 
 

 
Outside of front door
 Inside of front door
Row.txt_description: Helps children identify and verbalize what "Home" means to them individually. Provides a forum where the children can express their hopes and dreams for their future "Homes."
Row.txt_tips: Have children think about how their idea of "home" has changed since they arrived at the shelter.

Row.txt_code:
< br/>

Tupelo’s Superhero Power Pourer in action.


< span class="TextHeader2">Objective:
To provide the children an opportunity to see their present challenges in light of previous accomplishments. To encourage them to set goals, allowing time to define them.  To help them to remember how certain things seemed impossible at one time but are easy now, so that they can feel confidence in their learning process.

Materials:
Styrofoam cups (1 per child)
Oil pastels/Cray-Pas (sets can be shared)
Large water container
Drinking water (may substitute with juice or drink mix if the children would enjoy that more)
Labels
Markers
Pens/Pencils
Writing paper
Adhesive tape
Tape player
Inspiring music
Optional - Glue sticks, scissors, photo stock books for collaging the cups. Anything can be used that can withstand moisture. Collaging actually works quite well on the cups.





Cathy senses her superhero powers.



Timeframe:
Opening Circle:    15 minutes
Warm-up:        5 minutes
Creating Superhero Power Pourers:                    20 minutes
Drinking Superhero Power Activation Juice:    5 minutes
Closing Circle:    15 minutes
Total Time:        1 hour

Age Range: 4-12

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children
1 adult for 2 younger children

Space Setup/Preparation:
It's helpful to make a Superhero Power Pourer yourself so that you know how the art supplies work on styrofoam. Also, before the workshop, prepare the large water container so that it will be easy to label as Superhero Activation Juice during the introduction. If you are using bottled water from the store, you might tape paper around it to cover the original label, making it blank and ready to be renamed by the group.

Introduction:
“Today we are going to think about times when we have learned to do something that we
thought we would never be able to do. Do you remember a time when you've thought,
'I'll NEVER be able to do that! That's too hard for me! A Superhero could do it, but not
me. I could never learn that, no way!' Remember how you felt confused and frustrated?

“Today we are going to learn about our personal Superhero powers, and we are going to practice being Superheroes. We will be making Superhero Power Pourers to show the powers inside of us that helped us learn new things. We will fill our Power Pourers with Superhero Power Activation Juice so we can keep learning and growing in order to do the things we want to do.”

Opening Circle:
“For our opening circle let's each share something we have learned to do that might have seemed too hard at first. It could be a small thing or a big thing. Does anyone remember how hard it was learning to tie your shoes?  Before we learned, how it seemed impossible?"  As leader, you may want to choose another example that is personal for you to help encourage each child to share. Make sure your example is appropriate for even the youngest participant.




“Superhero Activation Juice,” labeled as
“trust” (you can label yours as you and your
group want to during the introduction).




As each child shares a learning experience, seek out the Superhero Power the child used to learn the new thing. Ask them how they finally learned the skill. They may not understand what Power they used. For example, if they say that they "just kept trying until they got it right,” the power might be patience or persistence.  If they say that they were scared at first, the power might be courage. If they “just figured it out,” the power could be intelligence or imagination. If they say, “someone showed me" the power might be good-listening or paying attention.

It might be helpful to think of skills as powers—such as reading, writing, being polite, spelling, adding, subtracting. Other ideas for Superhero Powers: courage, perseverance, remembering, patience, imagination, rhyming, intelligence, strength, being nice, confidence, caring, endurance, passion, faith, love, creativity, calm, and wisdom.

As the children discover their powers, help them see it as their special magical power and remember it.

Warm-up: 
Go around the circle and have the children each think of a Superhero name for themselves using their power uncovered in the Opening Circle; "Luis the Listener," "Strong Linda," "Tupelo the Shoe-tier." Encourage them to add a Superhero Term like Turbo, Awesome, Nitro,Wonder—“Super Strong Linda" or to add an animal name like Spider, Shark, Lion, Bat—"Luis the Listening Lizard."  They might want to use the name of their favorite Superhero.

"Now that everyone knows their Superhero Name it's time to grow into Superheroes and take flight! Everyone lie down on the floor and be very still.  Be very still and quiet, don't move a muscle.  Be Superhero still, as still as you can be.  Now, start saying your Superhero name very quietly over and over, but don't move.  Keep saying your Superhero name and rise up onto your feet slowly, slowly, slowly. You are getting stronger and stronger!  Your Superhero Name gives you strength.  You are standing up straight and tall.  Now push your arms out straight in front of you, don't stop saying your Superhero Name.  And now it's time to fly! Fly around the room saying your Superhero Name!  We're flying over the city.  Look at all of the cars and trees.  Look at the people, how small they look!  Watch out for tall buildings.  Now that we've flown all over the city it is time to fly back to the art table and rest. All Superheroes need to rest and rebuild their strength.  Superheroes fly to your seats!"

Superhero Power Pourer Creation: 





Drawing on the cup with Cray-Pas.





Collaging on the cup works too.



After the warm-up, it is Superhero Power Pourer creation time.  Explain how each participant gets to make their own cup, their Power Pourer.  Then it can be filled with Superhero Activation Juice, so you can drink it and keep your Superhero Powers healthy and strong.  (If the children have the focus and energy to help name the juice, help them do so:  “What shall we call our juice? Super Juice? Power Water?”  As the Children come up with ideas the leader can write them down, narrowing it down to create a label for the Superhero Activation Juice Container.)

Encourage the children to think about their Superhero Names and draw pictures or words onto their cups.  They can draw whatever makes them think of their Superhero Name and Powers. 

Suggest to the children that they begin drawing when they feel ready.  It is important to remind them to not draw around the lip of the Power Pourer or they will end up with pastels on their lips!  The oil pastels will smear a bit but they won't rub off or run if water gets on the outside of the Power Pourer.

Drinking:
As the children complete their Power Pourers, help them one at a time, to fill them with Superhero Activation Juice and enjoy taking a sip.

Finishing Up: 
If some children finish before others, give them drawing paper so they can draw and/or write the story of their Superhero self while the other children finish making their Power Pourers.

Closing Circle: 
Encourage each child to share about their experience of making their Superhero Power Pourer. They might share how it felt remembering previous accomplishments or any insights they have gained into their ability to handle the challenges they currently face in making their dreams a reality.






Pouring “Activation Juice” into the cup.

Dolores joins the Superhero Power Pourers.
Row.txt_description: Provides children an opportunity to see their present challenges in light of previous accomplishments. Encourages them to set goals, allowng time to define them.
