< /tr>


 Happy Jar created by Diane and Sylvia
  

This wonderful workshop was created by Diane Jauregui and Sylvia Magana at the San Diego YWCA. It was shared at the Women’s Windows Leader’s Retreat, where the Women’s leaders enjoyed it immensely. Here, Tupelo Hassman has adapted it to share with YOU, the Children’s Windows leaders. Enjoy!

Possible Mother’s Day Project:
The Happy Jars could be created as gifts for Mother’s Day, with each child creating a jar of happy thoughts for their moms.

Workshop Objective:
To provide each child with a special place to collect and store their happy thoughts, and a positive tool that can be used to reaffirm their ability to be in charge of handling their emotions.

Materials:

 
 
 Leader, Cheryl Davis shares
her Happy Jar.
  


Newspaper to cover tables
Baby food jars (Note: Tennis ball cans can be a nice alternative. The labels pull off easily and they can be decorated using the same techniques as the jars)
Tissue Patchwork supplies:
20% water / 80% white glue - mix together
Colored tissue paper (pre-torn)
Crayons (to add after paper is dry)
Painting supplies:
Puffy paints, assorted colors
Brushes and containers for water
Colored paper and ball-point pens
(for happy thoughts to go in the jars)
Relaxing music
Paint palettes or paper plates

Timeframe:
Total Time: 55 minutes
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Circle/WarmUp: 5 minutes
Demonstration: 5 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing Circle: 10 minutes

  


Baby food jars ready to become Happy Jars.
 
  
Setup/Preparation:
Make a sample in advance. Experiment with both the tissue paper technique and the painting to see which will be better for your group. Clean the baby food jars and remove any excess glue or paper left from the label. If you decided on Tissue Patchwork, tear the tissue paper into small scraps. Make the water and glue mixture by mixing 20% water with 80% glue. A paint palette works best but make sure the palettes are soaked in warm water after use. Cover the art area with newspaper and set the supplies around the table. Depending on the number of participants, you may want to have more than one container of the water/glue mixture to go around. Last but not least - prepare a happy thought about each child to put into their Happy Jar!

Introduction:
“Happy Jars are a place to keep any special thoughts or words that you want to remember. Your Happy Jar can stay on your dresser, by your bed, or you can carry it with you in your backpack, so you can use it when you want. You can store happy feelings and memories in your Happy Jar, and then, when you feel scared or worried, you can open your jar and be reminded of your happy thoughts.”

Opening Circle & Warm-up:
“Picture yourself when you are having a fun time playing, when you are making happy noises and faces, when you are thinking happy thoughts. What are some faces you might make when you are having fun? What are some happy noises? (Encourage the children to each come up with a happy noise, for example: Yippee! Yahoo! Bangzowie!) Now, what are some happy ways of acting? (Have each child show a happy action, such as clapping, jumping up and down, shimmying and shaking. After each child shares their happy action have the whole group copy it—like ‘follow-the-leader.’) Today we are going to make a special place to keep all of those happy sounds, faces, noises, and thoughts so that you can see and feel them whenever you want.”

Age Range: 5 and up


 
 
 Painted jar.
  
 
 Tissue patchwork with crayon added.
  

Ratio:
One adult for four children; one adult for two young children.

Demonstration/Creation:
Step 1.
The first step is choosing the jar you'll be using to create and keep happy memories.

Step 2.
The second step is to decorate your jar and lid. (Have an example of a Happy Jar to demonstrate how the technique was done. Share the Tissue Patchwork or Puffy Painting technique.)

Step 3.
Lastly, write or draw your happy thoughts and fun words and pictures (colored paper looks best and can be cut ahead of time into small pieces). Such as: “Swinging on the swingset.” or “Bangzowie!” What were some of your favorite noises, faces, and thoughts from today? Which ones do you want to find inside of your Happy Jar? (Younger children will need help with the writing.)

Closing Circle:
Give each child a chance to share his or her Happy Jar and what it means. They might also share what things they are keeping inside of their Happy Jar.


   



Yarn-covered lid: This is more difficult than
tissue or paint, but can give a neat effect.
 Stained Glass Glaze close-up
Row.txt_description: Provides each child with a special place to collect and store their happy thoughts, and a positive tool that can be used to reaffirm their ability to be in charge of handling their emotions.
Row.txt_notes: ER TO DO: Rewrite!
Row.txt_tips: You can also use permanent markers and acrylic paints on your jars.

Row.txt_code:
Jen Muhlbeier at the
AWBW training.



Jen attended the last Children’s Windows Leadership Training, and shared this project with the group.  Here, she has written it up and taken step-by-step photos, to share it with the whole circle of leaders.  Enjoy!

Objective:





Positive Crown Sample



To create an opportunity for the children to have positive things about themselves noticed and celebrated in the group.  To give each child a fun way to display and share their pride in themselves, after the workshop is over, by wearing their crown.

Materials:
Colored construction paper
Crayons/Markers/Colored pencils
Scissors
Pen
Stapler
Music
Optional: glue, glitter, buttons, any decoration you choose.

Timeframe:
Total Time:                   1 1/2 hours
Opening Circle              15 minutes
Explanation of Project:     5 minutes
Creating Positive Crowns:          1 hour
Closing Circle:               10 minutes





Picture 1:  Fitting both hands
on the paper.



Picture 2:  Tracing both hands.



Picture 3:  Cutting out the hands.



Picture 4:  Now you have six
cut-out hands.



Picture 5:  Cut a one-inch band along
the side of the paper.



Picture 6:  Stapling the strips together.



Picture 7:  Stapling the band to
the child’s head.



Picture 8:  Writing on one hand
for each child.



Age Range: 4-12 

Ratio:
1 adult for 5 children
More is always better!

Preparation:
Begin by laying all the needed supplies on the table where the children will create their positive crown so they are able to choose the colors of their construction paper and what decorations they want.

Opening Circle:
I call it “Circle Time.”  We introduce ourselves, state if we have had a good, medium, or bad day.  Talk about the worst and best part of our day.  Next do some stretching exercises starting with your toes moving up through your entire body, then back down to your toes.  Then do three “bubble breaths.”  Bubble breaths are breaths that you use to blow bubbles, not too hard, not too soft, but very deep.  We hold imaginary bubble wands to our lips.

Introduction:
“Today we are going to create a crown made from a very beautiful shape on our body, our hands.  Our hands are used for many fun things.  Can you think of something fun that you do with your hands?”  (Allow the children to talk about fun things they do with their hands.  Very typical responses are: coloring, cutting, drawing.  I like to help them out by steering them in the direction of loving appropriate touch.  For example: petting a cat or dog, giving your mom or dad a hug, etc.)  “We all have wonderful and beautiful things about us on the inside and the outside.  Sometimes people can’t see those wonderful things, or we try to hide the good things about us.  The crowns we are going to make today will tell everyone some good things about us and make us feel good at the same time.”

Creating Positive Crowns:
Begin by allowing the children to choose 3 colors of construction paper, help the kids make sure both their hands will fit on the papers (picture 1).  Trace both hands on the construction paper (picture 2).  Cut out both hands, it is less time consuming if they can cut all three pieces of paper all at once, if not, they will have to trace and cut out six hands one at a time (picture 3).  Now you have six cut-out hands (picture 4).  Cut a 1-inch thick band of paper together along the long side of the paper (picture 5).  Staple the separate 1-inch strips of paper together to form a band around the childrens’ heads (picture 6-7).  Allow the children to decorate the bands and 5 of the 6 hands as they choose.  Save one hand for positive comments.  After the children are done decorating their bands and hands, collect the plain hands from all of the children and write their name in the “palm” of the hand.  Choose one child’s hand and go around the table asking
each child in the group to name something positive, or something they like about _________________.  (I like to use the name of the child, I think it makes it more personal (picture 8).  Write those positive comments on the fingers of the hand.  Do this for every child in the group.  Staple the hands on the bands with the fingers pointing up to form a crown (picture 9, 10, 11).)

Circle Time:
Have all the children put on their positive crowns and process the project.  Allow the children to parade around the room showing off their strengths.








Picture 9:  Starting to staple
the hands on the band.

Picture 10:  Continuing to
staple the hands on the band.









Picture 11:  All done!
Row.txt_description: Creates an opportunity for children to have positive things about themselves noticed and celebrated in the group. Gives each child a fun way to display and share their pride in themselves, after the workshop is over, by wearing their crown.

Row.txt_code:
Rachel Rioux
  
 
 Antonia Glowacki
  

One thing that we would hope not to ever have to experience in the shelter setting is one of the children or mothers being badly injured and subsequently hospitalized. We, unfortunately, had such an experience at our shelter this past year. One mother and two children were hit by a car and badly injured. It became apparent to the counselors that many of the children were missing their friends. Their absence, and the sense that no one was talking about what had occurred, seemed to lead to many questions and worries for the children. We decided to take advantage of the safe environment that was created each week in our Window’s group to address these concerns. This Get Well Wishes workshop is what we came up with.

Objective:
To provide a safe place for children to work through the questions and worries they have when/if their friends are injured and unable to be with them. To acknowledge feelings about losing a loved one, and help reduce the children’s sense of anxiety about being injured and being in the hospital. To offer a positive way to reach out and have a sense of connection and/or closure.

Materials:
Part I:
Information from a book, coloring book, or created by staff about a trip to the hospital. This may include pictures of a doctor and a nurse, explanations of why people enter the hospital, and what happens there.

Part II:
Construction paper
Glue
Scissors
Crayons and/or markers

Part III:
Tape recorder
Audio tapes

Timeframe:
Total Time - 1 hour
Opening Circle/Reading Time
10 minutes
Making Get Well Cards
25 minutes
Audio Taping
25 minutes

Age Range: 3 and up


  


Crayons, markers, and a “Get Well Wishes”
card under construction.
 
  

Part I: Reading Time
Have the children do a short warm up, such as a Wiggle-Down (see manual), and have them sit in a circle. Begin by introducing the reading materials, relating them back to the child who is in the hospital. You may want to preface this by reminding everyone that this is a “safe place” and that it is okay to talk about the injured child and ask questions if they like. Read through the materials, using whatever you have. This may bring up a lot of questions about the injured child. We did not know very much about the child’s condition, and were honest about this, while addressing their frustrations and worries. Also, we found that many children had experienced visiting a family member, or were themselves, in a hospital at one time. It was important to address the fears and myths about being in the hospital, and we tried to let the children share their stories with the group.



 
 
 Cover of a “Get Well Wishes” card.
  
 
 Inside of a “Get Well Wishes” card.
  

Part II: Get Well Cards
At this point, we allowed the children to begin making “get well cards” for the injured child. Small children may need assistance with spelling. We talked about good thoughts and messages that we could write on the cards. We asked the children to imagine the injured child reading these cards and feeling better. We talked about what makes them feel better when they are sick.

Part III: Audio Taping
Because we were not allowed to visit the ill child, we addressed the children’s frustrations by allowing them the opportunity to send taped messages to the injured child. We gave the opportunity to tape these messages in private, in a nearby office, while the other children continued making cards. We also gave them the opportunity to tape group messages. We brought out our small collection of musical instruments and the children initiated singing songs on the tape. This turned out to be very creative and joyful! We found that many children opened up, becoming more extroverted, when they were singing. You may find that some children have a hidden talent as well! If you don’t have access to instruments, you could improvise some drums from coffee cans, or purchase inexpensive slide whistles and harmonicas at a discount store. One important step was allowing the children to listen to themselves on tape when they were done. We found that this helped them recognize that they have a voice, and are affecting someone else’s life in a positive way. We then delivered the audio tapes and cards to the children and mom, and were able to report back to the kids that their efforts had lifted their spirits and helped them get better.

Ending:
We ended our session with a final song and short check-in. Many of the children remember this group to this day! Some children in shelter have unrecognized and unresolved issues with grief and loss. This group reduced their general anxiety about being injured, being in the hospital and the uncertainty that is a part of life. In addition, it helped provide a safe, nurturing space to acknowledge feelings about losing a loved one. We gave the children follow-up on how the injured children and mother were doing, and although they were unable to return to our shelter, we were able to give everyone a sense of closure and a chance to say goodbye with more cards and audio tapes at a later date!

   



“We miss you!!!”
 “We love you!!!”
Row.txt_description: Provides a safe place for children to work through questions and worries they have when/if their friends are injured and unable to be with them. Offers time to acknowledge feelings about losing a loved one, and helps reduce anxiety about being injured and being in the hospital.
Row.txt_tips: Setting up a Girls Group and a Boys Group to meet once a month is a possibility if this workshop goes particularly well.

Row.str_author_location: Good Shepherd Shelter, Los Angeles, California
Row.txt_code:
Summer Wind Catcher


This workshop idea, and the Summer Wind Catchers appearing in this Update were contributed by the Sisters at Good Shepherd Shelter in Los Angeles.  The workshop was written by Cathy Salser, based on their idea and examples.

Objective:
To cool down together in the heat of the summer by noticing the wind around us and the wind inside us—our own breath.  To give the children an opportunity to explore and enjoy creating their own sense of peacefulness and beauty through the wind inside and outside them.

Materials:
Newspaper
Large, thin white paper (cut into strips)
Popsicle sticks
School glue
Tempera paints (for finger painting)
Paper plates (for dipping fingers)
Paper towels
Markers (especially green)
Hole punch
String
Wind outside, and/or a fan inside
Peaceful music & tape player

Timeframe:
Total Time:  60 minutes
Introduction:        10 minutes
Warm-Up:         10 minutes
Demonstration:    5 minutes
Creation:        25 minutes
Closing Circle:    10 minutes

Age Range: 3 and up

Ratio:
One adult for four children; one adult for two young children.

Setup/Preparation:
If possible, make a sample in advance so it’s easier to give a sense of what a Summer Wind Catcher might look like.  






Summer Wind Catchers


Cover the art area with newspaper.  Check out the wind situation and figure out which warm-up(s) you think might work best.  (Is there an area right outside the door where the children would be able to try the Wind Statues Warm-up?)

Introduction:
“Today, we will be making Summer Wind Catchers.  Did anyone get hot yet this summer?  When was the hottest?  Have you felt a nice breeze this summer, helping you cool down?  Where is the windiest? (Outside on a windy day? by a fan? near a big truck or bus? in the car? etc...)

“Did you ever notice you have wind inside of you too?  Can you make a nice cool breeze right now?  (Put your hand out in front of you and blow.)  Can you make a hot breeze?”  Note: the closer your hand is to your mouth and the more wide-open your mouth is, the hotter the wind will be!  

“The wind around you can be relaxing and peaceful.  The wind inside you can be relaxing and peaceful too.  Sometimes when you are upset, you can just take some nice slow breaths and it can help you feel better—even when you think you’re going to explode!”  (Sometimes it’s good for moms too!)




Popsicle stick attached to ends of paper.




Warm-Ups:
Here are three options for a warm-up.  Choose what you think would work best for your group, and use as many warm-ups as you like, to draw the children together throughout the workshop.

Ten Wind Warm-up:
“Sometimes when we need to relax, we can use our own breath.  It can be very special to take ten nice, deep, slow breaths.  Who here can count to ten?  Let’s try it together together.  Ready?  Can you count with me?  Let’s take our first breath in... and now let it out... and that’s one.  And now our next breath in... and out... and that’s two.   Let’s remember to go nice and slow and easy.  And three... etc.” (Encourage the children to count with you out loud, and at the end, ask them how it felt.)

Wind Dance Warm-up:
Play soft music.  “Today we are going to try the Wind Dance Warm-up.  As I play this music, we get to become the wind.  Did you ever notice how the wind moves?  Can you move like that?  Can you make wind sounds?  Where would you go if you were the wind?  Would you go along the walls?  Under the table?  Would you twirl around in a corner?  That’s good!  Now let’s be a stormy wind!  Wonderful!  And now let’s be a gentle breeze!  Beautiful!  And let’s blow all the way back to our seats and rest.”  (As you lead the children, guide and encourage them by dancing a wind dance with them.)






Holes punched and string attached.


Wind Statues Warm-up:  
(For this warm-up, you need to have access to a safe outdoor area where the children can go feel the wind.)  “Today we are going to be wind statues.  Have you ever seen a statue?  Can you imagine how it feels to be a statue, so still and quiet?  Can you imagine being a statue and feeling the wind moving across your face, your arms, your hair?  We will go out into the yard and each find our own spot where we can become a statue.  When you’ve found your spot, freeze, like a statue and just feel the wind moving around you.  The more quiet and still you are, the more you can feel the wind.  You can let us know you’ve found the wind by holding really still and quiet until we all find our spots.  Ready?  Let’s go!”  Note: You might need to define the area they can be statues in, so no-one will be running out of sight or into the street.

Demonstration and Creation:
Step 1. Construction
“The first step is doing the construction (for younger children, it might be simplest to prepare some in advance, so they can skip this part).  We can fold the ends of our papers around the popsicle sticks and hold them with glue.”

Step 2. Finger Paints
“The next step is the painting.  You get to pick the colors.  With just a finger print, we can create beautiful flowers to blow in the breeze.  (If you want to make something else on your wind catcher, that’s okay too.)  Just let me know what colors you want on your plate.”   

Step 3. Markers
“After the flowers are on, we can use markers to create the stems and leaves and vines.  Be careful not to put the markers into the wet paint!”

Step 4. String
“Finally we are ready to punch the holes and attach the string.  (This may take adult help.)  And then, once it’s all dry, your Wind Catcher is ready to hang!”

Closing Circle:
“Give each child a chance to share his or her Wind Catcher and anything about what it means to them.”







Variation:
Instead of summer vines and flowers, you might try the “hands are not for hitting” theme.  The children could create a vine of hand prints on the Wind Catchers, and think of how they want to use their hands in positive ways this summer.
Row.txt_description: Gives children an opportunity to explore and creating ctheir own sense of peacefulness and beauty through the wind inside (their breath) and outside of them. The end product are breezy strips of fingerpainted art, ready to hang outside or in.

Row.txt_code:
This project idea was contributed by Erica Poellot during her time as AWBW Children’s Windows leader at the Family Violence Project in Los Angeles.  The workshop was written up by Cathy Salser.




Dolores holds “I Am a
Bright Light” candle


Objective:
To create an opportunity for the children to think about someone who has been a “bright light” to them, and to notice how they themselves are a bright light to those around them.  To create candle holders symbolizing each child’s own bright light that shines on the world around them.  
In the midst of domestic violence, the children are facing a time that may feel especially dark and confusing.  This workshop provides a way for the children to talk about that darkness, and to notice the bright lights in them and around them that can help them through it.  

Materials:
Candle holders: You can use baby food jars, or purchase “ivy bowls” or small glass candle holders at a craft supply store (about $.79 each).
Food warmer candles  (can be purchased in bulk at Smart and Final)
Newspaper to cover tables (several layers—this is a messy project!)
School glue





Torn tissue paper, school glue, and brushes.


Water (in cups/bowls for rinsing brushes)
Water/Glue mixture (80% glue, 20% water)
Brushes
Tissue paper (pre-torn into pieces)
Paper towels
Peaceful music
Optional: glitter and ribbon

Timeframe:
Total Time:  60 minutes
Introduction:        10 minutes
Warm-Up:         10 minutes
Demonstration:    5 minutes
Creation:        25 minutes
Closing Circle:    10 minutes

Age Range: 5 and up

Ratio:





Baby food jar, before soaking and
removing label.



Food warmer candles in bulk
(above), in hand (below).




One adult for four children; one adult for two young children.

Setup/Preparation:
If you are using baby food jars, you will need to soak them and remove the labels before the workshop.  Also, you will need to tear the tissue paper into pieces in advance.

If possible, make a sample so it’s easier to know how to help the children with their creations.  

Cover the art area with newspaper.  This is a messy project!!  Create a separate drying area, also covered with plenty of newspaper.  If possible, you might want to choose a sunny or warm spot for faster drying.

Introduction:
“Today’s workshop is called I Am a Bright Light.  Each and every one of you is very, very special.  Today, our Windows time is a very special time for you to notice that.  Can you think of some ways you are special?  Can you notice how you are an inspiration to those around you?  Sometimes you make people smile, sometimes you make people laugh, and you fill their hearts with joy.  You make a difference to everyone around you.

“Today, we will each be making our own bright light (show sample).  We can each give our light to someone who has been a bright light to us.  Can you think of someone who has been a bright light for you?  Is there someone who has been your guiding light?  Is their someone who has hugged you when you’re sad?  Who might be your bright light?”  (Listen to the kid’s thoughts, and see “Note about Moms,” below.)

Note About Moms:
When Erica did this workshop, the children all wanted to give their light to their moms.  Focusing on the moms was very useful and therapeutic for the kids.  During the workshop, most of them talked about their mom’s reason for coming to the shelter.  After the bright light creations were completed, Erica said it was great to see the mom’s reactions and to hear the kids tell their moms why they wanted to share their “light!” with them.  It was also great to hear the kids tell their moms why they are so important to them and how their moms have been a “guiding light.”  

As you lead this workshop, notice if it makes sense for moms to be the natural focus.  If that works well for the kids, great.  However, be ready to notice and support children who may wish to focus on others besides their moms.  It’s fine for the kids to make their light for whomever they wish.  Even if their light was not created for their mom, the story of their light and who it’s for can be just as precious and important to share with their moms after the workshop. 




Step 2: Applying the tissue.


Also there may be children who have a hard time thinking of anyone at all who has been a “light” to them.  You can support them one-on-one, and encourage their thoughts.  Ask if anyone has comforted them when they’ve been sad.  Their bright light might be a shelter staff person, or a pet they miss at home.  They could even choose themselves to be their own bright light, or they could make their light for someone they might find in the days ahead of them.  

Bright Light Warm-Up:
“For our warm-up, we are going to practice being bright lights.  Has anyone here ever watched a candle burn bright?  How does it look?  Let’s all become candles.  (Stand straight with your hands up as a wick and flame.)  What color is your candle?  (Encourage the children to share what color they are.)  How big is your flame?  How bright are you?  When you shine your light on people, how do you want to make them feel?  (Encourage the children to share their thoughts, e.g. happy, smiling, warm, peaceful, loving, strong, hopeful, etc.)  Who wants to blow the candles out?  (See if one child will go around and blow each candle out.)  Any more candles still burning?  Are they all out?  That’s good!  (Thank whoever blew them all out.)  You were wonderful bright lights!”

Demonstration and Creation:
Step 1. Picking your tissue paper colors
“The first step is picking out which colors you want for your bright light.  Gather some pieces of tissue paper.  You can tear it into smaller pieces if you want.”

Step 2. Applying the tissue
“The next step is putting the tissue pieces on.  Dip your brush into the water/glue and paint it onto the glass.  Then you can stick the tissue on, and you can paint some extra water/glue over the top of the tissue to smooth it on.  Don’t worry if the colors run and get mixed up.  It’s beautiful when they do.”

Step 3. Ribbons and Glitter (Optional)
Ribbons can be attached with the school glue.  If the entire surface is sticky enough, glue may not even be needed.  Glitter can also be added, before the sticky surface dries.

Step 4.  Drying





Completed “I Am a Bright
Light” with candle.


Once the glass is as covered with tissue as the child wants, it may need to sit and dry for a bit.  Help each child move their creation to the drying area.  As the creations dry, you might encourage the children who finish early to continue working with tissue on paper, or white mat board, until you’re ready to bring the workshop to a close.  

Closing Circle:
Give each child a chance to share his or her “Bright Light” and anything about what it means to them.  Support them as they share their bright lights with their moms, whether or not they made it for their moms.  If it was made for someone who is not there, they can ask their moms to be the keepers of their light.
Row.txt_description: Offers an opportunity for the children to think about someone who has been a "bright light" to them, and to notice how they themselves are a bright light to those around them. The end product are candle holderes symbolizing each child's own bright

Row.txt_code:
Sample Pumpkin Heads: Mad and Happy


Objective:
To use Pumpkin Heads as an identification prop for self-expression for children deciding their choices on specific issues or feelings.

Materials:
Popsicle sticks
Construction paper (pumpkins don’t have to be orange!)
Markers
Oil pastels/Cray-Pas
Glue sticks
Yarn (if you want to add hair)

Timeframe:
5 minutes    Opening
5 minutes    Halloween Dance
20 minutes    Creation
20 minutes    Closing





Pre-cut pumpkin circles, stems, and leaves.



Age Range: 3 and up

Ratio:
1 adult for 6 children
1 adult for 3 young children

Setup/Preparation:
If you are working with young children it might be helpful to draw the Pumpkin Head for them and/or cut it out prior to beginning with the children.

Opening:
“Today we are going to make our own unique ‘Special Pumpkin Heads.’  These special pumpkins will help us in thinking about the choices we make everyday, how important our choices are, and how we feel about things.  How is everyone feeling today?  Did we have a good, bad, or okay day today?  What kind of choices did we make today? (Give examples of choices for understanding.)  What are some things that we did today that were good or bad?

“Our Special Pumpkin Heads will hopefully help us figure out how we feel about things.”




Beginning the pumpkin face with Cray-Pas.




Halloween Dance:
(This warm-up is similar to the “Monster Dance” warm-up.)  “Today, we are going to start with a Halloween Dance!  Has anyone ever dressed up for Halloween?  What was your favorite thing to be?  For our Halloween Dance, let’s start moving around the room together and think about Halloween costumes.  Have you ever seen someone be a ghost?  Let’s be ghosts.  What noises would you make?  And how about a witch?  (Move around the room as witches.)  And how about a fairy?  And how about a warrior?”  Dance around the room with the children, making the noises and motions for various characters.  You might want to end the Halloween Dance with everyone turning into pumpkins and walking their pumpkin-selves back to their seats. 





This Pumpkin Head is angry.





This Pumpkin Head is sad.



Creation:
Have the children pick what colors they want their pumpkins.  They can each make two different pumpkin heads to be glued together around the stick.  Once they’ve picked their colors, they can start drawing the circles and cutting them out.  The children may also choose to draw and cut their own stems and leaves.  The pumpkin faces can be done with oil pastels, markers, yarn, or buttons!  Encourage the children to make two different faces—one for each side.  Maybe they could make a happy and a sad face.  After the faces are done the pumpkins are glued together with the popsicle stick in the middle.

Closing and Discussion:
During closing circle have the children share their own individual faces.  

Ask them to share their feelings about issues by turning their sticks either to happy or sad pumpkins.  Remind the children that there are no right or wrong answers.  

Leader can raise issues to examine, for example:
1.  How do you feel when someone pushes you?
2.  How do you feel when someone hugs you?
3.  How do you feel when someone smiles at you?
4.  How do you feel when no one plays with you?

*Also leader can ask children to participate in sharing issues and asking all the participants.

Halloween Choices:
In closing, the group can talk
about Halloween and tie in the importance of safety and making good choices.  The children can use the finished projects to answer some Halloween scenarios.  For example:
1.  Do we eat candy that isn’t wrapped?
2.  Is it important to make sure you are with an adult while ‘trick or treating?’
Row.txt_description: Pumpkin Heads are created for use as an identification prop for self-expression for children deciding their choices on specific issues or feelings.

Row.txt_code:
“See who talks a lot and who is quiet!” Family Portrait.
  
Objective:
To give the children an opportunity to draw their families, with encouragement to see their family however they feel best about it. To give them the ability to frame their creations in something special and fun that they’ve made themselves. To help each child walk away with a sense of pride, having created their own framed family portrait—more satisfying and complete than a drawing with no frame.

Materials:
Construction paper
Popsicle sticks
Glue

 
 
 “My dog was who I felt safest
with!” Family Portrait.
  

Markers
Scissors

Timeframe:
5 minutes Opening
5 minutes Golden Ball Visualization
20 minutes Creation
10 minutes Closing

Age Range: 3 and up

Ratio:
About one adult to four children, depending on the age group.

 
 
 Popsicle sticks, ready to use.
  
 
 Finished frames, ready for drawings. One not
cut (on left), and one cut out (on right).
  


Setup/Preparation:
We have pretty crazy groups so we take the kids interested in the art program into a separate room to do our projects. We sit around a large table. The supplies and an already-put-together sample of the project with no decoration are set out, so the kids will do their own idea and not ours.

Opening:
“Today we are going to make our own unique Framed Family Portraits. Has anyone ever drawn a picture of their family before? That’s great! Today, we will be making our own frames to go with our drawings. (Share already-made sample.) We will start with the frames and then go ahead with the drawings and put it all together.”

Note: These are some questions you might ask, to encourage the children to think about their families, or you might dive right into the Golden Ball Visualization and creation.

Possible questions: Does anyone here have a family that includes a dog or cat? Today, in your picture, you get to decide who to put in your family. How do you feel about your family today? Does anyone feel good about their family? Does anyone feel mad? Does anyone feel sad? Does anyone feel lots of different feelings at once? You get to draw your family however you want to today.


 
 
 “See who talks a lot and who is quiet!” detail.
  
 
 “My dog was who I felt safest with!” with frame.
  

Warm-up:
Golden Ball Visualization (see manual)

Creation:
1. When the kids are ready, they can start by gluing the popsicle sticks around the construction paper. We made ours four popsicle sticks wide on each edge (see illustration, page 2).
2. Next, the kids can cut out the center of the frame. (If that’s too hard, or they don’t want to cut it out, their picture can be glued in, without cutting the center out.)
3. Next the kids can draw their picture which then can either be glued in the center of the frame, or glued from the back if they cut out the center. As the kids draw their families, encourage them to remember that it’s okay to include whoever they want in their family. There is no right or wrong. In our group, some of the kids did include the father and some included only the mother and children. It’s important to let each kid know that it’s okay to see their family however they feel best.
4. Once the portrait is in place, the finishing touches can be added by decorating their frame of popsicle sticks with markers.

  


Using markers to decorate the frame.
 
  

 
“My dog was who I felt
safest with!” detail.
 
  

Closing:
“This is the time to share what we made and discuss our familes and who we include in them. Anyone who wants to share can share, and anyone who doesn’t want to doesn’t have to. As we listen to each other, let’s all practice remembering that it’s okay to draw our families in any way we want to. There is no right and wrong.”

Variations:
Here are a few ideas for variations of this workshop: You could get pre-made frames and concentrate more on the creation of the picture. The kids could use magazine cut-outs instead of drawing their family. I’ve found that stencils also work well for children who have a difficulty with feeling comfortable about their art work.
Row.txt_description: Gives the children an opportunity to draw their families, with encouragement to see their family however they feel best about it, then gives them the ability to frame their creations in something special and fun that they've made themselves.
Row.txt_tips: Children could also draw out a small family tree in addition to their portraits.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:





“Good for 10 Hugs” Coupon.



To give the children an opportunity to create gifts that they don’t need to buy.  To help them notice how their presence, caring, and actions can be very special and wonderful gifts.

Note:
In leading this workshop, it was very rewarding to witness the children actually realizing that the most important gifts are those they don’t need to buy.  It was challenging, but important to help them face the reality that they may not have enough money for many of the things they want (and maybe even some of what they need at times).  It was also wonderful to see how this workshop helped a very angry eight-year-old focus briefly on how his behavior has been difficult for his mother to handle.

Materials:
Construction paper
Markers
Scissors (if you have “edger scissors,” it’s nice to give a special edge to the coupons)
Glue sticks
Glitter, stickers, etc.





“Back Rub“ Coupon.



Timeframe:
5 minutes    Opening
5 minutes    Warm-up
20 minutes    Creation
10 minutes    Closing

Age Range: 3 and up

Ratio:
About one adult to four children, depending on the age group.

Holiday Feelings Dance Warm-up:
“Sometimes, during the holiday season, we feel lots of different feelings.  Our moms sometimes do too.  Have you noticed that?  What feelings have you noticed inside of you during the holidays?  What feelings have you noticed around you during the holidays?   Have you ever seen people rushing, in a big hurry?  Have you seen people sad and lonely?  Have you seen people happy and singing?  What have you seen?”  (Encourage a sharing of thoughts and then have all the children stand in a circle for the Holiday Feelings Dance.  Begin to move around, like when we do the Monster Dance.)  “Now let’s make up a Holiday Feelings Dance together.  We can start by moving around in a circle together, slowly at first, and now faster and faster.  Can you become a rushing holiday person?  And now can you be a happy holiday person?  How about a silly holiday person?  And now, a sad holiday person?  And can you be a peaceful, relaxed holiday person?  So peaceful, so relaxed...  Let’s go slower and slower, peaceful and more peaceful, and find our way back to our seats to relax!  Beautiful!”   

For older kids:  Instead of a dance, have a circle of sharing thoughts out loud.  Ask each person to share the good and bad feelings they’ve noticed inside them and around them during the holiday season.  Whoever doesn’t want to share any thoughts can pass.





“Extra Chore” Coupon.



Creation:
“Today, we are going to make empathy “gift coupons.”   Has anyone ever heard the word empathy?  It means caring and understanding how someone else is feeling.  It’s a very wonderful thing.  When you are able to understand how someone else is feeling, you can be close and connected with them.  Empathy is what connects us to each other so that we can cooperate and enjoy being together.”  

“You can make ‘gift coupons’ to give your mom or someone else that you care about.  It’s a chance to think about something that would make that person happy, something that you can give them and that you don’t need to buy.  It could be a hug, an extra chore for the week, free T.V. time, a backrub... anything you think the person would enjoy.  Does anyone have any ideas?”  

When the kids are ready, they can start drawing their coupons.  Younger kids may need help with the writing.    

Closing:
“Share your coupon(s) and something you learned from doing this project.  How do you feel about giving it to your mom?”

Variations:
This workshop can be adapted to focus on giving at any time of year.   Any day is a special day to give someone you love a gift, and a Gift Coupon is one way the kids can always express their caring.
Row.txt_description: Gives children an opportunity to create gifts that they don't need to buy. Helps them notice how their presence, caring, and actions can be very special and wonderful gifts.

Row.txt_code:
Example Thoughtstopper



Objective:
To provide each participant with positive images to focus on when she is overwhelmed with negative thoughts or feelings.  These "thoughtstoppers" can be any image that reflects a personal sense of peace, relaxation or calmness.  The framed images are gentle reminders that these women have the ability to redirect negative thoughts to positive thoughts with visualization.



Materials:
Magazines
Photo stock books
Pre-cut mat boards
Glue
Scissors
Construction paper





Example Thoughtstopper



Setup:
Arrange magazines, books, frames, glue, scissors, and construction paper on the table, ready for distribution.

Timeframe:
Introduction: 5 min.
Opening Circle: 15 min.
Demonstration: 10 min.
Supply Distribution:  10 min.
Relaxation: 5 min.
Creation: 45 min.
Closing: 15 min.

Introduction:
“Today, we are going to think about those images that take you to that ‘special place’—images that produce a sense of peace and relaxation—images that are calming and soothing—or images that portray future goals or desires—goals that are obtainable or places you would like to visit.  This workshop will give us an opportunity to find those images that help us to relax when we're distracted by negative thoughts.”




Example Thoughtstopper




During the introduction, ask the participants to share about the images that bring them good feelings, peace, and serenity.

Opening Circle:
“Share how you are feeling today, and name a place, thing, or time in your life that reminds you of good feelings.”

Demonstration:  
Demonstrate the following steps in creating a thoughtstopper:
1.  Select a picture or image.
2.  Using construction paper for background, glue picture.
3.  Select frame and glue on picture and trim the edges.

Supply Distribution:
Make sure each participant has magazines, scissors, and glue in front of her.




Example Thoughtstopper




Relaxation:
Use your favorite visualization.  Here is a possible one to try:  “When you are ready, close your eyes, get comfortable, and take a deep breath...  and another...  As you let the air go, notice your body relaxing into your chair.  Notice the chair and the floor holding you up, gently...  Now begin to imagine that you are sitting in a forest.  There are many colors of green around you.  There are beautiful patches of warm sunshine coming through the green leaves.  You are sitting on a big, comfortable rock—a rock that is warmed by the sunlight.  Notice the warmth of the rock beneath you...  Notice the sense of peace and calm surrounding you.  This is your special place—a place that nourishes you and comforts you...  a place that gives you strength and clarity.  Take your time relaxing and soaking in your special place.  Remember this place.  It is yours...  When you are ready, open your eyes and begin to create.”

Creation:





Example Thoughtstopper



“Now, let's select pictures that remind us of those peaceful places.  Select an image that brings you a personal sense of peace and enjoyment.”

Closing Circle:
As the workshop comes to a close, encourage each participant to share her reasons for making the selections that she did.  

Remind each participant to use her “thoughtstopper”—to remember to look and focus on her positive images whenever those negative thoughts or feelings might appear.

Variations:
1. Collage images
2. Use pastels for background
3. Use plexiglass instead of frames (pre-cut)




Example Thoughtstopper
Row.txt_description: Provides participants with positive images to focus on when finding themselves overwhelmed with negative thoughts and feelings. The end product are framed images - gentle reminders of the ability to redirect negative thoughts to positive thoughts with visualization.

Row.txt_code:
Oceana Madrone


About the Author:
My name is Oceana Madrone. I'm a mother, grandmother, partner and sweetheart.  I make fantasy clothing, quilts, dolls, jewelry and other bead objects.  I also work at Humboldt Women for Shelter, as Children’s Services Coordinator.  My favorite part of the job is the art groups I get to do with the women and children.  Art has been a powerful tool in my life.  I feel honored to be able to  share art as a way of expressing oneself and exploring feelings.  I, too, am a survivor of domestic violence and sexual assault.

Objective:
To redisover and honor our intuition.  The inner voices that guide us and tell us what to do if we allow ourselves to become quiet enough to hear them.  The dolls are a visual reminder to listen to our intuition.

Materials:
-One and a half pipe cleaners per person (for body)
-Embroidery thread (for hair)
-Thin ribbon: 1/8" wide, 36" long per person  (for skin)
-4"x7" fabric rectangles  (wide range of colors, textures and patterns)
-Beads, fishing line
-Old jewelry
-Feathers
-Pin backs
-Scissors
-Jewelry pliers and wire cutters
-Paper and pens







Timeframe:
75-90 mins—Total Time

10 mins—Intro + Opening Circle
5 mins—Technical Demonstration
5 mins—Relaxation and Visualization
45-60 mins—Creation of Doll
10-15 mins—Closing Circle

Introduction:
“Today we are going to make intuition dolls.  The dolls are  symbols to remind you to listen to your own inner voice. 

“There is a Russian folk tale called Vassilissa.  It is the story of a girl who receives a doll from her mother, right before her mother dies.  She tells Vassilisa to always keep the doll close to her and to listen to what the doll tells her.  She also tells her to keep the doll a secret and tell no one.  Vassilissa keeps the doll in her pocket.  Through the story Vassilissa consults her doll, who always gives her good advice.  When Vassilissa comes to a fork in the road, the doll seems to tell her which way to go;  when she meets Baba-Yaga, the doll jumps up and down in her pocket to warn Vassilissa.

“Vassilissa's doll is like intuition. That voice inside ourselves that tells us which path to take and warns us of danger.  Can you think of a time when you've felt your intuition?  What happened?  Where in your body did you feel your intuition?  The participants may talk about a funny tummy feeling, a tightness in their chest, a voice in their head.  It is helpful for them to talk about where they feel their intuition.  Then, they can begin to recognize it  and learn to listen to it.”

Technical Info:
Body
1.  Fold full size pipe cleaner in half.  Twist 1/2"-3/4" into loop at top to make "head".
2.  Using 1/2 pipecleaner for arms twist on below "head"
3.  For smaller dolls, about 1/2 way down arms & legs fold pipe cleaner in (towards body).  Twist small loops for hands.
4.  For larger dolls, make head loop slightly larger.  Fold in arms and legs at desired length, leave full length if desired.



Hair
1.   Wrap embroidery thread around all 4 of your fingers to make loops.
2.   Insert loops through "head."
3.   Tie knot.  Clip loops.



Skin
1.  Using thin ribbon, tie an X over the chest of the doll. 
2.  Wrap the ribbon tightly! around the arms (leave the "hands" unwrapped), neck, head and chest area.  Legs do not need to be wrapped.
3.  Knot tightly.  Save any extra ribbon for belt.

Dress
1.  Use pattern to cut dress.
2.  Cut fringe, if you wish.
3.  Fold in 1/2 front to back, and then fold in 1/2 again side to side.  Just barely clip folded corner.  This makes the neckhole.  It will stretch, so make sure not to cut it too big.
4.  Slide dress over head.  Use ribbon to tie around waist. Adjust if necesary.

Final Touches
1.  Add beads, feathers, etc.
2.  Glue pin on back.  Or you can
     use a little piece of ribbon to
     tie it on.
3.  When you are done, take a few minutes to write a few words about your intuition doll, and what it means for you.






Deep rich colors
   
Dark & nurturing—
like soil is for seeds
   
Shell brings
wisdom of sea
   
Feathers—
flight & freedom
   
One arm holding close, protecting
   
Other arm extended, releasing...



Relaxation/Visualization:
Use your own favorite relaxation.  One of my favorites is Rose Rothwell’s Comfort Relaxation  (Comfort Journals Nov. 1996).
Near the end, I change talking about comfort to talking about intuition.  What does your intuition look like?....  What colors and images come to mind?....  If you look for your intuition in your body where do you find it?....  How does your intuition speak to you?...  When you are ready, gently bring your awareness back to this room.  You  can make your own Intuition Doll a symbol to remind you to listen to your own inner voice.  When you feel ready, open your eyes and begin.

I like to play the song  "Inner Voices" by Sweet Honey in the Rock while we make the dolls.

Closing Circle: 
Give each person a chance to share as much or as little as they would like to about their doll, or anything they want to share about the group.  Validate the unique creativity of each person.  Listen to and enjoy your intuition doll.
Row.txt_description: Allows time for the rediscovery and honoring of the inner voices that can guide us if we allow ourselves to become quiet enough to hear them. The dolls are a visual reminder to listen to our intuition.

Row.txt_code:
“This hand shows that there was a lot of sadness
for me and stress and my children were afraid a lot
of times.  Huge disappointments.  My hand.  Me
and my children are a lot more peaceful.  We’re
happy and I’m independent and I’ve grown a lot.”



Sister Carmelita and Sister Christina lead the AWBW art sessions at Good Shepherd’s domestic violence shelter in Los Angeles.  

Here, they share a workshop they developed in which each participant explores the differences between her own hands and the hands of her abuser.  

At Good Shepherd, the participant’s expressions, painted onto fabric squares, are being made into a quilt.







Strong, angry hands that once held our
hearts, dreams and future
are no more. 

Hands that hold our hearts, peace,
and happiness now are alone,
yet strong and powerful...
They are my hands. 

-Handprints workshop participant



Objective:
To give each participant the opportunity to draw two hands:  first, to draw the hand of her abuser/partner and what it meant to her and her children, then, second, to draw her own hand and what it has meant to her and her children.

Materials:
8 x 8 inch squares of cloth (2 squares per participant)
Acrylic paint (good to have the squeeze bottles for fabric painting)
Glitter
Glue (white school glue)
Slips of paper and pencils for writing
Setup:
Tape the cloth squares on the table.  Each individual uses two squares each.





“Left hand is the hand of anger, emptiness, rage, fear, sorrow,
and pain, sadness.  Right is the hand of healing, love, peace and
joy, strength, forgiveness.  The Hand of God.”



Timeframe:
1 1/2 hours

Introduction:
“Our hands are the most powerful “doing” part of us.  The hands tell much about us.  Look at the back of your hand and the palm.  They say that our left palm speaks of our past and potentialities while our right palm speaks of our present and our choices.  In the family situation of domestic violence, we see how the hands play a visible and strong sign in the human and family relationship.”

Warm-up:
“The Archer’s Hand is a part of the Shibashi exercise for focus, health and well being.  Stand straight with feet apart.  Stretch both hands forward.  Swing your left hand in an arc toward self and point with the middle and pointer finger to the left, while the right hand swings in an arc with the right’s middle and pointer finger aligned with the left hand, simulating an archer stretching the bow.  Stretch as if to hit a target and release the arrow.  Repeat the same exercise with the right hand taking the lead, pointing to the right.  Breathe in and breathe out as you do this exercise.”




Sample of handprints




Demonstration: 
“There are two pieces of squares on the table for you to trace your two hands.  Trace your hand with the acrylic or textile paint.  One of them symbolizes your abuser’s hands and the other one symbolizes your own.  Decorate or color it the way your partner’s hand meant to you and your children when you were together and do the same for your handprint.”

Supply Distribution:
Make sure each participant has magazines, scissors, and glue in front of her.





Participant works on her handprints.



Closing Circle:
Go around the table silently to view the different hands in front of you and absorb the symbol each one draws.  Those who feel free to share the meaning of the two hands and also the feeling they got in touch with, can now share.  A song on Hands and Blessing can then be played. All stand in a circle and in a silent gesture of support each person opens their right hand to receive from the person on their right.  And then each person offers their left hand to give support and join the circle together with all hands linked.
Row.txt_description: Gives survivors the opportunity to draw and describe two hands: the hand of her abuser and what it means to her and her children, and her own hand, and what it means to her and her children.
