Row.txt_code:
Detail from Rose Rothwell’s “Love Flows From Peace Within”



About this Workshop
Thanks to a generous donation from Sakura, each Windows Program has been given an ample supply of Cray-Pas for the year.  Cray-Pas are oil pastels that can be used in many diverse and fabulous ways.  “Inner Lilies” is the first in a series of workshops AWBW has developed to assist your workshop participants in fully enjoying and exploring the Cray-Pas.  The technique used here is “scratchboard.”  This technique, using the Cray-Pas in this three-step process, can be used to draw anything: landscapes, families, doodles, flowers, etc.  The “Inner Lilies” idea is just one way of using this technique.  Enjoy, and feel free to use this technique in whatever ways you wish.  Please join us in experimenting and sharing new project ideas.

Objective:
To give each participant an opportunity to reach inward for a sense of internal calm, serenity, and beauty.  To explore and express an inner place of peace, through words and oil pastels, and to work with the oil pastels in a way that is surprisingly simple yet utterly satisfying in the beautiful possible effects.





“Love Flows From Peace Within”
Inner Lilies  drawing
Artist:  Rose Rothwell



Materials:
Newspapers for protecting table
Cra-Pas sets
Toothpicks, forks, paper clips, pen caps (for scraping)
White paper, cut into small (4.25”x4.25”) pieces
Relaxing music
Writing paper and pens

Timeframe:
70 mins—Total Time

Introduction:  5 min
Opening Circle:  10 min
Technical Demonstration/Warm-up:  10 min
Relaxation:  5 min
Creation:  30 min
Closing:  10 min

Introduction:
“This workshop is going to be a chance for each of us to explore our inner sense of calm and peace.  We’ll be working with Cra-Pas and with words to express this calm place.  It turns out that Cray-Pas are really wonderful for drawing lilies floating on water.  Here are some samples of how they can look (share your samples).  Believe it or not, it’s not that hard to create the beautiful effect of water.  So that’s how the ‘Inner Lilies’ workshop was born.







“To begin, let’s think together about our inner calm.  Is it possible to find the strength to have a calm, powerful perspective in the midst of very difficult situations?  Can you think of any examples?  

“There have been people who have been able to stay very strong in spirit in the midst of being imprisoned.  I think of Nelson Mandela, who was able to maintain his vision in the face of tremendous challenges and systematic injustice.  He maintained his clarity, didn’t lose his center, and was not destroyed by the mistreatment.  As a result of his inner vision, he was able to emerge from prison intact, able to walk out with the clarity to lead enormous changes.  

“Can you think of examples in your life of individuals who’ve been able to maintain calm in the midst of challenges?  How is it for you?  When things are hectic and challenging around you, do you let it take away your sense of inner calm and clarity?

“This workshop, ‘Inner Lilies,’ is a chance for us to look at the place of calm inside ourselves that we want to remember and grow and strengthen.” 

Opening Circle:
“Whom do you know in your life that has a strong sense of inner calm?
or:
What do you do to remember your inner calm place?
or:
What words do you tell yourself to remember your calm?”

Technical Info:
(Note:  If you think it would work better for your group, you could skip this section and just encourage participants to use the pastels in whichever ways they want to.  However, if it’s possible to show them this technique, they might be pleasantly surprised and proud of what they are able to create.)





Step 1: Creating a ground layer





Step 2: Adding a “water” layer





Step 3: Adding the lilies



“Today, we will be working with oil pastels.  We’re going to do a guided warm-up.  As we do the warm-up, I want you to remember that you can work with the pastels in any way you want to.  There is no wrong way to do it.  We are going to do a warm-up together just to give you a sense of one thing that’s possible.  We will be working with a technique where you can scratch lines through the pastels to get interesting effects.  I want to share this technique with you because it’s especially beautiful.” 

Distribute the materials, so everyone has a box of pastels, toothpicks, and some paper.

Step 1:
Creating a ground-layer:
“Cover your paper with stripes of light and bright colors across the page.  Be sure to put it on thick and solid, covering every bit of the page.  Note that this won’t be the color your drawing ends up in. It will be the color you will always be able to reveal when you scratch. It’s okay to peel the pastels, so the paper wrappers won’t get in the way.” (Demonstrate, and then give everyone time to do this step themselves)

Step 2:
Adding the water-layer:
Turn your paper, so the horizontal stripes become verticle. Select an overall water color and begin drawing stipes across the page (across the ground-layer stripes).  This can be a darker color, like deep blue, green, purple, etc.  It can also be light colors.  With your selected color(s), cover your paper with a second coat of pastel.  Be sure to do your pastel strokes against the grain of the ground-layer stripes. This will create the water effect.  (It also helps to move the pastels in one direction only instead of back and forth across the page.  Going in just one direction helps smear the under-layer of colors and create the sense of water.)  (Demonstrate, and then give everyone time to do this step themselves)




“Stars, vessels of light”
Inner Lilies drawing
Artist: Rose Rothwell




Step 3:
Adding the lily-layer:
“Now that you’ve got your water down, you can add your flowers.  Decide where you want them and what colors.  Press boldly to create a sense of each petal.  Go ahead and add the lily pads too.”

Here are three tips:
1. Work light to dark (light colors first, dark colors last.  No black until the end.)
2. Work in layers, mixing the colors right on the paper. (Go ahead and mix opposite colors, put red into the green, to make a beautiful, dark brown.)
3. Work large to small: (Do the broad areas first. Work your way down to the               details later.)”  (Demonstrate, and then give everyone time to do this step themselves)

Step 4:
Adding the scratches:





Step 4: Scratching in
the lily-petals





Step 4: Scratching in the words



“To create details and fine lines, you can scratch through to your ground color.  Use a toothpick, or whatever you want to scrape with.  You can create the shapes of the petals with these lines, or whatever you want to do. With the scratching technique, you can add any words about your ‘Inner Lilies.’” (Demonstrate, and then give everyone time to do this step themselves)

“Any questions?  Are you more comfortable with the pastels now? Are you ready to do our relaxation and create your ‘Inner Lilies?’  I will guide a visualization, and then when we are done, you can go ahead and create a drawing of your inner lily. You can use this technique we’ve practiced.  Do you remember what the four steps are?  (Have the group say them back to you)  Remember that you can use the Cray-Pas any way you want to.  There’s no wrong way.  Also, you can use as many pieces of paper as you want, so feel free to experiment and be free with your drawings.  Ready for the relaxation?”

Relaxation:
“Get yourself comfortable in your chair.  Take a deep breath, and let your eyes close.  As you breathe in, notice your body relaxing and sinking into your chair.  Take another deep breath and just let the chair hold you.  Imagine that you are sitting by a beautiful pond, peaceful and relaxing.  Take a deep breath and notice the cool, refreshing air.  As you sit by the side of the pool, notice that this is your own, peaceful, private place.  With each breath, notice you are safe.  Notice the reflections in the water, bits of color, greens, blues.  You can see pieces of the sky reflected in the water.  In some places, you can see beneath the surface of the water, the roots reaching down. Near you, notice a beautiful water lily, floating on the surface of the water.  As you look at it, you know this is your own lily, a reflection of the calm beauty deep inside of you.  Notice the shape of each petal, vibrant, and strong.  Notice the color of your lily, delicate, and fresh.  As you watch it, you feel a sense of peace emanating from the flower.  You can absorb its strength and beauty, almost like a smell.  Go ahead and breathe it in deeply.  As you take another deep breath, notice that this peace and strength and beauty belong to you.  Stay as long as you like with your inner lily.  When you are ready, open your eyes and begin to draw.” 

Creation:
Assist and encourage the participants as they create their drawings.  As they finish, encourage them to scratch words about their Inner Lilies into their drawings. 

Closing Circle: 
Welcome each participant to share her drawing and words.  Invite each one to share anything that she discovered or anything she wants to take with her from this workshop.




Inner Lilies sample
Row.txt_description: To give each participant an opportunity to reach inward for a sense of internal calm, serenity, and beauty. To explore and express an inner place of peace, through words and oil pastels.

Row.txt_code:
< /tr>


 “Affirmation Gems” created during Lynda Campbell’s
workshop.  These two gems say “Courage” and “Love.”
   
 Stepping Stones
“I made little stones with words that were set as a
goal for me to use in order to learn more about myself
and to empower me to be able to escape the mental
and emotional, sexual and physical abuse that I
endured my entire life.”
  
Lynda Campbell has been leading art workshops for four years as a part of Haven House’s wonderful team of Windows Leaders.  Here, she shares a very simple, powerful, workshop she has created.  She also shares one of the “tricks” that the Haven House leaders have discovered: that it works better to use colored Sculpey, than to try to find the time for painting the clay.  As a result, Lynda’s workshop can be accomplished fairly quickly, yet is wonderfully beautiful and satisfying for the participants.  See “Materials List” for where to order the colored Sculpey (it even comes in beautiful iridescent shades!)  Thanks, Lynda!

Objective:
To provide each participant with a beautiful, tangible tool to help her focus on affirming that which is positive and growth-promoting within herself.  These Affirmation Gems can be displayed in a bowl of her creation.  She may choose one “gem” daily to be carried as a reminder of a special ideal or goal on which she will concentrate.


 
 
 “Affirmation Gems” can be
formed into many shapes
  

Materials:
Sculpey in a variety of colors--(may be ordered from Artcraft, Inc.: (800) 262-1948)
Fine point, permanent ink “Hi Jell” metallic roller pen, or similar
Clear nail polish or other gloss finish, to glaze the art after being baked
Fishing line, yarn or thin ribbon (optional)
Round toothpicks or thick needle (optional)
Relaxing music

Setup:
Arrange the Sculpey and other materials in a convenient manner for the participants.  This is a very simple project, requiring few supplies and minimal set-up time.

Timeframe:
50 min: Total Time

Introduction:  5 min.   
Opening Circle: 10 min.
Relaxation:  5 min.
Demonstration: 5 min.
Creation: 10 min.
Closing Circle: 15 min.

 
 

 

“When I am working
on the art, I feel peaceful,
my worries go away
and in these moments
it helps me...”

“Affirmation Gems” created during
Lynda Campbell’s workshop.  These two
gems say “Faith” and “Strength.”
  
   
Introduction:
“As you contemplate your life; envision the traits, goals, plans and ideals you wish to focus on and incorporate into your life.  It is a good time to consider old, negative, ideas you have held about yourself and replace them with positive, growth-promoting ones.
This worshop is your opportunity to begin affirming those aspects of yourself which you value, as well as specific ideals toward which you would like to strive.”

Opening Circle:
“Share how you are feeling today and include a trait about yourself that you particularly value.”


 
 
 Sculpted Bowl to hold the “Affirmation Gems”
  

Demonstration:
Step 1:
Demonstrate the making of a “gem” using one or more Sculpey colors. Make each about the size of a large marble.  They can be formed into balls or other shapes (cylinders, squares, etc.).  Part of the “gem” should be of a light color for writing an affirming word, i.e., “clarity,” “peace,” “play.”  Use the fine point pen mentioned in “Materials” for this writing.  The inscription is made prior to baking.

Step 2:
Have an example of a small, pre-sculpted bowl ready (4”x5” wide); or demonstrate how to make one.  This bowl can be decorated and inside the bowl, a magical affirmation already written, i.e., “I am a woman of beauty and courage.”

Supply Distribution:
Make sure each woman has selected an assortment of Sculpey colors with which to work.

Relaxation:
Use your favorite relaxation. Here is a possible suggestion: “Inhale deeply while raising your arms, joining your hands together. Exhale and bring your arms down. Repeat this process three times. At the fourth deep inhalation, hold your breath for eight-to-ten seconds, then slowly exhale through your mouth, letting go of any tension you might have been holding in your body, your muscles, your head, even down to your toes. Picture very specific areas of stress and tension and one by one let them relax, letting go... Every time you inhale, breathe in the light, the energy within; every time you exhale, blow the negative or painful tension out.  Once you feel you have reached a place of peace of mind, a ‘recharge,’ you are ready to begin creating your affirmation gems.  Enjoy!”


 
 
 “Overcoming domestic violence was hard, but my piece has
‘phenomenal woman’ written in it.
 It’s part of my favorite poem by Maya Angelou. It reminds me
that no matter what everyone else thinks,
I am truly phenomenal.”
  

Creation:
“Now, let us begin forming our gems as we lovingly think about our strengths, as well as the personal goals we have set for our lives.”

Closing Circle: 
Encourage everyone to share what she has written on her “gems” and her reasons for doing so.

   



“Affirmation Gems” in a
variety of shapes
 Close-up of one of the bowls
Row.txt_description: Provides participants with a beautiful, tangible tool to help focus on affirming that which is positive and growth-promoting within themselves. The Affirmation Gems can be displayed in a bowl also created during the workshop.

Row.str_title: What My Bunny Ears Want to Hear
Row.str_author_firstname: AWBW Staff with contributions by Leslie Sanchez
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To build the children’s  self-esteem by thinking about positive things that have been said to them by different people in their lives. By creating bunny ears as reminders of the nice things about themselves, the children have the opportunity to notice that they are special and cared for.

  
 Roxanne modeling the Bunny Ears!
 
Materials:
Card stock, assorted colors
Clear tape
Glue sticks
Markers or crayons
Scissors
Bunny Ear Template (click here)

Time Frame:
Warm Up and Introduction: 15 minutes
Creation: 15 minutes
Closing: 15 minutes
Total Time: 45

Age Range:
3 to 12 year old

S
  
 Cutting out ears from the template
 
et Up:
You might want to take the time to pre-cut the bunny ears and head bands, especially if the children in your group are too young to cut out their own.

Warm Up (optional):
It would be fun to ask the children to stand up and form a line.  Then you can lead them in the Bunny Hop! Remember; put the children in a conga line. Start the music and then, it is 2 steps right, 2 steps left, 1 step right, 1 step left, 1 hop forward with both feet together, 1 hop backward with both feet together, 1 hop forward with both feet together, 3 hops forward with both feet together.  Repeat the steps, holding onto the person in front of you, until the music stops. Continue around the room! 

Introduction:
Why do you think bunny rabbits have such big ears? You are right, it is so they can hear better.  Today we are going to decorate bunny ears that have on them words of all the things we like to hear. For example, I love to hear my mom tell me that she loves me or that I did a good a job on something. Can you think of things people have said to you that make you feel good?

Opening Circle:
Have each child share one thing that some one has said to them that made them feel good.  If you have help it would be great for someone to take some notes of what each child shares to help them get started during the creation process.


 
 Gluing inner ear
 
  
 Special words we want to hear
 
  
 Making the headband
 
Creation:
Step One:
If you didn't have pre-cut ears have the children cut the ears shapes using the provided templates.

Step Two:
Glue the inner ear onto the outer ear.

Step Three:
When the children are done gluing you can ask them to pick up a marker they like and write on their bunny ear what they shared during the opening circle (if you or a helper wrote the words down you may want to go around the room and remind them what they said.) Have each child start to write some of those positive and kind words about themselves around the ears.

Next, they will write words of all the things they WANT to hear or that make them feel good, all around the Bunny Ears. Encourage them to decorate their headband in any way that makes them happy.

Step Four:
The children will need some help to measure the headband around their head.  It will take two strips of paper that can get taped together so it fits on their head.  You can fold and cut one piece of paper into three sections to easily measure the head band strips.

Step Five:
Glue or tape the ears to the headband. Remember if you use glue, the ears cannot be worn until the glue dries!

If you anticipate that the children will have a hard time coming up with lots of words for the things they like to hear, you may use the following questions to keep going around in circles and have the children say out load, then write their answer.
  • What is the nicest thing someone has ever said about you or to you?
  • What is your favorite thing a family member has said to you?
  • What are nice things you would like to hear someone say about you?
  • What is a nice thing you can say to the person next to you?
  • What is something that you like about yourself that you would like others to notice?
  • What is something nice that you would like to hear from your mom, teacher, friend or sibling? etc.
Closing Circle:
It is important for the children to actually hear those positive and kind words.  You can ask the older children to pair up and have them read to each other the words around the ears.  For the younger children, the leader can read the words to each child so they can hear the kind words.  The leader can also add something special for each child to hear.
Row.txt_description: To build the children’s self-esteem by thinking about positive things that have been said to them by different people in their lives. By creating bunny ears as reminders of the nice things about themselves, the children have the opportunity to notice that they are special and cared for.

Row.txt_code:
“Respect,” “Life,” and a butterfly are some of the
words and images which show how inspired the
“Mini-Art Display Clip” participants felt during
Martha Contreras’ workshop.



Objective:
To make a small clip which will hold a small piece of artwork that is a daily reminder of something positive, an encouraging message, or a picture that reminds you of something beautiful.





“Mini-Art Display Clip”
created during Martha
Contreras’ workshop.



Materials:
Wire (“Guy Wire,” 4 strand/20 gauge from Home Depot)
Wire cutters
Mini-alligator clips (Part #270-380A from Radio Shack)
Art paper cut into 3”x3” squares or rectangles
Super Sculpey
Ruler
Acrylic paint
Gold/Silver paint markers
Mod Podge
Toaster oven

Setup:
Arrange the Sculpey and other materials in a convenient manner for the participants.  This project takes time for the various steps so you may need to keep the opening circle brief.

Timeframe:
Two-hour workshop




“Mini-Art Display Clip” created
for AWBW.




Opening:
“Today we will be making something special to encourage us and remind us of the positive.  It’s a Mini-Art Display Clip, and you’ll get to make your own stand and piece of art for it to hold.  We’ll start with the stands right away.  That way we’ll have time to bake and paint them.  I’ll share some examples and we can dive in.”

Activity:
Make a cube (or any other free-standing shape) from the Super Sculpey. The cube dimensions should be about one inch on all sides.

Cut wire into three-inch pieces.
Place an “alligator clip” at one end of the piece of wire.
Insert the wire/clip into your Super Sculpey shape.
Bake for 10 minutes @ 250 degrees.






Close-up of a “Mini-Art Display Clip” base.

Mini-alligator clip




While Shape is Baking:
Decorate the art paper squares with any message, picture, poem, etc., that you would like to be able to see every day as a reminder.







Once shape is baked, and it has had a chance to cool off, paint it.  You can choose a solid color, then decorate it with designs made with the gold/silver markers, or paint each side of the cube with different colors. You may also inscribe words or pictures on the cube itself by using acrylic paint and a toothpick.

Place your art paper on the alligator clip and you are done!

Wait until the paint is thoroughly dry to add a coat of modge podge on it to protect the paint. You might want to have this process done the next meeting. It’s optional.

Closing Circle:  







Go around the circle and ask who would like to talk about their clip artwork. What does it mean to them? Why did they choose particular shapes and colors for their clip base and artwork?




Love shines through in
this mini-clip example.





“Mini-Art Display Clip” created
during Martha Contreras’
workshop.
Row.txt_description: Mini-art display clips act as special reminders of the positive. Participants make their own stand and piece of art for it to hold.

Row.txt_code:
Cray-Pas Scratchboard technique
  
For those of you who were not able to be at the “Windows into Our Future” workshop, June 17th, this Update will fill you in on this project and how to be a part of it.  We don’t want anyone to miss out!  We’ve included a master copy of the release form for you to duplicate and use.  In addition, we’ve enclosed an invitation sample.  The invitation includes exactly the same info as the release form.  It’s just presented in a more inviting way, so that it will be easier for you to share with family and friends.  Let us know if you need copies.

General Format: Windows into Our Future
Note about this Format:
The following format is intended to be used with a range of materials
and techniques.  In this Update, three possible techniques are offered. 
Three more will be coming in the next Update.  As always, feel free
to make up your own workshops too.

Objective:
To provide participants with an opportunity to create a “window” into their violence-free futures.  To take the time necessary for each person to envision what their future free of domestic violence would look like for them personally.  To create art pieces that represent each person’s personal commitment toward creating this future.

Timeframe:
Two-hour workshop

  


“Windows into Our Future” sample:
Cray-Pas with acrylic technique
 
  

Opening:
“As we move towards the year 2000, this is a transition for all of us.  Hopefully, for each of us, and for the whole world, this will be a transition into a future free of domestic violence.  Together, we have an opportunity to make this happen.  Many people are working toward it, and it takes all of us, as a community, to end the violence.  Together, our commitment makes a difference.

“This workshop will be an opportunity for each of us to create a piece of art that personally expresses our transition toward a violence-free future.  This project is called ‘Windows into Our Future.’ 

“We are each welcome to share our art to be included in an exhibit that will help raise community awareness and involvement in ending domestic violence.  To be part of the exhibit, each artwork must have a window somewhere in it.

“In addition to creating art yourself, you are also encouraged to ask others to join you in making a creative commitment to end the violence.  Everyone may submit a window: women, men, and children.  This also includes families, creating their art piece together.  This includes aunts, uncles, friends.  Use your imagination, and let’s enjoy creating windows into our future—together!”

Technical Demo:
Demonstrate the technique you will be using with the participants.  (See following information on several suggested techniques.)  Remember that it’s good to try the technique yourself as part of your workshop preparations, so that when you demonstrate for the group, it will be easy to be clear, brief, and inspiring.

Setup:
Before the relaxation, make sure all the needed supplies are distributed and/or selected by participants, so that after the relaxation, they’ll be able to dive right into their creative process.


 
 
 Cray-Pas Scratchboard technique
  

Relaxation:
With soft music playing, and everyone seated comfortably, encourage each participant to let her eyes close and take a deep breath.  Remember that you may need to adapt this relaxation a bit to apply to the technique you are using that day.  (For example: If the workshop is a writing workshop, gear the visualization toward picturing words, as well as colors.)

“Take a deep breath... and let it go...  Take another deep breath, and as you let it go, notice yourself sinking into your chair...  Notice the chair holding you, supporting you, as you relax...  Take another deep breath and feel your feet sinking into the floor.  Feel the floor gently holding your feet, so that you can rest...  Take another deep breath, and as you exhale, notice yourself relaxing even more, sinking into your chair, resting...  This is your time—just for you.  As you breathe deeply and relax, picture yourself sitting in a room...  Notice the colors around you in the room.  This is your present world, surrounding you.  Slowly, you begin to notice there’s a window in the room.  As you look out, you know this is a window into your future.  Notice the color coming in the window.  Notice it welcoming you, showing you the way toward your future.  Notice what it’s like in that world, free to be yourself...  free from domestic violence.  This is your window.  When you are ready, open your eyes and let that paper become your window into your future.”

Creation:
Start creating.  As always, relaxing music makes a tremendous difference.

Closing Circle: 
Encourage each participant to share about what she has created.  What did she discover in creating?  What does her window mean to her?


Cray-Pas on Writing


 
 
 Step 1: Free writing about the future
  
 
 Step 2: Adding the Cray-Pas over the writing
  
 
 Step 3: Scratching through with the back end
of a brush
  

Materials:
Newspaper for table
White paper or board (4”x4”)
Ball-point pens
Cray-Pas
Toothpicks

Step 1.
Writing:
“Write down any words that come to mind as you think about creating a
window into your future.  What do you want?  Fill the page with your
words or thoughts.  The words don’t have to be written in straight
lines across the page.  Fill the page with them however you wish.”

Step 2.
Cray-Pas
window drawing: “Draw a window right over your words.  If the Cray-Pas
are applied thinly, the words will show through.  However, don’t worry
about it, because  if some get covered up with thick Cray-Pas, you can
always scratch through to get them back (see next step).”  

Helpful
Hint: It’s good to work in light colors first, then add the darker
colors (light colors don’t show when they are applied on top of dark
colors).

Step 3.
Scratching:
“After you do the drawing, you can use a toothpick to scratch through
the Cray-Pas.  If you’ve covered words by mistake, don’t worry, you can
scratch through and they will show again.  You can scratch designs and
details into the Cray-Pas surface.”


Cray-Pas Scratchboard


 
 
 Step 1: Starting with the light color(s)
  
 
 Step 2: Adding the medium color(s)
  
 
 Step 2 cont.: Completing the window
  
 
 Step 3: Adding the cover layer
  

Materials:
White paper or board (4”x4”)
Cray-Pas
Toothpicks

Helpful
Hint: It’s good to work with light colors first and then add darker
colors.  The reason for this is that light colors don’t show up on top
of dark colors.  So, it’s useful to use a light color for the future, a
medium color for the present, and a darker color for the cover layer.  

Step 1.
Future
Drawing (light color): “Select a color for your future.  This is the
color that will appear through your window.  Go ahead and fill your
window with this color.”  (It’s fine to do this really roughly.  The
definition of the window will come from adding the next color.)

Step 2.
Present
Drawing (medium color): “Select a color for your present.  With this
color, draw the window frame and the inside of the room.”   (It’s fine
to be rough about this step too, because you’ll be covering it all up
with a dark color anyway!)

Step 3.
Cover
Layer (dark color): “Go ahead and cover the entire surface of the
drawing with darker color.  It takes an emotional plunge to cover up
your drawing.  If you want to save your drawing without adding the dark
color, that’s fine.  You may want to start a second window drawing that
you’d feel free to cover over.”  

Step 4.
Scratching
Through: “Now go ahead and scratch through the surface.  You can
scratch lines, stripes, entire areas of color.  You can also scratch
words into your window.  Feel free to fill the drawing with words about
the violence-free future you want to create for yourself.” 

  


Step 4: Scratching through the cover layer
 
  

















Cray-Pas with Acrylic

 
 
 Step 1: Starting with the light colors
  
 
 Step 1 continued: Adding the darker colors
  
 
 Step 1 continued: Completing the drawing
  
 
 Step 2: Covering with acrylic paint
  


Materials:
White paper or board (4”x4”)
Cray-Pas
Acrylic paints: gold or silver suggested other colors work well too
Toothpicks
Brushes
Cups of water to rinse
Paper towels

Step 1.
Window drawing: “Use the Cray-Pas to draw a window into your future.  What colors would you see through the window?  What colors would be on the inside of the window?” 
Helpful Hint: With Cray-Pas, it’s good to work in light colors first and then add the darker colors.  The reason for this is that light colors don’t show up on top of dark colors.

Step 2.
Acrylic Paint Layer:  “Cover your drawing with a layer of acrylic paint.  Have fun with it.  You can put the paint on thin so that you don’t loose your drawing.  You can use your brush to make a texture you like.”   

Step 3.
Scratching through: “With a toothpick, or with the back of your brush, you can scratch lines through the paint.  Feel free to add words, lines, designs, whatever you’d like in your window.”  
  


Step 3:  Scratching through the acrylic paint
Row.txt_description: Provides participants with an opportunity to create a "window" into their violence-free futures using Cray-Pas techniques. Participants take the time necessary for each to envision what their future free of domestic violence will look like for them personally.

Row.txt_code:
Butterfly Mosaic window by Amanda
 
  
The following are three additional projects suggested for use in the “Windows into Our Future” pr oject.  Remember that all materials and techniques are welcome.  You don’t have to stick to these.  We wanted to provide some simple approaches to the making of a window image that you might find inspiring and easy to share.






Mosaic Collage Windows
This is a “bare-bones” collage window-making process, with each
participant selecting just one image, and making it into a window
simply by cutting and gluing.

Materials:
Photo stock books, magazines
4”x4” Backing boards or papers
Construction paper (assorted colors)
Newspaper to cover table
Scissors
Glue sticks


 
 
 Step 1: Selecting an image
  
 
 Step 2: Cutting your image
  
 
 Remember to keep the pieces in order!
  

Step 1.
Selections:  “Select an image that represents your future.  First thoughts are fine.  Select a color of paper for the background.”

Step 2.
Cutting:  “Cut your image into the 4”x4” size.  Cut your background paper into the 4”x4” too.  Then go ahead and cut your image into pieces that represent the panes of glass in your window.  Be careful to keep the pieces in order, or else you’ve got a puzzle on your hands!”

Step 3.
Gluing:  “First, glue your background color to the 4”x4” board.  Then glue the window pieces to it, arranged as you wish to represent your window.”






 
 
 Step 1, 2: Selecting images
 
 Step 3: Tearing a window hole
 
 Step 3 cont.: Making the hole fit the image
 
 Step 4:  Optional—water/glue mixture
 
 Step 4 (cont.): Applying the water/glue
mixture to the image
 
 Step 4 (cont.):  Applying the tissue
 
 Step 4 (cont.):  Adding more water/glue
 
 Step 4 (cont.):  Poking through the tissue
 
 Step 5: Putting the layers together
  

Collage Window with Tissue
This workshop provides a second “bare-bones” collage window-making process, with each participant selecting just two images, and collaging them into a simple window.  This one requires a bit more as far as mess and complications.  However, the results can be quite beautiful!

Materials:
Photo stock books, magazines
Tissue paper - assorted colors
Water/glue mixture (half and half)
Brushes
Paper towels
Newspaper to cover table
Scissors
Glue Sticks
4”x4” thick paper or board for backing
Optional: Paints and brushes, or metallic pens

Step 1.
Selecting image(s) for the present: “This will be the image covering the page.  For this reason, it must be large enough to cover your 4”x4” page.”

Step 2.
Selecting image(s) for the future: “This will be what appears through the window hole.  For this reason, it must be smaller than the image you picked for the present.” 

Step 3.
Tearing window hole in present image:  “Decide where, in your ‘present’ image you’d like the window hole to appear.  If you wish to cut into the middle of your image, you can tear your window hole, or cut it.  You can make it any size or shape you wish.  Keep in mind the ‘future’ image you will have showing through it, and how much of that image you want showing through.  That will help determine the size of your window hole.”

Step 4.
Optional Tissue: “To give a wonderful depth to the collage, you can apply tissue paper over the ‘present’ image.  This gives a distance between the present and future images, and makes the future image the clear focus of the piece.  To use the tissue paper, select a color, and cut it out to fit the size of your entire ‘present’ window.  Apply water-glue to the face of your entire ‘present’ image.  Lay tissue paper on it (this will temporarily cover your window hole).  If you like the interesting patterns created by the tissue, leave them.  If you want the tissue smooth, apply a layer of water-glue over the surface of the tissue.  To bring back the hole, apply water-glue to the tissue covering the hole.  This will help to dissolve it, so you can break through the membrane to clear the window. Leave the tattered edges, or fold them over the edge to make it smooth as you wish.” 

Step 5.
Gluing layers together:  “Once you have your present layer and window ready, it’s time to put all the layers together.  Decide how you want your future appearing through the window.  Use tape on the back to fix it in the desired position.  Then apply glue stick to the entire surface of your 4”x4” back board.  Press your image on.”

Optional Additions.
Optional additions:  Use metallic pens or paints to add final touches, such as a window frame, or words, etc.

  


Finished Sample: Collage Window with Tissue
 
  
































Cray-Pas over Windows

Materials:
Copies of windows
Cray-Pas
Toothpicks
4”x4” boards
Glue sticks

  


Step 1—3: Selecting copy window image and covering it with Cray-Pas
 
  
Step 1.
Selecting window image: “Choose a copy of a window that appeals to you for your future window. Remember that you will be using only a 4”x4” section of the image.”

Step 2.
Attaching to 4”x4” Board:  “Decide which 4”x4” section of the image you want.  Do you want your window in the middle?  Do you want it going off the edge?  Attach the copy to your board, and trim as necessary.

Step 3.
Coloring with Cray-Pas: “Go ahead and cover your window with color.  Feel free to blend and change the image as you wish.  Remember that Cray-Pas work best from light to dark.  It’s difficult to put light colors on top of dark ones, so you’ll want to put all the light colors on first, and then work your way to the darker colors.” 

Step 4.
Scratch into the image as desired:  “You may, at any time, scratch through the CrayPas with a toothpick, or fork, or other tool.  By scratching, you may be able to retrieve the covered copy image where you wish.” 

   



Step 4: Scratching  through
 You can always add more Cray-Pas
   


   



Finished Sample: Cray-Pas over copy
Row.txt_description: Provides participants with an opportunity to create a "window" into their violence-free futures using three more Cray-Pas techniques. Participants take the time necessary for each to envision what their future free of domestic violence will look like for them personally.

Row.txt_code:
Suzy Karcher Rogers
  

I'm a painter, and a survivor of domestic violence.  I've been running weekly workshops in a shelter in Columbus Ohio for a couple years now.  The workshops I lead usually have a spiritual overtone.  I believe art can be a spiritual endeavor, and that painting, drawing, writing, and other creative forms can bring us closer to God.  I've introduced this meditation focus workshop to the women in Columbus a few times, and it's been well accepted, so I wanted to share it with you also.

Workshop Objective:
To give participants and ourselves an experience of how art and spirituality can go hand in hand.  I've tried to bring the concept of God and art together in this workshop.  I study many religions, so I've tried to present this in a nondenominational way.  The goal of this art is to spend time thinking about uplifting qualities (spiritual qualities) that we want to become more in tune with.

Materials:
Card stock in light/bright colors
(packs of assorted colored card stock can be purchased in most office supply stores)
Scissors
Glue sticks
Oil pastels or acrylic paint
Optional - scrap book cut outs (these are available in craft stores, and they're basically just pre-cut colorful shapes)
Notebook paper
Pens
Tape player
Relaxing music


 
 
 Leaf Mandala: Meditation Focus Painting
  

Note to Facilitator:
The participants may not use all these mediums, but it's nice to have different supplies available so they can make their focus art in a way that's comfortable for them.  Example: some participants would rather make a collage with the various papers than use paint.

Technical Information:
I like to give the group a lot of space to create their art however they want, but for anyone who's not real comfortable just picking up supplies and beginning, I would suggest.

Step 1.
Pick out a color of card stock, and place note paper and pen beside that to write thoughts while you work on your focus.

Step 2.
Pick out one or more colored cut-outs, and use glue stick to attach these to the card stock.

Step 3.
On top of this we could layer oil sticks, add more cut-outs, scratch into the oil sticks (Cray-Pas), write into the oil stick with pencil—it makes a very nice dark line.

There so many ways to use these mediums. I would just remind the women that what we learn about ourselves during the process is as important and enjoyable as the finished piece. Have Fun!

Opening Circle:
“Today we will be making meditation focus art.  What's that?  In this instance we'll be making an image, using colors and shapes that make you feel peaceful, free, protected, happy, or any other quality you wish to strive toward.  A focus is a reminder of something.  One of the most famous examples of this type of art is the Statue of Liberty.  I had a chance to visit the statue this summer, and was able to see what a powerful focus it is for freedom and liberty.  There are so many ways to make a type of focus art, and I invite you to use any of the supplies we have here to make your piece any way you want, but here's a suggestion of one way to begin.  Think of a quality that you want for yourself (we'll say wholeness, for example) and imagine what color that idea is.  What shape is it?  To me it's a circle, so I would start with my circle of the color I imagined, and go from there.  This is a time to explore the quality you want.  Perhaps you spend your time here thinking about it while you paint, or maybe you write pages about it and make your focus out of these.  However you wish to investigate the quality you want is fine.  Your piece will be a record of your thoughts on the subject, and every time you look at your focus art you'll be reminded of a quality you’re striving for.”

The following is a prayer.  I sometimes include its reading as part of our meditation.  Do so if you feel comfortable with that, or maybe it could be a handout for the participants to read on their own.

 
 
 I AM LIGHT
by Kuthumi

I AM Light, glowing Light
Radiating Light, intensified Light
God consumes my darkness,
Transmuting it into light

This day I AM a focus of the Central Sun
Flowing through me is a crystal river
A living fountain of Light
That can never be qualified
By human thought or feeling
I AM a outpost of the divine
Such darkness that has used me is swallowed up
By the mighty river of Light which I AM

I AM I AM I AM Light
I live I live I live in Light
I AM Light’s fullest dimension
I AM Light’s purest intention
I AM Light Light Light
Flooding the world everywhere I move
Blessing, strengthening, and conveying
The purpose of the kingdom of heaven

Summit University Press  P.O. Box 5000  Corwin Springs MT 59030
  

Note to Facilitator:
The following is a list of qualities I pass out to the participants, and together in a discussion we make the list longer.  It also serves as ideas for anyone who can't think of anything at the moment.

Qualities
security prosperity
freedom calmness wisdom
ability to make wise choices in life protected peaceful centered assertive patient abundance happy light-hearted

Meditation/Relaxation:
“Take a deep breath, and try to imagine a calm place where your heart is. Concentrate on your heart, and take a deep breath for your heart.  For one moment think about the other people in this room. Imagine that you wish them the best. Imagine that they wish you the best. Imagine light comes down into the room. This light is from God or your higher self. You can breathe it in.  With it you feel calm and protected.  Imagine the colors that make you feel calm and peaceful.  Look at these colors and what shapes they are. Think about what colors make you feel happy, light hearted, comfortable protected, or any quality you want for yourself.  Think about these colors as light coming down from above.  They wash over you and you can breathe them in.  Take all the time you want to imagine these colors, and what they stand for.  Whenever you are ready, slowly bring yourself back to the room, open your eyes, and create your focus painting that represents what you just envisioned.”
  


Heart: Meditation Focus Painting
 
  

Closing Circle:
Give each participant a chance to show her art and talk about it.  I've found that the closing circle can be a very enjoyable and important part of this workshop.  If I'm able, I arrange a comfortable space for the workshop in the beginning.  Lately we've been running them outside in a play area with picnic tables.  The participants are not in a big hurry to leave, so we're able to have some good discussions.  I think this workshop lends itself to having long talks afterwards of what we have discovered during it.  I pass out a book list, and Survivors Art Circle flyers, and tell them some about AWBW.  It lets them know that there are people who care how they are doing even after they leave the shelter.

  


Sun and Window: Meditation Focus Painting
Row.txt_description: Gives participants an experience of how art and spirituality can go hand in hand and time to think about uplifting qualities that we want to become more in tune with. The end product acts as a visual focus for meditation.

Row.txt_code:
This wonderful workshop was shared at the Leader’s Retreat in August.
As part of our closing circle, we even wrote appreciations and wishes to each other and placed them in the jars. That way, we each took with us a pot of happy surprises to treasure and carry with us.

Our d eepest thanks to Diane and Sylvia for sharing such an inspiring, fun, and rewarding workshop.

   

“Anchor”Happy Jar created at Retreat
(left)

Happy Jar created by Diane and Sylvia
(right)

   
Workshop Objective:
To provide participants with memories of what make - them happy. A Happy Jar is a positive tool that can be used to reaffirm their strength and faith within themselves.

Materials:
Newspaper to cover tables
Baby food jars (Note: Tennis ball cans can be a nice alternative. The labels pull off easily and they can be decorated using the same techniques as the jars)

Tissue Patchwork supplies:

 
 
 Baby food jars ready to become Happy Jars.
  
20% water / 80% white glue - mix together
Colored tissue paper (pre-torn)
Crayons (to add after paper is dry)

Painting supplies:
Puffy paints, assorted colors
Brushes and containers for water
Paint palettes or paper plates

Colored paper and ball-point pens
(for happy thoughts to go in the jars)
Relaxing music

Timeframe:
Total Time: 55 minutes
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 5 minutes
Relaxation: 5 minutes
Demonstration: 5 minutes
Creation: 20-25 minutes
Closing Circle: 10 minutes


  


Leader, Cheryl Davis shares her
Happy Jar at Retreat.
 
  
Setup/Preparation:
Make a sample in advance. Experiment with both the tissue paper technique and the painting to see which will be better for your group. Clean the baby food jars and remove any excess glue or paper left from the label. If you decided on Tissue Patchwork, tear the tissue paper into small scraps. Make the water and glue mixture by mixing 20% water with 80% glue. A paint palette works best but make sure the palettes are soaked in warm water after use. Cover the art area with newspaper and set the supplies around the table. Depending on the number of participants, you may want to have more than one container of the water/glue mixture to go around. If you know the group well enough, prepare a happy thought about each woman to put into their Happy Jar!

Introduction:
“Happy Jars are a place to keep any special thoughts or words that have gotten you through hard times as survivors of domestic violence. Your Happy Jar can be placed on your dresser or carried in your purse, so you can be reminded of your ‘happy thoughts’ and goals throughout your day.”

Opening Circle:
“Picture yourself moving forward in the life you want ahead of you. Envision the happy times you are experiencing in your new life. Are there any particular words or phrases that keep you on track?” (Encourage them to each share their thoughts.)


 
 
 Painted jar.
  
 
 Tissue Patchwork jar with crayon added
after the tissue dried.
  

Demonstration:
Step 1.
The first step is choosing the jar you'll be using to create and keep happy memories.

Step 2.
The second step is to decorate your jar and lid. (Have your example of a Happy Jar to demonstrate how the technique was done. Share the Tissue Patchwork or Puffy Painting technique. Encourage the women to experiment and come up with their own ways of decorating their jars.)

Step 3.
Lastly, pick a piece of blank paper to write your thoughts, goals and inspirational words (colored paper looks best). Such as: “Beautiful sunny days," and/or “Tears are like a river, they can carry us forward.” What are some of your words or thoughts that keep you focused and confident throughout your day?

If time allows, encourage the women to write happy thoughts for each other and place them into each jar.

Closing Circle:
Give each participant a chance to share her Happy Jar and what it means to her.

Retreat Additions:
At the Leader’s Retreat, we had a few other supplies. It works well to share the various techniques and have participants select the supplies they want to use.

  


Sample jar with yarn on the lid.
 
  

 
Sculpey-covered lid.
 
  

Yarn on Lid: Yarn can be applied to the lid in a spiral. (Note: This can get a little frustrating when/if the yarn gets full of glue and starts sticking to fingers instead of the lid.)

Colored Sculpey Clay: Sculpey can be pressed onto the lid, covering it with 3-dimensional designs. The entire lid can then be cooked to harden the clay.
Row.txt_description: Happy Jars are positive tools than can be used to reaffirm the strength and faith within each individual.

Row.txt_code:
Catherine Marcotte, Community Solutions



Personal Statement:
Over a year ago I shared a vision that I had with my supervisor.  My fantasy was to facilitate creativity groups for women.  At the time I was working full time as a therapist exclusively with women who were victims of domestic violence.  I was also, at this time involved in my own journey of self discovery and was fighting burn-out from working with this population.  I was searching for a way to revitalize myself, reconnect with the passion I used to feel.

In a display of wonderful synchronicity, my supervisor described the presentation she had seen of "window between worlds" at a conference in Sacramento.

I now facilitate two groups per week; one in the shelter for residents, and one at the main office for victims of domestic violence who are not in shelter.

Although there are still many kinks to work out and we continue to problem solve and restructure things, I have enjoyed these groups very much. I not only enjoy creating the time and space for participants to explore their inner world, but I also enjoy using that time to explore my own creativity.





“Our Wishes...” on butcher paper



I am constantly amazed at the way in which art can express the inexpressible, how it can bypass analysis, and how deeply revealing and healing this forum can be.  

Some of the most challenging aspects of facilitating these groups have had more to do with logistics than with art. This workshop was one of the ways I attempted to address some of these issues.

Workshop Objective:
We found that in the beginning of providing these workshops in the shelter, there was very little "buy in" from shelter staff and therefore, residents. Several times we would arrive and there would be no residents there at the shelter to participate in group. On one of these occasions I decided that I needed to try something different. I wanted something which involved shelter staff and left a message to residents that they had missed something fun, as well as bring creative force and expression to the shelter.





Unrolling butcher
paper



Murals can be powerful tools to embody collaboration and strengthen a sense of community and common purpose, as well as individual vision. All of the above were objectives for this workshop.

Materials:
Long length of butcher paper; (you may need to tape several lengths together to make it wide enough as well as long.)
Tape
Felt tip markers (especially ones with thick tips)
Pastels (optional: kind of messy, and lessens the durability of mural, but fun for some.)

Introduction:
(This is for shelter staff as well as residents.  Write across the top of paper "Our Wishes for Women and Children in Shelter.")




Drawing on Butcher Paper




“This is a time to express your wishes for yourselves if you are residents, and for the residents if you work here. Any wishes, big or small for anyone here are important. Let yourself have fun. There is no right or wrong way to do this. You may use symbols, words, etc. If you are uncomfortable drawing specific images, you may draw borders around the paper. Have fun!! If you use symbols, consider writing words underneath for what it represents. You may use whatever language you are comfortable using. The most important thing is to have fun with your creation.”

Setup:
We set up the paper in the hallway near the bedrooms. We hang the paper on the wall with tape, out of the reach of the children. (We put another paper down there for them.)

We set up some chairs at various stages along the mural and set materials on those.

Activity:
Let participants move to a part of the mural and begin drawing what ever they wish. They may start out small and reserved, but our group warmed up very quickly and didn't want to stop!

Allow writing to be bilingual if possible. Model for them with your own creations on the paper. Encourage them to "Take up space."

Borders around the outside edges creates unity in the mural. Provide encouragement as people participate, (This activity is fairly interactive) Nice colors! Great wish! Beautiful poem! Etc. Be positive.
We left the mural on the wall for residents who were not there to see. We also left an invitation for them to share their own wishes on the mural and a flyer about the group.

Closing:
Have all participants share what they liked about the activity, the art they created, their own process. If possible give each person a chance to speak.

Note: We now have a beautiful mural to use at-various functions with the work of many hands united in one common vision.
Row.txt_description: Encourages participation in, and support of, art workshops by shelter staff and clients through the creation of a group art project focusing on wishes.

Row.txt_code:
“Wishes for the Holiday Season” card
 
  
  
Thanks goes to Rose Rothwell for suggesting this workshop.  

Workshop Objective:
To provide an opportunity for the participants to explore and express their own personal, positive perspective for the holiday season by choosing their own message of inspiration, and creating holiday cards which reflect this message.   

Materials:
White card stock, cut to sizes appropriate for cards
Masking tape
Cray-Pas
Toothpicks
Relaxing music

Timeframe:
Total Time:    70 minutes


 
 
 “Wishes for Warmth and Joy” card
  

10 min        Opening Circle
10 min        Demonstration
40 min        Creation Time
10 min        Closing Circle

About Holiday Diversity:
To effectively address holiday issues, it is important to be aware of the cultural and religious backgrounds of those in your group.  You may need to work on this ahead of time to find out who celebrates Chanukah, Kwanzaa, Christmas, etc.  If there is someone in your group who is in the minority in terms of what they celebrate, it can help if you do some research into the meaning of their traditions and share a bit with the group.  This can be wonderful for the whole group.  (However, don’t put them on the spot by asking them to be the one to explain to their traditions in front of the group, unless you know they wish to do so.)

Opening Circle:
“Share how you are feeling about the holiday season right now, and share one inspirational thought or personal perspective that you’d like to keep in mind during this season.”  It’s important to encourage sharing of the difficult feelings that participants may be going through in relation to the holidays.  By sharing the tough stuff, they can begin to work it through to a more positive perspective.


 
 
 Cray-Pas workshop participant, scratching
through the layers.
  

Demonstration:
Demonstrate the steps of the card making, to help inspire a comfort with the materials.  As you demonstrate, be sure to stress that each participant can use the supplies however she wants.  There is no right or wrong.  Let them know they can experiment and make many cards, to get a feel for working with the Cray-Pas.

Step 1: Taping
“Fold your paper into a card, and tape the edges to the table.  This will create a crisp border around your image and give it a ‘professional’ look.”  

   



Step 1
 Step 2
   
Step 2: Light Colors
“Add a layer of light colors.  These will be the colors underneath your drawing—the colors you will be able to find when you scratch through your drawing with a toothpick!”   

Step 3: Darker Colors
“Next, add a layer of darker colors.  Add whatever colors you need, to create your drawing.  Just remember to work light to dark.  It’s hard to put light colors over dark ones.”

   



Step 3
 Step 3 - completely covered
   
Step 4: Scratching
“Next, you get to scratch through the darker colors to reveal the light ones underneath.  You can create all kinds of beautiful detail with your scratching.”    
   



Step 4
 Step 5
   
Step 5: Remove Tape
“When you are ready, gently remove the tape.  If you pull too quickly, it may tear the paper, so be careful!   

Step 6: Borders
“After you remove the tape, you may wish to draw designs into the border.  Enjoy!”  
   



Step 6
 Step 7
   
Step 7: Your Message
“When your image is complete, decide where you would like to place your message.  Would you like to put the words inside the card?  Or would you like to use a toothpick to scratch them into the surface of your image?  Add them wherever you wish.”  

Creation:
After the demonstration, welcome everyone to begin their cards.  Remind them that they get to just “play around” with the colors.  They can experiment with the Cray-Pas and make as many cards as they wish.  If anyone is hesitant to begin, encourage them to start with a “warm-up” card—one where they just try to make a “mess.”  Sometimes making messes leads to the very best discoveries.  

Closing:
Have all participants share what they created, and what they want to remember to take with them into the holiday season.
Row.txt_description: Provides an opportunity for participants to explore and express their own personal, positive perspective for the holiday season by choosing their own message of inspiration, and creating holiday cards which reflect this message.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Adapt for Children and Teens.

Row.str_title: Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow/Growing Step by Step
Row.txt_code:
Workshop Objective:
To allow each participant a chance to begin to heal and release negative feelings from the past, celebrate the present and look forward to the future, by creating an image of yesterday, today, and tomorrow.





Past, anonymous artist





Present, anonymous artist





Future, anonymous artist



Materials:
Photo stock books
Chalk pastels
6”X6” squares of construction paper
Masking tape
Pens
Hairspray, or Fixit spray fixative
Scissors
Glue sticks
Relaxing music

Timeframe:
Total Time:    70 minutes

10 min        Opening Circle
10 min        Demonstration + Relaxation
40 min        Creation Time
10 min        Closing Circle

Introduction:
“As we grow in our lives, even difficult situations can be our teachers and help to make us into the strong, patient, wise people that we are.  Today, we will try an exercise designed to give us a chance to let go of any negative feelings from the past, look at the present, and celebrate the things that the future holds.  To do this, we will be making one picture for yesterday, one for today, and one for tomorrow.”

Note:
You can think about yesterday, today, and tomorrow in any way you wish.  Yesterday could be a memory from long ago, or it could be literally yesterday... however each participant wants to take it.

Opening Circle:
“For our opening circle, share one way in which you notice that you’re growing.  If that’s hard to think of, think of one way that you would like to grow.  Take a moment to think about it.  I know each of us is growing in many wonderful ways, even though it’s sometimes hard to notice.  Let’s give ourselves some time to notice.  Who would like to go first?”




Past, artist: Dede Douglas




Present, artist: Dede Douglas





Future, artist: Dede Douglas




Warning:
For participants in Outreach Programs, the present may feel very difficult to look at, because of the current challenges they are facing.  Be prepared for this.  For outreach participants, it may be especially important to be able to break the present down into yesterday, today and tomorrow.  Likewise, for some it may be difficult to think far into the past.  If looking at their lives this way (yesterday, today, and tomorrow) seems too problematic, see the variation at the end of this workshop.  

Demonstration:
(You might want to do the relaxation before the demonstration.  Choose whatever order you think will flow best.)  “I will demonstrate the steps for this project.  You can do it however you like.  These are just suggestions.”

Step 1:
“Take three 6”X6” squares and tape a border for each.  Label the first one ‘yesterday,’ the second one ‘today,’ and the third one, ‘tomorrow.’”  

Step 2:
“For each of your three squares, use the pastels to create a background that would best portray your feelings for that particular time in your life.  Try blending as many colors as possible.  Select colors that would best depict your feelings.  Spray pastels with Fixit, or hairspray to stabilize the colors and create a glossier finish.”     

Step 3:
“For each of your squares, find pictures that make a bold statement to best depict your innermost feelings at that particular time.”

Step 4:
“On each of your squares, arrange and glue the pictures to include your background colors.”

Step 5:
“Write something for each picture to express your reasons for selecting the pictures and colors you did.”  

Relaxation:
(from Lucy Rizo)  “Let’s all take a deep breath in and let all the air out with a very long breath (a couple of times).  Let’s all stand straight up and relax our shoulders (shake and roll your shoulders a couple of times).  Now let’s bend at the waist and just let our heads hang off the ends of our bodies.  That’s good.  Feel your head hanging there.  And now let’s stand up straight again.  Now imagine that all of our feelings and thoughts will be taken care of by our drawings in this hour.  Our drawings can feel and speak for us.”  

Creation:
“Now go ahead and create your yesterday, today, and tomorrow.  Let me know if you have any questions as you go.”

Closing:
“Share your yesterday, today and tomorrow.  Is there anything new you discovered during this workshop?  Anything you noticed about how you’ve grown or how you want to grow?
Row.txt_description: Allows a chance to begin healing, release negative feelings from the past, celebrate the present, and look forward to the future, by creating an image of yesterday, today, and tomorrow.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create version for Teens.

Row.txt_code:
Cora Ramirez attended our most recent Windows Leadership Training, and shared this project idea with the rest of the group.

Kori Taylor, who was there, has already used this project extensively.  In the Leader to Leader column (this page), she shares her experiences with “The Mask of Survival.”

We are very excited to be able to share Cora’s project with all the women’s leaders.
Thanks Cora!

Workshop Objective:
To give each participant an opportunity to let go of the past and reconnect with her true self, a survivor.  The Sculptamold will act as a visual reminder of her ability to create life.

Materials:
Newspaper for protecting surface of table and for the mold
Sculptamold 3 lb (1 bag for every 3 clients)
Deep bowls—plastic or glass (Sculptamold will wash off)
Container with water

 
 
 
 
  

Relaxing music
Writing paper and pens

Optional: (If you want to mount masks with stories, see page 4.) 
Dark mat boards
Liquid Paper pens
Elmer’s Multi-Purpose Glue

Timeframe:
Total Time:    1 hr, 40 minutes

5 min        Introduction
10 min        Opening Circle
10 min        Technical Demonstration
5 min        Relaxation
50 min        Creation Time
10 min        Timed Writing
10 min        Closing Circle

Note: The Mask Making process can bring up powerful emotions.  If you choose to lead this workshop be sure to allow time for adequate sharing, support, and follow-up as needed.

Introduction:
This workshop is an opportunity to let go of a piece of the past. This will be done by letting go of that which you are not, that which is a victim. The purpose of this project is to help survivors rediscover their identity. When a person is caught in an abusive situation a sense of self is lost—slowly but surely she ventures down a path of chaos and confusion. She will alter herself in order to avoid conflict, or simply to be loved.  She will cease to share her opinions or thoughts because they are only criticized and degraded. Hence, a loss of self.  When a person decides to leave an abusive situation, she has decided to stop being a victim. When she arrives at the shelter she finds herself with a sudden case of amnesia.  She has no recollection of who she is, what she wants, or what she likes.  She stopped thinking of her wants a long time ago.  The purpose of these masks is not to make her dwell in the past, but to help her let go and reconnect with her new identity as a survivor and to experience her intrinsic power to create.

  



 

  

Opening Circle:
“To love is to give, but how much does one give? Does it mean to give oneself entirely or only partly?  When did you begin to lose yourself in love?  What happened to make you decide to search for yourself?”

Technical Demonstration:
It is recommended that group leaders experiment with Sculptamold before facilitating a group so that you know what to expect. At first, the consistency should be like cottage cheese.  As time passes it will dry and harden slowly, making it easier to shape. Of course, once it dries it hardens and adding water will not soften it up again, but more Sculptamold can be mixed and added to the dry mask.  Therefore, it might be a good idea to mix a little at a time so you don’t end up wasting much Sculptamold.

Step 1:
Prepare Sculptamold when participants are ready to begin.

Step 2:
Make a ball with a piece of newspaper; sizes will vary depending on how big the client
wants her mask.

Step 3:
Begin to layer the newspaper ball with Sculptamold, adding to it until half the ball is
covered—There is no need to make it too thick. When you feel ready, just begin sculpting
the facial features.

Step 4:
When the masks are finished, you will want to place them somewhere safe to dry for at least a day. The next day they will need to be baked in the oven so they don't mold. (See
instructions on bag).

Timed Writing:
Once they have finished creating their masks have participants write what they feel as they look at their masks.  Encourage them to take a deep look inside and write about how they feel now that they have finally taken it off.

Closing Circle:
Each participant is welcome to share her experience.

Additions:
Have them mat their masks, after they are completely dry—which is by the following week.  Masks can be glued on the mat board with Elmer's Multi-Purpose Glue.  Aflerward, they can transfer on to the mat board what they wrote the day they worked on their masks. 

For this, you will need the mat boards (black looks good), glue, and opaque pens that will show up on the mat boards.  Liquid Paper pens work well.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants an opportunity to let go of a piece of the past and reconnect with her true self, which is that of a survivor. With the use of Sculptamold participants have a visual reminder of their ability to create life.

Row.txt_code:
Oftentimes I watch the women who come into our shelter and they are extremely frightened and stressed.  Many of them are so close to the breaking point emotionally that adding one more task to their "plate" can be the weight that breaks it. Immediately, they are faced with the need to "be strong" for their children, appointments to keep, looking for housing, work, etc. I often find myself repeating the words: "Yes, it's important, for your future, to accomplish all of these "tasks," but it is just as important, maybe even more so at this time, to really pay attention to how you are feeling.  Take the time, everyday, to allow yourself to "feel the sadness, the pain, etc., of your situation."

Workshop Objective:
This workshop was structured to help participants focus on the feelings they are experiencing in this very difficult and frightening time of leaving their abusive partners.





“The Coldest Day” by Kori Taylor



Materials:
Cray-Pas   
Heavy white drawing paper (cut to size) approximately 6x6
Practice paper (for Cray-Pas practice)   
Writing paper   
Pens/gel pens   
Mat boards (different colors) approx. 8”x10”   
Glue sticks   
Tooth picks   
Paper clips   
Plastic forks, spoons and knives
Musical tapes or CDs:
1. Instrumental relaxing music
2. (Optional) “As Bad As it Gets,” by artist Christine Lavin, from her CD entitled “Shining My Flashlight on the Moon.”

Timeframe:
Total Time:    2 hrs
10 min        Check-in
5 min        Relaxation
10 min        Technical
5 min        Playing the song
60 min        Creating
30 min        Discussion

Step 1: Check-In
I usually begin by introducing AWBW, and what it means to me, personally, to be able to share this process with them.  I share how important I think it is for all of us to have this “window” of time for ourselves.  Then we have a circle, with each person introducing herself, and sharing how she feels about doing the art workshop.  When difficult feelings are shared, (for example “I hate art,” “I was never good at it,” “Making art brought up such strong feelings last week, I’m scared”), I welcome these feelings, and encourage her to share more about them.  After everyone has “checked in” we are ready to begin.




Close-up of gel pens on
dark mat board






Step 2: Relaxation
(Choose relaxing music with no lyrics.)  I ask them to get comfortable and to breathe deeply in and out. To focus on the music  they are hearing and to let it take away the stresses of their day.  I ask for them to consciously make an effort to set aside all of their worries (e.g., finding a job, housing, appointments, etc.)  To let this be their opportunity to experience their feelings.  To focus solely on the feelings they are experiencing in their life at this moment.  The kids are taken care of, there is nothing they need to do for the next two hours, so they can allow themselves to focus on the moment.  They can take advantage of this time to devote to themselves and their healing.

Step 3: Technical
I give each participant a small piece of white paper to practice on.  I then demonstrate layering the Cray-Pas. First layer, the lighter colors, second layer, the darker colors, and then one final layer of black or a dark color of their choice.  As I am demonstrating I have them follow along with their practice paper.  I then have them use various objects that I have collected for them to scratch away at the surface colors to get to the brighter colors below.  I tell them that they can do this with a design/designs or a picture.





Close-up: scratching with forks to make grass



Step 4: Playing the Song
(Optional: “As Bad As It Gets” by Christine Lavin.)  I once again have them get comfortable and practice their deep breathing.  Before I start the song, I ask them to focus on the music and the words of the song, to let it speak to them each individually.  I then play the song.

Step 5: Creating
Start the first layer with light and bright colors. This layer will represent their future.  I then have them turn their work and add a second layer of dark colors.  This layer will represent their feelings of being in a violent relationship.  For the third and final layer I ask them to use black (or another very dark color of their choice).  This layer represents "The Coldest Day," representing what incident brought them to the shelter and/or just having to be at the shelter—what that means for them.

I then ask them to use whatever tools they would like to scratch away at the "surface" to get to their "future" layer below. This scratching away can be in the form of a picture or a design of their choice. I talk to them about how this "scratching away" represents the work they are doing, emotionally and physically, while they are at the shelter, and in the process of getting free of their violent relationship.

We then mount their work on a mat board, the color of their choice. Using gel pens I have them title their work and write how they felt while creating.

Step 6: Discussion
Completing the process with plenty of time for participants to share their experience is very important.  It is the final step in the healing journey of this workshop.

This has been an incredibly powerful workshop.  It seems that no matter where the participants are "at" when they come into the workshop, the song used, and the process of the art, never fail to bring up a lot of emotion.  I have watched this workshop have a great healing effect for clients who are participating simply by their being given the opportunity to "be where they are at at the present moment."
Row.txt_description: Helps participants focus on feelings they are experiencing in this very difficult and frightening time of leaving their abusive partners using interesting and powerful techniques.

Row.txt_code:
Sun Catchers as bookmarkers


Workshop Objective:
To create a Sun Catcher as a reminder of the sunshine we want in our future.  The technique can be used to create cards, bookmarks, or art to "frame" on paper.

Materials:
Plastic transparent report covers
Scissors
Gold and silver markers
Tissue paper (multi-colors)
Cray-Pas
Mod Podge (watered down a bit)
Feathers
Black string
Beads
Magazines
Rub-on letters
Sparkles
Small hole - hole puncher
Thick paper (different colors to mount artwork)
Photo corners

Timeframe:
This workshop takes 2 hours.





Sun Catcher sample created by Martha



Opening:
Opening circle (introduce all the participants and ask them to share: name, how they are feeling and their experience with art). Explain the project. Because this project can have many opportunities for individual expression, I suggest leaders have a couple of samples with multi-techniques on them, and let the members pick and choose what they want to work with.

Activity:
Sun Catcher Option:

Cut the report covers into 6 pieces or 4 pieces (discourage participants from using a full-sheet because somehow a full-sheet does not look as "cute" as a cut piece). Cut tissue paper in different shapes and sizes.

Method 1:
Write a word with a gold or silver marker on a piece of tissue, "glue" the paper with the Mod Podge to the back of the cut report covers arrange remaining cut tissue paper pieces around or behind this piece.

Method 2:
Get one of the feathers and "glue" it to the back of the cut report cover with a very thin layer of Mod Podge. Arrange cut tissue paper pieces around the feather or use a few more feathers. Try not to "glue" anything behind the feather part.




Method 1: Writing in gold pen on tissue


Method 3:
Rub a word with the rub-on Letters on a piece of tissue paper and "glue" the paper with the Mod Podge to the back of the cut report covers arrange remaining cut tissue paper pieces around or behind this piece.

Method 4:
Cut out letters/words and/or small pictures from magazines (don't use the thick art photo books for this project) and use these with a combination of tissue paper to create your art work.




Method 2: Working
with feathers



Method 5:
Rub different colors of Cray-Pas on the back of one of the pieces of the report covers.  Try to make an interesting design or color pattern. Rub a little to mix. Coat with a very thin coating of Mod Podge and place a second piece of report cover to protect the design. This method works well as a bookmark by making one small hole on top and putting a piece of colorful string through it.

Once you have created a few of these pieces you can now make your Sun Catcher. Make holes with the hole puncher and sew the pieces together with the black string (in any pattern that you want). The top piece should just have a piece of string to be able to hang. You can have beads or feathers stringing from the last piece to give it a more "breezy" effect. Also you can cut one of your finished pieces into a design or shape of some kind and use them instead of, or in addition to, the beads or feathers.

Special Tip:
If you want to place a second piece of plastic cover at the back of your artwork, you can. Advice here is that if you can do without one, do without one. Sometimes the Mod Podge does not dry between the covers and you'll have a white glob in your art work.  Allow art work to dry a little bit and allow the Mod Podge to get a little "tacky" before you try to place the 2nd piece of cover at the back of the artwork and see if by rubbing your art piece you can sort of distribute the Mod Podge evenly between the two pieces of plastic.





Method 3: Rub-on letters





Method 3: Collaging from magazines



Artwork/Card Option:
All of the above methods can be used on the artwork/card option, except that you probably will only be making one piece. After you get done with the piece you can use the photo corners to "glue" it to the card/art paper. Or you can make holes to the art piece and the paper and use the black thread to sew it to the card/art paper.

Closing:
Go around the circle and ask who would like to talk about their Sun Catcher and/or transparent artwork. Encourage them to share what it means to them and talk about the shapes, colors and/or words they chose for their artwork and any attachments that they chose for the Sun Catcher or transparent artwork.
Row.txt_description: Offers participants a chance to create a reminder of the sunshine they want in their future. The technique product can also be used to create cards and bookmarks.

Row.txt_code:
with extra special thanks to Cathy Salser and Suvan Geer for inspiration and assistance


< /td>


Tupelo takes charge of the magic,
and enjoys her Wizard Water.




Workshop Objective:
To provide participants a chance to view their present seemingly insurmountable challenges in the light of previous accomplishments. To empower them to reach for what they truly want in life by allowing time to define what their goals are, and the areas of their lives they can influence towards that end.  By helping them to remember how certain things seemed impossible at one time and how they now have become everyday, run-of-the-mill occurrences, the women can feel more comfortable and confident in their learning processes.

Materials:
Styrofoam cups (1 per participant)
Oil pastels/Cray-Pas (sets can be shared)
Large water containers to pour from (about 6)
Drinking water
Labels
Markers
Pens/Pencils
Writing paper
Adhesive tape
Inspiring music

Optional - Glue sticks, scissors, photo stock books for collaging the cups.  Anything can be used that can withstand moisture. Collaging actually works quite well on the cups.

Timeframe:
Introduction:              5 minutes
Opening Circle:        15 minutes
Naming Wizard Waters:    10 minutes
Creating Wizard Cups:    30 minutes
Enjoying Wizard Water/
Writing Thoughts:        10 minutes
