Closing Circle:        20 minutes
Total Time:            1 1/2 hours

Space Setup/Prep:
It's helpful to try making a Wizard Cup yourself so you know how the art supplies work on styrofoam.  Also, before the workshop, prepare the large water containers so that they will be easy to label as Wizard Waters during the introduction. If you are using bottled waters from the store, you might tape paper around them to cover the original labels, making them blank and ready to be renamed by the group.





Cathy with her Wizard Cup, sensing the magic.



Introduction:
“Today we will be taking time to think about times in the past when we have succeeded in overcoming a challenge that we thought we would never be able to surmount. Do you remember a time when you may have thought, ‘I'll NEVER be able to do that! I could NEVER accomplish that. I don't have what it takes. It's not within my power to do that.' “Remember how it felt to be challenged, confused and frustrated. Today we are going to learn about our personal power. Today we are going to practice being wizards. We will be making Wizard Cups to represent the magic inside of us that makes it possible for us to learn and grow and overcome new challenges. We will be able to fill our cups with special "wizard waters" and drink in just what we need in order to face what lies ahead.”

Opening Circle:
“For our opening circle, let's each share something we have learned to do that might have seemed too hard at first. It could be little or big, anything you overcame. Does anyone remember how hard it was learning to tie your shoes? Before we learned, how it seemed impossible?" The leader may want to choose another example that is personal for them to help encourage participants to share.





Dolores joins in the Wizard Water Drinking.



Naming the Wizard Waters:
“Before we make our cups we get to name our Wizard Waters. Let’s start by figuring out what makes it possible for wizards to do such amazing things. What kinds of powers do wizards have?" Or, if the group is not wizard sympathetic: "Remembering past challenges, what kinds of qualities did you have that helped you to be able to do the things that were hard to do?”

The group brainstorms powers while the leader writes them on a tablet or chalkboard. Then the group narrows down the options from the list to choose the powers that will become Wizard Water ingredients. (The power of magic doesn't go on a Wizard Water Container because this is the ingredient supplied directly by the participants.) Ideas for Wizard Ingredients: courage, perseverance, passion, faith, love, creativity, calm and wisdom.

Cup Creation:
"Magic is the most important ingredient because it is the one that we supply ourselves. We are in charge of the magic ingredient. We are going to take out the magic inside of us and draw it onto our Wizard Cups.

“Let’s remember those particular times in the past when we used our personal magic to overcome obstacles and begin thinking of the things we want for our lives now. The goals that seem too challenging today, out of reach or foolish. Then we’ll draw the pictures or words, whatever symbolizes this goal to us onto the cups. Anything that represents the new challenges we'll face as we work toward making our dreams a reality.






Labeling a Wizard Water, “Trust.”

Drawing on the cup with Cray-Pas.






Collaging on the cup works too.





“Once you've added your personal magic to the outside of your cup, it will be ready to be filled on the inside with the Wizard Water Ingredients. You can have a sip of Knowledge, a gulp of Creativity, half a cup of Love and half a cup of Faith. You get to fill your Wizard Cup with whatever you are thirsty for as you prepare yourself for the future you want. That's part of the magic. So when your cup is ready, fill it with the Wizard Waters and enjoy it until everyone has finished their Wizard Cups and then we’ll have a closing circle."

Encourage participants to take time visualizing their goals and reassure them that there is nothing too big or impossible. Suggest that they begin drawing when they feel ready.  It is important to remind them to not draw around the lip of the cup or they will end up with pastels on their lips! The oil pastels will smear a bit but they won't rub off or run if water gets on the outside of the cup.





Pouring Wizard Water “Trust” into the cup.



As they finish, encourage them to get their water and sip it.  As they sip, they may wish to write thoughts of the powers they will bring with them as they journey towards their goals.

Closing Circle:
Encourage participants who want to share something about their experience of making a Wizard Cup and being in charge of the magic. They might share how it felt remembering previous accomplishments, which Wizard Waters they filled their cups with, and/or any insights they have gained into their ability to handle the challenges they currently face in making their dreams a reality.
Row.txt_description: Provides participants a sense of empowerrment by creating a cup and enjoying a process that is a reminder of how they have accomplished many things in their lives which seemed difficult at first.

Row.txt_code:
Kelly Carter


Hello! My name is Kelly Carter and I have been volunteering with the AWBW program at the Shasta County Women's Refuge in Redding, California for about five months. The idea for the Gratitude Journal workshop came from watching my two daughters make collages on everything from folders to binders.   I used their idea to start making collages on hardcover composition books and sealing them with clear packing tape to preserve the collage. My youngest daughter had been keeping a gratitude journal for about five years. After a trip home from college, she had left her journal at my house. When she arrived back at school and discovered her journal was missing, she immediately called and asked me to send it to her as soon as possible. I realized what a powerful process keeping the journal had become for her and decided to introduce the concept of the Gratitude Journal at our monthly AWBW meeting. The next month we took the workshop into the shelter. The women at the shelter loved the process and appreciated creating something that they could use daily. By focusing on the positive aspects of our lives, we can lift our awareness and create a more positive life experience as well. Keeping a gratitude journal is something we can all benefit from.

Workshop Objective:
To give participants time to reflect on the good and positive aspects of her life. To create her own personalized journal as an expression of those positive aspects and to have a place to record daily the things, people, and personal strengths for which she is grateful.

Materials:
Magazines
Scissors
Glue sticks
Pens
Clear packing tape
Composition theme books (hardcovers, often black & white speckled)

Timeframe:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Openingand sharing: 10 minutes
Demonstration: 5 minutes
Relaxation/Visualization: 5 minutes
Writing: 5  minutes
Creation: 50 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Total Time: 1 1/2 hours

Space Setup/Prep:
Set out the supplies, with scissors, glue stick, and composition book at each place. Spread out the magazines for easy access.





Gratitude Journal sample cover



Introduction:
"Tonight we’re going to spend sometime focusing on what we are grateful for in our lives.  Along with the chaos that we may be experiencing right now, there are positive aspects in our lives that may be overshadowed by the chaos.  What we want to do today is to identify those positive aspects and spend some time in appreciation of them.

"The workshop is called Gratitude Journals. We will spend some time in a relaxation and guided visualization followed by a few minutes of journal writing. Then we will create our journals and end with a few minutes of sharing. You might use your journals as a daily reflection tool to record your blessings. Focusing on our strengths and blessings helps to keep us centered and grounded."

Opening Sharing:
Use the opening to have participants introduce themselves and briefly share if time allows. (This will be dependent on the number in your group.)

Demonstration:
This is a basic collage on the cover of a composition book. Participants can collage on front & back using images and words cut from the magazines. (Tip: Finding a background image that fills up the cover and then adding other images over the top makes it easier to cover the entire space.) When the collage is completed, clear packing tape (2 inches wide) is placed in vertical strips to seal the collage. Overlap the strips slightly and' fold the ends over to the inside of the cover.




Gratitude Journal sample cover




Relaxation/Visualization:
“Take the time to become very comfortable, notice your hands. Are they relaxed and loose? If not, take a moment to relax your hands. Now focus your attention on your face, is it relaxed? Take a moment and simply send the message to your entire body to relax. Focus your attention on your breath, not seeking to change it in any way but simply become aware of your in-breath and your out-breath. Now using your imagination, picture yourself in your favorite kind of place. This is a place you know to be safe, nurturing and uplifting. This is your special space, where you are at peace, empowered and centered. It is a place of beauty... one that sets your Soul free to soar. See it very clearly taking in every detail that makes this place special to you... Now if you are inside, move outside and if you are already outside, look around you and take in the beauty of your surroundings What is the weather like? Is there a breeze? What are the sounds and smells... Be fully aware with your whole being... Now notice in front of you a gentle pathway... You begin to walk along the path... feeling content and at ease...completely enjoying this time... soon you come to a small garden... and in the garden you find a bench... you find yourself drawn to this little garden and choose to rest here for awhile ... as you sit there among the flowers and trees on the little bench, I invite you to spend a few minutes reflecting on your life.... looking for the good that is there ... the things that bring you joy and happiness... it could be your child's smile .... or a hug from a friend...or the sunshine warm on your face ... or the smell of violets growing in the garden ... look for the things that you are thankful for in your life....maybe it is your courage and strength ... or your willingness to make changes in your life...perhaps it is a special person ... someone you deeply love and appreciate ... someone who supports and honors you... as you remember the blessings in your life, you begin to feel a greater sense of joy and connection to all life ... a sense of peace settles over you ...  as you remember what you are grateful for ... It is now time to leave the garden and return to the here and now ... take a few deep breaths... and feel yourself in your body... back here in this room ... and when you are ready, open your eyes.

Writing:
After the guided visualization, take a few moments to have each participant write down some of the thoughts that came to her during the visualization. Suggest that she date this first entry and use the journal on a daily basis to focus her thoughts in a positive direction.





Collage sample from Griffin and Sabine



Creation:
As the group begins to cut images for their collages, encourage them to focus on gratitude and the images that best represent their personal response to the visualization. It is easy for them to get distracted while searching for images in the magazines. By encouraging them to share during the creation of the journal, you might help to keep them on track and possibly give some ideas to those who may have been challenged in identifying positive aspects of their lives. Assist with taping of the books at the end of the project.

Closing:
Take a few minutes at the end of the session to allow each participant to share her Gratitude Journal. If the women have not fully completed the collages, encourage them to continue on their own after the workshop. Remind them that their journal is a place they can record their accomplishments and daily reflections. They could also use the journal to record uplifting poetry and quotes.




Collage sample from Griffin and Sabine
Row.txt_description: Gives participants time to reflect on the good and positive aspects of her life. The end products are individualized, personalized journals, expressions of those positive aspects and a place to record daily gratitude lists and strengths.

Row.txt_code:
Special Thanks to Tupelo Hassman for inspiring, encouraging, and editing this workshop, and for her special invention of the “Nap Goggles.”  Nap on, Tupelo!

Workshop Objective:
To allow each participant a time-out to nap, to reflect on how her sleep is going, and to create art that can help her sleep become as restful and beneficial as possible during this special transition and rebuilding period of her life.





Hard at work: AWBW staff tests out a mini-nap.



Note:
In this Update, we have provided a range of suggested variation projects that address the issues surrounding sleeping well.  As the main project, we have focused on the collage-making because it is probably most familiar to the clients and leaders, and requires the least amount of preparation.  However, if you would like to substitute one of the variations, go ahead!  Also, if focusing on sleep seems especially useful to your particular group, you might decide to stick with this theme for several weeks, using a different project each week.  That way, they can share their progress and support each other over time.  

Materials:
Magazines
Scissors
Glue sticks
Pens
3”X3” card stock, or heavy paper
Envelopes
Optional:  3”X3” plexiglass, matte medium, brushes

Timeframe:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Sharing: 5 minutes
Demonstration: 5 minutes
Relaxation/Nap-Time: 15 minutes
Creation: 50 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Total Time: 1 1/2 hours

Space Setup/Prep:
Set out the supplies, with scissors, glue stick, & 3”X3” card stock at each place. Spread out the magazines for easy access.




Sleep Collage sample in progress.




Introduction:
"Tonight we are going to spend some time on sleep.  Anyone ready for a nap?  Tonight we are going to share a nap and create a piece of art to help ourselves rest well.  Naps and sleep are very, very important—especially important in the midst of changing your life.  Changing your life and getting free from a violent relationship takes lots of energy.   There are so many things to solve and figure out.  There is so much to do that it might not feel possible to rest.  There are so many confusing feelings that sleeping might feel difficult.  Is anyone having trouble sleeping?  And yet sleep is especially important at this time.  Why do you think that is?  Answers can come to you when you are resting, not trying too hard.  Has anyone here noticed that?  Sometimes when your mind is just safe and free, that’s when you can gather the clarity and strength you need.  Resting is so deeply important to growth.”

Opening Sharing:
“How is sleep going for you these days?  Any thoughts you want to share about what helps you sleep well?”  (Remember that different people are very different, and what helps them sleep may differ considerably.  One person may find it peaceful and comforting to have the TV and radio on, while someone else might prefer quiet.  There is no “wrong” way to sleep well.)





“Time to Rest” Sleep Collage.



Demonstration:
“Tonight, to help our resting, we will be making Sleep Collages that we can keep by our beds at night.  They are something we can look at before going to sleep, or if we wake up in the middle of the night and want to relax again.  You can put together into your collage whatever images are relaxing and comforting to you.  There is a 3”X3” paper at each place for you to collage on.  It’s good to have the image small so it’s easy to put by the bedside, or store in an envelope if you want to keep it more private.”  (Tip: Finding a background image that fills up the 3”X3” and then adding other images over the top makes it easier to cover the entire space.)

Optional: When the collage is completed, 3”X3” plexiglass can be placed over with matte medium, to seal the collage (see manual).

Relaxation/Nap-Time:
You might want to play soft, relaxing music during this nap-time.  “Remember being in school and taking nap-time?  We get to do that tonight.  You can rest your head on the table and just relax.  I will turn the lights low and you can just take a break from everything.  You can listen to the sounds of your breath, the birds, cars outside, and know that you don’t have to do anything at all.  This is time for you to rest.  After about 15 minutes, I will let you know, and you can start collaging.  But you could keep resting if that’s what you need to do.  This workshop is your time, to honor the rest you need.  There is nothing you have to do.”  

Creation:
As they begin to cut images for their collages, encourage them to focus on rest and what would help them sleep well.  The images they chose may be very simple.  Let them know that’s okay.  If some complete their image quickly, encourage them to create more sleep collages, or to write their thoughts about their sleep and how they want it to be.   If you are doing the 3”X3” plexiglass, help each participant one-on-one as she applies matte medium and glass.

Closing:
Take a few minutes at the end of the session to allow each participant to share her Sleep Collage and the steps she would like to take to rest deeply during this time of transition.




Wishing all AWBW leaders and workshop
participants happy sleeps!




Guided Relaxation for Peaceful Sleep

Lay comfortably in your bed, ready for sleep. 
Adjust your arms and legs so that they are comfortable and settled.  Notice your breathing...  Now take in some deep breaths... 
As you let out each one, mentally say the word “relax”... 

When you are ready, become aware of your face. 
Notice your whole head and neck.  Now take a deep breath in,
and squeeze the muscles in your face, head, and neck.  Now let your breath go and release all the tension from your head.  As you relax your head, picture the relaxation spreading through your entire body...

When you are ready, become aware of your shoulders and back. 
Now take a deep breath in, and squeeze all the muscles in your shoulders and back.  Now let your breath go and release all the tension. 
As you relax your shoulders and back, picture the
relaxation spreading through your entire body... 

When you are ready, become aware of your arms and hands. 
Now take a deep breath in, and squeeze all the muscles in your
arms and hands.  Now let your breath go and release all the tension.
 As you relax your arms and hands, picture the relaxation
spreading through your entire body... 

When you are ready, become aware of your chest and stomach. 
Now take a deep breath in, and squeeze all the muscles in your chest and stomach.  Now let your breath go and release all the tension. 
As you relax your chest and stomach, picture the
relaxation spreading through your entire body... 

When you are ready, become aware of your legs and feet. 
Now take a deep breath in, and squeeze all the muscles in your legs and feet.  Now let your breath go and release all the tension.
 As you relax your legs and feet, picture the
relaxation spreading through your entire body... 

Now take another deep breath for your entire body. 
Gently squeeze the muscles from head to toe, one more time.  Squeeze your head, your shoulders and back, your arms and hands, your chest and stomach, your legs and feet...  And relax...  Feel the wonderful relaxation through your entire body. 

Rest comfortably in this position.  Just enjoy how relaxed your whole body is, as you drift off to a deep, peaceful and refreshing sleep.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants a time to relax and take a nap, followed by the creation of a collage filled with relaxing images that can help them sleep better during this difficult time in their lives. There are several variations to this sleep workshop: sleep rocks, nap goggles, etc.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
Healing from emotional abuse is a difficult task.  This workshop provides a space where each survivor can notice that, can reflect on words she finds to be affirming and encouraging, and can create hearts to use as a fun and beautiful support in the days ahead.

Materials:

 
 
 “Have respect for yourself, before anyone
else can respect you!”
  

Art Supplies: scissors, “edger” scissors, construction paper, pretty stationary, glue sticks, markers and gel roller pens, ribbon, string, or yarn, laminator (or clear contact paper) and hole punch

Books with affirmations or positive sayings, i.e., Louise Hay, Melody Beattie, Sue Patton Thoele, or any of the books you read with a daily affirmation

Relaxing music

Timeframe:
Introduction:         5 minutes
Opening Circle:      5 minutes
Demonstration:      5 minutes
Relaxation:            5 minutes
Creation:              50 minutes
Closing/Grab-bag:   20 minutes
Total Time:            1 1/2 hours

Introduction:
“This workshop is window into loving yourself and others more everyday!  We will be making two affirmation hearts for ourselves and three hearts to share with the group via a grab basket!  That means you will walk away with a total of five hearts of love with which to affirm yourself every day.  Emotional abuse is very difficult to heal from.  These hearts with positive affirmations on them are a fun and beautiful way to heal.” 

  


“Shout your joy, shout your sadness,
shout that you are here and alive...”
 
 

Opening Circle:
Begin by asking each participant to share what words are encouraging to her—anything that she likes to hear when she’s having a hard day.  (You might also include a “check-in” so they can share how they are feeling right now—good or bad.)

Technical Demonstration:
It might be helpful to make a few hearts ahead of time for yourself to enjoy and share with your group. Pass them around for everyone to see.

You want to cut your hearts about 3 1/2 by 3 1/2 inches, so you can fit at least three hearts in the lamination pouch.  If you do not have a laminator, you can have them all done at a copy center or use clear contact paper.

You can collage with scraps of paper and/or draw designs with the markers or gel rollers on both sides of your heart.  Next write or print an affirmation.  When you are all finished, the hearts can be laminated and hole punched.

Relaxation:
You can use this one or your favorite.  Play relaxing music and speak softly and lovingly!


 
 
 “I am strong and wise...”
  
 
 “Always be an angel-on-call for a friend...”
  

“I will now guide you through a color relaxation.  You can let everything go for right now, all you need to do is sit back and relax!  If you are sitting, it's good to sit with your feet flat, your back straight and your hands just lying loosely in your lap.  If it feels safe for you, you can close your eyes and picture the colors on the screen in your mind!

“Take a deep breath and as you slowly let it out, see yourself surrounded by peaceful sky blue ribbons drifting through the air.  Feel yourself calmly breathing in and out. Feel the tension in your body softening and melting away.

“Picture yourself floating on a soft pink fluffy cloud, feel beautiful music surrounding and caressing you. You feel very light, almost like cotton candy.  Your breathing intuitively is deeper as you begin to feel more and more relaxed.

“Visualize fresh yellow sunshine gently warming your body.  You notice all your muscles relaxing and all their knots untying.  You feel very free.  Take a deep breath, fill your lungs and as you let all the air out, you feel any last tension you have totally leave your body.

“Breath in and imagine you can smell the wonderful scent of fresh cut green grass and feel a slight breeze clearing your mind.

“Take a deep breath and go to that deep place inside of you and remember how strong you are...  Remember how absolutely wonderful you are...  And remember how beautiful you are... just soak these positive thoughts up holding onto them...  knowing that they are all true...

“When you are ready, bring yourself gently back to the room and begin to create your beautiful affirmation hearts.  Make sure to create two affirmation hearts for yourself and three hearts to share with the group.”

Closing:
Have everyone choose which hearts they are keeping and then put the other three in a basket or bag. Pass the basket or bag around the circle.  Have each participant pick one at a time until they are all gone.  If they pick their own, they of course have a choice, keep it or pick again.  I always feel if you pick your own, you must really need that affirmation.  There are no coincidences!  You can laminate before or after this process depending on time.

Participants can string them together creating a heart garland with knots keeping the hearts spaced on their ribbon, yarn or string.  Or they can tie a ribbon on each heart separately like you would an ornament or a bookmark.

Have them share their favorite heart and affirmation, or all of them, as time permits.

Close your workshop, suggesting everyone get two hugs before they leave, including you!

Enjoy!  Love, Rose

  


“You don’t have to study to become
an angel— just wing it!””
Row.txt_description: Provides a space where each survivor can notice that healing from emotional abuse is a difficult task and reflect on words she finds to be affirming and encouraging, and can create hearts to use as a fun and beautiful support in the days ahead.

Row.txt_code:
Workshop by Tupelo Hassman with thanks to The Naysayer for the inspiration and use of the song (visit them at www.naysayer.com).

Objective:
To offer an opportunity to consider fears in a new light.  To provide participants a chance to be in charge of their fears and to recognize that the "price" paid in facing them is not always as high as it seems.





FEAR MENU
Song by The Naysayer

Today I order from my Fear Menu
Because so many things
look tempting today.
Like laughing my head off,
Or dangerously close -
Leg veins exploding,
Teeth falling out.

Don't you worry
About my Fear Menu
I've had everything on it
And look at me, I'm fine.
I've had acceleration,
Deluxe palpitations.
A fine humming yellow,
That old insect feeling.

I'd be so bored without my Fear Menu,
But I rest so assured
I'm always invited
to the lunch with an unknown
His sneaking suspicions.
My see-thru composure
Utter exposure.



Materials:
Menu Paper:
Large pieces of construction or other paper that can be folded to create a menu effect, if participants are journaling they might also use pages inside their journals.
Menu Design:
oil pastels/Cray-Pas, watercolor sets, markers, crayons, colored pencils or pens (sets can be shared)
Scissors
Paper towels
Pens or pencils
Writing paper
Inspiring music





“Today’s Special—Thinking about what scares me. 
Cost: Butterflies in my stomach.”



Optional, if time permits you may want to collage the Fear Menus, in which case add: glue sticks and photo stock books and/or magazines.

Timeframe:
Opening Circle:          15 minutes
Warm-up:                   5 minutes
Creating Fear Menus:   20 minutes
Writing Thoughts:        5 minutes
Closing Circle:            15 minutes
Total Time:                1 hour

Space Setup/Preparation:
It's helpful to make your own Fear Menu and experience the process of examining your “Fears” and the “Costs” of meeting them. It might be helpful to examine menus from restaurants or take-out places (we all have stacks of these somewhere!). It can be fun to think about all of the special parts of a menu—Daily Special, Desserts, Lite Menu, Children's Menu, etc.

Introduction:
“Today we will be taking time to think about the fears we face, for example, before speaking in front of a group or when asking someone for help—and how we feel as we face them, emotions that come up, nervousness or worry that we won't be liked and the physical reactions our bodies have to these experiences—feeling sweaty or hot or short of breath.






“These responses, emotional and physical, are the prices we pay for taking these risks, for speaking in front of a group and being heard, for asking for the help we need.  Today we are going to create our personal Fear Menus to remind us that we have a choice to take these risks and to let us know that we are prepared for what it might cost us to take them, to remind us that whatever might happen inside our minds and inside our bodies when we order from our Fear Menus, we are prepared.

“First we are going to spend some time thinking of those things we want to be able to do without hesitation, without feeling afraid, especially those things we often decide not to do rather than run the risk of our fears.  These are the items that we will list on the Menus so that we can order them when we are ready. “Then we will think of how much these items cost us, the price we pay to take the risk, whether it be sweaty palms, a racing heart, or a sick stomach.

“Once we have decided what belongs on our personal Fear Menus we get to design them.
I have collected some examples of menus in order to give us ideas for design, you can look through them or create your own menu from scratch. Most importantly, remember that it is your menu and it can be designed in any manner that will make it accessible to you, what is important is that you are able to understand what you want to order and how much it will be.”







Opening Circle:
“For our opening circle, let's each share something that comes up for us when we think about our fears. Something that we really want to do, but we might talk ourselves out of doing because of our fear. It could be a smaller thing, like asking for help or a larger thing, like asking for love, anything that makes you nervous.

“As we each share something that causes us fear let us also also share how that fear manifests itself. Maybe you feel fearful sharing what makes you nervous!” (As leader you may want to choose an example that is personal for you to encourage sharing.)



Fear Menu Creation:
“We will take a few minutes to think of the items that will be included on our Fear Menus and what the price is for ordering them. Feel free to sketch how you would like your menu to look and don't forget to consider adding categories, such as the Daily Special or Seafood. Then when you feel ready begin to create your menu.”



Closing Circle:
Encourage participants who want
to share something about their experience of making their Fear Menu and understanding the risks they run when they take chances. They might share how it felt remembering nervous feelings, or deciding that taking these chances are worth the risks of feeling nervous and especially any insights they have gained into their ability to handle the challenges they currently face in making their dreams a reality.
Row.txt_description: Offers participants the opportunity to consider their fears in a new light. Provides a chance to be in charge of their fears and to recognize that the "price" paid in facing them is not always as high as it seems.

Row.txt_code:
“Skeleton Woman” sample created by Martha Contreras.
 
  
Objective:
To create a movable (and/or dancing) Skeleton Woman marionette as a way of exploring issues of life, death, love, and relationships. To use the “Skeleton Woman” story in the book Women Who Run With the Wolves to spark the creative process.

Materials:
Skeleton Woman pattern
Tag board
Scissors
Paper fasteners (each Skeleton Woman requires 12)
Hole puncher
Glue (and a glue gun if available)
String
Decoration materials like: pieces of cloth (and thread and needles) for making clothing
Feathers
Beads
Sparklers/glitter/sequins
Paint
Color pencils/markers

Timeframe:
This workshop takes 2 hours
(This workshop could run over and could be made into two workshops if more discussion is needed for the article of "Skeleton Woman.")

Opening Circle:
Introduce all the participants and have them share the basics (name, how they are feeling that day, experience with art and anything else they would like to share with the group).

Introduction:
Give them a brief overview of the "Skeleton Woman" myth from Women That Run With the Wolves (see below) and/or if you are doing this workshop in October or November you could make this a Dia De Los Muertos theme (Day of the Dead)—A Mexican Celebration where the dead members of the family are remembered, honored, and their lives celebrated by a big party. An altar is made with pictures, flowers, food, and articles of the person that passed away. The celebration is also a way to teach that death is a natural process and that you should enjoy life, of which death is also a part.

  


Group photo of “Skeleton Women.”
 
  
Activity:
Version 1 (Simple):
This version is more simple because it does not include attaching strings so the skeleton can “dance.”

1. Glue a copy of the model on tagboard (see attached “Skeleton Woman” pattern).

2. If the body of the skeleton is going to be decorated (painted), do it now before you cut the pieces out, otherwise painting the cut-out piece is harder.

3. Cut out all the parts.


 
 
  

4. You can make a "dress" for your Skeleton Woman (and you can give her a "bust" with small pieces of material glued to the body in a bust form and a strip of material could be placed on top and glued on back, like a "bra") or you can just decorate the hat (and other body parts) with colors, sequins, glitter, feathers, etc.

5. With a hole puncher, punch out each point marked with a circle or an “X.”

6. Connect the arms and legs to the body with paper fasteners. Make sure that they are very loose to allow for movement of the parts.

Version 2 (for the technically advanced):
This version is more advanced because you are attaching strings so that your skeleton can “dance.”

Do Steps 1 through 4 same as above and then do the following:

4A. Put a piece of thread, about 10 inches long, through the X's in the legs.

4B. Make knots on each end of the threads without making them very tight.

4C. Cut out any leftover thread.

Do Step 5 from Version 1

6. Tie a 13 inch piece of thread in the middle of the thread that connects the arms.

7. Tie the same 13 inch piece of thread to the thread that connects the legs in the middle as well.

8. With tape, attach a wooden stick to the back of the body (in the middle) in order to hold the figure in your hand. The stick must pass beneath the threads.

9. When you pull the thread, you will see how your skeleton woman dances.

Closing Circle:
Ask the participants to share about their Skeleton Woman and also to write what they felt about decorating her and giving her a form.

Note:
A Polaroid picture of the participants with their creations and/or a group picture as a keepsake goes well here.

  


  


----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Women Who Run with the Wolves (excerpt)
Chapter 5
Hunting: When the Heart Is a Lonely Hunter

Skeleton Woman:
Facing the Life/Death/Life Nature of Love

Wolves are good at relationships. Anyone who has observed wolves sees how deeply they bond. Mates are most often for life. Even though they clash, even though there is dissension, their bonds carry them over and through harsh winters, plentiful springs, long walks, new offspring, old predators, tribal dances, and group sings. The relational needs of humans are no different.

While the instinctual lives of wolves include loyalty and lifelong bonds of trust and devotion, humans sometimes have trouble with these matters. If we were to use archetypal terms to describe what determines the strong bonds among wolves, we might surmise that the integrity of their relationships is derived from their submission to the ancient Life/Death/Life nature.

The Life/Death/Life nature is a cycle of animation, development, decline, and death that is always followed by reanimation. This cycle affects all physical life and all facets of psychological life. Everything-the sun, novas, and the moon, as well as the affairs of humans and those of the tiniest creatures, like cells and atoms- has this fluttering, then faltering, then fluttering again.

Unlike humans, wolves do not deem the ups and downs of life, energy, power, food, opportunity as startling or punitive. The peaks and valleys just are, and wolves ride them as efficiently, as fluidly, as possible. The instinctual nature has the miraculous ability to live through all positive boon, all negative consequence, and still maintain relationship to self, to another.

Among wolves, the Life/Death/Life cycles of nature and fate are met with grace and wit and the endurance to stay tight with one's mate and to live long and as well as can be. But in order for humans to live and give loyalty in this most fit manner, in this way which is most wise, most preserving, and most feeling, one has to go up against the very thing one fears most. There is no way around it, as we shall see. One must sleep with Lady Death.

Skeleton Woman is a hunting story about love. In stories from the north, love is not a romantic tryst between two lovers. Stories from the circumpolar regions describe love as a union of two beings whose strength together enables one or both to enter into communication with the soul-world and to participate in fate as a dance with life and death.

To understand this story, we have to see that there, in one of the harshest environs and one of the most stressed hunting cultures in the world, love does not mean a flirtation or a pursuit for simple ego pleasure, but a visible bond composed of the psychic sinew of endurance, a union which prevails through bounty and austerity, through the most complicated and most simple days and nights. The union of two beings is seen as angakok magic in itself, as a relationship through which "the powers that be" become known to both individuals.

But there are requirements for this kind of union. In order to create is enduring love, one invites a third partner to the union. The third partner is Skeleton Woman. She is also called Lady Death, and as such she is the Life/Death/Life nature in one of her many guises. In is form, Lady Death is not a disease, but a deity.

In a relationship she has the role of the oracle who knows when it is time for cycles to begin and end. As such, she is the wildish aspect of relationship, the one of whom men are most terrified… and sometimes women also, for when faith in the transformative has been lost, the natural cycles of increase and attrition are feared as well.

To create enduring love, Skeleton Woman must be admitted to the relationship and be embraced by both lovers. Here, in this old Inuit story, are the psychic stages for mastery of that embrace. This story was given to me by Mary Uukalat. Let us peer at the images which rise from the smoke of this story.

Skeleton Woman

She had done something of which her father disapproved, although no one any longer remembered what it was. But her father had dragged her to the cliffs and thrown her over and into the sea. There, the fish ate her flesh away and plucked out her eyes. As she lay under the sea, her skeleton turned over and over in the currents.

One day a fisherman came fishing, well, in truth many came to this bay once. But this fisherman had drifted far from his home place, and did not know that the local fisherman stayed away, saying this inlet was haunted.

The fisherman's hook drifted down through the water, and caught, of all places, in the bones of Skeleton Woman’s rib cage. The fisherman thought, "Oh, now I've really got a big one! Now I really have one!" In his mind he was thinking of how many people this great fish would feed, how long it would last, how long he might be free from the chore of hunting. And as he struggled with this great weight on the end of the hook, the sea was stirred to a thrashing froth, and his kayak bucked and shook, for she who was beneath struggled to disentangle herself. And the more she struggled, the more she tangled in the line. No matter what she did, she was inexorably dragged upward, tugged up by the bones of her own ribs.

The hunter had turned to scoop up his net, so he did not see her bald head rise above the waves, he did not see the little coral creatures glinting in the orbs of her skull, he did not see the crustaceans on her old ivory teeth. When he turned back with his net, her entire body, such as it was, had come to the surface and was hanging from the tip of his kayak by her long front teeth.

"Agh!" cried the man, and his heart fell into his knees, his eyes hid in terror on the back of his head, and his ears blazed bright red. "Agh!" he screamed, and knocked her off the prow with his oar and began paddling like a demon toward shoreline. And not realizing she was tangled in his line, he was frightened all the more for she appeared to stand upon her toes while chasing him all the way to shore. No matter which way he zigged his kayak, she stayed right behind, and her breath rolled over the water in clouds of steam, and her arms flailed out as though to snatch him down into the depths.

"Aggggggghhhh!" he wailed as he ran aground. In one leap he was out of his kayak, clutching his fishing stick and running, and the coral-white corpse of Skeleton Woman, still snagged in the fishing line, bumpety-bumped behind right after him. Over the rocks he ran, and she followed. Over the frozen tundra he ran and she kept right up. Over the meat laid out to dry he ran, cracking it to pieces as his mukluks bore down.

Throughout it all she kept right up, in fact grabbed some of the frozen fish as she was dragged behind. This she began to eat, for she had not gorged in a long, long time. Finally, the man reached his snowhouse and dove right into the tunnel and on hands and knees scrabbled his way into the interior. Panting and sobbing he lay there in the dark, his heart a drum, a mighty drum. Safe at last, oh so safe, yes safe, thank the Gods, Raven, yes, thank Raven, yes, and all-bountiful Sedna, safe . . . at . . . last.

Imagine when he lit his whale oil lamp, there she—it—lay in a tumble upon his snow floor, one heel over her shoulder, one knee inside her rib cage, one foot over her elbow. He could not say later what it was, perhaps the firelight softened her features, or the fact that he was a lonely man. But a feeling of some kindness came into his breathing, and slowly he reached out his grimy hands and, using words softly like mother to child, began to untangle her from the fishing line.

"Oh, na, na, na." First he untangled the toes, then the ankles. "Oh, na, na, na." On and on he worked into the night, until dressing her in furs to keep her warm, Skeleton Woman's bones were all in the order a human's should be.

He felt into his leather cuffs for his flint, and used some of his hair to light a little more fire. He gazed at her from time to time as he oiled the precious wood of his fishing stick and rewound the gut line. And she in the furs uttered not a word—she did not dare—lest this hunter take her out and throw her down to the rocks and break her bones to pieces utterly.

The man became drowsy, slid under his sleeping skins, and soon was dreaming. And sometimes as humans sleep, you know, a tear escapes from the dreamer's eye; we never know what sort of dream causes this, but we know it is either a dream of sadness or longing. And this is what happened to the man.

The Skeleton Woman saw the tear glisten in the firelight, and she became suddenly soooo thirsty. She tinkled and clanked and crawled over to the sleeping man and put her mouth to his tear. The single tear was like a river and she drank and drank and drank until her many-years-long thirst was slaked.

While lying beside him, she reached inside the sleeping man and took out his heart, the mighty drum. She sat up and banged on both sides of it: Bom, Bomm! . . . Bom, Bomm!

As she drummed, she began to sing out "Flesh, flesh, flesh! Flesh, flesh, flesh!" And the more she sang, the more her body filled out with flesh. She sang for hair and good eyes and nice fat hands. She sang the divide between her legs, and breasts long enough to wrap for warmth, and all the things a woman needs.

And when she was all done, she also sang the sleeping man's clothes off and crept into his bed with him, skin against skin. She returned the great drum, his heart, to his body, and that is how they awakened, wrapped one around the other, tangled from their night, in another way now, a good and lasting way.

The people who cannot remember how she came to her first ill-fortune say she and the fisherman went away and were consistently well fed by the creatures she had known in her life under water. The people say that it is true and that is all they know.
Row.txt_description: Participants create a movable (and/or dancing) Skeleton Woman marionette as a way of exploring issues of life, death, love and relationships. Uses the "Skeleton Woman" story in the book "Women Who Run With the Wolves" to spark the creative process.

Row.txt_code:
String painting with chalk pastel added, by Robin Rea.



About String Painting:
String Painting is a great workshop for leaders who are looking for a simple, introductory workshop. It doesn’t require a lot of materials and it can be easily grasped by participants who might be new to the art process. It might also be a good workshop for a group who is art-phobic and possibly intimidated by more ambitious projects. String Painting is a reminder that art can be created by objects that we all have lying around in our "junk" drawers!

Objective:
To allow each participant to experience her own inner "flow" in a simple, creative way. 

Materials:
Masking tape
Paper
String (Thick, soft string works well.  If the string is very thin, it won’t hold much ink.)
Black India ink 
Pastels or crayons
Relaxing music





String and bottles of ink (left).    Using pencil to push the string
into the ink (right).





Samples of string paintings drying.



Timeframe:
Total Time:          50 - 60 minutes
Introduction:        5  minutes
Opening Circle:    10 minutes
Demonstration:    5  minutes
Relaxation:        5  minutes
Creation:        20 minutes
Closing Circle:    10 minutes

Preparation:
You might want to try doing a String Painting before you begin the workshop to show the group what it looks like. Also, with this workshop, music is important. Find music that will allow participants to slow down and relax. 

Introduction:
“Today, we will be trying our hand at String Painting.  It’s okay if you’ve never done this before.  This will be an opportunity to just appreciate whatever flows from us.  There’s really no way to control it or plan it out, so it will be a chance to appreciate things we can’t control or plan.  Sometimes life is like that, and it’s important to be able to flow with it and notice what is beautiful and wonderful in the surprises.”

Opening Circle:
“Let’s begin with a check-in circle, and each share something that’s going well today or something for which we are grateful.  Even on the hardest of days, it helps to notice something, large or small, that’s hopeful or good about the day.  Even when many things have been difficult, there is plenty to be thankful for if we stop to think about it.  Noticing what we are thankful for can help the day go better.”

Demonstration:
“String Painting isn’t about making a ‘pretty’ picture, but rather allowing the string to move across the paper in harmony with our own internal rhythms.  String painting can be related to a meditative practice, for it’s not so much about what we consciously try to create, but what we allow to appear on the page through the simple, unforced movement of our hand. The magic of String Painting is that the shapes the string and ink make are always a surprise.  Yet with a closer look, we see that they correspond to some internal movement or dance within us.  I will show you the steps, so you can see the process.”  Show each of the four steps below, giving a sense of the process.  Have participants tape their paper and set up their ink and string next to them, before the relaxation, so that they will be ready to go right into the creating when they are relaxed.

Technical Tip: 
Try soaking the string and then dangling it onto the paper, so it is laying there.  Then gently pull it sideways.  As you pull sideways, the ink makes amazing, fluid lines (see illustrations at right).

Relaxation:
It can be helpful to start with a short meditation or relaxation that allows them to close their eyes and become focused on their breath. (Note: This is optional.  Remember to always do whatever you think is best based on your particular group.) 

“Get comfortable in your chair and let your eyes close if you wish.  Take a deep breath in... and let it go...  Take another deep breath in and as you let it go, picture breathing out any tension.  Just let it go.  Take another wonderful, relaxing breath in, and notice that this is a special ‘window’ of time for you.  It’s your time to relax and let go of any stress and tension.  It’s your time, just for you, to become still and clear and notice how you are really doing.  It is your time to be completely free.  No rights or wrongs.  Free to just be yourself and explore.  You can keep your eyes closed and relax as long as you wish.  And whenever you are ready, you can open your eyes and begin to dip your string into the ink.”

Creation:
Step 1:





Laying the string on the page.





Pulling the string across the page.



(This step might already be completed during the demonstration.)  Have participants tape down their paper, if they wish to have a border around their picture. Tape will also help secure the paper while the string is being moved around on it.

Step 2:
Dunk a piece of string (about 12 inches long) into the bottle of ink. Be sure that the string is saturated with ink. You may need to use a pencil tip to push the string into the ink. 

Step 3:
With eyes closed, move the string across the paper.  Some might find having to close their eyes while "painting" with the string frustrating; others might find it liberating.  If they don’t like what they see when they open their eyes, allow them to re-soak the string and do it again.  Advise them that if they want larger areas of ink on the page, they only need to move the string more slowly and make sure the string is soaked in ink. 

Step 4:
Once participants are satisfied with their ink shapes, they can choose pastels (or crayons) to add another dimension to their drawing. Allow them time to play with colors that embrace or intensify the shapes on the page.  Often, the ink shapes may begin to take on a life of their own. Participants may try to describe or understand what they see.  Try to keep their verbal reactions to a minimum. Allow them to finish the creative process without judgement. Every picture is about an inner life that dances and glows on the page and is beyond words or description.




String painting with chalk pastel drawing added.




Closing Circle:
For the closing circle, allow participants an opportunity to share their String Paintings. You also might want to explore how it was to have their eyes closed and what reactions came up for them. Without the use of one of our primary senses, we may feel out-of-control or powerless.  Was that something they might have been experiencing?  It might help to think about other things we do with our eyes closed, in which we call on or visit deeper powers. Prayer, for instance. Or dreams. In String Painting, we get a glimpse of an inner dance that is totally unique and precious.  Celebrate that!

Variation:
Skip the taping and closed eyes, but make sure there’s plenty of paper for each person.  Encourage each participant to play with the string-painting with her eyes open, and start on a fresh page whenever she feels ready.  It is possible to create string drawings very quickly.  Each participant can develop her own rhythm as she moves from page to page.  Then when she’s ready to stop painting, she can choose to draw with pastels back into some of the designs, or she can write words about them.




String on the page, leaving its mark.
Row.txt_description: Allows each participant to experience her own inner "flow" in a simple, creative way focusing more on process rather than product.

Row.txt_code:
“I may be alone this holiday, but
I won’t be lonely...” collage.
  
Workshop Objective:
To give participants a time-out in the midst of this season so that she can identify and explore the mixture of feelings she might face as the holidays approach.  To help each participant find creative ways to be thoughtful and loving towards herself through the holidays.

Materials:
Magazines
Scissors
Glue sticks
Pens
Card stock or heavy paper

Timeframe:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Sharing: 5 minutes
Supply Set-up: 5 minutes
Relaxation: 15 minutes
Creation: 50 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Total Time: 1 1/2 hours

  


“Each moment of this season is
full of possibilities...” collage.
 
  

Space Setup/Prep:
Set out the supplies, with a pair of scissors, a glue stick, and some card stock at each place. Spread out the magazines for easy access.

Introduction:
"In many ways, the holidays can be tough for everyone.  In the midst of facing domestic violence, it can be even more challenging.  Tonight we are going to take a holiday season time out.  (Anyone ready for a rest?)  In this workshop we are going to rest together and then create a collage to help ourselves identify the mixture of feelings that are coming up for us around the holidays this year.  It will help us figure out ways to be loving to ourselves through all of this.” 


 
 
 “I will remember to keep my sense
of peace in mind...”  collage.
  
 
 “I am looking to the future that I
am building now...” collage.
  

Opening Sharing:
“What’s one good feeling and what’s one bad feeling that is coming up for you as the holidays approach?”  

Supply Setup:
Before starting the relaxation and rest time, make sure everyone has chosen some art supplies.  Encourage each person to choose a few magazines, a piece of paper, scissors, and a glue stick, so that once they’re ready to create, they can dive right in.

Relaxation Time:
(You might want to play soft, relaxing music during this little “time out.”)

“Sometimes people can get so busy during the holiday season that they forget to slow down and find a sense of peace within themselves.  We will start this workshop by just taking a rest together.  You can lay your head on the table and just relax.  I will turn the lights low and you can just take a break from everything.  You can listen to the sounds of your breath, the music, cars outside, whatever you hear around you.  Just know that you don’t have to do anything at all.  This is time for you to rest.  After about 15 minutes, I will let you know, and you can start collaging.  But remember, you can rest as long as you need to.  This workshop is your time, to honor the rest you need.  There is nothing you have to do.”  

Creation:
As participants begin to cut images for their collages, encourage them to focus on the holidays and trust their gut feelings about what images are relevant.  When the collages are complete, encourage the participants to write any thoughts that go with them and about how they would like to approach this holiday season.  Encourage them to make a list of ways they might be especially loving and thoughtful of themselves during this challenging time of their lives.  

Closing:
Save time at the end of the session to allow each person to share her holiday collage and any steps she would like to take to make this a positive time for her. 

  


“I may be alone this holiday, but I
won’t be lonely...” detail.
Row.txt_description: Helps participants identify and explore feelings about the approaching holidays. Helps each person find creative ways to be thoughtful and loving toward herself during the holidays.

Row.txt_code:
< /tr>


  
Workshop Objective:
To give participants an opportunity to notice how sometimes the difficult things in life can be chances to learn and grow. To help each participant find patience, compassion, and trust in facing the struggles and difficulties in her life’s path. If the workshop is held around the new year, it can symbolize a each participant’s new beginning.

Materials:
Paper towels
Construction paper
Scissors & hole punchers
Puffy paints
CrayPas
Paperclips (for scratching)
Pipe cleaners (chenille stems)
Newspaper (to cover tables)
Optional: Glitter, sequins
The Butterfly Story - Spanish Translation

Timeframe:
Reading The Butterfly:
5 minutes
Opening Sharing: 10 minutes
Supply Set-up: 5 minutes
Relaxation (optional): 5 minutes
Creation: 55 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Total Time: 1 1/2 hours


 
 
  

Space Setup/Prep:
Cover the tables with newspaper. Set up a drying area, covered with newspaper. That’s where the completed butterflies can go to dry. Try creating some butterflies yourself, just so you’ll be more ready to help the children with their efforts.

Introduction:
“Today, we’re going to take a look at how the difficult things in our lives can help us to grow. That’s how it is when a butterfly is trying to come out of a cocoon. The difficulties are very important. To start us off, I’m going to read The Butterfly out loud. Afterwards, we will be each creating a butterfly to express our own learning through the difficulties and challenges we face.”

Opening Sharing:

 
 
 Cutting the folded construction paper into a
half-butterfly shape.
  
 
 Open butterfly with paint drips added.
(The antennea have also already been added
with a stapler.)
  
 
 Refolding and pressing until the paint squeezes
out of the sides.
  
 
 Gently opening the paper again to see the beautiful
design that came out.
  

“What’s something that hard that you’ve been through in your life and what’s one way it helped you to grow?”

Demonstration:
Step One:
Fold a piece of construction paper in half and cut, to create a half of a butterfly shape. Open the fold to see your butterfly. (Note: You might want to cut out butterfly shapes that could be used as patterns by anyone who’s nervous about making her butterfly shape.)

Step Two:
If you want to have antennea on your butterfly, punch holes to put them through. (It’s easier to do before the paint is added.)

Step Three:
Now use CrayPas to cover your butterfly with colors. Use colors that represent all the hard things you’ve been through. When you’re ready, choose puffy paints to represent all the ways you’re growing strong. Add them to your butterfly!

Step Four:
Now fold your butterfly in half with the paint inside. Press so that some of the paint squeezes out the edges. Then gently open it back up. See the beautiful shapes and colors of your butterfly!

Step Five:
Optional: You can scratch through the paint to add words or lines. You can also add glitter or sequins. Lay your butterfly down in the drying area.

Creation Time:
After the demonstration, encourage the women as they create. Encourage them to trust their gut feelings about what colors to choose. When their butterflies are complete, encourage them to write any thoughts that go with them.

  


  

Closing:
Save time at the end of the session to allow each participant to share her butterfly and what it means to her.


The Butterfly
Author Unknown

One day, a man was walking and found a butterfly still inside of its cocoon. He looked closer and saw that the butterfly was working very hard to fit its body through a tiny, tiny hole in the cocoon so it could get out and fly around. The man decided to help the butterfly. He used scissors to cut a bigger hole in the cocoon.

The butterfly was free from the cocoon and the man thought it would fly away quickly. But the butterfly could not fly. Its body was too swollen and its wings were too shriveled for flying. It was out of its cocoon, but this butterfly would never be able to fly.

Although man was trying to help by cutting the cocoon, he didn’t realize one very important thing about butterflies. Even though it is very hard work, pushing its body through that tiny, tiny hole in the cocoon helps make the butterfly strong enough to fly. All that hard work makes its body trim and its wings big and strong. The challenge of fitting through that tiny, tiny hole makes the butterfly able to fly.

We’re a lot like butterflies sometimes too. We need to work hard to get through the challenges we face. And, like the butterfly, once we work through them, we’re stronger too. If we didn’t have those challenges, we would never get any stronger.

I asked for Strength...and was given Challenges to make me stronger.
I asked for Love...and was given People to help with Kindness.
I asked for Riches...and was given Brain and Brawn to work.
I asked for Wisdom...and was given Problems to Solve.
Row.txt_description: Helps each participant find patience, compassion, and trust in facing the struggles and difficulties of her life's path. The end product is a reminder of why the struggle that sometimes accompanies growth is worth the pain.
Row.txt_notes: ER TO DO: CS needs to meld with newer version in conference handouts.

Row.txt_code:
As a victim, I was empty.  I functioned
instead of living.  I felt my inner self being
torn away.  I felt myself dying inside. 

As a survivor, my inner spirit shines again.
I’ve rediscovered my talents.  My experiences
no longer have the power to hurt me.  They are
now my “special gifts” that I share as tools of
empowerment. 



About This Workshop:
We gave the Power Masks workshop a little face-lift.  This workshop by Cheri Grenfell came out in the October 1998 Leader’s Update and it involves creating a mask of your face by pressing aluminum foil over your face and then painting it.  In trying this workshop, we found many participants had reservations about putting the aluminum over their faces.  Many had experienced their perpetrators using various items to try to suffocate them.  So we decided to change the workshop using balloons and a material called Celluclay.  Celluclay is similar to crushed newspaper and, like traditional paper mache, it is mixed with water and becomes a moldable paper clay.  This became a two-part workshop as it took time for the Celluclay to dry.  

In the first workshop, the women created faces using the balloons as their base.  Then when the clay was dry, we popped the balloons and in the second workshop we painted our masks.  It was truly an empowering experience for all. The masks were put on display in our group room and have touched all who have had an opportunity to see them.





As a victim I felt gray, I felt blue.  I cried bloody
tears.  My eyes were closing with desperation to
survive...

As a survivor I’m grasping from some air from
the darkness of my soul.  I can feel the other
side of me bursting out to be free.  The tears
are melting away...



Objective:
In this workshop, each participant creates a mask of her face and divides it in half, painting one side to represent her feelings as a victim and the other to represent her feelings as a survivor.  This workshop allows participants to express feelings caused by their abuse on the victim side of the mask.  By acknowledging and identifying their emotions, the participants can then move on to the positive feelings of self-love and personal empowerment on the survivor side of the mask.  The completed masks become a visual validation of the power of choice.      

Note to Leaders:
This is a powerful workshop, and because it summons up many buried feelings, we allow as much time as possible for the closing circle.

Materials:
Celluclay (one pound per five women.  Celluclay costs about $21 for a five pound bag that makes about 25-30 masks.)
Water
One large plastic bag
Bowls (at least three, to share among the group)
Round-shaped balloons
Shoe boxes (one per woman)
Old rags or old clothing
Paints and paint brushes
Newspaper to cover table(s)
Optional:  Water-based paper varnish (We use “Water-clean-up Poly Urethane for furniture and decoupage.”)




Roxanne Mayo-Turner and three women holding Power Masks at the
opening reception of the exhibit.




Timeframe:
Total: 2 hrs per workshop
10 min. Opening circle
10 min. Introduction
10 min. Relaxation
60 min. Mask-making
    (or Painting in the second workshop)
30 min. Closing circle

Space Setup:
Hand mix water with Celluclay (enough for all participants) in a plastic bag until it is a thick mushy consistency. (We found trash bags work well.)  Cover the table with plenty of newspaper and fill bowls with water for dipping fingers while molding faces.

Opening Circle:  
We usually open with a seemingly silly question such as, "If you could be a telephone, what kind would you be and why?" Or, "What kind of animal would you like to be today and why?" These questions not only relax the group, but also serve to get them into a creative, right-brained frame of mind. The participants never fail to astound me with their insightful, pertinent analogies.




As a victim I remember feeling
Sadness
Fearful
Afraid
Scared
Anger

As a survivor I am now
Happy
Laughing
Calm
Peaceful




Introduction:  
“Today, we are going to be making a mask with two sides: a victim side and a survivor side.  We will be working with Celluclay (show the pre-mixed clay).  To mold the Celluclay, we will each blow up a balloon to use as a base.  We’ll each blow up our balloons after the relaxation, and then anchor them in a shoebox with rags around the edges to hold them in place (show a sample and distribute the balloons and boxes).  After the Celluclay dries, we’ll be able to pop the balloon, leaving just our masks.  Then at our next workshop we’ll be able to paint our masks.”


Relaxation:
“This is your special time.  It is yours to create, rest, explore, and enjoy.  Today’s workshop is called Power Masks.  We will create these masks with two sides.  One will represent what we remember it felt like and how we saw ourselves as victims of abuse.  The other side will represent our feelings now and who we have become as survivors.  

“You may close your eyes now or leave them open, whichever is the most comfortable for you.  Begin taking deep, slow breaths.  

“As you inhale, I want you to focus on the weight of the air that fills and expands your chest.  Allow this air to absorb any heaviness that you may be carrying within from the past or tension of the day.  

“As you exhale, slowly, gently release the air.  Feel the lightness that comes from releasing the heaviness inside you.  Receive the peace that you’ve chosen to give yourself today as a survivor.  

“When you feel ready, you may pick up your balloon and begin using these same breaths to gently blow and fill your balloon to begin your mask.”

(When using the relaxation for the second workshop, I change the word “create” to “paint” and ask them to begin painting when they are ready.)





As a victim I felt confusion, anger, sadness,
depression, lost, fear

As a survivor I have peace, contentment,
and happiness



Creation:
Assist participants as they blow their balloons into their desired head shape, anchor them on their sides in the shoeboxes, and stuff clothes or rags around the edges. Encourage them as they focus on the various feelings they felt when they were abused and the feelings they feel now as survivors.  At our workshops, many participants used the ends of the paintbrushes to help create some facial features.  It’s important not to make the clay too thick, as the weight may pop balloon.  Some put holes through the sides so they would be able to hang them with string later.  Many participants were able to mold the Celluclay to reflect feelings of anger and sadness from the past.  Many felt they looked much different then too, and showed that in their creations.  

Closing Circle:
Allow time at the end of the group for everyone to share about their masks.  If they want to write down any thoughts they want to remember for the painting session, encourage them to do so.  Allow the masks to dry overnight. (The thinner the layers, the quicker it will dry.)

Part II:
As with Part I, Part II takes about two hours.  You can start again with an Opening Circle and then pop the balloons and get ready to paint.  You can use the same relaxation as you used in the first workshop to help participants reconnect with their feelings as victim and survivor as they begin to paint.   

When we did this project, we painted the masks in halves.  One half of the mask had colors that were representative of how we felt and things we experienced as victims.  The other half represented how we feel and see ourselves now as survivors.  We also wrote out our feelings to mount with our masks.  At the end, when the paint was dry, we applied a thin coat of paper varnish.  This added extra gloss and protection to the masks.  As with Part I of the workshop, it’s important to allow plenty of time at the end for each participant to share her mask and the feelings that go with it.
Row.txt_description: Participants create masks which allow them to express their feelings about being a victim and being a survivor. The completed masks becomes a visual reminder of the power of choice.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To decorate a matchbox and place positive self-messages inside.  This matchbox can symbolize each survivor learning to “light her own inner fire” to keep herself warm in her journey ahead.  This workshop gives each survivor a chance to reflect on finding ways to keep her own inner pilot light burning bright through all the surprises that are to come.





Completed Matchbox Inspirations box, “I will always remember my
heart is my own.”
Materials:















Mod-Podge
Small size box-type matchboxes (brand name: "Diamond")
Gesso (liquid)  (I think white paint can be substituted, but Gesso is best because it covers well.)
Brushes
Paint
Ribbons
Magazines
Tissue paper (assorted colors)
Paper for the inside of box (this can be any type of paper)
Scissors
Glue sticks
One wax candle
Optional (for variation):
Super Sculpey
Rollers (you can use anything as a rolling pin: circular-long pieces of wood, smooth glass cups, a smooth small plumbing pipe piece, or long glue stick.)





Accordion-folded paper, cut to fit
inside the matchbox.



Timeframe:
This workshop takes 1 1/2 hours

Opening Circle:  
Introduce all the participants and have them share the basics (name, how they are feeling that day, experience with art, and anything else they would like to share with the group).
Introduction:
Briefly explain the workshop (see Objectives, page 1).  This workshop is short with no time pressure, so let the women know they can do multiple boxes.


Creation:
Step One  
Preparing the Boxes:





Diamond brand matchboxes





Painting the matchbox with Gesso





Cutting slits in the drawer.





Ribbon tied through the
slits to make a loop.



Cover the matchboxes with paper or paint them with Gesso liquid.  This will cover the match-box surface and create a blank surface like a “canvas” upon which to create.  Several THIN coats of Gesso (3 coats) will be necessary.  Allow a few minutes time between coats.  This is the time to mention that they can "prepare" more boxes now if they are going to be doing more than one.
 
Step Two
Preparing the Message:
“While waiting for boxes to dry, think about the inspirational messages you want to have in your special box.  You could write ideas down on scratch paper just to see what comes to mind.  To create an accordion-style message in your box, you will need to measure the box (width and length).  Cut a long (8 inches or so) strip of paper in the same dimension as the ‘length’ of your box, and fold it ‘accordion style’ with the same dimension of the ‘width’ of the box.  This strip of paper is going to be tucked inside the box—so you have to make sure that it fits inside.  Once you have tried out that it fits, write your ‘inspiration’ message on it.  For now, put the message aside and continue working on the box.’”

Step Three
Decorating the Box:
“Cut out small pieces of tissue paper (several colors) in different shapes. You will be using these pieces as "paint" to decorate your box.  You can cut out small pictures and words from magazines. (Don't use the photo stock book pictures, as they are too thick to use here.)  Using the tissue paper and the cut out magazine pictures/words and start gluing them to the box with Mod-Podge.  You can also use paint to cover any empty space or to accent a particular piece of your box.”

Step Four
Finishing the Inside of Your Box:
“Adding a ribbon loop to the drawer of your box can create a nice special way to pull the little drawer out of the box.  As you are letting the outside of your box dry, take out the inside drawer and make two (2) small slits on the bottom of the box (close to the edge) with an Exacto knife.  Then put a small piece of ribbon through (this will be in loop form).  Tie the two ends together inside the box.  Glue one of the "accordion" panels from your "inspiration" message to the bottom of the box to cover the ribbon piece where you tied it and also to hold your "inspiration" message in place.”

Step Five
Putting it Together:
“Once the box cover has dried, you can place the inside part of the box back with the cover.  You will be using the ribbon loop to pull the inside part of the box out (and also to hang your box if you want to make it an ornament).  To make it easy to open and close the box, rub a little bit of wax from the candle on both sides of the inside part of the box.  Give your box a coat of Mod-Podge to protect the paint/art work and also to give it shine.”
 
Closing Circle:
Ask participants to share about their Match-Box Inspirations and welcome them to share the messages inside.




Tissue paper cut to paste onto box.





Box decorated with issue paper.
Row.txt_description: Gives each woman a chance to reflect on finding ways to keep her own inner light burning bright by decorating a matchbox and placing postitve messages inside.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create a variation based on Kesa's samples.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To draw the face of a clock and instead of numbers we will be decorating the face of the clock to represent how we want to be living our life. This workshop gives us as a chance to decide how we want to fill our time, whether it’s a 24-hour time , the next 12 weeks, or the next 12 months!

  


 
  
Materials:
Large white construction paper
Pencils
Colored pencils
Markers
Inspirational poem - "I'm Special" (click here for handout)
Inspirational poem - "The Paintbrush (click here for handout)
Inspirational poem - "Risks" (click here for a handout)

Timeframe:
This workshop takes approximately 1 1/2 hours


  


 
  

Opening Circle:
Have everyone share their name and talk about what their favorite clock looks like...i.e. grandfather clocks, cuckoo clocks, Big Ben, an hourglass, a clock radio, or any other kind of clock—let the imagination juices flow!

Introduction:
“Every day we’re faced with deadlines, agendas, and things we have to do, and always there’s not enough time. And sometimes we don’t even have a choice about how we fill our time. Today we get to design our own time frame. We get to boldly choose how we want to fill our time by designing our own clock. We will be drawing a clock, and on the face of the clock we will be able to draw whatever we want in our life. Instead of numbers on the face at the clock, we’ll be using words, small pictures, or designs of how we want to be living our life.
Before we start drawing, I will guide you through a relaxation, to help us all center our thoughts within. For some people, relaxing is difficult and might even feel uncomfortable, but I encourage you to just give it a try—you might even find that you enjoy it!”

Relaxation:
(Speaking slowly with a calm voice)


 
  
 
  This clock helps me remember that it's " ok" to simplify my life.

“So just take a deep breath and then gently let all the air out. If you are sitting, it’s good to sit with your back straight, your feet flat on the floor, and your hands lying loosely in your lap. And if it feels safe for you, you can gently close your eyes. Take another deep breath and begin to feel all the tension flowing out. As you concentrate on your breathing, realize this is a time for you, a very special time for you where you can let everything go, just for right now.

“Breathing in, you start to feel your body intuitively becoming more and more relaxed. Begin to visualize the clock of your choice in your mind... take a few moments to notice the shape of your clock. Is it a tall clock like a grandfather clock? Does it have graceful edges like a mantel clock? Perhaps your clock is just a large round wall clock. Go ahead and visualize all the details of your clock.

“Breathing in and out you notice your body becoming more deeply relaxed and the shape of your clock is becoming more and more clear.

“Now visualize the face of the clock and picture all the numbers gracefully flying away and notice that this is entirely your clock and your time. Begin to visualize exactly what you need on the face of your clock. Tap into the boldness within you and feel your adventurous spirit. Start to visualize the clock of your life. Perhaps words come to mind or certain colors or shapes.

“Now with your clock still imprinted in your mind, gently open your eyes and bring yourself back to the room and begin to draw the clock you just visualized.”

Creation:
With soft background music still playing... Let the creative juices flow!

Closing Circle:
Ask participants to share about their clocks and welcome them to share how it felt to design and personalize their time!
Row.txt_description: Gives a chance to decide how we want to fill our time by drawing the face of a clock and substituting words and/or images of how we want to spend our lives in place of numbers.

Row.txt_code:
Leaders’ workshop participant Curtis holds
up one finished Dream Holder she created and
one empty bowl ready to be worked on.
 
  
About this Workshop:
This workshop was inspired by what I saw one day at a craft fair. It was beautiful collage-work done on the inside of glass bowls and vases. Seen through the glass, the collage looks amazing. I experimented until I figured out how to create the effect. Magic Bubble Adhesive does the trick. It can create a very smooth, glassy, clear surface to collage into without creating brush strokes. This wonderful technique gives a very professional looking result.

Objective:
To express hopes and dreams in shapes, images, and colors. To explore new materials and techniques for collaging onto glass as each participant creates her own Dream Holder.

Note: This workshop can follow the "Match-Box Inspirations" workshop (March 2001 Update). That way the Dream Holders can be used to hold the matches from that workshop.


 
 
 Large Dream Holder bowl collaged
with a hummingbird.
  

Materials:
Small glass candle holders (Actually, glass bowls of any shape or size may be used as long as they have a smooth surface and no ridges.)
