Magic Bubble Adhesive (Found at Michael's Craft Store seasonally. If it’s out of season they may special order it, or you might be able to get some from us at AWBW or search for it on the web, one site currently selling Magic Bubble is www.craft-ware.com.)
Brushes (Thick kind.)
Water for rinsing brushes
Paper towels
Small paper plates (to use as palettes)
Gold paint (I suggest Delta Ceramcoat Gleams in “Metallic Kim Gold” color or “14K Gold” color.)


 
 
 “Honor Diversity” Dream Holder with
black paint (step 5).
  
 
 Dream Holder created with tissue paper
shapes and gold paint.
  

Optional: Other colors of Delta Ceramcoat (Black can look especially wonderful)
Tissue Paper (assorted colors)
Colored Pencils
Magazines with small images (But not photostock books. For this project, they are too thick. If you want to use images from photostock books, you can color copy them. Same with family photos—you can copy them for collaging.)
Scissors
Small “Brizzle Brush” (You can make one by taping a 1 inch piece of pipe cleaner onto a bamboo skewer and bending the pipe-cleaner—see photo page 3.)
Chopsticks (1 set per participant)
Exacto-Knife
Blow dryer (1 for every 2-3 participants, plus extension cords if needed)

Timeframe:
This workshop takes 2 hours

Opening Circle:
Have each person introduce themselves, sharing the basics (name, how they are feeling today, experience with art, and anything else they would like to share with the group).

Introduction:
“Today we are going to be creating Dream Holders.
I will share the basic steps with you, but you can experiment and go wild. Use it however you like. Remember, there is no right or wrong way. Whatever you create is just right.” Briefly explain the steps. It can help to show a sample. Make sure that it is understood that steps 1 and 2 (the preparation for the collaging) will take most of the time. Once they get to step 3, the pasting will go very quickly and the rest will be just drying time.

  


Pressing the images on with brizzle brush
(to create your own brizzle brush, tape a piece
of pipe cleaner onto a skewer).
 
 

 
Dream Holder created from a square glass bowl.
 
  

Step One: (Selecting items to collage)
“Look through the magazines and colored tissue paper thinking about your hopes and dreams. Cut out whatever you like. Remember the size of your glass, and cut the images so they’ll be small enough to fit. Cut pieces of tissue paper in different shapes and sizes to match your theme. Remember that you can cut tissue paper in the form of hearts, squares, triangles, squares, letters, etc. And, actually, you can do that with the magazine images too! Use the exacto knife when needed. Remember to think about the bottom of your glass. What image or shape do you want to place there?”
diagram of
the cuts

  
Step Two: (Preparing the items)
“Next you must make sure that each image can fit smoothly against the glass. To help larger images curve to the form of the glass, cut slits in the image. Cut slits toward the center of the image, like the spokes of a wheel (see mini-diagram above). This will make the picture very flexible so it can totally adhere to the surface of your container. Do a trial run and see how each picture will react once you try pressing it against the background. This is very important. Otherwise you’ll have air bubbles that will interfere with your design. Plan where your pictures and pieces of tissue will be pasted. You can also use colored pencils on the tissue paper or images. The colored pencil color will bleed, but it will give a watercolor effect.”

Step Three: (Collaging)
Note: Participants may need individual help as they get ready to start this step. It’s great if you can check their collage pieces and walk them through using the Magic Bubble Adhesive. “Once you are sure of where everything is going to go, put a tablespoon of the Magic Bubble Adhesive into your container and very softly brush it all over the inside of the container. Turn the container upside down across your two chopsticks (see below) to drain the excess. While the liquid is still wet, start pasting your pictures and tissue. Try not to touch the inside of the container. Use your “brizzle brush” (see photo page 3) to place and smooth your pictures into place. The Magic Bubble Adhesive dries very quickly. If you want to work more slowly, paint only a section at a time.”

Step Four: (Drying)
“Once all of your pieces are in place, use the hair dryer to help dry the liquid.”


 
 
 Using chopsticks to let
excess liquid drain.
  

Step Five: (Sealing the inside)
“The next step is to paint the inside of the container with gold paint. Paint THIN layers; allow time between layers. It can take about three layers to get the desired effect. If you like, other colors of paint can be used. Black can be especially striking. However, if you’ve used tissue paper, the black can seep into it and make it almost invisible. If you want to avoid this, you can paint gold or some other color behind the tissue paper shapes before applying the black. Once you finish the painting, your container is done. If you want, you can coat the paint with Mod Podge for protection and/or you could place a small piece of tissue to protect the inside from getting scratched over time. Wait a few days before placing items inside to allow time to totally dry.”

Closing Circle:
Ask the group to share about their Dream Holders and what their design means to them.

  


Dream Holder collaged and
ready for step 5.
 
  

 
Step 5: Painting black into the
Dream Holder.
Row.txt_description: Participants express hopes and dreams in shapes, images, and colors and explore new materials and techniques for collaging onto glass.
Row.txt_tips: The fish bowl looked good, but hard to work with. I would choose a bowl with a wider opening. With a wider opening, it would be easier to work inside the bowl.

Row.txt_code:
About this Workshop:
I wondered if it might be helpful to leaders to have a couple of short workshops they could use as warm-ups. These workshops are light, inspired, not too structured, and they don’t require a lot of setup. Most importantly, they can quickly serve to help draw out emotions and feelings.




“Treasure” drawing in progress.



Objective:
To allow participants to play together and discover their differences and similarities.  To establish rapport by enabling the group to use color, shapes, and lines to draw out feelings.  To allow them to enjoy the freedom of capturing a feeling on paper.

Note of Caution:
This kind of workshop can often be more difficult for participants who have been traumatized or have been chronically under stress. They may have learned not to listen to or honor their feelings. It’s important to have time to allow them the opportunity to express any difficulties they may have had with these exercises and to validate all feelings that come up for them.  

Materials:
Any and all drawing/painting materials such as colored pencils, crayons, watercolors, acrylics, wax crayons, pastels, charcoal pencils.
A variety of paper, including different sizes and weights.
Small objects brought in by leader (used in workshop 2).

Timeframe:
Any of these mini-workshops can run from 5 to 45 minutes.





“Feeling Picture” in progress.



Opening Circle:  
Have each person introduce themselves, sharing the basics (name, how they are feeling today, experience with art, and anything else they would like to share with the group).

Introduction:
“Today we will be doing a couple of exercises which aren’t very long or complicated, but which I hope will be fun.  I really don’t want you to worry about not knowing how to do art or making it perfect or doing it right. This is about expressing your feelings through art, and there is no right or wrong.”  





Relaxation with hands on chest.



Relaxation:
“Close your eyes and start to focus in on your breath.  Relax into the rhythm.  You may want to put a hand on your chest or abdomen to feel the rise and fall as your breath enters, then leaves.  Let your thoughts come and go.  If you feel like your mind is too busy,  go back to the breath.  The simple rhythm—one breath in, one breath out—can be like a lullaby to your spirit.  I want you to remember a feeling, a feeling that you experience when you are doing something that you love.  Take your time.  It could be hugging your child, looking at the stars, listening to your favorite music or reading a book.  Experience that feeling.  Let it wash over you.  Where is it living in your body?  Is it curling up your toes?  Fluttering in your stomach?  Tugging at the corners of your mouth?  Does it swirl, float, or drip inside of you?  Is it moving fast, or spreading slow?  What temperature is it?  Is it like waves?  Or tiny ripples?  Is it one long swell or little bursts?  What color is it?  Is it a drumbeat?  Piano? Trumpet?  Let the feeling fill you.”

Mini-Workshop #1: “Feeling Picture”
The introduction can lead right into this workshop.  Each participant chooses a piece of paper and places it in front of her.  They can then choose what medium they want to use—whether pastels, colored pencils, crayons, watercolors, acrylics, etc.  The leader explains that they have a time period (the shorter the interval, the less time participants have to over-think about what they’re doing) to create a drawing of the feeling they were experiencing during the introduction.  They can also choose to put a word to the feeling and write it on the paper.  At the end of this the group can share, if they wish, how it felt to make their drawing and what feeling is represented in the drawing.




Pulling treasure out of surprise bag.




Or another variation might be a “Group Feeling Picture” where everyone adds to the same piece of paper, one at a time, very spontaneously and quickly.  Start with one participant sharing a word associated with a feeling that is important for her in that moment. It could be anything from “love,” “trust,” “light,” or “power.” She shares the word with the group and starts the drawing.  She could start it as simply as putting a drop of color or a line or a shape on the page.  The others wait for her to finish (again, set a time limit—something like 45 seconds to a minute is good).  Then she passes it on to the participant next to her.  The group can choose to pass it around as many times as they wish.  At the end, there is one completed drawing to which all have contributed. They can then share their feelings about what the word meant to them, what feelings it brought up in them, and how it came out in the drawing.

Mini-Workshop #2: “Treasures”
The art leader brings in a variety of small objects or “treasures” in a bag.  These could include something like a flower, rock, piece of music, photograph, or piece of clothing.  The leader passes the bag around with each participant reaching in to grab her “treasure.”  The leader then gives the women time to absorb the object (a couple of minutes) before asking them to draw or write what feelings the object brings up in them. It’s important to let them know that this exercise isn’t about drawing what the object looks like, but rather what it feels like to them. When they are finished, participants can share their drawings and how it felt to express themselves in this way.

Or a playful variation on this might be “Blind Treasure Drawing.”  The leader could choose one object and have participants close their eyes and pass it around.  Having the eyes closed could be very uncomfortable for some, so make sure they know this is something voluntary.  The leader could encourage them to explore the object with their senses and see what they can learn and say about it without using their eyes.  What does it feel like in their hands?  Is it cool, hot, smooth, rough, heavy, light, etc?  Is it wet or dry?  Does it have an odor?  Does it make a sound when touched?  (Sharing the exploration out loud can help everyone since sitting with your eyes closed in silence can be too difficult.)  After the object goes all the way around the circle, the leader hides it and lets the group know they can open their eyes.  Participants then create a drawing of what they experienced as they held the object in their hands.  It’s always fun for the women to see what they were holding after the exercise is over and to compare/contrast drawings.

Mini-Workshop #3: “Inner Self-Portrait”
Have participants draw the way they feel.  You might explain it as a picture of the way each of them would look if people could see inside of them.  What colors are there?  Is there one main color or lots of different colors?  Is it dark or light?  Can they see shapes?  Are they still or moving?  Are the colors and shapes bold or muted?  Sharp or soft?  Is it quiet or loud?  What kind of sounds are there?  Participants can then share their portraits with each other.





Holding “Treasure” with eyes closed.



Or another variation might be “Partner Portraits”.  Participants could pair off and draw inner portraits of each other.  They could ask questions (like the ones above) and then use shapes and colors to draw how their partner is feeling.  Participants can then share these portraits with their partner.  Note: This could be too intimate or invasive for some and would probably work best with those who have spent time with each other and have gained some trust.  If they know each other very well, then they could try doing inner portraits without talking out loud.  It could be a special challenge and surprise to see what they can feel or sense from their partner without talking—allowing time for each to absorb facial expressions, the feeling in the eyes and body posture.

Closing:
Be sure to save time to allow them the opportunity to express any difficulties they may have had with these exercises and to validate all feelings that came up for them.
Row.txt_description: Several short workshops ideas which allow participants to enjoy the freedom of expressing their feelings using drawing and painting. These workshops don't require a lot of setup and can quickly serve to help draw out emotions.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To help participants find their own voices and live their own lives through insights gained by journal writing.

Materials:
A pen, yellow highlighter, and journal for each person
Box of tissues, wat ch, timer, relaxing music (optional)
Handouts of “Beginnings,” “Privacy and Protection,” and “More Writing Exercises” (in English and Spanish as needed).
Timeframe:
Total: 90 Minutes
Introduction and agenda: 5 min.
Check-in: 10 min.
Game: 10 min.
First writing exercise & sharing: 25 min.
Second writing exercise & sharing: 20 min.
Review of privacy issues and other journal writing exercises: 5 min.
Closing circle: 10 min.
Feedback form: 5 min.
Note: Depending on how many people share their work you may only have time for one writing exercise.



Preparation Before Workshop:  
Before leading the workshop, try the free flow form in the writing exercises listed. What issues come up? What have you learned?

Introduction and Agenda:
“Journal writing enables us to find our true voices, beyond what our families, schools, religions, and laws dictate is true. As we release feelings, explore contradictions, and clarify goals, questions float to the surface. What words did we leave unspoken? Why did we not say them? Who are we beneath our masks? Journal writing takes us deeply into ourselves to find the answers. It serves as a sanctuary from the troubled world and as a place to write our troubles down. It serves as a meditative practice and as a place to reflect upon the world at large. Through the cries, complaints, shouts, sighs, prayers, and affirmations that flow in our journals, truths emerge. We find the words we’ve longed to say. As our words are voiced, we speak up for ourselves and speak out for others. 

  


  

“Today we’ll use an intuitive form of journal writing to find our own true voices. There is no wrong way to do this workshop and no prior experience is required. Whatever you write is fine; it doesn’t matter how it sounds to others. You aren’t here to meet anyone’s needs but your own. Don’t worry about spelling or grammar, but it’s nice if you write legibly so you can read what you wrote! And it’s good to date each journal entry for future reference.

“We’ll start with a check-in followed by a game, writing exercises, sharing work if you’re comfortable, a review of privacy issues and different writing styles, a closing circle, and feedback forms.”  

Check-in:
“Can we agree that everything said during this workshop remains confidential?”
(Look around to make sure everyone is in agreement.)

“Let’s go around and briefly say what you’d like us to know about yourself. Also, what would you like to learn from this workshop?”  

Game:
“Intuitive or free flow journal writing is when you write continuously without stopping to correct spelling, edit, or judge. The idea is to release distracting surface thoughts so deeper layers can emerge. Here’s a game to demonstrate the free flow form. The lead person says one word and then the next person says another one, whatever comes to mind, until everybody has said one word. If our words sound all mixed-up it’s fine! That’s the free flow, anything-goes form.” (Begin the word game). “Next, the lead person says one sentence and then the next person says another one, whatever comes to mind, until everybody has said one sentence. For example: 1st person—“I hope everybody likes me.”  2nd person—“I don’t understand what this exercise is about.”  3rd person—“There was terrible traffic on the 405 freeway.” (Begin the sentence game).
It’s best if the rounds go quickly. Encourage participants to look around the room if they need inspiration and say a word or sentence about something they see.

First Exercise with Sharing:
“There are several options for our first writing exercise based on the same free flow form. One option is to write on, ‘I am wonderful and amazing because…’. Another option is “The best thing in my life right now is…”. You can also write about anything else that feels important, but remember if you choose a serious topic strong emotions may arise. Please write the options down and chose one. As you write, release silly, irrelevant, or petty thoughts by putting them down on paper as you think of them and keep on returning to the option you chose. Insights will emerge when there is room for them to surface. Let’s work for ten minutes; try to keep writing the entire time.” (Wait ten minutes). “Please finish your sentence and stop for now. Reread your writing and highlight any words or phrases that seem interesting, strange, or important. Write for five more minutes on something you highlighted. This will deepen your work.”  (Wait five minutes).
Note: I don’t usually write during the exercise so I am emotionally available. If you notice someone has stopped writing you can approach her quietly to offer support.



Sharing:
“Who would like to share all or part of what you wrote? You can also ask someone else to read your entry for you or pass completely.” Don’t worry if no one wants to share. If they do share, thank each person after they read their work.
It takes a lot of courage. Let participants cry if they need to without interruption. They may have waited years to be able to release repressed emotions. Be with them in spirit and heart. Offer tissues in silent support.”

Second Exercise with Sharing:
“Here’s another way to choose something to write about. Close your eyes and relax your body with your journal in your hands or on your lap. Take a deep breath or two. Feel your jaw and eyes soften, let your throat relax, shoulders are loose and free. Feel your whole body sink into your chair, into the earth. Invite in an image of something that would be positive for you to write about right now. Don’t censor! If you choose not to write on your image that’s fine. Just let the image reveal itself and when you have one, come back into your body by wiggling your fingers and toes. Then open your eyes. Options include writing about something that happened in the past week and how you felt about it, or choosing another topic altogether. You are in control. Let’s begin.” (Wait ten minutes). “Reread your work and highlight words or phrases that pop out at you just like in the previous exercise. Write for five more minutes.” (Time permitting).  

Sharing:
Same instructions as before. An option is for the participants to talk about the journal writing process instead of what they wrote.

Privacy and Protection:  
“Thank you all for sharing. It takes a lot of courage. The following suggestions help create a safe and nurturing writing environment. Let’s review them together.”
(Read them out loud).
1. You may want to have a well-defined boundary to help you feel more in control. For instance, only write for ten minutes or three pages and then stop.
2. If you’re writing about something traumatic, you might want to meditate beforehand, be aware of body tension as you write, and plan a rewarding walk or bath for afterwards.
3. If you want to read certain pages only when someone is available to help you, fold the pages to alert yourself not to read them on your own. This can also serve as a bookmark to show the pages to your therapist if you have one.
4. Deliberately close your journal and leave the feelings inside.
5. Keep your journal closed and stored in a private place.
6. If you are living with an abusive person, hide your journal well or tear out relevant pages. This is important advice to those who will, unfortunately, return to an abusive home.

Other Journal Writing Exercises:
“Here are a few other writing exercises to try out on your own.” (Read them out loud).
1. Write lists of things that irritate you, beliefs that you have disregarded, short term and long term goals, or blessings in your life.
2. Write about yourself in third person (she said she was sorry instead of I said I was sorry). This will help you create distance from your feelings if necessary.
3. Write a letter to someone with no intention of sending it, just to release your feelings.
4. Write a dialogue with some event (like a lost job), person (friend or foe), or body part (my big belly) by giving it a voice that responds to yours, sentence by sentence.
5. Add drawings, photos, or stickers to personalize your journal.

Closing Circle:
“It’s time to close our workshop. Would everybody please stand? This is a call-and-response exercise based on the African American tradition. One person at a time calls out, ‘My voice is important because...’ and finishes the sentence. For example: ‘My voice is important because it’s time to be heard.’ The group responds to her by saying words of support such as, ‘Yes it is, You’re great’ or whatever comes to mind. Each participant offers her own unique response at the same time, just like baseball fans shouting out their individual responses, all at the same time, when someone hits a home run. Example: first participant calls out, ‘My voice is important because I have important things to say.’ Group responds to her, all at the same time. One participant says, ‘Yes, it is.’ Another says, ‘I believe in you!’ Another says, ‘Hallelujah!’ second participant calls out: ‘My voice is important because I’m tired of being silenced.’ Group members respond to her, all at the same time. One says, ‘You can do it!’ Another says, ‘You inspire me!’ Another says, ‘You’re amazing!’ Repeat until every participant has said why her voice is important.

Feedback Forms:  
Hand out feedback forms for workshop participants to fill out.  Enjoy your successes and learn from your mistakes by reviewing these forms after class.

Acknowledgments:
Many ideas and techniques in this workshop are from the following wonderful books: Way of the Journal by Kathleen Adams, A Voice of Her Own by Marlene Schiwy, The Artist’s Way by Julia Cameron, and The New Diary by Tristine Rainer.  You may want to read them!
Row.txt_description: Helps participants find their own voices and gain insights through journal writing.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for Teens.

Row.txt_code:
During the Closing Circle, participants have an
opportunity to symbolically and literally let their
burdens go.  


Objective:
This workshop is about freeing ourselves from experiences we carry that may have become burdens and obstacles to living completely and giving and receiving love. During the warm-up the participants will think of something they would like to be rid of and then write or draw it out on the inside of a grocery bag. I like grocery bags because they have an inside and because they are universally expendable—there is no pressure to be “artistic.” The act of cutting the bag open acts as a metaphor for accessing hard to reach feelings on difficult subjects.

About Creating Safety: 
To make sure things go well, please consider these safety issues:
1. Think about your group: 
Working on experiences from the past can be difficult and requires adequate safety and support.  Try this workshop only if you feel that you and your group are ready for this kind of work.  Also, feel free to change, adjust, or adapt the workshop as necessary to fit the needs of your group.
2. “Letting go” is voluntary:





A candle can help mark the
creation of safety.



Make clear that participation is voluntary.  Also, let the group know that they don’t have to “let go” of anything they aren’t ready to let go of.  Reassure them that we all put up our walls for a reason and they have served us well.  These walls help us survive.  We can honor them and thank them for the work they have done.  We don’t have to let them go before we’re really ready.
3. Light a candle:
One way an individual or a group can create a special sense of safety is to light a candle symbolizing protection.  When the candle is lit, it is safe to explore feelings that might be scary.  At the end, blowing the candle out symbolizes that we are done exploring and are coming back into our everyday selves.  (Special thanks to Kesa Kivel for sharing this added safety feature at her Journal Writing Workshop—see July 2001 Update.)





Brown grocery bag, cut open.



Materials:
Brown grocery bag, handle optional (1 per participant)
Scissors (1 per participant)
Markers
Tape and/or rubber-bands
Candle
Garbage can

Timeframe: 1 hour
Opening circle:       5 minutes
Introduction:           5 minutes
Relaxation:           5 minutes
Writing on the bags:       25 minutes
Releasing the burdens:   5 minutes
Closing circle:           15 minutes

Space Setup/Prep:  
Light a candle and place it where everyone can see it. Have a bag cut open and lying flat on the table as an example. At each place there should be a folded, uncut bag, scissors, and markers within reach.

Opening Circle:
“Share one thing that feels like it’s weighing you down today and
one thing that lifts your spirits - no matter how large or small.”

Introduction:
“This is a window of time to rid ourselves of emotions that block us from having the freedom to be ourselves. It is a time to explore letting down walls we have put up, creating space for growth, and the giving and receiving of love.  As we explore letting go of these walls, let’s try not to be hard on ourselves for having them.  They’ve served us well.  They are nothing to be embarassed about.”

Relaxation:
Have the participants open their bags and place them on the floor beside their chair. Have them notice how much room there is inside their bag, how much a bag can hold.




Writing onto the bag.




Ask them to sit comfortably and close their eyes or watch the candle flame. Then spend a few minutes on the following relaxation, encouraging stillness: “Take a deep breath and release it. Take another and notice if you feel that you could be breathing more easily. What are you carrying? Notice if there is something in the way, a block. Today we are going to look at our inner obstacles. We are going to see what we are carrying inside. Think of something you have been carrying, an experience that has been living inside you, using your energy. Trust your instincts, if something immediately came to mind know that this is the thing you can release today.

“Examine your obstacle, notice how long it has been weighing you down, and how draining it is to always have it inside. Pick it up and hold it in your mind. Imagine your hands holding it. Notice how heavy it is, it might take two hands to hold it. It might take all of your strength.

“Imagine using your strength to pick up your obstacle and drop it inside the bag next to you. Imagine letting go of this heavy, heavy burden. See yourself opening your hands and releasing it. Notice how light you feel, how open you are, notice the room that you have created inside yourself. Take a deep breath and notice how much more deeply you can breathe now.

“When you are ready pick up your scissors and cut open the bag so that it lies flat, but in one piece.”

Writing on Bags:
“Choose a marker(s) and if you wish begin by reminding yourself by writing (or saying), I can write anything here. No one will read this. I can put down my fear, I can put down my sadness, I can put down my anger. This is a safe place...





Preparing to let go, folding up the words.



“Now choose a marker(s) and write or draw anything that will help you to rid yourself of the experience on the inside of the bag. Write down any thoughts you have about this burden, write why you haven't let it go, why you've held onto it, and why are you deciding to let it go now. Release what you have been carrying anger, tears, sadness - feel free to use expressive language, the goal is to let go, you are safe to write the things you would never say.”

A Place for Future Thoughts:
“You might want to draw a circle somewhere on your bag and write around or next to it, ‘This space is for anything I might remember later, this space holds all future thoughts about this burden.’ This way, should feelings come up about this experience when the workshop is over, you do not have to carry them. You already have a symbolic place for them. You can be rid of them immediately and are not limited by the end of the bag or by the end of the workshop.”




Creating a circle for future thoughts.



Preparing to Let Go:
When finished, the bags can be prepared for the “letting go” closing circle.  Participants can choose whatever process feels right to them.  They can tear the bag up, roll it up (see illustration at left), or crumple it up.  They can seal it with tape or bind it with rubber bands (see page 4).  Whatever feels most satisfying for each woman is the best way to go.  If they bind it into a ball shape, the experience can be released with a sense of wholeness and completion when the ball is literally released in the closing circle.


Closing/Letting Go Circle:
When everyone has taped or bound their burden ask someone who appears ready, “Would you like to let that burden go?” Walk each participant to the garbage can, and have her stand with her back to the garbage can holding her burden behind her. After taking a deep breath have her let it go. After everyone has released their burden and is seated ask if anyone would like to share how it felt writing and releasing their burdens.




Taping up the burden.




Rubberbanding the burden.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants the opportunity to free themselves from experiences they may carry that have become burdens and obstacles to living completely and giving and receiving love. End product is a feeling of weightlessness.

Row.txt_code:
Feather pattern
(see attached
for master).


About this Workshop:
This workshop was adapted from an e-mail story we received via Denise Nyby who coordinates the Windows Programs in Redding, CA.  As with many internet inspirational thoughts, the message was anonymous.  We thank Denise for sending it to us and hope you and your groups will enjoy it!

Objective:
To give each participant an opportunity to identify the “storms” she is facing in her life, choose the perspective she wants to hold through it, and create a beautiful visual reminder to carry with her as she rises above these “storms.”

Materials:
Clear plastic wrap
Aluminum foil
Scotch tape
Copies of the feather pattern (1 per participant. See attached master copy)
Assorted permanent markers
Scissors
Glue sticks





Finished feather next to the original blank pattern.



Timeframe: 1 1/2 hours
Story/Opening circle:    15 minutes
Demonstration:       5 minutes
Relaxation:           5 minutes
Creating Feathers:       50 minutes
Closing circle:           15 minutes

Finding Markers:
Be sure to look for permanent markers in advance.  You may have enough around the office or you may need to purchase some. It’s good to have one black marker per participant since they may all be starting with black at the same time.  With other colors you don’t need one per person.  Just make sure you have a good assortment and enough to share.  (Staples sells sets of assorted colors and sets of black markers).  

If you purchase markers, hold onto them for holidays.  This project is a great way of making ornaments for all sorts of occasions.  Just use a different shape (instead of a feather).
 
Preparation Ideas:
Create a sample in advance, so you know what it looks like.  It’s exciting to try it out!    

Opening Circle:
“Today we are going to begin with a story about eagles.  I’ll read you the story (see left column) and then for our opening circle, we can each share anything it means to us or anything about how we’re doing today.”  (Read the story and listen to each person’s reflections.)

Introduction:
“For our project today, we will be creating our own eagle’s feather.  This project is a chance to notice the storms you are facing in your life and also to notice the beliefs and strength you want to find in yourself to help you use the winds of the storm to lift you high above it.  These beliefs and strengths are part of your eagle’s feather.”

Technical Info:
Prepare your supplies so you can do a quick demonstation of the process.  See “Creation Steps”.  Be sure to distribute the supplies before you start the relaxation.  That way, once the relaxation begins there’s no more explaining to do.  Each participant can simply follow her own intuition and create.

Creation Steps:
Step 1: Tape the feather pattern onto the table:


Step 2: Tape a piece of plastic plastic wrap over the feather pattern:


Step 3: Color with permanent markers (use black to trace the lines and bright colors to fill in):


Step 4: Crumble a piece of square tin foil, then flatten it back out again (or try leaving it smooth—some women may prefer the smooth effect):


Step 5: Once your foil is ready, use the glue stick to cover the back of your plastic wrap drawing with glue:


Step 6: Place the pplastic wrap onto the tin foil and gently press so the glue holds it together:


Step 7: Cut out the feather.  Be especially careful when cutting the narrowest end of the feather (the quill).  Once cut, the feather can be bent, cut or molded further:


Step 8: On the back of your feather, add words that go with your feather.  Include the date if you like.  (You may need to smooth out parts of the foil to write.):


Relaxation:
Play relaxing music as you lead the following: “Get comfortable in your chair.  Make sure your feet are securely resting on the floor, and your arms are comfortably in your lap.  Let your eyes close if you feel comfortable closing them.  Now take a deep breath in.  Hold it for a moment, and as you let it out imagine releasing any tension you are carrying from the day.  Take another deep breath in, and again release with it any tension you’ve been carrying.  Notice your body becoming more relaxed as you take another breath in...  and release...  As you take another deep breath and release it, imagine you are releasing any storms and turmoil you’ve been facing and feeling.  Imagine that with each breath you take you are finding calm and clarity, and with each breath you release, you are rising higher above any storms, able to find more peace and serenity.  Take as many breaths as you wish.  And whenever you are ready, you can open your eyes and begin creating your feather.”

Creation:
After the relaxation, the participants can begin to create their feathers.  It’s fine for each one to make as many feathers as she wants.  Encourage and support each participant individually.  

Closing Circle:
Give each participant an opportunity to share her creation(s) and any feelings that came up during the workshop.  Congratulate and validate them for their courage and their creations.

--------------------------------------------

Eagles in a Storm
-anonymous via the internet

Did you know that an eagle knows when a storm is approaching long before it breaks?  The eagle will fly to some high spot and wait for the winds to come.  When the storm hits, it sets its wings so that the wind will pick it up and lift it above the storm.  While the storm rages below, the eagle is soaring above it.

The eagle does not escape the storm.  It simply uses the storm to lift it higher.  It rises on the winds that bring the storm.

When the storms of life come upon us—and all of us will experience them—we can rise above them by setting our minds and our belief toward that which is deepest in our hearts: our sources of clarity and strength.  The storms do not have to overcome us.  We can focus on that which lifts us above them. 

We can find the clarity and strength to ride the winds of the storm that bring sickness, tragedy, failure, and disappointment in our lives.  We can soar above the storm. 

Remember, it is not the burdens of life that weigh us down, it is how we handle them.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants an opportunity to identify the "storms" faced in their lives, and choose the perspective they would like to hold through them. End product is a beautiful visual reminder to rise above the "storms."

Row.txt_code:
A Tunnel Book by a Joyful Heart participant.
 
  
About this Workshop:
This workshop was adapted from the Children’s Windows Program by Dolores Sanico. She wanted to make sure to put this captivating project into the hands of all of you Women’s Windows Leaders. Enjoy! It may become one of your favorites!

Objective:
To help participants get in touch with their feelings and express them in a safe way. This workshop can really help us understand the feelings we keep inside and the feelings we show on the outside.

Materials:
Picture frame mats 8 1/2 x 11 (3 per person)
Construction paper (4 pieces per person, folded so there are 8 sections—like an accordion.)
Magazines to cut out
Paper for free-hand drawing
Markers
Glue sticks
Scissors


 
 
 Some Tunnel Book supplies: scissors, glue, picture frame
mats, and accordion-folded paper.
  

Timeframe: 1 1/2 hours
Opening circle: 10 minutes
Demonstration: 5 minutes
Relaxation: 5 minutes
Creation: 60 minutes
Closing circle: 10 minutes

Setup:
Arrange the picture frame mats, construction paper, glue, scissors, and magazines so they are accessible to all.

Preparation Ideas:
Be sure to make a sample in advance so you know how the project works and the group can catch onto the construction process more easily. One simple trick for folding like an accordion is to fold in half, then in half, and in half again, so you have a 1-inch wide band. Then unfold, and refold (like a fan), using the creases as your guide.

  


Completed Tunnel Book by Joyful Heart participant.
 
 

Opening Circle:
“Today we’ll be making Tunnel Books. It’s a chance to explore all the different parts of ourselves—the ones we keep on the inside, the ones we show on the outside, and all the ones in between. You could also use your tunnel to show your journey into the future or whatever you want it to show. There’s no right or wrong way. Let’s start with a check-in circle. Share something you showed on the outside today and something you kept on the inside.”

Demonstration:
Share a sample Tunnel Books and the steps of creating it. Before you do the relaxation, have everyone pick their mats and construction paper.


 
 
 
 
  
 
  

Step 1: Glue the folded construction paper to the three picture frame mats on each side to make a tunnel with the construction paper forming the sides of the tunnel. You now have a tunnel-like construction and should be able to see directly through the mat frames.

Step 2: Select an image to put at the back—the end of your tunnel. Make sure this back image is large enough to fill in the space of the mat frame, like a picture in a frame.

Step 3: Cut and arrange images by gluing them onto the mats. The front mat is for images that respresent the “you” on the outside that you share with the world. Images on the insides of the ‘tunnel’ are for the things about yourself that you keep hidden—the real hidden inside you. You can paste them to the edges of the mat frames or to the folds of construction paper.

Relaxation:
Once everyone has selected some materials, play relaxing music and lead your favorite breathing relaxation. A possible relaxation: “Take a deep breath in. Hold it for a moment, and now let it go... Now take another deep breath in. Imagine that each breath is a wave of pure relaxation, washing over you. Take another deep breath in. As you let it go, feel it washing over you, from you face down to your toes. Each breath you take, imagine the relaxation washing over you, from head to toe, all the tension draining into the ground below you, leaving you calm and refreshed. When you are ready, open your eyes and begin to create your Tunnel Book.”

  



 

 
  

When you’re done, you’ll have a visual tunnel going from your outside self (in front) to your inside self (inside the tunnel).

Closing Circle:
Gather around to share the Tunnel Books. If the group is comfortable, they can share feelings that they hold inside. Remind them that this is a safe place to share feelings and all feelings are okay.


 
 
 Adding images to the Tunnel Book.
  
 
 Windows Leader Obbie Brown,
with her Tunnel Book.
Row.txt_description: Helps participants get in touch with their feelings and express them in a safe way. Can really help us understand the feelings we keep inside and the feelings we show on the outside.

Row.txt_code:
Mandala from The Picture of Health, Healing Your
Life With Art, a book by Lucia Capacchione.  “In this
mandala, we see various aspects of a woman’s life.
The outer ring evidences ‘suffering,’ the middle rings
show ‘understanding’ and ‘letting be,’ while the
center design indicates ‘peacefulness.’”


Objective:
To give each participant an opportunity to create a personal shield that symbolizes her power—abilities and strengths she has and/or hopes to have.  To provide a way for each participant to notice the variety of tools she uses to operate in our world and cope with the things around her (i.e. stress, work, relationships, family, children, spirituality, etc.).  To explore the difference between inner and outer strengths.  To notice the kind of boundaries one has or needs to have.

Materials:
Cardboard pizza rounds (16”) (Found at restaurant supply stores, i.e. Smart & Final)
Drawing paper (plain, colored)
Image books (magazines, photo stock books)
Drawing tools (Cray-Pas, chalk pastels, pencils)
Painting tools (watercolors, acrylics, tempera paints, brushes, water containers)
Tissue paper
Glue guns, glue sticks, Elmer’s Glue
Glitter, shells, feathers, nature items, beads, yarns, fabric
Scissors
Relaxing music
Optional:  Kilz paint for preparing the surface of the rounds in advance
Note:  Use fewer materials for a less experienced group.  It may be too daunting to have lots of choices. 




“Home is where my heart is; from it comes
spiritual, love, creativity, sharing, giving,
etc.”

(Mandala from The Picture of Health,
Healing Your Life With Art, a book by
Lucia Capacchione.)



Time Needed:
I recommend a minimum of 3 hours, but I prefer offering it in 3-4 sessions.  That gives the participants the opportunity to recognize and honor their strengths and abilities through the process and within the group.    Working with the large, 16-inch pizza rounds can take a long time, but creates a powerful, life-sized shield in relation to the size of the person.  For me, it’s not a process that I would offer for only one session with participants who have been battered or others who are dealing with great pain or injury.  

Depending upon your group you could have a variety of topics to offer for discussion related to personal power.  Some of related themes could be: beliefs of what power means; abilities in communication, interaction, personal care, child care, personal relationships, family, etc.; career, spiritual beliefs, education, personal experience, and physical and mental abilities.  As facilitators you can take your lead from what the group speaks of or asks about.  An initial discussion of the word “power” may be helpful.  Such topics will probably be brought up in conversation, imagery, or metaphor throughout this AWBW process.

If you are trying this project in a one-time workshop, try simplifying the process by working on smaller-sized rounds and limiting art supplies by using only one or two types of materials/tools. (For example, try smaller rounds and use only Cray-Pas on them.  Or use thick paper instead of rounds.)  You will not end up with life-sized shields, but will still have a very valuable creative process.  It’s important to make the creation part short enough to allow plenty of time for the women to share and process their feelings.





“This mandala shows a week in her life.  Each piece of the circle represents one day of the week and portrays her feelings through brightly colored abstract designs.  The center of the mandala contains an eye looking out and observing life.”

(Mandala from The Picture of Health, Healing Your Life With Art, a book by Lucia Capacchione.)



Setup:
Using a 16-inch round requires a bit of space for each participant.  Be sure to take this into account when planning and setting up.   

Preparation Ideas:
For those facilitators that have enough time, the pizza rounds can be painted before hand to aid the process. I use Kilz paint (used to cover up mildew or anything on walls) to paint the brown side of the round. The Kilz surface is good for drawing and gluing. It gives a basic white background which some may prefer to start with.  

Introduction:
“Today we are going to be exploring our personal power, creating a shield that symbolizes our strengths and abilities that we use to interact with ourselves, other people, and the environment around us.  We will use these pizza rounds as the base for our shields.  

“One side of your round can become the outside of your shield—the side that people out in the world usually see when they look at you. These are aspects of your strengths, abilities, and tools that you use as you interact in the world.   It’s okay to include tools and ways of coping that you hope to change and grow beyond (like yelling at our kids, eating too much, dependency, using alcohol or drugs, etc.).  Your shield can include imperfection, reality, and transition.  You can also include aspects that you are working on or hope to have someday.  

“The other side of your shield can become the inside—the side that few people see, only you and maybe those who are closest to you.  Only those closest to you might know of these strengths and abilities.  These may be strengths that you might want or need to keep to yourself.  These may be strengths that you’ve kept hidden for a long time.  They may be strengths your heart has been yearning to see and share.

“Since the shield is round, you could work as a mandala, starting in the center and creating circles around and around the center, representing your strengths.  You can work with you shield in any way you wish.  
These directions are only offerings and possibilities. Just follow your heart, your intuition, your gut feelings, and what is created will be just right.”

Opening Circle:
“Share one tool or ability that you feel proud of using in your life right now, share one tool or ability that you hope to let go of, and share one tool or ability you hope to have in the future.”  Or  “Share your thoughts about what the word power means to you.”




Cover of The Picture of Health, Healing
Your Life With Art, by Lucia Capacchione.




Relaxation:
“Get comfortable in your chair.  Let your eyes close if you feel comfortable letting them close.  And take a deep breath in.  As you breath in, imagine that you are drawing air up from the ground, through your feet, through your legs, through your whole body.  Take another deep breath in, and imagine bringing the air up through the earth beneath you.  And as you breath out, imagine that you are releasing all the tension and stress from your body.  Imagine it flowing out through your mouth.  You are like a fountain, drawing the air up from the ground and letting it flow out through your mouth.  The air is coming up from the ground, through you, cleansing your whole body as you let it out through your mouth.  Wonderful!  Notice yourself becoming more and more relaxed.  Letting all that’s stuck inside of you just flow out with your breath.  

“And now as you notice yourself becoming free, releasing all that was held inside, begin to notice the strength and clarity inside of you.  As you breathe out, imagine that you are breathing out your wonderful, powerful energy.  Your personal power and strength shows more and more with each breath.  As you breathe in and out, notice your sense of personal power.  What are your strengths?  What do you appreciate about yourself?  Notice the strength of your power to choose.  Notice the strength of your power to rest.  Notice the strength of your power to say ‘no.’  Notice the strength of your love.  Notice the strength of your courage.  Notice all of the powers that are yours personally.  Feel your strength growing stronger with each breath.

“And take a moment to notice the powers that you hope for in the future.  What strengths do you hope to grow?  What strengths do you wish for?  Take a moment to notice a strength you hope for.  Picture it in your mind and as you breathe in, imagine that it grows stronger with each breath.  It belongs to you.

“When you are ready, open your eyes and begin to create your Power Shield.”

Creation:
As the group creates, continue to play soft music.  Assist and encourage participants with their creations individually as they go.   

Closing Circle:
As they finish up, encourage them to write any words that go with their Power Shields.  When everyone is ready, have a closing circle where everyone has a chance to share her creation and what it means to her.  For those seeing a therapist you might encourage them to share with their therapist as it could provoke further processing.




Mandala from The Picture of Health, Healing Your
Life With Art, by Lucia Capacchione.
Row.txt_description: Provides a place for each woman to talk about her personal power: her abilities, boundaries, and strengths. End product is a shield which acts as a reminder and representation of this power.

Row.txt_code:
Group prayer ornament detail.
 
  
About this Workshop:
I think prayer ornaments are inspirational for all the residents and can help to see them through a difficult season.  When I did this project I was surprised by how much this idea brought them to a place of wanting to join the group.  I had about 15 people that night and they all wanted to put a prayer on.  

Objective:
To give each participant an opportunity to express her prayers in a beautiful way that those around her can see and appreciate.  To create a sense of community and connection by decorating the shelter with prayers.

Materials:
Hole punch
Ribbons (assorted colors)
Scissors
Markers
Glitter
Glue sticks, white school glue
Card stock:
For Variation I:
Metallic gold thick card stock cut into a 1-foot circle
Card stock cut into 2-inch circles (in assorted colors)
For Variation II:
Card stock in assorted colors cut into 3”X5” pieces—size of index cards


 
 
 In Variation I, the prayer ornament  opens
like an advent calendar to reveal the words.
  

Setup:
Prepare the card stock.  If you are doing Variation I, have all the circles cut in advance.  If you are doing Variation II, be sure to have the 3"X5" cards cut in advance.

Relaxation:
“Today, I’d like us to start our workshop by taking a time-out.  We’ve all been dealing with a lot, personally within us and with the world around us.  For just a few minutes, let’s take a time-out and put our heads on the table and just stop everything.  As you rest your head, it’s fine to let your eyes close.  Let go of all your worries as you rest your head.”  (Continue resting silently for a few minutes.)  “Now, with your head still resting on the table, take a few deep breaths.  Notice how relaxed you are.  Slowly begin to open your eyes, and when you’re ready, lift your head.  You might want to stretch a little bit as you sit up.  Can you stretch your shoulders?  Can you gently stretch your neck from side to side?  Wonderful!  Thanks for taking a time-out.”

  


Group prayer ornament (Variation I).
 
  

Introduction:
“The project for today is Prayer Ornaments.  We will be taking some time to notice our prayers.  They could be prayers for ourselves, our families, our communities, the world…  Feel free to think without limits.  Whatever prayers come to your mind and heart are fine.  To connect with your faith you might focus on the idea “with God all things are possible.”  If you do not usually pray or think in terms of God, you could think of your wishes instead.  Think about it however it’s easiest for you.  All prayers and wishes are welcome here tonight.”

Opening Circle:
“For our opening circle, I’m going to ask you one question: If you could get one good thing out of being in this group today, what would it be?  Say whatever comes to your mind first.  First thoughts are usually important, even if they seem silly.  So just say whatever you think of.”


 
 
 Prayer ornaments (Variation II).
  
 
  
 
  

Technical Info:
Share the process (Variation I or II, below).  Share the card stock and other materials.  If you’re using glitter, have some clean scratch paper available and show the group how to shake the excess onto the paper and then funnel it back into a bowl for re-use.  This will cut down on mess and waste.  Also, let them know they don’t have to put their name on their ornaments unless they want to (many will want to).

Journaling and Creation:
“To make our prayer ornaments, we will start by noticing our prayers and wishes in writing.  You can notice them by making a list or writing whatever comes to your mind.  Then when you are done with your writing, take some time to read over it.  When you’re ready, dive in a begin to create your Prayer Ornament.”  As they create, assist them individually.  As they finish up, they can attach their prayers to the large ornament (Variation I) or hang them individually on the tree or walls (Variation II).

Sharing the Prayers:
For the closing circle, give each participant a chance to share her Prayer Ornament and one thought, feeling, or discovery she takes with her from the workshop. 

  


“Peace” prayer ornament.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants an opportunity to express their prayers in a beautiful way that those around them can see and appreciate. Creates a sense of community and connection by decorating the shelter with prayers.

Row.txt_code:
“My Butterfly” samples
Objective:
To give the children an opportunity to notice how sometimes the difficult things in life can be chances to learn and grow.

Materials:
Paper towels
Construction paper
Scissors & hole punchers
Puffy paints
CrayPas
Paperclips (for scratching)
Pipe cleaners (chenille stems)
Newspaper (to cover tables)
Optional: Glitter, sequins
The Butterfly Story - Spanish Translation

Timeframe:
5 minutes Opening / Story
5 minutes Warm-up
20 minutes Creation
10 minutes Closing

Age Range: 3 and up

 
 
 The paint makes amazing, beautiful patterns
when it is pressed together.

Ratio:
About one adult to four children, depending on the age group.

Space Set-up:
Cover the tables with newspaper. Set up a drying area, covered with newspaper. That’s where the completed butterflies can go to dry. Try creating some butterflies yourself, just so you’ll be more ready to help the children with their efforts.

Opening / Story:
“Today, I have a story to share with you. It’s a sad story, but it’s an important story too. It’s about a cocoon. Does anybody know what a cocoon is? Did you know that’s how a butterfly starts out when it’s a baby? And then when it is ready, the butterfly comes out of the cocoon and spreads its wings to fly. This is a story about a butterfly coming out of a cocoon. Ready? (Read The Butterfly) After you read the story ask the children if they’ve ever been through something hard, but found out that it helped them to grow. (Like doing homework, practicing a sport, or learning to share with their brothers and sisters.) Encourage them to share their own stories.

Butterfly Warm-up:
(Optional, depending on age-appropriateness.) “For our warm-up today, let’s start out as baby butterflies. Do you remember how a butterfly starts out when it’s a baby? That’s right. It’s a cocoon. So let’s start as cocoons (curl up on the floor). Can you get curled up really tight? There you go! And now you’re growing, starting to wiggle, and you think maybe it’s time to start making your way out of your cocoon. Can you make a little hole? And wiggle, wiggle wiggle. Oh! I think I see some butterflies coming out (as the children wiggle their way into becoming butterflies)! Beautiful! Can you enjoy all the air and all the space around you as you stretch your new wings? And let’s stretch and fly until every little cocoon has turned into a beautiful butterfly.”

Creation:
“Today, we are going to make our own butterflies. Everyone gets to pick three colors for their butterfly. Think of colors to show the wonderful ways you have grown from the things you’ve been through. Can anyone think of a color? (Encourage them to share colors that represent how they’ve grown.)

Now here are the butterfly-making steps:
Cutting the folded construction paper
into a half-butterfly shape.
Open butterfly with paint drips added. (The antennea
have also already been added with a stapler.)
Refolding and pressing until the paint squeezes
out of the sides.
Gently opening the paper again to see the
beautiful design that came out.
Step One:
Fold a piece of construction paper in half and cut, to create a half of a butterfly shape. (See top of page.) Open the fold to see your butterfly. (Note: For younger children, you might want to cut out butterfly shapes in advance so they can go on to Step Two.)

Step Two:
If you want to have antennea on your butterfly, punch holes to put them through. (It’s easier to do before the paint is added.)

Step Three:
Now use CrayPas to cover your butterfly with colors. Use colors that represent all the hard things you’ve been through. When you’re ready, choose puffy paints to represent all the ways you’re growing strong. Add them to your butterfly!

Step Four:
Now fold your butterfly in half with the paint inside. Press so that some of the paint squeezes out the edges. Then gently open it back up. See the beautiful shapes and colors of your butterfly!

Step Five:
Optional: You can scratch through the paint to add words or lines. You can also add glitter or sequins. Lay your butterfly down in the drying area. (Younger children may need help if they want words written on their butterflies.)

Closing:
“Share your butterfly and any thoughts about how you are learning and growing just like a butterfly.”

Less Mess Variation:
To eliminate the messiness, this workshop could be done with colored markers instead of paints. (The only reason the paints are worth the mess is that the colors look so beautiful when they are pressed together this way. It’s definitely worth trying.)
Row.txt_description: Gives children an opportunity to notice how sometimes the difficult things in life can be chances to learn and grow.
Row.txt_notes: ER TO DO: CS needs to meld with newer version in conference handouts.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To create a safe space for the children to express their feelings about a time they felt scared and a time they felt safe. To honor the children’s experiences and expressions by putting them into a quilt which can help raise awareness about domestic violence in the community.

Materials:
8” X 8” fabric—two per child (muslin works well)
Fabric markers
Fabric crayons/pastels
Pen and paper (to write what each child shares)
After workshop: supplies (and a volunteer?) to turn the squares into a quilt.
Note: If sewing a quilt is not possible, you can also make a paper quilt by gluing squares onto a large piece of butcher paper. Enjoy!

Timeframe:
5 minutes Check-in Circle
10 minutes Scared Square Creation
10 minutes Sharing and Writing
10 minutes Safe Square Creation
10 minutes Sharing and Writing


 
 
 Completed Scared/Safe Quilt from
Humboldt Women for Shelter
  

Age Range: 3 and up

Ratio:
About one adult to four children, depending on the age group.

Space Setup:
Have fabric markers, crayons, pastels, and strips of printed fabric (for the square’s borders) laid out on the table.

Note:
Thinking about being scared can be sad and serious. That is why we like to do the “scared” square part of the project first. That way, when we do the “safe” square second, it leaves them on a positive note.

Check-in:
We start every group with a check-in circle. We usually ask some question. For example: “share something that was fun for you this week,” “share something you liked about today,” “share something you like about your family,” or “share something about how you’re feeling today.”

  


  
  

Creation:
“Today, we are going to make the squares for a quilt together. This is going to be a Scared/Safe quilt. We each get to think of sometime when we were feeling scared and sometime when we were feeling safe. We each get two different squares. Here they are. One square is for scared and one square is for safe.” Pass out two squares to each child. “So let’s start with the scared square. Think of a time when you were scared: What did you feel? Where were you? Was anyone with you? What colors, smell, sounds were present? Go ahead and draw it all on one of your squares.”

Sharing the Scared:
“Now let’s share the scared squares. Who wants to go first?” (As they share, I write down their stories on paper. This way, the words can be printed onto fabric later and then sewn under their square.)

Creating the Safe:
“Now, let’s try the safe square. Think of a time when you felt safe and protected: What was it like? Where were you? Was anyone with you? What colors, smell, sounds were present? Go ahead and draw it all on your other square.”
Sharing the Safe:
“Now let’s share the safe squares. Who wants to go first?” (Again, as they share, I write down their stories on paper to sew under their square later.)


 
 
 
 
  

About the Quilting:
To get the squares sewn into a quilt, it can be a great help if you find a volunteer, staff, or board member who loves sewing!
Row.txt_description: Creates a safe space for children to express their feelings about a time they felt scared and a time they felt safe. Honors their experiences and expressions by putting them into a quilt which can help raise awareness about domestic violence in the community.
Row.txt_tips: Puffy paints are also good to use with fabric.

Row.txt_code:
“Happy” Feelings Face
 
  
Objective:
This workshop is a time for the children to learn about feelings, identify with them, and express them as art.


 
 
 Three Feelings Faces: Satisfied, Aggressive, and Happy
  

Materials:
Poster Board Circles (Be sure to use light colors—white is fine. You can get about four or five circles out of one poster board, so you may need more than one sheet.)
Scissors (to cut circles)
Black marking pens (thick)—one per child
Elmers Glue
"How Do You Feel Today?" handout (click here for handout)
Note: If possible, get the little plastic eyeballs (see picture at right). The children really love gluing these on!
Optional: Other decorations (fabric, lace, feathers, etc.)

Timeframe:
Total Time: One Hour
Warm-up: 10 min
Check-in: 10 min
Creation: 30 min
Sharing: 10 min

Age Range: 3 and up


 
 
 The kids love using the plastic eyeballs.
  

Ratio:
1 adult per 4 children

Space Set-up:
Prepare the circles in advance (you can use the attached circle stencil) and make enough copies of the "How Do You Feel Today" sheet to hand out to everyone.

Warm-up:
Give each child a "How Do You Feel Today?" hand-out with the seventy feelings faces. Have everyone pick out a face they want to share with the group. They could show it on the page or they could also show it on their own face. If it’s appropriate for your group, have everyone join in making the face with each child.

  


More plastic eyeballs
 
  

Check-in:
After the Warm-up, we do a check-in, asking each participant how their week was.

Creation:
After the children look at the feelings faces handout and pick one feeling, they draw the face on the cut out circle with a thick marking black pen. Children each create their own Feelings Face. They can glue on the eyeballs. Use a strong glue. (Elmers will work.) Then they can share about their Feelings Faces.

Closing Circle:
Give each child a chance to show everyone their Feelings Face. Encourage them to share about the feelings if they want to.


 
 
 “Determined and Smug” Feelings Face
  

Variations:
If you can't afford poster board, use cardboard from boxes that are thrown away. It’s hard to cut cardboard with scissors, so you can use a rug cutter to cut out the circles. You can also glue construction paper on top of the cut out circle if you want a colorful face. Paper plates are another option, but I prefer making the circles for each child.
Row.txt_description: Offers time to learn about feelings, identify with them, and express them as art. The Feeling Faces can be helpful and fun reminders of what the children have learned.

Row.txt_code:
&ldq uo;Possiblities for Teens” workshop participants
with their Inside/Outside creations.
 
  


About this Project:
This project was brought to us by Karen Akamine who was trained at the Armory Center for the Arts in Pasadena. The concept was adapted into this teen workshop by the AWBW staff.

Objective:
To express the self that you let people see on the outside and explore the self that is on the inside, underneath.

    




Inside/Outside creation (closed,
opening, and open all the way)
from the “Possibilities for
Teens” Leaders’ Workshop.
   
    



  


Materials:
9"X12" Colored construction paper
Chalk pastels
Paper towels
Pens and writing paper
(Option: teens could use their journals)
independent project handout (for individual workshops) (click here for handout)
Alternative variations: This workshop could be done using collage instead of pastels. Plus if you are doing collage, you could do it on boxes or paper bags instead of construction paper.

Timeframe:
Total Time: 1 hr
Intro/Ground rules: 5 min
Check-in: 10 min
Journal Writing: 5 min
Creation: 30 min
Closing Circle: 10 min

Age Range: 3 and up

Ratio:
This workshop is geared for teens, so the ratio can be whatever the leader is comfortable with.

     





Door Fold
  Triangle Fold
 
Diamond Fold Open ... and Closed

    
Here are some examples of

ways to fold the paper so

there’s an inside and an

outside. Encourage the

teens to be creative in

their folding.
     Double Door Fold

Space Setup:
It helps things go smoothly when you have the supplies prepared and set up in advance. Try various folds (see illustrations below) so it will
be easy to show the teens some possiblilities. Use the pastels to make an example yourself. That way, you can make sure the supplies are ready and you’ll notice if there’s anything else needed.

Welcome:
When possible, try to individually welcome each teen and let them know you’re glad they’re there. One-on-one contact can help them get connected and feel safe and comfortable enough to truly use their Windows time for themselves.

  



Inside/Outside created with a
diamond fold: closed (above)
and open (below).

 

 
  

Introduction:
“This art time is a special ‘window of time’ for each of you. The project we are doing is called Inside/Outside. It is a chance to explore the ‘you’ that people see on the outside, and the ‘you’ that you know is on the inside. We will be using folded paper and pastels to create our inside and outside selves in shapes and colors.” (Optional: show samples.)

Ground Rules:
“For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? (See Ground Rules for teen workshops—attached.) Are there any other Ground Rules you’d like to add?”

Check-in:
“Before we start the art, we’ll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art.” (This is a time to reassure anyone who’s scared of art that it’s fine, and to tell anyone who “hates” art that’s fine too. Remind them that they don’t have to do it. They can just watch if they want to. If they are given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in, even if they say they’re just going to watch. If they don’t want to say anything for “check-in,” let them know that’s fine too.)

Journaling Warm-up:
(Note: The journaling is optional. If you feel your group would be better off just diviing in with the project, that’s fine too.)

"Let’s start with a journaling warm-up. Divide a paper into two columns. On the left side, write ‘Inside’ and on the right side, write ‘Outside.’ Fill the left side of the page with any words that describe how you feel on the inside, and fill the right side of the page with any words that describe the ‘you’ that people see on the outside."

Creation:
"Now pick a piece of construction paper and fold it to so it has an inside and an outside. Think about the outside of you, and then start with the outside of your paper. On the outside are you bright or dark? Are you sharp or soft? Are you foggy or clear? With the pastels, use shapes and colors to draw how you are on the outside. When you are ready, move to the inside. Open up your paper and begin to think about how you are on the inside. Are you bright or dark? Are you one color or many colors? Are you soft or rough? Use pastels to draw shapes and colors that show the inside ‘you’ on the inside of your paper. When you are finished, take some time to write any words that go with your drawing." You might want to encourage the teens to take a moment after they finish to think about how they might want to take care of themselves inside and outside.


 
 
 Inside / Outside creation
with diamond fold.
  

Optional Closing Feedback Exercise:
(10 minutes before the workshop ends) Pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You can even take them to copy and return them the next week. I think you will be pleased. (AWBW would love to receive copies too!)

Closing Circle:
Give each teen an opportunity to share what she/he created and talk about what it means and how it felt to make. Just like the Check-in Circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.
Row.txt_description: Opportunity to express the self that we let people see on the outside and explore the self that is on the inside, underneath.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for adults.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop is designed around Mother’s Day.  The handprint flower can make a beautiful keepsake for the mothers from their children.

About the Variations:
There are two variations:
A—using cut-out construction paper to make the hands, or B—using paint handprints.  The cut-out variation is wonderful because it’s less messy.  The painted variation is wonderful because there’s something precious about an actual print of a child’s hand.  And by using iridescent acrylic paint, you can make especially beautiful prints.





Mother’s Day Flowers created
using the “cut-out” technique.



Materials:
A: Cut-out
Colored construction paper
Scissors and glue
Markers, crayons, Cray-Pas
B: Painted
Colored construction paper
Brushes, water, paper towels  
Iridescent acrylic paint (You can buy one tube of iridescent acrylic paint for about $5 at an art store.  Then squeeze it into 6 bowls and tint it to create pink, orange, yellow, blue, purple and green by adding a touch of poster paint to each one.)





Mother’s Day Flowers created using
\the “painted” technique.



Timeframe: 1 hr
Warm-up: 10 min
Check-in: 10 min
Creation:  30 min
Sharing:   10 min

Age Range: 3 and up

Ratio:
One adult per 4 children 

Preparation Ideas:
A: Cut-out
If you are working with a lot of younger children, it can be difficult for them to maneuver the scissors.  It may be helpful to pre-cut the stems and leaves for the flowers.
(See patterns.)

B: Painted
Don’t forget the smocks or old
t-shirts to paint.  Be sure to mix the paints in advance and try out making a print yourself!

Growing As A Flower Warm-up:
(This warm-up is modeled on the “Growing as a Tree” Warm-up from the November ‘99 Update.) 
Have the children gather either in a circle or just ask them to find a favorite spot near you in the room.  Ask them to make space around them because they are going to grow from small to big.  Tell the children that they are going to be special flowers that are going to grow big and strong.

“Now I first want you to be a small plant but with strong roots.  So let’s make sure our feet are on the ground and we have good roots that will help us grow.  Let’s hunker down close to the ground so we can be small plants.  Now we are going to grow, little by little.  First let’s put our arms up above our head and our fingers are like little leaves, wiggling about and then little bit by little bit we are going to get bigger, and bigger, and bigger, reaching up towards the sun (until you are standing up fully).  Now we are a strong plant, upright and ready for anything.  Yes, let’s keep our arms and hands straight up in the air.  Now let’s imagine that we are growing a flower.  Put your hands together, up over your head.  Your flower is starting out all closed up.  and now notice it’s beginning to open.  And now it’s opening more, and growing so big and beautiful!!!  Look around at all the different flowers.  Each one is different!  And look at all the flowers smiling!  That’s wonderful!”




Mother’s Day Flowers decorated with markers.




Check-in:
After the Warm-up, we do a check-in, asking each participant how their week was.  During this time, the group can talk about the Mother’s Day holiday.  Examples:  1.  What it means to them.  2.  Past Mother’s Day holidays (if it seems appropriate for your group).  3.  Ways to honor the holiday by doing little things for mom.

Creation:
A: Cut-out 
The children begin by tracing their hand themselves or with help.  Then they cut the hand drawing and glue to a different construction paper.  The leaves and stem can now be added to make the flower.  The flower can be further decorated by using markers, crayons, or Cray-Pas.

B: Painted
To begin, the children will choose a color of paper.  Then they will choose a color or colors of paint, and then paint their hand completely (palm-side only).  Their handprint is then made on construction paper.  The leaves and stem can be painted next (or cut out with construction paper).     





More Mother’s Day Flowers
decorated with markers.



Closing Circle:
Give each child a chance to show everyone their flowers.  Encourage them to share something about their flowers.
Row.txt_description: Designed around Mother's Day, the handprint flowers make beautiful keepsakes for mothers from their children at an important time in their lives.
Row.txt_tips: This can be adapted for Valentines Day

Row.txt_code:
Baggie Book sample with decorated cover.





Ziploc baggie “pages” inside the book.





Ziplock baggie with “pleat” at the bottom.


Objective:
To help the children create their own “Baggie Book” out of Ziploc bags.  To support them in thinking creatively about how they might like to use their special book.  It could be their Treasure Book with special things in each pouch.  It could be a Family and Friends Book with each baggie holding something about each family member or friend (drawings, photos, notes, etc.).  It could be a My Favorite Things book with each baggie representing a favorite place, person, or activity.  It could be a Wishes book with a baggie for each wish.   The possibilities are endless!

Materials:
(You’ll notice the material set-up is more complicated than usual.  Don’t let that stop you!  It’s worth the effort.)
Cover—7”X7” railboard or chipboard (flexibility is important), 2 per participant
Ziploc-type baggies—size 5 7/8” X 6 1/2” pleated bottom, 3 per participant. (see photo)
Baggie dividers—5 7/8” X 6 3/8” Construction paper, 3 per participant.
Extra insert pages (optional)—5 5/16” X 6 3/8” colored paper, 3-6 per participant
Spine—6 7/16” X 11” cover stock (strong paper), 1 per participant
Staplers—approximately one for ever 4 participants
Staples, glue sticks, markers
Single hole punch (optional)
Scrap color paper for collage
Ribbons

Timeframe: 1 hr
Warm-up:  5 min
Check in:  5 min
Introduction:  5 min
Creation:  40 min
Closing:  5 min

Age Range: Ages 10 and up (For younger children, you’d need a ratio of one adult per child, or use a simpler way of binding the bags together.)

Ratio:
One adult per 3 children

Preparation Ideas:
Be sure the chipboard and papers are cut to the right sizes in advance.  Create a sample to share so you know how it works and the kids can get a sense of what a Baggie Book could be.  As you make your sample you can follow the instructions here or improvise. 

Simpler Binding for Younger Groups:
Feel free to experiment with different ways of creating/binding the book.  For younger groups one alternative could be to just directly staple the bags and cover and not use any spine. 





Close-up of the “accordion fold” spine
that binds the baggie book.



Warm-up:
Use your favorite warm-up to get the kids focused and together.

Check In:
(Optional, depending on age-level and group tone):  If it works for your particular group, have a check-in circle where each child can share about how they are doing today. 

Introduction:
“Today we are making Baggie Books.  Has anyone ever seen one before?  Here is one (show sample).  This is just a sample.  You can decorate yours any way you want, and you can use it however you want.  It could be a Treasure Book, Wishes Book, or My Favorite Things Book…  You could even make it a Family Book, with one baggie for each member of your family.  You could fill it with drawings, photos, and thoughts about each person in your family.  Or you could make it a Friends book with a page for each of your friends.  You get to use your book however you want.  Today we will begin by putting it together.  Then you can take it with you and put things in it.  Ready to start making it?”     

Directions:
