Gently guide the children through the following four steps:

Step One: Making the “pages”
To make the “pages” insert one of the page dividers into the baggie as shown below:















First, roll paper into a tube shape and insert into a baggie (above).

Second, gently unroll and flatten the tube.  Slip the divider paper all the way in, between one of the pleats.  (If baggie won’t zip shut, check that the paper is fitted into the pleat.)

Third, do this for all three of your “pages” (see all three “pages” above).

Step Two: Making the “spine”
To make the spine, use an accordion fold, shown below:

First, start with a 1/2 inch fold at one end of the paper. 















Then turn the paper over to make another 1/2 inch fold.  Continue flipping and folding until you have an accordion fold happening. 

Continue folding all the way to the end of the paper. 

Step Three: Putting the “pages” and “spine” together
You might suggest that participants pair up and work together to do the following:

First, separate the pleat and insert over the second fold from the end of your spine.  (Leaving one fold allows enough paper for attaching the cover later.)











Next, staple at two sides (the “page divider” adds strength).

Repeat with second and third pages, skipping one fold of the accordion between each page.  (This allows for expansion of the book when the baggies get full of things.)

Step Four: Attaching Cover
Apply glue to one end flap of the spine.  Attach the cover and then staple twice for added strength at the top and bottom. Repeat with other cover and decorate!




Cover added to Baggie Book.

Inside the cover, you can see where it’s
stapled to the accordion spine.




Closing Circle:
Validate the children for their hard work and patience, and give each of them an opportunity to share what they made and what it means to them.




When the book is finished, things can
be added inside the baggie pages.
Row.txt_description: Children create their own book out of ziploc bags and are supported in thinking creatively about how they might like to use their special book; it could be a Treasure Book, a Family and Friends Book, a My Favorite Things Book, a Wishes Book...

Row.txt_code:
Stained Glass Butterfly — Cut-out variation (see below)


About this Workshop:
This workshop is brought to us by Heather MacAdam, Children’s Windows leader at Good Shepherd Shelter in Los Angeles.  She adapted it from a school textbook.  The supplies are simple and the effect is beautiful.  Her only warning is to gather the permanent markers in advance.

Children’s Feedback:
“Ooooh cool!”  “This is easy!” 
“I added antennas on my butterfly.” 
“I wrote my name around my butterfly.” 
“I’ll put mine on the refrigerator.”

Objectives:
To give the children an opportunity to try new materials that give a rewarding visual effect.  To give the children a chance to think about the changes they are going through by thinking about how butterflies change. 





Stained Glass Butterflies —  Created using
cut-out variation (see below)



Materials:
Clear plastic wrap
Aluminum foil
Clear tape
Small paper plates (1 per child)
Copies of the Butterfly pattern (1 per child)
Assorted permanent markers
Magnets and glue (optional)

Note: If you’re doing the cut-out version, you can skip the paper plates and you’ll need:
Scissors
Glue sticks

Timeframe: 1 hr
Warm-up:  5 min
Introduction:  5 min
Creation:  45 min
Closing:  5 min

Age Range: Ages 6 and up

Ratio:
One adult per 3 children

Finding Markers:
Be sure to look for the permanent markers in advance.  You may have enough around the office, or you may need to purchase some. It’s good to have one black marker per child since they may all be starting with black at the same time.  With the other colors you don’t need to have one per child.  Just make sure you have a good assortment and enough to share.  (Staples sells sets of assorted colors, and sets of black markers). 

If you purchase markers for this workshop, hold onto them for holidays.  This project is a great way of making ornaments for all sorts of occasions.  Just use a different shape (instead of a butterfly). 

Preparation Ideas:
Create a sample in advance, so you know what it looks like.  It’s exciting to try it out!  You may also want to do step one and two in advance for the kids, depending on the group you’ll be working with. 

Introduction:
Begin with a discussion of the changing of butterflies from caterpillar to cocoon to butterfly.  Ask the children how they can change.  If it’s appropriate for the age-level of your participants, work the following Butterfly Warm-up into your introduction.  

Butterfly Warm-up:
“For our warm-up today, let’s practice changing as butterflies.   Do you remember how a butterfly starts out when it’s a baby?  That’s right.  It’s a caterpillar!  So let’s start as caterpillars.  Can you move along like a caterpillar moves?  And then something happens.  You’re ready to change into the next shape.  Does anyone remember what that is?  Yes!  A cocoon!  So go ahead and find a place where you want to become your cocoon (curl up on the floor).  Can you get curled up really tight?  There you go!  And now you’re growing again, slowly, slowly, starting to wiggle, and you think maybe it’s time to start making your way out of your cocoon.  There’s no hurry.  Can you make a little hole?  And wiggle, wiggle, wiggle.  Oh!  I think I see some butterflies coming out (as the children wiggle their way into becoming butterflies)!  Beautiful!  Can you enjoy all the air and all the space around you as you stretch your new wings?  And let’s stretch and fly until every little cocoon has turned into a beautiful butterfly.” 

Creation:
Step 1
Tape the butterfly pattern on the table:


Step 2
Tape a large square of plastic saran wrap over the butterfly pattern:


Step 3
Color with permanent markers.  Use black to trace the lines and bright colors to fill in:


Complete coloring the butterfly:


Step 4
Crumble a piece of square tin foil:


Step 5
Cover a small paper plate with the tin foil:


Step 6
Now put the saran wrap with the colored butterfly over the tin foil plate.  You might need to use some tape to keep it fastened onto plate securely:


Step 7 (optional)
Put a magnet on back (if small plate).  Could also be hung on the wall. 


Closing:
Give each child a chance to share his or her butterfly.  Does it have a name?  What is it feeling about the changes it goes through?  

Cut-Out Variation:
If the participants are old enough to use scissors to cut out their butterflies instead of mounting them on a plate, the effect is extra beautiful. 

Instead of putting the crumbled foil over a plate, flatten it out.  Then use a glue stick to apply glue to the saran wrap butterfly.  To make it easy, you can do this while it’s still taped down). Then pick up the saran wrap and attach it onto the foil.  Now you’re ready to cut out the butterfly!  (See below)


Holiday Possibilities:
For any holiday celebration, this technique can be a wonderful way to create decorations.  Instead of using the butterfly pattern, just create a different pattern or set of patterns.  Consider flowers, fall leaves, pumpkins, candles, trees, stars, etc., depending on the occasion.  Creations can be strung together with ribbon to decorate the shelter walls.
Row.txt_description: Gives the children the opportunity to try new materials that give rewarding visual effects and make beautiful butterflies. Encourages them to think about the changes they are experiencing by thinking about how caterpillars change into butterflies.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Expand on this workshop, i.e. by including patterns and suggestions.

Row.txt_code:
About this Workshop:

Set of “Midnight Star” handmade cards tied
with ribbon for a gift.


I was first introduced to flexi-foam by artist Karen Akamine.  With Flexi-Foam it’s easy to cut and create your own shape and then use it like a rubber stamp.  

We tried Creative Card Making with the Flexi-Foam at our last “Art in the Afternoon” event.  It worked out so well we wanted to share it with you.  

The Flexi-Foam printing is a bit messy, so for those of you who need a non-messy workshop, I’ve also included a no-mess variation at the end.  Enjoy!

Objectives:
To give the children an opportunity to create their own personalized set of cards and envelopes by making an original and reusable stamp.  (Note: Sets of cards can also be great for the children’s gift giving.  A set of cards can be a very personal and creative thing to give a loved one.)     

Materials:
Newsprint to cover tables





Flexi-Foam scraps to use for Creative
Cardmaking workshop.



Card-stock, heavyweight paper cut to 8 1/2 X 4 1/4 (to fold into cards)
Envelopes (Size A-6)—Assorted colors if possible
Iridescent acrylic paints (sparkly fabric paints can also be used)
Paper plates
Sponges
Water containers
Flexi-Foam (available at Michael’s)
Scissors and ball-point pens
Scratch paper
Optional: Glitter, feathers, sequins, glue sticks, and school glue

Time Frame: 1 hr
Warm-up:  5 min
Introduction:  5 min
Creation:  45 min






Shapes drawn onto Flexi-Foam (above) and
cut out with scissors (below).






Closing:  5 min

Age Range: Ages 4 and up

Ratio:
One adult per 3 children

Preparation:
Make sure you have a good selection of paints.  You may want to buy one tube of iridescent acrylic white paint and then mix colors with it to create a range of color choices.  Once you’ve mixed your paints, create some sample stamps, cards, and envelopes.  Tie a set with a ribbon as a sample (see photo, page 1). 

About Themes:
Having a theme is not necessary for this project but it can sometimes spark extra creativity.  Here are some possible themes and discussions you might have while working with the children:
Happy Hearts—What is in your heart that makes you feel happy?  What color would you make your heart?
Summer Suns—What do you like about the sun?  If you were a sun, what would you look like?   
Midnight Stars—At night, sailors used the stars to guide their course.  If you were a star, what would you look like and who would you guide? 
Spring Flowers—If you were a flower what would you look like?  Would you be big?  Small?  Many colors or just one color? 

Warm-up:
If you’re using a theme, it might be good to create a warm-up that gives the children a chance to explore that theme (i.e. being happy hearts, melting in the summer sun, twinkling like a midnight star, blooming like a spring flower, etc.). 





Assorted paper for cards.



Introduction:
“Today we will get a chance to make our own ‘rubber stamps’ using Flexi-Foam.  We can use them to stamp on paper and make cards and envelopes.  If you want to make a whole set of cards and envelopes you can tie them up with a ribbon.  Here are some samples.  It could be a nice present for someone, and would be very special because it’s made by you.”  Here are the steps:

Making Your Stamp Shape:
“Step one is to draw your shape on the Flexi-Foam.  You can draw it right on and then cut it out with scissors.” (Young children might neeed help with the cutting.)

Choosing Cards and Envelopes:
“Once the shape is made, choose the paper and envelopes you want.”




Paint spooned onto plate with sponges
and ready for printing.






Choosing Paint:
“Next choose the colors of paint you want.  Put small spoonfuls of it onto a paper plate.”

Sponging and Printing:
“Use your sponge to dab paint into a flat area on your plate.  Press your Flexi-Foam stamp onto the paint.  Then press it onto your paper.  (You can also dab with the sponge directly onto the Flexi-Foam.)   You might want to make some practice prints to get a feel for how the printing works, before printing it onto your cards and envelopes (see photos at right).” 

Optional-Extra Decorations/Ribbons:





Paint sponged onto the Flexi-Foam.





Printing onto the card.





Printed several times onto one card.



After printing with the Flexi-Foam some children might want to add decorations to the print.  With glue they could add sequins, glitter, or other decorations.  If a child wants to make a complete set of cards and envelopes as a gift, help tie the set with a ribbon.

Closing:
Give each child an opportunity to share his or her creations and any thoughts or feelings about them.

No-Mess Variation:
The children can create their own personalized sets of stationary using just black pens, copier paper, and a copier machine.  It helps to have an assortment of black pens available (thick and thin points) and a variety of paper colors to copy onto.  
1. Create design (with black pens on white paper).
2. Choose paper. (Printing on colored paper looks great!)
3. Copy!  (How many sheets do you want?)  Save the design to copy more in the future.








Star prints on card (top) and envelope (bottom).
Row.txt_description: Gives the children the opportunity to create personalized sets of cards by using stamps they have created and designed themselves. A set of cards can be a very personal and creative thing to give a loved one.

Row.str_author_location: Women's and Children's Crisis Shelter, Whittier, California
Row.txt_code:
Spiral mosaic
 
  
About this Workshop:
I have been leading this activity for almost a year now and every time the children make the mosaics they usually make lots of different pictures. The older children usually make their names, other children like to make flowers or volcanoes. The children use lots of concentration for this activity. They also learn to use their motor skills (especially smaller children). Overall I feel like this workshop is both fun and different for the children of any age.

Objective/Intro:
“Not all still lives are painted. There’s one that is made a single square at a time. One can create a dazzling still life with tiny colored paper ‘tiles.’ It’s like putting the pieces of your life back together again.”



 
 
 Sun and sea mosaic
  

Materials:
Colored paper in assorted colors
Ruler (to cut strips)
Pencils and erasers
Scissors
White glue
Black paper (about 7”X 9”)

Timeframe: 1 hr
Touch Blue! Warm-up: 5 min
Introduction: 5 min
Creation: 45 min
Closing: 5 min

Age Range: Ages 3 and up

Ratio:
One adult per 3 children



 
 
 Heart mosaic
  

Preparation:
If you are working with younger children, you might want to cut all the squares in advance (see step one) for the children to use.

Touch Blue!:
Touch Blue! is a playful warm-up game designed to get the group energized, cooperative, and focused on noticing all the colors around them.

“Are you ready for a special game? It’s called Touch Blue! The game starts when I say ‘Touch Blue!’ When I say that, all of us have to find something blue in the room to touch. It’s okay to help each other find things! Once everyone has found something blue, then we’ll be ready for another color. I’ll call out another color and we’ll keep going with all sorts of different colors until we come back to blue. Are you ready? Okay.”

“Touch blue! (Praise them as they find and touch blue things. Praise them for helping each other until everyone has found something blue to touch.) You guys did great! Are you ready for the next color? Okay.

“Touch red! (Again praise them as the help each other find colors. Praise them when they are proud of what they’ve found. And encourage them to help each other and be aware of when everyone has found the color. When they say they’re ready give them the next color.)

  


Volcano mosaic
 
  

“Touch yellow! (Etc... continue with colors... purple, brown, green, black, grey, white, silver, pink, etc. When you’re ready to finish, come back to blue and when everyone is touching something blue again, praise them for how well they did finding all the different colors.)

Note: Depending on the age-level and tone of your group, you might want to try these variations or make up your own:

1.—Make a rule that two people can’t be touching the same peice of color, they all have to find their own. That makes it more challenging for everyone to find something, and more fun for everyone to try to help out and make sure everyone else can find something.

2.—Make a rule that everyone must find colors on each other (clothing, earrings, hair, etc.) This will definitely change the game and since it involves touching, it would only be appropriate and enjoyable for a group that is comfortable with and respectful of each other.


 
 
 Flower mosaic
  

Mosaic Creation:
1. Preparing the Tiles
Cut the paper into 1/4” squares. The quickest way to do it is by cutting the paper into 1/4” wide strips first. The snip the strip into squares. (You can use larger squares but you won’t be able to get as much detail.)

2. Drawing your Design
Pencil the outline of the drawing on the black paper. Make sure you keep the design simple because it’s hard to keep a lot of detail with such a small mosaic.

3. Tile the Lines
Place the mosaic squares along the pencil drawing by using white glue. You can use many different colors to give it a vibrant look. It’s best to make a large picture and cover most of the paper with the little squares. (Make sure you don’t place the squares too close together or else you can lose the visual effect of the mosaic. Leave a little space around each square so that the black paper shows through.)

Hint: This has made it easier for the younger kids to paste the little squares onto the black paper without making a huge mess. First, squirt some white glue on a large piece of scrap paper. Dip just the tip of your finger into the glue, and then onto a square—it will lift the paper right up. Use your other hand to flip the square and place it on the outlines of your drawing and position it on your paper.

4. Filling in with Tiles
Once you have outlined the drawing, you can fill in the design and the background. Follow the outline of your design. You can even cut out smaller squares when filling in your design to fit any tight or irregular spots.

Tip: To help your design really stand out you can have the colors contrast each other. For example, light versus dark. You can make the background squares much lighter (or darker for a different effect) than those you choose to use in the design itself.

Closing:
Give each child an opportunity to share his or her creation(s) and any thoughts or feelings about them.

  


Flag mosaic
Row.txt_description: Gives children a chance to create beautiful art using the mosaic technique, exploring their motor skills and powers of concentration. Fun and rewarding for any age group.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for adults.
Row.txt_tips: Elmer's glue can get pretty messy, especially with younger children.  A glue stick might be easier for kids to use.

Row.str_title: The House of Wonders - Part I
Row.txt_code:
“The House of Wonders” writings and
collages on display.



Note:  This is a two-part workshop.  However, each part can be done separately.  

The first part is shared here in this update. Part II will be printed in the next Update.  

In the second part, the children express what they have “seen” in their visualization through collage and drawing.  The images throughout this Update are details from the collages the children created in Part II of the workshop.


About this Workshop:
This project was developed with the help of the children who participated.  It started as an exercise in teaching kids that they have the ability to calm themselves through meditation. The workshop evolved into an exercise in visualization, imagination, journaling, and concluded with art.  

Objective:





Detail from one “House of Wonders” collage.



Children need tools to calm themselves.  This workshop is an experience that can be used later by children when they are stressed or preparing for sleep. It can cure “being bored” and strengthen self-esteem through storytelling, journaling, and art.      
Materials:
Writing paper
Pencils or pens
Colored construction paper  (cut in half horizontally)
Scissors
Glue sticks
Computer (if possible)

Timeframe: 1 hr
Opening: 5 minutes
Introduction: 5 minutes





Detail from one “House of Wonders” collage.



Meditation: 10 minutes
Journaling: 10 minutes
Typing: 10 minutes
Cut and paste: 10 minutes
Closing circle: 5 minutes

Age Range: 6 and up.

Ratio:
One adult for four children. (More help may be needed with journaling for small children.)

Space Setup:
Make sure there is room for everyone to lie down comfortably.
After the meditation, there should be space for writing.

Opening Circle/Intro:
Sit in a circle and give children an opportunity to say how they are feeling today.  Anyone not willing to share can just say “pass.”  This is something I do at the beginning of each workshop.  Introduce the workshop as something the children can do whenever they need to calm down.  Let them know that they will be lying down, listening, and then writing.  Younger children may need writing assistance.  Let them know that they will have help and that clear penmanship will help later on.





Detail from one “House of Wonders” collage.




“My House” Meditation,  Visualization,  Imagination:
Note:  It is important that the children do not verbally express what they imagine DURING the meditation.  This can create a problem because once the children hear another’s idea they tend to copy it or try to ‘out do’  each other.

“Find a place in the room where you can lay down and get comfortable.  We’re going to do a little relaxing together.  Once you’re comfortable I’d like you to notice your toes.  Can you wiggle them?  And now let them relax...  And now notice your legs.  Wiggle them a little.  And now let them relax...  And now notice your tummy and back.  Can you wiggle them a little?  And now let them relax...  And now notice your arms.  Can you wiggle them a little?  And wiggle your hands and fingers?  And now let them relax...  And now notice your neck and your head.  See if you can wiggle them a little.  And now let them relax.  Now take a deep breath and notice how your chest rises.  And let your breath out, and notice how your chest goes down.  Take another deep breath in...  And out...  And again, in...  And out...  Notice your chest rising and falling.  

“Now, if you feel safe closing your eyes, let them close.  If you want to keep them open, that’s okay too.  The most important thing is to just take a nice rest and let your  imagination be free.  Picture yourself in a beautiful forest.  Notice the beautiful trees around you.  See all the colors of green and the golden light of the sunshine coming through.  Notice the sounds of the birds around you.  As  you walk along, you hear the sound of water.  As you come closer you see there is a little stream.  Notice how it sounds.  Notice how it looks... the rocks along it, the big ones, the small ones...  There is a trail along the stream and you can explore it.  Do you see fish in the water?  Are there flowers?  Notice all the sights and sounds.  
You are now walking through a foggy area.  It is wonderful soft fog.  This is your special place.  No harm can come to you here.  Breathe in the fog and enjoy your special place.





Detail from one “House of Wonders” collage.



“Now, it seems as though there is a cloud right in front of you.  Walk through the cloud and you will see your perfect house.  What does it look like?  Look at the porch and remember what you see there.  Next walk inside your house. What do you see?  Remember the colors and shapes.  Is there furniture? Are there stairs?”  

Lead the children through an exploration of the house.  Finally have them leave the house to meet their friends at a party in an open field just down the stream.  This process should not be rushed.

Journaling:
Have the children write their own personal story. Help them remember the meditation by giving them the opening line: When I was walking to my house I saw... (LET THEM FILL IN THE BLANKS). Then, remind them that they walked through a cloud.

Have them write this, let them write what the experienced inside the house.  End the story with them leaving the house to join their friends for a party down at the end of the trail by a stream.

Creation:
Type up and print it. Cut around the story and glue to a half sheet of construction paper.

Variations:
If you are unable to provide space for the children to lie down, then have them sit at a table, arms folded and heads down.  Eyes are to be closed only if that is comfortable for the child.  If you are unable to print the journal, glue the original hand-written story onto the construction paper. It is always fun to hang the story and have adults try and guess who is the author.

Closing Circle:
Children should be encouraged to read their story at the Closing Circle.  The circle can then recognize the individual as an author.

Part II to follow in next Update.




“House of Wonders” collage detail.
Row.txt_description: Offers an experience that can be used later by children when they are stressed or preparing for sleep; it can cure "being bored" and strengthen self-esteem. The end product (see Part II, November 2001) acts as a visual reminder of the meditative exercises learned.

Row.str_title: The House of Wonders - Part II
Row.txt_code:
< span class="TextCaption">“I went to each room and put flowers in each room.”



Part I was printed in last Update.
Note:  This is a two-part workshop.  However, each part can be done separately.  






“When I was walking to my house, I saw a big piece of
 paper.  The paper was eating candy...”


About this Workshop:
This project was developed with the help of the children who participated.  It started as an exercise in teaching kids that they have the ability to calm themselves through meditation. The workshop evolved into an exercise in visualization, imagination, journaling, and concluded with art.

Objective:
Children need to have dreams to use their imagination in expressing themselves. This workshop is ideal for children to show others their hopes and dreams through art.
      
Materials:
Colored construction paper
Colored pencils, Cray-Pas
Photos books for collage
Scissors, glue sticks
Copies of “blank house” (see attached)






“...Then I saw a little puppy and
 started playing with it...”





“I saw big blue flowers and big bushes... I swam
across a big pond to get to my front porch...”


Timeframe: 1 hr
Opening: 5 minutes
Introduction: 5 minutes
Distribute/read journals: 10 minutes
Demonstration: 5 minutes
Cut and paste: 30 minutes
Closing circle: 5 minutes

Age Range: 5 and up

Ratio:
One adult for four children

Space Setup:
Cover the table area with newspaper

Opening Circle/Intro:
Sit in a circle and give the children an opportunity to say how they are feeling today. Anyone not willing to share can just say “pass.” This is something I do at the beginning of each workshop. Introduce the workshop as way to express what they were SEEING in their minds during their meditation on their “House of Wonders.” If some children did not do Part One of this workshop, they may get ideas by listening to other children read their journal page.

Creation:
Distribute the journal pages that each child made to describe their “House of Wonders.” Ask the children to read their journals aloud to refresh their memories. Give a demonstration of the various forms of art that may be used to best describe their scene. Distribute a “blank house” that children can use to start their project. Have them decorate the house as their journal states, with whatever variables are described in their story.

Variations:
Paint seems unnecessary and a mess when doing a large project such as this, so you may want to avoid it. Markers and Cray-Pas do very well. Pictures cut from a photo stock book can be folded and then attached to the picture to give a 3D effect similar to pop-up books.

Closing Circle:
Children should be encouraged to share their pictures and pass them around the circle. They should also have the opportunity to say how they felt during the process.
Row.txt_description: Offers an experience that can be used later by children when they are stressed or preparing for sleep; it can cure "being bored" and strengthen self-esteem. The end product acts as a visual reminder of the meditative exercises learned.

Row.txt_code:
< /tr>


 “My guardian angel...”
  

Objective:
To encourage children to explore some non-violent words and ideas. To help children cope with past crisis and trauma and to foster their sense of safety and security by creating their own angel.

Valuing Diversity:
It is important not to assume that everyone celebrates Christmas. Have an alternative project planned for children who choose not to make a paper plate angel.

Materials:
Angel template (click here for template)
Paper plates (the template is designed for paper plates with a 9" diameter)
Angel words (click here for template)
Paints and brushes
Markers and crayons
Glue and feathers
Glitter and sequins
Stapler and scissors
Stickers and fabric scraps
Colored construction paper
Ribbons and string




 

Angels decorated with ribbons, markers, feathers, and glitter.
 
Timeframe: 1 hr
20 minutes: Opening circle
30 minutes: Activity
10 minutes: Closing circle



 
 
 Angels decorated with ribbons,
markers, feathers, and glitter.
  

Ratio:
1 adult to 3 children

Preparation:
Cut out the angel words (see enclosed copy) for the warm-up activity. Make the blank paper plate angels for each child in advance.  To make the angels in advance, cut out the template and place it over the top half of a paper plate.  Most of the template will line up with the outline of the plate.  Trace the design onto the plate, then cut out the parts that form the angel's head and neck as well as the two extra cuts as indicated on the template.  Make enough for each child plus some extras. They are beautiful to have around the shelter, so you might encourage everyone to make more than one. Cut and fold them to make the three-dimensional angels. Staple if necessary. It’s amazing how the simple cuts of the paper plate can end up creating such beautiful, graceful three-dimensional angels.

Space Setup:
Have cushions or pieces of rug available to sit on for the opening circle and tables for the activity.

Assembling the Angels:
Follow steps #1 through #6 pictured here to create a three-dimensional angel from a cut paper plate.


1. Begin with cut plate.


2. Bend sides of plate backwards.


3. Tuck point A through slit B, so wings cross in back.


4. Gently expand the skirt of the angel to make it circular.


5. Staple back if you’d like. This can help hold the wing position.


6. Pull and adjust neck and head position, and you have your assembled angel. Note: In step #3, it helps if you pull the two slits into each other as far as they can go so the ends of the slits touch. Doing this makes the wings rise higher.


Opening Circle:
Gather the children in a circle. Ask them to close their eyes while they draw one or more angel words out of a hat or bag. Help them to read and understand their words. Give them the opportunity to talk about angels by asking, “What are angels?” and having a discussion.

Activity:
Offer the paper plate angels and the art materials. Explain to the children that they have the opportunity to create angels as holiday decorations or gifts. They can also create an angel for themselves—their own guardian angel to watch over them and help things go well. Allow time for the participants to decorate and to personalize their angels.

Closing Circle:
Gather the children into a circle again. Encourage each to share what he or she created and discovered in doing this workshop.

Variations for Age Levels:
Younger children might prefer to hear a story about angels instead of discussing angel words. Older children who finish the activity quickly might be interested in journaling about the workshop until it is time for the closing circle.
Row.txt_description: Encourages children to explore non-violent words and ideas. Helps them cope with past crisis and trauma and foster their sense of safety and security by creating their own angel.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for adults.

Row.txt_code:
We’d love to have some samples of
My Footprints created by the children in your
workshops. Please send any that you can. Thanks!
  
This workshop was adapted from a Women’s Windows Workshop written by Lucy Tschachtli. Lucy is a Women’s Windows Leader at Haven House in Buffalo, New York.

A special “thanks” to Silvia Gutierrez for helping to adapt this project for children.

Note: The footprint collages throughout this update were created during Lucy’s workshops.

Objective:
To allow the children to validate and express feelings about their unique journey. If appropriate you can focus more specifically on their journey to the shelter, what they are learning, and where they want to go in their lives after they leave the shelter.

Note:
Note: Sometimes participants may want to create two feet: one to show where they’ve been and one to show where they’re going to. Encourage their creativity with this.


 
 
  

Materials:
Poster board and markers
Glue sticks and scissors
Magazines and/or stickers
Relaxing music
Laminating sheets and laminator (optional)
optional - "Footprints in the Sand" poem (click here for handout)

Timeframe: 1 hr
20 minutes: warm-up and opening circle
30 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult to 3 children

Space Setup:
Have an open space for the opening circle and tables for the activity.

Feet Warm-up:
(Alternative: Instead of using the following playful warm-up, you could start by reading the attached poem: “Footsteps.”)
“Let’s start with a Feet Warm-up today. Let’s stand in a circle. Find your spot in the circle and pretend your feet are glued to the ground. Get them glued down so you can’t lift them up. Wonderful! And now, slowly, slowly, start to pull them out of the glue. Can your stretch them out of the glue? Slowly, slowly! Like when you step in a pile of gum! Let’s walk around in a circle slowly slowly, like there’s gum on the bottom of our shoes! And now the gum is wearing off and we can walk easily. You can walk around outside of the circle. Walk wherever you want to go! And let’s see how your feet look when you are walking happily! Can anybody skip? Does anyone like to run? Wonderful! And now let’s see how they look when you are starting to get tired! Let go slower and slower, and come back towards the circle. Let’s go around in the circle again, slower and slower, getting tired. Let’s see what sleepy feet look like! And when your feet are really sleepy you might sit down and rest. Can you sit down? Anyone like to lay down and rest your feet? Let’s take a very quiet moment resting our feet! Beautiful!”


  
 





   

Introduction/Sharing:
“Our workshop today is called My Footprints. Our whole life is a journey and it is often our feet that carry us along—and sometimes it’s the feet of people we love when they are carrying us. Did your feet carry you here into this shelter? Or was it your mom’s feet?

“Today we are going to make a picture in the shape of our own feet! Think about your feet .... where have they carried you? What images, words, colors come to mind? Where would you like your feet to carry you? What images, words, colors come to mind? Every journey goes through hard times and good times. Along the way, it can help to notice where you’ve been and where you want to go next.

“I’ll help you trace your own foot and then cut it out. And then you can draw on it or glue things to it about your own journey. You can put anything on it. Try to include something about where you have been, and something about where you hope to go next.”

Step 1: Tracing
Trace the outline of each child's foot onto poster board and have him or her cut it out (if they are old enough). If you have younger children, they may need you to cut out the footprint for them.

Step 2: Creating
Encourage the children to use markers, stickers, and collage materials to illustrate their journey.

Step 3: Words
As the children finish their footprints encourage them to think of words that go with it. If possible, work with each child one-on-one as they are done. Ask for permission to write their words onto the back of their footprint. Be sure to include the date too. It can be meaningful as time goes by and the journey continues on.

Step 4: (optional) Lamination
If possible laminate the footprints. They look great and last longer! The leader will most likely need to do the laminating as lamination sheets can be tricky and unforgiving when you make a mistake. Note: After laminating, small pieces of magnetic tape (adhesive backed) can be added to the back of the collages so they can be hung on a metal surface.

Closing:
Encourage the children to share something from their Footprints. Affirm each child’s experience.

  


  


Footprints in the Sand

By Mary Stevenson

One night a man had a dream. He dreamed he was
walking along the beach with the Lord. Across the
sky flashed scenes from his life. For each scene, he
noticed two sets of footprints in the sand: one
belonging to him, and the other to the Lord. When
the last scene of his life flashed before him, he
looked back at the footprints in the sand. He
noticed that many times along the path of his life
there was only one set of footprints. He also noticed
that it happened at the very lowest and saddest
times in his life. This really bothered him and he
questioned the Lord about it. "Lord, You said that
once I decided to follow you, You'd walk with me all
the way. But I have noticed that during the most
troublesome times in my life, there is only one set
of footprints. I don't understand why when I needed
you most you would leave me." The Lord replied,
"My precious child, I love you and I would
never leave you. During your times of trial and
suffering, when you see only one set of footprints, it
was then that I Carried You."
Row.txt_description: Allows children to validate and express feelings about their unique journey, what they are learning and where they want to go in their lives, by creating drawings or collages using outlines of their own feet.
Row.txt_tips: Some children may not want to take off their shoes in order to trace their feet.  In case this should happen, leaders may want to trace their own feet in advance so that kids could also use a generic footprint pattern.

Row.str_author_location: Women's and Children's Crisis Shelter, Whittier, California
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
I think this is a great way to show kids that using ordinary kitchen items can create beautiful things.  It’s also a great way for the children to express themselves as they create their own flowers and vase.  

Materials:
Coffee filters—the kind with ruffled edges (3 per individual)
Markers and/or watercolors (young children are better off using markers)
Pipe cleaners
Bottles (water bottles, soda bottles, etc—plastic and glass are both fine)
Tissue paper cut into squares (different sizes)
Glue (white school glue)
Water and a bowl
Brushes
Newspaper to protect the table

Ratio:
1 adult to 3 children

Timeframe: 1 hr
20 minutes: warm-up and opening circle
30 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Space Setup and Prep:
Have an open space for the opening circle and tables for the activity.  Mix the glue/water in advance (Put glue in the bowl first.  Then slowly add water and stir until the glue is like heavy cream—about 1/2 glue and 1/2 water).  Be sure to make your own flower in advance so you know how the process works.  Have fun!

Flower Warm-up:
For younger children:  “Let’s start with a Flower Warm-up today.  Let’s all stand in a circle.  Good.  To do our Flower Warm-up, let’s take a minute to think together.  How do flowers start out?  What are they before the bloom?  What are they before they even have stems or leaves?  That’s right!  They start out as seeds!  So that’s how we’re going to start out: as seeds.  Can you make yourself into a seed?  Would you be a small round seed, like a poppy seed?  Would you be big like a sunflower seed?  Would you be a long stretched out seed, like a green bean?  As you rest on the ground being a seed, I’m going to walk around the room and sprinkle some magic water on you so you can begin to grow.  (Walk around the circle rubbing your hands together over each special seed to make the magic water sound.)  As I sprinkle the magic water on you, begin to grow.  Can you make a stem?  Can you make a leaf?  How tall can you grow?  And is your flower ready to open?  Lets see all of the flowers opening!  Beautiful!”  If you like, sit in a circle and have each child share about what kind of flower they were, what color they were, etc.    
For older children:  “If you were going to be a flower today, imagine what would you look like and why?  Picture what color you would be.  Would you be big or small?  Short or tall?  Would your flower be happy?  Shy?  Angry?   Wise?  Let’s go around in a circle and hear about each of the flowers.”
 
Introduction/Sharing:
“For our workshop today, we each get to make flowers and a vase.”   





Step 1:  Decorate three filters





Step 2:  Stack on top of each other





Step 3:  Dig finger in center to
close and tie on pipe cleaner





Step 4:  Spread filters to open flower



Flower-Making:
Step 1:
First, each individual will receive three coffee filters.  The older children can color in each filter with watercolors.  They can use all kinds of different colors, or just one color, whatever they’d like.  Younger children can use markers.  They can make designs, write words, or just color it all with the markers.

Step 2:
Next, when all three filters are done and dried, put all three filters together, one on top of the other in any order.  Then dig your hand in the middle of the filter to create a closed-like flower.  Keep the flower closed by pinching the bottom of the filters and twisting a small piece of all three filters.

Step 3:
Next, grab your pipe cleaner and tie a small part of the pipe cleaner on to the small twisted piece of the filter.  You can just wrap the pipe cleaner around.

Step 4:
Spread out the filters to create a bloomed flower.

Vase-Making:
Step 5:
Use an empty bottle (i.e. water bottle, soda drink, etc.).  It’s good to use a plastic or glass bottle. 

Step 6:
Cut out tissue paper in small square pieces, all different sizes and colors. 

Step 7:
Now using a brush, paint the bottle with the paste liquid we created.  Then place the tissue squares onto the bottle and add another coat of glue/water paste.

Step 8:
Let it dry and place your flowers in the vase.

Closing:
Encourage the children to share their flowers and vases.
Many things can come out as the children share about their flowers.  The colors they choose for their flowers can express a lot.  Remember that the same color might mean different things for different children.  (e.g. black could mean strength, anger, danger, etc.)  Affirm each child’s experience.

Variations:
I led this activity at a Mommie and Me class and both the mothers and the children really connected and bonded very well.  This could also be a great group activity as well.  I think it can work well for children of any age, as much can be expressed through the creation of the flowers.
Row.txt_description: A great way to show kids that using ordinary kitchen items can create beautiful things.

Row.txt_code:
Safe Rock samples
  
Objective:
To give the children a chance to think about times they have felt safe, happy, and secure. To create something strong and solid—their Safe Rock—that they can carry with them to reassure themselves and build their sense of safety. Note: You could also call them “lucky rocks.”

Materials:
Rocks (big enough to paint on). Get enough for kids to paint more than one each. You can find them at house and garden stores and some building supply places. Bourget Bros. in Santa Monica specializes in assortments of stones.
Gel pens/paint pens that can show up on rocks
Paints (acrylic paints, fabric paint, or puffy paints)
Brushes
Water and cups
Newspaper to cover table

  


“Roasting Marshmallows”
 
  

Background Thoughts about Rock Painting:
“People painted on rocks thousands and thousands of years ago. It was one of the very first kinds of art there ever was. They painted on the walls of caves where they lived, before there were even houses and streets. They painted pictures about what was very important to them. Sometimes is was pictures of what they wished for, like when they hunted to get their food, they drew pictures of how they wanted the hunt to go. Their paintings on walls of rock lasted for years and years so that people can see them even today. As you paint on your rock today, know that what you paint and what you express is important. And it can last a long time.”

Ratio:
1 adult to 4 children

Timeframe: 1 hr
20 minutes: warm-up and opening circle
30 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle


 
 
 “Friendly Trees”
  

Space Set-up and Prep:
Have an open space for the opening circle and tables for the activity.

Safe Rock Warm-up:
“Let’s start with a Rock Warm-up today. Let’s all sit in a circle. Good. To start our Safe Rock Warm-up, let’s take a minute to think about rocks together. Have you ever seen a rock you liked? What did it look like? Take a rock now and hold it in your hand. How does it feel? (smooth, hard, cold... etc.) Have you ever sat on a big rock? Or jumped off of one? Where were you? Have you ever felt how wonderful it can be to sit on a cool rock on a hot day? Or when you’re cold have you ever sat on a rock that’s been warmed up by the sun? As you hold your rock now, you might notice it warming up.

“How old do you think your rock is? Is it older than you? Is it older than your parents? And your grandparents too? Rocks are very old. They were here before there were TVs, computers, or even cars. They were here before this country was created. As you hold your rock, notice that it has been here a long, long time. Some people feel that rocks have wisdom in them. They have seen so much.


 
 
 “My Beautiful Night”
  

“Look closely at your rock. Imagine how old it is, old and strong. Imagine that your special rock wants to help keep you safe and happy. It has been around a long, long time. It knows many things, and now it’s happy to be meeting you for the first time today. What do you think your Safe Rock is thinking right now? If it could talk, what would it say right now?” (Encourage each child to share.)

Introduction/Sharing:
“Today each of us will get a chance to make our own Safe Rocks that we can carry with us, or give to someone else who needs help staying safe. If you need to make more than one rock, that’s fine. There are plenty.

You’ve already had a chance to hold your rock and ‘listen’ to what it might say. Now you get to use paints and pens to draw on it whatever colors and shapes it wants to have. What colors and shapes help remind you of being safe? Ocean waves? A party full of friends? The sunshine? Some trees? The moon? What gives you a sense of safety and peacefulness? Maybe it’s a special person who helps you feel safe. Or maybe there are words your rock would like to have on it, to help you feel safe. What words would your rock have on it?”

  


“A New Morning”
 
  

Painting:
Assist each child as they paint their Safe Rock or Rocks. They may need special help putting words on with the paint pens. Help them out as needed. Encourage them to create more than one rock so they can keep one for themselves and also give some to others. They make wonderful, meaningful gifts.

Closing:
For the closing circle, give each child a chance to share their Safe Rocks.
Affirm each child’s experience.



 
 
 “Love”
  
 
 “My Best Friend”
Row.txt_description: Gives the children the chance to think about when they felt secure, and to create something solid as an expression of that safe feeling.
Row.txt_tips: If available, bigger rocks would allow for more creativity and self expression.

 Expressing Feelings sample: Mad
  
Objective:
To let the children express themselves and their feelings. To allow them to create without criticism. To give them the opportunity to experience the magic and beauty of seeing something invisible become visible.

Materials:
White construction paper or watercolor paper
Watercolor sets w/ brushes
Cups of water (2 per participant)
Paper towels
White crayons
Children’s music
Feeling chart (see attached sample)
Spray bottle with water


 
 
 Happy feelings painting (using watercolor on
op of bubble letters drawn with white crayon).
  

Music Suggestion:
I love to use a children’s music CD called “On the Move with Greg and Steve.” My favorite song for this workshop’s Opening Section (see below) is “Friends Forever.” This CD is available at teacher’s supply stores. It’s a wonderful resource for the Children’s Windows Workshops.

Ratio:
1 adult to 5 children

Timeframe: At least 1 hr
20 minutes: opening circle
30 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle


 
 
 Supplies for this workshop: paper, white
crayons, and watercolors.
  

Space Setup and Prep:
Have an open space for the opening circle and tables for the activity.

Opening:
Introduce yourself and explain about the art project, “Expressing Feelings with Watercolor.” Show the chart to the children and talk about it as a group. Have each child introduce themselves and share how they feel at that time. Remind the children about respecting others’ work as well as their feelings.

Do an exercise with the children with music to shake their feelings out. Have the children share what they do when they feel a certain way. (For example: “When I feel sad, I cry in my room.”) Encourage the children to share their feelings.

  


Angry feelings watercolor.
 
  

Expression Time:
Allow the children to write or draw how they feel with the white crayons. If they are unable to write, they can dictate the words and have you or another leader write for them. Be sure everyone presses hard to make their crayon lines. The harder you press, the more the crayon will show up!

Because both the paper and crayon are white, it is sometimes hard to see exactly where you left off. Help the children know that that’s part of the creation and it’s okay.

Once they are done, let them paint with the watercolors.

If they wish to see more of the colors mixing together, spray the paper lightly with a spray bottle (set on light mist).


 
 
 Using bubble letters for “SAD.”
  

When the color appears, a white outline will appear where the crayon is. The writing or drawing will stand out.

Let the children know even if it’s not exactly what they expected, it’s okay.

Closing:
At the end, give all the children a chance to share how they feel then and what they think of the art they have created. You may need to remind everyone about respecting all the art and all the different feelings.
Row.txt_description: Allows the children time to express their feelings without criticism. Gives the opportunity to experience the magic and beauty of seeing something invisible become visible.
Row.txt_tips: Kids who are too young to write can use faces instead to express the emotions.

Row.txt_code:
Note: The images illustrating this workshop
are miscellaneous magazine pictures.


Objective:
To give the children an opportunity to express   all the things they feel about themselves in their own creative way.  To help them focus on positive things about themselves and each other.

Impact:
When I lead this project the children get very excited about it.  They enjoy having the freedom to draw and experience how they feel about themselves.  I can see them gain a sense of self-esteem, pride, and understanding of themselves.  I can see how they benefit from this project because it allows them to take control of themselves and their feelings. 

Materials:
Construction paper (assorted colors)
Coloring markers
Magazines or photo stock books
Pre-cut images (for younger children who cannot cut their own)
Scissors







Glue sticks
Ratio:
1 adult to 6 children

Timeframe: At least 1 hr
20 minutes: opening circle
30 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Space Setup and Prep:
Set up an art table with supplies for the project.  If possible, set up a separate space for the opening and relaxation where the children can sit in a circle, away from the distraction and temptation of the art supplies.

If you are working with younger children who cannot use scissors, it’s important to have pre-cut images for them to select and paste.







Opening:
For the opening circle, I like to have each child say one thing they like about themselves.  When I work with the children, I constantly tell them positive things about themselves, so it’s not hard for them to think of things they like.  Often they say “can I say two things?”  It’s wonderful to see them focus on the positive about themselves.  
 
Relaxation:
Every group, I lead a relaxation for the children.  I dim the lights and play soft music.  I have them all sit in a circle and close their eyes.  I tell them this is a “special time” out for them—a time they get to relax and learn how to calm themselves.  Each relaxation I lead is different.  Often I count backwards from 10 to 1.  I also use the breathing exercises from the Children’s Windows Manual (pages 34-35), Energizing Breaths, Breathe Hot/Breathe Cold, Butterfly Breaths, and Monkey Breaths are all exercises that can be adapted into the relaxation. 











For the “All About Me” workshop relaxation, I like to have the children focus on noticing things they like about themselves during the relaxation.

Note about resistance: There are sometimes children who have a hard time relaxing and can tend to be disruptive during this part of the workshop.  Our group is optional, so I ask any children who do not want to cooperate with the relaxation to leave and go back to class.  If I feel it’s appropriate, I invite them back when the relaxation is over.

Expression Time:
After the relaxation, it’s creation time.  I encourage the children to look through the pictures in the magazines and pick out what ever they think best gives a description of themselves.  They then paste it onto their construction paper.  
I encourage them to pick lots of pictures of all the things they like about themselves.  They can also use markers to write or draw things they like.  

Closing:







At the end, give all the children a chance to share what each of their pictures means to them.  Encourage them to especially focus on sharing the things they like about themselves.  

If time allows, during each person’s turn, have the other kids say something positive about that person too.   

It’s wonderful practice for them to focus on the good in themselves and in those around them.
Row.txt_description: Encourages children to express all the things they feel about themselves in their own creative way. Helps them focus on positive things about themselves and each other.

Row.txt_code:
This workshop came to AWBW from Bob Bowman of Free Arts for Abused Children (FAAC).  Bob has volunteered with FAAC for 12 years and has been leading this Life Masks project for 10 years now.  He led this project for AWBW during  our May Leader’s workshop where it was well received a nd enjoyed by all.






Leader’s Workshop participant holding
her finished Life Mask.



Objective:
To give the children the unique and powerful experience of having a mask formed on their own face.  To give them the opportunity to explore their feelings and sense of self by decorating their life mask.

Materials:
Quick dry plaster bandages, cut into strips
Vaseline
Large bowls/warm, salted water
Paper towels
Plastic garbage bags (1 per child, plus extras for trash)
Masking tape (to secure the bags)
Clear shower caps (1 per child)
Baby wipes
Assorted acrylic or tempera paints (watercolors can be used as a low-budget alternative)
Glitter, sequins and feathers
Brushes
Scissors
Elmers glue
Newspaper or butcher paper to cover tables (and maybe floor)

Sources:
3-inch plaster bandages can be ordered from McKesson (a medical supply company) at (626) 284-3221.  It’s about $33 for a box of 12 rolls.  Also, instead of shower caps, you can use bouffant caps from Smart and Final.

Ratio:
At Free Arts, the ratio is one volunteer per child.  In your group, you might have older children work on each others’ masks to lower the ratio.

Timeframe: At least 1 hour
10 minutes: opening
20 minutes: mask making
20 minutes: decorating
10 minutes: closing circle

Space Setup:
Cover all tables and the floor too, if you wish.  The plaster is messy.  It does turn to powder when dry and washes off easily.  Cut plaster bandages into strips.  Cut 3” diameter paper towel circles to cover eyes.  Place strips, vaseline, warm salted water (the warmth and salt make the plaster dry faster), 3” circles, shower caps, baby wipes, and garbage bags at each of the mask-making tables.  Have enough tables to set the vaseline and water on, plus one separate table set up for decorating.  Note: At the end of the activity, dump the plaster/water outside (not into the plumbing system).

Opening:
Tell the children what you're going to do: you're going to cover their faces with vaseline, apply strips of wet plaster gauze, let it harden, peel it off and then they're going to decorate it.  Ask them if this is all okay with them.  This enables them to agree to the process and grant you entry into their space.  Empower the children by letting them decide if they will do a mask or a hand.  If they do a mask, ask if they want their eyes and mouths open or covered.

Note:  Although it might seem like it would be scary for kids to have their faces covered with plaster, I’ve found that they actually enjoy it it greatly.  Once they decide they want a mask, they generally go along with the process and don’t get apprehensive or scared.  I have never seen a kid freak out and require removal of a partially completed mask.  They usually trust the volunteers and are enthusiastic about the activity.

Face Masks: 
Step 1: Check-in
With this project, we work in pairs, one volunteer per child.  When you are assisting a child, first check in about the different mask options: Does the child want their mouth open or closed?  Eyes can be left open or covered.  Or would they rather do their hand instead of their face?










Fig. 1: Protecting hair
with cap and shoulders
with trash bag.

Fig. 2: Applying vaseline
to face.

Fig. 3: Covering eyes with
cut-out paper towels.





Step 2: Protection
When they are ready to begin their mask, have them sit in a chair facing you (not laying down).  Drape the trash bag over their chest and tape it behind the neck.  (Cutting a hole and slipping the bags over the children’s heads is confining and can be uncomfortably hot).  Put shower cap over the child’s hair (see Fig. 1). 





Fig. 4: Applying and
smoothing wet plaster gauze
around edges of face.




Cover the child’s face with a healthy layer of vaseline (see Fig. 2).  Use LOTS of vaseline.  Add extra along hair lines.  This prevents plaster from adhering to skin and facial hair. 

If the child wants to have their eyes covered by the mask, first have them close their eyes.  Then cover each eye with a paper towel circlet (see Fig. 3).  Explain the importance of covering the eyes, as the plaster is painful and difficult to remove from them.  Once the eyes are covered, you are ready to begin with the plaster.









Step 3:  Plaster
Dip plaster strip into warm-salted water (the salt helps the plaster dry more quickly), squeeze extra water from plaster by running it through two fingers.  Frame jawline, then forehead to create a circle (see Fig. 4-5).  Framing first strengthens mask and reinforces the structure.





Fig. 5: Creating a circle of
gauze around face.



Frame nostrils and mouth (See Fig 6-8).  For example with open nose, see Fig 13.  Fill in rest of face area with plaster strips, leaving air space for nose and mouth.  Add 3-4 layers of plaster gauze.  When the plaster feels solid and does not give when touched, the mask is ready to be removed.  Ask the child to move his/her jaw back and forth as you slip your fingers under their lower jaw area.  Peel the mask up and off (see Fig. 9).

Step 4:  Decoration
Have the child wipe their face with baby wipes.  Once they have cleaned themselves off, they can take their mask to the decorating table (see Fig 10-11). 













Fig. 6: Working up
over mouth.

Fig. 7: Working down nose.

Fig. 8: Entire face is
covered with layers.










Fig. 9: Removing mask.

Fig. 10.: Painting masks
with acrylics.

Painting masks

with acrylics.





Hands Masks:
When doing a mask of the hand instead of face, have the child lay his/her hand flat on the table.  Apply vaseline.  For some reason, hands need a lot more vaseline than faces, so put extra.   At Free Arts, we require the hands to be flat (to avoid gang signs, etc.).  Apply strips of plaster to the fingers.  Apply only to the top surface.  Do not wrap around the fingers.  You will need extra layers in order to make the plaster solid (5-6 layers).





Fig. 11.: Completed Life Mask.





Fig. 12.: Completed hand mask.




Closing:
At the end, give all the children a chance to share their masks and what they mean to them.






Fig. 13.: Sample of mask with open nose.
Row.txt_description: Gives the children the unique and powerful experience of having masks formed from their own faces. Gives them the opportunity to explore their feelings and sense of self by decorating their masks.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for adults (appropriate for all ages).

Row.txt_code:
At AWBW we’ve been noticing how many children struggle with being extremely hard on themselves and afraid of making mistakes.  We looked into our files to find a project that could help the children to find a sense of humor, playfulness and acceptance about making mistakes.   We found this workshop from Erica Poellot.  We hope you enjoy it and have fun exploring mistakes with the children!

Objective:
To help the children learn to stop being so hard on themselves.  To give them a chance to build a sense of humor and acceptance about mistakes they (and those around them) have made.  

Impact:
When I led this project it was a very lighthearted group.  Everyone was very open and joked a lot about mistakes we had all made.  It was great to see the sense of camaraderie.  One of the children said “Erica, I think you are the biggest turkey!”    








Materials:
Construction paper (assorted colors)
Coloring markers
School glue
Feathers (lots)
“Googley” eyes
Scissors
Optional:  We did the workshop using pinecones instead of construction paper.  It took a lot of extra feathers to decorate them, but they looked great!!!

Ratio:
1 adult to 6 children

Timeframe: At least 1 hr
20 minutes: opening circle
30 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle









Space Setup:
Set up an art table with supplies for the project.  If possible, set up a separate space for the opening and Turkey Dance where the children can be away from the distraction and temptation of the art supplies.

Note:  If you are working with younger children who cannot use scissors, don’t cut out the turkeys.







Opening:
At the beginning of the workshop, I encourage the group to think about mistakes.  I help them be light about it.  It helps to have some silly mistakes in mind that I can share to inspire the group to be open and enjoy sharing their mistakes.

Turkey Dance Warm-up:
If you have a young group, you could begin with a “Turkey Dance”  Play up-beat music, and have everyone dance around the room as a turkey.  Ask: Would they be a big turkey?  A little turkey?  A fast turkey?  A slow turkey?  Encourage everyone to be silly and not worry about how they look!

Expression Time:
For making the Mistake Turkeys, begin choosing colors of paper and outlining hands with markers.  If the children are old enough, they could cut out their hand-tracing before decorating it and adding feathers.  If they are younger, it may be much easier and less frustrating for them to leave it on the full page.  After the Turkey is drawn, add glue, feathers, more drawing, and “googley” eyes to complete them.   

Closing:
At the end, give all the children a chance to share their Mistake Turkey and anything about what it means to them. 

Encourage them to remember that it’s okay to make mistakes, and it’s okay not to be perfect.  Remind them that it can be fun when they are not being too hard on themselves.
Row.txt_description: Helps the children learn to stop being so hard on themselves and gives them a chance to use humor to accept their mistakes and those of others.

Row.txt_code:
Introduction:







Color Discovery Maps is a workshop  adapted from an exercise in the book The Artist’s Way by Julia Cameron.  The exercise is called Color Schemes and is in the chapter—Recovering a Sense of Strength.

I feel this is a good exercise for all ages. I wanted to adapt and expand the idea for children.

Objective:
To gain a sense of strength in relating ourselves to a color.   To explore and accept our feelings in a different forum by noticing our own qualities—   as they relate to color.  When a child (or older person too!) begins to contemplate their favorite color, or a color they like, and relate it to themselves somehow, I’ve found that they naturally begin to associate the good in themselves with their color.  They can also accept aspects of themselves as true and “OK” by thinking about the color.  Because colors are strong, a sense of strength is gained in relating ourselves with a color.  (The following details and steps of this workshop will describe this idea better.)

Age Level:
Children age 4 to 104    







Materials:
Butcher paper - or any large white paper that can be put on the floor (like a map).
The idea is to be able to work freely with a lot of space around each person.
Acrylic paint or finger paint (many colors)
Large brushes (or children can use their fingers)
Water
Paper towels
Cray-Pas
Markers

Timeframe:
Total time: 1 1/2 hours
Relaxation—10 minutes
Painting shape—15 minutes
Drawing on and around the color (making the map)—30 to 45 minutes
Closing circle—15 minutes 







Relaxation:
This art work is a relaxation on its own—you may want to begin by explaining what we are doing and just letting the children begin while listening to relaxing music.  You can use this relaxation if they don’t seem able to jump right in:

“Imagine a box of crayons—it’s a really big box.  It has every color you can imagine.  The crayons are big and once you begin to draw with them they can turn into markers, they can turn into paint brushes.  The box has so many colors.  There is bright red, sky blue, pumpkin orange, lime green, bright green, dark green—like in a dark forest.  Bright yellow—like the sun, light yellow like a pretty small bird, light pink—like cotton candy, dream like and carefree, bright blue—very strong, but friendly and, there, there it is: your favorite color—what color is it?” 

Encourage the children to announce their color.  Ask them to try to describe it exactly.  Now we are going to try to make our color with paint in a shape on our paper.

Art Making Steps:
#1 Have the children paint a shape of the color they have chosen in the center of their paper (map). This is the color they have in their mind - it may not be straight out of the bottle.  Help them to mix their color—the exact color they want.

#2 Put the paint away (young children will get distracted and messy with paint for long periods of time).  We want to stay focused, so it’s best to introduce our new materials (Cray-Pas and markers) for that purpose.

#3 “We want to relate the color we have chosen to ourselves and our feelings.  This color you chose to put on your paper—does it have anything in common with you?
When you think about the color, how is it like you?  The map has our color in the middle and we can draw pictures and write around that, in order to discover what the color has in common with us.”

Examples:  I am blue like the sky—positive, expansive, full of hope.  I am red—wild, fun, sometimes I get mad.

The children should have a good amount of time to draw pictures and write things around their color.  Of course they may need help.  I would walk around and just talk to each child individually to help generate ideas.

Closing:
Allow a good amount of time to let children share and discuss their color map (15 minutes for the group). They will discover more as they talk about their color.

Note: I recently did a version of this exercise with a painting class I teach.  The group is mostly adults, but they came up with such beautiful writings about color and themselves that I wanted to share them with you:






I am blue, full of hope.
Sometimes I’m blue like in
the sky and free.






I am blue, strong.

I am blue - expansive.






Sometimes I’m a peaceful blue.





Emma:
I am Golden. I am lustrous; radiant in richness and splendor; of greatest value and importance. I am precious, marked by peace, prosperity and creativeness, very favorable, advantaged and excellent. I have a promising future, assured of success.

Lea:
I am blue. I come in many shades depending on the weather, time of day, or season. I am seen mostly in the sky. I represent cleanliness and hope. I am a calmer.

Angie:
I am blue/green. I am blue at times, yet strong and positive, and green at times, feeling clam and close to nature as the trees. Yet when blended I am the beautiful color blue/green.

Shari:
I am green, the life, breath and beauty of spring, I am green.

Carol:
I am taupe, neutral, flexible, compatible, almost rosy. I can stand alone, but prefer a colorful companion. 

About the Author:
I taught workshops at Choices in Columbus to women and children for almost five years.
I learned a lot about teaching with a spirit that comes from A Window Between Worlds.
I was involved in Women’s Windows training in 1997 and Children’s windows training in 2002. I basically teach classes that are not involved with the shelter now, but I keep the spirit of teaching that I learned with the residents. I learned to give the residents a window of time and freedom to enjoy and express themselves. I’ll take that idea and my experiences with me to all the students I teach in the future.
Row.txt_description: Helps each child gain a sense of strength by identifying with a color that he or she really likes. Offers time for exploration and acceptance of feelings in a different forum - by noticing our own qualities as they relate to color.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for adults (appropriate for all ages).

Row.txt_code:
Helping Hands artwork on these pages
by Olivia Tamayo and Cathy Salser
  

Objective:
To focus on the positive things that can be gained and learned from difficult experiences.
To notice the importance of giving and receiving help. To give participants an opportunity to reflect on the events of September 11th in an atmosphere
of safety and support.

Materials:
Heavy paper
Scissors
Markers, collage supplies, glitter, watercolors
Hole punch
Thread, string or ribbon

Age Level:
All ages. For younger children, you will need to help with the cutting, or else do the project without cutting out the hands. (You can just trace and draw without cutting.) Depending on the age-levels, range, and size of the group you might decide to limit the materials to just markers for simplicity.

Timeframe:
Total: 1 hour
10 min: Introduction
5 min: Warm-up Circle

 
 
  


25 min: Creation
20 min: Sharing

Caution:
Be thoughtful about whether or not to bring up 9/11. If it’s not already on the children’s minds, there’s probably no need to remind them or focus on it.

You can adjust the workshop by just leaving out all references to 9/11 and focusing on general feelings about helping others and being helped.

If 9/11 is on the children’s minds, then this workshop may provide a helpful way to channel worries and memories in a positive direction.

Introduction:
“With September here, I know people around us are talking about 9/11 and what happened last year. Have you heard people talking? Do you remember what happened last year?

“There were lots of scary and difficult things about what happened last year. There were also some good things. It might be hard to remember, but let’s try. Do you remember anything good? Did you see anyone helping anyone else? What do you remember that was good?”

  


  

Depending on the age of your group and what they remember seeing on television you might encourage them to remember some of these things: Do you remember the rescue workers saving people? Do you remember how people sent support from all across the country to help? Do you remember the dog that helped the blind man out of the building? What are the good things you remember seeing people do to help each other? Do you remember how special it was for the people who got to hear “I love you” from their loved ones for the last time? Little things people did make a very big difference.

“So today, in honor of all the ways people have helped each other since 9/11, we will be creating Helping Hands. You can make one, and if you want to make more after that, that’s fine.”

Warm-up:
“For our warm-up today, we’re going to go around in a circle and each share about someone who has helped us, and someone we have helped. It could be someone in your family, or someone far away. It could be something from today, or it could be something from a long time ago.”


 
 
  

Creation:
As the children create their hands, encourage
them to trust
whatever comes
to them and not
criticize it. Assist
them as needed with
the cutting. For those
who finish early, encourage
them to add any words that go on their hand. Let them know it’s fine to make another Helping Hand to give to someone else if they wish.

Sharing:
Give everyone an opportunity to share their Helping Hands, what they mean to them, and anything they discovered in the process.

Closure:
It is important to take special care to end the workshop on a positive and hopeful note, especially since this is such a deeply difficult subject. If you think it would help, have a final sharing circle. Ask each participant: What is one good thing you take with you from this workshop?

You might want to end with a celebration of hanging all of the hands in the shelter.
Row.txt_description: Offers time for focus on the positive things that can be gained and learned from difficult experiences and to notice the importance of giving and receiving help.
Row.txt_notes: TO DO: Create variation for adults (appropriate for all ages).
Row.txt_tips: One way to start out this activity that works well is to read kids the book "Hands are Not for Hitting", by Martine Agassi.

Row.str_author_location: Friendship Center of Helena, Helena, Montana
Row.txt_code:
Awesome Essence sample drawing.



Mary Huigen developed this project for a women’s group.  The goal was to work on creating and maintaining personal boundaries.  She wrote it to be adaptable for all ages, so here we share an adaptation for working with children.  Feel free to change and adjust it as you need.  Enjoy!

Objective:
To explore our “essence” by noticing who we are, what makes us special, and what makes us strong.  To see how this “essence” comes through whatever we experience, and all the challenges can make us even stronger, more special, and more amazing. 

Note:  If the word “essence” throws the kids off too much, you could call this workshop “Who am I?” and just leave the word “essence” out.   

Materials:
Large paper bags (brown grocery bags)
Cray-Pas oil pastels
Watercolors (Prang makes good strong colors)
Large container of warm water
Tea candle

Timeframe:
Total:        1 hour
10 min:  Introduction
10 min:  Visualization
30 min:   Activity
10 min:   Closing Circle

Setup/Prep:
It is optimal to have an open area that has plenty of space for movement, yet is near the area they will be working.  Place one of each item from the materials list for each participant.  Place the candle in the middle of the table, but don't light it yet.  Have the container of water near by, but in a location separate from the working table, so spills don't occur where the work is being done.

Be sure to experiment with this project prior to doing the workshop, so you know how it feels to go through these steps.





Step 1: Cut the paper bag to
the shape you desire.





Step 2: Draw an image of yourself.





Step 5: Paint with water
colors (after folded & wet).



If you are working with children who won’t be able to cut out their own shapes from the bags, you might cut the bags in advance.  You might choose one basic shape for the kids to work with (hearts, circles, squares, etc.)

Introduction:
“This workshop is an opportunity to discover the power at the root of ourselves.  One word for this is our “essence.”  Our essence is the wonderful strength and specialness inside of us that cannot be changed.  It is there no matter what we go through.  Today we’ll be making drawings with shapes and colors to show our “essence” and then we’ll see what happens when our drawings go through difficult changes.  We’ll actually be taking our drawings, crumpling them up, and dunking them in water.  Then when we open them up, we can add watercolor and see how amazing they look even after all they’ve been through.”  (Maybe do a demonstration of the Awesome Essence Making)

Visualization:
We did this standing and with eyes closed.  If a participant is too uncomfortable with eyes closed, perhaps they could stand near you or with their back to the wall and the exit door near them.  They may choose to do this with eyes open.

“First, it is important to feel centered in your body.  Find the center of the balls of your feet.  Find the center of your heels.  Rest in that place.  Find where your hips are square and comfortable.  Find where your shoulders are set and balanced.  Find where your head rests evenly on your neck.  Stay here for a moment.  This is a good time to thank your body for what it does for you.  In front of you, imagine there are four balls of energy: one blue, one green, one violet and one white. In a way that is most comfortable for you, bend, fold, twist, or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the blue ball.  This ball holds the question for you, ‘Who is in my family?’ Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball. In a way that is most comfortable for you, fold, bend, twist or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the green ball. This ball holds the question, ‘Who are my friends?’  Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball.  In a way that is most comfortable for you, fold, bend, twist, or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the violet ball.  This ball holds the question, ‘What makes me special?’  Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball.  In a way that is most comfortable for you, fold, bend, twist, or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the white ball.  This ball holds the question, ‘What makes me strong?’ Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball.  Now find and gather all the balls you have stored.  With the greatest care and with all the power you can muster, bring these balls together and merge them into one singular flame.  Remember to use your power, not force.  Rest with this flame.” 
 
For different age levels you might vary the questions.  You might include “What are my hopes and dreams?”  “What makes me feel happy?”  “What makes me feel peaceful?”  “Who do I feel supported by?”
