“And now picture it shining out from the room to the whole world.  Shining all the way from inside your heart out to the whole world around you.  

“Take a moment with your eyes still closed to notice how wonderful it feels, and when you’re ready, open your eyes, and stretch like a ray of sunshine, filling the room!”






Sample words of inner gifts (for older kids)


Adapting for Older Kids:
If you are working with older kids, you will probably want a different warm-up and you will want to encourage them to create their own shape person (not use the gingerbread-shaped pattern).  One idea for an alternate warm-up is to place words in a hat—words representing the inner gifts you think your group of kids/teens has in their hearts.  Have them each draw a word and then think about where that gift is inside of them and how they show it in their lives.  If you think it would work with your group, you could lead a visualization similar to the one for younger kids, but having them picture their word filling up their heart and shining out to the rest of the world.









Creation:
Show the example, and walk them through the steps as needed:

Step One:
Making the main person shape. (Could be traced, could be cut out and colored.)





Two pieces of paper to make
the inner window.





The first piece is glued down
and decorated.





The second piece creates the window.



Step Two:  
Making the Window into Your Inner Gifts

Step Three:
Decorating everything!

Closing:
Give each child an opportunity to share about his/her creation and Inner Gifts.

Optional:  As we end our workshop today, let’s notice what’s nice about having holidays here with each other in the shelter.   Can anyone think of something that’s nice about celebrating together?
Row.txt_description: Gives the children a chance to explore the gifts they have on the inside, and notice that they are their best gifts--better than anything money can buy.

Row.txt_code:
I Am Strong Because... puzzle drawings from a
participant in Ramona’s workshops.
 
  



Objective:
To build a sense of pride in oneself and build a sense of cohesion within the group about the obstacles and hard times that they have been through as a group. The finished artwork serves as a pride badge as well as a means to not give up when times are difficult. This project is especially good for teenagers.

Materials:
Construction paper, markers, crayons, colored pencils, and a ruler for each participant.


 
 
 I Am Strong Because... puzzle drawings
from workshop participants
  

Be aware that there is a lot of room for creativity so please have glue, scissors, pencils, and pens on hand they just might want to use them.

Also have writing paper available because they may want to write it out before doing the artwork.

You will also need an easel or a large poster board attached to the wall and a marker available for participants to write on it in a visible accessible part of the room.

Timeframe:
This workshop could take up to 2 hours, but the time can be adjusted by the leader depending on the amount of time spent on discussion.


 
 
 I Am Strong Because... puzzle drawings

from workshop participants
  

Age Range:
Designed for teen girls, but please adapt to others as needed.

Setup:
Make a sample before the group, so you have something to share and get them started. Also, prepare the large poster board entitled We are strong because... so it will be accessible during the workshop.

Introduction:
Begin the introduction by having the participants read the quotes and the poem “Still I Rise” (see attached). If you have male clients, possibly teenage boys, they can discuss the poem “Ability” instead because they will be able to relate to it better. As the clients read the quotes and poem ask them what they feel the overall message is that the poem and the quotes give. (If you are short on time you can have the clients read only the poem or fewer quotes.) From the discussion that has been generated the leader can make a transition statement by saying something like, “We all have been through good times and bad times and this makes us who we are today, strong. If we were not strong we would not be here today.” I also present a poem that I personally wrote. (See side bar.)

 
 

 
I Am Strong Because... puzzle drawings
 
   


 
 A Picture of Me

Vivid, lively, and imaginative,
Smiling, laughing,
Caring, sharing, and loving,
Always putting others before herself,
Always helping others
in any way she could,
Friends and family are
her pride and joy: #1 priority,
As a matter of fact, through her actions,
she shows that they come before her.

She is her own Women,
She's a nonconformist,
Her clothes: a vivid formulation
of the passionate color of purple,
A style that is unique to her and only her,
She's not about styling and profiling,
She dresses for her,
It must comfort her,
No validation is needed but hers,
The decision to change
is hers and only hers,
She does what she wants
when she and only she wants to.

To understand her,
Nobody does,
She's like a puzzle of many pieces,
Only she has them all,
Everybody else just has a few pieces,
So they can’t see.

What they can’t see,
is that the pieces
are all in the pictures of her
It’s not in the pose,
It’s not in the hair,
It’s not in the clothes,
It’s not in her eyes,
It’s not that she is conceited,
Every set of eyes has a different story,
A story of growth,
That only she knows and only she can see.

By Ramona Young
  
Project:
Next, you tell the clients that today we are going to create our individual puzzle pieces which represent all of the reasons we are strong. Tell the clients that they can design it anyway that they want to and the title is I am strong because... You can show them your example and present it as a way to help them get started. The rulers are there in case they want to draw straight edges.

As clients begin to work, point out the poster board that you have entitled We are strong because... and tell them to feel free at any time to come up and write something on that piece of paper or ask you to write it for them.

As clients complete their puzzle give them the opportunity to share their puzzle with the group. You can point out or ask the clients to point out similar points made and use those to add to the We are strong because... page.

If possible, post the clients’ work and post the We are strong because... page as well. You can format the We are strong because... page into a poem. (See attached for the example my group did.) Make sure when you format it that it is written in a way that applies to all.

  


  



Obstacles and Hard Times
We need the rock of the past under our feeet in order to spring forward into the future. -Madeline L’Engle

Obstacles are those frightful things you see when you take your eyes off your goal. -Hannah Moore

I’ve failed over and over again in my life. And that is why I succeed. -Michael Jordan

You need chaos in your life to give birth to a dancing star. -Friedrich Nietzsche

Obstacles don’t have to stop you. If you run into a wall, don’t turn around and give up. Figure out how to climb it, go through it, or work around it. -Michael Jordan

Being defeated is often a temporary condition. Giving up is what makes it permanent. -Marilyn vos Savant

It gets dark sometimes, but morning comes... Keep hope alive. -Jesse Jackson


Still I Rise - Maya Angelou

You may write me down in history
With your bitter, twisted lies,
You may trod me in the very dirt
But still, like dust, I’ll rise.

Does my sassiness upset you?
Why are you beset with gloom?
‘Cause I walk like I’ve got oil wells
Pumping in my living room.

Just like moons and like suns,
With the certainty of tides,
Just like hopes springing high.
Still I’ll rise.

Did you want to see me broken?
Bowed head and lowered eyes?
Shoulders falling down like teardrops,
Weakened by my soulful cries.

Does my haughtiness offend you?
Don’t you take it awful hard
‘Cause I laugh like I’ve got gold mines
Diggin’ in my own back yard.

You may shoot me with your words,
You may cut me with your eyes,
You may kill me with your hatefulness,
But still, like air, I’ll rise.

Does my sexiness upset you?
Does it come as a surprise
That I dance like I’ve got diamonds
At the meeting of my thighs?

Out of the huts of history’s shame
I rise
Up from a past that’s rooted in pain
I rise
I’m a black ocean, leaping and wide,
Welling and swelling I bear in the tide.
Leaving behind nights of terror and fear
I rise
Into a daybreak that’s wondrously clear
I rise
Bringing the gifts that my ancestors gave.
I am the dream and the hope of the slave.
I rise I rise I rise



Ability - Selina E. Matis

Ability is to look at a blank page,
And create a poem.
Ability is to stare into the eyes of fear,
And come out stronger because of it.
Ability is to walk into a room of strangers,
And come out with friends.
Ability is to admit you are wrong,
When you are wrong.
Ability is to get back up,
When you fall down.
Ability is to believe,
When everything seems lost.

Ability - a simple word, with complex meaning.
For many, ability is never found, but for all ability is within.
Ability stares everyone in the face at one time or another.
Whether your ability is how well you shoot hoops,
How well you flip at dancing,
How smart you are at school.
You have ability.
For some, ability is lost by never trying.
Whether never trying to shoot one more time,
Never trying to bend a little more,
Or never trying to score higher in school.

Ability is within.
Ability is yours.


We are Strong Because - The Poetry Club

We are patient (sometimes).
We all have experienced good times and bad times.
We are strong because we come from strong cultures.
We help each other even when we don’t all get along.
We’ve had similar experiences.
We’ve had similar pasts.
We come together to help each other through hard times.
If we weren’t, we wouldn’t be here today.
We are all loved and we need each other.
Row.txt_description: Offers the chance to build a sense of pride in oneself as well as a sense of cohesion within the group about the obstacles and hard times that they have been through. The finished artwork serves as a pride badge and reminder to not give up.
Row.txt_tips:
The collage technique is popular because it prevents frustration over not being able to draw.

The theme behind this workshop also works well with journaling and poetry projects.

Row.str_title: Children Throughout The World Are Victims Too
Row.txt_code:
Here’s how the final mural looks at Women-Shelter
of Long Beach.



Objective:
To educate, discuss and have the children share their feelings about being in a family with domestic violence. While doing the workshop, children learn that some children of all ages all over the world have had or have domestic violence issues within their families.






These are some of the paper
dolls made at WomenShelter
of Long Beach.



Materials:
Wall space of 6 by 5 feet
Construction paper (assorted colors)
Large white paper (for 2-foot diameter drawing of the globe)
Blue, black, green, yellow, & brown yarn for the globe & for the hair.
Cray-Pas and markers
Glue, scissors, masking tape and a white paper plate
Patterns of boy and girl (see attached templates)
Patterns of clothes for the boys/girls
Patterns of hearts (see attached)
Optional: Real globe for discussion

Timeframe:
We did this project during a whole week, taking about an hour each day to work on it.  Once it was up, we decided to leave it up (it’s been 6 months now) and make it an on-going project adding new dolls when new children come to the shelter.  They really like it, and when they leave the shelter, we give them their doll to take with them.  This makes space for new dolls to be welcomed as new families come to the shelter.

Age Range:
We’ve done this project with mixed groups, ages 3-17.

Setup:
It might be a good idea to have made all the patterns (world, letters, hearts, clouds, sun, children, and paper clothes) before you start this workshop. It is a little long for the children ages 3 to 5.  Decide based on your group how much how is realistic for them to help cut out.  You might want to use the clouds as something the younger children can help cut out so they will feel included while older children cut out the more detailed parts.  If you have a mixture of age-levels, the school-age children like to help the younger children.  

Introduction:
Throughout the days of this workshop, as you create the paper “mural,” you’ll be talking with the children about the world and about domestic violence.  Ask them if they know what domestic violence is.  Ask the older children to give some examples of what they think it is.  Let the children know what domestic violence and what abuse are.  Ask them to share about their families if they want to.  Ask the children if they can come up with different countries around the world.  Let them know that in every country children are victims. Ask the children how they think other children may be feeling in homes with domestic violence.  Go with the flow of the children.

These are the stages we did day by day.  You could try it this way, or change it to fit the schedule at your shelter.

Monday:  World
Talk about the world.  (It helps if you have a three-dimensional globe to show, and of course, how you talk about it will depend on how old the children are.)  The way we shared it was: “Throughout the world there are many victims.  Does everybody know what the world is?  Do you know what countries are?  Can anyone name a country?  (Point out the countries they name on the globe.)  And where do you think there are children in the world?  Are there children here (point somewhere on the globe)?  Yes, there are.  There are children everywhere around the globe.”




This is how the whole thing looks when it’s
finished.  It’s about 6 feet wide and takes
the whole wall, with the sun and clouds at
the top.  You can see how big it is compared
to the chairs.




As you begin the artwork, be sure you have a nice big area to work in. Take the large white paper and make an even circle 2 to 2 1/2 feet in diameter for the world.  Invite the older kids to help you cut out the world, draw shapes on the circle to look like land masses of the earth and water.  Cut and glue different colored yarn to the outlines of different landmasses.  Ask the children to color inside each land mass using the Cray-Pas that match the yarn around the land. Use blue cray-pas to color in the water inside the blue yarn.

After the world is all done, the children can help the leader hang it on the wall with masking tape.   Be sure the world is hanging up high enough so the younger children cannot reach the pins if you decide to use push pins.

Tuesday:  Letters
The next day, we make the letters to spell “Children Throughout the World Are Victims Too.”  This is a good day to talk more about what it means to be a victim.  We say: “We often think about how your moms are victims of violence, but you are also victims.  There are many kinds of victims.  Can anyone tell me what a victim is?”  The children are really smart as they explore and express the many ways kids can be victims.  Talking about how children are victims around the world can help them feel connected rather than isolated.
As we cut out the words, we made them all black except for the word “children” which we made in many colors.  Making the letters for “children” we asked “What color do you want the ‘c’ to be?  And how about the ‘h’?  We will use many colors because there are many of you!”  The letters are traced from alphabet stencils, which are 2 1/2 inches tall onto construction paper.  Leaders and older children can cut out the letters.

Have the children help the leaders to stick the letters up on the wall. They need to be about 14 inches from the world so the paper dolls go in between the world and letters.  Remember to leave spaces for the hearts—or make them the same day as the letters! (See photo.)

Wednesday:  Hearts, clouds, and sun
The next day, we work on the hearts, clouds and sun. Use red construction paper to make hearts about 4 by 4 inches and cut out. Do the same with the clouds 6 by 12 blue or white paper. The sun is a cut out from a paper plate and colored yellow. Keep your patterns once you made them so you can use them again. Have the children help the leaders to stick hearts, clouds, and sun up on the wall.   If the children are ready, you might get them started on making the children this day (see below), or you can start that on Thursday.

Thursday:  Children
Now it is time to make the doll patterns for the children of the world.  Leaders trace around each pattern on different colored construction paper according to how many are in the group. Younger children need help to cut out patterns, in some cases the leader can cut them out for them. Older children can cut out their own pattern. Leaders and older children can make patterns for the different clothes for the paper children. Different colors, and different pieces of clothes such as t-shirts, pants, dresses, blouses and skirts, and anything else the children might like. (This part is sort of like playing with paper dolls for the leaders who use to do that way back when.) Make a pattern of each piece of clothing then have the older children trace on to construction paper and cut out. Younger children can pick out what pieces they want for their paper doll and leaders will trace and cut out. The children then will glue each piece of clothing to the proper place on their doll.  

Friday:  Putting it together
The last day can be for finishing up the dolls and getting them ready to put on the wall.  “Now that the paper dolls all have clothes on, it is time to put them up on the wall!”  The dolls go around the world under the letters and hearts (see photo, page 3).  Attach masking tape on the back of the paper dolls (three inches rolled) and stick it to the wall.  Be sure to put the children’s names on the backs of their dolls before you put them up on the wall.

Have fun!
Row.txt_description: Offers a chance to educate, discuss and have children share their feelings about being in a family with domestic violence. While doing the workshop, children learn that children all over the world have experienced domestic violence issues.
Row.txt_notes: ER TO DO: Photograph and enter pages with "THE" and drawing of heart into Quark.

Row.txt_code:
Carlos Morales and Matthew Caldera of LACAAW at the AWBW
studio with some masks from their teen groups.
  
About this Workshop:
Survival Masks began in 1996 during a collaboration between AWBW and LACAAW. The goal of the collaboration was to bring the creative arts to teens at Monroe High as part of LACAAW’s “In Touch with Teens” curriculum. The program has grown and continues to thrive in four high-schools reaching 5,000 teens in the last two years. In February 2004, Carlos Morales and Matthew Caldera shared hands-on how this mask-making project has developed since it began. Here is what they shared:

Objective:
To give teens the opportunity to recognize and explore the ways they have survived violence in their own lives, the ways they found strength and courage, and the directions they want to go in the future. To create “survival masks” that tell their stories. To experience art as a safe space to look within and practice respecting themselves and valuing their own thoughts and feelings.


 
 
 AWBW leader Eva Felix shares her mask.
  

Materials:
Relaxing Music
Writing paper or journals and pens
Plaster mask molds (may be available through AWBW)
Sculpey clay — 1 lb makes 6 masks — available at:
Clay Factory of Escondido
1-877-728-5739
www.clayfactoryinc.com
Paper clips for detailing the clay
Toaster oven
Acrylic paints, trays, brushes
Water cups, paper towels
Optional: a pasta press or garlic press can help make hair.

Timeframe:
Carlos and Matthew lead this project in three parts: journaling/ mask-making/painting. You’re welcome to experiment with condensing it.


 
 
 AWBW leader Jessenia Garcia shares her mask.
  

Age Range:
This workshop is designed for teens. Feel free to adapt to younger groups.

Setup and Prep:
Try this project out yourself before leading it so you’ll be familiar with the materials and will be able to support the teens better. Also, you’ll have a sense of how long it takes so you can decide how many sessions to allow for the project. Make the Sculpey into mask-sized balls so you can hand it out easily. (The clay comes in blocks with 4 layers. One and a half layers is a good amount to make into a single mask.)

Introduction:
“Survival Masks” is a chance for each of us to explore the violence we have witnessed and experienced, and how we have survived. Growing up in this society, we have all survived violence. There are many different forms of violence, and we have each experienced and survived them in our own ways. Can anyone think of some of the forms of violence around us? You might have survived the violence of poverty. You might have survived the violence of racism. You might notice you’ve survived many difficult challenges. During this project, you will be creating a series of masks through which you get to explore what you’ve survived and where you are going. Each person will get to make three miniature masks.

“With your masks, you may show your survival in whatever way comes to you. Your masks might show your past, present, and future. They might show three different defenses you have used to survive or three wonderful ways you’ve found peace, clarity, and hope. You might decide to show it all in one mask instead of three.
You don’t need to plan it all out now.”

Day I: Journaling
“We want your art to tell us a story. It’s not just a mask—it’s your story. So today, we will not begin with the masks. We will begin with the ideas. We will start with journaling. Your journal is the safe place for your ideas, and we will be writing in the journal each time we meet.

“When we write, it’s a different type of writing than we usually do. It’s completely for the purpose of expressing and respecting ourselves. Spelling doesn’t matter. Punctuation doesn’t matter. Language doesn’t matter. You will write whatever comes to you, however it comes to you. It’s not for anybody else. It is just for yourself.

“For the journaling, we will begin with the phrase ‘I am…’ and write whatever comes to mind. This is your story. You can explore the past, present and future. Think about where you are now and how the past has affected you. Know where you’re at and know why you’re where you are. And then start thinking about where you’re going – your future.”

Closure and validation:
—Have the teens split into pairs to share anything they want about what they wrote and how they felt.
—Ask the whole group how it felt writing. Was it hard for anyone? Was it easy? Was anything surprising?
—Validate the courage of those who shared with the group.
—Validate the courage of each person for opening themselves up to their own creativity and not worrying about what came out.


 
 
 Pressing clay into the mold.
  
 
 Pulling clay from the mold.
  
 
 Out of the mold and ready to be worked on.
  
 
 Shaping the face.
  
 
 Painting the face.
  

Day II: Mask-making
“Let’s start with some journaling to get focused on our stories. You can begin with the phrase ‘I am...’ and see what comes out today. Or you can start with whatever words you need to. Remember, the journaling is a time to respect ourselves and whatever we need to express. There is no right or wrong. It’s important to just express whatever is inside of us.

“Today we will be starting our mask (pass out the balls of clay). Get the feel of the clay. Start to play with it. Get used to it. It’s okay to squeeze the hell out of the clay. A lot of feelings may come up. It’s okay to release the feelings into the clay – (just don’t throw it at me!) When you are ready to make your mask, this is how you can do it. Roll it into a ball and make it a little smaller on one end – where the chin will be. See if there are any lines or creases in the surface and smooth them out. Take the narrow end of your ball and put it into the chin of the mold. Press into it. Really squeeze it in there. Don’t be scared of it. It’s okay if you mess up the first time, because you can just pull it out and do it again. (Note: If the clay is too soft, it may stick to the mold. You might try a fresh piece and let the too-soft piece rest before using it again.)

“After you pull the face out, you’ve got a little face to work with. Your mold might be bubbly and make bumps on the face. Don’t worry about that. Set your mask down in front of you and start to work on it with your fingers. Run your finger over any scratches or bumps. Just get a feel for it. It’s okay to squeeze it up and start over. It’s also fine to change the shape of the face – make it as different as you want. The face from the mold is just a starting point you can work with and change.

“You could represent your whole story on just one mask, or make more than one mask to tell the story. It doesn’t even have to look like a mask. You can use paper clips, pencils, brush handles, whatever you want, to work with the clay.”

(Give the teens freedom to express themselves however they need. As long as they respect themselves and others, don’t restrict them.)

Closure and validation: (Same as in session I.)

Cooking:
Cook the masks for 7 minutes each at 350 degrees in a toaster oven. (If it burns a little, it’s okay, because you will be painting over it anyway.)

III: Painting
“Today, we will be finishing our masks by painting them and writing any words that go with them. Again, we’ll start with some journaling time.”

Paint Demonstration:
Here are the paints and trays. How do you think we can respect the paints and brushes so they will last a long time? (e.g. by not taking more than you can use, and by not letting paint dry on the brushes) Any questions about the paints? Go ahead and paint your masks so they express your story. When you are done, notice if there are any words that you want to write to go with your mask.

Closure and validation: (Same as in session I.)

If time allows and your group size is not too big, it can be powerful to give each person the opportunity to share their finished masks with the group. It can also be powerful to welcome the teens to display their work for others to see. Be sure to have release forms available so they can give permission to display their art, and write the title and any words they want displayed with it.
Row.txt_description: Gives teens the opportunity to recognize and explore the ways they have survived violence in their own lives and the directions they want to go in the future. The end product serve to tell their stories and serve as a reminder to respect themselves and value their own thoughts and feelings.
Row.txt_notes: Notes: children’s manual pg. 53

Row.txt_code:
“Letter to Fathers” participants holds
up his letter.
  
About this Workshop:
For the last five years working at Human Options, I (Daniel) have implemented an activity to help the children with communicating their feelings, expressing them without fear, amd feeling comfortable with their words to be able to speak with their father. I thought about this activity to write letters to their fathers because many children in domestic violence situations experience so much trauma and are fearful of their own fathers.

Often they are not able to express or communicate to their fathers for fear of being physically or verbally abused. Many children have been controlled throughout life by the abuser and may have much to say to him and need the support and confidence to be able to do so.

This workshop provides them that chance to do so or to work up to that point of feeling strong enough to do so. In some cases the children may have not been abused but have seen or heard it done to their mother and have never had the chance to tell their father or abuser how they felt about it and for what the abuser has done to the family and the circumstances around it by possibly splitting the family apart.

This is an opportunity for these children to finally express their thoughts and feelings of either good or bad to their father, and it’s an opportunity for the children to know that what they think is very important.

My experience doing this activity is that it has been helpful to some and has not visibly done much for others. Even those times when I don’t see the immediate benefits, I believe it will benefit them in time. I think this activity is an eye-opening experience and plants seeds for the children’s strength and communication in the future.

Objective:
To provide a safe place for children to release their emotions and feelings for their father.

Materials:
Cray-Pas/paints
Construction paper or writing paper (depending on age)
Markers
Envelopes
Pencils/pens (optional)


 
 
 “Letter to Fathers” participants at work on their letters.
  

When to Do this Workshop:
Please be advised that this workshop should be done with children that you know pretty well and are able to handle talking about their fathers. It needs to be done in a supportive environment with enough volunteers and staff.

Timeframe:
Total Time: 1 hour
10 Min. Opening Circle
30 Min. Activity
20 Min. Closing Circle

Age Range/Ratio:
This workshop is designed for children aged 7 and up.
The ratio is 1 adult to every 4 children, so that there is plenty of support for the kids to share their feelings.

Setup and Prep:
Cover table with paper. Place construction paper or writing paper in the middle of the table. Place Cray-Pas, paint, and markers in front of each child so they can have their choice of what they would want to use. Place an envelope in front of each child’s place.

   



Leader sharing paper for the letters.
 Letter to “Papa.”
   
Warm-up: Rain
Start with the warm-up in a circle away from the table and art supplies. “Today kids we are going to make rain. I want everyone to follow me and do what I do. We will be using our hands and feet. Everyone rub your hands together.” (When you have everyone in unison then move on to the next step). “Everyone tap your thighs with your hands” (Make sure everyone is in unison). “Now, we are going to hear the thunder, stomp your feet. Now we want the rain to stop so now lets tap our hands to our thighs again start getting slower. Now, let’s rub our hands together. Start getting softer and softer.”

  


Circle of children working on their letters.
 
  
Introduction/Opening Circle:
“Today, kids we are going to do something special. Does anybody know why you’re here?
Who is missing from your family? How does that make you feel?” Have the children answer if they feel comfortable. “At times we can feel sad that our father is no longer with us. We may often feel that we could have said something to our fathers but cannot say it right now. Well, today we are going to write a letter and I am going to give you two sentences to help you write a letter to your father.”


 
 
 Young participant shares her letter.
  

“I wish my father said… and What I want to say to my father….” When you are ready you can either write or draw your feelings. You can even just write whatever you want to say to your father. It is your choice. If you are not ready to express those feelings let us know. It is your choice to write the letter. When you are ready go to the table and begin.”

Leaders please note that if the children are not ready they can have the option to draw their family.

Closing Circle:
Have the children share what they wrote or drew if they are comfortable. Ask them if they would like to keep it, tear it up, or put it in their treasure boxes. We like to call them Daddy Boxes and they can have the choice to do what they would like with them.

Treasure Box Option:
Leaders may want to do the Treasure Box workshop before they do this workshop. We have modified the Treasure Box workshop and have called it Daddy Boxes for children to put the letters and special things when they miss their Dad.

  


One participant’s letter.
Row.txt_description: Provides a safe place for children to release their emotions and feelings for their father.

Row.txt_code:
Suzy Karcher Rogers



Objective:
To think about and explore our thoughts about ourselves in the past, present, and future by creating a New Year’s Garden.

About This Workshop:
While making this I found myself dividing my life into time periods—each flower in my garden represented me at a different time of my life.  I thought about what were really good times for me and what I was like during those times. I made flowers for my difficult periods also and I found myself looking for what I had learned during these times and how I had been strengthened during these periods.  As I represented my future, I was pleased that I had ended up making the flower very similar to my present flower.  It wasn’t some distant dream, which made me realize I was heading in the right direction.  





New Year's Garden daisy.




I hope those women who participate in this workshop are able to gain some valuable perspective about the different periods of their lives.  Sometimes the future seems a bit intimidating. This workshop is helpful in lightening up our thoughts about the future.

Materials:
Card Stock (heavy background paper) 81/2” by 11”
Construction paper
Tissue paper
Cray-Pas
Elmers Glue or glue sticks
Scissors
Yarn—various colors—(can be bought in one mixed color roll.)
Pen/Paper
Relaxing music

Setup and Prep:
Many shelters operate on a very tight budget. I know when I was running groups there always seemed to be a sense of lack in the shelter, lack of space, lack of basic needs for the residents. I didn't want that sense of lack to be part of my group, so I would set everything up in an inviting way before we began. The way I arranged out the supplies made it special and welcoming.
Place all papers, yarn and craypas in the center of the table or a nearby table.  Invite them to use as much as they need.  Each participant should have her own scissors and glue.  





Supplies set up on a welcoming way.



Timeframe:
Opening Circle /
   Warm Up

10 - 20 min
Demonstrations
5 min
Creation
45 min
Closing Circle
10 min

Opening Circle/Warm Up:
It’s definitely best if you make a New Year’s Garden yourself before running this group.  You will have an example to show and be able to share your own experience of making it.  When I ran groups I found that it was often our time of talking that was as beneficial as the creating time.  Start by showing your own piece and discussing what the different flowers represent.  Invite the group to share any ideas about what the garden and individual flowers could represent.  Get a discussion going.





Fig. 1.  Leaving the strip open at the top.





Fig. 2.  Adding strings for stems.





Fig. 3.  Completed New Year’s Garden.



Writing Time:
Participants could begin free writing ideas of what they want to represent in the garden.  “Is each flower a separate time period in their lives?  Do the flowers represent different people?  Does each flower represent themselves at different times—in the past, presently and in the future?  Are there flowers in the garden?  If not, what is in the garden?”

Creating Time:
Writing and art creation can be done separately or simultaneously.

Demonstration:
Demonstrate how to make different types of flowers if the group seems like they are having a difficult time starting and aren’t comfortable making things.

Possible demos:
—Draw different flowers
—Make cones out of tissue or construction paper.  (They can have different paper coming out of the center.)  “Does the way a flower looks symbolize something?
What do different colors mean?”

Ask them to try to have fun making this childlike picture. Try new things, because it doesn’t really matter what it looks like. Trust that still small voice that says:  “This might work and I’ll try it!”  

Possible step by step method:
#1 Pick a color of card stock (background).
#2 Glue 2” strip of paper (ground) at the bottom. Only glue the bottom and sides on—like an envelope (see fig. 1).
#3 Glue yarn on paper for stems.  Tuck the bottom of the stem into the envelope (see fig. 2).
#4 Draw or make flowers to attach to the stems.  (This can represent a time line.) (see fig. 3)

My garden has a flower for my childhood, my early twenties, my time in an abusive relationship, one for the last five years, one for now and one for the future.  I also added a sun to represent God.  I decided to give the sun a stem that went to the earth to show a connection.




Detail of flowers with sunshine.


Closing Circle
The closing circle was always a very important part of my groups.  Give each participant a chance to talk about her garden and share about the individual flowers and any thoughts that came up while she created it.  Is there a flower for the future? Let’s hear about that!
Row.txt_description: Offers participants the opportunity to think about and explore their past, present, and future by creating a New Year's Garden.

Row.txt_code:
Close-up of suvivor
working on creation.
 
About this Workshop:
The Panty Line is a project that was inspired by a cross between the Clothesline Project and the Vagina Monologues.  The Clothesline Project has proved to be an emotional and effective way to create awareness about violence.  The Vagina Monologues take the idea of speaking out on abuse against women to a unique level with V-Day activities around the nation.  I developed this project to be a part of V-Day at Cal Poly, Pomona, where we exhibited the Panty Line.

Objective:
To give each participant an opportunity to dare to expose her message(s) in a beautiful, even provocative way—on the AWBW Panty Line—a revealing look at the “Victorious Secrets” of survivors.  

Materials:
Writing paper, pens, pencils
Scissors and hole punchers
Lingerie items:  bras, panties, hosiery, camisoles, tank tops to paint and decorate
Or for paper cut-outs of lingerie items:  Use pastel colored paper and trace outline shapes
Image books if working with paper lingerie: magazines, photo stockbooks
Painting tools (acrylics, fabric paint, brushes, water containers)
Drawing tools (craypas, pencils, markers)
Glue guns, glue sticks, craft glue
Decorative items (feathers, yarn, ribbon, beads, sequins, glitter, bits of lace, etc.)
  


 “No More Shaving” created on
paper outline of panties.
  

Setup and Prep:
1-2 hours.  2 hours is better, but this workshop could be completed in a one hour session if needed, providing the prep work has been done and choices in materials kept to a minimum, especially the idea of using paper tracings of lingerie items.  These could be made into a limited number of paper/cardboard patterns ahead of time by the facilitator. The women could then choose their desired item, choose their paper, trace the outline, cut it out and start creating their messages on them.

Introduction:
“This project is called ‘The Panty Line Project: Victorious Secrets.’  We will be creating art on lingerie that tells of our Victorious Secrets of survival.  Lingerie is made for comfort and support as much as it also exists for its sheer beauty (and sometimes for its daring!)  We are survivors and we have hidden strengths that sometimes we fail to notice and appreciate.  How about the feelings we try to hide from ourselves, like anger, sorrow, even laughter at the sheer outrageousness of it all?  If my bra could only talk, what would it have to say?  Underwear?  Pantyhose? Now is your chance to let them speak.  Forget about doing the laundry. Let’s go shopping instead!”
  


Survivor works on Victorious Secrets slip.
 
  

Opening Circle:
“How do you feel “all under?” (As opposed to “all over.”)  Share one feeling or characteristic that you keep hidden that is/or has been a support or comfort in your life.  Is there an item of lingerie that best represents this?” OR “What things are most important when you think about your lingerie? Is it support, comfort, durability, beauty?  How are these things representative of who you are?”

Remind the group that just as there are no wrong items of lingerie, so there are no wrong feelings.  Each has a value and a purpose. This is a safe place to explore and share feelings.

Relaxation:
“Get comfortable.  Let your eyes close if you feel comfortable doing so. Notice your in-breath and out-breath.  No need to change it, simply notice the breath as it enters our nostrils, fills your chest. Notice the exhalation, the letting go.  Allow each out-breath to be a relaease of tensions, of thoughts, of any stress that holds you back from being fully present.
  


 The story unfolds in paint.
  
 
 “You can’t push my buttons” panties.
  
 
 “Power” spelled in yarn.
  


“Take a few moments to let the awareness of breathing in and out calm and relax you.  You may want to imagine a healing or calming color and with each in-breath feel that calm, healing color as energy filling your entire body, from your toes... all the way up your legs... into our pelvic area... into your back—from the lower back, through the mid- to upper-back.  Feel the healing and calming energy come into your belly... your lungs... your chest... feel it relaxing your shoulders... your neck... and gently feel your face muscles, your jaw, your eyes and ears relaxing.  Take another few moments and check to see if any part of your body is still carrying tension or stress.  Breathe into it a sense of calmness... Breathe out, letting the exhalation be a release of tension, a letting go.  Allow your mind to rest, letting all thoughts fall away with the breath.

“In this clear and safe space, begin to create and explore a place, a most wonderful place.  It’s a specialty store selling only the finest in intimate apparel.  You’ve just won a shopping spree at Victorious Secret.  That’s right.  Only it’s not Victoria’s. It’s yours. You are VICTORIOUS.  Your secrets have been with you through thick and thin. Underneath it all.  Under where, you might ask?  Yes, underwear in all its glory:  bras, panties, camisoles, full and half slips, hosiery, and more.  As you look around this wonderful store you notice that the selection of styles, colors, seem to be all your favorites.  No need to worry about sizes, everything is just the right size for you.  And get this—Price is no object!  The friendly and wise saleslady smiles and beckons to you to please come inside...  browse... shop... She hands you a beautiful gift bag and tells you to drop any items you would like to keep into it.  Keep only the items you want.  As you move from table to table, and rack to rack, think about how much lingerie items have at times held you up, held you in, or held you back.  Some have been uplifting and enhancing, while yet others have been restricting and minimizing.  Yet they all have a purpose and they are always with you. Now it’s your turn to choose.  It’s your time to shop.  What items will you choose today?  Each item has a meaning for you.  Some styles and colors may be pleasant, some not.  All have a purpose and you are the shopper and remember:  THERE ARE NO WRONG CHOICES HERE. Only Victorious Secrets!”

“Now that you’ve made you final selections, look at them carefully.  Which one is your favorite?  What does it have to say about you?  Put this item and its message in your gift bag and carry it back with you as you leave the store and come back to this present moment.  Take a nice breath.  Exhale and open your eyes.  You are now ready to create.”  

Creating Time:
“Now it’s time to create your message on your item of lingerie. You can use your own actual piece of intimate apparel, or draw your own, or use one of the templates provided for you to trace a bra, panty, etc. Choose your paper, drawing or painting tools and begin.  You can decorate your Panty Line item however you wish to display its message and function in your life.  Use your own words, pictures, colors.  Remember:  There are no mistakes.”

Closing Circle
As participants finish up, encourage them to write any words that go with their Panty Line item.  When everyone is ready, have a closing circle where everyone has a chance to share her creation and what it means to her.  Remind them that this is a safe place to share feelings and all feelings are okay.
Row.txt_description: Give each participants an opportunity to dare to expose her message(s) in a beautiful, even provocative way--on the AWBW Panty Line--a revealing look at the "Victorious Secrets" of survivors.

Row.txt_code:
Sample of My Road and the places that make me the
most happy.
 
   
   
   
   
  Materials for My Road
 
Objective:
This workshop gives participants the opportunity to visualize the different roads each of us take to find a place we feel the most happy, comfortable, safe, and peaceful. The goal of this workshop is for participants to think about where they go to feel safe, happy and comfortable. The landmarks they place on their road will be random images that they associate with getting one step closer to a happier place.

Materials:
Large Butcher paper
Pencils
Craypas or Markers
Watercolors
Acrylic Paint
Paintbrushes
Paint palettes/plates
Water cups (for brushes)
Scissors
Magazines (collage images)
Glue sticks

Time Frame:
Total time: 2 hours
Opening:15 minutes
Creation: 1 1/2
Closing: 15 minutes

Age Range:
Ideal for teenagers

Preworkshop Prep:
   
  Starting out on The Road
 
   
   
  Creating the Road
 
   
  Creating the Road
 

Creating a sample of a road taken will be helpful.

Set Up:
If possible give each participant a large working area. Have each of the materials set-up at each station. Journaling materials will make it easier for participants to write down what they see as they visualize their road.

Pre-cut images with places and words can be very helpful.

Opening Circle:
Have a simple one-word opening circle about how each participant is feeling today.  Thank everyone for sharing and introduce the project.

Introduction:
Today you get to create your very own road.  A road that will take you to a place that will help you feel good.  At this point it is good to share your sample or show the one from this workshop. This will help the children/teens to visualize their map during the warm-up.  You may want to encourage them to remember that this window of time is for them to make plans for their future and enjoy their freedom.

Warm Up:
Have the participants sit quietly for five minutes and write about a place they go to that makes them feel safe, happy and peaceful. Have them think of the different things they see on their way to get there…the different streets, parks, buildings, people, cars, or signs they see along the way to that place. If anyone has a hard time thinking of an actual place, tell them to feel free to come up with a place they think will make them feel happy and safe. Let your imagination run wild, this can be a completely made up place.   The only requirement is that you write about a place where you feel peaceful and free. At the end of the five minutes, ask if they need another minute or if they are ready to begin. If only a few participants need more time tell them they can start creating when they feel ready.

Creation:
Each participant should have enough space to spread out their paper.  Briefly share about the supplies you have available and how much time they will have to create.  Ask participants to begin to create their road map and encourage them to feel free to use all the materials available to them, they can paint, draw and collage. It is important to give them at least a 10-minute warning before the closing circle, as the participants can easily loose track of time during this project.  If anyone finishes early, encourage them to add a title to their piece and to journal about what it felt like to take a trip down "their own road".

   
  Sample of My Road
 

Closing Circle:
Have the participants share their road map and their final destination. Have them explain the different things they saw on their road and why they think these particular images stood out to them.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives participants the opportunity to visualize the different roads each takes to a physical place where they feel the most happy, comfortable, safe, peaceful, etcetera. The goal of the workshop is primarily for participants to think about where they go to feel safe, happy and comfortable. The landmarks they place on their road will be random images that they associate with getting one step closer to a happier place.

Row.txt_code:
All types of boxes can be Wish Boxes.
  
About This Workshop:
This workshop was created by a high school student who is volunteering with AWBW.

It is something Jordan does at the beginning of each year, and the box stays sealed throughout the year like a time-capsule.  

We felt it would be especially useful in the Windows workshops because in shelter, each day is really the start of a new year—not just January 1st. It is definitely a new beginning, and  a special and important time to think about new wishes for the year ahead.  

We hope you’ll enjoy Wish Boxes any time of year!

   

 
  Shoe box ready to be transformed into a Wish Box.
   

Objective:
This box is designed to guide you and set your mind for the bright new future. It is best done right before the New Year, but anytime will do. 

Materials:
Shoeboxes—one per participant (Cigar or other types of boxes are fine too)
Magazines (Ones with positive images and phrases)
Scissors
Glue
Decoupage
Paintbrushes
Pens
Paper
String and/or ribbons

Opening Circle:
Each day is a new beginning.  Share a wish that you have for yourself for your year ahead.

Creating Time:
Step 1:  Cutting
Start out by cutting images, pictures, and phrases from magazines. Think of goals or wishes that you want to conquer in the Next Year.
  


Decoupage gives shiny protective coating.
  
  

Step 2:  Gluing
Next, start gluing your images on the shoebox. Try to cover as much of the box as you can but, if you see a little cardboard, don’t fret. Layers are usually best.

Step 3:  Decoupage
Wait for box to be semi-dry before you begin to decoupage. Start by dipping your paintbrush in the decoupage and spread it all over your box. You don’t want it to be goopy. You want a nice thin coat of it.  Two coats are usually best.

Step 4:  Writing
Let dry for a few hours. (When it is finished drying, your box will have a beautiful shine and a wonderful hardness.) Next start to think of goals, wishes, and dreams that you want to conquer in the New Year.
Put all of your energy into it because the more you do the more it will come true.

Step 5:  Imagining
After you write down all of your wishes, goals, dreams, etc. on the piece of paper, sit with it and imagine it all coming true.

Step 6:  Sealing the Box
Fold the paper up and place inside box. Really see all of you goals. Close the box and tie it in a bow with string.
  


 Ribbons or string can be used to
seal the box for the year.
  

Step 7:  Date to Open
In a corner of the box (preferably on the bottom), write down the date in which you created the box and the date you will open it (a year and a day).

Step 8:  Saving
Keep your box in a secret place.  Don’t open until a year and the day.

Closing Circle
As participants finish up, encourage each to share her creation and what it means to
her.  
 

Choose relaxing, positive images.
Row.txt_description: Wish Boxes are designed to guide participants and set their minds for their bright new future. It is a perfect project for before the New Year, but anytime will do.
Row.txt_tips: Shelley Huff of Huff Art Center in Visalia, CA used instructions from this website for an easy, inexpensive cardstock paper box.

Row.txt_code:
A big square dream pillow with a diagonal pocket
and a little round dream pillow.


About This Workshop:
I have had this idea for a long time.  As part of my self-growth, I like to write about my dreams for the future or positive wishes for myself.  I shared the idea of Dream Pillows at the Fall 2002 training and Cathy encouraged me to share it with you.  A Window Between Worlds just received lots of donated fabric for you to use, so it’s a great time to begin Dream Pillows!

Objective:
To create a special pillow with a pocket that can hold messages—a place to honor our wishes and affirmations.

Materials:
Assorted fabrics
Stuffing material (Note, plastic Easter grass makes a stuffing that is surprisingly warm and pleasant to hold.)
Ribbons, bows, decorations to sew on
Needles and thread
Assorted papers and pens
Relaxing music
Candle light (if possible in your facility)

Timeframe:
2 hrs total
Introduction

5 min
Opening Circle
15 min
Relaxation

5 min
Creation
80 min
Sharing Circle
15 min







Introduction:
“Today we will be making dream pillows.  A dream pillow is a special pillow that has a special place to hold messages or wishes for ourselves.  As we make our pillows, we can sew on a little pocket with a front flap to cover that pocket and protect it.  Your pillow could be any shape or size and the front pocket could be small for small notes or bigger for letters to yourself (about the size that  a small note/small envelope could fit in). 




Sewing supply basket.




“As we think about our dreams and wishes today, let’s make this circle a special place where it is safe for all of our dreams and wishes.  Sometimes we might think our dreams are silly, but they are not.  There are no right or wrong wishes or dreams. Whatever is most dear to our heart is very important.  If your thoughts feel silly or impossible, they are especially important.  Together today, let’s create a special space where it is safe for them to come out, be supported, and find a home in our Dream Pillows.”  (If you are able to light a candle in your facility, you might light a candle to symbolize creating a safe place for all the wishes and dreams that we hold in our hearts.)

Opening Circle:
“Let’s start with a check-in.  Share anything you’d like to about how you’re doing today.  Also share if you can think of a special dream or wish you have for yourself.  If you could have one wish come true in your lifetime, what would it be?  Whatever thoughts come to mind are fine.  Your thoughts are important.  Remember, there are no right or wrong wishes or dreams.  Take this moment to honor whatever comes to your mind.  Who would like to share first?”



Here are three pieces of fabric to make a square
pillow.  The fabric is folded back so you can see
the inside piece folded diagonally.  This will
make the diagonal pocket after the pillow is
sewn and turned right side out.





Here the pillow is sewn.  Leave one open part
to turn right side out.





Here the pillow is completed with a dream
wish in the pocket!



Technical Info:
Ask if anyone has never sewed before.  Encourage participants that even if they’ve never sewn, they can do this project and they can have help if they need it.  Share the fabrics, needles, thread, paper and pens.  Let them know they can start with the writing if they wish, or they can start with the sewing.  Demonstrate any steps that would be helpful (depending on how much your group knows about sewing).  

If they need to do a pattern for the pillow, a square and rectangular design would be the easiest, but other fun shapes such as a circle or triangle would be great.  Let them know that however they do it, there’s no right or wrong about the sewing.  What’s important is the thoughts and feelings that are going into their pillow, not so much what it looks like. 

For the notes in their pillow, they can write about dreams, wishes, heart’s desires, positive affirmations they are working on or positive aspects about themselves that they would like to acknowledge to place in the pocket.  The pillow and notes are about believing in our dreams, affirmations, and strengths.

Relaxation:
“Before we begin our Dream Pillows, let’s take a moment to relax.  (Play soft music.)  As we take a moment to relax together, notice the candle flame in our circle. (If you aren’t allowed to burn a candle, you can have the women close their eyes and imagine a beautiful, warm, safe flame in the middle of the circle.)  It is like the flame deep inside our hearts.  No matter how difficult things get, that flame is still there, deep inside of us.  It is the flame of our wishes…  It is the light of our dreams.  As you notice the warmth and beauty of the flame, take a deep breath in…  And let it go…  Take another wonderful, deep breath in…  And let it go…  As you watch the flame, and breathe deeply, notice this is your time, just for yourself.  It is a time to honor your deepest dreams and wishes.  You can take as long as you like just to relax and notice your thoughts.  And whenever you’re ready, you can start to create your dream pillow.  You can start with the fabric or you can start with writing.  Start wherever is right for you.”


(folded pocket piece)



Steps 1+2.  Choose and cut fabric for your
pillow and pocket.  For your pocket, you might
cut the same shape as for the pillow, but just
fold it in half.  The folded edge can be where
the pocket will be!





Steps 3+4 . Position your fabric inside out and
sew together, leaving an open edge.





Step 5 . Turn it right side out.





Step 5 . See how the pocket appears when you
turn it right side out!





Step 6 . Stuff pillow and sew the open edge up
to complete it!




Creation:
Below are possible steps, but there is no wrong or right way.  Encourage each participant to find her own way.

1. “Choose the fabric.  Pick out whatever colors your are drawn to… whatever colors reflect your dreams and wishes.”

2. “Cut the fabric and decide your shape.  Square or rectangular is easiest, but you might also consider triangles, circles, hearts… whatever you like.”

3. “Position your fabric sides and pocket  If you want the stitching to be hidden, place the fabric inside out when you sew.  Then when you turn it right side out, the stitching is hidden. You might also want to place your pocket inside your pillow before sewing it together – so it will already be sewn into your pillow when you turn it right side out.”

4. “Sew it together.  Be sure to leave an unsewn edge so you can turn it right side out and stuff it!”

5. “Turn it right side out!”

6. “Stuff it and complete it by sewing the last edge up.”

7. “Write your dreams and wishes to store inside the pocket.”

Sharing Circle:
Save time so everyone has an opportunity to share her pillow and what it means to her.
Row.txt_description: Participants create a special pillow with a pocket that can hold messages - a place to honor their wishes and affirmations.

Row.txt_code:
Seeing Me mirrors.


About This Workshop:
This is a very powerful and inspiring workshop.  It’s amazing how in such a brief time, this project can impact how a person sees themselves.  This was developed as a children’s workshop by Mandy and Monique of Good Shepherd Shelter.  They led it in April for the Children’s Windows Leaders.  It was so powerful with the group of children that we knew it would be a wonderful project for adults as well.  So here it is for all of you!  

Note: We have extra mirrors in the AWBW art supply store, so be sure to come for “free shopping” soon.

Objective:
To give participants a chance to see the beauty within themselves and to know how others view them.  The goal of the project is for self-esteem to be raised each time participants look at the art they create in this workshop.

Note from Mandy and Monique:
Our shelter receives donations everyday and at times it is hard to decide what can be used for art and what should be passed on.  When we saw five boxes of small mirrors with plastic coating our creative side saw endless art projects.  The first project we created is "Seeing Me.”  When our children start to settle into the shelter they begin to see themselves in a different light.  This project gives the children a chance to symbolically and verbally express how they are feeling about their physical appearance as well as how the are feeling on the inside.  We were amazed at how hard it was for the kids to recognize their own beauty and how easy it was for them to recognize the beauty of their fellow classmates.  We hope you enjoy this workshop as much as we did!




Back of the mirror, collaged.




Materials:
Mirrors 3x4
Magazines/Art stock books
Mod Podge or watered down glue
Paint brushes (older brushes are the best because the glue is rough on them)                       
Sequins
Beads
Feathers
Scissors
Puffy paint
Glue guns (optional)
Music

Setup:
Set out supplies.  You can choose to let the group use all of the items listed above or just use collage-making materials.

Timeframe:    2 hrs total
Warm-up:          5 minutes
Introduction:     5 minutes
Opening Circle:  10 minutes
Technical Info:   5 minutes
Mirror Exercise: 15 minutes
Creation Time :  60 minutes
Closing Circle:    20 minutes

Introduction:
“Today we will be exploring how we see ourselves.  We will be looking at our own beauty – our inner beauty and outer beauty too.  Each of us is beautiful in our own special way.  We will be doing an exercise looking into our mirrors, and then we will be decorating the mirrors to express what we see.  Sometimes it can be difficult to notice the beauty in ourselves.  Sometimes we forget that we are beautiful at all.  If it’s difficult noticing your beauty, that’s okay.  You’re not alone.  Whatever you see today is fine.  And maybe you’ll even surprise yourself with the beauty you see.   After you’re done creating your mirror today, I want you to keep it in a special place.  When you are feeling bad you can pull it out and remind yourself of how wonderful you are.





Front of the mirror.



Movement Warm-up:
(Optional:  For the Children’s workshops we always start with an active warm-up.  Feel free to use it with your adult group too!)  “As we begin, let’s start by being mirrors for each other.  Stand up and choose a partner.  Face each other.  Decide who will be leader first and who will be the mirror.  Stare into the eyes of your partner and don’t talk at all.  If you’re the leader, begin making very, very slow deliberate movements.  If you’re the mirror, follow the movements with your own body.  Keep looking into each other’s eyes as you go.  (As you guide the group, remind the pairs to go really slow, so that the movement becomes synchronous.)  Wonderful!  And when you’re ready, go ahead and switch, so the other person gets to be the mirror!”

Opening Circle:
If you sense that your group needs a check-in, start with that.  Give each person a chance to share anything about how she’s doing and how she feels about doing art.  Welcome any fears or resistance about the art and the mirrors and reassure participants that whatever they discover and create is fine.  There is no right or wrong.

Technical Info:
Share the supplies you have available.  If they’ve never used Mod Podge, show them how you can paste it over the surface when you’re collaging and it dries clear, like a protective covering.  Remember to let them know there’s no right or wrong way.   Let them know that after the mirror exercise, they’ll be able to just dive in and decorate their mirrors. 

Mirror Exercise:
(Play peaceful, relaxing music for this exercise.)



Mirror decorated with collage, glitter, and sequins.





Front of mirror decorated with collaged words.



“Pick-up the little mirror in front of you and look at your own eyes.  Pull it back and look at your entire face.  Do you like what you see?  Just take some time to look and see what you like.  As you look into your eyes and notice your beauty feel free to say out loud one thing you think is beautiful about the way you look.  (Encourage participants to share.  They can go in any order, and it’s okay if some don’t speak.)  Now look at your eyes again.  Look really hard into the centers of your eyes.  Look into the black centers of your eyes.  What do you see all the way inside you?   Do you see the beauty that is inside of you?  Do you see kindness?  Do you see courage?  Do you see an open heart?  As you take your time to look at the beauty on the inside of you, go ahead and share one thing you like about yourself on the inside.  Share something you think is beautiful about your personality.  (Again, give the group time to share.  Any order is fine and it’s okay if some don’t share out loud.)  You can keep looking into your mirror as long as you wish, and whenever you’re ready, go ahead and begin decorating your mirror to express the beauty you see!”

Creation:
As the participants decorate their mirrors, you might remind them every so often that there is no right or wrong way.  If it looks like they need a time-reminder you can let them know when there’s a half hour left, ten minutes, five minutes, etc.

Closing Circle:
“Now that you have completed your project carefully bring your mirror to our closing circle.  Hold the mirror by the edges since it might not be all the way dry yet.”  (Have everyone stand in a circle facing the center.  Then ask everyone to turn to their left and hold up their mirror and use it to look over their shoulder so they can see the face of the person behind them.)  “Use your special mirror to look at the person behind you.  Do you see something beautiful in that person?  Take a moment to think of something you like about that person’s outside appearance and something you like about their inner beauty.  We will go around in a circle, looking at each other with our mirrors and sharing the inner and outer beauty we see.  Whoever wants to start can begin.”  (After the circle is complete, finish with one final circle where each person shares her own mirror and what it means to her.)


Some participants may also decorate the
front of their mirror.





Mod Podge over the collaged images looks
cloudy until it dries.
Row.txt_description: Participants are offered a chance to see the beauty within themselves and to know how others view them. The goal of the project is for participants self-esteem to be raised each time they look at the art they create in this workshop.

Row.txt_code:
This workshop was originally created as a Children’s Windows workshop by a previous leader in our program, Cathy Peverly. I felt it would be a really good workshop for adults too because it affords them the opportunity to think about themselves, sometimes for the first time.
  


"Me As I Shine" creation from Wings.
 
  

Objective:
To think about and have the opportunity to see yourself through your own eyes, by creating a sun full of rays with the words, images, and colors that make you you.

Materials:
Yellow copier paper (orange and red paper are fine too - any colors that would be nice for a sun)
Pattern with a circle drawn on
(see attached pattern to copy)
Pattern with sunrays drawn on (see attached pattern to copy)
Color markers
Glue sticks
Scissors
Relaxing music

Timeframe:
1 1/2 hrs
Opening Circle: 10 min
Relaxation:
 10 min
Demonstration:
 5 min
Creation:
 45 min
Closing Circle:
 20 min

Preparation:
Copy the circles and rays onto yellow, orange and red paper before the workshop. Make enough for each participant to cut out her own circle and 10-20
rays.

Introduction:
“Today we will be making a sun. Not a regular sun, but one that represents us. We will concentrate on the things that make us individual, as the unique person that we are.”
  


“Todo esto es lo que me hace feliz.” /
“All of this is what makes me happy.”
 

Opening Circle:
If you feel that the group needs a check-in, start with that. Give each person a chance to share anything about how she’s doing, feeling, and how she feels about art. Welcome their fears, and assure them that there is no right or wrong way to do the project.

Relaxation:
Dim down the lights and play relaxing music. Tell everyone to sit comfortably, to close their eyes, and focus on the music and your voice as you go.

“Take a deep breath and let it out slowly. Now, take another deep breath and hold it for a little longer, and as you breathe out, do so a little slower... Do these wonderful deep breaths a couple more times. At this point when you start to breathe out, start to relax your body. Each time you breathe out relax your body little more...

“As you are feeling more relaxed, start to imagine yourself sitting outside. Imagine that the sun is touching your face, arms and legs. The touch of the sun is soft soothing and comfortable.
You also can feel the warm breeze as it moves your hair a little to the side.
  


 “Esta es mi gran felicidad en el futuro con mis
hijos y yo. Felizes y alegres viviendo una nueva
vida...” / “This is my greatest happiness in the
future with my children and myself. Happy and
joyful, living a new life...”
  

“Slowly, as you continue to breathe in and breathe out, you start to feel a sense of comfort, security and happiness. Give yourself time to enjoy this feeling. Feel the sensation that it gives your body as you continue to breathe in and out.

“At this point you can feel yourself becoming very light. You almost have no weight. It’s as if you are starting to float in a very soft and comfortable cloud. As you float, continue to breathe in deeply and each time that you do so you can feel all the good energy passing through your whole body.

“Slowly you continue to float to a spot in the sky where you can see your favorite places. You are at a comfortable spot in the sky. Rest there comfortably and feel the soft breeze sway you gently and feel the warmth of your body.

“As you breathe in, notice how comfortable you are with yourself and your surroundings. Notice how good you feel inside and how your skin feels as if it is glowing. Imagine that your skin is now shining, glowing with all of the goodness that you have inside of you. It is becoming a brilliant shine that only makes you more aware of all the wonderful things, great emotions, and love that you have within you. Let it shine from within you. Feel it, welcome it. As you feel your glow, let this glow touch everything around you. Let yourself enjoy these feelings.

“Once you are ready, slowly open your eyes, and as you do so, keep feeling the sense of the glow. Allow the feeling of the glow to give you all the words, images or colors to do this project with.”
  


"This are the things that make me happy..."
 
  
  

Creation:
Allow participants to write all the words, or drawings, or just color each ray on the yellow (or other colors) paper. They should cut out the rays and the circle. Then glue each ray on the circle to make a sun.

Closing Circle:
Give the group an opportunity to share how they felt during the relaxation and then to explain what the rays of their sun say or mean.

You might want to end the group by asking participants to place their suns on a board for everyone else to see.
Row.txt_description: Participants are giving the opportunity to think about and see themselves through their own eyes, by creating a sun full of rays with the words, images, and color that make them who they are.

Row.txt_code:
Audrey is an AWBW Board member and author of The Money ToolBox for Women. The recent Leader’s Workshop she led gave participants a sense of inspiration about their finances.  Th ey left feeling they had the tools to make their dreams come true—some for the first time.  It was clear how these tools make a big difference!

  


Cookie Jar, Clarity Keeper, and Angel Envelopes from
one participant at the Leader’s Workshop.
 
  



This is a four-session workshop that can be used as individual workshops or together.  Each session shares a different “tool” — a creative process leading us to awareness about our wealth through observing, respecting, honoring and tracking.  They say “the rich get richer” and that’s no accident.  There is a focus and attention involved.  These projects are about finding creative, simple ways to build that focus and attention. 

Note: Each Tool takes about 45 minutes.  With Opening and Closing Circles added each session could stand alone as an entire workshop.

Money ToolBox Tool #1:  Clarity Keepers

Objective:
To create a tracking system to help us observe where we spend our money each and every day—a way of becoming conscious of that which we might overlook that cause the ‘holes’ in our ‘money buckets.’


 
 
 Participant shares her
Clarity Keeper.
  

Materials:
2”X3” spiral notebooks
Puffy paints, stickers
Ball point pens
Presentation pad
Music

Introduction:
“How many people here count their money?  How many count it when they get change?  How many count it when it comes out of the ATM?  Counting your money is a powerful thing to do.  Knowledge is freedom.  The Clarity Keepers we will be making today are a tool to give us knowledge and set us free.  This tool helps us track our daily expenses by giving us a place to list the items and the amounts we spend each day.  In a microscopic way, this will begin to help you become conscious of where you spend your money on a daily basis.  It will create money clarity.  This can be uncomfortable, but being uncomfortable is normal with growth.” 


 
 
 Participant shares her
Clarity Keeper.
  

Process:
Pass out the notebooks and supplies.  Before everyone starts decorating theirs, guide them to prepare the inside pages.  On a presentation pad, draw a chart of what goes on each page: 
At the top of each page:
Date:
Money Start:         $_____
Spending:         $_____
At the bottom of each page:
Money Spent:         $_____
Money Ending:    $_____

Walk the group through the chart and how the ‘Money Ending’ amount should be the difference between what you had in the morning for “Money Start” and what you have spent during the day.  Walk them through how they will use their Clarity Keeper: “Each morning, count the money in your purse.  Know how much you are starting out with today and every day from now on.  At the end of the spending day, recount the money.  This way you know how much you have for tomorrow.  This is not about being a miser and counting your money to hoard it.  This is about letting the energy flow of money find itself.  (If you have a secret money place, that’s fine.  However, keep it consistent so you can keep track of it, and count it with the rest of your money.)”

  


Participant shares her
Clarity Keeper.
 
  

Once they are ready, they can go ahead and decorate the cover.

I recommend that you use your Clarity Keeper every day for 60-90 days to bring clarity.  Then in the future, whenever you feel out of control with your spending, you can do another “dose” of your Clarity Keeper.







Money ToolBox Tool #2: Cookie Jars

Objective:
To give intention and rigor to the practice of nurturing ourselves.  To create a special way of saving for yourself, so that saving money can become a wonderful, joyous and sacred process, connected to treating ourselves well and appreciating the gifts in our lives.    

Materials:
Jars (6" high) (You can get these  from the 99 cents store.)
Puffy paints, sequins, glitter



 
 
 Cookie Jar decorated with words:
“my style” and “family.”
  

Introduction:
“This workshop is about paying yourself first.  It is about saving today for what you want tomorrow.  It is also about the magic of money magnets:  Money attracts money.  The concept of paying ourselves is normally foreign to us.  Women especially will tell you that they have to pay all the bills first and they make do with what is left over.  We share with others—but do we share with ourselves?  If we were with our best friend and had three cookies, we’d at least offer one of them to our friend.  Well, in this workshop we will each decide to offer some percentage of our paycheck to ourselves, as our best friend.  It doesn’t matter what percentage you begin with.  Start today.” (You could read the Cookie Jar story — see attached.)

Process:
Start by going around the table and sharing what you’d be saving for with your Cookie Jar.  The goal you’d be saving for could be big or small.  Here are some examples:  buying stocks one share at a time, a seminar, a vacation, a down payment for _______________, an anniversary present, flowers for garden, a spa day, a manicure, a dress, a sweater, a house in the country...”
(Note:  If people have more than one thought, encourage them to choose the one that has the most energy in it for them.  If they really need to, they could create two different jars, like one for something fun, and one for something very different, like real estate investments.)

  


Participant shares her Boat Jar.
 
  

Distribute the jars, paints, etc. and encourage them to begin.  “As you decorate you Cookie Jar, give it a name that represents your intention.  (For example, if you’re saving for a downpayment on a boat, it could be your Boat Jar.)  Your jar needs to know why you’re saving it.”   

“As you complete your jar, think about what percent you will put into it.  For example, you will put 10%—or whatever feels comfortable for you to do now—into your cookie jar whenever, wherever money flows to you (paycheck, unexpected gifts, tax returns… a percentage of any money that comes your way.)”

“As you use your jar, count the money in it and be grateful to have it.  Let the money know it’s honored and respected.  It is not a change jar where you throw coins in unconsciously, and it’s not a jar you can borrow from in a pinch.  It’s a jar where you consciously build toward your dreams.  It’s a way of honoring yourself, celebrating yourself, and loving the life you’re living.  Watch your riches grow.”  (I keep a slip of paper in the cookie jar with the total amount I am money-magneting towards.  I add in each amount that is put in the jar so that I know when I’ve reach the intended amount.)
 
Money ToolBox Tool #3: Angel Envelopes

Objective:
To help set up, divide and organize your expenses into segments, so that you have money put aside for emergencies, savings, and tithing.  To set up an easy way to become rigorous with your money and practice recognizing what you need and when you’ll need it so you can stay on the mark for monthly money requirements. 

Materials:
Envelopes (3 each)
Watercolors, crayons, markers
Optional: Have each participant decorate a box where she can store her Angel Envelopes—her Treasure Box.

Introduction:
“Today, we are going to create Angel Envelopes.  These are envelopes to divide and organize our expenses into segments and practice staying on the mark for monthly money requirements.  It’s an easy way to practice recognizing what you need and when you’ll need it.”







 





Decorated Angel Envelopes.


 

Process:
“What we’re going to do is decorate 3 envelopes each.  These envelopes each represent a different category of money.

One is for Savings (Think about building for your future.)
One is for Emergencies (Think about the expenses that creep up on you as
emergencies—oil changes, car insurance, medical bills, etc.)
One is for Tithing (Tithing is when you give back to the world around you.  It could be giving to a church, or an organization you love.)

Decorate each envelope, energizing it with Loving Energy.  The envelopes hold the monthly money focus.  They are your training wheels in the new money practice.

For each envelope, choose a percentage you want to set aside each time you get paid or you receive money, any money.  Example:
     Savings  10%
     Tithing   10%
     Emergencies  5%

When you decide your percentages, remember you are putting away money in your Cookie Jar as well for what you are aspiring to attain.
