Note that several of the pages have "pockets" where secret messages or hidden treasure can be kept.  When you open up the book you can lift up one side of the page (the side that contains the bottom of the bag) and write messages that will stay hidden there.  If time permits, take a moment and show the children where each of the pockets and hidden spaces can be found in the book.

Part Two - Cover Design
Save the cover for last, you can draw a shape, picture, or doodle that represents you, using a bold colored crayon. If you like you can also write your name or a title for your book on the cover. Cover with the Foam Paint like you did on the other pages.

Closing Circle:
After the children finish their books, ask them to partner up with a neighbor and share their books with each other, page by page.  Ask for volunteers and see if anyone would like to share their book with the whole group.
Row.txt_description: This workshop will teach the children about using a new and fun material while empowering them to think about positive sides of themselves. The books created can be an expression of themselves plus the hidden pockets can be used to save private messages or store special things.
Row.txt_tips: You can use the Foam Paint in many different ways.  For example you can tell the children more about how Michaelangelo spent four years painting the Sistine Chapel upside down.  Then tape a piece of paper underneath a desk (for each child in the group) and ask the children to create their very own masterpiece upside down!

Row.txt_code:
About This Workshop:







This workshop came about when another support group leader in the Haven House program (Marcia Young) approached me with a request for some colored markers.  Her support group participants were asking for name tents (folded paper name signs) to help them learn each other’s names.  She thought about offering them stickers or small pictures to decorate the Name Tents.  After we talked about it and tried it out in both of our support groups we came up with this workshop.  The participants were very excited with this project and put a lot of effort into making the name tents reflect who they were, what they liked, what they wanted the other group members to know about them.







Objectives:
To give each support group participant an opportunity to focus on and express her own identity by creating a “Name Tent.”  To build sharing and connection among the group members and help them learn each others names.

Materials:
Heavy card stock paper-size  8”x11” either colored or white paper
(I find that in the finished project, colors look better than white.)
Glue sticks and scissors
Markers
Small words/pictures cut from magazines
Relaxing music
Optional: glitter glue markers, stickers, etc.

Preparation:
Make the blank Name Tents by cutting the card stock in half (widthwise). Fold each half in half again—you can get two name tents out of each piece of card stock.

Introduction:
Explain that these Name Tents will be used in support group to help them learn each other’s names.  The collages on the tents will help the other group members to learn some important things about them.  When living in domestic violence situations they often loose sight of who they are and what is important to them.  This workshop will give them a chance to identify who they are and express what they like in a safe, non-judging atmosphere. 




Name Tents lined up on the table for a photo.




Step 1
Distribute Supplies:
Pass out Name Tents, scissors, glue sticks.  Make markers and magazine pieces available to all participants.

Step 2
Relaxation:
Using relaxing music, lead participants through a simple deep breathing exercise. Emphasize that this is to help them focus on the activity at hand, honoring their own unique identity. 

Step 3
Creation of Name Tents:
Have participants write their first names (no last names) on their Name Tents.  This allows them more room to collage while making the name large enough to be easily seen. Encourage the participants to choose pictures and words to collage onto the Name Tents.  These words and pictures should describe who they are, what they like, and what they want the others in the group to know about them, focusing on the positive. 





Shar’s Name Tent with colorful flowers.



As you can see by some of the pictures included, some participants chose to collage on both sides of the Name Tent. 

However they may need to be reminded not to cover up their names in their enthusiasm!

Closing:
Encourage everyone to share their Name Tents with each other. Focus on the positive words and images of each artist, the unique qualities and the similarities.




Chris’s Name Tent with keywords about faith and balance.




Further Use:
I keep the Name Tents in our group room so they can be used in each support group.

I have the materials handy at the beginning of support group (on a small table in the room) so as new members join the group they can create their own Name Tent.  To make this as non-threatening as possible (especially since my support group has some members that don’t attend the art program), I have them start by only putting their name on the tent.  I encourage them to add pictures/words as they become more comfortable with the group.  Other group members often add to/change their Name Tents as time goes by.

This is a new project for our groups, so we are finding new ways to utilize the Name Tents—our parenting program leader is adapting this idea for her classes as well. 

This workshop is a unique way of utilizing Art Empowerment in other areas of your domestic violence program!  I would enjoy hearing about your experiences with this workshop and any changes or modifications you find that work for you and your group.




Lynn’s Name Tent with flowers, stars, and words of confidence.
Row.txt_description: Gives each participant an opportunity to focus on and express her own identity by creating "name tents" that build sharing and connection among the group members and helps them learn each others names.

Row.txt_code:
“Recovery from the Heart and Living by
Spiritual Practices...” — Kimberly Lyon



Objectives:
To give each participant the opportunity to recognize what she treasures in herself and her life.  To explore the blessings, dreams, beliefs, friendships, hopes, and strengths that make her life special by creating Treasure Boxes to hold and protect them.  

Materials:
Boxes (1 per participant—I recommend the small wooden boxes you can get at Michael’s for $1 each.)
Paper and pens for writing
Paper towels
Newspaper to cover table
Painting supplies: acrylic paints, paper plates, small brushes, water cups
Specialty pens: metallic, gel-roller, or opaque paint pens
Collage supplies: photo stock books, magazines, stickers, scissors, glue sticks
Mirror paper (Mirror surfaced paper is available in the poster board section at Michaels.  One sheet can be cut to fill many boxes.)





Blank wooden boxes from Michaels,
ready to be made into Treasure Boxes.



Variations:
Have a look at the Treasure Box Variations at the end of this Update.  Think about the specific group you are leading.  Would it work well to use one of the variations instead of calling them Treasure Boxes?  Or would it work well to give your group all the variations and let them choose what their box will be?  Some groups may do better with more options.  Others may feel more comfortable with more simple directions, since too many choices can be overwhelming.  Feel free to adjust the intro, check-in, and relaxation as needed.  

Optional:
Participants could also make maps to keep inside their Treasure Boxes, maps showing how to find the treasure in their lives.

Introduction:
“Today we will each be making a Treasure Box.  When you picture a Treasure Box, what do you imagine? Pirates of the Carribean? Gold coins?  Treasure Boxes were built to protect valuable things.  They were made to be strong on the outside and filled with precious things on the inside.  As we make our Treasure Boxes today, we will be taking time to slow down and notice the things in our lives that are most precious and worth protecting: our selves, our strengths, our blessings, our dreams, our hopes, our beliefs...  These are treasures within ourselves, even more precious than gold.  To explore the treasures within ourselves, we will be doing a relaxation.  Try not to worry about what you are going to create on your box.  Try to trust that whatever comes to your mind through the relaxation will be just right.  This is a chance to treasure whatever happens.  It’s fine to make a mess.  (Having the opportunity and freedom to go ahead and make a mess is actually something to treasure.  It’s not often that we give ourselves that permission!) There is no right or wrong. Your Treasure Box can be whatever it becomes.  It will be fine.”    




Painted and collaged box with view inside.




Opening Circle:
“Let’s start by each sharing thoughts about what we treasure—whatever comes to mind is fine:  what’s one thing you treasure in your life or in yourself?”  

Technical Info:
“Before we begin the relaxation, I’ll share a little about the supplies we have.  You can use them and combine them any way you want.  We have a few different things for you to use:  There are paints, pens, and collage supplies.  (Demonstrate each technique as needed.)  Feel free to decorate the inside and outside of your box. Feel free to make parts of your box blank and open, or fill them with all sorts of shapes and images.  Feel free to create little notes or messages to put on the inside of your box.  What you create is up to you.  Again, don’t worry about what it will be.  You can let it unfold and trust whatever comes to your mind.  Take a box and place it in front of you. Open it and close it.  Notice all the sides of it.  It is your blank canvas upon which to create.  Ready for the relaxation?”    

Relaxation:





“I tried to include all of life’s experiences inside my box
such as friends, family, material things I ‘treasure,’
painful experiences, etc.” —Anonymous



“Get comfortable in your chair.  Let your eyes gently close. Make sure your feet are settled on the floor.  Now take a deep breath in…   And let it go…  Notice your breath going in and out.  No need to change it, simply notice the breath as it enters your nose, fills your chest.  Notice the exhalation, the letting go.  Allow each breath out to be a release of tensions, of thoughts, of any stress that holds you back from being fully present.  Take a few moments to let the awareness of breathing in and out calm and relax you.  Allow your mind to rest.  

“In this clear space, we will be taking some time to notice what we treasure.  Know that each person will imagine everything in her own unique way.  There is no right or wrong way, simply follow your own experience without judgment.  

“Imagine yourself walking on a beautiful beach.  Breathe in the fresh air.  Feel the ocean breeze on your face and notice the gentle warmth of the sun on your arms.  

“What sounds do you hear?  Can you hear the waves?  Can you see the colors in each wave as it rises and falls?  Do you see any birds soaring over the water?  As you walk, feel the sand beneath your feet, between your toes, wonderful and warm. 




“My Treasure Box means so much to me.  I
named it ‘my treasures’ because my life is
what I treasure today, and that’s what I did
on it.  My life today is free of abuse.”
   —Laura Nelson




“As you walk, you notice something shining in the sand up ahead.  It looks small, like a piece of metal.  As you come closer you see it is the corner of something larger underneath the sand.  As you kneel down and brush away the sand, you find that it is a beautiful box.  Notice the color of it.  Notice the details of decoration.  As you hold it somehow you know that it is safe and welcoming.  Take some time to hold it and know that it is your box.  You were meant to find it here on this beautiful beach.  

“When you are ready, open your box.  As you lift the lid, you see beautiful colors, your favorite colors.  And you see beautiful things.  What do you see?  Notice whatever things come to mind.  What do you find in your box? [Pause…]  

“As you reach further into your box you find photographs.  There are pictures of people you have treasured in your life.  Who do you see?  Look into their eyes and notice their warmth and love for you.  What do they want you to know about yourself? [Pause…]  

“As you reach further into your box, you see notes and you recognize the words.  They are the helpful things people have said to you— things that have stayed in the back of your mind and helped you through your life.  What are the messages you see? [Pause…]   

“At the very bottom of your box you find one more thing.  It is a beautiful mirror.  As you pull it out and look into it, you see yourself, but you see yourself in a way you’ve never seen.  In this mirror, you see clearly all the things that are precious and wonderful about you.  You see your strengths, you see your courage, you see your spirit, you see your caring, you see what a good person you are, what a treasure.  

“Take some time with your mirror, noticing what you see.  And take some time with all the wonderful treasures in your box.  With the sun on your back keeping you warm and relaxed, you know you can take as much time as you need with your box.  
“When you are ready, take this special box full of all your treasures and bring it with you, in your mind’s eye, back into this safe and special room.  Here, you will be creating your own box, using whatever colors, shapes and thoughts you want to from that treasure box in your mind’s eye.





“Look inside.  People tend to work on the
outside and then not have enough time or
energy for the inside, but my Treasure Box is
filled with work...”  —Loretta Pearce



“With your eyes still closed, take your time, slowly feel and wiggle your fingers and toes.  Find yourself present in this room.  When you are ready, open your eyes and begin to create your treasure box.”

Creation Time:
“As you begin to create your Treasure Box, remember there is no right or wrong.  You can just trust whatever comes to your mind.  Try to give yourself complete freedom, freedom to explore, freedom to make a mess.  You can work on the inside, the outside, you can make things to put inside.  It’s up to you.  Try to trust whatever comes to your mind.”  

Closing Circle:
Give each participant an opportunity to share her Treasure Box and what it means to her.
Row.txt_description: Gives each participant the opportunity to recognize what she treasures in herself and her life by exploring blessings, dreams beliefs, friendships, hopes, and strengths that make her life special by creating treasure boxes to hold and protect them.
Row.txt_notes: children’s manual pg. 43

Row.txt_code:
Crayon Feelings drawing: “So much going on, but I’m
finding my own center...”



About this Workshop:
This is a very simple and direct workshop—about as simple as you can get—but quite powerful.  It requires practically no set-up or preparation.  The supplies are very inexpensive and accessible.  

At AVDVC, our workshops are only one hour long, so we need projects that can be accomplished in an hour, including enough time for sharing.  This is an excellent workshop in a short time-frame.  If you have longer, it allows even more time for sharing, which is great!  

This workshop is a great one for clients who don’t want to participate.  They can just take all their grumbling and resistance and put it on the paper.  

This workshop is also effective with teen groups I lead.

Objectives:





Basket of crayons for
Crayon Feelings workshop.



To put feelings into shapes and color.  To experience a completely free, no-pressure, expressive process— free from worrying about creating a product or what it will look like.  To discover and explore how our feelings can change through the process of expressing them.

Materials:
White copier paper (enough for plenty of sheets per participant)
Crayons—in big shoe boxes (or baskets)
Optional: journals for the writing part of the workshop.  (It’s also fine to write on the copier paper)
Pens
Relaxing music




Simply supplies: crayons and paper.




Setup:
Place the paper, pens, and crayons in the center of the table.  Get your music ready, and you’re all set!

Timeframe:
Total:  1 1/2 hours
10 minutes    Introduction
10 minutes    Relaxation
15 minutes     Drawing
20 minutes     Writing
30 minutes    Sharing


Opening:
“Today we will be drawing our feelings in shapes and colors—no pictures—just whatever shapes express how we’re feeling.  It’s fine if you’re mad, tired, or don’t want to be here.  Whatever you’re feeling, that’s what you get to put on the paper in shapes and colors.  Remember, we’re not going to be making pictures—no drawings of things.  Just use the colors and shapes to represent what you’re feeling.  Don’t worry about what you’re going to make, or what colors you want to choose.  I’ll be leading a relaxation, and you can just see what comes to mind during that.  Take some white paper.  Take a few sheets in case you need more than one.  I’ll lead a relaxation and then we’ll dive in.”





Crayon Feelings drawing: “Letting out the anger and finding
tenderness surrounds me...”



Relaxation:
“Get comfortable in you chair and take a deep breath in.  Let your eyes close if you feel comfortable closing them.  Take another deep breath in.  As you let it go, try to let go of any tension in your body.  Let any tension out with your breath.  And take another wonderful, deep breath in.  And then let it go, breathing out any tension.  Take a few more nice deep breaths and notice yourself relaxing more and more with each one.”  (pause)   

“As you keep enjoying your relaxing breaths, picture yourself in a place where you feel safe and find beauty.  Are you inside or outside?  Notice your beautiful place.  Take some more deep breaths as you sit in your beautiful place...  (pause)  When you’re ready, notice how you are feeling.  Notice what colors come to mind.  Are you feeling blue?  Red?  Lavender?  Yellow?  Green?  What colors come to mind?  And what shapes?  Spirals?  Straight lines?  Swirls?  Scribbles?  Whenever you are ready, you can open your eyes and begin drawing in shapes and colors, however you’re feeling.”  




Crayon Feelings drawing: “Running into the
tough spots and finding joy too...”




Drawing:
As people draw, encourage them to keep trusting whatever comes to mind.  Encourage them to fill the whole page, and encourage them to use as much paper as they need.  

Allow them to continue drawing for about 12 minutes.  Then let them know “You’ve got about 3 minutes left, so start getting your thoughts together for writing.”  Then give another reminder when they have a minute or so left.

Writing:
“Now we’re going to take about 15 minutes for writing (in your journal or on a piece of paper). Write down how you feel now, and write about how you felt when we first started.”

Again, give everyone a 3-minute warning near the end, and then a 1-minute warning, etc.

Closing Circle:
Give each participant a chance to share anything she wants to about what she drew, wrote, or experienced.  Let them know it’s fine to pass if they aren’t comfortable sharing.  When you’ve gone all the way around the circle, come back to those who passed and give them a chance to share if they’ve changed their minds.
Row.txt_description: A chance to put feelings into shapes and color while experiencing a completely free, no-pressure, expressive process - free from worrying about creating a product or what it will look like.

Row.str_author_location: Sexual Assault Crisis Agency, Long Beach, California
Row.txt_code:
Christina Curtis


Objectives:
To give the clients an opportunity to explore feelings and issues and gain self-awareness by creating a brick wall to represent the emotional walls they have built in order to survive.  To notice what shows to the world and what stays hidden inside.  To explore the positive and negative aspects of having the wall, and consider what it might be like to take it down.     

Materials:
Clay or Supersculpey
Pens, needles, or something sharp for writing into the clay
Newspaper to cover the table (if you’re using messy clay)

Relaxation:
Guide the participants through a relaxation exercise that leads them to identify things they hide from others.  

Creation:
Tell clients that they are going to make a brick wall, where each brick they create will have writing on it.  The brick that will be placed on the bottom of the stack will symbolize the things they hide from the outside world.  The brick on top of the stack will symbolize what the outside world sees.  They are free to make as many bricks as possible to create their wall.  

Sharing:
At the end, ask if they would like to share.  Encourage them to express whatever they discovered about themselves and their issues through making their wall.    Encourage them to smash down their wall, if they wish.  

Note:  The poem below by an anonymous survivor illustrates one woman’s exploration and experience of the walls she created to survive.  Remember that everyone’s wall will be unique.  There is no right or wrong.  There are positive things and negative things about having walls.  There are reasons why we built them as we did. 




The Wall: Freedom in Three Parts

Part I
It took six months to build the wall

The first brick was laid when I decided that instead of being “again” in a never ending hell, this time would mark the beginning of a change.

The second brick was laid the very next day when I broke through the silence of shame and told a friend what had happened.

More bricks were added later that week when I raised the courage to call the Family Violence Project.







The next week I began a new weekly routine. Tuesday morning I walked to work, went in the back door, out the front door, got on the bus and ducked when it passed our street and rode for an hour to group.  It was worth it.  Every Tuesday I returned with an armload of bricks.

In the evenings I began to take my daughter out of the house and back to my office, our hideout, where she could play in peace and I could hear the clink, clink, clink of bricks sliding into place.

When the yelling started at home and my body ached from the blows, I would leave.  I would pull inside of myself and retreat to the wall.  Just feeling its coolness, its roughness, its solidness gave me hope.

One night, when the pain was too much to bear, I wrenched my heart out of my chest and buried it in the path of the wall, laying bricks over it and marking it with a pebble.  The pain had been holding me back.  Without it I could focus on building the wall.

As the wall grew I found I could push some of the chaos behind it.  When the chaos could not touch me, I grew stronger.

It took an attorney, a restraining order, four cops and more support than I ever thought possible to push the last few bricks into place.  When the wall was complete, the chaos was gone.  The silence was deafening, the peacefulness overwhelming. 
I could finally rest.  I had escaped.  I was free.

Part II
The wall in my soul is four feet thick

It contains thousands of bricks.

It has stood for a year.

Behind the wall is chaos.  Behind the wall is the screaming voice, the raised hand, the cold gray eyes.  Behind the wall is every assault, every insult, every coercion, every degradation. Behind the wall is the power that controlled me.

The wall protects me.  It is stronger than the power on the other side.  The wall is stronger than any one person because it is held together with the experiences and understanding of many women.  I add my experiences to the mix and make it stronger.  By making bricks and passing them on to other women, I strengthen myself.

The wall is cool.  It contains the heat.  The wall is strong.  It has withstood the violence of hurricanes raging on the other side.  The wall is high.  It shelters me as I grow stronger.  The wall is solid.  It protects me.

The wall has saved my life.

The safety of the wall is my freedom now.  With it, I am able to live each day.  For now, that is enough.

Part III
The wall will not stand forever

The wall that keeps me safe also restricts me.  It gives me room to breathe but not to move.  Sometimes I wish that the wall were gone, that I could stretch my arms all the way out.  Sometimes I wish I could hear music.  Sometimes I wish I could dance.

The wall separates me from the person I was “before.”  I don’t know her anymore.  In pictures, she looks like a stranger.  I can’t get close to her because the wall is in the way.

But the wall is only temporary. 
It will not stand forever. It cannot stand forever, because my heart is buried beneath it, healing in the cool dampness of the earth.

When I am stronger than the power on the other side of the wall, the wall will no longer be necessary.  I don’t know when or how, all at once or piece by piece, but the wall will come down.  And when it comes down, I will see the power on the other side of the wall reduced to ashes blowing in the wind, no more significant than crumpled bits of leaves I can kick out of my way.

When the wall comes down,
I will stretch.  I will dance. 
I will reach out and embrace the person I used to be.  When the wall comes down, I will find the place where my heart is buried and dig it up.  I know it will still hold pain, but I will be stronger than the pain.

When I reclaim my heart, I will be whole again.  I will be able to trust, to feel, to love.

When the wall comes down,
I will finally be free.

—anonymous survivor


Extra Workshop: Rules
Note: This project was adapted from a book called A Practical Guide to Art Therapy Groups by Diane Fausek.

Objectives:
To allow clients to examine the rules in their lives.  This activity is perfect for survivors who are in shelter.  They are suddenly living in an environment where there are a lot of rules that they have to follow. 

Materials:
Pastels and Construction paper

Activity:
1.  Begin a discussion about rules.  What kind of rules are there?  There are internal rules (morals) and external rules (“Stop at the red light”).  How do rules make you feel?  How does breaking the rules feel?  Ask each client to define her feelings about rules.

2.  Ask the clients to choose a color and pattern that reflects their feelings regarding rules and cover the entire paper.

3.  Now ask the clients what breaking the rules feels like.  Ask them to create the feeling of “no rules” over the existing picture.  Do not cover the original picture completely. 

4.  After they are done, ask the clients how rules or lack thereof coexist together.
Row.txt_description: Clients are given the opportunity to explore feelings and issues and gain self-awareness by creating a brick wall to represent the emotional walls they have built in order to survive.

Row.str_author_location: Based on O Magazine article 'After Great Pain' (Sept. 2002, pg. 121)
Row.txt_code:
Helping Hands artwork on these pages
by Olivia Tamayo and Cathy Salser



Objective:
To give participants an opportunity to reflect on the events of September 11th in an atmosphere of safety and support.  To explore what it takes to emerge from great pain and trauma such as this by creating a “helping hand.”  To notice the deep significance and impact of giving and receiving help.

Non-9/11 Note:
This workshop can easily be shifted
to focus on the importance of giving and receiving help, with no reference to 9/11.  Only focus on 9/11 if you feel it would be useful for your group.

Materials:
Heavy paper
Scissors
Markers, colored pencils, collage supplies, glitter, watercolors
Hole punch and thread/string

Timeframe:
Total:         2 hours
10 min:   Introduction
20 min:   Opening circle
10 min:   Relaxation
50 min:   Creation
30 min:   Sharing







Introduction:
“With September here, I know we have had the 11th on our minds.    This workshop, ‘Helping Hands,’ will be a chance to explore our feelings about what has happened and give ourselves and each other a helping hand in coping and moving forward.  It is a chance to trace our hands, draw, and write as a way of finding strength and clarity together.

“There are so many different ways to find strength and clarity.  Can you think of some?  Letting the pain out is an important part of recovering.  Looking for the positive can also be an important part of healing.  There’s an article about this in the September O Magazine.  It talks about how people who have survived some of the worst situations in history - even torture and imprisonment - survived best by focusing on positive things like making a difference in the lives of those around them.  The author shares:

“Perhaps the most difficult part of recovery is squeezing the good out of the horror.  Since we’re stuck with September 11, we should try to learn from it.  We should live more fully in the present tense because we have been reminded how fragile our lives really are.   We should remember the many cell-phone calls from the buildings and planes that were about to go down, and how much that repetitive cliché of three words meant to all the people who heard ‘I love you’ before the final moment...”

“So today as we create our Helping Hands, we will notice not only the hard things but also the good things.  The ways we have seen people helping each other so bravely and boldly in the face of this tragedy.  The ways we have seen people reach out to each other.  The ways we can all make a difference in the lives of those around us. 

Opening Circle:
“Share one thing you lost and one thing you gained because of 9/11.”  (Alternative non-9/11 opening: Share one time you remember being helped by someone, and one time you helped someone else.)







Technical Info:
“Thanks so much for sharing all your thoughts and feelings.  As we create our Helping Hands today, I want you to know you can trust whatever comes to your mind.  We’ll be doing a relaxation and then diving in.  Remember that whatever you create is just fine.  There’s no right or wrong.  You can trace, cut, draw, and write.  You could make your hand two-sided or work on just one side.  Your hand could be a place to let out all the pain, worries, and fears.  It could be a place where you count your blessings and look at what you are thankful for and want to remember because of 9/11.  It could be a place where you write and draw all the help you noticed, and the ways you’d like to be a help in creating a violence-free future.  Whatever you create, let it be a Helping Hand for you, helping to carry you through these rough times of so much change and uncertainty.  You don’t need to plan it out.  Just trust whatever comes to you.”  (Show the supplies - paper, scissors, pens, glue, etc. so that after the relaxation everyone will be able to just dive in.)

Relaxation:
“Get comfortable in your chair.  Let your eyes close if you feel comfortable closing them.  And take a nice deep breath in...  And let it go...  Good.  And now take another deep breath in...   And let it go.  As you breathe in, imagine pure relaxation is coming into your body, washing through you and draining all the tension away.  And take another nice deep breath in...  And let it go...  Good.  Now with your eyes still closed, put your hands together gently.  Put them together any way you like.  Move them together, noticing the warmth and comfort hands can give.  Imagine someone giving you a helping hand when you need it... a comforting hand.  Take a deep breath in and appreciate that comfort...  And now imagine how it feels when you give someone else a hand of comfort and help, and you know it is making a difference.   Take a nice deep breath and notice the strength and caring that come from your hands.  And now imagine how it feels when you are gentle and comforting with yourself.  Take another nice deep breath in and notice how wonderful and important it is - that comfort and help from yourself.   You can keep your eyes closed as long as you want.  As you breathe deeply, just drink in all these kinds of helping hands.  Take your time.  And when you are ready, open you eyes and begin creating your Helping Hand.”

Creation:
As the group creates, encourage them to trust whatever comes to them and not criticize it.  Let them know when there are 15 minutes left, 10 minutes, 5 minutes, etc.  For those who finish early, encourage them to write about what they have created and/or create another Helping Hand to give someone else. 

Sharing:
Give everyone an opportunity to share their creations, what they means to them, and anything they discovered in the process.

Closure:
It is important to take special care to end the workshop on a positive and hopeful note, especially since this is such a deeply difficult subject.  If you think it would help, have a final closing circle after the sharing of the artwork.  Ask each participant:  What is one positive thing you take with you from this workshop?

You might want to end with a celebration of hanging all of the hands in the shelter.
Row.txt_description: Give participants an opportunity to reflect on traumatic events (i.e. September 11th) in an atmosphere of safety and support, exploring what it takes to emerge from great pain and trauma such as this by creating a "helping hand."

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop was created with the intention of bringing forth the essence of the power of boundaries.  The group had been working on creating and maintaining personal boundaries, and I wanted to offer an opportunity to touch on the strength of power, not force.

Materials:
Large paper bags (brown grocery bags)
Cray-Pas oil pastels
Watercolors (Prang makes good strong colors)
Large container of warm water
Tea candles with containers

Timeframe:
Total:         1 1/2hours
20 min:   Visualization
50 min:   Activity
20 min:   Closing Circle

Setup/Prep:
It is optimal to have an open area that has plenty of space for movement, yet is near the area they will be working.  Place one of each item from the materials list for each participant. Place the tea candles too, but don't light them yet.  Have the container of water near by, but in a location separate from the working table, so spills don't occur where the work is being done.

Visualization:
We did this standing and with the eyes closed.  If a participant is too uncomfortable with eyes closed, perhaps they could stand near you or with their back to the wall and the exit door near them.  They may choose to do this with eyes open.





Step 1:  Cut the paper bag to the
shape you desire.





Step 2:  Draw an image of yourself.





Step 5:  Paint with water colors
(after folded & wet).



“First it is important to feel centered in your body.  Find the center of the balls of your feet.  Find the center of your heels.  Rest in that place.  Find where your hips are square and comfortable.  Find where your shoulders are set and balanced.  Find where your head rests evenly on your neck.  Stay here for a moment.  This is a good time to thank your body for what it does for you.  In front of you, imagine there are four balls of energy: one blue, one green, one violet and one white. In a way that is most comfortable for you, bend, fold, twist or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the blue ball.  This ball holds the question for you ‘What am I made of?’ Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball. In a way that is most comfortable for you, fold, bend, twist or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the green ball. This ball holds the question ‘Where did I come from?’  Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball.  In a way that is most comfortable for you, fold, bend, twist or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the violet ball.  This ball holds the question ‘Who am I?’  Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball.  In a way that is most comfortable for you, fold, bend, twist or manipulate your body to reach down and pick up the white ball.  This ball holds the question ‘What is my essence?’ Rest with this ball.  Now find a comfortable place to store this ball.  Now find and gather all the balls you have stored.  With the greatest care and with all the power you can muster, bring these balls together and merge them into one singular flame.  Remember to use your power, not force.  Rest with this flame.

(At this time you may want to go around and light the tea candles at each participants place.  Another option is to light the candles after they sit down. If you light them while they are still resting with their flame, be sure to let them know you will be moving about the room.)

For children:  You can use the same visualization, however, the questions can be adapted to the appropriate age levels.  For example:  for children in the 4-8 year range, the questions might be more concrete, such as “Who is in my family?” “Who are my friends?” “What makes me special?” “What makes me strong?”

For 9-12 year range, perhaps “What are my hopes and dreams?” “What makes me special?” “How am I strong?” “What feelings are in me that help me to understand myself?”





Step 3:  Crumple, fold, or bend.





Step 4:  Immerse in water.





Step 4:  Take out of water to begin painting.



Introduction:
I did this workshop without giving an introduction to the participants.  I did not explain to them the intended process or possible outcome.  The reason for this was that they requested a workshop that had to do with boundaries and it was my intent to allow them an individual expression of the idea and experience.  It allowed them to bring together the multitude of sensations and experiences in their lives under one umbrella of “power.” The formulation was entirely their own and was not contrived for them.

For children, youth, and adults who may not be able to grasp without guidance, introduce the workshop as an opportunity to discover that power is a root of boundaries.  Force does not make happen what you want to happen.  Power is all around and in you and comes from our pain.

Awesome Essence Making:

Step 1.  Cut the paper bag into the size and shape you desire. You may need to show younger children how to get into the paper bag and cut the bottom off so it lays flat.

Step 2.  Ask the participants to use the Cray-Pas to draw an image of themselves. I let them know they are not bound to making a body. Often the image is of abstract shape rather than an identifiable object. What ever the image is, is fine.

Step 3.  “Crumple, fold, or bend the image and the paper bag. This is often hard to do because we don't like to mess up our art!!! This portion may also be representative of the pains we have endured, times we have felt folded, crumpled or otherwise “mutilated.” The more the fold lines are accentuated (by pressing harder) the more vibrant the paint will appear on those lines.”  Note:  You should experiment with this part prior to doing the workshop.

Step 4.  “Immerse the crumpled piece into the water.  You may hold it there for about 15 seconds or more, swish it around, squeeze it, whatever.” (This part allows the paper to absorb moisture, thus allowing the watercolors to do their job.  The more moisture in the paper allows the paint to fuse across the paper.)

Step 5.  “Open the paper flat and begin painting with the water colors. This process is much like the healing process. Washing our experiences, our perceptions of ourselves with what we believe to be helping us heal. The areas covered by the Cray-Pas will repel the water colors, while the mist area will absorb the colors.”  (It is best to use Prang Professional water colors, as the pigment is more dense and shows better on the darker paper.)

Closing:
I like to allow enough time for participants to express their sensations about the process as well as what the piece expresses.  I ask “What did I notice in my body as I worked through each portion of this process?” “What were my struggles and what were my joys?” “Was there a cathartic moment while I worked?”

I ask if that individual wants to hear feedback from the other participants. If they do, I ask others to give their sensations about that persons piece, not an artistic critique.  

I ask them to ask themselves “What sensations or feelings come alive in me when I
I observe your work?”





Awesome Essence drawing before the
 water and paint.

Awesome Essence drawing after the
water and paint.
Row.txt_description: Brings forth the essence of the power of boundaries by offering an opportunity to touch on the strength of power, not force.

Row.txt_code:
Many leaders have created wonderful workshops focused on hearts.  In your reports, we’ve noticed that these heart workshops seem to always be your favorites (and the client’s favorites)!  Here we share some of these ideas, so everyone can enjoy them!

See also:  “Affirmation Hearts” project by Rose Curtis in the August 2000 Leader’s Update.

  



 
  




Objective:
To give participants a chance to explore their hearts and notice the many layers—inside, outside, hurt, hopeful, strong, vulnerable, beautiful, and healing.  To give them a chance to express all these layers and notice that their heart is beautiful as a whole.





Materials:
See variations below and decide which materials your group would like best: 
    1. Watercolor
    2. Collage
    3. Drawing 
    4. Heart Ornaments 
    5. Lamination 
Or come up with your own supplies and process!

Timeframe:
Total:         1 1/2hours
20 min:   Relaxation
50 min:   Heart-making
20 min:   Closing

Introduction:
“Today will be a special time for us to listen to our hearts.  As you listen to your heart today you might hear difficult things, and you might also hear wonderful things.  You might hear pain, strength, brokeness, hope, courage...  Today is a special time to practice having tenderness and compassion for all that our hearts hold.  This is a special time to care for ourselves and our hearts.” 

Opening Circle:
Begin with a “heart circle” check-in giving each participant an opportunity to share how her heart is feeling today:  light?  heavy?  foggy?  clear? 

Relaxation:
Before you lead the relaxation, be sure to explain the art supplies and technical aspects of the heart-making.  This way, when the relaxation is over, the group can dive right in a create without any further instruction.

“Get yourself comfortable in your chair and gently place both your hands over your heart.  Let your eyes close if you feel like closing them, and take a deep breath in.  As you let it go, picture letting go of any tension in your body... and take another nice deep breath in... and let it go.  As you breathe deeply, notice your hands resting on your heart.  Notice that this is a special time to care for your heart—all the good things, all the difficult things, all that your heart carries inside...  This is a time to protect and thank your heart.  And this is a time to listen to it.  Whenever you are ready, you can open your eyes and begin to create what your heart tells you.”


 
 
 “Shadows , darkness, and light... 
Falling apart...”
  
 
 “Nurturing, growth, beauty.”
  
 
 “My heart can be beautiful again with
patience and time.”
  

Heart-making:
1. Watercolor
Healing Hearts
from Kori Taylor, The Abbie

Materials:  Watercolor paper (three small pieces per person), watercolor sets, brushes, water cups, paper towels, relaxing music, pens and paper for writing.

Process:  Have the group use the watercolors to paint three pictures of their heart on its journey of healing.  Watercolors are a wonderful way to explore and express what’s happened to our hearts and then how our hearts are healing.  The way the colors move and blend can express so much.  (See illustrations this page.)

2. Collage
What’s in My Heart?
from Silvio Velasco, YWCA Wings

Materials:  Heart outlines copied onto colored paper (see enclosed outline), glue sticks, scissors, and magazines.

Process:  This is a very simple project.  Hand out copied colored paper with outlines of hearts and have the participants collage onto the paper to show what is in their heart.  (It’s fine if they don’t stay within the outline of the heart.)  They can make it however they wish in order to show what’s in their heart.  (See samples this page.)
Comments:  “The supplies are simple and familiar, so the participants really like it and feel comfortable with it.  It was not too hard for them and at the end of the group, everyone shared.”

3. Drawing
Both Sides of the Heart
from Jeanne Anderson and Caroline Castleforte, Good Shepherd Shelter

Materials: Markers, construction paper, pens, pencils

Process:  This project uses two sides of the paper to show two different sides of the heart.  Have them use the two sides to show their heart felt before they came into the shelter, and their heart now that they are here in the shelter.  (Note: Variation 4 also builds on this theme.)

Comments:  “Participants were able to recognize feelings that they help deep within.  They were able to see that their heart was beautiful as a whole.  One of them shared, ‘Sometimes I try to hide what is inside my heart, because I think it’s bad, or someone will take advantage of me.’”

    




“Remembering my children who are not
with me...  These pictures signify how
much I love them and wish to have them
with me very soon.”
  “I pray for things to get better for myself.
I put everything on the table.  I feel free,
standing strong today.”
    

4. Heart Ornaments
How Does My Heart Look? 
from Cecilia Bendimez, WomenShelter of Long Beach

Materials:  Hearts copied onto white paper (two per participant—see enclosed master or make your own), markers, colored pencils, beads, yarn, scissors and glue.

Note: It can also be helpful to have a chart of different colors and what they can mean in terms of emotions.

Project: Talk about how different colors can convey different emotions.  (You can use a color chart, or just discuss various feelings and what colors might convey those feelings.  Remember, there is not a right or wrong answer.  Different colors can convey different things for different people.)  Give them each two hearts and ask them to use colors on one heart to show how their heart looked when they were in the domestic violence relationship.  Ask them to use colors on the other heart to show how their heart feels now that they are in the shelter.  They can then cut out their hearts and glue them back to back with yarn in between so they can hang it and see both sides.  Encourage them to share the differences and the reasons.

Comments:  “It really worked well.  They ladies enjoyed it and at the end, they really opened up.  And their hearts were amazing.  You could see the transition they were making in their lives. 

5. Laminated Mixed-Media
Hearts of Soul
from Obbie Brown, Valley Oasis

Materials:  Construction paper, scissors, edger scissors, markers, craypas, glitter glue, contact paper or lamination equipment, yarn and hole puncher.

Process:  This workshop is the same as the Affirmation Hearts project (August 2000 Leader’s Update).  Each participant creates five cut-out hearts, decorates them, and writes something on each one that she would want said to her to help uplift her soul when she’s feeling down.  When all the hearts are made and laminated, they put them all into a bag, mix them up, and then pick 5 without looking.  Then each participant can string the five hearts she picked on yarn and hang them in her room as a reminder.  This way each woman will have something that speaks to her soul during those tough times when she might feel like going back to her abuser.  The heart messages come from deep inside your soul. 

Comments:  “This has to be one of the best projects that I’ve done.  The group sure loved it.  The sharing of the hearts reminded them of the saying ‘treat others as you want to be treated.’  They liked that they could give someone else a piece of a good part of their soul.”  (See samples this page.)

Closing:
Close with a special “heart circle.”  Give each participant an opportunity to share what she is carrying in her heart from the workshop. 


  



 

 
Hearts from the “Affirmation Hearts”
workshop (August 2000 Update)
Row.txt_description: A collection of heart themed workshops by different leaders, always favorites!
Row.txt_notes: ER TO DO: Get heart patterns photographed and entered.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give participants a chance to experience total artistic freedom. To allow the creative juices to really flow without any boundaries and at the end have a tangible symbol of that freedom and awareness. This workshop will allow the ladies to explore their feelings, instincts, talents, dreams, hopes, fears, likes and dislikes.

Materials:
Shrinky Dinks paper (Frosted Ruff N’Ready type – for use with colored pencils)
Permanent fine point markers
Colored pencils
Scissors
Magazines/stock books/coloring books, etc (for tracing)
Hole puncher
String
Doll template (click here for template master copy)
Grocery paper bags

Opening Circle:
Share how you feel about trusting your intuition.

Introduction:
Share the project with the group (see Instructions, page 3) so they will be ready to begin after the relaxation. It will help a lot if you have a sample already made to share.

  


  

Relaxation:
Dim down the lights and put a candle in the middle of the table. “Take three deep breaths. (If you feel comfortable close your eyes. If not, look into the middle of the table at the candle.) Now, take another deep breath and hold it for three seconds... and release your breath. Now, do this two more times. In your mind’s eye go to a place where you feel safe and calm and happy. This place can be a real place (a favorite beach, park, chair) or an imaginary place. Be there. Think of the sounds, smells, etc. of that place. Feel how comfortable and safe and happy you are. (This place can also be a place in your past where you were safe/happy.) Now become aware of the wonderful energy around you. (You can visualize energy as anything you want: light, small spheres, etc). Imagine you being aware now of all this positive energy around you and being willing to allow it to come inside you. In your mind’s eye see and feel it coming through your skin into you. Feel the warmth of it. Welcome it in – invite it in!”


 
 
 Martha Contreras holds three
intuition dolls.
  

“Now, when you are ready you are going to slowly open your eyes and you will remember the energy being inside you to guide you in this project and imagine yourself being in that safe/special place in your mind. Allow the energy in!

Instructions:
“Trace your doll template with a permanent fine point marker on the smooth side of your shrinky dinks plastic. This will be a guide only. You can alter the template as you are drawing it to make long hair, ponytails, a short dress, pant suit, etc. Anything you want your doll to be and/or have (hat, jewelry, etc). Once you have this outline (on the smooth side) turn the paper around to the "rough" frosted side and draw and/or trace (from magazines, coloring books, etc.) whatever comes into your mind with color pencils. Be creative, let yourself go, allow that energy that is inside guide you now! Even if you just use colors to signify different emotions, etc., your dolls will look great – that’s a guarantee!”

Once you are done coloring and drawing/tracing, you can cut out your doll. Think about how you are going to use your doll – a holiday ornament, earrings, pin, magnet, necklace, etc. If you are using your doll as an ornament or earrings, then your doll is going to need a hole on the top of her head for you to put a string through it. The hole needs to be done PRIOR to baking. If you are using your dolls as a pin or magnet, then no hole is needed. If you are using your doll as part of a necklace where more dolls are going to be “united,” then you want to put a hole on both of her hands so you can later unite the dolls by their hands with string or a “mini” paper fastener (these work very well).

  


Intuition doll sample before
baking and shrinking.
 
  

Now you are ready to bake! Follow the instructions on the package. Place a piece of the paper bag to line the toaster oven tray, plus make a small “handle” by tipping up one of the corners – this way you won’t get your hands burned. Most dolls will be “done” in 3 minutes. Be patient. Let the doll do her transformation and “lie down flat” before you take her out of the oven. Once you take her out, quickly put a book on top of her and press down hard for 15 seconds.

Technical Note to Leaders:
If the doll gets “stuck” within itself and does not want to “lie flat” at all even after 4 minutes, take her out while she still hot and soft and unstick her and put her back into the oven and see if that helps the process.

One of the dolls got her hands stuck when she was baking (like she was praying). We tried to unstick her hands twice and she kept putting her hands together. Well, after the second time around we decided to leave the doll be. Sometimes art has to be let be! The participant later on said that she will always remember the determination of her doll to be herself!

Closing:
Give the group an opportunity to share how they felt about the process of making their doll(s). It is okay if someone does not want to share, for these dolls can be VERY PERSONAL!


 
 
 Intuition dolls samples after baking and shrinking.
  

Children’s Corner:
A very simple variation of this workshop for children is for them to trace their hand – yes, their actual hand and color it in. It is o.k. to go outside the lines as you will be cutting the pattern out anyway. This very special hand can become a necklace, a zipper pull, a magnet, etc. Don’t forget to punch a hole before baking if you are going to use it as a necklace or zipper pull.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants a chance to experience total artistic freedom. Allows the creative juices to really flow without any boundaries and at the end hae a tangible symbol of that freedom and awareness.

Amazon.com's Best of 2001
The Blueprint may be Jay Z's most captivating record since Reasonable Doubt, but its predictably detached mood reflects the master hustler's superior ability to trick out lackluster subject matter with lyrical complexity and brief flashes of manufactured introspection. The Blueprint, a solid mix of preprogrammed radio hits ("Izzo," "Girls, Girls, Girls") and better-than-average mid-tempo compositions ("Never Change," "Song Cry"), confirms the Brooklyn rapper's legendary status. Blistering flames of the Queensbridge/Jay Z feud fan high with "Takeover," a direct attack on Nas, set over the Doors' rock & roll burner, "5 to 1." "Renegade" provides the album's only full-on guest appearance. Jay and Eminem take this opportunity to address haters (within the industry and in the general population) who don't understand the mind of an artist. Jigga spells it out on the title track: "Reasonable Doubt--classic, shoulda went triple." The Blueprint might not be quite on par with Reasonable Doubt but it is reasonably good. --Rebecca Levine

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
The purpose of this project is for each person to create a personal drinking glass or cup.  This glass can be used for self-empowerment, spiritual renewal or just to create a quiet time for self-soothing. By drinking from this glass each woman can “fill her self up with the power of her own life and nourish herself with positive reflection”.





Hand-painted glasses completed at the
“Taste of Life” leader’s workshop in June.



Materials:
Porcelaine paints (can order from Dick Blick)
Outliner pens.
Rinse cups (two per person)
Paint brushes
Paper towels
Q-Tips for wiping off drips
Popsicle sticks to dip into paint
Paint palettes
Glasses (packages of 4 juice glasses are at Big Lots for $1.29 to $1.79).
Plain coffee mugs (Big Lots $.59 to $.99)
Tiles form Home Depot are about .79 a piece and the tiles could be uses as trivets, paper weights or hanging pictures.

Introduction:
Drinking glasses have for centuries (as early as 2000 BC) been used symbolically. Whether to seal a bargain, signal allegiance, perform a spiritual ritual or simply enjoy nourishment, drinking from a glass has represented empowerment, commitment and determination.

Relaxation:
Because of the fact that all art projects have to be conducted in the kitchen at the dining room table, it is often impossible to do guided relaxation because of the distraction of people walking in and out. So, we normally just do some stretching and deep breathing. It helps the women to relax and lightens the mood of group.




Working on a “stained glass” effect.




Opening Circle:
Can you remember a time in your life when drinking from a glass held some symbolism for you? Have you ever had a time when you sat down with a friend or relative and shared deep feelings over a glass of iced tea or lemonade or even cold water? Have you ever just taken a break from a stressful day to sit by yourself and sip some form of nourishment to revive? Or, do you have memories of a feeling of spiritual renewal after a religious ceremony concerned with the power of sipping from a cup or glass?


Introduction:
Today we will be making our very own personal drinking glass. Take a minute to think about the things that are important to you. Think about the changes that have happened in your life and the lives of your children since you had the courage to enter a domestic violence shelter. Give yourself permission to be proud of those changes. Picture the power you are creating for you and your children as you find the strength to change your life.

Remember that change does not come with out challenge. There will be times when you feel doubtful and afraid. The glass you will be painting today will symbolize your strengths and the things in life that make you strong. Whether it’s your love for your children, your hope for a new future, or your desire to discover a new way of life, I want you to think about your ‘powers’ as you paint your glass. Visualize your energy. Go to that quiet place in your heart that holds the power of your spirit. And when you feel ready, start to paint.

It’s important to know that it does not matter what you paint. It can be a summer day at the beach or an image of your future or just colors and shapes and swirls. It doesn’t matter if the paint runs (you can always wash it off and start over!!) or if it doesn’t look like what you thought it would. The only thing that matters is that you hold the image of your own personal power in your mind as you paint you glass.





“Mi Casa” glass.



Process:
Each of you has one glass, two rinse waters and some paper towels in front of you. Make sure to take a few sizes of brushes, being sure to include extra small to medium in size. The glasses are small so smaller brushes work best.

There are several colors of paint. Paint with one color at a time. Pick you color, shake the jar and remove the cap. There is a little cup inside the cap top. You will be using the cap as a palette. (You can also use a popcicle stick to dab a bit onto a tile or palette instead of using the lids.)  This helps to keep your brush from getting too much paint on it and makes it easier to apply to the glass When you are finished using your chosen color, replace the cap, rinse your brush, dry your brush off with the paper towels and get another color.

You will also notice that there are some squeeze tubes (outliner pens) of various colors on the table. These are used to outline shapes. They can also be used to write names or encouraging words that mean something to you personally. It’s best to practice on the paper towel in front of you first. These tubes have to be squeezed very gently for maximum usage.

When the glasses are done, you are encouraged to share your thoughts and meanings with the other participants. I have been using this project for years and I have never seen an ugly glass! So don’t worry. Just the paint alone makes the glass pretty.




Participant painting flowers onto her glass.






Tips:
No water in the Brush:  Use a dry brush to apply the paint.  After you rinse your brush, be sure to dry the water off completely before dipping into the paint again.  Water in the brush will make the paint too runny.

Wiping off the paint:  You can use a paper towel or Q-Tips to wipe off the paint if it drips or if you don’t like what you painted.

Layers:  You can put many thin layers of color on for a beautiful layered effect.  The thin layers dry quickly and don’t drip.

Where to paint:  Don’t paint inside the glass or too close to the rim.  The paints are not intended to be in contact with your drink. 

Baking the glasses:  Let the glasses dry for 24 hours. After that drying period, the glasses are baked at 300 degrees for 30 minutes. After that, the paint is set and the glasses can be washed (hand washed preferred) without washing off the paint.

Closing Circle:
Give each woman an opportunity to share about her glass and what it means to her.  (Sometimes it helps to put a paper towel in the glass when sharing so the design can be seen by everyone in the circle.) 





Using the glass paints on tiles.



Variations:
Hand painted tiles can be hung on the wall for inspiration. Coffee mugs can be used for coffee, tea and other hot drinks. Also flower vases, teapots, kitchen storage jars and any number of other glass or ceramic items suitable for painting. The purpose will vary with the project; Vases – flowers can symbolize beauty and hope and serve as a reminder of spring and new beginnings. Storage jars – this can represent saving for the future and planning for family needs.

This glass can be used for self-empowerment, spiritual renewal, or just to create a quiet time for self-soothing. By drinking from this glass, each participant can "fill herself up" with the power of her own life and nourish herself with postive reflection.

Row.txt_code:
This Protective Shield includes "Family, Friends, Myself, Music."
  
Objective:
To give the children the opportunity to visually express valuable aspects in their life they wish to protect when they feel a sense of danger. To explore what it means to feel protected or safe and create something tangible that helps them feel secure.

Materials:
Poster board (Could precut out to the shape of a shield. It’s nice to have life-sized - about 27” tall and 18” wide.)
Glue sticks
Cray-Pas (Permanent markers optional)
Aluminum foil
Magazines and scissors
(Could precut images for younger children)

Timeframe:
  


 Protective Shield underway at Women's and Children's Crisis Shelter brings big smiles.
  

Total Time

1 1/2 hours
Opening Circle
 15 min
Activity
 45 min
Closing Circle
 30 min

Age Range / Ratio:
This activity is best suited for children 5 years and older. Recommended ratio is 1 adult for every 4 children.

Preparation:
There are two ways you can go about making a Personal Shield. You can have it as an individual project or a group project. The shield can be a collage or a drawing, whatever you feel the children will be most comfortable working with. You can precut the poster board into a shield shape or have the children cut their own desired shape. For younger children, be sure to precut the shields. Have them use the Cray-Pas and no foil. Even for older children, it can help to precut the shields and even the foil. Cut out long sheets of aluminum foil so those can also be ready for the children to cover the poster board with. Set up Cray-Pas, scissors and glue sticks for each participant. Finally, lay out magazines in the middle of the table for everyone to share.
  

 
Participant working on Protective Shield.

  

Introduction:
Some children may not know the history of shield in the medieval times. A brief history of the shield can be told in order to have the children more or less understand the shield concept:

Shields were once used as a main source of personal protection in war during the early ages. They were carried in one hand or on the arm to ward off enemy shots. Shields were not only for protection in battle, but also to identify its owner. The shields varied in size, shapes, and design. Can you think of a time when you felt you wanted to protect someone or something when you felt they were in danger? What kind of things do you wish to protect in your life? Why do you think you wish to protect them?

Opening Circle:
I feel it is important for the children to do a brief introduction of themselves. In this way everyone knows everyone’s name and it helps to break the ice if there are any new participants. They can also share their thoughts about protection.

The “Art Rule”:
We stress the importance of the “art rule.” The “art rule” at our shelter states, “There’s no wrong way to do art because we are all different. We cannot make fun of other peoples’ art.”

Activity:
“We’re going to start by wrapping the front sides of our protective shields with aluminum foil. Let’s try and get it on as smooth as possible and to put enough glue on the poster board before setting the aluminum on. Now divide your shield into 4 parts by using the Cray-Pas. Each section can be as big or little as you want. Each divided section can express a different valuable part of your life that you want to protect. You can select a title for each section and then begin to look through the magazines or precut pictures to present your valuables in a collage form.

Closing:
After the children are all done making their own shield or group shield, have them talk about why they chose that certain someone or something to protect. Encourage each to share, but make sure no one feels forced. They need to feel secure that no one will ridicule them in order to open up. Hopefully each child gets more than one opportunity to do the art workshops, bond with the other children and learn to trust the art facilitators.

You can also talk about how important it is to keep away from their parents’ fighting because they can get hurt. Discuss other means of protection such as calling the police when there is an emergency or talking to a teacher or friend as a form of protection and help.

Submitted by:
Rosalba Gonzales
Children’s Windows Leader for Women’s and Children’s Crisis Shelter (WCCS)

About this Workshop:
I am submitting this workshop to honor the legacy of Dolores Sosa, former
Children’s Windows leader at the Women’s and Children’s Crisis Shelter.
She has been promoted to be the new legal advocate for our agency, so
she will no longer be leading Children’s Windows. This is a workshop
she developed with a group of high school students at Santa Fe High
School who were working on their senior projects. I wanted to submit
this workshop to thank Dolores for the great legacy she left in the
Children’s Program at our agency. She began working as a Child Care
Aide for W.C.C.S. in 1999 and later got promoted to the position of
Children’s Advocate. I worked along side her for two years and have
never met anyone with such a strong work ethic. Dolores truly went
beond the call of duty and genuinely cared for the children.

Dolores’ idea for this workshop was to get the children thinking about things or people that they want to protect. As Dolores says, “I’ve always heard
children say ‘I’m going to protect my mommy’ when they speak about the
problems they have experienced at home. I’ve always wondered if their
mothers knew their children felt that way. Usually when parents are
fighting, children often get in the middle of the fight to try and stop
the fighting. Of course this is not a safe way for children to express
their feelings by getting involved because they could very well get
hurt. I believe if children are given the tools and time to create a
wonderful visual piece that represents what valuable things are
important to them, it could do wonders! Is also gives the mother a
chance to have an opportunity to speak to the child and have his/her
feelings validated.”

The group of students that Dolores did work with enjoyed it very much and put a lot of themselves into making it.

Special thanks to:
Diane Sanchez, Lupita Sosa, and
Joey Chavira at Santa Fe High.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives the children the opportunity to visually express valuable aspects in their life they wish to protect when they feel a sense of danger. To explore what it means to feel protected or safe and create something tangible that helps them feel secure.
Row.txt_tips: Be sure to have an example ready so the children understand the concept.

Row.txt_code:
“Depressed, Sad”
“Nice, Happy”

  
Objective:
To support children and teens in sharing their hearts and stories through art. To give them an opportunity to listen to their hearts, value the stories within them, and know that others want to hear them too.

Materials:
Cray-Pas
Thick white paper 5 1/2” X 7” (cover stock)
Brushes
Water cups / paper towels
Watercolors, tempera paints, or puffy paints:
Note: Watercolors work best for having the Cray-Pas show through.
Acrylic paints or puffy paints have the most bright and cool colors (but they stain clothes)
Tempera paints are good because they are washable (but they crack and get dull when they dry)

  

Heart Story in the shape of a tree.
 
  
  
  
  
  

Age Range / Ratio:
Here are two versions of the intro/warm-up to suit a range of age levels. Have a look at both and see what you think will work best with your group.

Introduction:
Today our project is called Heart Stories. It’s a chance to notice what’s in our hearts, a chance to notice what our hearts would say if they could talk.

Heart Talk Warm-up (for older children):
This is an interview-style warm-up the kids can do in pairs. Pick 1-3 questions from the list below (or make up your own questions). Consider the age level of your group when you choose the question(s). If you are working with an old enough group, pick three questions and write them up to show the group.

Possible Heart Talk Questions:
—What’s something your heart is proud of about you or your family?
—Share something that made your heart happy this week
—If your heart was a color today, what color would it be and why?
—What makes your heart laugh?
—If your heart could do something fun, what would it do?
—If your heart could do something it’s never done before, what would it do?
—What makes your heart feel safe?
—What makes your heart feel scared?
—What makes your heart strong?
—What makes your heart beat faster?
—What makes your heart happy?
—How do you look when your heart is sad?
—How do you look when your heart is happy?
After the kids interview each other, have them think about what their partner shared. Then go around in a circle and have them each share something they like about their partner’s heart.

Happy Hearts/Sad Hearts Warm-up
(for younger children):
“Today we get to listen to our hearts and notice what helps our hearts feel safe and happy. Does anyone know where your heart is? Can you show me? (Everyone puts their hands on their hearts) Good! What does your heart do? (Pump your blood around your body, bring oxygen to your whole self, tell you how you’re feeling, beat fast when you’re excited or nervous, etc.) Can you feel it beating? Your heart is right in the center of you. Sometimes you can feel feelings in your heart. Has anyone ever felt happiness in their heart? Or sadness, like your heart is breaking? When our hearts are feeling different ways, our whole body knows it.

When you have a sad heart what does your body do? (curl up, look down, cry, etc.) Let’s all be sad hearts with our whole body. Notice how it feels in your whole body when you are sad. It’s okay to be sad sometimes and let it out with our whole bodies. Now take a deep breath in and breath all the sadness out with your breath. Good.

And now let’s think about when we have happy hearts. What does your body do then? (smile, jump up and down, dance, etc.) Let’s all be happy hearts with our whole bodies. Wonderful! Take a deep breath in and feel your heart filling up with happiness. Good! Hearts need a lot of love. And they need to be taken care of and listened to. Today will be a chance to listen to our hearts and take care of them.”

Technical Info:
Today, we are going to make Heart Stories paintings to share the different feelings we have in our hearts. We each get to think about what our hearts would say if they could talk, and what color they’d be inside and outside. Does anyone remember the Windows rule? Remember, there’s no right or wrong way. We’ll just explore some steps you could try.

Step One: Cray-Pas
First let’s use Cray-Pas to draw a heart. Let’s do a sad heart. What colors should I use? (Use all the colors they say.) You can keep adding colors as long as they give ideas of what to add.

Step Two: Paint
Now let's add paint on top of the Cray-Pas. What colors should we use? If we use lots of water, the Cray-Pas show through. If we use thick paints, the Cray-Pas get covered up. Fill in all the paper so there's none showing!

Step Three: Words
Now let’s notice if there are any words that go with our heart. We can write down the story that this heart wants to share.

Closing:
At the end of the workshop, have a Heart Circle where everyone has a chance to share their Heart Stories. If the group seems sad at the end, be sure to leave things on a positive note by having each person share something positive. For example, they could each share a way they want to take good care of their heart. Or they could say something they like about the person on their left – in order to put a nice feeling into everyone’s hearts.
Row.txt_description: This workshop supports children and teens in sharing their hearts and stories through art. The workshop gives them an opportunity to listen to their hearts, value the stories within them, and know that others want to hear them too.
Row.txt_tips: Some kids may want to write stories to go along with their hearts.

Row.str_author_location: Women’s and Children’s Windows Leader Haven House
Row.txt_code:
“Mix Tape” and “My World, My Life, My Dreams”
   
About this Workshop:
I am really excited about this workshop! There are a lot of ways you can use this idea and if you have access to computers with your youth, you could actually create real CD’s for them too! There are so many possibilities to have this workshop be continued for their whole stay if they have access to a computer at your shelter. Sometimes staff have concerns about youth using computers, especially being able to go online, so if it is possible, have them work on the CD in session with you in your office. For shelters that have teens for longer periods of time, this workshop could be never ending! Here are just a few ideas for future workshops utilizing the computer and youth creating a real CD; they could write journal entries on the computer and then store it on their own CD, download pictures…create clipart collages, write poetry, write rap or other kinds of music, create computer generated art, and…of course download or copy their favorite music.

Objective:
For youth to create something about themselves…a CD jewel case insert for their debut album!

Materials:
Insert/Booklets (precut to fit in CD jewel cases)
CD jewel cases
Markers, gel pens, pencils
Glue sticks
Collage material
A few examples of CD inserts
Instant cameras
Scissors
Music
handout (click here for template)

Preparation:
It’s best to have the jewel case inserts already precut and stapled. You can use an insert from a purchased CD as a pattern. You will need a booklet stapler to staple the pages together.
Note: If you don’t have a booklet stapler, here’s a trick. It takes more time, but makes it possible without a special stapler:
>Open up the stapler completely
>Position the booklet on a pile of cardboard
>Staple it (the staples will go straight into the cardboard)
>Pull it off the cardboard
>Bend the staples by hand using a spoon

  


"My World, My Life, My Dreams" Inside Cover
 
  

 
“Mix Tape” and “My World, My Life, My Dreams”
 
  

Timeframe:
This workshop could easily be divided into two sessions or it can give them something to work on more on their own, which for teens in a shelter can be a great boredom reliever! It is good to set a goal of at least finishing the front cover in the first session.

Total Time: 1 to 2 hours
Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Photography for front cover…can be time consuming, especially if they want to go outside!
10 to 30 minutes
Creation: 45 minutes to hours…
(if they want to finish everything on the list!)
Closing Circle: 15 minutes


Introduction:
“Today we are going to find out more about ourselves and create a CD insert for our debut CD. Usually when an artist releases their first CD the insert tells the world something about them and their music. The insert sometimes has a photograph of the artist or some kind of symbol that will forever be linked with that particular artist. As you create your insert, think about what you want to say about you. Think about how you would pose if you were using a photograph, (you will be able to have an actual picture taken today), or think about a symbol or image that represents either yourself or the information you are willing to share with people about who you are. Remember that symbols can be codes about who you are or what you believe in.”

Opening Circle:
If this is a small group open with a circle, having each person share what kind of music they like and where they like to sing…in the shower etc.! (When I facilitate groups at schools I usually skip the opening circle for lack of time, unless it is an ongoing group.)

It’s easier if you already have supplies laid out but if that’s not possible begin to pass them out now. Have participants take a look at a few different CD inserts. (Try to only have ones that represent positive stuff… no drugs etc.) Some ideas are Norah Jones, “Come Away With Me,” & Christina Aguilera, “Stripped.”
Talk about the main topics that most CD inserts have:
1. Front cover
2. Track list…song titles + sometimes the words to songs are included
3. Thank you info: Every artist thanks someone in their life who inspired them to create the music or supported them through the process
4. Credits… CD mastered by…, Art Direction & Graphic Design by…, Photography by…, Art by…,etc
5. Dedications

Because there is a lot to remember I created a handout (see attached) to go along with the workshop so if a youth does not finish in the allotted time, they will have a reference of what else goes in the jewel case insert!

Relaxation:
I like to have at least a short relaxation even though they may giggle or squirm through out it!
It’s important to tell them that relaxing can feel uncomfortable but that it assists us in going within and centering ourselves. I also explain why I play “weird music” by saying that it filters out noise that can interrupt our creativity. I also explain that the music doesn’t have words because words can influence and even change the direction of our own art. The Golden Ball relaxation in the children’s manual is short and sweet but very powerful. Have it lead them into creating the front cover.

Creation:
Keep the music playing while everyone works on creating his or her front cover. You can offer assistance with the instant camera (or if you have a digital camera…they have even more options). Pass out the handout so that those who get their cover done quickly can continue working.

  


 Important people in my life
(my little sister, and older brother).
