Blank Duluth Power & Control Wheel (click here for template)
Duluth Equality wheel (click here for handout)
Duluth Power and Control Wheel (click here for handout)
Construction paper (large)
Markers and Colored Pencils
Paint and brushes
Glue
Glitter
Optional: Collage materials (in case participants want to collage as well as draw and write their wheel)

Timeframe: 2 hrs
Intro and Sharing: 30 min
Creation: 60 min
Sharing: 30 min

Introduction:
“Today we are going to discuss the power and control wheel. You can go around in a circle with each individual one by one sharing a section of the wheel and how it relates to her experience.

Sharing these experiences gives each person a chance to think about what she has gone through and also how other women have handled their abusive situations and how they were not alone in experiencing violence in their lives. They get a chance to vent, cry, to comfort each other and to definitely bond together.
  

 
Sample completed Power and Control Wheel.

  
  
  
  

Creation:
Step One: Each person is given a blank power and control wheel. They are encouraged to fill in each section of the wheel. The group leader should make the group aware that everyone’s story will be different and not all of the sections of the wheel will be filled. (Allow twenty minutes for participants to fill in the wheel.)

Step Two: Participants glue their wheels on large pieces of construction paper.

They are given the opportunity to use pictures, words, paint, glitter, etc. to describe how their story of violence affected them.

They can put whatever they are feeling on the construction paper or on the blank side of the power and control wheel.

Closing:
Each woman shares how the exercise has affected her. Encourage each to share how she plans to stay safe and to take care of herself.

The group leader should encourage each individual to give her statement of what she feels is a healthy relationship.

Each person is encouraged to write up a safety plan and what methods she will use to stay free of violence in her life. (This may relate to groups later in the week.)
Row.txt_description: The workshop was created to help each woman understand the cycle of violence and the dynamics of the power and control wheel. To give each person an opportunity to tell their own story of abuse by writing, drawing and collaging into a blank power and control wheel.
Row.txt_tips: It is also powerful to have participants create a Power and Control Wheel as a group, in addition to creating one individually. This is great for cohesion building. It can then be hung somewhere in the shelter which brings a great sense of accomplishment to the participants.

Row.str_author_location: Women’s Window Liaison at Laurel House, PA
Row.txt_code:
Sample of a “Letter to My Abuser” with glitter pen writing surrounding the letter, mounted onto the scrapbook page.
 
About this Workshop:
This workshop is the third in the “Creative Scrapbook” series created by Carolyn Coleman Manns of Laurel House in Pennsylvania. Through this series, Carolyn powerfully links creative expression to the shelter’s basic DV curriculum.

Objective:
To express what you could not say in person and to express how the abuse made you feel. To express how you feel about him after leaving him. This exercise officially puts closure on the relationship.
 

 

Sample of a “Letter to My Abuser.”
  






Materials:
Large writing paper (beige or white)
Large black construction paper
Pens
Glitter pens
Glitter (optional)
Staple gun
Glitter paint (optional)
Scissors
Markers
Music
White-out pens

Timeframe:
2.15 hrs
Introduction: 15 min.
Sharing: 30 min.
Creation: 60 min.
Closing: 30 min.

Preparations:
Staple gun needed to staple the letter on to the large black construction paper. Some of the women wrote the foul names their abuser called them or the woman can write their feelings on the construction paper circling the letter.

Introduction:
“Today you will have an opportunity to write a letter to your abuser. It won’t be the kind of letter you send. It will be a safe place to get everything out onto paper, express how the abuse made you feel, and say the things you could not say. It will be a chance to talk about your feelings and emotions during your abusive relationship.”
 

Sample of a “Letter to My Abuser.”
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Opening Sharing:
“Share about the feelings you dealt with during the relationship and share about your self-esteem during the relationship.” (The group can be encouraged to talk about the methods they used to express how they felt during an incident or an argument or a physical altercation. Some of these women were unable to express verbally how they felt. Their abuser may have seriously injured them.)

Creation:
“Now we will begin our letters. There is paper to write on, and then there’s black paper to mount the letter on, and add shapes, colors and words around it. Notice any feelings, words, or thoughts that come to your mind when you are writing your letter. These words or thoughts can surround your letter in any fashion. You can use a gel pen, white-out pen, glitter and glue stick. Write the words with glue and shake the glitter on the glue.”

Closing:
Save time to allow each woman to share her letter and how this activity made her feel. Try and get the women to express if this has empowered them in any way.
Row.txt_description: This letter-writing workshop was designed to help the participants officially put closure on their abusive relationship after leaving by expressing how they they felt about their abuser and how the abuse made them feel.

Row.str_author_location: Children’s Liaison, Haven House, Pasadena, CA
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To support children to notice things that they are proud of about themselves, and create a tangible reminder of their pride that they can wear and enjoy.

  

 This Pride Medallion says,
“I’m proud I know how to play basketball.”
  
Materials:
Shrinky Dink rough and ready type pre-cut circles or (4x4 squares)
Color pencils
Hole punchers
Ribbon / yarn
Toaster oven
Scissors
Pencils sharpener
Small paper plates (to collect pencil shavings)
Circle shape / stencil different sizes (plates, cups, etc. ranging in diameter from 3” to 4”. Note: anything smaller than 3” will be difficult to read or see due to shrinkage of the material when it cooks.)
Paper to cover tables

Timeframe:
Time frame: 1 - 1 1/4 hours

Age Range:
3 yrs. and up.
  

 
Pride Medallion table in action.

  
Set-up:
Younger children (under age 5) may have difficulty cutting on their own medallion circles, so depending on the age levels in your group, you will probably need to pre-cut circles. Cut them into circles varying in size from 3” to 4” in diameter. Older children will probably be able to trace and cut their own circles from 4”X4” squares of Shrinky Dinks (some may still need assistance.) Cover tables with butcher/newspaper. Set out the materials: color pencils, sharpeners, small plates (for pencils shavings) pre-cut circles and/or 4x4 squares for children to trace and cut.

Introduction:
You could begin by asking if anyone knows what a medallion is. You can use the Olympic Gold, Silver and Bronze Medals for the winning athletes, or the Medal of Honor for heroic deeds as examples.

Have the children imagine how it would feel to be awarded such a medal for something they have accomplished. Talk about different types of feelings we all have. Has anyone ever felt happy about something they did for themselves or someone else? If so, what was it? Have they ever felt excited about something they have done at home or school? Are they kind to others? Did they ever help another person? Did they want to help that person? If so what did they do? Did they show a new person around? Did they pick up after themselves and feel really good about it?

Explain that today they are going to make their very own medallions to honor themselves. They will be able to decorate their medallions with colors and symbols and then thread them with ribbons to wear around their neck to represent their pride in their accomplishments.

  

 Pride Medallions, after cooking.
They are ready to wear!
  
Creation:
Encourage the children as they begin work on their own medallions. Encourage the younger children to select their circle. Have the older children trace their circles. Next, they can trim the circles with scissors and begin to decorate using colored pencils and markers.
Be sure to hole punch for ribbons before baking the Shrinky Dink material.

Bake Shrinky Dink in the toaster oven at 300 degrees for about 30 seconds to 1 minute until Shrinky Dink has completely flattened.

Remove immediately to avoid scorching or bubbling. Allow medallions to cool about 1 minute before letting children handle.

String medallions with ribbons or yarn cut to approximately 28” long. Knot the ends and they are ready to wear.

There is plenty of time and material for each child to make more than one medallion.
  

This Pride Medallion reads,“I am proud to have a family.”
This picture was taken before cooking the medallion.
 
  

Closing:
Once you have finished making and baking medallions have all the children share one at a time, at least one of their pride medallions and what it represents to them.
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps children notice things that they are proud of about themselves, by creating a tangible reminder of their pride that they can wear and enjoy.

Row.txt_code:
Ready to create Guardian Jars,
with all supplies layed out.
  
Objective:
To find a place to store fears and worries so the children can have a sense of letting them go.

Materials:
Tennis ball cans – remove outer label
White glue (such as Elmer’s)
Paint brushes
Colored Tissue Paper
Small pieces of writing paper
Pencils

Timeframe:
30 to 45 minutes

Age Range:
4 years and up (This project can be adapted to children of all ages. Younger children will need help writing down their troubles.)

Set-up:
Mix the glue with water and stir ‘til it becomes very liquidy (about 3 parts glue to 1 part water). Give each child a small bowl or cup of the mixture. Rip the tissue paper into irregular size and shapes.

Introduction:
This is a very simple activity yet it can be used in many different ways. Talk to the children about things they worry about or discuss the times they feel scared. Often when someone is troubled by worries or fears they tend to dwell on them and think about them all day long. This workshop gives the children an opportunity to write down what is bothering them and put those thoughts away in a jar for safe keeping.
  

Adding the glue.
 
  

 
Adding the tissue, piece by piece.
 
  

 
Completing the tissue.
 
  

 
Writing the worries.
 
  

Creation:
Step One:
Dip the brush in the glue solution and apply to a small area of the Tennis Ball can. (Make certain that the outer wrapper has been removed.) Once the glue is applied you can start to layer the colored tissue paper onto the can. Layer each piece with a slight overlapping of the one underneath. You can use the glue on the brush to help smooth out wrinkles. As you continue you may choose to apply the glue on top of the tissue paper as well. The color on the tissue paper should bleed and the overall affect is that of a stained glass window. The outside will be colorful; slightly shiney and you will not be able to see what is inside. Cover the entire outside of the can with the pieces of tissue paper and allow to dry. Take care not to use too much of the glue solution so the jar doesn’t take too long to dry.

Step Two:
While the container dries have the children think about the things that are on their minds and troubling them. You can help them to write their comments on the slips of paper. It can be any way they want it expressed – just a word or two may be enough. Or they may wish to write a whole story, dream or memory. After that is done fold the pieces of paper up and each child can place them in the jar. You can talk about what it feels like to release these thoughts and how they can store them away for a later date.

Older children may want to add additional problems to the jar in the days and weeks to come.

Step Three (for later):
Take the jars out after some time has passed and read about the things that once were so worrisome. (These can be read out loud or privately.) Often people find that those particular issues have passed or that they are no longer scary or troubling. It is a good experience to show that sometimes time can make a difference. Even if the issues are still present sometimes we are able to look at them differently as time passes.
  


 Completed Guardian Jars drying.
  

Closing:
Assure the children that everyone has fears and worries and that sometimes expressing them out loud or writing them down on paper can be away of letting them go.

Variations:
The Guardian Jar can be used to hold joys and happy memories and children can look inside when they are feeling sad and be reminded of happy times.
You can also use these containers for children to write something positive either about themselves or about each of the other children in the group, or the other members of their family. Now each child will have their own jar filled with positive messages.

Special Thanks:
AWBW sends special thanks to Laura Slakey of Haven Hills, who shared the idea of making Guardian Jars at a 2002 training, and to Elda Unger, of Free Arts for Abused Children, who gave AWBW hundreds of tennis ball cans in 2004 and shared the similar project called “Worry Jars.”
Row.txt_description: This workshop was created to give the participant a place to store fears and worries so he or she can have a sense of letting them go.
Row.txt_tips: Depending on how many jars and much time is available, kids could make a positive dream or wish jar in addition to their guardian jars.

Row.str_author_location: Children’s Windows Liaison, Haven House, Pasadena, CA
Row.txt_code:
The Very Hungry Caterpillar, The Butterfly Kiss, and
The Caterpillar & the Tadpole are wonderful for focusing
on transformational changing and growth.

  
  
  
  
  
About this Workshop:
AWBW leader Melissa Falco facilitated a wonderful workshop at AWBW’s Venice studio, introducing her favorite projects for working with pre-school aged children. She shared how central reading and movement warm-ups are to her work with young children. In this workshop, we share her favorite story books and CDs, as well as how she integrates them into her art group.

To see Melissa’s three favorite workshops for young children check out Roller Derby Painting, Bugs and 'Mud' Workshops for Toddlers.

About Working with Young Ones:
I have worked with children at Haven House since 1989, and it has been the most rewarding work that I could have chosen for myself. I have also worked in the pre-school setting which was a great joy and extremely rewarding. Children are my favorite population to work with and I have applied a lot of my creative ideas from this period of my life to the art workshops. The children are open to learning new things and even when they’re unhappy and not quite ready to play, they still respond to my silliness, let loose and begin to enjoy just being kids. In watching them during Windows time, I have come to learn that the simple act of being a child is just a vague memory for some of the children---and for others, not a memory at all.

My own personal process in having a successful Windows Workshop is to take the time before I start the workshop to ask myself key questions:
— “What do the children want or need from me today?”
— “What kind of day are the children having?”
— “Do they want or need extra attention, maybe starting with a big hug?
— “Do I need to be a good listener?
— “Do they need an affirmation of their self-worth?

I never approach the workshop with the question
— “What do I want from them”?

The children trust me and know that the time they will spend in the workshop will be enjoyable. They will have the freedom to express themselves as kids and enjoy who they are and, more importantly, they know that it is a “safe place.” This becomes obvious when I occasionally see the children between the workshops and see their excitement and anticipation for the next workshop.

In every workshop, I start by getting on the floor with the children (which happens to be my favorite position). Just by physically lowering myself to the children’s level helps me in setting the tone for them to begin to relax and begin to rid themselves of any outside pressures and stress.

Here are some of the ways I have incorporated what I have learned from my Windows training, and some of my own ideas on Warm-ups.
  
 

 

Reading Warm-ups:
Reading is one of key missing components in the children who live at the shelter. It doesn’t matter if they are too young to read or are able to read by themselves. Reading is a vital part of childhood development and they just don’t get enough, generally due to living in a household in constant crisis. I have found that reading is a very powerful tool in helping the children to calm down and focus. It is also a great stress-reliever, especially when the story has a message pertaining to real-life issues. Further, reading to the children helps to increase the bond you will quickly establish with them.

The book titles I have listed are some of my favorites. I put them in categories to help you choose a book to match the mood of the children. Many of our children are exposed to terrible situations that are beyond their understanding. By reading and discussing stories about different point of views and cultures or familiar issues and concerns, they find a certain sense of relief and understanding. Reading is a valuable tool in getting their imaginative juices flowing and helps in opening up on some deeper anxieties. By taking the time to read slowly, showing the illustrations (also very important in choosing new books), I engage them in the story. I endeavor to make it inter-active by asking what they think of the pictures or story line and then listen to them. I always value their involvement in our reading time.

If the children seem to particularly enjoy the reading, you may want to have a couple of books handy to prolong the warm-ups at their request. Stories should be engaging, enriching and have a message. Imagination picture books are best for children between 3 – 8 years old. Board books and hard covers work well for toddlers. I have listed below a few book titles in connection with certain projects, themes, and messages. Very importantly, these are only my suggestions and you may have your own favorites. So, please feel free to choose a book based on what you think would most benefit your particular children’s group.
  


Tough Boris, Owl Babies, and Mama, Do You Love Me?, are
great for exploring separation anxieties and feelings.
 
  

 
Amazing Grace, William’s Doll, and Happy to be Nappy are
wonderful for dealing with stereotypes.
 
  

 
Caps for Sale and The Hat are great
project books for Hat Workshops.
 
  
  

Reading List:
Transformational Changing and Growth Titles:
—Butterfly Kiss, Marcial Boo (Author), Tim Vyner (Illustrator)
—The Very Hungry Caterpillar, Eric Carle
(Great story to go with “Water Color Journey Butterflies”)
—The Caterpillar & the Tadpole, Jack Kent

Separation Anxieties & Feelings:
—Owl Babies, Martin Waddell, Patrick Benson
—Mama, Do You Love Me?, Barbara M. Joosse
—Tough Boris, Mem Fox

Dealing With Stereotypes:
—William’s Doll, Charlotte Zolotow
—Happy to be Nappy, Bell Hooks
—Amazing Grace, Mary Hoffman

Enhancing Self-Esteem:
—I Like Me, Nancy Carlson
—Chicka, Chicka, Boom Boom, A,B,C (Fun Book), John Archambault
—Yoko, Rosemary Wells

Divorce:
Whenever children question a divorce with their parents, this is an excellent book to share:
—Dinosaurs Divorce, Laurene Kransy Brown, Mark Brown

Project books for Hat Workshops:
—Caps for Sale, Esphyr Slobodkina
—The Hat, Jan Brett

Dance Warm-ups:
Music is therapy in itself. How many times have we heard a song playing and start to move and sway or sing along to the music? It makes you feel lighter and happier. As an example, at my son’s school, they play music up and down the halls over the intercoms in the morning. It starts the day with a little pep and a sort of “Good Morning” to the kids and it works. The kids start walking a little faster, and become more animated. While I still use some soft music for the workshops as they are in progress, I love to utilize some terrific energizing children’s music for warm-ups. Depending on the mood of the children, I may combine Reading Warm-ups with Dance Warm-ups.

In Dance Warm-ups, I cannot stress enough how gratifying it is for me to watch the children open up and bloom like flowers, becoming joyful just by being able to jump up and down, wave their arms and legs, and use their energies in dancing and singing, often pretending to be animals with noisy sounds. In my experience, spending 5 - 10 minutes dancing and singing has a calming effect, not a nervous effect, on the children. I have listed below some of my favorite children’s music as well as different cultural music. These varied choices are invaluable in opening up the world of music for the children and teaching them respect for people’s diversity.
  
 

Getting to Know Myself, by Hap Palmer.
  
 
 We All Live Together, by Greg and Steve.
  
 
 Big Fun, by Greg and Steve.
  
 
 Samples of multi-cultural music from Putumayo:  Mexico, African Playground, and World Playground.
  

Dance & Music List:
Interactive and Background music:
—Getting to Know Myself, by Hap Palmer (Feelings music)
—Dream Land, by Putumayo (Relaxing music)
—Chant, Religious chanting very soothing for nap time

Dance and Warm-up music:
—Big Fun, by Greg and Steve (Loud dance music for warm-up)
—We All Live Together Vol 1,
by Greg & Steve (Great movement music with good morning song for A.M. workshops)
—The Amazing Adventures of Kid Astro (Fun, fast CD)
—The Kids Yoga Deck, by Annie Buckley (Yoga is wonderful for stretching warm-up)

Multi-Cultural Music:
Putumayo is the music publisher under the title “World’s Playground.” Types of music you might look for are:
—Mexico
—African
—Armenian
—Russian
—Celtic
—Cuban
—Irish/Scottish
—Australian
—Island Music
—Native American
—Reggae
—Any other multicultural music appropriate for young children

Popular Artists:
—Carole King
—Hap Palmer
—Ella Jenkins
—Raffi
—Greg & Steve

While, I have so many other ideas that I can go on and on, but these will surely make a difference with the children. Remember, just have fun and be a KID!

I’m looking forward to sharing some of my favorite Children’s Workshops in the next few months ahead.
Row.txt_description: This is an introduction to the use of story, music and dance as warm-ups for the Windows groups with children ages 3-8. Reading is used to help calm and focus the children. Stories are used as a catalyst for discussions. Dance is used as a stress reliever and has a calming effect for the kids.

Row.txt_code:
Windows participant models her new hat.
  
 
 “I feel like a cool dude in my best hat!”
Objective:
Encourage young children to celebrate themselves by exploring the world of hats and their many meanings and uses. Explain that each hat has its own special purpose. Encourage the children to imagine and create their own special hat that reflects who they are and what makes them special.

Materials:
Newspaper
Masking tape
Acrylic paints (dries faster)
Markers
Crayons
Brushes
Hair dryer (aide for drying the wet paint)
Pipe cleaners
Collage materials (glitter, gems, ribbons, feathers, etc.)
Tacky Glue
Stapler (to fasten loose edges at the rim of the hat) for leader only
Pictures or cut-outs of different hats

Timeframe:
1 hour - 1 1/2 depending on the size of the group and their ages

Age Range:
Children 3 yrs. old and up
This activity requires some assistants if the group is larger than 4 children.

Set-up/Prep:
Create a sample hat in advance. Cover the tabletops and have everything in the center of each table. Position an area for the newspaper, unfold the full sheets and stack them at the end of each table. Place masking tape next to the newspaper. You may need an assistant for each table where children will be working. No more than 4 children per table.
  


Windows group decorating their hats. 
  
  

Introduction:
“Today you are going to create your own special hat, a special hat just for you to wear. Your hat needs to be special just like each one of you. Your hat can be a fun hat or a silly hat, a work hat or a serious hat. When you are done creating your special hat we will show them off for everyone to see just how special they really are.”
(You may want to display real hats or cut-outs showing different types of hats along with your sample: cowboy, derby, bonnet, athletes, rescue personnel etc.)

Warm up/ Opening Circle:
Have the children close their eyes and imagine what their hat will look like? What shape will it have? How about the color? Will their hat be big or will it be small? Once you have asked the children these questions, have them open up their eyes and one by one share one of their feelings about their very special hat that they will wear. It may be nice to photograph the children (with permission) wearing their special hat at the end of the group.
  
 

Step 1: Putting newspaper on the head.
  
 
 Step 2: Circling with a band of tape.
  
 
 Step 2: Ready for rolling the brim.
  
 
 
Step 3: Rolling the brim.
  
 
 Step 4: Decorating!
  

Creation:

Now it's time for the children to create their special hat. Have the
children line up with the assistant at their table. (There should be no
more than 4 children to each table).

Step 1: Preparing the Newspaper: Layer 3 sheets of newspaper before placing it on the top of the child's head. You want to rotate the corners so the top and bottom piece are exactly the same. The middle sheet should be the only one shifted with the corners hanging out. Explain to the child that their face will be covered for only a few moments; if the child is uncomfortable you may ask them if it is ok to ask another child to assist them with this part. Once you have their permission to cover their head, place the 3 layers of newspaper on top of their head.

Step 2: Masking Tape: Holding the newspaper down with your hand, use the other hand and begin to roll the tape around outside of the newspaper in the center of the forehead area, do this about 3-4 times to create the inside dome for the hat to sit comfortably. Once you have completed this step remove the paper from the child's head have them return to their seats.

Step 3: Rolling the Brim: You will instruct the children to then begin to roll the ends of the newspaper creating a brim. When the children have finished rolling the brim the leader may have to go around and staple any loose ends that won't stay put. Once this is complete the children are ready to decorate their hats.

Step 4: Decorating: Have the children use glue and paint only on the outside of the hat. If the children are painting you may want to have a hair dryer handy to speed up the process. For really small children you may want to use markers or crayons to cover the outside of the hat. You can have the children color the top sheet of newspaper before you place it on their heads and tape around their forehead. This process takes less time and is great for really young children who just want to color.

Closing:
Have the children share with each other their special hat. It may even be nice to parade the children in a circle with music and let them celebrate being special and unique.
You may want to play some cheerful dancing music for the end parade.
Row.txt_description: This workshop encourages young children to create their own special hat that reflects who they are and what makes them special.
Row.txt_tips:
Have a lot of help for young children. Have kids lie down and think about why they are special and what makes them different from everybody else. Why are they loved?

Have students make hat that reflect who they are.

It may be helpful to bring in a variety of different hats for the children to try on or bring a book about hats to read to the kids.

Row.str_author_location: Women’s Window Liaison at Laurel House, PA
Row.txt_code:
Sample from “Funeral of ‘I Cant’s.”

  
About this Workshop:
This workshop is the fourth in the “Creative Scrapbook” series created by Carolyn Coleman Manns of Laurel House in Pennsylvania. Through this series, Carolyn powerfully links creative expression to the shelter’s basic DV curriculum.

Objective:
To help each woman realize how much strength it took to leave her abuser and come into the shelter. To affirm that she took the power with her when she left. To say “goodbye” to her “I Cant’s” — the fears she faces as she thinks about building a new life (I can’t drive, I can’t get a job, I can’t find a place to live, etc.)
  
 

“I can’t live without him... I can’t leave him. I can’t make it on my own... No more abuse!”
  

Materials:
Paper Shredding Machine (Some shred into confetti, some into strips. Check to see what kind you have. Either works for this workshop - they just look different.)
Off-colored writing paper (Beige, grey, off-white)
Construction paper (assorted colors)
Scissors
Glue sticks
Glitter or glitter paint
Bright paints and brushes
Markers
Popsicle sticks (Optional)
Music

Timeframe: 2 hrs
Intro & Writing: 30 min
Sharing & Shredding: 30 min
Creation: 45 min
Sharing: 15 min

Introduction:
“Today we are going to discuss the fears of leaving, and anything you felt you could not accomplish before entering the shelter and in your 1st few days in the shelter. This project is called ‘The Funeral of the “I Cant’s” (It’s useful to have samples to share, so they can see what will happen with the shredded “I Cant’s.”) Is there anything you felt afraid of or felt that you couldn’t do? Can anyone think of any “I Cant’s” she felt when she arrived here? We’re going to start out today be writing them all down.” (Each woman writes down on a piece of paper her list of the “I Cant’s.”)
  

 
“Rest Peacefully I Cant’s.”

  
  

Sharing & Shredding:
Each woman one by one shares her list. One by one, each woman shreds her “I Cant’s” and saves the shredded paper.

Creation:
Each person chooses a piece of construction paper, markers, paint, glue, glitter, and paint brushes. Encourage each woman to think about how she wants to bury her “I Cant’s.” Is there any style of burial that suits her religion or preferences? Support each participants to bury her “I Cant’s” according to her choice. Creativity is the key.

Closing:
Allow each woman to discuss how she felt burying her “I Cant’s,” and to share why she chose the method of burial she chose.

Workshop Variations
Funeral for My Past
Lupe Diaz and Jesucita Zuniga, from WomenShelter of Long Beach, changed the "I Cant's" to "My Past" to allow participants to choose what, from thier past, they're ready to let go of.
Row.txt_description: This workshop was designed to help each woman realize how much strength it took to leave her abuser and come into the shelter.

Row.str_author_location: Women’s Window Liaison at Laurel House, PA
Row.txt_code:
Mask of Abuse
About this Workshop:
This workshop is the fourth in the “Creative Scrapbook” series created by Carolyn Coleman Manns of Laurel House in Pennsylvania. Through this series, Carolyn powerfully links creative expression to the shelter’s basic DV curriculum.

Objective:
To help participants realize the power they have and identify their strengths and ability to survive in a difficult situation by identifying and creating the masks they wore to survive. To encourage them to use their power and strength in starting over, and living a free and non-violent life-style.

                                                                               






Mask of Abuse





Materials:
Paper plates
Markers
Paint
Glitter
Ribbon
Buttons
Glue
Felt pieces
Yarn
Hot glue gun
Paint brushes
Music





Timeframe:

                                                                   Sample mask


Total Time: 2 1/2 hours
Introduction: 15 min
Opening and Sharing: 30 min
Creation: 75 min
Closing: 30 min

Introduction:
“This workshop will be a chance to notice the masks you wore to survive during your abusive relationship. You survived an extremely difficult situation, and the masks you wore demonstrate your strengths and ability to survive. You get to notice these masks, explore them, and decide whether or not your old masks can have a positive role in starting over.”

Opening and Sharing:
Encourage each group member one by one to discuss the masks they wore during their abusive relationship. You can encourage the individuals to discuss why that particular mask was used, and how it helped them to survive. You can ask each woman, “How many masks did you wear, and how did each mask play a part in your survival?”

Creation:
The actual masks will be created on paper plates. Share examples of masks of previous group members to help your group envision their masks. Encourage each to remember an event that she would like to share with the group, and the mask that was worn during the incident. Ask them to take a few minutes to think of the mask they would like to share with the group. Each person chooses the materials she wants to use. Once they begin creating, put music on that is soothing.


































































Mask of Abuse (outside)

   












































Mask of Abuse (inside)
































If the women in your group have talked about many masks that they wear, encourage them to focus on one mask to create today.

Closing:
Each person shares her mask and her feelings about the incident. They are each encouraged to process how they felt during the activity. They are also asked, “Can this mask play a positive role in starting over or is this a mask that will be placed in their memory bank as a part of their domestic violence survival and struggle?” Support them as they consider whether this mask might play a part in a positive manner and situation, during their transition of starting over.
Row.txt_description: This workshop was created to help participants realize the power they have and identify their ability to make it in a difficult situation by identifing and creating the masks they wore to survive.

Row.txt_code:
This workshop is based on a Chippewa Tribe tradition.

Objective:
To allow children to feel more in control so that they can feel more secure and safer at bedtime. To help children cope with bad dreams and to feel less afraid about going to sleep.

Materials:
Paper or foam plates (or foam core cut into circles)
Yarn
Beads
Feathers
Markers
Stickers, glitter
Glue
Masking tape
Hole punch

Time Frame:
20 minutes: opening circle
30 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children

Opening Circle:
Gather the children in a circle and do the Energizing Breath. Before discussing dreams, have the children close their eyes (if they feel comfortable closing them) and pretend they are asleep, only they are awake (just like at night when they try to fool their mommies into thinking they are asleep). Tell them: "When we are dreaming, we are acting as if we are awake, but we are really asleep. Sometimes we remember these stories in the morning when we wake up."

Give children the opportunity to talk about some good and bad dreams. Discuss how all children have bad dreams sometimes, but often we will have bad dreams when something has happened during the day or evening which did not make us feel safe. Let children know that often they will remember more bad dreams when they come to the shelter.

Activity:
Introduce the dream catchers to the children. Tell them that it is a tradition on the Native American tribe, the Chippewa, to help catch bad dreams. The good dreams float through the web and the bad dreams get tangled up in the web. Children are to hang their dream catchers over their beds.

How to make a dream catcher:
1. Draw a large ring inside the rim of a paper plate (or cut out a circle with a hole in it using the foam core).
2. Cut out the center of the plate to the edge of the ring. You can also trim the outside rim to leave a neat edge.
3. Punch holes around the ring.
4. Wrap masking tape around one end of the yarn (about 12" long). Use this edge to poke the yarn through the top hole and pull through, leaving about 3" at the end. Using masking tape allows the child to thread without having to use a needle.
5. Create a web by criss-crossing the yarn through the holes around the plate. Leave the center of the web open.
6. Bring the taped end of the yarn back to the top hole and tie it to the other end.
7. Decorate around the rim with markers, glitter and glue, if desired.
8. Cut a piece of yarn about 8" long. Loop it through the bottom hole so that the yarn is double. Thread several beads up the yarn and slip a feather into the beads. Knot the doubled yarn to fasten the beads and feather.

Closing Circle:
Gather the children in a circle to talk about the making of the dream catcher and to show their dream catcher to the group if they choose to do so. Explain to the children that they hang the dream catcher above the bed and that it is there to help them feel safe while they sleep and to protect them from bad dreams. Discuss with the children the importance of talking about their dreams to their mothers or to an adult whom they trust.

Note:
If art therapy or counseling is available in the shelter, it can be useful for the children to draw their dreams in the therapy sessions.

Variations for age levels:
Older children can thread more beads into the “web” and punch more holes along the sides to hang feathers. A more sophisticated dream catcher is to use a wooden frame with hide and gut for the web (see picture).
Row.txt_description: This workshop allows children to feel more in control so that they can feel more secure and safer at bedtime. It also helps children cope with bad dreams and feel less afraid about going to sleep.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 45
Row.txt_tips:
Use the CD "Wind Spirit".

Kids might be very interested in Native American crafts and want to do medicine pouches, shields, arrows, etc...

It's a good idea to prepare the materials in advance so there's more than one of each colored yarn for each child.

Younger kids may need one-on-one assistance with this project, especially with the beads and the string.

If done in a counseling session, this workshop gives kids an opportunity to talk about and share the dreams they've had, and no longer be afraid if the dreams they've had are scary.

Be sure to have an example ready so that the children understand the finished project.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To allow children to create a figure that expresses how they are feeling in the present moment.

Materials:
Pliable wire or chenille stems
Wood scraps
Cloth (different colors and textures)
Beads
String
Glue gun
Markers

Time Frame:
10 minutes: opening circle
40 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 older children; 1 adult for 1 or 2 younger children

Space Set-up:
A quiet, spacious area to do the opening circle is needed and enough tables for the participants to spread out their supplies. All materials should be laid out in the middle of each table prior to the beginning of the group.

Opening Circle:
Begin with the Get Off My Back exercise.

Activity:
Using the various materials, each participant creates a figure representing how he or she feels right now. Examples can be figures expressing feeling free, caged, scared, etc. This activity can be broken up into several workshops to create how the child felt in the past, feels in the present, and would like to feel in the future.

Closing Circle:
Allow participants time to share their creations, thoughts, and feelings. Discuss the different feelings and ways that each child can support other children to get to where he or she would like to be. When children openly support and console one another, remark on the importance of such caring acts.

Variations for age levels:
Be sure not to use potentially dangerous materials with younger children (i.e., wire may poke them, beads may be swallowed). With younger children, it may be more appropriate to use chenille stem with pieces of cloth that can denote different feelings through color and texture. Do not have small pieces available as they might fall off and young children can choke on small things.
Row.txt_description: This workshop allows children to create a figure that expresses how they are feeing in the present moment.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 51

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To help strengthen the child's sense of self. Children relate to animals, and this workshop is a good way for them to gain a sense of power and identity through an animal.

Materials:
Paper
Markers
Magazine cutouts of animals
Playdough
Construction paper

Time Frame:
15 minutes: opening circle
25 minutes: activity
15 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 younger children; 1 adult for 5 older children

Space Set-up:
Arrange markers, playdough, and construction paper on tables, setting up work stations. Have a box of cut-out images of animals on hand for younger children.

Opening Circle:
Begin with the Monkey and Butterfly Breaths. Then have everyone sit in a circle. Explain that you are going to ask them to close their eyes (this is optional - let them know they can do it if they feel comfortable doing it) and imagine they are in an open field and that they are very safe. At the edge of the field there are some trees and bushes. As they look over to the bushes an animal comes out. This animal is very special to them, it looks after them and keeps them safe. Imagine that the animal can talk to them: What is the animal wanting to say to them? Does it have a special message? Ask them to open their eyes. Go around the circle and ask each child if he/she saw an animal. If a child did not see the animal, then he or she can choose an animal.

Activity:
After everyone has shared, they can go over to the activity table and either draw an animal or make one out of playdough and mount it on construction paper. They can also see if there is a cutout of their animal, which they can paste on a piece of paper. Children are to write a little story about their animal, how it can help them, and the special qualities that animal has.

Variations for age levels:
Younger children will need help with the writing and will need special attention to help them articulate the qualities of their animal and how it can help them. Having a box of cut-out images of animals can help them to visualize their animal.

Closing Circle:
Everyone has the opportunity to share the animal and how it has been a helper or can be a helper from now on. Children may want to act out their animal, so make floor space for the enactment.
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps strengthen the child’s sense of self. Children relate to animals, and this workshop is a good way for them to gain a sense of power and identity through an animal.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 55
Row.txt_tips:
You could also use paint in this workshop.

It could be fun to have kids dance or act out their animals.

For younger kids, it may be helpful to have various animal-shaped cookie cutters to help shape the Playdough.

Having a book or posters of animals in nature can really help kids visualize their animals.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To encourage introspection, communication, and self-expression with others.

Age Range:
This workshop is intended for children who are old enough to write.

Materials:
Ruled writing pads for each person
Pens or pencils for each person
6 to 10 small household objects (apple, magnet, knife, leaf, light bulb, tools, semi-precious stones, pine cones, glasses, teddy bear, doll, angel, action figure, etc.)
A timer or watch

Space Set-up:
Place a variety of objects on the center of a table with the writing supplies at hand.

Opening Circle:
Ask each person to identify with or choose something he or she likes. Ask each person to hold that item.

If two children fix on the same object, ask if one child will choose the object for the next round or have them hold the object together.

For a warm-up, try deep breathing relaxation exercises. You might use the Butterfly Breath.

Activity:
From the Butterfly Breath, facilitator leads a visualization: “Close your eyes and think about the qualities of this object (hard, soft, dull, sharp, warm, cold.) How could you be like this object? Or unlike this object?”

After a few minutes, ask them to open their eyes and write the question: "How am I like the ....." (object) for about five minutes. On the same sheet ask "How am I not like the ...?" At least 20 minutes should be allowed for journaling.

Closing Circle:
Invite each person to read their list and share what they got out of relating themselves to the object. Most will want to do this. However, sharing should always be optional.

Variations:
On another piece of paper, ask each person to choose another object, one he or she has not chosen before. Have them write their name and the object on their paper. Then the papers will be passed around to each other person in the group with the goal being to write down how this person is like or unlike the object they chose. When the papers get around the table and back to the owners, have them read them silently or they may choose one item to share. Or if time allows, they may read them all aloud.
Row.txt_description: This workshop encourages introspection, communication, and self-expression with others
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 57

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To help children identify and express different feelings. To help children become aware of how important feelings are and how empowering they can be.

Materials:
Poster board, paper or felt (to make the hat)
Markers or paints
Glitter
Feathers
Stickers
Stars for decoration
Cutouts from magazines
Yarn
Glue (optional)
Hole punch and stapler
Polaroid Camera and film (optional)

Time Frame:
10 minutes: opening circle
10 minutes: discussion
40 - 60 minutes: activity
If hats are done sooner, allow 20 minutes for children to roleplay their emotion hats.
If you do a full costume party with dress-up and face makeup, allow another hour or arrange for another day.

Optional: Photograph them using a polaroid and they can take the polaroid picture away with them.


Ratio:
1 adult for 3 older children; 1 adult for 2 younger children

Space Set-up:
Arrange the different materials on a counter and set up work stations.

Opening Circle:
Begin with the Wiggle Down exercise.

Activity:
Children discuss how faces look according to different feelings; they can draw these different faces on the chalkboard or on a flip chart. If the children find this too difficult, you may prompt them or draw the different feeling faces yourself.

Each child decides on a particular feeling for the hat. Adults will need to help each child measure the head size to determine how large to cut the hat. Hats may be of the chef type or crowns or bishop's hats, depending on the materials used. Encourage them to use their imagination, bearing in mind the materials you have on hand.

Once a child has had a hat measured and cut out, he/she will stitch it together, glue it or use staples to staple it together. Younger children will need this part of the activity done for them for safety and practical reasons.

Each child then works on his or her hat, decorating it to describe the “emotion” of the hat. Help children think about colors as related to emotion, as well as shapes, words or pictures.

Children put on the hats and verbalize or show by actions their feelings. You can also do face makeup as well as dress-up and have an impromptu costume party.
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps children identify and express different feelings. It helps children become aware of how important feelings are and how empowering they can be.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 61
Row.txt_tips:
It may be easier to do this activity in two groups because it can get a little chaotic and loud.

It can be helpful to have the hats already cut out before the workshop begins.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide a tangible outlet where participants can express their feelings of grief and vulnerability. To acknowledge the gains of leaving the violence and their hopes for the future. To help facilitate the grieving process and provide some control over their environment and their emotions.

Materials:
Butcher paper (for group scroll)
Large sheets of paper (for individual scrolls)
Markers
Pens

Time Frame:
10 minutes: opening circle
40 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children

Space Set-up:
You will need a large, blank wall to hang two group scrolls or enough table space for the individual scrolls. Put markers and pens in the middle so that all participants can share the materials. You will also need pieces of rug or cushions that the children can sit on while participating in the circle.

Opening Circle:
Begin with Get Off My Back exercise. Then, have everyone sit down in a circle to discuss issues of grief and loss. It will be important to normalize the feelings of sadness, anger or resentment that children may feel. Ask the children to discuss things they miss from home and reasons they are glad they have left the violent environment. Explain the purpose of the scroll and how this workshop is an opportunity for them to express some of their grief and their hopes for a better future. The scroll can also be a way for them to say their good-byes.

Activity:
Once the children are ready to write, have them move to the table or to the wall and begin writing their messages. Allow them to write as many things as they would like. In the meantime, have leaders in the nearby areas to talk to children who are having a lot of emotions come up. The children may need support when doing this activity due to the nature of dealing with sadness and anger.

Closing Circle:
Gather around in a circle so children can share what it felt like to write about the things they miss and the things they are looking forward to. Discuss the healing process and various ways that are appropriate ways of expressing grief.

Variations for age levels:
This workshop works best with children who can write. With children who are unable to write, this activity can occur with them drawing pictures or having leaders write what they would like to say. This can be a very powerful workshop with children of all ages and can create a forum to discuss what they want for their futures.
Row.txt_description: This workshop provides a tangible outlet where participants can express their feelings of grief and vulnerability while acknowledging the gains of leaving the violence and their hopes for the future. To help facilitate the grieving process and provide some control over their environment and their emotions.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 63

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give children an opportunity to express some of the rage they feel toward the batterer in a safe environment and to overcome the feelings of guilt and self-blame.

Materials:
Blank paper
Toilet paper
Crayons
Markers
Pens

Time Frame:
10 minutes: opening circle
40 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children

Space Set-up:
Have a quiet place where the children can sit comfortably on cushions or pieces of carpet, and table space for the writing part of the activity.

Have all the materials set up on the table before the group begins so that there is no distraction. If possible, space the chairs around the table so that each child can have privacy while writing his or her personal thoughts and feelings.

Opening Circle:
Play soothing music in the background and have the children do deep breathing exercises from the Breathwork section of the Children's Manual.

Guide them in focusing on their feelings now and how they felt being in the home with the batterer. Have the participants think about the things they would have liked to say to the batterer but were afraid to voice.

Some children may become very anxious or agitated with the memories. Be watchful throughout this workshop to help children process the feelings that come up.

Activity:
Once the children are ready to write, have them move to the table. On sheets of toilet paper, allow the children to write down hurtful things that were said to them and the things they would have liked to say. Begin the exercise with, “I didn’t like it when...” Be sure to tell the participants that they do not have to share these messages with anyone.

When they have finished writing, allow them to crumple up and throw away the sheets of hurtful words. They may choose to flush these messages out of their lives (the whole group may literally stand around the toilet to flush away all of the hurtful messages together). If they would like, the children can keep the sheets of what they would have liked to say, maybe to store in their treasure boxes. This can be very empowering to be able to verbalize the hurt and anger. State that this is a time when he or she can let go of the anger that goes along with the message if he or she is ready. Allow participants to share their feelings and/or messages with the group if they would like.

Closing Circle:
During the last 10 minutes, allow participants to discuss how they felt. Was the activity empowering or did it make them feel powerless? Discuss alternative methods to letting go of anger in safe ways where they do not hurt themselves or others. Discuss how everyone has the right to be safe and to live a life without fear.

Have participants stand in a circle holding hands. They can take turns saying: “I deserve to be safe.” Then the person talking should squeeze the next person’s hand to let him or her know it is his or her turn. Young children really enjoy this closing activity.

Variations for age levels:
With young children who may have difficulty working with paper, have them work with clay. Discuss what makes them angry, especially when Mom and her partner are fighting. Allow the children to pound on the clay and state that they can use their anger to be creative and make something.

Toward the end of the workshop, show the Video 10 Things to Do Instead of Hitting if your shelter has a copy (available through Sunburst Communications: 1-800-431-1934). Talk about alternatives to hitting. At a later date, the children can paint their creations.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives children an opportunity to express some of the rage they feel toward the batterer in a safe environmnet and to overcome the feelings of guilt and self-blame.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 67

Row.txt_code:
Objectives:
To offer children an opportunity to notice their inner and outer worlds. To assist children in discovering the beautiful and rewarding experience of watercolor.

Note to leaders:
With the use of watercolors, many beginners miss out on the beauty and ease of this material because they paint with the full strength of the pigment rather than using water washes. This workshop puts the focus directly on the water wash, having the children select the shape of the wash and define it on the page before adding any color. Once the water wash is in place, the rest flows easily and beautifully.

This workshop focuses on this single-wash process. It does not teach the children how to use multiple washes to render objects in a representational way. That sort of thing takes more time for the washes to dry in between and takes more training and patience than this workshop involves.

Be sure to try this process out with yourself before trying to demonstrate it for children. That way, you can make sure to keep the demonstration as brief as possible.

Time Frame:
10 minutes: opening circle
10 minutes: demonstration
30 minutes: relaxation and creation
10 minutes: closing circle

Materials:
6" x 6" watercolor paper (3 pieces per participant)
Masking tape (1 per participant)
Watercolor sets (1 per participant)
Brushes (1 medium sized brush per participant)
Cups of water (2 per participant)
Paper towels
Writing paper
Pens (1 per participant)
Tape player and relaxing music

Space Set-up:
Tape 3 pieces of paper per child down in advance (fig. 2 on page 70), especially if you are working with young children. If you have older children, they may wish to tape their paper themselves. Set up paints and brushes so that each child will have a set. Provide 2 cups of water per child (1 for rinsing the brush and 2 for getting clear water to paint with). For older children, have writing paper and pen available so they can write about their paintings (fig. 1).

Opening Circle:
Start with Wiggle Down exercise. Then ask the group: “How are we feeling today?  If you were going to be a shape, like a circle or square or triangle, what would you be today?”

Introduction:
Say to the group: "Today we’ll be painting ourselves as three shapes in water. We’ll each put a shape of water on our three papers. Then we get to add drops of color and see what emerges. It’s sort of like magic. It's fine to make a mess on the paper. It's fine to leave the paper blank. Whatever you decide to do is fine.

Your three papers can represent whatever you want them to represent. They can represent how you feel on the inside and how the world feels around you. They can represent your past, your present, and your future."

Technical Demonstration:
Tape down the 3 pieces of paper. Explain the various supplies, (fig. 1) especially the reason for the 2 cups of water (1 is to rinse the brush and 1 is a source of clear water to paint with).

To demonstrate the use of the water washes, paint a shape with pure water on all 3 papers (fig. 3). Use plenty of water so that the shape remains wet like a lake on the page.

Begin to drop color into the shapes (fig. 4). Notice how the beauty of watercolor comes from what the color does by itself as it is carried through the water. When the paint is dropped into it, the magic begins effortlessly.

Show what it's like to drop it near the edge. Show what it's like as the color spreads and runs into other colors (fig. 5).

Show what it's like to paint the area outside the shape with color, leaving a space of dry paper between the shape and the background (fig. 6).

Show what it's like if you join the 2 wet spaces. You can work the 3 papers at the same time or one at a time (fig. 7).

Creation:
Ask the children to imagine before they paint: “What shape would you be?" Once each has pictured a shape, the children can go ahead and create their shapes in water on the 3 pages and then begin to add color as they wish.

For older children as they begin to finish up, encourage them to write about their paintings. This gives them a way to process what they have experienced while the paint dries and the other children finish up.

Closing Circle:
When the children are finished, leave the papers taped down during the closing circle. This will give the water washes a chance to dry.

For the closing circle, encourage each child to share what he or she created and discovered in doing the paintings.

After the circle, the children can go ahead and take the tape off. If the paint is still wet, they may want to wait longer, or gently use a hair dryer to dry the water before taking the tape off.
Row.txt_description: This workshop offers children an opportunity to notice their inner and outer worlds. It assists children in discovering the beautiful and rewarding experience of watercolor.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 69

Row.txt_code:
Developed by Ellen Denninger, an AWBW art leader who specializes in groups for children and mothers together.

Objective:
This art workshop is designed to allow mothers and children a chance to create a very simple musical instrument with which to express and identify feelings concretely using movement and rhythm. Moving the body and making sound are two ancient techniques of human expression that can help facilitate active experiencing of feelings and sensations that may be difficult to put into words. Children instinctively express themselves with their bodies and respond to voice intonations more than word content, precisely because they are in the process of developing abstract language as a means of communication. Art-making serves as a natural bridge between our inner world of feelings and their embodiment in our behavior. Grounding expression of a wide range of feelings through physical action and sound vibration can help release blocked energy, which becomes more available for creative use in present awareness.

In working with families who have survived domestic violence, it can be very meaningful to focus on learning a feeling vocabulary. Often, family members have had to shut down their personal reactions to traumatic events. Being in the shelter is a unique opportunity of safety for them to explore stored memories that affect mind, body, and spirit. Sometimes it is usually the quiet and controlled children who will start to act out aggressively their feelings of anger and sadness once they feel comfortable in the stable environment of the shelter. The following exercise can teach mothers and children a safe and fun method to shake, move, and sound out their feelings with congruent actions.

Materials:
Cardboard paper towel rolls (1 for each participant)
Paper plates
Paint
Markers
Glitter
Paint brushes and/or sponge pieces
A variety of cloth scraps, cut into 5 x 6 inch squares
Glue
Scotch tape
Stapler
12 inch chenille stems (pipe cleaners) in a variety of colors
Dried beans or uncooked pasta shells
Old t-shirts for participants to wear over clothes
Snack provisions (because this workshop is extra long)

Time Frame:
The whole workshop will take approximately 1 1/2 to 2 hours. Allow the first hour to be devoted to the construction of the shaking instruments, giving each participant (mothers and their children) a choice of using either a paper towel roll or paper plate. If someone finishes the painting process quickly, they may want to do one of each. Before the beans/pasta are placed inside, the rolls or plates will need to sit and dry for about 15 minutes. This time can be used to clean up painting materials, wash hands, and provide a small snack of crackers and juice. The second hour will involve filling and sealing the instruments, which will then be used to express different feeling states in a guided movement circle.

Space Set-up:
I always strongly encourage families to sit together as a unit so that they can have a shared positive experience together and appreciate each other's creative process firsthand. It is good to have tables already set up with rolls, plates, and materials to decorate them (paint and glitter) when the families arrive. After the clean-up and snack break, you can then set out the cloth scraps, pipe cleaners, and beans/pasta. When construction of instruments is completed, create a common space for a movement circle. Depending on space availability and group size, this may mean pushing tables back against walls so that there is room for everyone to stand in a circle, or it may mean arranging chairs near each other and doing movements while seated. I don't recommend going outside merely because children tend to wander off and it is difficult to maintain a sense of privacy and sacred space.

Introduction:
Say to the group: "Today we are going to make a simple shaking instrument by placing beans or pasta inside a paper towel roll or folded paper plate. The first step is to choose either a roll or plate (I recommend plates for smaller children because they are much simpler) and decorate the outside with markers, paints, and glitter. This can be a messy process, so there are shirts here for those of you who want to protect your clothes. Let yourself apply any colors, shapes, or designs that pop into your head; there is no right or wrong way to do this. If you decide to use glitter, shake it on while the paint is still wet. Those of you decorating paper plates will want to fold the plate in half before beginning to decorate one or both sides. After your family has finished decorating rolls and plates, take a 15-minute break to clean up your table area, wash hands, and have a snack while the instruments dry.

For those of you making a roll, the second step will involve selecting 2 pieces of fabric and 2 pipe cleaners. Place 1 fabric piece on the end of your roll and secure it tightly by wrapping scotch tape several times around the edge of the fabric that meets the roll. Take a pipe cleaner and circle it around the layer of tape, twisting the ends together and tucking them in. Carefully put several handfuls of beans or pasta inside the open end of the roll until it is about a quarter full. Take the other piece of fabric and pipe cleaner and secure the end exactly like the first one. You are ready to shake your instrument!

For those of you making a plate, put a handful of beans or pasta inside the folded plate and carefully staple the two edges together. You will need to put a staple every 2 inches or so. Your instrument is now ready to be shaken or gently patted like a tambourine.

When everyone has completed their instruments, we will all come together in a circle and use them to create movements and sounds according to specific feelings."

Note to facilitator:
It is helpful to have examples of 2 different kinds of shaking instruments to show families while you are explaining the art workshop. The process of making them yourself will also help you to problem-solve any difficulties they may experience. Helpful hints from my own experience: too much paint makes the rolls and plates soggy, glitter must be applied while paint is still wet, stand the rolls upright when drying, and secure the fabric on the ends with a lot of scotch tape so that beans don't come flying out!

Sharing Circle:
Lead the circle by saying: "We can now use the instruments that we created to express ourselves with movement and sound. I am going to be the leader of this circle right now as we do some warm-ups, but all of you will have the opportunity to lead the circle a little bit later if you choose. The director of the circle stands in the center, like I am now, so that everyone can see what to do and stop when the director stops. Let's practice following directions and begin by shaking our instrument straight out in front of us so that everyone can see and admire what we have created. Now stop. Shake it up high and make a high sound with your voice. Now shake it down low and make a low sound. Shake it loudly and use a loud voice. Now shake it softly and make a soft sound. We can also use our bodies, our voices, and our instruments to express feelings. Let's start by doing “happy” and make happy sounds and movements with our bodies. Stop. Now let's do “sad” by making sad sounds and movements. Stop. Raise your hand if you can think of a feeling and would like to stand in the center and direct the circle."

Continue this process until everyone who raises their hand has had a chance to lead. Small children can be accompanied by their mother or an older sibling. To make sure that a wide range of feelings are covered, the facilitator may take an occasional turn in order to include the following suggested feelings: angry, excited, afraid, hopeful, confused, joyful.

Closing Circle:
To close the circle, the facilitator can lead a final goodbye movement using instruments and encourage everyone to take them home and continue expressing feelings. I find that the energy is usually so high that the circle dissolves into spontaneous dancing!
Row.txt_description: This workshop is designed by Ellen Denninger and is intended to let mothers and children create a very simple musical instrument with which to express and identify feelings concretely using movement and rhythm. Their physical action and sound vibration can help release blocked energy, which becomes more available for creative use in present awareness.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 73

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To assist children in exploring feelings about their stay in the shelter. This book is beneficial because it is something tangible that the children can take away with them about their shelter experiences. This is especially important because all children who come to the shelter have had to deal with numerous losses as explained in the Children's Manual section, "What Happens to Children When They Go to Shelters?" (page 3)

Materials:
String
Magazines
Scissors
Pictures (optional)
Paint
Markers
Crayons
Pens
Pre-printed A Book About Me booklet

The A Book About Me booklet should include a full page for each question listed in the activities below. You can create a master to photocopy and have spiral bound with a transparent plastic cover.

Time Frame:
5 minutes: opening circle
45 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children

Space Set-up:
You will need cushions or small pieces of rug to sit on during the opening circle plus tables and chairs for the activity.

Opening Circle:
The Wiggle Down exercise

Activity:
Workshop I:
Focus on the children’s feelings and experiences about entering the shelter. Have them decorate the cover page titled, “A Book About Me,” and fill in the pages titled “I came to the shelter on... with...,” “My hands were this big when I came to the shelter,” and “Things I miss from home are...”

Workshop II:
Focus on educational topics such as safety, prevention, and feelings. Possible entries can be: “Hands are not for hitting” (kids can talk about good and bad ways of using hands), “If someone touches me on a private part of my body, I can tell...,” “If scary things are happening in my family, people I can tell are...,” and “Things I like about myself are...” Focus on the positive to help raise self-esteem and on education and safety to empower the children by knowing what to do.

Workshop III:
Focus on the issue of leaving the shelter. Possible topics may include: “Things I learned from my groups are...,” “Friends I made at the shelter are...,” “When I leave the shelter, I will go...,” and a “Remembering Me” page. The “Remembering Me” activity is when each participant has a piece of construction paper that he or she chooses, writes his or her name on the page, and passes it around so that other participants can write something nice about that person or draw a picture for him or her. This last page allows the child to take something positive away that other children felt about him or her.

Closing Circle:
Allow participants to discuss feelings and to share their books. Discuss feelings of fear, grief, and loss. Have children discuss what has helped them with adjusting to new situations. This can be extremely helpful for new children at the shelter.

Variations for age levels:
If children cannot write, leaders can write for them if the children prefer. For young children, provide activities where they can draw instead of write. For older children, use a blank bound journal where the leader or the child can choose their own exercise.

Possible Journalling Exercises:
The following journalling ideas are adapted from Lucia Capacchione’s The Creative Journal for Children. You may wish to have these exercises available on 3” X 5” index cards so that older children can select their own exercise.

• Today
Draw a picture of the most special thing you remember about today. Write down your feelings about it.

• Myself
Draw a picture of yourself. It could be a picture of your appearance, or it could be abstract symbols, colors, shapes, or designs. When you are done, write a poem entitled “I Am...” (Your poem doesn’t need to rhyme.)

• My Name
Think about the letters of your name. Create your own design, logo, or symbol that uses the letters of your name and expresses who you are.

• A Letter to Me
What are all the wonderful things about you? What are the good things people have said to you? Go ahead and write a letter to yourself about all the things you like about you.

• Right Now
Draw how you feel right now. You can feel free to scribble, doodle, and choose any colors that express your state of mind. After you’re done, write about what you drew.

• It Scares Me
What scares you? Draw a picture of it. Write about what you drew.

• Very Mad
It’s okay to get mad. There are many ways to express anger without hurting anybody. See if you can fill a page with the colors representing your angry feelings. You may want to do angry scribbles, or you may want to do words or pictures.

• Can You See Through Me?
What would someone see if they could see through you, all the way inside to what you are feeling. Draw a picture of the feelings they would see.

• My Family
Who is a part of your family? Are there friends? Are there pets? Are there people younger than you? Are there people older than you? Draw a picture of yourself with your family. Include all of them.

• Hands are Not for Hitting
Trace your hand on the page. Decorate inside and around it to show all the good things you do with your hands.

• Treasure Map
Everyone has buried treasures inside of them. These are the gifts, feelings, and abilities that we have deep within us. What treasures do you have inside of you? Draw a map to the treasure. Are there things in your way? Are there any helpers?
Row.txt_description: This workshop assists children in exploring feelings about their stay in the shelter. This book is beneficial because it is something tangible that the children can take away with them about their shelter experiences. This is especially important because all children who come to the shelter have had to deal with numerous losses as explained in the manual section, “What Happens to Children When They Go to Shelters?”
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 79
Row.txt_tips: Children could also write a book about their families.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To help children feel connected to others and to help them identify and explore their significant relationships.

Materials:
Poster board
Magazines for cutout images
Glue
Scissors

Time Frame:
10 minutes: opening circle
30 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 younger children; 1 adult for 5 older children

Opening Circle:
Begin with the Birthday Candles exercise. Discuss the importance of relationships and that we are always in relationship to somebody or something. Have the group discuss their relationships, not only to people, but to animals as well. Explore the differences between family and friends. (You will need to adapt this discussion for younger children, keeping it more simple; the older the children, the more sophisticated the discussion).

Activity:
Children each take a board and find images in magazines that represent their different relationships. They are to put an image or drawing of themselves at the center of the board and place the different relationships around them with the most important closest to them and the less important further away.

Closing Circle:
Children have the opportunity to share their pictures and talk about relationships they like and relationships that have problems.

Note:
This activity can be done with young children keeping it at a more simple level; however, it is more suited to older children - seven and older - who can appreciate the differences and complexities of different relationships.
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps children feel connected to others and helps them identify and explore their significant relationships.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 83

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To help children explore relationships and express with pride their connection to others. (This can be a variation of the Relationship Collage. There is a similar set-up, including Opening and Closing Circle.)

Note:
Children love this project. They feel very creative and important making such a “professional” looking pieces of art.

Materials:
Plexiglass (pre-cut)
Backing (pre-cut)
Magazines for cutout images
Glue Sticks
Scissors
Matte Medium
Brushes
Pins for gluing on the back of Friendship Pins
E-6000 Glue to attach pins

Time Frame:
15 minutes: opening circle
30 minutes: activity
20 minutes: finishing and gluing pins
15 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult to 3 children. This activity is suitable for children ages 5 and up

Space set-up:
Set up mats on the floor or clear carpet space for an opening and closing circle. Arrange on tables the pre-cut plexiglass and backing, as well as magazines and scissors and glue. We suggest that the leader and assistants do the Matte Medium Gluing for the child since it is a bit tricky. Children under age 7 will need help with cutting out images. We recommend, due to time constraints, that diverse images of people and animals as well as evocative words are cut out beforehand so children can choose the images.

Opening Circle:
Children gather around and do the Pretend You’re a Snowman exercise, followed by a discussion of how we are connected to living things. Ask children to talk about important people and animals in their lives. Explain that they are going to make a Friendship Pin that they can wear.

Activity:
Explain to the children that they are to choose images and arrange them on the piece of cardboard and glue them. You will then brush Matte Medium on the picture so that the plexiglass will adhere to the picture. Glue the pin back to the back of the board so the Friendship Pin can be worn as a brooch.

Closing Circle:
Children gather around in a circle and show their pins (they may not be dry enough to wear). Encourage children to talk about why they chose those pictures and what these friends mean to them. Finish by talking about how important friendship is and that there is always a friend for us somewhere.
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps children explore relationships and express with pride their connection to others. (This can be a variation of the Relationship Collage. There is a similar set up, including Opening and Closing Circle).
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 85
Row.txt_tips: Have different sizes cut out and let them pick.

Row.txt_code:
Objectives:
This workshop is intended to help children build a stronger sense of self-esteem through self-image / body awareness.

Materials:
Large sheets of butcher paper (pre-cut into 3, 4, or 5 foot lengths, depending on the age group you are working with)
Scissors (a pair for each child)
Watercolor markers, pastels or crayons for each child
Band-Aids (for emotional or physical hurts)
A large space to work

Time Frame:
10 minutes: opening circle
40 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children

Space set-up:
Enough floor space for children to be comfortably spread out to do their body drawings.

Introduction to the leader:
Children who have experienced family violence and/or physical, emotional, sexual and spiritual abuse often have a strained or disconnected relationship with their bodies. As a defense against the violence, they disassociate from the physical and escape into a mental world, as an attempt to cope with pain or trauma.

Celebrating My Body is a window of time that allows the child an opportunity to reconnect to his or her body in a way that is safe and autonomous.
