This workshop is intended to stay emotionally “light.” The children may discuss some issues of abuse or violence. Please do not initiate this type of discussion. It is OK if the child shares some statements or remembrances. Just be near and listen. Any response from you should be only acknowledgment and should be limited. These issues are sensitive and deserve the focus of a therapist. You may want to have a follow-up discussion with the children's shelter therapist about any powerful or revealing statements.

It is important that children have the option not to participate. You may wish to have an alternative activity on hand.

Introduction to Art Activity:
Introduction and Wiggle Down, with each child calling out body parts. Tell the children they will be tracing their bodies and decorating them. Older children may choose partners to trace and cut out themselves.

Body tracing and cut-outs:
The children may trace each other’s bodies.  Adult help may be required for preschoolers. They can also trace their own bodies and ask for assistance when they need it. It can put them at ease to see the leader demonstrate tracing her own body.

After the bodies are traced, each child may begin to color it in to soothing, uplifting music.

Closing Circle:
Encourage each child to say, "I celebrate my body. My body is mine,'' while sharing their picture.
Row.txt_description: This workshop is intended to help children build a stronger sense of self-esteem through self-image/body-awareness.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 93

Row.txt_code:
Adapted from Lucia Capacchione’s exercise in The Creative Journal for Children: A Guide for Parents, Teachers, and Counselors

Objective:
To provide an opportunity for children to gain insight into the feelings they hide to protect themselves and the feelings they show to the public. To help children express what they are feeling as opposed to what others say they are feeling.

Materials:
Blank sheets of paper
Markers
Crayons
Pens

Time Frame:
10 minutes: opening circle
40 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children

Space Set-up:
Enough tables for the children to be comfortably spread out.

Opening Circle:
Begin with Breathe Hot, Breathe Cold exercise to help the children focus and relax.

Activity:
Explain that they will have the opportunity to draw a picture of how they think others see them and another picture of how they actually feel. If the children would like to draw several pictures of how they feel inside, allow them to do so.

Closing Circle:
Allow a forum where the children can share their drawings. Discuss how children hide certain feelings. Facilitate a discussion on how it feels to have to act one way when the child actually feels differently (i.e., acting happy when the child is actually scared). Discuss how everyone has the right to live a life free of violence and fear. This topic can also lead into a discussion as to why they came to the shelter.

Variations for age levels:
With younger children, the concept of how they actually feel on the inside may be difficult to grasp. Have the children talk or draw about how they feel and how others want them to act.
Row.txt_description: This workshop provides an opportunity for children to gain insight into the feelings they hide to protect themselves and the feelings they show to the public. This workshop helps children express what they are feeling as opposed to what others say they are feeling.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 95

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give children something tangible to take away with them -- a reminder of the friends they have made and of their time in the shelter.

Materials:
Self-hardening clay
Sculpting tools (optional)
Paint

Time Frame:
5 minutes: opening circle
45 Minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 2 children; 1 adult for 1 younger child

Space Set-up:
Enough table space for the children to be comfortably spaced apart.

Opening Circle:
The Butterfly Breath

Activity:
Hand out a good sized portion of clay which they can mold to create plaques of their own hands or include handprints of their friends. There should be enough clay to make the plaques about 1 1/2" thick, so that when they press their hands into the clay, it doesn’t become too thin or fragile. Allow the children time to paint their friendship plaques during this time if they want.

Closing Circle:
Allow participants to share their friendship plaques. Have each child share something he or she values about himself/herself or values about a friend made during the time in the shelter.

Variations for age levels:
With younger children, have the clay pre-made into plaques of the correct thickness. It will be easier for them to focus on the actual prints rather than focusing on the thickness of the clay. With older children, have them do a journalling exercise reflecting who they are, such as "A Letter to Me," or " I Am" (see page 81).
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives children something tangible to take away with them -- a reminder of the friends they have made and of their time in the shelter.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 97

Row.str_title: Let’s Make a Mess: Gloop and Slurch
Row.txt_code:
Developed by Ellen Denninger, an AWBW art leader who specializes in groups for children and mothers together.

Objective:
This art workshop, "Let's Make a Mess; Gloop and Slurch," can be a lot of fun for any family, but may be especially meaningful for families recently escaping domestic violence. I consider this art directive to be a kind of "mess therapy" in that it can help mothers and children overcome rigid controls on their behavior which were necessary in an atmosphere of constant potential danger, but now serve only to hinder self-expression. As a result, I have encountered the most initial resistance on the part of mothers when leading this workshop. However, the transformation from skeptic to enthusiastic participant can be quite astounding, and invariably, this proves to be the most popular and requested art activity in the shelter!

Mothers who had limited opportunities to be playful in their own childhoods seem to access a part of themselves that had been severely neglected. In turn, this makes them more emotionally available to their children's needs for creative art expression. Often, I end the group by handing out copies of the recipes for making these slimy substances so that families can repeat the experience at home.

This art directive is very process-oriented, with the focus being on a shared and cooperative family project. It is very important to designate the mother as the leader and decision-maker who assigns tasks and turn-taking for her children during the art process. This gives the mother an opportunity to practice exercising a powerful parental role as the new head of the family. It may be appropriate at times for the facilitator to assist her in this role by modeling how to designate tasks and ensure equal and active participation on the part of the children. This is a very exciting activity for most children, to be allowed to make a big gooey mess and get "dirty." Therefore, they can get impatient and are easily frustrated when having to wait their turn. I suggest having more than one facilitator available if conducting a multi-family group in order to provide a calming presence of structure and reassurance.

Materials:
Gloop:
4 ounce bottle of white glue, at least 2 per family so they can make more than one batch
1 1/2 cups of water
1 teaspoon of borax powder (you can find this among laundry detergents in grocery stores)
Food coloring, a box of four primary colors
Medium mixing bowl, 1 per family
Large spoon, 1 per family
Plastic 2 cup measuring containers, if possible 1 per family
Plastic teaspoon
Paper cups, for carrying gloop home

Slurch:
1 cup cornstarch
1/2 cup water
Food coloring
Mixing bowl, measuring cup, stirring spoon, 1 for each family
Paper cups, to carry slurch home

Optional:
It is always a good idea to have old t-shirts on hand for participants to protect their clothes! Also, it is fun to have small plastic animals, cars or other toys to stick into the gloop and slurch.

Time Frame:
It takes about 15-20 minutes to make gloop, and about 5 minutes to make slurch. However, families will probably want to make more than 1 batch of gloop according to how many children are in a family. You can split 1 batch in half for sharing in order to save time and materials. Allow about an hour for participants to explore and experiment with the delightful textures of the two substances. The complete workshop takes about an hour and a half.

Space Set-up:
This workshop requires that you have easy access to a sink for fetching water and washing out bowls between batches. If you conduct this group in a carpeted space, I suggest putting old sheets on the floor because gloop and slurch are easily removed from smooth surfaces but stick relentlessly to rough, porous materials like clothing or carpeting. It is impossible not to get floor, tables and self covered with oozing slimy stuff, so be prepared to make a mess!

Note to facilitator:
When you are setting up for this group, set out the bowls, spoons, and measuring materials on the tables before the families arrive. Do not set out the glue, borax, or food coloring because curious little hands will get into these before it is time to begin. I hand these materials directly to the mother in each family when it is time to use them. Also, when a family is ready to discuss what color to make their gloop or slurch, they may need some education about color mixing, i.e., yellow plus red makes orange, red plus blue makes purple, green plus blue makes turquoise, green and red makes brown, etc. Often the children want to mix all four colors, so it is important to warn them that this will create a brownish color. Also, tell the families that it isn't possible to make red; because the glue base is white, when you add red food coloring the mixture will turn pink.

Art Directive:
“Today we are going to make a stretchy, slimy material called gloop, which is similar to something called "gak" sold in stores. Your family can also make another oozing substance called slurch. I'd like you to sit together as a family because as I teach you the recipes, the mother in each family is going to give each child a turn to measure, pour, or stir. Everyone will have a chance to participate, unless you prefer not to. Mom will decide how many batches of gloop will be made, and you will talk together as a family when deciding what color to make each material. It is important to listen carefully to my directions and then wait for your mother to direct you to do a certain task. While you are waiting for a turn, it is a good idea to watch closely what other people in your family are doing. This is so that you can learn how each material is made and it will be easier to do next time.”

Making Gloop:
1. The first step is to have someone pour the 4-ounce bottle of white glue into the mixing bowl. Go ahead and take the entire cap off the glue bottle so that it pours out completely.

2. For the second step choose someone to put 1/2 cup of water into the measuring container and pour into mixing bowl with glue. Discuss as a family what color you want to make the gloop (at this time advise them about color mixing) and then have someone carefully and slowly squeeze either 10 drops of 1 color or 5 drops each of 2 colors into the bowl with glue and water. Choose someone else to stir the mixture.

3. The third step requires someone to measure 1 cup of water into the measuring container, but do not pour it into the bowl. First, choose someone to measure a teaspoon of borax powder, put it into the measuring cup of water, and stir for several minutes until the borax is mostly dissolved. (To ensure that several full minutes of mixing takes place, give each child in the family a turn to stir.)

4. The last step is to direct someone to pour the borax mixture into the mixing bowl of colored glue and stir. The gloop will immediately begin to congeal. There will be extra water in the bowl so it is necessary to scoop the gloop together with your hands and lift it out of the bowl onto the table. (The facilitator may need to do this herself because the gloop is pretty disgusting at this point.) The gloop will rapidly dry out with handling until it is a nice rubbery texture. Divide into portions for children to play with.

Suggestions for creative play with gloop:
Make handprints by pressing palm down, poke holes with fingers, 2 people can tug until it breaks, have dripping contests by holding a piece up high and see which one reaches the table or floor first, press objects into it to make impressions... the possibilities are endless! If stored in a sealed container, gloop should last for several weeks, but it does dry out with a lot of handling.

Making Slurch:
1. Measure 1 cup of cornstarch and pour into a clean mixing bowl.

2. Measure 1/2 cup of water, squeeze several drops of food coloring into it, and stir.

3. Pour colored water into a bowl of cornstarch and stir. You will probably need to use your hands for mixing because the concoction should be very stiff, yet liquid enough when scooped up and allowed to dribble through the fingers. Because it is fairly liquid, this mixture should remain in the bowl or put into a paper cup. Slurch may feel slightly warm to the touch and has a fascinating quality of being both hard and soft at the same time.

Closing Circle:
Putting different mixtures into paper cups for children to transport home, and cleaning up the room, is usually a good way to end this group. It is often easier to facilitate discussion of the mother's responses to this art process while they are either actively playing with the gloop or slurch, or avoiding the materials altogether.

Children usually have no problem letting you know how they feel about this workshop and are eager to show their newfound toy to everyone they see. So be prepared to receive inquiries about gloop and slurch from other shelter residents and staff who were not lucky enough to participate!
Row.txt_description: This workshop is especially meaningful for families recently escaping domestic violence. I consider this art directive to be a kind of “mess therapy” in that it can help mothers and children overcome rigid controls on their behavior which were necessary in an atmosphere of constant potential danger, but now serve only to hinder self-expression.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 99

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide an arena where the children can express their hopes and dreams in a safe way.

Materials:
Poster boards
Magazines
Pre-cut images (for younger children who can’t cut)
Scissors
Glue
Markers
Pens
Soothing music (optional)

Time Frame:
5 minutes: opening circle
40 minutes: activity
15 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children; 1 adult for 2 younger children

Space Set-up:
Have a quiet, spacious environment for the children to spread out their magazines and boards. If possible, provide some soft background music while the children do the Opening Circle and begin their activity.

Opening Circle:
Have the children begin with the Golden Ball Visualization exercise. Move into a visualization of the kind of person each participant would like to be or of what that person wants for his or her future. Begin the exercise with, “I want you to imagine the person you would like to be, either now or in the future. Think about what kinds of things you would like in your future. When you are ready, open your eyes, and move to the table.”

Activity:
Have the participants look through magazines and cut out words and pictures that appeal to them which represent the kind of person each one wants to be. Have them glue the words and pictures on a poster board in a way that is pleasant to them.

Closing Circle:
Allow participants to share their Dream Boards. Make sure to tell them that this is voluntary, and that she or he can choose to keep the Dream Board private or to share it with the group.

Variations for age levels:
For younger children who have difficulty with scissors, the leader can provide pictures and words that have already been cut out to facilitate that aspect. This activity requires more adults to work with preschool-age children as they would probably need help gluing the pictures and words.
Row.txt_description: This workshop provides an arena where the children can express their hopes and dreams in a safe way.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 107
Row.txt_tips: To enable the children to hang their dream boards, they could punch holes on the top and use pipe cleaners to make a handle.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To allow a window of time where the child can express her/his wishes for the past, present or future. Depending on which age group you are working with, you can modify the complexity of your direction and focus.

For example:
Preschoolers (ages 3-6) should be able to make one simple wish for the present. You will need an assistant available to help with writing the dictation for the children.

School-age children (ages 7-12) may be able to create one, two or three wishes, and they may be able to draw and write their own words (instead of dictating). This will depend on the maturity of the group and their writing abilities. Many children of domestic violence miss a lot of school and may need help writing, so be sure to make that OK. You can modify the number of wishes you ask them to create depending on the level of the group.
Pre-teens and teenagers (ages 13-19) will be able to be fairly autonomous in creating their three wishes.

Materials:
Non-toxic watercolor markers for each child
3 pieces of construction paper for each child
Manilla envelopes to hold the completed work

Time Frame:
5 minutes: opening circle
40 minutes: activity
15 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children

Space Set-up:
Prepare tables with supplies for the creation of the wish drawings. The opening circle can be held on the floor or somewhere separate from the tables, and the children can move to the tables when they are ready to create.

Introduction to the leader:
Children who have experienced family violence and/or physical, emotional, sexual, and spiritual abuse often experience feelings of hopelessness. Their hopes, ideas, and dreams are often left unheard. In the shelter, most of the attention is focused on the mother. At this time, it is especially important to validate the significance of the wishes of children.

Opening Circle:
Begin the workshop with the Wiggle Down or Pretend You’re a Snowman exercise. Remember: the younger the age group, the less words will need to be used. The purpose of the Wiggle Down is to release tension, bring attention and focus to the objective, spark creativity, and create a fun environment.

Activity:
At the end of the Wiggle Down, ask them "Make up three wishes.” (Remember to modify the number of choices depending on the age group):

• One wish for your past (this might be something you wish happened or didn’t happen)
• One for your present (this might be how you wish things were for yourself now)
• One wish for your future (this might be wishing for how you want things to turn out for yourself in the next five years)

Ask each child in the circle and help them to say the wishes aloud if they want to.

Then ask the children to move from the circle to the tables where you can assist them in the dictation of the wish to be written on the top of the page. While playing soft music (like light piano by George Winston) ask them to work on the first wish, drawing a picture or shapes or colors that go with the wish. Give them about 15 minutes for creating each wish.

Closing Circle:
Ask each child to hold up his or her drawing and share the wishes with the group. Some children may only want to show the picture and say nothing at all. This is OK -- participation must always be optional.

Thank everyone for their good work and give each child a manilla envelope to take their pictures home in. Laminating the pictures would also be great, if possible.
Row.txt_description: This workshop allows a window of time where the child can express her/his wishes for the past, present or future. Depending on which age group you are working with, you can modify the complexity of your direction and focus.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 109
Row.txt_tips: Give the children an option to use paints or markers.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop is intended to help children have the opportunity to express their dreams and wants, to bask in some individual adult attention, and to experience magic and fantasy in a safe place.

Materials:
2 child-sized balls of red or gray clay per child
Cardboard or clay-board for each child
Clay tools (popsicle sticks, toothpicks, dull butter knives, small sponges, several small water bowls)
A piece of large construction paper (to record each tale)
Small black permanent markers (for the facilitators and volunteers to record what the children say)

Time Frame:
10 minutes: opening circle
40 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children

Space Set-up:
Prepare tables with supplies for the children to create their fairy tale figures.

Opening Circle:
Begin the opening circle with the slow breathing exercise such as the Breathe Hot, Breathe Cold. Ask the children to close their eyes and imagine they are in a fairy tale. (Assure them that it’s okay not to close their eyes too, if they are uncomfortable.)

This fairy tale starts out "Once upon a time.......” and this fairy tale is about themselves and it has a beginning, a middle, and an end. Imagine. Who could be in it? Do they live in a castle? If not, where then? What does it look like? Who lives in it?

Activity:
When they open their eyes, they will play with their clay to make their fairy tale. The facilitator and volunteers will go around to each child and record the story. Starting with once upon a time, then moving to the beginning, the middle, and the end.

Closing Circle:
The children wash their hands before coming to the circle. Then they may choose to tell their stories.

The clay pieces should stay in the children's room to dry and, if possible, to fire. The children can take the story back to their rooms. (Make sure the child's name is written on the clay piece.)
Row.txt_description: This workshop is intended to help children have the opportunity to express their dreams and wants, to bask in some individual attention, and to experience magic and fantasy in a safe place.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 111

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To offer children a “private space” in order to foster a sense of self-power and magic, to create a special place keep their artwork, and to encourage the gift of imagination.

Materials:
Large handled paper bags -1 for each child (such bags are used at Trader Joe's markets)
Paintbrushes for each child (1 small and 1 large)
Tempera paints - a variety of colors mixed with white glue (will dry glossy and can be easily washed)
Painting smocks (large men's dress shirts from a thrift store)
Newspaper to cover the floor (make it thick)
Glitter and ribbon for the handles

Time Frame:
15 minutes: opening circle
35 minutes: activity
10 minutes: closing circle

Opening Warm-up:
Begin with rhythmic clapping, with everyone in turn saying “My name is ___, what’s your name?” After the name clapping, share a breathing exercise like Butterfly Breath or Breathe Hot, Breathe Cold.

Activity:
Say to the group: "Today we are going to make a magic bag! This magic bag will be your powerful place to keep all of your artwork together. This magic bag is just for you! It is magic because it belongs to only you and you can put whatever you want in it. You can even use it for a hiding place that will help you make-believe a daydream.

"First you need to have your magic word..... think of it and say it out loud or only in your head if you want to. Next we will decorate it however you want! We have shiny paint, glitter, ribbons etc."

List the choices and pass out the bags, and painting smocks. Invite each child to find a spot of newspaper on the floor (spaces should be far enough apart so the child has room to paint). Assist with smocks and sleeve rolling up, then watch the magic.

Closing Circle:
The bags will be wet with paint, so ask each child to stand by their bag to hold up and show the others their magic bag and say their magic word. Of course, sharing is always optional.

Variations:
• Donated pillow cases to decorate with permanent markers.
• Sewing cloth bags for children to decorate with fabric paints.
• Felt bags with lacing. See Emotion Hats for stitching and gluing decorations (page 61).
Row.txt_description: This workshop offers children a “private space” in order to foster a sense of self-power and magic, to create a special place to keep thier artwork, and to encourage the gift of imagination.
Row.txt_notes: Children’s Manual pg. 113

Row.txt_code:
Overview and Objective:
This is the simplest and clearest, expressively focused exercise of "A Window Between Worlds." It is basically the title exercise, during which we literally practice creating a window with the chalk into the world of present fe elings and needs, and then another window into the world of visions and hopes for the future. It is an exercise during which we literally practice putting our hopes and dreams into a tangible form, and the piece of paper literally becomes a window between worlds.

Materials:
Alpha-color pastels (A wide assortment, including fluorescent colors is desirable, if affordable.)
Colored Construction Paper- Pre-cut to frame size (Colored pastel paper can be nicer, if affordable.)
Masking tape- a roll for each woman, otherwise, too much time is spent passing tape around and waiting for each woman to get set up for the exercise (Drafting tape, magic removable tape, or blue painter's tape are all easier to remove without ripping the paper, but are more expensive.)
Frames (Simple 8X10 frames can sometimes be purchased for a dollar.)
Tape-player, relaxing tapes
Paper towels

Set-up:
It is helpful to lay out a spread of paper of various colors to choose from, a box of pastels within reach of each woman, and a roll of masking tape for each woman.

Opening:
[Circle of Introductions:] (See "General Format")
[Set the tone of safety:] "This is a separate space for you, for you to feel, relax, and take time out from everything else. This is a time for you to practice respecting your feelings, your needs, and your visions and your hopes- respecting them enough to put them into a tangible form. Respect whatever you feel, even if you feel like putting your head down and resting, or going to get a drink. This is a time for you. None of this is required. It is all offered to you as a window of time for you to respect your own needs."

Technical Demonstration:
"What we will be doing today, is making two windows with the pastels- one window into how you are feeling in the present moment, and one window into how you want to feel in the future. The point of this is not to worry about how it looks, but rather to concentrate on really giving yourself freedom of expression. If anger is what you are expressing, there is no need to make it 'look nice.' So this is a demonstration of how to make an absolute mess (and enjoy it)! It is not a demonstration of what you 'have to' do." (Begin taping the paper down, and ask why they think you're taping it. Then demonstrate vigorous strokes and smearing and how much fun it is to be free with it. Then remove the tape and show the crisp edge.) "The wonderful thing about this material is that the crisp edge seems to pay respect to the depth of the emotion expressed. Angry scribbles, done in this technique, end up looking as important as they truly are (which somehow doesn't seem to happen if it's done in crayons.)"

Pass out materials (if they aren't already passed out.) Have each woman choose a color of paper to represent the future, and tape it down. Then a color of paper to represent the present, and tape it directly over the other piece. Then pick a third sheet of paper for practice, and tape that directly over the two previous sheets. Once everyone has their three papers taped, begin the technical demonstration. (It's good to get all the taping done first, so that this activity doesn't interrupt the flow of creative expression once it starts.)

Warm-up:
"We are all fairly used to putting our feelings into words, but we rarely practice putting them into shapes and colors. To get used to the process of putting emotions into shapes and colors, we are going to try a very loose, quick warm-up. We're going to move quickly, so that no-one has time to think to carefully, and you can practice grabbing your first, fresh thoughts, without having time to criticize them."

"Ready? OK, first look at the pastels in front of you. Go ahead and grab whatever color you're instantly drawn to. Go ahead and cover the page with that color. Cover it however you feel like- in big scribbles, in smooth strokes, however you want. Then see what it's like to smear it in with your hands. Now think of anger- what color, what shape comes to mind for anger. Go ahead and grab your first thought for anger and put it onto the page. If there's any anger in your body, feel it and let it come through your body onto the page. And now think about peace. What color and what shape come to mind? Go ahead and grab your first thought and make a mark on the page for peace. And now think of sadness. What color and what shape come to mind for sadness? Go ahead and put your first thought on the page. And now think of joy. What color and what shape come to mind for joy? Go ahead and make a mark for joy on the page. And now think of masculine. What color and what shape are masculine to you? When you're ready, go ahead and make a mark for masculine. And now think of feminine. What color and what shape are feminine to you? First thought- grab it, and put it on the page. And now think of your father- make a mark for your father- first color and shape that come to mind. And now think of your mother- make a mark for your mother- first color and shape that come to mind. And now think of your self. What color and shapes come to mind for your self? Make a mark for your self on the page. When you're ready, remove the tape."

"How did that feel? Was it difficult? What it strange to put feelings into shapes and colors? Is it something you've never done before?"

Relaxation:
"Now we are ready to begin the windows. I'd like to begin with a relaxation, to help each of us really notice that this is time for us, time apart from the rest of the day. Like everything we are doing today, this is optional. For some people, a relaxation is the most unnerving thing they could do- not relaxing at all. If you are one of these people, respect that and don't feel odd about it. There is no need for you to feel obligated to do it."

"Ready?" (Begin to play relaxing music) "Go ahead and get comfortable- let your eyes close and take a deep breath."(See "Relaxation Techniques", and follow the general relaxation of the body. Then at the end of it, add the following in order to guide the women into the drawing process.) "Notice that this is time for you, time for you to notice how you are feeling. Take a moment to notice the world on the inside of you. What does it feel like? Notice if any colors or any shapes come to mind. Would the world on the inside of you be many colors? Or just one? Would it be dark? Would it be light? Would it have sharp lines? Or curves? Would it be foggy? Or clear? And take some time to notice what the world around you feels like. Do any colors or shapes come to mind? Would the world around you be dark? Or light? Would it be foggy or clear? Would it have many colors or just one? Whenever you are ready, go ahead and begin to draw a window into your present world."

Pastel Window Into the Present:
(Relaxing music continues, the women begin to draw when they are ready. As they begin to draw, it can be helpful to throw out some reminders:) "If you notice yourself worrying about what your drawing looks like, see if you can remember that this is free time. See if you can send the critical thoughts out of the window- see if you can let yourself be as free and bold as you were during the warm up." (As the first women look like they are feeling finished:) "When you are ready, go ahead and remove the tape from your drawing. Notice if there are any words in your mind that go with this image, and take a few minutes to write the words on the back of your drawing." (This gives the women who aren't yet finished a signal that we are wrapping up that drawing, while giving the ones who are already done a way to continue their expression while waiting for the others to catch up.)

Transition:
(Stop the music) Before going on to the drawing of the future, it can be important to share what was felt and discovered in the process of this drawing. If there is a small group, and time allows, it is wonderful to give each woman an opportunity to share whatever she wants to share of what she made and how it felt to make it. If the group is large and time is too tight for such in-depth sharing at this point, it is helpful to have each person think of one word to describe how it felt to do this drawing, and have each share their one word. Then ask if everyone is ready for the future.

It can be helpful to share a note about the future: "It can be quite difficult to ask ourselves what we really want in our future. As important as that question is, we don't spend a lot of time with it, and it can be disconcerting to discover that we really aren't sure what we want. Be patient with yourself during this exercise. This is a window of time for you to consider this question and to practice respecting your true feelings about it. If you are uncertain, respect your uncertainty. Don't feel like you have to 'make something up'. It is most important to honor what you really feel, and it is wonderful if even at the end of ten minutes you have only clouds of uncertainty on your page. That is valuable, and important. That is what this time is for. So see if you can take the risk of being as honest as possible with yourself during this time."

Relaxation:
(Begin music again) "Go ahead and get yourself very comfortable again- let your eyes close and take a deep breath. Notice if there is any part of your body that has become tense in doing the drawing you just completed. Take another deep breath, and imagine any tension flowing out of your body with the air. Now picture the drawing of your present world. Picture in your mind's eye the colors and shapes you just created. Notice if there is anything in that world that you are ready to leave behind as you move ahead into your future. Are there any shapes and colors that you would like to leave behind? Imagine breathing those colors out with your breath. Imagine exchanging the old air with fresh, new air."

"Now, with your eyes still closed, take some time to ask yourself 'what do I want in my future?' As you ask yourself this question, notice if any shapes or colors come to mind. Imagine how you want to feel on the inside. What colors would do you imagine for your inner world? Would it be dark or light? Clear or foggy? Curving or straight? And take time to notice how you want the world around you to feel in your future? Would it be dark or light? Foggy or clear? Curving or straight? Take as long as you want, just to imagine your future. Whenever you are ready, go ahead and open your eyes, and begin to draw your window into your future."

Pastel Window Into the Future:
(Music continues, the women begin to draw at their own pace, you may want to remind the women to send their critical voices away. As the first women wrap up their work, let everyone know that they can remove the tape whenever they feel complete, and they can take time to write any words that go with their image on the back.)

Closing Circle:
If you asked for one word about how the Present Window felt, it is good to ask for one word about how the Future Window felt. Remark if the words are different from the previous round of words. It is important to give each woman time at the end of the drawing session to express anything she wants to share about her drawings, and about how it felt to create. It can be wonderful to hold up each woman's drawing (if she is willing) so that everyone, including her, can see it from a distance as she talks about it.

Giving the women frames for their images can be a wonderful conclusion to this project. The content of the drawings is so valuable. They deserve to be honored in this way. The framed images can serve as tangible reminders for the women of where they are and where they are aiming to go in their lives.

Variations:
This exercise can be used to explore many areas other than present and future worlds. It can be wonderful to use the pastel windows to explore a negative feeling and a positive feeling. (This can be great with younger children- a feeling you don't like, and a feeling you love) This exercise can follow a writing session during which each woman writes about herself. She can circle the most positive thing and the most negative thing in her writing, and use the drawing as an arena to explore those poles in depth.
Row.txt_description: This workshop allows the participants to create a window with the chalk into the world of present feelings and needs, and then another window into the world of visions and hopes for the future.
Row.txt_notes: Women’s Manual pg.46

Row.txt_code:
Overview and Objective:
Jewelry Making is one of the most popular sessions I have offered. When I first began to work in battered women's shelters and was uncertain of what the women would be interested in doing, I brought SuperSculpey to the kitchen table and began making jewelry. Before we knew it, a group of curious observers had become eager participants. This activity has an inherent appeal. It is an excellent and non-threatening way to get to know a new group of women, and for them to get to know you. When I worked in shelters, I was living in them, staying at each one for a week and working intensively with the women during my stay. I had several nights in progression to get the know the women. I usually began with the jewelry making as a way to build the safety of the art-making process. During the session, I had a chance to get to know each woman: to see who was afraid of art, and who was confident, to see who was quiet, and who was vocal. It was an opportunity for the women to get to know me as well, and to sense that they could trust me to encourage and listen to them without pressure or judgment. During the Jewelry Making, they were able to venture into new territory and succeed.

Before I began working in shelters, I had little understanding of the power of crafts. For many women I've worked with, the process of making a pair of earrings has been as transformative an experience as the more expressive Mask Making workshop (see next "Focused Workshop"). Making beautiful jewelry can be an incredible self-esteem builder. It shows the women that they are capable of learning new things and of creating beauty in their lives with their own two hands. It never ceases to amaze me how powerful, simple craft activities can be as healing tools in the shelters. A process which can seem more superficial than a focused, expressive session, can be incredibly empowering.

Materials:
Examples- completed jewelry to inspire ideas
Tape Player and relaxing tapes- to set the tone of the session
Acrylic Paint- including Iridescent paints (pre-mixed)
Wet Paint Box (in which the mixed paints are stored)
Brushes- enough for each person to have a large and smaller brush, if possible
Water Jar
Paper Towels
Old Cloth Sheet- to cover the table (newspapers also work)
SuperSculpey, rolled into walnut-sized balls for distribution
Jewelry Findings (pin backs, earring backs, jump-rings, magnets)
E-6000 Glue- for attaching pin backs to cooked and painted clay
Aluminum Foil Pans
Conventional Oven or Toaster Oven (not microwave)
Ribbons- to hang the jewelry from

Introduction:
The introduction, like the entire format of this workshop can vary greatly depending on the attention level and focus of the group. It can be conducted with structure. You introducing yourself (why you do this), introducing the project (making jewelry) and introducing the philosophy of the art-making (that this is a window of time for you). It can also begin more casually. Simply laying out a cloth full of examples can be enough to encourage the women to grab a ball and begin to explore.

Whether casually or formally, I usually explain: "This workshop is a time for you to make whatever you want. I have these examples here to give you some ideas of what is possible, and I can certainly show you how to make any of these things, but don't feel like you have to stick to what I show you. Let your imagination go wild, and ask for all the help you want!"

Opening Cirlce:
If the group is focused, it is helpful to begin with an opening circle during which each woman can share her name, how she feels, and how she feels about art. It can also be fine to skip such structure and check into how everyone is feeling and how they feel about art more casually. The casual approach is usually the one I take in getting to know the women for the first time.

Technical Demonstration:
On the most informal level, the best technical demonstration is having examples available for the women to see and to be inspired by. If the women see anything they wish to know how to make, they can ask. You can grab a piece of clay and demonstrate, step by step, how it is made, with them following each step as you go.

If the group is focused enough, I find it most helpful to begin with a step by step, follow-along demonstration of how to make a rose. It is something very basic and very beautiful, and lets the women begin to feel the clay and create something that surprises them without having to agonize over what to make. It's a good warm-up. I always explain that they can crumple it up as soon as it's done, but I just want them to know how to make it. I am also careful to make it clear that this is only one way to make a rose- not the only way and not the "best" way.

Some women enjoy the rose making immensely and continue exploring it for the entire session. Others enjoy it and then move on to create other things at their own pace.

Note: Unlike many of the other workshops, this is one during which it can be helpful to continue giving technical assistance to each woman individually throughout the creation process.

Relaxation:
This project can work well without any structured relaxation. The tactile process of working the clay seems to automatically provide a sense of nurturance and peace, so even without any guided relaxation, the tone of the workshop can be very calming and rejuvenating. If the group wants a formal relaxation, it can be a wonderful part of the Jewelry-Making process. (For details on Relaxations see "A Note on Relaxations".)

Regardless of whether or not there is a formal relaxation, it is helpful to have relaxing music playing during the session. Without any formal explanation, this helps set session apart from the rest of the day, as a window of time for the women to re-energize, play, and create.

Creation:
The creation of the work progresses naturally as each woman works at her own speed and asks for assistance as she needs it. It is helpful to let the women know how much time they have to create. It is important to leave the final 45 minutes to cook and paint the jewelry.

Note: Pre-heat the oven as the women create so that it will be ready for the cooking.

Cooking:
Begin cooking everything 45 minutes before the end of the session. Generally 10 minutes is a good length of time to cook small objects (directions are on the SuperSculpey package). This will allow the women 25 minutes to paint and 10 minutes to clean up.

Painting:
I have found it important to have the colors pre-mixed for the women to use. To teach about color mixing would take much longer and the women wouldn't have much time to paint.

I highly recommend Iridescent Gold, White, Bronze, and Silver as the base of all the colors, mixing them with a palette knife and storing them in an air-tight, moist paint storage box. The iridescent paints make each color sparkle and make the jewelry look much more professional and beautiful than flat paints.

As the clay cooks in the oven, I get out the paints and explain the toxicity, and demonstrate how a thin, dry coat of paint looks much smoother than if you use lots of paint and/or lots of water. I also explain how to care for the brushes (not letting paint dry in them and not letting them stand in the water).

When the jewelry is cooked we all begin to paint.

Closing Circle:
Usually the women keep creating and painting up until the very last instant, so we don't have a formal closing circle. When time allows, it is nice to have a circle during which each person has an opportunity to share what she created and how it felt to her, especially noticing if she feels any different about herself or about art from how she felt when she began the session.
Row.txt_description: This workshop is a non-threatening way to help women informally speak about their feelings. The jewelry making process demonstrates the safety of the art-making process. Building beautiful jewelry can also be an incredible self-esteem builder.
Row.txt_notes: Women’s Manual pg. 53

Row.txt_code:
Overview and Objective:
This is one of the most intense workshops I have developed. The idea was partly inspired by Kathryn Trenshaw's mask work with survivors of incest. Because of its potential to stir up deep emotions, I recommend that it be offered in the presence of a shelter staff person, who will be available to the women after the session if necessary. As with all expressively focused workshops, it is crucial to discuss with the staff whether or not they want this level of emotional work to occur with their residents.

This workshop consists of guiding the women to create two masks out of SuperSculpey: one representing the present, and one representing the future. During this workshop, the women often surprise themselves with their strong emotions and profound reflections.

To set the tone for this workshop, it is especially important to make it clear that the whole process is voluntary. It is an opportunity for each woman to express as much as she can of whatever feelings come up for her. It is also important to make it clear that the product is not important at all. What is important is only that she use the time to experience her feelings and to put them into the clay.

With the rare atmosphere of safety and openness established in the beginning of the session, it is very important to allow ample time for the closure of this atmosphere. Allow plenty of time after the completion of the masks for a relaxed discussion of the experience -- a chance to share discoveries and verbally release what the process brought up for each woman.

Materials:
SuperSculpey (two walnut-sized pieces for each woman)
Pan and Oven (portable toaster-ovens work fine)
Tapeplayer and relaxing music
Utensils and/or paper clips to form the clay
Optional: Ribbons and Jump-Rings (to make the masks wearable)
Optional: Acrylic Paint / Brushes / Water / etc. (if there's extra time afterwards to paint the masks)

Opening and Relaxation:
Circle of Introductions: "Share your name, share how you feel about art, and share how daring or not daring you feel today."

Set the tone of safety: "This is a separate space for you, for you to feel, relax, take time out from everything else. A time for you to get a sense of how you're feeling. This is also totally voluntary. Do only what you want to do. This is a safe space for you to feel- this session may bring feelings in you. Respect whatever you feel, and respect the feelings of others too."

Pass out the sculpey clay, and ask the women to begin to squish it around as they get themselves really comfortable. Then begin the guided relaxation (see "Note on Relaxations" for detailed description).

After the relaxation, with the women's eyes still closed, begin to guide them into the mask-making:

Present Mask-Making:
"Begin to visualize your present world. Picture all of the things you feel ready to let go of in the present... all of the things you are ready to leave behind. Picture them however they come to you- as images, or as along list of all of the things. As you imagine these things you're ready to leave behind, notice how it feels in your body. Does your body get tense anywhere? Are there any wrinkles on your forehead? As you keep imagining all of these things from your present, notice how you feel and see if you can begin to mold these feelings into a mask. We will take ten minutes to work on this mask of the present."
Play soft music during the 10 minutes to help the women get into it.

"You can make this mask with your eyes closed, or you can open your eyes, but remember that it does not matter what it looks like. All that matters is that you keep feeling whatever you're feeling about the present, and that you keep putting those feelings into the clay. At the end of the 10 minutes, you may have a squished up ball into which you've been squeezing all of your anger. That squished up ball would be the perfect thing to end up with. Just focus on letting your feeling into the clay as much as you can, and whatever you make is absolutely perfect. It does not have to look like a face. Your mask can be any shapes at all that express your feelings."

 
A Leader Sharing the Present
 
Sharing the Present:
When the 10 minutes is over, turn the music down slowly, and ask if anyone needs more time: "Take a few more minutes if you need."

When everyone's ready: "How are you feeling? How would you describe your feelings in one word?" (Listen to everyone's words.)

Usually everyone feels pretty low at this point. Take time for everyone to share whatever the Present Mask brought up. Ask them to share their mask and anything they wish to tell about it or about the process of creating it. This is voluntary, but usually all of the women want to share. Often there are tears shed and profound experiences to relate. It is often wonderful to see how much the women are able to appreciate and respect their own creative process. It is wonderful to see a group of women let go of the need to create a perfect product, and to hear them relate all that they were able to discover in a twisted mound of clay. Once everyone has had a chance to express how they're feeling, move on to the Future Mask.

Future Mask-Masking:
Pass out new sculpey, and guide a brief second relaxation: "Close your eyes again and take some deep, deep breaths. Imagine all of the negative things from the present being breathed out of them in the air you exhale. Imagine hope and strength coming into you with the air you breathe in. Now, slowly, begin to visualize your future."

"It can be as great a risk to truly imagine what you want in your future. It can be scary to imagine the good things you want, or to realize that you aren't sure what you want. So as you begin to imagine your future, be gentle with yourself. Respect whatever ideas come to mind, even if they don't seem realistic, and don't worry if you feel blank. Appreciate how valuable it is just to realize that you're not sure what you want."

"Take the risk to picture what it is you really, really want. Let it appear however is most comfortable to you- as images, or as a long list of all the things you want. As you imagine all of the good things in your future, notice how it feels in your face. When you're ready, begin to form a mask of all of those feelings. Again, we will create these for 10 minutes. Again, what is important is not what it looks like, but rather the process of staying with your feelings of the future, and letting them emerge in the clay."
Play music during the 10 minutes.

 
 A leader sharing the future.
Sharing the Future:
When the 10 minutes is up, turn down the music, and see if anyone needs more time. When everyone's ready, ask again how everyone is feeling in one word. Usually the words are quite different at this point from how they were after the Present Masks.

Have everyone share what they want to about their mask and the process of creating them.

Closing Circle:
To wrap up the session, share how powerful objects such as these can be. Taken away from the session, they are precious reminders of where we are in our lives, and where we want to go.

They can be made into jewelry, or hung on the wall, or saved as clay to work with later.
Close with a circle giving each woman the opportunity to share what she personally will take away from the workshop to use in her everyday life.

Variations:
Other themes could also be used as focal points for the masks. Each participant could choose two emotions to explore through the Mask Making. Two of her strongest emotions, or two opposite emotions, or a "positive" and a "negative" emotion she feels.
Row.txt_description: This workshop allows women to express their feelings and identify their emotions. The women have a chance to look at their own profound reflections and thoughts.
Row.txt_notes: Women’s Manual pg. 57

Row.txt_code:
Overview and Objective:
Collage Pins have been a terrific exercise for all levels, especially women who have not considered themselves capable of creating art. When the art session results in an object each woman can proudly wear, this art can take on a particular importance that extends far beyond the session itself. Each time she wears her art, and each time someone comments on it, she is reminded of her creativity and capabilities.

Each miniature, wearable collage can serve as an intentional reminder for the woman who creates it -- a reminder of her dreams and hopes, a reminder of her strength, a reminder to relax, a reminder to take time for herself. Each woman can use the session to think of what she wants to remind herself of as well as to create a pin representing that thought, dream or quality. Such a pin can literally function as a window for her -- a window through which she reaches for a new world.

Each pin can be as simple or complex as each woman wishes. They can also be as playful, as beautiful, as expressive, as meaningful as each woman envisions. One young woman was so thrilled to realize that she was capable of creating something that looked so professional, that she considered taking the Pin Making on as a way to raise money.

Materials:
Example Collage Pins- to inspire ideas
Newspaper or Old Sheet- to cover table surface
Pin Backs- to glue on to make the pins
Magazines- be sure to have an adequate variety
Sharp Pencils- to outline the plexiglass onto the board
Scissors- to cut the images and the poster board to size
Glue Sticks- to collage the magazine images to the poster board
Poster Board/Heavy Cardstock- to make the backing for each pin
Matte Medium- to attach the magazine images to the plexiglass
Soft Brushes- to apply the Matte Medium
Water Jar- to rinse the brushes (Don't let the Matte Medium dry in the brushes. It's permanent.)
Paper Towels
Self Adhesive Magnets- in case anyone would prefer a magnet to a pin
Plexiglass- cut into appropriate sizes and shapes for pins
Exacto Knives- for any intricate cutting of the magazine images (optional)
Card Board- to use beneath the exacto knives (optional)

Note: The plexiglass store will often cut the glass for a minimal charge or as a donation.

Opening:
As with the Jewelry Making session, the Pin Making need not be formally structured. If appropriate, a formal introduction can be offered (See "General Format"). Likewise with an opening circle. If the women are focused, it would be appropriate to have a circle during which each shares her name, how she feels, and how she feels about art. If not, then these issues can be explored throughout the session more casually.

The display of examples can be enough to interest a woman in participating in the session. Sometimes that is the only sort of introduction necessary.

Technical Information:
The creation of the pins is a step-by-step process which can be most efficiently explained and demonstrated once for everyone to see before they begin to create their pins. The basic steps are as follows:

1. Select an image or images you wish to collage and select a piece of plexiglass of an appropriate size.

2. Trace the shape of the plexiglass onto the poster board. Then cut a piece of poster board to the exact size of the plexiglass.

3. Cut the magazine images you like and collage them onto the poster board piece. Make sure that you are attaching the images to the correct side of the poster board piece so that you will be able to put the clear glass right over the images. Use the exactos and scissors and the glue sticks for the collaging.

4. When the collage is complete on the piece of poster board, remove the protective paper from the plexiglass.

5. Check the fit of the board and glass. Trim the board and magazine images if necessary.

6. Use a brush to cover the face of the magazine images with Matte Medium. It will look like you're ruining the collage by making it all white. Don't worry -- the Matte Medium dries clear.

7. Press the plexiglass onto the surface of the magazines. Squeeze excess Matte Medium and air bubbles out to the sides of the glass. Be careful to not get Matte Medium on the front surface of the glass- it will show. Also, be careful to match the edges of the board and glass up as you press. Once they are pressed together, you won't be able to slide them into alignment.

8. Hold the board and glass together for about 3 minutes as if begins to dry. When you are able to lift your pressure without seeing a whole bunch of air bubbles enter the image, take your hands off and let it sit.

9. Attach a pin back or magnet to the back of the board with a generous dab of E-6000. Let the pin dry for 24 hours before wearing. (Use E-6000 only in well-ventilated areas.)

Creation:
After demonstrating this process, assist each woman in making pins for herself.

Closing:
This exercise can be closed as informally or formally as seems appropriate. If possible, it is powerful to have a circle during which each woman can share what she made, what it felt like to her, and what she gained from the session.

Variations:
Larger collages could be made with larger pieces of plexiglass. Also, rather than collaging pins, boxes could be created in another playful workshop. Cigar Boxes in particular make wonderful objects to collage. To increase the expressive focus of such a workshop, the collaging of a box could represent the inner and outer worlds of a woman.
Row.txt_description: This workshop allows women to see their creative potential and express their emotions and dreams. The pin is a reminder to relax, and to take time out of the day to unwind.
Row.txt_notes: Women’ s Manual pg. 62
Row.txt_tips:
Optional Journaling
"Write for five minutes about your vision for the future.  What comes to mind?  Write anything at all that you think of."

Row.txt_code:
Overview and Objective:
This workshop was developed by one of the first artists and coordinators of A Window Between World's pilot program. Watching her lead this workshop opened my eyes to the beauty and depth of collage work. Collage is her preferred art form. As she shared her own beautiful collages with us, we were all able to see the tremendous potential of this medium.

During this Intuition Collage session, women are encouraged to explore the process of creating something guided by their intuition rather than by a conscious and intentional thought process. It is a deeply engrossing workshop, and always the women want to continue longer than the usual 2 hour time.

Materials:
Example Collages if possible- to show the wonderful potential of collage
Poster Boards- Large enough to be the backing for each woman's collage
Newspaper or old sheet- to cover table surface
Magazines- be sure to have an adequate variety
Sharp Pencils
Erasers
Scissors- a pair for each participant
Exacto Knives- for any intricate cutting of the magazine images (optional)
Glue Sticks- to collage the magazine images to the poster board
Cardboard- to use beneath the exacto knives (optional)
Paper Towels
Tape Player
Relaxing tapes

Introduction:
In addition to sharing the usual introductory information (See "General Format"), it is helpful to bring up the concept of intuition. What does the word mean? Has anyone ever known something by a gut-reaction or intuition?

Opening Circle:
Share name, how you're feeling, how you feel about art and / or intuition.

Technical Demonstration:
"Today we will be creating a collage by using this intuition rather than analyzing. We will be using a relaxation to get in touch with our intuition, and then we will be tearing out all the images that we have a strong, intuitive reaction to. Then we will be collaging them together, again, using intuition rather than analyzing."

It is useful to demonstrate a variety of collaging possibilities, regardless of how basic they may seem. Here are some of the basics you might demonstrate:

1. The process of cutting out an image and gluing it carefully to a different background.

2. The process of cutting a shape that is different than what's printed on it (like cutting a heart shape out of a page of flames).

3. The process of tearing pieces out, without trying to have them be an identifiable shape.

4. The process of tearing pieces out of various colors and using them for their color, like a mosaic.

5. The process of turning your work upside down and continuing in this new orientation.

6. How to put glue on the back of a given shape, against a piece of wax paper, so that the table doesn't get covered with glue.

7. The process of smoothing the glued-together pieces out with wax paper and a popsicle stick rubbed over it.

(The processes are endless. Demonstrate what you're excited about.)

Distribute Materials:
Each person selects a variety of magazines from which to tear (maybe 10 or so per person). It is important for each person to select the magazines before the relaxation so that once they open their eyes, they can dive right into the intuitive selection of images.

Relaxation:
Once everyone has their magazines, go ahead and lead a general relaxation (See "Notes on Relaxationl") Music helps to create the tone of peacefulness. At the end of the relaxation, while everyone still has their eyes closed, begin to guide the women to notice their intuition. "With your eyes still closed, notice that this is a time for you... It's a quiet, peaceful time for you to notice your gut feelings... With the world quiet around you, take a moment to focus on the world inside of you... This session is a time for you to practice respecting your gut reactions... When you look through the magazine images, see if you can remember your gut feelings... When you open your eyes and begin to tear out images, see if you can be guided by your inner senses... Whenever you are ready, go ahead and open your eyes and begin to tear out whatever images you have a gut reaction to."

Image Gathering:
Each woman begins to tear out images that she responds to intuitively. Based on her intuitive pulls, she will rip out entire pages, not worrying at all about how the images will be arranged or relate to each other- simply collecting.

Image Synthesis:
When it looks like most of the women have ripped out quite a stack of images, encourage them to begin going through their selected images. As they do this they can begin to arrange and collage them together, still being guided by intuitive impulses rather than analysis or conscious planning. This process can take quite a while. When there is only 45 minutes left for the session, let them know they have 15 more minutes to create. This will leave 15 minutes for sharing of the creations and the insights, and 15 minutes for clean-up. (It's usually quite a mess by this point!) Encourage women who want to continue working to borrow a glue stick and some scissors so that they can continue working on their collages after the session.

Closing Circle:
Even if the women aren't all finished with their work, it is very important to have a closing circle of sharing. After such a journey into the unpredictable territory of intuition, it is particularly valuable to take time for each woman to sit back and look at her work from a distance, to share what she sees in it. I usually hold up each woman's work for the whole group to see (with her permission), as she shares what it means to her and what it felt like to do. This process of intuitive collaging lends itself to wonderful and useful surprises.

Variations:
Rather than intuition, the collages could be used to explore a different issue. For example, love and hate. The women could rip out images that relate to their love and to their hate. They could then create a single collage combining the two or two separate collages.
Row.txt_description: This workshop encourages women to explore the process of creating art guided by their intuition.
Row.txt_notes: Women’s Manual pg. 65

Row.txt_code:
Overview and Objective:
This simple and playful exercise can be revealing. Each woman chooses her own one-word theme about which to write. She begins by writing down that word and then making a list of all of the words that pop into her mind in association with her theme word. The structure of jotting down words by free association, without composing sentences, breaks us out of ordinary paths of thought. This allows us to discover surprising connections and often profound meaning.

Materials:
Pens
Paper
Tape Player (optional)
Relaxing music (optional)

Introduction:
When introducing a writing exercise, it can be important to explain that this writing, unlike most of the writing we ordinarily do, is purely a space for self-expression: "This is an opportunity for each of us to respect whatever wild and unexplainable thoughts come into our heads. This writing is for each of us, not for anyone else."

"Today we will each choose a single word, whatever word feels most important to us in our lives right now. That word might be hope or pain, or change or marriage, or whatever is the center of your life at this time. Then we will be writing a list of whatever words come to mind in association with this theme. Without thinking about it or analyzing it, we will each list what comes into our heads. Then we will have a chance to look back over the list and think about it and write down any comments or observations."

Opening Circle and Theme Choice:
"To begin, I'd like you to remember that this entire session is a time for you. It is a time for you to respect what you feel and think and need. You do not have to do this for anyone else, or share it with anyone else. You do not even have to participate. So really notice that this is your time.

To begin, let's take a moment to go around the circle. Take time if you want to to share your name, to share anything you'd like about how you are feeling today, and to share your theme word, if you've thought of it." (Circle of sharing, then pass out paper and pens)

Writing:
"Go ahead and write your theme word at the top of the page, then begin to write the chain of whatever other words come to mind." (Take about ten minutes for this. Then, as the women seem to finish their lists:) "Take some time now to read back over your list. Write down any thoughts or comments that come to mind about the words you've chosen."

Sharing and Closing Circle:
"How did that feel to write?" (Take time to hear everyone's reactions and discoveries. Anyone who wishes can read what they wrote to the group.)

Variations:
There are countless variations of simple and powerful writing exercises. The "Word Chain" is an exercise I've seen in use in writing groups around the country. Many useful writing exercises can be found in The Creative Journal by Lucia Capacchione. Her exercises in that book include:

"Looking Back" (In which you ask yourself: "What king of day was it? What were the highlights?" and you draw or write about the highlights of the day, asking yourself, "How did I feel about it at the time? How do I feel about it now?" The exercise can be used to focus on whatever block of time makes sense- a week, a month, a year, etc.)

"Do Like and Don't Like" (In which you ask yourself: "What do I like about myself and my life right now?" List it, study it, add to it, and then ask: "What don't I like about myself and my life right now?" List it, study it, and choose one thing to work on changing during the up-coming week.)

"What's in a Name" (In which you go back in your memory as far as you can to remember all of the things you've ever been called. Write the list in chronological order and write down any reactions you have. Then you create a "name design" and poem or wordplay about your name.)

"I Believe" (In which you ask yourself: "What do I believe about myself? What personality traits do I have? What are my patterns of behavior? My talents and potential? My limitations?" You write them in two columns, with the first being "Beliefs about myself" and the second being "Where they came from." Include positive and negative beliefs. As you review it, select any beliefs that you want to change. For those beliefs, begin a new page with columns: "Old Belief" and "New Belief." Write a new alternative belief to replace each old one.)

"Love Letter to Myself" (In which you meditate on all of the things about yourself that you love. Write a letter to yourself that describes each of these things in detail.)

"My Support System" (In which you think about the people in your life and ask: "Who are the people I turn to in time of need when I want understanding, encouragement, support, and assistance or any kind?" Then you create a graphic design showing them, and words explaining the support each provides.)

"I Wish" (In which you imagine that you have been given the necessary things to enable you to have any wish. You decide what your wish would be and you write it out.)

Concise and wonderful descriptions of these exercises and many more appear in Capacchione's book, The Creative Journal.
Row.txt_description: This workshop allows the women to discover surprising connections and profound meaning in their lives and the lives of others. It is an opportunity to respect the wild thoughts that pop up, and encourage honest self-expression.
Row.txt_notes: Women’s Manual pg. 70

Row.txt_code:
Overview and Objective:
Timed Writing is a tool aimed to give us a chance to tap into our creative, playful, expressive selves. It is designed to cut right through the sense of pressure, the doubts, and the self-criticism that can block our flow of expression . It gives each woman the opportunity to focus her attention to create something spontaneous and powerful. Timed Writing is adapted from Natalie Goldberg's book Writing Down the Bones.

The following focused exercise is a session during which each woman practices listening to her own thoughts without judgment, and being listened to by the rest of the group without judgment. As the process of writing is guided by the "rules" of Timed Writing which help everyone to suspend criticism, so the process of listening is guided by the "rules" of Echo Listening.

Echo Listening is a form of listening which is structured to be completely non-judgmental. After listening to a woman read her piece, everyone in the room simply repeats at least one thing they remember the person saying, word for word, so that she hears the entire room "echo" her words to her, rather than judging them. It is one structured way to try supportive listening.

This process of sharing can be just as powerful as the writing itself. Since the women spent the time writing intentionally not reflecting on what they were creating, it's often quite surprising and extremely gratifying for them to read what came out of them. It can feel as if they are discovering it for the first time as they read.

Because of the extreme vulnerability encouraged in this entire situation by the non-judgmental atmosphere, it is important to stress throughout the session that all parts of it are optional. The intention of the entire session is that each woman can practice respecting her own needs, feelings, and visions. If she feels the need to skip any part of the exercise, she is more than encouraged to respect that need.

Materials:
Paper
Pens
Tape Player and music (optional)

Introduction:
As is detailed in "General Format", it can be helpful introduce yourself, the exercise you'll be leading, and the philosophy of the session as a "window of time" for each woman to practice respecting her own needs, feelings, and visions.

Opening Circle:
To build an atmosphere of safety in the group an opening circle is quite useful. Give everyone an opportunity to share her name, how she is feeling, and how she feels about writing. If people share any insecurities about writing, that is an opportunity to explain that this writing experience, unlike most times we write, is purely for ourselves. Grammar, punctuation, spelling, etc. don't matter. This writing is a chance to have it feel completely free.

Technical Information:
"We will try an exercise designed to give us a chance to let out our deepest, strongest feelings. We will begin writing with the phrase 'I am...', and then write whatever comes to mind. We will write for just ten minutes, that's all, and during that time, all you have to do is grab the very first thoughts that come into your head. During this ten minutes, anything goes, absolutely anything."

"First thoughts have tremendous energy. We usually censor them, change them, criticize them, so here are some rules to help you let them out without criticizing them:
1. Don't cross out, change, correct, or judge anything you write. Let it be. I mean it when I say 'anything goes.' Keep going.
2. Go for the jugular- the first, fresh thoughts, whatever they are, those have the most energy. Write them! Even if they're strange, even if they're embarrassing, even if they're private, even if they're true, even if they're untrue. You don't have to share what you write. Just let it out.
3. Don't stop writing. Write for the entire 10 minutes. To decide it's 'done' is a judgment. We're going to suspend judgments for 10 minutes, and see what happens, so don't stop. If you can't think of what to write, just keep writing "I am, I am, I am..." until something comes to mind."

"These rules are aimed simply to help us feel free as we write. This freedom can sometimes feel like being out of control. You may feel out of control. Try it for this 10 minutes and just see what happens!"

Relaxation:
Depending on the attention level of the group, how safe they feel with each other, and how they feel about guided relaxations, it can be effective to begin the Timed Writing with a relaxation. After explaining the "rules" and before beginning the writing, guide a relaxation (See "Notes on Relaxations" for detailed description). At the end of the relaxation, while the women still have their eyes closed, guide them to picture the words "I AM..." Then say "Notice the first words that pop into your mind when you picture the words "I AM..." And when you're ready, go ahead and begin to write."

Write! If you didn't lead into the writing with a relaxation, just begin the writing with: "Ready to begin?... What are the 3 "rules"? Any questions? Go..." (Time the 10 minutes. If you notice people stopping or seeming self-critical, remind the entire group to just keep writing, no matter how silly or strange the words are- whatever comes to mind.) "Now finish up whatever thought you're in the middle of, and put down your pens. How are you feeling now?" (Move on to Echo Listening.)

Echo Listening:
"Just as we wrote without judging what we were saying, we're going to try to listen the same way. Since we are used to judging things immediately, and saying that's good, or that's bad, it can seem impossible to stop judging. In Echo Listening, you don't give any feedback. Rather than saying 'that was good', we're going to appreciate what we've heard by simply echoing back whatever stuck out in our minds when they were reading. Say their words right back to them when they're finished reading. See what you can remember! For each person's writing, be sure to remember at least one phrase that you can echo back to them. If you remember more than that, feel free to say more."

The first woman reads her piece. Then, one at a time, everyone echoes back to her what they heard, word for word. When the echoes slow down (like popping corn), ask the woman if there's anything she wants to say. This is the first time she has heard for herself what she wrote, and she may have strong emotions to share about what it means to her and what it felt like to hear it spoken back to her. It is important to give her time for this, before the group moves on to the next woman.

Be sure to leave an ample amount of time for this. I've found that it generally can take about 4 minutes per person, depending on how long and how much they wrote. This circle of sharing and echoing can be the closing circle for the session, or you can add a final closing circle for everyone to share whatever they feel like saying about the whole experience.

Variations:
The Timed Writing can be offered for varying lengths of time, and can be used in groups or by an individual. It's a technique that anyone can use at any time to break through a creative block, explore an idea, or vent an emotion. "I am..." is a very basic, but evocative theme. Other themes to try include "I feel...", "I am proud of...", "I remember...", "I hope...", "I hate...", "Family is...", "Violence is...", etc. Groups of survivors working with The Courage to Heal can use the book's themes as the basis for timed writings. Those in 12 Step Programs could try the 12 steps as themes about which to write.

Timed Writing can stand alone as a creative workshop in itself in conjunction with the Echo Listening. It can also be used as a 10 minute launching point for a visual art-making session. It is wonderful to create drawings, sculpture, and photographs, based on the writings. I often have each woman circle the most positive thing in her writing and the most negative thing (or the most powerful and the most difficult) and then have everyone create a drawing in shapes, lines, and color, of the world of the negative thing and the world of the positive thing. The words and visual imagery often combine to produce an expression more powerful than either one alone.

Other variations of Timed Writing exercises can be found in Natalie Goldberg's Writing Down the Bones.

Another writing technique that I recommend for focused creative writing sessions is Lucia Capacchione's non-dominant hand writing, in which women carry on a dialogue between their two hands. Her powerful non-dominant hand techniques can be found in The Power of Your Other Hand and Recovery of Your Inner Child.
Row.txt_description: This workshop taps into a woman’s creative, playful, and expressive self. It cuts through the sense of pressure, the doubts, and the self-criticism that blocks creative expression. It gives each woman the opportunity to create something spontaneous and powerful.
