Row.txt_notes: Women’s Manual pg. 73

Row.txt_code:
Overview and Objective:
This empowerment workshop combines the Relaxation, the Timed Writing Exercise, and Photography to create a Self-Portrait Book. The time frame for this project is three separate 1 1/2 hour sessions. These could be spread out once a week for three weeks, or occur on three consecutive days.

Session One: Timed Writing Exercise
Session Two: Creative Photography
Session Three: Book-Making

Materials List:
First Session:
Paper
Pens
Timer

Second Session:
Camera and Tripod
Film (3-4 shots per woman)
Props to Pose with (large newsprint paper, or blankets and sheets work well for the women to wrap themselves in, break out of, etc.),

Third Session:
Photographs (Developed from the Second Session)
Colored Construction Paper
Scissors
Glue Stick and Elmer's Glue
Ribbons to Decorate and Bind the Books
Colored Pens, Metallic Pens, Fancy Pens


Description of Session One:

Introduction:
Explain the process of the three nights, and show an example book if possible. "We will be using writing and photography to express ourselves. How do you feel about writing and about photography? We will be doing expressive photography- unlike most of the photography we're used to seeing in magazines and on billboards. In other words, there's no need to make it beautiful, or make it look like any of what we see. If you're trying to express anger, rage, desperation, aggravation, etc., there's absolutely no need to look pretty! You already look perfect to express your feelings- you have exactly what you need."

Opening Circle:
Have everyone introduce themselves: "Share how you feel about art and how you feel about trying something daring today."

Set Tone:
"See these art sessions as a time just for you- a time to feel however you're feeling, and express whatever you want to. Together, we will create a separate space. Doing art is a time for you to relax and get in touch with yourself. A time to give yourself time out. So I'd like to begin by relaxing. Get yourself as comfortable as possible. Lay down, if you like. Close your eyes and take a deep, deep breath..." Proceed with the relaxation detailed in "Notes on Relaxations."

Timed Writing:
While they are opening their eyes, pass out the pens and paper to write with. Proceed with the Timed Writing "I am..." Exercise detailed in the "Creative Writing" Section. Follow through with the Echo Listening. Now ask them how they feel. Then ask them to look at their writing one more time to circle what is the most positive thing in it, and the most negative thing they find in it, as well as other things they find particularly important. These are the sections we'll focus on next session when we begin the photographs.

Closing Circle:
Complete the session by going around the circle giving every woman the opportunity to say how she feels and something she gained from the experience.


Description of Session Two:

Relaxation:
Recreate the special art space by repeating the same relaxation process as last night. Vary it if that feels right.

Opening Circle:
Give everyone the opportunity to say how she's feeling now.

Introduction:
"Today we move into transforming our words into photographic images. I'd like you to take another look at your writing. Look at the parts you've circled, or read all of it, and see if any images come to mind. As you read, imagine what position you'd be in to express what you wrote. What would be the expression on your face? Is your face showing, or is it hidden? Each woman gets up to three photos. These can illustrate a transformation that she is going through, perhaps a transformation expressed in the words. We have paper, tape, and whatever else you can find to use. Imagine what it expresses to show someone wrapped in a blanket and then show them coming out. Imagine a blank piece of paper, then a hand punching through it, then a person coming out of it. Read what you've written, and think about what you want to do in your photos." Give them a few minutes to read and think.

Photography:
Take time to develop ideas for the photos. If it feels like everyone is ready to begin taking their photos, have them begin one at a time, in front of the group. The group can provide encouragement, suggestions, and help to compose the pictures. The picture-taking tends to be an exciting process that involves everyone. If everyone seems to need time to think about what they want to create, them have them split into pairs to help each other figure out what they want to do. Then regroup for the picture taking.

Closing Circle:
Again, wrap up the session by going around the circle to give everyone the opportunity to say how it felt and what they got out of the session.


Description of Session Three:

Relaxation:
Begin with another relaxation to recreate the special environment of the workshop.

Opening Circle:
Ask how everyone's feeling today.

Introduction:
"The hard work is done. Today is a fun time to see what you've got and to make it into your book." Hand back the photographs, developed earlier at a one-hour place. Discuss and share how they came out.

Demonstration:
Show techniques of book-making like how to split the construction paper into various sizes by folding/licking/tearing. Show various methods of binding a book. Show the ribbons, papers, glues, and pens available. Discuss how the words and photos can be arranged in the book.

Book-Making:
Make the books, helping individuals as needed, to clarify what they want and create it.

Closing Circle:
Everyone can share her book, and say how she feels and what she got out of the entire workshop.

Variations:
A book could be made to address any theme. The Timed Writing and the photography could focus on anything at all: Recovery, Violence, Hope, the Family, Spirituality, My Life Story, Memories, Goals, etc. The content can be varied infinitely within the structure, and of course, the structure can be varied as well. Instead of photographs, the women could draw. Instead of creating books, the women could combine their words and images into collages.
Row.txt_description: This workshop combines relaxation and a sense of empowerment through the form of self-reflection.
Row.txt_notes: Women’s Manual pg. 78

Row.txt_code:
A beautiful butterfly kingdom was
created at Miss Julie's Preschool and Childcare.
Objective:
To give younger children an opportunity to be a part of a creative process. The children will experience the use of various art materials as well as engaging in a group activity to create something that is unique and special.











Close-up of watercolor butterfly.





Materials:
Wooden clothespins (w/ springs or not)
Large coffee filters
Pipe cleaners (metallic or multi-color)
White or tacky glue
Small google eyes
Fabric squares 4x4 size (Can be used in place of coffee filters for children who are not able to maneuver the markers or watercolor brushes.  For example, children with fine or gross motor (skill) difficulties. Children enjoy mixing the patterns of fabric and creating their very own butterfly colony.  This version also works well with children with short attention spans.
Yarn (for stringing)
Markers
Watercolors
Wire hangers (mobiles for 3 butterflies) optional
Tooth picks (for gluing the eyes)
Hair dryer
Masking tape (for mobiles and to station the coffee filters for really small children)





 Coffee filter painted with watercolor.





Using a hair-dryer to dry more quickly.





Gathering in the middle.





Securing with a clothespin.





Preparing the pipe-cleaner antennae.



Timeframe:
1 hour - 1 1/2 (depending on the size of the group and their ages)

Age Range:
This activity can be done with children as young as 2 yrs. of age with adequate supervision (suggested 1 adult with 1-2 toddlers).  For children 3 yrs. and up in a small group setting, the suggested ratio is 4 children to 1 adult.

Set-up:
Place newspaper on the tables or covers (tape down for small children).  Set out watercolor trays, markers, brushes, one coffee filter at each setting, pipe cleaners, wooden clothes pins, small paper plates or container with a tbsp. of glue, 2-3 tooth picks (to apply the glue for the eyes, dries faster.  Too much glue can be very messy.  Place the google eyes in a bowl to pass around towards the end of the process.  For the smaller children use a maker for the eyes.  This will prevent choking.  Allow enough space between each child for them to create.

Introduction:
Today we are going to create a colorful butterfly.  We are going to begin by reading a story called " The Very Hungry Caterpillar."  You may ask the children questions about the book or about the butterfly. Has anyone ever seen a butterfly? Get them involved. What makes butterflies special? What color is a butterfly?  What do butterflies eat? For smaller children have them physically act out the 4 stages of a butterfly's life: first, a tiny egg, so very small; second, a hungry caterpillar, searching for food; next finding a dry safe place to build a comfortable cocoon; and finally emerging as a beautiful butterfly, spreading its wings and flying for the first time. If the area is spacious allow the children to follow you around the room flying.  This is a wonderful workshop to do outdoors if the weather permits. Young children will enjoy being a part of dramatic play.

Creation:
You want to begin the group by going step by step with the children. Have them begin to decorate their coffee filter using watercolors, markers or crayons. You may have to tape down the sides of the filter for the aggressive movement of crayons and markers. Use a hair dryer to dry the wet paint. This speeds up the process. Have the children gather the center of the coffee filter and placing it in between the clothespin.  Once they have done this have them pick out a pipe cleaner of their choice and bend it down the center and curl the ends around their finger.  Some children may want to bend it themselves, that's fine. The eyes should be added on as the very last step.  Use the toothpicks, dipping the end into the glue, and placing a drop on the area where the eyes will be going.   This helps you avoid using too much glue.  Children often choose the location of where they want their butterfly's eyes to be.  Give them the freedom to be in control of their art.  It's important they take ownership for their work.

To create mobiles use the yarn to tie around the opposite ends of the clothespin to balance the butterfly and string onto a wire hanger. Use masking tape to cover the tip of the hanger to prevent injury.




Butterflies suspended from a wire hanger.




Closing:
Have the children share their work one by one.
Row.txt_description: This workshop was designed to give younger children an opportunity to take part in a creative process. The children will experience the use of various art materials as well as engaging in a group activity to create something that gives them the freedom to take ownership of their artwork.

Row.txt_code:
My Happy Self creations.
 
Objective:
To give young children an opportunity to express happiness through their art. To help them focus on themselves and share their feelings with others. The end result will create a “People Rainbow” of happiness for all to see.



Materials:
Lg. & sm. white paper plates
“People Color” paints, markers, and crayons (found at Lakeshore Learning Store, or choose colors from your materials that can be used for different types of skin tones. Choose enough to represents the cultural rainbow of life. You can also experiment with the children by mixing different skin tones using the paint (white, brown, red and yellow).
Wide popsicle sticks
Tacky glue
Google eyes
Yarn, shredded or crinkled paper for the hair (brown, black, red and yellow)
Hair dryer
  


 My Happy Self creation.

Timeframe:
1 hour

Age Range /Adult to Child Ratio:
1 adult to 6 children

Set-up:
Cover the tabletops with newspaper. Place the following items at each setting: plate, popsicle stick, crayons, makers and glue. Place the different colors of paint, yarn, crinkle or shredded paper for the hair, and the google eyes in the center of each table. Allow the children to choose these materials on their own.

Introduction:
“Today we are going to create our ‘Happy Selves’ and share our happy faces with each other. This workshop is about celebrating our smiles and good feelings.” (You may want to begin by asking is there anyone who has a happy thought or story and would like to share? You may begin to explore other feelings and talk about those as well but center the workshop on creating a happy place.)
  


David's My Happy Self creation.
 

Optional Warm-up or Opening Circle:
You may lead this part of the group with a song, "If You’re Happy and you Know It Clap Your Hands." The children will enjoy opening with a song that spreads cheer to everyone. This is great for younger children (3-6 yrs. old). For children who are a bit older you may want them to go around the room and introduce themselves and share a happy thought or feeling with the group.

Creation:
Have the children begin by choosing paint, crayon or maker for their skin tone. Once they have made their choice it's time to color in the face (white paper plate). You may want to experiment by having the children take one finger and dip it into the color they think is closest to their own skin tone. The children will enjoy matching the paint to their skin. You can share with the group how each of us is different and unique. We all are very special because we are different. We are all Beautiful. Once the children have chosen their colors they can begin to paint. (You may want to speed up the drying process by using a hair dryer.) They can follow with adding eyes, a nose and a mouth. Then have the children choose their hair color. Once their face is complete, they will attach the large popsicle stick to the backside of the plate (flat side). If you are working with the younger children it may help to adhere the sticks prior to the group.
  


 My Happy Self creations.

Closing:
Close with a final thought from children about their work. Have them express one thing they enjoyed most about creating their Happy Face.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives young children an opportunity to express happiness through their art. To help them focus on themselves and share their feelings with others. The end result will create a “People Rainbow” of happiness for all to see.
Row.txt_tips: Make sure there is enough glue.  If this workshop is done with younger children who tend to be messier, glue sticks may be a neater alternative to tacky glue.

Row.txt_code:
Sock puppet.
Objective:
To help children of all ages voice feelings, emotions, fears and inner thoughts. To empower children and give them new confidence, freedom and joy through puppetry.  

Note:
Puppets have been around for over 3000 years and they can be made out of almost anything.  We will explore 2 techniques in this workshop.  Feel free to try other techniques as well (like paper plate puppets, paper bag puppets, etc.




This spoon puppet is a fork!!


Materials:
Yarn
Feathers
Buttons
Fabric Scraps
Glue
Sequins
Pom Poms
Pipe Cleaners
Markers
Wood Pieces
Wooden Spoons and/or Socks
    (depending on which type of puppets you are        making)

Timeframe:
45 minutes to 1 hour

Age Range /Adult to Child Ratio:
3 and up.  One adult to every 3-4 children.
Set-up:
Lay out all the materials for the children to select–since each puppet will have its unique look it is helpful to have a wide assortment of materials.  Feel free to add to the list above including paper cups, sponges, egg cartons, old gloves, paper towel rolls and clothes pins! Be sure to use a strong holding glue (or glue gun if you have enough adults).





This sock puppet has shades made out of
buttons and pipe cleaners.

Introduction:
You can start by talking about puppets; ask the children if they have seen a puppet maybe even a shadow puppet.  You can explain that a puppet is any object that appears to be alive when it’s set in motion by a human hand.  A puppet can have its own personality, voice and even it’s own language.  Half the fun of the workshop is watching the puppets come alive and in that process the children discover a new way to be expressive.

Optional Warm-up or Opening Circle:
To get the children used to the idea of a puppet you can have an opening circle and ask each participant select a sock out of a pile and then put that sock on their hand.  Ask each person to name the “sock” and say how the sock is feeling – shy, excited, scared, angry, happy etc.  Then you can begin to decorate.  The puppets name may change once more of the personality evolves and the feelings may change as well.  This will be reflected in the closing circle.




This spoon puppet has a full set of
clothing made from felt.


Creation:
You may want to begin with the sock puppet, as it is the easiest for children of all ages to make and operate. Show how when you put your hand in the sock, with the thumb in the heel and your fingers in the toe section – you have the beginnings of a puppet already! Next is adding eyes, mouth, hair and any accessories like glasses, hats etc.  You can practice talking by having the puppet count to 25 – experimenting with the different ways the mouth moves for each number.  If you have the time you can have the children stand in front of a mirror and study how the mouth movements change with each number.  As you feel more comfortable you can enhance the sock puppets with things like construction paper beaks for birds, floppy felt or cloth ears for dogs, a cup paper cup to extend a nose of a dragon or inset red fabric or paper to make a large mouth (you can even add teeth)!  An old sock can easily be converted to a simple or complex puppet!

Spoon puppets can also be made with anything with a long thin handle – like wire wisks, feather dusters or paintbrushes.  The bowl of the spoon makes a perfect head, gluing a yarn wig makes the hair and you can use pipe cleaners for the arms. Dress the spoon with a piece of fabric with a hole cut in the middle for the head. As the puppet develops a personality you can build a story about who she/he is and where she/he came from!





This sock puppet has big lips made out of red felt.

Closing:
Ask each participant to have their puppet introduce him/herself using the voice of the puppet stating something about themselves like telling a story, talking about a hobby or a made-up adventure the puppet has had.

Additional Steps:
You may even want to plan for a puppet show.  Making up a story with all the characters the children created and performing in a show can be great fun. The possibilities are endless!!

Be prepared, often children will act out their own story or secrets – pretending it to be the puppet’s story. The puppet can give a voice to pain, it can empower shy children and it can be a great tool to nurture creativity.  Have fun!
Row.txt_description: This workshop was designed to help children of all ages voice feelings, emotions, fears and inner thoughts through puppetry. To empower children and give them new confidence, freedom and joy.

Row.txt_code:
Sample "Safe Place" worksheet made into a collage.

About this Workshop:
This workshop is the sixth in the “Creative Scrapbook” series created by Carolyn Coleman Manns of Laurel House in Pennsylvania.
Through this series, Carolyn powerfully links creative expression to the shelter’s basic DV curriculum.

Objective:
To support participants in creating a safe space they can go to in their minds when they are facing stressful situations, and in identifying ways to build safety and security in their lives.

This project can be a good compliment to working on a domestic violence safety plan.

Materials:
Markers and colored pencils
Large black construction paper
Glue sticks
Magazines (could consist of travel
magazines, children’s
magazines, family magazines, ebony and essence magazines, etc.)
Scissors
“Safe Place” Handout (optional - click here for handout)
Puffy paints (optional)

Timeframe: 2 hrs
 
 Sample "Safe Place" collage.
 

Intro & Sharing: 30 min
Sharing: 20 min
Creation: 60 min
Closing 30 min

Intro & Sharing:
“Sometimes stress arrives or a stressful situation arises and we cannot escape. If it is appropriate, you can escape by creating a safe place in your mind. Think hard about that picture. What would a safe place look like to you if you could go there in your mind?"

When that discussion is over as a group, have them think about options and remedies to relieve stress. You can start out by giving a few examples: running, journaling, a hot bath with candles, music, walking in the woods, etc.

Creation:
Play soothing music. Ask each resident to write for ten minutes about what her safe place would look like, smell like, etc.

You can use the “Safe Place” handout (attached), or just use any paper. Give each person a paper for writing, as well as the construction paper on which to put their project and word descriptions. Encourage everyone to write down a complete description.

Have each participant turn her words into a picture on paper by drawing, cutting out pictures or words, and mounting her drawing and words onto the large black paper.
        
        
      
      Safe PLace Sample
 
        
        
       
 Safe Place Sample Collage
      




















Closing Circle:
Have each person share her creation and discuss how it felt to create a safety zone for herself. Talk about the highlights and any not-so-positive thoughts as well.
Row.txt_description: This workshop was designed to support participants in creating a safe place where they can go to in their minds when facing stressful situations, and in identifying ways to build safety and security in their lives. This project can be a good compliment to working on a domestic violence safety plan.
Row.txt_tips:
Window's leader Mercedes Brown created the following poem during the Safe Place workshop.  Feel free to use it as a warm up or part of an introduction when you do the workshop.

A Safe Place
by Mercedes Brown
My place is in the universe, amongst the heaven and the earth.
A place where I can be me, without others complaining how they think I should be.
Where I should be — when I am me.
A safe place to be on earth in this place called me.
A body, a mind and a soul exploring what it means to be free, in this world called me.
My safe place is inside of me.

Row.txt_code:
About this Workshop:
          
          Life Line unfolds from a Scrapbook

This workshop is the seventh in the “Creative Scrapbook” series created by Carolyn Coleman Manns of Laurel House in Pennsylvania. Through this series, Carolyn powerfully links creative expression to the shelter’s basic DV curriculum.

Objective:
To have each participant examine her Life Line and identify any abuses in her life. To set up a plan not to accept abuse from anyone: on the job, home, place of worship, mutual friends, and community.

Note:
This workshop invites participants to think about their entire life history and memories. It is important to consider carefully whether or not this would be appropriate and useful for your group of clients. It is also important to set up a support system so that participants can have follow-up support after the group if they would like it. 

Materials:
Newsprint rolls or large sheets of newsprint of rolls are hard to find. (We get the ends of
     the rolls of paper from a newspaper company donated, since they usually throw them
     away.)

 Life Line of events of a surviver's life

Markers
Colored pencils
Paint
Paint brushes
Scissors
Magazines (For people who don’t like to
    draw, they can use words, pictures, and
    letters out of the magazines.)

Timeframe:  2.5 hrs
Introduction: 30 min.
Creation: 90 min.
Closing Process: 30 min.

Intro & Sharing:
This project will give you a chance to reflect on your life from the beginning of your memory of childhood until you walked into this shelter. It’s a chance to examine your
  
Life Line sample
 
Life Line and notice any abuses in your life.  Doing a Life Line can be a very powerful experience. By looking at their whole lives, some survivors realize that the cycle of violence started from a young age. The Life Line can sometimes display how abuse has a pattern and how it may continue if the cycle is not broken. Looking at your Life Line can be a useful step in seeing the whole picture and setting up a plan not to accept abuse from anyone: on the job, home, place of worship, mutual friends, and community.

Creation:
Give each resident a roll of paper that they can use to document each event with a drawing and short story about the event. Each event will be connected by a line, the last event will be entering the doors of the shelter and the event that caused them to come into the shelter. They can be as graphic as they want. Encourage them to take a minute to reflect on their entire life. Have them think about events in their life that they have not forgotten, both positive and negative. Encourage them to remember the year. The events will be connected by a date, year, age, and a line: event to event.)




 Early memories in a Life Line

 Later memories in a Life LIne

 Recent memories in a Life Line








Closing Circle:
Get each participant’s comment on how this project made her feel. Discuss feelings that are hard to deal with, and set up a support system for sharing any feelings beyond the timeframe of the group. Some feelings may be processed with the group leader or one on one with a counselor. Process all feelings about the project.
Row.txt_description: This workshop was created to have each participant examine her Life Line and identify any abuse in her life. Seeing the whole Life Line picture can help participants as they set up a plan not to accept abuse from anyone: on the job, home, place of worship, mutual friends, and community.

Row.txt_code:
A beautiful Inspirational Scroll, created by Anna Reyner.
Objective:
This workshop helps participants access their deepest feelings through the use of writing and Liquid Watercolors to create an Inspirational Scroll.

Materials: (Workshop supplies can be purchased at www.discountschoolsupply.com )
Liquid Watercolors in primary or assorted colors
Metallic Liquid Watercolors in silver and gold (optional for added accents)
Spray bottles
Squeeze bottles to use with Metallic Watercolors
Mural Art Paper/ Paper Drop Cloth (any size - we made ours 12x20)
Dowels or chop sticks (2 inches wider than the Mural Art Paper to be used)
Permanent markers
Colored ribbon cord
Scissors
Tacky Glue
Card stock or natural fiber paper for words and stencils
Paper towels
Plastic stencils (Optional)
Bell or chimes (Optional)
Poetry writing prompts (word prompt on strength, or prompt with different themes)

 
  The poem can be decorated too!
Timeframe:
Intro: 5 minutes
Warm Up: 10 minutes
Meditation: 5 minutes
Demo/Creation: 1 hour
Closing: 10 minutes
Total Time: 1 to 1 1/2 hours

Note: It may be helpful for this workshop to be done in two sessions. The first focusing on designing the scroll with the Liquid Watercolors, and the second focusing on writing the poetry and mounting it on the scroll.

  
An assortment of fun materials.
  
Set Up:
Prepare the supplies by placing the Liquid Watercolor paint in spray bottles and the Metallic Liquid Watercolors in squeeze bottles (the metallic colors will be drizzled or dripped as accent colors). Cut the Mural Art Paper in any size you like; ideally the Mural Art Paper should be at least 60% longer than the width to make a panel shape.

Spraying the Liquid Watercolors can be messy, so prep the tables with washable table cloths or newspaper. You may even want to do the spaying outside where there is room to spread out and where the sun will accentuate the colors!

Introduction:
Make sure to take time to welcome everyone, and let them know that their presence is really appreciated. Have soothing music on as people settle in. "This art time is a special 'window of time' for you, where we will be using words and watercolors to access deep feelings of strength and inspiration, creating beautiful Inspirational Scrolls. We’ll begin our workshop by spending quiet time together and honoring those in our life who have given us strength. We’ll begin our art project with a demonstration of how to spray the Liquid Watercolors to get beautiful color effects. Then we’ll mount our messages onto our art panels and add rainbow silk cord and beads to make Inspirational Scrolls!"

Warm Up:
Pass around a chime, or bell, and have each participant take turns striking the bell as it is passed around the circle. As they strike the bell have them say “In honor of ..." and name someone who gives, or has given, them strength. Pause between each person so they can reflect on who they will chose to honor.

The leader can begin, setting the example by making the bell tone and saying something such as, “I ring this bell in honor of my mother Betty whose loving support gives me strength.” Then the leader will pass the instrument for each participant to take a turn ringing the chime and saying her own words of honor.

When all are finished, have the women hold hands, while the leader says “we gather here today to honor ourselves, to honor the process of healing that lives in us, and to honor those in our lives who have given us strength. We are all stronger today because of your presence. Thank you for being here."

Meditation:
Ask everyone to sit comfortably for a brief guided meditation. In a calm, nurturing voice, guide participants with this dialogue: “If you are comfortable, close your eyes gently, if not you may keep them open, as you join me on an imaginary journey. Pay attention to your breathing, as you breathe in and out. Relax and let your imagination be your guide. Join me in a bright green meadow on a sunny day and feel the warm sun on your body as you walk through the meadow, safe and happy. Watch the sparkle of sunlight on colorful wildflowers all around you. Hear, see and feel the beautiful nature surrounding you. Find yourself completely at peace. (pause)

As you walk in the sunlight through this meadow, notice a small stream of water bubbling swiftly over small rocks as it flows through the meadow. Walk along the stream, and continue to feel the warm sun on your back (pause). How do you feel? (pause) What sounds capture your attention? (pause). Continue along this stream of water until you find yourself at the edge of a small forest. You peer inside the forest and see that it’s safe and inviting. You continue to follow the stream that leads into the lush, beautiful forest with sunlight beaming through the trees. Listen to the sounds of the birds. Listen to the sounds of the bubbling stream as it meanders farther into the forest. Sit down nearby to take it in. Notice how you are feeling and settle in and make yourself comfortable.

Allow yourself to experience this "scared space" fully. Know that this scared space lives within you, and that you can draw upon it again whenever you need to. Invite whoever you honored today to join you. Allow yourself to feel strong, compassionate and well cared for. Allow yourself to feel loved.

Keep this sense of relaxation and peace within you, and slowly open your eyes. You’ve come here today to join with others in healing, to find strength in a community of people who genuinely care about you and your needs."

 
 Spraying the Liquid Watercolors to layer colors.
  
 
  You can use stencils to create designs of all shapes!
  
 
  Shade and layer stencils to create beautiful effects.
Demo:
Introduce how to use the Liquid Watercolor sprays on a “scratch” panel of Mural Art Paper. Demonstrate how to use the "mist" spray option rather than the "stream" spray option on the spray bottles. This will give a much more fluid effect.

Demonstrate how by layering primary colors there are lots of possibilities. Demonstrate by spraying first yellow then overlapping with blue to show how the colors blend to make green where they overlap. Then add a stencil, either a plastic pre-made stencil or hand-made stencil, and spray over that. Repeat this process by lifting, overlapping, and re-spraying with various colors.

A hand-made stencil can be made by using the card stock paper and tearing it into the desired shapes. One can then use the "negative" or "positive" of the stencil (the cut out itself or the paper it was cut from). One can also use leaves or other objects as stencils too, which is especially fun if the project is taking place outside. When using the stencils spray from the side (not straight on) for a better effect and more options. For a "shading" effect spray one side with a darker color, then spray with another color from a different side to make it two toned.

When layering a lot the stencil image can disappear. If the participant wants to see the stencil pattern encourage them to not layer too many colors on the scroll, and to make sure to use the stencil towards the end.

Keep in mind, this project is all about abstract color, so there are no "mess ups." Play with the paint until you like the blending and patterns that are created. Even the darker "muddy" areas can be turned into something beautiful by adding the metallic colors. Take gold and silver watercolors and drizzle or drip those as accent colors on top, or you can even paint them onto the scroll. When your are finished painting lay the Mural Art Paper to dry on paper towels.

Creation:
Now, we will create Inspirational Scrolls or wall hangings, that help us remember our strengths, our time together today and our ability to create a scared space.

 
 You can even use a real leaf as a stencil!
  
 
  Add accents with Metallic Watercolors.
Step 1:
Spray entire panel with a variety of colors. Use stencils to create patterns, layer, and overlap colors.

Step 2:
Add gold and silver Metallic Watercolors by dripping, drizzling, or painting them on as accent colors.

Step 3:
Put the scroll aside to dry.

Step 4:
While the scroll panel dries we will do a writing exercise. Ask the group to reflect on the people and things that give them strength, hope and courage. Then have participants write a poem, message or words about those people and things that have inspired them in their lives.

If you choose to you may want to pass out writing prompts (see links in materials section) to help participants focus their writing. The word "strength" can be substituted with the words "hope," "courage," "inspiration," or "power."

When they have finished writing down their words of strength, hope, courage, and/or power, have each person transfer their words, or "poems" onto card stock or other heavy weight paper such as natural fiber paper.

When the messages are finished, use Tacky Glue to attach the card stock onto their painted Mural Art Paper.

Step 5/ Final Step:
To create your scroll you will glue in place two dowels or chop sticks (depending on the size of your scroll) at the top and bottom of the scroll. Fold over the top of the scroll to create a small (1") flap to insert the dowel into. Then have them put glue onto the back side of this fold, then lay down the dowel and fold the flap over to secure the dowel inside. Leave a small section of dowel (1" or less out from each side) to later hang ribbon from. Repeat at the bottom with a second dowel. To finish the scroll tie the ribbon cord to each end of the dowel, adding beads onto the cord for added flair.

Closing Circle:
When everyone is finished have each of the participants share their scrolls with each other. Give each participant an opportunity to share with the group and congratulate them on their beautiful creations and for sharing their strengths!

Encourage them to keep these scrolls as a special reminder of their strength and what inspires them. They can be hung on a wall, kept near a bed, or rolled up and carried with them.
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps participants access their deepest feelings through the use of writing and Liquid Watercolors to create an Inspirational Scroll.
Row.txt_tips:
Elvira Barnard of Chicana Service Action Center asked clients to bring their favorite poem to group to use in their art piece.

Wendy Ball of Equinox, Inc. used these Inspirational Quotes as an examples:
A Friendship Blessing: (adapted from Anam Cara – a book of celtic wisdom by John O’Donnohue)
May I be blessed with good friends.
May I learn to be a good friend to myself.
May I be able to journey to that place in my soul
where there is great love, warmth, feeling,
and forgiveness.
May this change me.
May it transfigure that which is negative,
distant, or cold in me.
May I be brought in to the real passion, kinship,
and affinity of belonging.
May I treasure my friends.
May I be good to them and may I be there for them;
May they bring me all the blessings, challenges,
truth, and light that I need for my journey.
May I never be isolated.
May I always be in the gentle nest of belonging
with my soul

A Blessing of Solitude: (adapted from Anam Cara – a book of celtic wisdom by John O’Donnohue)
May I recognize in my life the presence, power, and light of my soul.
May I realize that I am never alone,
that my soul in its brightness and belonging connects me intimately
with the rhythm of the universe.
May I have respect for my own
Individuality and difference.
May I realize that the shape of my soul is unique,
that I have a special destiny here,
that behind the façade of my life there is something beautiful, good and eternal happening.
May I learn to see myself with the same delight, pride, and expectation with which God sees me in every moment.

DV Affirmations: (some affirmations from Melody Beattie)
I’m no longer willing to lose my self esteem, self respect, my children’s well-being, my job, home, possessions, safety, credit, my sanity or myself to preserve a relationship.

I don’t have to be willing to lose everything for love.

I can learn to make appropriate choices concerning what I’m willing to give in my relationships of myself, time, talents, and money

As I develop healthy boundaries I am learning to respect others and myself.  I am learning not to use or abuse others or allow them to use or abuse me.  I no longer abuse myself!  I am learning not to control others or let them control me.  I am learning to stop taking responsibility for other people and stop letting them take responsibility for me.  I am learning to take full responsibility for myself.

I am proud of myself for accepting to take care of myself no matter what happens, where I go, or who I’m with.

I am proud of myself for believing that I deserve a better life and for acting on this belief.

I have the right to take care of myself and to be myself.

I am learning to value, trust and listen to myself.

I am able to choose and to alter the direction of my life.

I own and treasure my life!

I am not stuck or trapped in a relationship.  I have choices.  I may not be able to see them clearly right now, but I do have choices.  I am responsible for my choices.

Row.txt_code:
Purpose:
To create a bead or beads that represent how you want your future to be.

Materials:
colored SuperSculpey (If you only have plain SuperSculpey, you will need painting supplies to add colors)
toot hpicks and plastic utensils (to create holes and form the clay)
toaster oven
embroidery floss, string, wire, thread, or ribbon (to thread the beads)
large needles
optional: gel roller pens
optional: clear nail polish (to add shine at the end)
pens and writing paper (teens could also use their journals instead)
independent project handout (for individual workshop) (click here for handout)

Set Up:
Set the supplies on the table, making sure that the supplies are accessible from each place at the table.

Welcome and Ground Rules:
It can help create a safe environment if you take time to individually welcome each teen, connect with them, and let them know you are glad they are there. Introduce the project and the philosophy of Windows time: "This is a special "window of time" for each of you. For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? Are there any other Ground Rules you'd like to add?" At this time you can mention any pre-established ground rules you have.

Check In:
A good example of an appropriate check-in would be: "Before we start the art, we'll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art." This is a time to reassure anyone who's scared of art that it's fine, and to tell anyone who "hates" art that's fine too. Remind them that they don't have to do it, that they can just watch if they want to. When given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in even if they say they're just going to watch. Let them know that it's fine if they don't want to say anything for "check-in", too.

Optional Journaling:
"Write for five minutes about your future. Write whatever thoughts come to mind. You could start with the words, 'My future...' and grab whatever thoughts come to mind first."

Project Suggestion:
"This workshop is a chance to create a bead (or set of beads) that represent your future. What is important to you in your future? How would you like to be as a person? What are the qualities you'd like to have? What colors would you use for each thought? What shapes? Go ahead and make as many beads as you would like for your future. As you form each one, use the toothpick to make holes. Be sure to make the holes large enough for whatever thread or string you want to put through them. Once the holes are all ready, go ahead and cook your beads (about ten minutes at 275 degrees). When you are finished, take time to write any words that go with your beads. If you have gel-roller pens, you can write directly on the Sculpey."

Optional Feedback Exercise:
Ten minutes before the workshop ends, pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You could even take them to copy and return them the next week, so that the teens can add them to their journals.

Closing and Validation:
At the end of the project, a Closing Circle can be a way to give each teen an opportunity to share what she or he has created and talk about what it means to them and how it felt to make it. Just like the check-in circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives teens an opportunity to create a bead or set of beads representing how they want their futures to be.

Row.str_title: Footprints in the Sand and other Sand Painting Workshops
Row.txt_code:
Joanne Webb and sample Sand Painting
Objective:
Gives participants an opportunity to explore the footprints in their heart, regarding the journey that is their life and the challenges that have been overcome or are being dealt with now. Through using the technique of sand painting, inspired by a Native American tradition, participants explore their journey and a vision for a brighter and more productive future.

Materials:
Colored Sand (can be purchased in jars from Oriental Trading)
Plastic tube containers with pour spout (for the sand)
White glue
Glue stick
9” – 12” heavy black construction paper
Colored construction paper
Fiskars foot paper puncher (used for scrap-booking)
Colored pencils
Toothpicks
Tablecloths or placemats
Music (Please let us know if you would like us to send you a copy of Baby Blue,
Native American Music by Carlos Reynosa)
Native American Sand Painting background handout


 
Sand Painting Materials 
Timeframe:
Intro: 5 minutes
Relaxation: 5 minutes
Journaling (optional): 5 minutes
Creation with pencils: 25 minutes
Creation with sand: 35 minutes
Closing Circle: 15 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour 30 minutes

Set Up:
Transfer the different color sand into smaller plastic tube containers to be used in the workshop. It is best to do this with a funnel. Have tablecloths, or placemats, on the tables for this workshop so that clean-up is easier. You may want to create small footprints with the foot paper puncher before the workshop so that they are ready for the participants to use. This can be done with different color construction paper to create variety. Have a minimum of 10 pairs of feet per participants. Lay out an assortment of the colored sand and other materials. Lay out an assortment of the colored sand and other materials.

Introduction:
What we are going to do today is a sand painting journey called Footprints in the Sand. This project has been inspired by the Native American art form known as sand painting. In the Native American tradition sand paintings were created to heal a person during a healing ceremony. Today we are going to create our own type of healing ceremony by using our sand paintings to tell a story of our journey (you may want to use the Native American Sand Painting Background Handout provided).

In life, in everything we go through, there are challenges and positive experiences, setbacks and things we overcome. What we are going to do is tell this story in a simple way using symbols and words. Your story can be anything it needs to be. You can look at where your path has gone and where you want it to go. The main objective will be to look at your story in a way that helps you explore a vision for a brighter future. This is an experience just for you.

 
  Sketching symbols from their story
 
  Outlining images with glue
 
  Sprinkling sand on images
Meditation/Relaxation:
I like to focus on the chakras, spiritual spaces in the body. Take a breath in each one, starting from the base of the spine, lower abdomen, belly, heart, throat, third eye (between eyebrows) to the crown of the head. We then go back to the heart and treat it as if it were a piece of canvas for us to paint on. The meditation in the heart is a form of creative visualization and can go like this:

"Take a moment and breathe deeply in your heart three times. (Feel your heart and the stories it holds.) Then begin to envision how far you have come in your life to this healing place. Rediscover yourself and the future you would like to co-create. When thinking of the past, think about symbols that could best express that particular moment in your journey. If it is a negative experience involving abuse or any other kind of pain, you might want to look at it as a lightening rod, tornados, fire, monsters, etc. When you reach areas where you have positive experiences or visions for the future, those symbols could be that of sunshine, rainbows, a butterfly, a sunset along the ocean, a house or a flourishing garden. These symbols are just suggestions, they will vary for each person as you may come up with something that is more creatively powerful for you. Just take this time to concentrate on your breathing and begin to envision a picture that takes you on your journey. "

Give them about 5 minutes to explore, then take them through their chakras again with a deep breath through each one. From the crown of the head to the third eye to the throat to the heart to the belly to the lower abdomen and finally to the lower part of the spine. They can then open their eyes.

Journaling (optional):
It may be helpful to allow the participants to journal about what came up for them. They can start with the prompt "my journey is..." or "my journey begins..." or "I would like my journey to lead to..." Put on relaxing music, possibly Native American music, softly in the background.

Creation:
Begin by taking 2 pieces of black construction paper and with a glue stick glue them together (one on top of the other) to make the paper stronger. We are going to use a lot of glue and don't want to paper to wilt! Next take a light colored pencil and begin to
 
Adding the footprints
 
 
Mapping out our journey
 
 
A finished sample
 
draw and sketch out your journey on the construction paper. Draw about six different symbols that are a part of your story, let it unfold. Use as many colors as you want. Think about where you've been and where you want to go. Don't worry about getting it perfect, just focus on the symbols for now. Enjoy the journey...

Once the drawing is completed demonstrate how to work with the sand with a sample drawing. First you squeeze the white glue to outline or fill in the first shape of your drawing. Choose the color of sand you want to use and place some in the palm of your hand. With your index and thumb fingertips sprinkle the sand onto the glue. Then lift the paper and shift it around to fill any gaps, next curl the paper to empty any loose sand back into your hand. If there are still gaps repeat this again and again with the remaining sand in your hand. You can even mix and blend colors by the way you sprinkle them.

Keep in mind that sand painting is a Native American art form and that respecting nature, earth and the materials are a part of their culture. Therefore any extra sand of a particular color should be placed back in its container when done. Once the project begins they will get into the rhythm of this process. This makes for a very meditative experience.

When clients have completed their sand paintings pass out tiny colored footprint shapes (which you have punched out of colored construction paper using the Fiskars footprint puncher). They can use these footprints to track their journey, placing them right, left, right, left into the sand to show the path they walked. The clients can glue stick the tiny footprints onto their sand painting, emphasizing their journeys through their challenges to a place of hope and new possibilities.

Closing Circle:
At the end give all of the participants a chance to share their sand painting and take the group through their individual journeys. This is a very powerful art project and the participants come away with a stronger sense of where they started on their journey, how far they have traveled, and a stronger vision for their futures.

Share with them that when we take time to explore our own stories we learn so much from them. And when we share our stories it often helps others. It's powerful and empowering to share our own stories. Thank them for exploring their own stories and where their footprints have taken them. This life of ours is a journey and it's empowering to know that we can choose which way we want our path to lead next!
Row.txt_description: Gives participants an opportunity to learn new ways of telling their story. Through using the technique of sand painting, inspired by a Native American tradition, participants will use symbols to tell a story they would like to share.

Row.txt_code:
Purpose:
To create a three-dimensional figure representing yourself.

Materials:
fabric scraps
yarn
newspaper
masking tape
feathers
beads
pipe-cleaners
markers
white school glue
pens and writing paper (teens could also use their journals)
independent project handout (for individual workshop) (click here for handout)

Set Up:
Set out the supplies on the table, making sure the supplies are accessible from each seat.

Welcome and Ground Rules:
It can help create a safe environment if you take time to individually welcome each teen, connect with them, and let them know you are glad they are there. Introduce the project and the philosophy of Windows time: "This is a special "window of time" for each of you. For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? Are there any other Ground Rules you'd like to add?" At this time you can mention any pre-established ground rules you have.

Check In:
A good example of an appropriate check-in would be: "Before we start the art, we'll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art." This is a time to reassure anyone who's scared of art that it's fine, and to tell anyone who "hates" art that's fine too. Remind them that they don't have to do it, that they can just watch if they want to. When given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in even if they say they're just going to watch. Let them know that it's fine if they don't want to say anything for "check-in", too.

Optional Journaling:
"Write for five minutes starting with the phrase 'I believe...' and notice whatever comes to mind."

Project Suggestion:
"This workshop is a chance to create a spirit self - a three-dimensional figure representing yourself. It could represent the you that you show the world. It could represent the you that's hidden on the inside. Whatever part of yourself you want to express is the right part. There is no wrong way to create your figure. Use your imagination!
If you like, you can roll up pieces of newsprint into shapes for the body or head, and use the masking tape to secure the paper. Then wrap it in fabric to cover the newsprint. You can add anything that comes to mind. When you feel finished, take some time to write any words that go with your spirit self. Does it have a name? Does it have a message for you?"

Optional Feedback Exercise:
Ten minutes before the workshop ends, pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You could even take them to copy and return them the next week, so that the teens can add them to their journals.

Closing and Validation:
At the end of the project, a Closing Circle can be a way to give each teen an opportunity to share what she or he has created and talk about what it means to them and how it felt to make it. Just like the check-in circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives teens an opportunity to imagine and create a three-dimensional figure representing themselves.

Row.txt_code:
Purpose:
To start a journal by collaging the cover. To make this journal a safe place to write or collage thoughts and feelings anytime.

Materials:
Journals (you could use spiral-bound notebooks, or create journals with a comb binder. For low budgets, a three-hole-punch and twine can work.)
Magazines/ photostock books
Glue sticks
Scissors
Clear Contact Paper or Clear Packing Tape (to protect the cover once it's done)
independent project handout (for individual workshop) (click here for handout)

Set-up:
Set out the supplies, with a journal, glue stick, and scissors at each place. Spread out the magazines for easy access.

Welcome and Ground Rules:
It can help create a safe environment if you take time to individually welcome each teen, connect with them, and let them know you are glad they are there. Introduce the project and the philosophy of Windows time: "This is a special "window of time" for each of you. For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? Are there any other Ground Rules you'd like to add?" At this time you can mention any pre-established ground rules you have.

Check-In:
Check-in is a brief opportunity for everyone to share their names, how they're feeling, and any apprehensions they may have about doing art. A good example of an appropriate check-in would be: "Before we start the art, we'll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art." This is a time to reassure anyone who's scared of art that it's fine, and to tell anyone who "hates" art that's fine too. Remind them that they don't have to do it, that they can just watch if they want to. When given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in even if they say they're just going to watch. Let them know that it's fine if they don't want to say anything for "check-in", too.

Project Suggestion:
"In this workshop, you will have a chance to begin a journal for yourself by collaging the cover. To create your collage, select images from the magazines and photostock books. Choose whatever images you feel drawn to. You don't have to understand why you choose them, just rip or cut out whatever pictures seem important to you or catch your attention. When you are ready, begin to collage them onto your journal. It helps if you start by covering the whole front of your journal with soem images or a big image to be your background. Then it's easier to add pictures on top. When you are done, take some time to begin writing in your journal. You could start with writing about what you'd like your journal to be. At the end, use clear contact paper or clear packing tape in strips to protect the cover of your journal. Wrap it around the edges of your collage."

Optional Feedback Exercise:
Ten minutes before the workshop ends, pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You could even take them to copy and return them the next week, so that the teens can add them to their journals.

Closure and Validation:
At the end of the project, a Closing Circle can be a way to give each teen an opportunity to share what she or he has created and talk about what it means to them and how it felt to make it. Just like the check-in circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.
Row.txt_description: Give participants a chance to start a journal by collaging the cover and making the journal a safe place to write or collage thoughts.

Row.txt_code:
Door design depicting a sunny spring day
  
 
  Door design depicting apple harvest
Objective:
To provide children an opportunity to decorate the doors of their residence, creating a unique and fun environment that celebrates a special occasion, holiday, or season.

Materials:
Butcher paper
Construction paper
Drawing materials and/or paint
Scissors
Novelty trim (such as stickers, ribbons, etc.)
Glue sticks/tape
Plain paper for sketching
Photos (optional)

Age Range:
5 years old to Adult

Time Frame:
This activity can be accomplished in 1 - 1/2 hours or it can be an on-going activity over several sessions.

Introduction:
We are going to have the chance to decorate our doors. The doors can reflect any occasion like a birthday, holiday or season.

Opening Circle:
Think about what you would like your door to look like and what you want it to tell others. Make a decision about what theme the door should be, for example if it is in December you can make the door look like a ginger bread house or a fireplace with stockings hanging. If it is your birthday month you can decorate the door to look like a giant cake, or if it is the start of the spring season you can do a garden with lots of beautiful flowers. You might want to think about several ideas so you can decorate another door in the months to come. Perhaps brothers and sisters in the same family would like to create a door together or groups of children may want to work on a door in teams. Once the theme is decided, ask the children if they want to share what theme they selected.

 
Door design depicting a sunny
spring day		  
Creation:
The children can choose to cover the entire door with butcher paper or just cover a section of it. Before you begin decorating, discuss what the theme is going to be. Next you might want to do a simple sketch of your plan. When working in a group you may want to have the whole group make a design plan, including what materials to use, who will work on which part of the design and what steps need to be taken to complete the project. The children may want to create a large collage, drawings, a painting or all of the above. Anything is possible – it is their door! The child or group might want to decide how long the decorated door will stay up - a week, a month or longer?

Closing Circle:
Once the door is complete, ask the children to discuss why they chose the theme and what it felt like to complete a task that everyone can see on display.

Note: You may want to make this project monthly or seasonally or you might want to hold a door-decorating contest. When holding a contest you might want to have different ways of acknowledging each "winner" in order to not have anyone feel left out. For example, if there are three doors their could be three awards, one for best teamwork, one for most colorful and one for most dedication (hard work).
Row.txt_description: To provide children an opportunity to decorate the doors of their residence, creating a unique and fun environment that celebrates a special occasion, holiday, or season.

Scissors


 
 
Creation:

To start, have each person draw a name of someone else in the group, Then make a card for that person, once that is done each participant can make additional cards for family and friends. Row.str_title: Take a Walk in My Shoes
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To give participants an opportunity to communicate what it is like to walk in their shoes and tell the story of their experience.
 
Setting up the room with all the supplies.
 
 
Embellishments to decorate the shoes.
 
 
Prepare the shoes with a white primer.
 

Materials:
Shoes (enough for participants to select from)
Acrylic paint /puffy paints
Spray paint if you have a well ventilated area
Embellishments like chains, glitter, buttons, flowers, beads, letters, feathers, rhinestones
Glitter glue
Collage materials
Tissue paper
Glue gun
Fabric/Tacky glue
Mod Podge
White Primer for the shoes – spray Gesso works well

Time Frame:
This project is best when done over several sessions.

Age Range:
9 – 18

Set-up/Prep:
We sprayed all shoes with a primer spray paint like Gesso– this eliminated the branding and creates a base for painting. Everyone can start with a blank “canvas.”

To avoid participants from all wanting the same shoe, you may want each child to draw a number that corresponds to a shoe – explain to the children that even if they didn’t get the shoe they originally wanted, it will be the images and decoration they create that will be important.


Introduction:
Experiencing domestic violence can be difficult to talk about. This workshop gives us the opportunity to tell people what it is like to be you. The idea is If others could walk a in your shoes they could better understand your life. We all want to be understood and not feel so alone. Your shoe can speak for you. You can use what ever you need to tell your story. Your shoes can tell the story of life at the shelter or before you got here.
Feel free to use all the materials you want!

   
 
  Shoes can be collages with tissue paper.
  Shoes can be painted.
 


Warm-up or Opening Circle:

 
Painting a large area -
like a boot shaped canvas!
 
  
Here are several suggestions:

1. Show a slide show of images of embellished and/or sculptural shoes that can be found online– ask the participants “What do these shoes mean to you?”

2. Pass around a box of shoes and have the children make up a story about the shoes they selected - show how shoes have personality!

3. Have the participants look at their own shoes and think about why they chose those shoes. You can ask “What does the shoe say about you?” or “Think about where those shoes have been with you, and what story they would tell?” You might even want to ask the participants to journal these stories.

4. Play the Telephone Game – one person picks up a shoe and whispers one thing about it to the person next to them then each person adds a little more to the story, and then go around the room until the end – the last person tells the story about that shoe.



   
 
  Added embellishments like feathers.
  Added embellishments like flowers.
 

Creation:
Suggested beginning:
Have the children start by drawing a shoe and adding images of things that are important to them, then brainstorm about their idea. This gives a framework and organizes the intention.

1. Explain how each material works, for example: to collage on a shoe you will use a material called Mod Podge.  This will allow you to glue paper to your shoe as well as seal and protect the collage.  Also to add heavier items to your shoe you will be using a glue gun.  Be very careful since glue guns get very hot so you will need help.
2. The first step is to paint the shoes.  The paint takes some time to dry, you might want to use a hair dryer or place them in the sun.  Also if you are going to do this workshop in more than one session, this would be a great place to end, the shoes will be all ready for the next time you meet.
3. Then add decorations. With young children give them only 2 embellishments or decorations at a time, otherwise they could get too overwhelmed with too many choices.
4. Ask the children to discuss their shoe. You could hold individual interviews – ask the kids if they would rather do it 1 on 1 or if they are comfortable in front of peers.
4. Take notes about their stories so you can document each piece.

 
  Shoes with a message.

Closing:
Ask each person to share what it was like to create a shoe, and ask them if they would be willing to tell their story.
At sharing time, wrap-up with an inspirational talk about the importance of this project and how telling their stories will help to educate others.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives participants an opportunity to communicate what it is like to walk in their shoes and tell the story of their experience.

Opening:
If you are beginning these workshops in November, you can take this opportunity to talk about what the holidays mean and discuss things to be thankful for. Also note, these workshops can be adapted to any time of the year - not just for the holidays.
Creation:
In this update we are sharing three activities - you can choose one each week. Feel free to adapt, change or modify to fit your group.

 
 
Holiday Card Making
Making and giving a personal home made card is a wonderful way to make someone feel special. To start, have each person draw a name of someone else in the group, Then make a card for that person, once that is done each participant can make additional cards for family and friends. You can add materials to make the card more detailed, such as magazines for collage, doillies, vellum papers and ribbons. (You could also skip the drawing names and just have everyone make cards for people they love!)

Materials:
Construction Paper
Colored Pencils
Markers
Craypas (especially great for getting bright colors on colored paper)
Glitter Glue or Paint
Scissors


Shrinky Dink Blessing Charms
Taking the time to think about what is good in your life and what you are grateful for is a powerful exercise especially at this time of year. You could open with a circle of blessing-sharing and then make Shrinky Dink charms. These charms can be used to hang in the window or on a tree. They can even be made into jewelry – such as a necklace, pendant, or earring.

Materials:
Shrinky Dink Material
Permanent Markers and/or Color Pencils
Scissors
Ribbon or Yarn
Beads (Optional)
Toaster Oven

(Feel free to call for more details if you’ve never used Shrinky Dinks before. They are fabulous!)

 
  For sculpey beads colors can be
swirled together
 
  Use a toothpick to create holes
before baking.
Bracelet Making
Beaded bracelets make a special a gift. They can be as simple or detailed as you like. You can string regular beads or you can make your own beads. Here are 2 methods: roll small pieces of scuply, mixing colors if you like, make a hole all the way through and bake for 10 minutes. (Feel free to experiment with the size and shape of the bead). You can also make beads from paper by cutting long narrow triangle shapes from color magazine pages. Roll the shape starting from the widest end and glue the narrow end to the rolled paper. This is an inexpensive and colorful way to make a unique beaded bracelet or necklace.

Materials:
Beads
“Home Made Beads” out of sculpey or rolled magazine paper triangles
Elastic Sting or Ribbon



To create paper beads, cut magazine pictures into triangular strips,
wrap around a toothpick and glue at the end.
Row.txt_description: This is a series of workshops with holiday themes including Holiday Cards, Shrinky Dink Blessing Charms and Bracelet making to help children find art in the holidays. The idea is to create something special to show loved ones that we care and perhaps even begin new family traditions. Creating with art during the holidays as a family can be a relaxing way to connect, bond and celebrate.

Row.txt_code:
The “Monster in Me” idea was inspired by the quilt made by Megan Torrey and the children at Good Shepherd Shelter in Los Angeles, CA.  Thanks Megan!





“Monster in Me” sample



About this Workshop:
Thanks to a generous donation from Sakura, each Children’s Windows Program has been given an ample supply of Cray-Pas for the year.  Cray-Pas are oil pastels that can be used in many diverse and fabulous ways.  “The Monster in Me” is the first in a series of workshops AWBW has developed to assist your workshop participants in fully enjoying and exploring the Cray-Pas.  The technique used here is “watercolor-resist.”  This technique, using the Cray-pas and watercolors in this three-step process, can be used to draw anything: landscapes, families, doodles, flowers, etc.  The “Monster in Me” idea is just one way of using this technique.  Enjoy, and feel free to use this technique in whatever ways you wish.   Please join us in experimenting and sharing new project ideas.

Objective:
To give the children an opportunity to be playful in exploring some of the more difficult emotions they experience.  To offer a process that will look bold and powerful, and be rewarding and satisfying for the children.  

Age-Range: 3 and up

Ratio:
1 adult for 6 children; 1 adult for 3 young children.





Cray-Pas set



Materials:
Craypas sets (one set per child)
Thick white paper (8 1/2” x 11” is good)
Spray bottle filled with water
Watercolor sets (one set per child)
Watercolor brushes (one per child)
Newsprint to cover the table
Cups of water for rinsing the brushes
Paper towels for drying the brushes

Timeframe:
Opening:  5 min
Monster Dance warm-up:  5 min
Technical demonstration:  10 min
Creation:  30 min
Closing:  10 min

Space Setup:
Cover the table with newspapers.  Open the Craypas sets in advance.  Open each watercolor set and spray lightly with water.  The water helps soften the colors so that they will be easy to use when the children paint.  Prepare the cups of water for brush rinsing.  Place supplies out of reach, (if necessary, depending on the age level), and bring out when needed.   Have a space for the “Monster Dance” to occur, away from the art supplies.






Step 1: Drawing the Monster (Cray-Pas)

Step 2: Watering the Monster (spray bottle)



Opening:
“Today, we’re doing a workshop called ‘The Monster in Me.’  Have you ever felt like a monster?  How did you feel?  What kind of monster would you be today?  Who has a mean monster in them?  Who has a happy one?  Who has a sad one?”





Step 3: Coloring the
Monster (paint brush)



Monster Dance Warm-up:
“Let’s do a Monster Dance.  First we can start by moving around in a circle being monsters.  Now let’s all be scary monsters!   Now let’s be happy monsters!  Can you be really loud monsters?   Can you be really quiet monsters?”

Note for Teen Workshops:
If you are working with a group of teens, the Monster Dance won’t be the best way to start.  You could try something more theatrical, like walking into the workshop with a scary mask on and asking them what they see.  Talk about how we all have monsters inside of us and it’s really important to take a look at those monsters and see who they are and what they need.

Technical Demonstration:
There are three steps.  Demonstrate them to the children, but get them involved in the demonstration.  Ask them to guide you as you go through the three steps, so you’re creating the monster they are telling you to make.

1. Drawing the Monster:
“What kind of nose should I put on this monster?  What kind of eyes?  What kind of ears?  How about big teeth?  Anything else I should add?   How about a neck for the monster...   Notice that I’m pressing really hard to make the lines.  This is important because it makes the lines strong enough for when we put the paint on.”  

2. Watering the Monster:  
“Now we get to make the monster all wet.  (Spray the entire page with a spray bottle.)  Did I get the whole monster wet?  Is there anywhere I missed?  (Keep spraying until the whole surface is wet.  You could call the water “Monster Juice.”)”  

3. Coloring the Monster:  
“Now we get to add the colors.  Tell me what colors to use.  We can just drop the colors into each space and see them spread.  (Demonstrate how the watercolors spread in the water.)  Isn’t that beautiful?  What color should I make the eyes?  How about the mouth?  How about the space around the monster?” 




Painted Monster




Creation:
“Now it’s your turn.  Go ahead and draw your monster.  What kind of eyes do you want to make?  What kind of mouth?  Teeth?  Ears?  Does your monster have hair?  (Encourage the children as they draw.)  When you are ready, raise your hand, so I can come water your monster.  (Probably, you will want to be in charge of the spray bottle, and spray for the children.  If a spray bottle is not available, you might use a big, broad, house-painting brush.)   

“When your monster has been sprayed, you get to drop in the colors and watch them fill the spaces.  Beautiful!  (Encourage and assist the children as they add the watercolors.)”
Closing Circle:  
Each child has an opportunity to share his or her monster.  You might encourage the children to share with questions like: “What does your monster feel like?  What is it thinking?”  If time allows, ask the children to think about what their monster needs, to feel better.  Does it need to be loved?  Does it need to be understood?  Sometimes monsters have important things to say if you listen to what they need in order to feel better.





“Monster in Me” sample

About this Workshop:
This workshop is the eighth and final segment in the “Creative Scrapbook” series created by Carolyn Coleman Manns of Laurel House in Pennsylvania. Through this series, Carolyn powerfully links creative expression to the shelter’s basic DV curriculu
  

 “Day By Day” — detail from “Hands that Respect.”
m.

Objective:
To discuss parenting objectives and give participants an opportunity to explore how their hands can be used positively in molding a child’s future. To explore how hands can be used in a loving and compassionate manner showing respect, love, support, and guidance.

Materials:
Construction paper (all colors)
Markers
Glitter
Magazines
Scissors
White-out pens
Stick-on jewels, stones, etc.
Glue sticks
Paint & brushes
 "I will love and respect my children even when I'm upset."
  


Timeframe: 2 hrs
Introduction: 30 min.
Creation: 60 min.
Closing: 30 min.

Intro & Discussion:
Share examples of “Hands That Respect” from previous groups. Discuss how parents need time out when they become overwhelmed, and discuss how there are other options besides spanking. Discuss what type of message spanking sends to a child. One message is that when you are angry it’s okay to hit. Discuss other facts that your agency shares in terms of parenting (eg. Discipline should be a learning experience, not punishment. / A child can be given options for their negative feelings, like talking, communicating, and expressing. / Time out should be only used to calm down, not to isolate. / Time out should only be minutes matching age - a four year old would get 4 minutes of time out.)

"I will promise to raise my child in a non-violent household." — Trisha, January 31, 2001
 
Creation:
Participants
begin by tracing their hand or hands. They can decorate the hands
however they prefer. They are asked to take a minute to think about a
message that they want their hands to send to their children or loved
ones. They can then glue their hands on to construction paper. The
messages can be creatively placed anywhere on the page.

Closing Circle:
Encourage each individual to describe her project and share how she felt while completing it. Encourage each to discuss how she would like to use the information, feelings, and options in her life.
