Closing Circle:
Give the teens time to share their art piece with the group or how the experience as a whole was for them. After the teens have shared, you can share with them that: "If we open ourselves to the possibilities that all we encounter and opportunities for joy and learning, then we can make all circumstances useful and fruitful."

Share with the teens before they leave that we each have our own wisdom and medicine to share with the world. What we have experienced and what we have learned from our so called "mistakes" can become this wise medicine that we have to share. This wheel can become a reminder of this for them.
Row.txt_description: Teaching everything in terms of circles or wheels is a Native American spiritual tradition. The "mistake wheel" shares the keys to self-acceptance and acceptance of the universe. The five sections of the wheel hold five messages about "mistakes," leading us to reflect on what we can learn from them and how we can accept them.

Row.txt_code:
An example of a Peace Wreath
Objective:
To have the women contribute to the holiday decorations by creating a personal Peace Wreath made from their own hand shapes. This activity motivates the women to think about what creates peace in their lives and in the world and in what ways they can use their own hands to create a more peaceful world.

This is a great workshop for community building or as a family activity!

Materials:
Lots of green construction paper
Red construction paper
(one for each participant) or red ribbon
One paper plate for each participant
Pencils
Scissors
Glue
 
  Tracing hands to create the wreath
Glitter glue (optional)
Quotes on kindness

Timeframe:
Under an hour

Set-up/Prep:
This is a very easy activity with no real set up or prep except for laying out the supplies!

Introduction:
Speak with the women about the many ways we can share something special with others for the holidays. Today we are making decorations for the holidays that we can share with our friends and family as a way to promote peace durring the holidays. When you are kind to others it not only changes you, it changes the world. What acts of kindness can each of us do to change the world to create a more peaceful place to live?

"Don't wait for people to be kind, show them how." Unknown

Opening Circle:
Begin the workshop by having the women share what they think they can do to create more peace in the world. Pass out a handout of quotes on kindness and have this spark conversation of how all of us can bring peace into the world even through small guestures. Things such as showing love, kindness, smiling, forgiveness, reaching out to others, being nice to someone who is having a bad day, etc. always have an impact on others and the world.

As Archbiship Desmond Tutu states, "Do your little bit of good where you are; it's those little bits of good put together that overwhelm the world."

 
Cutting out and glueing hands to wreath
 
 
Putting the wreath together
 
 
Creation:
Have the women trace one of their hands on a piece of green construction paper. Then have them cut the hand out and trace the cut hand 9 more time on the green paper. Once this is done they can cut-out the rest of the hands.
Next have them glue the hand cut-outs together, using the plate as a base, in a wreath shape. Tell them to glue the wrists so that they are overlapping a little creating the center of the wreath. The fingers then flar out at the edges and look like leaves!
Make a large red bow, either from construction paper or the ribbon, and glue it to the bottom of the wreath.
Speak with the women again about how their hands can create a more peaceful world and have them write on the wreath some of their ideas of how they can create peace. They can then use the glitter glue to decorate the hands further.

Closing:
Check in with the women and ask them if they would like to talk about their creation and what might have come up for them durring the creative process. After they have shared you can further motivate them to think about what they can do today to create more peace in the world, or have them share who they might want to give their wreath to as a gesture of peace and love durring the holidays.
Row.txt_description: To have the women contribute to the holiday decorations by creating a personal Peace Wreath made from their own hand shapes. This activity motivates the women to think about what creates peace in their lives and in the world and in what ways they can use their own hands to create a more peaceful world. This is a great workshop for community building or as a family activity!
Row.txt_tips: This is a great workshop for community building or as a family activity!

Row.txt_code:
This workshop was inspired by two of AWBW's
friends and supporters, Karalee Hayes and
Lina Paredes.
 
  Sample Spirit Candle and Materials
Objective:
The Spirit Candles workshop gives participants the opportunity to search for the strength and energy or light that nurtures and guides our spirit as we prepare for new begginings. We will decorate candles by collaging onto them our biggest dreams and deepest hopes.

Materials:
Glass candles (glass should be clear for decorations)
Photostock books
Magazines
Colored tissue paper (non-bleeding)
Scissors
Mod Podge
Brushes
Paper and pen for journaling
Note: The glass candles can be any shape and size you choose. A great place to purchase this kind of candle is at local discount stores such as The .99 Store.

Opening Circle:
Have the women share their name a happy dream they had growing up.

Introduction:
As we prepare for the beginning of a new life and all it's possibilites, we go through a winding down period, which is meant to release what we no longer need and to collect and gather the energy to face our new experiences. During these quiet times, we dream and imagine what is to come. We will honor these wishes by creating a tangible reminder of the will that allows us to make these dreams a reality.

Candles have different uses all throughout the world, but at their most basic, they are meant to bring forth light. In this case they will also assist us in honoring the fire within us, our inner spirit. With our collages we bring to life the hopeful and strong spirit that gives us the strength to face change. In order to connect to the emerging light in our lives, we will be decorating candles. We hope you will light these candles to celebrate new beginnings.

Note: If there is a policy against using candles within the shelter stay, you may want to encourage the women to keep it for the future.

 
Painting with Mod Podge
 
Warm Up:
Let's begin by taking a few deep breaths. With every slow breath, allow your body to relax. Try to be patient with yourself as you become centered. Continue to breathe in and out and when you're ready, begin to think about the new stages in your life. How do you feel about them? How are you preparing for them? What hopes emerge with this new beginning? What fears might be blocking your way?

Now let's consider this new year. What visions do you have? What do you imagine for your life? What experiences would you like to have? As you consider and process these questions, you may want to journal.

Timeframe:
Total: 2 hrs per workshop
10 min. Opening circle
10 min. Introduction
10 min. Relaxation
60 min. Mask-making
(or Painting in the second workshop)
30 min. Closing circle

 
  Finished Spirit Candle Samples
Creation:
Step one
If you purchase candles that already have stickers and images you can remove them by soaking with warm soapy water for about one hour.
Step two
Participants can use tissue paper to cover glass and/or to prevent the back of the images from showing through when the candle is lit.
Step three
Gather images and words.
Step four
Paste images and words by using a medium brush to spread the Mod Podge evenly on the glass to ues as glue and then directly over the pictures to protect and provide a clear glossy finish.
Caution: Do not to apply too much Mod Podge as the ink may run.

Let the images dry and your Spirit Candle is ready.

Closing:
Ask the women to share their creations and how they think they will feel when they light them.
Row.txt_description: The Spirit Candles workshop gives participants the opportunity to search for the strength and energy or light that nurtures and guides our spirit as we prepare for new beginnings. We will decorate candles by collaging onto them our biggest dreams and deepest hopes.

Row.txt_code:
"Sometimes I am sad or happy but
I am always beautiful and strong."
 

Masks are a very powerful technique for self-expression. We were so excited at AWBW when Sandra Mueller shared this new mask-making process with these plastic molds and tissue paper. This project was designed to provide a simple, accessible, inexpensive way to create life-sized masks.

Objective:
To allow participants to speak out about and against Domestic Violence, as well as express personal stories, for the purpose of creating awareness.


Materials:
Part 1:
Plastic mask molds
(set of 10 “Multi-Cultural Face Forms” can be ordered for $6.69 from Dick Blick:


 Example of a Speak Out Mask with the eyes cut out

1-800-447-8192)
Elmer’s glue or white glue
Tin foil
Bowls
Paintbrushes
Non-bleeding colored tissue paper – all
colors, including skin tones
Paper towels
Newspaper

Part 2:
Matte board 1 for each participant
– cut 8 1/2 x11
Tape
Wire
Scissors
Crayons or markers
Construction paper
Hot glue gun
Pipe cleaners and/or wire
Paper clips

Timeframe:
Plan for at least 2 hours. While the glue/water solution and tissue paper dry, work can be done on the framing. (Or, you may want to consider this a 2 day activity).

 
 Example of a finished Speak Out Mask
  
Set-up / Prep:
Pour glue into a bowl and add water slowly, stirring as you go. Consistency should not be too thin. Prepare pieces of tissue paper in various colors by cutting into thick strips. Prepare wet paper towels (or wipes) for hand cleaning during the project. Cover the tables or workstation with newspaper. It is a good idea to have one or two made for examples so the women can begin to plan how they want their mask to look. Expect a pleasant mess!

Introduction:
Masks provide a wonderful way to express feelings, fears and emotions that are hidden or suppressed. This activity gives an opportunity for the words to pour out of the mouth of the mask! Identifying feelings is a critical step in awareness of the things that we fear and are angry about. In time for Domestic Violence Awareness Month, Speak-Out Masks are a great vehicle for self-expression.

Opening Circle:
Take this time to talk about things the women fear or are afraid to say out loud. Explain that the Speak-Out Masks can speak for them - show an example and help them to understand that the mask is a safe way to express themselves and that everyone has fears and anger – they are not alone with their feelings.

Creation:
Part One:


  A mask covered in foil

Begin by wrapping the tin foil over the face of the mask mold. Before you begin to add the colors, encourage the participants to think about how they want their masks to look. The tissue can be applied to the masks in several different ways – here are 2 suggestions, feel free to explore new techniques.
1. The glue mixture can be applied to the tin foil first and the paper can be layed on top. You can continue to layer by using a brush or your fingers dipped in the glue mixture. 2. You can place the tissue on the foil and apply the glue with the brush over the tissue, and continue to layer in this fashion.
The paper can be applied in clumps or strips and the features of the face can be built up by using thick layers or you
can leave the surface of the mask as it
is on the mold – just

 Glue can be applied with fingers or a brush
make certain to
have enough layers of tissue paper to cover the foil. Encourage exploration and experimentation.
Allow the mask to dry.

Part Two:
Once the mask is completely dry carefully lift the foil with the tissue from the mold. Each mask can be left as it is or the features, such as the eyes or mouth, can be enhanced by cutting them out.
You can have your mask “say words” by attaching a pipe cleaner or wire that has been wrapped around a finger to make a spiral – insert one end in the mouth and glue a piece of paper with words on the other end.

  
 
 Apply tissue to the tin foil

 
 Curl pipe cleaners around a
finger

 Attach words to the mask








Part Three:
Carefully glue the mask to the Matte Board, a hot glue gun works best. If desired, additional words can be added to the surrounding Matte Board.

 
 Sample Speak Out Mask
Closing:
This is a very powerful workshop. Try to allow enough time for sharing the finished masks with the group. Encourage participants to discuss what their masks have to say. Celebrate and validate the uniqueness and creativity of each piece of work. Be sure to have release forms available so the participants can give permission to display their work. Make certain to write the title of the work and the words that go with it.
Row.txt_description: This is designed to allow participants to speak out about and against domestic violence, as well as to express personal stories for the purpose of creating awareness.

Row.str_title: What Good Fortunes Have Come Your Way?
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To provide every child with an opportunity to realize that despite their situations they do have "good fortunes" in their lives and to help them begin to appreciate the little things that they do have.
 
Pot of Gold Good Fortunes
 
 
4 Leaf Clover Good Fortunes
 

Materials:
Thick white paper (card stock works well)
Crayons, colored pencils, markers
Scissors
Glitter glue or puffy paints
4 leaf clover patterns
Lined paper
Click here to see template

Timeframe:
Opening circle: 10 minutes
Activity: 1 hour
Closing Circle: 10 minutes

Ratio:
1 adult for 3 children

Set-up:
Prepare tables with the various supplies to create the 4 leaf clovers. Have clover patterns cut out and dispersed amongst the tables.

Introduction:
Begin by discussing St. Patrick's Day and the symbols that we use to represent the holiday.

Have children brainstorm the various symbols (Pot o' Gold, Rainbows, 4 Leaf Clover, Leprechauns, the color green etc.) You may want to discuss the word fortune and how it often relates to money. Then explain that fortunes are also things we are lucky to have. Ask the students if any of them know what a 4 leaf clover symbolizes - then explain to them that it too represents good luck.

Have the children close their eyes if they are comfortable, or put their heads down. Have them pretend that they are leprechauns in a field and that they can see a beautiful rainbow. Have them picture the rainbow and each color in it. When they get to the end of the rainbow, rather than finding good fortune in the form of gold coins, they find a beautiful green meadow filled with 4 leaf clovers. Each one of the clovers represents the good fortunes in their lives; the things they are lucky to have. Begin asking questions to help them realize what their fortunes might be. Do you see your family on one of the clovers? Maybe a pet or your clothes? Your mom's hugs or good friends? The list goes on and on. Tell them that when they are finished thinking about all of the good fortunes they can open their eyes again.
Ask the children to share what fortunes they saw on their 4 leaf clovers.

     
My clothes are a good fortune
to me because I won't be
dirty and have on the same
clothes. Clothes are important
because I can change my clothes.
  My dog spot is a good fortunte
because I like to play with him
and he plays with me. Spot is
a broen dog with blue eyes. My
dog spot is the best friend to me.
He is the best dog I ever had.
  My family is a good fortune
to me because they're very
special to me. My mom is
special because she loves me.
My broter and sister are
special to me because their
laughing is very cute.

 


 
Place the words on the back of the 4 leaf clover
 
Creation:
Walk the children through the process of tracing the 4 leaf clover pattern. Explain to them that they are to write the fortune on the front in large lettering and then decorate their clovers however they like. Afterwards they cut it out.
Next, on the lined paper ask the children to write a paragraph or sentence (depending on the age of the group) to describe why this is a good fortune in their life. You may have younger children use these sentence starters.
________________is a good fortune because...

It is a good fortune that ______________because...

Then glue the descriptions on the backside of the clover. Display the clovers from the ceiling for the remainder of the month of March.

Closing Circle:
Have students share their 4 leaf clovers and explain why it represents something they are lucky to have, despite the situation they are in at the present time.
Row.txt_description: To provide every child with an opportunity to realize that despite thier situations they do have "good fortunes" in their lives and to help them begin to appreciate the little things that they do have.

Row.txt_code:
Puzzle Piece Paper Doll Template
Objective:
By writing and coloring emotions on a paper doll made up of puzzle pieces participants are able to reflect on their current emotions and where they feel these emotions in their body. Through journaling and reflecting on their present emotions and envisioning what they wish to feel in the future they will begin to deepen the process of "putting themselves back together" after all that they have been through.

Materials:
Colored markers - for coloring
Pencils - for coloring
Permanent markers - for writing words
Blank paper for journaling
Handout of paper doll made up of puzzle pieces - 2 for each participant
- click here for Paper Doll Template
Relaxing music

 
  Materials for "Putting Myself Back Together"
Timeframe:
(feel free to break this workshop into two sessions if needed)
Intro: 5 minutes
Relaxation: 5 minutes
Creation, Part 1: 10 minutes
Journaling: 15 minutes
Creation, Part 2: 10 minutes
Closing: 15 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour

Set Up:
Lay out blank paper, colored markers, pens, and pencils around the table. Make sure that there are two paper doll handouts at each seat, or you can to hand them out at the beginning. Have relaxing music ready to be played during their relaxation and journaling time.

Introduction:
Today we are going to use these paper dolls to get in touch with the emotions we hold within our body. We often go through each day without slowing down to really feel how our body feels, to notice what emotions may be surfacing, and to listen to what our body may be telling us. When we stop to listen we notice that we may tend to hold certain emotions in different places in our body. Maybe in our chest, or our stomach, or our heart. Each feeling may even have a different intensity. At times we may feel one feeling really strongly, or we may feel lots of feelings all at once. Sometimes we may not even know what we are feeling, and that is okay too.

By really noticing our feelings and how our body holds them we can begin to work with them. We can begin to feel and process each emotion and eventually transform them. Sometimes we may feel both happy and sad at the same time. It can be confusing to have so many varying emotions at once, yet we may find that it can be a large part of being human. We all have feelings, and these feelings change with each day and each experience. Through nurturing and loving ourselves we can begin to transform old feelings and start fostering the feelings we wish to have.

 
Writing feelings where we may feel them 
  
 
Connecting colors with feelings
 
  
 
Reflecting on the process
 
Relaxation:
Put on relaxing music silently in the background and begin to lead the women through relaxation...

"Set yourself in a comfortable position and begin to take a few deep breaths. You can close your eyes or keep them open, do whatever is going to make to feel relaxed. We rarely slow down and focus on ourselves, so know that this time is for you. Bring yourself into this present moment and feel your breath move in and out. Send the message to your entire body to relax. Focus your attention on your breath, not seeking to change it in any way but simply become aware of your in-breath and your out-breath. With each breath allow your body to relax further. Begin to focus on how your body feels. What feelings do you have in the present moment? Become aware of them. Notice if you feel different feelings in certain places in your body. Maybe there is a certain feeling in your chest or your heart or your stomach. Breathe into those places and simply notice how your body feels. Are there certain colors that come to you when you feel each emotion? See what comes to your mind naturally with each breath. Continue to breathe slowly, in and out. Remember that it is safe to feel these feelings, that you are in a safe place. Begin to breathe in love and compassion for yourself, and know that you are surrounded by love and support. Now when you are ready you can slowly open your eyes if you closed them."

Creation, Part 1:
Have the women begin by reflecting on what feelings and colors came up for them in the relaxation. Inside each puzzle piece they can write a word that describes a feeling that they have right now or even a feeling that they have had sometime today. Encourage them to think of where in their body they might feel these different feelings, they can then write that feeling in the place that they feel it.

After the puzzle pieces are filled with the words of their emotions they can then color in each puzzle piece with a color that portrays each feeling.

Journaling:
After the women have created their dolls they can move on to journaling about how to process and look at all of these feelings that came up for them. They can reflect on why they put certain words in certain places, what the different colors meant to them, what came up for them in the relaxation, and how it feels to look at their doll made up of all of their present emotions.

They can reflect on how to make peace with conflicting emotions. For example how for some of the women in their heart they may still feel love for their batterer, but everything else is telling them to run.

 
  Close-up of feelings in the present
  
 
  Close-up of feelings wanted in the future
Share with them how these dolls help us see that all human beings can feel fragmented at times. That at some point in our lives all human beings experience brokenness and are left to rediscover their sense of self and sense of the world again. If they are feeling fragmented and broken how can they, and how do they want to, put themselves back together again? Have them reflect on what this next step would be for them. What feelings do they want to replace other feelings with. What do they want to replace fear with? What do they want to replace loneliness and sadness with, etc?

What kind of nurturing self-loving things can they begin to do to piece themselves back together? What would help them create a more empowered sense of self?

Creation, Part 2:
Once the women have journaled they can create a second doll to "put themselves back together" with nurturing and loving feeling words and colors. Encourage them to see this as actually taking a step to create this transformation in their lives! Through nurturing and loving themselves they can begin to transform old feelings and start fostering the feelings that they wish to have.

Closing Circle:
At the end, give all of the women a chance to share their paper doll. If they don't want to share be sure to let them know that that's okay.

After the women have shared encourage them to see how strong they are and to have compassion for the times that they feel broken or lost in their emotions. They are doing the work here and now to "piece themselves back together again" in loving and empowered ways! Congratulate them for doing such wonderful work and sharing their feelings!

Variation:
Lupe Diaz & Debi Barrett of WomenShelter of Long Beach had participants write, color and cut the pieces before gluing the pieces on construction paper. They felt that doing this had a demonstrated how difficult it is to put your life back together after a traumatic event, however with great care and patience it can be done.
Row.txt_description: By writing and coloring emotions on a paper doll made up of puzzle pieces the women are able to reflect on their current emotions, where they feel theses emotions in their body, and how they envision themselves "putting themselves back together" after all that they have been through.

Row.str_title: Footprints in the Sand and other Sand Painting Workshops
Row.txt_code:
Joanne Webb and sample sand painting
Objective:
Gives participants an opportunity to learn new methods of story telling. Through using the technique of sand painting, inspired by a Native American tradition, participants will use symbols to tell a story they would like to share.

Materials:
Colored Sand (can be purchased in jars from Oriental Trading or Discount School Supply)
Plastic containers with pour spout (for the sand)
White glue
Glue sticks
9” – 12” heavy black construction paper
Colored construction paper
Fiskars foot paper puncher (used for scrap-booking)
Colored pencils
Toothpicks
Tablecloths or placemats
Music (Please let us know if you would like us to send you a copy of Baby Blue,
Native American Music by Carlos Reynosa)
Native American Sand Painting background handout


 
Sand Painting Materials 
Timeframe:
Intro: 5 minutes
Warm Up: 5 minutes
Journaling (for teens) 5 minutes (optional)
Creation with pencils: 20 minutes
Creation with sand: 30 minutes
Closing Circle: 15 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour 20 minutes

Age Range:
7 years and older

Set Up:
Once you have ordered the sand you will want to transfer the different colors into smaller plastic containers to be used in the workshop. It is best to do this with a funnel. Have tablecloths, or placemats, on the tables for this workshop so that clean-up is easier. You may want to create small footprints with the foot paper puncher before the workshop so that they are ready for the participants to use. This can be done with different color construction paper to create variety. Have a minimum of 10 pairs of feet per participant. Lay out an assortment of the colored sand and other materials.

Introduction:
What we are going to do today is a sand painting adventure called Footprints in the Sand. This project has been inspired by the Native American art form known as sand painting. In the Native American tradition sand paintings were created to tell stories (you may want to use the Native American Sand Painting background handout provided). Today we are going to use our sand paintings to tell a story of our adventures.

Everyones experiences are different. Some things that happen to us can be happy, exciting or fun and sometimes things that happen can be sad or difficult. What we are going to do is tell a story in a simple way using symbols and words. Your story can be anything you want it to be. You can decide where your story starts and where you want it to go.

 
  Sketching symbols from their story
 
  Outlining images with glue
 
  Sprinkling sand on images
Indian Rain Dance Warm Up:
First gather the group into a standing circle. Leader starts a rhythm beat using clapping, snapping, slapping on thighs, etc. Example: Leader starts with a 1-2 1-2-3 clapping beat, participant to left mirrors the same clapping beat and once she has it, the participant to her left follows suit. This goes on throughout the circle and when it reaches the leader again, a new beat is introduced such as clap 1-2 and snap 1-2. However, the rest of the participants continue doing the rhythm beat they were doing originally, until the person to their right introduces the next beat. This can go into five or six rounds depending on the number of participants. It works well to soften the sound towards the end to create a different level of energy in the room.

This exercise also works well adding vocal sounds along with different movements to make it more playful.

Journaling (optional for older children and teens):
It may be helpful to allow the participants to think about their story. They can start with the prompt "my adventure is..." or "my adventure begins..." or "I would like my adventure to lead to..." Put on relaxing music, possibly Native American music, softly in the background.

Creation:
Begin by taking 2 pieces of black construction paper and with a glue stick, glue them together (one on top of the other) to make the paper stronger. We are going to use a lot of glue and don't want to paper to wilt! Next take a light colored pencil and begin to
 
Adding the footprints
 
 
Mapping out our journey
 
 
A finished sample
 
draw and sketch out your adventure on the construction paper. Think about where you would like your story to begin, it could at the beach, a park, the forest or maybe a playground... Think of where you want to go next. Is it sunny out or maybe it is cold and raining, maybe there is snow on the ground... You can keep adding to your story by drawing about six different symbols that are a part of your adventures. For example if you are talking about a forest you can draw several trees, if you are on a playground you can draw swings...Use as many colors as you want, you can even write words on your paper if you want. Don't worry about getting it perfect.

Once the drawing is completed demonstrate how to work with the sand with a sample drawing. First you gently squeeze the white glue to outline or fill in the first shape of your drawing. Choose the color of sand you want to use and place some in the palm of your hand. With your index and thumb fingertips of the opposite hand sprinkle the sand onto the glue. Then lift the paper and shift it around to fill any gaps, next curl the paper to empty any loose sand back into your hand. If there are still gaps repeat this again and again with the remaining sand in your hand. You can even mix 2 colors and blend colors by the way that you sprinkle them.

Keep in mind that sand painting is a Native American art form and that respecting nature, earth and the materials are a part of their culture. Therefore any extra sand of a particular color should be placed back in its container when done.

When clients have completed their sand paintings pass out tiny colored footprint shapes (which you have already punched out of colored construction paper using the Fiskars footprint puncher). They can use these footprints to outline their adventure, placing the feet right, left, right, left into the sand and drawing to show the path they walked. The clients can glue stick the tiny footprints onto their sand painting, emphasizing their adventure.

Closing Circle:
At the end give all of the participants a chance to share their sand painting and story. This is a very powerful art project and the children come away with a stronger sense of their personal journey, and a look at how far they have traveled.

Share with them that when we take time to explore our own stories we learn so much from them. And when we share our stories it often helps others. It's powerful and empowering to share our own stories. Thank them for exploring their own stories and where their footprints have taken them.
Row.txt_description: Gives participants an opportunity to learn new ways of telling their story. Through using the technique of sand painting, inspired by a Native American tradition, participants will use symbols to tell a story they would like to share.

Row.txt_code:
Project Overview:
This project started as AWBW’s Unmasking Me/Unmasking the Future multi-media project designed to enable teens and women that have experienced domestic violence, to express themselves and educate their communities in a powerful and unique way. This is a great project for Domestic Violence Awareness Month.

Objective:
Through a combination of journaling and mask making this workshop gives participants an opportunity to explore their feelings about the abuse they have experienced and think about who they want to be in future relationships. This workshop is also a great way to share personal stories for the purpose of creating awareness.

 
  Mask molds and materials
  
 
  More materials for the masks
Materials:
Plastic mask molds (set of 10 “Multi-Cultural Face Forms” can be ordered from Dick Blick)
Sculpey (approx. one -pound per person)
Various rubber stamps with letters, numbers, textures, etc.
Acrylic paints (assorted colors)
Spray paint (assorted colors) - Optional
Assorted craft wire (20 to 22 gauge)
Assorted beads (plastic, metal, wood, etc), rhinestones
Foil (to ball up into a form to place under mask while working on them and during cooking)
Feathers, Yarn
Toothpicks, or paper clips (for making holes in the face for the wire to pass through for decoration)
Popsicle sticks (for smoothing, cutting the clay, etc.)
Toaster oven/s (Due to toxic fumes from the clay, toaster oven should be one dedicated or baking the Sculpey: for non-food use)
Tongs, potholders, timer
Scissors
Markers, gel pens, pencils, sharpies
Hot-glue gun, glue sticks
Music
Pre-made Journal with questions listed (click on this link to print Journal)

Preparation:
The journals should be prepared in advance. Feel free to make copies on nicer paper to make it more special. Three hole punch and assemble with ribbon or yarn. Tip: put sculpey in the refrigerator to keep it cool before workshop.

 
  Sample Masks shown before workshop
Time Frame:
Total Time: 2-3 hour workshop plus a break in between or 2 separate days 2 hours each day
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 10 minutes
Journaling Time: 20 minutes...if you have a group with teens and women you may choose to adapt the journal questions and talk about them as a whole group instead of writing about them. We recommend putting on some light music while they are journaling.
Sharing Circle: 6-10 minutes
 
  Finished mask
Creation Time: 35 to 45 minutes

45 minute brake/lunch: It’s nice to have a brake or lunch while the masks are cooking…it gives time to clean up a bit, get ready for painting and gives the women a break from a tough topic

Cooking Time: 20 to 30 minutes (depending on how thick the mask are)
Painting Mask: 30 minutes
Sharing/Writing about mask: 15 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Pictures: 10 to 20 minutes
Times will vary!

Introduction:
Today we want to create a safe window of time for you to express your thoughts and feelings about the violence you have lived with, experienced and witnessed in your own home. We are going to ask some tough questions but you will be choosing which questions to answer and how you answer them. The journal is to get you thinking about what you have seen, heard and experienced and the mask you will be creating will be an outlet for all those feelings and answers.

Opening Circle:
(If you are a survivor or an adult survivor of childhood abuse, it is possible to share a bit of your story to create a safe atmosphere, only do so if you can share the past and still remain in the present!)
Let’s start with checking in about how we feel about sharing out loud such personal information, if you could choose one feeling or one word about how you are feeling about this process today what would it be?

Relaxation:
Doing a simple breathing relaxation before journaling could be helpful. It will assist them in going within, getting in touch with what they are really feeling, and getting in touch with their creative power within.

Journaling:
The relaxation guides the participants into the journaling part of the workshop. Remind them that the journals are confidential. They do not have to share the journals with anyone; they won’t be expected to read them out loud, although they are welcome to. They can write or draw their answers. Remind them that the journals are a safe healing space to let the feelings out so that the feelings no longer have any power over them. They don’t have to answer all the questions, if one becomes particularly difficult they can skip it and come back to it later or even on their own on another day, or they can just totally skip it! The journals ask some hard questions but they are just for them, they are theirs to assist them in figuring stuff out!

Sharing Circle:
Have the women share whatever they are comfortable with regarding their journaling or choose a question or two for them to pick from. You can have them share about how it felt to write about what they experienced and what feelings came up for them. So that sharing is less intimidating have them pair up with each other and share in pairs. Give each partner two minutes (use a timer) to share while the other listens, then have them switch. Let them know that when they are the Listener, they only need to listen.

Remind them that they do not have to share anything that they are not comfortable sharing. Afterwards there may be a few that want to share with the whole group.

 
  Molding the mask in the plastic mold
 
  Pressing the sculpey firmly in the mold
 
  Putting mask on foil to hold its shape
Creation:
Talk about all the materials available. Show some examples of masks that have been made free form, compare to using the plastic mask. You can show pictures of masks from history and remind them there isn’t a right or wrong way to create a mask. They don’t have to look like a human face. Before they begin creating their masks have them think about the questions, their answers, and what they might want their mask to share with others. Encourage them to pick one of their journal question answers to create the mask about. Remind them that there is no right or wrong way to create their mask.

Step 1- Molding:
Have them begin molding their masks, either with the plastic mold or free form. If they use the plastic mold they should press the sculpey firmly inside the mold to create the mask’s shape, no more than an inch thick. Warn them that if the Sculpey is too warm from handling it might stick to the molds.

Step 2 - Removing from Mold: Carefully remove the clay from the mold form. This takes some patience. They may want to rest the clay on preformed foil for support and to hold its desired shape (the foil will be left under the mask for the baking).

Step 3 - Decorating:
Textures, glitter, wire, beads, sequins and rhinestones can be added by pressing into the soft clay. Remind them if they want to add wire…they need to create some holes in their masks prior to baking, this can be done with toothpicks or straws.

Step 4 - Mask cooking time/ Lunch/or break for the day:
Set the toaster oven to 275 degrees and cook the masks for 20 minutes, depending on how thick they are. Check the masks every ten minutes and pull out any masks that are turning tan so that they don’t overcook. Make sure the toaster oven is not on toast or broil. Set the timer so you don’t forget, while you are taking a break or eating, to pull the pans out of the toaster oven!

 
  Decorating mask before it's cooked
 
  Painting mask after it's cooked
Step 5 - Painting/Decorating the Mask:
Talk a little about the painting materials available. Since the masks are clay, even though they are baked, they should not get too wet with paint – do not add water to the acrylic (you might not even want to put water on the table) – if spray painting do not saturate. Have an assistant spoon out acrylic paint so participants don’t take too much. Have an assistant help with the spray painting, which is good to do outside or in a well-ventilated spot! Feathers, rhinestones, beads, wire can all be added using a hot glue gun.

Sharing/Writing about the Mask:
Celebrate the completion of the dialoging mask with each other!
If you are planning on using the masks for an exhibit here are a couple of options for sharing and writing about the mask:

1. Have them share with the group about the process and/or anything about their mask. If the participants are comfortable you could ask if it’s ok if volunteers or other group members write down what they say when they share about the mask. This will allow you to keep track of words that go along with their masks.
Or
2. You could have them work again in partners and have one partner write while the other shares and then switch places. Have the women figure out together what words can go with the mask when they are displayed. This also creates a unity or partnership for future sharing between the participants outside of group!

 
Finished mask
 
Closing Circle:
Have everyone hold their masks in the circle so that they can all be seen. Ask the women to share whatever they want about the mask or about the process of creating the mask. They could also give a one-sentence title for their mask to sum up their feelings. (Have paper ready if they want to write down other/more words that can go with the mask if the masks will be exhibited).

Pictures:
You might want to take a picture of the women with their mask so they can glue it into their journal. This will give them a visual record of the whole process and their creation.

Note to Leader:
If you are choosing to facilitate this workshop using the two separate workshops it would be best to do the journaling and the mask creation on the first day, and the mask painting/decorating and writing the words to go with mask the second day. This is a very powerful project!
Row.txt_description: Through a combination of journaling and mask making this workshop gives participants an opportunity to explore their feelings about the abuse they have experienced and think about who they want to be in future relationships. This workshop is also a great way to share personal stories for the purpose of creating awareness.

Row.txt_code:
Freedom Flyer Windsocks blowing in the wind
 
 
Getting supplies ready
 
About the Project:
Windsocks were once were actually used as a tool to help measure the direction of the wind. People have also made windsocks for hundreds of years as a way of making decorations for the outdoors, like flags or wind chimes. They were often used as a symbol of good luck or longevity. They can be colorful symbols for any holiday or special occasion. For this project we will call them Freedom Flyers, and they help commemorate the freedoms for which we are thankful.

Objective:
To make an outdoor decoration for the 4th of July, which will give children the ability to express what freedom means to them.

Materials:
Card stock or construction paper cut to 6x11 (toilet paper rolls work as well)
Glue stick
Hole punch (novelty shaped punches are available at craft stores)
Scissors
White craft glue
Stapler
Strips of tissue paper or ribbons
Cord, twine or yarn
Markers
Stickers (optional)
Glitter (optional)

Time Frame:
    Age Range:
45 minutes to 1 hour    6 - 12




Set Up:
Set up supplies for the workshop. If you have younger children, you may want to precut the paper for the body of the windsock and for the strips (which can be made from tissue paper, or ribbons). This is also a great activity to do outdoors.

   
 Cutting shapes to glue on to the windsock. 
   
   
 Drawing and decorating the windsock. 
   
   
 Glueing the streamers.
 
   
   
 Attaching the hanging loop. 
   
Introduction:
Today we are going to make Windsocks! Windsocks are used to decorate the outdoors and when they hang from trees they blow in the wind. We are going to make windsocks to help us celebrate the 4th of July. Let’s think about the 4th of July -- and what the holiday means. This holiday is the celebration of the date that The United States was established as a nation and it represents freedom and independence. Let’s think about the things that we are free to do:
We are free to change our minds, we are free to make decisions, we are free to pick our friends, we are free to read what we want or learn what we want, we are free to have our own opinion about things – ask the children to name other things that are freedoms. The 4th of July is the time to celebrate our freedoms. Our windsocks can be decorated with words, colors or designs that show all the freedoms that are important to us.

Warm Up:
Since the windsocks will be used outdoors, you might want to do any of the breathing exercises that are in the Children’s Manual – such as The Butterfly Breath, Energizing Breaths, Breathe Hot, Breathe Cold or Monkey Breaths (page 34-35). Breathing exercises can be a powerful tool in helping children get in touch with their feelings and by showing the strength of breathing this also shows an example of the power of the wind’s movement.




Creation:
Cut the paper to be 6 x 11, card stock works best, you can use construction paper or toilet paper rolls (you may want to prepare this ahead of time, especially for younger children). We like this size but you can be flexible and make them larger or smaller.
Decorate the paper with stickers, drawings or words – you can pick themes for a holiday or special occasion like 4th of July.
Glue ribbons or strips of tissue paper along the inside of the bottom edge.
The strips or ribbon could be pre-cut and could be up to 20 inches long and approximately 1/4 to 1 inch wide.
Roll the rectangle so the short sides overlap and glue or staple the edges together.
Punch 3 holes along the top edge that are in thirds around the windsock (younger children may need help with getting the holes evenly spaced).
Loop the cord, yarn or twine through the holes creating a way to hang the windsock by tying a sting in each hole and then tying the three together.
If it is possible to take the children outside – find a place to hang the windsock and see how they blow freely in the wind.

Closing Circle:
Ask the children to discuss their freedoms and what it was like to be able to make a decoration just about their liberties, free will and ability to make choices. You can also talk about what it felt like to create special decorations for the outdoors and to see them hanging in the trees.
Row.txt_description: To make an outdoor decoration for the 4th of July, which will give children the ability to express what freedom means to them.
Row.txt_tips:
1. Use toilet paper rolls or even oatmeal containers instead of making your own roll. You can also vary the size of the paper to create a variety of windsocks.
  2. If you plan on using glitter, apply it AFTER the entire windsock is stapled and completely decorated.

Row.str_title: A Bridge to a New World
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
 
 "Full Circle," An example of a finished collage pin
This workshop, A Bridge to a New World, is based on Sandra Beckwith's work, Your Life as a Masterpiece. A Bridge to a New World allows participants to reflect on steps to move forward with hope: from survive to thrive. Participants journal and create multiple collages to discover their inner selves, look at their own gifts, skills, and unique design to envision their own path moving forward into a more fulfilling life.

For more info on Sandra's work check her website: www.yourlifeasamasterpiece.com

Materials:
Newspaper to cover table surface
Magazines (Oprah's, National Geographic, and travel magazines are great for collaging)
Photo stock books
Scissors
Glue sticks
Plexiglass- cut into appropriate sizes and shapes (we recommend 3x3 inches)
Poster board or card stock cut into corresponding size of plexiglass
Matte Medium
Soft brushes- to apply the Matte Medium
Water cups- to rinse the brushes (Don't let the Matte Medium dry in the brushes. It's permanent)
Pin backs- to glue on to make the pins
Magnets- to glue on to make a magnet
E-6000 Glue- (Use in well-ventilated areas only)
Pens and journals to write throughout the workshop
Handout with journaling questions for Part 1 (click on this link for What is Your Unique Design? questions)
Handout with journaling questions for Part 2 (click on this link for The Bridge questions)

Note: If you do not have journals to use for this workshop participants can create their own if you provide them with nice paper, hole punchers and ribbon to bind the journal pages together.

Time Frame:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Part 1: 25 minutes
Part 2: 25 minutes		   Creation of the collages: 25 minutes
Closing Circle: 10 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour and 30 minutes
     





Introduction & Process:
Many of us are asking and searching for our own life's purpose, as if it is something outside of us to be found. What if it was a part of you from the very beginning? Is it possible that "your purpose " is a natural expression of the most profound experiences of your life?

  
"Healing Touch," another beautiful example
  
Today we are going to reflect on a series of introspective questions, journal on them, and then create a collage, collage pin, or collage magnet that is inspired by what the questions evoke within you and your vision that emerges.

This workshop is divided in two parts: "What is Your Unique Design?" and "The Bridge." Each part follows a process of questions and answers that are meant to provide you with clues of how to uncover deeper aspects of yourself and the steps you wish to take to move along your path. As I share these questions with you allow them to spark your imagination as they aid you in uncovering the steps of your journey. As you consider each question write your thoughts in your journal, and remember that the answers are just for you. You can also begin to gather the images for your collage as you process each question.

Note: Participants can create one or more collages for each part of this workshop. It is fine if you feel the need to have them complete this project in more than one sitting, making Part 1 and Part 2 separate workshops.

Part I: What is Your Unique Design?
No one else has walked your journey, seen what you've seen, and is the combination of your skills, gifts, talents and perspective. You are the only piece to the human puzzle that is you. I'm going to share these questions with you and give you a handout with them, consider the following questions to uncover your unique design:

What are your skills? What have you always been good at doing?
What are your gifts? What are you talented at doing, feeling or expressing?
How did you play as a child when no one told you what to do?
Everything you have ever been through and experienced gives you a special compassion for others. For whom do you have compassion?
Trends of all questions: What do these characteristics all have in common?

Remember that we are trying to uncover the ESSENCE of why each of us do what we do. We are all good at doing something. Allow your imagination to guide you as you recall the gifts and skills that make you, YOU!

The Questions, Journaling, and Image Gathering:
Share the above questions with the women and encourage them to let the questions guide them to uncover their own unique design. Before the women begin to journal provide each of the women with a handout with the questions to guide them through their journaling and reflection. Encourage them to follow their own timing with each question for this will allow the answers to come to them more genuinely. Remind them that they can gather images for their collage as they process each question and that they can choose which questions they want to answer and reflect on, it is up to them.

Part II: The Bridge
The second set of questions is called The Bridge and can help you uncover the steps of your journey in a new light.

B Balance.
R Re-invent yourself.
I Invite new experiences.
D Discovery.
G Guidance.
E Emergence.
    Be patient with the process
Be open to new perspective
Investigate what's possible
Delight in life, simple pleasures
Ask to be lead across the bridge
Evolve, Experiment








 
  
 
  
 
We have heard many times: "I want a new life, I just don't know how to get there!" Let's consider the following questions to help you uncover the steps of your journey:

BALANCE
How do you relax, get centered, or calm down after an upset? When you feel anxious or have anxiety, what is a healthy way for you to process your feelings and become peaceful? What balances you? (Writing, walking, gardening, dancing, creating, designing, singing, etc.)

RE-INVENT
You're not the same person you were yesterday, last week, or last year. Who are you now? Are you willing to express new sides of yourself? What are some new things you could shift or try doing? (Your look, your job, your home, taking lessons, etc.)

INVITE
Can you open your heart and being to new experiences? At your own pace, and one step at a time, invite change to be your friend.

DISCOVER
It's time to rediscover finding delight in life. Like a child, what reminds you that this world can be a truly wondrous place? What delights you and creates a sense of wonder? (A walk on the beach, blowing soap bubbles, visiting a beautiful garden, etc.) Let the wonders of nature guide you.

GUIDANCE
You don't need to cross that bridge alone. Ask for help and it will appear in the most unexpected and extraordinary ways. Your challenge is to become humble and ask for assistance. Then, be open to receive the help with a grateful heart. Who can I ask to nurture and support me as I walk the bridge?

EMERGE
Allow the transformation to happen. Nurture the new you. Butterflies take time for their new wings to dry as they leave the cocoon. They don't fly immediately. Acknowledge what is happening and that it will have a time frame all it's own. Enjoy the process. Your new wings will grow stronger and you'll fly when the time is right. What will the new me look like?

The Questions, Journaling, and Image Gathering:
Share the above questions with the women and encourage them to let these questions help them discover the steps they wish to take on their journey. Remind them that they can move forward with hope, from survive to thrive. Before the women begin to journal on this second set of questions provide each of the women with a handout with the questions to guide them through their journaling and reflection. Remind them that, like before, they can gather images for their collage as they process each question or they can choose to look for images after they have finished journaling.

 
  Plexiglass and collage before being attached
  
 
  Painting the Matte Medium on the surface of the collage
Creation and Technical Info:
Have the women select images (some of them may have already started to while journaling) to create a collage, pin, or magnet that relates to the above questions and what visions they evoked within them. Once they select the images they wish to collage, have them follow the steps below:
  1. Select a piece of plexiglass of an appropriate size.
  2. Trace the shape of the plexiglass onto poster board. Then cut a piece of poster board to the exact size of the plexiglass.
  3. Arrange and collage your images onto the poster board piece. You will put the clear glass right over the images. Use scissors and glue sticks for the collaging.
  4. When the collage is complete on the poster board, remove the protective paper from the plexiglass. Check the fit of the board and glass. Trim the board and magazine images if necessary.
  5. Use a brush to cover the face of the magazine images with Matte Medium. It will look like you're ruining the collage by making it all white. Don't worry -- the Matte Medium dries clear.
  6. Press the plexiglass onto the surface of your collage. Squeeze excess Matte Medium and air bubbles out to the sides of the glass. Be careful to not get Matte Medium on the front surface of the glass- it will show. Also, be careful to match the edges of the board and glass. Once they are pressed together and dry, you won't be able to slide them into alignment. Hold the board and glass together for about 3 minutes as it begins to dry.
  7. If you want to create a pin or magnet attach a pin back or magnet to the back of the board with a generous dab of E-6000. Let the pin or magnet dry for 24 hours before wearing or using. (Use E-6000 only in well-ventilated areas.)

 
A finished collage framed by the plexiglass 
Closing Circle:
Provide the women with time to share what is was like for them to reflect on both sets of questions and what these questions uncovered within them. Encourage them to share their process and art with each other if they are comfortable.

Thank them for sharing and encourage them to remember these questions when taking each step of their journey, these very answers can become their bridge to where they wish to go.
Row.txt_description: This workshop, A Bridge to a New World, is based on Sandra Beckwith's work, Your Life as a Masterpiece. A Bridge to a New World allows participants to reflect on some steps to move forward with hope: from survive to thrive. Participants journal and create multiple collages to discover their inner selves, look at their own gifts, skills, and unique design to envision their own path moving forward into a more fulfilling life.

Row.txt_code:
Purpose:
To explore, express, reflect, and record your feelings through journal entries. Remember that you don't have to share your work. You're in charge!

Materials:
Journal books
Pens for wr iting and colored felt pens to illustrate journals
Yellow markers or highlighters
Magazines, scissors, and glue (optional items to personalize journals)
independent project handout (for individual workshops) (click here for handout)

Set Up:
Set out the supplies around the table. Make sure there is a journal and pens at each place.

Welcome and Ground Rules:
It can help create a safe environment if you take time to individually welcome each teen, connect with them, and let them know you are glad they are there. Introduce the project and the philosophy of Windows time: "This is a special "window of time" for each of you. For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? Are there any other Ground Rules you'd like to add?" At this time you can mention any pre-established ground rules you have.

Check-In:
A good example of an appropriate check-in would be: "Before we start the art, we'll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art." This is a time to reassure anyone who's scared of art that it's fine, and to tell anyone who "hates" art that's fine too. Remind them that they don't have to do it, that they can just watch if they want to. When given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in even if they say they're just going to watch. Let them know that it's fine if they don't want to say anything for "check-in", too.

Note to Leaders:
Always offer options and thank teens for their courage. Having colored markers and collaging supplies can give the teens more options for exploring their feelings if they are having a hard time writing.

Project Suggestion:
"Write three pages in a non-stop manner about something that happened this week and how you feel about it. Don't worry about spelling, punctuation, or how it sounds. If you get stuck, write, 'I don't know what to write' and keep coming back to the topic at hand. Remember, don't stop writing!"
Sample:
"I don't know what to write but the topic is to write about today and today was a good day but also a hard day and a day I'll always remember and I might wish to someday forget. My clothes are a bit tight but that is not the topic and I don't know what to write but I'll come back to how my day went and I didn't like it when Mom yelled at me but I love her and can I love her and not like what she does?"
Second Section:
Re-read what you wrote and highlight with the yellow marker anything that seems particularly interesting, powerful, or strange. Write three more pages based on the words or sections that you marked using the same non-stop format. This second section helps deepen your self-awareness.
Third Section (time permitting):
Use colored felt pens to illustrate your journal entries.

Optional Feedback Exercise:
Ten minutes before the workshop ends, pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You could even take them to copy and return them the next week, so that the teens can add them to their journals.

Closure and Validation:
At the end of the project, a Closing Circle can be a way to give each teen an opportunity to share what she or he has created and talk about what it means to them and how it felt to make it. Just like the check-in circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.
Row.txt_description: Give teens an opportunity to explore, express, reflect, and record feelings through journal entries.
Row.txt_tips:
Some kids may close down during this workshop, especially if they're used to journaling during their therapy sessions. Have some more "hands on" alternatives ready in case this happens.

Have a definite topic ready when you begin this project.

If you're doing this project with younger kids, glue sticks may be less messy than Elmer's glue.

Row.txt_code:
Purpose:
To explore writing in a way that helps you feel especially free from all judgment - even your own judgment.

Materials:
Timer
Journal books
Pens for writing and colored felt pens to illustrate journals
Magazines, scissors, and glue (optional items to personalize journals)
independent project handout (for individual workshop) (click here for handout)

Setup:
Set out the supplies, with a journal and pens at each place.

Welcome and Ground Rules:
It can help create a safe environment if you take time to individually welcome each teen, connect with them, and let them know you are glad they are there. Introduce the project and the philosophy of Windows time: "This is a special "window of time" for each of you. For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? Are there any other Ground Rules you'd like to add?" At this time you can mention any pre-established ground rules you have.

Check-In:
A good example of an appropriate check-in would be: "Before we start the art, we'll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art." This is a time to reassure anyone who's scared of art that it's fine, and to tell anyone who "hates" art that's fine too. Remind them that they don't have to do it, that they can just watch if they want to. When given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in even if they say they're just going to watch. Let them know that it's fine if they don't want to say anything for "check-in", too.

Note to Leaders:
Always offer options and thank the teens for their courage. You can offer a theme for the whole group to work with, or encourage each teen to chose his or her own theme. Having colored markers and collaging supplies can give the teens more options for exploring their feelings if they are having a hard time writing.

Project Suggestion:
"In this workshop, you can explore writing freely, without judgment or criticism. You can start with a theme phrase (such as "I am..." or "I feel..." or whatever theme seems right to explore). Begin with your theme phrase, and write whatever comes to mind. To help you be as free as possible, there are some rules. You don't really have to follow them, bu tif you do, you might find that they help you write. Here are the three rules: 1) Write for the full time without stopping (that's why we have a timer); 2) Write whatever your first thoughts are, even if you don't like them; and 3) Write without crossing out or changing anything. Just let it be. Let this writing be different from anything you've ever written. Spelling doesn't matter. It's even fine if you just scribble the whole time. The only important thing is that you give yourself freedom and practice respecting whatever comes out.
Decide on the amount of time for writing (5-10 minutes is usually pretty good to try out). Set your timer. Get ready. And go! After the timer goes off, you can take some time to read back over what you wrote. Reading it out loud to someone can be powerful. If you don't want to read it all, you can read parts of it and share your thoughts and feelings about it."

Optional Feedback Exercise:
Ten minutes before the workshop ends, pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You could even take them to copy and return them the next week, so that the teens can add them to their journals.

Closing and Validation:
At the end of the project, a Closing Circle can be a way to give each teen an opportunity to share what she or he has created and talk about what it means to them and how it felt to make it. Just like the check-in circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.
Row.txt_description: Teens explore judgment-free journaling by completing timed writings.

Row.txt_code:
Purpose:
To explore three different feelings by creating three pastel drawings.

Materials:
9" by 6" Colored Construction Paper (standard 9" by 12" paper cut in half)
chalk pastels
masking tape
paper towels
pens and writing paper (optional: teens could use their journals)
independent project handout (for individual workshops) (click here for handout)

Set Up:
Set out the supplies around the table. Make sure that there are three pieces of construction paper and pastels at each place.

Welcome and Ground Rules:
It can help create a safe environment if you take time to individually welcome each teen, connect with them, and let them know you are glad they are there. Introduce the project and the philosophy of Windows time: "This is a special "window of time" for each of you. For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? Are there any other Ground Rules you'd like to add?" At this time you can mention any pre-established ground rules you have.

Check In:
A good example of an appropriate check-in would be: "Before we start the art, we'll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art." This is a time to reassure anyone who's scared of art that it's fine, and to tell anyone who "hates" art that's fine too. Remind them that they don't have to do it, that they can just watch if they want to. When given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in even if they say they're just going to watch. Let them know that it's fine if they don't want to say anything for "check-in", too.

Optional Journaling:
"Write for five minutes about whatever feelings you've been having lately. Can you remember any good feelings? Any bad feelings? Write about them."

Project Suggestion:
"This workshop is a chance to explore feelings with chalk pastels. Pick three feelings from this list: love, hate, peace, anger, sadness, joy. Notice which feelings you would like to explore today. Write them down. If you want to pick a feeling that's not on the list, that's fine too! Now choose three pieces of paper to represent these three feelings, and tape the edges down with masking tape in front of you. When you are ready, begin with one of the feelings. Use the chalk pastels to create whatever shapes and colors express that feeling. Try covering the page with a color and smearing the pastels with your fingers. See how smooth it can look when you blend the colors together. When you are ready, move onto the second feeling. Use the shapes and colors of the pastels to create the world of that feeling. Remember, if you notice any critical thoughts coming into your head, send them into the Self-Critical Trash Can. When you are ready, explore the third feeling, and when all three are finished, take some time to write any words that go with your pastel windows."

Optional Feedback Exercise:
Ten minutes before the workshop ends, pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You could even take them to copy and return them the next week, so that the teens can have them or add them to journals they might be keeping.

Closure and Validation:
At the end of the project, a Closing Circle can be a way to give each teen an opportunity to share what she or he has created and talk about what it means to them and how it felt to make it. Just like the check-in circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.
Row.txt_description: Teens explore three different feelings by creating three pastel drawings.
Row.txt_tips: If you or your clients need resources to help address Teen dating Violence issues use the Teen Dating Violence Resource Page.

Purpose:
To create a bookmark-sized collage that reprsents your journey from where you are now towards where you want to go in the future.

Materials:
2" X 6" paper or card stock
magazines/photostock books
glue sticks
paper towels
scissors
clear contact paper (if possible) to protect the journey-marker once it's done
pens and writing paper (or teens could use their journals)
independent project handout (for individual workshops) (click here for handout)

Set Up:
Make sure there is one piece of 2" by 6" paper, a glue stick, and scissors at each place. Spread around the magazines and photostock booths so that they're accessible to everyone.

Welcome and Ground Rules:
It can help create a safe environment if you take time to individually welcome each teen, connect with them, and let them know you are glad they are there. Introduce the project and the philosophy of Windows time: "This is a special "window of time" for each of you. For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? Are there any other Ground Rules you'd like to add?" At this time you can mention any pre-established ground rules you have.

Check-In:
A good example of an appropriate check-in would be: "Before we start the art, we'll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art." This is a time to reassure anyone who's scared of art that it's fine, and to tell anyone who "hates" art that's fine too. Remind them that they don't have to do it, that they can just watch if they want to. When given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in even if they say they're just going to watch. Let them know that it's fine if they don't want to say anything for "check-in", too.

Optional Journaling:
"Write for five minutes about your journey. How is your journey going right now and where do you want it to take you?"

Project Suggestion:
"This workshop is a chance to create a journey marker-a bookmark-sized collage that marks your place in your journey. Where are you now? Where do you want to be going? Collage whatever images and words remind you of the path you are on and where you'd like it to lead you. When you are done with your collage, take some time to write any words that go with it. Optional: you may be able to laminate your journey marker or cover it with clear contact paper to protect it. That way, you can carry it with you to use as a reminder of where you are going during the ups and downs of the journey ahead."

Optional Feedback Exercise:
Ten minutes before the workshop ends, pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You could even take them to copy and return them the next week, so that the teens can add them to their journals.

Just like the check-in circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.

Row.txt_code:
Purpose:
To explore different feelings by creating three small watercolor paintings.

Materials:
4" X 4" watercolor paper (three per person)
watercolor paint sets (one per person)
brushes
cups of water (two per person)
paper towels
masking tape
pens and writing paper (teens could also use their journals instead)
independent project handout (for individual workshop) (click here for handout)

Set up:
Make sure that there are three pieces of watercolor paper, two cups of water, and a watercolor paint set and brushes at each place. If possible, tape down the pieces of watercolor paper at each place with masking tape before the workshop begins.

Welcome and Ground Rules:
It can help create a safe environment if you take time to individually welcome each teen, connect with them, and let them know you are glad they are there. Introduce the project and the philosophy of Windows time: "This is a special "window of time" for each of you. For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? Are there any other Ground Rules you'd like to add?" At this time you can mention any pre-established ground rules you have.

Check In:
A good example of an appropriate check-in would be: "Before we start the art, we'll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art." This is a time to reassure anyone who's scared of art that it's fine, and to tell anyone who "hates" art that's fine too. Remind them that they don't have to do it, that they can just watch if they want to. When given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in even if they say they're just going to watch. Let them know that it's fine if they don't want to say anything for "check-in", too.

Optional Journaling:
"Write for five minutes about whatever feelings you've been having lately. Can you remember any good feelings? Any bad feelings? Write about them."

Project Suggestion:
"This workshop is a chance to explore feelings with watercolor paints. With watercolors, it can be very beautiful if you start by creating a shape out of pure water, and then add colors into it. You can't control what the colors will do, so it's amazing to just watch. Take three pieces of watercolor paper and tape the edges down. This will help hold them flat while you are painting. Now pick three feelings from this list: love, hate, peace, anger, sadness, joy. If you want to pick a feeling that is not on this list, that's fine too!
Start with your first piece of paper and begin by making a shape on your page out of clear water - a shape that represents the first feeling you picked. Put enough water so it's like a little lake. Then begin to add colors into the lake, and around it. Notice how the colors move. Flow with them to express the feeling.
When you're ready, move onto the next feeling you chose. On a second piece of paper, create a shape of water representing this feeling and add colors in and around it. When you are ready, move on to the final feeling and create your third watercolor window. Let the watercolors dry before removing the tape. As they dry, you might write down any words that go with your three windows."

Optional Feedback Exercise:
Ten minutes before the workshop ends, pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You could even take them to copy and return them the next week, so that the teens can add them to their journals.

Closing and Validation:
At the end of the project, a Closing Circle can be a way to give each teen an opportunity to share what she or he has created and talk about what it means to them and how it felt to make it. Just like the check-in circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.
Row.txt_description: Teens explore three different feelings by creating three small watercolor paintings.
