Row.txt_code:
Purpose:
To notice and express the story that lives in each part of our faces - our eyes, our nose, our mouth, our ears, etc. To honor the knowledge and strength each part has to offer.

Materials:
4" X 4" smooth cover stock paper
oil pastels (such as CrayPas)
paper towels
toothpicks, plastic utensils
pens and writing paper (teens could also use their journals)
independent project handout (for individual workshop) (click here for handout)

Set Up:
Make sure that there is a piece of stock paper, oil pastels, and toothpicks or utensils at each place.

Welcome and Ground Rules:
It can help create a safe environment if you take time to individually welcome each teen, connect with them, and let them know you are glad they are there. Introduce the project and the philosophy of Windows time: "This is a special "window of time" for each of you. For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? Are there any other Ground Rules you'd like to add?" At this time you can mention any pre-established ground rules you have.

Check-In:
A good example of an appropriate check-in would be: "Before we start the art, we'll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art." This is a time to reassure anyone who's scared of art that it's fine, and to tell anyone who "hates" art that's fine too. Remind them that they don't have to do it, that they can just watch if they want to. When given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in even if they say they're just going to watch. Let them know that it's fine if they don't want to say anything for "check-in", too.

Optional Journaling:
"Write about your face. Write about your eyes, your nose, your mouth, your ears...What have these parts of your face been through, seen, and heard? What have they learned? What do they know?

Project Suggestion:
"This workshop is a chance to notice the special story of your own face. It's a chance to think about your eyes, your nose, your mouth, your ears - any part of your face. What have these different parts of your face been through? What have they learned? What do they know? To explore this we will be creating a CrayPas mask with three layers that you can scratch through and and write into. Your drawing can be symbolic with shapes and colors representing the parts of your face. It doesn't need to be realistic, and you probably will want to wait until the scratching at the end to add much detail.
Begin with the first layer: cover your paper with a bright color - whatever bright color represents you as a very young person. Now add a second layer of colors - darker colors this time - choose colors for each part of your face to represent what your eyes and ears and nose and mouth went through as you grew. Now add a third layer of color - pick a darker color this time. This layer can represent anything difficult that you went through, and you can layer it over what ever parts of your mask you wish. It's okay if you layer it over all of it.
Now that you have added all these layers, the last step is using a toothpick or a utensil to scratch through them. Scratch through to draw eyes, nose, mouth, ears, etc. As you draw, notice the wisdom that each part of your facehas gained through all the layers it's been through. Take time to think about any words or stories that go with your mask. You can scratch these words into the drawing, or you can write them on separate paper or in your journal."

Optional Feedback Exercise:
Ten minutes before the workshop ends, pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You could even take them to copy and return them the next week, so that the teens can add them to their journals.

Closing and Validation:
At the end of the project, a Closing Circle can be a way to give each teen an opportunity to share what she or he has created and talk about what it means to them and how it felt to make it. Just like the check-in circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives teens an opportunity to create masks that express the stories that live in each part of their face, from their eyes to their ears to their nose.

Row.txt_code:
Purpose:
To notice different sides of yourself, and know that the sides that feel easy and the sides that feel hard are both okay.

Materials:
4" by 4" smooth cover stock paper
oil pastels (such as CrayPas)
paper towels
toothpicks, plastic utensils
pens and writing paper (teens could also use their journals)
independent project handout (for individual workshop) (click here for handout)

Set Up:
Make sure that there are two pieces of precut stock paper and an assortment of oil pastels at each place, as well as paper towels and toothpicks or plastic utensils.

Welcome and Ground Rules:
It can help create a safe environment if you take time to individually welcome each teen, connect with them, and let them know you are glad they are there. Introduce the project and the philosophy of Windows time: "This is a special "window of time" for each of you. For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? Are there any other Ground Rules you'd like to add?" At this time you can mention any pre-established ground rules you have.

Check In:
A good example of an appropriate check-in would be: "Before we start the art, we'll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art." This is a time to reassure anyone who's scared of art that it's fine, and to tell anyone who "hates" art that's fine too. Remind them that they don't have to do it, that they can just watch if they want to. When given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in even if they say they're just going to watch. Let them know that it's fine if they don't want to say anything for "check-in", too.

Optional Journaling:
"Divide a paper into two columns. On the left side, write 'easy', and on the right side, write 'hard'. Fill the left side of the page with any words that describe the 'easy' sides of yourself, and fill the right side of the page with any words that describe the 'hard' sides of yourself."

Project Suggestion:
"This workshop is a chance to explore different sides of yourself. We all have sides of ourselves that feel easy and wonderful, and we have sides that feel more difficult and troublesome. In this workshop, we get to notice both sides and explore them with CrayPas.
Take two pieces of paper: one for the 'easy' and one for the 'hard'. Start with one piece of paper and think about the side of yourself that feels difficult. Use colors of CrayPas to represent the feelings. You'll find that if you start with lighter colors and then put darker colors on top, you can scratch through with a toothpick afterward to add lines, designs, and words to express the tough side of you. As you write, try to be nice to yourself. Remember that even the hard parts of ourselves are there for a reason, and they can help us become stronger.
When you are ready, put this first drawing aside and take a deep breath. As you let your breath go, try to release all the hard things. As you breathe in, begin to think about the sides of yourself that feel easy and wonderful. Use colors of CrayPas to represent these sides of you, again using the CrayPas layers and scratching through to add details and words."

Optional Feedback Exercise:
Ten minutes before the workshop ends, pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You could even take them to copy and return them the next week, so that the teens can add them to their journals.

Closing and Validation:
At the end of the project, a Closing Circle can be a way to give each teen an opportunity to share what she or he has created and talk about what it means to them and how it felt to make it. Just like the check-in circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives teens an opportunity to notice and accept different sides of themselves by creating two contrasting CrayPas drawings.

Row.txt_code:
Purpose:
To use the art process to safely work out feelings of anger. To explore what you can learn from your own anger.

Materials:
8 1/2" by 11" smooth, thick paper
oil pastels (such as CrayPas)
paper towels
toothpicks, plastic utensils
pens and writing paper (teens could also use their journals)
highlighter pens
independent project handout (for individual workshop) (click here for handout)

Set Up:
Make sure that there is paper, oil pastels, and toothpicks or other utensils available at each place.

Welcome and Ground Rules:
It can help create a safe environment if you take time to individually welcome each teen, connect with them, and let them know you are glad they are there. Introduce the project and the philosophy of Windows time: "This is a special "window of time" for each of you. For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? Are there any other Ground Rules you'd like to add?" At this time you can mention any pre-established ground rules you have.

Check In:
A good example of an appropriate check-in would be: "Before we start the art, we'll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art." This is a time to reassure anyone who's scared of art that it's fine, and to tell anyone who "hates" art that's fine too. Remind them that they don't have to do it, that they can just watch if they want to. When given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in even if they say they're just going to watch. Let them know that it's fine if they don't want to say anything for "check-in", too.

Optional Journaling:
"Write down any words that express your angry feelings. After writing, read back over what you've written. Highlight any parts that seem most important. Then write more about the parts you've highlighted.

Project Suggestion:
"This workshop is a chance to let anger out in a way that will be safe for you and those around you. And as you let your anger out, you might find that it is there to teach you something. This workshop is a chance to let it out and listen to what it is able to teach. Take a pile of paper and a set of Craypas. Pick a piece of paper and a color that represents your anger. Make marks on the page that express your anger- whatever shapes come out. Let any anger in your body come through your arm onto the page. Add more colors. Fill the page.
You can make one drawing, or as many as you need to. You can scratch through with a toothpick afterwards to add lines, designs, and words to express the feelings and thoughts that come to mind. When you feel like you've gotten enough out onto paper, put the drawings aside and take a deep breath. As you let your breath go, try to release all the anger. As you breathe in, imagine breathing in relaxation and peacefulness. Now write on scratch paper (or in your journal) about any positive things you'd like to learn from your anger or from letting it out in the drawings."

Optional Feedback Exercise:
Ten minutes before the workshop ends, pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You could even take them to copy and return them the next week, so that the teens can add them to their journals.

Closing and Validation:
At the end of the project, a Closing Circle can be a way to give each teen an opportunity to share what she or he has created and talk about what it means to them and how it felt to make it. Just like the check-in circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives teens the opportunity to safely work out their feelings of anger by creating drawings with oil pastels.
Row.txt_tips: When doing this workshop with younger kids, the word "mad" may help them grasp the concept more than "anger".

Row.txt_code:
Purpose:
To create a collage pin representing your vision for your future.

Materials:
3" by 3" card stock
larger card stock (in case anyone wants to collage bigger)
3" by 3" plexiglass
Matte Medium and brush to apply it
magazines and photostock books
scissors
glue sticks
optional: magnets or pin backs and E-6000 glue (supervise the gluing for proper ventilation)
pens and writing paper (teens could also use their journals)
independent project handout (for individual workshop) (click here for handout)

Set Up:
Spread out the supplies on the table. Make sure there is a piece of card stock and a piece of plexiglass at each place. The magazines and photostock books should be spread out so they're accessible to everyone. It may be a good idea to set out some newspaper or paper towel before covering the collages in Matte Medium because it can be messy.

Welcome and Ground Rules:
It can help create a safe environment if you take time to individually welcome each teen, connect with them, and let them know you are glad they are there. Introduce the project and the philosophy of Windows time: "This is a special "window of time" for each of you. For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? Are there any other Ground Rules you'd like to add?" At this time you can mention any pre-established ground rules you have.

Check In:
A good example of an appropriate check-in would be: "Before we start the art, we'll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art." This is a time to reassure anyone who's scared of art that it's fine, and to tell anyone who "hates" art that's fine too. Remind them that they don't have to do it, that they can just watch if they want to. When given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in even if they say they're just going to watch. Let them know that it's fine if they don't want to say anything for "check-in", too.

Optional Journaling:
"Write for five minutes about your vision for your future. What comes to mind? Write anything at all that you think of."

Note:
It's helpful to have a sample of how the collage looks with the plexiglass attached.

Project Suggestion:
"This workshop is a chance to create your own vision pin or magnet (see sample). You don't have to know in advance what you want it to look like. You can let it evolve as you go, just like your life evolves as you go. Look through magazines and tear out whatever pictures jump out at you. When you've collected a bunch of them, go ahead and begin to cut out the parts you want to use.
When you start gluing them down, it can help if you glue something over your whole 3" by 3" board. That way, you will have the background you want. If you need to use a bigger board, go ahead, but know there might not be large enough plexiglass for it. When you are finished collaging, you are ready to attach the plexiglass. Remove the brown paper from both sides of the glass. Then cover your collage with a thick layer of Matte Medium. Press the glass onto your collage. Matte Medium will squeeze out the edges as you press. Hold it into position and squeeze the air bubbles out as you press. Try not to get the Matte Medium onto the surface of the glass. When it is complete, take some time to write any words that go with your vision. If there are pins and magnets available you can glue them on the back."

Optional Feedback Exercise:
Ten minutes before the workshop ends, pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You could even take them to copy and return them the next week, so that the teens can add them to their journals.

Closing and Validation:
At the end of the project, a Closing Circle can be a way to give each teen an opportunity to share what she or he has created and talk about what it means to them and how it felt to make it. Just like the check-in circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives teens an opportunity to create a collage pin representing their visions for their futures.
Row.txt_tips:
It's possible to use the vision pin as a frame by getting a frame stand for the back of the plexiglass.

If this workshop is done towards the end or beginning of the year, participants could collage their pins according to their New Year's resolutions.

Row.txt_code:
Purpose:
To create a mask or series of masks representing what you have survived

Materials:
Colored SuperSculpey (if you only have plain SuperSculpey, then you will need painting supplies to add colors)
toothpicks and plastic utensils (to form the clay)
toaster oven
optional: clear nail polish (to add shine at the end)
pens and writing paper (teens could also use their journals instead)
independent project handout (for individual workshop) (click here for handout)

Set Up
Set the supplies out on the table, making sure that there is SuperSculpey available from each seat at the table.

Welcome and Ground Rules
It can help create a safe environment if you take time to individually welcome each teen, connect with them, and let them know you are glad they are there. Introduce the project and the philosophy of Windows time: "This is a special "window of time" for each of you. For Windows time, we have some Ground Rules to help create respect and safety. Can anyone think of a Ground Rule that would help? Are there any other Ground Rules you'd like to add?" At this time you can mention any pre-established ground rules you have.

Check In
A good example of an appropriate check-in would be: "Before we start the art, we'll have a check-in circle so everyone has a chance to share their name, how they are feeling today, and any feelings about doing art." This is a time to reassure anyone who's scared of art that it's fine, and to tell anyone who "hates" art that's fine too. Remind them that they don't have to do it, that they can just watch if they want to. When given the freedom, they will probably choose to join in even if they say they're just going to watch. Let them know that it's fine if they don't want to say anything for "check-in", too.

Project Suggestion
"This workshop is a chance to create a mask, or series of masks, representing yourself as a survivor. You might not always notice, but you probably survive many challenges every day. Since the time you were born, you have survived difficult moments and you've learned and grown from them. Those experiences helped make you the wonderful, unique person that you are today.
As you work with the clay, create a miniature mask that represents yourself as a survivor. Use whatever colors and shapes that express all that you've come through. When you are finished, cook your mask (about 10 minutes at 275 degrees). As your mask is cooking, take some time to write any words that go with your mask. If you want to, use a coat of clear nail polish to add gloss to your mask after it's cooked."

Optional Feedback Exercise
Ten minutes before the workshop ends, pass out one sheet of paper per person. Ask the teens to write a paragraph about what they learned from the workshop. Ask permission to read these papers so you can learn about the effectiveness of the workshop. You could even take them to copy and return them the next week, so that the teens can add them to their journals.

Closing and Validation
At the end of the project, a Closing Circle can be a way to give each teen an opportunity to share what she or he has created and talk about what it means to them and how it felt to make it. Just like the check-in circle, give each teen a chance to speak. Validate their courage for opening themselves up to their own creativity and respecting whatever came out.
Row.txt_description: This workshop allows teens an opportunity to create a mask or series of masks representing what they've survived.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To explore the creative process by allowing participants the freedom to sculpt whatever they would like using sculpey.

Materials:
colored sculpey (if you only have plain sculpey, you will need painting supplies to add colors)
toaster oven
optional: clear nail polish (to add shine after baking)

Set Up:
Set the supplies on the table, making sure that the supplies are accessible from each place at the table.

Project Suggestion:
"Today, we will be using Sculpey clay to express ourselves. After we sculpt we will be baking the clay so that it hardens. Then we will be able to paint it many colors. feel free to create whatever you would like to create. Enjoy the feeling of clay in your hands and just see what happens as you play with it. It's okay to make something "ugly" or "beautiful" or whatever comes out. It doesn't matter what it looks like to anyone else. Enjoy!"
Row.txt_description: In this workshop, participants explore the creative process of sculpting and the freedom of imagination by using sculpey to sculpt whatever they would like.

Row.txt_code:
Here are a few creative ideas that children can write about in their journals.

Materials
Pens and pencils
colored pens or markers
Journals (or looseleaf paper)
creative journaling idea handouts (for handouts, see below)

Today
Draw a picture of the most special thing you remember about today. Write down your feelings about it.

Myself
Draw a picture of yourself. It could be a picture of your appearance, or it could be abstract symbols, colors, shapes, or designs. When you are done, write a poem entitled "I Am..." (Your poem doesn't need to rhyme.)

 For a handout with the prompts "Today" and "Myself", please click here.

My Name
Think about the letters of your name. Create your own design, logo, or symbol that uses the letters of your name and expresses who you are.

A Letter to Me
What are all the wonderful things about you?
What are the good things people have said to you?
Go ahead and write a letter to yourself about all the things you like about you.

For a handout with the prompts "My Name" and "A Letter to Me", please click here.

Right Now
Draw how you feel right now. You can feel free to scribble, doodle, and choose any colors that express your state of mind. After you're done, write about what you drew.

It Scares Me
What scares you? Draw a picture of it. Write about what you drew.
For a handout with the prompts "Right Now" and "It Scares Me", please click here.
Very Mad
It's okay to get mad. There are many ways to express anger without hurting anybody. See if you can fill a page with the colors representing your angry feelings. You may want to do angry scribbles, or you may want to use words or pictures.

Can You See Through Me?
What would someone see if they could see through you, all the way inside to what you are feeling? Draw a picture of the feelings they would see.

For a handout with the prompts "Very Mad" and "Can you See Through Me?", please click here.

My Family
Who is a part of your family? Are there friends? Are there pets? Are there people younger than you? Are there people older than you? Draw a picture of yourself with your family. Include all of them.

Hands Are Not for Hitting
Trace your hands on the page. Decorate inside and around it to show all the good things you do with your hands.

For a handout with the prompts "My Family" and "Hands Are Not For Hitting", please click here.

Treasure Map
Everyone has buried treasures inside of them. These are the gifts, eelings, and abilities that we have deep within us. What treasures do you have inside of you? Draw a map to the treasure. Are there things in your way? Are there any helpers?

Your Own Project
Can you think of your own Project? What do you want to write or draw about in your journal? Go ahead and do it! Your ideas are important.

For a handout with the prompts "Treasure Map" and "Your Own Project", please click here.
Row.txt_description: A variety of interesting journaling prompts for kids

Creation:
Beaded bracelets make a special gift. They can be as simple or detailed as you like. You can string regular beads or you can make your own beads. Here are 2 methods: roll small pieces of scuply, mixing colors if you like, make a hole all the way through and bake for 10 minutes. (Feel free to experiment with the size and shape of the bead). Row.txt_tips:
Gingerbread Recipe

Ingredients
1 cup butter at room temperature
1 3/4 cups brown sugar
1 1/4 cups white sugar
2 tablespoons molasses
6 eggs
6 cups all-purpose flour
2 teaspoons baking soda
1 tablespoon ground ginger
1 tablespoon ground cinnamon
1 tablespoon allspice

Directions
Line several cookie sheets with aluminum foil. Butter and flour the foil. In a large bowl, cream the butter and sugars. Beat in the molasses and the eggs.

In another large bowl, sift together the dry ingredients. Combine mixtures and knead into a smooth ball. Cover and refrigerate at least 30 minutes.

Preheat the oven to 325F. On a well-floured surface, roll out a small amount of the dough until it's 1/4 inch thick. Cut into desired shapes using cookie cutters. Gently, using the spatula, lift the dough and place it on the prepared cookie sheet.

Bake 15-20 minutes or until slightly firm. Le tcool on racks until firm enough to handle. Peel the foil off the pieces and set aside the pieces to dry thoroughly overnight.

To make icing:
3 egg whites
1 1/2 teaspoons cream of tartar
3 - 3 1/2 cups powdered or confectioner's sugar

In a large bowl, beat the egg whites until they begin to foam. Add the cream of tartar and beat until the whites are stiff but not dry.

Gradually beat in the sugar, beating for about 5 minutes until it reaches spreading consistency. Keep it covered and refrigerated until needed.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To have participants create a charm bracelet or necklace that helps them recognize the importance of using language that directs them to take positive actions and then to focus on solutions rather than problems. This charm bracelet or necklace encourages group members to see what skills and gifts are working for them even in the midst of despair and chaos when moments of success are often forgotten or unnoticed. Participants are empowered as they recognize their strengths and envision themselves accomplishing measurable goals.

Materials:
 Pens
Writing paper
Scissors
Stapler
String
Yarn
Ribbon
Glue
Construction paper
Colored cotton balls		 Markers
Hole puncher
Paint
Flexi-foam
Pipe cleaners
Felt
Wire
Faux gems
Buttons
     












Note to Leader: To make the bracelet or necklace more durable and wearable you may want to use jewelry making materials and beads. Shrinky dinks with words can also be added to create charms.

Time Frame:
Warm Up:
Introduction:
Journaling:
Creation:
Closing:
Total Time:
5 minutes
10 minutes
15 minutes
40 minutes
5 minutes
1 hour, 15 minutes







Warm Up:
Sit comfortably with your back upright but not rigid. Close your eyes or look at a place on the floor in front of you. Focus all your attention on each breath. Observe the movement of your belly—up and down. Don’t change your breath in any way — just observe it. After a few minutes of conscious breathing, hold in your mind the image of yourself sitting by a place you find relaxing (i.e. the ocean, a river, a lake, the forest) as you watch your thoughts and fall. Notice that when a thought disappears, another thought comes to take its place. This is okay. Just notice the experience, let it go, and return to your breath. Then simply focus on sitting, breathing and watching your thoughts.


 
Sample bracelet with positive qualities and strengths
 
  
 
Another sample bracelet with different materials  
Introduction:
Today we are going to do a workshop called "Words are Like Charms." Charms can be reminders of things that are important to you. Today we will have a chance to create our own charms using the powerful words that describe us. Before we start we are going to think about our strengths and positive qualities, although this is not always easy. We’re always eager to think about our negative qualities. Right now, though, I’d like all of you to take a few minutes and bring to mind something you’ve done lately that opened up your heart—did you speak kindly to someone, give someone a compliment, did someone share a kind word with you? Do you remember how it felt to hear or speak those kind words?

(Give the group time to talk about this--usually one group member points out another member’s positive qualities and this opens up the discussion).

Reflection and Journaling:
Then encourage participants to think about their strengths by asking them how they managed to do certain things they accomplished (for example leave an abusive partner--this shows courage, growth), how they account for some of the changes they are making in their lives (for example finding a job which shows resilience, courage, determination). Other ideas include taking a parenting class, this underscores someone’s willingness to learn, and a loving spirit and on and on.

Have the women each take a piece of paper and a pen and come up with a list of words that reflect their strengths and accomplishments. Remind them to be patient and that a few words can be enough to express what an amazing person they are. Then have them think about and set some of the goals they want to achieve in the future. (To help them focus on goals, you can ask them “What” questions such as, "When you are being patient with your daughter, what will that look like to you?” or “When you are organized, what will your house look like?”)

Once the list of strengths and goals is finished, ask the women to share one of their positive qualities and one goal. While everyone shares, keep track of the adjectives they use, and once everyone has had a turn read the collection of adjectives aloud. Encourage the women to notice how powerful these words are--the words can be seen as “charms,” “talismans.” If we string our positive qualities together along with our goals, the words become actions or formulas that empower us--just like the charms on a charm bracelet. Positive words can also be seen as amulets--items that have “magical” benefits.

 
  Sample charms
Creation:
Now you get to design a bracelet, necklace or amulet and add “charms” to it. The “charms” can be depictions of goals you want to achieve or of your personal strengths. You may decide to design a “charm,” and then write on it. Remember you can use paper, wire, pipe cleaners, beads, ribbon, or string—anything you like. As they create, remind them to focus on the positive words that describe their strengths.

Closing:
Once the women are finished with their necklace or bracelet, have them think about the words they used to describe themselves and the goals they've identified. Ask them to notice throughout the week how focusing on the positive feels. Have them think about the “charms” they created which describe their strengths. Remind them that the more they focus on these "charms" and goals, the more they will help bring them into their lives! Each day their thoughts and words can become new "charms" they wish to bring into their lives.

Variation:
Make a bracelet with two sides to it, one side representing something or someone they wanted to leave behind, the other side representing something they would like to gain or accomplish in the future. Towards the end of the day, ask participants to set a short-term goal for themselves and promise they would do something for themselves in the next week.
Row.txt_description: Participants will have the opportunity to recognize the importance of using language that directs them to take positive actions. This encourages us to see what skills and gifts are working for us even in the midst of despair and chaos when moments of success are often forgotten or unnoticed. We can be empowered as we recognize our strengths and envision ourselves accomplishing measurable goals.

A table set with footprint templates and other materials
Objective:
To provide a creative opportunity to explore what footprints you want to leave in the world and how all of our journeys combined can create a non-violent future.

Materials:
Shrinky Dink plastic (Ruff-N-Ready type)
Colored pencils
Individual pencil sharpeners
Small paper plates for shavings
Permanent markers
Scissors
Hole punchers
Craft wire
Wire cutters/pliers
Assorted beads
Assorted findings (fishhook earrings, key chains, jump rings)
Assorted ribbon
 
  Tracing and coloring the footprint on the shrinky dink
Toaster oven
CD player
CD's of relaxing music
Paper to journal on
Foot template
(click here for template)









 
   Feet with ribbon and beads


Preparation:
You'll need to make enough photocopies of the various foot templates for all the participants. Pre-cut the Shrinky Dink into 3 1/2"x4" squares to fit the size of our template (AWBW sells pre-cut Shrinky Dink material, $5 for 100 sheets). Make sure all colored pencils are pre-sharpened. It's good to have all the materials set up prior to beginning the workshop.

It’s important to try this project in advance so you have some samples to share, and also so you can get a feel for how the Shrinky Dinks cook. It’s very exciting to watch!

Timeframe:
1 1/2 to 2 hours

Introduction:
Today you are going to create Journey Keepers to explore what footprints you want to leave in the world and how all of our journeys combined can create a non-violent future.

How you choose to live your life makes a difference in the world, the path you choose to walk leaves its imprint. What imprint do you want to make on the world? What footprints do you want to leave in your life and in the lives of those around you? What steps do you want to take?

Creative Writing Warm-up:
Lets begin by journaling about these questions and what steps you want to take in your life to create a non-violent future.

This Journey Keeper can be used as an opportunity to make one commitment to yourself about your life, the steps you want to take in your life, and the footprints you want to leave.

Think of one commitment that you will make to yourself. It could be a personal promise to yourself such as "I will trust myself and be gentle with myself," "I will be kind to others," "I will live a peaceful life," or "I will try to make the world a better place by the choices I make." You can make a personal commitment to yourself that will become a global one if we all work together to create the change we wish to see in the world.

 
  Baked and decorated Shriny Dink Journey Keepers
Creation:
Once you have decided what commitment you want to make to yourself you can begin to create your foot. You will be writing this commitment on your foot as a reminder of the footprints you want to leave in the world.

Choose one of the foot templates in front of you. Start by tracing the foot on the rough side of the shrinky dink. You may choose any of the colors on the table. Begin to color and create the design that will fill in your foot. (Be sure to draw on the rough side of the plastic.) When you are finished coloring, decide whether you want to add wire and beads to your foot. Cut out your foot with scissors. At this time you will need to use the hole punch to place holes for wiring and beads. If you need help, please ask for it.

Now the feet are ready for baking. Place the Shrinky Dink on a flat metal tray and place inside the toaster oven. Bake at 300 degrees until Shrinky Dink has completely flattened (this will take about one minute). Watch the amazing transformation! Remove your Shrinky Dink and allow it to cool. Now your foot is ready for decorating with wire and beads if you wish. Repeat this process as time permits.

Closing Circle:
Have participants share their finished feet and say a few words about the commitment they are making to themselves in working to create a non-violent future.
Row.txt_description: To provide a creative opportunity to explore what footprints you want to leave in the world and how all of our journeys combined can create a non-violent future.

Objective:
This workshop teaches the children to create a charm bracelet or necklace that encourages them to notice their positive qualities and how to link them creating a brighter, more optimistic world for themselves.

Note to Leader: To make the bracelet or necklace more durable and wearable you may want to use jewelry making materials and beads. Shrinky dinks with words can also be added to create charms.

Age Range:
6-16 years old
 		 
  
Time Frame:
Relaxation:
Introduction:
Warm-up:
Creation:
Closing:
Total Time:

5 minutes
10 minutes
15 minutes
40 minutes
5 minutes
