Today we will be exploring this connection through journaling.
 
 
  Sample set up
 
Creation:
As the participants sit quietly and comfortably, light a candle and say a few words of inspiration, a mantra or prayer. You may also read: "Surrender to the beauty, surrender to the light, rest, restore, reunite." which is Patricia's own prayer.

The Power of Prayer, and Meditation:
Have each participant go around the room and say one word to describe what they intend to get out of this workshop.  It could be peace, comfort, strength - each person will have their own word.

Start playing soft and gentle music, preferably with no words and encourage participants to begin to journal by taking your one word intention from the introductions, write it down and allow other words to tumble onto the page. Keep your hand flowing, even if you write the same word over and over. If you feel you want to develop your own prayer through this process do so. We'll take about 10 minutes to do this.

Ask a few participants to read what they wrote. As they share thank them for their willingness to share or courage to change.

  
 workshop participants during meditation
Guided Meditation #1: Up a Flight of Stairs
To begin the creative process, say or read the following:

If you are comfortable, close your eyes, and breathe, just breathe, for breath is like magic…
Your breath holds the knowledge of your pleasure; it holds the knowledge of your pain. 
It knows what you are afraid of, what you dream of.  It holds the knowledge of all your identities, all that you would like to be and how you would like to be seen. And, it holds the truth. Your breath goes everywhere…it is part of everything that you are.

Imagine yourself walking down a hallway, with your most favorite clothing on (Patricia says, "I imagine a long flowing gown of gossamer – light, airy, like wings.")

At the end of the hall is a set of stairs.  Ascend the stairs one step at a time, while watching and feeling yourself step up, up and up, knowing that at the end of the stairs is a door.  Notice the energy in your step – is it heavy?  Is it light?  Are you looking forward or looking back?  Simply notice how you look and feel as you ascend the stairs.

Open the door and see the entire universe before you – what does this look like to you? This is your journey and your universe, your favorite place to create - it can look and feel any way that you want it to look and feel.

Imagine taking that first step through the door, into the vast space and being suspended in the most beautiful place you’ve ever seen.  You are light, surrounded by light – you can do anything, and you can create anything.  You are completely supported…imagine the freedom of being completely supported by the universe…imagine being supported by your hopes and dreams and all that you want to be…

Knowing that you are supported, let’s take a walk, deeper into your universe.  What do you see? How do you feel?  Describe this experience to yourself.  See every detail – allow yourself to fly from star to star, if you would like. Take note of everything … even if all you see, feel and hear is silence… as you journey deeper into your universe…what do you see?

Now, gently remind yourself to return to the door…walk back through, and descend the stairs one at a time until you reach the bottom.  Slowly open your eyes, pick up your pen and write about your experience, doodle about what you saw and felt and heard.

Take about 10 minutes to write and/or doodle your thoughts.

Ask a few participants to read what they wrote. As they share thank them for their willingness to share or courage to change.

  
 Art from A Woman With Wings
 
Guided Meditation #2: Finding Your Genius Seed
Next we will meditate then write about our own individual genius seed.

We all have one – what is yours?  This image and symbol of your brilliance will remind you of the creativity and healing within.  This guided meditation allows for discovering and claiming the participant’s "genius seed".  If ever stuck in the writing process, or need motivation to journal, this visualization and journey helps to unlock and guide you.

Imagine yourself once again, walking down a long hallway…noticing your dress, your movements…at the end of the hall is your flight of stairs, that takes you directly to your universe, your place of creativity, your place of power.  Take each step one at a time, noticing your energy, noticing your feelings, noticing you.  You can either go up the stairs or down the stairs, your choice.  You are free to decide where you would like to go today.

You are now at the end of the stairs about to open the door – pause and ask to be greeted by a being that knows and loves you, an angel perhaps. Open the door; step out into your favorite place where you are greeted by your angel, this most loving being, and say: 

“I want to find my "genius seed", will you take me there? Will you support me in my journey?”

Imagine your angel saying: “Yes!  Absolutely!  Of course!”

And off you go.

Notice your loving being in great detail…how they move, what they look like…
see every step of the journey they take you on. Imagine the smells in the air, how your skin feels. Remember to breathe in and out, and go deeper into your adventure, as you step closer and closer to finding your "genius seed".

Your angel, your guide, stops and points – there it is, you’ve found it!  What do you see?  Reach for it, touch it, smell it, feel it.

Now ask your "genius seed" to show you all of your talents and abilities – your gifts…ask it tell you all about you.

Take the time to really listen…to hear all that is said about you…later you will write about this journey in great detail…
 
Your angel gently reminds you it’s time to return home…this time, with your "genius seed" in hand.  Now that you’ve found it, it will never leave you.

The journey home is a quick one….back to the flight of stairs, stepping out of your adventure, taking one step at a time, noticing how you feel, what you see.  You are at the end of the stairs; preparing to enter the hallway home…you slowly open your eyes and start to write – about your "genius seed", the journey to find it, what is it, and what it tells you about you…

Take about 10 minutes to write and/or doodle your thoughts.

Ask a few participants to read what they wrote. As they share thank them for their willingness to share or courage to change.

  
  Listening to that inner voice.
Closing:
Intention Card Quotes
Have strips of paper with the Intention Card quotes available in a pile or in a basket or bowl for participants to grab from.

Have each participant take a quote and read it to themselves. What does this mean to you?  How does it make you feel? When you feel your feelings, and emotions, they become the precursor to great insight and personal wisdom.  Now we'll spend about 10 minutes to write and doodle.

Depending on time, allow participants to tell the group what their own quote prompted in them, they can also share what creative expressions they included during journaling?
Row.txt_description: This workshop takes the participant on their own journey of creativity, where the product is their own wisdom. The journal or sketchbook becomes a point of reference for their lives, and lends perspective on their fears and challenges, joys and enthusiasm, and every emotion and feeling in between.
Row.txt_tips:
The following is a list of tips for leading journaling workshops provided by Patricia Varga

1)  Ceremony
Begin the journaling process as you would begin a ceremony, for this is sacred time for self – to connect with the creativity and imagi nation within.  Lighting a candle, saying a few words of inspiration sets up the journey.  

If writing one’s own prayer or words of inspiration is too daunting, too scary, develop one together…or give them one and encourage them over time to develop their own.

They can use a poem from a book – a line from a play – a passage from the Bible…whatever they feel a connection to, whatever comforts or inspires them.

2) Write and doodle every day.
Creativity is a process, it is a practice.  Writing and doodling everyday – even if you write your name a hundred times on a sheet of paper and that’s it – gets the creative muscles in shape.  The physical act of picking your favorite pen, putting it to paper and letting the words and doodles tumble onto the page, is meditative.  It takes you to another world where possibilities are endless.  

Once you get your rhythm, you never lose it, for you know what it feels like to write, to doodle, to let go.  Your creative memory is in place.

3) Creativity only knows how to create.
There is no right or wrong, no judgment, only joy.  I encourage you and your clients to be “disobedient” during meditation…to know that it’s ok to be different. There are no expectations.  If your mind takes you in a different direction, not the one you are being guided to, go with it.  Following your imagination is a beautiful thing - flow with it and feel blessed.  

4) Share your own journey, your humanity.
I tell people about my own fears and criticisms, doubts and challenges and how I use writing and doodling to overcome them.  People want to feel safe and comfortable during the process and that it’s ok to be creative.  Sharing allows for this comfort.  

5) Tell them what you’re going to tell them, tell them, tell them what you told them.
Sounds crazy, but illuminating what’s about to take place, can be reassuring, and soothing. Allowing the journaling take place, then giving a quick recap of what took place invites greater participation and helps reinforce the process.  Please forgive me if this seems facile and understood – I always have to remind myself to do these!

6) A Beginning
Please know that this workshop is a beginning for what could become a life-long journey of creativity. There are more workshops, more techniques, more meditations, but for now, this is a great place to start.

“In this journey of creativity, the product is wisdom… wisdom that reminds you of your talents and abilities, and that all that you dream and hope for is possible.”

Patricia Varga, A Woman with Wings

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop is inspired by the words of wisdom and illustrations from "A Woman with Wings" by Patricia Varga.  Through this unique approach to journaling, the workshop shows the power of keeping a journal or diary. 
 
  Art from "A Woman With Wings"

Materials:
A journal or diary with lots of blank pages
A pen, special pens that the participants can keep is a great idea!
An open mind and heart
A candle, preferably soy (optional)
Relaxing music
Writing prompts (click here)
Journaling Tips to give to participants (optional)
(click here)

Time Frame:
Power of Your Word: 20 min.
Up A Flight of Stairs Meditation/Journaling: 20 min.
Finding your "Genius Seed" Meditation/Journaling: 20

Total time: 60- 75 minutes depending on length of sharing time

Age Range:
13- 18 year olds

Introduction:
To set the mood you may want to ask the teens to sit quietly and comfortably, they might want to close their eyes and light a candle and while listening to soft music and a few words of inspiration.

Patricia Varga created "A Woman with Wings" from a journaling exercise in July of 1993. She says, " I wrote my name a 1,000 times a day, even if I couldn’t write anything else – the act of selecting a pen and connecting with paper became a meditation that allowed me to connect with "The Divine" within – once I trusted this connection and allowed for my own abilities to come through, I found my voice, my place, my ability to create and heal….

Once you trust this connection, (some call it God, some call it The Divine, some call it the Goddess of Creativity, some call it Self, some call it nothing at all,) the creativity and ultimate healing is limitless.

Today we will be exploring this connection through journaling. Even the younger teens can experience meaning and growth through writing their thoughts and emotions without censoring themselves.
   
 
 
  Sample set up
 

Creation:
We will begin a journey together through some meditations and writing.  During this experience, remember that there are no judgments, only joy. What you write, think and feel belong to you alone and each of those thoughts and feelings are personal, there are no wrong thoughts or feelings!

Step One
The Power of Your Word:
Have each participant go around the room and say one word or phrase that is something positive about them.  It could be kind, caring, loving, good at school, likes to write, helps others ...  each person will have their own word or phrase.

Start playing soft and gentle music, preferably with no words.

Begin to journal by taking your one word or phrase and write it down and allow other words to spill onto the page by thinking about what that word means to you. Don't worry about creating sentences or spelling, just keep your hand flowing, even if you write the same word over and over.

Note: These words can be anything that is meaningful to the individual creating them… there is no right or wrong, only joy for the process.

Ask if anyone wants to share what they wrote, keeping in mind that teens are often relucktant to share personal things and that is fine, they don't have to share if they don't want to.

Step Two
 
 Reading from the journal
 
Guided Meditation #1: Up a Flight of Stairs
If you are comfortable, close your eyes, and breathe slowly and deeply, just breathe, for breath is like magic…
Your breath holds the knowledge of your joy, it holds the knowledge of your pain. 
It knows what you are afraid of, what you dream of.  It holds the knowledge of all that you would like to be and how you would like to be seen. And, it holds the truth. Your breath goes everywhere…it is part of everything that you are.

Imagine yourself walking down a hallway, with your most favorite clothing on, in your mind, picture how you look.  See your shoes, your outfit, how your hair looks. 

At the end of the hall is a set of stairs.  Go up the stairs one step at a time, while watching and feeling yourself step up, up and up, knowing that at the end of the stairs is a door.  Notice the energy in your step – is it heavy?  Is it light?  Are you looking forward or looking back?  Simply notice how you look and feel as you climb the stairs.

Open the door and before you see the entire universe!  What does this look like to you? This is your journey and your universe, your favorite place to create - it can look and feel any way that you want it to look and feel as you continue to take slow deep breathes.

Imagine taking that first step through the door, into the vast space and you find yourself in the most beautiful place you’ve ever seen.  You are light, surrounded by light – you can do anything, and you can create anything.  You are completely supported…imagine the freedom of being completely supported by the universe…imagine being supported by your hopes and dreams and all that you want to be…

Knowing that you are supported, let’s take a walk, deeper into your universe.  What do you see? How do you feel?  Describe this experience to yourself.  See every detail – allow yourself to fly from star to star, if you would like. Take note of everything … even if all you see, feel and hear is silence… as you journey deeper into your universe…what do you see?

Now, gently remind yourself to return to the door…walk back through, and gently down the stairs one at a time until you reach the bottom.  Slowly open your eyes, pick up your pen and write about your experience, doodle about what you saw, felt and heard.

Take about 10 minutes to write your thoughts.  If your would rather draw or doodle your thoughts that is fine also.

Ask if anyone wants to share their experience with their journey so far.

Step Three

 
 Leaders during the meditation
 
Guided Meditation #2: Finding Your "Genius Seed"
This image and symbol of your brilliance will remind you of the creativity and healing within.  This guided meditation allows for discovering and claiming the participant’s "genius seed".  If ever stuck in the writing process, or need motivation to journal, this visualization and journey can help to unlock and guide you.

Imagine yourself once again, walking down a long hallway…noticing your dress, your movements…at the end of the hall is your flight of stairs, that takes you directly to your universe, your place of creativity, your place of power.  Take each step one at a time, noticing your energy, noticing your feelings, noticing you.  You can either go up the stairs or down the stairs, your choice.  You are free to decide where you would like to go today.

You are now at the end of the stairs about to open the door – pause and ask to be greeted by a being that knows and loves you, an angel perhaps. Open the door, step out into your favorite place where you are greeted by your angel, this most loving being, and say: 

“I want to find my "genius seed", will you take me there? Will you support me in my journey?”

Imagine your angel saying: “Yes!  Absolutely!  Of course!”

And off you go.

Notice your loving being in great detail…how they move, what they look like…
see every step of the journey they take you on. Imagine the smells in the air, how your skin feels. Remember to breathe in and out, and go deeper into your adventure, as you step closer and closer to finding your "genius seed."

Your angel, your guide, stops and points – there it is, you’ve found it!  What do you see?  Reach for it, touch it, smell it, feel it. It can be a favorite doll from when you were little,  a sea shell, a feather, a charm from a bracelet or anything you like.

Now ask your "genius seed" to show you all of your talents and abilities – your gifts…ask it tell you all about you.

Take the time to really listen…to hear all that is said about you…later you will write about this journey in great detail…
 
Your angel gently reminds you it’s time to return home…this time, with your "genius seed" in hand.  Now that you’ve found it, it will never leave you.

The journey home is a quick one….back to the flight of stairs, stepping out of your adventure, taking one step at a time, noticing how you feel, what you see.  You are at the end of the stairs; preparing to enter the hallway home…you slowly open your eyes and start to write about your "genius seed", the journey to find it, what is it, and what it tells you about you…
  
  

Take about 10 minutes to write and/or doodle your thoughts.

Closing:
Encourage  participants to share about
their experience. Some may be willing to share about the journaling but if not they could talk about the mediations and what they saw, how they felt.
Row.txt_description: Through a series of guided meditations and journaling exercises, participants learn how to find their inner strengths.
Row.txt_tips:
The following is a list of tips for leading journaling workshops:

Be Spontaneous:
Just grab a pen. When the spirit moves you, jot down a few words or a few pages. Enjoy expressing yourself without judgment. Be free.

Be Ritualistic:
Create a special setting for your writing.
Light some scented candles, soak in the moonlight, or sit by the fire. Begin with a prayer or speak aloud words of personal meaning. Write slowly and let the moment fill you.

Be Formal:
Make a writing date with yourself and stick to it. It could be on Sunday mornings, every full moon, or Wednesday nights.  Mindfully develop a regular habit of reflection and honor it.

Be Emotional:
If you are in an emotional crisis or simply overflowing with feelings, carry your book close to your heart and use it throughout your day. Use a thick or colorful marker to express yourself better. Be generous in your writing, and fill as many pages as you need.

Be Specific:
You may have a special challenge, issue or event you want to address. Maybe it it your sixteenth birthday or your are about to have a baby or are beginning a new job. Celebrate and honor your life's turning points in writing.

Row.str_title: Reclaiming Denim- A Denim Day Workshop
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To learn about the history of Denim Day, define sexual assault, and empower women to know they can make change. This workshop also gives participants the opportunity to look at their own lives and make a personal commitment to protect themselves.

  
  Reclaiming Denim supplies
  
 
  Different pocket options
Materials:
Denim pockets or pieces of denim (two for each person)
Button backings or safety pins
Permanent markers (silver sharpies look great on denim)
Hot glue gun, with glue OR FabriTac glue
Ribbon, including rickrack
Puff paints
Foam Shapes
Assorted embellishments such as buttons, sequins, letter beads etc.
Embroidery needle (optional)
Embroidery thread (optional)
Denim Day Action kit from Peace Over Violence click here
 Scissors (fabric scissors are preferred)
Pocket template click here
 Paper (for participants to write messages on)
Pens
Glue sticks (if making pockets out of paper)

Preparation:
It is helpful to have the pockets already cut out before the group begins to expedite the creation process. 

If you do not have enough pockets you can make your own out of denim, fabric or paper.  Simply use the pocket template provided and trace it onto whatever material you have available. If you are doing paper pockets, use heavy cardstock.

Post statistics around the room or on the table for participants to use on their pockets if they choose to.

  
  Break the silence. Silent no more.
Some statistics from the Denim Day in L.A. toolkit include:
•    1 in 5 female students reported being physically and/or sexually abused by a dating partner (JAMA Vol. 286 No.5 2001)
•    Teens 16 to 19 were three and one-half times more likely than the general population to be victims of rape, attempted rape, or sexual assault. (U.S. Department of Justice, 1996)
•    In 3 out of 4 incidents of sexual assault, the offender was not a stranger. (DOJ, 1997)
•    One in 5 girls and 1 in 10 to 20 boys will be sexually abused at some point in their childhood, according to most reliable studies of child sexual abuse in the United States. (Finkelhor, 1994)
•    Only 3% of high school students who had been physically or sexually abused by a dating partner reported the abuse to an authority figure; only 6% told a family member. 61% of the respondents indicated that they told a friend and 30% indicated that they told no one at all. (The Prevention Researcher, 2000)
•    Most people know at least one person who has experienced or will experience sexual assault or rape. Everyone has a role in preventing sexual assault.

For a single page printable version of these statistics from the Denim Day in LA toolkit, click here, for a page of Common Misconceptions click here.

  
 Don't forget your prep time!
  
Time frame:
Introduction:15 minutes
Opening Circle:10-15 minutes
Creation: 45 minutes
Closing Circle: 15-20 minutes
Total: 1 hour, 20 minutes

Introduction:
Take some time to define sexual violence and rape. You may want to use the Denim Day Toolkit linked above or click here for one page of definitions.

Sexual assault is one of the most common, and most under reported forms of domestic violence.  Every 2 minutes, somewhere in America, someone is sexually assaulted, and the victims often blame themselves for the attack.  Unfortunately, victims are often blamed by society for the assault and even blame themselves.

In 1998, an Italian Supreme Court decision overturned a rape conviction because the victim wore jeans, reasoning she must have helped her attacker remove them.  People all over the world were outraged.  Wearing jeans became an international symbol of protest against erroneous and destructive attitudes about sexual assault. Denim Day was created to unite against the sexual assault of girls, women, boys and men.  People who participate in Denim Day stand in support of survivors, break the silence to end sexual violence, and wear jeans as a visible sign of protest against the myths that still surround sexual assault!  Today we will create our very own pins to wear in support of, and increase awareness about Denim Day.  Denim day falls at the end of April and this year Denim Day is April 22.  To learn more
  
  
 Christy and SACA leader Ana
about Denim Day please visit denimdayinla.org. 

For further information about sexual assault, you may want to use Peace Over Violence’s curriculum and make copies of their handouts for group members. Click here for the Action Kit.

You can also show an educational video regarding sexual violence from CALCASA.org or Peace Over Violence .

Opening Circle:
Ask the participants to close their eyes and imagine that they are making a public service announcement that informs people about sexual assault (you may want to have the scratch paper and pens for them to make some notes). Ask them to think about what words, symbols, or catch phrases they would use in their commercial.  For example, "Sexual Assault is Never the Victims Fault," "Got Consent?," "No Means No," or "Rape free Zone".  Give the participants some time to create their commercial. After about 5-10 minutes, ask the participants to share about the commercial they created in their minds eye.  Ask them to focus on a quote, statement or symbol that encompasses the message behind their commercial.  

  
POV leader Isabel reclaiming a pocket
  
Creation:
Have everyone choose two pockets, one to keep for themselves and one to give another person to help educate their community about Denim Day.

Let each person know they can use any of the materials laid out before them and if they need help to ask. They may need help gluing the pinbacks. If they so choose, the participants can use the color turquoise, which represents Sexual Assault Awareness. It is also fitting for April, Sexual Assault Awareness Month.

Have each person create the first pocket for themselves. Remind the group that the purpose of their pin is to help spread awareness about sexual assault. Once they have created their pocket, have each participant write a personal commitment on a piece of paper.  The personal commitment should be related to how they will protect their bodies from abuse.  For example: "I promise to trust my instincts and leave any situation where I feel unsafe.” This
   
 
 
  My body is sacred.
 
can be a letter they write to themselves or a simple one-line statement.  The participants will then place that commitment inside their pocket to keep it close to their heart. If you are using paper pockets or one piece of denim, you can have them write this commitment on the back of the piece. Make sure each person has a way to pin the denim so they can wear their creation.

The second pocket will be a pocket to make for someone else.  Inside this pocket the participant will place a message they hope the person who receives the pin will adopt as a commitment to himself or herself to avoid abuse in their lives. For example, "firmly assert your boundaries". The pin and personal commitment are intended to not only increase awareness about denim day, but also to encourage the recipient to protect and respect their body.


 
 Different examples of Reclaimed Denim
  
Closing:
Ask each participant to share something about the pins they created and why they chose the particular messages they displayed on their pocket or ask participants to share about how it felt to create this project. They may also want to share who they made their second pin for and why. Encourage the group to commemorate this event yearly by wearing their pin on Denim Day and continuing to share their commitment against abuse with friends, family co-workers etc.
Row.txt_description: This workshop covers the history of Denim Day, defines sexual assault and empowers women to know they can make change. This workshop also gives participants the opportunity to look at their own lives and make a personal commitment to protect themselves.

Row.str_author_lastname: Kestner with Contributions by Linda Sparks
Row.txt_code:
Workshop Objective:
To help promote the visualization of a new beginning. To plant seeds that reflect what we want in our lives or our hopes for the future.

Materials:
< td> 
 
  Completed Garden's from CCFCC
Small Clay pots (around $1 at Michaels)
Acrylic paints
Paint brushes
Colored markers
Planting soil or dirt
Wooden stakes or skewers
Cardstock is preferred)
Scotch tape
Flower seeds
Tending Your Garden Poem (click here)
Relaxing music


 
 CCFCC's seeds of Peace, Family, Self Will
 and a New Start!
 
Time Frame:
Intro: 5 minutes
Demonstration:  5 minutes
Creation: 40 minutes
Closing Reflection: 10 minutes
Total Time: 60 minutes

Introduction:
As we grow, each person has the opportunity to create the future that they want for themselves. What do you want to grow in your future? Love, patience, understanding, strength, freedom to overcome obstacles? Do you want to start a new beginning with more self-trust, self-esteem, and self-love?

Take a moment and try to visualize what it takes to grow a garden.  A garden requires a lot of nurturing to thrive.  It needs the proper nourishment such as rich soil. A garden's environment is also important. Plants and flowers can't grow without sunlight or water. Plants also need protection from weeds and slugs. It takes pulling the weeds out so that the seeds will grow and produce. It also takes caring and dedication and protection from harsh weather conditions.

If we visualize our own lives as a garden, what do we need to thrive? Don’t we need some of the same things to grow and blossom? This garden belongs to you. The outcome depends on how much commitment you have to nurturing your garden. There will be days when we do not feel like working on our garden or we might even feel like giving up and letting it go back to weeds.  It takes love and dedication and patience, so that the end result is something rewarding whether it be a harvest of fruits or even a colorful flower garden.

Warm Up/Relaxation:
Read the excerpt from Tending Your Garden (Workbook for victims of domestic violence). Participants can close their eyes and relax while you read the poem with relaxing music in the background or participants can read the poem to themselves.  Watch the movie "Being There".
                                                
Creation and Demo:

 
 Planting your seeds
 
Today we are going to create the beginning of a garden by planting seeds in a flower pot to represent what we want in our future. We will also add messages to ourselves as a reminder of the things we want to grow in our new lives.

Step 1: Paint the flower pot
The pot is our base. It can represent who we are at our core. You can paint your pot with pictures or words that represent you! You can choose to focus on the obstacles that you have overcome, and have made you who you are today or who your are becoming. 

Step 2: Create messages
When you are ready, cut paper into 2" X 3" strips and then fold it in half. Write on the front of the paper words or messages that represent the seeds that you want to plant in your life, like prosperity, self-worth or freedom. You can also date the paper with today’s date to mark your commitment. You may also choose to represent significant dates in your growth journey such as when you left your abuser. Add as many seeds as you feel ready to and remember you can add more later.
 
  Taping your skewer

Next, you will want to tape the the inside of the folded paper to the wooden stake or skewer. If you'd like, you could cut the sticks so that you have different heights.

Step 3: Planting your seeds
Like each of us, every flower has different needs to grow. Fill the flower pots with dirt and add the flower seeds according to the directions on the seed packet.  When you are finished  planting add the messages that represent how you want to grow.

Closing:
Ask all clients to share some of the seeds they chose to plant for their lives during this exercise. Ask each client to share what they think would be some of the rewards of committing to nurturing these seeds for their future.

Remind participants that keeping these flower pots in a place they can be seen everyday reinforces the positive messages, strengthens our self-esteem and reminds us that each day can hold the promise of new directions.
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps promote the visualization of a new beginning. Participants plant seeds that reflect what they want in their lives and what they hope for the future.
Row.txt_tips: This workshop can also be used for parenting groups. We can plant seeds that we would like to teach or instill in our children or plant seeds to becoming better parents.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop is a great way to introduce new group members to the art workshops and allow them to integrate themselves and feel connected with the group.  This workshop can be an on-going art project that encourages the children to create art o utside of the group while promoting teamwork and building cohesion.

Materials:
White Butcher paper
Plain white paper
Construction paper
Drawing materials: markers, crayons, craypas
Paint and paint brushes
Scissors
Novelty trim (such as stickers, ribbons, etc.)
Glue sticks/tape
Ruler or tape measure

Time Frame:
This activity can be accomplished in 1 - 1/2 hours or it can be an on-going activity.

Age Range:
4  to 18 years old

Pre-workshop prep:
  
 Village of Houses
 
  
 Village of Superheros
 
  
 Village Under the Sea
 
Depending on the age-range and time-frame of your group you may want to create the background of the village before the group begins.  However, whenever possible allow the children to choose the type of village they want to create and have them contribute to the background.

Remind them that this is their village and it can look however they want it to. Pink skies and purple grass are okay too!

For the background, cut out a large piece of butcher paper and lay out your background depending on what kind of village you are going to create.  Three options include: Village of Houses, Village of Superheroes, and Village Under the Sea. 

Village of Houses:
Divide the paper into quarters (horizontally), mark with a pencil.  Take a large paintbrush and paint the top ¼ of the paper blue (for the sky).  Paint the rest of the paper green (for the grass).

Village of Superheroes: This variation requires more preparation time as drawing the background of a city is more labor intense than the other variations.  The background can include sky in the upper portion, the remaining area can be utilized for buildings, roads, sidewalk, grass, bridges, etc. 

Village Under the Sea: Divide the paper into quarters (horizontally), mark with a pencil.  Take a large paintbrush and paint the top ¾ of the paper blue (for the water).  Paint the bottom ¼ beige or brown (for the sand).  You can also draw coral, rocks and plants to add to the background. 

Introduction:
Have you ever heard of that saying, “it takes a village?”  When adults say “it takes a village” they mean that it takes more than one person to make big things happen.  For example the art project we are doing today is so big that we all have to work together to get it done!  Every single one of you is part of this art group and I need all of you to work on this project together to create our very own village. After we create our village, I think it would be great if we welcomed new kids by asking them to add something to the village. 

If appropriate you can then ask the children to think about how they felt when they first came to the group, maybe they felt alone, or separated from the group. 

Before your begin give the children a choice of which village the will be creating. Very briefly introduce 3 types of villages, village under the sea, village of super heroes, village of houses and show them the background.

Opening Circle:
For the Village of Houses: If you could live anywhere, what kind of house would you live in, and why?  Haven Hills II, leader David Nott wore a pair of bunny ears and made a carrot house as an example of where he would like to live.  Other examples include a tree house, a rocket ship house, castle, farm, houseboat, skyscraper, or teepee.
 
   
 
  Carrot House
  River, boat and bridge in the village
  Spaceship House
 

For the Village of Superheroes:  If you could be any super hero, who would you be and why?  Would you like to be Super-Man, and fly through the air?  Would you like to be Wonderwoman, and help people in need? Other examples include Batman, Robin, Captain America, Iron Man, Superwoman, Wolverine, Hulk, Cyclops, Green Arrow, Storm, Iceman, Professor X, Jean Grey or Catwoman.

 
   
  Superman  Supergirls 

For the Village Under the Sea: If you could be any sea creature, what creature would you be and why?  Would you like to be a sea turtle and stroll around the ocean floor?  Would you like to be a dolphin and leap into the air?  Would you like to be the captain of a submarine?  Other examples include a sea snake, fish, shark, starfish, jellyfish, whale, stingray, sea urchin, oyster, shrimp, octopus, crab, or lobster.
 
   
  Fish in the Under the Sea Village
  Octopus in the Under the Sea Village
 

Creation:
Step One:
If you have not already made the background, have the children help you with creating it.  Place the poster paper on a table, stand next to the table and ask the children to help select colors, shapes, and additional features to include in the background.  This is a great way to interact with the children and have them work together as a team!

Step Two:
Instruct the children to create their addition to the village.  Remind the children that it doesn’t matter what their creation looks like.  For example their house doesn’t need to look like a house at all.  In our village anything is possible!

Step Three:
Help the children add glue or double-sided tape to the back and then ask them to place it wherever they like on the background.  As they add their creation, remind them about the theme, it takes a village, and that they are an important part of the village.  If they are having a difficult time knowing where to add their piece, remind them that it's their part of the village and only they know where it belongs.

Step Four:
If time allows encourage the children to add lots of different things to the village.  For example, they can create trees, cars, animals, bridges, restaurants, rivers, boats, roads, buildings, billboards, even aliens!

Step Five: (for new comers to the group)
When you have new children enter the group you can briefly explain the project to them and invite them to create their own piece and add it to the village (or villages).

   
  Children can add to the village at any time
 

Closing Circle:
Have each child talk about what they created and why they placed it where they did on the background. Encourage the children to create more pieces on their own to add to the village.
Row.txt_description:
This workshop is a great way to introduce new group members to the art workshops and allow them to integrate themselves and feel connected with the group.
This workshop can be an on-going art project that encourages the children to create art outside of the group while promoting teamwork and building cohesion.

Row.str_title: Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence Workshop (Paper Version)
Row.str_author_firstname: AWBW Staff - Adapted from Pearls of Wisdom Workshop by Kim Abele
Row.txt_code:
I have the power to chose how I see myself. Claiming one’s self worth is empowering and life changing. This helped me crystalize what I have learned from my experiences.
Objective:
This workshop is designed to help women and their children recognize their personal strength, and uses the metaphor of "pearls" as treasures that form inside an oyster in response to an irritant. Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength and wisdom as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence.

Project Background:
Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence is a two year community project organized by A Window Between Worlds in collaboration with artist Kim Abeles and AWBW Community Art Advocate Sandra Mueller. 

The Pearls of Wisdom project will culminate with an exhibition, online blog, catalogue and related events commemorating A Window Between Worlds’ 20th Anniversary at the Korean Cultural Center in March 2011. As the only national organization using art to help end domestic violence, this project affirms AWBW’s pioneering work in bridging the realms of art and social change.

About Kim Abeles: Abeles’ art crosses disciplines and media to explore and map the urban environment and chronicle broad social issues.  Her body of work gives the community a voice to address social issues in a positive, constructive way.  Both her personal experience as a survivor and her broad experience with large scale collaborative installation work position her well to conceive and implement this statewide collaboration weaving the voices of survivors and community members around the issue of domestic violence.

To see Kim talk more about her background and this project, click here.

  
  Love should never hurt!  Keep moving forward, beautiful, INSPIRE, resilient
Timeframe:
1 hour to 1 1/2 half hour

Materials:
Collage materials including different kinds of paper-doilies, tissue and natural fiber papers work well.
Magazines for images or words (use sparingly)
Scissors
Glues Sticks
Mod Podge and thick brushes
Acrylic or Biocolors paint
Make it Shimmer by Biocolor(this is an additive for a pearlized look)
Paint brushes
Paint palettes
Water cups
Paper towels
Colored pencils
Permanent Markers
Found objects (see Preparation/Set-up for details)
White card stock or watercolor paper 
Circle to trace 5-inch diameter or larger (Bowls, cds etc. work well)

Preparation/Set-up: 
We encourage and welcome all workshop Leaders to create their own “Pearl” and explore the creative process of this project. Leaders who do create a Pearl of Wisdom are encouraged to submit their creation for inclusion in the final exhibition. Provide small objects in the middle of the table (or pass around a basket) that the group can pick from to represent their irritant. Found objects such as symbolic items, charms, stickers, keys or images, Mexican Loteria cards and other knick-knacks. If possible you may want to welcome participants to bring a personal object that represents a significant irritant in their lives (i.e. letter, photo, etc.) prior to the workshop. 

Our story, our journey is not over.
Forgive to reclaim your power.
Workshop Introduction:
A pearl is a wonderful metaphor for the survivor’s journey. Do you know how a pearl is formed? Basically, it starts with an irritant that enters an oyster; protective layers transform that mollusk and create a pearl. Throughout our lives, we all have challenges and difficulties (irritants). There are lessons to be learned in all these challenges(pearls).

Sharing your story as a survivor, from pain to wisdom, can empower and inspire an individual or even a community to help end the violence perpetrated against our innocence, our hearts, our souls and our bodies.  What you’ve experienced (these difficulties and challenges) and the ways you survived are valuable and essential in helping to end the cycle of violence.

As you reflect and create your pearls, notice your strength, beauty and wisdom. Embrace the ways you are transforming and growing. Thank you for being here to share your story.

Demonstration:
Share about the materials you provided for this workshop and the different techniques that can be used for their creations.  As you share, pass around the workshop sample images. If you haven't already done so and it's feasible, this might be a good time to share the dvd created by Kim Abeles that goes with this project.  After the demonstration suggest that it is important to make a commitment to one idea for their Pearl.  Let the art become their voice.

Opening Circle:
  
Ask participants to choose a symbol of their "irritant" from the found objects provided. Ask why they  chose that object to represent their irritant.

Journaling:
From an irritant a beautiful pearl emerges. We are now going to take some time now to journal about your pearls of wisdom. 

A. How did the irritant affect your journey?
B. What has helped you through tough times? What helped you survive? What gave you strength?
C. What advice would you give your younger self?
D. What advice would you share with another person to give them strength?  It can be very practical things, a simple idea, or something more philosophical

E. In an oyster, a beautiful pearl emerges from an irritant. From the irritant you find a treasure.  From difficulties we gain so much wisdom. That wisdom is something you can share to help others get through their own issues. What wisdom would want to share?

 
 Journey through pain towards hope and serenity. Love Yourself.
Relaxation(optional):
Begin...This is your window of time. This is a time to honor yourself as a wise and strong survivor. Get comfortable in your chair and if it feels safe, let your eyes close.  (Read slowly) Now, notice your breath (pause). With each breath notice that your breath has been with you in pain and in joy. Your breath and you are one. Your breath is your life force. Continue to breathe and connect with how you are feeling right now.  Notice how strong and courageous you are to be sitting in this room.  Give yourself permission to feel whatever you may be feeling.  Notice that you are safe, that you are taking important steps to heal the parts of you that are hurt and to honor the parts of you that are strong, courageous and authentically you. Take a few deep breaths and when you are ready open your eyes.     

 
 I am breaking the cycle 
Creation:
Create artwork that shares your pearl of wisdom. As you create, remember to illustrate your message in any way that feels right. You can create an image, use words or both.

Throughout the creative process, remind participants that there is no wrong way to create their story of survival and wisdom.

Toward the end of the creating time start to encourage participants to think about their pearls of wisdom. Ask them to look back at the process of creating, what they learned today and what they may want to share.
      
Closing Circle:
 
  
Option A: Share about your pearl and the wisdom you represented on it.

Option B: What would you tell yourself today or what would you share with a younger friend who may be going through something similar. 

Option C: If the participants have good relationships with one another, have them share with a partner.  After sharing in pairs, go around the circle and have the listener speak the 'wisdom' from her partner and vice versa.  It makes it more of a 'wisdom circle'. 

Submit Pearls to AWBW:
Using a release form have participants share the words of wisdom that go with their Pearl. Take high resolution photographs and attach them to the corresponding release. Submit your pearls through AWBW's blog starting January 1st, 2011 and receive a new shrinky dink project in the mail. If you prefer you may send original artwork or a high resolution image with releases to AWBW for inclusion in the Pearls of Wisdom blog.
Row.txt_description: This workshop is designed to help survivors recognize their personal strength, and uses the metaphor of a "pearl" as a treasure that form inside an oyster in response to an irritant. Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength and wisdom as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence.

Row.txt_code:
< /td>
  Corn husk dolls/figures created by Refuge House, Inc.
Spanish Support group members & leaders (Tallahassee, Florida).
Background:
Corn husks can be interesting and fun to work with. They can be crunched or stretched in a variety of ways. They can be made round and tied or curled. And they can be left in their natural color or painted or dyed.

Some Native American tribes used corn husks to weave clothes and for storing food. They act as natural packaging, keeping in moisture and flavor. Perhaps you've eaten tamales, a Hispanic food steamed in corn husks.

Objective:
To remind the participants that they have made the right decision to leave their abusive situation and can take this opportunity to continue harvesting goodness in their new life.

Materials:
Dry corn husks (at least 5 per participant). These are available in most grocery stores.
Large water bowl to soak the leave in.
Paper towels at each station to soak the water from the corn husk when they are first pulled out from the water bowl.
Raffia, twine, or thin yarn for hair.
Scissors
Step by step Handout
Optional:
Paint
Paint brushes
Cups of water to wash paint brushes.

Note: Some suggestions may require additional materials. You may also use fresh corn husk leaves. If you want to save them until you are ready to do the workshop store them to dry.

Timeframe:
1- 1 1/2 hrs.
If broken into two workshops (first one creating, second one painting), workshop can take up to 3 hours total, which includes painting the dolls.

Preparation:
If you have time prior to your group, start soaking the corn husks so they are ready when your group arrives.

Introduction:
Autumn/fall is harvest time in the Northern Hemisphere and also fall equinox, when day and night are equal, essentially a balance of time. What a better time for us to bring balance in our lives. Harvest timing is a critical decision, a balancing act of weather conditions. If you harvest too early, crops may not be mature, but if you harvest too late the crops may be damaged. We can be like crops in that leaving our batterer was a critical step we had to make to begin harvesting goodness in our lives. While others may have told us we "harvested" too early or too late, we know that our timing was right for us, we are a special crop. These dolls can be an important reminder that you are taking steps to harvest goodness in your life. Whatever shape that takes can be up to you.

Demonstration:
To soften the corn husks before working with them, soak in warm water for several minutes, and then put on a folded paper towel, ready for use.

Hint, to keep in mind: Make every knot with the twine or raffia on the same side for a more finished look. All knots can be cut at the end or as you see, just make sure you double tie knots before each crop.

1) Layer 4 corn husks on top of each other. Larger leaves work best. Optional: To add "hair" place about 20 threads of raffia, twine or thin yarn from the middle of this layer with the extra length out the wide end of the leaves. The braids may be added at the end as another option, see instructions at the end. 

2) Join the upper inch of the husks and tie tightly with raffia or twine.

3) Take 2 leaves on each side and pull over the knot reversing the outside in.

4) To make a head, draw a string around approximately one inch below the top view of the folded back husks which should then envelop the knot hidden underneath. The raffia or string bow makes the doll's neck.

    
1
 2
 3
  4

5) To make the arms, fold a new sheet in half lengthwise coiled (corn leaves work better if you roll with the grain of the leaf rather than against the grain). Tie each end.

6) Place the arms between the two sets of corn husks into the body of maize leaves. Slide your arms as high as they will rise up towards the neck loop.

7) With a string of raffia, tie a belt under their arms. Tie it tightly enough to hold the arms firmly in place.

  
5
 6
 7

Warm-up/Relaxation:
The fall equinox mark opportunities to meditate and reflect on the choices we have made and the balance we want to bring to our lives. To begin the harvest meditation have the participants sit as comfortably as possible. Ask them to close their eyes if this feels safe to them. Ask them to put their hands on their laps and to begin taking a few even breaths to settle down.

Say, "Take 3 quick breathes in through your nose; hold 3 counts, breath 4 breathes out through your mouth." (You can count along out loud). Do this several times until the room feels still and quieted. Then, "Begin thinking about this special of year when day and night are equal, bringing a balance of time. This is our opportunity to start anew and bring balance to our own lives. Take 3 quick breathes in through your nose; hold 3 counts, breath 4 breathes out through your mouth. We've all had to make hard choices, but know that we did them in our own time, when the timing was just right for us. Just like nature, where timing is so important, we're here now because we found that perfect time. You are a special crop. Only you knew when the harvest was ready. Take 3 quick breathes in through your nose; hold 3 counts, breath 4 breathes out through your mouth. We all knew when we were ready and now is a chance to continue to trust our instincts as we keep taking steps forward. Steps toward harvesting goodness in our lives. Take 3 quick breathes in through your nose; hold 3 counts, breath 4 breathes out through your mouth. Reflect on each positive step you took. Now think about the steps you are taking, and how each leads to another and builds on a life full of contentment and happiness. See yourself bathed in a radiant harvest glow. This radiant glow comes from within you. Trust yourself.  Believe in yourself. Take 3 quick breathes in through your nose; hold 3 counts, breath 4 breathes out through your mouth. Remember the fall equinox is a time of even hours of night in day in both hemispheres, a time of balance, balance we can now bring to our lives. Autumn is a time of harvesting and a time to remember that only we know the right time to harvest in our lives. We are all here in perfect timing to harvest goodness. Let's take advantage of the time we have together, a time to support each other as we are reminded to trust our instincts and look towards our future harvest. Now for our last time, take 3 quick breathes in through your nose; hold 3 counts, breath 4 breathes out through your mouth.
Slowly bring yourself back to the room and begin to create your corn husk doll. Remember your doll can serve as an important reminder that you are taking steps to harvest goodness in your life. What ever shape that takes can be up to you."

Creation Process:
Remind the clients to follow the same steps as in the demonstration; they can use your sample to follow along. If needed participants can follow the steps again via the handout.

Optional:
-Make a doll/figure with braids Using 3 strings of raffia tied at each end. Tie the braid onto the doll or figure's neck.
-Make a doll/figure in pants rather than a short skirt by tying each side off at the ankle.
-Paint doll/figure.

Closing:
Go around and ask participants to share their corn husk doll and how their doll will remind them to continue to harvest goodness.
Row.txt_description: This workshop reinforces they made the right decision to leave their abusive situation. Corn husk dolls serve as an important reminder that the participants are taking steps to harvest goodness in their lives.

Row.str_author_lastname: Kestner with Contributions by Linda Sparks
Row.txt_code:
Workshop Objective:
Introduce kids to the idea of self-care and help them identify the things in life that help them grow, or nurture them.  This workshop reinforces that the children must communicate their needs to a safe person, which in turn will allow t hem to grow.  Participants will identify what they want in life, what they want to grow in the future, and will create a potted plant to represent all of those things.

Materials:
  
  Completed Super Size Me Plants
Small Clay or Plastic pots (around $1 at Michaels)
Acrylic paints*
Aprons or T-Shirt
Paint brushes
Colored markers
Ribbon (optional)
Planting soil or dirt
Tall Popsicle sticks or straws
Construction paper / Cardstock (preferred)
Scotch tape
Flower seeds
Relaxing music
*Acrylic Paints are not washable. Be sure to warn parents before the workshop or provide Aprons or old T-shirts to protect their clothes.

Time Frame:   Age Range: 
Intro: 5 minutes
Demonstration:  5 minutes
Creation: 40 minutes
Closing Reflection: 10 minutes
Total Time: 60 minutes		       
6 to 18 year old



 
 

Workshop Prep:
Pre-cut paper into 2" X 3" strips and then fold them in half. The paper will be attached to the straws or Popsicle sticks to display words that help the children grow and what the children want to grow for the future.  

   
  Seeds of family, hugs, happy times, and the beach
 
Introduction:
Does anyone know how a plant becomes a plant?  What makes it grow?  A plant starts out as a seed, but the seed can’t grow on it’s own.  It has to have some important things; otherwise the plant will just stay a seed.  Seeds need dirt and its nutrients, water and sunlight to make them grow.  You also have to make sure to protect the seed from bad things that can keep the keep the plant from growing, such as weeds or not enough food or water or lack of sunlight.

We are a lot like plants because we cannot grow without having some important things and without the people who help protect us.  What helps you to grow?  Who helps you grow? Is it your mom and the enormous amount of love she gives you?  Is it the yummy food that you eat? Is it playing and your friends?

As crazy as it sounds you also help yourself grow! Each of us is unique so we may need different things to help us grow.  That is why it is so important for you to speak up and ask for the things that help you to grow.  After all, you know what you need better than anyone else. For example, if you are feeling sad and don’t tell anyone, then how can anyone help you?  They can’t.  You must be brave and share how you’re feelin,g and what you need, with a safe person.  Today we will make our very own, Super Size Me Plant to show what makes us grow.

Warm Up/Relaxation:
Have the children sit in a circle, leaving enough room for them to move and stretch.  Inform them that you are going to lead them in a warm-up where they will get to use their imagination and move, grow and wiggle like a plant.  We are all going to grow, change, and transform from being a tiny seed into a big, strong plant. First, I want you to curl into a ball, try and curl up so you are short and round just like a seed.  Now, close your eyes and pretend that you are a seed that just got planted in the dirt.  You can feel the cool dirt all around you.  Pause.  You roots start to grow into the dirt.  Now it is starting to rain!  You can feel the rainwater.  Pause.  You feel yourself getting stronger and stronger as the rain pours all over you, feeding you, moving you gently from side to side.  Pause.  Here comes the sun! You feel the branches of your plant start to slowly grow and move with the warmth of the sun.  Stick out one arm and wiggle it around.  Now stick out your other arm and wiggle it around.  You are growing bigger and bigger, now your seed is changing into a plant.  Have the children sit up.  Our plants are still growing, being fed by the wet soil and the sun.  Here comes the wind.  It is so windy that the branches of your plant sway and move. You can feel the cold from the breeze, it feels good and stretches your plant helping it grow even bigger (have the children kneel on their knees), and bigger (have the children squat a bit higher), and bigger (have the children slowly stand up).  Take a moment and feel the sun on your back and feel how wonderful and strong you are!  You are a strong plant, standing tall, reaching up (have the children reach for the ceiling) to the sky.  You feel loved and cared for by the sun, rain and wind who all came together just to help you grow up big and strong!            
                                                
Creation and Demo:
Today we are going to create the beginning of a garden by planting seeds in a pot to show what we want in our future. We will also add messages to ourselves as a reminder of the things that help us grow and that we want to grow in the future.


 
Planting your "seeds"
 
Step 1: Paint the Pot
The pot is what holds the plant, and since we are a lot like plants we are going to pretend that the pot is you!  You can paint the pot your favorite colors, write your name on the pot, and decorate the pot any way you like!  Remember that the pot is you so there is no wrong way to decorate it!

Step 2: Create Messages
Pass out the 2" X 3" strips of paper (folded in half) to the children. Instruct the children to write colors, words, messages, or symbols (on the front of the paper) that represent the 'seeds' that they want to plant for their lives (what they want for the future), like happiness, kindness, love, smiles and friendship. 

Take a minute to think about what the 'seeds' need to grow and write words, colors or symbols to represent all of those things.  Remember that it is important to figure out what helps us grow, that way we know what we need and can tell safe people what they can do to help take care of us.  Some things that may help you grow include, family, friends, talking, food, sleep, kindness and love.      
  
  Taping your straw to the paper

Demonstrate how to tape the inside of the folded paper to the straw / stick or tape it for them.  You can also cut the straws or sticks so they stick out of the pot at different heights.

Step 3: Planting Your Seeds
Like each of us, every seed needs help to grow.  We will help our seeds grow by giving them what they need.  We'll start by burying them in the dirt.  Remember that dirt is one of the most important things a seed needs to grow into a plant. Help the children to fill the flowerpots with dirt and add the seeds according to the directions on the seed packet.  When they are finished planting, add the messages the children just created.

Closing:
Ask the children to share some of their messages or seeds.  Ask the children who their safe person or people are? Ask the children to share their creation with that person or people.

Finally, ask the children to put their Super Size Me Plant in a place where they will see it to remind them to ask for the things that help them grow.
Row.txt_description: Introduce kids to the idea of self-care and help them identify the things in life that help them grow, or nurture them. This workshop reinforces that children must communicate their needs to a safe person, which in turn will allow them to grow. Children identify what they want in life, what they want to grow in the future, and will create a flower pot to represent all of those things.

Row.str_author_lastname: Hughes with contributions by AWBW staff
Row.txt_code:
A completed safety planning mandala.
 
  
Special thanks to Karen Hughes of Life Crisis Center (LCC) in Maryland for her fabulous idea!

Objective:
To create a safety planning mandala containing colors, shapes, and symbols that can only be understood by the person creating it. The mandala will serve as a reminder to the participant about their plan for safely exiting their abusive relationship. Participants will also complete a safety plan worksheet to use in the future, and to guide their creation.


 
 Simple Supplies!
 
Materials:
Safety Plan Worksheet — short version. (Click here)
Safety Plan Worksheet— long version, good for one-on-one sessions. (Click here)
Construction paper (white, black and colored)
Choice of Markers, Colored Pencils or Cray Pas
Pens
Pencils
Mandala Templates (Blank, Circles, Seed of Life, Flower of Life, Center Flower)
Relaxing Music
Glue Sticks (optional)
Scissors (optional)
Samples (optional) (Click here or here for samples)

Timeframe:
1 - 1 1/2 hours

Opening Circle/ Worksheet:
The most dangerous time for a victim of domestic violence occurs once they have left their abusive partner.  So today our workshop focuses on safety planning, which is a back up plan that you can use in the future.  Whether you are currently in an abusive relationship or find yourself in an abusive situation in the future, this plan will enable you to leave your
 
  Creating a Safety Planning Mandala
relationship in a safe, quick and efficient manner.  Being in an abusive relationship is very unpredictable, and we never know when we will need to leave the relationship.   When the time comes we are often so overwhelmed with emotions that we are not able to think clearly, much less come up with an effective safety plan.  Making a safety plan today will provide you with the tools and resources you will need to keep you and your children safe.

Pass out the safety plan worksheet of your choice. Ask each person to complete the worksheet. You may want to play relaxing music while the participants work on their worksheets.  Once the majority of the group appears to have completed their worksheets, ask the participants if any of them had to leave their batterer in a hurry, and if so, is there anything they would like to share with the group about the experience.  This is a great opportunity for the group to bond over shared experiences, and to learn from one another.  If no one volunteers to share, you may want to share an anonymous story about one of your clients who successfully implemented a safety plan.

  
 Coloring a Mandala Template
 
Mandala Introduction:
Today we are going to create a Safety Planning Mandala.  A mandala is a drawing done in the shape of a circle.  You can fill your circle however you like. You can start at the center and make layers of rings, either making each one different, or keeping them the same.  You can also create slices, and divide the circle like a pie.  Remember there is no right or wrong way to create your mandala. Your circle is simply a place where you can express whatever shapes, colors, and images you choose to represent your safety plan.  For example if your code word/phrase for your family and friends is “how is your garden doing this time of year?”, you can draw flowers to represent and remind you about your code.

Mandalas have been used throughout history as a meditative and healing activity. In some parts of the world, people create mandalas as a form of prayer. Mandalas can be very intricate, circular designs. Sometimes people look at mandalas in order to meditate and find clarity.  Your mandala does not have to reflect traditional mandalas, just focus on respecting whatever thoughts and feelings come up for you, and let go of trying to make it look “good.”  Remember, it doesn’t matter what it looks like!

Creation:
Keeping your safety plan in mind, choose a template for your mandala. Remember to
  
  A completed Safety Planning Mandala
include colors, shapes, words, or symbols that reflect important aspects of the safety plan you just created, so you can hang your mandala somewhere where you will see it to remind you about your safety plan.

Closing:
Ask each participant to share something about their safety plan, their mandala and how it felt to create both of them.  You can also ask the participants to share about where they plan to hang or keep their mandala.  Before the participants leave the group you may want to remind them that it is their responsibility to keep themselves safe, and congratulate them on taking an important step in doing so.
Row.txt_description: Participants get to create a Safety Planning Mandala containing colors, shapes, and symbols that can only be understood by themselves. This Mandala will serve as a reminder for safely exiting their abusive relationship. Participants will also complete a safety plan worksheet to use in the future, and to guide their creation.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
For participants to learn and take part in a discussion about the Cycle of Violence and create a piece of art to reflect their own experiences with domestic violence and more specifically the "Cycle of Violence".

Materials:
 
 Completed Shrinky Dinks using
a keychains, ribbon and beads.
 
Pens and paper for writing
Cycle of Violence handout
Cycle of Violence worksheet
Shrinky Templates (optional)
Shrinky Dinks material (Ruff-N-Ready)
Permanent markers
Colored pencils and sharpeners
Scissors
Hole Puncher
Toaster Oven
Ribbon or Craft Wire
Beads (Optional)
Key Chain Ring (Optional)

Timeframe:
Introduction: 20 minutes
Discussion: 20 minutes
Creation: 40 minutes
Closing: 10 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour 30 minutes

Prep:
Set up the table invitingly with the all the supplies except the worksheet, Shrinky Dinks material and templates. If you pass out the Shrinky Dinks material too early, the participants may not be able to resist and you might loose everyone for the beginning portion. Also make sure to check that toaster oven is working.

Introduction/Journaling: 
Pass out the Cycle of Violence handout and briefly introduce the Cycle to the participants.  Give participants a few minutes to review the handout and ask questions. 

Once the participants appear to have grasped the concept, pass out the Cycle of Violence worksheet and ask them to write about their personal experience related to the Cycle of Violence as you are presenting it.  Ask the clients to write about whatever comes to mind, they can focus on their experiences as a child, as an adult or both.  Remind them not to worry about grammar or spelling, and to try not to censor themselves as they don’t have to share about what they wrote.


 
 Using the Cycle of Violence worksheet
 
Some important things to note about the Cycle of Violence:
o    The cycle can happen hundreds of times in an abusive relationship. Each stage lasts a different amount of time in different relationships. The total cycle can take anywhere from a few hours to a year or more to complete.
o    It is important to remember that not all domestic violence relationships fit the "Cycle". Often, as time goes on, the 'making-up' and 'calm' stages disappear.
o    This insidious repetitious Cycle will break you so smoothly, there's an excellent chance you won't even realize you've lost yourself. For some people it may take years... but it will break you.
o    The heavy weight of abuse weighs upon you a little bit more each time you travel around the Cycle, until you are physically, mentally, emotionally and spiritually drained.
o    Emotional abuse is present in all three stages.
o    Domestic violence increases in frequency and severity.  It is never an isolated incident or a one-time occurrence.


 
 A completed Shrinky Dink without beads
Viola- it's magic!
 
Discussion:
Have each participant share one sentence (or one word) about how the Cycle of Violence has affected their life.

After everyone has shared, take some time to congratulate everyone in the room for coming to this group and thus taking an important step towards breaking the Cycle of Violence.  You could say something like this, "while the Cycle violence is inter-generational, each of us has the power to heal from the past and move towards a violence free future.  Coming out of an abusive relationship we tend to focus on what we haven’t done verses recognizing all of our accomplishments.  The fact that all of you are here is a testament to your commitment to care for yourself and build a healthy future!  With that in mind, take a moment to think about an action you have taken to break the Cycle of Violence and / or an action you want to take in the future." 

 
  Creating without a tempate
 
  Creating using a template
 
  Cutting out the Shrinky Dink
 
  Don't forget to punch a hole!
Generate a discussion about what they have done to break the Cycle of Violence in their life and what actions they would like to take in the future.(Depending on your group dynamic you can either conduct this portion as a discussion or as another writing exercise.) Offer a few examples from your own experience or from past clients. After a few clients appear to have completed their writing or after the discussion, ask if a few of them would be willing to share their experience with the group.

Creation:
Now that the participants have learned about the Cycle of Violence, and recognized the strides they have made to end abuse, it is time to create a Shrinky Dinks key chain that will serve as a reminder of their accomplishments and their commitment to a future free from abuse.

Inform the participants that they must color on the rough side of the Shrinky Dink, using only colored pencils or permanent markers.  You may choose any of the colors on the table.  Whenever participants are ready, ask them to fill the Shrinky Dinks with colors, shapes, words or even doodles to represent how they have or plan to help stop the Cycle of abuse in their, and their family's life.  When they are finished coloring, they may use scissors to cut thier Shrinky Dink into a shape.  Then they will use the hole punch to cut a hole in the Shrinky Dink.  Remind them to be sure not to punch the hole too close to the edge of the Shrinky Dink paper (as it will not be sturdy enough to support the weight of the Shrinky Dink). Once the group members are done coloring on, cutting out, and punching a hole into their Shrinky Dink, they are ready for baking.  Place the Shrinky Dink on a flat metal tray and place inside the toaster oven. We've found it's best to place a cut out of a paper bag inside the oven with a corner turned up to grab. Bake at 300 degrees until Shrinky Dink has completely flattened (this will take about one minute or less). Watch the amazing transformation! Remove the Shrinky Dink and allow it to cool. Now the Shrinky Dink is ready for decorating with wire and beads, and attached to a key ring (if you like). Thread either wire or ribbon through the hole and add beads.  Next take the ribbon or wire and attach it to the key ring.  If you do not have access to key chain rings you can just have the clients string the Shrinky Dinks from ribbon, wire, embroidery thread, or yarn.  Please note that the Shrinky Dink may break off key rings.

Closing Circle:
If time allows, have each of the participants share about their Shrinky Dink, and anything they discovered or learned in group today.  Congratulate the participants for taking a time out today to honor all they have done to break the Cycle of Violence and encourage them to keep their key chain as a reminder of their strength, courage and commitment to a violence free future.
Row.txt_description: This workshop combines a basic DV101 curriculum topic, the Cycle of Violence, and art as a healing tool. Participants will learn and take part in a discussion about the Cycle of Violence and will create a piece of art to reflect their own experiences with domestic violence and the Cycle.
Row.txt_tips: You may want to do this workshop with your staff to reflect on their work as advocates & how they have individually and collectively worked to break the cycle of violence.

Row.txt_code:
"Inner Me" Artist: Rose Curtis
 Objective:
To learn more about yourself by going within and discovering your inner self through creating a portrait.

Introduction:
This workshop will assist the women and even teens to look inside and discover more about their inner self. We are used to looking at our outer selves, our looks, our clothes, our appearance, the image we try to portray. This workshop gives us an opportunity to go to a deeper level and get more in touch with our inner-self. You will have 3 options of materials, you can also combine them.

  Materials:   
 Timeframe:    
  Large Head & Body Template Introduction: 5 min
  Small Template Opening Circle:10 min
  11x14 Thick white paper (recommended)
 Journaling/Sharing: 20 min 
Technical: 5 min
  Journal Questions (You may want to print them on novelty paper   
Paper or Journals & Pen		 Relaxation: 5 min
Creation: 1 hour
Closing: 15 min
     
Below is a list of materials you may need  based on which medium you want to use:
 Collage
Option One
 Paper Mosaic
Option Two
 Oil Pastels Resist
Option Three
Magazines with images and words
Scissors
Glue sticks
Embellishments as wanted -
butterflies, flowers
Markers
 Novelty papers - patterns, textures, metallics
Pre-cut mosaic shapes are available at
Discount School Supply
Glue Sticks
Mod Podge with brushes
Scissors
 Oil Pastels
Watercolors         
Brushes
Cups
Spray Bottle
Water pitcher

Prep:
Have body and head templates ready, one for each participant. Print journal questions on special paper. Have samples on hand if available. If you are using watercolors, be sure to pre-moisten them with a spray bottle before the participants use them.

It's great to make an example of each medium so the participants get an idea of what they can create.

 
  Pre-collage Without a background image
 
  Adding a background image
 Collaging with layers
Technical Demonstration:
Explain to the participants the materials that will be available, especially if you are giving all three options. It is important to demonstrate all of the materials you give to them.

Collage - You may want to show your participants the different effects you can get by layering. You can show them how adding a background image can add hidden meaning and also make a collage "pop"!

Another wonderful collage technique is to not use scissors. Tearing the paper creates a cool effect.

Finally, encourage participants that while choosing images they should try to follow their intuition. This process can be quite surprising and freeing.

Paper Mosaic
You may not need to show a technical demonstration of how to do a paper mosaic, but it's good to at least show an example of what a mosaic is. Participants may choose to use a pencil to outline the spaces they would like to fill with mosaic pieces. It's also important to remind them that mosaics don't necessarily have to be squares, they can do long strips for hair and use lots of shapes.


 
 Notice how the white oil pastel was used
 in the bubbles of this Inner self portrait		 
  
Oil Pastel Resist
Give a demonstration to the participants by drawing a shapes with oil pastel on card stock  then using the watercolor over pastel to show how the pastel resists the watercolor. Remind them to use a lot of water and a lot of paint on their brush to create richer color effects. Using a spray bottle is an easy way to add water to the paper to help the watercolors flow.

Opening Circle:
Remind the group that anything shared in this circle is anonymous and should not be shared with anyone outside of this room.  Have the participants introduce themselves and share one thing that others don't know about them!  Ask the clients to be brave when deciding what to share and remind them that everything that is said in group stays in group.

Journaling & Sharing (optional): 
If you plan to use the journal questions provided, realize it takes a lot more time to write
and then share. If you have the time use this step as you may notice participants tend to go
to a deeper level when they write and share before they create.

Have participants journal on the questions provided and then share
 
 Combination Collage and Paper Mosaic Inner-Self Portrait
what they feel comfortable sharing. It is sometimes helpful to give participants a time frame and play soft music to get them writing. When it looks like most people are done, ask a volunteer to begin the sharing circle and ask them to share whichever answers they are comfortable sharing.

Relaxation:
Feel free to adapt this relaxation to work with your group and timeframe. Read slowly, pausing in between sentences to create a relaxing atmosphere.
