Row.txt_code:
A Loving Lily
 
Objective:
To give participants an opportunity to recognize what they like about and appreciate in themselves.  It also gives them an opportunity to share a lily with a loved one -even if they are that person!

Materials:
Pipe cleaners: 1 yellow, 3 green per person
Green masking tape
Tape
Scissors  
Cray Pas, crayon, pencil or marker
White heavy construction paper (or soft pastel colors)
Yellow construction paper for flower center (optional)
Pencil (optional to curl fingers)

Introduction:
It is a generous and loving custom to receive flowers from people, but why should we wait for other people to make us feel special?  Today we are all going to make flowers for ourselves!  This flower is called a Lily, and we will have the opportunity to fill each petal on the Lily with positive things about ourselves.  

Opening Circle:
Go around the room and have each participant share one thing that they love or appreciate about themselves.  It can be anything, from something big such as, "I love how nice I am to my friends," or something small such as, "I am good at soccer!"  If the participant is unable to think of something, you can assist by affirming them.  It can be a short phrase or a whole sentence; there is no wrong way.
   
  Create a Loving Lily
 


  
  Cut out your hand shape and write loving words
 
   
  Create  pipe cleaner leaves
 
   
  Add the leaves to the stem
 
   
  Loving Lilies bouquet
 
Creation:
Step One:
Have each participant trace their hand onto the white paper with a crayon or pencil. Have them cut out as many as they want for the lily blooms.

Step Two:
Remind participants to keep in mind some of the things they said in the opening circle; ask them to write at least one positive thing about themselves on each of the fingers.  You can say, "remember, you can write anything you like as long as it celebrates you!"  If they so choose, have the children decorate their hand using Cray Pas and/or markers.  There is no right or wrong way to decorate the lily. Encourage the participants to feel free to go wild and decorate their lily in any way they like.

Step Three:
Roll the hand print vertically to form a funnel shape, and secure the side with clear tape. 

Step Four - the Lily:
Roll each finger down to form the curls of each bloom.  You can wrap the fingers around a pencil or scrape against the side of a scissors to create the curls.

Step Five - stamens: 
Loosely curve the yellow pipe cleaner to form a ‘U' shape.  Wrap the top of a green pipe cleaner at the center of the ‘U'. Curl the ends of the yellow pipe cleaner to form the center of the bloom.
If you prefer you can also use strips of yellow construction paper and curl them using scissors. (see A Loving Lily Photo above)

Step Six - stem:
Insert the completed green stem into the center of the bloom and pull through.

Step Seven - leaves:
Use the green tape to secure the stem into the Lily and add another green pipe cleaner to create the leaves.  An easy technique you can use to make the leaves is to attach each end of the pipe cleaner together to create a circle, then pull the circle from opposite sides to make the circle look like an oval, then pinch the middle of the oval shape, and wrap it around the stem to create two leaves.

Step Eight - bouquet:
If time allows, have the participants make more lilies for themselves or for their loved ones.

Closing Circle:
Have each participant share their lily and some positive things about themselves.  After everyone has shared, remind the participants that it is important for them to recognize and appreciate all of the wonderful things that make them who they are.
Row.txt_description: This workshop will give participants an opportunity to recognize what they like about and appreciate themselves. It also gives them an opportunity to share a lily with a loved one -even if they are that person!

Row.txt_code:
An Aggressive Crayon example 
Objective:
To allow the children to release some of their feelings and/or energy onto a piece of paper.

Materials:
Crayons or Cray Pas
Paper

Prep:
Put out a large piece of paper, and have the children take out several crayons of their choosing.  You can instruct them to choose colors that represent how they are feeling that day.

Warm-up:
Have the children scribble as hard and fast as they can to get a mess of color.  You can instruct them to choose colors that represent how they are feeling that day. Encourage the children to keep scribbling until they feel satisfied that they have gotten that feeling out, and then switch colors.  You may want to use music to set the pace - fast upbeat music to start and switch to slower music to calm things down at the end.

Follow this warm-up with a workshop about discovering feelings, dealing with anger, etc using the "Emotional Theme" search tool on the AWBW website.
Row.txt_description: A great warm up that will allow the children to release some of their feelings and/or energy onto a piece of paper.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To get the children moving and reinforce the power of positivity.

Materials:
Paper
Scissors
A parachute or sheet (you may want to borrow this from your children's program; for an example of a parachute, click here)
Affirmation confetti words click here

Prep:
Make a list of positive or affirmation words (using different fonts and sizes is ideal), or use the above template and cut out each word. 

Introduction:
Let the children know that today we're going to have fun.  Remind them to try their hardest to just enjoy this time and take each affirmation they hear to heart.

Warm-up:
1. Place the affirmation in the middle of the parachute.

2. Lay the parachute (so it is open completely) on the ground.  Have the children sit around the edges of the parachute so there is equal distance between people.   

3. Have the children grab the edge of the parachute with both hands.

4. Have the children stand up and lift the parachute up to their waist.

5. Ask the children to move their arms up and down (while keeping them straight and extended in front of their body) at a quick pace over and over again, so the parachute and affirmation words dance in the air.

6.  One at a time, have the children grab a word from the parachute and say it out loud.

7.  To add a discussion to the warm-up, have then children share about a time when they felt the feeling they just read out loud.

8.  Follow this warm-up with a workshop that focuses on the positive attribute of the women.  Do this by doing a find for workshops using the Emotional Theme (i.e.self-care, self-esteem,discovering my feelings, etc) search tool.
Row.txt_description: The warm-up gets the children moving, but also reinforces the power of positivity.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
To help capture the inner childlike voice of the participants, and bring out their playfulness.  The movement releases stress and gives permission to be silly and carefree.

Materials:
Assorted scarfs or pieces of sheer, flowing fabrics
Upbeat music

Warm-up:
Have each person select a piece of fabric and form a circle.  You can have soft music playing at first as the children walk slowly in the circle gently swaying the fabrics - gradually increase the pace and the beat of the music, walk a little faster and have the leader call out things to do with the fabric.  Encourage the participants to be carefree, playful and free to move and dance around the room.

Here are some suggestions of scarf movements:
Swing over your head
Bend over and dust your shoes
Wave it up in the air
Hold it over your head with two hands and sway side to side
Dust off your knees
Dust off the person to your lefts feet
Pretend you are an animal like a butterfly or a bird
Make it become an elephant trunk by swinging up and down
Cover your face (and play peek a boo)
Throw it up in the air and catch it
Wrap yourself in it and give yourself a hug
This warm-up is great to use with a playful workshop such as those found using the search tool on AWBW's website (including My Body, Self-care and Self-esteem workshops).
Row.txt_description: This workshop helps to capture the inner childlike voice of the participants and is a way to bring out playfulness. The movement releases stress and gives permission to be silly and carefree.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
 
   A personal Red Flag Banner
To give teens an opportunity to identify "red flags", or warning signs, of an abusive relationship.  Participants will discuss what they see as "red flags" and then write on one side of a red flag to help them identify abusive partners and behavior.  On the other side of the red flag participants will create a collage to illustrate aspects of a healthy relationship to serve as a reminder for what they should look for in a potential partner.  The project can be done individually or collectively and once the flags are completed they are connected together to create a red flag banner.

  
  Large banner for group project
Materials:
Large flag template
Small flag templates
Red Flags of Abusive Relationships Handout
Teen Dating Violence Resource Page
Red paper (cardstock works best)
Glue
Scissors
Beads (optional)
Collage materials
Permanent markers (dark colors and metallics)
3 to 5 yards of twine, string or clothesline
  
  Smaller Individual Red Flag Banner
3 foot pieces of ribbon or yarn
Pens 

Time Frame:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 20 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing Circle: 20 minutes
Total: 1 hour, 15 minutes

Note to leaders:
  • Teens learn about relationships from the adults they live with, the media, the Internet and their friends. As adults we have the responsibility to be open to discussing relationships with teens, to hear their questions with respect and give them real answers. Being honest without judgment, no matter what they share with us, goes a long way to making you a child or teen's "safe adult".
  • To help establish boundaries with the teens you may want to create Ground Rules as a group. 
  • While you may feel like you can't be both a friend and an advocate to the teens, keep in mind that all you need to be is their trusted adult.
  • For more tips and information about working with teens please visit the FAQ section of AWBW's website.
  
 Cutting out your Group Project Template 
  
  
 Cutting out your Individual Project Template 
Preparation:
First decide if you will create this project as a team project, individual project or both. For the team project, we recommend using the large template and the smaller template for individual projects.
Print or copy the flag template(s) onto red paper. Or, hand out multiple templates and allow participants to trace. You may also want to pre-cut the flags in order to reduce the length of the workshop.
Print out copies of the Red Flag handout for each participant.  To save time you may want to read through the Red Flag handout and highlight the points you want to cover.

Introduction:
Teen Dating Violence isn’t an argument every once in a while, or a bad mood after a bad day, it is a pattern of controlling behavior that someone uses against a girlfriend or boyfriend.

Abuse can cause injury and even death, but it doesn’t have to be physical. It can include verbal and emotional abuse – constant insults, isolation from family and friends, name calling, controlling what someone wears-and it can also include sexual abuse.

Teen dating violence is very difficult to identify.  Have you ever had that gut feeling that something wasn't right?  Have you ever thought, “I saw all the writing on the wall and looked the other way”?  Just like those walls you walk by that are filled with tagging, often times we fail to see what is right in front of our face. We know it's there, however we don't really see it.  Red flags are intuitive warnings that let us know something is wrong.  All too often we silence that little voice inside of ourselves that warns us of a potential danger.  Abusive people are skilled at manipulating us into believing them and doubting ourselves.  Over time, abusers may convince us to automatically defer to what they think and want and to disregard our own needs, wants and opinions.  Today we are going to take a look back at the red flags from abusive relationships handout, and then create our own red flags to honor and allow our inner voice, needs and desires to be heard. We can save ourselves a lot of frustration and pain in the future by practicing identifying our red flags. During this workshop you will also have an opportunity to notice the things you want in your future relationships.

Opening Circle:
Begin by passing out the Red Flags of Abusive Relationships handout and go over it as a group. Ask the participants to share any thoughts about red flags, they can share personal experiences (that happened to them or someone they know), thoughts about how this issue is portrayed in the media (i.e. Rhianna and Chris Brown), and/or what the handout made them think about. 
 
 Writing out the Red Flags
 
 Creating a background image for the collage
 
 Gluing the inside of the flag together
 
  Tying a knot between each flag

Make sure to identify and explain how what they shared is an example of a red flag of a specific type of abuse.  For example, “I knew something was off when he/she said that I should not talk to boys/girls at parties”.  Just because you are talking to someone doesn't mean you two are hooking up.  This is an example of excessive jealousy.  Start the opening circle by asking someone to volunteer to share first and then have the rest of the group share one at a time.

Creation:
Now that we have identified some red flags, we are going to create a banner made of “red flags”.   Be sure to show a sample as a reminder of the two steps of the project. On one side you write down words, or symbols to remind you about some of the red flags we spoke about today.  You can write on as many flags as you want, they will serve as a reminder for what you should look out for in the future.  Allow about 10 minutes for everyone to write on one side of a flag.

Once the participants have written on  at least one flag, explain the collage portion of the workshop.  Now that we know what we don't want in an intimate relationship, lets look at what we do.  If time allows ask each teen to share one thing they think helps make a relationship healthy before they begin collaging.  Turn your flags over and cut out words and/or images and glue them to the blank sides of your flags to create a collage that shows what a healthy relationship looks like. While they are collaging you may want to remind the teens the reason why they are making this collage. Remind them that these flags will serve as a reminder of what to look for in an intimate relationship.   

If everyone is doing individual red flag banners, explain that they can begin to put their banner together by looping the first flag over the ribbon or string, gluing the insides together and then tying a knot or adding a bead between each flag. They can then take it home and hang it up as a reminder!

Closing:
Ask a volunteer to start the closing circle by sharing something about their red flag banner.  Ask the teens to speak about some of the red flags they wrote about and why they chose the images on their collages to represent what they believes makes a healthy relationship.  If you are doing this as a group project, after each person shares, have them loop their flag over the clothesline or ribbon and glue the sides together. Then add either a knot or a bead before the next flag. Once everyone has put their flag on the line, ask for someone to volunteer to help you hang the red flag banner! Thank everyone for sharing, participating and for creating an important reminder to pay attention to red flags. We teach people how to treat us, and what we will and won't allow in our relationships. Teach your partners that you won't accept abusive behavior, ever!
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives teens an opportunity to identify "red flags", or warning signs, of an abusive relationship.
Row.txt_tips:
Note:
You may also choose to do this workshop in two sessions.
First session: Discussing red flags using handout and creating on one side of the flags.
Second session: Discuss healthy relationships look like and create collage side.

Row.txt_code:
Objective: To allow teenagers to explore the difference between healthy and unhealthy relationships.  This activity also gives teenagers opportunities to think about what steps to take if they know someone, or are themselves, in an abusive relationship.

Materials List:
Teen Power and Control Wheel & Teen Equality Wheel
Participant Relationship Quiz
Facilitator Relationship Quiz Q&A
  
  A completed Healthy Relationship Collage
 
Tri-fold people form template on 8 1/2 x14
Single people form template on 8 1/2 x 11
Card stock or heavy weight paper (see prep)
Magazines
Scissors
Glue sticks
Sharpies
Pens
Music
Timer

Note to leaders:
  • Teens learn about relationships from the adults they live with, the media, the Internet and their friends. As adults we have the responsibility to be open to discussing relationships with teens, to hear their questions with respect, and give them real answers. Being honest without judgment, no matter what they share with us, goes a long way to making you a child or teen's "safe adult".
  • To help establish boundaries with the teens you may want to create Ground Rules as a group. 
  • While you may feel like you can't be a friend and advocate to the teens you serve for a myriad of reasons, keep in mind that all you need to be is their trusted adult.
  • For more tips and information about working with teens please visit the FAQ section of AWBW's website.
Prep:
Print out the handouts provided, including this workshop.
To print the tri-fold template provided, set your printer to print at 8 1/2 x 14 (legal size) on heavy weight paper, and click print. If this is not an option or you would like a larger template use the 8 1/2 x11 single person template.  Whatever size you pick, you may choose to make stencils on card stock for the students to trace onto large construction (12x18) or similar paper(11x17).
Depending on how much time you have and how much volunteer help you have, you may want to precut the people forms for each participant.

 
Collaging the tri-fold
 
Timeframe:
Prep: 15 min to 1-hour
Intro: 5 min
Warm-up/Discusson: 15 -30 min
Creation: 1-hour
Closing:10 minutes
Total Time: 2 hours

Introduction: Dating or domestic abuse occurs when one partner uses different types of abusive behavior to gain POWER and CONTROL over the other partner.

Dating or domestic violence is a pattern of behavior that can include emotional, mental, verbal, financial, physical, sexual, and social abuse.

Abuse can happen to anyone! Teens and adults experience abuse in their relationships at the exact same rate! Dating abuse can happen to anyone, no matter their sexual orientation, gender identity, ethnicity, income level, educational and/or national background!

Today we are going to talk about healthy relationships, unhealthy ones and what steps you can take if you or someone you know is in an abusive relationship.

Before we get started, I want to share some startling statistics about dating violence and teenagers. Did you know...
  • About one in three high school students have been or will be involved in an abusive relationship.
  • One in five or 20 percent of dating couples report some type of violence in their relationship.
  • One study found that 7 percent of all murder victims were young women who were killed by their boyfriends.
  • Teen dating violence most often takes place in the home of one of the partners.
  • One study found that 38 percent of date rape victims were young women from 14 to 17 years of age.
  • A survey of adolescent and college students revealed that date rape accounted for 67 percent of sexual assaults.
  • More than half young women raped (68 percent) knew their rapist either as a boyfriend, friend or casual acquaintance.
  • Six out of 10 rapes of young women occur in their own home or a friend or relative's home, not in a dark alley.
Warm-up: Share the Teen Power and Control Wheel or Relationship Quiz provided. Generate a discussion or create a list with the teens of what they believe is considered "abuse" in a relationship, then using the list below, fill in the blanks.

Emotional/Mental/Verbal

  • Using put-downs, insults, name-calling, humiliation
  • Threatening to harm or kill family, friends, a new partner, pets, etc.
  • Threatening to commit suicide if a partner leaves
  • Making threats like, “If you leave me I’ll … spread rumors about you, tell your parents we had sex”, etc.
  • Blaming the person who is being abused for the abuse or for all the problems in the relationship
  • Minimizing or denying abusive behavior, playing mind games
  • Possessiveness and/or constant accusations of cheating

Physical Abuse

  • Hitting, grabbing, pushing, shaking, restraining you physically etc.
  • Intimidation (blocking exits/doors, hitting things or throwing objects at or near partner)
  • Using or threatening to use weapons
  • Stalking
Social Abuse
  • Spreading rumors or using blackmail to control a partner’s actions
  • Keeping a partner “in check” by monitoring their cell phone constantly or using friends to keep tabs on them
  • Isolating a partner from her/his friends and family
  • Using religion/culture to control partner
 
 Creating the collage

Sexual Abuse

  • Ignoring partner’s sexual choice(s) through pressure, manipulation, coercion (e.g. saying, “You’d do it if you loved me”)
  • Rape: Forced penetration without consent (including use of intimidation, threats, weapons etc.)
  • Sexual Assault: Forced sexual contact
  • Sexual Harassment: Unwanted sexual attention

Financial Abuse

  • Controlling possessions like: a car, phone, clothes, jewelry
  • Excessive gift giving with strings attached, for example “I gave you this, now you owe me”
  • Using gifts to make up for abusive behavior
  • Controlling all money, using money to threaten or manipulate
  • Sabotaging a partner’s work or school career, for example harassing a partner at work and causing them to get fired or refusing to give a partner a ride to work or school, etc.
End the discussion by sharing information on steps they can take to help themselves or a friend in an abusive relationship. For example (from safespace.org ):

If you or a friend is being abused:
  • Don’t be afraid to reach out to someone who you think needs help. Tell them you are concerned for their safety and want to help.
  • Be supportive and listen patiently.  Acknowledge their feelings about their relationship.
  • Help them recognize that the abuse is not “normal” and is not their fault. Everyone deserves a healthy non-violent relationship.
  • Focus on your friend or family member, not on the abuser. Even if your loved one stays with their abusive partner, it is important that they still feel comfortable talking to you about it.
  • Be respectful of your friend or family members decisions about the relationship.
  • Connect them to resources in their community that can give them information and guidance. Remember, Break the Cycle is always here to help.
  • Help them develop a plan to end their relationship safely.
  • If they break up with the abuser, continue to be supportive of them after the relationship is over.
  • Even when you feel like there’s nothing you can do, don’t forget that by being there and by being supportive and caring – you are already doing a lot.
If you or a friend is being abusive:
  • Learn about domestic violence yourself so you can help your friend or family member recognize his or her abusive behaviors.
  • Your friend or family member may try to blame the victim for the abuse. Don’t support these feelings or help to justify the abuse.
  • Help the abuser focus on the victim’s feelings and the serious harm the victim is experiencing because of the abuse. Don’t support the abuser’s efforts to minimize the severity of their abusive behavior.
  • Don’t ignore abuse that you see or hear about. Your silence helps the abusive person to deny that their behavior is wrong.
  • Convince the abuser that getting professional help is important. Encourage him or her to find a program about ending domestic violence and have a list of resources ready.
  • Stay in touch with your friend and family member about the abuse. Be there to support the abuser to change long-term.
  • Remind your friend or family member that change will create a better, healthy relationship for both partners in the relationship.
  • Set an example by having healthy relationships in your own life.
 
 Moving towards a healthy relationship
Creation:  Give everyone the template or a stencil and paper to create a 3 body outline.  Explain that they will use collage and writing to illustrate healthy vs. abusive relationships and the steps we can take to help ourselves or a friend to leave abusive relationship. Give them one prompt at a time and allow them 1-hour to create their project.  Tell them that you will help the workshop move along by telling them when it's time to move on to the next collage. Give the teens 20 minutes to create each collage using the following prompts.
  1. On the first outline, use the collage materials to illustrate what the healthy relationship you deserve looks/feels like to you.
  2. On the second outline you will illustrate what an abusive relationship looks/feels like to you.
  3. On the last outline, collage and write your action plan to help yourself stay out of abusive relationships or to help a friend you believe is in an abusive relationship.
Closing:  Have the teens share what ever they feel comfortable sharing about their collages.  Ask each teen to share one thing they learned today that they didn't know.
Row.txt_description: This workshop will allow teenagers to explore the difference between healthy and unhealthy relationships. This also gives teenagers opportunities to think about what steps to take if they know someone or are themselves in an abusive relationship.
Row.txt_tips: If you or your clients need additional resources to help address this issue use the Teen Dating Violence Resource Page.

Row.str_title: A Kiss is Not a Promise
Row.txt_code:
The kiss journal
Objective: To assist teens in thinking about their own personal boundaries when it comes to intimate relationships.  To help them become aware of what a “kiss” means to them and how people have different expectations.

Materials for Journal:
Kiss template
Mylar or similar reflective silver paper
Copy paper
Hole puncher
3/4 inch white polyester ribbon
Ballpoint pen

Preparations: Have the Kiss template
precut for all participates to trace onto
Mylar and paper
     
Time Frame:
1 to 2 hours

Note to leaders:
  • Teens learn about relationships from the adults they live with, the media, the Internet and their friends. As adults we have the responsibility to be open to discussing relationships with teens, to hear their questions with respect and give them real answers. Being honest without judgment, no matter what they share with us, goes a long way to making you a child or teen's "safe adult".
  • To help establish boundaries with the teens you may want to create Ground Rules as a group. 
  • While you may feel like you can't be a friend and advocate to the teens you serve for a myriad of reasons, keep in mind that all you need to be is their trusted adult.
  • For more tips and information about working with teens please visit the FAQ section of AWBW's website.

Introduction: Today we are going to think and share about what exactly a kiss means to us and what our boundaries are when it comes to physical intimacy by creating a Kiss Journal.


 
 Cutting the kiss out of cardstock or paper
 
  
 Cut the Mylar for the front and back
 
  
 Write a message on the ribbon
 
  
 Use the pages as a journal
 
Journaling & Discussion:
Have the teens construct their journal by cutting out their kiss template and their Mylar front and back covers. Ask them to align all the pages and punch a hole at the top. Finally hand the ribbon out and tie it to hold the journal together.

Have the teens write about the following questions in their Kiss Journal. Explain that at the end of the journaling exercise you will ask everyone to turn them in so you can read their answers anonymously. No one will know who wrote what, so please be as honest as you can be. Ask them to write their name discretely on the back page of the journal so you can give them back after your are done reading them.  If someone does not want to submit their journal to you, they are still welcome to participate. Tell the teens that you will ask them questions and give them a few minutes to write about it (about 3 minutes per question). Give them one question at a time.
1.  Why do people kiss?
2.  What does kissing mean to you?
3.  What are your expectations once you have kissed someone that you like?
4.  What do you think the person your kissing expects from you after you kiss them?

Have everyone submit their journals and anonymously share the answers to any of these questions. Point out differences in expectations and meaning for each person.

Start a discussion about the importance of communication in a relationship. First, you should know what you want and don't want in a relationship. If you are in a healthy relationship, communicating these needs should not feel scary.  Explain that a healthy relationship always has open communication, trust, respect and equality. If you don't feel safe to communicate your needs or feel that your boyfriend/girlfriend treats you with respect or as an equal, you need to reevaluate your relationship.

Ask the group if they feel teens have good communication?  Do teens explain expectations or boundaries to each other before hooking up? Is it important for teens to speak more openly to each other about expectations or boundaries? Why?

Hand back the journals to each person. Ask them to each write themselves a message or words on the ribbon to remind them to always be true to themselves.  Give an example, "I will write, 'I will always respect myself and my boundaries'."

Closing Circle:
Have the participant’s each share about their message and anything they have learned today.
Row.txt_description: This workshop assists teens in thinking about their own personal boundaries and how becoming physical in a dating relationship can change everything. This workshop also helps them become aware of what a “kiss” means to them and how people have different expectations.
Row.txt_tips:
The Mylar can rip easily when cutting it out. Be careful.
If you are preparing the journals in advance, it is easier to use a standard 2 or 3-hole puncher to punch through all the layers.

If you or your clients need resources to help address this issue use the Teen Dating Violence Resource Page.

Row.txt_code:
A NOTE ON RELAXATIONS
A brief relaxation exercise at the outset of an art session can be a key factor, a sort of "rite of passage" into a creative session, helping everyone to make the transition from the customary chaos of the shelter into a separate, constructive time and space.  The relaxation exercise establishes the session as a chance for the women to get in touch with themselves.

BE AWARE:  For some women, closing their eyes and breathing deeply is the furthest thing from relaxing.  Many women who have experienced various traumas (of which they may or may not be consciously aware) find the process of "relaxation" disturbing rather than peaceful.  This condition can be similar to the experience of war veterans.  There are many parallels between war veterans, and the veterans of the "war at home".  For the purposes of conducting a relaxation it is helpful to keep this in mind.  Sometimes it can take the survivor of such a traumatic experience quite a long process of deep work to be able to relax intentionally.

One staff woman with whom I worked in Washington has personally experienced this sort of difficulty with relaxation.  She has undergone intensive work with an expert who generally works with war veterans.  In learning to guide herself into a relaxed state, developing the ability to create a bodily sense of safety has been a challenge.  Although she can now create a sense of safety for herself with her eyes closed, for a long the experience of shutting her eyes was terrifying for her.  When she would try to participate in guided relaxations, she always felt crazy and different because it was to opposite of relaxing to her.  I asked her if I should skip the relaxation part of the art process because of how it could re-stimulate that trauma for some women.  She emphatically answered "No", and explained that although it can be difficult for many women, and some may not be able to do it, relaxation is one of the most important things for each woman to learn.  She felt that the shelter needed to provide more opportunities for the women to learn to relax, and she certainly encouraged me to use the relaxations as a part of the art. 

She explained that the important thing is to make it clear that:

1. THOSE WHO DON'T FIND THE RELAXATION RELAXING ARE NOT CRAZY.  

2. THE RELAXATION IS COMPLETELY OPTIONAL. 

3. THOSE WHO WISH TO KEEP THEIR EYES OPEN OR EVEN TO LEAVE THE ROOM ARE ABSOLUTELY WELCOME TO DO SO.

With these warnings taken into consideration, and addressed, the relaxation has often been one of the most enjoyed and eagerly anticipated parts of the sessions.  Many women appreciate being guided to feel the peacefulness they so badly need, and so rarely feel.  It is definitely worth every slow, unhurried moment it takes to establish this atmosphere. 

RELAXATION DESCRIPTION

Note:  The words are to be read slowly, and calmly.  The three dots in the text (...) indicate a generous pause before continuing to speak.  It is helpful to accompany the relaxation (and the entire art session) with soft, relaxing music.

Opening:  This art session is a time for you to relax, and to get in touch with yourself, so we're going to begin with a relaxation.  I'd like you to get yourself as comfortable as you can.  You don't have to worry about anything.  This is a time-out from all of the things you have to do, a time-out from the children, a time for just you.  So see if you're comfortable.  Lay down if you like, put your head down on the table if you like, and let your eyes close. 

Breathing:  Now take a deep breath- a very, very deep breath.  As you breathe in, feel your lungs filling with air.  Imagine the air going all the way down into your stomach, and let your stomach stick out as far as it wants to go...  Then let the air go. [exhale] 

Body Relaxation:  As you take another breath, imagine the air going all the way into your toes and relaxing them...  Now breathe all the way into your calves, and let them relax...  Now breathe into your thighs, and imagine the air relaxing your legs...  Now notice your stomach.  Is it tense?  As you breathe in again, imagine the air soothing your stomach muscles.  Let any tension flow away with your breath...  [Continue these instructions using breath to relax the back, the neck, the shoulders, the arms, the head- scalp, forehead, eyebrows, eyes, nose, mouth, and jaw.]

Closure:  Continue to breathe deeply...  Take one final deepest breath to let your whole body relax, and give yourself a chance to notice how you're feeling right now.  Are you sleepy?  sad?  peaceful?...  When you are ready, you can open your eyes and stretch however you want.  

Variations:  This relaxation can be greatly varied in terms of length and detail.  The deep breathing is the most important part.  For a short relaxation, introduce the deep breathing, directed down into the stomach area, and then simply accompany it with head and shoulder rolls to relax the body.  For a longer variation, try having the women imagine the air coming into their bodies as a healing, relaxing force.  Have them imagine it as a color, like a colored fog. Have them picture that color relaxing their body from head to toe throughout the guided visualization. 

Materials:  None necessary.  A peaceful state of mind helps, and soft, "new-age" type music can enhance the experience.
Row.txt_description: A brief relaxation exercise at the outset of an art session can be a key factor, a sort of "rite of passage" into a creative session, helping everyone to make the transition from the customary chaos of the shelter into a separate, constructive time and space. The relaxation exercise establishes the session as a chance for the women to get in touch with themselves.

Row.txt_code:
Crowned With Esteem
 
Objective:
To help the children identify strengths in one another.  Each individual will then take this information and create a crown for themselves to give them a self-esteem boost. A sense of pride within oneself and a cohesion within the group.

Materials:
Card stock crowns (Discount School Supplies) click here for link  Note: you might need to adjust the size for smaller heads
(Card stock or construction paper can be substituted)
Markers
Index cards- enough for each person
Word list for spelling and positive word choices
OPTIONAL MATERIALS
Glue, glitter, scissors, rhinestones, feathers, beads, pom poms, various other embellishment

Time frame:
Intro and Warm-up — 15 min
Creations — 30 min
Sharing — 15 min

   
  Using the Discount School Crowns
 
Set—up/Prep:
Have the crowns punched out of their forms.  Have markers out and index cards, enough for each person.  You might want to include a word sheet to help those who struggle with spelling and ideas for positive words for their peers.

Introduction:
Today I want you to think about all of your peers in the room.  Some of them you may get along with while others you may struggle with.  We are going to be sharing a lot of ideas about each other today. The project we are going to do is called Crowned with Esteem. The word Esteem means to regard highly or favorably; regard with respect or admiration. 

Today you will be challenged to come up with one positive thing to say about each of your peers and write it on their note card.  Once your card is returned to you, you will use the positive words to create your crown.  You can color your crown in any way that you like,  making certain to sure to use the words given to you by your peers.

Warm-up/Opening Circle:
Ask each participant to say their name and then check in as an art supply. For example, “I am Kate and I feel like a pair of scissors, they are sharp and I am in a poor mood.” This can help to see where the children in the group are at emotionally.

   
  Words of esteem for each person
 
   
  Adding your special words to your crown 
   
  Decorating your crown
 
Creation:
Each person will have a card in front of them.  Have each child write their name at the top of the card. Then have each child pass the card to their left. The person who has the card will write one special thing about that person. (It can be helpful to instruct about the importance of being kind and how it would feel if someone did otherwise, this will be helpful to avoid critical messages.) You can use words like  - fun, happy, smart, friendly, energetic, fair, honest,strong, kind, sweet, funny, creative, good friend, helpful, positive.... Keep passing the card around to the left, so that everyone has had an opportunity to say something kind and positive about the person whose name is at the top of the card, until it comes back to the original person.

Once this is done encourage the children to start on the decoration of their crown using the words that were said about them and any embellishments available.  Let them know the amount of time left for their creation.

Closing:
It is important that each person get a chance to share about how this process made them feel and what things came up for them while doing the index cards and the crown itself. How did they overcome those feelings or deal with them. In the end make a statement about how important team work can be. Ask them to notice how support can be helpful to smooth out any feeling that arise during the process
Row.txt_description: To help the children identify strengths in one another. Each individual will then take this information and create a crown for themselves to give them a self esteem boost. A sense of pride within oneself and a cohesion within the group.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
 
   A personal Red Flag Banner
To give teens an opportunity to identify "red flags", or warning signs, of an abusive relationship.  Participants will discuss what they see as "red flags" and then write on one side of a red flag to help them identify abusive partners and behavior.  On the other side of the red flag participants will create a collage to illustrate aspects of a healthy relationship to serve as a reminder for what they should look for in a potential partner.  The project can be done individually or collectively and once the flags are completed they are connected together to create a red flag banner.

  
  Large banner for group project
Materials:
Large flag template
Small flag templates
Red Flags of Abusive Relationships Handout
Teen Dating Violence Resource Page
Red paper (cardstock works best)
Glue
Scissors
Beads (optional)
Collage materials
Permanent markers (dark colors and metallics)
3 to 5 yards of twine, string or clothesline
  
  Smaller Individual Red Flag Banner
3 foot pieces of ribbon or yarn
Pens 

Time Frame:
Introduction: 5 minutes
Opening Circle: 20 minutes
Creation: 30 minutes
Closing Circle: 20 minutes
Total: 1 hour, 15 minutes

Note to leaders:
  • Teens learn about relationships from the adults they live with, the media, the Internet and their friends. As adults we have the responsibility to be open to discussing relationships with teens, to hear their questions with respect and give them real answers. Being honest without judgment, no matter what they share with us, goes a long way to making you a child or teen's "safe adult".
  • To help establish boundaries with the teens you may want to create Ground Rules as a group. 
  • While you may feel like you can't be both a friend and an advocate to the teens, keep in mind that all you need to be is their trusted adult.
  • For more tips and information about working with teens please visit the FAQ section of AWBW's website.
  
 Cutting out your Group Project Template 
  
  
 Cutting out your Individual Project Template 
Preparation:
First decide if you will create this project as a team project, individual project or both. For the team project, we recommend using the large template and the smaller template for individual projects.
Print or copy the flag template(s) onto red paper. Or, hand out multiple templates and allow participants to trace. You may also want to pre-cut the flags in order to reduce the length of the workshop.
Print out copies of the Red Flag handout for each participant.  To save time you may want to read through the Red Flag handout and highlight the points you want to cover.

Introduction:
Teen Dating Violence isn’t an argument every once in a while, or a bad mood after a bad day, it is a pattern of controlling behavior that someone uses against a girlfriend or boyfriend.

Abuse can cause injury and even death, but it doesn’t have to be physical. It can include verbal and emotional abuse – constant insults, isolation from family and friends, name calling, controlling what someone wears-and it can also include sexual abuse.

Teen dating violence is very difficult to identify.  Have you ever had that gut feeling that something wasn't right?  Have you ever thought, “I saw all the writing on the wall and looked the other way”?  Just like those walls you walk by that are filled with tagging, often times we fail to see what is right in front of our face. We know it's there, however we don't really see it.  Red flags are intuitive warnings that let us know something is wrong.  All too often we silence that little voice inside of ourselves that warns us of a potential danger.  Abusive people are skilled at manipulating us into believing them and doubting ourselves.  Over time, abusers may convince us to automatically defer to what they think and want and to disregard our own needs, wants and opinions.  Today we are going to take a look back at the red flags from abusive relationships handout, and then create our own red flags to honor and allow our inner voice, needs and desires to be heard. We can save ourselves a lot of frustration and pain in the future by practicing identifying our red flags. During this workshop you will also have an opportunity to notice the things you want in your future relationships.

Opening Circle:
Begin by passing out the Red Flags of Abusive Relationships handout and go over it as a group. Ask the participants to share any thoughts about red flags, they can share personal experiences (that happened to them or someone they know), thoughts about how this issue is portrayed in the media (i.e. Rhianna and Chris Brown), and/or what the handout made them think about. 
 
 Writing out the Red Flags
 
 Creating a background image for the collage
 
 Gluing the inside of the flag together
 
  Tying a knot between each flag

Make sure to identify and explain how what they shared is an example of a red flag of a specific type of abuse.  For example, “I knew something was off when he/she said that I should not talk to boys/girls at parties”.  Just because you are talking to someone doesn't mean you two are hooking up.  This is an example of excessive jealousy.  Start the opening circle by asking someone to volunteer to share first and then have the rest of the group share one at a time.

Creation:
Now that we have identified some red flags, we are going to create a banner made of “red flags”.   Be sure to show a sample as a reminder of the two steps of the project. On one side you write down words, or symbols to remind you about some of the red flags we spoke about today.  You can write on as many flags as you want, they will serve as a reminder for what you should look out for in the future.  Allow about 10 minutes for everyone to write on one side of a flag.

Once the participants have written on  at least one flag, explain the collage portion of the workshop.  Now that we know what we don't want in an intimate relationship, lets look at what we do.  If time allows ask each teen to share one thing they think helps make a relationship healthy before they begin collaging.  Turn your flags over and cut out words and/or images and glue them to the blank sides of your flags to create a collage that shows what a healthy relationship looks like. While they are collaging you may want to remind the teens the reason why they are making this collage. Remind them that these flags will serve as a reminder of what to look for in an intimate relationship.   

If everyone is doing individual red flag banners, explain that they can begin to put their banner together by looping the first flag over the ribbon or string, gluing the insides together and then tying a knot or adding a bead between each flag. They can then take it home and hang it up as a reminder!

Closing:
Ask a volunteer to start the closing circle by sharing something about their red flag banner.  Ask the teens to speak about some of the red flags they wrote about and why they chose the images on their collages to represent what they believes makes a healthy relationship.  If you are doing this as a group project, after each person shares, have them loop their flag over the clothesline or ribbon and glue the sides together. Then add either a knot or a bead before the next flag. Once everyone has put their flag on the line, ask for someone to volunteer to help you hang the red flag banner! Thank everyone for sharing, participating and for creating an important reminder to pay attention to red flags. We teach people how to treat us, and what we will and won't allow in our relationships. Teach your partners that you won't accept abusive behavior, ever!
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives teens an opportunity to identify "red flags", or warning signs, of an abusive relationship.
Row.txt_tips:
Note:
You may also choose to do this workshop in two sessions.
First session: Discuss red flags using handouts and creating on one side of the flags.
Second session: Discuss what healthy relationships look like and create the collage side.

Row.txt_code:
Objective: To allow teenagers to explore the difference between healthy and unhealthy relationships.  This activity also gives teenagers opportunities to think about what steps to take if they know someone, or are themselves, in an abusive relationship.

Materials List:
Teen Power and Control Wheel & Teen Equality Wheel
Participant Relationship Quiz
Facilitator Relationship Quiz Q&A
  
  A completed Healthy Relationship Collage
 
Tri-fold people form template on 8 1/2 x14
Single people form template on 8 1/2 x 11
Card stock or heavy weight paper (see prep)
Magazines
Scissors
Glue sticks
Sharpies
Pens
Music
Timer

Note to leaders:
  • Teens learn about relationships from the adults they live with, the media, the Internet and their friends. As adults we have the responsibility to be open to discussing relationships with teens, to hear their questions with respect, and give them real answers. Being honest without judgment, no matter what they share with us, goes a long way to making you a child or teen's "safe adult".
  • To help establish boundaries with the teens you may want to create Ground Rules as a group. 
  • While you may feel like you can't be a friend and advocate to the teens you serve for a myriad of reasons, keep in mind that all you need to be is their trusted adult.
  • For more tips and information about working with teens please visit the FAQ section of AWBW's website.
Prep:
Print out the handouts provided, including this workshop.
To print the tri-fold template provided, set your printer to print at 8 1/2 x 14 (legal size) on heavy weight paper, and click print. If this is not an option or you would like a larger template use the 8 1/2 x11 single person template.  Whatever size you pick, you may choose to make stencils on card stock for the students to trace onto large construction (12x18) or similar paper(11x17).
Depending on how much time you have and how much volunteer help you have, you may want to precut the people forms for each participant.

 
Collaging the tri-fold
 
Timeframe:
Prep: 15 min to 1-hour
Intro: 5 min
Warm-up/Discusson: 15 -30 min
Creation: 1-hour
Closing:10 minutes
Total Time: 2 hours

Introduction: Dating or domestic abuse occurs when one partner uses different types of abusive behavior to gain POWER and CONTROL over the other partner.

Dating or domestic violence is a pattern of behavior that can include emotional, mental, verbal, financial, physical, sexual, and social abuse.

Abuse can happen to anyone! Teens and adults experience abuse in their relationships at the exact same rate! Dating abuse can happen to anyone, no matter their sexual orientation, gender identity, ethnicity, income level, educational and/or national background!

Today we are going to talk about healthy relationships, unhealthy ones and what steps you can take if you or someone you know is in an abusive relationship.

Before we get started, I want to share some startling statistics about dating violence and teenagers. Did you know...
  • About one in three high school students have been or will be involved in an abusive relationship.
  • One in five or 20 percent of dating couples report some type of violence in their relationship.
  • One study found that 7 percent of all murder victims were young women who were killed by their boyfriends.
  • Teen dating violence most often takes place in the home of one of the partners.
  • One study found that 38 percent of date rape victims were young women from 14 to 17 years of age.
  • A survey of adolescent and college students revealed that date rape accounted for 67 percent of sexual assaults.
  • More than half young women raped (68 percent) knew their rapist either as a boyfriend, friend or casual acquaintance.
  • Six out of 10 rapes of young women occur in their own home or a friend or relative's home, not in a dark alley.
Warm-up: Share the Teen Power and Control Wheel or Relationship Quiz provided. Generate a discussion or create a list with the teens of what they believe is considered "abuse" in a relationship, then using the list below, fill in the blanks.

Emotional/Mental/Verbal

  • Using put-downs, insults, name-calling, humiliation
  • Threatening to harm or kill family, friends, a new partner, pets, etc.
  • Threatening to commit suicide if a partner leaves
  • Making threats like, “If you leave me I’ll … spread rumors about you, tell your parents we had sex”, etc.
  • Blaming the person who is being abused for the abuse or for all the problems in the relationship
  • Minimizing or denying abusive behavior, playing mind games
  • Possessiveness and/or constant accusations of cheating

Physical Abuse

  • Hitting, grabbing, pushing, shaking, restraining you physically etc.
  • Intimidation (blocking exits/doors, hitting things or throwing objects at or near partner)
  • Using or threatening to use weapons
  • Stalking
Social Abuse
  • Spreading rumors or using blackmail to control a partner’s actions
  • Keeping a partner “in check” by monitoring their cell phone constantly or using friends to keep tabs on them
  • Isolating a partner from her/his friends and family
  • Using religion/culture to control partner
 
 Creating the collage

Sexual Abuse

  • Ignoring partner’s sexual choice(s) through pressure, manipulation, coercion (e.g. saying, “You’d do it if you loved me”)
  • Rape: Forced penetration without consent (including use of intimidation, threats, weapons etc.)
  • Sexual Assault: Forced sexual contact
  • Sexual Harassment: Unwanted sexual attention

Financial Abuse

  • Controlling possessions like: a car, phone, clothes, jewelry
  • Excessive gift giving with strings attached, for example “I gave you this, now you owe me”
  • Using gifts to make up for abusive behavior
  • Controlling all money, using money to threaten or manipulate
  • Sabotaging a partner’s work or school career, for example harassing a partner at work and causing them to get fired or refusing to give a partner a ride to work or school, etc.
End the discussion by sharing information on steps they can take to help themselves or a friend in an abusive relationship. For example (from safespace.org):

If you or a friend is being abused:
  • Don’t be afraid to reach out to someone who you think needs help. Tell them you are concerned for their safety and want to help.
  • Be supportive and listen patiently.  Acknowledge their feelings about their relationship.
  • Help them recognize that the abuse is not “normal” and is not their fault. Everyone deserves a healthy non-violent relationship.
  • Focus on your friend or family member, not on the abuser. Even if your loved one stays with their abusive partner, it is important that they still feel comfortable talking to you about it.
  • Be respectful of your friend or family members decisions about the relationship.
  • Connect them to resources in their community that can give them information and guidance. Remember, Break the Cycle is always here to help.
  • Help them develop a plan to end their relationship safely.
  • If they break up with the abuser, continue to be supportive of them after the relationship is over.
  • Even when you feel like there’s nothing you can do, don’t forget that by being there and by being supportive and caring – you are already doing a lot.
If you or a friend is being abusive:
  • Learn about domestic violence yourself so you can help your friend or family member recognize his or her abusive behaviors.
  • Your friend or family member may try to blame the victim for the abuse. Don’t support these feelings or help to justify the abuse.
  • Help the abuser focus on the victim’s feelings and the serious harm the victim is experiencing because of the abuse. Don’t support the abuser’s efforts to minimize the severity of their abusive behavior.
  • Don’t ignore abuse that you see or hear about. Your silence helps the abusive person to deny that their behavior is wrong.
  • Convince the abuser that getting professional help is important. Encourage him or her to find a program about ending domestic violence and have a list of resources ready.
  • Stay in touch with your friend and family member about the abuse. Be there to support the abuser to change long-term.
  • Remind your friend or family member that change will create a better, healthy relationship for both partners in the relationship.
  • Set an example by having healthy relationships in your own life.
 
 Moving towards a healthy relationship
Creation:  Give everyone the template or a stencil and paper to create a 3 body outline.  Explain that they will use collage and writing to illustrate healthy vs. abusive relationships and the steps we can take to help ourselves or a friend to leave abusive relationship. Give them one prompt at a time and allow them 1-hour to create their project.  Tell them that you will help the workshop move along by telling them when it's time to move on to the next collage. Give the teens 20 minutes to create each collage using the following prompts.
  1. On the first outline, use the collage materials to illustrate what the healthy relationship you deserve looks/feels like to you.
  2. On the second outline you will illustrate what an abusive relationship looks/feels like to you.
  3. On the last outline, collage and write your action plan to help yourself stay out of abusive relationships or to help a friend you believe is in an abusive relationship.
Closing:  Have the teens share what ever they feel comfortable sharing about their collages.  Ask each teen to share one thing they learned today that they didn't know.
Row.txt_description: This workshop will allow teenagers to explore the difference between healthy and unhealthy relationships. This also gives teenagers opportunities to think about what steps to take if they know someone or are themselves in an abusive relationship.
Row.txt_tips: If you or your clients need additional resources to help address this issue use the Teen Dating Violence Resource Page.

Row.str_title: A Kiss is Not a Promise
Row.txt_code:
The kiss journal
Objective: To assist teens in thinking about their own personal boundaries when it comes to intimate relationships.  To help them become aware of what a “kiss” means to them and how people have different expectations.

Materials for Journal:
Kiss template
Mylar or similar reflective silver paper
Copy paper
Hole puncher
3/4 inch white polyester ribbon
Ballpoint pen

Preparations: Have the Kiss template
precut for all participates to trace onto
Mylar and paper
     
Time Frame:
1 to 2 hours

Note to leaders:
  • Teens learn about relationships from the adults they live with, the media, the Internet and their friends. As adults we have the responsibility to be open to discussing relationships with teens, to hear their questions with respect and give them real answers. Being honest without judgment, no matter what they share with us, goes a long way to making you a child or teen's "safe adult".
  • To help establish boundaries with the teens you may want to create Ground Rules as a group. 
  • While you may feel like you can't be a friend and advocate to the teens you serve for a myriad of reasons, keep in mind that all you need to be is their trusted adult.
  • For more tips and information about working with teens please visit the FAQ section of AWBW's website.

Introduction: Today we are going to think and share about what exactly a kiss means to us and what our boundaries are when it comes to physical intimacy by creating a Kiss Journal.


 
 Cutting the kiss out of cardstock or paper
 
  
 Cut the Mylar for the front and back
 
  
 Write a message on the ribbon
 
  
 Use the pages as a journal
 
Journaling & Discussion:
Have the teens construct their journal by cutting out their kiss template and their Mylar front and back covers. Ask them to align all the pages and punch a hole at the top. Finally hand the ribbon out and tie it to hold the journal together.

Have the teens write about the following questions in their Kiss Journal. Explain that at the end of the journaling exercise you will ask everyone to turn them in so you can read their answers anonymously. No one will know who wrote what, so please be as honest as you can be. Ask them to write their name discretely on the back page of the journal so you can give them back after your are done reading them.  If someone does not want to submit their journal to you, they are still welcome to participate. Tell the teens that you will ask them questions and give them a few minutes to write about it (about 3 minutes per question). Give them one question at a time.
1.  Why do people kiss?
2.  What does kissing mean to you?
3.  What are your expectations once you have kissed someone that you like?
4.  What do you think the person your kissing expects from you after you kiss them?

Have everyone submit their journals and anonymously share the answers to any of these questions. Point out differences in expectations and meaning for each person.

Start a discussion about the importance of communication in a relationship. First, you should know what you want and don't want in a relationship. If you are in a healthy relationship, communicating these needs should not feel scary.  Explain that a healthy relationship always has open communication, trust, respect and equality. If you don't feel safe to communicate your needs or feel that your boyfriend/girlfriend treats you with respect or as an equal, you need to reevaluate your relationship.

Ask the group if they feel teens have good communication?  Do teens explain expectations or boundaries to each other before hooking up? Is it important for teens to speak more openly to each other about expectations or boundaries? Why?

Hand back the journals to each person. Ask them to each write themselves a message or words on the ribbon to remind them to always be true to themselves.  Give an example, "I will write, 'I will always respect myself and my boundaries'."

Closing Circle:
Have the participant’s each share about their message and anything they have learned today.
Row.txt_description: This workshop assists teens in thinking about their own personal boundaries and how becoming physical in a dating relationship can change everything. This workshop also helps them become aware of what a “kiss” means to them and how people have different expectations.
Row.txt_tips:
The Mylar can rip easily when cutting it out. Be careful.
If you are preparing the journals in advance, it is easier to use a standard 2 or 3-hole puncher to punch through all the layers.

If you or your clients need resources to help address this issue use the Teen Dating Violence Resource Page.

Row.txt_code:
Objective:
The goal for this workshop is to empower families to share their story of surviving domestic violence by illustrating their journey through the metaphor of a tree. In creating their trees, families will be asked to reflect on where they came from, how they escaped, and the kind of future that they envision for themselves.

Materials:

 Materials Sample Set-up
Windows will provide a basic kit including:
Assortment of acrylic paints (Biocolors), s cissors, glue, 18 x 24 flat canvas, brushes, oil pastels, watercolors and various collage materials.  You are welcome to donate the use of your supplies and/or we can reimburse up to $20 per family for supplies you contribute.
 
Windows will also provide all of the materials for the optional warm up of your choice.  Please let your AWBW Representative know which warm-up (if any) you will use so they can pack the appropriate supplies.  

In addition to the basic kit we'd love your help making sure each family's expression is unique in size, shape, color, etc.  Please feel free to add any supplies that you would like to include.

Note on Materials:
Instead of limiting everyone to a uniform size canvas and selection of materials, we realize it would be much stronger to have individually unique pieces.  We are very fortunate to have a gallery where we will be able to display a range of pieces. 

To help make each family's experience different we want to invite you to supplement this project with materials based on your unique expertise on materials for the workshops you will be co-facilitating.

 
 
Introduction:
Introduce the Guest Artist, AWBW Representative, and anyone else the family is not familiar with.  Reinforce that all of the previously mentioned people are there to help the family have a good experience with the workshop. Thank the family for being willing to create with your team and help them feel comfortable. Begin to share with them what this project is about and that it will lead up to an art exhibit open to the public.  Inform the family that their tree can be completely anonymous to ensure they feel comfortable to create without censoring themselves. 

Create, discuss and review any Ground Rules.  Make sure to include a statement about the importance of confidentiality.  It is also important to let the family know they may not like or agree with what the other participants say and create, which is just fine.  However, no one is allowed to critique or censor anyone.  Talk about trees in general and how they survive many things in their lives including drought, floods, fires, lightening, and even abuse from humans. Explain how the family can use this tree to represent their journey through domestic violence. For example, the roots might represent where they have come from and thus the foundation that allowed them to become the person they are today.  The trunk could represent where they are now, the  branches reaching out for help, and the leaves and blossoms, new growth or what they want to have in the future. The environment can also help illustrate the families’ story. For example, falling leaves, dead branches on the ground or roots buried underground could symbolize the bad memories or experiences they want to leave in their past.

It is important to share with the family that you hope this project helps to create more open communication between family members as they reflect and discuss their own unique experience so that they can begin to heal as individuals and as a family. Also, you will need to inform the family that as they tell about their journey out of domestic violence that it important that they explore and share all of the experiences and feelings in their story.  Including what they've been through at home, in the shelter, how they escaped, what they left behind (fear, sadness, anger, Dad, home, etc.) & what they're moving toward (safety, love, growth, rebuilding family together, etc.)  Leaders may consider asking the families to bring family pictures and significant documents to include in their piece.

Explain that sometimes when there is domestic violence in the home, parents and their children don't discuss what happened, what each person experienced, and the differences between each person’s point of view, feelings, and memories. Talking about it may seem scary and counterproductive, but it actually ends up taking the power away from the pain to talk about it together.  Moreover, sharing our pain with others helps us heal and let go. Remind everyone how courageous and important it is to talk about the pain and the abuse.  Expressing feelings, both negative and positive alike, in a healthy manner, takes practice and today we will all experience how it feels to open up lines of communication.    

 
  Stand Up Version of Tree
Warm Up/Opening Circle:
Option 1: (For mixed age groups or younger participants)
Using the Foam Tree and leaves provided by AWBW, set up a tree form in the middle of the each family's table. Give at least two foam leaves to each person to hold. Have the participants close their eyes if it feels safe for them and ask them to think about their journey through domestic violence, (pause) and ask them to think about a word that represents their past, (pause). Then ask them to think about their future (pause) and what they want in their future.

Ask everyone to open their eyes and put a word or words or even a drawing on a leaf for their past.  Give them time to do this. Then ask them to put a word or symbol on the other leaf to represent what they want in their future.  If the younger ones are struggling with this task encourage the parent to assist their children.  Pass the tree and two adhesive dots to the person who volunteers to share their leaves first.   Have the person share their name and whatever they feel comfortable sharing about their leaves.  Then instruct that person to attach the leaves to any part of the tree (including underneath).  Then pass the tree to the next family member who wants to share and repeat the process until everyone has had a chance to share their leaves and attach them to the tree.  After everyone has shared let them know that this tree represents letting go of the past and celebrating the future. Encourage the family to clap and cheer to recognize the significance of opening up about the past and looking to the future!


 
  
Option 2: (For more advance participant or families with older children)
First do a brief demonstration of the materials they will use for the warm-up (participants will be using watercolor crayons, water, and 5 x 7 pieces of paper). Explain to the family that during this warm-up you will be asking them some questions and giving them directions for putting marks on their paper.  If they don’t feel comfortable with the warm-up they can simply use the watercolor crayons to see how they work.

“We are going to try a very loose, quick warm-up. We're going to move quickly, so that nobody has time to think too much, and you can practice focusing on the thoughts that first come to mind without having time to criticize them."

If it feels safe for you, close your eyes and picture yourself as a tree.  Now look beyond the tree and see what color the sky and background are.  Is it night?  Is it morning?  (pause) Is there blue a sky? Sunshine?  Rain? Or a glowing sunset?  Open your eyes and choose the color that you just saw and cover your entire page with that color. (pause)  

Now think about the bark of your tree… What color is the bark?  What shape comes to mind for the bark? Is it rough or smooth?  Curly? Bent?  Or straight?  Go ahead and put on your page the first thought you had for the bark.  (pause)  Now think about the leaves of your tree. What colors and what shapes come to mind for the leaves? Choose a color and draw a leaf. (pause)  Does your tree have flowers or seeds? What color and what shapes come to mind for your flowers or seeds? Go ahead and put your first thoughts on the page. (pause)  Now think about how many branches your tree might have...Does your tree have lots of branches?  Are they little branches or big branches? Make a mark for the color and shape that come to mind.  (pause)   Is your tree an angry tree?  What color and shape come to mind for anger?  Make a mark on your page for anger.  (pause)   Now think about if your tree is happy.  What color and shape come to mind for happy?  Make a mark on your page if your tree is happy.  (pause)   Now think about if your tree is sad.  What color, and what shape come to mind for sad?  When you’re ready, make a mark on your page if your tree is sad. (pause)  Now think about if your tree is peaceful.  What color and shape comes to mind for peaceful.  Make a mark on your page if your tree is peaceful.    Now begin to think about if your family is part of your tree.  What shapes and colors would they be?  Think of your mom.  What shape and color comes to mind?  Make a mark on your tree for your mom.   Now think of your dad.  What shape and color comes to mind for your dad?  Make a mark on the page for your dad.  Now think about any brothers and sisters you have.  What shape and colors would they be?  Make a mark on your page for them.  And now think of yourself.  What color would you be?  What shape?  Make a mark on your tree for yourself...Now think about the future you envision and wish for your tree - think of a color or shape for your wish, and make a mark on your page for the future."

Have everyone take a minute to share their name and anything they would like to share about their tree.

 
Option 3: (for participants that respond to visualizations)
(Speaking slowly with a calm voice) Before we start our project I am going to guide you through a relaxation. All you have to do is sit comfortably with your hands on your lap, close your eyes, and imagine you are sitting in a very special tree.  Picture yourself swinging back and forth on a very comfortable swing on one of the branches.

As you are swinging back and forth begin to look around….glance up through the tree branches and notice the sky ….Is your sky bright or dark?  Are there fluffy clouds, or do you just see a blue sky?  Perhaps you see a rainy sky.  Maybe it’s night time.  Keep breathing deep breathes as your body relaxes more and more. Now turn your attention to the branches of your tree (pause)… feel sunshine bouncing warmly off the leaves, notice the color and shape of your leaves….Are they a dark color or a light color?  Are they all the same or are some leaves different? Now take another deep breath and notice if your tree has a special scent…can you smell flowers or maybe even pine needles?  Keep breathing and imagining your tree. Now begin to notice if your tree has lots of branches or just a few. Are the branches on your tree reaching up or down… are they chunky branches or skinny branches? And lastly while you are still swinging on your special swing notice the bark on your tree …is it wrinkly or smooth…. notice the color of the bark on your tree…Is the bark only one color or lots of colors?… Just keep swinging and imaging your tree...  
          
Whenever you are ready you may open your eyes and create a drawing of what you saw in your imagination using construction paper and colored pencils.


 "Family" Proudly Displaying Their Tree
Option 4: (simple relaxation)
Have everyone take off their shoes and gather the participants in a circle. Ask the family to begin to imagine if they could be any kind of tree, what kind of tree would they choose.  Then recite the following relaxation: Ok everyone let’s breathe in a deep breath and as you release your breath, let’s stretch up towards the ceiling and let out your big breath! Ok now let’s spread out a little and begin to pretend you are a tree. Look at your feet and spread all your toes out.  Feel your toes breathing and expanding into the floor.  Focus all your attention on your feet and allow them to feel the floor as if they were the roots of a tree and you are taking hold of the ground. Now bend down, and then slowly run your hands up your calves and thighs and imagine that those parts of your body are your trunk. Feel the bark - is it rough or smooth?  Now stretch your arms up as if they were branches reaching towards the sun. Feel the warmth of the sun nurturing your leaves, your branches and your bark! Now position yourself as a stationary tree, remember to keep breathing.  Begin to envision the shape of your trunk (pause) and your branches (pause).  What do they look like?  Are they reaching up towards the sky, across the room?   Are some sloping down? Imagine you are now a tree growing in a very safe forest filled with trees just like you ... A forest where you are taken care of, protected and loved. Just stand for a moment and hear the peaceful silence of the forest. (Pause)  Now give your tree a big hug (everyone hugs themselves) and give your tree and nice squeeze.  Take another deep breathe in. As you let your breath out slowly begin to bring yourself back to the room and begin to create your Family Tree.

Technical Demonstration:
Now begin the transition to each family working together on their tree. Give the family a tour of all the supplies along with a few options or possibilities of what they may create. If appropriate you may give each family only one option.

Give a demonstration on how to use all the materials. Never assume the family knows how to use a material. Some may have never used a paint brush or even a crayon.


  
 Planning Sheet 1
  
   
   
 Planning Sheet 2
  
   
Creation Possibilities:
Depending on family size and the ages of the children, there are different options for what to do next!  Share the creation process with the families based on the artist and leaders plan.  Have the parent direct the family to reach a consensus on how they will create their tree.  Be sure to reinforce that the parent is the lead designer, or creative supervisor for the project.

Here are some new possibilities to consider:
  • You may start by giving the parent a planning sheet (provided).
  • Different materials (watercolor, acrylics, assemblage, textiles, pastels...)
  • Different shapes and size canvas or paper (it may even be cool to have some mini-trees!!)
  • Creating a dyptych (i.e. dark & light, mother & child) or triptych(i.e. past, present & future)
  • Focus on one part of the tree(i.e. just the leaves, or the roots rather than creating a whole tree).
  • Selection of a color palette (i.e. a monochromatic tree or black and white tree).
  • A Mosaic tile tree.
  • A tree made out of words
As they consider the different options you may want to keep the following age related family dynamics issues in mind:
• Teens: Some teens might want to just create their own tree or section to add onto the bigger tree, that is fine! They may not be used to having mom/dad in charge or they may just be vying for independence as teens typically do.   Try to channel their energy in a positive direction. Sometimes teens just want to know they have choices, and they like attention just like we do!

• Very active children/or a family that can't seem to work together: For this family it might be easier for each participant to have their own separate piece to work with such as: leaves, flowers, trunk, or branches.  They can write, paint, or collage on them.   Then give the family the option to have mom/dad piece it all back together.  You can make a ceremony out of each person gluing their creation on the tree which will enable the family to put their separate creations together to form one family tree!

• Toddlers (under 3) and younger: The hand print option will probably be the easiest for this age! Don't forget footprints work too! Or a combination of the two.

Closing:
