Share about the materials you provided for this workshop and the different techniques that can be used for their creations.  As you share, pass around the workshop sample images. If you haven't already done so and it's feasible, this might be a good time to share the dvd created by Kim Abeles that goes with this project.  After the demonstration suggest that it is important to make a commitment to one idea for their Pearl.  Let the art become their voice.

Opening Circle:
  
Ask participants to choose a symbol of their "irritant" from the found objects provided. Ask why they  chose that object to represent their irritant.

Journaling:
From an irritant a beautiful pearl emerges. We are now going to take some time now to journal about your pearls of wisdom. 

A. How did the irritant affect your journey?
B. What has helped you through tough times? What helped you survive? What gave you strength?
C. What advice would you give your younger self?
D. What advice would you share with another person to give them strength?  It can be very practical things, a simple idea, or something more philosophical

E. In an oyster, a beautiful pearl emerges from an irritant. From the irritant you find a treasure.  From difficulties we gain so much wisdom. That wisdom is something you can share to help others get through their own issues. What wisdom would want to share?

 
 Journey through pain towards hope and serenity. Love Yourself.
Relaxation(optional):
Begin...This is your window of time. This is a time to honor yourself as a wise and strong survivor. Get comfortable in your chair and if it feels safe, let your eyes close.  (Read slowly) Now, notice your breath (pause). With each breath notice that your breath has been with you in pain and in joy. Your breath and you are one. Your breath is your life force. Continue to breathe and connect with how you are feeling right now.  Notice how strong and courageous you are to be sitting in this room.  Give yourself permission to feel whatever you may be feeling.  Notice that you are safe, that you are taking important steps to heal the parts of you that are hurt and to honor the parts of you that are strong, courageous and authentically you. Take a few deep breaths and when you are ready open your eyes.     

 
 I am breaking the cycle 
Creation:
Create artwork that shares your pearl of wisdom. As you create, remember to illustrate your message in any way that feels right. You can create an image, use words or both.

Throughout the creative process, remind participants that there is no wrong way to create their story of survival and wisdom.

Toward the end of the creating time start to encourage participants to think about their pearls of wisdom. Ask them to look back at the process of creating, what they learned today and what they may want to share.
      
Closing Circle:
 
  
Option A: Share about your pearl and the wisdom you represented on it.

Option B: What would you tell yourself today or what would you share with a younger friend who may be going through something similar. 

Option C: If the participants have good relationships with one another, have them share with a partner.  After sharing in pairs, go around the circle and have the listener speak the 'wisdom' from her partner and vice versa.  It makes it more of a 'wisdom circle'. 

Submit Pearls to AWBW:
Using a release form have participants share the words of wisdom that go with their Pearl. Take high resolution photographs and attach them to the corresponding release. Submit your pearls through AWBW's blog starting January 1st, 2011 and receive a new shrinky dink project in the mail. If you prefer you may send original artwork or a high resolution image with releases to AWBW for inclusion in the Pearls of Wisdom blog.

Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength and wisdom as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence.

Row.str_title: For Participating Programs Only - Pearls of Wisdom:End the Violence Workshop Draft
Row.txt_code:
Objective:
This workshop is designed to help women and their children recognize their personal strength, and uses the metaphor of "pearls" as treasures that form inside an oyster in response to an irritant. Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence.

Materials:
Collage materials (different kinds of tissue and natural fiber papers work well)
Magazines for images or words (use sparingly)
Watercolors, Acrylic or Biocolors
Biocolor Shimmer paint additive for pearlized look
Water cups
Paint brushes
Paint palettes
Sandpaper(provided in toolkit)
Color pencils
Yarn, string, buttons
Scraping tools (paper clips, toothpicks,screwdrivers, spoon, knives etc)
Tacky glue
Mod Podge and thick brushes
Hand wipes
Images of Kim Abeles Pearl Disc Samples:
1. Braille Collage / Safe Place Carving Image
2. Pencil Drawing and Woven Words
3. Woven Collage and Iridescent Paint
4. Paint and Collage with Nylon Stocking
5. Simple Layering Technique

Timeframe:
Plan for this workshop to take between 1 and 3 hours.


 
Project Background:
Pearls of Wisdom: End the Violence is a two year community project organized by A Window Between Worlds in collaboration with artist Kim Abeles and AWBW Community Art Advocate Sandra Mueller. 

The Pearls of Wisdom project will culminate with an exhibition, online blog, catalogue and related events commemorating A Window Between Worlds’ 20th Anniversary at the Korean Cultural Center in March 2011. As the only national organization using art to help end domestic violence, this project affirms AWBW’s pioneering work in bridging the realms of art and social change.

About Kim Abeles: Kim Abeles has been described by Artscene’s, Orville O. Clarke as “one of the most acute observers of the state of our region's body and soul.”  Abeles’ art crosses disciplines and media to explore and map the urban environment and chronicle broad social issues.  Her body of work gives the community a voice to address social issues in a positive, constructive way.  Both her personal experience as a survivor and her broad experience with large scale collaborative installation work position her well to conceive and implement this statewide collaboration weaving the voices of survivors and community members around the issue of domestic violence.

 
Preparation/Set-up: 
We are offering several options for warm-ups and creation. As always we want you to make this workshop your own. Feel free to use some or all of the different options presented to facilitate this project.  Each step will have an approximate timeframe to help you plan.

If you would like, you could do this workshop in stages. For example, you could spend the first session exploring the process of 'becoming a pearl' as it relates to each survivor using the journaling exercises suggested below. In the second session you could choose to offer a relaxation and/or opening circle of revelations or discoveries from the first session and create your pearl. 

We encourage and welcome all workshop Leaders to create their own “Pearl” and explore the creative process of this project. Leaders who do create a Pearl are asked to submit their creation for inclusion in the final exhibition.

After you decide how you will present this workshop, collect the materials you would like to offer and create an art supply buffet table or different supply stations with material laid out by supply type.
 

 
Workshop Introduction:
A pearl is a wonderful metaphor for the survivor’s journey. Do you know how a pearl is formed? Basically, it starts with an irritant that enters an oyster; protective layers transform that mollusk and create a pearl. Throughout our lives, we all have challenges and difficulties (irritants). There are lessons to be learned in all these challenges (pearls).

Sharing your story as a survivor, from pain to wisdom, can empower and inspire an individual or even a community to help end the violence perpetrated against our innocence, our hearts, our souls and our bodies. What you’ve experienced and the ways you survived are valuable and essential in helping to end the cycle of violence.

As you reflect and create your pearls, notice your strength, beauty and wisdom. Embrace the ways you are transforming and growing. Thank you for being here to share your story.

Opening Circle:

 Basket of "irritants"
Provide small objects in the middle of the table (or pass around a basket) that the group can pick from to represent their irritant. Found objects such as symbolic items, charms, stickers or images, Mexican Loteria cards and other knick-knacks. If possible you may want to welcome participants to bring a personal object that represents a significant irritant in their lives (i.e. letter, photo, etc.). 

Choose one:
A. Have participants share why they chose their object(s). How did this irritant/challenge affect your journey?
B. Ask participants to say the first thing that comes to mind about what they would say to a friend or complete stranger, right now, about getting out of a DV relationship or staying safe.
C. Go straight to journaling and share after.

 
 Oyster Journal
Demonstration:
Before the creation process on the pearl disc, share about the materials you provided for your workshop and the different techniques that can be used for their creations.   As you share, pass around the workshop sample images. If you haven't already done so and it's feasible, this might be a good time to share the dvd created by Kim Abeles that goes with this project.  After the demonstration suggest that it is important to make a commitment to one idea for their pearl project. Let the art become their voice.

 

Journaling (using the journals provided):
You may want to offer several journaling times (about 5 minutes each) to help participants reflect through the irritant on the process of transforming it into a pearl. They can use words, phrases, or draw symbols, whatever they feel like doing.

A. Using the mirror paper, have participants write about the irritants that have affected their journey to today.  They can write about why they chose the object during the opening circle or write about the people or experiences that affected their journey.  

B.Using the bandage paper, participants can reflect the ways they are healing or what has helped them through difficult experiences in their lives.

C. The extra sheets can be used at any time as a place to put thoughts, write personal notes or continue the creative process. 

Relaxation(optional):  
Have participants hold the unsanded pearl in their hands during the meditation and with their eyes closed. Begin...This is your window of time. This is a time to honor yourself as a wise and strong survivor. Get comfortable in your chair and if it feels safe, let your eyes close.  (Read slowly) Now, notice your breath (pause). With each breath notice that your breath has been with you in pain and in joy. Your breath and you are one. Your breath is your life force. Continue to breathe and connect with how you are feeling right now.  Notice how strong and courageous you are to be sitting in this room.  Give yourself permission to feel whatever you may be feeling.  Notice that you are safe, that you are taking important steps to heal the parts of you that are hurt and to honor the parts of you that are strong, courageous and authentically you. Take a few deep breaths and when you are ready open your eyes.     

 
Creation:
Start in any of the ways described above. Have participants select a plaster disc.  Invite them to choose the material they will need and tell them how much time they will have to create.

Explain that they will now sand their disks as their 'Pearl' begins to take shape. After sanding they will begin to create using the materials provided. 
With sand paper provided welcome participants to sand the disc/pearl’s jagged edges and/or rough surface or if they prefer they may leave it rough. 
(They could use this opportunity to think of this process as symbolic of letting go of their irritants, the challenges, the pain and struggles. Remind them that it is okay not feel ready to take this step at this time and that they can just notice how it feels to sand the rough edges.  It is also important to remind them that it is okay to leave it rough. What is most important is that they trust what feels right.)

When they have complete the sanding process they are ready to create.

Throughout the creative process, remind participants that their is no wrong way to create their story of survival and wisdom. The messages on their pearls of wisdom are meant to inspire, educate and encourage others in their healing journey.

Toward the end of the creating time, start to encourage participants to think about their pearls of wisdom. Ask them to look back at the process of creating, what they learned today and what they may want to share as part of this exhibit. 
      
Closing Circle:

Option A: Share about your pearl and the wisdom your represented on it.

Option B: What would they tell themselves today or what would they share with a younger friend who might be going through something similar?

Option C: If the participants have good relationships with one another, have them share with a partner.  Then, when we go around the circle - the partner speaks the 'wisdom' she heard and vice versa.  It makes it more of a 'wisdom circle'. 

Submit Pearls to AWBW:
Using release form have them share their words of wisdom to go with their pearl.
Pack the Pearls using the Pearls Handling Instructions provided in your toolkit.
Row.txt_description: This workshop is designed to help children recognize their personal strength, and uses the metaphor of "pearls" as treasures that form inside an oyster in response to an irritant. Similarly, survivors of domestic violence gain strength as they create healthy, violence-free lives that, in turn, offer stories that inspire and nurture others to mobilize the community to end domestic violence.

Row.txt_code:
Corn husk dolls/figures created by Refuge House, Inc.
Spanish Support group members & leaders (Tallahassee, Florida).
Background:
Corn husks are an interesting and fun material to use during the month of November as we celebrate and decorate for Thanksgiving. They can be crunched or stretched in a variety of ways. They can be made round, ruffled, tied, braided or curled. You can also leave them in their natural color or they can be painted or dyed.

Objective:
To look at the things that help the children to grow into strong, healthy adults while creatively using simple, natural materials.

Materials:
   
  Cornhusks
 
Dry corn husks (at least 5 per participant). These are available in most grocery stores or craft stores.
Large water bowl to soak the husks in.
Paper towels at each station to soak the water from the corn husk when they are first pulled out of the water bowl.
Raffia, twine, or pipe cleaners.
Scissors
Step by step Handout
Optional:
Paint
Paint brushes
Cups of water

Note: Some suggestions may require additional materials.You may also use fresh corn husk leaves. If you want to save them until you are ready to do the workshop store them to dry.

 Age Range:        
 Timeframe:
 Ages 6 - 16
 One hour.  If you choose to paint the body or create
clothing you can do this is a separate session.





 Preparation:
You may want to start soaking the corn husks in warm water prior to the group session so they are ready when your group arrives. You can dry them by laying them out on a folded paper towel.

Introduction:
Corn husk dolls have been around for centuries are seen in most all cultures that harvest and use corn.  Native Americans produced dolls of varying styles to look like members of their tribe. Later, European settlers learned from the natives and made corn husk dolls for their children too.  Corn also plays an essential role in Mexican culture, using different parts of the plant for medicine, food and crafts, like the corn husk dolls. Some cultures use the dolls in ceremonies to help heal people who are ill or to help stop evil dreams.

Corn husks dolls are perfect to make during this time of year since corn is a traditional food for Thanksgiving and the husks can make beautiful and creative decorations.

Today we are going to create a corn husk doll that can tell our story of growth.

  
 
Corn Husk dolls from
El Salvador
  Corn Husk doll from
Mexico		  Native American
Corn Husk doll

Warm-up/Relaxation:
To begin this meditation have the participants sit straight and as comfortable as possible. Ask them to close their eyes if this is comfortable to them. Ask them to put their hands in their laps and to begin taking a few even breaths to settle down.

Say, "Breathe in for 3 counts; hold 3 counts, breathe out 4 counts." (You can count along out loud). Do this several times until the room feels still and quiet. Then say, " Think about what corn needs to grow big and tall and healthy - like water and sunlight, now think about all the things that will help you to grow into a strong, healthy and happy adult. Breathe in 3 counts; hold 3 counts, breathe out 4 counts. It could be a family member who loves and supports you, close friends you can trust, a special teacher that encourages you to learn and explore new things, or someone who believes that you can do anything you try to do. Try to picture all the different ways people can help you as you grow up. Breathe in 3 counts; hold 3 counts, breathe out 4 counts. Think about the things in your life that make you feel proud. Breathe in 3 counts; hold 3 counts, breathe out 4 counts. Notice how good it feels to take a few minutes to think about the ways you can grow and learn and develop. Breathe in 3 counts; hold 3 counts, breathe out 4 counts.

Creation Process:
Create a doll that represents the person you would like to become when you grow up, remembering some of the positive influences on your life that you were just thinking of.

1) Layer 4 corn husks on top of each other.

2) Join the upper inch of the husks and tie tightly with raffia or twine.  Note, if it is easier for the younger children you can use pipe cleaners and twist around to tighten.

3) Take 2 leaves on each side and pull over covering the knot, reversing the outside in.

4) To make a head, draw a string around approximately one inch below the top view of the folded back husks which should then envelop the knot hidden underneath. The raffia, string, bow or pipe cleaner makes the doll's neck.

 
   
1
  2  3  4
5) To make the arms, fold a new sheet in half lengthwise, coiled (corn leaves work better if you roll with the grain of the leaf rather than against the grain). Tie each end. You can also braid the leaves for the arms.

6) Place the arms between the two sets of corn husks into the body of leaves. Slide your arms as high as they will rise up towards the neck loop.

7) With a string of raffia (or pipe cleaner), tie a belt under their arms. Tie it tightly enough to hold your arms firmly in place.


 
 
 5  6  7

Optional:
-Make a doll/figure with braids using 3 strings of raffia tied at each end.
-Make a doll/figure in pants rather than a skirt by tying each side off at the ankle.
-Make a doll/figure by painting the body by creating clothing.

Closing:
Go around and ask the participants to share their corn husk dolls and how these dolls represent the things they want for themselves in their future as they grow into healthy strong adults.
Row.txt_description: This workshop gives participants the opportunity to look at the things that help them to grow into strong, healthy adults while creatively using simple natural materials.
Row.txt_tips: Keep in mind: Make every knot with the twine or raffia on the same side for a more finished look. All knots can be cut at the end, just make sure you double tie knots before each crop.
